Volume front matter

Series title page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical—of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared from the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and most diligently corrected; continually elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indices following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indices: the first, of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the second, of Sacred Scripture, from which it is readily evident to the reader which Fathers, and in which places of their works, have commented on the texts of the individual books of Scripture. An exceedingly accurate edition, easily preferable to all others when one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the entire work, and the low price; above all, this collection is a single, methodical, and chronological gathering—first in our library—of six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works concerned with every age, place, language, and form.

SECOND SERIES, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning. Patrology was printed in two editions, namely one Latin and the other Greek-Latin.—The Latin edition is sold at one thousand francs for two hundred volumes; the Greek-Latin edition at one thousand eight hundred francs for three hundred volumes.—The Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; in the latter edition, however, the Eastern authors are supplied in Latin translation only.

[Column 0009]

PREFACE TO TOMES V AND VI.

I. Since all the genuine works of St. Bernard have been gathered into the first volume, it remains for us to conclude in this second one the spurious and foreign works. The manner and order in which this will be done must here be explained briefly.

II. This later volume consists of two tomes. One contains Gilbert’s Continuation on the Song of Songs, together with other little works and letters of that abbot, and at the same time doubtful or controversial works falsely attributed to Bernard. In the other are found the sermons of Guerric, abbot and disciple of the holy Doctor, akin to Bernard’s style and piety; certain letters of Guigo, his friend; various books on the life and miracles of St. Bernard; certain little works of Geoffrey, abbot; some writings on St. Bernard’s canonization; finally, testimonies of illustrious men concerning that same holy Doctor, as well as various Lives of St. Bernard, and so forth.

III. The first place in Tome V is claimed by Gilbert’s continuation of his Exposition of the Song of Songs, so that this Continuation may follow as closely as possible the Sermons on the same Song by Bernard, which occupy the final place in the preceding volume. Gilbert’s surname was of Hoyland, the name of an island or small province bordering England and Scotland, around which the rivers Veland and Lindus flow. In this island stood the monastery of Swinhet, to which Gilbert was abbot and which belonged to the diocese of Lincoln. That monastery seems to have been twofold, for men and for women; this may be inferred both from Aelred, abbot of Rievaulx, and from some sermons of Gilbert himself delivered to those same women. For Aelred, in his second sermon on Isaiah, mentions the monastery of virgins “who, under the venerable holy father Gilbert, whose name is spoken with the highest reverence, send rich fruits of chastity daily to heaven.” Gilbert himself, indeed, preached certain sermons on the Song among those virgins, namely sermons 17 and 18. For in the former, among other things, these words are read in section 8: “To you, Lord, I commend this Lebanon, this distinguished choir of virgins, this sacred company of women.” Thus these forty-eight sermons were delivered partly to monks and partly to nuns; they possess somewhat less richness, sublimity, and persuasive force than Bernard’s. At our request, the religious and pious man Dom Jean-Baptiste de Noinville, prior of that place and my friend, carefully collated these sermons of Gilbert, which appear in this new edition cleansed of innumerable errors, with an old copy from Clairvaux. He also supplied us, from a codex of Longpont, with Geoffrey’s booklet against the errors of Gilbert Porretanus, the notary of St. Bernard. As for what remains concerning Gilbert the abbot, the Chronicle of Clairvaux records that he died in the French monastery of Ripatorium, in the diocese of Troyes, in these words: “In the year of the Lord 1172, Gilbert, formerly abbot of Hoyland, who composed Sermons on the Song of Songs in the manner of blessed Bernard, died at Ripatorium.” Some treatises and several letters by the same author follow these Sermons. John Pits in his book On the Illustrious Writers of England listed them, along with other commentaries by Gilbert himself on the Psalter, on Matthew, on the Pauline Epistles, and so forth; following Gesner, he also ascribes to him a book On the Life of St. Bernard. That book may perhaps be none other than William of St-Thierry’s book on this subject. For more about Gilbert, see Sixtus of Siena and Manrius, under the year 1163, chapter 3.

IV. In these sermons of Gilbert there are many passages especially worthy of reading and observing for the formation of morals, not only for monks but also for clerics. Against those who give more to reading than to prayer, there are excellent observations in sermon 7, section 2. Sermon 16, section 5, teaches what the prayer of preachers ought to be. The sermon that follows teaches that no one should eagerly seize the office of preaching on his own initiative. In sermon 26, section 2, the author sharply rebukes preachers who pursue applause and empty glory. In the same place he gives them the useful warning to adapt their sermons to the understanding and benefit of their hearers. Sermon 31, section 4, and sermon 36, section 5, are relevant here as well. Sermon 23 presents an admirable model of the religious life; and in sermon 45, section 8, prelates are most aptly reproved for being excessively devoted to cares and temporal affairs. In addition, sermon 47 commends the practice of writing among monks, while adding that permission to write should nevertheless not be granted to everyone. Finally, various passages in these same Sermons support the praise of Gilbert as a theologian that more recent writers attribute to him, especially the passages on free will in sermon 39 [column 0011], and those on the sacrament of the most holy Eucharist in sermon 7, section 8. Sermon 30 commends the author’s ardent and pure zeal: there he does not hesitate to rebuke Pope Alexander III. Finally, his Treatises and Letters are no less important.

V. It is not necessary to preface the subsequent little works at greater length here, since Admonitions have been placed before each of them and can take the place of a longer Preface. The subjects of all these works will be explained more fully by the Index appended to each of the two tomes at its conclusion.

THE FIFTH VOLUME OF THE WORKS OF SAINT BERNARD, ABBOT OF CLAIRVAUX, COMPRISING SPURIOUS AND FOREIGN WORKS.

[WORKS OF GILBERT OF HOYLAND.]

[Col. 0011]

SERMONS OF GILBERT OF HOYLAND, ABBOT OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER, ON SOLOMON’S SONG, from the place where blessed Bernard, overtaken by death, ceased.

SERMON I. “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs III, 1).

[Col. 0011A]

1. The feelings of lovers are various, because their circumstances are various. Therefore the bride’s words sometimes seem interrupted, just as she either enjoys her beloved according to her desire or is deprived of him contrary to her desire. Now she invites him to return over the mountains; now she seeks him after he has slipped away on the bed. What sequence of continuity will you assign here? What account of the order will be taught? It does not seem to be order, but interruption. The wishes of love are not uniform. Therefore the sermon is not held to a single sequence. Feeling speaks in love and interrupts the words, because it too does not always remain joined to itself in one state. The bridegroom himself is rightly compared to a fawn, [Col. 0011B] deceiving and fleeing from his beloved in this way. This variety is lacking neither continuity nor reason. Although the words are changed so suddenly, they preserve continuity by serving the order of the feelings. See now what sequence of continuity exists within this variety. Her beloved had slipped away over the mountains, like a wandering and flying fawn; and she herself, having fallen back upon herself from those mountains on which she had been wondrously illumined and enlightened by the vision of her beloved, [Col. 0012A] had fallen back, I say, from those mountains to the valley of tears, to the bed of sorrow—to the bed and night from the luminous mountains. Why should she not fall back in this way, when her beloved withdraws in this way? For he is the salvation and illumination of his bride. Therefore, when he withdraws, she falls back to the little bed of weakness and the night of ignorance. Now she lies upon the bed of her weakness. Yet upon this bed she remembers her beloved; and now she meditates on him not in the mornings but at night, seeking him whom her soul loves. She does not act sluggishly on this bed to which she has fallen back. She does not indulge herself or delight in a bed of desire, but rather struggles, remembering the one beloved; she is subject not to weakness but to love. Let the matter be interpreted in this way by whoever thinks it so. I, however, do not understand the bed of sorrow here, unless perhaps it is that sorrow which [Col. 0012B] love gives birth to over an absent bridegroom: she seems to wish to delight herself rather than be healed, and to have sought a friend, not a physician. According to this sense you may continue as follows. He had hastily come down from the mountains to the little bed of the bride, where she, exercised and exhausted by the abundance of delight, fell asleep, spent amid the embraces of her beloved. Delighted, she fell into sweet sleep, but when she awoke this woman of delights did not find him in [Col. 0013A] her hands. Passing over those joys—ineffable joys—in silence, she finally burst into these words: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves.” Let this now suffice for the continuation.

2. Let us now consider the individual words. “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves.” It is sweet enough to seek you, good Jesus; sweeter to hold you. In the one there is devout labor, in the other perfect joy. Your touch is certainly sweet, for touch itself is not without fruit. That woman in the Gospel touched the fringe of Jesus by a blessed theft, and at once the flow of blood in her stopped (Matt. IX, 20–22)—that carnal flow of enticement, carnal delight, and care; and what had previously been fluid within her was checked and dried up. All this happened through touching the fringe. What if she had happened to embrace his very head? Not only would the flow of blood have stopped and been dried up, but the force of that river which gladdens the city of God would have poured forth (Ps. XLV, 5). Touch is therefore good, but contact is better. Jesus is scarcely touched in a crowd, in public. Therefore the bride, who desires not merely to touch but to embrace and handle the Word of life, avoiding public places, chose secrecy—the secrecy of both the bed and the night. It is a good work either to seek Jesus or to hold him; but the suitability of place and time must be applied to this work. What opportunity is greater and more suitable for the practice of love than the opportunity of bed and night? Unless it is sought with a quiet mind, the delight of wisdom cannot be sought, nor can one’s gaze be directed toward it without disturbance. Nothing defiled enters into it, nor anything unsettled. But it readily enters a quiet and pure soul and flows into it freely. “For his place is in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. LXXV, 3), that is, in contemplation. Peace is set first, as a kind of preparation for contemplation. How will an eye disturbed by anger or care behold that inaccessible light, which is reached only by serene minds, and not always even by them according to their wish? What, you will say, has peace to do with a bed? It has a great deal to do with it in this respect: just as one sleeps and rests in bed, so one sleeps and rests in peace. “In peace, in the same place, I will sleep and rest” (Ps. IV, 9). Why should a holy soul not willingly rest where the beloved’s place is? For his place is in peace. First acquire this place for yourself, then, so that in it you may either hold him whom your soul loves when he glides near, or seek him when he has slipped away. In bed, and in a certain secret quiet of the mind, he can be investigated more freely, found more quickly, and held more safely—perhaps also for a longer time, if one can remain longer in those delights which usually are interrupted at their very beginnings. For when, as it were, he has slipped from her embraces, and she pursues the delights that flee, she anxiously seeks her beloved again, and does so in bed. You are well placed in bed if, in a kind of leisure from occupations, your mind is freely at rest. What is more suited to the practice of love than freedom and leisure? Freedom gives birth to enticement. In leisure the feeling is both freed and devoted to it in no small measure. So it is: the freer the mind, the more intensely it will be devoted to what it loves. Experience shows that when we have been given over to leisure, then we feel the sharper bite [Col. 0014A] of divine love. Conversely, constant concern with the world makes feeling almost insensible and lays a kind of callus over the mind. Care entangles the mind; rest unravels it. Once desires are disentangled, what growth do you think they spread toward?

3. Do you see how many good things are contained in the little bed? Rest, freedom, and enticement. In the little bed, the desires for rest and release burn more intensely. A place suited to the delight of charity urges the bride to seek more ardently. There she is more painfully without her beloved, where she was able to enjoy him more abundantly. “On my bed,” she says, “and by night.” She who seeks by night seems to me to pursue embraces rather than sight. She wishes more to hold than to see. Vision is good, certainly, but attachment is closer. For “he who clings to the Lord is one spirit” [Col. 0014B] (1 Cor. VI, 17). Yet both are better, since when joined they mutually increase one another with gifts of grace. If you do not think you can grasp both, pursue what the bride pursues. Seek the embraces of the beloved. The night of your ignorance—or rather, the nights of your ignorances—takes from you the serene vision of heavenly secrets. Follow what is sweet. If you cannot know those things, seek to feel them. Night does not prescribe an end to delights, for it is sometimes illumined by them. “Night,” he says, “is my illumination in my delights” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 11). He says “in delights,” not “in knowledges.” So you too, if you cannot illumine night with knowledges, try to illumine it with delights. Whatever we see here through a mirror and in an enigma is all in night. In this night my Jesus can be felt sweetly by a certain tender affection more than he can be known perfectly [Col. 0014C]. Therefore, although she is not yet admitted to direct vision, she still pursues contact, seeking her beloved on the little bed and by night.

4. What if night also contributes to finding the beloved? It certainly contributes, and very suitably. Just as on the bed of holy rest you receive leisure, so in night understand a kind of forgetfulness. Both provide an opportunity for the work of wisdom and contemplation. Solomon does not want you to write wisdom except in a time of leisure (Ecclus. XXXVIII, 25), nor does Paul stretch forward to what lies ahead until he has first forgotten what lies behind (Phil. III, 13). Are you surprised that night is good and day is bad? “The day of man,” says the prophet, “I have not desired” (Jer. XVII, 16). I do not know how it happens that the day of the Lord and the day of man oppose and obscure one another [Col. 0014D]. When one rises, the other is hidden. “The day of man I have not desired”—that is, human favor, human glory, and, among the rest, indeed above the rest, the desire to appear distinguished. The prophet rightly rejects this day, which supplies material for disturbance. This night is therefore better than day: night hides from disturbance, whereas day exposes to it. In the end, as soon as the eyes of our first parents were opened to this light, they were ashamed and confused (Gen. III, 7). How much more happily had they previously kept their eyes closed, covered by a better night, unaware of the itch of sin! From that point this evil day took its origin: it stripped bare the paths of vices, displayed enticing forms, and thrust before the eye the material that provokes lust [Col. 0015A]. Alas, how this day surrounds me with light, how it drags my feeling toward itself! How clearly all things appear before the eyes of the mind—and most intrusively, both unsettled and immodest! There is scarcely anywhere to turn aside, scarcely anywhere to hide; no hiding places are safe enough. Thus everything that may disturb or disfigure the spirit bursts forth and rises into thought everywhere, whether touched carefully or only lightly. For although the mind may repel such things with a stricter resolve, it is still soiled by the mere touch of invading thoughts. “He who touches pitch will be defiled by it” (Ecclus. XIII, 1). Indeed, according to the precepts of the Law, even a slight touch of certain things defiles (Lev. IV–VIII). When they are forcibly thrust upon the mind, they are not counted as guilt and such thoughts do not bring blame; nevertheless they inflict some injury on the purity being pursued. What happens when bodily images spread themselves before a contemplative mind? Perhaps they do not provoke carnal desire, but they still delay spiritual vision. Some disturb, some disfigure, some delay; that is, they tear, entice, and mock. Would it not be better for all such things to be darkened, enveloped in the blind gloom of forgetfulness, than to be brought into the light and reviewed in memory?

5. Good, then, is the night which, through prudent forgetfulness, conceals all temporal things, providing and clearing the way to seek the One who is eternal; the night which hides worldly desire, care, and thought. This is to keep the world hidden, or to be hidden from the world. Thus we too may be hidden in the hiding-place of your face, Lord—not, I say, with full understanding, but with complete devotion, free investigation, and some measure of discovery. I believe that the bride now calls this concealment, this secrecy, these hiding places by which we avoid the love or image of the worldly day; by which we neither retrieve the human day when it has been taken away nor accept it when it is offered—by the name of night. For earlier she says: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song of Songs II, 3). This fruit feeds sweetly, provided that the shadow has first protected us. Good is the shadow which darkens the prudence of the flesh and cools desire. Do you understand what the shadow is? From it the occasion shines upon you, showing how you should understand night here as well, except that certain more hidden and more secluded retreats, better suited to investigation and contemplation, are expressed under the name of night than under that of shadow. In shadow, understand a partial forgetfulness of visible things; in night, a complete one. Who will give me such an evening? Who, I ask, will cause the memory of temporal things to decline into this evening of forgetfulness? Good indeed is the night when vain images do not trouble the mind or move within it, when they are hidden from the eyes of one seeking the beloved. Love itself brings on this night: intent upon the one it loves, it neither regards nor counts as known the things left behind, while it sighs for him.

6. “By nights,” she says. There are many nights for her; her night is not one uninterrupted and continuous night. Her nights are frequently broken by the presence of the bridegroom. When he is present, there is light; when he is absent, there is night. Therefore the bride has many nights, because the bridegroom has many withdrawals and there are many hiding places. Blessed indeed is she who clings to her beloved all day and seeks him throughout all her nights. Let those who hear this stir your zeal; instructed by the bride’s example, rise up in the night yourself, at the beginning of your vigils, and pour out your heart (Lam. II, 19), so that it may melt and run, and run onward into the presence of your God. Offer him the first beginnings of your vigils; let no foreign care tear anything away from you. Seek your beloved through each night. What do I mean, through each? Continue all your nights in this work. Do not [Col. 0016B] cease or rest until your beloved comes forth like a brightness, and a lamp is kindled for you. Then you will be able to say with Paul: “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near.” For what follows—“Let us cast off the works of darkness” (Rom. XIII, 12)—cannot be adapted to this night. This night does not know works of darkness; rather, it supplies light to those who remain engaged in the struggle of seeking the beloved. Good indeed is the night when you are hidden from disturbance and from the invasion of images. And although you have not yet been hidden in the hiding-place of your beloved’s face, it is still good that the face and display of empty and carnal thoughts be hidden from you. It is night when you do not attend to or see them; yet in this night your lamp will not be extinguished, so that you may seek the beloved.

[Col. 0016C] 7. Would that I could count such nights for myself, so hidden and so luminous! And who among us will boast that he has all his nights like these? Whoever he is, he is happy: all his nights pass in such use, and in his hidden place he does nothing worthy of concealment. Let each person meet with his own conscience. Why should I strike the conscience of another, which is weak? I neither strike nor even examine it; but though it is weak, let it at least not be foul. Let it do nothing in secret, and not even think what is shameful to say. Jesus does not know how to turn aside to such a bed. A confused conscience offends him and puts him to flight. Confusion of conscience does not invite him, but rather avoids him. “Charity from a pure heart and a good conscience” (1 Tim. I, 5) is what seeks him. [Col. 0016D] Thus you have: “I sought him whom my soul loves.” Nothing is safer than a good conscience. A good conscience dares, and charity burns. The one does not fear; the other inflames. The one is not ashamed for the beloved; the other is confident in the beloved. Great is the power of love. It does not rely on another’s support, but is content with its own merits. It always presumes itself loved when it feels itself loving. Finally, without considering the other titles of majesty, the bride remembers only the beloved, for inwardly she uniquely endures the heat of love.

8. We should observe how frequently she repeats the name “beloved,” in whatever mystery. “My beloved is white and ruddy,” and “Such is my beloved” (Song of Songs V, 10, 16); and here, “whom my soul [Col. 0017A] loves.” Certainly this gives great grace to the speech. It is no wonder that what burns in the heart is frequently on the lips. Therefore she also mentions the soul. She does not love with words alone, but with desire; not by action alone, but still more by feeling. But what does it mean that she says “soul,” not “spirit”? Perhaps because she did not yet cling to the beloved whom she was still seeking: for “he who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. VI, 17). Indeed, nowhere in this entire Song does she name the spirit, but says, “My soul melted” (Song of Songs V, 6), and “My soul troubled me” (Song of Songs VI, 11), and very frequently this same phrase, “whom my soul loves.” She scarcely uses it except when she seeks one who is absent or complains that he is absent. These names commonly distinguish certain degrees of the more perfect and less perfect soul. The Apostle says: “The animal man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. II, 14). I would never call this soul—loving, burning, fervent, and seeking—anything but spiritual; for although it did not yet possess full vision, it clung by a stronger desire to the one it loved intensely. We may appropriately understand in “spirit” a subtle and refined intellect, and in “soul” a sweet and tender affection. Through the prophet, in his promise, the Lord says: “I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. XI, 19). If the name of flesh is accepted somewhere in a good sense, why not even more so that of soul? To speak freely, I would judge this soul blessed, not stony but rather fleshly, with nothing rigid or hard in it, but soft, tender, tractable, and sensitive to each [Col. 0017C] prick of the divine word. In the end it says: “Nor is my flesh bronze,” but rejoices that the spiritual sword passes through it and that it has been wounded by charity. Rightly, therefore, she says that her soul loves, wishing to express a certain intimate, vivid, and living affection for her beloved, Jesus Christ the Lord, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

SERMON II. “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song of Songs III, 1).

1. We renew for you today a feast from yesterday’s chapter. For not everything that could be said was said there; some things were not even touched upon. In this sermon we undertake to examine them: namely, why she says “on the little bed,” and not “on the bed,” and why “on my little bed.” For elsewhere she is accustomed to call it “our little bed” (Song of Songs I, 16). Consider these matters as your portion. If I add anything new to what has already been discussed, count it, so to speak, as profit. What mystery do you think is signified by this very expression, “on the little bed”? Does it contain some hidden praise, or a reproach? Although it can bear either meaning, I prefer to take praise here; therefore let us first bend the sermon toward this sense. In this word I plainly understand a certain narrowing, so that she is sufficient with the beloved alone. Why should narrowing not be understood in a good sense, if the widening of the bed is turned into a disgrace? “You have widened your bed,” the Lord says through the prophet; “you have received an adulterer beside me” (Isa. LVII, 8). You see how the widening of the bed is charged against and reproached to the adulterous soul. It is good, then, not to widen but rather to contract the bed of thought and the little bed of the heart. Therefore the bride rightly congratulates herself on the little bed. “The bed is narrowed,” says the prophet, “so that one falls out, and the short cover cannot cover both” (Isa. XXVIII, 20). Both means the husband and the adulterer. The human heart is short and narrow for conceiving the delights of God’s word, even when it is stretched out entirely toward them. How much shorter if it has been stretched toward other things? Let this smallness be enough for your beloved. Do not make it shorter by sharing the little bed with another. Good is this shortness of the little bed, which knows how to receive no one but its beloved, that is, Christ. There is a shortness which knows how to receive only him, and there is a shortness which cannot receive him fully. The former belongs to charity and discipline; the latter to weakness and nature. Both kinds of shortness may be understood in the little bed: either the shortness by which it does not receive several together with the beloved, or the shortness by which it cannot receive even him fully. Great indeed is the pleasure of the little bed, but great is its narrowness; and therefore it is rightly called a little bed rather than a bed.

**2.** The delightful little bed is that of which you read in Proverbs: “A secure mind is like a continual feast” (Prov. 15:15). Outside is night, outside disturbance; but within is tranquility, like a little bed of rest. Here one does not say that lamentable thing: “Outside the sword kills, and at home there is death like it” (Lam. 1:20) [Column 18C]. On the contrary, if outside there is a sword, inside there is joy. “Rejoicing in hope,” he says, “patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12). Tribulation belongs to the night; hope and joy to the little bed. Perhaps for this reason he calls it not a bed but a little bed, using a sparing—that is, diminutive—word, because almost all our joy is still only in hope and in part.

The little bed of conscience, then, is good: rest and purity. “The heart of the wicked is like a seething sea which cannot be quiet; its waves overflow into trampling and mud.” Thus the wicked heart is turbulent, decayed, muddy, and always struggling with itself. “There is no peace for the wicked” (Isa. 57:20–21); but the kingdom of God is justice and peace (Rom. 14:17). “In peace,” he says, “in the selfsame I will sleep and rest, because you, O Lord, have singularly established me in hope” (Ps. 4:9–10) [Column 18D]. The name of hope embraces both the little bed and joy, because in hope we rejoice and in hope we rest. But whence comes hope except from the security of conscience? I rightly call a secure and free mind a little bed: secure because of the good of conscience; free from temptation, free from external occupation, free from trivial thought.

Yet how great can the mind’s rest and freedom be in this body? Brief and slight, like a narrow little bed. Much is taken from it by the body’s need for restoration, much by the care of seeking necessary things, much by the passing of time, much by the imminent fall of the soul, much by a hidden cause. “This is our glory,” says Paul, “the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12) [Column 19A]. Certainly he had placed himself sweetly in the little bed. “I am conscious,” he says, “of nothing.” But how much he enlarges and extends him, this other statement rather narrows and contracts him: “Yet in this I am not justified. He who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:4). You see how Paul ventures to say: “Our heart is enlarged” (2 Cor. 6:11). You see how the regard of the divine judgment constrains glory and the testimony of conscience.

**3.** Thus the little bed is a secure mind, but not in the least proud; quiet, not exalted; thinking well of itself, but not thinking high things, and always suspecting the night of uncertain judgment. “On my little bed,” he says, “through the nights.” The nights are many, but the little bed is one. “Many are the tribulations of the righteous” (Ps. 33:20), yet as though neither feeling nor regarding them, they sleep and rest in the one little bed: in the one hope of our calling to which we were called [Column 19B]. Night after night passes, but they do not leave the little bed of their tranquility until all iniquity has passed away. The nights are many and the darkness deep; but they neither fear nor are disturbed by the depth of night, because they hope in the Lord. Those who rest in this little bed of hope do not fear the nights. For he knows how to give songs in the night of tribulation (Job 35:10), and “in the night he commands his song” (Ps. 41:9). You have received why the bride says “nights,” and why more than one; why it is called a little bed, and why one.

**4.** Now receive why the bride says “my.” It is her bed [Column 19C], and as it were singularly hers, as long as she is singularly in hope. But when the reality comes to hope—or rather succeeds hope—when she has already partly held the Beloved, this bed is no longer the bride’s own, but rather common to bridegroom and bride. It is hers when, as though alone without the Beloved, she rests; it is common when he is present. It is the bride’s when, gathered within herself in quiet, peaceful, ordered character, she rests; it is common when she begins to delight in the bridegroom. Perhaps there is also one proper to the bridegroom, when, wholly forgetful of herself and putting herself off, she passes altogether into him and, as his beloved, is as though clothed with him.

On her own bed she neither pours herself outside herself nor is disturbed within herself. On the common bed certain delights flow to her from the bridegroom’s presence [Column 19D]. On that which belongs to the bridegroom alone, stirred by the fire of the bridegroom’s love, she boils and swells, poured out and flowing forth. She is wholly transfused into him and absorbed into a similar quality. In the first she is with herself; in the second the bridegroom is with her; in the third she herself is wholly with him and, if it can be said, is only he. In the first she seeks; in the second she clings; in the third she is united to him. In the first she possesses her own tranquility; in the second she merits a certain communion with the Beloved; in the third she is taken up and absorbed into a certain unity of love and grace. This third bed is better than the second, as unity is more complete than communion. Yet the first is good, for through it access to the others is prepared.


**5.** If you wish to turn the sense of the bed toward the allurements of carnal weakness [Column 20A], you neither err nor labor in assigning it thus. Under this interpretation the bed belongs to the bride alone and is not shared with the bridegroom. For although we know Christ according to the flesh, we do not know him according to the concupiscence of the flesh. The nature of flesh is shared, but the allurements of flesh are not shared by him. He did not reject the bed of our pain, but he did not recline as far as the experience of our pleasure. Therefore, when the bride signifies this bed, she says “on my bed,” not commonly, “on our bed.” Elsewhere, indeed, we read: “Our bed is flowering” (Song 1:15). That which is shared is flowering, having nothing of age or corruption. But when she calls the bed her own, there is no mention of flower. This is the bride’s, but it is unpleasant; not flowering [Column 20B], but dreadful to her.

It would be a hard condition even if there were corruption alone. But now adversity is added to weakness: a doubled hardship, bed and night, weakness and adversity. Yet love has a great power, restrained by neither—the one innate, the other imposed. The bride is not held by the bed or frightened by the night; on her bed and through the nights she seeks him whom her soul loves. This seems especially the voice of cloistered brothers, who are at rest from anxiety and, as it were, lost and hidden in the multitude, possessing in one respect a bed and in another the darkness of night. For even a very exalted life is in some way hidden when the entire multitude of brothers rises to an equal height, according to the prophecy concerning the Savior: “They walk in [Column 20C] darkness and have no light”—that is, no light of human praise—“that they may more freely hope in the Lord’s name and rely upon their God” (Isa. 50:10).

Their face is hidden. Thus we did not esteem them—rather, they do not esteem themselves within; they do not adapt themselves outwardly to the world’s uses; they do not desire glory from human speech, but that which comes from God alone, as is written: “I do not seek my own glory” (John 8:50), and, “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17). That is, let him not rest in human favor because of the Lord’s gifts; let him not adulterate the joys of spiritual glory by mingling this worldly end with them; but let him refer thanks to the Lord and seek glory in him—for this is what seeking him itself is. Such a man has a bed in tranquility and night in humility [Column 20D]. Biting cares do not fly round him, injuries of unrest do not exasperate him; all is bed and night, all peace and quiet and hiding.

**6.** Is this enough? Perhaps it is enough for one who labors, but not enough for one who loves. “Sleep is sweet to one who labors” (Eccl. 5:11). The anxiety of one who loves does not let him sleep; it shakes off drowsiness and brings on vigils. Love is made more restless by rest itself. Temptation rests, occupation rests, affliction rests, but love does not know how to rest. Then the sweet fire exercises its strength more, and the devouring flame, escaping from its hiding places, wanders more freely through the unoccupied mind, possessing it more deeply and feeding more eagerly. Love does not know how not to exercise its own work when given the opportunity [Column 21A]. For the one it loves, it always delights in while present or desires while absent.

“In the day of my tribulation I sought God with my hands” (Ps. 76:3). The bride now proposes a manner of seeking far different. Affliction does not drive her; affection draws her. The Psalmist seeks against tribulation; she seeks for the use and delight of love. For this end she relates both the bed of rest and the hiding place of night: that she may recollect without disturbance, savor sincerely, and feel sweetly him whom she loves. Therefore the reason for seeking is much more powerful in one who loves than in one who needs, although holy love can rightly be said always to suffer a kind of avarice. It always burns toward more hidden things; counting not the things it holds, it carries itself in a revolving movement toward those before it. Like a living wheel, with spiritual lightness it lifts itself with all effort to higher things, scarcely touching anything of earth [Column 21B]. Thus Paul also thinks he has not yet grasped it; stretching himself toward what lies ahead, like a rational wheel he follows where the spirit of burning desire carries him (Phil. 3:13). “When man has finished, then he will begin” (Ecclus. 18:6). So too the bride, while she possesses the bed, not content with it, seeks the Beloved more ardently. He is her bed; he is her Beloved: bed, while he receives her weak and weary; Beloved, while he inflames and kindles her. He is bed and Beloved because she rests in him and desires and faints into him.

**7.** Are you surprised that I call him a bed? I will dare to add something humbler [Column 21C]—indeed, something more exalted than all the glory of his praise. For the lower things he did for me, the greater the indications he gave of his goodness. He is a bed for little ones, a nest for fledglings: “For the sparrow has found herself a house, and the turtledove a nest where she may place her young” (Ps. 83:4). Do you wish to hear what kind of bed? Cast your thoughts, still unfledged and weak, upon the Lord, and he will nourish you until Christ is formed and strengthened in you and you reach the perfect man who cannot be tossed about. He is rightly a bed, who “has been made for me by God justice and peace and redemption and wisdom.”

Who will grant me to be placed in such a bed? Who, I ask, will give me these cushions and such pillows to be sewn beneath my elbow and head? Blessed is the pillow which the bride puts beneath herself: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6) [Column 21D]. She already possesses one and promises the other to herself. She holds the left, but seeks the right, for “delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15:11). As though from bed to bed she reaches. Your crown of thorns, good Jesus, is a most sweet pillow to me; that wood of your cross is a sweet bed. On it I am born and nourished, created and recreated, and on the altars of memory of your Passion I gladly place my nest again. If one is granted to perceive greater and more hidden mysteries of divine majesty, that differs in nothing from bed and night if one considers the future fullness rather than the form of human perfection. For even our most perfect state is imperfect—or, to speak more truly, scarcely yet begun [Column 22A]. Thus we are called a certain beginning of God’s creation (Jas. 1:18), and are said to have received only the firstfruits of the Spirit (Rom. 8:23).


**8.** Perhaps I seem rash in trying to explain things unexperienced and to speak of the bride’s bed, which she perhaps arranged more sweetly and secretly than our conjecture can attain. Let us therefore descend from mysteries to morals. Let us say that to seek the Beloved on one’s bed and through the nights is, after the tumult of heart and movement of flesh, to forget rest and present things and seize certain first delights of future sweetness. Thus, to summarize briefly, this chapter contains an opportunity, an action, and a cause. The cause is in the lover, the action in the seeker; the opportunity and occasion are indicated by the bed and night [Column 22B]. The chapter is short, because the bed is good: on it the tired mind receives refreshment—indeed, a burning fire—in which love, finding no obstacle, exercises the use of desire more ardently. But let us now rest here a little, and may it be on that bed where, while the bride rested, she sought the Beloved, so that by the sense of experience in ourselves we may learn what we now try to teach others: how sweet it is to rest on this bed and seek the Beloved, Jesus Christ our Lord.

## Sermon III: “I sought him and did not find him” (Song 3:1)

**1.** The bridegroom is not accustomed always to answer the desire of the soul that seeks him, whether because of the time or according to its measure. “I sought,” she says, “and did not find him.” “I sought” is certainly a welcome word [Column 22C], but “I did not find him” is grievous. Why should it not be grievous and intolerable to one who seeks and loves in this way? No one lacks without anxiety that which he ardently seeks, and the distress is more intense when one is deceived by a nearby hope that is about to grasp it. How much more is this true of one whose hunger is excited by inward sweetness once experienced and now lost. It is credible that the more such sweetness is recalled and rolled about in the heart, the sharper the blow by which the lover’s mind is driven to seek. The affection of one who does not find must be measured by the measure of love. Whoever has experienced such a sense of love or desire in himself can estimate from the example of his own conjecture with what plaintive heart the bride uttered: “I did not find him.”

There is nowhere consolation, nowhere refreshment; everywhere I found tribulation and pain while I did not find him whom I ardently love and diligently seek. “You have made me,” I say not, contrary to you, but as though a stranger from you, and I have become burdensome to myself (Job 7:20). She is plainly burdensome who is weary of life, weary of this light, because “the light of my eyes itself is not with me.” Where will there be outward consolation if, with you absent, there is disturbance within me? “My heart is troubled, my strength has left me, and the light of my eyes, even that is not with me” (Ps. 37:11). These three departed with you: strength, truth, and identity. For how could there be strength on a bed of pain, light in night, or the same thing in division and separation [Column 23A]? Now that prophetic reproach looks to me: “How long will you be dissolved, wandering daughter?” (Jer. 31:22). Thus Cain too, after he went out from the Lord’s face, became a wanderer and fugitive. I am not so much a wanderer and fugitive; I am more seeker than fugitive. Indeed, to speak more freely, flight better befits you. Is she not wandering who passes from the narrowness of the bed to the circuit of the city, running through streets, lanes, and guards? “He who clings to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). This sameness is sweet, and therefore separation is hard.

**2.** How has this identity been scattered, the union burst, and I returned to myself divided in half? For I did not depart wholly from you. By desire I am borne into you, but I am delayed from your presence. I have some consolation in desire, but the punishment of delay hides and absorbs all of it [Column 23B]. How can all consolation not be hidden while you hide your face from me? As the prophet says, “Consolation is hidden from the eyes,” because division has been made between beloved persons (Hos. 13:14–15). But it is hidden from me because this union had been granted to me. You have no need of my goods; my goods are your gifts. Therefore desolation presses upon me when separation from you occurs. You are my strength, you the light of my eyes, you my very self, you my all. “My flesh and my heart have failed,” so that hereafter neither carnal affection nor my heart’s feeling may breathe in me, but “God may be the God of my heart and my portion forever” (Ps. 72:26).

If I lose this portion, I shall remain empty and void, like thirsty earth and a lost vessel [Column 23C]. Take up, take up the thirsty one—you who are drunk—and pour into the empty vessel a portion of your fullness. Why spare that torrent of your abundance? Alas for me, how swiftly that torrent passes through our valleys! It passes quickly indeed, but the delights imparted draw me after them into eternal desire. The delights go away, but leave desire; they run onward, and it torments. The sweeter the privileges bestowed, the more troublesome the delay. Lord, will it seem sweet to you to torture a wretched soul by such delay and to laugh at the pains of one who loves and seeks you? If majesty draws you away, let mercy incline you. If you do not yield to your beloved, pity at least the afflicted one.

I am afflicted and humbled beyond measure, and this roars with me from the groaning of my heart: “I did not find him.” Where now is the multitude of your bowels and mercies? They have held themselves back from me too long and excessively. Your beloved pours herself out into pain from desire for one absent, and do you restrain yourself? Joseph, pitying brothers who had wronged him, could not restrain himself; his bowels were moved, and he gently made known who he was (Gen. 45:1–3). The bridegroom’s tenderness should surely be more ready for grace than a brother’s. You are more to me than Joseph: you are brother, you are bridegroom. Who will give you to me as my brother? I spend my whole self in seeking you, and you suspend me, bridegroom and brother? Will you then be less in love who are greater in majesty? Love and humility correspond more than love and majesty [Column 24A]. Forget your majesty a little, that you may remember mercy. All my desire is in you. Why is it not before you? Why is my groaning hidden from you, when it is wholly for you? You pretend, delay, turn your face from me, and I am troubled. Therefore I complain, plead my cause, and cry: “I did not find him.”


**3.** Happy is the condition when it is granted to say: “My Beloved is mine, and I am his.” But now, “I am my Beloved’s, and his turning is not yet toward me” (Song 6:16; 7:10). This is indeed a bitter exchange for one who loves. Therefore in turn I change my voice: “I did not find him.” All things have their time, and all things under the sun run through their allotted spaces. When will they remain with the sun and before the changeableness of the moon, standing in eternity [Column 24B] instead of running with time? Now all things have their time, and perhaps eternity itself has its own time. For eternal times are spoken of. Eternal things are eternal in themselves, but for us they are prepared in their own time. All things have their time: “a time to embrace, and a time to be far from embraces” (Eccl. 3:1–8). What time, then, will be more fitting than night for embracing? Indeed, what place is more fitting for embracing than a bed, or what time than night? “In peace is your place”; therefore it is a time of rest, and I have prepared in my heart a bed of peace for you. Let my Beloved come, let my delight come, and rest in his chamber.

Perhaps you delay by dispensation; but impatient love receives no consolation from dispensation. I know that it is laid up for me in its own time, but love complains of the slowness of fleeting time [Column 24C]. You delay; I can bear it no longer, and will rise and go about the city. I despise the bed and leave the beginning of the discourse behind, that I may be carried to more perfect things.

**4.** For though I am a bride and perfect according to the measure of the human rule, I count myself to have received only a beginning, looking toward what remains: “I will rise and go about the city; I will seek through lanes and squares” (Song 3:2). Good Jesus, how is it that you are not found somewhere, you who are believed everywhere? There are many mansions in your Father’s house; but do you leave some and pass to others, you who are infinite and immeasurable? In every creature you are wholly present, creating and containing; but no creature can express your infinity [Column 24D], though none fails to suggest your power in part. You are wholly everywhere by existence, but not equally in each by operation. Though you work wholly everywhere, you do not work everywhere all that belongs to your power—indeed, nowhere do you do so. By an undivided power you effect least things in the least and greater things in the greater. Thus, although your power works everywhere and wholly, it is nowhere wholly expended: when you wish, greater things are available for you to effect; nor is it wholly expressed, because images cannot imitate truth completely.

All things show you to me for knowledge, but not all can move me inwardly to devotion. Everywhere I encounter you, but I am not everywhere pierced with compunction. Everywhere the appearance, use, and order of things present you to me [Column 25A] as the Word of wisdom, but not as the Word of salvation. The Word who is wisdom and salvation—Christ Jesus—is found only in the city of our God, on his holy mountain. Therefore I will rise and go about the city. “Rise,” says Paul, “you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5:14). I will rise, not from dead works or evil conduct, but from good to better things, from conduct to mysteries, from mysteries to manifest things, from serenity to sweetness. I will rise and go about that city of which it is said: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly to be praised in the city of our God, on his holy mountain” (Ps. 47:2).

One must rise who wishes to ascend into the hill country with Mary (Luke 1:39). The prodigal son too, returning to himself, said: “I will rise and go to [Column 25B] my father.” He wisely said “I will rise,” since he was going to the Father who is in heaven. But he had placed in his bosom a hope too scanty and thin, intending to ask his father for a hired servant’s condition. It was modest in view of his merits, but he thought too humbly and injuriously of the abundance of paternal mercy, truly giving in this a sign of a hungry heart exhausted by want. “I will say to him,” he says, “Father, make me as one of your hired servants” (Luke 15:18–19). He could not stretch his fasting and meager hope to greater things. “I will rise and go to my father.” He is moved by nothing concerning seeking his father, anxious only to bend him. But the bride, certain of grace, asks only for presence: “I will rise and go about the city and seek him whom my soul loves,” counting discovery enough [Column 25C].

**5.** See whether this distinction cannot be observed in the present: the father’s forgiveness is displayed and prepared for all, whereas delights are fleeting and hidden, rejoicing in secret places. Therefore he says, “I will rise and go”; she says, “I will rise and seek.” The father runs to meet the penitent; the bridegroom withdraws from the lover. Mercy is more lavish of itself; delight more sparing. It is also fittingly understood of both that they say, “I will rise.” Paul does not allow you to seek the things above unless you have first risen (Col. 3:1). You cannot savor the things above unless you have first sought them. What is finding those good things above except perceiving them by some taste [Column 25D] of sweetness and experience? Therefore she surveys and searches everything so that she may taste somewhere what she loves.

“I will rise,” she says, “and go about the city; I will seek through the lanes and squares him whom my soul loves.” Holy love takes much confidence to itself. How greatly, do you think, did she love who dared so much? “I will rise,” she says, “and go about the city.” No hypocrite, Lord, will come before your sight. Adam hid himself after he lost the boldness of a good conscience (Gen. 3:8), and grieved to be found when he should rather have sought. One who loves falsely flees your sight; but one who is a bride and endowed with the gift of love pursues even the fleeing one. Where will you go, good Jesus, from the face of vehement desire? If you ascend to heaven, she is there; if you descend to hell, she is present [Column 26A]. Everywhere the eager searcher follows you and runs through every stage of your works, striving to pour into affection what she holds by faith and to answer wondrous majesty with devotion. She brings forward every teaching of the Gospel as an incentive to love, so that in those things in which she receives truth she may feel power—your very self, Christ Jesus, her bridegroom, who live and reign through all ages of ages. Amen.


## Sermon IV: “I will rise and go about the city; through the lanes and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:2)

**1.** This circuit is not wandering abroad but investigation. Even if she who goes about wanders, she does not stray: she does not go beyond the city’s boundaries or the places [Column 26B] which the Beloved is accustomed to traverse. She walks in a circuit, but within, through the lanes and squares of the city. For Wisdom shows herself joyfully in these ways and gives her voice in the squares. She therefore goes about in them because she knows where the Beloved is wont to meet her more abundantly. “I will go about,” she says, “seeking through lanes and squares.” O happy soul, such a circuit and familiar approach are frequent to you; all the courses and inner retreats of this city are known to you, its narrow lanes and broad squares. The king has brought you into the wine cellar; has he not also brought you into all the other more secret retreats? All is open and passable to you, and by a certain practice you find yourself made ready for this blessed circuit. Therefore she says, like one not hesitating but confident: “I will go about the city.”

And how much consolation, brothers, do you think it brings in the meantime to visit and often tread [Column 26C] the places in which the feet of him whom she loves used to stand? In some way, places in which we have experienced something good imprint that very thing more deeply on memory, set it in order before the eyes of the mind, and make us hope again in those places for what we have already experienced. I would understand these places not as bodily but spiritual, fitting for the spiritual exercise of the soul; therefore let us understand the circuit in them.

**2.** This circuit is either one of recollection or of investigation. One goes about who either recalls things known or gathers from known things what is not yet known. In some way one goes about who remembers things known or searches out [Column 26D] new things. There is a circuit when we reconsider in order things already held by faith and understanding. There is a circuit when from the things we already hold we tend and penetrate to more hidden things. The former circuit belongs to delight, the latter to reason; the former is more friendly, the latter more keen. Although the former circuit seems more suited to the bride, we will deny her neither. Whether she revisits what is known and discovered or investigates new things, in all she seeks only the fuel of love.

The circuit of reason is good when reason itself keeps within the rules of faith and does not exceed its bounds, attaining from faith to faith or from faith to understanding. Understanding indeed, although it surpasses faith, does not look upon anything other than what faith contains [Column 27A]. Understanding has not greater certainty than faith, but greater clarity; neither errs or hesitates. Where error or hesitation exists, there is no understanding; where hesitation exists, there is no faith. If something appears able to admit error, it is not true and Catholic faith but erroneous credulity. Faith, so to speak, holds and possesses truth rightly; understanding beholds it unveiled and naked; reason endeavors to unveil it. Reason runs between faith and understanding: it raises itself to the latter but is governed by the former.

Reason wants something more than believing. What else? To behold. Believing is one thing; seeing another. Yet it does not endeavor to behold anything other than what it conceives by faith. Even if it cannot yet see sincerely, it nevertheless tries by certain fitting experiences [Column 27B] to infer what it has already conceived by solid faith. Reason endeavors above faith, yet relies upon faith and is restrained by faith. In the first it is devout, in the second prudent, in the third sober. Thus, so to speak, faith holds, reason guards, understanding beholds. This circuit is good, in which the mind proceeds in investigation under reason’s guidance but does not depart from faith: instructed by faith and restrained within faith. It is plainly erroneous if it does not refer all things to faith’s test and correct the swift course of reason by the maturity of faith.

The circuit is good where God’s justice is revealed from faith to faith. The circuit is good where one is transformed from glory to glory as by the Spirit of the Lord (2 Cor. 3:18). The circuit is good where one, forgetting the things behind, stretches himself toward those before, if somehow he may attain them (Phil. 3:12–13). The circuit is surely good not only when new and more hidden things are always grasped, but when things already grasped are reconsidered with a continually new and fresh affection; not only when what remains is penetrated, but when what has already been penetrated is often repeated. It is a delightful circuit, and not unknown to the bride. Therefore she confidently says: “I will rise and go about the city.”


**3.** What city could be more fitting than that of which it is said: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3)? The universe of creation can indeed fittingly be called the city of God, created and ordered by him. It is glorious, certainly, both in beauty [Column 27D] and in order. Through less just acts, which the freedom of a depraved mind produces, it is, as far as those acts are concerned, less [alias, very much less] glorious; yet it is not through those acts that it fails to escape the order of divine disposition, an order they do not intend. Only those are truly glorious who submit their effort to the divine disposition, being solicitous to preserve the grace of their first condition whole or restore it when corrupted. These are made glorious in a twofold way: by their natural condition together with other creatures, and by voluntary conformity, beyond the other creatures, to the will of God who orders and directs.

The universe of creation is therefore called the city of God, because it is administered by the laws of his dispensation. He gives the whole creation the beauty of existence in its proper kind, effectiveness in its use, and coherence [Column 28A] in its order, so that each thing may be beautiful in itself, not superfluous in the universe, and not incoherent or contrary in relation to the rest. Whether a thing is done by natural motion, by the free choice of will, by the prompting of divine grace, by each of these reasons singly, or by their conjunction, it receives both its measure and its motion from the divinely effective power working invisibly within: its measure and, as it were, a law of order; its motion and the activity of action. For from him comes not only the native capacity of every motion, but also the motion of every capacity is governed, so that both the power and the motion of the power come from him. But the motion of a perverse intention has from him what makes it motion and does not have from him what makes it perverse. For it is not from him that it is directed to a less ordered end; but it is from him that the disorder itself is, by a truly marvelous reason, brought back into order [Column 28B].

4. Consider Joseph’s sale, his descent into Egypt; the departure thence and Pharaoh’s pursuit, the drowning of the army, and Israel’s deliverance—how these serve the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation and passion, and of our own deliverance. A diligent reader will find similar things in many places. Thus the ancient sins could not serve the new sacraments unless divine providence, secretly operating within, did so by a hidden rationale. For those ancient events did not happen accidentally or indifferently, so that new mysteries might later be fitted to them by a prudent disposer and careful observer. Rather, those events were prepared for the signification of these mysteries—though not intended by a human being, but disposed by God—more than these mysteries were adapted to them. What, moreover, of the fact that the Lord was committed to his passion at precisely that time, at that hour, on that day, and by that kind of death? Who would either deny that these are mystical, or believe them accidental? On the day on which humankind was created, it was restored; at the hour at which it received sentence, it obtained pardon. Through wood death was introduced; through wood life was restored. And yet someone contends that these things were arranged not divinely but humanly.

You have the time of the Paschal lamb; you have the spotless victim; you have the hour of Israel’s deliverance from Egypt; you have the grace of your own deliverance from the world’s error, from vanity, from corrupt birth. And do you believe that this happened merely by chance, God not disposing it but a Jew acting—though without understanding? These convergences, I say—the wood of the cross, the time, the hour, the day, and the remaining circumstances which may wisely be observed—do you attribute them to Jewish madness rather than divine wisdom? Indeed, in this saving remedy, converging with the ancient sacraments into one form, both accidental occurrence and human intention are excluded—but not the divine will.

And in Isaiah’s prophecy you will find it said to Hezekiah: “All these things have been given into the hands of the Chaldeans” (Isa. 39:6). In saying that they were given, he shows that they were not merely foretold prophetically but also decreed by a certain judicial equity. From these and similar matters scattered throughout the whole text of the Scriptures, who can still doubt that divine power and wisdom, by just laws, does not indeed inspire the perverse wills of rational creatures, but governs them? If this is so, still less can one doubt that the movements of the other living creatures—led by natural impulse and governed only by sense or imagination, not by rational choice—are by no means exempt from divine ordering.

And, to conclude once for all: the most just, most powerful, and most wise governor moves, changes, and sustains, by the eternal and immutable rules of his decrees, both the essence by which all things belong to this or that class of beings, their existence by which they are, and their use by which they effect something; and he governs all creation with justice that nowhere deviates, as though it were a city most perfectly ordered and arranged.

[Col. 0029B] 5. Is this, then, the city—the totality of creation—which the Bride proposes to traverse? The wise men of this world traversed the natures of things and observed the wisdom of God at work in its craftsmanship. I say “at work,” but not the work of which we read: “But God, our king before the ages, wrought salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12). They knew the craftsman in his work, but did not glorify him or give thanks (Rom. 1:21). The faithful soul unfolds and recounts everything in praise of God, and summons all creation to glorify him, so that it may stir itself up to thanksgiving and, by contemplating the universe, be incited to divine love.

Solomon traversed it, and “spoke of the cedar of Lebanon even unto the hyssop” (3 Kings 4:33). He traversed it in Ecclesiastes; and, after discussing the circuit of the elements, he turned the discourse toward human acts, so that from the passing vanity of things he might pass to abiding truth. Job traversed it—or rather, he was led about by the Lord—through the foundations of the earth, its measure, line, bases, cornerstone, morning stars, and the rejoicing of the sons of God; through the gates of the sea, its womb, garment, and the dark swaddling-bands of its infancy; through its bounds, bars, and gates; through the dawning of day, the place of the dawn, and certain fixed natures of other things (Job 38–39). To enumerate them all would be lengthy; yet all of them, to the prudent observer, inspire wonder at the Creator, and, to the devout contemplator, love.

These things are commonly set before all who use reason, and by the manifest beauty of their form they commend the majesty of their Creator. Yet beneath so beautiful a covering lie hidden more beautiful things: the sacraments of our salvation and the manifold gifts of spiritual graces.

6. Finally, David too, at the end of the Psalms, after stirring all creation to praise God, says: “Sing unto the Lord a new song; his praise in the assembly of the saints” (Ps. 149:1). Truly new: its matter knows no antiquity, its grace no weariness; it is ever fresh in love and ever fresher in use. Truly new, because it renews human minds unto eternal blessedness. For we read: “Remember not former things, and look not upon things of old; behold, I make new things” (Isa. 43:18–19). Rightly new, since they are not at all confined by the laws of nature’s ancient course.

“His praise in the assembly of the saints”: surely by a certain privilege of excellence—not merely through the dispensation of equity, but through the free gift and endowment of holiness. “His praise in the assembly of the saints,” because the actions of the saints display his praise in such a way that their affection attends to it. For the saints receive the gifts of grace excellently, experience devotion, and render thanksgiving. Therefore he is praised in the Church of the saints by a certain privilege; outside the Church he is praised by the mute and insensible service of things, and vainly by human beings. In insensible things there is creaturely condition; in unregenerate people, some knowledge; but in neither is there love. For love of their Creator is absent altogether in the former and unholy in the latter.

“His praise in the assembly of the saints.” For the saint investigates and appraises, as far as is granted, all things created, that they may naturally be; all things ordered, that they may not be unfittingly and disorderly; and all things predestined, that they may be blessed. Through these things, according to his powers, he gathers knowledge of the Author, passes into emulation, and is carried away into affection.

7. This, then, is the spiritual city; this is the Church of the saints, which the Bride undertakes to traverse. Good God, what an abundance of profitable contemplations is here! Who could adequately estimate how beautiful and how numerous are the spectacles everywhere—in sacraments, examples, and miracles? The first concern salvation, the second conduct, the third testimony.

What, indeed, when the mind rises from mysteries and moral conduct to admire the eternal rewards of temporal merits? How much joy is repaid there for lavishly poured-out vows! “Sons of men, why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3). Why do you turn your mind toward alien delights and laboriously seek pleasures that pass away? You hold, as though in your hand, the mysteries which are the material of our faith: ready for memory, abundant for meditation, everlasting for abiding in, and full for sufficing.

Sons of men—rather, sons of the Most High, foster-children of religion, you who tread the thresholds of regular discipline—why do you thirst with a dry throat for muddy waters, while scorning heavenly ones? Why do you admit into your mind thoughts to whose deeds you do not put your hand? What you utterly refuse to do, why do you reconsider with an intent mind? You have often experienced how swift repentance usually follows all this empty display of imagined shamefulness. Finally, it is shameful to disclose it and punishment to conceal it.

Change, therefore, the matter of your meditation, but preserve its constancy. How shameful it is for your studies to diminish when they are changed for the better! This is what I say: as you have offered your mind to impassioned thoughts of foul shamefulness, so now offer it to fruitful circuits of beautiful truth. “Surround Zion,” says the Psalmist, “and embrace her” (Ps. 47:13). Surround her by meditation; embrace her by love. Embrace her, so that both your comprehension of her may be whole and your lodging in her intimate.

An embrace seems to signify something more than a circuit. An embrace holds the whole together at once; a circuit moves from one thing to another. Yet in this respect a circuit seems superior: what we embrace, we clasp indiscriminately and in a mass; where there is a circuit, however, we examine each thing in sequence. The one is content with the whole; the other ranges over particulars.

14. For a hungry and searching soul, since particular things do not satisfy it, is always carried on to others; it rolls, as it were, in a circuit, drawn around by the extended revolution of its running desire, until love’s hunger is filled with good things and finds the resting-place of its course in him in whom it finds no limit. For none of the things created is infinite within the condition of its own being; and therefore the mind that makes the circuit passes through them all, finding rest nowhere, because everywhere it finds an end.

He alone is rest and refreshment for the lover: he who is the end of all things and has no end. Therefore the Bride passes through all things in her circuit so as to attain to him: “I will arise,” she says, “and go about the city.” I shall go through all things, seeking him whom I love, but finding him nowhere. “His invisible things are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Rom. 1:20); nevertheless, by the testimony of no creature, however excellent and however close it approaches imitation of him, am I fully instructed; nor am I enkindled by its service. For the service rendered by created things in commending the Creator proves as feeble, slow, and ineffectual as the image is known to be distant from the truth.

Therefore I shall go about the city, reaching all things and passing through all things: reaching them insofar as they bear his image in diverse ways; passing beyond them where they stop short of perfection. I shall go about the city, everywhere receiving refreshment and everywhere enduring weariness. For how can that which bears some pledge of my love, displays a sign, awakens remembrance, and introduces knowledge fail to refresh me? Yet again, how can I avoid weariness when I reflect that I am being entertained by an image and held by a shadow, not holding naked and simple truth? I shall go about the city, because throughout its whole beautiful circuit I am refreshed everywhere, but satisfied nowhere.

9. Nor will this circuit weary me until a fuller entrance is opened, so that I may enter into the sanctuary of God “and understand in his latter things” [*in novissimis eius*]. There the circuit will reach its end, when we have been filled with the good things of your house, Lord; when I understand, in his latter things, him who is first and last, beginning and end.

Oh, what a circuit there will be: to proceed from him into him, to go and return; to go in desire and return in delight, while his presence always satisfies what experience desires—so that the mind of one who possesses and contemplates him may both be fixed upon him in longing and be sufficiently content in him! Thus those winged and many-eyed living creatures are said to be “in the midst and around the throne of God” (Rev. 4:6). They are in the midst because they are brought to the inner reality of their desire; they are around it because, with desire ever renewed, they are borne toward that same reality. They are in the midst because their desire has now been fulfilled; they are around it because they are not sufficient to comprehend the whole. They are admitted into the midst by grace, and excluded into the circuit by difference of nature. They are in the midst because they are united by contemplation, and around it because they are separated by comparison.

For what is this throne but that of which the Apostle speaks: the inaccessible light in which God dwells (1 Tim. 6:16)? However many-eyed those blessed creatures may be, he both illumines them so that they receive as much as they can, and surpasses them so that they are not adequate to the whole. Oh, how broad are the watchtowers there; how wide the streets standing open in that infinity of light; how closely confined, united, and extended are the lanes in that simplicity, charity, and eternity! Those ways—beautiful ways, peaceful paths. In those paths there is neither error nor toil. Everywhere the Bridegroom meets them there, and, with a glad countenance, so to speak, offers and pours himself into the heart of his beloved, so that Jesus Christ need no longer be sought—he who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON V. “Through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves.” (Song 3:2)

1. Yesterday’s sermon extended its limit at length while pursuing the Bride’s circuit. I give you thanks, Lord Jesus Christ, because you have made your words sweeter to my mouth than honey. Therefore things once tasted scarcely leave the mouth, so that others may succeed them; while they are delayed, they are chewed over again, and, if swallowed, they return once more to be chewed over with a certain sweet belching. All these things could have been said briefly and quickly; but the material under discussion pleases the palate of one who eats it and creates a certain appetite for itself, which does not easily yield once it has been brought into examination.

For even the bread which a nurse crushes for an infant to chew, once sufficiently softened by the diligent tooth, she holds in her mouth for a time, attracted by the savor of its taste. And we, breaking up the solid food of this Song for others who may perhaps need it, cannot forfeit the sweetness we have tasted. We serve another’s use in such a way as also partly to satisfy our own desire. Finally, when I think the sermon ended and concluded with an appropriate close, the feast of the word returns to my lips in impatient exhalation; and, while memory pours forth the abundance of its sweetness, the subject is recalled for examination.

Why indeed should not a fig tree be shaken frequently, whose fruit is never completely shaken off? What wonder if it is often plucked—a tree made more fruitful by its own stripping, seeming to contend with the hand that plucks it and to overcome the picker’s avidity by its abundance? Not like that fig tree which the Lord Jesus cursed, finding no fruit in it and condemning it, for its barrenness, to eternal dryness (Mark 11:13–14).

2. See how faith in Christ has made dry the traditions of the Jews and the doctrines of philosophers; how it has dried up the rivers of Egypt. In their teachings and interpretations one cannot find the fruit of which the Psalm says: “Our land shall yield her fruit” (Ps. 84:13). Christ cannot be found in their lanes and streets. Now, O Jews, he has departed from your bonds; he has left his house and abandoned his inheritance (Jer. 12:7). Indeed, you have become “like a booth in a cucumber-field, like a city laid waste” (Isa. 1:8). And it is likewise written concerning the streets that “truth has fallen in the street” (Isa. 59:14). For it was said of the philosophers of the Gentiles that they “held the truth of God in unrighteousness” [or, “suppressed the truth of God in falsehood”] (Rom. 1:18, 25).

Does it not seem fitting to understand Israel according to the flesh by the “lanes,” since they were of one seed of Abraham, compacted and confined into one rite, bound by one law? The wise men of the Gentiles, however, are rightly represented by the streets, because in unbridled freedom and license they wandered beyond the path of truth, maintaining and professing concerning the divine majesty things no less discordant with dignity than contrary to truth. The Jews, restricted by poverty of understanding concerning the singleness of the divine substance, could not extend the growth of faith to the persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Gentile philosophers, spread abroad upon an open plain and held back by no restraint of divine instruction, introduced a multiplicity of gods in their natures and infinity in their persons: each holding various opinions, all holding vain ones.

3. But what soul now seeks the Bridegroom in such lanes or streets? It is a concubine, if there is one, or an adulteress: the one does not have enduring fellowship with the Bridegroom, the other has faithless fellowship. What could she seek there, where chaste wisdom does not meet her, but alien and prostituted wisdom? Such a woman is depicted for you in Proverbs: meeting a foolish young man as he passes in the street near a corner, at evening twilight, in the darkness and gloom of night—a woman in prostitute’s dress, prepared to ensnare souls, talkative and wandering; now outside, now in the streets, now lying in wait near the corners (Prov. 7:7).

Such a street is suspect to me, in which a woman so changeable and deceptive contrives the snares of her enticements for a foolish young man.
