For I do not know what dark, distorted, and painted-over thing night, corner, and prostitute’s dress signify to me. Every doctrine is suspect to me—or rather, contemptible—that introduces no mention of Christ; that neither renews me by his sacraments, forms me by his precepts, nor inflames me by his promises. The Jews indeed have him on the page, but not in their interpretation. For the veil still lies more in their mind than upon the Law. Nor can it be removed unless they turn to the Lord.

I find suspect alike, in divine understandings and human practices, the freedom of the one group and the restriction and obstinacy of the other; the multiplicity in divine nature of the former, the singleness of the latter, and the blindness of both. Therefore I would not grant to the Bride that she should seek her Beloved in these lanes and streets. Let us assign her other lanes and other streets—those which Christ has espoused to himself in faith and truth.

4. There is, indeed, a certain twofold manner of life among the faithful. Some follow a broad way; others give themselves to the strictest discipline. For although it is written, “Narrow is the way that leads to life” (Matt. 5:14 [probably 7:14]), there is nevertheless some distinction within this kind of life, and one way is reckoned broader in comparison with another that is stricter. Does it not seem to you to be breadth of command where no one is compelled to perfection, but permission is granted not only to frail health but even to the will of one at a lower grade?

I thank you, Lord Jesus Christ, because you prepare occasions of salvation for us and propose counsel to the vigorous and eager in such a way that you also provide a remedy for the sick and make an ascent available to the sluggish. Your holy city Jerusalem has not only the lanes of those who live strictly, but also the streets of those who pursue humbler and more level paths. Thus, in every profession and order, the Bride seeks the footsteps of him whom she chastely loves, so that she may have from every quarter both an example of action and the flame of love. She does not disdain to borrow marks of virtue even from those who are outside, who are bound by no rule of stricter discipline, judging that affection is often more fervent where the rank of the order is lower.

5. What shall we say of those who seek occasions of salvation nowhere, everywhere making excuses—leniency in the streets and indiscretion in the lanes? Indeed, there are many such people: they examine every profession and order, but find in them nothing to draw themselves onward, only matters for their own detraction, alleging that strictness in some is excessive and in others nonexistent. It is their saying, and as wretched as it is true: “I did not find him.” It is certainly a perverse understanding to say, “Behold, Christ is here”—or rather, “Behold, he is there.” But it is worst of all to say, “Neither here nor there.” The Bride seeks in both, here and there: “Through the lanes and streets I will seek him whom my soul loves.”

Understand strictness by the lanes and dispensation by the streets. Interpret neither malevolently in ministers of the Church. The Church receives both; in both the Bride seeks Christ. Do not seek him in one only: seek Christ in both. Join lanes and streets together within yourself. Do you ask how? If affliction restricts you, whether voluntarily undertaken or violently imposed, expand yourself inwardly in the heart through spiritual joy, and you have already joined streets to lanes. Does not the person who rejoices at being enlarged in tribulation seem to you to possess both? (Ps. 4:2). The Apostle desired a certain breadth within the narrowness of tribulation for those to whom he said: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12).

Breadth, finally, is referred to hope: “Having such promises, beloved, be enlarged also” (2 Cor. 6:13). The present situation is narrow for us, but hope is broad. Possession is constricted, whereas expectation is more expansive. Therefore refer these streets to the breadth of hope. The Apostle says, “Rejoicing in hope.” But the Prophet says: “Your streets shall yet be filled with companies of those at play” (Zech. 8:5). You see how the Apostle and Prophet agree in what they mean by hope and streets: both assign joy to them.

6. At the same time, another distinction should be noted: in lanes there is dwelling for domestic needs; in streets there is a certain holiday leisure for delight. For in streets there are choirs and gatherings of those at play. Thus leisure and joy have their place in streets. Good indeed are those streets in which the spiritual soul, with lively enough agility, exercises itself in the light dances of contemplation.

In the streets, therefore, the Bride seeks him whom she loves when, freed from domestic cares, made external to the dwelling of the body, and abandoning, as far as is granted, her earthly house, she strives to contemplate as freely as joyfully. In lanes dwelling is more enduring; in streets it is brief, but sweeter. In lanes are the practice and exercise of virtues necessary for us while we remain in this dwelling of the body; in streets are certain holiday anticipations of future blessedness.

Now observe the sequence of the words. First he places the lanes, then the streets. You have something similar in the Psalm: “How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts! My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:2–3). Do you imitate the Bride’s diligence? Follow her order. Do not presume yourself wiser or readier than the Bride. First exercise yourself in virtuous action; then ascend to the watchtower of truth. Why do you prepare to enter there by the way that is an exit? Come with the Bride through the lanes to the streets, and with the Psalmist after the tabernacles of virtues to the broad courts of truth; otherwise, if you reverse the order, you pervert it.

The more closely confined the lanes are, the richer and freer are the inward leisure of the mind. What do I mean by leisure? More rightly, I should say devotion. Outwardly strict discipline inwardly enlarges the soul. Whether you understand freedom or joy by streets, where will you find streets broader than in our Order? Nor could you easily say where lanes are narrower, where there is greater freedom both for the use and exercise of virtue, than in this holy Order and community. Therefore liberty for good is greater because license for evil is less. The greater the strictness, the greater the right direction. Narrower lanes make broader streets.

What, then, is it to seek Jesus through lanes and streets, except to restrict and extend oneself in this manner so as to receive the joy arising from his illumination?

7. Do you wish me to assign both streets and lanes within the mind? Does not a person whose patience is troubled, whose chastity is hemmed in, whose charity is constricted, seem placed in a kind of lane and in narrow quarters? Does one who does not freely and without labor engage in any pursuit of virtue—without labor and anxious striving of soul—seem to you to be located, as it were, in lanes? And although they seek not without labor and effort, nevertheless even those who are such seek rest in him whom their soul loves, as though through lanes. Of them the Prophet says: “Lord, in distress they sought you”; and, “In the path of your judgments, O Lord, we waited for you.”

This happens more often to beginners and novices, who are accustomed to toil either under diverse temptations or under a certain weariness, when fleshly desires constrain them or the delight of virtues does not cheer them. Blessed is one who is not scandalized in these things, who is not offended, who does not lose Jesus but rather seeks him through such lanes; who seeks in distress, not like those of whom it is said: “In distress they sought you; your instruction to them was in the tribulation of murmuring” (Isa. 26:8, 16). Rather, he understands both the exercises of virtue and the instruction of the Father in those constraints, and stretches from end to end with strength until he escapes from the lanes into the streets.

Even those more perfect and accustomed to the streets are sometimes suddenly allowed to fall back into the constrictions of the lanes. And who is more perfect than she who is called the Bride? Yet even she seeks her Beloved through lanes and certain narrow passages. This difficulty of seeking is not idle. Through it her humility is exercised and her desire aroused. How often have I felt myself wandering as though in inextricable lanes and shut in by the constraints of mind, when suddenly I escaped into neighboring streets and the good Lord led me out into a broad place! In the lanes I almost expired, but in the streets I immediately breathed again. In streets there is commended to you a certain breadth and freedom of a mind unoccupied and unencumbered.

8. But take care not to give this freedom as an occasion for the flesh; do not heap mud in your street, the mud of unlawful thought. Otherwise the Lord will destroy you like the mud of streets. “They made our steps slippery in the streets,” says the Prophet (Lam. 4:18), wishing us to understand streets as muddy, where walking is slippery. Let your streets be paved not with mud but with gold. Let there be no mud there; yet let there not be in you a certain dryness and aridity. Rather, let rivers of living water flow there: a certain spiritual stream of meditation.

In the streets, O Wisdom, distribute these waters in the breadth of a free mind: “I was exalted like a plane tree beside waters in the streets” (Ecclus. 24:19). “Not only in the streets, nor only beside waters, but beside waters and in the streets I was exalted,” she says. For the joyful production of wisdom’s offspring, how much do you think both free leisure and the frequent watering of holy meditation contribute? Rightly is she exalted like a plane tree who is planted in this way.

O truly blessed streets, in which wisdom so grows, is so exalted and preeminent, displaying herself openly and needing no search! And observe how some people devote the whole breadth of their heart to worldly prudence, how they stretch and expand their mind into a street in order to plant there an unfaithful planting—that is, an alien shoot—and how they water it by continual exercises, frequent meditation, and instruction. Therefore you may see among them a joyful, abundant, exalted wisdom of the world, bearing fruit in worldly understanding; while the wisdom which is from God remains humble, obscure, and impossible to find among them.

9. Go out into the streets and lanes of the city. Examine the leisure pursuits; investigate the business of those occupied with lawsuits, who hold the chair, who sit on tribunals. Consider what they do in public and what in private. Does pure and true heavenly wisdom stand forth among them? Is that wisdom which appears in speech expressed in their conduct? Will you find it visible to view? Will you find it “exalted like a cedar in Lebanon and like a cypress upon Mount Zion”? For she glories that she is exalted upon those mountains also (ibid., 17).

The very names contain a mystery, and even the order of the words is not idle. Lebanon comes first in wisdom’s praise and Zion follows: after the whiteness of a pure heart, you ascend to the radiance of contemplated truth. Purity merits knowledge—not merely literary knowledge, but a kind of sweet and inward knowledge poured into the very marrow of the soul. Indeed, purity is truth’s companion, its attendant, and its forerunner. Therefore Wisdom joins these mountains, Lebanon and Zion, in her own praise.

Where among those occupied either in conducting or deciding lawsuits can you assign these mountains? Wisdom cannot be found among those in whom the place of wisdom is not found. She loves Lebanon; she loves Zion; she loves streets; she delights in freedom and loftiness. What perversity it is if wisdom occupied with litigation, wisdom pursuing profit, is prominent, while divine wisdom is hidden! The contentious wisdom rises above, while that which is chaste, peaceful, and compliant with good things lies neglected as if in darkness. The former is cultivated, the latter neglected as though barren and unprofitable. A neglected planting does not grow tall. Rarely will you find wisdom exalted like a plane tree in the streets. It is not readily encountered; it is not common. Therefore she says: “I sought, and I did not find him.”

10. Everywhere he is handled, everywhere turned about in inquiry; everywhere the name of Jesus is honored. And would that what the voice sounds forth, life brought forth; that imitation expressed it; that it stood out and shone in conduct! Let one who seeks Wisdom sitting beside you find her at your very doors, in your very senses, in the modesty and composure of the outward person. For these are like doors through which the signs of the inner inhabitant come forth. By the fruits it is known whether Jesus dwells with you.

The Bride comes to you, turns over the leaves of your fig tree, seeks fruit in you, seeks her Beloved. For this is fruit sweet to her throat. You are blessed when you abound in this fruit, when you satisfy your Lord’s Bride with this food. Her food is choice food. Her delight is that her Beloved should be with you. She does not envy or begrudge it. She wants her Beloved to be the Beloved of all. Therefore she seeks him among all, so that she may either find him among all or invite him to all. For she seeks Jesus among those whose progress in him she seeks.

She seeks through lanes and streets, but cannot find him in everyone. “I sought,” she says, “and did not find him.” Paul thirsted for the salvation of all; he wished to find Christ in the hearts of all, desiring all to be in the heart of Christ. But hear what he says, how he laments some: “I have no one like-minded. All seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:20–21). Do you think Christ can be found among those who do not seek him in order to find him?

You will indeed find many who seek something other than Christ, yet through Christ. He is treated in councils, debated in courts, discussed in schools, and sung in churches. These are religious activities; but go to their outcomes and weigh which end of such works is the more general. See whether, through all these things, a kind of trade in Christ is not being carried on. The name of Christ is a profitable commodity. Nothing is more valued; nothing more desired. Blessed, nevertheless, is the one who pursues the power of this name. Let this name be treated, debated, and disputed among them. It is enough for us if, at least in our cloisters, he is loved. Nowhere is the opportunity greater; and therefore nowhere is the shame greater if Christ is not found among us.

The form of righteousness is not found if the intention of pious works is not pure. For joy itself is a certain divine gladness of mind, commonly conceived from his presence, and which we may truly interpret as his presence. This heavenly and surpassing affection, I say, is not easy or commonly encountered. This, I think, the Bride especially signifies when she says: “I sought and did not find him whom my soul loves”—Christ Jesus, who lives and reigns unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VI. “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” (Song 3:3)

[Col. 0038B] 1. The Bride suffers delay in seeking, and the Bridegroom casts over her a certain shadow of difficulty, not immediately granting her the abundance of his presence. Yet she, with her zeal warm, continues her diligence and repeats her complaint: “I did not find him.” Brothers, if diligence is driven away, when will idleness be admitted? If love does not find him, when will lukewarmness find him? When will infrequent prayer, when slackness?

Why then should I now argue among you against infrequency of prayer and slackness? There is no need to apply a remedy to a disease from which you do not suffer. These vices are foreign to you. For who among you is not both frequent and fervent in prayer? Yet if torpor is absent, see lest weariness caused by delay exhaust you and break your desires. There is fault in either case if your soul is either slack in petition or failing in expectation.

You hear that the Bride’s desires are deferred, and you, at the first stirring of your prayer, complain because the delights of divine inspiration do not flow abundantly upon you? You have only now begun, and so quickly is your spirit broken from its proper course? What if that saying from the Gospel were reproached to you: “Could you not watch with me one hour?” (Matt. 26:40). Watch, therefore, and pray, because you do not know at what hour your Beloved will come. Persistent prayer reaches its end.

Even if in its beginnings it seems dry and as if stony to you, you will nevertheless draw forth the oil of graces from this very hard rock—provided only that you persevere, that prolonged delay does not dissolve you, that your vows do not grow languid through postponement. Delay is certainly painful to one who loves, but prolonged desires are accustomed to grow stronger. Why do I press upon you matters already known? Frequent distress itself will give you understanding of this, or rather, has already done so—often. I have often found you exercised in studies of this kind. I cannot boast that I have begotten these dispositions in you, yet I rejoice that I found you in them. And if I did not form these pursuits in you, would that I might be able to cherish you in them!

I too am a watchman; therefore you often repeat to me the Bride’s words: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” O blessed soul, exercised by desires so holy! Desires of the Beloved—of her who knows how to ask only concerning Christ, who, finding such a one, bursts forth into the words: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”

2. Finally, the bride is she who is found engaged in such inquiries: “The watchmen of the city found me” [Col. 0039A], she says. Those who are false and deceitful shrink from nothing so much as being found by such watchmen; and if they are caught, they are not easily convicted. Cain became a fugitive and wanderer upon the earth, afraid of being found. “Everyone who finds me,” he says, “will kill me” (Gen. 4:14). Sin does not wish to be killed; it does not wish to endure the salutary shame of confession or the healing correction of a master. It does not wish to be found, because it does not wish to die. For where an undisciplined affection does not fear being slain, but rather hopes to be indulged, it brazenly displays itself. But the bride offers herself of her own accord and gladly meets the bridegroom’s companions. Why should she not be glad? She is found not as one fleeing an avenger, but as one seeking a lover. “The watchmen found me”: they were not found, but found her. Their diligence is commended in this.

[Col. 0039B] Sluggish and unfaithful watchmen employ no diligence in this matter: they do not go about; they do not seek whether they may find someone with a seared conscience, betraying by the sign of chaste love and the zeal of seeking the fire of love. They do not visit those subject to them, and perhaps regard it as troublesome if they themselves are summoned by them. Some utter a word of consolation only when questioned—and not even then. They merely set forth what the letter has upon the page, adding nothing of their own zeal or diligence. Entirely different is the office of a watchman: he ought to anticipate, not merely answer; to awaken rather than wait for those who will ask; as though looking down from a watchtower upon the children, to see who is wise and seeks God. “I am your watchman: grant me, Lord, a learned tongue, that I may know how to sustain him who has fallen [Col. 0039C] with a word, and direct him to the Word.”

3. And what else does the bride desire when she says: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” You see that she is not so much wearied as stirred up by spiritual pursuits. You have understood her persistence in seeking the beloved; now observe her humble prudence. She does not know how to despise the watchmen. For she does not think it safe to pass them by without consulting them, knowing that they are aware of the Lord’s secret and messengers of his command. “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?”

Yet what does this question, put in ambiguous terms, mean? Did she wish thereby to admonish you not to believe every spirit, but to test whether the spirit is from God? For it is not granted to everyone who has either undertaken [Col. 0039D] or seized the office of watchman to provide certain evidence of the bridegroom. There are many, indeed, whose eye is “over the whole earth,” and, according to the proverb elsewhere, “at the ends of the earth” (Prov. 17:24). Their light is not with them; nor can they extend it beyond the boundary of earth or raise it to heaven. They are sufficiently faithful and diligent—but only in accumulating earthly things and guarding earthly things. “Their eye,” he says, “is over the whole earth.” Insatiable greed extends itself over the whole earth; therefore the mind, swollen with earthly cares and serving the table of him who perishes, does not know how to dispense provision for the heavenly banquet, or to temper for those subject to it something serene from the higher contemplations.

For even if persons of this kind are perhaps questioned concerning spiritual mysteries, they reply that the plain way of faith and morals is sufficient; thus consoling [Col. 0040A] their own barrenness, or measuring another’s desire by their own lukewarmness. For languid and slack love, with a certain blameworthy patience, does not so much desire future goods as wait for them. But more fervent love is borne along by burning desire, attempting secretly and in part to pluck the fullness laid up for it. Since the bride knows that there are very many watchmen of this sort, she weighs her question with a certain ambiguity: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” Let a man be prudent, faithful, and a diligent watchman; let him, by zeal for discipline, restrain the irruption of enemies from the sheepfold. Yet he will not immediately know how to sing of love, reveal the bridegroom’s presence as his messenger, or, being swiftly admitted into the secret recesses, distil something of the inward sweetness.

For it is a very unequal grace to detect the furtive and painted seductions of the adulterer [Col. 0040B] and to bring about the lawful comings of the bridegroom. Since experience of evils is common, knowledge of them is easy. But because spiritual perceptions are rarely exercised and judgment is slight, the evidence concerning them is rather tenuous; nor can spiritual things be judged except by spiritual persons. And therefore they can be shown only by spiritual persons, such as those of whom it is written: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those announcing peace, announcing good things!” (Isa. 52:7).

4. “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” The bridegroom is not seen in one single, simple, or uniform way. Abraham rejoiced that he might see his day; he saw it and was glad (John 8:56). Jacob saw the Lord face to face, and his soul was saved (Gen. 32:30). Moses saw, but saw his back [Col. 0040C] (Exod. 33:23). Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a high throne (Isa. 6:1). Ezekiel saw (Ezek. 1); Daniel saw him in the likeness of a man (Dan. 7:13–14), when he had not yet assumed humanity. But every vision of this sort before the incarnation was shown in a bodily appearance, not in the reality of a human body. The Apostles saw him in the very reality of flesh, and handled and touched him. Yet both inwardly saw God by faith.

It was said to Philip: “He who sees me sees my Father also.” That this vision is referred to faith is made clear by what is added: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise believe because of the works” (John 14:9–12). What connection could there be in adducing the fact that Philip saw him to prove that he saw the Father, unless Christ intended the same vision in both cases—the vision effected through faith? Therefore he immediately adds concerning belief: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise believe because of the works themselves.” If Christ dwells through faith in our hearts, and if our hearts themselves are cleansed through faith, why should he not also be seen by faith in our hearts?

The former visions, one of which occurred in an image and the other in flesh, are both full either of delight or of usefulness; yet the integrity of the third vision, which is through faith, is preserved.

5. To speak, then, of the Word’s appearance in the flesh: apart from the words of life that proceeded [Col. 0041A] from his mouth, how great a mark of power, do you suppose, shone forth in his outward bearing itself? How manifest were the indications given by eye, voice, and countenance of that which was within? Indeed, how did every gesture breathe divine grace? That was surely a delightful vision—but for one who believed God to be in the man.

And indeed, the vision granted to prophets and fathers before Christ’s incarnation breathed something divine in the appearing image and, as my faith holds, poured into the mind and senses of the beholder an inestimable delight. It appeared to the gaze only of those whose mind was pure. For after the resurrection also, it is written that he appeared in the very reality of his flesh only to witnesses preordained by God (Acts 10:40–41). Happy are those watchmen, if any frequently and familiarly receive such a vision—especially that vision which is the sight of flesh now glorified, such as Peter and John saw when he was transfigured upon the mountain [Col. 0041B] (Matt. 17:1–2). Yet the former was not true, and the latter not full.

For Moses was delightfully detained by that former vision, but was not satisfied: “Show me,” he says, “your very self” (Exod. 33:13, 18). Of the latter, moreover, the Lord himself says: “It is expedient for you that I go away; otherwise the Paraclete will not come” (John 16:7). Good, then, is the vision which the coming Paraclete brings: it is spiritual, because it is made inwardly through the Spirit. Indeed, “the spirit before our face is Christ the Lord” (Lam. 4:20). This vision comes either through understanding in truth spiritually unveiled, or through sweetness infused by grace. For to experience this itself is to see. “Taste,” he says, [Col. 0041C] “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9 [Vulgate]).

Certainly this vision is most sweet; and although, in relation to what is to come, it is not yet full in measure, it is nevertheless near—near in quality, not in equality. This vision is not subject to human ability or set before human endeavor, though it is sometimes freely granted to desire. Indeed, it is not such a vision as can be conceived by the powers of understanding and prolonged in an unbroken course within the memory of the mind. It is sudden and under its own authority, coming and going in a mighty spirit. It is sudden and momentary, arriving suddenly and departing suddenly. Yet, if it is momentary, remnants of thought remain—so kindled, so serene—and they keep festival in the mind of one remembering.

The memory indeed remains [Col. 0041D] of the vision tasted and swallowed; those able to taste its sweetness know how to pour it forth, especially at this hour. For the heart, still warm with recent grace, “utters a good word,” and fervent meditation pours out corresponding discourses. For words have a strong savor of inward sweetness, and the utterances that burst forth from abundance of grace are most pleasing.

6. If you are a watchman, know that you ought to prepare such things for meeting the bride. Why do you meet her if you come to announce nothing sweet, nothing new? If you cannot produce new things, bring forth old ones. Offer familiar things if you have no new things. Yet what is offered is not what she asks. She does not ask what sort of one you have seen, but whether you have seen him. It is enough to announce him as she knows him. [Col. 0042A] Nevertheless, you bring an increase of graces if you proclaim something new. For what is neither unknown nor unusual to meditation is accustomed to become sweet to the bride through a certain new grace. The ear does not grow weary when desire burns: only speak of the bridegroom, and you have brought forth new things in the bride’s ears.

You are not always able to answer concerning that excellent and surpassing mode of vision. It is lofty and subtle, and usually seizes suddenly upon a mind it finds pure and unoccupied. It seizes suddenly, but does not occupy it long. Since such subtle matters are not available at will, bring sweet things forward. Each article of simple faith, tempered by a certain sweetness of discourse, gives rise in the hearer to the most sweet affections and transports of mind. The bride is delicate: she wants sweet things rather [Col. 0042B] than strong ones—except that she can do all things in the bridegroom who strengthens her.

Let others tell tales and meditate controversies. Let your mouth meditate wisdom and your tongue speak delights, you who speak to the bride. For she too desires such persons as will relate and announce matters concerning the beloved. “The lips of priests ought to preserve knowledge”; therefore she seeks the law from their mouth (Mal. 2:7)—the law of seeing and finding the beloved. “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” From their vision she presumes that she herself will see; therefore she diligently investigates the watchmen’s vision, hoping by their conversation either to be led into more secret things or to be affected by sweeter ones. For this is to see him whom she loves: to conceive God’s wisdom and power with an inclined affection and a pure mind. He sees him well who conceives him in both ways: seeing purely [Col. 0042C] and feeling devoutly.

Sweet, I think, is the whispering that passes between the bride and the watchmen, and pleasant the interchange—if indeed there is an interchange. For none of their answer is mentioned here. If there is one, it is very secret, since she thinks it should be hidden beneath deep silence. “My secret is for myself; my secret is for myself” (Isa. 24:16). Nor do we dare here to conjecture anything about that which the bride took care to leave unspoken. Let us now close our discourse with their silence, postponing until tomorrow the bride’s passing on, by which she says that she passed the watchmen a little way and found him whom her soul loves.

## SERMON VII

“After I had passed them a little way, I found him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:4).

[Col. 0042D] 1. You are importunate creditors, demanding payment from your debtor with excessive insistence; yet you deserve pardon, provided that what you demand is just. But you require me to pay what I never bound myself to pay. I was intending to treat of the bride’s passing on. For to this I am bound both by the order of our discourse and by my promise; yet you still press upon me, along with the bride, that question: “Have you seen him whom my soul loves?” (Song 3:3). But she more modestly frames her question like one in doubt, seeking rather than urging. For she knows that discourse concerning this vision is not present for everyone or at every time. “Since he has hidden his face, who is there that beholds him?” Yet you press me to prescribe for you a rule for contemplating the beloved and to impart the discipline of finding and seeing him. What then? [Col. 0043A] Do you wish me to confine the bounty of a divine gift beneath a rule? This vision belongs not to effort but to grace; it is of revelation, not investigation.

Yet if effort can cooperate at all in these matters, observe first what is written: “Wash yourselves; be clean” (Isa. 1:16). Second, write wisdom in a time of leisure. “He who is lessened in activity shall receive her” (Sir. 38:25). Third, be violent and seize the joy of the kingdom which is withheld from you too long (Matt. 11:12): that is, have a heart purified, prepared, and importunate. By the first you will become worthy; by the second devout; by the third vehement—that is, fit, ready to meet, and pressing: fit to receive grace, ready to meet it when it comes, and pressing upon it when it delays. By the first you are prepared; by the second you are made like the bride awaiting [Col. 0043B] the beloved when he returns from the wedding; by the third you hasten. And the bride does not wait but hastens, and even passes the watchmen.

I would have spoken better if I had said, “She passes through.” For what we pass by, we do not look back upon or touch, but despise; whereas by what we pass through, we understand that we examine it, inquire into it, and as it were penetrate it. Nor is this passing through useless. For after she had passed through them a little way, she found the beloved. You see, brothers, what profit comes from consulting the watchmen: it leads a devout but wandering soul to the discovery of the beloved. Consultation is indeed useful; and often the humility of the consulter merits what the learning of those consulted does not provide.

It is good that you be diligent in seeking, but not continually so. For the bride questions the watchmen not so much deliberately as on an occasion, and while passing through. The love of the beloved drew her further on and did not permit her to spend idle leisure in conversing with them. She ran in the thirst of her heart, perhaps having drunk in a spirit from the bridegroom’s nearness; and thus she gave less attention to those who blessed with the mouth, stretching toward him who blesses in the Spirit, who is God blessed above all for ever.

2. Mark this, you who pray while passing through and read with delay: you who are fervent in reading but lukewarm in praying. Reading ought to serve prayer and prepare the affection; it ought not to steal the hours or cut short the intervals. When you read, you are instructed concerning Christ; but in praying you enter into familiar conversation with him. And how much sweeter is the grace of speaking with him than speaking about him! If those who devote themselves more vigorously to reading suffer certain losses of spiritual visitations because they pray too rarely, what shall we say of those whom undisciplined conversations dissipate or anxious questions divide?

For monks ought to pursue not conversation but silence, not questions but quiet. Or if disturbance is to be admitted, it ought to be of love, not contention. Holy love has its own disturbance, but such as you read in the prophet: “I will not be silent and I will not rest until the righteous one goes forth as brightness and the savior is kindled as a lamp” (Isa. 62:1). Does not she disclose a similar passion of soul when she says: “After I had passed them”? She was borne along by the force of burning love, and therefore declares that she had passed through, as though surpassing in eagerness [Col. 0044A] and desire whatever could be said. “After I had passed them, I found him whom my soul loves.”

She passed through them either by sifting their teaching or by estimating their nature. She passed through both what they could say and what could be seen in them. For whoever these watchmen may be—whether you interpret them as Cherubim or Seraphim—they cannot wholly set forth by speech, or express by imitation, all that belongs to Christ. “All things are difficult, nor can a human being explain them in speech” (Eccl. 1:8). If there is such difficulty in created things, who shall describe the Creator of things, worthily or fully? Therefore she says: “After I had passed through them.”

3. Would that we might be such hearers of the word of God as do not succumb to what is said, whether through slowness [Col. 0044B] of intellect or lukewarmness of desire; lest such things pass beyond us, surpassing both our desire and our capacity. Rather, let us pass beyond the effort of the teacher or admonisher, casting our minds toward greater things—even if we do not yet grasp them, at least desiring them. For in a certain sense one passes beyond what is proposed to him who seeks greater things, even though he does not at once attain them.

But the bride attained them; therefore, being chosen [variant: glad], she sings: “After I had passed through them, I found him whom my soul loves.” Why should she not pass through those whose knowledge is numbered and whose nature is limited? But he whom she seeks is great and immeasurable, and none other shall be reckoned equal to him. Therefore he cannot be weighed equally by another’s teaching or example. All others can be passed beyond [Col. 0044C]; he alone cannot be passed beyond. Indeed, he says: “Come over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my generations” (Sir. 24:26). He says, “Come over to me,” not, “Pass beyond me.” For how can what is immeasurable be passed beyond?

“A good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, shall be given into your bosom” (Luke 6:38). Immeasurability is dispensed to you in measure; for in itself it is immeasurable. He does not say, “Filling,” but “overflowing.” If, then, even the measure cannot be contained, when will immensity itself be contained? How can that be passed beyond which cannot even be fully grasped? Indeed, the bride does not wish to pass beyond him, but says: “I held him and will not let him go.” “After I had passed [Col. 0044D] them a little way, I found him whom my soul loves.”

Perhaps these watchmen, whom she passed a little way, were near the bridegroom, and thus she found the beloved. But if we understand this to be said according to his divine nature, which of created spirits comes near that immensity and majesty? For even if likeness is understood to be present, it is nevertheless known to be far inferior and unlike. “There is none, Lord, like you.” Perhaps, then, knowledge permits this nearness which their created condition excludes.

4. But who would dare to define, as perceptible to the intellect of a created spirit, that abyss of divine wisdom “which has no number”? “He dwells,” says the Apostle, “in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16). This light is inaccessible to us, but we are not inaccessible to it. Therefore he says: “I have brought my righteousness near, and my salvation shall not be far off” (Isa. 46:13). It was made near because it was incarnate; nearer because it was revealed; nearest because it was bestowed.

Christ Jesus, the righteousness of God the Father, was made near by assuming our flesh; but by a twofold privilege he surpassed the whole human race, so far as concerns the condition of human nature: in righteousness and integrity, because apart from him none is clean from defilement and none free from corruption. Therefore he was endowed with this double gift and went before his fellows. Let your faith, then, pass beyond all others, so that in him alone you may discern both the equity of righteousness and the integrity of like nature. Yet pass only a little way beyond, because as he far surpasses us in righteousness and incorruption, so he was made near by the condition of a nature not different from ours.

[Col. 0045B] The Jews did not know how, in their assessment of him, to pass beyond Moses, Abraham, or the other patriarchs and prophets: they regarded him as one among the rest and as possessing no surpassing grace. Thus they said: “Abraham and the prophets are dead, and you say, ‘Whoever eats my flesh shall not die for ever’? Whom do you make yourself?” (John 8:52–53). They were unwilling to pass beyond John, but said that John himself was the Christ (Luke 3:15). John, however, did not allow them to remain in that belief about himself, but turned aside from himself the opinion wrongly presumed: “I am not the Christ,” he said; “but one stands among you whom you do not know” (John 1:20, 26).

5. The Synagogue does not know how to pass beyond, but assessed him according to the measure of others; and it charged him, as though with blasphemy, that, being a human being, he made himself God. But the faith of the Church passed beyond and found him “anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44:8 [Vulgate]). And with what abundant oil was he anointed, from whose fullness he poured into the wounds of us all! For we are that wounded man who went down to Jericho, fell among robbers, was stripped, wounded, and left half dead. Many passed by, and there was none to save.

[Col. 0045C] That great patriarch Abraham passed by: he was not the one who justifies, but was only justified by faith in the One to come. Moses passed by: he was not the giver of grace, but the lawgiver—and of that law which brings no one to perfection. For righteousness is not from the law. Aaron passed by. The priest passed by, and by the same sacrifices which he offered without ceasing he could not cleanse the conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Heb. 9:14). Patriarch, high priest, and prophet passed by, dry alike in soul and in deed; indeed, they too were wounded in this wounded man.

That true Samaritan alone, seeing him, was moved by mercy, because he is wholly mercy; and he poured oil into his wounds, himself into hearts, cleansing through faith the hearts of all. Therefore the faith of the Church passes beyond all, reaching him whom it alone could not pass beyond; he placed [the wounded man] upon his own beast (Luke 10:30–34), and himself also became a beast of burden. And it passes a little way beyond so as to find him whom it believes to be so exempt from corruption as to proclaim him a sharer [Col. 0046A] in the common condition. Thus it holds him to be the prince of grace while confessing him a participant in nature.

6. And if we say that, in view of the most holy soul allotted to him, he surpasses even those heavenly angelic spirits, this will not be contrary to faith, but entirely fitting to the dignity of his person. For if he was made a little lower than the angels with respect to the part in which he was clothed with flesh, he is nevertheless equal to them in spiritual substance and superior in the prerogative of power. Pass beyond these also, therefore, O bride. For they too are your watchmen and caretakers, who say in the prophet: “We treated Babylon, and she was not healed” (Jer. 51:9).

Pass beyond these, I say, and contemplate in your beloved the endowments of singular privilege. They are ministering spirits, not workers of salvation; but he is the Angel of Great Counsel, who worked salvation in the midst of the earth. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name above every name. It is a delightful contemplation to behold in the heavenly household simplicity of essence, serenity of mind, and the sweetness of mutual love. It is a delightful contemplation to behold their perpetuity of being, purity of understanding, and depth of knowledge; and also their humility in obedience, tranquility in diligence, and power in effectiveness. Yet pass beyond them all and behold how great is this one who enters to save the nations. When he enters the world, angelic praises usher him in; and, returning triumphantly, they bring him back with a song of wonder: “Who is this who comes from Edom, [Col. 0046C] with garments dyed from Bozrah? This one, beautiful in his robe” (Isa. 63:1)—that is, in the robe of his flesh.

7. Rightly indeed is he beautiful in his robe: it was conceived without admixture, born of a Virgin, preserved free not only from all corruption but even from the tinder of corruption; it was not dissolved in the tomb, was raised on the third day, was taken into heaven on the fortieth, and every day—what is more wonderful and lovable than all else—is set before believers as food for salvation. Who would not lovingly marvel at each of these things and say, “Who is this, so beautiful in his robe?” You have run through all these kinds of wonder—or rather stood astonished at each one—and behold, fresh material for wonder rises for you again from this source. You have been sufficiently exercised in those things; here again you are stirred to amazement, as though that word of the prophet were said to you: “Do not remember the former things; behold, I do new things” (Isa. 43:18–19; the citation is printed as “Id. LXIII, 18, 19”).

8. What is more new than that in the mystery of the Lord’s body the matter is changed while the appearance is preserved? The former form remains, but a new grace is present, because there is a new substance—new not in itself, indeed, but under an appearance of this kind. Truly new is the fact that the substance of the Lord’s flesh, received under another appearance, gives the soul the power of sanctification; and, in the mystery of the altar, immaculate flesh cleanses the spiritual substance.

This is new, indeed, and beyond the manner of the other sacraments: not only is a new grace of sanctification given, but natural substance is changed. For [Col. 0047A] by the blessing of the sacrament the offered bread receives this ineffable change; and through mystical consecration and union with the living Word this life-giving grace passes over into Christ’s flesh. “For the flesh profits nothing; it is the Spirit that gives life” (John 6:64), granting to the most holy flesh in the solemn sacrament spiritual efficacy for giving life to those who partake of so great a mystery.

Beautiful, then, in his robe—that is, in his flesh; but much more beautiful in the assumed spirit, which is certainly superior to flesh because it is nearer to the Word. And understand him to be anointed above his companions in this spirit: that is, not only above the children of human beings but also above the ranks of angels. Why should he not be anointed above them with the oil of grace, when he is joined to that most abundant olive tree, from which all anointing flows, not as others are by participation, but by personal union? Does not Truth and the Word of God seem to you like an olive tree, whose anointing teaches us concerning all things, whose words are softened beyond oil, whose name is poured-out ointment? To this olive tree is joined by personal union the wild olive of our condition—not of our corruption, so to speak—and it has become a participant in its richness.

9. The signs of his works proclaim what light, sweetness, pleasantness, and every kind of power he received—except that what he perceived in the spirit far surpassed what he expressed in action. Thus, with regard to every sign of power, you may say: “Your name is poured-out oil,” apart from what lies hidden within (Song 1:2). For it is not fitting that even the most wondrous outward work of that soul should equal its powers. [Col. 0047C] “I cannot, Lord, comprehend all your works that are before me. For they have been strengthened, and I cannot estimate them”; and how shall I experience the grace hidden within?

No eye has seen, most blessed soul of Christ, except yours, the gifts divinely bestowed in you. Therefore the angelic spirits, failing to comprehend, do not cease to wonder; and, as though ignorant but amazed, they burst forth in praise of the one set above them: “Who is this, so beautiful in his robe, advancing in the multitude of his strength?” Considering this prerogative of powers in the beloved, the bride rightly says that she passed beyond the watchmen, and passed them a little way: for she so marvels at his singular grace that she nevertheless establishes a common nature, and regards that blessed soul of Christ as being, with the rest, of the same kind, though of different and surpassing power.

I had been preparing to explain to you yet another passing beyond; but the subject, which fittingly suggests it—or rather demands it—now presses the discourse toward its end. Meanwhile let us remain in what we have reached, so that from this step, when leisure is granted, we may pass on to the higher mysteries of the bridegroom of the Church, Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON VIII

“After I had passed them a little way, I found him whom my soul loves” (Song 3:4).

1. You have passed beyond, O bride of the Lord, your watchmen, his companions and participants: companions in nature, participants in grace. You have passed beyond them and reached the Beloved. Why should you not pass beyond those who would themselves pass away like smoke unless they stood in their Beloved? You found the Beloved, and found him anointed with the oil of the Spirit above his companions. In him you discerned certain privileges of powers in a like nature. You found that his holy soul possesses some gifts singularly and others supremely. Therefore you passed beyond them because you preferred him; and you say that you passed only a little way beyond because, in this preference, your consideration has not yet departed from the common nature of the same kind.

But will you stop here? From this step the advance must be pressed onward to further and higher things; one must reach the end. “For wisdom reaches from end to end” (Wis. [Col. 0048B] 8:1). Indeed, the heretic, in order to assign a higher rank to your Beloved, removes this rank. In Christ he joins only flesh to the Word and denies a soul; or, if he does not dare to deny this because of Christ’s clear testimony—“No one takes my soul from me, but I lay it down and take it up again”—he grants a sensing soul but removes the reasoning spirit. He corrected the error in part, but could not depart further from the Egyptian darkness. He could not complete the journey of three days.

The faith of the Church establishes neither a humanity alone nor a half-humanity in Christ. It places both natures in Christ. And because the divine nature is simple and admits no distinction, in the human being it confesses the threefold distinction set forth by the Apostle: the entire body, soul, and spirit (1 Thess. 5:23). Otherwise he did not assume the human being whom he was to reform in himself. Indeed, the rational part of the soul required the remedy of the human mediator, because it was darkened by the cloud of ignorance and inflamed by the spark of desire. The Church confesses both natures, human and divine, whole in Christ; and, like the woman of the Gospel, hides the leaven of divine wisdom in the three measures of human flour (Luke 13:21).

2. But what? Did Christ need a rational spirit—he who is himself the Father’s Word, wisdom, and truth? Nothing could be hidden from him; rather, he enlightens every human being coming into this world (John 1:9). By what reasoning, then, could the light that creates and enlightens need a created and enlightened spirit? [Col. 0048D] By none at all. He does not need it; this is my need. This concerns my blindness, not his brightness; not the Word that assumes, but the spirit assumed. I needed it, so that this part also of my nature might be united to the Word and so that the merits of this portion glorified in God might flow back through faith upon all.

All of us are reformed in Christ through our consubstantial mediator, approaching him through faith. Therefore the whole had to be assumed, so that grace might be poured back into the whole, because corruption had leavened the whole. Thus the two natures remain in one person, as whole, so also unmixed. For the divine nature is unchangeable [Col. 0049A] and immutable: it cannot be changed into another nature, nor does it permit another to be changed into itself. It cannot fail out of itself into another. Every change would indeed be a defect in it; nor can another advance into it. We can communicate with it, not change it; certainly by using it [variant reading: “by enjoying it”], not by existing as it.

3. Therefore to each of these natures remains its own integrity and property. Consequently, the perceptions, affections, contemplations, and blessednesses proper to them are also unmixed, distinct, different, and innumerable without number in the one person. For who would assert either that Christ’s most blessed soul feels absolutely no sweetness and joy, or, conversely, that it is allowed the inward taste of that sweetness, savor, and blessedness by which the most blessed Trinity enjoys itself? For it is of greater excellence to be that living good than to participate in it; and experience is far more direct and domestic in essence than in the use of it.

To be that very reality is indeed to enjoy it, yet enjoyment does not confer essence. How then is essence not greater even than enjoyment alone, because it is nearer? Further, although this soul sees all things in the Word and sees the Word itself in the Word, it has not been admitted, nor can it be admitted, into partnership in the divine essence or equality of knowledge. For the fact of being God essentially, of being wisdom, the highest good, the supreme, sole, and eternal power—what delight and joy this contains—whom shall we grant to know it except one to whom it has also been granted to be it? Therefore the Word of the Father knows himself and all things through himself all the more inwardly, sincerely, and simply, insofar as essential unity rests upon a better privilege than personal union.

4. We have repeated these points in order to distinguish the powers of the one Jesus Christ according to the twofold nature in Christ: that is, of the Word essentially begotten of the Father, and of the spirit created in time; especially on account of those who, from unity of person, infer equality—or rather unity—of both power and knowledge. Yet, while they say that the soul possesses by grace everything that the Word possesses by nature, they themselves seem, by distinguishing these terms, “nature” and “grace,” to introduce certain differences and degrees, so to speak. How much do those deny who do not grant that it has or knows this very thing by nature? For even if the soul of Jesus, united to the Word, is pre-eminently illumined by grace, will it also be said to possess by grace that it is naturally, essentially, and simply light, and illuminating? Or how will knowledge belonging to nature be superior to that belonging to grace, unless it is more explicit?

But they adduce what is written—and most truly written—that “all wisdom is from the Lord God, and has been with him always, and is before the age” (Ecclus. 1:1). If all wisdom is from God, with him, and before the age, how then are there many wisdoms together with that Wisdom which is from God and coeternal with him, because it is with him before the age? There are not many, various, and different wisdoms; but one alone and unchangeable Wisdom.

[Col. 0050A]

5. This question is now not confined to the one soul alone of the Lord Jesus, but extends to all souls that participate in any wisdom. Thus one may likewise ask whether all have one wisdom with the Word of God; indeed, whether they have no wisdom other than the wisdom which is the very Word of God. But if this is so, the wisdom of all will now be one and undivided. And why is it called “all,” if there is only one? What if it is spoken of numerically, not because it is itself countable, but because of the multitude of those possessing it? For faith too is called one because of the one thing believed, though each person has his own faith. Why then should not one thing be spoken of numerically, when many are spoken of individually?

Finally, many knowledges and many wills are attributed to the same person, and at the same time, because of the multitude of things which he knows or wills even simultaneously. Looking, therefore, to the things known, not to the power of the mind itself by which each person knows all that he knows, we say both that one person has many knowledges and that many persons have one knowledge. Therefore, when it is said, “All wisdom is from the Lord God,” this does nothing against establishing the unity of wisdom: for the word “all” refers not to wisdom itself, but to those things which are known through it. For the fact that there are many things illumined so that they may be seen, or many persons so that they may see, does not make the light multiple—the light which illumines things seen and shines upon those who see.

What then? Shall we say that the knowledge of the soul of Jesus is one and the same as that of the Word—indeed, that the wisdom of all rational spirits, both among themselves and with the Word of God, is one because it is the Word of God? Then this dispute will no longer concern the soul of Jesus alone, and we shall have no way of maintaining the difference of knowledge, set forth above, between the Word and the soul of Jesus. And how can a way appear, when by this argument the wisdom of all is proved one, because there is one light that illumines all?

Or perhaps, because illumination occurs in different ways, the illuminations themselves are also different from one another and differ from the light by which they occur. Thus, even among rational souls divinely illumined, the light by which they are illumined and the illumination itself which occurs through the light will be distinguished from one another. For illumination occurs in that which is illumined, and it occurs in time; but the light itself does not come into being, but is, and is from eternity.

[Col. 0050D]

In this way, who would deny that there are many knowledges in one mind, when he understands that there are many acts of comprehension in it, although there is one power of mind which comprehends and sees, and one illuminating light by which it is able to comprehend and see? These things, then, must be carefully distinguished: the light, and the illumination produced through the light in the mind of the one who understands. For to understand, to be illumined, and to know are one and the same thing. Who, then, does not see—unless these things are distinguished with the utmost subtlety because of a certain resemblance—who, I say, does not see that the light through which illumination occurs differs from the illumination which occurs through the light in whatever is illumined? The one is created, the other creating; the one illumined, the other illuminating. Nor can the wisdom which comes about through grace be essentially the same as that which exists through nature; nor that which comes about in time the same as that which was begotten from eternity.

[Col. 0051A]

6. If you, O bride, have distinguished these things in the Beloved, and from those powers which are in him according to the condition of human substance have passed over to the riches of the Word, then you may rightly and excellently say: “When I had passed by them a little, I found him whom my soul loves.” But how shall we fit in the word which is added, namely, “a little”? Divine majesty surpasses every creature beyond estimation, and yet, as though it were near and familiar, she says: “When I had passed by them a little, I found him whom my soul loves.” For a great abyss has been fixed between our nature and his. What kind of abyss do you ask? Surely, that of our emptiness. “All nations,” says the prophet, “are before him as though they were not; and are reckoned by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40:17).

Our substance is rightly reckoned empty, since that fullness is said to have emptied itself in assuming it. What proportion or nearness, then, can be assigned between emptiness and solidity, between nothing and immensity? On what ground, therefore, does she say: “When I had passed by them a little, I found him whom my soul loves”? Perhaps love is winged, and by the swift flight of burning desire flies past the intervening void of which we speak? Certainly I agree. For to love is already to possess; it is also to be made like and to be united. Why should it not be so, since God is love?

[Col. 0051C]

7. But here I offer another explanation. When one ascends after contemplating rational creation, divine nature immediately presents and meets itself at the first step; no distinction of any other, more excellent nature intervenes. For what middle thing can be assigned between image and truth, the one above and the other below? How can that which is not truth approach it more closely than by being its likeness and impress?

In what, then, is that in the rational spirit which is an image of the divine nature to be observed? First, because it is capable of truth and justice. Second, if it receives them and through grace becomes true and just—which God is by nature. Here I distinguish three things: being capable of the highest good, possessing that good itself, and being that good itself. The image is seen in the first, likeness in the second, truth in the third. The first belongs to all intellectual spirits; the second, only to the elect; the third, only to the uncreated Spirit.

In the first we come near; in the second, most near; the third is himself. We come near through aptitude; most near through fitting conformity. Near through the original nature; most near through the privileges of virtue. Near because we are capable; most near because we receive. For how can immortality fail to come near immutability, incorporeality simplicity, non-locality immensity, reason truth, virtue goodness? And, to speak more expressly, what can be nearer and more similar than wisdom to Wisdom, justice to Justice; than that which is illumined to that which illumines, that which is justified to that which justifies? What is more like another than an effect to its cause, what is formed to its form? For in what is formed, almost nothing other than the form is perceived.

[Col. 0052A]

Finally, what is sweet seems above all things like sweetness, and what is luminous like light. Therefore that which is matched with such eager rivalry to it seems not unjustly to be near—near because nothing intervenes. For although the infinity of divine immensity incomparably exceeds our finitude, nevertheless a certain kinship of image with truth is recognized.

8. Therefore she rightly says: “When I had passed by them a little, I found him whom my soul loves.” O how happy, how joyful an outcome of so long a circuit! Blessed are those steps by which one escapes into such an end. She sought in her bed, went about the city, questioned the watchmen. First she seeks through herself and within herself. Secondly, outside herself, but through herself. Thirdly, neither through herself nor within herself. And at this point, the more humbly she seeks, the more effectively she does so; and the farther she withdraws from confidence in herself, the sooner she finds.

“I found,” she says, “I found him”—him who first sought and found me, like a wandering sheep and a lost drachma, and whose mercy went before me. He first found me lost, went before me when I had deserved nothing. He found me wandering, went before me despairing; found me wavering, went before me distrustful; found me by showing me what I was, went before me by calling me back to what was his; found me roving in errors, went before me, empty of grace, with gifts. He found me so that not I but he might choose me; he went before me so as to love first.

Thus, being chosen and loved, sought and gained, found and anticipated, how should I not both love and seek him—by effort according to my strength, and by affection above my strength? I shall seek until, having obtained my desire, I utter the voice of joy: “I found him whom my soul loves.” I refer this finding not to the beginning of truth and grace, but to their increase. For as the soul advances and progresses from virtue to virtue, from truth to truth, while everywhere it is shaped by new mysteries and filled with joys, at each stage of progress it may say: “I found him whom my soul loves,” the Word of the Father, Christ Jesus, “who is God over all, blessed for ages of ages.” Amen.

## SERMON IX

“I held him and will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house” (Song 3:4).

[Col. 0052D]

1. “I held him and will not let him go.” I wished to refer the sense of this chapter only to future blessedness, when the Bridegroom will grant his Beloved the manifest fullness of his presence, so that nothing may interrupt its perpetuity. For what precedes—“When I had passed by them”—is not incongruously referred to that time: “When he has abolished every rule and authority, that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:24, 28). Before that time, who can truly say: “I will not let him go”?

But what follows constrains and overturns this interpretation, and makes it refer to the present: “Until I bring him into my mother’s house.” Let us now consider each point attentively. First observe how full of joy these words are: “I found,” she says, “I held, and I will not let him go.” That great patriarch Abraham is recorded to have seen the Lord, not to have found him. For the Lord appeared to him of his own accord, as he stood at the door of the tent at noon. Abraham then went out from the tent to meet him and diligently rendered service beneath the oak tree (Gen. 18:1–8); but he was not granted to bring him into the tent, much less into the chamber.

Moses also saw the Lord appearing to him on Horeb, but was not granted to hold him, since he was not even permitted to approach more closely (Exod. 19 and 34). Jacob saw the Lord, but saw him in a dream and from afar, standing upon the ladder (Gen. 28:12–13). For although he seized the angel, he nevertheless did not retain him; rather, by a certain violence of wrestling he wrung from him the grace of blessing (Gen. 32:24–29). He lost the presence, and therefore could not say: “I will not let him go.”

Mary Magdalene found him, but was forbidden not merely to hold him, but even to touch him (John 20:16–17), because she sought life beside the tomb. The aged Simeon received into his arms the long-awaited one, unexpectedly found, and joyfully burst into a song of thanksgiving; but he did not presume to use this saying: “I will not let him go.” For he says: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace” (Luke 2:28–29).

[Col. 0053B]

Certainly he is dismissed in peace when, released and separated from the flesh, he no longer lusts against the spirit or resists it. At the embrace of the new child, that man laid aside the oldness of the ageing man, and either asks or rejoices to be dismissed into a more tranquil condition, from the punishment of the corruptible body and the conflict of the flesh. But the bride presumes that the Beloved is not to be dismissed by her. And how much more excellent a grace it is not to let go what one loves, than to escape what one dreads!

2. Although all these saw while in the flesh, or in an appearance of flesh, certain degrees either of vision or of apprehension distinguish them in human minds. What we do not read as granted to any of them, she claims whose words we are attempting to unfold: “I found, I held, and I will not let him go.” I found him through inspiration; I held him through recollection in memory; I shall not let him go through unbroken continuance. “I held him.”

And you, when you have found Christ, when you have found wisdom, when you have found justice, holiness, redemption—for Christ has become all these things for us (1 Cor. 1:30)—when you have found these, hold them with affection, hold them with zeal. Hold by love what you have found by understanding; and, so to speak, bind the resisting virtues and slippery forms to yourself in a tighter embrace, until in turn they voluntarily cling to you, embrace you freely, hold you without the labour of your own striving, and do not permit you either to withdraw farther or to remain absent longer.

And if at any time you turn aside to the offices required by human necessity, may they pursue you there, recall you, and seize you back to themselves, so that, if they cannot have your effort constantly, they may always have your affection bound to them. For there seems to me to be some difference between your holding Christ, the power and wisdom of God, and your being held by him. “Love wisdom,” he says, “and she will embrace you” (Prov. 4:5–8). Indeed, it is said even of some that pride held them. What does “held” mean except: it ensnared them, entangled them, and bound them with the indissoluble bond of an ingrained habit [or, “a delicate habit”]?

[Col. 0054A]

For this is what follows: “They are covered with their iniquity and impiety” (Ps. 72:6), so that they cannot easily free and disentangle themselves from it. And to say more: if some persons are covered and wrapped, as it were with a skin, in the evil habit of vices, so that unlearning and disaccustoming themselves from it is less like taking off a garment than being flayed. Perhaps the ordinance of the Law that the skin of the sacrificial victim be removed indicates this (Lev. 1:6).

3. Conversely, when the priest is commanded to be clothed in close-fitting linen, the Truth who sprang from the earth wishes you to be more tightly bound in his garment, so that the virtue of chastity, purity, and innocence may cling to you and be joined to you through itself. And the Law wishes all the priest’s garments to be fastened and bound together, whether by little chains, belts, or bands (Exod. 28), so that, when you have put on our Lord Jesus Christ, when you have put on compassion, kindness, love, and the other virtues which you read of in the Apostle (Col. 3), when you have mindfully clothed yourself in faith in Christ and lodged deep within yourself the desire to contemplate truth, all may be fitted and joined together for you, held firmly, and nothing about you may wander or fluctuate or be puffed up by the wind of temptation or dissipation.

One who has clothed himself in such a habit of virtue that it seems transformed into his nature—I should say that this person is not so much holding as being held. “You have held my right hand, and in your will you have guided me” (Ps. 72:24). You held me lest I go into failure; you guided me into manifold progress. “In your will you have guided me”: that is, in the will which is from you and according to you; in a will which draws rather than is drawn. For sometimes we strive with much labour to draw a good will, and pursue it more as though it were fleeing than follow it as leading. Thus it is written: “I have desired to desire” (Ps. 118:20). Such a will is good, but not yet pleasing; just, but not yet delightful. “In your will you have guided me”—in that will which consists in the sweet taste of the good itself, and which, so to speak, relies not so much upon sluggish reasoning as upon the devout delight of the good itself.

[Col. 0054D]

4. “I held him and will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.” The sense would seem much plainer if she had said: “I will not let him go when I have brought him into my mother’s house,” namely, that heavenly Jerusalem above, which is the mother of us all. For before that time all things here are uncertain, fluctuating between hope and fear, and supported by an unsteady step. And what certainty can there be concerning grace while nature is mutable?

Indeed, that person says: “I said in my abundance, ‘I shall never be moved.’ You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. 29:7–8). Do not the Psalmist and the Bride seem to have said similar things to you? For what else is “I shall never be moved” than the “I will not let him go” found here? Yet there it is manifest presumption, because punishment is near: “You turned your face away from me,” he says, “and I was troubled.”

Since, therefore, while in this flesh falling is easy, assault frequent, slipping swift, and toil certain, how will these words of the bride—“I will not let him go”—not seem to be words of presumption and excessively ready devotion? For who here can remain in one state, especially that state of most subtle contemplation, which can scarcely be reached by the faintest stroke of the mind? Perhaps, therefore, these words express not security but anxious care. For there can be no security until she brings the Beloved into her mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore her.

[Col. 0055A]

Then there will be no anxious effort to retain him, because there will be certainty of remaining in that state of blessedness. Without the exercise of our effort and the guardianship of discipline, streams of living water and tireless delight will flow freely to us—indeed, inwardly—from a certain inexhaustible womb of the soul. Then there will be no need to dig deep, no labour either to cleanse wells which the Philistines have filled up (Gen. 26:18), or to defend them lest they fill them again. That labour is required here; there it is excluded.

Therefore, when she says, “I will not let him go,” she seems to promise effort and diligence, so that she may always be watchful, until she can be fully secure: lest from now on her Beloved, the Lord Jesus, slip away from her—he who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON X

“I will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house” (Song 3:4).

[Col. 0055C]

1. In the previous sermon we applied to the bride examples of weakness; today let us apply from the sacred Scriptures examples of strength. Of Hannah it is written, when she prayed with intent and overflowing affection, that “her countenance was no more changed in different directions” (1 Sam. 1:18). The countenance interprets the mind and receives its expression from the inward affection. Therefore from its constancy an argument is drawn for the inward perseverance which is in the soul. “Her countenance was no more changed in different directions,” because nothing was diminished from the desire once conceived.

And what else does her saying, “I will not let him go,” mean except, “I will not change my countenance in different directions, nor turn the gaze of my mind elsewhere from him”? The Apostle also gives similar exhortations: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17); likewise, “Giving thanks always” (Eph. 5:20); and again, “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Phil. 4:4). The Apostle wishes prayer, thanksgiving, and joy in the Lord to be continual and uninterrupted. But who could fulfil these by the very disposition of the mind and with untiring affection, except one permitted to say: “Who shall separate us from the contemplation of Christ?”

The Apostle says: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. 8:35). He could not say, “from contemplation.” For love sometimes compelled him to be separated from the contemplation of Christ. “Whether we are beside ourselves,” he says, “it is for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you. For the love of Christ constrains us” (2 Cor. 5:13–14). Thus love, by a certain dispensation, withdraws itself from contemplation, although contemplation is its proper and familiar sphere.

[Col. 0056A]

Everything love does has something of the place and efficacy of untiring prayer and thanksgiving. But it performs these more abundantly and excellently when it is exercised specifically in them. “Hide almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will pray for you to the Lord” (Ecclus. 29:15). Under the name of almsgiving may fittingly be included everything mercifully bestowed on the needy: not only bodily food and clothing, but also teaching, exhortation, correction, consolation, and all things which seem to concern solely the benefit of the soul. These are works of love, and they possess the force of prayer when done solely for God’s sake; but they are not love’s special and proper acts.

For what is so proper as to attend only to the Beloved and freely occupy oneself in the business of love? To become sober from this ecstasy and intoxication of spiritual delight, and for the necessities of brethren to moderate one’s alienation of mind—what is this except to change one’s countenance in different directions? Martha, indeed, was anxious and troubled about many things. That disturbance about many things appears to be a certain changing of the countenance in different directions. Mary chose the best part, which shall not be taken from her (Luke 10:41–42).

2. The exercise of contemplation and love is the best part. For although the things Martha did are works of love, there love serves necessity, not itself. In relieving the needs of others the work is good, but the cause burdensome. Mercy is good, but misery burdensome. Treatment is good, but the sickness around which it is occupied is not good. The affection of compassion in such cases is good; but the other’s suffering, which provides the occasion for compassion, is not good. In the needs of brethren, love considers whom it may pity, by what it may be moved to mercy, and what it should endeavour to remove. But when it contemplates the virtues of the Beloved, everything pleases, everything delights, everything attracts; it sees there nothing to dread, but only that to which it may sweetly cling.

[Col. 0056C]

This is love’s proper exercise, its office: to be wholly occupied in loving. Such, indeed, is the case when one undivided delight enfolds and embraces all things: office, end, and cause. Love is the office; vision the cause; both together the end. Nor can there be any happier end than the vision and love of God itself. To this end all the desires of the saints aspire. This end is its own end, content with itself and unable to extend expectation toward anything better.

This is the one thing called necessary, which is not taken from Mary, in which the Psalmist rejoices: “It is good for me,” he says, “to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28). This is that ecstasy of mind which caught Paul up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2). This intoxication produced in Hannah a countenance resembling that of a drunken woman (1 Sam. 1:13). With this new wine the apostles were drenched when the mighty Spirit had filled them (Acts 2:1–21), and when they first experienced the power of that new wine which Jesus promised (Matt. 26:29). Filled with this wine, Noah underwent an ecstasy of spiritual sleep and set aside care for the flesh (Gen. 9:21), becoming wholly spiritual, scorning what is behind, though what was before had entirely held him.

[Col. 0057A]

Happy would he have been if, like Hannah, he had never digested the power of this wine. For she suffered intoxication of mind while her body was kept disciplined outwardly, and a holy drunkenness which she afterwards did not lose. For this is what is meant by the words, “Her countenance was no more changed in different directions.” By saying, “I will not let him go,” the bride seems to promise herself such an unbroken continuance of the presence she has apprehended.

For what excellent, spiritual, or bride-worthy statement would it be if she referred her words, “I will not let him go,” to faith, justice, humility, self-control, beneficence, and the other virtues which Christ is said to be? For she must not be thought devoid even of these while she sought the Beloved. Indeed, such common virtues are advantageous to those who possess them, and to lack them must be regarded as sinful.

[Col. 0057B]

3. Therefore this finding signifies something exceptional and singular, by which she rejoices that she has found and apprehended the Beloved, and presumes that she will not let him go. Perhaps these are certain first-fruits of future contemplation and glory, which is why she adds: “Until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me”—into that heavenly Jerusalem which is the mother of us all, whose walls are occupied by salvation, whose gates by praise, and whose boundaries are set in peace.
