The virtues of this laborious life cannot be brought into that place of light and joy: if they enter by merit, they are nevertheless excluded in respect of their exercise. Therefore, having experienced in the Beloved some heavenly affection and supramundane savor, she says, not boastfully but joyfully: “I will not let him go until I bring him into my mother’s house.” But has he not already ascended to the Father? Has he not entered beforehand for us as forerunner? And how will you bring him into the place to which he ascended first? You rather need him to lead you, as it is said: “Lead me in the way of your commandments” (Ps. 118:35). “I go,” he says, “to prepare a place for you; and when I have prepared it, I come again and take you to myself” (John 14:2–3).

How, therefore, will you bring him into the place to which he has already ascended? He ascended indeed by himself, but in you he still remains outside; he is brought into you, to the place to which he himself first ascended. Why not? Is he born in you, formed in you, and not brought into you? “My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

[Col. 0057D]

Therefore Christ is both brought to birth and brought to completion in us—not once but often, and, I believe, by repeated travail. Nor can we adapt to ourselves all Christ’s virtues at once, indeed not even any one virtue completely. Therefore we must always persist, because the spiritual bringing-to-birth of Christ in us occurs only gradually. He who is born in his members, in his bride—why should he not be brought in? For neither this bringing-to-birth nor this bringing-in can be referred to Christ’s person, but to virtues and grace. Therefore, as the bringing-to-birth is frequent, so is the bringing-in.

Indeed, we are said to sit in heavenly places with Christ (Eph. 2:6). But just as there is one true and eternal sitting in heaven, so also there is one true and eternal bringing-in. Abraham travelled through the land of promise before possessing it (Gen. 12–17). Blessed indeed is the one who is granted to travel through those blessed regions, and, like a visitor, to tread every place with a flying footstep which he is to receive as a possession; to whom, although he is not permitted to stand there, it is yet granted to ascend the mountain of the Lord and, although still through a shadow and swiftly, to survey all things and be refreshed by such a sight.

[Col. 0058A]

4. But the true and full bringing-in seems to be indicated here when it is said: “Until I bring him into my mother’s house.” Blessed indeed is she who has been able so to bind the Word of God and join him more tightly to herself, and to keep him by her side in exile, until it is granted her to be united with him in the chamber. “I will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me.” This will happen when she fully bears the image of the heavenly one in body and mind, so that you may refer the meaning of “house” to the body and of “chamber” to the mind.

Or, if you prefer: understand secure possession in the house, secret possession in the chamber; everlasting possession in the house, inward possession in the chamber; eternity, as Ecclesiastes says, in the house (Eccles. 12:5), and love in the chamber. In the chamber, where, the door being shut, you no longer pray to the Father, but thereafter adore in spirit and truth. She does not say, “into the house of my father,” but “of my mother”; and “into the chamber of her who bore me.” That mind knows its measure and therefore extends its hope to that eternity, truth, and love which the Church of the firstborn has attained in heaven.

For, as regards the things of God, he alone possesses immortality, and he himself inhabits inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6:16); and the fullness of Christ’s love surpasses knowledge, that he may fill us into all fullness in himself (Eph. 3:19), he who is blessed God and reigns unto all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XI

“I held him and will not let him go, until I bring him into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me” (Song 3:4).

1. The affection of love is a delicate disposition, and spiritual joy is wounded by a slight occasion. Love is impatient of outward occupations; it has enough to serve its own concerns. It rejoices in leisure, is nourished by quiet, and wishes to have free time for inward delight. Does not the bride herself seem to suggest this to you, as she draws her Beloved into the secrecy of the chamber?

[Col. 0058D]

She knows that her Beloved cannot be securely possessed outside, nor indeed possessed whole. And how hard it is for one who loves to divide the mind between Christ and the world! How hard, I say, to admit foreign anxieties into the claims of love and infest the heavenly secret with worldly crowds! “I remembered God,” he says, “and was delighted; I was exercised, and my spirit failed” (Ps. 76:4). If delight in the remembrance of God becomes occupied with a task and exhausts the Prophet’s spirit, how can it embrace many other and foreign concerns together with this one?

The bride rightly seeks the chamber with the Beloved, that she may attend to him with free devotion, enjoy him according to the will of her soul, and wholly embrace him with a quiet breast. It is clear that she is led by the spirit of love and has spoken from a bride’s affection, seeking an opportunity to exercise love.

[Col. 0059A]

2. And how is it that, if we touch even slightly upon Christ, wisdom, sweetness, or the savour of contemplation, we are not content with grace nor attentive to our measure, but immediately strive to break out, and, disdaining the chamber, hasten to depart from rest and from that rest of which it is said: “In peace, in the selfsame, I will sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:9)? Mary, sitting at the Lord’s feet, held to that one thing; Martha was troubled about many things. In many things there is disturbance; but one thing is necessary (Luke 10:39–42), indeed also delightful. For “how good and how delightful it is for lovers to dwell together as one!” Otherwise, there is no dwelling as one except in love, which causes those of one manner to dwell in a house (Ps. 67:7). What does “of one manner” mean except conformed by the covenant of love?

Love reconciles and unites the human mind to God. “We shall be like him when he appears” (1 John 3:2). Why should we not be like him? The inestimable beauty of divine majesty, revealed to pure minds, commends itself and draws the affection of the beholder into itself; and in a certain manner makes it like itself, while allowing it to think of nothing else. We are drawn by fragrance, but transformed by vision.

[Col. 0059B]

Good, therefore, is the exercise of contemplation, which makes the human mind and the supreme Majesty of one manner and conforms them. This is a good dwelling, beyond which neither our desires draw us nor ought anything short of it to hold us. Who will grant me that this may be my rest for ever and ever? Blessed is the one who can say from the heart: “Here I will dwell, for I have chosen her” (Ps. 131:14). Mary chose the best part, which shall not be taken from her (Luke 10:42). Knowledges shall be destroyed, prophecies shall be made void, tongues shall cease (1 Cor. 13:8); contemplation alone will not fail in the future.

Therefore choose this part for yourself in the present, which will never be taken away, so that your soul may say: “The Lord is my portion; therefore I shall contemplate him.” The Prophet says: “Therefore I shall wait for him” (Lam. 3:24). And rightly so: for he waits for the fullness of the good, of which he already holds a portion. One who enjoys here the good of contemplation—what more can he expect of this kind, except something other, which he ought not to seek?

3. These good things, these goods, are laid up for many years—indeed, for all years. Therefore, happy soul, you who enjoy this good: feast, eat; for this portion will not be demanded back from you, but will be poured forth and restored more abundantly. “This is your rest for ever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen her.” Dwell here, so that you may dwell with him who sits above the Cherubim, above the fullness of knowledge, who inhabits inaccessible light. Therefore let your place be in the light of contemplation.

[Col. 0059D]

This is the proper and domestic place of your mother, the Church; this is her house. All the other things which perform the offices of temporal necessity look toward this end. The offices of action pass away; those of contemplation remain. It is good for you to be here; make your tent here. Make not one for yourself and one for your Beloved, but one for yourself and him together. Bring your Beloved into this chamber; enter into your rest, that you may rest from your labours, as God also rested from his.

On the seventh day he rested from the work of institution; on the seventh day he rested from the labour of restoration: in the former, after creating the world; in the latter, when he was laid away in the tomb. In the former, after founding worldly things; in the latter, after restoring human things. If you have sought, found, and held your Beloved, hold him whom you hold; hold him, cling to him; impress yourself upon him, so that his image may be re-formed in you as though stamped there, and you may be made conformed to this seal. And you will be so if you cling to him: “For one who clings to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). Perhaps, as in hard material, his impression is at first formed in you with difficulty; yet though the impression is laborious, the clinging is sweet. The sixth day of your re-formation is laborious, but the sweet sabbaths of rest follow.

4. Therefore, through this sabbath-rest, be buried with Christ into death. “Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord: henceforth,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labours.” The Spirit says this, assuredly by the bestowal of the rest conferred and by the effect of grace, just as he himself bears witness to our spirit. The Spirit says this because the Spirit accomplishes it. He says it because he gives it. “Henceforth,” says the Spirit, “that they may rest from their labours.” From their labours, he says—not from their works: “for their works follow them” (Rev. 14:13). Works follow the spirit as heat follows fire, shadow the body, light the sun, effect its cause. Whoever keeps sabbath in the Spirit need not pursue works, for works follow him. “Their works.” What are their works? What are the works of those at rest, the works of those dead in Christ, buried with Christ, the works of those keeping sabbath? They are festive; they are holiday works: these works have the value of leisure. Hasten to enter into this rest, into this sabbath-rest. But see that sabbath-rest is left only to those buried with Christ; it is left only after the sixth day—that sixth day on which either the old man is crucified or the new man perfected. For the former it is said that those who have died in Christ may rest from their labours; and for the latter, that, when the new man had been created on the sixth day, God rested from his works on the seventh (Gen. 2:2). You too prepare a sabbath for yourself: redeem the time, and claim for yourself hours set free from outward occupations.

5. But take care lest enemies mock your sabbaths; lest your leisure serve them, lest you be at leisure for them, though you ought to have been at leisure for God. “Be still,” he says, “and see that I am God” (Ps. 45:11). Leisure is good; but “write wisdom in the time of your leisure” (Ecclus. 38:25). Write it upon the breadth of your heart. For the heart is broad when no anxieties constrict it. Impress upon the inmost part of your heart letters that cannot be erased, and engrave upon spiritual tablets the marks of wisdom, so that you may say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been sealed upon us; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:7). Rejoice, keep festival with the Beloved, and feast, as is written, upon entering this glory. The sabbath, according to Isaiah, is “delightful, holy, and glorious” (Isa. 58:13). “Delightful,” he says, “and holy.” “Every idle person is in desires” [Col. 0061A] (Prov. 21:25); yet not every desire is holy—such as the desires of those who wish to become rich and thereby fall into many useless and harmful desires (1 Tim. 6:9). You see how the Apostle places a multitude of desires among vices. What if they are also unclean? For many who cannot act think secretly of things shameful even to speak of, consoling themselves in this by a meagre remedy.

To distinguish these people, Isaiah was not content merely to call the sabbath delightful; he added, “holy and glorious to the Lord,” so that your glory may not be in confusion. If you are at leisure, you have a sabbath. If you are at leisure and see, and contemplate the delights of the Lord, your sabbath is already delightful and holy, and a sabbath glorious to the Lord: a sabbath from sabbath—that is, leisure from leisure. The first leisure is good [Col. 0061B] if you are not at leisure for the world. The second is better if you are also at leisure from yourself and consider how you may please God. The third is best if, forgetting even yourself, you are at leisure for God alone and consider the things of the Lord—how he himself may please you. Let your sabbath not be idle: perform God’s works on your sabbath. For the work of God is that you believe in him. By faith you see. “For now we see through a mirror”; therefore be at leisure so that you may see. Vision—indeed, the vision of God—is a delightful work. You no longer need to contend for the faith, but only to delight in it. It has now been rescued from the objections of a persecuting people and of a perverting heretic. Establish it at the head of your thoughts, so that you may think the ancient faithful thoughts. Amen (Isa. 25:1).

## SERMON XII

[Note: [Col. 0061] In the Clairvaux manuscript this sermon is continued with the preceding one.]

“I have held him, and I will not let him go, until I bring him into the house of my mother” (Song 3:4).

[Col. 0061C]

1. Those do not know how to hold ancient thoughts who seek novelties of words, who forge new dogmas, who do not turn away from youthful desires, who possess nothing of gravity, nothing of authority, nothing full of antiquity. There is no *Amen* where there is either disputation or deceitful thought; where there is either unbelief or faith itself wavers. Enter into the secure retreats of faith; bring the Beloved into your mother’s chamber, so that whatever you understand of Christ, whatever you think, you may confine within the Church’s rules and correct according to her judgment. Perform such works on your sabbath. Otherwise, if you are at leisure and do not devote yourself to such pursuits, vain thoughts and poisonous counsels will easily burst forth in an empty mind.

For, as you have it, “nettles and thorns overrun the field of a sluggard” (Prov. 24:30–31); and the Gospels tell you that “two shall be in one bed: one shall be taken, the other left” (Luke 17:34). The idle and tranquil life of those living in the Church’s bosom is like a certain bed: those occupied by no burden of ecclesiastical office, nor stretched by anxiety over governance and stewardship, but enjoying free leisure under another’s rule. Yet not all rightly and lawfully enjoy this leisure; rather, they make the freedom of time which they possess an occasion for temporal things.

2. For the bed is good if anyone uses it lawfully [Col. 0062A] and turns the opportunity of outward quiet into the pleasure of inward vision. These are those who will be taken from this chamber of the Church into that heavenly one, that where Christ is, there they too may be with him. For “where the body is, there the eagles also shall be gathered” (Matt. 24:28). Be like an eagle, and use keen sight. Accustom yourself to spiritual contemplation; dwell among rocks and abide upon steep crags—indeed, enter into the caverns of that single Rock, which is Christ. Enter, according to Isaiah’s word, into your chambers; shut your doors, and hide yourself for a little moment until indignation has passed by (Isa. 26:20). Rather, hide yourself so that delight may remain for eternity.

Enter into the chamber of peace, into the powers of the Lord, for peace is in his strength. Remember his righteousness alone, so that Peace and Righteousness may meet within you. Remember his righteousness alone, because “what have you that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). His righteousness alone. Good is that righteousness which you defend against the solicitations of vices by a kind of battle. Happier is the state in which you do not fight for righteousness but delight in it: where you devote yourself not to conflict but to delight; where you do not wage strife with vices but establish fellowship with virtue. You possess this righteousness; you do not assail that righteousness, when, forgetting the things behind, you think not of human things but of the things of the Lord, and remember his righteousness alone, once righteousness and peace have kissed one another within you. For “the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy” (Rom. 14:17). If it is a kingdom, why should it not be a house and a chamber? For “in peace is his place made, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3).

[Col. 0062C] Enter into the chamber of peace—of this outward peace indeed, but still more of that inward peace—into the dwelling of contemplation; for Zion is interpreted “Contemplation.” “In peace,” he says, “in the selfsame I will sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:9). He refers “the selfsame” to contemplation, because this is the better part that shall not be taken away. Thus the Bride too fell asleep with the Beloved in her mother’s chamber, and in the Bridegroom’s embrace underwent a certain ecstasy of the sleeping mind. Hence follows: “I adjure you,” and the rest.

3. Therefore, if you have laid hold of the Bridegroom, hold him and do not let him go until you bring him into the house and chamber of your mother. Why should I now persuade you to do what experience itself, by the sweetness perceived, much more strongly invites and draws you to do? For if anyone, with a mind at festival, has been able furtively and almost in rapture to taste beforehand the festive joys of free meditation, I do not know whether he ever does anything more willingly than wholly and completely to give and devote himself to this pursuit. Thus the first allurements of beautiful contemplation drew the Bride and summoned her to the chamber of rest, into which she rejoices that she will bring the Beloved. “I will not let him go until I bring him.” Does it not seem to you that by these words she says what the Psalm says: “If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, until I find a place for the Lord” (Ps. 131:4–5)? I let go of everything, lest I let him go. I count everything as loss, that I may gain Christ, because of the surpassing joy of his presence. “If two sleep together, they shall keep one another warm; but how shall one be warmed alone?” [Col. 0063A] (Eccl. 4:11). Ecclesiastes says this.

It is good to be warmed and kindled in the Word’s embrace—for the utterance of the Lord is exceedingly fiery—and to burn with spiritual desires. Therefore I shall not give sleep to my eyes or slumber to my eyelids until I bring him into my mother’s chamber. Then I shall rest, and my sleep will be sweet. John, reclining on Jesus’ breast, as it were slept, where all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge are hidden. There is the place of true rest, the serenity of understanding, the sanctuary of piety, the chamber of delight. Sleep here, that you may see what he saw: the Word in the beginning, the Word with God, and the Word God (John 1:1); and understand Christ’s coeternity of existence with the Father, distinction of persons, and consubstantial unity. What seems more like sleep to you? Human sight cannot venture here, nor reason break in. For “man shall not see these things and live.” It is good, therefore, for you to fall asleep and be lulled by forgetfulness of human senses and affections, so that you may dream dreams of this kind.

This is the chamber of the Apostles, who begot us in Christ. Paul is as a mother when he says: “My little children, with whom I am again in labour until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19). You have a mother; do you wish to have a chamber? “Our citizenship,” he says, “is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Do you wish for sleep? “We are beside ourselves,” he says, “for God” (2 Cor. 5:13).

4. Pass here, then, with the Beloved; remain here; meditate upon these things; be occupied with them. Or, if you cannot attain this [Col. 0063C], proceed more moderately. If you cannot recline on Jesus’ breast, where is the inexhaustible well of wisdom, rest between his shoulders, where you may contemplate the examples and mysteries of his patience. “Between his shoulders,” because “government has been made upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9:6). And of Benjamin it was said that the Lord’s most beloved one “shall rest between his shoulders.” Jesus indeed rested and fell asleep on the cross, so that you too may sleep with him in faith and remembrance of his Passion. Or rather, move between these portions—from breast to shoulders, from the mysteries of faith to the manifestation of truth. In the one make yourself a house, in the other a chamber. “Benjamin, the Lord’s most beloved, shall dwell as in a bridal chamber all the day, and shall rest between his shoulders” (Deut. 33:12).

[Col. 0063D] Do you see how he places the bridal chamber between the shoulders? What then will be upon the breast? Certainly in both places there is a place of beautiful contemplation, both between the shoulders and between the breasts. But grace is more abundant on the breast, where there is the place of love, the seat of thoughts, the occasion of embrace, and the fullness of seeing the face. Rightly, then, is there a bridal chamber—indeed, a treasure—on Jesus’ breast. For there are both the Bridegroom’s delights and the Word’s riches, because “in him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge of God.” Enter into these treasures; hide yourself in the hiding-place of his face from the disturbance of men; and let no one awaken you or make you wake until you yourself will it. For this too is contained in the Bridegroom Christ Jesus’ following adjuration, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XIII

“I have held him, and I will not let him go,” etc. (Song 3:4).

[Col. 0064A]

1. We are still held by the examination of this chapter: “I have held him, and I will not let him go.” Must such care and effort be applied that, once your Beloved has been grasped, he may be retained? If he is the Bridegroom, he responds to his lover in equal measure. How is it that he does not of his own accord cling to you and bind himself freely? For impatient lovers are so jealous that, even when expelled, they intrude importunately, and harsh rivalry unlearns shame. Yet now you say, “I will not let him go,” as though he wished to withdraw unless he were held more urgently. How, if he loves, will he either wish to withdraw or allow himself to be torn away?

Or perhaps you are troubled by a lover’s suspicions, and by a certain needless fear of losing him, arising from great affection for retaining him? Yet fear is not needless where the outcome hangs in uncertainty. Fear is not needless amid dangers. But you must fear more your own inconstancy, which is near at hand. For he is God and does not change. Your inborn fickleness is close to falling; by some unstable motion of a wandering mind you are most easily swept away unless you cling firmly.

2. But let us now refer these words to the primitive Church. For they seem to belong to her, as, by a kind of prophetic confidence, she defends to herself the rights of faith and charity against the injuries of persecutions. See how many attempted either to tear apart or to adulterate this spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church. Consider the beginnings of the nursing Church, when, like a newly wedded bride, she hastened into Christ’s first embraces. What fury, what deceit she endured in those days, good Jesus! Heresies indeed had to exist, and persecutions had to exist, so that she might cling all the more tenaciously to the Beloved in proportion as she saw herself more violently torn away from either her faith in him or her confession of him. “Who,” says one person on behalf of the whole Church, “shall separate us from the charity of Christ?” (Rom. 8:35).

Thus among them neither was the truth of faith corrupted nor the freedom of confession silenced. “For Zion’s sake,” he says, “I will not be silent; and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest” (Isa. 62:1). When the disciples had been beaten in the synagogue, they were ordered to be silent. But for Zion’s sake they are not silent, and for that carnal Jerusalem’s sake they do not rest (Acts 5:40–42). Truly carnal is the Synagogue, which extinguished within itself the life-giving Spirit and strives to tear him from the Church. It did not approve having Christ in knowledge; therefore it was given over to a reprobate mind. For it rejected the approved stone, the chosen stone. It held the Law but did not know Christ; it took away the key of knowledge, neither entering itself nor allowing others to enter. Why do you shut us out, to whom Christ has opened? Upon his shoulder is the key of David’s house, which opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens (Isa. 22:22). He opened to the Gentiles and shut to the Jews. For blindness has happened in part to Israel, that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter. Judea is blind and, beneath the veil of the letter, does not know how to find the door.

The Synagogue proclaims the veil and rejects the truth, neither offering nor dividing rightly. For it would divide rightly if it distinguished observance of the letter [Col. 0065A] from its interpretation; if it assigned one time to the antiquity of the former and another to the newness of the latter. “There is a time to sew and a time to tear” (Eccl. 3:7). For those precepts were at once commanded, and these things foretold. But in the former there was figure; these were beneath figures. The Church now divides and tears apart what had been sewn together; and, although it once knew the letter according to the flesh, it no longer knows the one whom the Synagogue held as though wrapped up and now lets go revealed.

3. The Church says, “I have held him, and I will not let him go.” The Synagogue rejects him—indeed, reproaches him; but the Church does not fear the voice of one reproaching and speaking against her, nor the face of the enemy and persecutor. Thus that wicked servant says in his heart: “My lord delays [his] coming” (Matt. 24:48–49). And so he beats the Lord’s servants because they now know and announce his coming; but for Zion’s sake they are not silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake they do not rest. They can strike the body; they cannot strike Christ out of the mind. By scourges their affection for Christ was bound more firmly in their hearts. They were scourged in synagogues, handed over to prisons, dragged before tribunals; but amid all these things they rejoice because they were counted worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus.

“I have held him, and I will not let him go.” She held him because she did not fear. She did not fear when the whole earth was shaken and the greater powers of this world were moved against her into the heart of bitterness. She was glued to the Bridegroom by a cord that could not be broken, the cord of charity which does not know how to fail, for charity never fails. She acted confidently because she clung by charity. “For whoever clings to God is one spirit” [Col. 0065C] (1 Cor. 6:17); “and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17). Therefore she acted freely and held fast the unwavering confession of her hope.

At that time faith indeed appeared a thing of folly, and confession something worthy of shame. Why do I call it shame? It was a matter of extreme danger. Yet they could not fear those who kill the body. For “the spirit of life before their faces is Christ the Lord” (Lam. 4:20). Therefore they suffered themselves to be torn from the flesh more readily than from his charity. She retained nothing of herself for herself, that she might hold him. Therefore she says: “I have held him, and I will not let him go.” Certainly she held firmly amid so many who perverted and persecuted, while the age of our faith was still tender.

[Col. 0065D] 4. “Until I bring him into the house of my mother.” Our faith has now been brought into safety. There is no one openly attacking it; those who had been persecutors have become compliant, and those who were perverters have become guides. It has been brought from the field into the house, from the sea into harbour. The rage of persecuting rulers has now turned into favour; the crafty quibbles of heretics, refuted by the uncorrupted truth of catholic faith, have fallen silent. Our faith has now been rescued; Christ has been rescued from the objections of the people. He has now been established as head of the nations, and is no longer set as a sign to be contradicted.

After the many struggles endured by martyrs for Christ’s faith; after he broke so many violences of persecutors and refuted the craftiness of heretics; after the cross of Christ is no longer a scandal but a joy, and we have become for this world not a spectacle of disgrace but a triumph of grace; after so many dangers have been sailed through—does it not seem to you that Christ’s Church has brought her Beloved, as it were, from a field of battle and toil into the chamber of peace and rest?

5. You see, therefore, the necessary diligence in the beginnings of the Church’s birth, lest the Beloved, long desired and at last grasped, could be snatched away. But what shall happen henceforth, now that he has been brought into safety and, as it were, into the bridal chamber through faith? Shall there henceforth be room for sloth, and shall we bid diligence farewell? Will one be endangered in calm who could not be endangered in storm? Or is not one in danger who dies? “Faith without works is dead” (Jas. 2:20). The Apostle commends faith, but faith “which works through love” (Gal. 5:6). Where there is the work of love, or love of work, there is life of faith. But what if there is truth in belief, freedom in confession, and no life through love? This is not a threefold cord and is easily broken. For that freedom is imaginary which does not arise from the root of charity; nor does such confession depend so much upon its own freedom as it makes use of another’s licence. It is precarious, not its own; it depends on rulers’ favour, not on the warmth of faith. Faith is animated into life by the fervour of charity. It is plainly sluggish when danger threatens, unless, by love’s assistance, it claims for itself freedom of confession. Otherwise confession perishes from the dead, as from one who does not exist. Thus without charity both faith is dead and confession vain.

[Col. 0066C] The Apostle says that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. 3:17). Does he dwell through dead faith? If truth is within and life outside, Christ is divided; for he himself is truth and life. You have not yet brought your Beloved in completely if half of him remains outside. What if he is not even Beloved? For how can he be Beloved if charity is not joined to faith? “Christ, risen from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. 6:9); but he does not die to himself. Take care lest he die to you—or rather, lest you die to him. Otherwise, what love can there be of the dead, or with the dead? On what grounds, then, will he be called Beloved where there is no love? If Christ dwells in your heart through faith but is outside through charity, I fear—indeed, it is true—that he is either half within you or dead. “I live,” says Paul, “yet no longer I; but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20).

6. You too may claim the use of this saying, provided that with him you can say: “The charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). But in some this life is laborious; in others it is free, living amid certain spiritual delights. But if you have still wholly passed under the jurisdiction of the flesh, if the rulers of darkness have easy and familiar access to the recesses of your heart, and if you have prostituted your soul to unclean lovers, what agreement can you have with Christ and Belial? What fellowship has light with darkness?

But if, for Christ’s charity, you have declared war on vices and on the instigator of vices, [Col. 0067A] you do indeed hold the Beloved, but your condition is not yet secure. You are still troubled and do not enjoy the tranquillity of the bridal chamber. Faith is in harbour, but you must still break—or at least flee—the assaults of perverse habit and the mass of temptations, whether newly arising or frequent. Hold fast amid dangers lest he escape from you, until you bring the Beloved into your mother’s house and into your mother’s chamber. Hold him with labour, lest he slip away more quickly from one insufficiently watchful and insufficiently attentive. You hold him by faith; you hold him by profession. Hold him in your morals; hold him in your manner of life, and do not let him go.

There is now no longer a struggle for the truth of faith; but the heat of this spiritual contest has wholly flamed up against good morals and an honourable life. In these last days dangerous times are at hand, when people are lovers of themselves, covetous, proud, inventors—indeed, instigators—of evils (2 Tim. 3:1–5). At the rising of Christian faith, a great persecution of this name broke out; today a foul and all-too-slow pestilence of morals exhales. For bad examples corrupt good morals. Draw us, good Jesus, in the fragrance of your ointments, lest the pestilential air breaking forth from near at hand make the salt of wisdom in us tasteless. Paul says: “Let your speech always be in grace, seasoned with salt” (Col. 4:6). Is speech alone meant, and not rather sight, hearing, gait—in short, every outward bearing—which ought to be seasoned with salt? “Please all people in all things,” he says, “as I also [do]” (1 Cor. 10:32–33). But if the leaders of the Church have become tasteless, with what shall the people be salted [variant: *salient*, “be salted”]?

[Col. 0067C] 7. And we, brothers, who profess the religious life, ought to be the salt of the earth. If salt has also lost its savour in us, with what shall it be salted? Priest and people alike: so that the people may more freely become like the priest. Monks diligently conform themselves to the world; and those who are in the world defend their error, quite cleverly and all too truthfully, by our example. Shepherds and people, secular and religious, mutually either form or foster one another in vices by their examples. Storehouses are full of such things, vomiting from one into another the pestilential spirit of either shameful or lukewarm conduct. Alas! With what eager mouth of heart do we inhale this perverse spirit and drink in this corrupting air! This pestilence flows everywhere through our windows.

Good Jesus, when will it be—if indeed it will ever be—that, as faith is whole, morals too may be uncorrupted? When will it happen that, as peace is with truth, so there may be no conflict for virtue? When shall we embrace you whole and entire, at our will, in the chamber of contemplation and rest? Few in the Church have reached this state, yet they profess it in part: “I have held him, and I will not let him go, until I bring him into the house of my mother and into the chamber of her who bore me.” The whole face of the Church is not such, but much of it is such, so that it may say: “I have held him, and I will not let him go, until I bring him into the house of my mother and into the chamber of her who bore me.”

Faith is more widely spread; the works of charity have been contracted. Must we observe this distinction only in the whole body of believers, [Col. 0068A] and not also in each of us? For who is there whose integrity of devout affections is as secure as his true and undoubting faith? Great indeed is anyone, if such a person exists, who never wavers in faith and is likewise troubled by no passions of the soul. Certainly I would call such a one an entrant into the secret places of the chamber. The tranquillity of the heart is a good chamber. Wisdom labours with some; but the Spirit of the Lord rests with the humble and tranquil, and his place is in peace.

But let our discourse rest here for the present; or rather, may our understanding rest, I pray, in this secret of the chamber, so that what experience has taught it may more fully pour forth in the discourse that follows, through the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the stags of the field, that you do not awaken or rouse the Beloved until she herself wills” (Song 3:5).

[Col. 0068B]

1. It is evident that she has fallen asleep, for whom such an adjuration is made. Why should she not sleep when she has entered with the Beloved into her mother’s chamber, the retreat of delights? She sleeps when she undergoes an ecstasy of mind through the Beloved’s approach. “I adjure you,” he says, “do not awaken the Beloved.” Blessed indeed is she who is permitted both to hold this Beloved and not compelled to let him go. Hold what you hold; hold, and linger over the word of life carefully and diligently. Unroll the scroll of life, the scroll which Jesus unrolls—indeed, which is Jesus. Wrap yourself in him; wrap yourself in that linen cloth in which he himself was wrapped, for “he is clothed with light as with a garment.”

Put on your Beloved, our Lord Jesus Christ. Carefully carve for yourself a memorial in the rock, a new tomb in which no one had yet been laid. For Christ is the Rock. New things can always be found in Christ. One may penetrate into new things. There are many recesses in him, innumerable treasures of wisdom. One fleece does not suffice; he can be shorn repeatedly. Mystical meanings and consecrated affections are good fleeces. Jesus abounds in such things; he cannot be stripped or despoiled. “I will rejoice over your words as one who finds much spoil” (Ps. 118:162). Clothe yourself in this spoil; wrap yourself in fleeces, so that, as it is written, your sides may be warmed (Job 31:20), for “his word is fiery” (Ps. 118:140).

[Col. 0068D] Rest in these things, that your sleep may be sweet, as Solomon says (Prov. 3:24). Thus the Bridegroom also guards and cherishes this sleep of his Beloved, forbidding her to be awakened. “I adjure you,” he says, “by the gazelles and the stags of the field.” This is indeed a new adjuration, containing no more matter for wonder in its outward form than in the power of its mystery.

2. Asking what sacrament these animals contain, hidden within themselves, I understand them to portray a certain cheerfulness of free mind and agility of spirit, which runs and leaps, so to speak, toward higher things. Do not those seem to you to be like certain gazelles and stags who, although remaining in the body, have nevertheless escaped the body’s inconveniences, and by spiritual lightness scarcely feel the burdens of flesh or know the weight of earthly mass through the mind’s power? These are those who, walking in the Spirit, no longer feel the desires of the flesh; or, if they feel them, feel them languid and, as it were, gasping their last breath. To such people the Apostle says: “You are not in the flesh but in the Spirit” [Col. 0069A] (Rom. 8:9). And so, “though we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him [so]” (2 Cor. 5:16). He has now become wholly spiritual; he has withdrawn to heavenly solitudes; he has ascended to higher things.

Therefore the Church says: “My Beloved is like a gazelle or a fawn of stags upon the mountains of Bethel” (Song 2:9, 17). He who says, “If you have risen with Christ” (Col. 3:1), and so forth, invites you to these mountains. Paul wishes you to become like a spiritual gazelle when he summons you to those heavenly mountains and clothes you in the image of that singular fawn. “As,” he says, “we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of him who is from heaven” (1 Cor. 15:49). Paul himself is a good stag when he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Certainly a good stag is one whom the Spirit of the Lord quickens and moves; for the Spirit of the Lord is subtle and mobile. Good are the stags whom the voice of the Lord prepares, to whom it reveals the dense thickets of mysteries, within which that blessed fawn lies hidden. Certainly a good gazelle is one who can say with untiring and indefatigable devotion of spirit, in all things either proposed or imposed upon her, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56:8), and who, forgetting the things behind, stretches toward those before.

[Col. 0069C] 3. You have heard what is common to both; hear what is distinctive, that we may assign some distinction between these animals and our discussion of each may not be confused and indiscriminate. In stags, observe antiquity of life; in gazelles, keenness of sight. Stags are said, by a certain natural skill, to protect themselves from old age and to recall a life tending toward decline from destruction by a renewed freshness. Christ is singularly called not so much a stag as a fawn: he flourishes with eternal newness and has nothing of oldness mixed in him that would continually need renewal. He alone is a gazelle by privilege of sight. For “no one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom he wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). But all things are naked and open to his eyes.

Thus those too are understood as certain spiritual gazelles who have the eyes of their mind unveiled in the knowledge of God; who, having become spiritual, judge and search all things; who contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face. Stags, on the other hand, are those who are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord; who, putting off the old man, put on the new, who was created in righteousness and holiness of truth; who restore devotion growing old and languishing, as it were, with weariness, to renewed fervour; and who, through frequent renewal, know no weariness of perseverance. “Those who trust in the Lord,” says Isaiah, “shall renew their strength”—not to lose the old strength, but to add new strength. They shall renew strength by frequently restored increases. “They shall renew their strength,” he says: “they shall run and not labour; they shall walk and not fail” [Col. 0070A] (Isa. 40:31). This change seems to be an unceasing renewal of progress without failure or weariness. Good indeed is strength which, though running with labour, nevertheless does not know how to decline into failure. Better certainly is strength which does not even feel the discomforts of labour, but leaps over the obstacles of opposing difficulties and, as though on the level expanse of a field, moves with unimpeded steps, according to what is written: “The swift runner makes his paths clear” (Jer. 2:23).

4. This is why he here calls them stags of the field: all rough and all steep things are level and passable to them, and are laid open to unobstructed running like the plains of a smoother field. It is the voice of the Lord, the voice of inward inspiration gently entering the ears of the mind. It is this voice, certainly, that prepares stags of this sort and reveals the thickets. For if there are any thickets, thickly overgrown as though with the prickles of repeated obstacles, they are not thickets to those whose feet the Lord makes like the feet of stags; who can be delayed by no barrier of injuries, but rather glory in tribulations and know how to regard injuries received as welcome—or to pay no attention to them at all—because of the vehemence of desire hastening toward higher things and straining toward those before.

O wretched times of ours! How almost all of us recoil from this rule into its opposite, interpreting even things full of the appearance of piety as injuries! Nearly everywhere we encounter obstruction; we stumble on level ground; and our steps have become slippery in the streets, as Jeremiah says [Col. 0070C] (Lam. 4:18). We complain that all things are blocked against us, since “the way of the slothful is like a hedge of thorns” (Prov. 15:19). We rejoice in occasions for complaint and stand ready for suspicions, so that, as Scripture says, “the sound of a flying leaf” seems to frighten us (Lev. 26:36), and we strive to summon up troubles of mind by hands and words. Hence we too often disturb the rest of spiritual persons, interrupt their leisure, trouble the sleep of a mind intent upon higher things, and tear them from the Bridegroom’s most pleasing embrace.

5. Therefore the bridegroom turns away from his beloved disturbances of this kind—whether perversity seeks them out or weakness produces them—inviting the daughters of Jerusalem to a certain spiritual cheerfulness. This is the meaning of his adjuring them by the gazelles and the stags: that they may be stirred to emulate spiritual men [Col. 0070D], and cease their importunate harassment of the beloved. “I adjure you not to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.”

It is beneficial to you that the beloved should wake; but wait until she herself wishes. Her choice must be awaited, for whose care your service is intended. Then she will wish, when the Spirit has taught her to wish. The Spirit’s anointing will teach her. For, cleaving to the beloved, she has become one spirit with him. Therefore she can say: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to preach the gospel” (Isa. 61:1).

Therefore she will preach the gospel to you when she has received the time from the Spirit. Meanwhile, let her drink deeply, so that she may pour forth more abundantly. The grace of contemplation does not empty out compassion, but gives it form; and the ecstasy of the mind makes one temperate toward the weak. Thus, while Adam sleeps, the manly rib softens into the weaker [Col. 0071A] sex; and for the sake of social union woman is formed from the man’s side; indeed Adam himself is transformed into a companion-woman, and by a certain conforming passes into the spouse. Therefore, when he awakes, he first utters the voice of love, recognizing himself in his counterpart: “This now,” he says, “is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:21–23).

Does not Paul seem to you to bend manly dignity toward the humbler sex when he says that he became weak to the weak? (1 Cor. 9:22.) Like a spiritual Adam, apostolic steadfastness becomes Eve when it has compassion on those subject to it; and the loftiness of power and knowledge is tempered, with a certain sobriety, to the capacity of the weak. And although he is beside himself in mind for God, he nevertheless becomes sober for others (2 Cor. 5:13). Ecstasy of mind is a good sleep: [Col. 0071B] it does not induce pride, but teaches sobriety.

“I adjure you not to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes”; and though meanwhile she is beside herself in mind for God, she will nevertheless become sober again. If she is now asleep, she will awaken once more and will pour out to you, with a certain moderation, the wines she has found. She herself knows when to distribute spoil to the household and provisions to the maidservants. How will she not have compassion on the daughters of her own womb, when she does not even pass over the maidservants? Yet good daughters regard themselves as maidservants, and do not know natural freedom, since they reckon themselves to have been set free by the Spirit of truth. For those whom truth sets free are truly free; and therefore they know no other freedom, rejoicing that they have been set free through adoption. Finally, the more gratuitous the adoption, the more devoted is the self-abasement. Thus they are both maidservants and daughters; because where [Col. 0071C] the condescension shown in adoption is greater, there devotion in subjection is more fitting.

6. “Do not awaken her until she herself wishes.” She herself knows when to distribute spoil to the household and provisions to the maidservants. There is no need to fear of her what is written: “The daughter of my people is cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness” (Lam. 4:3). The ostrich has the appearance of feathers, yet lacks the power of flight. It does not know how to fly through ecstasy of mind; therefore it does not care for its offspring, but leaves its eggs upon the ground. It forgets that a foot may trample them or a beast crush them. The ostrich does not know how to rise into the sleep of contemplation; therefore it does not clothe itself with compassion.

For the mother’s sleep in ecstasy of mind serves the daughters’ advantage, [Col. 0071D] and every prolongation of her spiritual sleep is for their profit. Therefore he says: “I adjure you not to awaken the beloved until she herself wishes.” It is a good adjuration, by which both the mother is spared and the daughters’ progress is sought. For the more freely she is at leisure and sees, the more abundantly she revisits the young women. The more loftily she is suspended, the more humbly she comes down and the more profitably she condescends.

Why do you wish to regulate times which the bridegroom has placed under the beloved’s will? “Do not awaken her,” he says, “until she herself wishes.” Then she will wish when the vision of the beloved has flown away from her eyes. His presence is fleeting and suddenly slips away: “I belong to my beloved, and his turning is toward me” (Song 7:10). Why do you attempt to tear apart before its time so holy a communion? Blessed is the encounter, but its hour is brief. Let its brevity suffice for her: why [Col. 0072A] do you wish to shorten it? Nothing should be taken from so small a moment. Let her freely enjoy meanwhile the passing hour.

Do you wish to awaken her and draw her away to yourselves—her whom Christ awakens and makes wake in himself? For although she sleeps, her heart keeps watch in Christ. Peter and those with him on the mountain were weighed down with sleep, and when they awoke they saw Jesus’ majesty. Well were they weighed down with sleep, since in them human perception was restrained. What was from themselves was weighed down and restrained in them, so that, blind and dull toward things of the world, they might awaken, stirred by the divine Spirit, only to know the things of God. “When they awoke,” he says, “they saw his majesty” (Luke 9:32).

He keeps watch well who sees such things: who sees the glory of the Only-Begotten from the Father; who hears secret words which it is not lawful for a human being [Col. 0072B] to utter. A vision cannot be spoken to one in whom the Son of God has not yet risen. “See that you tell the vision to no one,” he says, “until the Son of Man has risen from the dead” (Matt. 17:9). A vision cannot be spoken to one in whom Christ has not yet risen. Thus it was likewise said to Mary: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20:17).

It cannot be spoken to one who has not been snatched up into paradise, into the place of delights, into the place of which Peter said: “It is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:4). He is well awakened who, with Paul, is snatched up into this paradise (2 Cor. 12:4); who goes up the mountain with Peter; who can keep watch with Christ even for one hour; whom no human being touches in order to awaken and make him watch, but Christ does. Christ himself touched Peter; therefore [Col. 0072C] he awoke and saw his majesty. Finally, see what sort of rising this beloved makes from the bridegroom’s embrace. “Who is this,” he says, “who ascends like a slender column of smoke?” (Song 3:6.)

7. But let us now call back the discourse that is ascending here, and reserve this chapter for another beginning—indeed, for him who says of himself: “I am the beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25). May he be for us both the beginning of discourse and the Word of the heart, so that he himself may first speak within us those things which we are about to say concerning him. Speak, Lord; speak to me, and speak for me. Rebuke for me the daughters—not of Jerusalem, but of Babylon. Tell the daughter of the Chaldeans to sit and be silent.

Good God, how many daughters of Babylon there are today who do not know the songs of Zion, on account of whom we hang up our instruments! [Col. 0072D] How many sons of Edom there are who empty and drain us of spiritual joy! You restrain the daughters of Jerusalem from harassing the beloved. Would that you might spare me, Lord, from the daughters of Babylon. For the harassment of the malicious is different from, and much more troublesome than, that of the loving. Yet, by some misery of our present age, the loving themselves have become malicious.

How maliciously does a friend act today against a holy person? I should have said, “an enemy”; but I said what hurts more. Friends themselves have become enemies: friends by profession, enemies in affection; friends in appearance, but denying the power of friendship. Absalom was a friend, because he was a son; but how maliciously did that wicked man act against the holy one—son against father, Absalom against David! Absalom means “the father’s peace.” Certainly a good name; but he himself denied the force of this name. He sought the kingdom and defiled the bed.

Yet David was fortunate: among so many sons, only one persecutor arose. Whom can you give me today among teachers [Col. 0073A] against whom only one Absalom plots? Are not certain people like Absaloms, who, as it is written, “proclaim peace and bite with their teeth”? (Mic. 3:5.) They seek the father’s place; they foul the bed while corrupting companions by wicked whisperings; and they overthrow the hearts of the innocent, in whom the father’s spirit had rested sweetly. He is an Absalom by imitation who both arrogates to himself the teacher’s place and detracts from his life; who preaches peace and bites with his teeth.

Detraction is an evil bite, an evil food of which it is said: “For evil is sweet in his mouth, and he hides it under his tongue” (Job 20:12). He hides it until, at the proper time, he vomits out the poison [Col. 0073B] he has gathered. How maliciously does a friend act against a holy person! Indeed, what he does not see he suspects. “They set up their signs as signs, and did not understand” (Ps. 73:3–5). They posit what they do not find; they posit what they later explain perversely. “Their signs,” he says. For they make themselves the standard when they measure others by the rule of their own perversity. “Signs”: as though he said, “Signs only, not truth; signs not of certainty but of suspicion.” “And they did not understand,” for they rely not on knowledge but on conjecture.

An enemy acts maliciously against a holy person (Ps. 73:3–5). Against which holy person? Against the Holy of Holies; against the Holy One who says: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). It is rash, as the Apostle says, to judge another’s servant (Rom. 14:4). Who then are you, that you judge your [Col. 0073C] master? For whoever judges authority judges God’s ordinance.

8. Finally, he complains and says: “Men have taken away my judgment from me.” [Note: [Col. 0073] On this passage see *Doctr. PP.*, book *Against Rash Judgments*.] “Children of men, why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” You surely love the vanity of precedence, and therefore seek in your prelates the falsehood of perverse suspicion. For the children of men are vain, deceitful in the balances (Ps. 61:10), deceitful in their judgments. And would that it might be of little consequence to me to be judged by a human day, while I await the judgment of the eternal day: “When,” he says, “I receive the appointed time, I will judge justices” (Ps. 74:3).

The righteous Judge himself says that he waits for the time in order to judge justices; and do you assume judgment for yourself before the time? The Father has given all judgment to the Son; and do you assume for yourself a judgment which you have not received, [Col. 0073D] and that against a father? Take care lest perhaps it be against that Father “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.” A viperous brood devours its mother and with a venomous tooth gnaws away the teacher’s life. These are not daughters of Jerusalem, daughters of peace, but of Babylon.

When will you rebuke them and say: “Daughters of Babylon, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves”? For the reproaches of those who act in your stead fall back upon you; and their murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord. Therefore refrain from murmuring, which does you no good and harms others. You, Lord—rather, stop the mouth of those speaking iniquity, and do not shut the mouths of those singing to you.

But why do I now [Col. 0074A] linger any longer over these complaints? My present purpose is not to lament what is ours, but to sing what belongs to another. Let it suffice that I have bewailed our own troubles briefly. Now I return from laments to songs, he granting us mind, speech, and leisure—Christ Jesus, who restrains the restless from the bride’s sleep, reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages. Amen.

## SERMON XV. “Who is this who ascends through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke from spices?” (Song 3:6.)

1. “Who is this who ascends through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke from spices?” See, brothers, as you also see, how effective tranquillity of mind is for the growth of graces; what fruits Christ’s beloved harvests from inner rest. See, I say, what kind of person she comes forth from the bridegroom’s embrace. But do not ask me what sort of person she advances as; consult rather the bridegroom’s companions about this. What if she comes forth even to them, as though new and unfamiliar, from the secret recess of the beloved’s bosom? New indeed. For newness itself produces wonder. “Who is this who ascends?”

Observe her progress. Above, she questions the watchmen and asks about a vision of the beloved. Here she bursts forth before the very watchmen, marvellous and new in appearance. Why should she not come forth new from the beloved’s embrace? For he is the one who says of himself: “Behold, I make all things new” (Rev. 21:5). Even things that are new he renews. Suppose he is a furnace: bring gold near; if it is pure, he makes it purer and draws forth shining metal from the furnace with a fresh brilliance. Is not Christ a furnace? [Col. 0074C] “Your utterance,” says the Psalmist, “is exceedingly fired” (Ps. 118:140). Whatever has been refined in this furnace cannot come forth except new, and as though a second creation in Christ.

Thus, while he prayed, his appearance itself was made other (Luke 9:29); but when you pray, his appearance becomes other in you. For remaining one in himself, he renews all things. The Lord’s bodily appearance was made other while he prayed; and by this he wished to commend to your mind the power of prayer, because it is prayer that makes you inwardly another, changes you into a new human being, and renews you by meditation. “We,” says the Apostle, “beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image” (2 Cor. 3:18): that is, we are transformed into the image which we behold.

2. Perhaps the bride also came forth from the secret place of contemplation clothed in the image of the bridegroom whom she beheld. [Col. 0074D] New indeed. For the companions’ wonder concerning her proclaims her newness: “Who is this who ascends?”—as though to say, “She is not as she was yesterday or the day before.” She no longer circles the city; she does not run through lanes, squares, and among watchmen. She does not wander aimlessly, but ascends by a straight path.

What is this sudden newness in her? “Who is this who ascends, and ascends through the wilderness?” She truly considers the whole world through which she ascends a wilderness—dry and barren. By what reasoning has the scent of this wilderness become for us like the scent of a field full and as though the Lord had blessed it? How many does the scent of this wilderness draw to itself [Col. 0075A] and hold so that they cannot be torn away? This scent is “the scent of death unto death.” What you imagine to be abundance is emptiness. Indeed, it is a land of thirst and an image of death, as Jeremiah the prophet says (Jer. 2:6): “A land,” he says, “of thirst.” For it irritates rather than satisfies worldly desires. This fullness which you suppose is fruitless; and if it contains any fruit, that fruit is fleeting and, by its changeableness, bears the image of death. How can you think that you smell the fragrance of life where you see the image of death?

The abundance that breathes Christ’s fragrance is the scent of life. For he himself is the field truly full, the fertile field, the field which God the Father blessed. The bride knows no field other than this; she considers all else wilderness and a salt land.

3. “Who is this who ascends through the wilderness?” Certainly the wilderness will be good if your heart has not been furrowed by the enemy’s plough; if it has not been watered by his drippings or enriched by his dew; if the tares that he sows over you do not luxuriantly grow—or rather, grow again—as in fertile soil. Let your heart be barren, lest it either produce such a shoot or receive such seed. “My soul,” he says, “is like a land without water before you” (Ps. 142:6). Such a soul is a good wilderness. Likewise, whole flesh is a good wilderness: flesh untouched, flesh not furrowed by unclean desires, flesh ignorant of the seeds of carnal pleasure. “For whoever sows in the flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh” (Gal. 6:8).

Finally, a virginal womb is a good wilderness. Such was the womb of that blessed woman, possessing singular virginity, which no unclean injury of any shameful stirring or impure desire violated. Her flesh was like a wilderness land, pathless and waterless, in which Christ appeared. Yet it was not wholly desert, since it bore Christ: it was watered, but with streams of virtues. Therefore it is called a well of living waters flowing with force from [Col. 0075C] Lebanon, because the brightness of virginal purity pours forth spiritual graces. Her womb was a garden enclosed by the discipline of virginal chastity, because the heat of carnal desire did not break down the hedge of integrity. Therefore, being watered with such waters, it yielded its fruit in its season.

Do you wish to hear what fruit this wilderness land bore? Hosea teaches you, saying: “The Lord will bring a burning wind from the wilderness, and it will dry up the veins of death” (Hos. 13:15). Who else dried up the veins of death but Christ Jesus, whom the wilderness of an undefiled womb gave forth to us? And rightly is he a wind, because “Christ the Lord is Spirit before our face” (Lam. 4:20). Finally, he was called the second Adam, “a life-giving Spirit” (1 Cor. 15:45). By his breath the apostolic clouds fly, at which Isaiah marvels (Isa. 60:8). What wonder if he is called wind, whom you also read to be called a cloud? “The Lord,” he says, “will ascend upon a light cloud” (Isa. 19:1).

Do not understand “light” here as wandering and unstable. Rather, apply the idea of lightness to spiritual fitness: the incorruptible body brought no heaviness to the soul, nor did earthly dwelling weigh down a mind contemplating many things—indeed, all things. Are not all those like holy winds who, escaping earthly things through spiritual lightness, establish their citizenship in heaven? But he is wind in a special sense, who rides upon the wings of the winds of the rest and surpasses the powers of all spirits. Rightly therefore he calls him wind, and a burning wind, because by his breath the chill of sin has been melted in us, and our captivity has been turned like a torrent in the south. The disciples felt themselves burned by his heat when they said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke?” (Luke 24:32.)

And I do not know whether he breathes more willingly anywhere than in the wilderness and pathless place of chaste and uninjured integrity. He gladly blows through such places; he refines the soul of a chaste body with the heat of love; dissolves it, melted by spiritual desires, into subtle vapours; and makes it rise like a slender column of smoke.

[Col. 0076B] 4. “Who is this,” he says, “who ascends through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke?” And flesh exhausted and dried up by the strength of chastity is a good wilderness: flesh which breathes out no cloud of unclean pleasure, does not extinguish but nourishes the fire kindled by the Lord’s breath. If this fire finds an aromatic soul, it kindles it, changes it into another appearance, and breathes it out upward like a slender column of smoke.

“Like a slender column,” he says, because through the discipline of thoughts she is gathered from outward things to inward and directed from lower things to higher; “like a slender column,” because she both gathers herself into herself and stretches herself above herself. But what does it mean that he compares her to a column of smoke? Did he perhaps wish thereby to suggest that the grace of this spiritual sweetness and the mind’s ascent are neither lasting nor firm, but melt easily like smoke?

Sweet indeed, and altogether spiritual, is the vapour of smoke into which burnt spices release themselves. But I fear whirlwinds for this tender and delicate column, lest gusts of wind beat it, lest a storm of cares carry it about, lest a breeze of temptation dissolve it and make it yield to every wind. Examples urge fear upon us. For we see, and grieve over, many who have yielded as unexpectedly as they suddenly burst forth. They are subtle in meditation, earnest in the practice of prayer, rich in grace, abundantly fruitful in a certain sweet devotion, poured out in tears—when suddenly any slight occasion of impatience saddens and drains these spiritual delights. Is not glory, then, like smoke, so easily vanishing? Rightly is such an ascent like a slender column [Col. 0076D] of smoke, since it fails through its own mutability or yields to an intervening distress.

Yet I do not dare to interpret smoke as failure in reference to the Bride. But if you obstinately disagree, I grant you to understand by failure the failure which the Psalmist commends to you: “My eyes have failed for your word”; “my soul has failed for your salvation” (Ps. 118:82, 81).

5. Would that, Lord, my eyes might grow faint and fail with this failure. Would that my soul might fail with this failure—fail and melt away; warmed by your word, by your word exceedingly kindled; loosened from every gross understanding into the subtler air of spiritual disposition. Would that, if there is in me anything of bodily [variant: sluggish] understanding and dull desire, it might fail into the exercise of subtler grace and, by a certain thinning and spiritual sharpening, be changed from its grossness into a column of smoke. Would that the power of my soul might fail into such smoke; and not fail as smoke, lest it say: “My days have failed like smoke” (Ps. 101:4).

It is altogether different to fail like smoke, so that you are altogether no more, and to fail in such a way that, thinned like smoke in mind, you become spiritual. The Psalmist had failed well when he said: “My soul longs for and fails for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. 83:3). For how does one not fail whom Christ sets on fire? He himself is fire, as it is written, even “a consuming fire” (Heb. 12:8, 29). “Whoever approaches me,” he says, “approaches fire.” Who will grant me that I may bind this fire in my bosom, so that it may inflame my heart, transform my reins, and reduce me to nothing?

Rightly she ascends like a slender column of smoke who has proceeded from the warmth of the chamber, from the embrace of the kindled Word. Your flame, Christ, is accustomed to breathe forth sweet vapours and to produce smoke with the fragrance of spices. “Like a slender column,” he says, “of smoke from spices.” I also read of smoke proceeding from the mouth of Leviathan (Job 41:11), and likewise smoke coming forth from the pit of the abyss (Rev. 9:2); but there I do not read of a slender column or spices. There is nothing straight, nothing sweet, but utter horror and no order. It is the smoke of error which comes forth from the pit of the abyss. Of this smoke the ungodly are recorded as saying: “Smoke has been breathed into our nostrils, and speech is a spark to move our heart” (Wis. 2:2).

Would that, good Jesus, smoke might be breathed into my nostrils—the smoke driven by your fire; and from [Col. 0077C] your furnace, speech might be a spark to move, indeed to transform, my heart. Your fire is a consuming fire: if it finds vices, it consumes them and emits the smoke of confession. Yet this smoke is not from spices. “He touches the mountains, and they smoke” (Ps. 103:32). Good is the fire which diminishes the swellings of souls and by its touch causes earthly pride to vanish through the smoke emitted by repentance. Yet the smoke which burnt spices of virtues give forth is of another fragrance and grace. This fire—the fire which the Lord sent upon earth and wished greatly to be kindled (Luke 12:49)—not only consumes vices, but changes virtues themselves into the affection of a sweeter grace. When spices are whole, they smell sweet; but melted by this fire, they breathe a far different fragrance.

[Col. 0077D] 6. Sensing this fragrance in the bride, the bridegroom’s companions marvel and say: “Who is this who ascends through the wilderness like a slender column of smoke, from spices of myrrh and frankincense and every powdered perfume?” In myrrh you have the virtue of continence; in frankincense, zeal for prayer; in powdered perfume, amid the abundance of virtues, the humility of a contrite heart.

Myrrh is good when it restrains carnal wantonness, does not permit unrestrained impulses to play the wanton, and strives to compel flesh not to be fleshly. But the myrrh of our continence seems bodily, insufficiently chastened, and as though close to the flesh, unless it has been melted by this heavenly fire, by this fervour of divine love. The myrrh of continence is indeed good, since it restrains the appetite moving toward unlawful things; but it is of another sweetness and grace when, melting with the ardour of love, it knows no gross and carnal affection.

And what of frankincense? Does it not itself possess only a slight scent as long as it retains its wholeness and bodily substance? But when it begins to flow, overcome by flames, it breathes itself out wholly in fragrant smoke. By the same reasoning, does not prayer seem to you gross and sluggish, slow with a kind of bodily heaviness, unless it has been kindled by the power of the fiery and inward Word? Certainly, in frankincense I understand the material of prayer, and in smoke its grace. “Let my prayer be directed before you like incense” (Ps. 140:2). Prayer which has not been kindled does not know how to proceed by a straight way to God. Prayer forced out from a cold heart immediately falls back; nor can what is not prompt be constant. It suffers compulsion and is not its own master.

But kindled prayer is plainly not its own master either. The former is restrained against its effort; the latter is carried away beyond its effort. The former strives and falls back; the latter rises beyond striving. The former is directed by force; the latter is borne willingly. The former is barely offered; the latter cannot even be held back. The former is laborious; the latter free. The former sad; the latter joyful. The former good; the latter best. Finally, there is a prayer moderately midway between cold and fervent prayer, surpassing the former but not attaining the latter. And, if I may put it so, the first is compelled; the second directed; the third carried away. The first, if I may say so, is thirsty; the second sober; the third drunk. For this is the prayer that is beside itself in mind for God; therefore it ascends like a slender column of smoke from spices of myrrh and frankincense and, he says, every [Col. 0078C] powdered perfume.

7. He wonderfully expressed the virtue of humility in “powdered perfume,” because it knows how to think nothing great of great merits and not to be high-minded; but, by humble estimation, diminishes the merits of the other virtues and brings their solidity down, as it were, to the smallness of powder. And fittingly, after commending prayer, he added humility under the figure of powdered perfume. For “the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the clouds” (Ecclus. 35:21). Indeed, without the grace of humility, prayer, however sharp, is nevertheless dull; and the proud myrrh of chastity gives forth a sad fragrance, nor does the myrrh of continence well restrain the loose movements of carnal thoughts if it permits the soul to indulge itself in the smoke of pride.

Many spices are reduced to powder by crushing. And crushing is good, because “God will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19). Indeed, the crushing is good which leaves nothing unexamined, nothing swollen, nothing unhumiliated—not even among the virtues themselves; which judges even justices and rebukes not only concerning sin, but also concerning righteousness and judgment. Is not what is rebuked, as it were, ground down? Is not the righteousness that is judged, as it were, humbled? “In your truth,” he says, “you have humbled me” (Ps. 118:75).

Not everyone can say this. The weaker are humbled in their own vanity; the more perfect in God’s truth. Vanity cannot judge truth, but truth judges vanity—and truth judges truth. For the Spirit judges [Col. 0079A] all things. What seemed sound and whole to human judgment, when the Spirit of truth comes, he empties and grinds down. For in the vehement Spirit the spices of virtues are crushed into powder, and righteousness is judged. “In the whirlwind,” says Job, “he will crush me”: in the whirlwind of his Spirit, of the vehement Spirit, in the whirlwind which carries away my spirit. “In this whirlwind he will crush me, and,” he says, “multiply my wounds” (Job 9:17). My righteousness seemed whole to me before the vehement Spirit came; but he judges, he crushes, he wounds, and in many ways breaks the presumption of good merits, teaching human virtue to be wounded and weak.

8. Would that I might be crushed in this way, reduced to the powder of every good affection and devout meditation. Would that, good Jesus, the whirlwind of your Spirit might blow such powder upon my soul from the streets of the heavenly Jerusalem, that in this powder I might be warmed, sit, and sleep—yet in powdered perfume. Blessed is the one who dwells in this powder, to whom sweet thoughts, spiritually powder-like, flow in from every side. “Awake and praise, you who dwell in the dust” (Isa. 26:19).

Finally, the bride, awakened from her blessed sleep, rises like a slender column of smoke from spices of every powdered perfume. “Every,” he says. Truth itself teaches you to reduce the totality of good works to a kind of powder and, as it were, sterility. “When you have done all things,” he says, “say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought [Col. 0079C] to have done’” (Luke 17:10). Blessed is the one who gathers for himself so much and such powder: who does all that is commanded and considers it as though it were nothing; who crushes by humility all the good things which he gathers.

Paul enumerates many spices of his works to the Corinthians: “In journeys,” he says, “often; in dangers from rivers, dangers from robbers, dangers from my own race, dangers from the Gentiles, dangers at sea, dangers in the city, dangers in the wilderness, dangers among false brothers.” What follows? His daily care for all the Churches. “Who,” he says, “is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (1 Cor. 11:26, 28, 29.) Does not the Apostle seem, in recounting these and many similar things, to have gathered for you, as it were, a powder of good works?

Would you hear still more exalted forms of his virtues? Come with him to visions and revelations of God, to being snatched up into paradise, into the third heaven, to that blessed ignorance of not knowing whether that ecstasy occurred in the body or outside the body: no longer powder, but smoke. Yet lest the smoke of self-vaunting mingle with this smoke of spiritual contemplation, hear what follows: “Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me, a thorn was given to me in my flesh” (2 Cor. 12:1–7). Paul is goaded lest he be exalted; and how do you, who hear this, shrink from being goaded? How, amid the abundance of gifts, do you either cease to crush yourself or refuse to allow yourself to be crushed? The thorn is troublesome, but affliction gives humility precedence over advancement. [Col. 0080A] The thorn in the flesh is troublesome, but not the thorn of love. The suffering is bitter, and the chastening severe: both humble virtues.

9. But all things proceed more sweetly and more effectively from a kind of furnace of kindled love. This flame not only humbles virtues, but changes them, converts them into a new appearance, and makes the spiritual still more spiritual. The myrrh of continence, the frankincense of prayer, and, in powdered perfume, the humble awareness of all virtues: all produce a more serene countenance and a pleasing appearance when they come forth from this workshop.

For contrition is good, but burning-up is better. Powdered perfume is sweet, but smoke excels it. For I do not know what is signified as more sweet and more spiritual in smoke than in powder. Therefore, by a certain benefit of the fiery Word, amid the bridegroom’s burning embraces she melts from the powder of perfume into the fineness of smoke: from the powder of humbled virtues into the smoke of glory.

What, do you suppose, is the arrival when the ascent is so delicate? Whither does she go who ascends in such a manner? How great is the place of delights in which she establishes these ascents? Perhaps it is the beloved’s bed. For to it above all the bride ought to aspire. It is indeed so. Therefore it follows: “Behold, sixty of the mightiest of Israel surround Solomon’s bed.” And the order is beautiful: that she may come from bed to bed—from her bed, from her mother’s chamber, to Solomon’s own bed. Nor is the variety less fitting because he mingles strength with these delights, and Solomon surrounds his bed with so fortified a guard.

But let us now draw back the reins of the discourse rushing onward, about to dedicate a new discourse to a new chapter, through the aid of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVI. “Sixty of the mightiest of Israel surround Solomon’s bed.” (Song 3:7.)
