1. O how delicately the bride ascends—almost without the weight of a body, and altogether without the corruption of flesh! What bodily mass can there be where she is compared with smoke? What corruption, when it is not decaying flesh but burnt spices that breathe out that fragrance? Delicately she ascends, and worthy of Solomon’s bed. I read that Esther was both washed and anointed, so that by the sweetness of royal perfume she might delight the king’s embraces (Esther 2). But this bride no longer uses perfumes [Col. 0080D] to please the bridegroom; rather, she has been melted into the very fragrance of the perfume.

Yet not everyone receives this saying; not everyone can enjoy such delights. If all enjoyed them, all would be deprived of them. Herein lie both a beautiful diversity and a loving charity: one enjoys, another guards. The rest of some are secure and glad because others maintain a fortified watch. Therefore sixty men from among Israel’s mightiest surround Solomon’s bed. Our Solomon does not wish the delights of his bed to be disturbed, its sweet affections diminished, or even assailed. He who is called Peaceful loves what is at peace.

And who is our Solomon but Jesus Christ? He is our peace; he who made the two one (Eph. 2:14). By his blood he made peace not only for things on earth but also for things in heaven (Col. 1:20). “The chastisement of our peace was upon him” (Isa. 53:5). He endured the discipline of the punishment owed by us, that he might repay to us the peace of righteousness. He was punished; you were reconciled. For when you were punished, your punishment could not give birth to peace for you. An unclean sacrifice could not cleanse those who were defiled—not others, nor even itself. Thus the discipline was upon us, but it was not a discipline bringing us peace. A sentence of mortality and affliction had been imposed upon us; but injustice had not been removed. You were indeed bound under a judicial sentence, yet your guilt was not released: there was punishment, but no peace.

O wretched and grievous discipline laid upon the children of Adam! You crush, but do not protect; you punish, but do not cleanse; you consume, but do not reconcile. You consume the substance of the flesh, not guilt. What have you to do with peace? [Col. 0081B] When will you confer peace, being in commerce with sin? When will you bestow grace, who do not take away guilt? “Righteousness and peace have kissed each other” (Ps. 84:11). The chastisement of our peace was upon him who brought us the peaceful fruits of righteousness.

He alone is called our Solomon, our true Peaceful One, because in his days righteousness and abundance of peace arose for us (Ps. 71:7). Truly abundant is the peace which not only sufficed to reconcile past sins, but also abounds for ever. For it abounds until the travail of our changeableness is removed: the travail of our mortality, the travail of alternating failures. Truly abundant is the peace not given according to the measure of merit. For it did not find merit, but bestowed it. How could that peace fail to be abundant which both remitted the offence [Col. 0081C] and heaped up a former grace?

The first human being had peace in paradise, so that he could not be led away against his will; but he did not have the strength whereby afterward he could return when he wished. There was grace enabling him not to leave; but not grace enabling him, once he had left, to return when he wished. Now the peace in Christ’s grace is richer: after repeated transgressions it is freely offered, and it does not reject the repentant but calls them back. Well may it be called abundant peace, which no injury can exhaust, readier to pardon than to avenge. This peace, beginning from the remission of sins, has abounded even to participation in the divine nature. “He who is joined to God is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17).

2. You see how great is the abundance of reconciliation: it may now be called not merely peace with God, but rather unity with him. O blessed borderland, where the dividing wall of enmities has been removed! Blessed indeed is that borderland, but not yet secure. Our enemy still tries to penetrate these boundaries and tear down the frontiers. In Christ we have peace with God the Father, but not yet peace from the common enemy. Yet this peace will abound until the last enemy, death, is destroyed.

Meanwhile, though there is not peace from him, there is protection against him. “He shall be our peace when the Assyrian comes into our land and treads within our borders.” The Assyrian can attack the spiritual frontiers nearest to him; he cannot reach those farther within. He may tread upon our borders, but he cannot stand within them. Christ will be our peace when the Assyrian has trodden our borders.

We have borderland and borderland: borderland [Col. 0082A] with God, and borderland with the world; borderland with the spirit, and borderland with the flesh. Even if it was said to some, “You are not in the flesh but in the spirit” (Rom. 8:9), nevertheless they border upon the flesh, either by the nature of their substance or by the care of the flesh. Thus the enemy, using our flesh as though it were a fortress, attacks the regions of the spirit from nearby and lays snares from an adjoining stronghold.

But he—that is, Christ—will be peace when the Assyrian treads our borders. He is our Solomon, our Peaceful One, who grants us peace upon peace: peace with the Father and peace from the enemy. “He shall make your borders peace” (Ps. 147:14). O borderland and borderland, how greatly you differ from one another! With what joys you abound, and how near and exposed you are to stumbling-blocks! O boundary and boundary! How gladly the one is held, and how laboriously the other is governed! Christ is the middle boundary in both: on this side dividing, on that uniting; on this side beginning, on that completing. For Wisdom “reaches mightily from this end unto that end, and disposes all things sweetly in that end” (Wis. 8:1).

That final end is the bed. Therefore it is said of the valiant woman: “Her price is from afar and from the uttermost bounds” (Prov. 31:10). It is her price: that for which he spends himself, at which he values himself, by which his longing is fulfilled. What else is this but the bridegroom’s embraces and bed? It is the final end beyond which longing cannot extend itself and capacity cannot suffice to comprehend. It is the end where you cease to be yourself, where you are exhausted, where you begin to be another: wholly in Christ, and Christ alone in you.

O true peace, [Col. 0082C] and full peace, when stumbling-blocks are removed from the kingdom of God; when there is no fear within our borders; when there are no longer boundary and boundary, but one boundary only—the boundary spoken of above: the end that unites and conforms one to God alone; the end that enjoys the delights of the bed, not one that wields swords.

3. But now, so that the joys of the bed, however slight they may be, may remain undisturbed, a strong guard is necessary. Therefore sixty men from among Israel’s mightiest surround Solomon’s bed. The Gospel likewise says: “When a strong man, fully armed, guards his own court, the things he possesses are in peace” (Luke 11:21). A more abundant guard is mentioned here because the grace of the bed is more abundant than that of the court, and concern for the bride is greater than concern for a possession.

And at the gate of paradise I read that an angelic guard was stationed with a flaming sword (Gen. 3:24). Is not Solomon’s bed itself a kind of paradise? “Our bed is flowering,” it says (Song 1:15). Indeed, he himself is the flower of the field; he himself is the tree of life. Rightly is the paradise of delights such a bed. You see how ample delights are enclosed by a strict guard. For sixty strong men from among Israel’s mightiest surround Solomon’s bed.

I shall not now discuss at length the reason for this number. Yet it seems to signify those who excel both in righteousness of deed and knowledge of the law. They are among Israel’s strong men who are strong in faith, who stand firm in faith and act manfully; who can do all things, but in Christ who strengthens them. He is badly called strong who exalts himself against the knowledge of God, who is inflexible and rigid against it, [Col. 0083A] whose strength is the strength of stones and whose heart is bronze, so that not even affliction gives understanding to his hearing. Such are those to whom Paul says: “Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than he?” (1 Cor. 10:22).

He is not among Israel’s strong men who, when wounded, does not feel pain; who, when struck, does not perceive it; who remains dull under every thrust of the penetrating two-edged sword of the word, and glories if he kicks against the goads of wisdom. Mary was not like this: a sword passed through her soul as though through soft material. May the powerful word readily prevail over me; may its efficacy work in me, and may this sword penetrate my soul here, so that it too may be transformed, as it were, into a sword to fight against spiritual wickedness.

4. Why do you stretch out your hand toward mighty things, when you are not among the mightiest? Why undertake a guard when you do not shake off sloth? Why surround the bed when you have no sword? Or, if you have the sword of the word, why do you have it in a sheath [variant: “page”], rather than on your tongue? You do not hold in the hands of your tongue the versatile sword of God’s word.

The discourse is mobile; it is a fiery spirit. Yet somehow, contrary to its nature, it grows sluggish in your hand. It is restrained and blunted, though it is sharper and more penetrating than every two-edged sword. The word is not swift in your mouth; it does not run quickly. It is not versatile in your hand according to the variety of the occasion, though it is fully sufficient for every use of spiritual warfare.

Why do you usurp an office whose practice you do not possess? “All hold swords and are most skilled in war” (Song 3:8). You carry a sword in vain if you do not have adequate skill in fighting. Or if you are trained for war, you exercise yourself more in the affairs of the world than in the affairs of Christ; you employ civil law more than ecclesiastical law, and are more versed in secular than spiritual combat.

The Prince of the Church desires an ecclesiastical man to be ready: he desires him to be ready to give an account of the faith and hope that are within us (1 Pet. 3:15). And since you are slow and unskilled in these matters, do you boast if you answer readily concerning public law? Sacred learning sounds far more fittingly in the mouth of a cleric or monk than secular learning. Why do you wish to speak the Egyptian language in Jerusalem? Isaiah does not speak thus: “There shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan” (Isa. 19:18). That is, since they could not speak wholly Hebrew, they should speak what is near to Hebrew; since they could not speak the holy language, they should at least speak a language akin to the holy one.

Why do you wish to speak half in the language of Ashdod, when you ought to speak Jewish? Thus you have it in Ezra (2 Esdras 13:24). Speak with tongues not of men but of angels. For you are an angel of God, professing the ministry of the sacred word. “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 2:7).

5. Speak wholly in an evangelical manner, since you are an evangelical man. Let your speech, therefore, breathe of the Law, the Prophets, and the Apostles. Sharpen your tongue with their words; borrow from them weapons mighty through God for demolishing strongholds and bringing into captivity every understanding that exalts itself against the knowledge of God [Col. 0084A] (2 Cor. 10:4–5). Let the sword of the Spirit be versatile in your hand, that it may serve every need which arises for you; and let no lack of sacred speech leave you helpless when a temporary and sudden occasion requires it.

Let the strong and effectual word be upon your lips, not in your pages. For the lips, not the pages, of the priest guard knowledge. Let the sword of the word be at your side, not in hiding; let it be close to you. Gird it upon your thigh, that you may be powerful and ready both to exhort in sound teaching and to refute those who contradict. Let the sword not be beneath your thigh: do not subject study of the sacred word to the prudence of the flesh. “Each man’s sword upon his thigh” (Song 3:8).

To one is given the word of knowledge, to another the word of wisdom; and to each teacher grace is given by the Spirit [Col. 0084B] (1 Cor. 12:7–10). “Each man’s sword upon his thigh”: so that where there is occasion for temptation, there may be a greater anticipation by the word, a more frequent admonition. “Each man’s sword upon his thigh”: so that he may first rebuke himself, guard himself, judge himself. Paul teaches you, as it were, to keep the sword upon your thigh: “Consider yourself,” he says, “lest you also be tempted.” Each person’s sword is upon his thigh because of fears by night, sudden falls, unexpected accidents.

The Apostle suggests a nocturnal fear when he says: “If a person is overtaken in some offence” (Gal. 6:1). For nocturnal is what is unforeseen, what is sudden; nocturnal also is what is deceitful. Therefore [Col. 0084C] he says: “That we may not be outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his schemes” (2 Cor. 2:11). The same Paul elsewhere feared a fear by night: “I fear,” he says, “lest, as the serpent deceived Eve, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:3).

Good is the simplicity in which, cleaving to Christ, one is one spirit with him. Simplicity is where there is unity. Simplicity is when you no longer live, but Christ lives in you; when the wisdom of God devours you; when spiritual joy absorbs you and is stored in your innermost being. And where is such great simplicity except in the bed?

6. “Each man’s sword upon his thigh.” Upon the thigh—not for the thigh, but because of fears by night: perhaps because those whom the thigh signifies do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers of this darkness of the world (Eph. 6:12). Therefore it is because of fears by night: against spiritual wickedness.

How much happier is the contest allotted to her who is held in Solomon’s bed! It is not against carnal wickedness, nor even against spiritual wickedness, but with spiritual joy, with Solomon, who is distinguished by the name Peaceful. Thus her wrestling with him is peaceful. Solomon bears both the name of the Peaceful One and the person of Wisdom. “Love wisdom,” he says, “and she will embrace you.” An embrace presents a certain likeness of wrestling. Embrace her, that she may embrace you. “You shall be glorified by her when you have embraced her,” as he says in Proverbs (Prov. 4:5–8).

Embrace the Word; use him as in a bed, not as in war. [Col. 0085A] In a bed there is room not for swords but for close embraces. Do not be strong, lest it happen that you are outside. Use the Word within, not like a sword but like a bridegroom, so that you may wrestle with the Word himself. Wrestle with truth itself; do not wrestle against errors and vices. Leave that service and office to others. What have you to do with conflict, when your whole being ought to consist in affection? The bride does not pursue the work of disputing and fighting, but the repose of embracing. Let others surround the bed; you, enjoy your desired embraces.

7. Yet why does he tell us nothing of the furnishing of the bed itself? Why does he set forth none of its delights, even in small measure? Perhaps this saying is ineffable, a saying which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. Whoever experiences it understands; and while experiencing it, does not even wholly recall in memory its past delights.

Scripture expressed what it could. It said “bed,” and “Solomon’s bed.” Enough has been said—for the wise. I also read of Solomon’s throne (3 Kings 10:18–20) and his litter (Song 3:9), but both are furnished with splendid display, as befits royal delights. Shall we then understand the bed to be neglected? Far from it. But it was enough for the writer to call it a bed, since he was speaking to the bride. For she will love nothing in the bed except its being a bed, and the abundance there of embracing her Solomon.

You will find a great and manifold mystery in beds throughout the whole text of the Scriptures, but no comparison can be made with Solomon’s bed. There is the bed that Job makes for himself in darkness [Col. 0085C] (Job 17:13), and the bed that David drenches with tears (Ps. 6:7); there is the bed in which the sick man lies (Matt. 8:6), and the bed in which the dead man rises (Mark 5:40). Such was Elisha’s bed, and such Elijah’s bed. Each raised upon a bed the dead son of his hostess (4 Kings 4:32–37; 3 Kings 17:17–23).

The one stretched himself out over the dead man; the other bent himself down. Christ is one in both. He emptied himself to receive the form of a servant and contracted the length of his eternity within the temporal brevity of nature. He spread himself out when he poured the Holy Spirit abundantly into us. That bosom of the mother could press the dead man, but could not make him alive. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life. But the true Elijah carried him into the upper chamber, raising him to spiritual understanding. The bosom of the letter was cold, and its understanding could not breathe life-giving warmth. Good was Elijah’s bed, which imparted the warmth of life to the dead man.

“The righteous lives by faith” (Heb. 10:38). Therefore he measures himself three times, that the Trinity may confer knowledge and apportion the measure of faith. The law mourns the extinct sense of the letter, the carnal sense; but Christ took away this sense and restored the spiritual one. He gave back to the letter a new and life-giving understanding, one which Elijah himself—who restores all things and makes them new—may truly recognize as his own. And Paul says that he died to the law so that he might live in Christ (Gal. 2:19–20).

It is good that you also should die not only to the old law but also to the old human being, so that he may give you life in his bed, [Col. 0086A] he “who bore our sins in his body, that, dead to sins, we might live unto righteousness” (1 Pet. 2:24). “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies.” We all are understood in this one who was raised; and therefore this is a common resurrection. But in Solomon’s bed there is a certain private grace, reserved for the bride’s privilege alone.

8. Even now, good Jesus, if any son of our mother—of this holy community, the widow at whose house you are somehow sustained—dies, raise him up. Dead is the person overwhelmed by the burden either of weariness or despair, in whom there remains nothing of living devotion or fervent spirit; who, though he does not abandon the commandments of the law and confines himself within the bosom of the Rule, nevertheless languishes with a cold and dying affection, sensing no sweetness in holy work.

The sad appearance of the whole Order drains the life from him. He must be cherished in the soft and womanly bosom of his mother, lest, exasperated, he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. It is not expedient for him to be found outside the bounds of his mother’s bosom, lest perhaps the true Elijah not take him into his chamber. Those whom Christ raises, he everywhere gives back to women’s tears: thus he raised the widow’s son (Luke 7:12–15), the brother of holy women (John 11:11–14), and the girl at her parents’ prayers (Luke 8:49–55).

Take up, good Jesus, this dead man of ours from his mother’s bosom. This regular and external observance brings no one to perfection. Bring him into the softer bed of a better hope, by which he may draw near to God. Let him experience what he awaits, for “the Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul that seeks him” [Col. 0086C] (Lam. 3:25). The experience of a single hour makes glad the labours of many years.

Then he is restored to the mother whom she had previously lost, when she no longer held his affection but lamented his dead devotion. He returns to us renewed, after you have clothed him with yourself. Therefore you stretch yourself out over him, that you may cover what is foul in him and clothe what is naked. Good is the use of this bed, which in a brief hour pours life-giving alacrity into the times that follow. Greater is the grace in Solomon’s bed, in which the bride, leaving her carnal mother, cleaves to her beloved by an everlasting right and becomes one spirit with him.

9. Good, therefore, is the bed in which there is no languor except perhaps the languor of love; which is concerned not with weakness but with delight. Good is the bed not drenched with tears, not made in darkness, having nothing sad in itself and nothing dark, but being altogether light and joy. It has no need to be spread with Egyptian tapestries, with which the adulterous woman spreads her bed in Proverbs (Prov. 7:16). For Solomon’s bed has in itself no foreign ornament, nothing painted, nothing worldly; but all is holy delight and solid truth.

There is a great and varied mystery in the beds of the saints, but the bride’s bed may be compared with this one. In her own bed she seeks her beloved and does not find him; therefore she rises and goes about until she reaches this one. Hasten, daughter, consecrated virgin; hasten to enter this rest. Do not fear the drawn swords surrounding it. These swords, swords of the word upon the thigh and because of fears by night, in others either pierce the lust of the flesh or cut away the cowardice of a timid heart. But they wound you more sweetly, so that, pierced by charity, you may know no nocturnal fear and may have no admixture of cold fear; rather, pass wholly into the affection of burning love—you who are consecrated solely for the use of love and are to ascend into the pool of charity, the couch of the beloved, the bed of Solomon, the true Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVII. Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon. (Song 3:9)

1. You heard yesterday, sacred virgins, brides of Christ, concerning the bed of your Solomon. Today you proceed to inquire further into the mystery of the litter. You wish to turn every utterance of this Song toward the service of love and interpret it according to your delights. Do you think these songs were written for you alone? No discourse has savour for you unless it blossoms with loving affections and breathes the sweet fragrance of charity.

Here, then, you have something that sounds like a loving endearment: the divine discourse alludes to the litter. Your beloved leaves you no excuse for remaining behind. The promised joys of the bed are indeed pleasing, but some suspicion concerning the difficulty of reaching it might still murmur within you. Therefore the discourse describes, with beautiful variety, the adornment of the sacred vehicle by which you are to be carried to the bed. Even on the journey the bridegroom himself provides delights for you.

This litter is pleasant indeed in material, but more pleasant in its maker. For Solomon himself is the author and craftsman of this litter. “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon; he made its columns of silver, its backrest of gold.” Hear, daughter, with what glorious equipment you are carried to the bed. The bridegroom does not permit you to be without a backrest, and a golden one—perhaps of that gold of which you read, “His head is finest gold” (Song 5:11).

The backrest has many uses, but it is inferior to the bed. In the backrest, weary hope has pleasant support; in the bed, delight. Here the bride’s desire is cherished; there she enjoys what she has desired. What an array, do you suppose, awaits you, who are led in such adornment? Why should I now enlarge every detail with extended speech—cedar wood, wood of Lebanon, silver columns? These things commend themselves to us by their very sound, and bodily beauty, drawn into a spiritual figure, seeks to indicate a certain intelligible beauty and to designate the vehicle of the holy soul. The context of the passage does not allow these things to be understood bodily. For what material gold would charity be spread upon? All are spiritual, because spiritual is the love to which so splendid an equipment of the litter lends its charm.

2. I could apply these and similar features of this litter to our own meaning. Let it suffice to have discussed them briefly, either to satisfy or to stimulate your longing. What? Do you want these songs to serve you alone? Allow the young women to be fed; allow them, for their own benefit, to bend at least a few chapters to their use. Christ is debtor to wise and foolish alike. Nothing is taken from you if others abound according to their own understanding. Be content with the bed; allow those below you to make use of the litter. The grace of the former is more restricted; that of the latter more public. In the former Christ is enclosed; in the latter he enters.

He indulges you more abundantly and with a certain special privilege, yet he does not forget others who cannot yet attain your measure. You too can share in the mystery and function of the litter if you, as it were, carry back to us the Bridegroom whom you hold enclosed: if you bear peace, proclaim good things, and preach outside the joys which you see within. Why should those not have been a litter of whom the Church sings: “Bearing peace and enlightening their country”? (Office of the Apostles.)

But let no one assume the office of preaching, and let no one take honour to himself unless called by God (Heb. 5:4). Why do you place yourself upon the lampstand when you do not kindle yourself? Let him place you on high who made you a lamp. Ascend through him who kindled you. Indeed, no one makes himself a litter: Solomon himself made a litter for himself from the woods of Lebanon.

There is also a litter if someone bears Christ not only in his mouth but also in his body. “Glorify and bear Christ in your body,” says Paul (1 Cor. 6:20). Christ wishes to be borne by you gloriously—not with weariness, murmuring, indignation, or vacillating resolve; in short, borne, not dragged. For Christ is burdensome to one who drags him; chastity is burdensome, humility burdensome, obedience heavy, poverty repulsive. You carry him disgracefully when you live in this way. Faith seems to you a great burden and piety a heavy weight. You cannot say, “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh” (Song 1:12).

What? Does your faith seem hay to you, under whose weight you creak, groan, and murmur as a cart creaks when loaded with hay? Christ is not hay; he is flower, fruit, and the tree of life—the tree that gives its fruit in its season. And do you not wish to wait? “Blessed are those who eat in their season” (Eccl. 10:17). Therefore patience is necessary, that you may receive the promises (Heb. 10:36). Bear, then, burdens patiently—indeed, the burdens of piety. For piety itself already has a share in the promise, as it is written (1 Tim. 4:8).

3. Therefore bear the image of him who is from heaven, and bear it gloriously. For his burden is light. Be not a shameful stumbling-block, but a glorious vehicle, such as King Solomon made for himself. In a remarkable way he distinguishes the diversity of virtues so as first to exclude the vanity of self-exaltation. For “what have you that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

If you are a litter, you did not make yourself: he made you. “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon.” And who made the woods themselves? Was it not he? He planted the cedars of Lebanon. If you are a tall cedar of Lebanon, do not think proudly, but fear lest you be uprooted from the place where you were planted by election because of self-exaltation. [Col. 0089A] For you did not choose yourself: he chose you for the work of ministry. He gives both the office of ministry and the grace of ministering—that is, ability and dignity.

Acknowledge by whom you were planted, and let not the root of pride arise in you, lest the hand of the tempter shake you. Let not the axe of the enemy rise up to cut you down—the enemy whose razor did not even come upon the heads of the saints. He is eager to seize God’s litter for himself and to cut down woods from Lebanon for his own uses. Thus in Ezekiel he boasts and says, “I sat in the seat of God” (Ezek. 28:2). Take care, therefore, lest through self-exaltation you become, from a seat of righteousness, a seat of pestilence and a litter of scandal; and lest through you either examples or evil speech spread like cancer to the ruin of many.

Be God’s litter, that you may bear his image in yourself and that through you he may manifest the fragrance of his knowledge. Such a litter was Paul, concerning whom the Lord himself declares: “This man is for me a chosen vessel, to bear my name” (Acts 9:15). He who chose him also made him a litter.

4. “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon.” These woods are cedar woods; both their nature and the name of their place commend something great. Lebanon signifies whiteness; its woods are subject to no corruption. As they do not admit decay in their substance, so they breathe forth a most sweet fragrance.

Paul was rightly Lebanon: as he says, he served God with a pure conscience (2 Tim. 1:3). What is whiter than a pure conscience? What more incorruptible than one whom no creature could separate from the charity of God? Fleeting virtues, which endure only for an hour, seem to me not so much woods as vegetables, which quickly wither. But in Paul there was a certain incorruptibility of tireless charity. Therefore he fought the good fight, completed the course, and thereafter awaited the crown of righteousness (2 Tim. 4:7–8): a crown of sheaves, whose fragrance he already drew, as it were, from nearby.

Indeed, he too breathed forth a good fragrance: a fragrance of life unto life, the fragrance of the knowledge of God (2 Cor. 2:14–15). Good repute is a good fragrance; a good conscience is also a good fragrance. The former smells sweet to others; the latter to oneself. For this is the glory of the saints: the testimony of conscience (2 Cor. 1:12). The fruits of future blessedness have already begun to smell sweet to us in goodness of life. And rightly is good fragrance joined to incorruptibility; for, conversely, decay gives off a stench. Whoever sows in the flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh, and from corruption a sorrowful odour, just as from integrity comes a sweet one.

5. And integrity is aptly mentioned, because the virgin’s brightness seems to be expressed by the woods of Lebanon. Virgin continence too breathes forth a good fragrance, and its use is perpetual. Whether the service of marriage is abolished or the desolation of widowhood ceases, the liberty and grace of virginal integrity shall never fail; for those who neither marry nor are given in marriage are already like angels in heaven (Matt. 22:30).

Indeed, in Scripture virginity is compared to Lebanon: “I breathed forth my dwelling like uncut Lebanon, and my fragrance like unmixed balsam” (Ecclus. 24:21). Rightly is Lebanon an immaculate womb, an undefiled womb, an untouched womb, an uncut womb. It is uncut whose integrity remains, whose enclosures of modesty have not been unsealed. Lebanon because of purity; uncut because of integrity.

Rightly is she uncut who is not divided. Do you wish to hear of one who is cut? “A married woman thinks of the things of the world, how she may please her husband, and is divided”—divided, surely, between God and husband, and perhaps not divided equally but leaning more toward her husband. “But the unmarried woman and the virgin think only of the things of the Lord, how she may please God” (1 Cor. 7:34).

“I breathed forth my dwelling like uncut Lebanon.” These words seem to belong especially to the Mother of the Lord. She is truly Lebanon, and uncut Lebanon. She breathed forth her dwelling to you, sacred virgins: a heavenly dwelling, an angelic dwelling, when she poured into you examples of virginal life and inspired the love of perpetual chastity. She adequately expressed the grace of her dwelling when she said that she breathed it forth. For what is more like vapour than virginal life? This manner of life has nothing fleshly, nothing worldly; it is entirely heavenly, entirely above the world, entirely spiritual, and therefore like vapour.

But like what vapour? “And my fragrance,” she says, “is like unmixed balsam”: like balsam not mixed, like balsam not corrupted, like balsam not adulterated. There is a mixture that imitates balsam and falsely claims to be it; and there is a mixture which, though it has no resemblance to balsam, nevertheless spoils a good fragrance. Thus, so to speak, there is balsam which is true and unmixed; balsam which, though true, is not unmixed; and balsam which is neither true nor unmixed.

The first is found in the perfect; the last in those deceived; the middle in those who, though no deceit misleads them, are nevertheless lacking in some grace of virtue. Rightly, therefore, she who alone was full of grace calls her fragrance like unmixed balsam.

6. But if you breathe forth virginity, if persistence in prayer, if the abstinence of fasts, you breathe forth a good fragrance, and you breathe forth balsam. But if you still suffer from the disease of impatience; if empty talk, if rashness of counsel, if the burning urge to fulfil your own will, if sadness, if weariness—if any one of these is named in you—then your fragrance is already mixed, and you do not breathe pure balsam [Col. 0090D]. For a small drop of foreign admixture spoils the whole mass of balsam. Yet it goes well with one who, if by chance and as it were suddenly he gives off some unpleasant odor, immediately removes it. “For we all stumble in many things,” says the Apostle (James 3:2). No fragrance ought to be judged from a sudden fall that is immediately corrected, but rather from that fault in which a person is diligently occupied. It is a dangerous and most evil mixture when any vice counterfeits the appearance of virtue; when the angel of Satan transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11:14), and makes poison breathe forth as though it were balsam. Satan is a perfumer: do not buy oil from him. For he is not so much a maker as a corrupter of ointment. Finally, as it is written: “He makes the sea boil like a pot, and makes it as when ointments boil over” [Col. 0091A] (Job 41:22). There is death in this pot. Jeremiah saw this heated pot, “and its face from the face of the north” (Jer. 1:13). What sort of maker of ointments is he who pretends that vapors of life issue from the pot of death? What sort of artisan is he who makes the face of the heated pot boil as though from the south, through which evils rather blaze forth into the land from the north? He is either a son of a prophet, or certainly a prophet, who detects death in the pot and its vapors coming from the north. The vapors which your heated pot of flesh ejects are sulphurous; and do you think that in them you smell the fragrance of balsam? If you do not know by yourself how to distinguish unmixed balsam from mixed, come to the Prophets; come to the Apostles, the sons of the Prophets, that they may teach you the differences among mixtures and in which pot death is found. Such was Paul, who dared to say: “We are not [Col. 0091B] ignorant of his devices” (2 Cor. 2:11). If your own hand is not sufficient to keep balsam pure, let the saints teach you how to mix it. Nicodemus brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds (John 19:39), and the Marys bought ointments (Mark 16:1). But Mary, the Mother of the Lord, does not so much procure ointments as breathe them forth, she who bore Christ himself, anointed with the oil of gladness. “My fragrance,” she says, “is like unmixed balsam.”

7. If you do not know the principle of mixture, come to the doctors of the Church, to those who are in some sense pillars and the foundation of truth, and silver pillars in the Lord’s sedan-chair, and dispensers of the sacred word. Learn from them how to think of the things that are the Lord’s, and how to be concerned for Christ, so as to please him. Then [Col. 0091C] you too will have silver pillars within yourself, if you are supported by the knowledge of both Testaments. Therefore, here too, after the timbers of Lebanon, the divine discourse adds silver pillars, so that you may have the mystery of faith in a pure conscience. The mystery of faith which the sacred word sets before you is a silver word: so that, upheld by evangelical and apostolic precepts, you may meditate upon these things, preserve them, and ponder them in your heart; and may not allow the silver of the divine word to cling in idle stagnation, be effaced, and be blackened by the rust of forgetfulness.

8. But we cannot now insert these pillars into today’s discourse. For the timbers of Lebanon have already occupied this treatment; and, drawn on by the sweetness of the subject, our discourse has ranged more widely in their fragrance than I had thought. To you, Lord, I commend this Lebanon [Col. 0091D], this excellent Lebanon: this virgin choir, this assembly of holy women. Guard it, that it may not be felled or cut down, but that its integrity may be preserved; that the brightness of chastity may be preserved, since Lebanon signifies whiteness; that purity of mind may be preserved, so that they may be holy both in body and spirit. Guard this Lebanon, whose timbers you have dedicated to the fabric of your sedan-chair. Far from it be the prophetic threat: “Open your gates, O Lebanon, that fire may devour your cedars” (Zech. 11:1). Let these gates be closed to others and opened to you alone. Be to it its key and its bar; seal and unseal it, so that it may receive neither seal nor key apart from you, Christ Jesus, God blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XVIII

*King Solomon made himself a sedan-chair from the timbers of Lebanon.* (Song 3:9)

[Col. 0092A]

1. In the timbers of Lebanon, incorruption of the flesh and the brightness of purity are set forth for you. Chastity is indeed good; but “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). “By faith,” Scripture says, “purifying their hearts” (Acts 15:9). For chastity is not judged by bodily continence alone; it is much more to be valued by purity of heart. “Already,” Jesus says, “you are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you” (John 15:3). Good is the word of faith which cleanses. Therefore, in this construction of the sedan-chair, after the timbers of Lebanon it brings forth silver pillars, and summons the mind of virgin purity to meditation upon the sacred [Col. 0092B] word: a chaste word, a word compared to silver tested in the fire (Ps. 11:7).

The pillars raised in the breasts of virgins are good if they are supported by sacred Scripture, faithful understanding, and frequent recollection. You are a good Lebanon if you have a clean heart: clean from a shameful thought and from an unbelieving thought. Corruption of faith is a great foulness of spirit. But if within you there is the sound and firm form of faith, you already possess one pillar. Yet do not be content with this one; add the other: meditate in the law of the Lord day and night. Regard it as unbelief and fornication if your mind turns away even a little from recollection of faith. Divine knowledge and memory of the law are good pillars: right belief and recollection of faith. You are a pillar if you are firm in faith; silver, if you are trained by constant use of the divine [Col. 0092C] word. “The word of the Lord is upright,” he says, “and all his works are in faith” (Ps. 32:4). Faith and the word of faith are good pillars. Let this word be near in your heart; for it is near in your mouth. Let it be near, and remain there continually. Let the speech of your mouth break forth from the abundance of your heart. “Seven times a day,” says the prophet, “I have given praise to you” (Ps. 118:164). You, holy virgins, speak always: offer praise seven times, indeed, for the solemn hours; but sing and make psalmody in your hearts always.

2. Let your tongues be silver. They are silver if they sound forth Christ from the sacred page. Let no mass of lead be put into your mouth. A leaden mouth speaks nothing subtle, nothing keen, nothing from on high; rather, it is wholly slack, wholly dull, wholly [Col. 0092D] concerned with low things, perhaps even with wicked things. For “wickedness sits in a talent of lead” (Zech. 5:7–8). That Gospel man who went abroad did not distribute such talents to his servants (Matt. 25:14–15). Do not trade with such talents; let none of this sort be found in your treasures. Attend to Paul’s saying: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for the building up of faith” (Eph. 4:29). “For building up,” he says, “not for overthrowing faith.” An iron mouth is one that overthrows faith, ruins holy conduct, is an instrument of war and a seedbed of strife, and sounds forth grumbling and bitterness. Such a beast is described in Daniel, having iron teeth and claws, devouring and crushing [Col. 0093A] everything (Dan. 7:7). Let no such beast be found among the Lord’s little sheep—indeed, among his beloved ones. In this virgin flock let none be venomous, none violent; in this paradise let no serpent’s hiss be heard. Poisonous words do not befit a virgin’s mouth. What? Will you offer a mouth polluted with depraved words for a kiss upon the bridegroom’s lips? The very brightness of eternal light touches nothing defiled. Remember that your mouth has been consecrated by heavenly kisses and oracles. Count it sacrilege if it gives forth anything not sweet, not divine, not drawn from the sacred page. “Sound the trumpet at the new moon, on the notable day of your solemn feast” (Ps. 80:4). Every day ought to be solemn for you; always a new moon, always a Sabbath. Therefore let your mouth be like a beaten trumpet, a silver trumpet: a trumpet that sounds not quarrels, but joy [Col. 0093B], solemnity, and spiritual songs.

3. I do not know how our discourse turned aside from silver pillars to trumpets, unless it is because one who bears such a mouth is an excellent pillar in the house of the Lord. A good pillar is one by whom the weary are supported. You have in Isaiah: “The Lord gave me a learned tongue, that I may know how to support by a word one who has fallen” (Isa. 50:4). Truly the learned tongue of Christ Jesus, announcing peace and preaching good things. “A gentle tongue is a tree of life” (Prov. 15:4), a pillar and foundation of truth. And you, virgin, bear in this the image of the bridegroom, that you may have a learned tongue, a gentle tongue: not erring, not wandering, not prone to idle things, but one that speaks judgment, offers a word of consolation, and is a kind of pillar and foundation for the building up [Col. 0093C] of faith, whether your own or another’s. “The word of faith is near in your mouth and in your heart” (Rom. 10:8).

Do you wish to hear of a silver pillar? “The law,” he says, “of his God is in his heart”: behold silver. “And his steps shall not be tripped” (Ps. 36:31): behold a pillar. Rightly a pillar, since it cannot be overthrown. “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established,” says the Psalmist (Ps. 32:6). Let the heart of the virgin be strengthened by this word, so that it may be heaven, may be God’s seat, may be made a golden couch. In silver, understand the account and knowledge of faith; in gold, the radiance of understanding and truth. This golden couch is set upon pillars of this kind. “Unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9, LXX). Instruction in faith provides a step toward purity of understanding [Col. 0093D]. The grace of contemplation rests upon this foundation. While you meditate faithfully upon the word of God, and raise yourself through the patience and consolation of Scripture toward heavenly hope, you show yourself to be a pillar. You then become a golden couch when truth, stripped bare of the covering of words, begins suddenly to flash upon you.

4. But now consider more perfectly the order and a certain progress from the timbers of Lebanon to silver pillars and a golden couch. In Lebanon is purity of heart; in silver, knowledge of the divine law; in gold—whether through the ministry of the word—the sacred mysteries shine openly. In the first, you cleanse the eye of the mind; in the second, you look ahead; but in the third, you see clearly. Or, if you prefer it so expressed: you are cleansed, you meditate, you contemplate. “Confession [praise] [Col. 0094A] and beauty are before him” (Ps. 95:6). In Lebanon is beauty; in silver, confession; in gold, the sight of the divine presence is commended to you. How great is the grace of this confession and beauty, which is admitted into the presence of so great a majesty!

Do you wish to hear this distinction elsewhere in the Psalm? “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Do not cast me away from your face” (Ps. 50:12–13). You see how deep calls to deep; how different chapters of Scripture harmonize with one another. Refer the first to the whiteness of Lebanon: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Refer the second to the pillars of silver: for “the word of the Lord is upright.” Refer the third to the golden couch, where the Lord’s [Col. 0094B] face is sincerely seen without a veil, and royal majesty gleams in gold. That is, he asks that a spirit be given to him cleansed, instructed, and, so to speak, dazzled. In Lebanon it is cleansed; in silver it is instructed; in gold it is dazzled. For in contemplation the sight of every purified mind is truly dazzled, and for a brief while bears the flashes of inward light. Review these stages of progress, you who aspire to the grace of contemplation. Let nothing foul, nothing unbelieving, remain in you, so that naked truth may flash upon you. First cleanse; second, train; third, behold. Cleanse yourself from the law of the flesh; train yourself in the law of faith; behold and see clearly in the law of perfect liberty, in the spiritual law. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty” (2 Cor. 3:17): in the law which lacks the veil of the letter, in which [Col. 0094C] there is no room for error, ignorance, or enigma. Where error is, it misleads. Where ignorance is, it does not lead. Where an enigma is, even if it leads, it does not bring one to the goal. Who could err there? For it is a couch, rest, and the end of desires. Who could be ignorant? For it is gold, and shines toward the light. What enigma is there? The end of desires and serene truth admit no figures of enigmas. There is nothing false, nothing hidden, nothing figurative: it is gold, and it shines; it is a couch, and it cherishes; a sweet kindling, but a fleeting hour. And this flash is compared with a flash of lightning. It happens in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. The last trumpet is when knowledge is given no longer upon the page, but in the presence itself; when one becomes taught by God; when, after the words of the Apostles [Col. 0094D] and Prophets, at last the Son of God, the Father’s Word, speaks within the person himself. This trumpet does not know how to give an uncertain sound; it sounds only for solemnity, only at the new moon and at the beginning of new light.

5. Sound for us the trumpet, good Jesus, at the new moon, on the notable day of our solemn feast. Truly notable is the day on which divine majesty manifests itself: nothing more notable, yet nothing briefer. I called it a day: it is an hour. Truly a notable and truly solemn hour. Pour forth to us, good Jesus, some hours of that eternal day. You immediately make a day of the one to whom you pour forth the word of your light, for you are the eternal day. Flash such gleams upon us. The one upon whom you flash becomes lightning. You make like yourself the one whom you illumine: “We shall be like him when he appears” (1 John 3:2). The mountains which you touch with such a ray [Col. 0095A] do not smoke, but flash. They become golden when your gold shines upon them. Your head is finest gold; it does not find a golden couch but makes one wherever it reclines. It is no longer fitting to say of it, as in the Gospel: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58). Do you see, Lord Jesus, how many couches you have here? Never does the head of your majesty recline more willingly than in the golden bosom of virginity. Look upon these virgin breasts, breasts open to you: in them you often recline, rest, and lie at noon, and in a certain golden serenity of brightness. Here foxes have no dens, nor do birds of heaven make nests. This couch is too solid for a cunning fox to burrow beneath it. No place is left for heretical guile where serene truth flashes forth [Col. 0095B]. It is too lofty for either the cunning fox or the proud bird to approach. These things have been hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones, who follow the humble ascent, the purple ascent, and tread in the footprints of Christ’s Passion. Truly purple is the ascent, marked by Christ’s blood and colored by faith in his Passion.

6. But one must notice how—indeed, how fittingly—the silver pillars and the purple ascent harmonize with one another. In the former you are wise in faith; in the latter you feel humbly. In the former is meditation; in the latter, imitation. For the kingdom of God is not in word only, but in power. What will you say here, you who think humiliation to be servitude? That which royal [Col. 0095C] purple ennobles is not servile. Purple is indeed a royal adornment. If you either disdain or shrink from these steps, consider that they are purple. Humility undertaken for Christ bears royal dignity. But you, bride of Christ, press the purple steps with a white foot. Noble is the path which your Beloved first trod. How beautiful are the purple steps which Christ first marked with his sacred foot—with those feet to which no dust clung, snow-white feet marked by the trace of his own blood! Eagerly trace these footsteps; remove the fleshly shoe from your feet. For holy is the ascent which you prepare for yourself. Stand with bare and unencumbered foot upon these steps. This purple was dyed not by shellfish, but by Christ’s blood. Gladly place your foot here, so that your foot may be dipped [Col. 0095D] in Christ’s blood. Let not the foot of pride come upon you, if you follow the humble ascent marked by the sacred blood of your Bridegroom. Dip in it not only your foot, but also your hand and head, that, wholly purple, wholly royal, and wholly ennobled by Christ’s Passion, you may ascend. For if you suffer with him, you reign with him.

Do not think yourself illustrious through the nobility of the world. You will be more base if you look to that, if you reckon your birth to your Bridegroom, if you prefer yourself to others because of worldly distinction, or suppose that you possess some privilege. Against the humility of your profession, through the lineage of the flesh you are emptied of Christ’s glory if you presume to be ennobled by another thing. Let this purple suffice for your distinction, suffice for your ascent, suffice for your glory, so that you may glory in nothing except the cross of your Lord Jesus Christ. The purple ascent will bring you [Col. 0096A] to the golden couch, because the grace of contemplation is owed to the humble and the quiet, but is hidden from the wise and prudent and is to be revealed to little ones.

This purple is a great pledge of love which your Beloved has given you. The Passion of his death is indeed a great pledge of love. “No one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). His Passion, your humiliation, asks in return a pledge such as it has given. Let memory bring back to you what he endured for you and how greatly he loved the one for whom he so humbled himself. Love, then, him who loved first and more greatly. These times do not demand that you shed blood. Pour out your soul; pour out your heart like water. For even “if you deliver your body to be burned, but do not have love, what does it profit you?” (1 Cor. 13:3). Finally, in the last place, as though the final conclusion of all graces, love is set; and the middle is said to be spread with love, as with a certain ornament, for the daughters of Jerusalem.

## SERMON XIX

*He spread its middle with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.* (Song 3:10)

1. You want to hear something new, but I have nothing new except that love may make you new. “I give you this new commandment”: nothing is more familiar to you, and nothing newer. You are not inexperienced or untrained in this matter. This is your own proper office. For you have been especially dedicated to the ministry of love. Consequently, Solomon’s sedan-chair is said to be spread in the middle [Col. 0096C] with love for your sake. “He spread its middle with love for the daughters of Jerusalem.” This discourse has, by a kind of privilege, assigned to you the practice of love. Emulate, daughters of Jerusalem, the better gifts—but above all, that you may love. Love surpasses every grace; and in this description of the sedan-chair, love is placed over the other graces as both their ornament and their conclusion. Many graces are enumerated in this sedan-chair, but all are completed by love. Love is the summit; love is the foundation. “Rooted and founded in love” (Eph. 3:17). It is at the beginning, at the end, and in the inmost part; it begins, it completes, it communicates itself to the other gifts. Therefore it is placed in the middle as [Col. 0096D] a kind of common ornament and the conclusion of the entire sedan-chair. Purple color and golden brightness would be dimmer if they were not clothed with love. How great is the grace of that which adorns the very gold of contemplation! Love itself is the middle and, as it were, the marrow of the other graces. Yet no virtue is so inward, none so penetrates and bathes minds, and fills the hidden recesses of the heart. Love is absorbed into the very marrow of the soul and flows into its secret veins. “In the middle with love.” Rightly in the middle, for it is thus inmost. Love is the fulfilment of the law. Therefore the law is emptied if it lacks love. Love is a kind of vital vein of the law and of the other virtues. The others contract, as it were, into a part; love is common to every rank. Whether you exceed in ecstasy or become sober, everywhere the use of love is both necessary [Col. 0097A] and delightful. The offices of the other graces vary and alternate in turns; the claims of love continue in an unbroken course. “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, the love of Christ presses us” (2 Cor. 5:13–14). Truly, I think, Christ’s love presses you. To what does it press you? Into itself. Others have other duties; your special gift is love. Love is an insistent provoker of itself and exercises a sweet tyranny over those who undergo it. Love always urges itself toward richer advances.

2. “Emulate, daughters of Jerusalem, the better gifts—but above all, that you may love.” May this emulation always urge you more and more. Let this commandment always be new to you. It is new unless sweet Jesus has grown old in your affection. Would that he may always be fresh within you, and that no delay of time may diminish anything of grace. Surely your Jesus is fresh within you. He is always fresh, but not an alien God. Truly fresh is he for whom you always yearn with anxious love. Indeed, you have this alone in your desires: that he may always please you more. How much he pleases, who cannot please enough! You can please him in no way more than by his pleasing you. He wants the heart; he seeks nothing else. He alone suffices, provided that he is wholly bestowed. It is enough according to your powers, but little according to his merits. If you compare yourself with yourself and measure what is yours by your own rule, it suffices; but if you give of yourself, nothing remains for you. But if you measure yourself by his rule and place yourself, as it were, in the balance, what weight can you have against him? [Col. 0097C] If love holds and restrains itself below your powers, it is unjust; if it is according to your powers, it is scant. What then? Will you stretch yourself above your powers in a vain endeavor? Why not? Love admits no remedy drawn from impossibility. No services are great enough for love, provided love itself has not grown lukewarm. How will one who is faithful in another’s affairs be sparing in his own? How will one be eager in offices yet sparing of himself? Love spends nothing more willingly than itself, and can offer nothing more abundantly. What abundance is greater than that in which nothing is cut away? Love boils over; it cannot contain itself; it overflows itself; it strives after immensity because it knows no boundary to set for its affection. It is oil, which does not stop until the vessel fails (4 Kings 4:6), except that not even then does it know how to be restrained. Love bears the mark of new wine, which grows and overflows with a certain fervor of its birth and, as it were, the exuberance of youth, unable to be contained; and it always boils and ferments with new affection. Love does not plead weakness, but rather accuses it. Nothing is enough for love, nothing less than itself. Love cannot be satisfied with itself, and yet cannot be nourished except by itself: it is its own sweet and sufficient food. Love wants nothing more than to love. What exchange shall a man give for love? What shall he give—or what shall he receive? Nothing is offered more graciously than love; nothing is felt more sweetly. [Col. 0097D] Love desires sweetly and enjoys sweetly; it delights sweetly and grieves sweetly. Truly love is sweet, and love alone is sweet; every sweet love is sweet, but it is not love compared with Christ’s love.

“For his beauty is above all beauty. Above all beauty,” he says, “I loved wisdom” (Wis. 7:10). How could he not be beautiful, who is the brightness of eternal light? “My brother Jonathan, how lovable you are, and exceedingly beautiful!” (2 Sam. 1:26). I intended to say Jesus, but from habit I brought forth Jonathan’s name; yet it is a pleasing error, which expressed grace. There is error in the name, but the proper meaning of this name has been retained in the thing itself. Jonathan is “Gift of the Dove,” signifying him who is full of spiritual grace, the child given to us. Whether I say Jonathan or Jesus, I mean Jesus. “How lovable you are, my brother Jonathan, and exceedingly beautiful!” Do you think it presumptuous that I call him brother? These words express not my rashness but his [Col. 0098B] love. It would be presumption if he himself had not granted me this boldness. For he himself both assumed the condition of this kinship and showed its affection; and according to the Apostle, “he is not ashamed to call us brothers” (Heb. 2:11). If he is not ashamed, why should you not also say confidently, “My brother Jonathan”? Or, if you prefer to use the more familiar name: “My brother Jesus, you are lovable and exceedingly beautiful; you are lovable beyond the love of women.” Your desires, holy women, burn toward Christ with anxious and vehement affection; but he is much more lovable than he is loved by you.

3. Therefore emulate the better gifts, but above all that you may love. He enumerates the timbers of Lebanon, silver pillars, a golden couch, and a purple ascent, finally completing everything with love [Col. 0098C]. Why not? “Still,” Paul says, “I show you a more excellent way.” Silver pillars are good indeed, and great is the grace of sacred discourse. But “if I speak with the tongues of men and angels, but do not have love, I have become like a ringing cymbal,” giving the empty sound of a voice without the meaning of love. Great is the glory of the golden couch, by which the secrets of mysteries are signified to you. But what then? “If I know all mysteries and all knowledge, but do not have love, I am nothing.” Do you ascend by the purple steps and rejoice that you bear the marks of Christ’s Passion? But “if I deliver my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing,” says the Apostle. “Love is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own things” (1 Cor. 12–13:5); it delights in what is held in common and, as it were, makes its own goods public. For “he spread its middle with love.” “It is not puffed up,” he says; “it is not ambitious.” The good of love is not exclusive; if it has something, it loves; if it does not have it, it desires it. It does not wish to excel others, nor does it wish itself to possess more good. Many recognize the weakness of their own merits. Therefore, feeling nothing great about themselves, they are not puffed up; but perhaps they are ambitious. They have nothing from which to be puffed up, but they eagerly wish to possess what might puff them up. These also love private excellence, whether they desire it to exist or waste away because it cannot exist. But love has no path alongside envy that wastes away; it does not seek what is [Col. 0099A] its own. And how could it snatch away what belongs to another?

4. Why do you wish through envy to corrupt another’s good? Will you add to yourself what you cut away from another? Perhaps so, if you take away some material wealth. I therefore do not fear this fault of rapacity among those in a cloister; there is a subtler sort of envious rapacity. Why do you not consider it rapacity if you spare money but tear away reputation? You do not covet another’s possession, yet you lacerate the person’s repute. What profit does another’s diminution bring you? If you gnaw at another’s goods, what grows in you from that? Perhaps, in the evident truth of another’s virtue, the teeth which you had prepared for detraction are ground down in your mouth. You do not dare to gnaw, yet you cannot praise. [Col. 0099B] You no longer pluck at another’s good with words; does this mean that you do not steal? How is it not rapacity when you rob a manifest good of the testimony owed to it, and, though you do not corrupt another’s true glory with a lie, nevertheless suppress it by silence? Do you wish to hear that there is rapacity even in appraisal alone? “He did not consider equality with God a robbery,” says the Apostle (Phil. 2:6). A good opinion of another’s goods cannot enter an envious soul. For it does not wish to understand that another acts well; and even if it does not dare openly to do so, inwardly it either disguises or diminishes another’s merits. Why is this so, except because envy, always thinking of private excellence, darkens another’s? But love “does not think evil” [Col. 0099C], “does not rejoice over iniquity”—or, so to speak, over inequality—“but rejoices together with truth” (1 Cor. 13:5–6). It does not think privately; it rejoices in something held in common and shared. It does not seek its own things, but those of Christ Jesus. In all things it either loves or desires his glory. Christ is common to all, for he is mediator (1 Tim. 2:5); and therefore those things are not his which are not held in common, but are restricted to a part. Why do you wish through envy to reduce Christ to a private possession? Do you wish the grace of the Spirit to be miserly, whose benefits you desire confined to yourself alone? Allow the Spirit of the Lord to grow and overflow, to pour himself out upon all flesh and fill the whole world. Do not imprison the beneficence common to all within the narrow confines of your heart. For he is rich toward all (Rom. 10:[Col. 0099D] 12); and do you try to diminish the abundance of grace and reduce immensity to trifles? Christ disdains the miserly narrowness of a jealous heart. His goodness does not know how to be held back by your envy. It flows freely: his oil is poured not only into your vessel, but also into neighboring vessels. Make it so that those vessels are yours reciprocally. They will be, if you rejoice in the common good; otherwise you empty the oil of your own soul, while Christ the mediator is nonetheless poured into them. Therefore he wishes his own things to be held in common. “By this,” he says, “all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

5. Do you see how love is a special mark of Christ’s discipleship and a singular indication of his teaching? Therefore here, in the final place, it is introduced as an ornament [Col. 0100A] of the other graces: “He spread its middle with love.” O how soft is love’s bedding! Love of neighbor is without envy; love of the Lord is without fear. Love contains nothing punitive; fear has punishment. Therefore fear is not in love, but “perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). What indeed will love fear? Old offenses? But “love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). Will it fear the weakness of its own conscience, lest it fall away? But “love is strong as death.” Love casts out both fears. Nor will perfect love fear temporal troubles for Christ. But even if they were eternal, consummate love could not grow weary and vanish away. Once it has tasted knowledge of such sweetness, it cannot fail to delight in it. [Col. 0100B] Love does not love in order that it may not perish; rather, it prefers to perish outwardly under punishment forever than to be deprived of the enjoyment of eternal love. “For if a man gives all his substance for love, he will regard it as though it were nothing” (Song 8:6–7). Truly this is a soft bed, in which, even amid injuries, one rests as sweetly as one does holily.

Grant me, good Jesus, that upon this bed I may remember you and meditate on you in the morning watches. Truly sweet is the remembrance which love brings; pleasing is the meditation which love suggests. For there is now nothing concerning Christ which is not thought sweetly and pleasingly. Love of neighbor has compassion and a somewhat less sweet flavor, since it knows how to suffer with those who groan. But what is there in Christ over which you might suffer compassionately? Though “he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives from the power of God.” In every respect he furnishes you matter not for compassion but for shared rejoicing. He is wholly desirable, wholly desire, and, as it were, spread with love. What will you see in Christ that does not both show us his love and demand ours? He is wholly an allurement of love for us, an incentive to love. He leaves no place within himself for fearful affection. He who wholly deserves to be loved wishes to be loved wholly. Virgin, do not look toward torments when such delights are set before you in the Bridegroom. Fear ought to be idle where so many marks of love shine forth. Love disdains commerce with fear: it cannot be compelled, because it cannot be restrained.

6. Therefore perfect charity casts fear out as useless and superfluous; yet not that fear [Col. 0100D] which remains pure for ever and ever (Ps. 18:10). For there is a fear which charity casts out; there is a fear which truth sends; and there is a fear which both charity and truth bring in. The first is cautious; the second pure, but not abiding for ever and ever; the third both pure and abiding. The first dreads punishment, the second offense, the third is wholly a certain free and secure reverence. The first indeed fears offense, but because of punishment; the second fears offense for its own sake. And truly it is in some measure an injury to justice if one comes into its favor from fear of penalties. Justice itself sufficiently possesses merit in itself to awaken people’s zeal for it and win their affections. Therefore perfect charity excludes this fear. For how can charity be perfect if it needs the spur of fear in order to worship justice? [Col. 0101A] Perfect love wholly possesses the mind, wishing all services to be assigned to justice alone. Fear is cold and moves sluggishly, content merely to escape with impunity. Love knows no weariness: it is fervent and stretches toward what lies ahead. Fear is more contracted, undertaking the offices of justice only under necessity. Perfect love owes to justice alone what it does, leaving no claim in justice for fear. Why should it not? Does justice not possess enough worth in itself for every good work? For Christ was made justice for us. What then? Does Christ not have in himself sufficient endowment to please? Does he therefore need another’s aid in order to please? If one does not obey him on the strength of him alone, how can one’s love for him be perfect?

I will love you, good Jesus; I will love you, my strength—whom I cannot love without cause, and yet cannot love sufficiently. Let my efforts be directed wholly toward you, and let my affections not be led away and distracted by an alien attachment. Yet how slight are our efforts toward you, even when they are whole! How then shall I diminish what, even whole, is so small? With all my desire I shall be borne toward you, good God. Draw me into yourself, so that I may need no impulse of fear, but perfect charity may exclude its use.

7. What then? Are eternal punishments not to be feared? They certainly are to be feared and avoided. For no one ever hated his own flesh (Eph. 5:29); but a stronger love of Christ needs no movement of fear in order to produce devotion to justice. This love fears nothing so much as offense—but because of the offense, not because of the punishment. This, however, holds so long as human affairs fluctuate in uncertainty [Col. 0101C] and no person’s praise is secure during life. But when, after life, one has been brought into truth, fear of this kind will thereafter cease, making room for the third fear. It succeeds the earlier fears, yet yields to none; for it remains for ever and ever.

The first fear, then, dreads having to pay for the offense of rashness; the second, offending through weakness; the third has nothing to fear. For what could completed blessedness and perfected charity fear? This fear springs from the nursery-bed of charity. I do not dare say that it is charity, yet neither do I dare deny it. For what but love does that strive to be which no longer knows the affection of fear? How is it not love, when it has almost ceased to be fear? For in what sense [Col. 0101D] is fear that which fears nothing? I would bestow upon that fear, so secure, the name of love, were it not that God himself loves us there, while in so great a majesty no place is allowed for fear. But how can that fear in us be separated from charity? And what else is it there to fear, except not to be swollen with pride against the Lord of majesty? What is that fear but willing subjection, unforced obedience, reverence freely rendered? How can it be fear if it does not fear to offend? It cannot. Yet again, how is it not fear, if it does not dare to offend? Thus it does not seem fear, because it fears neither sin nor danger; and it is fear, because it presumes nothing boldly or rashly.

What is that fear but humble reverence rendered as though from the necessity of duty, while experiencing nothing of necessity? For there is a necessity of obedience by the right of one’s created condition; but the freedom of love knows no necessity. [Col. 0102A] What is that fear but rather the absence of rashness and negligence than the compulsion of necessity? You see how nearly this fear approaches charity: it is almost charity, but not wholly. Their grounds differ; their affection is the same. Do you ask on what ground? On account of the lower creature’s condition, bound to obey the slightest nod of so great a majesty. A just necessity lies upon you; but charity does not look to that consideration. It is carried away by admiration for divine majesty and does not contemplate the lowliness of its created condition. Therefore charity does not know the reason which fear regards, being forestalled by stronger motives.

8. Fear and love therefore differ in their grounds, but are kindred in obedience and free affection. The first fear fears punishment; the second deprivation; the third neither. Perfect charity drives out [Col. 0102B] the first, tolerates the second for a time, and sets the third inseparably beside itself.

Seek this fear, daughters of Jerusalem. Beware the first, which charity casts out. “He paved the midst with charity” (Song 3:10). Where it says “the midst,” it gives us to understand the whole. Let charity pave the midst of your heart; let charity clothe it. This garment is also the bridal adornment. If it is required of a guest at a wedding, how much more of the bride? Charity alone wishes to occupy and possess every recess of your mind. Do not share them with a degenerate and alien affection. The bed of charity is indeed soft and delicate; it does not wish to be distressed even a little by burdensome fear. “For the daughters of Jerusalem,” it says. Rightly so: “Great peace have those who love your law” (Ps. 119:165).

[Col. 0102C] If anyone boasts of grace freely bestowed, how much more may you? For although the riches of spiritual gifts are great, charity has surpassed them all. It has not merely surpassed them; it has also embraced them. Charity is both sweet and rich. Finally, as the Psalm says, “among the lots of virtues” (Ps. 68:14), in the common possession of spiritual graces one sleeps upon the bed of charity. Charity, as though in the midst, communicates itself to all; and, as though better, enriches all virtues. Therefore, daughters of Jerusalem, seek eagerly the greater charisms. But rather, that you may possess charity—and possess it more abundantly—pass wholly into the affection of love. For our beloved Jesus Christ is wholly lovable, he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XX

“Go forth and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” (Song 3:11)

[Col. 0102D]

1. You have heard to what the daughters of Zion are invited; but you have not yet heard from where they are commanded to go forth. For the text does not state this. From where, then? From Zion? But “the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 84:8). Therefore he does not call them from Zion when he calls them to see God. Or perhaps they are called not to see God, but to see Solomon alive in the diadem with which his mother crowned him? Thus nothing prevents his commanding the daughters of Zion to go forth from Zion. But was that man not born in Zion? Therefore, if they are summoned from Zion, still they are summoned only to Zion: from the higher Zion to the lower Zion. For it does not seem worthy or fitting [Col. 0103A] that the daughters should go forth from it—especially in order to see him whose dwelling is in Zion and who was born in it (Ps. 87:5, 7).

I remember a certain eloquent and learned man who, discussing this passage, said: “They seem poorly situated, since they are commanded to go forth.” He spoke quite aptly for the occasion, directing what he had proposed to the benefit of his hearers. Yet to me those toward whom the exhortation of the present discourse is directed seem exceedingly well situated. Where, you ask? Upon the golden couch of which yesterday’s sermon spoke. That place is delightful and richer in joy than human affection can contain. Excess of pleasure drains itself away, and overflowing delight drinks up the soul. This joy alternates in turns and cannot be continuous, because it is excessive. [Col. 0103B] Yet these are good turns, where one does not depart from the Bridegroom. One who remains in the flesh is not granted by inheritance to possess the golden couch. Therefore the daughters of Zion are commanded to go forth—but as if he were saying: Do not go too far away.

2. “Go forth,” he says, “and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” He does not wish them to depart from Christ, whether they rise in mind or return to sobriety. Good sobriety is the simplicity of faith, which the sight of those who behold may bear, and by which it may be nourished. Blessed is one who, descending by this step, is received; and who, ascending, begins. For this place of contemplation first meets those who ascend. The emulation of contemplation is good; but knowledge is necessary. You will be kindled and girded for that golden couch, a place truly fit for watching. I approve your zeal, [Col. 0103C] but wait while I set your foot in order and place a step for you. It is a watchtower—truly a lofty watchtower—having passed beyond the clouds of every earthly vapor. Being unaccustomed, why are you preparing to leap there? “Support yourself with your hands,” as it is written, so that you may grow accustomed to dwelling in the palace of King Solomon (Prov. 30:28). Meanwhile crawl, until you are caught up. For, says the Psalm, he “has set ascents in his heart,” not leaps. Yet there will come a time when ascent will be transformed into a leap—or rather, into assumption. What are these ascents but certain purifications of the mind? Therefore they are in “the valley of tears” (Ps. 84:6–7), because sins that are wept over are cleansed. Blessed is one who has sufficiently washed the bed of his heart, who has wept enough; [Col. 0103D] whose sorrow is complete, whose heart is addressed by the inspiration of divine consolations and summoned from the valley of weeping; whose eye is not troubled by fear of the Judge, so that he may see King Solomon with tranquil gaze on the day of his heart’s gladness.

3. “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon.” Those are deemed worthy of this joyful vision who have enclosed themselves under a certain law of repentance and restricted themselves within the guard of discipline, whose soul refuses consolation. Do you wish to know how good enclosure is? “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). “Arise, hasten, my friend, and come” (Song 2:10). Do you see how he now invites and calls “friend” the one who knows how to enclose herself? But if you are enclosed, do not go forth until Christ invites you. Dinah went out—not led out, but went out—and she went out not to see King Solomon, but to see the women of that land [Col. 0104A] (Gen. 34:1). You know what she found. Do not go out unless either the Bridegroom or the Bridegroom’s companions invite you.

Lazarus went out when the Lord summoned him to life (John 11:43–44). Noah went out from the ark that had enclosed him unharmed amid the waves of this world; but he went out when the Lord opened its doors for him (Gen. 8:16). Abraham went out from his land in order to see the land of promise; but he went out when called (Gen. 12:1). You also, daughters of Zion, go forth, invited to the grace of a more blessed vision. Miserably enclosed is one who neither strives nor deserves to go forth to this blessed vision. Servile is such enclosure; free is the going forth. [Col. 0104B] “When you turn to the Lord,” it says, “the veil shall be removed”—the veil of ignorance and ignobility; for the Lord is Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.
