Where there is a greater abundance of the Spirit, there is fuller freedom. One who is shut in and wrapped about has scant freedom to breathe.

4. Therefore go forth, daughters of Zion, so that with Paul you may say: “But we all, beholding the glory of God with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image” (2 Cor. 3:16, 18). The vision of God must always be received with a certain affection. And truly your vision is effective and compelling, good Jesus, for it draws the affections of those who behold into itself. Did Moses not undergo a sweet compulsion of desire, so that he might turn aside and see that great vision? (Exod. 3:3). Do you wish to understand [Col. 0104C] how effective it is? “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). But what when you have been humbled to the earth? Do you not draw the minds of all to yourself? Good Jesus, I do not await the glory of your resurrection, nor reserve my wonder for the power by which you ascend into heaven. Rather, at the very beginning of the annunciation or your birth, angelic voices strike my ears, a new report astonishes me, and an unfamiliar light arisen in darkness draws me to itself.

A bare vision, which does not translate itself into fitting affections, is to be numbered with ignorance and blindness. Do you wish to receive a fruitful vision? “The islands saw and feared; the ends of the earth were astonished and drew near,” says Isaiah (Isa. 41:5). You see [Col. 0104D] what fruits of virtue the vision of God produces: fear, astonishment, love. “They saw,” he says, “and feared; they were astonished and drew near.” They saw you unto understanding; they feared unto reverence; they were astonished at novelty; they drew near through conformity. Vision apprehends; fear restrains; astonishment suspends; drawing near carries away and unites. For those draw near who are inflamed with emulation. Fear humbles the mind of the beholder, astonishment renders it almost senseless, and love binds it fast. Vision is empty, and undeserving of the name contemplation, if it is not clothed with such affections. Will you call that person one who sees, if from knowledge of the mystery he neither fears, nor is astonished, nor burns? Through fear the mind becomes sober; through astonishment, absorbed; through approach, joined and associated.

The grace of contemplation consists in virtues of this kind, [Col. 0105A] but especially in astonishment and love. For by astonishment and admiration the mind goes beyond itself; by love it draws near. The power of contemplation is to be judged not so much from its matter as from its manner. Both must be considered: both the kinds of things contemplated and the degrees of their effects. Yet it is better to be affected more deeply in a lower kind than less deeply in a higher. This vision is hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones (Matt. 11:25). Therefore he says: “The ends of the earth were astonished and drew near.”

5. What the humble are capable of grasping commonly affects them more deeply and brings with it a certain admiration and love of itself. “When I am lifted up from the earth,” he says, “I shall draw all things to myself.” Everything that is in you, good Jesus, has a certain power [Col. 0105B] of attraction and stirs those who think upon it toward affection; but not all of us can attain to everything. High things belong to the high alone; lowly things to all. What humility is greater than being lifted up upon the cross? Even of this he says: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself.” This humility is effective in drawing. Why should it not be? Who is not filled with astonishment and ecstasy at the simple thought of this event? Whose affection does not this faith drain and render almost senseless, making it inadequate? It is an easy subject for contemplation, yet fruitful for grace. This simplicity of faith has less of intellectual understanding, but provides a sufficiently great stimulus to admiration and love. It is an accessible subject, yet produces the sweetest excesses. Do not disdain this place of contemplation. [Col. 0105C] It is not difficult to recall, and it is rich for glory. “Far be it from me,” says Paul, “to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). And what do you wish to hear? The cross itself is the crown of glory, the diadem of kingship. For on the cross he triumphed, stripping principalities and powers, and cast out the ruler of this world. Glorious is the vision of his triumph.

6. “Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him.” See the flesh which he took from the human race, triumphant upon the wood. Happy is the flesh which Christ took to himself not as a prison but as a crown; which served as adornment, not burden. All of us are hidden in the flesh as in prison-houses, fettered and serving the law of sin. [Col. 0105D] “Wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from this body of death?” “The grace of God through Jesus Christ” (Rom. 7:24–25). For God, sending his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, condemned sin in the flesh on account of sin (Rom. 8:3). The reality of Christ’s flesh, feeling no burden of sin, brought to us all the victorious palm over sin.

Rightly is the immaculate body understood as a diadem: the body of triumph, honor, and glory; the body by whose blood the bond-record of sin is erased, the written record of justice and salvation is sealed, and the documents of marriage are drawn up. For this is the day of betrothal, when, repudiating the old rites, he instituted the new sacraments of the Church; when, as the sign and bond of an everlasting marriage, a mingling of blood [Col. 0106A] and water flowed from his side. Today he gave the Synagogue a writ of divorce and passed from the former woman, whom he hated, to the latter, whom he loved. He passed from the old to the new, which he presented to himself glorious, “without spot or wrinkle or anything of the kind” (Eph. 5:27). Its freedom from wrinkle is a sign of newness. Christ unfolded the wrinkles of the letter and drew forth the newness contained within it.

Why do you, daughters of Zion and of the Synagogue, wish to gather wrinkles which Christ has unfolded? Why do you still glory in the old things when the new have come? Go forth, daughters of Zion, from the caverns of the letter, from a narrow and ignoble understanding. Go forth and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him. The Incarnation is a crown to us; you think it an insult. And see now how he has blessed [Col. 0106B] the crown of the year of his goodness, how his fields are filled with abundance (Ps. 65:12). See the crown, and see also the abundance: the crown of victory, the abundance of virtues. Whence comes this, except because the grain of wheat, falling into the earth, died? For “this is the victory that conquers the world: our faith” (1 John 5:4). The very multitude of believers is a crown and adornment for Christ. “You shall be,” he says, “a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.” Do you arrogate this saying to yourselves? Or is it not through you that the name of God is blasphemed? Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see how glorious God is in his saints, if perhaps this vision may lead you to emulation and make you pass from your solitude to the multitude of the Church. “Though you have been deserted,” he says, “you shall no longer be called Forsaken, [Col. 0106C] nor shall your land any longer be called Desolate” (Isa. 62:3–4).

7. But let us now cease to direct our discourse toward those outside. Let us rather delight in seeing how the beauties of the desert now grow fat, how Christ is girded in the Church with the crown of believers. “What is our hope and crown of glory? Is it not you before the Lord?” (1 Thess. 2:19). If Paul says this, how much more Christ? “As I live,” says the Lord, “you shall put on all these as an ornament” (Isa. 49:18). Have you noticed how he declares that the ranks of believers are Christ’s adornment in the Church? Why are they not also a crown? But the crown has a certain exceptional and illustrious dignity above other [Col. 0106D] adornments: since the others belong to the body, this belongs to the head. The consideration of time also contributes something to its distinction. Its use is reserved only for solemn feast-days.

I see your eagerness already aroused; already you turn this interpretation of the word toward yourselves. You recognize in the privilege of the crown your own prerogative—you who are bound by a purer life and profession, equipped by practice, untiring in zeal, and festive in leisure. Those are rightly reckoned under the name of diadem whom conflict now troubles less than triumph gladdens; who no longer wrestle against flesh and blood, who no longer watch for the serpent’s head, but adorn Christ’s. You are Christ’s crown and joy; and therefore, as you have begun, so stand, beloved: so stand [Col. 0107A] in the Lord—indeed, so hold the Lord as your head. It is an exalted place; bring there nothing of baser material. See your calling; see for what use you have been taken up. Do not wish to weave any hay, wood, or straw into the Lord’s diadem—nothing, in short, that deserves or fears fire. Let intertwined thorns be burned with fire. Do not emulate evildoers, nor envy those who placed a thorny crown upon the head of our King. Such a diadem brings not honor but horror. Christ recoils more from harshness of character and the stings of the tongue than from thorns’ prickles—especially in those called to the simplicity of silence, the work of charity, the quiet of leisure, the school of humility, the vow of submission, and the bond of unity.

But the bond is not good [Col. 0107B] when people band together among themselves and join hands in disparaging others, saying, after the manner of the Jews: “Let us remove the just man, because he is useless to us and contrary to our works” (Wis. 2:12). But you, always emulate the good of peace in what is good.

8. Finally, the shape of a crown presents a certain indication of unity. Not only the material of the crown is to be considered; its form too supplies grounds for a beautiful understanding. For the crown’s form is such that it coheres in a circle and rises upward. Do you wish to possess a common coherence and this very unity? “The believers,” it says, “were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). What is the end of this unity? Certainly hope, laid up in heaven. Thus you already have coherence in unity and upward elevation in [Col. 0107C] hope. And the Apostle says: “Take up the helmet of salvation” (Eph. 6:17). The mention of the helmet is well introduced because it has a certain affinity with the crown. Both belong to the head; but one is defense, the other adornment. Therefore nothing prevents hope from being referred to both: for “we were saved in hope” (Rom. 8:24).

Let these brief remarks on the form suffice for now. What do you ask about the material? You yourselves know that an exalted place disdains fragile and obscure material. It requires gold and precious stones: “For you have placed upon his head a crown of precious stone” (Ps. 21:4). In the Apocalypse you read of golden crowns (Rev. 4:4). Precious is the material, whether it is gold alone or some mixture of gold and gems. [Col. 0107D] Yet I do not know whether something of greater grace is not signified by this: the mention of gold is omitted, and it says, “You have placed upon his head a crown of precious stone.” And I shall show you a yet more excellent material: “A great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and upon her head a crown of twelve stars” (Rev. 12:1). You are shown the choir of the Apostles both in number and in kind. “Those who instruct many unto wisdom shall shine like the stars unto perpetual eternities” (Dan. 12:3). This crown of brothers stood around Jesus, as it is written (Luke 24:36). And in the Apocalypse, many diadems are upon the Bridegroom’s head (Rev. 19:12), according to the diversity of graces and ranks; but that one is preeminent with which he was crowned on the day of his betrothal, on the day when, in [Col. 0108A] his disciples, he betrothed the Church to himself.

He betrothed her in faith; he betrothed her by giving into their hearts the earnest, pledge, and first-fruits of the Spirit. Participation in the Spirit is called betrothal, when one who clings to God is no longer two, but one spirit (1 Cor. 6:17). Finally, he himself is the man who left father and mother, clung to his wife, and the two became one flesh (Eph. 5:31–32). O blessed exchange! As bride, you have become one flesh with the Bridegroom; and you yourself have become one spirit with him.

9. How you ought to rejoice in such a marriage, faithful soul! How you ought to be glad and keep festival! “Put on, put on the garments of your glory, holy city” (Isa. 52:1), bride of the Lamb; rejoice and be glad, Zion, joined to Christ. How [Col. 0108B] can you fail to rejoice when he himself rejoices? “The bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride, and your God shall rejoice over you” (Isa. 62:5). But with how great a joy? “On the day,” it says, “of his betrothal, and on the day of his heart’s gladness.” He indicates no slight movement of joy when he expressly calls it the heart’s joy. Do I say joy? It is delight. “My delights,” he says, “are to be with the children of men” (Prov. 8:31). At what a cost to you, good Jesus, those joys were secured! You do not possess them without cost, since you bought them by the suffering of your flesh. Therefore he calls this joy a joy of the heart alone. It is an injury to the Bridegroom if he rejoices and you do not applaud from the heart, congratulate him, and rejoice with him. Not to rejoice with one who rejoices—especially on the day of betrothal—is like disdain or contempt.

What beauty can draw your affection, if [Col. 0108C] not that of him who is “fairer in form than the children of men”? Rejoicing, rejoice in the Lord, and let your soul exult in your Bridegroom, in your God. Even if he were not God, but a mere human being, what attractions to love would such a man nonetheless possess, abounding in so many gifts of grace? For if you begin to recount from the root of his conception, he will appear wholly star-studded to you in relation to human condition, both in the singularity and in the excellence of his virtues: a man innocent, unstained, separated from sinners—to say nothing for the present of his having been made higher than the heavens (Heb. 7:26), able to sympathize with our weaknesses, tested in all things in likeness to us, yet without sin (Heb. 4:15). Grace was poured out upon his lips, mercy in his inmost parts, power [Col. 0108D] in his hands; singular in conduct, accessible in speech; prudent in answers, life in his words. What more? He was conceived from faith, born of a Virgin, not consumed in death, and taken up in glory.

10. I now pass over the number of believers and the merits of the peoples whom, by sending the Spirit, he joined to himself in faith and charity. O Christ, truly the great mystery of godliness, incentive to love, who was manifested and assailed in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was proclaimed among the nations, believed in throughout the world, and taken up in glory! (1 Tim. 3:16.) Who will grant me often to run and run again through these lines, and at every degree of virtues and works to say: “Lord, who is like you?” (Ps. 35:10.)

[Col. 0109A] Who will grant that these discourses may be written in my heart, engraved with a stylus, and, as it were, inscribed on flint so that they may not be erased? Your finger is a good stylus, Lord—the finger with which you wrote on the ground secret words, words whose power those who slandered could not endure (John 8:6–9). Bend yourself down, my God, and cut the tablets of your law into my heart. My heart is stony; yet the hard stone of nature forgets its hardness under the impression of your finger, yielding easily where you engrave. But we have now said much concerning why the Bride ought to rejoice and be glad on the day of betrothal and on the day of her beloved’s heart-gladness. The ground of joy on this day is great and exceeds the bounds of the human heart and affection. No foreign joy need be introduced here; this day has sufficient joy of its own. You are sweet, [Col. 0109B] Lord, and your spirit toward us is upright, a gracious spirit. Through faith and love you join human souls to yourself with a Bridegroom’s affection, and you rejoice in their conversion. Hard is the heart that withdraws from itself the matter of this joy, weakens its occasions, and diminishes its grounds. O how shameless and ungrateful I should be if I did not love one so free from corruption, so closely bound in compassion toward me, not subject to necessity, and steadfast in loving-kindness! I will love you, sweet Lord, even if not for myself, yet for your sake: that I may satisfy your desire, furnish you with causes of delight and grounds for joy on the day of your betrothal and on the day of your heart’s gladness.

## SERMON XXI

“Go forth and see King Solomon,” etc. (Song 3:11)

[Col. 0109C]

1. And I dare confidently invite you also to the joy of this vision, daughters of the heavenly Zion, Jerusalem which is in heaven. You are the true and full daughters of Zion, who always behold the face of the Father. You, I say, the multitude of many thousands of angels—you I invite and summon. Go forth and see; go forth from that hidden bosom of intimate vision, from the secret place of inaccessible light. Our earth offers you a new spectacle: for the Lord has made something new upon the earth. I call you from eternal things to earthly ones. This invitation is wonderful; yet somehow those eternal realities, ever new and wonderful in themselves, shine forth newer and more wonderful in this new thing accomplished on earth. O blessed temporal newness upon earth, which made that ancient [Col. 0109D] and eternal newness still newer for angelic sight!

“The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). What man? “Behold,” he says, “the man whose name is the East” (Zech. 6:12). The East, the brightness of eternal light, is encompassed by a woman’s womb—yet a virgin’s womb—and clothed in flesh. This is that new thing which, by the very greatness of its newness, would bar belief, if faith had not been elicited beforehand by unheard-of signs. Indeed, amid so many evident testimonies both of prophecies and of miracles, the minds of some were so astonished by this newness that, while they deny belief to the novelty, they do not grant belief to the clearest signs. But why do I invite you to go forth, when you everywhere even precede [Col. 0110A] and instruct the Apostles themselves? Everywhere you are diligent in admiring and proclaiming this newness.

An angel announces the conception to Mary (Luke 1:26–38); an angel announces the birth to the shepherds—indeed, the angel seems to have announced it to the angels themselves as well, not only to the shepherds. One proclaims; the others applaud. “There came to be with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host, praising and saying, Glory to God in the highest” (Luke 2:9–14). One announces what the others knew equally well, and yet they hear as new and recent what could not have been unknown to them. O blessed newness, which gives joy to angelic hearing and, so to speak, delights them to hear from another and as though to learn what Truth itself had taught them from the beginning! O humble and untiring devotion, both toward God and toward one another!

[Col. 0110B]

2. Here is something which we ought, if only we would, observe—indeed, preserve. What is it? That, following the angelic example, we should offer humble and attentive hearing to another’s discourse, even in matters we do not ignore. Yet one who speaks of God is not alien, unless we regard ourselves as alien from God. And if he is alien, the divine subject grants him authority. To disdain listening is a sign either of curiosity or of obstinacy. Angelic spirits, to whom the mystery of the Incarnation was known from the beginning, do not refrain from wonder at this newness when it is displayed; and their ancient knowledge rejoices and is glad not only at a new vision, but also at a new hearing.

Christ came forth at the end of the ages; therefore they too go forth. And “his going forth is from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5:2). But at the end of the ages he came forth from the womb [Col. 0110C] of the woman who encompassed him. Therefore the daughters of the heavenly Zion go forth, to marvel in fulfillment at what they had always marveled at in expectation. An angel at the annunciation (Luke 1:26–38), an angel at the nativity (ibid. 2:9–14), an angel at the baptism (ibid. 3:21); an angel appeared while he prayed (Luke 22:43), is witness at his resurrection (Luke 24:4), and stands by at his ascension (Acts 1:10). How ardent lovers do you think those are who are such diligent heralds and untiring admirers? Throughout every stage of this mystery they go about and offer the sacrifice of admiration, the sacrifice of loud acclamation; they sing and chant a psalm to the Lord. And all this reverence is outwardly displayed, apart from that which lies hidden within.

And if the Lord made [Col. 0110D] something new on earth, nevertheless the fragrance of this newness filled heaven. “A woman shall encompass a man,” just as a crown encompasses a head. For Christ is the head of the Church (Eph. 5:23). Certainly he is glorious in that splendor of glory and image of the Father’s substance; but with a certain added tint, as it were, of our nature, and a color put on, while that splendor shines through, he is more pleasing—not only to those who could not bear it otherwise, but even to those upon whom that splendor is poured out in purity.

3. But what I mean is this: this very condescension by which he willed to be incarnate seems to have brought a certain beauty to the dignity of majesty. For how could humbled sublimity, emptied immensity, and incarnate divinity not please more? What is more beautiful than this variety? Do I say “variety”? It seems rather a contrariety, and is the more beautiful to contemplate [Col. 0111A] because these contraries do not oppose one another, but are harmonious with one another. Divine simplicity is wonderful in itself; yet, if I may so speak, this composition is much more wonderful, because it is newer. I cannot sufficiently marvel at the art of this union, and I think neither can the angels.

Indeed, their reason for wonder is greater, for the pure simplicity of the divine nature is more sincerely made known to them. That nature is incomparably pure, and therefore makes this union more wonderful. What is this union, when the integrity of each nature remains intact? For neither passes into the other, nor does some third and new thing, as it were, arise from the two. Yet it is new that they meet in one person.

Each contemplation is, as it were, a wine-cellar. Into that nectar-filled cellar of eternal majesty the angelic spirits were introduced—indeed, placed there from the beginning of their creation. But now, at the end of the ages, this our cellar upon earth pours forth new wine. O storehouses full, storehouses overflowing and pouring forth from this into that! Come forth, daughters of Zion, from the cellar of pure wine to this new wine which Wisdom has mingled in a new bowl. O cup that intoxicates, how splendid you are, and therefore intoxicating by your splendor! The eternal liquor poured into this new cup is drunk with greater love, though tempered with clarity; and therefore love too ought to be untempered. For who could restrain himself from loving, when immeasurable Majesty has accommodated itself to the measure of our capacity? O cup intoxicating the minds not only of human beings but also of angels, and turning them toward itself, from the contemplation of pure divinity, by this new union!

[Col. 0111C] Come forth, daughters of Zion, from that abundance of pure wine to this tempered cup. Come forth, and taste how sweet the Lord is. There the simple nature of divine sweetness is beheld; here its workings and evidences are set before us. There he is seen in himself; here in his affection. In this latter respect both are wonderful; and I do not know whether I should marvel more at the union of natures in one person or at the cause of that union. Why should we now marvel that three persons exist in the unity of the divine essence? Marvel instead that several complete natures exist in one person. What is there here that is not sweet to contemplate, or that does not move the affections?

4. Finally, the cause is added to the fullness of our wonder. This cause lacks neither rational coherence, nor efficacy for salvation, nor the grace of compassion. Do you wish to hear its coherence? “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22); and again: “As through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man many are made righteous.” What could be more coherent? The coherence is great, but its efficacy is greater from the standpoint of justice. Finally, “where transgression abounded, grace also superabounded” (Rom. 5:19–20). Where there was transgression, seduction and deception intervened; and so it does not appear voluntary in every respect. But in grace nothing is without purpose, nothing is unwilling. How then are voluntary goods not more effective than evils compelled, as it were, in some respect? Grace is truly effective and artful. I do not know whether I should marvel more at the art of the fitting together [Col. 0112A] or at the efficacy of salvation. In the benefit, both are welcome: both the will and the result.

Add also a third consideration: the very manner and rationale. Nothing is more affectionate than this will. “Greater love has no one than this, that one lay down his life for his friends.” Yet he did this for enemies. And they were enemies in themselves, and friends because they were loved before the foundation of the world. What could be more fruitful than the outcome of this work? The lavish outpouring of the Spirit upon all flesh makes this sufficiently clear. The outpouring of Christ’s blood obtained for us the spiritual outpouring. How could he fail to pour his Holy Spirit upon those whom he washed in his blood? Therefore he first cleansed them, so that there might be persons upon whom the Spirit afterward might flood more deeply. What could be more coherent in its order?

I am constrained in considering this matter, and do not know which of the three I should choose chiefly for contemplation: mercy, prudence, or result. These contend with one another in our contemplation; when attention is directed toward one, it is drawn toward another. They delight me and caress me with diverse affections. I burn, I am amazed, I rejoice. I rejoice at the benefit; I am amazed at the prudence; I burn because of the love of mercy bestowed upon me.

5. Why do I divide these things? They are intermingled with one another and are frequently blended in every category. For manner, benefit, and affection—or, if you prefer to say so, prudence, result, and mercy—these three, I say, whether considered together or separately, both draw my mind to themselves more swiftly, hold it longer, and transform it into a kind of wonder and exultation.

The faith of Mother Church has woven her diadem from the variety of such virtues. [Col. 0112C] They assign to it this number, this weight, this measure. In the rationale and coherence of order, number is discerned, along with the measure of harmony. In weight there is the more vehement affection of mercy. And indeed the weight of grace is mighty, drawing immeasurable Majesty down from heaven to earth. This immensity, incomparably exceeding every creature, contracted itself to a measure: a measure sufficient to reach us. For it did not stretch itself over us as though not condescending to us; rather, in measure it distills to us the gifts of the Spirit.

I understand “measure” as the effect of the gifts. For God gives us the Spirit according to measure: measure against measure—measure of grace against measure of injustice. For “as transgression abounded, [Col. 0112D] grace also abounded.” Is this not measure against measure? Certainly, and beyond measure as well. For grace also “superabounded.” Did it superabound only beyond the measure of transgression? Certainly not merely beyond the measure of transgression, but even beyond the measure of grace. Grace abounds both against and beyond the measure of injustice, so that it abounds beyond the measure of grace, but not against grace. For where one abounds, the other must also superabound, and more is given to one who has abundantly.

This measure is a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing. There seems to be abundance when not only necessities are supplied, but luxuries also overflow. Among the gifts of the Spirit, some are useful, some instruct, some delight, heal, adorn, [Col. 0113A] and gladden. How could things that grow so greatly not overflow? But this is enough now concerning the number, measure, and weight of the diadem which his mother fashioned for King Solomon. For she confers upon him a kind of garland of glory, while she joins together what he took from us and what he bestowed upon us.

You see of what gifts of grace this diadem consists. But what have graces to do with a diadem? “He will give,” Proverbs says, “increases of graces to your head” (Prov. 4:9). The Father gives, and the mother crowns. She crowns, because she believes; she surrounds; she, the Mother, crowns. Church adorns you, good Jesus, with herself; she clothes you with herself; she shoes and crowns you with herself. Footwear belongs to the journey; the crown, to perfection. A wondrous change: when the dust, if any has clung to one, has been shaken off, a crown is made from footwear.

[Col. 0113B] 6. “On the day of his betrothal and of the joy of his heart.” Observe the order. One day is spoken of for betrothal and coronation. If you understand this, blessed are you if you follow it. You reverse the order if you wish to be betrothed before you are crowned; if you wish to be bound to Christ first in delight and rest, rather than to conquer with Christ. Such anticipation is indeed blessed, but not orderly, if you desire the bridal chamber to be prepared for you before triumph, if you presume upon joy before labor. One day is appointed for these three things: the diadem, the betrothal, and the joy of the heart.

And what is the heart of our Solomon? “You,” he says, “are the body of Christ, and members of a member” (1 Cor. 12:27). Any member whatsoever of this head is surely blessed; but one that is his heart is among the chief members. And see whether he is not the heart who is cherished in a certain [Col. 0113C] womb of God’s secrets, in the living warmth of affections, in the midst of meditations. For from the heart come thoughts, not actions (Matt. 15:19). Rightly, then, he is the heart who is placed in the midst of spiritual thoughts, in the richness of graces, in a certain womb of truth, in the womb of wisdom, of which Solomon is presented as a type.

And indeed one and the same Church or soul is both crown, heart, and bride: a crown on the head, a bride from the side, a heart in the womb; the crown at the summit, the bride nearby, the heart in the innermost place. What here is not most fittingly placed? What is not festive? Come forth from here, daughters of our Zion, and see, so that you too may pass into the affection of this heart, the grace of the bride, the beauty of the diadem. Do not boast in an empty name. Be what you are called: daughters of contemplation. Let practice itself bear witness to the name. For this day of betrothal is festive, worthy of receiving God; and from it one comes to the still more festive day, the day of the wedding. On that day no certificate of divorce is given, no divorce intervenes; the husband does not depart on a very long road—nor even on a very short one—but Christ Jesus the bridegroom is always in his house, he who lives and reigns with God the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXII

“How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful! Your eyes are those of doves, apart from that which lies hidden within” (Song 4:1).

1. She is not afraid that she may swell with her own praises and forfeit humility, she whose bridegroom himself commends her beauty [Col. 0114A] with such emphatic expression. Often, beneath a great desire to please, there lies fear of displeasing; and more earnest devotion diminishes and steals away the security of conscience. What wonder, then, if the bridegroom applauds her beauty and soothes with gentle address the affection into which fear had entered? For on what grounds would any human soul, admitted into marriage with our Solomon, not fear her own deformity? She had heard him in his diadem, on the day of his betrothal and the joy of his heart, more festive than usual in that abyss of glory; and she could rightly fear rejection if she looked to the cause of her own deformity and lowliness.

It was necessary, therefore, that when made more secure she should recover courage, and that the gladness infused into her mind should suffuse her face with a certain living warmth. [Col. 0114B] For cheerfulness of mind greatly adds beauty to the countenance of one’s whole life and works. Therefore the bridegroom addresses his friend in this way: “How beautiful you are, my friend!” Nearly similar words were said above in the preceding passage, where we read: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful” (Song 1:14). “Behold, you are beautiful,” and “How beautiful you are,” seem almost the same. In both places her beauty is praised, and the repeated commendation indicates confirmation.

Yet, as far as I can perceive, a certain distinction is suggested here. Where he says, “Behold, you are beautiful,” he speaks only of beauty; but here he speaks of an excess of beauty: “How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful!” There it is a simple attestation of beauty, as though suddenly discovered; here it is wonder at the abundance of that beauty. [Col. 0114C] There he attests how beautiful she is; here he delights that she is so beautiful. For here it is uttered with greater weight and with the affection of one who marvels, and the manner of utterance declares the movement of a delighted mind: “How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful!”

In the progress of the Song, moreover, it was fitting that more perfect things should be said to the bride. This is what we have to say regarding the distinction between similar words. For the matters that had to be interpreted concerning the bride’s beauty have been fully and carefully explained in their proper places. And what a certain man—whether more learned or more eloquent, I do not know—has discussed in his homilies (BERNARD, Sermon 40 on the Song), it would not become us, so to speak, to touch even with the smallest finger for examination.

2. This, however, must not be overlooked: after his general commendation of her beauty, when he is about to portray his friend feature by feature, he begins first with the eyes. Wisely indeed, since “if your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. 6:22–23). He therefore compares her eyes to doves, in order to teach his friend, in accordance with the Gospel’s teaching, to be simple as a dove (Matt. 10:16).

For the eye of intention, if simple, illumines the whole body of action and causes works to shine before God which might of themselves shine before human beings. When a good work shines outwardly, but the mind does not intend the goodness of the work, then, as it were, the eye is blinded while the body is bright. The works themselves may indeed sometimes be good in kind and useful to others; yet the goodness of the works does not return to the doer, who has no single eye [Col. 0115A] in them. Therefore they are dark, because they lack the light of sincere intention.

The good eye, then, is single, having no part of darkness, and making the whole body of conduct bright. For the eye is either wholly dark, wholly bright, or has some admixture of darkness. It is wholly dark when it intends an evil work for an evil end; wholly bright when it intends a good work solely for the good. But when, in a good work, intention is directed not only to the good itself but also to some other end; or when, in a work that is not good, something mistakenly believed to be good is loved—then the eye is darkened in some respect and is not pure with unmixed simplicity.

What if a good work is pretended, but not the good itself—something altogether different—is intended? Is that eye to be called wholly dark, or only partly obscured? To me it seems rather wholly dark. For even if light is reckoned to be in the work, none is discerned in the intention. How can an intention be good if it does not desire the good? Or how can it be simple if it conceals itself under the covering of good?

But in the bride’s eyes both simplicity and spirituality are commended; therefore they are called dove’s eyes. And fittingly, in his friend he first commends light, to show her like himself, who is also called “the light of the world” (John 8:12), and in whom there is no darkness at all (1 John 1:5). In the creation of the six days, light is said to have been created before all things (Gen. 1:3); and in describing the bride’s beauty, mention of light is fittingly introduced first.

[Col. 0115C] 3. “Your eyes are those of doves.” How do you presume to be a friend, you who do not know how to have a dove’s eyes? However good your works may be, if your mind is impure, you applaud yourself in vain for beauty. How are you a friend if you are not beautiful? But how are you not an enemy if you malign what is holy? He maligns what is holy who maligns what is good, whether it be his own good or another’s. You malign your own good when you do not regard the good itself; another’s, when you suspect evil of good. Both a depraved intention and a perverse interpretation are maligning; both are bitter, both false, having nothing in common with the nature of doves.

Doves’ eyes are those that neither wish to be deceived nor know how to deceive. Do you not know that your bridegroom is truth? How then will he say to you, “My dove, my friend” (Song 2:13–14)? Simplicity is a friend to truth; therefore “his converse is with the simple” (Prov. 3:32). Finally, he applauds friendly simplicity, saying, “Your eyes are those of doves.” For clear-sighted simplicity is good: it excludes pretense without becoming dim-sighted concerning truth.

This bird is rare on earth today; and if it has any abundance anywhere, it is sufficiently hidden and concealed in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall, and beside the streams of waters. How has the dove-like eye become darkened or hidden? Who does not pursue the shrewd devices of the age? Who does not delight in employing them? Who does not love to possess them, or at least not wish to be named as lacking them? Who is not ashamed of dove’s eyes [Col. 0116A] and proud to possess kite’s eyes?

If you desire to be called Christ’s friend, what have you to do with the prudence of the flesh, which is hostile to God? (Rom. 8:7). Or are you trying to do away with these enmities, so as to house in yourself both the prudence of flesh and that of spirit? “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5:6). What then will happen where there is much leaven and only a small lump? What fellowship is there between the law of desire and the law of charity? The former ought not to be joined to the latter, because it cannot be subject to it (Rom. 8:7). For the prudence of the flesh either resists the law of God and is hostile to it, or perishes altogether and is nothing: it either resists or wholly ceases. It can be killed, so that it is no longer at all; it cannot be subdued so as to be accommodated to it.

Yet you desire to have both mouth and heart trained in a prudence that can neither be associated with nor subjected to the law of God. The prudence of the spirit is life and peace. For the prudence of the spirit is life-giving, having use for the life that now is and for that which is to come. But the prudence of the flesh is exercised only in the present life and will have no place in the life to follow. For among the dead there are neither the riches nor the use of desire, but torment. The one is peace; the other, conflict. And it is rightly called peace when its task is to abolish what does not serve peace.

Christ recalls such prudence in speaking of the bride’s beauty. It is portrayed in the eyes of doves, which breathe simplicity and spirituality, because the Holy Spirit is commonly understood under the figure of a dove. Such simplicity is not usually empty; much hidden grace lies beneath it.

4. “Your eyes are those of doves, apart from that which [Col. 0116C] lies hidden within.” That is some great thing, I know not what, and truly great: something that either ought not manifestly to have been said or could not have been said; something that was not to be figured by any likeness, as other graces are, but is left only to suspicion and conjecture for those who perhaps undergo similar experiences. “Apart from that,” he says, “which lies hidden within,” as though there were not other graces and gifts of the Spirit within. And how is “all the glory of the king’s daughter from within”? (Ps. 44:14).

Moreover, the dove’s eyes themselves are inward: there simplicity of faith purifies hearts and makes the eyes of the heart enlightened; there not merely the eye, but the whole hidden person of the heart is spoken of (1 Pet. 3:4). Yet although all glory is inward in relation to outward glory, and just as in the outward person, so also in that [Col. 0116D] inward person some things are more inward than others and wholly hidden, known only to the beloved: perhaps some things are unknown even to the bride herself, who does not possess a full knowledge of the gifts divinely bestowed upon her. For what if sublimity is concealed so that humility may be preserved?

“Your secret is for yourself, good Jesus, your secret is for yourself”; and you alone delight in the hidden places of the bride. Why do you not share with us, even a little, that hidden something, and portray for us the concealed beauty in which you delight? You draw us on more to seek, by saying that it lies hidden within; and you stir our curiosity more strongly by pressing so great a mystery down in silence. By your silence you draw us more. How great is the abundance of this sweetness, which you judge should be concealed by not explaining it! Whatever it is lies hidden within; yet from those hiding-places a most sweet fragrance breathes forth. For in some way, while I conjecture that it is wonderfully sweet, I already feel it to be wonderfully sweet. Affection already weighs that to which understanding does not penetrate. This is stored with the bride and sealed in her treasures; only the beloved has the right to enter them and unfold the secrets of hidden glory.

5. But I say this because it is not easy to define anyone’s virtue from its indications. For often, when the outward signs are slight, the hidden secrets within are outstanding. Therefore we ought to praise manifest virtues in such a way as to use this addition in each case: “apart from that which lies hidden within.” Look, finally, at this dove-like simplicity commended [Col. 0117B] in the bride, of which we are speaking: how gracious, how sweet and pleasing it is in itself! Yet it has greater treasures hidden within it, and is, so to speak, made rich in marrow by a sweet secret.

Do you ask what that is? I have already said it; and if you still wish to hear, I confess that I do not know. I could commend to you this devout simplicity and urge you to emulate it, since it contains, and perhaps also confers, so inexplicable and sweet a mystery. Yet if I attempted to unfold that very thing, perhaps by experience or conjecture I might reach some hidden and concealed matter; but would it be that which the bridegroom has mentioned so enigmatically in his praise of the beloved? However much hidden matter I might uncover, something would still lie hidden within. It lies hidden in deep darkness and is not subject either to our pen [Col. 0117C] or to our study.

I shall venerate the very silence of so great a mystery. For although it has not been granted to us definitely to know what it is, because it is kept silent, enough has been left us to believe that it is something singularly sweet and pleasing to the bridegroom. Its quality cannot be investigated; yet one may judge its greatness from the very fact that such an arcane matter could not be spoken.

6. Yet, so that I may seem to have said something and not to have been wholly silent—for this is what you press me to do—receive what seems to me truly capable of being said on this point. Whether it is suited to the present chapter, you must judge. Virtues themselves are by their nature situated inwardly in the soul; but the exercise of some is vigorous in outward matters, while others exercise their power within. The former avoids carnal enticements; the latter embraces the hidden places of spiritual delights. The former either flees enticing occasions or restrains unruly affections, and, though necessary for the time being, labors in a burdensome exercise. The latter delights in such material as excels not more in pleasantness than in honorableness.

The former, with a simple gaze and a dove-like eye, passes over outward appearances and either hates or despises them; the latter, with a more searching vision, surveys heavenly forms and burns more ardently after seeing them. We may frame a certain distinction, saying that some virtues are outward, others inward, others innermost. Some withdraw themselves from carnal things; others attend to spiritual things; others now possess certain firstfruits. The first restrain themselves from the world’s enticement, which they despise; [Col. 0118A] the middle sort still dispose themselves toward that which they desire spiritually; the last—or rather, the innermost—now eagerly enjoy the things they desired.

Good God, how much light and delight there is in those hidden places! What ecstasy in those recesses! Would that such hiding-places might enclose me, so that I could say with the Psalm: “This night is my illumination in my delights” (Ps. 138:11).

7. Behold, I have now touched upon something hidden in this final degree; and perhaps this is it, or something like what the bridegroom has marked. Henceforth I wish to yield to mysteries. For it is not lawful to uncover the sacred secrets with bold speech, or with the less holy hands of the tongue to unfold delicately wrapped forms within the Holy of Holies, or to touch the hidden manna which the golden urn contains and the ark encloses.

The very name of manna reveals something mysterious, something of which one may more aptly ask, “What is this?” than say what it is. And to what could I better compare that hidden thing than to manna? Manna is indeed sweet and heavenly food; but you see how secretly it is enclosed in the urn, in the ark, in the Holy of Holies, so that the curious and less worthy eye may be shut out from such a sight—the eye that does not know how to be dove-like, one not guided by devout faith and pure intention.

But we ask you, brothers, embrace holy simplicity, tranquility of mind, pure meditations, and free prayers. For in such vessels—and, so to speak, in the ark of holy meditation and the inner urn of prayer—divine refreshment has been placed for us, and that portion of glory of which it is written: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. [Col. 0118C] 16:15). May its fullness bestow eternal life upon us through Jesus Christ, to whom be honor and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIII

“Your hair is like flocks of goats which have ascended from Mount Gilead. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep,” etc. (Song 4:1–2).

1. As you well know, these endearments are spoken to the Church, and her spiritual eyes were discussed in the preceding sermon. But since they are such, are they rare? See how her whole body is full of eyes before and behind. Her eyes are the Prophets; her eyes are the Apostles, who either foretell future things or proclaim things already done. Her eyes are the interpreters of both, and the teachers of peoples: through whose office we both see and discern the soul’s spiritual benefits and scandals.

But I do not know whether all who hold the office of eyes also retain its use. Blind guides, and not only of the blind but, what is more shameful, of those who see—do they not seem to have the place and appearance of eyes, but to lack their power? Would that even this were all: that they lacked the power to foresee good things and were blind to common benefits, while not being shrewd for private advantages. But now they are both blind and cunning: dull toward the Church’s gains, sharp toward their own.

But how can he be a dove’s eye who does not serve the dove, does not see for the dove, does not provide for the dove; who does not lead the dove, but rather leads the Church astray and, so far as he can, precipitates her by evil [Col. 0119A] examples? The Apostle speaks of such people: “All seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21). Such people occupy the place and pervert its use.

Conversely, there are others who do not possess the office of eyes by promotion, but arrogate it by presumption. This crowd is indeed numerous. Whom would you now name from among the disciples who, as though placed upon a tribunal, does not criticize, correct, and censure the works of prelates? These are no longer the eyes of the members, but a kind of eyes of the eyes—like feathers and down on a dove’s body wishing themselves to direct the very lights of its eyes.

I do not wish to press this point too hard, lest I seem to harass you, brothers. Be content with your own measure. In the dove’s body nothing is without an office, nothing lacks honor; and those parts that are hidden have more abundant honor. Finally, the bride’s hair also has its own honor. For if the prelates are understood by the eyes, who are to be understood by the hair except the disciples? And good disciples: those who, like hair, show themselves pliant and flexible to every nod of the teacher, as to the movement of the wind; who are slender and made fine by spiritual disciplines, almost without body and wholly without flesh, insensible to every injury, so that they do not feel even the wound of the shearing instrument. They endure the pains of suffering only in this: if they happen to be plucked away from the head to which they cling. For when the rest of the body is dead, they retain living sensation only there where they are joined to the head from which they arise. Being close to the brain itself, where the recess of wisdom is said to be, [Col. 0119C] they strive, as it were, to enter its innermost secrets. To be uprooted and, as it were, plucked away from there seems to them to be called away to outward cares on any occasion. For if they flow away from there without any sense of pain, how will they be believed either to have been born or rooted there?

2. Finally, hear what follows, showing that the bride’s hair does not fall but rises: “Your hair is like a flock of goats which have ascended from Mount Gilead.” Like a flock of goats, because they graze and dwell in high places, ever tending upward like goats; yet they do not think lofty thoughts, but are conscious of carnal weakness. For pride itself descends; humility ascends. They are therefore like goats because they both seek heights continually and look back upon their own lowliness.

And fittingly they ascend from Mount Gilead, but only from Mount Gilead, which is interpreted “Heap of Testimony.” And who is that but Christ, upon whom all the testimonies of the Prophets have been piled up, to whom the Prophets, John, the Father, and his very works bear testimony? This mountain is the head of the Church. Do not flow down from this mountain if you are a hair. Why do you threaten us with separation, as though you would be torn away from the flock of the remaining hairs? Will your fall bring baldness upon the Church? She does not know how to become bald. For all her hairs are numbered. That threatening was addressed to the Synagogue in the prophet: “Instead of curled hair there shall be baldness” (Isa. 3:24).

The Church’s locks are curled, always returning to their own head, winding around it in a friendly circuit and striving to enter the head’s hidden places. Therefore her hairs do not fall, but ascend [Col. 0120A] from Mount Gilead, continually piling up for themselves greater examples from Christ’s works to imitate. Would that all my works bore witness to the faith that I have in Christ, and that, heaped together through continual progress, they formed for me a heap of ascent. How few stones of this testimony I have gathered for myself! Indeed, I fear that I have piled up many to the contrary.

For what? Do they not seem to you to have amassed testimonies not for faith but rather against faith, who live in such a way as to appear to belong to a faith other than the Christian? Finally, how many such persons we see, of whom it may rightly be said: “These do not live as people who believe themselves redeemed by Christ’s blood, who hope for another life, who fear the future judgment, who, finally, acknowledge that the evangelical precepts were given by God!” May few such testimonies be found in my possession; I would prefer none, lest a little leaven blacken the whole heap of faithful works.

3. And, my brothers—to glory a little in our common life, since I cannot do so in private—if you consider the order of your whole life and the course of regular observance, the heap of good testimony which you build up will not be small. For if, beginning with the night Vigils, which with tireless affection you taste as certain firstfruits and pour out your heart like water before God’s presence at the beginning of the watches—if, I say, beginning from the head, you are willing to proceed in sequence through each degree of divine conduct, what will be found there that does not speak of discipline, that does not harmonize with our faith, [Col. 0120C] that does not either wear down the body, raise up the mind, or direct it when raised?

During psalmody, how great is the discipline of the body, and how much greater that of certain persons in the mind, while they do not allow it to depart even briefly—or at least only very briefly—from the sense of the words. For there, that is, in the very words which are sung, they either keep their mind bound or let it range toward related matters, but never toward foreign ones. And if this happens—for the human mind is fleeting—how sternly they immediately punish it, and demand from themselves payment for the loss of time! Nor are the very intervals of the common night-hours idle.

Good God, how that hour of night is without night, how that night is illumination amid delights! Those prayers are offered privately, but do not seek private things. The voice is lower, indeed, but the mind more intent, and silent prayers have much sharpness. Indeed, vehement prayer often tears out the voice; it neither needs nor uses words, being borne forward by pure and full affection. Love alone, sounding in the Lord’s ears, scorns the noise of bodily words, which, as they are incentives to one beginning to pray, so they are usually impediments to one praying perfectly.

What follows? At the very morning hours they renew their prayers as if freshly begun, multiply confessions, and by a modest but open disclosure cleanse even slight transgressions. Yet they do not count it slight if their recollection of Christ falters even faintly. If the enemy’s cunning has suggested anything through wickedness, they blame themselves, unfair judges in this respect, considering their own fall what was only an ineffectual provocation by another’s fraud.

What of their daily labor with their hands, by which the body is sufficiently worn down and meagerly fed? They do not eat the labor of their hands alone; from their insufficiency they share with the needy, so that they themselves may have hardship, provided others have abundance. At certain intervals they lighten their labors, but though the body is weary, affection burns fervently. There silent tears flow abundantly, groans emerge, sighs break forth, so that those sitting nearby, if perhaps cold in themselves, may be kindled by their neighbors’ sparks.

Finally, what of the fact that they think not of tomorrow, nor even of today? Casting all care upon him who presides over them, they seek not a reward but the kingdom of God alone. What of this, which I had almost passed over: every day in chapter they stand to be examined by the abbot’s judgment, as though presented before Christ’s tribunal. There each person is first his own accuser, hastening to forestall others in accusing him. What of their unbroken silence itself and a certain gravity of demeanor? Does it not beautify their whole conduct and clothe it with a fair countenance of holiness?

Sleep itself also bears testimony to holiness, nor is it without confession in so great a heap of testimonies. For the remnants of thoughts confess Christ when sleep overwhelms the body. How indeed could the images of one’s whole daily conduct, impressed before the eyes, fail to move about in the mind and remain awake while one sleeps?

4. Does not this great heap of testimony seem to you to be raised up, except that these things are not done in a heap and without order, but in a definite sequence, each distinguished by its proper times? [Col. 0121C] Have not these testimonies been rendered exceedingly credible because such holiness befits your house, O Lord? Would that the roots of my heart might thicken upon this heap. So great a mass of good conduct cannot be barren. It is a high and fertile place, such as the prophet mentions: “A vineyard was made for the beloved upon a horn, in a fertile place” (Isa. V, 1). And truly the more abundant yield of fruits is a great proof of fertile soil; just as, conversely, the fertility of the place rebukes a tree for its fruitlessness. Is not that tree evil which, occupying good ground, bears no worthy fruit, nay, does not even put forth any flowers of good promise? Perhaps the fruitful vines nearby condemned that barren fig-tree which the Lord commanded to be cut down (Luke XIII, 7).

It is exceedingly unjust [Col. 0121D] to be planted in holy conduct and to undertake nothing holy; to plead excuses and be convicted by the examples of one’s brethren; and from that very place whence others arrange ascents in their hearts, to arrange descents. Let your descent suffice you, whoever you are. Why do you seek to pull down the heap of good works which others climb with gladness, and to alter the regular observances, complaining both of their number and their strictness? Do not hinder those who do well; if you can, climb yourself. Hear from what a great and what a kind of heap the saints ascended. “The saints experienced mockings and scourging, moreover also bonds and prisons; they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted; they died by the slaughter of the sword. They wandered in sheepskins, in goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted, wandering in deserts and mountains and caves, and [Col. 0122A] caverns of the earth; and all these were approved by the testimony of faith” (Heb. XI, 37–39).

You see by how great a testing their faith was approved, by what testimonies it was examined. What such thing is either demanded or expected of you? Yet even these testimonies of yours, of a lower kind, are sufficiently credible—indeed, more credible in this respect, that necessity did not impose them, but the will submitted itself to them. Therefore let will be will, relying upon the right of its original freedom; let it show itself free to persevere, not regard itself as free to withdraw. Let it acknowledge the debt due to necessity, but not feel its yoke. Let it be free in the good, and likewise free toward the good: in that which it already possesses and toward that to which it ought to tend; but let it judge that no permission to return to what lies behind has been granted it.

5. Hear at last from what a great heap of testimony Paul ascended. [Col. 0122B] “The Spirit himself,” he says, “bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God” (Rom. VIII, 16). What a great heap in this one testimony! But did he not also bear testimony outwardly? “God,” he says, “attesting by signs and wonders and various powers and distributions of the Holy Spirit” (Heb. II, 4). And yet, established amid so great a heap of powers and attesting graces, he says: “I do not yet reckon that I have apprehended. Forgetting indeed the things behind, I stretch forth to those before me” (Phil. III, 13).

“Therefore we also, having such a cloud of witnesses placed upon us, laying aside every weight and the sin surrounding us, let us run with patience the contest set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and [Col. 0122C] finisher of faith, who, for the joy set before him, endured the cross, despising shame, and sits at the right hand of God. For consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, lest you grow weary and fail in your souls. For you have not yet resisted unto blood” (Heb. XII, 1–4).

For the testimonies of those who shed their blood for Christ’s faith are called testimonies by a certain prerogative—that is, martyrdoms. See how Stephen himself, the first martyr, ascended to Christ from so great a heap of stones; and all righteous souls follow him. “Like a flock of goats,” he says, “which have ascended from Mount Gilead.” They carried the treasure of faith in earthen vessels, but the sublimity of their power was God’s. Thus they are called as though ascending because enormous torments did not so much break them as strengthen them to render testimony with great power.

What spirit is there here in those who cannot endure even a single reproof from their superiors, though mild and friendly; but at one rather stern word the whole rigor of their good resolution, which they had established for themselves, melts away? The testimonies of these persons, supported by so many aids, can scarcely stand; [Col. 0122D] those of the martyrs, restrained by so many torments, burst forth more abundantly. Is not the number of punishments as great as the heap of testimonies? Though “put to death all the day long, and reckoned as sheep for slaughter,” yet in all things they overcame, and as it were ascended beyond Gilead, from the heap of martyrdom.

For the saints entered the contest not for preserving bodily life, but for the life of faith, from which the righteous person lives. Therefore they overcome in all things in which their cause remains safe. For how do they not overcome, when either, by persisting in confession, they are restored to eternity, or, by persuading, they form their persecutors in the truth? Finally, though reckoned as sheep for slaughter, yet with certain harmless teeth they cut off their enemies from the root of unbelief, so that they might lay them up among the living inward parts of the Church.

6. Or is this not the meaning of what follows? “Your teeth,” he says, “are like a flock of shorn sheep.” Do you observe what sort of sheep these are, which indeed can be shorn, but whose teeth cannot be broken? They can be slain, yet cannot be bent. Rather, they themselves broke their persecutors and, having softened them with the words of invincible teaching—as though chewing them with teeth—transferred them into the unity of the faithful. [Col. 0123B] Peter was told: “Kill and eat” (Acts X, 13). And Moses’ teeth “were not moved” (Deut. XXXIV, 7). For “their teeth are weapons and arrows”: spiritual weapons, mighty through God for overthrowing strongholds.

Are there not certain teeth of the Church, of whom the Apostle says: “If an unbeliever or uninstructed person enters, he is judged by all, convicted by all; the secrets of his heart become manifest, and so, falling upon his face, he declares that God is truly among you” (I Cor. XIV, 24–25)? Brothers, do not fear the bite of these teeth: they are not canine, but ovine. For they are compared with a flock of shorn sheep. In dogs, not tearing apart but barking is commended. Isaiah says: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark; most shameless dogs, knowing no satiety” (Isa. LVI, 10–11). It is as though he reproaches certain persons because in one respect they strip themselves of the office of dogs, while in another they show themselves dogs: unable to bark, and never ceasing to tear apart. Such are those who bite and devour one another, and are consumed by one another.

Would that it might suffice them thus far to bite and devour one another, and that they would not attempt to tear apart the very teeth of the shorn sheep. Do not the teachers and superiors of the Church seem to you to be certain teeth, who by the bites, as it were, of kindly reproof convict, judge, expose, and soften those subject to them into a better condition? But if you are excessively hard and cannot be softened, why do you prepare to bite back? Do you not bite back when either you slander in secret or openly contradict? Why prepare tooth against tooth—an evil tooth against a pious tooth? You can bite, but you cannot consume. [Col. 0123D] For they are teeth: hard and firm. They do not fear slanderers, remembering that with the prophet they dwell among scorpions and unbelievers (Ezek. II, 6), and that, like sheep, they are sent among wolves (Matt. X, 16), in order by rational endurance and exhortation to change the wolves themselves into sheep. And they are aptly called shorn, because one need not fear the bites of those to whom subjects offer examples of good works, like certain fleeces.

7. Yet the use of teeth is not reckoned to consist only in reproving and convicting others’ errors. There is another and higher use of them, for those who are fit to chew the solid bread of heavenly food, and to judge and distinguish the hidden meanings of loftier teaching; who no longer need milk, but solid food; and who can in some fashion break down and soften it, and by a certain moderation either of dispensation or disputation render it soberly suitable for those who were insufficient by themselves for solid food and capable only of milk.

For those who have their senses trained for the discernment of good and evil employ the service of a stronger instrument for chewing—indeed, for discerning even good from good: judging not merely between night and day, but judging every day. And rightly he says that they ascend from the washing, in order to show them diligent in cleansing the heart, because knowledge of divine things is promised to the pure in heart.

You see how clean and blameless those must be who ought to bite back at [Col. 0124B] and correct the transgressions of others; how clean and pure in heart those must be who ought to dispense the nourishment of the divine word, examine the hidden senses of the more secret word, search out the inner things of wisdom, and chew over its inward parts.

8. “Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep.” Why then “like a flock”? Certainly because the teeth of the Church do not fight or oppose one another, but agree and harmonize in the simplicity and unity of their understanding: “like a flock of shorn sheep which have ascended from the washing.” For, putting off the old man and lightened and washed of their superfluous burden, they climb more eagerly to what is above. Indeed, the old hairs themselves begin to be a burden when new fleece first sprouts, [Col. 0124C] when winter has passed, when the rain has gone and departed.

Therefore, if you still judge it necessary to be wrapped in the old and superfluous fleece of trivial and vain things, the wintry cold of a frozen mind has not yet passed from you. Thus they are rightly shorn and ascend from the washing, as having nothing old either of burden or of filth. Do you observe that it does not suffice for you to be shorn, does not suffice to be unburdened, does not suffice to be washed and made new, unless at once you ascend and walk in the Spirit, you who are renewed in spirit? “If,” he says, “we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit” (Gal. V, 25).

Therefore, if you intend to ascend, always ascend from the washing, always new and clean. Wash your bed every night with tears. Or, if sin does not envelop you like night but passes over like a cloud, nevertheless wash every night: erase with tears even the traces of light faults. For here, in the valley of tears, is the place of washing. Why do you reserve accumulated filth and the dregs of sin for the washing of the age to come? What do you know whether there will be there a refining furnace rather than a washing? For things which here could easily have been washed away are there cleansed not so much in mercy as in a spirit of judgment and burning. And blessed is the one who ascends from the world not as from mud but as from a washing, having no need to wash anything in himself, but being wholly clean.

Such a person will plainly be judged worthy, with whitened teeth—that is, with the senses of the soul—to eat the bread of angels: no longer the bread of sorrow, but the bread that gladdens the human heart; namely, that bread which the prophet signified in saying, “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI, 15). For that glory, while it does not appear, feeds; when it is revealed, it refreshes. What indeed is the full revelation of that glory but true wisdom? Inviting us to eat it, it is eaten by us only when we meditate upon it as the life-giving delights of a pure mind and unfailing refreshment.

Therefore let us here possess purified and exercised senses of the soul, no longer for discerning good and evil, but only for perceiving so great a good. Let us do frequently here what we shall do there continually; let us often anticipate that with which we shall be occupied without ceasing. Let that be our supreme business here which alone will exist there. For the contemplation of wisdom is eternal refreshment. [Col. 0125B] Nothing is chewed more sweetly by the spiritual teeth of the soul than that Living Bread who says to the Father: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII, 3), who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXIV. All bear twin offspring, and none among them is barren. Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon (Cant. IV, 2–3).

1. In the preceding sermon you heard the bride’s teeth commended—and rightly, because the teeth contribute no small element of beauty if they are white and evenly set. Nor is beauty alone pleasing in teeth, but usefulness also. For how could John in the Apocalypse eat the scroll, offered him by the angel and rolled up, without teeth fit for such food? (Apoc. X, 9–10). The whole book seemed hard food; therefore teeth were needed to break it all into pieces and soften its hardness, so that it could be swallowed more easily.

And certainly a good tooth is trained understanding, spiritual understanding, which judges all things, investigates all things, chews over and searches all things, even the deep things of God; which eats even the marrow of the rolled-up book, and consumes the innermost parts of wisdom. “The fool,” as it is written, “folds his hands and eats his own inward parts” (Eccl. IV, 5). This food is bloody food, fleshly food, food which perishes—indeed, which kills. How much sweeter and more useful it is to eat the inward parts of wisdom and the hidden things of the sacred word! They cannot be reached by bloody teeth, but by washed and white ones; for whiteness is that of eternal light itself, and the bridegroom’s own teeth are said to be whiter than milk. Therefore he commends in the bride such teeth as resemble his own: “Your teeth are like a flock [Col. 0125D] of shorn sheep which have ascended from the washing.” One must have not only washed but also free senses of mind, if one prepares them for searching the divine word.

2. “All bear twin offspring, and none among them is barren.” You are reckoned barren if you are content with only one offspring. If you have been able to attain some sacred understanding in the Scriptures, you have already borne one offspring. It is good and great progress, but insufficient for sacred understanding if affection does not answer to it. Understanding is barren when devotion, contemporary with it and of the same birth, does not accompany it. Everywhere in Scripture a kind of seed is scattered for you, from which you may conceive this twin offspring. There all things are not merely subtle, but sweet. The Lord’s command is luminous, and his utterance is fiery.

The word of God is barren in you whenever it does not work one or the other of these effects. If you see by understanding but still remain frozen in affection, is not the fiery power of the word of God reckoned barren and ineffective in you? For though it belongs to fire to give light, it belongs much more to it to kindle. The Lord says: “The word which shall go forth from my mouth shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish and prosper in those things for which I sent it” (Isa. LV, 11). For what things? You have it in the Gospel: [Col. 0126B] “I came to cast fire upon the earth; and what do I will but that it be kindled?” (Luke XII, 49).

The word of God is seed, and in it, as you read in Job, both light and heat are scattered over the earth (Job XXXVIII, 24). But I know not how light has sprouted more abundantly, and people have loved light more than fervor—unless it is because those who do not embrace the very thing that shines take greater pleasure in the light itself. Does not fire that fails to kindle seem to have lost, or unlearned, its nature? When you hear someone speaking as if boasting and saying, “That word of Sacred Scripture does not edify me,” what else does he seem to say but: “The fiery word has lost its efficacy in me; it does not kindle me, inflame me, or exercise in me its generative power”? He attributes his barrenness to the word which, so far as it is concerned, grows and bears fruit. What a glorious boast, brother, to say that the divine word does not edify you!

Perhaps the old things have not yet been thrown down and rooted out; therefore new things cannot be built upon them, cannot sprout or be born. Blessed is the person in whom the moisture of worldly love has dried up and its vigor fails: in that person the power of the fiery word works easily. The word of God both shines and burns. Let neither power be absent from you; conceive from this seed a double offspring. A womb which is not pregnant with these offspring is reckoned barren. “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. V, 6).

Love is certainly a good offspring, because charity is numbered among the fruits [Col. 0126D] of the Spirit. Finally, as twin offspring, there is a twofold charity: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” The one is first, the other second; both are greatest, because the latter is like the former. These are good and sufficient twin offspring, because “on them hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII, 37–40). Finally, “the end of the commandment is charity” (I Tim. I, 5), which elsewhere is also called “the bond of perfection” (Col. III, 14).

3. And fittingly there follows the scarlet bond from which the comparison used in praise of the bride’s lips is drawn: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon.” For those lips bind and glow red which speak from such fruit of the womb. Charity conceived in the heart, like a flame-bearing fire, stains red the lips through which it bursts forth. Heat sent from above into the heart gives the lips a kindred color. For what else does it mean that they are called scarlet, but that they are shown to be flaming, because scarlet dye glows with a fiery redness?

These lips no longer need to be purified by altar-coals or seared by an external fire. Already flaming from the inner flame, they sow among others the fire conceived within the inward parts. They disseminate saving knowledge—the fiery law which the Lord came to cast upon the earth. Blessed are the scarlet lips that send this fire not only to earth but also to heaven. Indeed, they kindle the Lord of heaven himself. Therefore he commends scarlet lips because they are scarlet to him, appear warm to him, and are felt by him to be flaming; and they kindle one another yet more in mutual charity.

A wondrous thing: he himself is fire, and yet he burns with our sparks. Why should he not? The Word of God is also a sword (Eph. VI, 17), and yet it is wounded: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes” [Col. 0127B] (Cant. IV, 9). Thus he is fire, yet is inflamed. He is wounded by an eye, inflamed by a lip, and even bound; therefore he is compared to a ribbon. But charity is a wound, charity is a ribbon, charity is scarlet. You see how sharp, how tenacious, how fiery charity is.

Use such lips in prayer. With the tenacious bond of memory, like a ribbon, bind your beloved tightly to your heart; fasten him there and kindle him by kindled affection. How sweet if he should say and allude to you: “Your utterance is exceedingly fiery, and your bridegroom loves it! Kiss me with the kiss of your mouth, because your lips are beautiful like a scarlet ribbon.” For commendation of the lips suggests the desire for kissing. He desires his lips to be impressed upon yours, so that there may be one mouth and one lip; and after the impression he may say to you: “This now is mouth from my mouth, and lip from my lip.” The grace poured out upon his lips flows back into yours, and from his scarlet yours have become scarlet. A good impression, which expresses so great a grace in the bride’s lips.

Remember, however, that I do not now mean bodily lips, but spiritual and inward lips—those of which the Apostle speaks: [Col. 0127D] “Singing and making melody in your hearts to the Lord” (Eph. V, 19). If you are a bride, your lips ought to be bound and kindled for this one purpose: to entreat your beloved, converse with him, sing to him, and say with the prophet: “My lips shall exult when I sing to you” (Ps. LXX, 23). In so holy a conversation let there be nothing loose in your lips, and then they are like a ribbon; nothing cold, and then you have scarlet lips.

Who will grant me, good Jesus, to have such lips in conversing with you—so ready, so open, so kindled; kindled and exulting, that they may sing only to you and sing of you? Would that my lips might be such, expressing through a subtle course and the kindled affection of unbroken meditation the likeness of a scarlet cord.
