[Col. 0128A] 4. Christ commends such a lip in the bride, not only in prayer but also in exhortation, that it may be able to exhort in sound doctrine. For lips which bind themselves in his address rightly pour forth and disseminate saving knowledge if they use speech that is sweet and fervent, so as to stir the hearts of their hearers: they are scarlet because they kindle. But if they exhort and teach at once, and teach things suitable to sound doctrine, things consonant with the rules of faith, then they are like a ribbon and disseminate not only saving but also indissoluble knowledge. For what is so coherent, so tenacious, so woven together by an indissoluble knot, as the reasoned account of faith? Paul instructed his disciple in this way, saying: “Attend to exhortation and doctrine” (I Tim. IV, 13).

But even in ordinary speech, where mysteries of faith are not treated, your lips are compared to scarlet ribbons if your speech is restrained by a fine measure, discerning and sparing, colored by the pleasing blush of modesty; if it gladly and frequently makes mention of Christ’s Cross. O blessed lips, truly worthy both of Christ’s kiss and of his converse—lips so sincere and so kindled: sincere in faith and kindled in love. This kindling comes from the inward and the highest places; it contains nothing from the lowest.

5. For there is a kindling that bursts forth from hell. James says: “The tongue, a small member, sets on fire the wheel of our birth, itself set on fire by [Col. 0128C] Gehenna” (James III, 5–6). How can a tongue so badly inflamed set anything on fire well? The moving corruption of a vitiated birth turns of itself too much toward evil and, by its own rolling motion, is carried headlong. What need is there to set on fire this wheel, which cannot stand firm but is carried by itself toward evil? Indeed, it is carefully added: “The heart of man is inclined to evil from his youth” (Gen. VIII, 21). Impelled from its first birth, it does not know how to bend its course; and do you, with an evil tongue, drive and inflame it further?

An evil tongue seeks occasions for anger and indignation. It either invents false injuries or exaggerates true ones which it ought to have overlooked. It interprets even kindnesses as offenses, and applies sparks of poisonous speech to stir its own heart. Why, wicked tongue, do you apply such a flame to your heart? Let its own flame suffice it; let the burning of fleshly desire and the heat of innate fickleness suffice it—by which your heart, like a revolving wheel, is driven. Your first birth implanted this flame in you, but the grace of rebirth restrains it. Do not apply fire to fire or add malice to desire.

The fire which you vomit forth you draw from Gehenna. From there it begins and there it carries you. “The tongue,” he says, “set on fire by Gehenna.” This evil tongue is scarlet, but it is not a ribbon. It does not bind, but scatters. It kindles badly because it cuts apart what is united, scattering words of discord; and such flame is from hell. But the flame that is from above is chaste, peaceable, consenting to good things and making people good. For a sweet word multiplies friends and softens enemies.

As flame consumes flame, the higher consumes the lower, the heavenly the infernal: when wise and gentle speech conquers malice, and sweetness softens hardness. Therefore he says: “Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet.” For only sweet words befit the Bride: words of love, words serving in place of delicate cords, words which entangle and draw the Bridegroom in the bonds of charity. Blessed is the soul that knows how to weave such nets of sweet words, by which it may ensnare Jesus, bind the Father’s Word with the affections of the soul, enclose Christ as it were by speech, hold him by loving discourse, and delight him—so that its speech may be sweet to him who has the words of eternal life and is the eternal Word, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXV. Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate, etc. (Cant. IV, 3).

[Col. 0129B]

1. How sweet, do you suppose, are the bride’s cheeks, which can be eaten and possess the attractiveness of health-giving fruit? And indeed you may see even someone’s bodily cheeks so filled with pleasing beauty that the outward face itself can refresh the minds of beholders and feed them from the inward grace which it suggests. Beauty of countenance interprets the mind, and among us the face speaks affections.

You see how fittingly, after the white teeth and scarlet lips, mention is made of the cheeks. The cheeks are sufficiently akin to the lips and, even while the lips are silent, reveal the hidden things of the mind by a kind of visible word. The cheeks themselves have the use of speech: they either supply the function of the mouth or adorn it further. However sweet and fervent speech may be, a bold countenance makes all its grace harsh and diminishes the gravity of utterance by its frivolity. Therefore the cheeks follow, because their modest gravity adds grace to the scarlet lip. Indeed, he seems silently to suggest a certain maturity in them by comparing them to fruit; for fruits always possess a pleasing maturity.

And earlier he described her cheeks as those of a turtledove, because nothing wanton, light, or impudent appears in her face, but the heat of her desires lowers her cheeks with sweet seriousness. Anxious affections do not allow the face to be wanton, and loving meditations banish every frivolity from the cheeks. For the turtledove is an anxious bird, a mourning bird. Paul wishes the virgin to be such a person, “anxious how she may please God” (I Cor. VII, 32), accustomed to say: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” [Col. 0129D] (Ps. XLI, 3). Does this not seem to you the voice of one mourning? Your groaning is sweet, because love has begotten it. How could cheeks not be grave and mature when a mourning affection forms them?

These groanings possess not merely groaning, but also the grace of refreshment. “You will feed us,” he says, “with the bread of tears” (Ps. LXXIX, 6). And in the present passage he compares the bride’s cheeks to a pomegranate because anxious and loving affection, by a kindred maturity, both clothes the face and feeds those who behold it. For the grace of the mind shining in the face refreshes those who see it, as though it sweetly affects them and pours its own passion into others. I cannot help being sweetly moved when I picture such a face before myself; loving cheeks, when recalled, produce in me a similar affection. How much more when they are seen? For sight is more vivid than thought.

The cheeks are altogether beautiful, in which such loveliness shines forth, and which pleasing humility commends: having nothing lofty or harsh in themselves, but softened by a certain exercise of discipline into the composed form of modest humility.

2. “Your cheeks,” he says, “are like a fragment of pomegranate.” Does not he seem to you to have had cheeks as though broken, who “gave them to those striking him, gave them to those plucking them, and did not turn away from those spitting upon him” (Isa. L, 6)? This is a good breaking, by which inner strength began to stand forth and the grace enclosed beneath the rind of flesh to break out. So great a dignity seems as though broken when it gives itself up, emptied, to the outrages of suffering; but through these [Col. 0130B] fragments the abundance of salvation poured itself out for us.

And if you “fill up what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings in your flesh” (Col. I, 24), if you bear “the marks of Christ Jesus” in your body (Gal. VI, 17), Christ now says to you: “Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate.” If your cheeks have been broken and, as it were, crucified; if they have been subdued and cultivated by a certain discipline, do they not seem to you like fragments of some good fruit? And later it is said of the bridegroom that his cheeks are “like beds of spices” (Cant. V, 13), because they are ploughed, cultivated, and arranged for fragrant consolations. Thus here too he says that the bride’s cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate. And it is a good breaking through which not death enters, but the appearance of spiritual fruit shines forth.

Therefore good are those cheeks which are so broken by humility that they do not lose, but rather disclose, the grace of inward fruit. Indeed, pomegranates themselves signify the pleasing modest shamefacedness of the countenance by the red color of their rind. Modesty is certainly the finest adornment in Christ’s bride. Modesty, like a kind of dawn, colors the beginnings of every action and beautifies all the other virtues with virginal shame. Modesty does not boldly boast of its goods, but speaks sparingly, content to give only a slight indication, and then only when necessity presses.

Good Jesus, how great is the modesty everywhere in your utterances! How sparing you are in your own praises, which you could state sufficiently, as without loss to humility so without injury to truth! Even when he expressed what was his own, he suppressed the name. He could have spoken more fully, but he himself assumed, as an example for the bride, the color of modest shame.

I do not now commend only that modesty which commonly suffuses the face with a bodily blush, but that which beautifies the face of one’s whole conduct. For just as the body has cheeks, so conduct too has certain cheeks, in which no color is more pleasing if the whole bearing of one’s works smells of humility, if one conceals more in the heart than one displays in the face. Therefore he says here also: “Your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate, apart from your hidden things.” Good cheeks are those which, as they have nothing feigned, so have much hidden; which, as they pretend nothing, [Col. 0131A] so do not pour out everything; which display less in appearance than they possess in power.

3. These things may be referred to the inward cheeks of the soul, which are in the face of conscience, where not a human being but God sees. Each person’s conscience has, as it were, its own particular face. Its cheeks glow with the modest color of humility if it does not boast of its works to itself, magnify its merits, or judge them outstanding, but is ashamed that they are so small. For “who shall boast that he has a pure heart?” (Prov. XX, 9). If one has received it, how shall one boast as though one had not received it? Yet who understands even the gifts that one has received? For if one does not understand one’s faults, how much less one’s gifts?

Gifts are from above; they descend from the Father of lights. But no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. Therefore, if God reveals something to someone through his Spirit, it is not so much that person who knows as the Spirit of God within that person. Paul says: “We have received the Spirit who is from God, that we may know the things given to us by God” (I Cor. II, 12). All of them? Or even if one could know all, could one know them wholly? Not even one, I think, in its entirety; and in chastisement one could not understand the gift.

It is useful that conscience itself is hidden from itself in part, and that the excessive love of progress is ignorant of the increase of its own advancement. Finally, not the whole fullness of virtues, as though of fruits, but only fragments are said to stand forth in the bride’s cheeks, because what is in the cheeks is manifest. And even if someone knows within himself the true grace of some virtue, does he know its intensity, its constancy, its perseverance? “My bone,” he says, “which you made in secret, was not hidden from you” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 15). And though it is hidden from me, it is not hidden from you. For your Spirit searches all things, even my hidden things.

Would that I had many such hidden things in myself, known to you, good Jesus, and laid up in your treasures. To lay them up in my own knowledge is dangerous; therefore I entrust them more safely to yours. But it is not so much I who entrust them to you as you who do not entrust them to me. More safely still you cherish with yourself what you made in secret. Nor is the bride’s perfection permitted to be so great that it lies open to herself and comes forth into her cheeks.

4. “Thus,” he says, “are your cheeks, apart from your hidden things.” There are certain hidden things which, at the fitting time, are to be brought forth into the light and set in the face. Meanwhile they lie hidden in seed, to receive in their own time their full form. Thus now you are the bride, but it has not yet appeared what you will be. Who, do you suppose, will be like me when I shall have appeared? Even now you possess likeness in part, because you know in part. With unveiled face you now behold my glory as in a mirror, yet you are still being transformed from glory to glory (2 Cor. 3:18). While you are being transformed, you do not yet possess it wholly. To be transformed is to make progress, not to be perfect. But your perfection is not yet yours; nevertheless my eyes already see it: with me you already are what you are to become. You are already inscribed in the book of life, and I have painted you upon my hands. Your face is always before me; before me it shines, though now it is darkened within you. I have already found in you the coin bearing my image, but it is still tarnished by a certain rust, and its appearance is hidden. [Col. 0132A] Faith already glows red in your cheeks and pours into them the color of life; yet the reality of faith is still hidden. Therefore, “your cheeks are like a fragment of pomegranate, apart from your hidden things.” The countenance of faith is altogether pleasing; but because of your hidden things you appear still more worthy of approval to me. The virtue of patience, evident and, as it were, already in your cheeks, pleases me greatly; but I value you more by your later glory. And indeed, brethren, not only the sufferings but even patience itself of this present time is not worthy to be compared with the glory to be revealed in us (Rom. 8:18). Of that glory certain seeds have already been cast within us; by a hidden operation they bring themselves to maturity and to the reality of perfect fruit. This reality is now hidden in us through a kind of seminal grace. “My substance,” he says, “is in the lower parts of the earth” [Col. 0132B] (Ps. 138:15).

Do you see where he says it is hidden? In the lower parts of the earth. Happily, with him it is not in the lowest parts. I understand certain things to be upper, certain lower, and certain lowest regions of the earth. The upper region is the very nature of the human body; the lower is the corruption of that nature; the lowest is a certain wickedness and guilt proceeding from corruption and corrupting it still further. Therefore he does not say that his substance is in the lowest parts, because spiritual grace—which is the Prophet’s highest substance—has no commerce with wickedness; but it is in the lower parts of the earth. “My substance”: because the grace of the Spirit is hidden medicinally in the weakness of the flesh, like leaven concealed, healing and working until mortality is swallowed up by [Col. 0132C] life. For the lump ought not to corrupt the leaven, but rather be changed by the leaven into a like savor.

5. But elsewhere the same man says: “My substance is with you” (Ps. 38:8). Thus his substance is both in the lower parts of the earth and with the Lord. It is hidden in distant places: in the heights of heaven and the lower parts of the earth; in eternity and in weakness—there through providence, here through grace at work. And grace is good which so works the progress of virtues that it in turn breathes into us some taste of perfection, and brings forth things hidden from the foundation of the world, hidden from the world, and hidden in God, where our life is hidden with Christ. And truly great is the multitude of your sweetness, [Col. 0132D] Lord, which you have hidden—but for those who fear you, not for those who love you. Perhaps this stolen sweetness is therefore not even the bride’s own. These are the bride’s very hidden things, concerning which he says: “Thus are your cheeks, apart from your hidden things.”

Thus this utterance was made not only for her sake, but for those standing round her; indeed, more particularly for those standing far off and for those opposing her: for those who timidly draw back from holy conduct, and for those who maliciously disparage it. Some of these think the hidden life, the life of the saints, empty and without honor. Others, although they do not think it empty, regard its whole course with the utmost dread; yet they dare not suspect that its end is without honor. Some think religion vain, others bitter. The former do not reverence it; the latter fear to approach it. Therefore he took care gently to hint at the bride’s hidden things, as though touching the former obliquely and drawing the latter, while thus secretly reminding them of her inward delights: “Thus,” he says, “are your cheeks, apart from your hidden things.” As though he said: If others too knew by what hidden things your belly, O bride, has been filled, how readily they would count all things loss in order to gain them! How gladly they would lose good things and endure evil things in order to become sharers in hidden sweetness! But now that which visits holy souls in secret by turns is hidden from their eyes. Yet it is a pleasing alternation, which softens the troubles of many seasons; and these are no scanty delights, which abound for the time to come. Why do you fear want in her? Her delights are hidden, and they are abundant delights. For “there is abundance in your towers,” O bride. [Col. 0133B] Finally, “your neck is like the tower of David”: though the delights are hidden, strength stands forth. How could it fail to stand forth when compared with a tower? But let us defer this matter until tomorrow’s discourse, when we shall speak concerning this tower, whose author and guardian is David himself—Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVI

“Your neck is like the tower of David, built with battlements. A thousand shields hang from it,” etc. (Song 4:4).

1. He now speaks strong things to the bride and concerning the bride; for above he spoke tender things, where he said: “Your neck is like necklaces” (Song 1:9). You have something similar in the Psalm: “The Lord has clothed himself with splendor; he has clothed himself with strength” (Ps. 92:1). These are good garments, [Col. 0133C] one of which adorns and the other arms. He placed first that which seems more proper to the bride. Now he turns to a certain strength of hers. The virtue of strength is so much the more precious in the bride because it is rarer. It is indeed rare: “Who shall find a strong woman?” (Prov. 31:10). And even if one can, yet you, good Jesus, do not so much find one who is such as prevent her beforehand from becoming such. This tower does not build itself; rather, it is built by him without whom builders labor in vain.

See how strong he wishes her to be understood, whom he compares to the tower of David: “Your neck,” he says, “is like the tower of David.” Do not take this neck to mean inflexibility and hardness. Such qualities cannot be turned to praise, but call forth a sentence of curse. “Cursed,” he says, “be their fury, [Col. 0133D] because it is stubborn; and their obstinacy, because it is hard” (Gen. 49:7). “Your neck,” he says, “is an iron sinew” (Isa. 48:4). These words are twisted toward condemnation, not offered in commendation. Rigid obstinacy commonly counterfeits freedom; but I understand freedom in these words: “Your neck is like the tower of David.” It is truly a free neck, ignorant of servile condition, so erect and so fortified as the tower of David. I do not think this neck is chafed by any yoke of abject slavery. “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth” (Ecclus. 40:1); but this woman no longer appears to be among the daughters of Adam. By the newness of regeneration she has changed the old birth, knowing not the carnal Adam, from whom she has passed over to Christ; to whom, having adhered as to the second Adam, she has become one spirit with him. Therefore she is free, because “where the Spirit [Col. 0134A] of the Lord is, there is freedom”; the freedom by which Christ has set us free—a freedom given, not innate. For from the day of their birth a heavy yoke lies upon the children of Adam. Truly heavy: it had bent over that woman of the Gospel for eighteen years, so as not to allow her to look upward (Luke 13:11). How unlike her is this bride, who has raised her neck heavenward in the fashion of a tower.

2. Truly heavy is the yoke which the entire human race could not shake off in that bent woman. It could not lay it down and did not cease to add to it: iniquity upon iniquity, weakness upon weakness, and each upon the other—very fruitful indeed, but in a most unhappy fruitfulness. Do you wish to hear someone adding yoke upon yoke? Hear with what excuse one of those invited withdrew himself from the Gospel banquet: “I have bought five yokes of oxen” (Luke 14:19). O foolish soul, with so feeble a neck and so chafed a collar! You bear the one yoke which corrupted birth imposed upon you, and you purchase more? You have no need to buy what is born within you without charge. You add other things by purchase, and yet you cannot free your neck from that by which you are oppressed. “I have bought five yokes of oxen,” you say; and you cannot shake off without charge this one yoke, so heavy and so universal. Yet you do not possess the price by which to redeem yourself. Do you not know under what heavy yoke you are held? It cannot be taken away except by the blood of Christ. You abound sufficiently to buy more; you do not abound sufficiently to redeem yourself from this. O your wretched riches! You are rich enough not to soften, but to multiply the bonds of your neck and make your fetters heavier. Let that heavy yoke by which you are oppressed suffice you. This yoke, if you do not know it, [Col. 0134C] is a certain necessity of sinning and an inability to rise again. This yoke is difficulty in doing good and eagerness for evil. This yoke is both the iniquity by which you are held guilty for punishment and the weakness by which you are drawn prone toward vice. These are original to you, arising from the defect of propagation; and you still heap up voluntary burdens! While through the curiosity of the five senses you attend to external forms, you stir up the inward flame of desire, which cannot be extinguished except by the blood of Christ. Desire, when alone, burns fiercely enough; but when outward matter is added, it rages madly. A twofold evil: corruption of nature and a curiosity that explores external provocations. A doubled evil: one’s own impulse and the enemy’s prompting. A doubled evil: the flame of desire and the breath of the instigator.

3. “I have bought five yokes [Col. 0134D] of oxen,” he says. Appropriately, indeed, of oxen, since the labor of curiosity wears down brutish minds. If you desire a yoke, you have no need to purchase one. Take upon yourself the yoke of Christ: a freely given yoke, a pleasant yoke, not a heavy one. For he says: “My yoke is sweet, and my burden is light” (Matt. 11:30). This is not a yoke of oxen, because it is a rational yoke; a yoke that does not impose toil but provides rest. And see how he calls this yoke light. For that former yoke is heavy, which lies upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth until the day of their death. Of what death do you suppose this is said? Surely of that concerning which you have: “You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” [Col. 0135A] (Col. 3:3). This is a good death, which buries the old birth and introduces the new. A good death, which swallows up slavery and produces freedom. For the children of this birth are free. This is a good end: that, putting off the old Adam, we may at the same time cast away the heavy yoke. This end of carnal life breaks the yoke of our captivity; it can no longer weigh us down, but wastes away before the oil, from the time we began to be called by another name and the name of the second Adam was invoked over us—he whose name is “oil poured out” (Song 1:2). Do you wish to hear that this heavy yoke is both broken and wasted away? “Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your weaknesses” (Ps. 102:3). All iniquity is forgiven wholly and at once: the yoke is broken. Weakness is still being healed: the yoke wastes away. Finally, what wastes away declines slowly; it does not cease all at once. The purpose of the will can indeed be cut off and, as it were, broken; but an inveterate passion is not so much cut off as unlearned. When the impossibility of working salvation is removed by grace, then the yoke of captivity is, as it were, broken. But the difficulty in good that still remains, while it is gradually healed, seems to have its yoke wasting away. “It shall waste away,” he says [Col. 0135B] (Isa. 10:27): this indicates that, although it is not wholly removed at once, it will nevertheless at some time be consumed by decay. What wastes away is certainly corrupted. How then is one not free whose yoke is either broken at once or gradually corrupted? A yoke and a bond that have been corrupted both seem deprived of their function: they neither weigh heavily nor bind tightly. Truly happy is the person whose bonds have wasted away so as to be of no use, whose chains too have wasted away and been corrupted before the oil.

4. But you will say: You had begun a discourse about the bride’s neck; why do you now linger over the yoke? What has the yoke to do with the neck? Would that it had nothing to do with it. But now the crushing is great. For what is a yoke for except the neck? Yet not for the bride’s neck, because the bonds of her neck have already been loosed: she no longer knows how to be held under the yoke of slavery. “Your neck,” he says, “is like the tower of David.” By this is shown a most abundant freedom, free from every depression; yet not bare, but having strength mixed with it. In a tower one considers not merely its height, but the strength of its fortification against the enemy. Freedom has indeed been restored, but security is not yet permitted you. The snare of captivity has been broken. The enemy seeks to entangle you from another quarter: he has lost his right, but has not laid aside either the hope of recovering it or the stubbornness of assailing you. You have become free; henceforth the business of preserving your freedom rests upon you. Do not expose the neck given to the bridegroom’s embraces to even the slightest ignoble yoke. Thus, when the son returned, his father met him and fell upon his neck. A loving burden and a sweet yoke—yet he deserved to bear and not feel it only after first coming to himself and breaking the condition of slavery within himself, and thus returning to his father [Col. 0135D] (Luke 15:20). Your neck has been raised up: be strong like the tower of David, so that you may say, “I will keep watch for my strength toward you” (Ps. 58:10). For David himself, Solomon himself, is Christ—the power of God and the wisdom of God. You are his tower if you do not think meanly or weakly concerning him, but recognize the sublimity of God’s power, not from yourself. One who, puffed up in the mind of his flesh, exalts himself against the knowledge of God is like a tower—not David’s tower, but rather one against David. This neck is lofty; but Wisdom tramples the necks of the proud and lofty and raises the humble. Humility itself supplies the necessary expense for building the Gospel tower. Nor need one fear that the bride will lack the means, since she may borrow them abundantly from the bridegroom’s treasury. [Col. 0136A] “Learn from me,” he says, “for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). Do you not yet understand how humility supplies the cost for building the tower? “He who humbles himself,” he says, “shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). And humility was fittingly suggested in secret in the preceding chapter, where he mentioned the bride’s hidden things; for it is a beautiful form of humility to hide the praises of one’s merits. If humility was discussed there, he consequently adds sublimity here. A tower founded in humility cannot remain hidden long.

5. “Your neck is like the tower of David.” See the bride’s privilege. The apostle Peter exhorts us to be built together into spiritual houses (1 Pet. 2:5); but she is built not merely into a house, but also into a tower. Paul desires that we be built together into a dwelling place of God (Eph. 2:22); but the bride, not content with this, [Col. 0136C] adds battlements, so that her dwelling may be lofty and more secure. Perhaps she too is one of those towers of which it is said: “May peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers.” It is entirely fitting that a tower should not lack plenty. Need is hard when it is doubled: a siege outside and famine within. What advantage is there in all entrances being closed and fortified if within a savage enemy—famine—makes all things sorrowful? Famine is an evil; so is disgust. The doors are shut and the outer approaches fortified if death does not enter through the windows of your senses, and if the experience of undisciplined senses does not admit from outside the material incentives of evil. If you cast off greed arising from oppression, if you stop your ear lest you hear blood, if you close your eyes [Col. 0136D] lest you see evil, you are already enclosed; you already dwell on high, and the strongholds of rocks are your height. Is that enough? What profit is such fortified height if cruel lack, famine and disgust, lays waste what is within? What profit are hard rocks and inaccessible elevation if there is no bread there, if there are no sure waters? Protection is good, provided refreshment is not lacking. The fortifications of rocks are good, provided they are such that honey and oil may be extracted from their hardness. Indeed, the very severity of observances and the rock of discipline frequently pour forth abundant streams of oil; a certain stony rigor of the Order ministers the sweetness of devotion to the throat of the mind. Finally, you have: “May peace be in your strength, and abundance in your towers, O Jerusalem”—but abundance for those who love [Col. 0137A] you (Ps. 121:6–7). Otherwise, one who does not love, though within, is still hungry.

But how can there be want in this spiritual tower, in the tower of David, in the bride’s neck, in which by constant interchange the vital spirit is drawn in and breathed out; in which there is an unceasing supply of the sacred Word and the voiced spirit moves? How can there be famine in a neck through which abundance of sweetness is uttered and a good word from the heart’s freedom? The neck seems to be a certain exchange and a certain bond, both between heart and mouth and between body and head, each toward the other. In the neck there is both a bond and a way. What else can the bond be but charity, through which the body cleaves to the head, the Church to Christ? What other way of the spirit is there but charity? For this is the more excellent way; indeed, this is the spirit going and returning, running back to its own source—returning where it was born. From it hang the Law and the Prophets.

6. Therefore a thousand shields hang from it. For every word of the Lord is a fiery shield, and the battlements themselves are referred to discourse. In what follows he says: “If she is a wall, let us build upon her silver battlements” (Song 8:9). Battlements are customarily of the tower’s own material and, as it were, of one body with it. See how charity bears battlements consubstantial with itself and incorporated with it. See how an innate concern, a certain prudence, and ever-watchful caution for avoiding or repelling hostile assaults and devices belong naturally to charity. Battlements have something closed and [Col. 0137C] something open: through the latter charity spies out ambushes; through the former it wards off attacks—there provident, here protecting itself. Charity is built with such battlements because such strong and prudent concern is innate to it. It is itself a great support to itself. Finally, love is strong as a tower. It knows occasions of temptation, when it is necessary to flee, and, where no opportunity of flight is available, to endure bravely. Although it seems to possess so much strength in itself, it does not reject outside aids. Fortified with battlements, it also takes up shields. The order of one’s conduct and a law handed down by men are a good shield. Though such order is not necessary to charity, it is nevertheless not considered superfluous, nor indeed burdensome. Charity is spiritual: it does not need law, yet it does not scorn law, but uses it lawfully, protected by it rather than oppressed. Meditation on the sacred Word is also a good shield. For every word of the Lord is a fiery shield (Prov. 30:5).

7. Charity is not content with the spiritual meditations it itself produces. Though it is itself the Lord’s law, it nevertheless meditates upon the very words of the law; from them it takes testimonies for itself, from them it [variant: protects its convictions] defends itself, and with a manifold shield protects itself. Though it has the great inward testimony of the Spirit, it nevertheless plucks safeguards for itself from the sacred writings. Good is the protection which either the experience of charity suggests or skill in sacred discourse hands down. Paul in his Epistle depicts certain battlements of charity for you. “Charity,” he says, “is patient, is kind.” Run through [Col. 0138A] that entire passage on charity: do not as many battlements seem to rise for you as there are distinct graces enumerated? “It does not envy, does not act perversely, is not puffed up, is not ambitious, does not seek its own, does not rejoice in iniquity but rejoices together with truth,” and so on, down to “it never fails” (1 Cor. 13:4–8). Do you see with how many battlements it stands tower-like? Do these not seem incorporated with charity and, as it were, to rise from its foundation? Yet doctrine directs, discipline governs, and exercise raises these affections, which charity produces almost naturally. This order, prescribed by the experienced, either cherishes that good native principle, so far as charity is concerned, lest it fail, or advances it that it may grow. Therefore charity, not content with inward inspiration, hangs upon itself from every side the teachings of sacred discourse as shields.

Look upon the Bridegroom himself, who is a mediator and a kind of intermediary between human beings and God, like a neck between body and head, a tower of strength against the enemy. Look, I say, upon him who abounded in resources of his own: how he took up the shields of Scripture and, as it were, appealed to its authority, repelling the deceitful snares of the evil interpreter by the shield of truth.

8. You also, if you are a mediator and intermediary between human beings and God, and like a neck joining body and head, let a thousand shields hang upon you—shields of every kind drawn from the divine Word. Let sacred authority be ready to hand for you and lend support in every matter, [Col. 0138C] not merely so that it may suffice for you, but so that it may overflow for others. “Be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason concerning the faith and hope that are in you” (1 Pet. 3:15). A person seems to ask for an account of your faith when he tries to persuade you of things contrary to faith and to break faith itself. Thus a good shield hangs from your neck if you are armed with the shield of faith, the shield of truth, the shield of good will, the shield of sacred discourse. You read of all these shields in the Scriptures.

But if you are raised aloft through charity like a tower; if, by the grace of contemplation, like a neck surpassing the rest of the body, you approach the Lord who is the head, and are hidden in the hiding place of the Lord’s face, in the Bridegroom’s inner chamber, in the bridal chamber of truth—do you not seem to yourself to be protected by a delightful shield? I do not know [Col. 0138D] whether any shield is more effective in protecting than such an embrace of the beloved. It is fiery, and therefore extinguishes all the fiery darts of the wicked one; fire consumes fire. If the shield of faith extinguishes those darts, how much more is the person protected by the good shield of truth who is hidden in its warmth? For fervent meditation upon truth extinguishes the enemy’s maliciously kindled suggestions before they reach the mind. Amid the bridegroom’s embraces and the business of charity, the bride has no leisure to receive alien darts. Such a shield fittingly hangs from the bride’s neck, because love alone experiences the grace of such inflamed embraces, and love alone knows such ecstasies; making the mind adhere to God, it makes it one spirit with him for a time. Blessed indeed is the neck in which the fiery Word of the Lord dwells; from which the Word, truth, and power hang as a shield, freely bestowed by the Father’s embraces. [Col. 0139A] Does not the one who is crowned and surrounded on every side by such shields, before and behind, seem to you delightfully protected? It is a peg for the faithful, upon which so many different kinds of vessels hang. These things fittingly hang from the neck of charity, because charity is the anointing that teaches us concerning all things and suggests everything; because in it all graces are bestowed, referred back to it, and weighed and measured by its measure. “A thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty.” Truly armor, which Paul enumerates for the Ephesians (Eph. 6:13–18). “All the armor of the mighty,” that is, of those who love. For “love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). What then? Are there only the weapons of the mighty there, and not breasts for infants? If charity rises beyond itself like a tower, does it not condescend? “Whether we are carried beyond ourselves, it is for God; whether we are sober-minded, it is for you. The charity of Christ urges us” (2 Cor. 5:13–14).

9. You have heard of the bride carried beyond herself. Do you wish to understand her as sober-minded and condescending? “Your breasts,” he says, “are like two twin fawns of a roe.” The bride is a good tower: through the discipline of her conduct she closes herself on every side; through the teaching of the Scriptures she hangs abundant shields upon herself; through contemplative ecstasy she rises aloft. Her continence too is strong, her doctrine trustworthy, and her ecstasy heavenly. Yet even her loftiness has learned to condescend; her abundance of doctrine to be brought down to sobriety; her rigor to melt into the sweetness of a certain rational milk; [Col. 0139C] and the weapons of the mighty to be transformed into breasts for the weak. Everywhere the charity of Christ urges her, drawing her upward to him and drawing her downward on account of him; yet it does not hold her below for long, as she repeatedly returns in ecstasy to her own delights. Therefore he says, “Your breasts are like twin fawns of a roe,” because she ever looks toward the mountains of her pasture; because familiar refreshment turns and draws her to the place of pasture; because she suddenly springs back with a light leap to the Bridegroom, from whom, delightfully refreshed with the juices of heavenly herbs, she brings back her full breasts again to the little ones. But what must be said concerning these breasts perhaps cannot now be borne by weary ears and the fleeing hour, nor can the drink of milk be pressed from these breasts. If you pray for more abundant leisure and a freer hour, when the Lord grants it I shall not deny the office of my mouth—he himself providing abundance for his own praises, who grants affection: Christ Jesus, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXVII

“Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe, which feed among lilies, until the day breathes forth,” etc. (Song 4:5–6).

1. You see, brethren, how even the bride’s breasts are not deprived of praise. Indeed, the image of breasts is frequently employed, both elsewhere and especially in these Songs. He prefers breasts to wine (Song 1:1), compares them to a cluster (Song 7:7), likens them to a tower (Song 8:10); and now, in the present passage, he says: “Your two breasts are like [Col. 0140A] two twin fawns of a roe, which feed among lilies.” You see how manifold is the commendation of breasts. If she is a mother, it is unfitting that a mother’s breast should lack breasts. Paul knew that he had breasts when he said: “We became little ones in the midst of you, as though a nurse were cherishing her own children” (1 Thess. 2:7). Does he not seem to you to have become like a fawn, who became like a little child? Whence did he cherish his children like a nurse, if he did not have breasts? The two fawns of a roe are the two sons of the Church: one from the Circumcision, the other from the Gentiles. See how Paul adapts breasts to each alike. “I became,” he says, “as a Jew to the Jews; and to those who were without the law, as though I were without law. I became all things to all people, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9:20–22). Did he not adapt breasts to these fawns by becoming all things to all people? He became all things to all, not by the craft of pretense but by the affection of compassion and by a fitting adaptation of manner. Finally, he conformed himself to both: now restraining himself with them from lawful things, now condescending to lawful things; everywhere avoiding the scandal of either, where no injury to faith opposed it. He became all things to all: neither removing at the outset from Jews a rite that was lawful, nor compelling Gentiles to it in order to provoke the Jews. He became all things to all, both prescribing moral teaching and expounding mysteries according to his hearers’ capacity. In this twofold subject matter he offers, as it were, two breasts, tempering the milky breasts of plainer teaching for little ones. Inward compassion has breasts indeed, but outward adaptation displays the breasts. The former pities; the latter heals. What benefit is it to me if you merely [Col. 0140C] sympathize, yet do not conveniently know how to adapt yourself to my weakness and, as it were, my infancy? What benefit is it if, by compassionate feeling, you take my cause upon yourself, but do not bring the care you owe? Both are necessary: compassion and a certain ordering of discipline and teaching. Compassion conforms the affection; adaptation usefully bends you down to nurse little ones. Holy teachers do not fail their hearers in either respect: becoming like them both in the affection of piety and in the practice of adaptation.

2. Would that those who are about to address the assembly of the brethren would heed this. They study to say lofty rather than suitable things, making a display of themselves before weak understandings, rather than working their hearers’ salvation. They are ashamed to teach humble and plain things, lest they appear to know only these. They are ashamed to have breasts, to uncover the breast, to nurse little ones. What is this? Have you taken your seat in the midst, holding the chair, in order to parade knowledge, or to nurse the tender infancy of those subject to you? You weave subtleties: those who hear admire the art and praise the eloquence. This is well enough, provided they feel grace, provided that while you argue the hearers’ affection is moved and their understanding instructed. Otherwise, why bring forward at the present task certain alien matters which the listeners cannot grasp? A great praise of eloquence is to pursue fittingly the case one has undertaken, to refer everything to its advantage, and to serve the task undertaken. Nowhere will you give a clearer sign of your eloquence than if you treat a humble subject [Col. 0141A] elegantly; raise by the measured quality of your speech things which seemed low in themselves; and make seemingly contemptible thoughts more commendable. You should attend not so much to what befits you, a learned person, to say, as to what those whom you instruct ought to hear. What do they gain if you move among great and wonderful things—not, I say, above yourself, but above those who sit before you? “Do not think high things in a high manner, but condescend to the lowly.” By speaking sublime things, but not at the fitting time, what else do you seem to seek except that people may be silent for you alone and that it may be said of you what was said of the Savior: “Never has a man spoken thus” (John 7:46)? You have ascended the chair in order to build up others, not to puff yourself up; in order to fill, not empty yourself—unless perhaps in the way in which the Savior emptied himself, [Col. 0141B] taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), so that he might nourish us for salvation with the milk of his flesh. Paul, the good imitator of the Master, does not hide his breasts, but boasts that he has them. “I gave you milk to drink,” he says, “as to little ones in Christ, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:1–2); and again, “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Cor. 2:2). He knows himself for whom he prepares a table and to whom he offers breasts. Therefore his breasts are like fawns, because the words of his teaching [variant: breasts] are softened into such things as little ones in Christ can receive.

3. You have now heard who these fawns are and why they are two. Do you wish to know why they are twins? Because in faith “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Rom. 10:12). Privileges of merits have no place for you, and regeneration, which absolves all equally, distinguishes no one. “For all need the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” [Col. 0141C] (Rom. 3:23–24). Faith equally ennobles both peoples; but the Jew reckons otherwise: within common mercy he demands private rights for himself. What wonder if he wishes to be first, when he wished to be alone? He cannot be the only-begotten, so he aspires at least to be the firstborn. See what objections were made against Peter in the Acts of the Apostles: that he had entered among uncircumcised persons and admitted them to the mysteries of faith (Acts 11). See how hard Paul labors against the Jews in the Epistle to the Romans because they claimed for themselves certain privileges in the grace of faith and distinguished by ranks those whom one faith had joined. There they aspired to be alone in grace; here, to be supreme, unwilling to have equals where they could not avoid having fellow-sharers. But God made the Gentiles one body with Israel and fellow-partakers of the covenants, making no distinction at all, cleansing their hearts by faith. Therefore they are called twins, because faith separates by no ranks those whom it regenerates equally. Otherwise, those who do not know themselves to be twins have become nothing; and, taking the first place at the banquet, they no longer even possess the last. This principle concerns not only them but extends to all, so that no one, in whatever rank he may be, may begrudge another either participation in grace or equality in it. For who can put forward merits where grace alone is at work in the gift? Old things ought not to prejudice where all things have become new. The newness of regeneration is indicated in the fawns, [Col. 0142A] as equality in regeneration is indicated in the twins. They are aptly called roes—that is, children of the Church—because, like roes, they see keenly. For the Church’s eyes are keen, contemplating not things seen but things unseen.

4. Your breasts are like two twin fawns of a gazelle, feeding among lilies—provided, however, that they perceive the sweetness of the lilies; provided that the lilies themselves smell sweet to them as lilies, and do not give back an unpleasant odour. The lily’s fragrance is good and pleasing; yet the lily itself smells of lily to some, of wormwood to others. Christ, the lily of the valleys, is the unique lily; his imitators too were lilies. Hear what one of the lilies says: “We are the good fragrance of Christ: to some, an odour of death unto death; to others, of life unto life” (2 Cor. 2:15–16). You see how that unique lily [Col. 0142B], in which the fullness of every good thing gave forth its scent, nevertheless seemed to breathe a sorrowful odour to certain people. These are those who turn sweetness into bitterness and light into darkness.

But he truly feeds among lilies who enjoys the lilies’ fragrance. Lilies are examples of chastity, which give forth an excellent scent not only in the present age and close at hand, but also in the past and far away. Lilies also are sacred words, in which we smell the joys of eternal life and draw in the breath of their perfumes. By how many such lilies, brothers, are you surrounded! Although all are children of the Church, you have them more abundantly: at almost every moment the chaste utterances now of prophets, now of apostles, now of evangelists breathe upon each of your nostrils like lilies; and both their words and their lives are fragrant with a pleasing scent. What lilies [Col. 0142C] could smell more sweetly? What could equal their fragrance? What a scent Mary gives back to you; what John, what Peter, what the other Gospel men; and, finally, what Jesus himself—who alone gives fragrance uniquely in himself, and who alone is perceived in all the rest: whatever sweet fragrance is in them is his.

His words scatter a new fragrance through the world when they disclose the mysteries of the Trinity, the grace of redemption, the abundance of virtues, the glory of the Resurrection, and the condition of eternal life. “You have the words of eternal life,” Peter says, “and to whom shall we go?” (John 6:69). Let us say the same, drenched in his sweet fragrance. In you, good Jesus, the Godhead of the Father who is in you is fragrant. In you is the grace of the Spirit who anointed you; in you the virginity of your Mother [Col. 0142D]; in you the integrity of your own flesh; in you the healing of our sickness. All these things are fragrant to us in you; and to whom else shall we go, whether in love or in remembrance?

It is plainly an injury to such lilies if some foreign scent mingles with them, saddening their sweetness, corrupting the breath of the soul in its nostrils, turning it toward the world, and making it run after the stench of mire. It is an injury if vices smell sweeter to you than the lilies of virtues. He is truly fastidious who takes no delight in feeding on milk and among lilies. For not every milk is for little children. Does not every teaching, every devout affection gently entering the soul, seem to you like milk? Whatever is sucked in easily and sweetly seems like milk.

5. The Bride’s breasts abounded in such milk; and therefore they are called like fawns, because in them is a fresh and [Col. 0143A] ever, as it were, new and renewing harmony of word, together with a lively abundance of teaching. These breasts possess nothing of old age; therefore they are better than wine (Song 1:1), yet like new wine. “Your breasts,” he says, “are clusters” (Song 7:7): that is, they do not have the harshness of wine, but the fresh sweetness of must. Other breasts feed; these intoxicate. Thus the breasts are rightly like fawns, because they are unbroken by any old age.

It is a great adornment of the Bride’s breast if she has breasts whole—not slack, not broken—in this Egypt of the present age. Therefore she said: “My breasts are a tower” (Song 8:10). These breasts are impregnable and swollen with abundance of milk, having grown to the stature of a tower. Good, then, are breasts so full: breasts of piety, twin breasts, because piety has the promise of consolation for the life that now is and that which is to come. [Col. 0143B] “Rejoice with great joy,” he says, “that you may drink of her milk and be filled from the breasts of her consolation. And when you have been weaned from the milk, feast from the entrance of her glory” (Isa. 66:10–11).

Do you see to what the use of milk brings us? “That you may feast,” he says, “from the entrance of glory.” Do not the Bridegroom’s breasts seem to you to feast from the entrance of glory—those which, like fawns, feed among lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline? How sweetly breasts are suckled when they feed in this manner: breasts full of heaven, because refreshed among lilies with heavenly things! The very fragrance of the lilies feeds them. Their scent possesses the attractiveness of food. For fragrance is a kind of fruit: “Like a vine,” he says, “I have borne the fruit of sweetness of fragrance” (Sir. 24:23). See how Wisdom reckons its fragrance among its fruits.

This is spiritual food, having nothing bodily about it [Col. 0143C], neither touched by the tooth nor chewed with labour, but drunk in by the spirit, immediately flowing into the breasts themselves and filling them. Why are they called fragrant with the choicest ointments (Song 1:2), unless because in them the spirit drawn from nearby lilies gives forth its scent, until the day breathes and the shadows incline?

6. It is sweet indeed to await the rising dawn among lilies. Perhaps the day is near to these lilies, and among the lilies a certain breeze and breath of it is frequently drawn in. The Bridegroom himself feeds among the lilies—he who is himself both the lily of the valleys and the light of day. It is sweet, therefore, while feeding with him, to await him; to await him among lilies until the light of day breathes.

This indicates that time of which it is said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15). Then the true and [Col. 0143D] eternal day will breathe, when the shadows of the enigmas in which we still see are inclined. There are several shadows here: the shadow of deception, the shadow of refreshment, and the shadow of figure. In the first the serpent sleeps; in the second the Bride rests; in the third the Bridegroom lies hidden. Of the first it is said: “He sleeps in the shade” (Job 40:16); of the second: “I sat in his shadow whom I had desired” (Song 2:3); of the third, that wisdom is hidden in mystery (1 Cor. 2:7).

All these shadows will be laid down when the day breathes: the shadow of deceit, the shadow of faith, the shadow of mystery. Then there will be no shadow, because truth will be naked. Then, therefore, those things that are now raised up will be laid down. Do you wish to know how high they are? “His shadow covered the mountains” (Ps. 79:11). Paul is a great mountain; yet he says that he is covered by this shadow, seeing only “in a mirror and in an enigma” (1 Cor. 13:12). He is a great mountain, and yet was easily caught up into the third heaven. Blessed rapture—and far more blessed than that by which the Gospel mountain is cast into the sea at the apostles’ command. He was caught up because the wisdom of God changed his mind. Therefore he was caught up into the third heaven, into the heaven of pure understanding, whence shadows and enigmas have been banished far away.

The shadows are lower, and in a manner laid down by comparison with him who is caught up into heaven. He was caught up into heaven, and caught up into paradise. Heaven is a place of serenity; paradise, a place of delights. He is beautifully caught up into both, because contemplation is half-full when it lacks either. Finally, that person who [Col. 0144B] feeds among lilies until the day breathes seems to be placed in a certain paradise of delights and pleasures. Before the day breathes, it is night. Yet this night seems to possess something of day: “Night,” he says, “is my illumination in my delights” (Ps. 138:11). For delights partly take the place of illumination.

A most beautiful place of contemplation is where the simple consideration of faith sprinkles heavenly and sweetly fragrant affections and breathes the grace of eternal light. These are not the delights which blessed Job, speaking of wisdom, recalls when he says that it “is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job 28:13). In these delights there is a certain share of wisdom. How is there not a share of wisdom where truth itself, not yet understood but already believed, tastes sweet? Spiritual delights themselves sufficiently teach by their own experience both how greatly what remains beyond them is to be sought [Col. 0144C] and how greatly whatever obstructs them is to be rejected.

7. Three things here call for attention: time, activity, and place. The time, that is, night, is a time of repose and leisure. The activity is refreshment, because they feed. The place is delight, because it is among lilies. One who feeds thus—who feeds freely, abundantly, delightfully in meditations upon faith—rightly carries back distended breasts to little children. Do you suppose Solomon, in all his glory, was clothed as the Bride who feeds among lilies? How could she not be gloriously clothed, surrounded with lilies? For although the shadow obscures her appearance, she nevertheless perceives the scent; she perceives the fragrance of the garments; and in these she smells, as it were, the renown of wisdom, until the day breathes and the shadows incline—that is, until the day, the everlasting day, breathes.

So long as day and night alternate in their turns [Col. 0144D], the shadows do not appear wholly laid down while they retain their position. Where, then, are they laid down? Surely with the Father of lights, with whom there is no shadow of changeableness (Jas. 1:17). Every change has the likeness of a shadow; and while one thing succeeds another, it in some manner hides and casts a shadow over what preceded it. This, therefore, is what he says: “until the day breathes and the shadows incline”—that is, until the day and the full, everlasting noon breathe, which annihilates every shadow. “Who feed,” he says, “among lilies until the day breathes and the shadows incline”; that is, those who delight and feed upon the scent of wisdom, until the brightness of eternal light itself dawns.

Both things are commended in lilies: whiteness and fragrance. And what is the fragrance except the grace of faith? What is the whiteness except the glory of sight? In the night the fragrance is perceived, but the whiteness is not seen, until the day breathes; for that whiteness itself is day, having no share at all in shadows. When that day has breathed, breasts will no longer be necessary. For all will be taught by that day itself. Meanwhile the Bride’s breasts are like two fawns feeding among lilies, until the day that comes from Day, Christ Jesus, breathes.

91. SERMON XXVIII. “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense” (Song 4:6).

1. “Your breasts,” he says, “are like twin fawns of a gazelle.” You see how great is the Bride’s grace: she is little and, as it were, a young maiden, yet she has breasts. For what does he indicate except a young maiden when he compares her with fawns? Thus she is both a mother [Col. 0145B] and little: feeding others and needing to be fed. Even if someone is like Paul, while dwelling in the flesh he has not yet put away the things of childhood. And even if he abounds for others, he does not yet consider that he has attained. He sees in a mirror; he sees in an enigma. Therefore, like a little child, like a fawn, he feeds in the shadow until the day breathes.

He feeds in the shadow, but among lilies. Plainly wretched is the person who, though placed among lilies—among the lilies of the holy assembly, where varied virtues give fragrance on every side—nevertheless knows how to smell nothing sweet, nothing like lilies. On the contrary, good is the one who rejoices in the Bride’s privilege, in whom lilies of virtues themselves are born inwardly; who feeds among lilies, is refreshed among lilies, hungers for lilies. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst” for the lilies of righteousness, the lilies of chastity, the lilies of every grace. If it is blessed to hunger [Col. 0145C], much more so is it to feed among lilies. Even hunger for virtues feeds, and eagerness gives delight. The scent nourishes, but does not yet satisfy. “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15).

Indeed, even the glory of the virtues themselves, if one may so speak, still lies hidden. Everything you draw from them is in fragrance. Their form is concealed, but we hear their renown. Food in renown, in smoke, in scent, is thin—sweet, but thin. Yet we are already filled, already made rich, content with the scent of virtues alone. I do not know, however, whether we even draw in their scent if we are not drawn by eagerness for perfection. The lilies’ scent is sweet indeed, but grace amassed in direct vision is sweeter. The lilies’ scent is sweet indeed, but the sweetness is thin if it is only scent. Thus he says, “who feed in lilies”: that is [Col. 0145D], among lilies, not upon the lilies themselves; sensing their nearness, not enjoying their substance. In scent is expressed a scant use of virtues, not abundant, solid, and, as it were, bodily refreshment. For one who feeds is not in every respect refreshed; therefore he does not say, “who are refreshed,” but “who feed among lilies until the day breathes.”

Yet it is a delightful expectation of light among lilies. And observe among what kind of lilies the Bride feeds. They are lilies not subject to decay, lilies that do not wither, lilies, finally, made fragrant with myrrh by a certain incorruptibility. For myrrh signifies incorruption.

2. Myrrh is rightly joined after lilies, in order to commend the Bride’s lilies by a certain enduring perpetuity of incorruption. “I will go,” he says, “for myself to the mountain of myrrh.” What is this, good Jesus? Your Bride, your beloved, waits in one place, while you go elsewhere. She feeds and waits among lilies, and you go to the mountain of myrrh? Why do you not rather go to the lilies, where the Bride remains until the day breathes? Perhaps these lilies are not foreign to the mountain of myrrh or far removed from it, but instead grow upon it. Indeed it is so: nowhere do lilies grow more joyfully than on the mountain of myrrh, nowhere are they preserved more uninjured. On the mountain of myrrh no place at all is left either for corruption or corruptibility. There, on the mountain of myrrh, where every affection of the flesh is mortified, lilies of chastity and lilies of graces both arise in purity and flower perpetually.

Thus you see that the Bride is placed quite delightfully both among lilies and on the mountain of myrrh. For the present discourse has explained one of these to you; you may explain the other yourself through interpretation. In what other direction would he say that he was going than where he knew his beloved to be? As she waits eagerly, so he hastens ardently. “I will go,” he says, “for myself.” What then? Does he not go to the Bride? Or does he go for himself precisely because he goes to her? “I will go, therefore,” he says, “for myself. I shall go for myself, not for her alone. She is not alone in receiving joy from my coming; she in turn gives joy back to me as well. It is sweet and pleasant to me to go to her. Now I shall go for myself. Going in this way benefits me and affects me delightfully; therefore I shall go for myself. Already the sweet fragrance of the mountain of myrrh breathes upon me; therefore, drawn by the scent, I shall go. I shall go for myself, because my delights are to remain with the Bride.”

Is it so, good Jesus? Do you take pleasure from conversation with the Bride, and therefore go for yourself? When excluded, you do not turn aside like a fastidious lover, but stand [Col. 0146C] at the door? You stand and knock; having suffered, as it were, the injury of rejection, you nevertheless stand and knock, if only it may be opened. Sprinkle, O Bride, sprinkle your bed with myrrh and aloes. Christ runs after the fragrance of your ointments. Sprinkle your bed with the myrrh which Paul mentions: “You have died,” he says, “and your life is hidden with Christ” (Col. 3:3). With such myrrh sprinkle, water, drench your bed—or rather, be yourself a mountain of myrrh. For grace is more abundant where myrrh grows than where it is sprinkled. Place your bed on this mountain—or rather, the bed of your Beloved—in a certain abundance of myrrh, where this aromatic kind more truly arises than is brought in.

3. In many places of Scripture the use of myrrh is applied to mysteries. The Magi come to Christ with myrrh (Matt. 2:11). Nicodemus also came, bringing a mixture of myrrh, about one hundred pounds (John 19:39). There is a great quantity here; but what is it compared with a mountain? “Bringing,” he says: that is, bringing it with him, not producing it from himself; carrying it, not bearing it within himself. Both are good—the myrrh that is offered and that which grows—but the latter is superior. Indeed, the former is brought to Christ, while he himself goes to the latter. For he goes for himself to the mountain of myrrh.

A mountain of myrrh is rightly so called when it bears Christ’s death within itself, not in part; not as something sprinkled upon it, but abundantly, continuously, and eminently; not for an hour and, as it were, growing old, but rather continually renewed. A mountain of myrrh is rightly so called when it does not merely carry within itself Christ’s mortification, a certain incorruptibility, and an image of the future resurrection, but brings them forth. Can a place seem to you a mountain of myrrh in which nothing magnificent or eminent of future incorruptibility appears, nothing except something temporary? Plainly blessed is the mountain which is clothed on every side in the growth of this myrrh, not sprinkled in parts; having nothing bare within itself, nothing sterile, but wholly fertile with this blessed kind.

How could one not be blessed who draws Christ to himself through the scent of his own aromatic spice? This is a good fragrance: not merely filling the house of the Leper [Col. 0147A] (Matt. 26:6–7), but also the heavenly palace, the Bridegroom’s chamber. It is plainly a good fragrance to Christ the Bridegroom, pleasing amid the very delights of deity. Indeed, beyond so many delights, his delight is nevertheless to be on the mountain of myrrh. Therefore he says: “I will go for myself to the mountain of myrrh.”

[Col. 0147B] 4. O blessed mountain to which you go, good Jesus—to which you come, which you walk through, which you inhabit, and inhabit unto the end; which you alone inhabit, even to the boundary of the place. Come, Jesus; begin to take possession of this mountain. Let no one raise an objection against you; let no one say, “Will you dwell alone on this mountain?” It is a rich mountain, a fertile mountain, an abundant mountain, a mountain overflowing with ointments. These ointments cannot be exhausted. For there is a great store of ointment on the mountain of myrrh. The ointments will not fail from this mountain; therefore one who goes to the mountain of myrrh will not need ointments, nor even spices, when he goes to the hills of Lebanon. For frankincense will not fail from Lebanon. Indeed, they say that Lebanon is understood as frankincense.

Come, good Jesus, to [Col. 0147C] these hills, that frankincense may flow at your presence. O how great a smoke of incense rises from these hills when they have been kindled with your fire—or rather, with you as their fire! Your fire has in the hills of frankincense a great supply of fuel and an abundant material for burning. This frankincense is not quickly consumed. The smoke of this burning does not easily vanish. So great a mass of frankincense, so great an abundance on the hill of frankincense, cannot be enclosed in a fist or contained in a censer. It is not held by a small vessel; it knows no measure because it knows no interruption.

Thus rightly is it a hill of frankincense: one who prays without interruption—and, what is better, without slackening; who has in prayer nothing lax or scanty, but, as the smoke of some great furnace grows thick, sends forth billows of swelling prayers and overflowing desire. Come, therefore, good Jesus, to the hills of frankincense: the mountains which you touch send up copious incense of prayer. What have our prayers, brothers, that is like this? How quickly our frankincense is exhausted! It is scarcely kindled, as it were, and immediately extinguished. Why is this? Surely because we have gathered for ourselves only a scant supply of material for incense.

5. I interpret the angelic spirits—and any among human beings who are their imitators—as certain hills of frankincense, whose prayer is always set before God like incense; who produce the sweetest vapours of devotion and gather clouds of heavenly affections. Blessed indeed is the priest who offers such abundant frankincense, whom the vapour of such sweet mists covers and envelops. In the Apocalypse you read of bowls full of fragrances, which are the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8). [Col. 0148A] But what relation have bowls to hills of frankincense? What bowl could hold a hill of frankincense? A bowl full of fragrances is good. But behold, here is more than a bowl: “The smoke of the aromas,” he says, “ascended before the Lord from the hand of the angel” (Rev. 8:4). Yet what hand would suffice for an entire hill? What hand, I say, except yours, good Jesus—your hand, you who weigh mountains and enclose the earth in your palm, who weigh mountains by weight and hills in a balance?

In your hand, Lord, are all the ends of these hills; and, if it is permissible to say so, in your bosom. Indeed, the prayer of the saints turns in your bosom and enters into your presence; there it dwells, there it is turned: they are in you, and you in them. Therefore you say, “I will go for myself to the hills of frankincense.” Come then, Lord; come and do not delay; come and do not leap over these hills. What if the hills of frankincense also leap to you? The mountains of myrrh and hills of frankincense are mobile where you yourself have come. How could they not be mobile, when they melt, flow, smoke, and ascend like the smoke of aromas before the Lord from your hand?

Go then for yourself to the hills of frankincense, where there are many incense-offerings, where all are incense-offerings; for on the hill of frankincense nothing is without incense. These incense-offerings have been given to you; therefore come, that you may burn them in your presence.

6. “I will go for myself to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. Come from Lebanon, come.” It has now been made clear why he goes: for why, except to call, to enter, to say, “Come”? Behold how good and pleasant it is to dwell among these hills, to which the Word of God goes [Col. 0148C], which he visits again; from which he calls the Bride, and calls her to a crown! “Come,” he says, “from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned.” Lebanon signifies whiteness. How could it not be white with heavenly snow? For, as it is written, “snow shall not fail from Lebanon” (Jer. 18:14): that snow which comes down from heaven, waters and drenches the earth, and makes it germinate. Blessed are the mountains upon which this snow falls, and the hills which it covers. “So,” says the Lord, “shall the word be which goes forth from my mouth: it shall not return to me empty” (Isa. 55:11).

Does the word which goes to the mountains of myrrh and hills of frankincense, which falls upon these mountains and covers the hills, seem to you to return empty? It does not know how to return empty. Therefore he calls and says, “Come from Lebanon, come.” Do you suppose it is without mystery that, after the mountains of myrrh and hills of frankincense, he mentions [Col. 0148D] Lebanon? What renders the mind as clean and white as the practice of prayer? First myrrh mortifies; then frankincense purifies. For prayer cannot go forth pure unless every wicked scent and exhalation of the flesh has first been restrained.

In the ointment of myrrh the mind is constrained, so as to contract itself into a certain—indeed, complete—unity. By burning frankincense it is directed, enlarged, and poured out, filling the heavenly regions with the fragrance of incense. There it mingles and is blended with the breezes of free truth; and the soul which was first contracted into itself there becomes rarefied, attenuated, and fails away, suspended and looking upward on high.

7. Prayer performs the service of both myrrh and frankincense. At first it gathers the affection of the one praying and constrains it into yourself; then it pours it out and transfuses it into God. What is more like myrrh, where there is so great a transfusion into divine union? What is more like incense, where there is so great a diffusion of a certain divine perception? She is rightly called altogether beautiful and without blemish whom the ardour of prayer has made glow, whom the brightness of eternal light has coloured and made white. “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish in you.”

You are wholly beautiful, because at this hour above all you are wholly beautiful: the hour of prayer, the hour of incense. You are wholly beautiful, my friend, wholly beautiful, because you are wholly a friend, glowing only with the affection of love. You are wholly beautiful and without blemish, having no foreign colour mingled with you. “Come from Lebanon, come from Lebanon, come from Lebanon.” Come from Lebanon because you are without blemish; come from Lebanon because you are wholly beautiful; come from [Col. 0149B] Lebanon because you are fully washed. Come from Lebanon, wholly enlightened; come from Lebanon, free from fault; come from Lebanon, radiant with grace; come, you shall be crowned.

Entirely blessed is one who is called from Lebanon of radiant affection, from the hill of frankincense, from the abundance of intent prayer, to a crown. Blessed, I say, is the soul which ascends to the Father in the hour of incense; which is called without interval from Lebanon to a crown—the crown of glory, which the righteous Judge and sweet Bridegroom Jesus Christ will render to it at the hour of departure, with God the Father, through all ages of ages. Amen.

94. SERMON XXIX. “You are wholly beautiful, my friend” (Song 4:7).

1. “You are wholly beautiful, my friend, and there is no blemish [Col. 0149C] in you. Come from Lebanon, my Bride; come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned.” Who will grant me to complete this journey of three days, so to speak? Who, I say, will grant me to traverse this path with untiring progress? These ways are beautiful ways and peaceful paths: to come from Lebanon to Lebanon, from Lebanon to the kingdom. For the Bride, summoned to the crown, seems invited to partnership in reigning. The end of the way is sweet, but the passage itself is no less sweet. How could it not be sweet, since it does not know how to turn aside from Lebanon? This is not the broad way; this is not a worldly way; nor can one who is defiled pass through it. It is not of the one who runs or wills, but of God who has mercy (Rom. 9:16).

Why do I say “who has mercy”? I might better have said, “who desires.” Does not the threefold calling signify the longings of burning desire? Calling her a third time is evidence of vehement affection. Run through in your mind the preceding parts of this Song: nowhere will you find the Bride either called so frequently or her beauty commended so expressly. Three times he calls her, and says that she is wholly beautiful. Indeed, in the preceding passages you have this: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful” (Song 1:14). And elsewhere again: “O how beautiful you are, my friend! How beautiful you are!” (Song 4:1). But in this third passage he declares her to be wholly beautiful.

In those passages he either shows that she is beautiful or wonders that she is so beautiful; he does not, however, definitely determine that she is entirely beautiful, as in the present passage: “You are wholly beautiful, my friend.” How could she not be wholly beautiful, entirely conformed to Beauty and to total Beauty? How could she not be wholly beautiful, she into whom the immeasurable brightness of eternal light flows? She is rightly wholly beautiful, indeed surpassingly beautiful, into whom all the Lord’s beauty has poured itself in a rich inflow. He has indeed been exalted above the stars, yet the form of his beauty is in the Bride. “His form,” he says, “is in the clouds of heaven.” So long as the Bride is a cloud of heaven—bright and light, as if approaching the sun and receiving it—so long in her alone does the Sun’s brightness shine forth, and the form of his beauty remain.

2. The Bride is plainly then a cloud when she possesses the lightness of spiritual affection and the light of understanding. So long as the spiritual soul is suspended in heavenly things through the practice of prayer and contemplation, like a bright and light cloud, so long she is wholly beautiful, because wholly a friend; and free from blemish, because she has been transformed into the colour of ardent [Col. 0150B] love. This hour presents to him a glorious Bride, having neither spot nor wrinkle, cleansing her not so much in blood as in his own light.

How could she not be wholly beautiful, in whom the form of divine beauty appears so clearly? Show me a soul which you would dare to call wholly beautiful, except only at this hour, when by the heat of love she is more imbued than clothed with the form of the Bridegroom. At other hours she is counted without blemish, while guilt is not imputed. But at this moment, when she is called without blemish, it is not a matter of pardon, but of love, desire, and devotion. For where the vows of love burn so intensely, what place can there be for forgiveness? Love does not need pardon; for where it alone is, everything is gracious.

See, therefore, how both offence is excluded and grace alone is commended—grace alone. “You are wholly beautiful,” he says, “my friend, and there is no blemish in you.” Such endearments do not appear to belong to one pardoning, but to one cherishing, loving, admiring. Delighted by beauty, he desires her presence. “Come from Lebanon, come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned.” The repeated invitation reveals affection and manifests longing.

3. Let others investigate the mysteries and assign the stages of the threefold calling. For my part, it is enough to marvel at the affection of the divine Majesty toward the human soul. This is enough, yet I myself succumb. Would that I had no task resting upon me but continually to marvel in rapt astonishment at the grace bestowed—yet so that vows may be joined to this admiration and love may be genuine. For affection merits affection, and “deep calls to deep with the voice of your waterfalls” (Ps. 41:8). Good indeed are the waterfalls which, good Jesus, distil your affection and pour in love.
