Love is not mute; it has the use of a voice. For “that which contains all things has knowledge of voice” (Wis. 1:7). This is written of the Spirit; and you know well how great is the kinship—if not rather the identity—of love with the Spirit. Love contains all things, because “love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13:10). The Spirit speaks mysteries (1 Cor. 14:2), and surely speaks words of love. The Spirit himself bears witness to our spirit (Rom. 8:16); certainly he can also speak endearments. His sound is the meaning of love and desire, vows having the likeness of a voice. The very experience of grace speaks, invites, says: “Come from Lebanon.”

He calls three times, perhaps because “a threefold cord is not quickly broken.” For love is a tenacious cord. Love draws affectionately; for it is the same thing to address as to attract. Nothing is more tenacious than the bond of love, nothing more drawing. Hear how the divine law displays this threefold bond of the cord: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matt. 22:37). It is as though it said: You shall love the Lord your God with the purpose of the heart, the vital affection of the soul, and the whole and rational judgment of the mind—so that in you love may have both purpose, inclination itself, and discernment.

A devout intention of heart toward God is good; but what if it is sluggish, lifeless, containing nothing vital, nothing animated? Therefore a pure intention is good, made living and, as it were, animated by fervent and sweet affection. Meditation gives form to this affection, which is like a soul of good purpose, if it is discerning; and nourishes it if it is frequent. With the cord thus bound in threefold fashion, what is more abundant for the merit of the crown laid up, or more manifest for experience? Does not this threefold love seem to you to invite and, as it were, say “Come” three times?

4. Finally, it invites, as it were, by giving both courage through merit and eagerness through experience. “Come from Lebanon,” he says, “come, you shall be crowned.” In the Apocalypse you read, as it were, of those coming from Lebanon: “Who are these clothed in white robes, and from where have they come?” [Col. 0151C] “These are those who have come from great tribulation and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7:13–14). They made their robes white in the blood of the Lamb, certainly by faith in believing and by the manner of their conduct: they follow, in their tribulation, this Lamb who did not open his mouth when led to slaughter and was silent before the one shearing him (Isa. 53:7); they are neither sad nor troubled until they bring judgment forth unto victory (Isa. 42:4; Matt. 12:20), and conflict to its crown. “For no one shall be crowned unless he has contended lawfully” (2 Tim. 2:5).

And because the crown comes from conflict, perhaps he thus invites his beloved to the crown in order to state the cause. For he says: “You shall be crowned [Col. 0151D] from the summit of Amana and Sanir, from the mountains of leopards, from the dens of lions.” In these names and natures I know not what harsh, savage, and deceitful thing is suggested. Therefore she is said to be crowned from them, since, once conquered, they furnish the material for her crown. He is crowned through enduring tribulation who comes from great tribulation gentle, meek, like a lamb; who comes clothed in white in love, not worn out, whom no stain of impatience or murmuring blackens.

These are they who come from Lebanon and are crowned from the summit of Amana and Sanir, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards. For they are crowned through these things by which they are tested through kinds of temptations. Do they not gather grapes from thorns and figs from thistles? “The momentary and light affliction of the present,” says the Apostle, “works in us beyond measure, in exaltation, an eternal weight of glory” (2 Cor. 4:17). Therefore the sufferings of this time cooperate toward—although they are not comparable to—the future crown of glory reserved for us.

It is plainly an accumulated material of rewards when, amid merits of the utmost purity, a person is worn down by varied sufferings. A most beautiful bond for the crown is formed when purity of life and humble endurance of pressures cling to one another. The burden of pressures is great indeed; therefore perhaps it is expressed by the names of mountains. It is a huge mass, but faith rises above it and does not know how to be crushed. It treads upon the summits of these mountains and strikes “the head from the house of the wicked.” Thus the very head, triumphing, is rightly crowned from the head [Col. 0152B], because it both crushes the beginning of temptations and does not yield to the violence of tribulations.

In every matter, “head” is, as it were, what is either first or greatest. Thus understand “head” here as signifying either the beginning or the height of the things figured by these mountains. One is crowned from the summit of Amana, from the summit of Hermon and Sanir, who overcomes a certain height of injuries and the mass of tribulations that raises itself against the humble knowledge of Christ. Yet this mass seems to have so much the less weight because everything that swells is temporary.

5. Finally, though it is a mountain, you nevertheless read that it is written: “A falling mountain melts away, and a rock is removed from its place” (Job 14:18). See how these mountains have melted away, how they have been removed. They have been removed because they have been transformed. The Apostle points to them as, as it were, removed and conquered when he says to those whom he addresses: “And such indeed some of you once were; but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified, but you have been justified” (1 Cor. 6:11), by that washing and cleansing which takes place through the word of faith. The leopard has laid aside its spots, becoming wholly unblemished, wholly of one colour—that is, of one faith and manner of life. A person sprinkled with the variety of heretical doctrine seems like a kind of leopard. Yet a person unlike himself, variable and inconstant, and continually changing his plans, is no less like a leopard. For, so to speak, the leopard both wills and does not will. Apply these things to the conversion of the Gentiles, and at once you will understand how those who have been converted to the Lord appear, through unity of faith and hope, to have put on one colour; and you will see that they have laid aside not only their variety but also their savagery, and that they dwell not in lions’ dens—not, I say, in dens of debauchery—but in beds and gardens of spices; and that they abide in beds not bestial, not foul, but flower-strewn. For the bed of bridegroom and bride is flower-strewn. The bride does not appear willing to leave Lebanon and pass from Judaea to the Gentiles. She departs unwillingly, though called so often; she does not wish to leave Lebanon in order to cross to Mount Amana, to the summit of Sanir and Hermon. Yet by her passage she herself turns these barren, barbarous mountains into Lebanon.

6. But now consider the names of these mountains. Amana is understood as “a vain people” or “a people making narrow”; [Col. 0153A] Sanir, “rough”; Hermon, “anathema.” What is more vain than that people whose very teachers “became vain in their reasonings,” and “claiming to be wise, became fools”? What is narrower than those who, despairing, “gave themselves over to uncleanness”? Narrow indeed is the heart that confines the end of its desires within the bounds of temporal pleasure, not knowing how to enlarge its hope toward eternal things. What is rougher and more disordered than those of whom the Apostle says: “Without natural affection, without covenant” (2 Tim. 3:3), living in malice and envy? (Tit. 3:3.) Are not these to be regarded as Sanir? Hermon, moreover, denotes those who are alienated from the mind of Christ, having no hope of the promise, neither fellow citizens of the saints nor members of God’s household, but altogether without God in this world. And indeed, [Col. 0153B] you Gentiles were such; but you have been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of our Lord Jesus. Therefore the bride is crowned from among you, she who glories in your transformation. A good transformation, when Sanir is converted into Lebanon.

And Lebanon itself—that former Jewish Lebanon—now seems to have been converted into Sanir and Hermon. Therefore, “Come from Lebanon; come”; and see, in place of that small and short-lived Lebanon, how many Lebanons arise for you. Lift your eyes round about and see: all the mountains of this world are to be converted for you into Lebanon. It is indeed distressing to see the losses and desolation of your people; but so profitable a transformation compensates for this distress that a more abundant yield redeems the loss of one people. Do not therefore delay, but come from Lebanon, which now ceases to be Lebanon; [Col. 0153C] come, that you may be crowned through the faith and conversion of the Gentiles.

Do you wish to understand all these mountains not in Judaea and the Gentiles, but in the Church alone? The interpretation will not be discordant if you choose to turn it in this direction. Here you will find Lebanon, Amana, Sanir, and Hermon. Here too you will find the mountains of leopards and the dens of lions.

7. Would that in this our Lebanon, in this holy assembly of monks, made fair and white by both profession and manner of life—in this Lebanon, I say—one might not be allowed to see the head of Amana, nor the summit of Sanir and Hermon. Whenever you see among the gathering and congregation of saints someone exalting himself, puffed up with fleshly understanding, vain in boasting, [Col. 0153D] swollen and agitated within and without, anxiously occupied with the vanity of idleness—for idleness breeds acedia—when you see such a person, what else do you behold but the head of Amana in Lebanon? Nothing is more vain than idleness, nothing more anxious than acedia, nothing more disorderly than swelling pride. For Amana also signifies a vain or troubled people; thus one comes from Amana to Sanir, “the rough and hairy.” For where there is acedia, there is swelling; where there is disturbance, there is nothing gentle, nothing composed, nothing ordered, but all is harsh. And one who is such is without covenant, without affection, of hostile and alienated mind—indeed, accursed, which is what Hermon signifies. Such a one is not of God’s household, not a citizen, not even a stranger or guest; therefore no grace bends toward him, no devotion turns aside to him. The bridegroom does not turn in to him, even to visit him in passing and, [Col. 0154A] as a guest, to stay there.

Yet leopards dwell in him—demons, diverse and deceitful—and lions lie there. They do not roam about merely to fly past; they possess the place securely and establish their dens. But such persons must not be despaired of. For many of this sort are predestined for the bridegroom’s adornment. Therefore he says: “Come, you shall be crowned from the head of Amana and from the summit of Sanir.” “Come,” he says, “from Lebanon, come.” Observe whether she does not leave Lebanon slowly, she who is called so often. Yet this delay is not obstinacy but caution. For who gladly leaves the brightness of contemplation, the serenity of inward rest and purity? To whom would it not be burdensome to withdraw, even for a moment, from a place of delights? Perhaps the hoped-for gain in disciples attracts her; but the labour is burdensome. The gain is desirable indeed, [Col. 0154B] but falling is to be feared. Gains whose outcome is uncertain are suspect to me, when the danger to one’s own salvation is near, and the loss of inward sweetness certain. What wonder if she is slow to come, when it is burdensome to leave Lebanon and fearful to approach those barbarous and beastly mountains?

Perhaps the bride’s delay reproves and censures our own haste, who, all too ready and insufficiently prudent, giving too little consideration to our strength, hasten to undertake the labours of prelacy, the burdens of cares, and occasions of falling. We do not wait even to be called once, but ourselves take honour for ourselves, either forestalling the call or securing it by contrivance. There should be neither reckless presumption toward so great an office nor stubborn fear.

8. Yet one must venture when Christ commands, when the Bridegroom calls and promises abundant results, as in this place: “Come,” he says, “you shall be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Sanir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards.” [Col. 0154C] When barbarity of conduct is changed in subjects; when beds are transferred from dens and debauchery to beds that are flower-strewn and honourable, and into gardens of spices; to beds in which there is no roaring but weeping; to beds in which there is compunction of heart rather than warfare of thoughts; when the covering of stained variety is taken away and naked simplicity succeeds, conduct being transformed for the better through its ministry—then the bride is most fittingly understood to be crowned. She is rightly crowned from such persons when those whose conduct she formerly abhorred are now turned into adornment, and when those formerly divided by beastly affections adhere together as one in a certain order of charity. This cohesion of unity is indeed pleasing to the Bridegroom. Therefore perhaps what follows is said: that he is wounded in one of her eyes, in one lock of her neck—namely, the bride’s.

The treatment of this chapter must be postponed to another time. But it will suffice to have warned, at the end, anyone whom concern for another’s advancement prompts toward a higher rank: I neither dissuade nor positively advise. Yet I urge one thing: whoever you are, emulate both the bride’s hesitation and her purity. She is not content to be called once, nor does she come forth worthy at all except from a certain Lebanon of pure and whitened conscience. For Christ Jesus, her Bridegroom, calls his beloved to the crown only from Lebanon—[Col. 0155A] he who is God, blessed for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXX

*“You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes,” etc.* (Song 4:9).

1. O hard heart—and wickedly hard—in which these words produce no wounds! Truly dull is the heart that does not feel the force of these words, that is not astonished at so great a condescension. Why do I call it condescension? It is even more than that. And how great a thing would it be if it were only condescension? For it would be a great matter, worthy of all wonder, if such majesty merely deigned to grant human weakness the title of sister and bride. But now it is not so much condescension as devotion.

Do you wish to hear the proof of a devoted and eager affection? “You have wounded my heart,” he says, “my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart.” The wound of the heart signifies the vehemence of love. O truly sweet heart, moved by our affections to repay love in return! There is both kinship and reciprocity here: kinship in the name of sister and bride, reciprocity signified in the wound. Great is the kinship of sister; greater that of bride: the former is of kindred, the latter of love. There it is signified that they are from one source; here, that they are one. She is sister because she shares the divine nature; she is bride because she has been assumed into the uniqueness of his person. These are plainly terms of relationship, expressive either of nature or grace. How greatly ought she to love who knows herself united to Christ by so great affinities? [Col. 0155C] However much she loves, she does not simply love, but loves in return. For he first loved us (1 John 4:10). However earnest our love toward him may be, it is not bestowed but repaid; it is owed, not gratuitous. It cannot equal the love already bestowed upon her. How can one merit or bind another when one cannot even fully pay what is due? You cannot, bride, render full reciprocity to your lover. Yet he does not cease to bestow still more. What he has bestowed on you has not yet been fully repaid, yet he considers himself indebted. Whatever love you repay to him, he receives not as owed, but as a gift. He perceives himself as provoked to love when he confesses that his heart is wounded.

2. What miracle is this, brothers? Do you not judge blessed that soul which pierces and penetrates the very heart of our Lord Jesus Christ with devout affections? That affection is keen and effective, truly forceful, which wins and moves your affection, good Jesus. Great and forceful is the power of charity: it reaches and penetrates God’s very affection, and, like an arrow, pierces his liver. What wonder if the kingdom of heaven suffers violence? (Matt. 11:12.) The Lord himself endures the wound of violent love. But see with what darts he is wounded: “You have wounded my heart,” he says, “with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.” Do not spare, bride, to assail the Bridegroom with such weapons. Use devout glances as little darts. Do not act too slackly in this undertaking; do not be content to wound your beloved once, but strike him down with wound upon wound. Happy are you if your arrows are fixed in him and your loves do military service in Christ, if your eye remains tirelessly fixed upon him.

A good wound is that from which power goes forth. A woman touched the hem of his garment, and Christ felt power go out from himself (Luke 8:43–46). How much more, when his heart is touched not lightly but wounded, does he feel grace flow forth from himself? This wound is not without awareness. Therefore shoot the darts of pure gazes toward him; regard him as a target set up for such arrows. He receives such arrows favourably because he himself shoots such arrows. He looked upon Peter, struck his heart, and pierced him with compunction unto repentance (Luke 22:61–62). The tears of a wounded heart give proof of this. Finally, [Col. 0156B] by a merciful look he wounds that heart which he moves toward some affection of virtue. Would that he multiplied such wounds in me from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, so that there might be no soundness in me. For it is evil soundness when the wounds inflicted by Christ’s devout gaze are absent. One gaze provokes another; therefore attempt to wound him by your own look. Let your eyes always be toward the Lord, so that he may be caught by the signals of your love and ensnared by your little locks.

3. Yet he does not say “with your eyes” and “with your little locks,” as though with many, but as though with one: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.” If you have many eyes, close all the rest, that you may use this one alone, with which you are accustomed, and with which alone you are able, to gaze upon your beloved. Those who wish to look more directly close one eye and fix the other upon the object; and they narrow even that eye with which they see, so that, narrowed, they may contemplate more effectively with a sharpened gaze.

Your eye is one if it is pure; it is one if it is not directed toward many things; it is one if, in a manner, it is made simple, narrowed, and directed to one thing—not split, not diffused, not scattered among many things. Your eye is one if you direct it and look always toward one thing, and toward that One. Finally, if it is the eye of love, it is one. “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the length of my days, that I may see the delight of the Lord” (Ps. 26:4). This eye is one, asking one thing and looking toward one thing. And “with one lock [Col. 0156D] of your neck.”

The locks ought not to hang loose, wandering without rule, scattered and straying across the brightness of the eyes. It is unfitting that the eye should be narrowed while the lock is loose. For the eye is offended when the lock is spread out. If intention is understood in the eye, what is signified in the lock but thought? Do you wish to have both—lock and brightness, intention and meditation—made one? “His delight is in the law of the Lord, and on it he meditates day and night.” Such a person also possesses one eye in uniformity of will and one lock in meditation. Otherwise, if you lack a uniform and simple intention toward God, if your thoughts wander without discipline, they blunt the focused eye, batter the keen edge of simple intention, and scatter the heart through the restless movements of an undisciplined mind. Let thought correspond to pure intention: let it be one, as that intention too is uniform. For good is the lock that is not spread out—not unkempt, but gathered into one and clinging to the neck, namely that neck of which it is said: “Your neck is like a tower, from which a thousand shields hang” (Song 4:4).

4. Understand this neck as Sacred Scripture, through which the words announcing the divine will flow down to us. Therefore the lock of the neck is a thought constantly engaged with God’s law. It is called a lock of the neck because all your thought, all your perceptions, and your understanding ought not to prejudge the sacred utterance, but must depend upon its prescription and proceed from it. If your locks are divided and, as it were, torn apart, possessing no harmony in themselves, then, though they cling to the neck, they do not please the Bridegroom or wound his heart; they move no affection [Col. 0157B] and merit no grace. He requires both: that they be gathered into one and cling to the neck, possessing in themselves both order and authority.

For what advantage is it if your meditations are upon God’s law but are themselves lawless? Those are lawless which lack order and are carried about everywhere. “With one lock of your neck,” he says. In the neck is understood the authority of the sacred word, which gives form to thoughts; order, however, lies in unity. For good order exists where they are gathered into the same thing, directed toward one thing, and toward that One which shall not be taken away. Or perhaps he says, “with one lock of your neck,” in order to signify the bride’s free and unveiled face. For locks are regarded as a covering. Thus he desires in the bride a face bare and unveiled for beholding the glory of God, and an eye of contemplation fixed without obstruction; therefore he commends locks that are orderly and drawn back from the face to the neck.

5. Why do we understand this only in one individual soul? Let us extend this meaning to the condition of the Church. For what is shared is more pleasing. Indeed, nothing is more pleasing to the Bridegroom than the community—rather, the unity—of believers and the compactness of the Church. He has heaped many good things into his praise of the bride, by which he shows himself delighted; but he has never expressed the affection of one rejoicing with her as he does here, where the unity of eye and lock is mentioned. How could his joy not be greatest where the greatest commandment is kept? “I give you a new commandment,” he says, “that you love one another as I have loved you.”

The eyes of the Church are its teachers; whoever touches them touches the pupil of the Lord’s eye. The locks, however, are the multitudes of believers. Unity in both is pleasing to the Bridegroom. “By this,” he says, “all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34–35). The agreement of two or three makes prayers effective in obtaining their request (Matt. 18:20); how much more the agreement of the whole Church in Christ? How can unity fail to obtain, when it penetrates the very heart of the Lord? “You have wounded my heart,” he says, “my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart with one of your eyes and with one lock of your neck.”

For what in all a woman’s adornment more draws and affects the lover’s feeling than well-arranged locks? But why do we attempt to pile praise upon the bride’s locks, arranged and gathered with elaborate adornment? There is more material here for lamentation than applause.

6. In these days we see the bride’s locks miserably torn apart and rent, and the peoples of the Church fighting among themselves over the Church. You see this too, good Jesus: does this division not move you? Does so grievous a wound of your bride not wound you? If unity wounds your heart to rejoicing, dissension ought to wound you to compassion. The arrangement of unity and uniformity moves you; let the scattering of things once united move you. Your locks are divided and separated from one another—indeed, set against one another. Both parties boast that they hang from the bride’s [Col. 0158A] neck, and glorying in their own possession, strive to tear others away from themselves.

“The Lord knows those who are his; and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” (2 Tim. 2:19). Possessing this twofold seal, as Paul says, his bride remains unmoved amid the impious hands that on every side pull her apart and tear her. “The kings of the earth and the rulers assembled together against the Lord Christ” (Ps. 2:2), and against his bride. But the bride knows the Bridegroom, so that she does not follow a stranger, but him. She is not ignorant of herself; she does not ignore whose bride she is. Therefore she does not wish to go out or go away after the flocks of her companions. And if they were companions, they are so no longer. “They went out from us, but they were not of us.” How are they companions who are not friends? For “the friend of the Bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices greatly because of his voice” (John 3:29). But these men neither hear nor rejoice at the Bridegroom’s voice, but rather at the voice of the Roman Emperor—[Col. 0158C] unless, as we more truthfully confess, they do not so much rejoice as fear his roar. But the Lord knows who are his, not who belong to the Emperor. Therefore they cannot be moved by the roaring of Leo.

> [Note: [Col. 0157D] An allusion to Peter of Leo, the antipope.]

For they are held fast by the immovable seal of divine knowledge.

7. For the knowledge of God is a good seal: knowledge according to the purpose by which the saints are called. This seal of his knowledge is firm because nothing escapes it. Not only does nothing escape it; it itself brings forth those to be saved, itself predestines, itself marks those whom it wills to be its own. The seal is twofold: divine purpose and human endeavour; divine providence and human diligence. [Col. 0158D] For the Apostle adds concerning diligence: “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.” Observe the two parts of this seal: one belongs to grace alone; the other to both grace and freedom; the former to purpose, the latter to assistance. This second part directs the weak choice of our freedom; the first makes disposition by predestination. In the first, the Lord knows those who are his by foreknowledge; in the second, they become known to us. The former is the cause; this is its effect. That seal is immovable; this one is evidential. That is the seal; this is the sign of the seal. That is the root; this the fruit; and by these fruits you will know those who name the Lord’s name. For in his good pleasure he himself knows who are his and appoints them to bear this fruit abundantly. Therefore he says: “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity.” Whoever says that he belongs to him must not depart from unity. Nor can any of those whom divine knowledge has formed and confirmed depart.

Finally, not even a hair from the head of the Church shall perish. For all her hairs are numbered, all marked with the seal of predestining knowledge. This knowledge is without repentance; therefore the foundation stands firm, having the Lord’s seal: the aid of divine purpose and the striving of our will. No one will be able to snatch from the bride’s head the locks bound by this seal. In your hand, Lord, are all the bride’s locks, and no one shall snatch them from your hand. Hold fast, good Jesus, those whom you hold, and gather again those whom you know. And let whoever knows himself to be yours, who says, “I am the Lord’s,” who names the Lord’s name, depart from iniquity and draw near to the unity of the Church, to the unity of head and body—that is, let him be a lock of the neck, and one lock.

8. Nothing wounds the Bridegroom’s heart, nothing stirs his affection and penetrates his mind, as does the bride’s unity, maintained amid those striving to tear her apart and, as it were, made solid against their efforts. Religious bishops abandon their own sees and flee from city to city before the persecutor’s face. Clerics and monks devoted to God, afflicted by tribulations and insults, gladly endure the plundering of their goods, knowing that they possess a better and enduring substance in the unity of fraternal and ecclesiastical charity. For if a man gives all his substance for charity, he will regard it as nothing (Song 8:7).

Some, indeed, buy the freedom of ecclesiastical communion with gifts. It is a good redemption, but a disgraceful sale. Why do you sell what you yourself condemn? If you regard those separated from you as schismatics, you ought not, induced by a price, to have allowed them liberty in their error. If you consider it schism, why do you sell its liberty for gifts? But if the truth of ecclesiastical unity is with us, why do you attempt to tear it apart? If by right of succession you hold Peter’s seat, why do you not enforce Peter’s judgments against those whom you judge schismatics? “May your money perish with you” (Acts 8:20). But now you say: “May your money be safe for me, but let the soul go to perdition.” For how is it not perdition where there is separation from the unity of the body? “Let it be neither mine nor yours, but divided” (3 Kings 3:26). Thus you take the money when you cannot take the souls. Take what you take: take the gifts for yourself; leave the souls to the Church. For the Church herself seeks nothing but souls. Let temporal goods be scattered among you, lest you scatter with them the goods of souls. For whoever does not gather with the Church scatters. Significantly enough he says: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters.” For gathering embodies the principle of unity, just as scattering indicates separation. The Church knows how to say with the Bridegroom: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matt. 12:30). [Col. 0160A] He leaves nothing in between: either you gather with her, or you surely scatter; either you are with her, or against her.

But you are accustomed, as they say, to reply: “If you do not wish to scatter with me, at least do not gather with them. If you are not with me, at least do not be against me. It is enough if you are neither ours nor our opponents’.”

> [Note: [Col. 0159D] No one other than Alexander III seems to be attacked here in section 8; the Emperor Frederick set the antipope Victor against him. The author desires Victor’s overthrow at the end of the sermon. There “avenger” was formerly printed instead of “Victor”; the latter is the authentic reading from the manuscript of Clairvaux.]

9. But our Jesus is not so, who says, “Are you ours or our opponents’?” (Josh. 5:13?), leaving no middle position. Is there no balm in Gilead, good Jesus? Why then, Lord, is the brokenness of your bride not healed (Jer. 8:22)? Why is her wound and bruise and swelling sore neither bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor soothed with oil? (Isa. 1:6.) Have you given your beloved enough to drink of the wine of compunction, Lord? When will you soothe her with oil—with your holy oil? [Col. 0160B] Yet “the oil of the sinner shall not anoint her.” For those on the opposite side also boast that they have oil. What do they sell but oil, when they flatter, promise honours, and offer gifts? This oil does not heal but rather tears apart. Therefore, as their wine, so also their oil. Their words and blows must be weighed in an equal balance. “My soul refused to be comforted” by the breasts of their consolation. For they, like sea-monsters, have laid bare their breasts and there nurse their young (Lam. 4:3), not the children of the Church. But the Church has her own breasts. Therefore immediately in her praise follows: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!” Recall, Lord Jesus, your wandering children to the sweetness of this milk, that from the mouths of nursing children you may perfect praise when you have destroyed the enemy and Victor. Therefore hasten and bring judgment forth unto victory, so that those who call upon your name may dwell as one; for in this unity you command blessing and life through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXI

*“How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride! Your breasts are more beautiful than wine,” etc.* (Song 4:10).

1. We must now touch the bride’s breasts lightly, for above they have already been pressed with particular care in more than one place, and I do not know whether they have been completely expressed. Perhaps, even when touched now, they will pour forth something new for us. [Col. 0160D] Who would not run eagerly and in good hope to breasts which the Bridegroom has taken such care to praise? These are the breasts of which Peter exhorts us, like newborn infants, to desire milk (1 Pet. 2:2). Does not this present praise seem to carry a certain force of invitation? “How beautiful are your breasts,” I say, “my sister, my bride!” Such abundant praise is not poured out simply and without emphasis; the very manner of utterance displays the speaker’s wonder and delight.

What, however, is the rationale of this sequence? Why, after the eye and the lock, does his discourse turn at once to the breasts? Or why is unity commended in the former, plurality mentioned in the latter? In the preceding chapter, to my mind, a certain ecstasy of mind and thought toward God is indicated; here, sobriety and moderation toward little ones. There one thing is necessary; here concern and doctrinal speech must be apportioned among many. There the unrestrained ardour of love, gathered into one, constrained and penetrating, wounds the very breast of the Beloved; here measured teaching and sober speech satisfy little ones with a kind of milky drink. You see how nothing intermediate is left out of the bride’s praise: with Paul, she either is beside herself for God or accommodates herself to us. “For charity urges us,” he says (2 Cor. 5:13–14). To what does it urge us? Surely not to ecstasy, but to accommodation. The former is a matter of desire; the latter, of service—there the summit of unrestrained affection, here of affection made temperate. It is good indeed to drink deeply there and to pour out here; first to be filled there, then to pour forth here; to be intoxicated there and to intoxicate here. Such reciprocity is good, if only it is such as it ought to be.

2. By your ordering, Lord, this alternation endures: the alternation of contemplation and consolation. Is not that person blessed whose every moment of life is spent either in inflicting the wounds of charity upon Christ or in offering breasts of mercy to those under his care? Whenever I—if ever, indeed, that happens—seem, intoxicated by the abundance of your house, Lord, to return from there with full breasts, they are dried out by so many various and burdensome tasks that rush upon me, so that breasts which had previously streamed abundantly with the milk of instruction and grace are soon returned parched. Blessed indeed is one who by some holy alternation keeps up such pursuits in himself, so as either to penetrate, if I may so speak, into the very heart and inner chamber of wisdom, or to bring back breasts filled from the abundance of that delight.

The bride indeed knows how to vary such turns. Therefore, in her praise, immediately after the ecstasy of contemplation comes discourse concerning the breasts of consolation and teaching: “How beautiful are your breasts!” The eye is pure, and the breasts are beautiful. The former is for the Bridegroom, the latter for the Bridegroom’s children. The former is therefore called one; the latter, many, because the breasts’ provision must be varied according to the diverse condition of those nursing. See how Paul became a Jew to the Jews, and as though himself without law to those without law, weak to the weak (1 Cor. 9:20–22). Does he not, as it were, apply as many breasts to disciples as he transforms himself into kinds of people? What else did he accomplish by such manifold adaptation than gently to infuse his teaching, like milk, into the tender minds of his hearers? He seems to abound in as many breasts as the ways in which, by ingenious art, he adapted himself to the capacity of the weak. “I became,” he says, “in your midst like a little child among little children, as a nurse cherishes her children” (1 Thess. 2:7).

3. And if you wish, I shall assign you two breasts of maternal mercy; indeed, Paul himself assigns them when he says that godliness is useful for all things, “having the consolation of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4:8). With these twin breasts a person who occupies in the Church the place of teacher and father ought to abound toward those under his care; he ought to be furnished with these breasts on right and left, so that those entrusted to him may drink milk and be satisfied from the breasts of his consolation. Regard one of them as the left and the other as the right: the left in temporal assistance, the right in spiritual consolation—“the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness; the one who gives, with simplicity” (Rom. 12:8).

One who, following the prince of the Apostles, provides for the flock entrusted to him not under compulsion but willingly (1 Pet. 5:2), offers here the left breast. And in Isaiah’s prophecy the Church is promised that she shall nurse at the breast of kings (Isa. 60:16). He says “breast,” not “breasts,” because it chiefly belongs to kings to nourish the Church with temporal goods; for this is her left hand, in which are riches and glory (Prov. 3:16). Paul instructs us concerning the right breast: “Comfort the fainthearted” (1 Thess. 5:14); and “Comfort him who is such a one, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow” (2 Cor. 2:7); likewise, “You who are spiritual, instruct such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. 6:1).

And, so to speak, there are some whose office provides only the left breast, such as the kings and princes mentioned above. And there are others whom the right of their office chiefly obliges to provide the right breast, such as the Lord’s priests and teachers, whose lips preserve knowledge and from whom the law of the Lord must be sought (Mal. 2:7). For these reap carnal things more particularly from the peoples subject to them, to whom they sow spiritual things. But those who renounce all possessions, take leave of temporal affairs, surrender themselves and all that is theirs to a monastery, pass entirely under an abbot’s authority, and henceforth leave themselves no concern for themselves—such persons must surely be nursed with the twofold breast of consolation. Therefore those who preside over such persons ought to lack neither breast, lest they seem to bear a mutilated and, as it were, truncated breast, content in an unbecoming way with one breast alone.

But those deprived of both hold this place in the Church to their own condemnation and, as regards others, dangerously, lest perhaps the tongue of the nursing child cling to its palate while the mother’s breasts are dry. This praise, uttered at present to the bride, is indeed foreign to them: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride!” Observe likewise that not all breasts are beautiful. “Praise is not comely in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15:9). “My son,” he says, “if sinners offer you milk, do not consent to them” (Prov. 1:10). See how he does not merely refuse to have certain breasts regarded as beautiful, but wishes them to be suspected. Therefore he commends these, so that you may know well to which you ought safely to have recourse.

4. “How beautiful are your breasts! Your breasts are better than wine.” He sets forth two things in praise of these breasts: beauty and efficacy. The former befits one who loves; the latter, one who suckles. For what does it matter to one being nursed if the breasts are beautiful, provided that they are breasts and overflow with wholesome milk? Thus he mentions beauty for his own sake, and the pleasantness of the milk for the sake of his own people. And if you do not understand this more aptly yourself, refer beauty to the loveliness of conduct; and what remains in the praise of the breasts, to teaching and instruction. Milk is sucked more sweetly where a life adorns the power of speech.

And if you wish to hear something spiritual, and a direct explanation of their beauty, I refer you to the pursuits of women who devote care and effort to bodily beauty and adornment, and have acquired the art. For what do they seek more earnestly in arranging the breast than that the breasts should not grow excessively large, end in an unshapely way, and occupy the space of the breast itself? Therefore they bind breasts that protrude and hang loose with breast-bands, remedying nature’s defect by art. For breasts are beautiful when they rise a little and swell moderately [Col. 0163B]: neither raised too high nor level with the rest of the flesh; as though restrained, but not pressed down; gently confined, not freely hanging loose.

By this example, whoever ought to utter good words, spiritual words [otherwise: consoling words], should imitate both women’s attention and their skill. Let him employ disciplined speech. Let not the breasts of his words hang loose; let them not be carried along without rule. Let them not occupy the breast and the inner chamber of the mind more than they adorn it. Let them not have more matter than grace, nor more flesh than milk. Let speech be pure and prudent, suited to the occasion. Let devotion be added to it, and let it preserve the proportions of beauty. Let it not have more of the mouth than of the breast, nor suffer an uncontrolled flow of milk. The breasts ought to come forth from the breast and remain attached to it, rather than the breast itself being transformed into them. “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks”: let it speak from that abundance [Col. 0163C], but not pour it all out.

The breasts must be restrained lest they overflow too greatly. You may see some, while they pursue consoling words beyond measure, lapse into trivialities; and while they want to cheer hearers wearied by a long silence and made, as it were, somewhat sad by listlessness, after useful things they let the wanton frivolity of their tongue flow into buffoonery. Thus they either sow beforehand or sow over a little wheat with much darnel. They speak pleasing things and turn the bread of teaching into laughter, as it is written: “For laughter they make bread” (Eccles. 10:19); but shortly after the laughter there is no bread—no bread of the saving word. The word of God must not be adulterated (2 Cor. 4:2), nor corrupted by an alien admixture.

Let it be content with its own breasts—the breasts of the two Testaments. Let these be fixed in your breast and memory [Col. 0163D]; let these supply you with consoling, milk-like speech; let these suggest what others may suck. Let them spring from your breast by the root, so that what you say is not affected, but uttered from pure and heartfelt feeling, according to that saying:

> If you wish me to weep, you yourself  
> Must first feel grief.

(Horace, *Art of Poetry*, vv. 102–103.)

Let the feeling of compassion and shared joy be born within you; but let it flow out for the instruction of hearers through the words of Holy Scripture, as through certain breasts. Let it do so modestly, because the matter is serious: let wantonness be absent and serenity present. For the beauty of breasts is enhanced if they rise a little and swell, [Col. 0164A] yet only moderately, so that they have as much authority as is sufficient and nothing of harshness.

5. For this reason the breasts are also called better than wine. Thus the praise of them immediately continues: “Your breasts are better than wine.” The breasts of grace, the breasts of consolation, are better than the wine of severity and harshness, because they are more effective and more suited to changing sorrowful and embittered dispositions, and to cherishing the weak and tender. They move more readily and nurture more sweetly. “A sweet word both softens enemies and multiplies friends” (Ecclus. 6:5). The word of the Gospel is sweet; that of the Law, harsh.

See how a sweet word converts the savage hearts of the nations, changing waves that are, as it were, marine and salty into the flavour of milk: “They shall suck the abundance of the sea as milk” (Deut. 33:19). This was said of the apostles under the figure of Zebulun and Issachar. Who today flows bitter and turbulent? Do not despair: apply the breasts, instil milk; perhaps tomorrow he too will flow milk-like. Who knows whether a small drop may not transform the whole mass? For “the Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power.”

The severity of the Law is barren and weak: it commands without grace and punishes without pardon; it lacks both breasts. It contains these things in prefiguration, but does not display them in action. Remember that you are a minister not of the Law but of the Gospel, a minister of Jesus, who in his Passion rejected the sourness of vinegar and at supper that of old wine. Novatian has no breast of pardon, nor Pelagius that of grace. The former proclaims the goodness of nature grown old and corrupted, and says that it suffices for righteousness; the latter removes the goodness of the divine nature [Col. 0164C] by denying repentance. The former, so to speak, calls back those who seek; the latter does not receive penitents. The former serves up oldness; the latter, severity. His teaching does not possess the milky newness of grace, nor this man’s sweetness.

“You, O God,” says the Psalmist, “have prepared in your sweetness for the poor” (Ps. 67:12 [68:10–11]). Pelagius is rich; he does not need this sweetness: it is born in him, not prepared for him. Pelagius says, “I have no need”; Novatian, “I grant no pardon.” One is excessively rich; the other excessively harsh. Prepare, Lord, prepare in your sweetness for your poor one, O God. You prepare; you restore; and only in your sweetness. Great is the abundance of sweetness sucked from your breasts, Lord. How often, after grave transgressions, have I approached these breasts and pressed them more earnestly; and how great an abundance of milk I drew forth, you, Lord, know. “Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20). It was enough for me to have riches reckoned to me if only I might deserve pardon; and behold, grace also abounded. I pressed one of the breasts, and both flowed in abundance [Col. 0164D].

Therefore your bride, made to drink the milk of grace and filled from the breasts of consolation, has herself learned to offer breasts rather than wine. For her breasts are better than wine. Wine turns sour with age; the breasts pour forth what is wholly new and wholly sweet. Finally, fear is cast out, and love never fails (1 Cor. 13:8). This is his new commandment, ever-fresh sweetness. Love cannot exist without being sweet.

6. Therefore your breasts are better than wine. Wine is not evil, but breasts are better. They are indeed better, yet they do not reject an admixture of wine. For a little later she will say: “I drank my wine with my milk” (Song 5:1). Yet it is better if she drinks milk alone and without wine, because wine contains terror, while the breasts contain the gentle caress of compassion and grace. Although wine can rightly and customarily be understood in a good sense, here, in comparison with breasts, it seems to signify something harsh, perhaps.

Her breasts are better than wine, because sweet and brotherly compassion is better than the hard and merciless disposition of an angry mind. Paul marks out as though they lacked breasts those whom he calls “without natural affection” (Rom. 1:31). The bride who clings to her Bridegroom cannot lack the breasts of devotion in a human breast. For he himself is a mountain full of breasts, a mountain of curds, a mountain rich in fatness. How could the bride receive nothing from so great an abundance of milk, when it has pleased him to dwell on this mountain? And if we cannot yet dwell on this mountain without interruption, let us return to it frequently; let us ascend and become intoxicated by its breasts. For Scripture says: “Let her breasts intoxicate you at all times, and delight continually in her love” (Prov. 5:19). See to what meaning it directs the interpretation of the breasts: to intoxication and the delight of love.

7. Why must we linger longer in seeking an explanation of the breasts? Let us rather seek to be intoxicated by them. For breasts are better than wine, because “mercy is better than lives” (Ps. 62:4 [63:3]); the affection of love is better than the affliction of the flesh, and the milky drink of spiritual newness is better than the wine of compunction. For there harsh things are displayed and tasted, while the old man [Col. 0165C] is repelled and destroyed; here, in newness of life, we receive the milky caresses of divine favour, signifying not flight but refuge. Wine is good indeed, but breasts are sweeter; compunction is good, but anointing is better.

“For the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” I see that your eagerness to listen has now been renewed. The fragrance of the bride’s ointments has stirred your desire. With an indiscriminate kind of hunger, today you wish ointments to be added to the breasts. Grant a postponement until morning. Let the breasts suffice today; tomorrow we shall come to the ointments, he granting fulfilment to our prayers who is both the commender and giver of the breasts and ointments of his bride, Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXII

“Your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments above all spices” (Song 4:10).

[Col. 0165D]

1. Brothers, I have only a little oil and ointment, while today you bring vessels so large and so empty? Do not take it as an insult that I call your vessels empty. By this I do not mean that they are void, but rather that your minds are eager and capable of receiving, and thus more capacious. Who could suffice to fill them? You attend to the bride’s ointments and to the abundance of her spices, as though account need not also be taken of the instrument through which they must flow to you. The material is abundant, certainly; yet nevertheless consider what the minister can do.

Let what you wish be done. I shall not plead poverty, lest you accuse me of failing to observe my promise. I shall pour the little oil I possess into immense vessels; and would that some Elisha might command it, whose power would grant a good outcome to our effort (4 Kings 4:1–7). What then? Are there not many Elishas sitting here, many prophets, or at least sons of prophets? All these command; and, if their merits were lower, their very number could supply the place of some one great person. Therefore I shall pour out something from the remnants of the ointments. For you remember that at the beginning of the book they were poured out abundantly and sufficiently, and perhaps their dregs have not yet been emptied. Am I now to exhaust them? Do not expect that from me; I do not presume it. The bride’s storehouse of ointments is fertile. There is no occasion for you to say of it: “Lay it bare, lay it bare even to its foundations.” Would that it might be granted me to be fixed in these dregs [Col. 0166B], and not merely to dip my foot in oil, as is written of Asher (Deut. 33:24).

Brothers, if we do not deserve to be immersed, with John the Evangelist, in a vessel of oil or an abundance of ointments; if we do not deserve so rich an anointing, shall we despair even of a dipping? Shall we despair at least of the fragrance? For it is precisely the fragrance that is so highly commended here: “And the fragrance of your ointments above all spices.” Breasts are beneficial that you may grow; ointments, that you may not fail. “Your breasts are better than wine, and the fragrance of your ointments above all spices.” And, to join today’s chapter to yesterday’s, let us say that breasts belong to the tender, ointments to the strong.

2. Let us compare these three things with one another: wines, breasts, and ointments. In wine lies the weakening of the old man; in the breast, the restoration of the new; in ointments, a certain delight. By wine the carnal sense is intoxicated, lulled to sleep, and overwhelmed; by the breast the new man is nourished; by ointments the mature person is delighted. In the first, the old man is brought to an end; in the second, the new man is restored; in the third, one now approaching perfection is affected with inexpressible joy. Is this not a good order: that you proceed from restoration to delight, from the first offerings of milk to the delights of ointments?

From the beginning of this Song, both of these—ointments and breasts—have been mentioned and joined together in the bride’s praises. Their grace is no small thing, since he repeats them so often in praise of his beloved, not content with mentioning them once. Do you not suppose that he took delight in these praises, which he recounts so affectionately and so frequently? There is also something for you to draw from such diligence in repeated praise: regard this repetition as an invitation to you. Run also in the fragrance of these ointments; rather, take care that these ointments should give fragrance in you, so that you too may be worthy to hear: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” Nor should you hear this only once; let the mouth of the Beloved repeat these praises to you.

Let the ointments in you be fresh and always, as it were, new: let them not dry up, wither away, or be emptied. The emptied oil is the name of the Beloved. But see that it may be emptied out into you, not emptied away from you. It is good if you begin with the bride from ointments; but it is not good unless you are brought to completion in ointments. Otherwise Paul says to you: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being completed in the flesh?” (Gal. 3:3). [Col. 0167A] You are well anointed if you are anointed in the Spirit. Therefore be so anointed that the flesh in you is changed because of the oil. Let not the oil be changed or diminished because of the flesh.

Let the oil—indeed, the ointment—not depart from your head, but overflow and descend even to the feet; for both in Christ Jesus were not so much anointed as drenched with ointment. Let the oil enter your inner being and be absorbed by your very affections, so that all carnality in you may be changed because of the oil. For the time will come when the flesh also will be changed because of the oil. “He was anointed and drenched with the oil of gladness above his companions” (Ps. 44:8 [45:7]). Therefore, before the time of resurrection, he alone could say: “My flesh has been changed because of oil” (Ps. 108:24 [109:24]). Rightly did flesh free from carnality anticipate the common hour of transformation. O desirable hour! O sweet ointment! When and through which flesh dissolved shall ascend into incorruption! Before that condition, why should it not descend into corruption?

3. Yesterday, brothers, you saw—you looked upon with tearful eyes—wretched flesh changed, flesh descending from corruptibility into corruption; descending indeed slowly and with delay, and unable to decay altogether. Corruption itself seemed to wish to take possession by inheritance of the body it had occupied; and, lest it cease to rot, it did not allow it to have entirely rotted away. It held back its own powers, as though unwilling quickly to consume the substance, so that it might infect it longer. For when flesh has been reduced to dust, what more is there for corruption to do? “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass. The grass has dried up, and the flower has fallen” (Isa. 40:6–7).

By these words the prophet expressed the swiftness of the decline by which flesh, flourishing and vigorous with vital warmth, beautiful with rosy colour, yet cut off from the land of the living, dries up suddenly indeed but does not rot so quickly. Thus, by comparison with grass, he showed the speed of sudden change; he did not depict the horror of slow and putrid decay. In that corpse you could see bones that had been covered: some laid bare, others not so much still covered as defiled and wrapped in decay. Prolonged corruption raged in the wretched flesh and, reaching mightily from end to end, miserably scattered everything. I too could have said: “He ordered all the things of his flesh,” since that scattering served the will of divine ordering [Col. 0167D].

A wretched transformation, but a beautiful purpose: God was pleased that the glory of the flesh should be brought to dust only through decay. Let death rage; let corruption itself rage and spread through human flesh. Let it despoil it as much as it can; let it bring it first to pus, then to ashes. For it can reach this point and no further: it can bring the glory of the flesh to dust. It cannot consume the substance of the flesh into nothing, nor consume it utterly, nor possess it for ever. “Until the heavens are worn away, he shall not rise” (Job 14:12); yet then he shall rise. For then “the Lord will pour out of his Spirit upon all flesh” (Joel 2:28); then the flesh of the saints will be changed because of the oil, because the Spirit of the Lord has anointed it. “For we shall all rise, but we shall not all be changed” (1 Cor. 15:51).

4. O how great is the power of that ointment, before whose face the yoke of such ancient corruption shall decay, and flesh consumed by sufferings shall return to the days of its youth—a youth that will not pass away as another age succeeds it. Certainly effective is the ointment through which such inveterate brokenness will be healed and such long-standing putrefaction transformed into incorruptible health.

This ointment belongs especially to the Church. Therefore Christians are called her children after her Bridegroom, Christ—that is, the Anointed One. And we have already received this ointment in Baptism. But as there it worked for sanctification, so at the end of time it will work for that glorious transformation, when the flesh will be changed because of the oil. Who knows whether, meanwhile, disease is permitted to rage, so that the power of the remedy may be revealed from the violence of the disease? Rightly, therefore, is the fragrance of this ointment commended, because we smell its grace as though still from afar.

What other antidote could you give, so effective for soothing every desolation that may come upon the mind, as the most certain hope of the resurrection to come and of that blessed transformation? The teaching of the Gentiles does not have belief in resurrection, and the Jewish tradition does not possess its character [Col. 0168B]. The former do not believe; the latter think less fully, and not altogether rightly, concerning the spiritual glory of resurrection and likeness to the angels. The Gentiles do not draw the fragrance of this ointment; the Jews draw not its own proper fragrance, but—I know not what—another and counterfeit fragrance in its place. With the Church alone the fragrance of that ointment exists both whole and proper. Therefore the fragrance of her ointments is above all spices.

5. Impassibility and patience are good ointments. By the former, resurrected flesh will be unable to suffer harm; by the latter, the devout mind remains uninjured amid provocations and injuries. By the former, in the peaceful and unshaken right of our flesh, we possess the earth as an inheritance; by the latter, we possess the soul itself. “In your patience,” he says, “you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21:19). What else is patience but a certain fragrance, as it were, of future impassibility? There no evils are inflicted; here, by the benefit of patience, as by some soothing ointment [Col. 0168D], even the evils inflicted are not felt.

This is certainly an effective and useful ointment: amid the afflictions of the flesh it guards the mind against injury, and keeps it from being broken down, failing, or wearying. I proclaim the usefulness of this ointment; perhaps you seek its pleasure. I shall not fail you even in this, and shall show you a still more excellent anointing. “Count it all joy, my brothers, whenever you fall into various trials” (Jas. 1:2). Does not one who knows how to rejoice in adversity seem to you drenched with a more excellent ointment than one who has merely learned not to be saddened by it? For it is less to exclude pain than to introduce joy.

Finally, the bride of Christ is commanded not merely to endure enemies but also to love them: “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:35). Therefore her ointments are good: in sorrowful circumstances they breathe joy, and toward enemies they offer love. For love is greater than all sacrifices and burnt offerings. Therefore the fragrance of your ointments excels all spices. The spice of prayer is certainly good, and incense is good; but hear what the Gospel prefers: “If you offer your gift at the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled with your brother” (Matt. 5:23–24). You see clearly how the ointment of reconciliation is preferred to the spice of prayer.

What is reconciliation except the renewed bringing together of minds that are at variance? And concerning concord and brotherly love the Psalm says to you: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132:1 [133:1]). This is, according to Paul, the more excellent way, greater than other gifts of grace (1 Cor. 12:31 and ch. 13), as though greater than all spices. This ointment descends from the head to the beard and to the edge of the garment (Ps. 132:2 [133:2]). For Christ our head first loved us, that we might love him.

6. Therefore the bride says that she runs in the fragrance of the anointing—that is, in the emulation of love. She does not say, “of ointment,” but “of ointments,” because love is twofold. One love is that by which we love him because he first loved us; the other is that by which we love one another, just as he loved us. From him we have both the example and the gift of each love. For he both shows the way of love and supplies its power. Therefore it is written: “We shall run in the fragrance of his ointments” [Col. 0169C] (Song 1:3).

Does not that very union and sweetness—the love of Father and Son, and their mutual embrace through the Spirit of both—bathe us in a welcome fragrance and invite us to a like emulation, that we too may be one as they themselves are one? Blessed indeed is the person who follows and runs in the fragrance of that love, that sweetness, that affection, that anointing. For the Spirit himself anoints, as it were, both parties whom he joins in so great a sweetness of love. Let us imitate this anointing; let us run in its fragrance.

Brotherly love is an emulation and, as it were, an image of that divine and essential unity; it is a kind of shadow of that ointment, sweetness, and mutual love. “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! Like ointment on the head, which descends” (Ps. 132:1–2 [133:1–2]), and so forth. And would that some shadow of this ointment might descend upon us from our head which is above, so that we too may deserve to hear: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.”

Run through the other virtues in your mind and recount the use and works of each. Nothing in them breathes as sweetly as love from a pure heart. What fragrance can fasts breathe for you, what fragrance almsgiving, if love does not give fragrance to them? Even chastity and endurance of sufferings—if they are not seasoned with love—what sweet fragrance can they pour out for you? “If,” Paul says, “I hand over my body so that I may burn,” and melt wholly in the fire like incense-spice, “but do not have love, I gain nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3). What is not offered with grace cannot be received graciously. Love is the root; the other virtues, like branches, spring from it and therefore ought to share in its richness. What use is a branch in a good olive tree if the richness and grace of the root is not felt in it? So also virtues and the works of virtues are of no use unless the power of love and affection breathes in them.

7. Mary, whose name from the Gospel has just now also sounded in your hearing—what other fragrance was there in her but love? “Many sins were forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:37, 47). Good is the fragrance of this ointment, whose grace utterly removed the stench of old corruption and filled the whole house of the Church with welcome sweetness. While the King was at his table, she broke an alabaster vessel of genuine nard and poured it over the head of him who reclined there (Mark 14:3). That nard gave its fragrance, still gives it, and will give it until the end of the age.

She burned on the altar of her breast a good spice for Christ the Lord, as though her heart had been emptied out as ointment and melted by the flame of love. When the Lord had been buried, see how devotedly and diligently she visits the tomb. She goes and returns; she sees angels; she summons the apostles; when they depart, she does not depart. “My heart burns,” she says; “I desire to see my God; I seek him and do not find him.” Does not this anxiety of one seeking seem to you to breathe the fragrance of exceptional love? As these words are sung in memory of her, are not those who sing them also inflamed?

Finally, Jesus himself, whom she desires, smells the fragrance of that ointment and, as it were, runs to her in the fragrance of vehement love. Why should he not gladly return to kindred ointments? As if in the early morning he hastens to her, and “rising early on the first day of the week, he first appeared to Mary” (Mark 16:1–9). He anoints her with the oil of gladness above her companions by revealing himself to her now risen in glory. He changes her spices into ointments and transforms her desires into delight.

8. It seems to me that the person who prays and longs offers a spice. But that person is drenched with ointment when he obtains an abundance of the one he loves, when he delights in that one's presence. It is indeed good to pray for and desire the Lord; but it is better to love, possess, and enjoy him. And, if I may put it so, when you do not have him, it is good to beg, but better to eat. If you can love him while absent, how much more when he is present, when he grants you an abundance of himself, when experience supplies sweet nourishment to love?

For then the soul is anointed more spiritually and more abundantly, when it is joined more closely to him who was anointed with Spirit and power. Then it is especially pleasing to the Beloved; then it breathes a sweeter fragrance, when it has wholly poured itself into him and, clinging to him, breathes the ointment of union—the ointment that overflows from the Bridegroom into the bride. That dwelling together in unity breathes a wholly pleasant and sweet fragrance, “like ointment on the head, which descends,” and so forth. Therefore the fragrance of her ointments is above all spices.

And even if the bride herself has other ointments, none is such as that which descends into her, especially at the time when she clings to the Beloved, when she remains between his breasts, when she lies in the inner chamber of the heart. Finally, when the King is at his table, then the bride’s nard spreads its fragrance: a fragrance good above all spices, the fragrance of the Bridegroom—or rather, the Bridegroom as fragrance. For he himself is the ointment of his beloved; he himself is the fragrance. For in his beloved he is pleased with himself; he breathes fragrance. And would that this ointment might not depart from our head, and that the smoke of its fragrance might rise from our hearts for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIII

“The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices” (Song 4:10).

1. This day, solemn through the annual celebration of the Lord’s Resurrection, compels me to renew my discourse by taking up again the subject of ointments. Today the women come with spices (Mark 16:1); Nicodemus also comes, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about one hundred pounds (John 19:39); Mary Magdalene herself comes beforehand to anoint the body of Jesus for burial (Mark 14:8). You see how great are the mysteries celebrated in ointments. Great mysteries indeed; and who is fit for them? Who will worthily determine the distinctions among ointments or explain their particular character? This discussion belongs to one who has experienced, not one who guesses. For it is not easy for anyone to speak about ointments unless anointing itself has taught him.

Today the Lord has been anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, yet not without his companions. For how is one a companion who does not congratulate, does not rejoice together, who does not rise with the Risen One into new joy? The occasion is fitting indeed for discussing ointments with you, but far more fitting for breathing their fragrance. You demand a discourse from me, and I ask from you the fragrance of ointments. On what grounds do you, together with the holy women, visit the tomb of the Lord Jesus if you bring to it no spiritual ointment? Today the Lord’s flesh has been gloriously changed because of the oil. Does it not seem fitting that our hearts too should be changed and transformed into spiritual oil, into oil of exultation and joy?

I had begun a discourse on ointments, and behold, our discussion has stuck upon oil. What has oil to do with ointments? Much indeed; and although it is not identical with them in every respect, it approaches and resembles them in some measure. For oil, though it does not give fragrance, nevertheless softens: it does not smell pleasantly, but you are well anointed by it. Here, however, he commends in the bride’s ointments not so much their anointing as their fragrance: “And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.”

2. Not every soul abounds in fragrant ointments, just as the woman in the book of Kings says to the prophet: “There is nothing in my house except a little oil with which I may be anointed” (4 Kings 4:2). This woman has no ointments composed of fragrant ingredients, but simple, scant oil for anointing. Mary Magdalene—the woman of the Gospel, not of the Law—brings ointment of costly spikenard, not a little, but a whole pound (John 12:3). Simon himself is rebuked by the Lord because he did not even anoint his head with oil, while she drenched his head with ointment (Luke 7:46).

You see how ointments, and fragrant ointments, are preferred to oil. For in addition to their effect of anointing, ointments confer a certain benefit of spiritual fragrance. Anointing is more limited, but fragrance spreads itself to more people. Even one who alone is anointed does not alone smell the fragrance. This power is communal if it diffuses itself to all. Thus, anointing belongs to you; fragrance belongs both to others and to you.

He is well anointed and gives good fragrance who loves what is good before God and provides what is good before human beings. “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your modesty be known to all people” (Phil. 4:4–5). Refer joy to ointments, and the being known for modesty to fragrance. Hear how Paul himself connects fragrance with knowledge: “He makes manifest through us in every place the fragrance of his knowledge” (2 Cor. 2:14). Thus spiritual rejoicing in the Lord and modest outward conduct—joy and being known—are both good ointment and good fragrance.

He is well anointed to whom the Lord is pleasing in the inward joy of conscience, who delights in him; and he gives good fragrance who, with Paul, pleases all people in all things (1 Cor. 10:33), and pleases them only in the Lord. In his modest bearing, judicious action, and learned speech, the ointments of inward cheerfulness and grace breathe fragrance. He is well anointed who glories in the Lord; and he gives good fragrance through whom the Lord is glorified before human beings. The fragrance of the one who gives fragrance itself breathes sweetly, if he does not glory in commending himself, but in commending the Lord through himself.

3. “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” Do you wish me to set out for you the difference between ointments and spices? The very wording of the Song appears to make the distinction, not rejecting spices but preferring ointments. As far as I can find a difference in things so similar and joined together, ointments may seem to be gifts of graces conferred in the Holy Spirit, while spices are the services themselves devoutly rendered. In works and offices of honourable conduct there is a certain natural attractiveness; in ointments there is the grace of the Spirit.

You read that the Lord Jesus was anointed with Spirit and power; so it was fitting that his bride should be made like him in this, that she too should be anointed with Spirit and power. The spices of virtues are indeed good and seem to give fragrance in themselves; yet they breathe a fuller fragrance when they are sprinkled with the sweet fragrance of the Spirit’s anointing. Works themselves and virtues may be shared by us with those outside; ointments cannot be. Finally, although such works are beautiful in themselves, they please more when they proceed from the Spirit.

How do those who see good works glorify God except because they understand that the good work both comes from God and returns to him? If there are any good things in me, they are more pleasing to me when they are reckoned to Christ’s grace, when his anointing in me is commended, when the Spirit breathes fragrance, than when the capacity of free choice by nature or the fruit of industry is praised. Finally, without the anointing of the Spirit, both nature is deprived of freedom [Note: [Col. 0171D] See Sermon 39, nos. 3–4.], [Col. 0173A] virtue is deprived of truth, and work of merit. For without the grace of the Spirit and faith in Christ, both the effort of the will lacks effect, the virtue that appears to exist is counterfeit, and the work does not attain the fruit of eternal reward. Therefore the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices. For whatever the spices may be, they do not spread a fragrance of unmingled sweetness unless the ointments of spiritual grace breathe fragrance and overflow within them.

4. Do you wish me to set before you some ointment whose fragrance surpasses all the spices of ecclesiastical gifts? What scent in the Church gives forth a sweeter fragrance than that of mercy and forgiveness? How many have run after the fragrance of this ointment, and by it have been incorporated and united to Christ? It rightly gives forth fragrance, because in a moment it removes the stench of former corruption and of sin long established from of old [Col. 0173B]. How foul-smelling was that woman in the city, named Mary, when she came to Jesus’ feet in the house of Simon the leper! How much she stank to Simon himself, who could not bear the horror of her presence! How foul-smelling, I say, she came to Jesus; and behold, now throughout the whole world the fragrance of her repentance, love, and the grace which she received is spread abroad. Christ’s grace is not tardy: at the very banquet at which this woman washed, wiped, and anointed the Lord’s feet, she herself was washed, cleansed, and anointed, and by the Lord’s own testimony is preferred to the Pharisee (Luke 7:37–50). For Christ’s mercy is neither sparing nor slow: it repays more, and repays within the hour. What wonder that pardon comes to meet one who repents, when patience itself leads to repentance? Consider the woman caught in adultery and left standing in the midst: how she gave forth the fragrance of Jesus’ mercy, though formerly she stank from the guilt of adultery (John 8:3–11). Read through the Gospel: everywhere you will find Jesus swift and abundant in forgiveness. Finally, even if a man has been dead four days and the report of his notorious crime already stinks: where Jesus calls him forth and brings him out from the tomb of depraved habit, where Jesus unbinds him and pours in the ointment of forgiveness, immediately every stench of old decay flees from his face. For who will charge again what the Lord does not impute? Who will retain offences which he himself forgives? What he wipes out cannot smell foul. “Lord,” says Martha, “he has been dead four days, and already he stinks” (John 11:39–44). You are mistaken, Martha: Jesus does not so much flee foul smells as he is accustomed to drive away the stench itself [Col. 0173D]. He gave his Church an example: as he did to us, so we also should do to one another. These are the ointments he left to her.

5. How many, despairing of themselves, would have given themselves over to every uncleanness and avarice, and hurled themselves headlong into the abyss of every vice, had they not been drawn back by the fragrance of this remedy? “I should be afflicted,” he says, “if I did not know the mercies of the Lord” (*Responsory for the First Sunday of Lent, according to the Roman Breviary*): mercies in the Head, and mercies in his body, which is the Church. For she too received from the Lord what she hands on to her children: she, I say, received mercy [Col. 0174A] as a gift, and also as a command, that she might be a minister of compassion. It is good indeed to administer mercy, but better to be merciful. Render mercy, which you owe by reason of your office, from your heart. Express within yourself Christ’s disposition, whose office and place you have assumed. You are the minister of him who is rich in mercy. Do not prove harsh in what belongs to another. Dispense to those converted by you a measure of this ointment in due season. “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?” Let your disposition be merciful, for the effect of pardon belongs to the Lord. One who bears a wounded conscience, a covered [variant: blind] wound beneath the breast, will safely entrust himself to you if he perceives with you the fragrance of this ointment. “If you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice,’ you would never have condemned the innocent” [Col. 0174B] (Matt. 12:7). Not so, Lord, not so: you condemn not merely the innocent, but not even the guilty; rather, you correct them. “The righteous man will correct me in mercy; but let not the oil of the sinner make my head fat” (Ps. 140:5 [Vulgate]).
