Here the Psalmist distinguishes oil from oil: the oil of flattery from the oil of compassion. The former softens and wounds; the latter softens and heals. Does not the ointment through which all sins are so easily erased give forth a good fragrance to you beyond all spices? That younger son, coming to himself, caught from a far country and among herds of swine the rich abundance of this ointment in his father; his father’s clemency began to fragrance him. Therefore he was drawn and began to run to his father in the fragrance of his ointments. See the ready, see the overflowing [Col. 0174C] grace of the Lord Jesus: he ought to rejoice and feast with his repentant son (Luke 15:11–32). He remains in Zacchaeus’ house and admits the tax collector to discipleship (Luke 19:2–10); and with Lazarus, after the tomb, he restores a banquet (John 12:1–2). He does not know how to reproach those to whom he is gracious; he does not know a divided clemency; those whom he pardons he receives into the favour of intimacy.

6. Good, therefore, is the ointment of mercy: it forgives sins, goes before merits, accompanies them, and adds to them. It gives forth fragrance above all spices, because the entire Church of saints depends more upon mercy than upon merits. Finally, the ointment of forgiveness is the last sacrament. This ointment is common and beneficial both to sinners and to the righteous. For there are certain other ointments peculiar to saints and suited to them alone [Col. 0174D]. There are ointments which heal; ointments which nourish; ointments which sanctify; and ointments which delight. The first drive away sickness; the second give liveliness to those already well; the third sanctify for the work of ministry, as do royal and priestly ointment; the fourth are no longer for work but for repose, not for administration but for love, glory, delight, and the use of bridegroom and bride. It is good to linger among ointments; but since elsewhere there has been sufficient discussion of the distinction among ointments [Note: [Col. 0173D] Bernard, *Sermon 10 on the Song of Songs*], let us now briefly distinguish the ways of anointing. Some are touched, some sprinkled, some anointed, and some drenched [Col. 0175A]. Reread the Pentateuch; turn again to the Gospel; and apply to moral dispositions these differences of anointing which you observe performed bodily and outwardly. I am not now speaking about the nature of ointments, but about the measure of anointing. Some indeed make use of ointments once, others more often, others always. Abundance is good, provided grace is present too. Neither seems lacking in the bride’s ointments, neither sweetness nor abundance, whose fragrance surpasses all spices.

7. We have applied this praise to the Church in general; let us turn our discourse to some particular person in the Church, who, by a singular benefit of love and intimacy, ought to be reckoned worthy of the name of bride, one in whom ointments breathe abundantly not merely for necessity, but [Col. 0175B] for dignity and delight. I would not suppose that she has been merely touched in part by the sacred unguent, or sprinkled piecemeal, but drenched and more richly anointed for the bridegroom’s delights. With this bridegroom are copious storehouses of spices, pouring forth from this one into that one, as royal wealth ought to do. Yet it is credible that the queen breathes forth the fragrance of more excellent ointments. Nevertheless, nothing is stated to us regarding the efficacy of these ointments, except that their fragrance alone is commended. The text does not say what the anointing accomplishes, content merely to mention delights—delights especially suited to kindle spiritual love. Anointing is felt by touch alone when poured upon the flesh. Fragrance, escaping touch, permits itself to be perceived only by the spirit. The liquid [Col. 0175C] of ointment gradually flows downward; its fragrance, however, with complete ease rises upward, enters the brain, and refreshes as it occupies the seat of the senses. Therefore the fragrance of ointments is much subtler and loftier, much more so than their liquid. And in flattering the bride, it was fitting to mention what is more delicate, more adapted to spiritual delights, and less burdened with sediment. Others need ointments and oil in order either to soothe or alter the movements of the flesh. But this bride, now no longer in the flesh but in the spirit, as befits the Lord’s bride, abounds in spiritual delights. “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” Even if fragrance alone is mentioned, perhaps it does not work alone: the anointing works as well. “Those who belong to Christ,” says the Apostle, “have crucified [Col. 0175D] their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24). Where there is anointing, crucifixion does not seem necessary. The one mortifies; the other transforms. Crucifixion indeed entails the sensation of pain, but anointing gentleness. Sweet is the anointing, yet effective: without injury, it preserves the flesh unharmed from corruption by the oil of exultation and gladness; it removes corruption and causes no torment. Ointments precede and follow the passion of the Lord Jesus, so that you too may learn to ease whatever suffering there is in your flesh by the abundant pouring out of ointments. He was anointed twice, both that he might not feel the violence of the cross and that he might attain the newness of his resurrection, and that by this, as it were, sacrament he might commend the grace of spiritual anointing. Good, then, is the ointment [Col. 0176A] whose liquid, so to speak, transforms the flesh and whose fragrance refreshes the spirit.

8. To summarize: anointing is the mind’s exultation; fragrance, prayer. Anointing is spiritual joy; fragrance is an outward knowledge, through reputation, of things borne in the soul. Anointing is inward delight; fragrance is a kind of desire sweetly flowing from the experience of joys. Therefore, “the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” For every incense of prayer, and every vehemence of desire, is surpassed by that desire born from the delight of heavenly joys, and by the longing which, from the Spirit’s anointing, breathes out abundantly like a certain most sweet fragrance. Good is this desire: it possesses the power of prayer and lacks the burden of affliction. The bride [Col. 0176B] is she to whom this privilege of ointment and fragrance is assigned. What wonder if she gives forth a more excellent fragrance, she who is more specially anointed? What wonder if she longs more eagerly, she who tastes more sweetly? For it is fitting that she pray more abundantly who clings more closely. Cleaving to the Bridegroom, she has become one spirit with him. Therefore none but the Spirit gives forth fragrance in her—the Spirit who anointed her and intercedes for her with inexpressible affections. For this reason the fragrance of her ointments is above all spices. And in the Apocalypse you read of bowls full of fragrances, which are the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8). As Exodus teaches, spices are assigned to two uses: namely, chrism and incense (Exod. 25; 30).

9. Do not these two things seem even now to be joined in the bride’s praises? Her ointments are both ointments and very fragrant; for their fragrance is above all spices. Ointment, as has been said, is the reception of gifts; fragrance is thanksgiving arising from that reception, desire for eternal things, and a certain humble disposition amid sublime goods [Col. 0176C]. For the prayer of one who humbles himself penetrates the very clouds (Sir. 35:21). Do you see how the fragrance of humble prayer rises? That Pharisee went up into the temple to pray, but the fragrance of his prayer did not know how to rise. He recounts to himself the gifts of graces divinely bestowed upon him, and as it were enumerates his ointments. “I am not,” he says, “like other men—robbers, unjust, adulterers.” Do you hear above whom he boasts that he is anointed? His glory lies in the shame of others. It is no great glory, though it seems great to him. It smells sweet to himself, yet not above spices but above the sulphur [Col. 0176D] of others. You have heard above whom he is preferred; now hear what graces the ointments in which the Pharisee boasts bear in themselves. “I fast twice in the week; I give tithes of all that I possess; and if I have defrauded anyone, I restore fourfold.” These give forth the fragrance of the elementary observances of the Law, not evangelical teaching [variant: perfection]. He does not fast at all times; he does not renounce all that he possesses, so as to have nothing from which he may give either firstfruits or tithes. He restores what he has defrauded fourfold; he does not allow himself to be defrauded; he does not give up the remainder to one who takes away a portion; he does not say that he counts injuries received as favours. Pharisee, among feeble works you swell beyond measure. Pharisee, you do not ask, but inflict insults on the tax collector standing near. [Col. 0177A] You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is slight. Concerning your works it is slight; concerning your pre-eminence it is untrue. Two things in your prayer do not so much give fragrance as stink: pride and lukewarmness. Pride lies in your reproaching the tax collector; lukewarmness, certainly, in your asking absolutely nothing. For how could a prayer not grow lukewarm when it is filled with the wind of self-exaltation and emptiness? Pharisee, you do not pray, but display yourself. You bear witness concerning yourself, and your testimony is not true. Hear, then, the testimony of Truth: “Amen, amen, I say to you, this man went down to his house justified rather than that man” (Luke 18:10–14).—“For it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom God commends” (2 Cor. 10:18). Therefore blessed is the soul to which so excellent a commendation is pronounced by Truth itself [Col. 0177B]: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” A great testimony was rendered to the tax collector; but to this woman, to whom these praises are sung, a far greater one is rendered. He went down justified rather than the Pharisee—that is, rather than a proud man, an unjust man—to his own house; but the fragrance of this woman’s ointments surpasses all spices. A mighty commendation; yet she receives testimony not from a human being, but from him who searches hearts, who both dwells and works in her heart through faith and love. She does not commend herself; she does not disparage others. For her lips are a dripping honeycomb. This chapter follows in order, but it cannot be treated today. Tomorrow’s discourse will give your hearing and eagerness joy [Col. 0177C] and gladness in the Lord Jesus. May he deign to grant this, he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XXXIV. “Your lips, O bride, are a dripping honeycomb,” etc. (Song of Songs 4:11)

1. “Your lips, O bride, are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue; the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense.” Very sweet indeed are the words now addressed to the bride. But you ask how these fit with what precedes. Let it suffice that I have once reminded you that the law of praise is free from the necessity of continuity. It does not maintain a sequence, but employs a wandering freedom. Where the rationale of praises is in question, order cannot indeed be demanded; yet neither should it be rejected if it can be supplied. Immediately after the praise of ointments, the grace of her lips [Col. 0177D] is brought forward. For what do you know whether this grace poured out upon her lips comes from the power of ointment? Turn again to the Gospel, and you will find something similar said of the Bridegroom himself. “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim good news to the poor” (Isa. 61:1; Luke 4:18). Thus it was fitting that the bride also should be made like the Bridegroom in this: that she too should be anointed by the Spirit’s anointing for the work of the Gospel. For the Spirit anoints both for office and for effectiveness. Both come from him: the rank of ministry and the grace of ministering. Without grace, rank is useless; and without rank, the exercise of grace is presumptuous. “How are they to preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10:15); or how are they to be sent unless they are anointed? As it is written: “The Spirit of the Lord anointed me; he sent me to proclaim good news to the poor.” The Spirit ordains [Col. 0178A] to office; the Spirit also opens the mouth and forms it for use. Therefore, in the bride’s praises, he first treats of her ointments and then of the sweetness of her lips: because, though she speaks sweet things, it is not she herself who speaks, but the Spirit of the Bridegroom speaking in her. Finally, hear what the Bridegroom Jesus himself promises to the first bride, that is, to the Apostles, who received the firstfruits of the Spirit: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist” (Luke 21:15). Great indeed is the power of divine speech: it can overcome opponents and draw those who do not oppose. And this itself belongs to her praises: what is now under discussion pertains more to tender persuasion than to the effect of refutation. “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” It is familiar to her, and almost innate, to speak sweetly. But whenever she rebukes harshly, that is foreign to her, brought in from afar rather than implanted; she is not so inclined, but rather constrained. When she speaks sweetly, she speaks from what is her own; but when she speaks harshly, this belongs not to the quality of her mouth but to the perversity of her hearers. Therefore the Bridegroom praises the bride for what is her own and familiar when he says: “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb” [Col. 0178B].

2. But since you have now heard something concerning the connection, do you wish me also to explain the content of this praise? This praise embraces three things: sweetness, fullness, and restraint. Sweetness is considered in its kind; fullness in its abundance; restraint in its outflow. Why do I say outflow? It is dripping rather than pouring out. For, “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” What need is there to dwell in assigning each point? You yourselves know that a honeycomb pours out nothing but sweetness, and pours it out only from fullness. And even from that fullness it does not pour out the whole. Therefore it is not, “Your lips are a pouring honeycomb,” but, “a dripping honeycomb.” Thus in the bride’s lips there are sweetness alone, full sweetness, and temperate sweetness. It is possessed fully, yet not poured forth in full [Col. 0178C], but according as the capacity of the hearers requires. Do you wish also to have the bride’s own testimony concerning her lips? “How sweet are your words to my palate,” she says, “more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118:103 [Vulgate]). The bride’s lips are indeed sweet, for the Lord’s utterances drip from them. This sweetness belongs to the Lord’s utterances. For she does not speak from herself, but as the Lord’s sayings; therefore grace has been poured out upon her lips. Receive now, in part, what kinds of honeys the sacred honeycomb of utterance drips, and the measure which, as God has apportioned to each vessel, it pours into it. It forgives, permits, promises, and sends beforehand. It forgives offences, permits weaknesses, promises eternal things, and sends ahead certain firstfruits of those very things. Among the perfect it speaks wisdom—not the wisdom of this world, but God’s wisdom hidden in mystery—and among those less spiritually wise it judges itself to know nothing but Christ Jesus, and him crucified. It exhorts to perfection, but does not compel; rather, it consoles the fainthearted, supports the weak, and, if it rebukes the restless, the rebuke itself tastes of maternal sweetness. It has compassion upon one who sins, pardons one who turns back, and sets no number or, as it were, fixed boundary to its pardons which it may not overstep, since it is commanded to forgive seventy times seven times in a day the sins of one confessing so often [Col. 0179A] (Matt. 18:22).

3. See how great is the abundance of sweetness in the bride’s lips: as often as you yourself overflow into evil, so often, if you turn back, she drips good upon you and is not exhausted by repeated acts of pardon. Finally, after the likeness of God’s angels, she does not insult but rejoices over a sinner doing repentance (Luke 15:10). It is good, then, to give an attentive ear to her lips. For the Lord also inclines his ear to her prayers, and thus summons and invites your affection in such a way as to reveal his own. Speak, bride, what you speak, because your beloved listens with desire whether you are discoursing about him or conversing with him. But when the bride speaks to the Bridegroom himself, [Col. 0179B] she then speaks in the speech of a sweeter lip and with another tongue. Then the lips of the heart truly drip the honeys of divine delight; indeed, they do not so much drip as flow, because at that moment the entire soul is transformed into honeyed affections. Blessed interchange, when certain streams of honey flow from the bride’s heart into the beloved, and from him overflow into the bride. For these rivers of honey return to the place from which they go out, so as to flow again. Good honeycombs in the lips of Bridegroom and bride, pouring forth from one to the other and mutually sprinkling the sweetness of love. He sprinkles grace from above; she offers thanksgiving from below. Jesus himself produced drops of this honeyed dew within the beloved soul. Utterly sweet are the drops of dew: those affections of divine love, when the bride, wholly melted, drips in the presence of him [Col. 0179C] whom she loves, in the presence of her God. Therefore her lips are as a dripping honeycomb, because the kindling of a mind so disposed is intensely sweet, yet quickly cut short, owing to that sweet rapture of the mind into ecstasy and its swift interruption.

4. “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb.” I would certainly judge these lips to have been cleansed, from which Jesus himself judges that he draws honeyed sweetness. Isaiah’s lips are cleansed by tongs and a coal from the altar touching them (Isa. 6:6–7). “The Lord,” says another, “sent forth his hand and touched my mouth” (Jer. 1:9). She who is the bride desires neither a coal nor a finger, but the touch of a mouth. “Let him kiss me,” she says, “with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1): lips are owed to lips. For sweetness would not be expressed from the bride’s lips [Col. 0179D] unless the lips of the beloved were impressed upon them. And what but the sweetness of a kiss makes him rejoice that he is delighted by what he draws from the bride’s lips, when he says, “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb”? For both reasons: for the kiss of love and for the oracle of truth. “Your lips,” he says, “are a dripping honeycomb; honey and milk are under your tongue.” This now properly concerns the grace of speech. The use of lips is also for kissing; that of the tongue, however, is only for speech. Not sweetness alone resounds in the tongue, but “honey and milk are under your tongue.” A sweetness which merely resounds on the tongue and is not felt beneath it is feigned. That is a scant sweetness which is wholly on the lips and tongue and whose greater part is not under the tongue. Sweetness is not merely in her tongue, nor is it all on her tongue; rather, as he who knows bears witness: [Col. 0180A] “honey and milk are under your tongue.” Therefore she pours forth a good word: a word as honeyed as it is milky, because of the majesty of the Godhead and the mystery of the Incarnation. Tongue and lips are like a silver channel through which streams of milk and honey burst forth from the fountain of the heart. Both are sweet, but their sweetness is distinct. Milk is for little children, as Paul says (1 Cor. 3:1–2). And the same Apostle teaches among the perfect a sweet, divine, and, as it were, honeyed wisdom (1 Cor. 2:6).

5. Some have honey alone under their tongue, and not milk; others milk alone, and not honey. But both honey and milk alike are under the bride’s tongue. Nor does the honey flow, but rather drips. For she does not indiscriminately and intemperately pour out those lofty and hidden meanings of heavenly secrets [Col. 0180B] and mysteries of the Godhead, nor does she serve the drink of milk without discernment. “Honey and milk are under your tongue.” For her speech is neither empty of inward sweetness nor equal to that inward sweetness. It is easy for her to speak sweetly, under whose tongue are honey and milk. Blessed is the tongue which drips like a honeycomb and, like breasts, is swollen with milk for little ones; which drips honey and lets milk flow. Every cry, bitterness, and blasphemy is banished far from these lips, as the Apostle exhorts (Eph. 4:31). Nor, according to the Psalm, is “toil and sorrow under her tongue” (Ps. 9:7 [Vulgate]); but, he says, “honey and milk are under your tongue.” “The lips of a harlot drip honey, and her throat is smoother than oil.” Yet honey and milk are not beneath her tongue, not in her inward parts [Col. 0180C], not in her end; rather, “her end is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword” (Prov. 5:3–4). But of the valiant woman Proverbs says: “Strength and beauty are her clothing, and she shall laugh in the last day” (Prov. 31:25). Her mouth even now brings to birth that spiritual and truly blessed laughter; and, as it were, her sweetness lies hidden beneath her tongue. But the honey and milk now beneath it will bubble up into full joy on the last day. Then no part will be held, as it were, beneath the tongue in silence; joy long pressed down will break forth, and her mouth will be filled with laughter—the mouth, I say, of the woman whose clothing is strength and beauty. See how she who waits for the joys promised to her must not be found naked.

6. Who knows whether these are not the very garments [Col. 0180D] of which, in this same passage of the Song, the text goes on: “For the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense”? “I covered my soul,” says the Psalmist, “with fasting” (Ps. 68:11 [Vulgate]); likewise: “I will humble my soul with fasting, and my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. 34:13 [Vulgate]). Fasting is a good garment, in whose hidden bosom prayer dwells. A garment has a bosom: “My prayer shall return into my bosom.” Here, if you observe it, you have both: in fasting the garment of strength, and in prayer the fragrance of incense. “My prayer,” he says, “shall return into my bosom.” But why does he say, “into my bosom”? Does he perhaps indicate the failure of lukewarm and weak prayer, which vanishes in its very first movement and is therefore said to return into its own bosom, dying there where it is exhausted? But how does that which perishes turn back [Col. 0181A] and return? Rather, prayer seems to return into the bosom when it swiftly receives the effect of petition: though not yet fully, it nevertheless gains in part the fruit of humble and devout request. For fervent and devout prayer has great sweetness, and as it is directed before the Lord like incense, it draws in the sweet perception of its own fragrance. Is not that a good garment, when the vapour of such a cloud covers and clothes the soul of the one offering it? Certainly it is good. But let us, as we began, pursue the interpretation of garments according to outward acts.

7. Good works cover former deformity, lest it be imputed for harm; and they confer a certain beauty and comeliness, so that it may be reckoned for grace. Good garments, therefore, are good works, which at once adorn and pray. That they adorn is manifest; but the adornment of all does not breathe the fragrance of incense or bear the mark of prayer. Finally, the works and patience of one who performs them publicly give forth the smell of display and empty vainglory, not the urgency of supplication, concern to please the Lord, or vows for obtaining grace. How, then, could it be said, “The fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of incense”? But one who does everything to please the God to whom he has committed himself, in order to merit his favour, certainly has garments whose fragrance is like incense [Col. 0181B]. Indeed, incense is not customarily offered, nor ought it to be offered, except to God alone. Therefore the fragrance of her garments is like incense when whatever she does, whether openly or secretly, she directs toward obtaining divine propitiation. The oil in the vessels and the fragrance of incense in the garments seem to be the same thing. What else is meant than that a person prays to God for those spiritual joys and eternal delight who renounces and abhors every other? “My soul has thirsted for you,” says the Psalm, “how greatly has my flesh thirsted for you?” (Ps. 62:2 [Vulgate]). You see in these words how even the garment of the flesh itself serves, as it were, the role of prayer, when it is said to thirst for God. When the flesh is afflicted by voluntary disciplines, does it not seek to bend God toward propitiation? Its sufferings undertaken for God are themselves certain supplications to him. Alms mercifully bestowed upon a poor person intercede; and why should not the prudent restraint of one’s own fleshly pleasure itself have the effect of prayer? The restraint of pleasure [Col. 0181C] is a certain expression of vows and of desire sighing for another delight. The effect of fervent prayer turns and returns in the bosom of the heart. Incense gives forth a sweet fragrance in the garment of outward abstinence. And it is altogether a good garment when the soul is clothed not so much with flesh as with a kind of fasting from fleshly pleasures and with temperance. Virgin continence is altogether a good garment: it breathes a sweet fragrance, like that of incense, both to him whom it loves and to the woman who loves. Whatever is offered with love cannot fail to let the very one who offers it enjoy its delight. For all this sweetness which is praised in her is felt by her also. It flows from her and remains in her. In her lips is a honeycomb; beneath her tongue, honey; and in her garments the fragrance of incense. All these things, whose sensation is so pleasing and enjoyment so sweet, are near to her [Col. 0182A]. “May the words of my mouth be pleasing, and the meditation of my heart always before you,” says David (Ps. 18:15 [Vulgate]). Here you have both these things; and, lest anything should be lacking to complete the abundance of grace, the quality of works is brought forward in third place under the designation of garments. In the lips utterances drip; beneath the tongue honeyed meditations flow; the adornment of the garments breathes the fragrance of incense.

8. What do you think is lacking for glory in one in whom these three things are pleasing: mouth, mind, and work? All things are contained in this number, but their order is reversed. For one must begin with works, not speech. In Cornelius the centurion, works and prayers were first heard; hearts were cleansed by faith; then the Spirit fell upon him and his household, and they spoke in tongues (Acts 10). The Apostles themselves, after the Lord’s Ascension, continued unanimously in prayer. When the days of the promise were fulfilled, they were filled with the Spirit; afterwards they went forth and preached everywhere. First they poured themselves out in prayer, then the Spirit was poured into them; and thus they themselves poured out to others the grace they had received. First, by expectation and desire, they were turned toward God; second, God was turned toward them; third, having been turned, they conform and strengthen their brethren. But whether you consider holiness of life, divine visitation, or ministry of the word in the Apostles, all these things perform the office of garments: by all these they were covered and adorned [Col. 0182B]. What was left in them naked or stained with former age, they who shine with so festal an adornment of word and virtue? Their adornment, then, is outstanding, and its abundance no less. What fragrance do these garments give forth? What kind is their fragrance? Is it not like incense? When they dispense the Lord’s money to their fellow servants, they permit none of it to remain secretly with themselves, taking nothing from it deceitfully for their own use. They even shake their hands free of the recompense of praise, referring everything to God’s glory. They are clothed as it were in heaven’s splendid light, but “the heavens declare” not their own glory but God’s glory. Paul himself weaves for you, in his words, certain subtle and seamless garments and fits you with a covering of light and understanding proportioned to your capacity, yet not in the persuasive words of human wisdom but in the teaching [Col. 0182C] of the Spirit (1 Cor. 2:13). Therefore the garments with which he is covered, or which he weaves for you, have no fragrance but that of incense. For affected wantonness of words and ornament seems to give forth the odour of vain and frivolous glory. Those who pursue not elegance of speech but slippery and deceptive disputations on subtler subject matter, while stretching themselves too far for empty favour, sometimes weave blasphemies into their work. Therefore the fragrance of such garments is not like the fragrance of incense. He appears to exempt none among the bride’s garments when he declares without qualification: “The fragrance of your garments [Col. 0182D] is like the fragrance of incense.” O that I were fortunate enough that even one or two garments in me might give forth the unalloyed fragrance of incense, uncorrupted by some foreign admixture! For I think no one has attained the measure in which all his garments smell like incense, unless he has already merited to be enrolled by the Lord Jesus, the Bridegroom of brides, among the company of brides [Col. 0183A].

## SERMON XXXV. “You are an enclosed garden, my sister, my bride,” etc. (Song of Songs 4:12)

1. “You are an enclosed garden, my sister, my bride; an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain.” First weigh, from his words, the affection of this praiser. He appears delighted, since he is not content with having praised her once. And how great would it have been if he had merely and without repetition expressed the praises of the one he addresses? But now he employs choice endearments toward her and doubles them in rejoicing. Why should he not? Will he not rejoice in the outstanding endowments of one whom he has chosen for the grace of marriage? She could not have been chosen as worthy of the rights of so sweet a union, nor, once chosen, could she be loved coldly. Is it not fitting that she too should strive to please him in such matters, since he has approved her so highly? He approves her; he makes her such; he plants for himself a paradise of delight. He who makes her such compares her to a paradise of delights. “Behold,” says Isaac, “the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a field full of blessing from the Lord” (Gen. 27:27). But she is compared not to a field but to a garden, where a spiritual planting of flowers and a richer cultivation of spices are apparent. Into this garden, good Jesus, you gladly descend to the beds of spices, that you may rest in it, cultivate it, and guard it. “An enclosed garden,” he says, “my sister, my bride; an enclosed garden.” By “garden,” brothers, understand inward delights; [Col. 0183C] by “enclosure,” the discipline of guarding. To what garden will you compare one whose soul breathes forth spiritual affections as a garden does aromatic flowers? How pleasant an inner chamber, how sweet a retreat, is in the bride’s breast—in a breast so full of flowers that it is compared to a garden! There is no root of bitterness springing up in it, by which the delights of this garden might be hindered. Every plant which my heavenly Father has not planted will not be found in it. Finally, he himself planted this garden of delight, that he alone might cultivate and guard it. He cultivates it in a twofold way: planting and cleansing. He plants it so that every seed in it may be true; he cleanses it so that it may bear more fruit. It is planted that its seed may be true, and cleansed that it may not be only half-full [uncertain reading: *semiplenum*]. What benefit will planting unto truth bring if cleansing unto abundance is lacking? Diligent cultivation by discipline will contribute nothing if guardianship is lacking. The one who is likened to a garden—and to an enclosed garden—is deprived of neither [Col. 0183D].

2. “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride.” Adam guarded badly the garden in which he had been placed, against the slippery entrance of the deceitful serpent. Pleasant indeed was that paradise of bodily trees; but I understand a far better one, planted in his soul. It would have done no harm for the serpent to burst into that bodily paradise, if it had not crept into this inward one. The serpent was admitted, and immediately Adam felt its poisons. “Whoever breaks down a hedge, a serpent shall bite him” (Eccles. 10:8). A hedge is a good guard: cultivated, it separates the cultivated from the uncultivated and keeps the former unharmed.

Therefore surround this garden of yours with a hedge, lest, if the hedge be removed and the wall broken down, you become exposed to plundering and trampling. That garden was not closed against the enemy; but, once he was cast out and exiled from it, how severely was it closed against him! With difficulty he returns to the place from which he fell through heedless ease. By the sweat of his face he eats his bread, though in paradise he freely plucked fruit from the tree of life at will. Here he eats his own bread; there, the fruits of life. In paradise the Lord brought forth every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food. Adam, cast out, labours upon the earth; and not the Lord, but the earth itself brings forth thorns and thistles for the labourer. Paradise gives its fruits freely; the earth gives not even its own fruits to one who labours. A wretched exchange—but you, Lord, “destroy, and rightly so, all who commit fornication away from you” (Ps. 72:27 [Vulgate]). Rightly is one destroyed who, by fornication, destroys such dear relationships; nor does he thereafter deserve to hear these tender names: to be called sister, bride, garden, and enclosed garden, admitting no one except the Beloved.

Let the gate of your paradise always remain shut, open only to the Prince. Let its door not be struck down by axe and hatchet. Let there be one entrance only, entrusted to the Cherubim. Let nothing be admitted unless first examined by the flaming sword: nothing that the word of God rejects, that charity does not approve, that does not advance toward the perfection and fullness of the Law. For the fullness of knowledge is the Cherubim, and the fullness of the Law is charity, in which all commandments are enclosed. Let this be your flaming guard, so that whatever unworthy thing attempts an invasion may be consumed at once and without delay. [Col. 0184C]

Is not enclosure fittingly assigned to love, since it always binds together the bride’s affections and shuts them into one thing, ever turning them inward, where her delight is to be with the Son of God? Love is a good wall; yet this wall has an outer rampart. Love is as a wall; regular strictness is its outer rampart. The former encloses holy thoughts and sweet affections; the latter repels and excludes occasions of sin. The latter provides leisure for the duties of love; the former enjoys it. That wall is pleasant; this one necessary. The former encloses you amid heavenly delights; the latter banishes worldly ones. If it is your desire to offer your heart to Christ as a garden of delights, do not take it ill that you are enclosed by this outer rampart. He wishes to lose the delights he has—if indeed he has them—who murmurs against the fortification. He does not know how to be a garden who does not know how to be enclosed.

3. “A garden enclosed, a fountain sealed. Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates, with fruits of the orchard.” In three things he completes the praise of this garden: it is enclosed, watered, and aromatic. The first provides security; the second fertility; the third concerns both the shoots it produces and their grace. Does not this garden seem pleasing to us—so intact, so fruitful, so useful? Nor is it merely useful: it also abounds in fragrant delights. Which of us would dare to claim these praises for himself? Who would presume that such endearments were spoken of him? Yet would that, just as we desire the watering and germination of aromatic plants, we did not refuse to be enclosed [Col. 0185A] and sealed. For only an enclosed garden, watered by the flow of a sealed fountain, produces those infusions of aromatic plants.

Therefore let your fountain be sealed, lest it be wholly dried up by lavish spilling; sealed, so that it may suffice you for watering. “Divide your waters in your streets; have them for yourself alone, that strangers may not share with you” (Prov. 5:16–17). In your streets, I say, divide your waters—but in your own streets—so that the fragrances of virtues may increase within you, as though beside water in the streets. How could that fountain fail to be sealed which flows from that fountain of life sealed by God the Father? “Whoever drinks of this water which I give shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:13–14).

In this fountain, which he calls sealed, understand a teaching that is sealed in a certain sense: spiritual, personal, and separated from the world; or at least a devotion marked by the privilege of sweetness, as though unique, flowing abundantly and continually. This is what makes all the growths of virtue joyful. This is the gladness of strong deeds, a kind of watering of the bones. For this distinctive and eminent devotion to God gladdens the heart, like a sealed and personal fountain set apart for this service: to water the bride’s heart as a garden for the Bridegroom’s delight.

Let it therefore be sealed, lest what is written come to pass: “Your fountain [is] troubled by a foot, and your spring corrupted” (Prov. 25:26). Otherwise your Beloved does not know how to drink from a pure fountain. “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been sealed upon us; [Col. 0185C] you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:7 [Vulgate]). Direct that gladness toward watering. For “in the drops of the fountain the garden shall rejoice in germinating” (Ps. 64:11 [Vulgate]). Do you not recall from Genesis that a fountain rose up and watered the whole face of the earth? (Gen. 2:6.) The earth still gave its fruits; it did not yet know thorns and thistles. Who will give my little garden this water, and my beds this sealed fountain? Who will grant that the whole surface of my little garden may be watered by rivulets of joy and light, so that nothing in it may be either barren or saddened by a kind of lack of devotion? Sad activity, lacking the watering of spiritual joy, seems close to barrenness. Even if something grows, it rises “like a root out of thirsty ground”—like a root, not like flowers, not like fruit; like a root, that is, having little or nothing beyond the root. [Col. 0185D]

4. For this reason mention is made of a fountain: that you may believe joyful shoots break forth in a watered garden. There is indeed a garden whose waters are accidental and, as it were, brought in from outside—not perennial, not its own. But a good garden is one in which its fountain springs up within. “A fountain sealed” and its own fountain: “a fountain,” he says, “and a fountain sealed”—that is, continually bubbling forth within and incapable of corruption. A fountain, because it flows abundantly; sealed, because it by no means flows away completely. Or it is called a sealed fountain because, although different people have different fountains, the sister and bride has one fountain special and proper to herself, sealed by a certain prerogative.

The fountain of wisdom is altogether good, yet it still flows forth to us under a seal: it tastes sweet, but is not yet known clearly. It is sealed and closed beneath [Col. 0186A] figures. In the Apocalypse, a book is shown in the hand of the One seated upon the throne, sealed with seven seals (Rev. 5:1). The meaning of both—the fountain and the book—belongs to the understanding of wisdom; but both are sealed by figures and wrapped in enigmas. It is sealed: for by certain indications it is made known to us and concealed in those very indications. And as in the Apocalypse there are disclosures of the sealed book of the Law, so here there are outpourings of the sealed fountain.

“Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard.” This fountain is indeed sealed, but it is not dried up, since its streams are so gracious. The fountain of wisdom is sealed, but you will know it from its outpourings. “There shall be an open fountain for the house of David, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman” (Zech. 13:1). That fountain is open; this one is sealed. That washes; this bathes. That cleanses; this waters. That purges offences; this produces delights. That is common to many; this is special to the bride. There are remissions there; here, outpourings. In the Psalm “for the eighth,” see how he first washes the bed and then waters it (Ps. 6:7 [Vulgate]). For it is not enough to be washed from filth unless fruitfulness follows.

5. “Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates.” Yes, good Jesus, so it is. These outpourings are your infusions, infusions through good angels. The garden could not send forth such delights unless you had poured inwardly the delights of living water into it. “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been sealed upon us; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4:7 [Vulgate]). It is sealed upon us because it has been impressed upon us from above. Upon one whose image of divine light is impressed from above [Col. 0186C], an abundance of spiritual joy is expressed inwardly in the heart. Thus the glorious outpourings of the king’s daughter are from within. “Your streams are a paradise.” The inward abundance of delights from which a whole paradise is sent forth is no small thing.

You possess both: a paradise enclosed and a paradise sent forth. The former lies in affections of purity; the latter in works of piety. The former is inward; the latter proceeds from it and proves it. Both the bride’s conscience and her conduct are delightful. For she both proposes all things usefully and orders them sweetly. Thus in her outward bearing and action you may behold a kind of paradise, while propriety pleases in individual things, order in things brought together, and sweetness in things arranged. She does everything modestly and tranquilly, so that the serenity of virginal shamefastness in her may not be violated. Finally, when he is about to enumerate the gifts of paradise, he begins with shamefastness: in signifying it, because of their similar colour, he puts forward pomegranates. “Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates.”

6. In the pomegranates one may also understand the patience of martyrs, because they are reddened with their own blood. Patience is a good companion of chastity; in the praise of wisdom they are joined together, as it is written: “The wisdom which is from above is first indeed chaste, then peaceable” (James 3:17). Chastity regulates itself modestly and according to propriety; patience bears another’s immodesty with equanimity. The former shapes one’s own impulses; the latter breaks the assaults of others. The former is beauty; the latter [Col. 0187A] strength. Thus it is said: “Strength and beauty are her clothing” (Prov. 31:25). “First,” he says, “chaste, then peaceable”; and a little later he adds: “Full of good works.” For it is good to suffer persecution, but for the fruits of righteousness. Therefore her outpourings are of pomegranates, but with fruits of the orchard. Chastity is good indeed—but only if it is not idle, affected, or feigned, but bears fruit in patience. The former orders sweetly; the latter protects strongly. The former is modest; the latter long-suffering. Therefore the fruits of the orchard, as the completion and end of works, are now joined to these two.

7. We should now have passed on to a discussion of the aromatic trees, to the more delicate kinds, to the outpourings of cypress with nard—unless the pomegranates still drew us by their fragrance and detained our discourse as it hurried to other matters. The parable of the pomegranates concerns us, who keep regular assemblies, who are held together under one Order, like seeds beneath a rind. Would that we might imitate these seeds: unanimous in the union of our hearts, just as we are in a certain enclosure of the Order. The seeds of this fruit cling together, almost indistinguishable in appearance from one another; they differ more by the distinctness of their number than by kind.

Let us also learn to differ from one another in number, not in spirit. They do not quarrel with one another; they do not murmur against the rind; they do not try to break through it. Patiently they allow themselves to be enclosed as in its womb, so that they seem in some manner to say: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” (Ps. 132:1 [Vulgate]). Is not, brothers, the colour of Christ’s Passion made red in our Order, as in a pomegranate rind, through imitation? Finally, those who regard it as natural for themselves to be held beneath the skin of regular discipline are like seeds of this fruit; they think themselves not so much pressed as protected. Let love of private possession be absent; let love of private power be absent—and you show yourself a seed of this fruit. Let others, invited by our example, learn how good and pleasant it is to dwell in a certain close fellowship and beneath the protection of a rind. Let charity unite, and let the rind protect.

As many ordered communities as you see, understand so many pomegranates flowing from the fountain of Baptism. For, as we read, the believers “were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4:32). From those original seeds came forth pomegranates: great congregations living in order and unanimity. Those first gatherings of believers were not yet bound by an institution of an Order, but by love’s impulse. They judged dwelling together to be not merely useful, not merely good, but also pleasant—like “ointment descending upon the beard, the beard of Aaron, down to the hem of his garment” (Ps. 132:1–2 [Vulgate])—from Christ Jesus himself, the Head, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVI  
“Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates,” etc. (Song 4:13)

1. “Your streams are a paradise of pomegranates with fruits of the orchard, cypress with nard; nard [Col. 0188A] and crocus, cane and cinnamon, with every tree of Lebanon; myrrh and aloes, with all the choicest perfumes.”

We must begin with cypress, for there we ended. Seven aromatic trees are enumerated here, said to be sent forth from the sealed fountain. These words indeed seem to be words of a sealed book. So they are: sealed and shut up. What praise of your bride do you set before us, good Jesus, unless you yourself unfold what virtue [variant: truth] they contain within? You hold the key of this enclosed garden; you have sealed it: unseal it, open it; loose, I say, these seven seals. No one knows those inward things of the bride, those hidden things of yours with which her womb is filled, except you and whomever you yourself choose to reveal them to. Would that we too might be among those who can, with unveiled face, contemplate the bride’s glory, which is from within.

Great is her glory in the mystery of both the number and the names. Here, indeed, insofar as we can perceive by the Lord’s gift, the mystery of seven signifies either the spirituality or the universality of graces. It is frequent and customary in sacred Scripture for the number seven to signify gifts that are perfect and from above. “There are divisions of graces, and divisions of ministries, and divisions of operations; but the same Spirit, dividing to each one as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:4–11). He distributes different gifts to different persons, but in the bride he gathers and bestows them all together. They are not divided out to her piecemeal, as though divided within her. To others he both distributes and gives; to her he does not so much distribute as give the whole—unless you understand him to distribute to her in this respect: that he bestows upon her, selectively and by prerogative, either more abundantly within the same class of graces or something specially in another. He could have listed other aromatic trees; but seven suffice because of the significance, as we have said, either of spirituality or of universality. [Col. 0188C]

2. Let us now bring the names and natures of these trees under examination. It seems pleasant to linger under their shade, and their fruit will be sweet to our throat. By shade I mean the figure itself; by fruit, their truth. How could the fruit of their meanings fail to be sweet, when even the leaves of their words are pleasant? You know how much feeling and gladness the abundance of such sweet names gives to your hearing. These might suffice to stir the affections; indeed, this simplicity suffices for affection, but it cannot suffice for understanding. We must comply with the understanding, which wishes to be fed with the truth of meanings.

It is sweet to hear this repeated utterance of sweet words: “Cypress with nard; nard and crocus; cane and cinnamon; myrrh and aloes.” Yet far sweeter is it to understand them. Great are the bodily delights in the trees enumerated here; but how much greater are the spiritual delights figured by them! “Your streams,” he says, “are a paradise of pomegranates; they are also cypresses with nard.” There is a good order: after the labours of patience and the modesty of chastity, one proceeds to perfumes—and royal perfumes. For a royal perfume is customarily prepared from cypress seed. And because in the pomegranates we interpreted regular unanimity, understand consequently in these words and royal perfumes a certain outstanding loftiness. “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14:11). What is patience and unanimity but humility? Humility neither swells against those who wrong it nor stretches itself above its companions. Thus humility is in pomegranates, loftiness in cypress; labour in the former, delights in the latter.

Cypress seed, they say, is customarily boiled in oil so that perfume may be extracted from it. Others sow in tears, but the bride sows in oil. Our seeds are our works. If these possess gladness, they are, as it were, boiled in oil. It is not enough for them to be dipped in oil unless they are cooked and perfected in oil, and as though changed into oil itself. What is boiled in hot oil is imbued with the nature of the oil itself. Cypress seed and oil are cooked and made into one quality of perfume. A wonderful preparation of labour and joy, and all the more wonderful because in labour no labour is felt, but joy alone. For a work of exultation, boiled in oil, passes into its nature. The work itself, so to speak, forgets that it is work, while it is wholly steeped in the richness of love. Yet inward exultation itself also receives increase from the work: thus both the seed contributes to the oil and the oil to the seed, when the bride works with exultation and exults still more in the work itself. [Col. 0189B]

3. This perfume is royal. Jesus himself gladly receives anointing from it: “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9:7). Although God the Father anointed him with spirit and power, although he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions, he nevertheless wishes to be anointed by his companions and desires the perfume of our devotion. Who will give me such an abundance of oil that all the fruits of my works may be boiled in it and my whole heart crushed? John the Evangelist, under the type of the contemplative life and in the figure of the bride, descended into a full barrel of boiling oil (Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*). Who will give me such an abundance of oil—and boiling oil—that I may be wholly immersed and prepared? Who will give me such abundance of oil and cypress seed as may suffice for the preparation of perfume?

Not every seed receives this boiling in oil; it does not want every fruit. For not every work can be mingled with the joy of contemplation. Works of outward concern and the practice of contemplation cannot be prepared together or coagulated into one quality. What fruits, then, does this preparation receive? Precisely those enumerated by the Apostle: “But the fruit of the Spirit [is] joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, faith, gentleness, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5:22–23). These fruits suit the oil of contemplation and grow, as it were, into one nature with it.

That seed also is especially suitable for this preparation, of which it is written: “The seed is the word of God” (Luke 8:11). Cypress seed likewise bears a certain resemblance to manna, in which we understand the word of God to be figured. For both manna and cypress seed are white and like coriander seed. “The law of the Lord is undefiled” (Ps. 18:8 [Vulgate]). It does not wish to be investigated by the water of worldly wisdom or confirmed by its arguments, but by the oil of the Spirit, so that spiritual meaning and the anointing of the Spirit may be extracted from it. Meditation upon it and the joy of contemplation are most readily mingled when study of the word is joined to the oil of grace in contemplation; and while the former is boiled by the latter, spiritual understanding and the anointing that teaches concerning all things are readily extracted from this preparation. Observe that he does not say merely “cypress,” but “cypress with nard.” The Lord declares that he was anointed beforehand with nard for burial (Matt. 26:3, 8). What, then, do you understand in nard except repose of mind? Therefore it is joined to cypress, because every practice of contemplation needs mental repose. [Col. 0190B]

4. “Cypress,” he says, “with nard; nard and crocus.” A good connection. For crocus is a flower of almost golden colour, referring to the glowing colour of wisdom. Thus in cypress is understood investigation; in nard, repose; in crocus, the vision of wisdom. Nard is rightly placed in the middle, necessary to both—that is, to investigation and vision. For truth can neither be sought out without leisure of mind nor be seen when found. Understand, therefore, study in cypress, repose in nard, and the fruit of both in crocus.

No longer, bride, do not say, “Because I am dark”; do not call yourself discoloured any more (Song 1:5). For now, by the Bridegroom’s own testimony, you shine with crocus colour, you who send forth crocus. She rightly gleams with crocus colour whom foolishness does not darken, whom the deathly pallor of weariness and a failing spirit does not stain, but whom the radiant wisdom and glowing colour of charity gladdens.

5. If we wish to refer these things to the person of Christ, a fitting interpretation follows. Who has been more thoroughly boiled in the oil of grace? He is understood in manna; he bears the likeness of cypress seed; pressed by the cross of the Passion, he poured forth the mysteries of salvation and perfumes of grace. He suffers in cypress, is buried in nard, and rises from the heart of the earth in crocus—like a new and glowing flower, when through his resurrection [Col. 0190D] the flesh blossomed anew. Perhaps in cane he ascends to heaven, for this tree grows upward to a height. And his bride, as it were, suffers with him in cypress, is buried with him in nard, and rises with him in crocus. What follows, then, except that she ascends with him in cane? For if she has risen with the Bridegroom, she ought to seek the things above and savour the things above, where her Bridegroom sits at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1–2).

“Cane and cinnamon.” Cane rises high; cinnamon rises only a little from the earth. In cane she beholds lofty things, but in cinnamon she does not savour lofty things. The one ascends; the other descends. Cane is when the bride is carried beyond herself toward God; cinnamon, when she accommodates herself to us. Yet, though she accommodates herself, everything she brings forth remains spiritual. For cinnamon, when broken, gives off a visible breath. When is it broken, except when it is opened, when it is expounded? Thus Jesus, when he took bread, broke it and gave it (Mark 14:22).

Therefore a teacher accommodating himself, as it were, breaks himself when he begins to open himself, to draw out those secrets hidden within concerning heavenly things, to pour forth the remembrance of abundant sweetness. This is what it means for broken cinnamon to be said to emit a visible breath. Why “breath,” and why “visible”? Breath, because what he says is spiritual; visible, because he teaches plainly. One who falls from lofty matters into trifles and vain tales does not descend; he falls. He may speak in a broken manner, but he does not emit a sweet breath.

Like cane growing among waters, so you rise to heights amid the tears of prayers. A beautiful ascent—but see that your descent resembles cinnamon. When some reasonable cause calls you back and restrains you from that ascent and transport, be like cinnamon. Let your conversations and ordinary intercourse breathe grace. And if you are sometimes turned back from your own will and purpose, let your will, turned back and as it were broken at a superior’s decision, utter no murmur and no complaint. Be cinnamon: emit the breath of grace, not an answer of injury. Therefore, when broken, it emits a visible breath, because the virtue of humility grows and is proved in the weakness of vexation and, as it were, breaking. It is called both breath and visible: breath, because tranquillity is preserved in the heart; visible, because it shines forth in the face. [Col. 0191C]

6. To these he adds all the trees of Lebanon. Observe that he includes no trees except those of Lebanon, and omits none that belong to Lebanon: “with every tree of Lebanon.” The trees of Lebanon possess incorruptibility because they are cedar trees, and purity because they belong to Lebanon. Only the trees of the Church possess the mystery of faith in a pure conscience and a certain incorruptibility of continence; only her trees possess both purity and permanence. A churchman is indeed a good tree, in whom the strength of discipline and the beauty of faith meet and encounter one another. “Strength and beauty are her clothing” (Prov. 31:25).

In these days certain trees have sprung up which the heavenly Father did not plant, trees not planted in our Lebanon. They display strength in works, insensibility to injuries, endurance of austerity. They seem like cedars, but they are not of Lebanon, because their mind and conscience are unclean. “To the unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus 1:15). The strength that they display and that flourishes in their conduct decays in their confession. What seems to shine there stinks here. Piety appears in action, but unbelief is exposed under questioning. “Their strength is the strength of stones, and their flesh of bronze.” Clearly they do not degenerate from their father, of whom it is written in Job: “His heart is hardened like a stone; it is bound fast like the anvil of a smith” (Job 41:15 [Vulgate]). They are evil strong men: strong not for faith but against faith. For the Almighty has not softened their hearts, has not softened or cleansed them, nor made them white through faith. Therefore they are not trees of Lebanon. “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23): how much more is what is against faith? They are not trees of Lebanon whose faith is not watered by purity. Virtues not made fruitful through faith are barren; but faith itself without virtues is dead. No rot of incontinence defiles its whiteness. In the trees of the Church both meet together: the beauty of faith and the strength of work. Such a cedar is planted in our Lebanon. Here, and nowhere else, are purity of faith and enduring, almost incorruptible perseverance in virtue. [Col. 0192A]

7. For here myrrh and aloes are sent forth with all the choicest perfumes. These substances are known to preserve from corruption, unharmed, even things that are corruptible in themselves. Why would these perfumes be produced after the trees of Lebanon if there were no difference between them? Though they seem alike, they nevertheless admit a distinction. The former—that is, the trees of Lebanon—possess incorruptibility in themselves; the latter—that is, myrrh and aloes—bestow it upon those who do not possess it. The former are incorruptible; the latter confer incorruptibility.

Therefore that is a good tree, truly planted in the paradise of the Lord, on that excellent mountain, Mount Lebanon, which both restrains itself lest it flow away through unlawful things and, by the myrrh of its speech, renders others immune from such a flow; whose body is like cedar and from whose lips myrrh distils. “Myrrh and aloes with all the choicest perfumes.” We may also direct these things, by interpretation, toward the four cardinal virtues, if we understand strength in cedar; faith in Lebanon, faith which itself gives form to prudence; temperance, continence, and justice in myrrh; purity in aloes. For the gum of this tree is said to cleanse the stomach. Thus by myrrh outward things are restrained; by aloes inward things are not feigned in hypocrisy.

You now have these four expressed here. First, constancy, lest you believe only for a time and fall away in time of temptation. Then prudence, so that your service may be rational. Thus myrrh for the mortification of the flesh will follow when you have zeal according to knowledge. In the fourth place, aloes, when the heart itself is offered and burned: so that there may be at once mortification of the flesh in myrrh and cleansing of the conscience from dead works in aloes, in order to serve [Col. 0192D] the living God—not serving merely before the eye, nor as pleasing men, but rather pleasing God.

Is not the bride truly blessed, to whom so many endearments are spoken? Much has been poured into her who sends forth so many gifts pleasing to the Beloved. For in all these things Jesus Christ himself glories and applauds the gifts of his bride, he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XXXVII  
“A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters,” etc. (Song 4:15)

1. “A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow swiftly from Lebanon.” At the beginning of this chapter the bride is called a fountain; now at the end her Beloved bestows upon her the name of fountain. He begins from fruitfulness, and in a fruitful old age she is multiplied: the end corresponds to the beginning. Her outpourings are many, but she is not exhausted by her outpourings. She does not dry up through delay; she is not exhausted by flowing forth. At the beginning of this chapter she is called “a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12); here she is indicated to be undried. There it is taught what her outpourings are like; here, how tireless they are. Abundant streams of graces flow from this fountain, yet the fountain always remains. It does not restrain itself from that from which it begins; therefore it is called a fountain here and there.

But now observe where its waters flow: where but in gardens? For it is “a fountain of gardens,” flowing gently, which does not go out from the gardens, does not wash but waters; whose whole use lies in this, not to remove filth but to bring fruitfulness. To cleanse is indeed a good use of a fountain, but to make fruitful is better. One washes away defilements; the other, as by a kind of alluvial deposit, brings increases of graces. One makes shoots washed; this one makes them joyful. One is open for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman; this one is sealed for the bride’s delights. “You are altogether beautiful, my friend, and there is no spot in you” (Song 4:7). Therefore she is called only a fountain of gardens, a fountain of delights. [Col. 0193B]

2. Finally, as varied and manifold as is the manner of heavenly delights, so great also seems to be the number of gardens. In one roses redden; in another lilies shine white; and violet flowers yield their purple colour. There are as many gardens as there are plantations of virtues gathered together. Where there is only one flower, who would judge that a garden exists? Thus not even one plantation of chastity, nor one of justice, can fill out the completeness of a garden.

Solomon, who is called delicate and tender (Prov. 4:3), made for himself gardens and orchards, and planted them with trees of every kind. He does not say, “I planted a tree,” but “trees”; nor, “of one kind,” but “of every kind.” “I made for myself pools of water,” he says, “that I might water the forest of growing trees” (Eccles. 2:5–6). Rich indeed in delights was he who possessed not sparse trees, which could be counted and written down because they were few, but an entire forest—a forest of growing trees. In the garden of wisdom there is nothing barren, nothing not growing.

Thus the bride also has several gardens and is abundantly planted with shrubs of every kind of virtue. And later the Bridegroom applauds the bride, saying: “You who dwell in the gardens, friends listen to you; make me hear your voice” (Song 8:13). Most fittingly indeed. For what could be sweeter than to listen to her who dwells in gardens and speaks of gardens? Her voice is not heard outside, nor beyond the garden; therefore he is a friend who dwells in the gardens with her. Nor is she so much in the gardens as she herself is the garden. She is the garden, and he is the fountain, watering these gardens with the streams of his teaching. Blessed is the bride who has nothing to water but gardens.

3. Are there not, in this numerous assembly, as many gardens as there are souls? Because of unanimity, one garden; because of differing graces, many gardens. Would that in these gardens no root of bitterness might spring up, that there might be no useless tree, none unworthy of the bride’s garden; that there might be here no vegetable garden, because the vegetables of the herbs will quickly fall away (Ps. 36:2). “For he who is weak,” he says, “let him eat vegetables” (Rom. 14:2). But you do not need vegetables as though you were weak. For what is weak in you is stronger than secular persons. Their weakness rests content with permitted things; yours strains toward perfection. Their weakness is to make use of what is allowed; yours, indeed, is to stop short of perfection. What is it for weakness to be in you except not to be perfect? What is it for weakness to be in you except not to attain the highest? And what is strength, except striving in order that you may attain it? Therefore our weakness is stronger than secular persons; and, so to speak, the weakness of a monk is better than the good conduct of a secular person. Works regarded as weak among us—how great would they be thought if secular persons were seen doing them? Solid food belongs to the perfect; yet however many among us are imperfect disdain the eating of vegetables. Things permitted to weak secular persons are neither offered to ours nor demanded by them. Among us the profession is perfect, though its fulfilment be weak. The plantings are perfect, but the growth is very slight. They must be watered if they are to grow, but with spiritual waters.

Paul well knows with what waters he should water each kind of garden. To married persons he grants the use of marital union (1 Cor. 7:5–6); he consoles the fainthearted, supports the weak (1 Thess. 5:14), gives milk to drink to the carnal (1 Cor. 3:2); he speaks wisdom to the spiritual, who judge all things—not wisdom of this age, but wisdom from God, wisdom hidden in a mystery. And if anyone else speaks of the beauty of the house of the Lord, the place where his glory dwells, the delights of the bridal chamber, the joy with which the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, and with which she, rejoicing in turn, rejoices in the Lord—certainly he ought not, with waters such as these, to water a vegetable garden. For the natural person does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:6–7, 15, 14). In short, whoever either commands spiritual things to be done or sets them forth to be understood—does he not seem to you like a pure fountain flowing in aromatic gardens? And rightly pure: since, because of the perfection of his hearers who listen in the gardens, he need speak only of the purity of spiritual life, and offer them, as inhabitants of paradise, draughts from the streams of paradise.

[Col. 0194D] 4. In accordance with this meaning, understand the hearers as the garden and the teachers as the fountain. But if they are a fountain, how are they also a well? For you know how greatly these familiar fountains and wells differ from one another. A well is dug; a fountain flows freely. In the former the waters are stored away; in the latter they are, as it were, set forth and spontaneously offer themselves. The difference between them is great, and the two properties cannot be found in either one. Neither a fountain can claim for itself what properly and naturally belongs to a well, nor a well what belongs to a fountain: each is confined within the limits of its own nature. Bodily and earthly things are narrow; spiritual riches abound.

If we refer these things to spiritual realities, we shall find fountain and well in the same place, and the distinctive properties of each shared with the other. Let us therefore, if you wish, share these distinctive properties with one another and assign both to the same subject. Let us understand in the fountain sufficiency of teaching; in the well, secrecy; in the one, abundance; in the other, deep mysteries. Indeed, a good teacher is one who, as though from a deep well, brings forth abundantly from the hidden treasure of wisdom things new and old. He is a well, because no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. For the Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God (1 Cor. 2:11, 10); and, like a certain fountain, brings them forth into the open and makes the gardens of virtues well watered. Thus in the well you have hiddenness, in the fountain abundance; lavish outpouring in the fountain, and depth of meanings in the well. The well is deep, but it needs no bucket: it is a fountain, and flows freely. Let the thirsty come and drink from the waters of the bride, from the waters of Beersheba, that a new Solomon may be born from her. And Beersheba is interpreted “the seventh well”: that is, the well of rest, the well of wisdom. For wisdom appears seventh as one ascends in the catalogue of spiritual gifts.

5. Just as “well of wisdom” is read, so also is “fountain of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:5). Perhaps in these two its twofold mode is expressed: one arising through inquiry, the other through inspiration. The waters of a fountain burst forth of themselves; but in a well the mass of earth is broken through and its solidity penetrated, in order that you may reach living water. Each is necessary to the other: industry to grace, and grace to industry; and they lend each other reciprocal aid. For one who digs a well labours in vain unless the fountain of life itself flows freely into it. Yet you too will dig your well in vain and prepare a reservoir for waters if your well is neglected and foul with stagnation: living waters will not descend into it; they will not flow with force from Lebanon.

The waters descending from Lebanon do not know how to be gathered except into a white well; and waters that flow with force wish to have a capacious well. You will make the well of your heart deep and capacious if you cast out earthly cares; if you make room in your soul for spiritual joy; if you open your mouth so as to draw in the Spirit, and rivers of living water may flow into your belly. Your openings were prepared for this work on the day of your birth, as is written concerning the prince of Tyre (Ezek. 28:13). The capacity of natural understanding, by which on the day of your creation you were privileged above other living creatures, serves as a vast receptacle for receiving and holding the waters of vision and life. For we read of “the well of the Living and Seeing One” (Gen. 16:14). If after sin it seems blocked by vices, whether inborn or added, let faith open it, let hope diligently dig it deep, let love enlarge it. Let leisure and freedom from business not allow it to adhere to shameful stagnation. For festive joys wish minds free from anxious cares, and the vision of God claims leisure for itself. Does not that one in whom all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge are hidden seem to you a deep well? Or will you deny that Mary was like a well of most pure water, she who kept all the words concerning Christ, pondering them in her heart? (Luke 2:19, 51). Be such a well yourself according to your measure: a deep and broad well.

[Col. 0196A] 6. After the well of Accusation, after the well of Enmities—after leaving, I say, these two wells—Isaac dug two wells: the well of Breadth and the well of Satisfaction (Gen. 26:20–23). In the former he began not to contend with vices; in the latter he began to delight in the fruit of virtue. He would not have a well in common with the Philistines, whose name is interpreted “Falling by drinking.” He left the wells of enmity and accusation to the Philistines. Surely those who drink from the well of error and schism fall. Such wells their authors dig; their hearers drink from them. Thus Arius dug; thus Donatus. The one introduced an accusation against the faith; the other divided the bond of brotherhood into parties. The former distinguished the equality of the Trinity by ranks in a heretical definition; the latter tore the unity of the Church into parts by his presumption. Dathan and Abiram dug wells of accusation against Moses and Aaron, and themselves fell into the pit they had made; the earth swallowed them alive (Num. 16:1–33). They were cast down by the drink which they themselves had dug, thus fulfilling in their fate the interpretation of the name Philistines.

But a good well is one from whose waters whoever drinks will lift up his head, not fall through drinking. He digs, as it were, a pit who, with the sharpness of earthly understanding, penetrates the solidity of Scripture and violently rends the little garden of the Church, producing some unknown doctrine and obscure mysteries. So too does one who, by subtle scrutiny and deceitful contrivance, pierces the solidity of brotherly love [otherwise, unanimity] and opens a vein of discord; one who shuts and seals himself in the well of conspiracies, refusing to come out, but entering ever more deeply into the interior of schism and digging out its abyss. This is a Philistine well; let nothing be common between you and it. At first such things grow gradually and secretly, breaking out from the bowels of an earthly and brutish mind, until afterwards they flow with force; but they do not flow from Lebanon. These waters are not faithful; they are not living waters. Discord cannot remain consistent with itself; perpetual peace cannot be kept among those who produce schism. Schism itself is faithless to itself; it cannot remain joined to itself for long, since it attempts to dissolve the glue of love. If anyone invites you to these wells, break up, if you can, the wells of the Philistines and dry up the pestilential waters. Leave the Philistines their own wells, wells of enmity.

7. Pursue the wells of heavenly delights, wells of faithful waters and living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon. Be a flower of the garden, and of the enclosed garden, that you may not be plundered; and you will see how the Lord will break open for you fountains and torrents. Live in the garden, so that perhaps you yourself may be transformed into a well, and rivers of living water may flow from your belly. What are living waters except waters that do not fail? Good indeed are those waters, whose draught cools the heat of desire without failing. The delights of the world universally offer a false appearance of refreshment and quiet worldly desire only for an hour; but, as if immediately upon their rising, they dry up, and do not flow in a perennial vein. Like a torrent they pass swiftly, and living waters cannot be found in this torrent.

Another Isaac dug in a torrent and found living waters (Gen. 26:19). For there is a torrent that seems pleasant but is not health-giving, nor indeed everlasting: such is the worldly flood of pleasure mentioned above. And there is a torrent that is indeed health-giving but not everlasting; yet, if you dig in it, you will find living waters. “We have,” Peter says, “the surer prophetic word, to which you do well to attend, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (2 Pet. 1:19). This lamp will not be extinguished in the night; for meanwhile its use is necessary. But when the eternal day has dawned, the teaching of the prophetic lamp will cease, and the torrent of written discourse will be dried up. For whether prophecies are abolished, or tongues cease, or knowledge is destroyed, the discourse of sacred Scripture flows, in view of the future manifestation, troubled, so to speak, in the manner of a torrent, instructing us through a mirror and in an enigma. But the waters of that vision which is face to face are true, pure, and perennial (1 Cor. 13:8, 12). They will not fail you, nor you them. When the torrent of this mortality has passed, cloudy mysteries will pass with mortality; and unveiled, serene truth, for whose sake you dug here in the torrent, will burst forth joyfully. Here is the place for a mirror; there, for direct contemplation.

Yet this contemplation is accustomed in some way to penetrate a foreign place; and, cheerfully showing itself to travellers in the place of exile, it invites them to their homeland. Truly festive, but still furtive, is this ray and rivulet of the eternal light. It does not shine forth or emerge except in gardens, and in aromatic gardens. O depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how like a well you are! You cannot be exhausted: you pour out living waters, health-giving and abundant waters.

8. Who will give my little garden these waters, and my heart this well of delights? “Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord, and spare your servant from strangers” (Ps. 18:13–14). Make me Lebanon: sprinkle me and I shall be cleansed; wash me and I shall be made whiter than snow (Ps. 50:9). Cleanse me from the great offence, and then “the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart will be pleasing in your sight always” (Ps. 18:14–15).
