Make me Lebanon, that I may always pour out these waters for you. “They will be pleasing,” he says. What does “be pleasing” mean, except that both may please and may please both parties? Whom are the two parties, except you and me? What are the two things, except words of praise and meditation of the heart? These waters are living because they always please and always flow; but they flow only from Lebanon, and not slowly either, but with force.

The mighty impulse of the feeling of love has approaches that are sweet, yet not difficult. Its force is great because it reaches effectively even to the affections, and sweetly exhausts them. Great is the force whose vehemence nothing can resist: “With force,” he says, “from Lebanon.” He expressed the cause of this overflowing by the name Lebanon. Purity is the place of overflowing joy, and it pours forth waters of saving wisdom: they burst from what is white and make yet whiter. Gather these delights together into one and heap them up, as it were, in a pile. See and consider the well, Lebanon, force, and living waters. You will discern in these, if you attend in mind, that these waters are serene, hidden, powerful, and unfailing. The well signifies hiddenness, Lebanon serenity. In force every other affection is exhausted; living waters do not know how to be exhausted.

Faith also is a good Lebanon, because hearts are cleansed by faith. From this Lebanon flow the living waters of serene understanding, because “unless you believe, you shall not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint). Good is that understanding whose contemplation remains for ever and ever. This is truly living. For eternal life is this: that we may know the one true God and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17:3). And Christ himself is our Lebanon, pouring living delights with force into the bosom of his beloved. He himself is Lebanon, and he himself the stream; for he is the brightness of eternal light and the most pure emanation. Truly delightful is the well of the bride’s affection, into which the rays of eternal brightness, like little streams from Lebanon, are both gathered and poured forth to water the bridegroom’s flowers and gardens. Good, therefore, is Lebanon, into which nothing defiled enters; and great is the force which no barrier can restrain.

9. Finally, those waters flow with a force that neither persecution, famine, peril, nakedness, nor sword can separate from the love of God. So many barriers of scandals were thrown before the peoples who believed, so many masses of torments were set against them, and yet the waters always flow from Lebanon. For “the waters are peoples” (Rev. 17:15). Great are the barriers, but greater is the force. If you try to restrain it, it grows the more and breaks through the obstacles. Repelled, it rises into a swelling mass; gaining advantage from its impediment, it spreads itself more abundantly. To pure love even the barriers themselves work together for good, and virtue, assailed by injuries, gains increase.

Could not these things, even while I say nothing, strike the consciences of those whose love flows according to uncertain places and times—who love for a time, indeed, and withdraw in the time of tribulation? What do I say, “tribulation”? They never endure even the mass of a slight and doubtful temptation, but only its barrier; they are easily restrained and, with their purpose turned back, rush with irresistible force toward worldly things. If you cry out with the prophet, “Stand, stand!” (Nah. 2:8), there is no one who returns. No persuasion recalls them—not the pious rebuke of a teacher, nor misfortune, which is often and almost always in their paths. They flow, rush, and collapse, in order to drink on the way from the torrent of pleasure, which will not lift up their heads but dash them to the earth. Blessed indeed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of love, who walk in the force wherever the force of the Spirit may be, and do not turn back; nor are they separated by any obstacle from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

128 SERMON XXXVIII. “Arise, north wind; and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden.” (Song 4:16.)

1. The bride’s spices are sweet and holy affections. For she herself is a garden. When the south wind blows, these flow forth into the bridegroom’s delights; but the harshness of the north wind again checks them. For the north wind is cold, and at its blast the spices freeze. How long, Lord, will the north wind of adversity press upon our regions? How long will it hang over our little gardens? How long, good Jesus, will the rigor of the north wind bind our spices? Spare, Lord, spare your bride from the north wind. Long has this hard and violent spirit been urging, pressing, and hanging over us. Adversity, amassed on every side, presses upon us. Tell it, Lord, to arise, withdraw, and allow room for breathing. The poverty of misfortune is barren and brings forth grievous disasters on every side. Weak things are easily injured, and the abyss of misfortune calls to another abyss at the sound of your cataracts (Ps. 41:8). Secretly you call adversities against us, as though you said to the north wind: “Rise up, press down, take possession.” “Smoke,” Isaiah says, “will come from the north” (Isa. 14:31). But for us not so much smoke as flame now hangs over the boiling pot from the face of the north. From the north comes cold, and from the north flame. Thus it is, Lord. In the harshness of your hand you oppose me; you restrain the veins of your mercy. Therefore my soul boils, and in my meditation fire will blaze. This is the grievous fire of anxious care; and in its heat the spices do not flow, but rather, if you allow any to flow, their streams are dried up—especially when the occasion for adversities seems to open more and more.

2. Lord, my sorrow is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you. The cause of my anxiety is known to you; but I ought rather to have said sorrow, for anxiety has now begun wholly to pass into sorrow. Where no prospect of counsel shines forth, where not even a shadow of good hope presents itself, there is no longer anxiety but sorrow. My groanings are many, and my heart is sorrowful. “Little children ask for bread, and there is none to break it for them” (Lam. 4:4). For there is no one to break bread—not, I say, the bread of the word, but this daily food for the body. Yet my soul cannot be filled with the richness of that heavenly bread while the lack of this daily bread brings upon it a certain leanness of sorrow. At the voice of this groaning I have forgotten to eat that heavenly bread. Harsh is the north wind, outward adversity; but far harsher is the anxiety of the mind. One presses you, brothers; both press me. I suffer in you from the common wearing-down, and beyond you from a domestic burden, because it is for you. On one side are the blows of misfortune; on the other, lawsuits arise in accusation. Some murmur, others insult; and what human diligence cannot ensure will never happen, they reproach us with once it does happen. Some provoke, some mock, making adverse fortune an occasion for folly. The good successes in which they abound they ascribe to themselves, believing them to be the result, as it were, either of foresight or merit, not a divine gift. “The tents of robbers abound,” says Job, “and they boldly provoke God, though he himself has given all things into their hands” (Job 12:6). Some are both robbers and provokers, who take for themselves what belongs to God by attributing it to themselves; and they bend the gift of divine grace to the effect of their own industry. Why do you reproach us with benefits bestowed on you from above? Or because the eye of divine mercy is good toward you, is yours therefore evil toward us? Why do divine benefits make you readier to disparage than to give?

3. You see, Lord, from how many quarters the blasts of the north afflict us; troubles, murmurings, and reproaches blow upon us from every side. Amid pains of this sort, the soul, divided and constrained, does not know how to receive the gentle breezes of the south wind. Arise, Lord; let not the north wind prevail. It is enough that it has now long risen and hung over us. Bid it arise, depart, and give way to the south wind. The pot has long been kindled from the face of the north (Jer. 1:13); but send, Lord, the south wind that will make the midst of this furnace like a wind blowing with dew. I do not dare to ask for continual blasts of the south wind. It is enough if its alternation tempers the malice of the north wind. You stretch out, as we read in Job, “the north over the void” (Job 26:7), not over a garden. The bride’s little garden is not void, in which so many species of aromatic plants, enumerated above, are planted. And how can the joyful spices of meditation flow freely where pursuits are not free from sorrow, where adversity causes grief and the north wind binds them?

Be jealous, Lord; be zealous for your bride. Tell the north wind to arise, and to divide its seasons with the south wind. Thus indeed it will happen, according to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, if your consolations make my soul glad. You see, brothers, how the north wind gives birth to the south wind in proportion to itself; and perhaps where the north wind has abounded, the south wind will abound still more. For the south wind will blow prosperously and compensate for the injuries the north wind has inflicted. Therefore let the north wind arise, rage as much as it wishes, and roar, provided that it gives occasion and, as it were, force [otherwise, material] to the blasts of the south wind.

Do those whom Paul addresses in the Epistle to the Hebrews not seem to you to have endured grievous blasts of the north wind? “You endured,” he says, “a great conflict of sufferings: partly being made a spectacle by reproaches and tribulations, and partly becoming companions of those so treated. For you also,” he says, “had compassion on those in bonds.” But amid so many blasts of the north wind, did the south wind claim no turn for itself? Indeed it did. Hear, finally, what follows: “You received with joy,” he says, “the plundering of your goods, knowing that you have a better and abiding possession” (Heb. 10:32–34). Again, when the Apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41), does it not seem to you that, against the severe assaults of the north wind, the south wind gently blew upon them? Consider those sorrowful Sabbaths of the Lord’s burial. Did not the hearts of the Apostles stiffen with unbelief and a certain fearfulness, as at a blast of the north wind? When the Lord rose again, the gentle south wind began to breathe through his garden. During all those forty days, finally, faith in the Lord’s resurrection and truth, and confidence in freedom, gradually gained strength through many proofs. On the very day of Pentecost, when a mighty spirit arose in the upper room where the Apostles were sitting, all the coldness of their frozen minds was released, like a torrent in the south wind; and thereafter the spices of word and virtues flowed forth.

4. But did the harsh north wind therefore rest? Did not the storm of persecutors rise much more violently, together with the onrush of heretical tempest? Did not the north wind, in a kind of jealous rivalry of temptation, set itself against the grace of the south wind? As though it alone were striving to blow through the garden, it seeks by a certain harsh rigor to bind the spices so that they may not flow; yet they flow all the more broadly. By the alternating movements of adversity and prosperity, now provoked, now calmed, the bride of Christ, his Church, has not ceased and does not cease to bring forth the spices of virtues. In persecution virtue shone forth; in peace the number increased. In the former the strong are tested; in the latter the weak are nurtured.

Why then do I recall the primitive Church, when even now the bridegroom’s garden endures frequent, though less violent, assaults of the north wind? Around it the south and north winds take alternating turns. A grievous assault has struck the Church in this time, and indeed from the north. For there is the origin of schism; from there it arises and there it remains. The north wind alone oppresses there. Tell it, Lord, to arise and depart. Call also to the south wind and say: “Come, breathe upon my garden, and let its spices flow.” I do not mean the south wind of earthly happiness and security, for this south wind often binds and dries up the spices; rather, call the south wind of your grace. And if it is necessary, send even the north wind into that barren garden—not the north wind of obstinacy, but of affliction, so that affliction itself may give understanding to the ear for obedience. Scourge your garden with the cold of the north wind; rouse its torpor, as it were, with this lash, that it may more eagerly turn toward the gentle breathings of the south wind.

Both by regions and by seasons, south and north winds alternate turns around our garden. For just as now the south wind blows and now the north wind, so here there is a south wind and there a north wind. Sometimes both blow at once; but one is outside and the other inside. Outside is the north wind, inside the south: the one raging, the other warming. Let the north wind roar and make tumult outside; only let it not blow through the garden within, let it not enter, let it not bind the innermost joy of the heart which is in Christ. When, Lord, will that cold spirit finally rest altogether? When will it be that we are no longer afraid at the sight of its cold?

Your city is founded, a garden planted on the sides of the north. This wind is called “right-hand” in the Scriptures. Thus Job makes this complaint concerning it: “At my right hand,” he says, “my calamities immediately rose from the east” (Job 30:12). Rightly he called that wind right-hand, since it could inflict nothing sinister upon him; indeed, it brought an increase of glory to the righteous man, when virtue both shone forth by being tested and grew by being challenged. It strikes your garden from nearby, for it is situated on the sides of the north. Make it right-hand for us, Lord; temper it with the blasts of the south wind. For even the north wind cooperates for our good in your love, even while the south wind blows. Whether commanded or permitted to arise, let the north wind of tribulation not frighten us. For soon the south wind of consolation will follow, even if it does not meanwhile interrupt it. For where affliction abounded, grace also abounded.

5. But why, brothers, do I speak to you of outward tribulation? Another north wind is accustomed to assail you. From this north wind God spares you, interposing others to receive the frequent shocks of secular turmoil and tribulation. No grievous external care constrains you, because none comes to you by right; yet he does not allow you to be exempt. Those whom outward care cannot affect, inward weariness afflicts. In this respect it goes well with those who are not exposed to outward troubles; yet they do not escape the north wind, since they do not please themselves inwardly. Festive joys first turn into distaste, and sadness changes the cheerful countenance of the mind. Happy is the person for whom there is no such change. But who is that? For who is there whom weariness does not sometimes consume and sadness wound?

Finally, where we were carried in a favourable voyage, shortly afterward we run into shoals; and against a breeze that bore us onward, a storm bursts out. Even where no cause appears, disturbance presses in. The cause is not evident, yet anger threatens. A person is angry with the anger which he suffers irrationally and whose movement he detests, but whose origin he does not know. This harsh spirit blows where it wishes: you do not know whence it comes, nor perhaps where it goes. Or rather, where it escapes? For such an affection proceeds from itself toward evil, but often escapes into good. It does not reach the destination toward which it goes, but God even brings an outcome from temptation. When he wishes, he himself brings on the north wind; when he wishes, he says, “North wind, arise.” And if meanwhile you complain of its distress, know that through such instruction you are both reminded and admonished. You are reminded to attend to the nearness of the north wind, admonished to escape its harshness. Since you are situated upon the sides of the north, it is not in your power to flee its proximity; yet you can escape its violence. As long as we are here, it is always near. It is not always violent; but after we have gone around by the north, we often turn back by the south. Even when you do not feel its assault, regard its nearness with suspicion.

6. Yet when will you escape its whirlwinds unless the gentle south wind, called upon, comes, and you thus spread your wings toward the south that you grow feathers for heavenly flight? If, however, the north wind tries to mingle itself in and bind with its cold spirit the wings newly growing in renewal, it restrains wings from flight and spices from flowing. It restrains them, I say; it does not take them away. For violent weariness and bitterness of heart exercise virtues themselves; they do not overthrow them. This whirlwind indeed shakes a holy purpose, but does not take it away. It restrains joy, but does not take away constancy. The soul is affected by weariness, but not consumed. It is saddened, but struggles against its sadness. Virtue thus affected is no less strong, but less happy.

What has it to do with the vice against which it contends and declares war? The distaste with which it makes no pact is not its own. It suffers the trouble; it does not make peace with it. Finally, it is not the soul itself that effects this, but rather the north wind, on whose sides it dwells. It therefore detests it because it feels its efforts against its virtue. Whoever feels this knows how great is the weariness with which he endures that weariness of good conduct; how he loathes that distaste; with how great bitterness he struggles against that bitterness—against a violent bitterness which intrudes itself unwillingly from the continuance of disciplined exercise. The soul turns by desire toward the south wind; and behold, the north wind intrudes upon it importunately, against its will and in opposition to it. It is hard to endure before this cold and not have it in one’s power to flee according to one’s wish. The soul labours under both the weariness of discipline and hatred of this weariness. Both affections are troublesome: not to find sweet what one has chosen, and to feel what one hates. Both are burdensome: to defend discipline and to repel sloth.

7. How, good Jesus, do you endure for so long such vexation of your beloved bride? She suffers sloth against her will, and persecutes it in herself as though it were voluntary, punishing it thus. With the greatest difficulty she bears that she cannot, as she wishes, delight only in you, who are her good. She imputes to herself what she suffers unwillingly. A goad comes to her from the north wind, but this goad urges the bride to prayers. Chastened by this goad, she gives herself to supplications, though she had earlier prepared herself for embraces. Mitigate, good Jesus, these evil days for your bride. For unless you help her, her soul will dwell in the north wind. Who indeed will rise against the north wind except you, O God, who come from the south?

A holy purpose and a pure conscience are a good spice; yet it does not flow for one who does not enjoy the delights of this good. Come, good Jesus, come; breathe through your garden, that its spices may flow like a torrent in the south wind. She is the garden; be yourself the south wind. When you water her, her soul will be like a watered garden; and when you blow upon her, her spices will not fail—you who live and reign for ages of ages. Amen.

SERMON XXXIX. “Arise, north wind; and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and let its spices flow.” (Song 4:16.)

1. Fulfil, good Jesus, what you command: bring the south wind from heaven and lead it into your garden, into the soul of your bride. By this gentle breath loosen weariness; loosen sadness from her affections. For both are a vice and bear the appearance of the north wind; both bind the mind and hinder it from a certain free outflow of pure joy. What of fear? Does it not also bind the affections with icy rigor? “Spare your bride from strangers, O Lord.” What is more alien to her than fear, which is not in love, when she is wholly in love? That fear is slavish; she is called to freedom.

You saw yesterday, brothers, in the sermon, a man advancing fearfully so that he might undertake the first elements of the religious rule; how, with purpose lingering and wavering, he allowed himself to be marked with the rudiments of discipline. And you know well how, while he was still secular, his hand poured forth abundant streams of alms. What was the reason, except that the north wind of fear had bound his mind in this respect? The south wind had indeed breathed upon it in part, but had not blown through it; therefore it readily poured forth the spices of almsgiving. But that most precious and aromatic liquid of renunciation, after many efforts, could scarcely at last be squeezed very thinly from his soul. Clearly he was like the rich young man in the Gospel, who boasted to the Lord of keeping the law but, when the restraint of evangelical perfection was set before him, went away sad (Matt. 19:16, 22)—except that he went away sad, whereas this man, though sad, nevertheless came forward. See the north wind of fear blowing under the Law: therefore its choicest and most selected spices flowed only sparingly. Therefore, on the day of Pentecost, when the mighty Spirit blew from the south, so many thousands of people flowed forth spiritually in truth, word, and life (Acts 2). Thereafter the care of worldly property did not bind them.

2. Freed from this rather harsh north wind, hearts flow more abundantly in contemplation and love of God. “You did not receive,” he says, “the spirit of slavery again in fear; but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom. 8:15 [Col. 0204B]). That was the spirit of the north wind; this is that of the south: the former harsh, the latter welcome. Therefore the former, as heavy, weighty, and oppressive, is told, “Arise”; but the latter, as cheerful and pleasant, is invited to come and blow through the bridegroom’s little garden. The former bears punishment; this one flowing joys. The former threatens; this one pours out caresses and delights. “I will ask my Father,” he says, “and he will give you another Paraclete” (John 14:16): that is, to invite the south wind and bid it come and blow through his garden. “Blow through my garden, and its spices will flow.”

Some fruits do not yield their liquid unless they are pressed and forced. But the fruits in the garden so delicately described do not await pressure: they do not know how to be compelled, but, when the south wind blows through them, they flow freely. Consider worldly wisdom. Does it not seem violently squeezed out, laboriously wrought by prolonged practice and study? Yet in the authors of our philosophy a swift and mighty abyss of wisdom burst forth. Do you wish to hear its swiftness? “When you stand before kings and governors, do not prepare beforehand; for in that hour it will be given you what you are to say” (Matt. 10:18–19). Do you wish to hear its force? “I,” he says, “will give you a mouth and wisdom which none of your adversaries will be able to resist” (Luke 21:14–15). How could these things flow forth so suddenly and serenely unless this south wind were breathing upon them? You have now heard whence came the spices of truth, so abundant and ready in their season.

3. Is not charity itself also “poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5)? Many spices flow forth [Col. 0204D] through the Spirit, and only through the Spirit: joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, faith, gentleness, modesty, self-control, chastity (Gal. 5:22–23). These have not merely sprung up, but have also flowed forth. Their flowing signifies abundance; their flowing at the breath of the south wind removes compulsion. Charity cannot be forced; it flows gratuitously. It moves not by necessity but by choice—yet while the south wind breathes.

For what would freedom of choice contribute if the south wind of grace did not breathe upon it? Although choice, wherever it is, is always free, we do not grant that it is thereby free for all things. It does not possess free election or free execution in all things. In choosing there is always freedom, but not always freedom to choose. For it cannot choose except freely; yet there is something which it cannot choose of itself. The will is its own master; it is free when it is present. But the mind is not free to possess every will which ought to be present when that will is absent. Nor is it more within its own control that it should have the intense will which it has, or that it should have a good will.

Yet, so far as freedom of choice remains after the Fall, whatever the mind wills, it always wills freely; but it is not free for it to will whatever it pleases, even what it ought to will. There is a freedom which does not exist without will, and without which there is no will; and there is another freedom which will does not always accompany. The former is in the will; the latter is in a certain capacity for willing. The former is in the thing itself; the latter is, as it were, directed toward it. We can possess the latter, and we compel the former.

There is likewise a certain power of seeing in the eye, and yet sight is also a certain affection or act in seeing. So too [Col. 0205B] in the mind, “understanding” is said both of the natural power for understanding and of the exercise of that power. A similar distinction occurs in choice, so that under one name both aptitude and act are understood. In both cases there is freedom of choice: both for choosing and in choosing. Yet when it is in evil, it is always enslaved. The former is enslaved precisely because it is weak, both for good and against evil. An evil will is free precisely insofar as it is will; but it is servile precisely insofar as it is evil. “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). For sin seizes, binds, and fetters the person whom it occupies; it enslaves while it compels.

4. “But you, O Lord, restore our captivity like a torrent in the south” (Ps. 125:4). Send forth your Spirit, and the ancient freedom will be renewed—renewed, I say, not re-created. For although it has been obscured, it has not been taken away [Col. 0205C]. What was created remains, but cannot move itself toward that for which it was given; it lives, but does not flourish.

Thus in those who are delirious, innate rationality is not diminished; but in persons so affected, no movement of it can arise. When the grave condition has been cured, reason is not given anew but awakened from sleep. So also the freedom of choice created together with humankind has not been wholly or partially removed, but bound by sin. It is the same as it was made, but differently affected.

And, if I may put it so, there is freedom of condition, freedom of disposition, and freedom of affection. The first belongs to nature and is therefore always good; but unless it is healed, neither the second will be directed toward good nor the third established in good. The first consists in natural aptitude; the second in the disposition of a mind established either well or ill; the third in use. Therefore, unless natural aptitude is aided by grace, neither the disposition nor the act of the will will tend toward virtue.

The freedom of choice is weak. Therefore, where choice succumbs, let the south wind breathe, and immediately the spices will flow. It does not possess that noble and truly free liberty, which is toward good and in good, unless the Spirit has set it free. Therefore, Lord, send forth your Spirit, that he may grant both ability and willing through grace—he who first granted the possibility of either, when he created human nature.

We have listed above three freedoms. In the third, willing is present; in the second it underlies; in the first, the natural power with respect to the other two is considered. Let the first, then, be called *potentiality*; the second, *power*; the third, *will*. It does not seem the same thing to possess a natural capacity for something and actually to be able to do it [Col. 0206A]. For many things which we are naturally capable of, we cannot immediately do when the inborn capacity is hindered by weakness or lacks skill and practice. Often, for a time, the eye cannot see, although its natural power of sight has not failed: the disposition is present, but the exercise is absent. It is naturally capable of seeing, but cannot actually see.

Likewise, the natural freedom of choosing remains, though impeded by sin. Therefore it cannot possess that third freedom which is in good, nor the second which is toward good. The first remains—changed indeed, but not diminished; the others ought not even to be said to remain. For after sin it is not left free to us to will the good; hence no remaining freedom consists in good will. But by grace this final freedom is inspired [Col. 0206B], the second is repaired, and the first is naturally created.

5. Let this be said concerning the freedom by which we will the good, because it is from grace. Yet there is another freedom likewise through grace, by which we not only will well, but desire the good itself with affection. That freedom is always in the will; this one is not so. For we always will freely, but not always affectionately. Affections do not belong to the freedom of choice.

Nevertheless, the freedom of a good will is not altogether free if it is not affectionate; but when the south wind breathes, aromatic affections immediately flow. They are not pressed out; they flow freely. Holy will is often accompanied by a certain weariness and sadness; but sweet affections do not travel with these. They are aromatic in fragrance and equally pleasant to the touch: they are sweetly felt and sweetly recalled; they flow sweetly and overflow sweetly. They flow for themselves and for others. Both the inward affections and the outward utterances are aromatic. Freedom of choice may aspire to these, but they do not depend upon freedom of choice.

Just as evil affections are often contrary to good will, so good affections, when present, although they accompany it, do not arise from it. The will is free without them, and is rendered, as it were, generous by them. They make the will itself freer, but they do not flow from its freedom. Rather, they flow when the south wind has blown through.

O sweet south wind, truly desirable, by whose spirit the grim face of winter’s cold is dissolved; in the gardens the spring mildness of welcome newness smiles; there comes a new mildness and autumnal abundance! For in the flowing of spices the ripeness of fruits is signified. Behold how good and pleasant it is, in chambers and gardens of spices, to await this breeze—so sweet, renewing and restoring the fruits of the Spirit, pouring forth spices, scattering fragrances! Send us, Lord, this Spirit, who after the north wind’s terror may clothe our little garden with a new face and turn our mourning into joy.

Or, if the north wind signifies something good, invite it together with the south wind. Let them join their offices, and let each accomplish its part. Let the north wind bind tight; let the south wind loosen. Let the former restrain wantonness; let the latter release the mind into overflowing joys. Let the former grant continence; let the latter gladden the conscience. Let the former contain, and the latter fill. “I have become like a wineskin in the frost, yet I have not forgotten your statutes” [Col. 0207A] (Ps. 118:83). Good is the wineskin thus frozen and filled: outwardly, the frost of continence; inwardly, the fullness of righteousness. Both winds blow well when outward things are stiffened by the cold spirit of continence and inward things are watered with flowing joys.

6. And that you may direct the south wind’s breath inward, he says, “Blow through.” Whoever blows through blows in the innermost places, and nothing is impenetrable to him. This Spirit is subtle, keen, and mobile: blowing through, not puffing up. “Knowledge puffs up” (1 Cor. 8:1); charity blows through. Charity is more inward than knowledge and reaches more secret places. The Spirit who searches even the depths of God blows through every inward place.

Where he has blown through, and as it were permeated those things, there the spices of knowledge flow beneficially: meditations, prayers, sighs, sobs, tears, and the very conversations themselves [Col. 0207B]. All things which derive their origin from charity flow like spices. Everything that proceeds from it is, as it were, aromatic, full of grace. They are dear and abundant; aromatic and flowing. Those things which proceed from the fullness of charity are full. They are full, not squeezed out; nor do their spices suffer the violence of the winepress.

You do not read that a winepress has been built in this garden; for the south wind performs the office of the winepress. They flow better when breathed upon than when trodden. For, as we have said, they are gratuitous: poured out by the Spirit, not extorted by fear.

There are those who refer the north and south winds to this world’s adversities and prosperities. And indeed, though the Church of God is vexed by this double temptation, it always abounds in spices of good affection and good repute. Therefore it allows itself to be blown through by these temptations, because it knows how both to abound and to suffer want [Col. 0207C]. This passage calls for fuller treatment; but let it suffice, at the conclusion, to have touched upon these matters only lightly. The following sermon will turn to the mutual invitations of the bridegroom and bride, if Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God, deigns to grant us grace.

## SERMON XL

[Note: [Col. 0207] Delivered on the feast of St. Lawrence, as appears from the context.]

“Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple trees. Come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have gathered my myrrh,” etc. (Song 5:1.)

1. How far, brothers, are the words of these desires from my own manner of life. The Lord knows my longing, but I lack boldness. Why should I not? I do not have a garden such as Christ described above: there are no fruits [Col. 0207D] upon which he may feed eagerly; no aromatic fruits; no irrigating spring; no deep well of living waters. Rather, a horror of thorns and brambles rises up in my garden. I do not dare invite you, good Jesus, into such a garden—unless perhaps that you may first pluck up, destroy, and scatter, and afterwards plant; and thus, at the fitting time, eat of the planting of your right hand.

Happy is the soul worthy to invite you to fruits already ripe, fruits prepared and containing nothing bitter. And would that only bitterness were charged against our fruits; would that they were unripe, provided that they were not evil. Fruits that are good by kind are frequently not yet pleasant in season; they displease only through immaturity [Col. 0208A]. Happy is the garden whose fruits are all good by nature and seasonably ripe. The bride knows that neither quality is lacking in her fruits, to eat which she invites her beloved: “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple trees.”

See how cautiously and modestly, and only after many praises, this invitation is made. For she does not presume to invite her beloved; she does not thirst for delights until she knows herself sufficiently described as delightful. What then? Do you suppose that Jesus grants the delightful coming of his presence to those who are not endowed with the virtues mentioned above and worthy of praise? Regard it as rash presumption if, before you are fit for the exercise of contemplation, you invite Jesus. Do you urge him to delight himself with you, while perhaps you are still defiled by sins? Your garden bristles with thorns and lies barren, and do you invite Jesus there? Invite him, not that he may already delight himself, but that he may destroy what your own right hand has planted. Invite him first to cleanse, then to plant. There is labor in both; but he will come with delight to pluck ripe fruits.

2. “Let my beloved come,” she says. Not only does she flatter and rejoice in him when present; her desires also burn toward him when absent. False and feigned love forgets the absent and flatters the present. Not so the bride, not so: she desires him when absent and rejoices in him when present. “Let my beloved come,” she says, “into his garden.” Why should she invite the south wind to herself? Let him himself come; he is enough for me. He himself is my south wind; he himself is my spice. He himself is my south wind; he himself is my love. God comes from the south, and the south wind comes with him [Col. 0208C]. For he himself is full of grace and truth. Well indeed is Christ my south wind: serenely he illumines and sweetly enters. Christ is my south wind; he blows through the garden; he eats its fruits. “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple trees.”

The time of pruning has now passed; the flowers have borne the fruits with which they were pregnant; winter has gone; spring has withdrawn; riper autumn is driving onward the now-declining summer. Let my beloved now come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple trees. Behold, the fullness of time has come; therefore let my beloved come into his garden. The fruits are early ripe; therefore let him eat the fruit of his apple trees.

The fig tree produces its first fruits early. When it was not yet the season for figs, he came to the fig tree [Col. 0208D] by the roadside, turned over the leaves, and found no fruit (Mark 11:13). Before the time of eating and before the time of fruits, he approached it hungry in the morning. I know a fig tree that bore morning fruits from earliest childhood—the fruits of first-fruits, the fruits of virginal grace. This fig tree was not planted by the roadside, but in a garden, indeed in an enclosed garden: a garden surrounded by the wall of discipline and the close hedge of guardianship. Truly it was a fruitful fig tree, and most beautiful in appearance among the rest. The Lord Jesus frequently turned aside to it, perhaps saying: “Under his shadow, whom I had desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2:3).

3. But would that she had preserved the fruits which she bore [Col. 0209A]. Would that the wicked hand of a thief had not plundered them. But now it has taken the best fruits, those which cannot grow again. Others have grown in their place: that is, bitter penitence in place of virginal continence. How much more sweetly did you feed both yourself and your beloved with that native fruit than with this subsequent one! Woe to you, poor woman! When your beloved comes, what mind, what face, what expression will you have? Where will you turn in shame, you who have lost the fruits of chastity? Where will you turn when he approaches, when he turns back your leaves and does not find the fruits he was accustomed to find? He will be ashamed because of your confusion.

Recall the words of your virginal vow; recount the words of your consecration. Beneath these leaves observe that there is no longer your own fruit—the fruit of integrity, the fruit of virginity. Such fruits were consecrated, but have now been taken away [Col. 0209B]. Consecration and corruption do not fit well together. Injured virginity is customarily forgiven, but it cannot be given back. “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God,” but shameful things have been done in you. Henceforth, in double confusion and shame, acknowledge your portion in mourning.

“Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” And I shall weep for one who has fallen—not an insignificant woman of the common people, but one who was, as it were, foremost in the virginal flock. Who, I say, will give me a fountain of tears? For she herself who has fallen wholly overflows with tears; through her moist lips streams of tears run down. Deep sighs and anxious groans reveal that confusion, ever attendant upon guilt, oppresses her. I saw in that unhappy face a cast-down countenance and broken cheeks. Sobs interrupted her speech. She was unwilling to restrain herself from falling; she is unable to restrain herself from tears [Col. 0209C].

Do what you are doing: bear fruits worthy of repentance. Let grief renew you; let sorrow consume you. Say with the prophet: “Do not press upon me to comfort me; I will weep bitterly” (Isa. 22:4). I too will weep with you. Perhaps your beloved himself will weep with you, he who wept for Lazarus (John 11:35). Perhaps he will weep more. He who loves more grieves more. His mercies are many; therefore, says the prophet, “we are not consumed” (Lam. 3:22). Indeed, neither will you be consumed, because your counselor is a comforter, restoring your soul.

How, to say what can scarcely be understood, will the pitiable appearance of your mourning not move his affection—though in a different way—when I myself, reviewing the course of your sorrow, am inwardly touched by grief of heart? If you bear fruits worthy of repentance, your beloved will again return to his garden. For he gladly eats the fruits of repentance. Yet happier is the one who preserves untouched the fruits of original purity. It is good to be early in ripeness and to persevere therein.

4. Therefore the bride is early in ripeness and says: “Let my beloved come into his garden, that he may eat the fruit of his apple trees. Come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” The Lord Jesus is a vehement lover: at one word of invitation he gladly flies to the bride’s little garden. As though he flies ahead and anticipates her in ripeness, he says, “Come.” Let this word be understood in the imperative sense, and what follows will fitly cohere: “Come.” He is neither slow nor a sparing rewarder, but immediately invites the bride in return: “Come into my garden, my sister [Col. 0210A], my bride. I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.”

Hard is the heart which these invitations and return-invitations, so sweet, do not move. What is more pleasant than this interchange? What is more wonderful than this commerce? O wonderful exchange! The beloved of God the Father, the glory of heaven, the delight of angels, allows himself to be invited into our little gardens, and does not fail to invite us again into his own. And the garden which is ours is more truly called his. For she does not say, “Let my beloved come into my garden,” but “into his garden.” Rightly indeed, into his own: because it was given by him, owed to him, and certainly dedicated to him.

“Let my beloved come.” “Come, my sister, my bride.” Great sweetness, and a fitting distinction: she desires, while he commands. She says, “Let him come”; he says, “Come.” “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter and dine with him, and he with me” [Col. 0210B] (Rev. 3:20). You need not, good Jesus, linger at the bride’s door; for she herself eagerly addresses you with her desires. Return the exchange; invite her again. You have sat at her table; see how much she has set before you, knowing that you too ought to prepare so much. So much, I say—and it is enough for her.

But I say this: she expends her whole self; repay your whole self. How will it be whole if she gives herself wholly and you give yourself by halves? Your little is more than all of hers. All that is hers is some portion of your grace; therefore her garden is yours, and yours is hers.

5. “Come into my garden.” Brothers, I gladly understand the bridegroom’s garden as that abundant, delightful, and gloriously planted paradise of Christ’s virtues [Col. 0210C], which according to his twofold nature he either possessed from eternity or received in time. According to this interpretation, then, understand the bride’s garden as the state of the soul or of the Church, together with the endowments of virtues and affections with which it is enriched by the bridegroom. In the latter, the goods of the body are considered; in the former, those of the Head. In each there is a beautiful nourishment of contemplation. But what is the former compared with the latter? By as much as the glory of Christ surpasses the virtues either of the soul or of the Church, so much more delightful is entrance into the latter garden.

Action pertains more to that garden; to this, contemplation alone. Though the bride rejoices in the former, she labors in it and eats its fruits in sweat. When she has been brought into this garden, nothing remains but delights alone. She tends her own garden and contemplates this one. Nor is she admitted [Col. 0210D] into this one except from the former—that is, from action to the exercise of contemplation.

Or, if we admit contemplation into that garden of the bride, it resembles action. Certainly through those many things one arrives in fitting order at this myrrh. For one does not enter into the garden of the beloved except amid an abundance of virtues. “You will enter the grave in abundance,” says Job (Job 5:26). Yet here “garden” sounds better. In the grave rest and a certain concealment from cares are suggested; in the garden contemplation and feasting are expressed. In the grave we rest; in the garden we enjoy. Therefore, just as we enter the grave only in abundance, as Scripture says, much less do we enter the garden otherwise. Thus he invites the bride from garden to garden: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride. Enter, enter, bride, into the contemplation [Col. 0211A] of the virtues of your beloved. Enter into his delights; remember his righteousness alone.” There God, your God, will teach you in joy and will wondrously lead you by his right hand. He will feed you with the fruits of life and understanding. He has gathered myrrh and spices for you.

6. “I have gathered,” he says, “my myrrh with my spices.” For after death he gathered immortality and incorruptibility. By the benefit of myrrh, the bodies of the dead endure unharmed. “My myrrh,” he says. Rightly his own: for he first received it and alone imparts it. “Christ the first-fruits, then those who belong to Christ.” Through him comes the resurrection of the dead, since he, the first to rise, now dies no more.

Such myrrh is good, and better than the common kind which prevents dead flesh from decaying: for this prevents living flesh from failing. His myrrh was also that surpassing and unique virginal chastity which felt no rising movement of sensual solicitation and possessed no tinder of concupiscence. In him no such movement was repressed, nor was any tinder merely restrained; for he was anticipated in anointings of myrrh, and of his own myrrh.

The myrrh and continence of others are effective only to the extent that they preserve from corruption; this preserves the Lord’s flesh untouched from corruptibility. The myrrh of others follows the corruption of the fleshly incentive; this one anticipates every incentive. Theirs excludes it; his precludes it. In Jesus there is neither cause nor corruption; in his Mother, though there is cause, there is nevertheless no corruption; in all others there are both cause and corruption. Our myrrh represses the rising movements of carnal desire [Col. 0211C]; Mary’s myrrh knew no such movements; Jesus’ myrrh had neither cause nor origin for being so moved. “From his fullness we have all received,” and myrrh from myrrh. The myrrh of our chastity is by his gift and imitation; therefore, when he gathers myrrh in us, he gathers his own.

Would that he might find much myrrh in me to gather. “Myrrh with spices”: that is, abstinence from evil with affections toward good; sternness toward the flesh and devotion of heart; or, whether we understand temperance from lawful things or endurance in injuries. In myrrh the spices of both virtues are fittingly joined. For this is grace: if, while doing good, we are scourged; if, while ourselves afflicting ourselves outwardly, we are thereby sweetly affected inwardly.

From the field of the martyr Lawrence, whose feast we now celebrate, he gathered much myrrh [Col. 0211D] and many spices: the myrrh of confession and the spices of confession. Set to the fire, he confessed Christ; he gave his body that it might burn; he distributed his possessions to the poor. His flesh was burned for Christ, but his heart even more in Christ; therefore he is called from the gridiron to the garden. While he was on the gridiron, he was not absent from the garden. Now he is only in the garden, but not wholly there. His flesh is still held in corruption and has not yet blossomed again; but it will blossom again when the body of our humility has been made conformable to the body of Jesus’ glory.

Then he will gather the myrrh of immortality, which Christ himself gathered beforehand, and the spices of manifold glory. Then he will truly invite and say: “Come into my garden, my sister [Col. 0212A], my bride.” Then he will glory fully that he has gathered myrrh with his spices. For then he will obtain the effect both of his passion and of his prayers, which are signified in the spices. “Offering prayers with loud crying and tears, he was heard for his reverence; and, being made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him” (Heb. 5:7, 9). “I will,” he says, “that where I am, there also my minister may be” (John 12:26). Where, unless in his garden? This will be at the consummation of the general resurrection; nevertheless, it also happens now through contemplation.

7. We enter, as it were, into his garden when with affection, worthily, and desirefully we contemplate what we shall be through him, and what he himself, now risen, has already become for us and as an example [Col. 0212B] to us. What do I say—“now risen”? Even before the resurrection, all his conduct bore the grace of a most beautiful garden; but what he planted before, he gathered afterwards. In the resurrection there is the time both of ripeness and harvest, when each person will receive the fruit of his labors.

Therefore, when he calls us into his garden and adds that he has gathered his myrrh and spices, he exhorts us to contemplate the glory of the resurrection: the resurrection which will occur in us through him, or which has already gone before in him for us. Is it not a pleasant and truly delightful progress to enter Christ’s garden, to enter by a certain prospect into the Lord’s plantings, from virtue to virtue of his? By a prospect, I say; I do not dare call it advancement. For who promises himself advancement toward the truth and fullness of his virtues? It is plainly a pleasant and fitting excursion. Nowhere is the pride of the human mind more restrained by humility; nowhere is hunger more satisfied by contemplation; nowhere is weariness more stirred by emulation [Col. 0212C]. Comparison humbles; imitation exercises; contemplation delights. The first presses down; the second urges on; the third feeds. Immensity humbles; excellence provokes; truth nourishes.

8. Finally, a little later the beloved himself, the bridegroom himself, invites his friends and those most dear to him to eat, drink, and be inebriated. And that a greater appetite may be born in them, he first entices them with, and sets before them, his own banquet: “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey.” Both are yours, good Jesus: both the honey which you give and the honey which you are. But in this place the honey which you yourself are presents itself more readily to our understanding. Why do you not say “your honeycomb,” as you say “my honey”? Why do you now use this distinction? The honeycomb too is yours, just as your honey is, though you plainly state the latter while keeping the former unspoken.

Both natures are yours; but the divine nature is yours and naturally yours, while the human nature is not naturally yours in the same manner, but rather assumed and made natural to you through condescension. “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey.” Before the conception of the sacred Virgin there was, as it were, honey alone and without honeycomb: divinity not yet incarnate. Afterwards, honey was in the honeycomb—God in man. But now the honeycomb is in the honey: humanity clothed with divinity. “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now,” says the Apostle, “we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). As God was hidden in flesh, so now, conversely, the flesh itself is hidden in God. And although that flesh has been glorified, so that it is now spiritual and has nothing of weakness, yet it is in some sense hidden, since we attend to and worship him more in that he is God [Col. 0213A].

In a certain sense, the honeycomb of flesh is hidden in the honey of divinity, because the reverence of majesty, wholly manifested, has drawn our admiration and faith to itself. Therefore, after the glory of the resurrection, Christ eats his honeycomb with his honey; and, without the liability of fleshly weakness, he enjoys in the substance of assumed flesh a divine delight native to himself alone. “I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk.” Now you say that both milk and wine are yours. For the rights and properties of both natures are yours, not the defects of another; and as he drinks new wine, so also new milk. “With my milk,” he says: that is, with the milk of your newness, not of our weakness.

9. Run, bride; hasten to so sweet a banquet, where there is the bridegroom’s wine, where there is milk, where there is a honeycomb not empty or void but full of honey. You have found honey: eat what is sufficient, for you are not sufficient for the whole. But Jesus does not eat by measure; he eats all, he who is sufficient for all. To you it is said, “Do not be a searcher into majesty, lest you be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:16, 27); he searches all things, even the depths of God. “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). He eats all; he imparts to whom he wills and as much as he wills. By glorying that he is himself fed, he promises you, as it were, a share of this food.

If gall is given you for food and you are given vinegar in thirst, remember that Jesus suffered such things. He tasted them on the cross but did not drink [Col. 0213C] (Matt. 27:34), signifying the swift passing of bitterness. But he drank his wine with his milk. No longer is he troubled at Lazarus’s tomb; no longer is he sorrowful unto death; no longer, under death itself, is he given vinegar and gall to drink. Old things have passed away; new things have succeeded. That disturbance, sorrow, and weariness, assumed in the dispensation for a time from the old human being, have passed into the new sweetness of milk.

It is good wine: when it has been drunk, former distresses are consigned to forgetfulness and do not rise into the heart. Instead, in flesh now resurrected, he is refreshed with new, pure, and milky affections, when no injury or distress is any longer either assumed or endured, in soul or body, as before. Rather, the vinegar mixed with gall, which he tasted beforehand but did not drink, has passed into the flavor of wine and milk.

You too, faithful soul, who exercise the dignity of the bride, trust that this change will come to you. He proclaims these things fulfilled in himself so that you may learn to hope for like things concerning yourself. For he wishes to feast with you and drink with you: “I will not drink,” he says, “of this fruit of the vine until I drink it new in my kingdom” (Matt. 26:29). This signifies the kingdom for you when he calls you to the garden: to the garden of delights, to the paradise of pleasure [Col. 0214A], to ripe fruits, to fruits already received by him and to be received by you. Then you will drink wine with milk, so as to forget former distress and taste the sweetness of the new resurrection, through the grant of our Lord, who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

## SERMON XLI

“I have gathered my myrrh with my spices,” etc. (Song 5:1.)

1. “I gathered my myrrh with my spices; I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk. Come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” Suppose, brothers, that this summons refers to the end of the age, when all the mysteries of the Church have been fulfilled and she herself is invited into the kingdom; when the Lord will send angelic reapers, because then the fields will be white for harvest [Col. 0214B]. O happy days of the primitive Church! How fertile was her field then, how abundant the fruits it produced! How great was the fruitfulness of myrrh in the martyrs; how many bees were making honeycombs of more perfect and mystical teaching! One might have thought, amid the very beginnings of the faith, when the seeds of the word were being sown, that the time of harvest had already come and that the fields were whitening, ripe for the sickle.

Why do you delay, good Jesus? Why do you not invite the bride into the garden? Can you not already say: “Because I gathered my myrrh with my spices, ate my honeycomb with my honey, and drank my wine with my milk”? Where now are the martyrs in myrrh, the teachers in the honeycomb, the fervent in spirit signified by wine, and the simple whom the sweetness of milk figures [Col. 0214C]? Does not the field of your Church now seem stripped of such glory? “You have multiplied the nation, but have not magnified its joy” (Isa. 9:3). There are many fruits of believers, but few spices. The autumnal abundance came first, in those first days of the Church’s birth; now winter’s harshness presses upon us. Years of plenty came first; years of barrenness now loom over us. After flowering and joyful ears of grain, barren stalks rise up, consumed by blight.

Why do you not now say, good Jesus: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride”? What are you waiting for? Why prolong the delay? Is it that, after this winter, autumn may return? “They shall yet rejoice before you as they rejoice at harvest.” Then you will bless “the crown of the year of your goodness,” and your fields will be filled with abundance. “The lovely places of this desert of ours, which is now seen, shall grow fat” [Col. 0214D] (Ps. 64:12–13); and the heat of the final persecution will bring the gray-white ripeness of maturity to our harvests. They will multiply in an old age that does not fail, is not exhausted, is not barren, but fruitful; and they will be patient, so as to proclaim (Ps. 91:15–16). Patient, because of martyrdom; proclaiming, because of the word. In the patient you will reap myrrh; in those who proclaim you will eat the honeycomb. Then you will give your elect the wine of compunction to drink, mingled with the milk of consolation. For unless the Lord had shortened those days, no flesh could be saved.

2. Even now the Lord reaps: not indeed as much myrrh as then, yet much myrrh of voluntary affliction. He eats honeycomb with honey and, through the expressed sweetness of spiritual meanings [Col. 0215A], makes us delight in its containing figures. He drinks wine with milk, because he tempers and sweetens exalted perceptions and surpassing contemplations with the simplicity of faith and conduct. He loves the fervour of zeal, provided that there are also certain milk-like supports for little ones.

When all these things have been spent; when the times of martyrs have passed; when teachers, like certain honeycombs containing wisdom hidden in mystery, have completed their ministry and, pressed by the disputations of heretics, have poured forth honeyed doctrine; when both the little ones nourished by milk and those fervent in spirit, who, intoxicated by the wine of grace, forget what lies behind, have completed their numbers and their days—when all these things have been fulfilled—for “not one apex or one iota shall pass from the law until all things are fulfilled” [Col. 0215B] (Matt. 5:18)—then the whole Church of the saints will rejoice at that most sweet hearing: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I gathered my myrrh with my spices; I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk.”

“I gathered, I ate, I drank”: these are words of the past tense, and they signify a finished completion, as though he said, “It is finished.” “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I gathered my myrrh with my spices.” Into that garden where no nettle, ready to burst forth, will sadden the grace of the lilies; where the harshness of thorns will not wound the blooming rose; where there is no tree whose access is forbidden. “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I gathered my myrrh with my spices.”

Hear that he reaps only what is his own, only what he himself sowed beforehand [Col. 0215C]. Truly that servant was wicked and slothful who, by a malign interpretation, cast the cause of his own sloth upon his master: “I know that you are a harsh man, taking up what you did not lay down and reaping where you did not sow” (Matt. 25:24). Well may he be called slothful, in whom the master found nothing to reap; and truly wicked, who converted the care of his reaping master into harshness through a perverse interpretation, preserving fruitlessly what he had received and thinking unjustly about a good master.

The Lord Jesus reaps only what he has sown; he reaps only what is his own. What the enemy-man oversows upon his wheat, he does not reap; rather, he will send angels to gather the tares and make bundles for burning [Col. 0215D], to gather out of his kingdom all scandals (Matt. 13:24–30, 37–42). Therefore he first cleanses his kingdom of scandals, his field of tares, and his garden of useless growth, so that he may reap and gather only what is his own.

3. If Jesus should come now; if the voice of the angel should sound; if the final trumpet should thunder terribly; if judgment should be brought forth; if fire should blaze before him; if heaven above should be summoned, and earth, to judge his people (Ps. 49:3–4)—if all these things should suddenly overtake you now, what judgment would you hold concerning your merits? Where would you be placed at your judgment? Among his saints [Col. 0216A], who will be gathered there, or among those who will be gathered together into the assembly of one bundle in the pit? Among the tares or among the spices? Or perhaps does even your own judgment concerning yourselves hesitate?

“Who shall glory that he has no tares in his field?” Happy is the person in whom there is only a little of them, and that little neither cultivated nor fostered, but stolen in and lurking amid a certain abundance of spices—and which, as soon as a person notices it, he plucks from his garden. Woe to me, Lord, because of my imperfection, if you are a hard man, a stern exactor, taking what you did not lay down and reaping what you did not sow! Woe to me if you reap everything that you sowed, without remission and without regard for mercy! For not everything that you sowed in me has grown up.

Would that you might deign to receive my little bundle of myrrh [Col. 0216B], that it might remain between your breasts. Would that the slight vapour of my spices, yielding a little fragrance, might ascend to you. For when shall I offer you an entire honeycomb? When shall I offer you continual meditation on your law? When a pure and full understanding of spiritual mysteries? When the honeyed wisdom which Paul speaks among the perfect (1 Cor. 2:6)?

For just as a honeycomb contains honey in its cells, so heavenly wisdom is contained in the most pure mysteries of figures, so that, through their reciprocal comparison, the figured mysteries may commend the truth, and the truth itself may draw no small measure of grace by being expressed in such cells, as it were. When shall I be able to mingle, in some vessel of my heart, that tempering of wine and milk? This mixture is rare: that one who surpasses himself in mind toward God may learn to be sober; that one who knows lofty things may consent to the lowly; that one intoxicated by purer understanding may become a little child [Col. 0216C].

4. How great, how vast, how fertile a honeycomb has in these days been carried over to the heavenly banquet: I mean Lord Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx.

> [Note: Aelred, Abbot of Rievaulx in England, who died in the fiftieth year of his age, under Henry II, king of the English, in the year of the Lord 1166. See the notes to the first letter of St Bernard, [Col. 0215D; Col. 0216D]. The works of Aelred may be found in the *Bibliotheca Sanctorum Patrum* and in the *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, vol. III.]

While we are expounding this passage, news of his departure was brought to us. It seems to me that, when he was taken away, our garden was stripped bare and surrendered a great bundle of myrrh to God the husbandman. No honeycomb like him remains in our hives. In him one could see both the honeycomb of honey and the bundle of myrrh with good spices. Who was purer than he in life, or wiser in teaching? Who was more infirm in body, or more cheerful in spirit? His speech, like wax, poured forth honeyed knowledge [Col. 0216D]. Though weak in body, he nevertheless languished more inwardly in spirit from love of heavenly things. With his body steeped in myrrh and his mind fragrant with spices, through continual mortification he offered the sweet-smelling incense of tireless love.

Though his body was dried and parched, his soul was filled as with fatness and richness; therefore his mouth would always praise the Lord with lips of exultation—his lips a dripping honeycomb. For, wholly transformed into lips, he displayed tranquil dispositions of mind in his modest expression and in the peaceful bearing of his whole body. He was penetrating in thought, not hasty in speech. He asked modestly [Col. 0217A], replied more modestly, bore with troublesome people, and troubled no one; keen in understanding, deliberate in reporting, even-tempered in bearing.

I remember him often, when someone sitting by had importunately interrupted a discourse he had begun, suspending his words until the other had poured out his whole mind. When the rushing torrent of the importunate speech had subsided, he resumed the suspended word with the same calmness with which he had endured the interruption: speaking when fitting and being silent when fitting. He was swift to hear and slow to speak, but not slow to anger (Jas. 1:19). How can he be called slow to anger, when he was found, so to say, to have none at all?

5. Rightly a honeycomb: for, composed and planted throughout with uncorrupted cells, he seemed in every act, word, and deed [Col. 0217B] to sweat forth the honey of inner sweetness. Happy is he in whom Jesus finds a whole honeycomb to eat, thick and not dried out.

Consider the nature of the honeycomb: it has, as it were, a helmeted head, because of the shape of the vessel in which it grows. Then it hangs from above and comes forth from above. According to Paul, the good helmet is hope of eternal salvation (1 Thess. 5:8). From the hope of heavenly things, indeed, the head of every action and the whole purpose of life ought to begin; it ought to cleave to that hope, tend toward it, and defend itself by it against every temptation.

If you see a person who, because of hope in heavenly things, is filled in every action—even under adverse circumstances—with joy of spirit sweeter than honey, what would you judge him to be but a honeycomb overflowing with honey in all its cells? But what if you see a person capacious in understanding, disciplined in conduct, consistent with himself in the even proportion of his actions and life, fitted together everywhere with such vessels, but empty and drained of the honeyed liquid of hope laid up in heaven [Col. 0217C]? Does this portray for you anything other than the dryness of a parched honeycomb?

The disadvantage is indeed doubled if he is at once scattered by dissipation and dried up by a certain lack of devotion. Yet it is one thing if he preserves the appearance so as to counterfeit virtue; another if he exhibits the form of integrity and the favourable capacity for hope to be poured in, so that vessels fit to receive the gift of spiritual sweetness may not be lacking, and cells suitable for the heavenly honey.

6. But this honeycomb of ours, of whom we speak, was whole and overflowing with inner liquid. He was full of cells; here and there he distilled sweetness; as an assiduous worker in the divine word, he fashioned honeycombs [Col. 0217D]. Good honeycombs, by which the throats of many are daily sweetened while they are still whole. He did not pursue an annoying subtlety that supplies more material for contention than for instruction. Industrious in moral teaching, he committed it to the most polished cells of words. He was prudent in mystical discourse, which he dispensed among the perfect. His milk-like teaching overflowed for the salvation and consolation of little ones; yet he often secretly mixed into it the wine of speech that gladdens and intoxicates.

So it was: his milk possessed the power of wine. His simple instruction and milk-like discourse habitually seized the mind of the hearer, imperceptibly, into an intoxicating ecstasy of an alienated mind. Hence the one who drank from him could rightly say: “I drank wine with milk.” Indeed, he knew how to mix these temperately in milk and to provide both in either. He used material easy for edification, but in his words one felt the force of intoxicating grace. His understanding was easy, but his affection was powerful [Col. 0218A].

7. Certainly we must grieve that we have been deprived of the abundance of so great a man; nonetheless, we must rejoice that we have sent beforehand from our little gardens such a bundle of myrrh to that heavenly garden. There he is an ornament, who here had been our aid. And although our hives seem emptied and our garden stripped bare, he left many handfuls from which God is able, through the increase of virtues, to create bundles.

This he does also throughout the whole Church [Col. 0218B], until, through unbroken successions and the completion of the dispensation of every rank, he says to his bride, now perfect and consummated: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I gathered my myrrh with my spices; I ate my honeycomb with my honey; I drank my wine with my milk. Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, dearly beloved.”

Although this is most perfectly hoped for in that universal introduction of the Church into the Lord’s joy which will take place after the resurrection, nevertheless we believe that the citizens of heaven are daily invited to the banquet of mutual rejoicing whenever any holy soul—whether one such as we have mentioned above, or one of lesser perfection and grace—is transferred into the loveliness of paradise, into ever-green gardens, “to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God” [Col. 0218C].

8. Recall these things, brothers; remember them, and pour out your souls within yourselves. This remembrance is inflamed: it will make your soul melt and pour itself out in delights and longings when you pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle. For “in the voice of exultation and confession is the sound of one feasting” (Ps. 41:5). Sweet there is each sound: that of the feasting friend and that of the inviting Lord. For the inviting voice says: “Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, dearly beloved.”

“Friends,” he says, “and dearly beloved.” These are names of endearment; yet these endearments do not savour of flattery but are full of duty and love. And the very endearments uttered by the Lord do not lack the effect of intoxication: they are efficacious in softening the affections of those to whom they are made [Col. 0218D]. Yet there is a distinction between them, and the title “dearly beloved” conveys something more of grace than “friends.”

The Lord says to the Apostles: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you. I will no longer call you servants, but friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John 15:14–15). See here also a certain distance. There they are called friends, and here also, but differently: there because they do; here because they know; there because of service; here because of mystery; there they eat, here they also drink. In both places they are friends, but not yet dearly beloved. To the dearly beloved intoxication is granted in drinking.

The very form of the name secretly suggests a certain superabundance and signifies the fullness of charity. The *charissimus*, “dearly beloved,” is one most full of charity. The *charissimus* is one infused and imbued with charity [Col. 0219A], whose marrow, bones, and all inward parts are watered by the liquid of charity. Nor is he intoxicated because he is dearly beloved, although he is dearly beloved because he is intoxicated. For what else is it to be intoxicated except to be filled with the delight of most perfect charity?

Or perhaps we may distinguish thus: the dearly beloved are those loving most fully; the intoxicated, those delighted most perfectly. “Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, dearly beloved.” Friends are those who either act or hear; the dearly beloved are those who cleave. Friends act for him and hear from him; the dearly beloved are intoxicated by him. Friends are those to whom he has made known what he heard from the Father; the dearly beloved are those into whom he has poured full knowledge of the Father himself. There many things are taught [Col. 0219B]; here one thing is loved. In the dearly beloved there is no dispersion into works or doctrine, but only the outpouring and summit of love. Friends are those conformed to the divine will; the dearly beloved are those intoxicated and imbued with the delight of divine love.

9. “Eat, friends.” It is no longer said, “The poor shall eat and be satisfied” (Ps. 21:27), but, “Eat, friends, and be intoxicated.” How are those poor who are intoxicated from the abundance of the Lord’s house? How can poverty exist where abundance is? “Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, dearly beloved.” You are friends and dearly beloved to me: friends because of social love; dearly beloved because of bridal love. “Be intoxicated, dearly beloved. I brought you into the wine-cellar, that I might set charity in order within you.”

Charity is not ordered unless your mind has been intoxicated by the force of charity [Col. 0219C]. It is not ordered unless it has been set above all other affections. The pre-eminence of love is a good order; pre-eminent love makes persons dearly beloved. The dearly beloved are those in whom there is nothing empty of charity or occupied with another concern. The order is full when one passes from the rank of the beloved to that of the most dearly beloved. The order is full when nothing can be added to the abundance of charity.

“Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, dearly beloved.” There all are friends and all are dearly beloved. All are given drink and all are intoxicated. But it is not so in this valley of tears, not so. Many are friends; few are dearly beloved. Many are given drink, but not all are intoxicated; and those who are intoxicated become sober again. For an hour they pass beyond themselves in mind, and again return to their customary sobriety [Col. 0219D]. They fall asleep and awaken; they become drowsy and shortly afterward are awake again. Therefore it follows: “I sleep, but my heart watches.”

Yet these watchings do not seem to succeed sleep, but to accompany sleep itself. May the Lord Jesus grant us to understand vigilantly what must be said further on these matters, and grant you to hear it—he who lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLII

“I sleep, but my heart watches. The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me, my sister,” etc., “for my head,” etc. (Song 5:2).

1. “I sleep, but my heart watches.” After yesterday’s chapter, by what sequence of reasoning is the discourse of such a response introduced? There was a general invitation; this is an answer, as it were, from an individual. There many are invited; here one responds. There it is said, “Be intoxicated, dearly beloved”; here she who is most dearly beloved because she is the bride reports that she sleeps. “I sleep.”

What wonder if a singular response is given to a common invitation? Many are dearly beloved, but for all of them there is one heart and one soul. “My dove is one,” he says (Song 6:8). Love unites, and love intoxicates. Do you see how justly one answer is made by all those whom the powerful common draught of charity fills? Truly mighty is the power of love, intoxicating and estranging. Do you wish to hear how charity estranges the mind which it intoxicates? “I sleep,” she says: as though she said to her beloved, “You summon me to intoxication, and I devote my whole self to this gift [Col. 0220B]. I sleep, but my heart watches. I sleep and rest from other occupations; therefore my heart watches more freely in pursuit of this intoxication and in drinking wine.”

A wonderful order: from intoxication, sleep; and from sleep, watchfulness. He says, “Be intoxicated”; and she says, “I sleep.” A good sleep is an ecstasy of the mind and estrangement from the affections of the flesh and—if this may also be said—from the senses of the body. Then spiritual love flourishes and watches more keenly when every animal passion and affection has been entirely lulled to sleep. Sleep and intoxication alike perform the role of estrangement. They have this in common with one another: each seizes the mind for itself and does not allow it to remain in its own possession. Each steals, as it were, the soul’s former state and fashions new affections [Col. 0220C].

“I sleep, but my heart watches.” Others sleep their own sleep, and their delight rests in their own will and pleasure. From such persons I sleep, and my heart watches for you. “Others sleep at your rebuke, O Lord” (Ps. 75:7); I sleep from drunkenness. This rebuke is harsh enough when, by overlooking a person, you permit him to remain in his own sloth, since such overlooking is a great sign of the rebuke of abandonment. He sleeps from this rebuke who, through divine overlooking, gives himself up to drowsy security and does not perceive that the patience of one who overlooks him brings forth the rejection of one who remains unrepentant. The long-suffering patience of one who does not meanwhile strike has force in modest minds; and the same tolerance of the Lord which makes honourable minds anxious makes hard hearts secure.

2. “I sleep,” she says, “but my heart watches.” I sleep, not rebuked, but made heavy with wine, to which you call those dear to you.
