The surfeit of your intoxication raises me above the world and gives me to you: it lulls me to sleep and awakens me; it makes me forget worldly matters and does not permit me to forget you. “I sleep”: sleep with me, according to what you yourself declare in Solomon, “If two sleep together, they shall keep one another warm” (Eccl. 4:11). Thus, through the presence of my beloved and the force of love, my heart will watch all the more. My heart watches when your love flourishes more strongly in it.

“I sleep, but my heart watches.” I sleep for the repose of my friend; I watch because of rapture. In the sweet sleep of my repose, the solicitude of one who watches dreams of you more watchfully. Sweet sleep and sweet dream: to know no other things, to know you alone; to be free for you and to see you—as this is granted here in a dream, so to say, and in shadow and enigma. This is a good surfeit: an abundance of this freedom and vision [Col. 0221A].

This vision has something like a dream, because it comes about neither by human choice and effort nor from our investigation, but by the visitation of the Dayspring from on high. Paul is as though asleep when he dies to the world; as though awake when he lives to Christ. May my soul sleep, brothers, in this sleep; may my watchings become like these. Would that they were continual and uninterrupted. But now, by a reversed order, I watch and my heart sleeps: the spirit sleeps, the flesh watches. And if the flesh sleeps, the spirit does not immediately watch. The soul is granted rest, yet it is not as yet drunk and carried away by that glorious intoxication. It sleeps as regards temptations, but is not yet awakened by those intoxicating endearments. Although these are often tasted, nevertheless with renewed freshness they awaken the soul which they intoxicate [Col. 0221B].

3. Those are rightly called watchers who never digest that intoxicating wine, who are always wet with the abundance of eternal delight. You read of such watchers in Daniel’s book (Dan. 4:10). Rightly watchers, in whom there is nothing that needs to be lulled asleep, but everything watches for God. Rightly watchers, whose watchings are not interrupted. No animal affection is felt in them which ought to be put to sleep so that the watchings of the heart may be freer.

There are certain watchings filled with the trouble of anxieties, of which Peter says: “Be sober and watch, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). And Paul says: “Watch and stand firm in the faith” (1 Cor. 16:13). Yet these watchings are not free from anxiety, by which teachers of the Church are troubled, like those evangelical shepherds “watching and keeping the watches of the night over their flock” [Col. 0221C] (Luke 2:8). These watchings are tormented by a certain trouble through caution against impending evil.

The watchings of the sleeping bride do not contain caution against evil but an abundance of good. For vehement love imposes watchings of unfulfilled longing on a mind freed from occupation. The watchings are either desire for the hoped-for presence or delight in the presence attained. Good watchings are vigorous and undrowsy devotion, whether in the abundance of the beloved who is present or in longing for one absent. This neither watches nor flourishes unless the mind is restless and, as regards the pursuits and desires of the age, lulled to sleep. Therefore she says: “I sleep, but my heart watches.”

And in Job we read that “in a vision of the night, when sleep falls upon people and they sleep upon their beds, then God opens their ears” (Job 33:15–16); then he speaks, then he knocks. Therefore it follows here:

4. “The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me.” She rightly watches, not knowing at what hour her beloved comes. The bride’s watchings and the beloved’s voice are, as it were, continuous. “My heart,” she says, “watches”; and immediately she adds, “The voice of my beloved knocking: Open to me.” My heart watches, and my beloved does not sleep. His voice knocks and says: “Open to me.” My heart watches, and he at once flies to me, and his voice is heard: “The voice,” she says, “of my beloved.”

This voice is known to me; this voice is welcome to me. I am deaf to other voices; at this voice I have awakened. As soon as it sounded in my ears, I leapt for joy. Many voices commonly make noise and whisper false blandishments, but not as the voice of my beloved. Great, brothers, is the prudence of the bride, rich in discernment of spirits, who knows so well how to distinguish between the tricks of demons and the true endearments of the beloved. “The voice of my beloved knocking.”

What voice is such as Jesus’ voice? Is it that of philosophers? Of heretics? Of the Law? Of the Prophets? His is a powerful voice: “He has made foolish the wisdom of this world” (1 Cor. 1:20). The Law and the Prophets brought no one to perfection; the voice of Jesus embraces the sum of perfection, contains the precepts of perfection, and moves the affections [Col. 0222B]. “The voice,” she says, “of one knocking.” It knocks and penetrates, effective like a two-edged sword; it glides in gently and sweetly persuades what no other teaching could obtain.

It is not lofty speech, but lofty mysteries. What disputation or severity ever conveyed in speech, or persuaded by inspiration, humility of conscience, moderation of conduct, obedient compliance, purity of the flesh, contempt for the world, longing for eternal things, and knowledge of divinity? Under this teaching we have learned to hope and sigh for the grace of resurrection, the impassibility of the risen, the eternity of life, and the revelation of majesty.

“God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75:2). But is it only so? Is it so explicit? So deeply impressed? So widely spread? “His name is great in Israel,” but it was not great to that extent in evident teaching, vehement devotion, or the numerous multitude of believers [Col. 0222C]. “Formerly God spoke to the fathers in the prophets; in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son” (Heb. 1:1–2). Therefore this is a powerful voice, a voice of strength, a voice of the beloved; but it could not prevail in Jewish ears. The Gentile world heard it, confessed it, and did not deny it, saying: “The voice of my beloved knocking.”

I recognize both to belong to my beloved: voice and knock, word and power. In both my beloved is pleasing to me; in both he caresses and moves me—by voice and knock, and, so to speak, by song and psalm. He rightly knocks and, as it were, beats a drum, who sets in motion the harmonious symphony of word and deed. Think of Jesus as a drum: approach, touch, strike, sound out his character, deeds, words, and life. Every string in him is stretched and resonant; when touched, each gives back sweet melody.

Jesus himself knocks upon himself. “No one,” he says, “takes my life from me; I lay it down, and take it up again. I have power to lay it down and power to take it up again” [Col. 0222D] (John 10:17–18). Consider what this laying down, taking up, and power over both sound forth to you; consider how these themselves provide the occasion for such knocking. Do they not most of all knock upon and awaken our hearts, so that we, made like a kind of lyre, may strive to sound in harmony with this music?

5. “The voice of my beloved knocking.” She rightly says “of my beloved,” as though he speaks and knocks solely out of love and grace. “Open to me, because my head is full of dew, and my locks of the drops of the night” [Col. 0223A]. Charity grows cold in Judaea; now, according to Scripture, the passage is being made to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46). The word of salvation was sent to them, but they rejected it, judging themselves unworthy of eternal life. I have been shut out by her; you, open to me, “because my head is full of dew, and my locks of the drops of the night.”

The head of Christ is God. The Jews glory in God the Father and boast that they have knowledge of him; they reject and blaspheme the Son. You, open to me. “My head is full of dew.” He does not desire such persons, nor thirst for them, but rather finds them repugnant; therefore it is full. It is full of dew because they are light in understanding, lacking the weight of reason, having no force in their assertion: light in reasoning, heavy in obstinacy; like dew and drops, ineffectual yet persistent. “And my locks are full of the drops of night,” which are cold and dark.

For there is a dew which is not of night. Isaiah says to God: “Your dew is a dew of light” (Isa. 26:19). “And my locks are full of drops of night.” They clung to figures, knowing the letter but not knowing the spiritual sense. The Jews glory in knowledge of the one God and in figurative observance of the Law, while denying the mystery of the Trinity and the truth of prefiguration; they boast in superfluous and lifeless signs [Col. 0223B]. They are troublesome to me; they oppress my disciples, who are like a certain ornament and glory of my head. Therefore I flee: open to me.

6. Certain heretics try to extinguish Christ’s divinity, which they neither wish nor are able to reach by faith or reason. They contaminate, corrupt, and overwhelm the subtle and harmonious testimonies of the Scriptures, which rest upon divine authority—like certain locks of the head—by the incoherent sophistries of their arguments and by tiny quibbles, as it were, resembling drops of dew [Col. 0223C]. These also, presuming upon knowledge of God and subtle spiritual perceptions, as though proudly situated upon the very head and hair of God, are compared to dew and drops of night, so that you may understand them to be minute, cold, fluid, and inconsistent with themselves.

But if you see someone holding a sound faith, as it were the head itself; sharing in the sacraments only superficially; and flourishing in subtle understanding—yet he is cold because of an evil conscience, dark because of hypocrisy, and fluid because of swift passing away. For “the joy of the hypocrite is like a point” (Job 20:5). Jesus judges such a person to be outside and flees from one who oppresses him and is, as it were, burdensome to him.

Persons of this kind do not so much walk as fly about in great and wonderful matters above themselves, wandering suspended in the air through proud exaltation. In ambitious commerce they walk about in darkness: hunting profit from religion, pretending to possess spiritual teaching, offering discourse fluid like dew, claiming to know uncertain, hidden, and night-like mysteries, claiming to hold the head and summit of the wisdom and holiness of God and to cling to the very crown of Christ; they seek to excel rather than to enter [Col. 0223D].

7. Jesus, bearing these persons with difficulty and fleeing them, says: “Open to me, my sister.” You who are within, who do not wander outside, who do not fly about in lofty things, who wish not so much to stand out externally as to remain within—open to me [Col. 0224A]. “Open to me, open to me.” Whom do you seek except me? You are wholly mine: wholly mine, and mine by many claims. By how many? Hear how many: “My sister, my near one, my dove, my spotless one.”

“My sister,” because in the assumed flesh you are my kinswoman. “My near one,” because from my side, while I slept upon the cross, the new Eve was created from the second Adam, so that they are no longer two but one flesh. There is natural kinship; here, personal union. There, sister; here, bride. “My dove,” through the grace of the Spirit; “my spotless one,” through forgiveness and discipline. In the flesh, sister; in the sacraments, bride; in spirit, simple; spotless in holiness: in all these ways mine. “Open to me.”

Do what you are doing: open to me. I am within, but open to me in those among whom I still remain outside. Open to them; invite them; bring them into the place of the wonderful tabernacle. Knock, that a great and manifest door may be opened to you, as Paul says (1 Cor. 16:9), so that entrance may be given to your persuasions into their affections. Penetrate to them so that afterwards you may bring them in to yourself. Go out to them so that those who outside grow cold with frozen affection may enter in to you. Redeem the losses of your going out by the introduction of others.

What do you say? “I have put off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” You have put off your garment—the garment of fleshly care, certainly a troublesome garment and perhaps a defiled one. You have put off your own garment: put on mine. “The zeal of my house has consumed you”; therefore, according to Isaiah, put on “the cloak of zeal” [Col. 0224B] (Isa. 59:17). Insist, rebuke, preach, exhort, in season and out of season (2 Tim. 4:2). It is not to defile your feet to walk this path. If any dust clings to you, shake it from your feet. Isaiah commends not defiled but beautiful feet when he says: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those proclaiming peace, proclaiming good things!” (Isa. 52:7).

Do not delay. Let the examples of my works move you. Let my hand touch you if you are sluggish at my word. I am zealous; you also be zealous for me. Put aside sweet leisure; involve yourself a little in my concerns. Everyone who serves as a soldier for God ought, when commanded, to involve himself in such concerns. Though I was rich, I became poor for all; equal with God, I emptied myself, taking the form of a servant. I died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for me [Col. 0224D].

8. The bride, considering such things in her Beloved and moved by these examples to emulate them, says: “My Beloved put his hand through the opening, and at his touch my inmost being trembled.” Through the narrow opening of poverty, persecution, and death, he has introduced to me examples of his works. These touch me; these move me. For the trembling of the inmost being is the movement of the mind. Hear, finally, the effect of this movement. For it follows: “I rose to open to my Beloved.” Listen and understand, you who rush too hastily and with excessive forwardness toward honours in the Church. For the bride to whom the caresses of this Song are sung approaches slowly and hesitantly, even after hearing herself called sister, near one, [Col. 0225A] dove, immaculate one. Consider whether these things are in you; and if they are, fear lest you lose them; if they are not, fear still more lest you fail to receive them. Notice after how many invitations and commendations she says: “I rose to open to my Beloved.” It is vain for you to rise before you are called, though you eat the bread of that holy delight and drink the wine of which it was said above: “Eat, my friends, and drink; become intoxicated, beloved ones.” Indeed, unless you have been invited, you should regard it as vain—and even dangerous—to rise from your sweet sleep before your Beloved says to you: “Open to me.” Let not the voice of ambition, greed, restlessness, or pride stir your mind or entice it by deceptive flattery. Let these voices be unknown to you; let such things not urge upon you a good work. Rise only at [Col. 0225B] the voice of your Beloved, who lives and reigns, etc.

## SERMON XLIII

“Open to me, my sister,” etc. “My head is full of dew. I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” etc. “He put his hand through the opening,” etc. (Song 5:2–4).

1. In the preceding sermon we examined this passage so as to say that Jesus implored from his bride consolations against the vexations of those who attempt to infect the purity of our faith with the corruption of human and faithless teaching, and to soak it with the nocturnal dew of subtle persuasions, which the prince of darkness, the prince of this air, secretly and gently instils. For elsewhere in Scripture he complains that “waters have overflowed above my head” (Lam. 3:54). Yesterday, therefore, the Lord Jesus was presented by us as fleeing troubles; today he will be presented [Col. 0225C] as bringing joys. Yesterday he was presented as seeking consolations; today as carrying consolations with him: yesterday, full of injuries; today, of graces. That interpretation concerns the few; this one relates to the many. Not all are either fit for, or appointed to, the work of preaching. For not all are able to repel corruptions of the faith, nor are all set over this office. Not all can be mothers and brides; all can be sisters and brides. Not all can endure the injury of childbirth; all ought to embrace the grace of an embrace. In yesterday’s interpretation the liquid of that nocturnal dew was troublesome; let today’s be welcome. There Jesus speaks, uttering complaints; here he speaks, offering endearments. There he flees hostile persons; here he hastens only to the bride [Col. 0225D].

2. “Open to me, my sister, my near one.” Observe here the discipline of guarding, where the door does not stand open indiscriminately. Who may enter there at will, where Jesus himself does not enter without knocking, nor except when his voice has been heard and recognized? O happy am I, if it may be said of my soul: “This gate is shut,” and through it no undisciplined impulse is admitted, whether stealthily or casually! It lies open to the Prince alone, if I set a guard upon my mouth, so that it may lie open to the Prince alone when he stands before it. “Open to me the gate of righteousness”; and, entering through it, I will feast with you: I will eat there and drink and become intoxicated; finally, I too will intoxicate you with my drops. I do not come barren, but moist with the sweetly descending dew of graces. Open to me. I am already within you [Col. 0226A] now; but open to me, that I may enter more fully. Open to me. I approach now as though new, and dripping with fresh affection. My speech will flow upon you like dew, when I instil into you the mysteries of my divinity. My head abounds with dew, and contemplation of the divine nature in me brings forth subtle and fruitful meanings.

Why do you linger only around the mysteries of my humanity? Why do you remain seated so long only at the feet? Rise; ascend to the head; open to it. Open to me in this, because my head is full of dew. Humanity obtains grace; divinity bestows it. Humanity shed blood; divinity pours in love. My head is full. It itself is the very dew. It descends into the soul and waters its marrow. I have entered to a certain point; open to me, that I may reach the innermost places, that the sweet knowledge of my divinity [Col. 0226B] may flow in and permeate all that is within you. Open to me, that the subtle dew of my divinity may soak the soil of your heart and make it drunk.

And indeed it is so, brethren. Where the subject-matter has greater glory, there meditation has greater grace. What possesses greater excellence demands greater reverence and returns greater grace. What by a certain merit of its nature is pre-eminent bestows a fuller delight in its apprehension. That which surpasses all things pleases more than all things. A special mode of beholding is owed to a singular subject-matter. It is not within human power, for it is not a human practice. It is granted to a tranquil and vigilant mind, yet not at its own wish, but when he himself wills and says: “Open to me.” What is it to say, “Open to me,” except by a certain enticement to draw the affection, to move desire, [Col. 0226C] so that a mind touched in part by the radiance of so great a light may present itself purified for fuller perception? Thus light says, as it were, to the eye: “Open to me”; and from a slight perception it begets an appetite for a greater participation in itself.

3. “Open to me, my sister.” What is it, good Jesus, that you ask to be opened? You yourself have the key of David: “You open, and no one shuts” (Rev. 3:7). Your appearing is an opening. Appear, and no one shuts you out. When the glory of your majesty begins to shine upon someone even in the smallest degree, it immediately turns and carries the soul to itself. While it shines, it does not permit itself to be shut out. The heart you penetrate, you open for yourself; you keep it open so long as you do not withdraw yourself. Perhaps both are necessary, and the opening of the Bridegroom and that of the bride are kindred. The opening [Col. 0226D] of the Bridegroom is his appearing; the opening of the bride is her preparation and fitting disposition for such sweet employments.

“My head is full of dew, and my locks with drops of the night.” The head is full, and those who cling to it are moistened by it. God is delightful in himself and delightful in his saints, who arise from him by grace and, through his ordering, remain in him like certain distinct locks. Both contemplations are beautiful: that of God himself and that of the graces proceeding from him. “There are divisions of graces” (1 Cor. 12:4), as though there were a distinction of locks. For his invisible things appear to exhibit a certain distinction, though only in proportion to our capacity. Since distinct signs and words endeavour to signify one thing and another, what is one in him becomes known to us as though multiple and varied.

Some things refer only to his greatness: regard this as one lock. Some refer only to power: understand this also as, in a sense, one. Likewise, what pertains to wisdom, goodness, predestination, providence, grace, forgiveness, counsel, and the thoughts of God generally—whatever is comprehended by one mode of signification and as it were belongs to one—interpret as one lock; what pertains to another, believe to be another. “His invisible things,” says the Apostle, “are perceived by understanding through the things that have been made; even his eternal divinity” (Rom. 1:20). He expressed the former in the plural, the latter in the singular. Take the latter, then, as the head; the former as the locks. For divinity in itself is one and simple; but in accordance with its effect in subjects, and with the particular image impressed upon subjects, it receives a number of diverse significations [Col. 0227B].

Therefore essential names can be said reciprocally of one another, but denominative names cannot. God’s essence is his knowledge, by the truth of convertibility and identity of substance; yet, though it is true that God knows something, it does not consequently follow that he is that thing. Likewise, power and will in God are one and the same essentially; but names denominated from them do not mutually follow one another. For these denominations, since they contain some effect with respect to creatures, draw from those effects a related multiplicity and cannot accompany one another. A wondrous identity, and a wondrous diversity: both inexplicable, both full of wonder, containing the most hidden and efficacious causes of devotion and reverence [Col. 0227C].

4. Draw near, bride, to this head of the Beloved, to his locks; press the dew-laden hair, and you will draw forth from it much sweetest liquid. They are full of drops of night—hidden drops, drops refreshing with a sweetness not unknown. A time will come when such drops, pressed forth more frequently, will produce the rush of an entire river—a good river indeed, which cools the desire of burning love.

Whether you understand the head and locks in the ways stated above, or understand by the head that bare knowledge of divinity which is face to face, and by the locks that knowledge which comes through a mirror and under the veil of an enigma, in both you will find an abundant dew of refreshment. Perhaps this is why dew is assigned simply to the head, while drops are attributed to the locks with the addition “of night”: because this vision through mirror and enigma has something of the quality of night—less brilliant and less ardent.

Emulate the Bridegroom, holy soul: let head and hair be moistened with the dew of devotion—the head, of intention; the locks, of thought. Like wet hair, let them be drawn tight, let them be stretched out, let them be glossy: thinned by the discipline of continence, extended by the perseverance of continuance, glossy with exultation of spirit, lest they be infected even briefly by the dark and cold dew of malice and wickedness, which the prince of this air gently and secretly sprinkles. Beware his deceptive infections: he falsely claims to possess the heavenly dew of your Bridegroom. Shut him out; and if he says, “Open to me, my sister,” answer that you have no kinship with him [Col. 0228A]. She who is related to him is not immaculate. A perverse kinship, followed by contagion. Whom Christ calls sister, he adds as immaculate. Listen for when you may say: “The voice of my Beloved knocking.” At his first attack the enemy acts timidly: fearing to be caught as a tempter, he strokes rather than knocks. Your Beloved, wishing to make himself known, knocks boldly: “Open to me, because my head,” he says, “is full of dew, and my locks with drops of night.” As though he said: “Open to me, because I come in full of the dew of grace. Open; prepare yourself fittingly for so great a presence.”

5. Then she says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I soil them?” You say, “Open to me.” Behold, I have opened; I am ready. But I shrink from being disturbed again by domestic concerns. I do not wish to put on again the tunic [Col. 0228B] I once took off. How shall I put it on? How? In no way. I do not consent; I cannot hear without distress the word “putting on again.” I took off the woollen garment, being clothed in fine garments. I know how laborious Martha’s tasks are, how burdensome her garment of business is; how, by running about continually in frequent service, she must have feet defiled in affections and steps of works. I cannot decline from Mary into Martha. I have chosen the better part: to make my heart open and ready for the coming of the Beloved. He does not seem to be distressed by the labours of Martha’s tasks who, once released from them, hastens to return to them again.

Naked of every worldly matter, and without the impediment of a veil, free and with face, as it were, unveiled, I shall rise to contemplate the glory of the Beloved, and to open to him. This way is a beautiful way: no defiled foot can walk upon it, nor can it be defiled upon it. It is a short way, for the Beloved stands at the door, crying out and knocking, as though unable to bear delay. He knocks at the door, seeks an entrance, and, loving more ardently, anticipates me as I hasten [Col. 0228C].

6. “He put his hand through the opening, and at his touch my inmost being trembled.” What does it mean here that the bride, who had shut the door of her chamber [variant: little chamber], did not also stop up this opening, lest anything enter her through it unawares? Since she acted more cautiously in other matters, why did she leave room here for negligence? Or perhaps she herself knows this opening in herself less fully? For who can know all the openings in oneself, all entrances, all susceptibilities, except him who, as is read in Ezekiel, “prepared openings in a precious stone” (Ezek. 28:13)? He himself prepares openings where he wills, because where he wills he himself puts his hand through the opening, through a fitting entrance, the power of hidden inspiration. “Through the opening,” he says—that is, through a fitting, hidden, narrow entrance. For the entrance is narrow enough when Jesus puts in only his hand, as compared with the way by which he seeks the opening of the door to be made for him.

The bride’s inmost being would not be moved, she would not rise, she would not open to the Beloved, unless he himself had first inserted the hidden hand of his inspiration. The principle of the first calling is hidden, its cause concealed, and its entrance not yet broad. But it is widened when the soul cooperates with the Bridegroom who works first: she strives, rises, and opens. The first hand is recognized as God’s alone; the second as God’s and the human being’s together [Col. 0229A]. And although it belongs more to God because it is his gift, it is nevertheless attributed to the human being alone as merit.

Narrow also, and as if conceived through an opening, is that knowledge of God which is received through contemplation of his works: it is like the touch of his hand, not the vision of his face. Notice a threefold mode of contemplation: in the head, in the locks, and in the hand. In the head, nature; in the locks, form; in the hand, workmanship. Of this last the Psalmist says: “You have made me glad, Lord, in your workmanship, and I will exult in the works of your hands” (Ps. 91:5 [92:5]). We may also call them thus: essence, signs, works. Signs express, through a certain likeness in their own kind, knowledge of that divine nature; works prove it. Signs, so to speak, portray it; works establish it. This last mode of contemplation belongs to the simple; the second, to the learned; the first, to the most pure. Nevertheless, as we have already said, the putting of the hand through the opening signifies that hidden and secret infusion of inspiration which the touch of divine power effects.

7. Here also three things are to be observed in the bride. What three? First, that she trembles; second, that she rises; third, that she opens. The first indeed takes place in her, but not from her; the two following take place in her in such a way that they are also from her. In the first she is anticipated; in the second she strives; in the third she lays hold. When she trembles, she does nothing herself, but rather undergoes something; when she rises and opens, she applies something of her own effort. She trembles when she sweetly feels the hidden movement of holy inspiration; she rises when she consents and follows where it leads [Col. 0229C]; she opens when the mind gives itself wholly to this work and renders itself capable of it.

Yet the more it opens itself to this use, the more quickly it fails through excessive affection and intensity. “I remembered God,” he says, “and was delighted; I was exercised, and my spirit failed” (Ps. 86:4 [77:4]). Relate “remembrance” to the inmost being, delight to trembling, and exercise to rising, and the correspondence is apt. For his saying, “my spirit failed,” concerns what follows in this passage: “I opened the bolt of my door to my Beloved, and he withdrew.” He withdraws when you fail, unable to endure him. When you are affected more vehemently, then he flies away more swiftly. The more affectionately you seek the embrace of the Beloved, and strive, as it were with an opened heart, to swallow and consume him whole, the more swiftly the fleeting presence of your Beloved withdraws.

[Col. 0229D] 8. But let us now return to the sequence of the text. “I rose to open to my Beloved. My hands dripped myrrh; my fingers were full of the choicest myrrh.” Why, when she is about to speak of opening, does she first mention the hands? Perhaps she wished to suggest with what hands you ought to open to your Beloved, by what merits of works you should prepare an entrance for the truth to be contemplated. Myrrh-bearing hands are indeed good hands: hands which work the mortification of the flesh, restrain its excess, and check wantonness, so that delight in the Word may flow in more abundantly.

Do you not regard these works of regular observance, succeeding one another in turn, as drops of myrrh which anoint the mind and restrain the flesh? Vigils, fasts, a chastened and spare diet, rough cloth and [Col. 0230A] dark bread, blows of rods voluntarily accepted, loud psalmody in the morning, and silent prayer—both in the vehement spirit of the heart, but the latter all the more vehement because the bodily spirit is less restrained—why should they not drip upon us as they succeed one another in turn? They are rightly compared to myrrh because they bring the bitterness of affliction to the flesh and soothe the mind, as with an ointment, by devotion.

And so that you may understand that discernment and rational service are present: “My fingers,” she says, “were full of the choicest myrrh.” The hands are works; the fingers, discernment. Myrrh is both the bodily practice and the ointment-like gladness of the heart. This myrrh is approved; for there is a certain myrrh which is reprobate. When you see the fingers of certain childish people everywhere dripping forbidden signs, the hand of a wanton or perverse impulse scattering indications on every side, you will not, I think, deny that such persons pour out the bitterness of undisciplined conduct as though it were reprobate myrrh [Col. 0230B]. Is not such wantonness like myrrh, since it grieves the disciplined conduct of the brethren and will bring forth for itself in the future the sorrow of shame and repentance?

But the choicest myrrh is that found praiseworthy in many proofs of regular exercise. Both regular discipline and hostile affliction are approved when the virtue of patience, preserving its integrity, is not corrupted and degraded by excessive bitterness. Recall the times when the Church, still a young maiden, knocked at the ears of the Gentiles so that the door might be opened to their hearts for her Beloved Christ and an entrance made available: how countless struggles she endured, 150 how many martyrdoms she accomplished, how unceasingly she was vexed by punishments! Truly her fingers were full of the choicest myrrh, since her virtue was adorned in her labours by proofs of every kind of suffering.

9. With hands of this sort, brethren, strive to open to the Word and prepare an entrance for the sweetness of contemplation. By the merits of good actions you will open more abundantly the inner recesses of your minds to Christ. See whether the myrrh of your labour and weariness has been found praiseworthy through many trials, like gold tested by fire. “My fingers,” she says, “are full of the choicest myrrh.” The subtlety of discernment and abundance of anointing are signified: for she calls them fingers, and full ones.

They drip and are full: they have alternation, not depletion. Fasts are interspersed with refreshment, labours with rest, vigils with sleep. Alternation brings restoration, not failure. “My fingers,” she says, “are full of the choicest myrrh.” Do you desire the delights of contemplation, to enjoy in leisure the embraces of the Bridegroom, to contain him alone in the secret place of your heart? Do not come to open with empty hands; do not come with dry hands. Action precedes contemplation. The more you have mortified animal impulses by the myrrh of continence and affliction, the more abundant an entrance you will prepare for the Beloved.

Finally, it follows: “I opened the bolt of my door to my Beloved.” In the narrow compass in which we must conclude this sermon, we cannot open the door of this chapter. Let us defer it to another discourse, seeking and awaiting grace from him who [Col. 0231A] has the key of David, without whom no one opens—Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLIV

“I opened the bolt of my door to my Beloved; but he had withdrawn and passed on. My soul melted when he spoke” (Song 5:6).

1. Today, brethren, we shall speak to you about the opening of the door. For yesterday’s sermon, concerning the activity which is as it were a path toward opening, set forth the final point of our discussion. Good indeed is that activity which always displays the hope and likeness of immortality and incorruption, which does not sow in the flesh lest it reap corruption from it. Would that I could truthfully say that myrrh is always in my hands! “If anyone,” says Jesus, “does the will of my Father, he shall know of my teaching” (John 7:17). See how an act of devotion provides an entrance to truth. Good indeed are actions which are distinguished by a certain balance and moderation and filled with the devotion of anointing. Christ is rightly opened to by anointing hands, for he received his name from anointing. Perhaps he does not know how to enter except through an anointed door. Therefore, in the Temple, small doors were made of olive wood, through which an entrance might lie open into the Holy of Holies (1 Kgs. 6:31). Such wood is suited to supply anointing liquid. They are called little doors, and the entrance of olives is narrow; but in the richness of grace you will enter without difficulty, where understanding is subtle and the mystery hidden. The entrance will not be laborious if you are willing to use the oil of devotion and charity as a door. I think the testimony drawn from the Temple is fitting: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17).

Have, then, doors in your temple through which the High Priest alone may enter into the innermost recess of your heart. Shut the door; put on the bolt, except when your Beloved knocks, wishing to enter. If there is no door, an entrance will lie indiscriminately open to every passer-by. If the door is shut but not fastened with a bolt, it will easily yield and open to an attack, having no firmer closure. Have both the door of circumspection and the bolt of constancy. Watch circumspectly; resist steadfastly. Let forgetfulness and ignorance not creep in; let wickedness not break in. Or, if you prefer to distinguish them in this way, regard thoughtful forethought as the door, prayer as the bolt. Strengthened by such a bar, your door will not lie open to hostile attack. “He has strengthened,” says the Psalmist, “the bars of your gates” (Ps. 147:13). Do you not seem to hear in bars and gates, as it were, the door and bolt? Both are necessary against the enemy’s snares. But where you hear the voice and knocking of the Beloved, where through the opening you feel the subtle touch of his hand, remove the bolt, open the door, let every obstacle yield. If possible, remove the whole middle wall, so that your Beloved may pour himself freely into you. Turn anxiety against demonic temptations into security because of the Bridegroom’s presence; turn the caution by which you repel the enemy into an abundance of enjoyment of the Beloved. He knows that he has opened the door who said: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 107:2 [108:1]).

2. How does Jesus need a door, when he says in the Gospel: “I am the door”? A wondrous consideration: he is a door, and he knocks at a door. He wishes us to enter through him through whom whoever enters will be saved and find pasture (John 10:9). Great is the difference between doors. There is a door in the evidences of nature, a door in the sacraments of the Church, and a door in experiences of grace. At that first door, by the guidance of natural reason, the wisdom working through its works becomes known to us, and we are admitted to some degree of truth: we infer knowledge of divinity, yet not a personal distinction within the Godhead. At this door the person is not distinguished, nor is grace bestowed. Therefore one should not knock constantly or excessively at [Col. 0232B] this door.

Through the second door, when we are initiated in saving sacraments, we enter into the unity of the Church and communion of the saints. At this second door, some are within in such a way that they are nevertheless, as it were, outside, until they approach the third. We interpret this as familiar access through the affection of charity, into a certain abundance and contemplation of the Beloved. This door, so secret and so inward, does not stand open to all, but grants entrance to the bride alone. In Ezekiel you read of many differences of doors (Ezek. 40 and 41), which it would now take too long to pursue. Yet I judge there is little difference whether you enter to him, or he himself enters to you—except that you seem then to enter to him when you anticipate him and ask first; but he enters to you when he anticipates you, knocks upon your affection, comes in unexpectedly, and moves you by the touch of an unforeseen sweetness while you are contemplating nothing of the sort [Col. 0232C].

3. When he knocks at your door in this way, do not delay: rise, hasten, lest perhaps he withdraw. For in this passage you have: “I opened the bolt of my door to my Beloved; but he had withdrawn and passed on.” Why do you depart, good Jesus? Why do you withdraw? Why do you deprive the Beloved of her desire? You bring on desire; you take away delight. Or perhaps in this manner you stretch desire toward a greater hunger and a more ardent longing by withdrawing abundance? It is so. Certainly it is so. These deceptions of love inflame love itself more and advance it toward fullness precisely by deceiving it thus.

How brief, sudden, and interrupted were those appearances of the Lord’s resurrection! To some he was scarcely recognized before he immediately slipped away. He does not permit himself to be touched by some. To others he enters while doors are shut, needing no opening of the door. For the door most fully opened to him is the one closed to every other business. When he seems to be held, he as it were steals away his welcome presence: coming secretly and departing secretly. For the joy of contemplation is like a point. It swiftly departs and transcends, in an eminent manner, every power of human capacity. We cannot follow it with equal steps in this flesh where it goes. “I said,” says Solomon, “‘I shall become wise’; and it withdrew farther from me, much more than it had been before” (Eccl. 7:24–25). Its apprehension teaches better than its deprivation [Note: [Col. 0233D] See whether the reading should be: “Its deprivation teaches better than its apprehension.”] how transcendent its majesty is. By that very fact that it is more intense, it passes more swiftly: “He,” she says, “had withdrawn and passed on.” Did you withdraw toward the bride, good Jesus, only to withdraw from her so quickly? “He had withdrawn and passed on.” What is “passed on”? He passed beyond me, passed beyond my powers, passed through me. Therefore he passed through me as one unable, as it were, to bear and sustain him.

“The word of God is a sword” (Eph. 6:17); Jesus is a sword. He passes through the soul without delay or difficulty, not remaining when the melted mind cannot sustain his intensity. This is a flaming sword. Therefore, as wax melts before fire, so the soul is kindled before his presence. “My soul melted when the Beloved spoke.” You see how his fiery speech melted the soul [Col. 0233B].

4. “I opened the bolt of my door to my Beloved; but he had withdrawn and passed on.” Thus, in the manifestation of the Lord’s resurrection made to those two going to Emmaus, when their eyes were opened to recognize Jesus, at the very hour of that opening he vanished from their sight and, as it were, passed through their hearts, as they themselves confess: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke?” etc. (Luke 24:13–32). Their hearts burned in conversation, but in the appearance they melted under that intense vision, unable to retain solidity and constancy. For what is it that Jesus vanished except that they could not remain under the glory of his appearance? He withdraws toward the Beloved like a river of peace, but passes through like a torrent of glory [Col. 0233C], like a fiery torrent melting the soul which it floods, refreshes, and passes through.

How sweet is the hour when the soul melts and mingles with this fiery torrent! How subtle it is in that moment, how attenuated, how mobile! Then it has no lukewarmness, no hardness remaining, no rigidity: it is only warm and melting. Fluidity and warmth are kindred to each other. In these two consists the exercise of contemplation. What is fluid receives heat more readily; and heat once received, conversely, renders what it finds fluid more fluid. What I call warm and fluid may be called by other names: enkindled and pure. It is warm because it loves; it is pure and fluid because it represents in itself a certain likeness [Col. 0233D] of the Beloved. It is warm because it burns; fluid because it sees. It is warm because it is inflamed; fluid because it is formed by the image of the Beloved.

What is fluid has nothing impure, nothing sluggish; it readily sees and readily follows. But so great a grace of fluidity is not present where there is no warmth. Well fluid is that which both receives brightness from the Beloved’s purity and, as though stirred and made ready, pours itself forth beyond itself and hastens after the Beloved who has already passed on. “He,” she says, “has already passed beyond me”—he who has passed through all of me. His passage is swift; yet his touch has no little force. He left my soul melted behind him, poured forth more abundantly and striving to pass as far as the Beloved’s passage, presuming nothing in his presence. “I melted in the voice of exultation as soon as he spoke.” “My soul melted,” she says. What is “melted”? It is made expanding, running, brightening: expanding beyond itself, running to him, brightening from him. Expanding in power, running in desires, brightening in truth: that is, broad, flowing, shining [Col. 0234A].

5. Perhaps from this melting it was granted her that her hands drip myrrh: her mind has melted. Why do we pass over the third point which that song adds? For it has this sequence in order: the inmost being trembles, the hands drip, the soul melts. One may also, passing lightly through this reading, observe a certain ordered increase; yet it is neither easy nor plain to assign the rationale of the graduated distinction. In all, a certain measure is indicated, but greater in the second than in the first, and greater in the third than in the second. For dripping is more than trembling, just as melting is more than dripping. The Bridegroom’s presence bestows all this upon his bride: her inmost being trembles, her hands drip, her soul melts. All comes from the touch of his hand and the hearing of his voice; all comes from his touch and, so to speak, from his passing through. Because he touches, she trembles; she drips because he strikes through and passes through her in a vehement spirit, whose voice you hear but do not know whence it comes or where it goes. Therefore her soul melted when he spoke.

The voice is subtler than the hand: it moves more powerfully and passes more swiftly. The speech of Jesus, containing subtler and loftier teaching, contains more than any examples of works can display. Every example falls short of the word concerning the majesty of divinity which he poured out among the disciples; every experience falls short of the promise of future glory to be revealed in us. If you open the door to this understanding and perception so as to grasp it, it immediately withdraws and passes on. Therefore you too pass into the affection of a melted heart. At this voice of the Beloved say: “Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me; it has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to attain it” (Ps. 138:6 [139:6]). And my soul has melted, failing to comprehend and unable, because of vehement and overwhelming sweetness, to endure and remain in admiration. For these and similar reasons, she says: “My soul melted [Col. 0234D] when the Beloved spoke.”

6. What do you think—if I may presume to add something outside the sequence, as it were by way of surplus exhortation—what, I say, do you think? Does not this passage rebuke the hardness of certain persons, whose bowels are stiffened by the cold disposition of excessive severity; whose hearts distil no moisture of mercy, nor tremble or are moved, even slightly, by compassion for penitents; who do not feel the touch of the merciful hand, are not kindled by the address of most compassionate Jesus, and do not hear Jesus knocking outside in the penitent? I fear lest he turn away from them and pass by, lest, when they seek him, they fail to find him, and when they cry out he does not hear them.

Why are your bowels hardened toward your children, as though they were not yours? Perhaps you might look upon your own with an unmerciful eye and pass them by in proud disdain, if only they were yours and not also your Lord’s. How hard you would be, if you had to give from what was your own, when you distribute your Lord’s substance with such miserly and diminished affection, even to his children! “He has scattered abroad; he has given to the poor” (Ps. 111:9). But perhaps you do not recognize the poor. What if God should say to you: “Your eyes did not see my imperfection”? In your book only the perfect are written (Ps. 139:16); you are not accustomed to care for those who must be perfected. You are a bad physician, useless to the sick and perhaps even wounding those in health.

If you are unwilling to seek the wandering person, at least meet the one returning. Open the door of mercy; and, if you will not receive the penitent for Christ’s sake, receive at least Christ in the penitent. Let your soul melt with the dew of mercy, and be kindled by the speech of Jesus who cries out and knocks. The voice of the penitent, the voice of the poor, is the voice of Jesus. Therefore, when you hear this voice, let your soul melt in a merciful disposition, so that you too may say with the bride: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke.”

Listen and recall what he said to Mary Magdalene; what to the woman caught in adultery; what to the Samaritan woman, the Canaanite woman, Zacchaeus, Peter, and the centurion. Whose disposition would not be softened and whose heart melted by so many words of compassion and mercy? At such vehement south winds, even ice of however many years’ standing might be thawed from the hardest breast. I feel myself bathed in a stream of flowing oil, and melt in a like disposition whenever I recount the works, words, and commandments of your mercy. “Your word is exceedingly fiery, and your servant loves it” (Ps. 119:140). He loves it because he needs it; therefore my soul loves, and melts for joy where you speak.

7. Every holy person ought to experience this melting. For that melting discussed above belongs only to the perfect, and not even to them always, but at the fitting time. And lest I withhold in unfruitful silence what is suggested to me, I shall briefly set forth for you what I have so far understood concerning this melting.

Do you not see how what melts begins to move away from a certain stiffness and immobility; how it tries to leave and abandon itself; how it flows and descends from its former swelling and bulk, and disappears; how it readily follows what draws it toward lower places; or even pursues that same course of itself, often running ahead of the effort of the one drawing it? In things melted there is great mobility in following, and readiness of will. You now understand, I think, in melted things a great aptitude for obedience and the pliant disposition of a humble soul.

This humility is not imposed by fear, but formed by the warmth of love. Fear violently breaks the mind; love softens it and, making it tender and fluid, shapes it as it pleases. Humility flowing from charity suffers no trouble; of its own accord it tends downward and rests when it has reached lower things. In this melting, then, you have the nature, briefly expressed, of that noble humility; you have also the nature of obedience.

Do you want testimonies? “The Lord opened my ear, that I might hear him as a master” [cf. Isa. 50:5]. You have heard the Lord speaking; hear the disciple’s melted disposition: “I do not resist; I have not turned back.” You hear how he follows; now hear to what depths: “I gave my body to those striking me, and my cheeks to those plucking them; I did not turn away my face from those reproaching and spitting upon me” (Isa. 50:5–6). Did not he descend, as it were, to harsh and lowly things—not resisting rigidly, but melted and made pliant in hearing the warming speech?

Therefore, one who melts in the disposition of such humility and obedience—not cold, swollen, immobile, and stiff—may rightly and gloriously claim for himself the use of this saying: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke.” O wonderful force of the word, exceedingly fiery! It inflames the heart, transforms the inward parts, reduces the soul to nothing in the sight of its God; it makes the soul melt away from itself and fail, so that the soul is no longer with itself but, as the following words of the verse declare: “I am always with you” (Ps. 73:21–23). Therefore it is not in itself, not with itself, but with its God: always obedient, and following as far as it is enabled, though not always attaining according to its desire, nor in that sublime manner proper to the bride with the bridegroom.

For here too it follows: “I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me.” But this chapter requires treatment at another time, when leisure permits examination. These things will suffice—not according to their own grandeur, but according to the strength available to our discussion—concerning how the bride’s soul melts at the speech of her beloved Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLV

“I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me. The watchmen of the city found me; they struck and wounded me; they took away my cloak,” etc. (Song 5:6–7).

1. When your beloved has slipped away from you, he does not return at your pleasure. This distress gives understanding to love and increases its affections. Now he visits; now, by withdrawing his visitation, he afflicts his beloved. This vanishing carries away the lover’s heart and desire, and restores it to readiness. When the beloved speaks, your soul melts. Your melted soul fails, unable to endure; and your beloved turns aside. Your failure is his flight.

With the beloved present and speaking, you melt, fail, and expire; when he is absent, you are permitted to recover breath. His absence repairs the strength which his presence exhausts. Intervals moderate the violence of delights whose continual duration you cannot bear. Why do I say their continuance? Does not their very beginning leave you exhausted? For as soon as the beloved speaks, your soul melts. Thus she says later: “Your eyes made me fly away” (Song 6:4). How did they make the beloved fly away, except because, in excessive affection for him, they failed away into him? You do not know measure; therefore your beloved moderates and dispenses to you, in due season, the measure of his presence. Hence you seek and do not find; you call and he does not answer.

Attend, brothers, to the vehemence and force of love. It cannot endure the beloved’s absence, nor is it equal to his presence. There, panting desires labor; here, exhausted, they suffer faintness. O happy love, which in a continual alternation either melts in him or, seeking, pants toward him! “I sought him and did not find him,” she says; “I called him and he did not answer me.”

Elsewhere this is written in this manner: “The wicked will seek me and not find me; they will call and I will not hear” (Prov. 1:28). What is this, that the very same thing is common to good and evil? Why, good Jesus, do you withdraw yourself indiscriminately from both? Yet not indiscriminately, but very differently. Of the wicked it is said: “They will seek and not find.” But the bride does not despair that she will find; she complains only that she has not found. “I sought him and did not find him; I called him and he did not answer me.”

2. O how often I have sought the Lord Jesus in meditation and called upon him in prayer, yet neither has meditation become sweet nor prayer rich! Therefore I did not find him, nor did he answer me. I did not find either himself or what was his; yet what he has answered me is exceedingly sweet. Would that he might answer me often when I read or pray! Thus, good Jesus, answer me: show me how many iniquities and sins I have; show me my crimes and offenses. “Hide your face for a little while” (cf. Job 13:22–24), so that my own foulness may become salutarily known to me, whether in my meditation or in the reading of Holy Scripture.

For then the watchmen of the city—the holy teachers—find me, when I find my own conduct in their writings. Then they find me when they portray my conduct and vices; they strike when they examine; they wound when they rebuke. Holy writers, like certain watchmen of the holy city Jerusalem, which is the Church, investigate the varied dispositions of minds and discover each person’s passions, good habits, and the disease from which each suffers: no one’s thought escapes their discovery. Whenever I read these things, I think myself found and caught. They strike me with the darts of exhortation; they wound me by proving that what I had thought sound is wounded. They remove the veil of pretence, the covering of ignorance or forgetfulness, and the cloak of false glory. They strip me, as though of a cloak, of the covering of dissimulation and the ornament of pride. They strip me of a cloak of falsely assumed glory, by laying bare the weaknesses of my conscience.

Thus I am usefully found by the watchmen in this manner, though I cannot find the beloved as I desire. And so I now have less in myself in which to glory, less in which to boast; and, finding this, I burn more readily with love for the beloved.

3. “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell the beloved that I am sick with love.” I do not dare to approach by myself; I do not presume upon such familiarity; Jesus does not yet grant me the enjoyment of himself. Therefore, daughters of Jerusalem, I come to you, solicit you, commend my cause to you, entrust the business to you: tell the beloved. He acts as though he does not know, while he conceals himself.

Let the watchmen strip me; let the daughters report; let the teachers exhort; let the daughters intercede. “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell the beloved that I am sick with love.” Report it, urge it upon him: frequent representation will move the beloved. I am now stripped; I am now despoiled of myself; I am now fit to be clothed by the beloved. A mind stripped and emptied of occupation grows sick with love. “Tell the beloved that I am sick with love.”

Brothers, if the rebuking speech of a teacher seems specially to touch you, explicitly to strike at your conduct, to lay bare your mind’s wounds, or to remove the cloak of a hidden or blinded conscience, turn it into fuel for love, not for hatred. Why do you take as a private injury what is publicly set forth for everyone? Perhaps what is said concerns you, yet does not name you expressly. Let general correction bring you the sickness of love, not the passion of murmuring.

And if you do not yet languish with desire for that sweet love, it is good if in the meantime you languish with shame for sin; if you languish in penitence; if your flesh is pierced by fear of judgment. Be turned to affliction while your thorn is being driven in: confess your sin, and allow the cloak of covering, by which you deceitfully conceal your injustices, to be taken from you. Do not more stubbornly, do not more tightly, clothe yourself in the cloak of hypocrisy or wrap yourself in its covering.

Jesus will not turn toward you unless the veil of pretence and deceit is removed from you, a veil which a certain shame and fear of displeasing have spread before you. Shame has covered the face of your conscience: remove the veil of shame; put on confession. For the Lord too puts on confession—not his own, but yours. He counts this as an ornamenting cloak; he borrows it from you. Hand him this cloak, which he lovingly takes as a pledge of love and a sign of reconciliation.

Then you will begin to languish with love, when you have first languished in the affections of penitence. Then the daughters of Jerusalem will begin to commend you to the beloved; then heavenly spirits and spiritual souls, rejoicing with you, will report your sickness of love.

4. But we have treated this passage in an additional sense concerning the state of penitence, though its whole aspect seems to breathe something more perfect, consonant with that grace which deserves to be regarded as the bride’s condition. “I sought,” she says, “and did not find him; I called and he did not answer me; the watchmen of the city found me.” In meditation she seeks; in prayer she calls; by hearing teachers she is found, struck, wounded, and stripped. And, lest anything be lacking for the fullness, she is aided by the commendation of the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, faithful souls.

Observe four things here, either in her or concerning her: searches, desires, instructions, and prayers. Searches of meditation; desires of longing; instructions of teachers; and prayers of saints [or: companions]. Are not teachers’ instructions and exhortations often fittingly felt by those whom anxious searching and sincere prayer might weary? Are not sluggish desires often roused by the spur of words? Indeed, what is fervent is made more fervent by these incentives.

“The watchmen of the city found me.” Good and prudent masters employ a wandering, almost hunting, manner of speech; they direct their discourse toward the varied states of minds, if perhaps they may find someone to touch, spur, or move—someone among the hearers who may rejoice and say: “The watchmen of the city found me; they struck me and wounded me.” The more perfect a person is, the more readily he is wounded; and a tender disposition feels the barbs of words more swiftly.

O happy mind, to which such lofty darts of exhortation come, which they find suited to their wounds, when they do not go back repelled by the hearers’ hardness or stupidity! Such darts must not be cast everywhere, nor before every multitude, but only where minds are believed to be found capable of receiving such excellent teaching. These are like lightning: they strike the heights; lower things escape; they find the heights and strike the heights.

5. Therefore she says: “The watchmen of the city found me; they struck me; they wounded me; they took away my cloak.” They took away the cloak in which Adam was wrapped as a penalty, stripped of the brightness of his former simplicity; they took away the coverings of imaginations by which he was inwardly hindered; they took away the veil, the cloak, of figures, and brought in truth. Truth, unveiled, laid bare, and simple, gives birth to the fervor of love. Therefore: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell the beloved that I am sick with love.”

As long as perceived truth does not please, it does not carry away the affection or kindle it. However sincerely someone may think himself to enjoy the sight of understanding, he still suffers from a veil, a covering of dim-sightedness, a cloak laid over him. But when this veil has been removed, then truth gleams, then it flashes, and kindles love; then the person undergoing this can invite others to rejoice with him, saying: “Tell the beloved that I am sick with love.”

Look at Judaea. So long as truth lay hidden beneath the covering of the Law, so long as she herself endured the veil of blindness, she was numb with fear; in a rigid disposition she could feel nothing sweet, nor be wounded by the dart of charity. But when, converted to the Lord, she put aside the veil, when this cloak was taken away from her, then she began to use the words of this glorious confession: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell the beloved that I am sick with love.”

Then, rejoicing in the taste of a new and unfamiliar sweetness, she invites the daughters of Jerusalem to give thanks and urges the members of her people by her example. Hear, finally, what those stirred by such urging reply: “What is your beloved like? And we will seek him with you.” You see how they desire to become sharers in this faith and teaching. “Teach us what your beloved is like, and we will seek him with you. Make us sharers in so great a grace, that through zeal in seeking we may begin to languish in the disposition of love.” Let it suffice briefly to have touched on these matters by mystical interpretation.

6. Let us now return to that from which, by occasion, we have slipped into this passage, while explaining the usefulness of the cloak taken away. For the occasion arose from the words: “They took away my cloak.” Let us remain a little longer at this point and explain this cloak. It is not a simple cloak in which even holy minds are wrapped. It is a *diplois*, that is, a double cloak—perhaps even triple and quadruple.

How many kinds of cloaks have we set before you? Is not the care of souls and the anxiety of administering necessities still a heavy and burdensome cloak enough? I shall speak more expressly of my own difficulties. I know what it is to be pressed by this cloak; what parched ground and barren fig tree have fallen to my lot. Many years have now passed since I came—or rather since I have stood—seeking fruit upon it and finding none. How often has it mocked our hopes, deceived our labor, and frustrated our expectation? I rightly call this cloak burdensome, and all the more burdensome because it is less useful. For burdens of anxiety are lighter when the abundance of yield relieves them.

Woe is me, because the watchmen of the city found me, because they thought they had found in me something worthy of such a burden! They struck me, wounded me, took away my cloak, and went away after inflicting wounds, leaving me half alive. They took away my cloak: the cloak of simplicity, the cloak of light, the garment of joy, the clothing of fervent affection. How often was I once wholly wrapped in cloaks of this sort, warmed amid saffron-colored garments? But now all day long I embrace in my mind and turn over things which Paul counts as dung. They took away these sweet and glorious cloaks from me and clothed me with burdensome ones. When will these be taken away from me? When shall I cast them off, if indeed it is permitted to cast them off?

Happy the day when, stripped and freed of this cloak, I shall invite you with freer affection to rejoice with me, daughters of Jerusalem; when you, who have experienced nothing like what I now lament, will give thanks for the renewed sickness of love in you. Miserable indeed is the person who, stripped by such a cloak, wastes away in sorrow and trouble rather than languishing with love. The bride, when thus stripped either by the duty of care or by its exercise, does not languish in disgust but in zeal of love. Therefore elsewhere she calls upon others to rejoice with her and give thanks to the beloved.

7. When the early Church sought Christ in Judaea and met rejection—finding no place for him in them, finding no Jesus there—it passed to the Gentiles. It sought among them and called; in many it did not find him and received no answer except the answer of death. Finally, how were our martyrs, at the beginning, wounded by the rulers of this world, as by watchmen of the city; despoiled of their goods, torn in body, stripped of the cloak of their flesh? Amid so many rivers and torrents of torments, charity was not extinguished in them, but they languished even more with a certain increase of love.

It seems indeed pleasant, from the present occasion of the text, to recall the tireless charity of the martyrs amid so many kinds of affliction and death: how they moderated bodily sufferings by the inward suffering of love. For if you apply this passage to them, the words, “The watchmen of the walls struck me, wounded me, and took away my cloak,” are not a voice of complaint but of glory.

In the same way, we ought not to take it ill if at any time the watchmen of the walls strip us of the cloak either of burdensome care or of an action that is not good or is perilous, a cloak in which we are tightly wrapped. Elijah cast off his cloak when he was taken up (4 Kgs. 2:13); Joseph fled when he was being held (Gen. 39:12); the bride bore it while it was being taken away. Elijah, caught up to face-to-face vision, cast aside the veil of mirror and image. Joseph, sensing its inducement, fled the ornaments of the world as great burdens. Stripped of anxiety, the bride more freely seeks the favor of her beloved.

The intellect is held by imagination as by a cloak, lest it contemplate sincere truth. The affection for honors and dignities is wrapped in a cloak, lest it proceed freely toward the things of God. Anxiety clouds every joy in the soul; imagination obscures it; honor tempts it. In the first are darknesses; in the second, enticements; in the third, toil. In the first, obscurity; in the second, desire; in the third, care.

“The watchmen of the walls took away my cloak.” Good watchmen: they know well from whom to remove the hindrances of cares, whose soul to unburden, and whom to render free to delight and be delighted with her beloved, and to seek him. For he often slips away and cannot be sought except by an unencumbered disposition. Thus good watchmen know whom to spare from burdens, straits, and troubles of activities, so that they may run more freely to meet and embrace the Word; they know from whom to take away the cloak by their counsels. “I have taken off my tunic,” she says (Song 5:3).

8. She said this in the preceding verses, but now she says: “They took away my cloak.” She makes herself known as one of naked and pure simplicity, and as free in the business of love. “They took away my cloak,” saying in a manner: “Why do you seek the beloved while fettered by cares? Why do you wrap yourself in these troubles? If you do not entirely lay aside your office, why do you not at least put aside anxieties for an hour? We do not withdraw you from studies, but we want you to lessen your preoccupation. Do not cover excessive gain with the name of necessity.

“Why do you permit your good natural ability to be overwhelmed by earthly things? Why imitate those who, placed in honors, are compared to beasts: they gape after earthly things, chew earthly things, ruminate on them in thought, devour them in affection; they are placed on high but roll in the mire? Do not envy the violent in these matters, nor be jealous of those who practice iniquity. Is there not great injustice and inequality in devoting intense attention to transitory things and slack attention to eternal things? What of the fact that they do not always give attention to business? What of the fact that some, under the pretext of providing necessities, excuse themselves both from the work of their hands and from meditation and the study of searching out truth? They give more to commerce than to quiet, more to frivolous talk than to the reading of Holy Scripture, more to idleness than to work. They go about the workshops and cells of the brothers idly, curiously, and talkatively. Do not envy those who transact business in this way, nor those who are idle in this way.”

Turn every leisure, whether offered or arranged, wholly to the service of love: to the meditation of wisdom, to the zeal either of seeking the beloved or of embracing him when found. By these and similar exhortations the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak. These are the watchmen of whom Isaiah says: “Upon the walls of Jerusalem I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall not be silent” (Isa. 62:6).

But let us now be silent here; let us be silent from this discourse, paying the debts of prayers and praises—sometimes to be silent in speech, but always in mind rendering the solemn offices of praise to the Lord Jesus, king and heavenly bridegroom, through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVI

“I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find the beloved, that you tell him that I am sick with love,” etc. (Song 5:8).

1. The order is fitting. After the exhortation of teachers, she seems to ask the support of prayers from her companions; and she asks not simply, but with the solemnity of adjuration: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find the beloved, that you tell him that I am sick with love.” The adjuration shows the vehemence of her petition. Anxious desires do not know how to be content with their own merits; therefore they beg the assistance of another’s prayer. Perfect humility always relies upon another’s merits.

“I adjure you,” she says, “daughters of Jerusalem, if you find the beloved.” This condition does not belong to one in doubt, but moderates her request—as though she said, “if you find him,” that is, “when you find him.” I suspend the words conditionally, not doubting that you will find him, but rather preserving modesty. For you hear these things more gently when spoken under a doubtful condition than if they were said definitively: “When you find him.” She does not fear that they will take the suspended request as an insult. She knows the modesty of the daughters of Jerusalem, knows their humble spirit, and knows that a tender sense of shame would be more hurt by a definite assertion than by a suspended condition.

“If,” she says, “you find him.” I say, “if you find him”; I do not say, “when you find him.” I say the former, but mean the latter. This apparent uncertainty does not arise from my own disposition; rather, I accommodate myself to your disposition and to your most humble estimation of yourselves. “If you find him”—that is, when you find him—remember me when things go well with you. Then remember me, that you may urge the matter and report it to the beloved. There is no need to linger in discussing this passage; brothers, I leave it to your conduct.

2. Recall how you beg from one another the consolations of prayers—with what humble disposition, what urgency of desire, and what adjuration. Not all of you would dare ask that it be reported of you that you are sick with love; you are accustomed to lament one another’s other sicknesses, not to glory in this one. And if anyone can glory in it for an hour, it is not expedient, lest perhaps, through the onset of vain glory, your glory come to be nothing.

Yet there are some who cannot conceal within themselves the sickness of divine love, both by the evidence of their conduct and by the service of their speech. The mouth of one who loves cannot fail sometimes to bring forth the desires conceived within. For the inward-filling Spirit secretly draws out a word for the consolation of others and pours forth the abundance of infused grace. Indeed, in this passage the bride herself does not speak; it is the Spirit who speaks in her.

In holy conversations, are not sighs, sobs rising from the depths of the heart, and frequent groans certain outpourings of the Spirit and of grace conceived? Do not such signs reveal the sickness of love? The sickness is not hidden when the groan is not concealed. The sickness reveals itself when it produces these signs. What then of signs perceived? Do they not possess a certain force of wonder, moving those who detect them to the disposition of rejoicing with the person? Even if speech is silent, the holiness of devout conduct asks. It wishes to be commended while revealing itself through certain signs.

For when I detect this heavenly love in someone, should I not regard myself as adjured to give earnest thanks for that person? Shall I commend with devout prayers a conceived sickness which profound groaning reveals? I would be hard if I did not, with all the earnestness of prayer I can, foster such holy and divine suffering in my brothers, commend it by supplication, repeat it, and report it to the beloved, if opportunity is given.

What of you, who prefer to count your brothers’ vices rather than their virtues, their losses rather than their gifts, to condemn rather than commend? If you do not feel yourself adjured to commend them, you are no longer a daughter of Jerusalem but a daughter of Babylon. Miserable daughter of Babylon, who will repay you this repayment? For it shall be repaid to you. Unlearn being a daughter of Babylon; lay aside barbarous manners. Cease to count losses in the saints more than gains. Let your malice in counting at least suffice for you. Do not carry it abroad; do not proclaim it to your companions.

For the companions of the bridegroom do not lend an ear if you disparage the bride. The bridegroom himself hears injuries to his beloved with pain. Whoever you tell, you tell him; “for the ear of jealousy hears all things” (Wis. 1:10). It is rash to condemn the beloved before her beloved. He prefers to hear good things reported of his bride and more readily gives ear to commendation.

3. The bride knows this; therefore she says: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find the beloved, that you tell him that I am sick with love.” “That you tell him,” she says. The reporting of affliction has the effect of a petition. Consider ordinary human practice in asking. Is it not itself a request, when one mentions someone’s misery to a compassionate person? It is an effective prayer modestly to set forth the weakness of the oppressed, the unhappiness of their condition, and the insolence of enemies. To set these matters forth, I say, in the ear of one powerful—what else is it but to incline him, by a certain modest petition, to give assistance?

How often you find this manner of prayer in the Psalmist! In the Gospel Mary says to Jesus: “They have no wine” (John 2:3). She does not ask the Lord, nor command her Son; she is content merely to report the lack of wine. This is how one should act with benefactors inclined to generosity. Favor is not to be forcibly extracted; an occasion must be presented.

Commend the bride to the bridegroom; enumerate her gifts. Is this not to inflame his desire and apply spurs? “Tell the beloved.” To tell him this is to provoke him to return love and refresh one sick with love. He arranges consolations in his heart, but waits to be pressed by our prayers. What he will do, he will do sooner if we knock, perhaps more abundantly as well. This delay causes me torment, but gives birth to an abundance of consolation. When prayers are multiplied, he will pour forth the awaited consolations more abundantly.

“Tell the beloved that I am sick with love.” You tell him, who have familiar access to the beloved. You tell him, who have experienced how great is the power of sickness in one who loves; how “love is strong as death” and “jealousy hard as hell” [cf. Song 8:6]. “I adjure you to tell the beloved that I am sick with love.” Relate and report it, and he will hear your voice to refresh my desires. “Tell him that I am sick with love.” Love does not languish; the lover languishes. Where love is vigorous, there also languor is vigorous, if that which is loved is absent. What is this languor except an affection caused by the absent beloved, which wastes away the lover?

4. Vehement love simultaneously affects the sufferer’s flesh and mind. It extinguishes the flesh’s wantonness and checks the mind’s joy. It extinguishes movements of the flesh; it checks the mind’s cheerfulness with a certain sorrowful affection and longing for the absent beloved. The flesh languishes when its movement becomes weaker and more relaxed; the spirit languishes when it is exhausted by the excess of burning desire. The languor of flesh is its movement being either absent or very slight; the languor of soul is its movement being excessive.

Is not the flesh itself exhausted when the mind, withdrawn from its love, turns toward other things? The movement of the flesh is not felt when the soul has become more vehement and can scarcely be sustained. At times it cannot even be sustained, when excessive burning love exhausts the strength of the suffering soul. For what strength has the human mind to endure when that heavenly love of the bridegroom restlessly agitates it? In this exercise the melted mind flees itself, unable to bear the violence of love.
