For so, when fuel is consumed and already failing, the burnings of the fire become weaker. “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). Certainly one who languishes with a more vehement affection, delighted, exercised, and failing in meditation upon his God, feels the force of this saying. O powerful and most powerful passion of charity! If it is not moderated, it cannot be endured. It is rightly powerful, because it makes the mind which it has possessed powerless over itself. Once kindled in the mind, it reaches “mightily from end to end”; it accomplishes what it came to do, prospers and grows, and does not fail until it has made the soul fail.

For just as this bodily languor is not always equally intense, but at times becomes a more severe suffering, so the affection of love—although it continually stretches itself toward the beloved in desire—sometimes burns more intensely with desires, especially at the hour of prayer. Then the lover languishes, because a vehement spirit passes through him and does not remain. At the end of that hour he may say: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell the beloved that I melt with love.” Before that hour there is languor, but at its end languor is transformed into melting.

Therefore, when you pray, do not permit your mind to fluctuate or turn aside to other things, so that, when it has been touched by this happy passion, it may cling to it until it is more fully infused, traversed, and consumed. For it will not cease until it has run through and drunk up the whole spirit of the human being. Thus Daniel, “a man of desires,” languished from the heavenly vision so that no strength remained in him (Dan. 10:1–11).

When that vehement passion has passed through, the bride returns to a more tolerable and more human languor, which is continual for her because it is not so violently stirred. This, indeed, though it does not bring failure, nevertheless makes her waste away from love for the absent beloved. This is a good languor, through which the carnal affection moves sluggishly. It is one thing when an impulse of the flesh rises strongly and is repressed by a stronger force coming upon it; another when, languishing and as though expiring with a dying pulse, it makes a gentle attempt.

5. I still feel certain other troublesome languors, all nevertheless useful: the languor of fear, the languor of weariness, the languor of sorrow. Why should I not be consumed by fear and grief over the consciousness of a life wickedly spent—by fear because of the ease of falling amid the snares through which life must be lived; by weariness of life, as life passes away like an image? “For every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38:7, 6). Would that some daughters of Jerusalem might report my languors to you, Lord, if there be anything in me worthy to be commended to you! For many things in me need healing. O happy me, if some heavenly centurion should say to you: “Lord, my servant lies paralysed at home and is grievously tormented!” Would that, Lord, you would at once answer: “I will come and heal him!” Speak, Lord, the word, and I shall be healed. For you are present by the Word, because you are the Word. Great is the healing power in the Word—both in what you are, Lord, and in what comes from you through your own. The centurion perceived this when he said: “Lord, speak only the word, and my servant shall be healed” (Matt. 8:6–8). Yet every discourse of a teacher is empty unless you, Lord, speak inwardly. Speak the word, and my languor will be healed; perhaps, as you speak, languor will also be begotten in me, so that I too may dare to say: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I languish with love.”

Both languors are good: whether vehement and excited, or this one continuous and tempered. Except that this latter is not continuous in such a way as not frequently to return to itself, growing through the lack of restraint of burning desire and not containing itself. It does not turn back until it fails again. If you love for an hour and cease after the hour, it is not love; if you love and do not waste away from love of the absent beloved, it is not languor. Therefore, for love to be languor, it must possess both continuity and exhaustion. “Tell my beloved,” she says, “that I languish with love.” Those who are sick wish their languors reported to a physician; those of love, to a friend: the former so that they may be healed, the latter so that they may be refreshed. Rival, brothers, this better languor: as desire for the beloved who makes himself absent creates it, so the delight of the Lord Jesus, who makes himself present, refreshes it—Jesus, the Bridegroom of the Church and of the holy soul, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVII. “What is your beloved more than another beloved?” etc. (Song 5:9)

[Col. 0245D]

1. “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us?” These exceedingly emphatic questions seem to pour forth from great feeling. I think that in the daughters of Jerusalem, from their conversation with the languishing bride, a similar languor was either produced, or stirred up so as to become greater. And subsequently they say: “Where has your beloved gone? And we will seek him with you” (Song 5:17). As if they said: We will seek with you, but we will seek for ourselves also, desiring to enjoy him together with you. For they do not say, “We will seek for you,” but “we will seek with you,” desiring for themselves also a share in the blessed discovery.

Great is the humility on both sides, both in the bride and in the daughters of Jerusalem. She asks to be commended to the Bridegroom; they ask to be instructed concerning the Bridegroom. Nor do they do so simply: she with an adjuration, they with repetition. For neither her adjuring nor their repetition belongs to one who asks lightly. “What is your beloved more than another beloved,” they say, “O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us?” Usefully were they adjured, since they were thus encouraged. The usefulness of holy conversation is not slight. It is a word both through which the languor of love is generated and through which the languor of weakness is healed. The centurion knew the effective healing power in the word; therefore he says: “Speak only the word” (Matt. 8:8).

161 2. It is good for words to be spoken, but it is nevertheless good for words to be written. For a word flies away irretrievably unless it is read in writing. Writing makes the word both stable and visible; what is committed to the page may be reclaimed whenever you wish. A book is a good guardian of a deposit, returning intact what it has received: when you wish, you may take it up; where you wish, you may read it; as long as you wish, you may dwell upon it. Writing restores memory because it represents the word. There you safely store the remedies of the word, for they are kept unharmed. If the word has the power to heal when spoken, why does it not have it when read? If there is good healing when you speak, why not when you read?

Let my languor not be healed in this way. That is to say: let the first hearer receive the word’s benefit, and let it not reach those who come after or those far away; where it first sounds, there let it be choked; let all its usefulness be exhausted in the first hearing and crushed beneath everlasting silence. Let it not fall again into good ground to bear fruit. Let the sick person who first receives this remedy recover; after him let no one experience its power. In that pool, after the stirring of the water, one person was healed; but in that one person charity, not singularity, was signified. After the first person was healed, it was not said of that pool: “Empty it, empty it, even to its foundations; let not a trace of the saving water remain.” The stirring of the water is good: it is the disputation and examination of the sacred page. For it is rightly stirred when, through discerning winnowing, it is advanced toward spiritual understanding; it is rightly stirred when, through its investigation, the hearer is advanced.

The word is food as well as medicine. And how can you say: Let the food which you work perish and not remain? Yet this freedom is not to be permitted indiscriminately to everyone; nor did the stirring of the water heal except when the angel descended and stirred it at its appointed time (John 5:2–4). Certainly this is the angel whose lips preserve knowledge, from whose mouth knowledge of the law must be sought. Therefore—this must indeed be acknowledged—there is great benefit in composing the saving word, but when this work is permitted to someone, or rather required of him. Hence the caution of our elders ought not to seem blameworthy—a caution which does no harm by being excessive—which generally imposes silence: lest a permission usefully granted to some become for others an occasion of rash presumption; and lest anyone, while occupied with a burden not imposed upon him, be idle from the burden that has been imposed.

3. To return to the matter proposed: the daughters of Jerusalem were greatly stirred and encouraged by the bride’s conversation and adjuration. How could they fail to be encouraged to ask about his beauty, for love of whom they see the bride languishing and almost lifeless? The languor of love perceived in the bride drew them into this curiosity of seeking. For, seeing that the bride’s love is vehement, they suppose that the causes and incentives of so great an affection are in the Bridegroom. With feeling they ask what beauty is in the Bridegroom, of whom they cannot but suppose that he is wonderfully beautiful; and they take the bride’s beauty as evidence of the most beautiful Bridegroom. “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women?”

The Church is the most beautiful among women, since she is the beauty of individual souls. She is most beautiful, because every beauty is in her and no deformity is in her. Indeed, insofar as they belong to the Church, they are not deformed. If any deformity seems to be present in some, even though a foul stain may for a time be sprinkled upon some of her members, it is not imputed while it does not remain. Perhaps, once the stain has been wiped away, she acquires more beauty than the deformity she suddenly contracted when stained. Rightly, therefore, is she most beautiful: possessing every beauty and lacking every ugliness.

Many faithful and spiritual souls also are most beautiful insofar as they either admit no stain through holy conduct, or continually wash it away through vigilant and sincere confession. In a sense she is most beautiful—not surpassing all others, but not exceeding them. There is, as it were, no excess where there is swift return. Therefore she is most beautiful, putting on beauty and confession, clothed with light as with a garment. She is most beautiful, whether she is light itself or clothed with light: clothed with light through confession; becoming light itself through her conduct.

4. “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved?” This repetition is not without great feeling, nor is it without mystery. If it had been said thus, “What is your beloved more than another beloved woman?” just as it says, “What is your beloved more than another beloved?” no one would doubt that one expression should be referred to that generation which is from the Father, and the other to that which is from the Mother. For in each he is wonderful and exceedingly desirable, but from their conjunction he is much more wonderful.

He has one or the other of the two natures in common, either with the Father or with the Mother. This conjunction is proper to him alone. His personal property is considered jointly in these things because it is integrally constituted from them. For he consists of two natures; yet he nevertheless subsists in those two: he consists from the joined natures and subsists in each separately. The completeness of his property consists in the joined natures, and not in either separately; through it he differs at once from both Father and Mother. For he differs from each not in either one alone, but in their union—and from anyone who is not himself. His natural essentiality in a certain respect consists in each separately, and not in the joined natures: simply and in himself he is God, as is the Father; simply and in himself he is man, as is the Mother.

He is not God in part and in a qualified sense, nor is he man in part and in a qualified sense. Therefore he is called wholly God and wholly man: not because everything belonging to him is God and man, but because he himself is wholly so; nor as though in every part he were God and in every part man, but because he is not God in part and man in part. Thus, to say that he is wholly God and wholly man excludes parts rather than gathers them, affirming essential simplicity in each nature—not that each essence is simple, but that he himself is simply each. Therefore he is said to have been “found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:7), because, although humanity is not connatural with divinity, yet by assumption in the person of Jesus it is, as it were, a garment clothing and covering it.

Human nature is not connatural with the divine nature, but only with the person of Jesus himself; what belongs to human nature is naturally present in him. Thus it belongs to the nature of a human being that he is naturally human, true man, and truly man: true man by reason of the reality of the soul and human flesh; truly man because he truly consists of a human soul and flesh—consisting of real things and truly consisting, not merely possessing real parts of humanity and possessing them truly, but also truly existing from them. Possessing natural things and possessing them naturally: as he is naturally God, so also he is naturally, and not merely by a garment, man. Rightly, therefore, as Jesus is said to subsist in the reality of the divine nature, so he is believed to subsist [perhaps: “also”] in the reality of human nature, possessing both natures, and possessing them naturally.

5. Therefore the daughters of Jerusalem ask separately what he is like according to each generation, desiring to be instructed about his nature: “What is your beloved more than another beloved? What is your beloved?” In the divine birth he is beloved from beloved; in the human birth the beloved came from a beloved woman—except that he is not so much beloved from the Mother as she herself was made beloved through him. He has everything which beloved-from-beloved has, but not everything from the beloved woman; rather, she has everything that she has from him. Hence, when the daughters of Jerusalem first ask, “What is your beloved more than another beloved?” they do not similarly add, “What is your beloved more than another beloved woman?” but simply, “What is your beloved?” Their desires first stretch beyond the powers of their capacity, but they immediately correct themselves, turning to a more human and more modest question.

We may also understand this in either sense: either that the question is doubled because of Jesus’ twofold nature, or that the former question, as though unanswerable, is recalled by the following one—as if they said: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women?” The truth of this faith which you hold concerning the generation of the beloved from the beloved makes you, among all professors of every sect, most beautiful. This faith cleanses you; this makes you beautiful: you maintain that your beloved is equal to the beloved from whom he is. He is such as he from whom he comes is. Wondrous equality, and wondrous quality. That equality signifies identity; the quality, substantiality. If there were two natures, each supreme, one in the Father and another in the Son, there would indeed be equality but not identity; yet the divine nature admits no other equal to itself. The quality in both is numerically one, and it is substantial quality—indeed, substance is quality.

Thus, that the Son is such as the Father is means precisely that the Son is what the Father is. As the Father is, such is the Son; and each is that very quality: the Son is consubstantial with the Father and is the same substance with him. Substance does not merely grant subsistence, but itself subsists—living, powerful, and understanding.

6. Such is the beloved whom you proclaim as beloved from beloved; such do you define him to be. If possible, explain to us the reason of this faith, and it is enough for us. “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” How shall we know what your beloved from beloved is like, unless you teach us what the beloved from whom he comes is like? Yet this is not for our present time or our present capacity. It is enough to believe that he is such as the Father is. Although we are not sufficient to comprehend what that quality is, teach us what he is like according to his humanity, according to which the beloved is from the beloved woman. Teach and say what your beloved is like. We delight to hear again what we have already heard concerning him. Repeat for us what ought to be believed about your beloved, or what can be grasped.

Both kinds of things heard delight us greatly: even those things which we cannot grasp nevertheless grasp us. We are seized by that very heat of wonder and love, seeing you so seized, so carried away, so aflame. O what he is like! O how lovable is your beloved! His love in you continually increases; the beloved is ever more beloved to you because of the beloved—indeed, ever dearer because of the most dearly beloved. His love makes you beautiful; experience makes you eager; eagerness makes you anxious. For the feeling of one who is anxious and full of desire is shown by your thus adjuring us: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have thus adjured us?” How beautiful he is, who allows nothing foul to remain in you and therefore has made you most beautiful among women! How lovable and gracious he is, without whom you cannot endure even for an hour, and because of whom you thus adjure us!

7. I ask you, daughters of Jerusalem, daughters of this earthly Jerusalem: why do you not repeat these questions to the Church? Why do you neglect to learn this twofold birth in Christ, whom you disdain to believe? Why do you not perceive yourselves adjured by the Church—when the testimonies of your own Scripture are brought forth against you with faith; when the gifts of the spirits are displayed in faith; when the sufferings of the martyrs are endured for faith? Why do you not feel yourselves, as it were, adjured by the Church through the more fitting ceremonies which she observes, the keener doctrines which she handles, the loftier rewards which she awaits, and the stricter vows by which she disciplines herself?

A stricter discipline, fuller instruction, more expedient rite, and more eminent virtue could have generated zeal in you, stirred affection, and had force enough to move you to emulation through adjuration. But a time will come—for it is not yet—when, after you have turned to the Lord, the veil of ignorance and dissimulation will be removed. Then, made perceptive as it were, having received the Spirit of the Lord, you will feel the force of these adjurations. Then, awakened to a holy curiosity, you will eagerly repeat these questions, saying: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved, that you have thus adjured us?” For my Jewish brothers, the time has not yet come; but ours is always ready. Therefore, setting aside frivolous and deceitful discourses, let us cultivate in our assemblies exchanges of such admiration and inquiry.

8. Would that you might be such daughters as desire to hear such doctrines! Would that I too might be such a bride, from whom you might be able, being prepared, to ask such things! O truly blessed mother, who deserves to hear said to herself: “O most beautiful among women!” Blessed indeed, if she preserves so great a beauty intact. “Her Nazarites,” he says, “were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, more ruddy than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphire. Their faces have become blacker than coals.” Great indeed was the praise, but wretched the change. The whiteness of snow, the brightness of milk, the redness of ivory, the purity and beauty of sapphire, are covered with the blackness of coal. “Their faces have become blacker than coals, and they were not recognized in the streets.” Certainly they were no longer recognized in the streets as Nazarites.

I shall be silent about others. Look at the men of our own order: how admirable was their name throughout the whole earth. At the beginning, when they had scarcely been seen in the streets, they were immediately recognized by the mark of holiness upon them. But now, distinguished and marked from others neither by any difference of religion nor by any privilege of conduct—or by none, or by one too slight—they are not recognized in the streets as Nazarites. The frequency of the streets discolors Nazarites and gives them an alien appearance. “The best color has changed; the stones of the sanctuary have been scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4:7, 8, 1); therefore they were not recognized in the streets. Their native whiteness, brightness, redness, and beauty are not recognized in them. Whatever these signify, they portray great beauty. Therefore they were not recognized in the streets.

These are the colors of the Nazarites; they are also those of the bride and the Bridegroom. For here the bride too speaks and says: “My beloved is white and ruddy.” Such is our Nazarite, to whom the color of the Nazarites is conformed, and to whom the bride’s color is also conformed. For she is a Nazarite, dedicating and betrothing herself to the Lord Jesus the Nazarite. When we find her such, let us praise her beauty and consult her discernment: “What is your beloved more than another beloved, O most beautiful among women? What is your beloved, that you have thus adjured us?” But now she herself unfolds the praises of her beloved, the Lord Jesus, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XLVIII. “My beloved is white and ruddy,” etc. (Song 5:10)

1. “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from thousands.” She interrupts the pursuit of her beloved for a time—but only for a short time—in order to instruct the daughters. She interrupts delights for necessities; yet her recollection from memory of the Bridegroom’s praises is not without love. For praises of the Bridegroom are sweet to the bride’s palate. A devout mother and prudent bride forms her daughters and commends the beloved. Rightly prudent, having so ready and abundant a store of speech concerning the Bridegroom. All his individual features have been diligently noted and reconsidered by her, since they are so ready to hand. Each draws her affection, since it clings so tenaciously to her memory.

His color, head, hair, eyes, cheeks, lips, hands, belly, legs, feet, and throat—these are all described figuratively in praise of the Bridegroom. Then, as though in a conclusion and a short chapter, summing up everything, she says: “He is altogether desirable”; and, to teach that in these things she has ready nourishment for her love, she says: “Such is my beloved, and he is my friend.” See in all this the bride’s instruction; see her devotion; see her diligence, whether in seeking the beloved, instructing the daughters, or recalling his praises. Earnestly she adjures; readily she answers; gracefully she figures; distinctly she divides; briefly she passes through; summarily she embraces—and I do not know whether she adequately expresses it. I know at least that she concludes affectionately: “Such is my beloved, and he is my friend.” The scope of these praises is great, and clearly great is the love of the one who praises.

2. Let us now examine each point in this praise. “My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen from thousands.” This is a singular mixture of colors, which by divine operation came together in the one person of the Lord Jesus alone—not so that they are one, but that they are in one. O gracious and exceedingly lovable Bridegroom, in whom the divine generation shines white and the human is red! For he is “the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26); and although he was born neither of bloods, nor of the will of flesh, nor of the will of man, he was nevertheless born of the Mother’s blood, and nothing in him has that redness of which Isaiah says: “Though your sins be red as scarlet, they shall be white as wool” (Isa. 1:18).

The whiteness of wool and the redness of scarlet do not accord and do not endure one another. There is another redness, found together with whiteness in the garment of Jesus. “Why,” Isaiah says, “is your garment red?” (Isa. 63:2). The garment of the Lord Jesus is the nature of his virginal generation, white with the purity and innocence of holiness; yet it becomes much more beautiful through the color of voluntary suffering, red in the affections of believers. What redness is this, which does not lack the power to whiten? “They washed their robes,” he says, “and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (Rev. 7:14).

3. This redness in my Jesus found whiteness; it did not make it. In us it makes whiteness; it does not find it. This redness, laid over the hue of bloody birth and personal iniquity, changes that redness into whiteness, cleansing hearts by faith. “For we have been justified by faith in the blood of Jesus.” The blood shed for you rightly reddens for you if it kindles in your soul an affection of return. It rightly reddens for you if, in the blood shed for you, the excessive love of God shines red for you. For Jesus so loved his bride that he washed her in his own blood. Love is flaming; this makes the Lord Jesus ruddy to me. In him truth shines white for me and love shines red. “My beloved,” she says, “is white and ruddy.”

Why should he not be white? For God is light, and there are no darknesses in him. Why should he not be ruddy? For God is fire, and he came to cast fire upon the earth. If he supplies you with the light of understanding, he is white to you; but if he does not kindle your soul to love, you do not experience him as ruddy. Both are in himself; but they are not in you unless you experience their effect in yourself. If you are a bride, emulate in your Bridegroom this mixture of the twofold color, so that you too may be white and ruddy—that is, sincere and enkindled. For he has power both to make bright and to kindle. Whoever approaches him approaches fire.

*Here end the sermons of Abbot Gillebert on the Song of Songs, which, being likewise overtaken by death, he was unable to complete.*

[Col. 0251]

## ASCETICAL TREATISES OF THE SAME GILLEBERT

### TREATISE I, TO A CERTAIN RELIGIOUS R.  
[Note: [Col. 0251D] Perhaps Roger, to whom Treatise VI is addressed.]  
Written to a friend: *On the contemplation of heavenly things.*

[Col. 0251D]

1. Do I seem to you to have spun out my discourse sufficiently, and in this one to have supplied what was shortened in the preceding pieces? Perhaps I have been excessive in this respect too, and our prolixity is now burdensome to you, who formerly complained of brevity. For, my R., you complained that I gave you not letters but mere clauses of words, cut off while they were still beginning; adding that it would be very pleasing to you if a more extended page compensated for the infrequency of a friend’s conversation. While I excused myself on the grounds of your occupations and the need to spare the reader’s weariness, you commanded me henceforth to be unconcerned about that.

For my part, I confess that nothing is more delightful to me than this exchange, nothing sweeter—provided that we have as the subject of our discourse him who is the cause of love; provided he may sound in the mouth and bring serenity to the heart, inwardly conceiving what it may bring forth outwardly. Indeed, you read: “If anyone speaks, let him speak as the utterances of God” (1 Pet. 4:11): as though given by God and as though referred back to him. For grace is from him, the cause lies with him, and in him is matter abundantly available. Who can unfold it? Who, to say nothing meanwhile of his essence, can speak of his benefits and his judgments? No discourse here is excessive; none is sufficiently abundant. “Exalt the Lord,” Scripture says, “as much as you can; for he is greater” (Ecclus. 43:33). Rich indeed is this subject, and sweet this occupation. What is sweeter? What is more pleasing than this activity, which alone clothes and overlays us with an image of angelic enjoyment and of the life to come? “It is good,” says the Psalm, “to confess to the Lord, and to sing to your name, O Most High. For you have made me glad in your creation, and I shall rejoice in the works of your hands” (Ps. 91:2, 5). If your magnificence thus delights and gladdens, Lord, what will your essence do? If you please us in your works, what will you be to us in yourself?

2. Happy are those who can taste this beforehand: who can be free to behold how sweet the Lord is! Alas for me, that time does not flow freely into this very pursuit; that, with my mind distracted by gnawing cares, in some manner eaten away and halved, I approach so devout a spectacle; that I may not boast with the prophet of constancy in it: “I stand continually by day upon the watchtower of the Lord, and I stand upon my watch throughout the nights” (Isa. 21:8). Time did not flow away vainly for him; rather, he did not himself wander and flit about with time, since he held back passing time in his watch, spending it upon that watchtower of the Lord. The former watch is indeed salutary, but this contemplation is sweeter. Observe, indeed, that the former is compared with night and the latter with day. For what does the Apostle say? “But we all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory” (2 Cor. 3:18).

It is altogether excellent to keep oneself undefiled and not to be conformed to this age; but it is far more excellent to be re-formed for the age to come and transformed from glory to glory. To attend to this contemplation is to stand upon the Lord’s watchtower and to stand by day. “Standing,” he says, “continually by day.” What then? Have your knees not been weakened, blessed prophet, by such constancy? Have they not been weakened by fasting? Yet this contemplation is not fasting but rather a sweet banquet. Indeed, “he who dwells on high: bread is given to him; his waters are sure.”

3. Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly to so trustworthy and fruitful a station, where there is rest and refreshment? My access to it is rare, if indeed there is any. Rare—and perhaps immediately interrupted and taken away like a declining shadow—until once again, in the manner of locusts, I am suddenly shaken out into a leap. This is indeed a good leap, of which you read in the Psalm: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days” (Ps. 38:5). Indeed, this Psalm is entitled “For Idithun,” that is, “for the one who leaps over” (Ps. 38:1). He had leapt over all things that pass away, migrating in mind to those things which are and remain. That number is without number; that end without end—an end banishing misery but not ending happiness. For “Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4); and that same one is the end of faith for joy to everyone who beholds.

For he is Wisdom, “reaching mightily from end to end, and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1). From end to end: reaching from faith to hope, as a way; ordering, as life. “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6): the way leading, truth teaching, life sweetening. “This is eternal life,” that they may know you, the true God (John 17:3). This knowledge is full of sweetness. “You will fill me with joy with your countenance; delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15:11). At this end we shall be sweetly ordered, when he himself is all in all; when every remnant of the old man has been destroyed; when mortality is swallowed up by life, weakness by power, blindness by truth, and fleshly desire by spiritual abundance.

4. Since these oppose one another while life is lived here, we must fight bravely in order that we may rest happily, and that battle may be turned into peace, as it is written: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:9). O true peace and full peace—more true the less various, more full the more everlasting! “The selfsame” excludes diversity; peace excludes opposition. “They shall not labor in vain, nor bring forth in disturbance” (Isa. 65:23). It is as though he said: They shall not labor without fruit, nor shall they labor for fruit. Here no fruit is without labor, and labor without fruit is frequent. “When you cultivate the ground, it shall not yield its fruit to you” (Gen. 4:12). Now we travail and groan; then we shall rejoice in the birth. “A woman does not remember the distress once she has borne a child” (John 16:21), for she has borne a male, “who is the image and glory of God.”

But when will this occur? When will what we read be fulfilled: “We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2)? For this vision all creation groans, longs, and travails even now (Rom. 8:22). This is truly Wisdom, sweetly ordering us into the divine image. Now we are afflicted in many ways; then we shall be well ordered in all things (Wis. 3:5): not through successive times, not through stages of progress; not from virtue to virtue nor from glory to glory, but simultaneously and once for all in every virtue and every truth. Does not Isaiah say precisely this: “Before she travailed, she gave birth; before she travailed, she bore a male” (Isa. 66:7)? Who is she, who bore with such speed and without any weariness? Surely it is that Wisdom of which we speak, who says: “I am the mother of beautiful love and knowledge” (Ecclus. 24:24). In this birth she will bring us forth fully, when without difficulty we shall contemplate truth in eternity and be conformed to charity. “My little children, with whom I am again in travail until Christ is formed in you,” says Paul (Gal. 4:19). Therefore the Apostle now labors in birth; then the Lord himself will bring forth. “Shall I, who make others bring forth, not myself bring forth? Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren?” says the Lord (Isa. 66:9). Rather, we shall all be taught by God, conformed to him.

5. Finally, in this conformity born from the vision of him, we are renewed into a male offspring: “for man is the image and glory of God.” Therefore a man ought not to veil his face (1 Cor. 11:7), prefiguring in the habit of the body what will then exist in the spirit, when with the unveiled face of the mind we behold the glory of the Lord and are transformed into the same image, without any stage of progress or danger of falling away. This is what is said in wonder: “Who has ever heard such a thing? Or who has seen anything like it? Has a nation been born at once, or has a land travailed in one day, because Zion has borne sons?” (Isa. 66:8).

For truly Zion, whose name means “watchtower,” gives birth in the day—and in that single day which is better in the courts of the Lord than thousands. Of it the Prophet says elsewhere: “There shall be one day, known to the Lord: neither day nor night; and at evening time there shall be light. For your sun shall no more go down, nor shall your moon diminish; but the Lord shall be your everlasting light” (Isa. 60:19–20). This is the day known to the Lord; for this day is the Lord. “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom he chooses to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). His revelation will also make us day: we shall be like him when he appears. “Days shall be formed, and no one in them” (Ps. 138:16): namely, those to whom it is said, “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:14).

You now possess the prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp, until the day dawns (2 Pet. 1:19). The lamp is already put away when the morning star rises. For prophetic speech will be brought to nothing, and apostolic speech and understanding likewise. “For we know in part”; but “that which is in part shall be brought to nothing when that which is perfect has come” (1 Cor. 13:9–10). Therefore Philip says: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). You, he says—and the Father. None other than you; nothing other than him; and it is enough for us.

6. “For your invisible things are perceived and seen through the things that have been made—your eternal power also and divinity” (Rom. 1:20). Yet it is one thing to see you with no intermediary, another by another’s aid. Why do you light a lamp for me? That I may behold the sun? The lamp is good, but for a weak eye; breasts are good, but for infants in Christ; a mirror is good, but a kiss is better. Therefore, kiss me yourself with the kiss of your mouth—of your mouth, I say, not of your work. Within is the mouth; without is the work. “Who will give you to me as a brother, suckling the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you outside and kiss you?” (Song 8:1). She who longs to kiss him when found outside calls him also one suckling breasts, signifying something of the self-emptying of the Incarnation.

In another way, although in the unity of the person, Wisdom the artificer nevertheless shines forth outwardly through the indications of its work. Outwardly it delights, though sweetly, not sufficiently. Do what suffices: show yourself. I diligently seek you outside; I find you late, retain you with difficulty, and in some manner devoutly kiss you as you flee and slip away. These kisses are good, but as in an image, as in a shadow; they are good and refresh for a time, but do not suffice. Do what suffices. Kiss me yourself with the kiss of your mouth: with the kiss of the Word, not of flesh; of truth, not of image; with a kiss freely granted, not violently extorted; with the kiss of your manifestation and my conformation, so that, ordered toward you and joined to you, I may be one spirit. “For whoever cleaves to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17). This indivisible embrace of love and union is rightly designated by the name of a kiss. And therefore I assign to you the office of kissing and attribute to you the authority—where the whole is your work, not my labor; your gracious gift, not my diligence; your manifestation, not my investigation.

7. Therefore I say: Manifest yourself to me through yourself, as you are, and that suffices me. “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15): when you have poured me full of that wine, the new wine which you yourself drink and yourself dispense in your kingdom. I desire that wine unmixed, pure and without milk, because milk belongs to infants. The things of infancy shall pass away. Breasts are indeed better than wine—but not than this wine; rather, this excellent wine is better than breasts. For breasts do not intoxicate, but that wine does, and carries the mind’s state over into certain new and unfamiliar perceptions. While breasts are suckled, they are dried up; but that which intoxicates overflows continually. I do not wish its heat to be tempered by the coldness of milk; I await it pure and perennially flowing.

For thus we read: “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, because with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:9–10). This is plainly an unfamiliar intoxication, effected by light, not liquid; by purity, not by strong drink. Therefore send forth your light and your truth: fullness, not the pledge that delays your presence, moderates grace, and casts a shadow over the light. Let what is promised in shadow be bestowed in light. In shadow is what the prophet says: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who wait for you” (Isa. 64:4).

And the daughters called Zelophehad in Numbers (Num. 27:1–6)—that is, “Shadows”—do not possess an inheritance but ask for their father’s inheritance. For Zelophehad, “Shadow,” could not beget men, in whom are the image and glory of the Lord. This indeed will not be so while we believe; but when we see, then we shall be like him. For this reason, while we are in the body and away from the Lord, we petition with Zelophehad’s daughters; for “we do not know what we should ask for as we ought” (Rom. 8:26). We ask for our father’s inheritance; for “the Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5). We ask with the apostle: “Show us the Father, and it suffices us” (John 14:8). I press no farther, nor do I stop short of this: here I set the boundary of my desires and establish the end of my prayers.

What, then, is that end? The one of which the Apostle says: “But the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:22). What is this eternal life? That which Christ says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

8. To this end, as though to the conclusion of all things, he had passed in desire who speaks in the Psalm: “Make known to me, Lord, my end”—the end of good and the end of evil: of the latter because it is consumed; of the former because it is brought to completion. Therefore truly an end: pure, full, perpetual—pure from evil, full in good, perpetual in both; it affects purely, satisfies fully, and fails in neither. This is what he adds: “And the number of my days, what it is” (Ps. 38:5). For those days are truly simultaneous and do not succeed one another; their number is neither diminished nor changed. Therefore it is called “what is.”

How can my day fail if my sun does not set? “Your sun,” he says, “shall no longer set, and your moon shall not diminish” (Isa. 60:20). I am the moon and he the sun; and therefore the moon shall not diminish, because it is not moved away from the everlasting and everywhere-present sun. Thus, by a new mode of reckoning, those days will have no end and yet will have a number: there will be for us there unceasing and unfailing eternity, but not the absolute simplicity conformed to the divine unity. For all other things, although everlasting, are by no means simple: for them, to be is not the same as to be this or that; nor is to be this or that the same as to be whatever they are.

For in spiritual creation, those things which are in themselves infinite through unending continuance are nevertheless, in relation to one another, in a manner determined and defined because of a certain fixed difference of natures and affections. Thus: “In my Father’s house,” he says, “there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2)—dwelling places, plainly, of lights, because God himself “dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16). Thus what is here called the number of days may there be understood as the multitude of dwelling places: not because there is one dwelling place for each individual, but because one person may have many, according to the saying, “And you, have authority over ten cities” (Luke 19:17). For “star differs from star in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41). In whatever degree the number of virtues has preceded, the number of splendors will likewise be multiplied, as the prophetic promise says: “The Lord will fill your soul with splendors” (Isa. 58:11). Blessed indeed is the soul filled not with one splendor only but with many—the splendors of which it is said: “With you is dominion in the day of your power, in the splendors of the saints” (Ps. 109:3). These most serene splendors are days, and the power of brightness.

9. Who will grant that my spirit may be illuminated by the ray of this threefold splendor, so that this most blessed number may fill, complete, and contain my days? Who, I say, will grant that they may extend themselves to the measure of eternity, shine in the splendor of truth, and burn in the spirit of love? For then—not as at the world’s first creation, when the reciprocal recurrence of evening and morning marked off many days—there will be one continuous day, wholly noon. There, so to speak, the unhappy night has been driven out from between morning and evening; in that day, unchanging noon will occupy both limits, according to what is written: “At the time of evening there shall be light” (Isa. 60:19), because there will be neither change of time nor the shadowing of alternation.

But when will this be? When, good Jesus, will you manifest yourself to us in that noonday, as you are? For in you we shall see the Father, and it will suffice us. O sluggish times, and slow hearts—slow to behold, though ready to believe!

10. Draw near to us, Lord, that we may be able to say: “Behold, he comes, leaping upon the mountains, skipping over the hills” (Song 2:8). Draw near, and anticipate our slowness. For it was read just now how you drew near to those two as they went to Emmaus, rebuking their slowness of faith and interpreting yourself to them from the Scriptures; opening within and appearing without, but disappearing too quickly—perhaps because you did not manifest yourself in full noon, but at evening itself and when the day was already declining. Indeed, in all that appearance of the blessed resurrection, I do not remember reading of noon anywhere, but rather either of day scarcely begun or already declining, so that you may understand all light of truth here as moderated by a certain obscurity of ignorance.

At the same time, there is a pleasing distinction to observe: at dawn he appeared at the tomb to the women who diligently sought him; but late on that one day of the week, to the disciples shut up in the house (Luke 24; Mark 16; John 20). Would that, Lord, you might appear to us too, whether at this dawn or this twilight—you who are plainly the best of either, noon! But there we shall repose in our homeland. Meanwhile, while we are on the way, we pray, Lord, that you may refresh us with the shade of evening light. But now we close our discourse with the day, though we do not exclude you; rather, ending in you and beginning from you, may we give you thanks in the morning, breaking out into that saying of the Song: “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat” (Song 2:3).

## TREATISE II. On seeking Christ, and on the contemplation of wayfarers and of the blessed.

1. Our Beloved has withdrawn a little amid the shadows of night. Where, then, shall we seek him? Which one? Surely the one who says: “I am the flower of the field” (Song 2:1). If, then, we seek him, let us go out into the field—indeed, let us enter the garden, since he “went down into his garden, to the bed of spices” (Song 6:1). Mary too, when she sought in the garden, found him (John 20:1–16). She sought him in lamentation; let us seek him in praise. Sweet indeed is the undertaking, but sweeter the reward. What reward? That of which we read in the Psalm: “The sacrifice of praise shall honor me; and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23). Therefore Jesus is to be manifested to those who praise. Let us seek with praise, but let us seek in the garden: in the garden he was betrayed, in the garden he suffered, and in the garden he appeared.

She who saw him therefore says: “You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening: make me hear your voice” (Song 8:13). The friends are Peter and John; the friends are the disciples, who heard: “You are my friends” (John 15:14). Make me hear what I may announce to them; they are in the field, I in the garden. They, as men, put their hand to mighty deeds; I to sweet things. Blessed is the woman who merited to hear you; more blessed she who saw you. For your voice is sweet and your face beautiful. But most blessed would she have been if she had touched, held, and retained the hand toward which she had stretched out; whereas now it is said: “Do not touch me” (John 20:17). What one woman could not do, several could do—those to whom he said, “Greetings.” “And they came and held his feet” (Matt. 28:9). What singularity cannot accomplish, community accomplishes; love accomplishes. Let us therefore seek unanimously, and we shall seek profitably. For those who came with ointment found him. Good is the ointment of which we read: “Behold, how good and pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity! Like ointment upon the head” (Ps. 132:1–2).

2. Perhaps he did not so much allow himself to be found as offer himself to them of his own accord. “They held his feet,” it says, yet they did not pour ointment upon him. For they had found alive him whom they had sought among the dead. They came to anoint Christ—to anoint thoroughly the Anointed One—and he came to them, wholly breathing the life-giving fragrance of immortal spices. Before his passion he wished to be anointed; afterward he allowed himself to be buried; but once raised he had no need. For he now abounded not merely in the ointment of immortality but also in that of royal and surpassing authority, as he himself testifies: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18); and: “God gave him the name which is above every name” (Phil. 2:9). Therefore it is said: “Your name is poured-out oil” (Song 1:2).

Accordingly he invites her to his own ointments: “Come into my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices” (Song 5:1). “What I sowed from what was yours, I have harvested from what was mine—for myself, indeed also for you: for me in actuality, for you in hope. Therefore I invite you: Come into my garden, my sister, my bride.” These are welcome names, full of sweetness, expressing the bond either of nature or of grace. Having become a sharer in nature, I return the recompense of grace. Therefore I call you sister in the flesh, but bride in the Spirit: in the flesh, in which full humanity was assumed; in the Spirit, through whom love was infused. Come, then, my sister, my bride. Come, assured by so great a pledge, secure of fullness. “I have gathered my myrrh with my spices.” Myrrh belongs to the sister; spices to the bride. Myrrh to the flesh; spices to the spirit. Myrrh of incorruption; spices of truth. “You shall know the truth,” but when my anointing teaches you.

You come with ointments, but I have others which you do not know: new ointments, indeed also old; for I have heaped up for myself all things new and old. For in me the beginnings of the resurrection to come at the end of the world have already budded forth, and the glory of that ancient, eternal brightness endures. For “the Father has glorified me with the glory which I had before the world was made.”

3. Truly, Lord, these are excellent ointments, and already their fragrance has reached your bride. Hence she says: “Behold, the fragrance of my beloved is like the fragrance of a full field” (Gen. 27:27). And where you go before, she follows after; for thus she says: “Draw me after you; in the fragrance of your ointments we shall run” (Song 1:3). O blessed times, when they will hear this said of them: “Who are these that fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8). Now the spirit is willing, but the flesh is slower; weak powers do not equal the desire. Therefore, “Draw me after you; in your fragrance we shall run.” Running is good, but being drawn is more effectual. Wait for one who lingers; draw one who is willing. I shall run more devoutly if you run with me. Let us run together: you in ointments, I in their fragrance.

Blessed is the soul which, after its labor, now rejoices in the ointments—into which the anointing of your knowledge and love pours itself; or rather, which the torrent of delight and abundance of sweetness has taken up and absorbed into itself. Blessed indeed is one hidden where it is stored away, buried with Christ—indeed, in Christ—and whose tomb is, as we read, glorious (Isa. 11:10): glorious indeed, for “his place is made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3). Those who are there behold you directly. But what do we behold except in a mirror—in the mirror of created things and in the enigma of Scripture? We are amid figures and obscurities; they are in truth and sincerity. They are at leisure and see; they stand and listen; and they rejoice with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice and the bridegroom’s face. For his voice is sweet and his face beautiful. Thus a constant longing and tireless eagerness stretch the sharers in the ointment toward such sweet hearing and contemplation. For your name is poured-out oil in them. Rightly oil: for your name and knowledge are light and joy—joy poured out, joy diffused in the heart, not of those still believing but of those already beholding. There is not there “a heart and a heart,” but one heart of all.

O how good and pleasant it is to dwell in unity—and there, in unity! There the Lord commands and pours forth: he commands openly and pours forth abundantly; he lavishly pours out blessing and life forever.

4. Woe to me, because I do not fully pour out what I in some measure receive! Woe for the barrenness of my speech, and still more for that of my perceptions. For neither speech satisfies affection, nor affection faith; nor does faith suffice, since it does not fully refresh. “We shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15). When, therefore, the vision comes, hunger will depart—not abundant hunger but needy hunger; fasting hunger, not refreshed hunger. Yet that refreshment is good which removes disgust and sharpens desire; good is the appetite which satiety produces. “Those who eat me,” he says, “shall still hunger” (Ecclus. 24:29). What is feasting except contemplating? “Let the righteous feast in the sight of God” (Ps. 67:4), that is, by beholding God. What is hungering except always seeking? “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. 104:4).

Seek the face always, you who see face to face. But we who are in the body—what do we behold except his back? Draw us after you. Draw us from the back to the face, from faith to vision, from fragrance to anointing; for we walk by faith and run in fragrance. Blessed are those who so ran that they have now attained and have nowhere further to run, but stand in truth and do not waver, wholly drenched in the ointments of immortality and anointed with the myrrh of immutability. There they praise you all the more abundantly because more freely. “You shall know the truth,” he says, “and the truth shall set you free” (John 8:32). Therefore vanity shall vanish before the flashing brightness of truth; for “creation was subjected to vanity unwillingly” (Rom. 8:20), and the heavy yoke of corruption “shall rot away before the oil” (Isa. 10:27), before the abundance of ointment. For “a good measure, pressed down, and overflowing, shall be given into your bosom” (Luke 6:38).

You, Lord, will give—and you will give us yourself, for the Lord is my portion. But how is it that you give yourself by measure, when you yourself are great and immeasurable? Do you also pour oil according to the capacity of the vessel? Why, then, do you call it overflowing? Is it because you pour out more than we receive? For even if with every effort we stretch ourselves to receive you, we do not comprehend you wholly. God is able to do beyond what we ask and understand; how much more does he himself—who is and was not made—exceed the measure of our desire and the limit of our understanding? “Behold,” he says, “I will turn toward them like a river of peace, and like an overflowing torrent of glory” (Isa. 66:12). Can a human being absorb the river whose rush gladdens the city of God, or drain the Jordan so that it may flow whole into his mouth? Truly, Lord, we are not constrained in you, for you give abundantly; you give neither to few nor little, nor with a sparing and grudging mind; you anticipate merits and exceed desires. We are not constrained in you; we are constrained in our own inward parts. Having such promises, beloved, let us also be enlarged—enlarged in desire, that we may be enlarged in attainment.

5. Rather, Lord, by the gentle and mild flowing-on of your abundance—for “I ran the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32)—you who stretch out the heavens like a skin, gently stretch out the skin of my heart, made old and contracted by torpid neglect. Unfold its wrinkles, draw out its folds, widen its receptacles, that I may desire you without measure and receive without measure. Let this holy desire make me more capacious. For thus, having first tasted the slender foretaste of experience to which faith persuades, affection will fly ahead; fervent eagerness will not wait for reason’s prompting. Thus amid the hard and prolonged trials, the constancy of a holy purpose will labor less, sustained by the expectation of ardent desire and devout hope. But let us wait here and catch our breath a little, sparing the weary spirit, so that, refreshed by a brief interval, it may rise more fervently.

## TREATISE III. How unlike is the joy of the way and that of the homeland.

1. Refreshed by you in the night’s rest, it is fitting, Lord, that we should stand before you in the morning. Stand—or follow? Blessed is one who finds you seated by his doors in the morning, so that he may stand, and stand until evening, lest he seek you, suddenly slipping away in flight, with wandering gaze amid the thin air. For “you make darkness your hiding place” (Ps. 17:12). You are light, and yet a hiding place; for you dwell in inaccessible light (1 Tim. 6:16). Therefore you are darkness to us, because inaccessible; yet inaccessible not to the voice as to sight, because prayer passes beyond where reason cannot approach. “My cry,” he says, “entered before him into his ears” (Ps. 17:7). Therefore let our cry also enter before you, so that you yourself may come forth before us and graciously allow yourself at least to be seen, though you do not allow yourself to be held.

“Return, return, that we may behold you” (Song 6:12), until we hold you. Return: “Be like a gazelle or a young stag, my beloved, upon mountains of spices” (Song 2:17; 8:14). “Be like a gazelle,” she says: let yourself be seen, and fly away; be present, and withdraw; present to sight, while absent from touch. Thus it is said to the woman: “Do not touch me” (John 20:17)—as if she might touch by some trustworthy hand of experience. Behold, Lord, I withhold my hand and direct my eye. “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Ps. 5:5). Woe to me if I hear also this: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me flee” (Song 6:4)! Or perhaps, as you flee the gaze, you kindle desire, so that you may be anxiously sought as you are loved more deeply. Indeed, your flight spurs us eagerly to run.

2. Who will make my feet like the feet of deer, that I may lightly and eagerly follow this young stag? Who will enable me to unlearn domestic cares and become wild in heavenly solitude? It is good to unload oneself of oneself, the heaviest burden, and gradually to fail into the lightness of the wild goats. Therefore the prophet says: “I have not labored, following you, Lord.” What you say, blessed prophet, is true—true, but still too little. Not laboring does not suffice unless you also rejoice. Therefore what you express less fully another explains: “Let them sing in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord” (Ps. 137:5); and likewise: “Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118:54). All is done within, for singing is in the heart; and there also one runs. “He has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears” (Ps. 83:6–7).

Yet what is this mode of ascending with lamentation and journeying with song, when one can neither lament in the homeland nor rejoice in a foreign land? “How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?” (Ps. 136:4). But perhaps—indeed certainly—those who sit and remain by the rivers of Babylon weep, while those who go forth rejoice. And one who ascends in the valley of tears also ascends out of the valley of tears; and though he comes from tears, he does not ascend with tears. For it is sweeter to be on the mountain of joys than in the valley of sorrow. If he does ascend with tears, it is rather because he ascends sluggishly and has not yet drawn near. For one does not immediately accomplish the ascents merely because one arranges them in the heart. But when the lawgiver has bestowed blessing, then “they shall go from strength to strength, that the God of gods may be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:8), proceeding and hastening in gladness of heart toward the prize, like one who enters with a flute upon the mountain of the Lord—the mountain of which the prophet says: “The Lord will make on this mountain a feast of rich things, a feast of vintage wine, of rich marrow-filled things, of wine strained clear” (Isa. 25:6).

The joy of one ascending is still tempered, not yet clarified, and mingled with tears. For “a cup of unmixed wine, full of mixture, is in the hand of the Lord” (Ps. 74:9). It is mixed for those on the way; pure for those who arrive; the dregs remain for the sluggish. Here Wisdom has mixed wine in the bowl, where it will clarify the new vintage. There is one occupation for the blessed spirits, one festal rest of the year of jubilee: to rejoice with the Lord and praise him. For “joy shall be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of praise” (Isa. 51:3).

3. Rejoice, Jerusalem: break forth and praise. Praise majesty; render thanks to the bountiful giver. This obligation is always fulfilled by you and always required of you; it is readily fulfilled and devoutly required. The very requirement is delight. The desired apprehension of blessed truth commends itself; and serenity breathed upon the perceptions pours joy in together with light. “Light has risen for the righteous, and joy for the upright in heart. Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous.” What return will they make for joy? “And give thanks,” it says, “at the remembrance of his holiness” (Ps. 96:11–12). Thus joy comes from light, praise from joy. Growing joy breaks out into praise; and inward parts soaked with luminous truth cannot but belch forth the blessed fullness, nor, intoxicated by the torrent of sweetness, restrain themselves from song.

For sweetness awakens appetite, abundance supplies sufficiency, and eternity perpetuates the instant. Thus sweetness, abundance, and eternity themselves testify: “Whoever drinks the water that I give shall become in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John 4:14).

4. O blessed spirits and souls of the righteous! O Church of the firstborn, you who are enrolled in heaven! You are truly the firstborn, who taste beforehand the firstfruits of future blessing. “Eat, friends, and drink; be intoxicated, dearly beloved” (Song 5:1). Drink from your own cistern; let the streams of your well increase and overflow. Let the waters of your delights flow abundantly and run through the streets of your hearts. Let strangers not share with you; nor let even all members of the household be admitted. For we are fellow-citizens of the saints and members of God’s household: citizens enrolled, but not yet received; citizens rejoicing, yet citizens on pilgrimage; wandering and scattered citizens. For “our iniquities, like the wind, have carried us away” (Isa. 64:6).

But you sit in the beauty of peace, in tabernacles of confidence, and in abundant repose (Isa. 32:18). Woe to the inhabitants of the earth, where peace is rare, security nonexistent, labor unceasing, and labor brings forth poverty! For “the life of man upon earth is warfare” (Job 7:1), as long as flesh desires against spirit; and “our adversary goes about like a lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). In the sweat of our face we eat our bread, and the earth of our heart produces thorns and thistles for the worker. Therefore, scattered, torn apart, and wasting away in heart, we have more cause in our hands to groan anxiously over ourselves than securely to rejoice in the Lord—except that good hope, looking ahead to the end on the evidence of the firstfruits, presses from the winepresses of tribulation the oil of consolation. With face brightened and head anointed, we then glory with the Apostle in tribulations and take pleasure in insults, “knowing that tribulation works patience; patience, proof; and proof, hope” (Rom. 5:3–4). And what is hope except that it seems already to taste beforehand some firstfruits of the joys of the glory that is to come upon us? “We were saved in hope” (Rom. 8:24), and “rejoicing in hope” (Rom. 12:12). For devout faith knows how to fly ahead of slow time and be affected as by something present by that which unwavering confidence depicts for itself—yet it is hope born from the purity of a tested conscience, not presumption.

5. “Wash yourselves; be clean.” Wash yourselves, and be tested by fire, so that, refined to purity by the double furnace of penitence and patience, the heavenly regard may refresh you with a sprinkling like dew of its delight; and you may soon gratefully and exultantly break out into those words: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93:19). Wash yourselves and rejoice; wash yourselves more often, that you may rejoice more fervently. Claim more frequently what you cannot yet claim forever.

Unhappy mountains of Gilboa, condemned to eternal dryness: you have not been drenched with this willing rain, nor has a drop of early [dew, supplied] descended upon you. Therefore you are not fields of firstfruits, nor is a late harvest expected from you. Would, Lord, that my head were full of this dew and my locks with drops of the night! For what else are we doing but passing through the night, until the day breathes and the shadows decline? In the noonday which we await, neither is a shadow feared nor a drop desired. Here a drop flows from Jacob’s bucket; but there his seed shall be in many waters. Blessed times, when the whole face of the earth shall be watered—watered from above—and no barren dryness shall possess anything; watered both above and below, when my flesh and my heart shall rejoice in the living God.

Good indeed is the fountain which will then rise and cleanse our heart, better than that first fountain because it cannot dry up. “They shall be intoxicated with the abundance of your house, and you shall give us drink from the torrent of your delight; because with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:9–10). Certainly good is the fountain from which such streams flow: delight, abundance, life, and truth.

6. Sprinkle from there down to here. Extend mercy to those who know you, though not yet wholly; extend mercy, pour in grace, pour out your Spirit upon us—your ruling Spirit, who may renew our spirit in our inward parts, reform and conform us to himself, conform and strengthen us, gladden and illuminate us. For “the ordinances of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts; the commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening eyes” (Ps. 18:9), insofar as it belongs to us here to be enlightened and gladdened. Otherwise we shall truly rejoice before you as those rejoice in harvest, as victors exult over captured plunder when they divide the spoil (Isa. 9:3). There we shall rejoice as possessors; here as those who set before themselves, presume, and pursue until we attain. There, then, from possession; here, from promise. There, from fullness; here, from a portion.

For what is sprinkled from there to here is a drop, not a river; a spark, not a furnace. Alas, how quickly even this spark vanishes and the drop dries up! “Remember us, Lord, in the favor of your people; visit us in your salvation, that we may see your goodness and rejoice in your joy, that you may be praised with your inheritance” (Ps. 105:4–5). Visit us for seeing, rejoicing, and praising; visit us in salvation and light, in joy and praise. Good are these droplets, although rare and like falling dew. “Drop down, heavens, from above; eternal mountains, distill sweetness for us”: in your droplets the seedling shall rejoice.

7. Be to us, Lord, like dew, that we too may bud forth like a lily. Your word, once sent out, does not know how to return empty, but shall prosper in those things for which it is sent. Thus, through its watering, “instead of the salt shrub shall grow the fir tree, and instead of the nettle shall grow the myrtle” (Isa. 55:11, 13): while it raises and exalts the downcast; while it softens and moderates the incitements of the flesh; while it establishes the despairing and makes them dwell in heavenly places; while it softens those made harsh and brings them into harmony with the meek.

This visitation is pleasant, yet “like a morning cloud and like dew passing away in the morning” (Hos. 6:4). Any contemplation in the flesh and ecstasy of mind, however great, is rightly compared to morning dew. For it has something—indeed much—of the night’s cold, because affection is less fervent; and of the night’s darkness, because understanding is somewhat obscure. But if it is morning dew, why does it pass away? Does it pass from us, or does it pass into and penetrate us? “The word of God is living and effectual, and more penetrating than any sword”: so that it not merely marks the skin outside, but penetrates inward, passes into the marrow, and becomes irrigation for the bones. For his words are smoother than oil, yet they are arrows.

Or is it because, if the heart of a human being is spread out like heaven, it shall be folded up like a book and melt away like smoke? Let each interpret according to the judgment in which he experiences it in conscience: the perfect person, that it is poured into and penetrates him; the person making progress, that it passes through and flies past him. It passes from us in order to draw us after itself and, as if by its very flight, make us pass over to it, saying: “Pass over to me, you who desire me” (Ecclus. 24:26).

Perhaps, Lord, we pass from you more often than you pass from us. For you light the lamp, sweep the house, and search us, according to the prophet (Zeph. 1:12), in case you find hidden filth within—us immersed in vain and wandering, soft and troublesome cares and thoughts; not merely dividing our mind between God and the world, but more inclined and ready toward the latter part, if not out of covetousness, at least from habit. For even cares rightly admitted force themselves upon us; and thus, when necessity does not press, superfluity still occupies us. Indeed, we seem to flee the wood that flows with silence, in order to pursue the rivers of Babylon.

But we have now spoken with you, Lord, and about you, for some while; and we have been sweetly refreshed, like little dogs from the crumbs falling from your table. If you affect us thus while passing and moving through, what do you do while remaining and abiding? Alas for me, because we are unworthy of such sweet abiding! “Remain with us, Lord, because it is toward evening and the day is already declining” (Luke 24:28–29). It truly declines when you withdraw. Constrain him, brothers, by the urgency of your prayers. Those two going to Emmaus used force upon him when he pretended to go farther. Why, then, does Truth pretend what it does not do? He pretended to go, but was compelled to remain—yet not to remain permanently, for while they ate he vanished. But that pretense of departure is an occasion for remaining. He seems to pretend to leave, diminishing spiritual joy; yet he remains hidden, continuing righteousness and increasing humility.

## TREATISE IV. On discourse and meditation concerning divine things.

1. You have what you asked for, but you have it with a certain accumulated interest. Yet I count this interest among my own gains and reckon it as profit. I simply cannot fail to count it among my happy successes whenever an occasion somehow arises to converse with you. Perhaps you object that I have used the word “talking” [*fabulationis*; Col. 0266B], and that, since we are accustomed to speak almost of nothing except serious matters, I have done an injury to the majesty of our thoughts by such a term. Does it not seem conversation to you when we speak of what we do not see and testify to what we do not hear? “Eye,” says the prophet, “has not seen, O God, apart from thee, what thou hast prepared for those awaiting thee” (Isa. 64:4): for those hoping and awaiting, but not yet beholding. “For what a man sees, why does he hope for it?” (Rom. 8:24). And if even what we see is through a mirror and in an enigma, how much more what we speak of! For speech, however eloquent, cannot fully unfold the secrets of the mind.

Indeed, to speak according to my own understanding, every figurative parable seems to me, in comparison with the truth to come, to be a kind of fable, intended to make that truth known. All created things may be pleasing in appearance, harmoniously joined in unity, useful in employment, and effective in power; but what are they beside that immense, simple, and eternal unity of the divine essence—beside the beauty of wisdom, the weight of love, and the strength of power? For he himself is “He Who Is” (Exod. 3:14); “there is no number of his wisdom” (Ps. 146:5); and the fullness of his charity surpasses knowledge. And who shall speak the mighty acts of the Lord? Everything assumed in the service of speech in order somehow to suggest those realities to us is incalculably unlike them by nature and admits of no comparison. “Gold from Ethiopia shall not be compared with it, nor shall the purest dyes be set beside it” (Job 28:19).

And yet by gold and dyes, flower and fruit, and every created beauty, that which is above every beauty is coloured and painted for us, so that, because it is utterly inward, it may wholly elude us as to what it is; and, through the superimposed colours of figures, may in some measure shine through beneath a shadow. It is indeed a good shadow, refreshing for an hour. Therefore it is said: “Under his shadow whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2:3).

2. O how much more delightfully, how much more lovingly, would she sit not beneath the shadow but above the shadow, in thee thyself, good Jesus, and, having attained this end of her desire, rest! But now she rests beneath a shadow and refreshes herself beneath a shadow. Yet what sort of refreshment is that which failure follows? “For we know in part; but that which is in part shall be done away when that which is perfect has come” (1 Cor. 13:9–10). These are meanwhile supports for those who are falling and remedies for the languishing. Thus it follows: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2:5).

Happy is the one in whom holy love is a languor, not a passing passion. For there are some who are suddenly wounded by charity, only to be healed again shortly afterwards—like Jonah’s ivy, which withered in the same hour in which it flourished (Jonah 4:6–7). Passion, then, is the stirred-up emotion of desire; languor is continuous. O heart poorly sound—indeed, truly mad—that does not know how to be wounded by this wound! “I am wounded by charity,” she says (Song 5, according to the Septuagint). Love not only wounds but even kills: “For love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). Accordingly the Apostle says: “You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3).

While life is hidden and longing is kindled, truth lies concealed and strength languishes; the anxious heat of desire is cooled by shadows of figures and sustained by earliest flowers. These figures are beautiful enough: they refresh the striving affection and revive it with childlike allurements, so that through familiar and sensible delights we may apprehend experiences of unfamiliar joys. “Your streets, Jerusalem, shall be paved with pure gold” (Tob. 13:22). “I will lay your stones in order and found you upon sapphires” (Isa. 54:11). “I will make your desert like delights and your wilderness like the garden of the Lord” (Isa. 51:3), and very many other things spoken by Prophets and Apostles as types of the heavenly Jerusalem.

When its gates and streets, walls and metals, stones and woods, springs and rivers are described, how deeply they move and delight us! How gladly they are heard, though they are expressed with little clarity! For incomprehensibly more, and incomparably greater things, are left to conjecture than are put forward in comparison. Jonah rejoiced greatly beneath the shadow of the ivy; but that ivy withered and the figure passed away. Therefore, when comparisons drawn from figurative discourse are woven together, I may freely call them a kind of conversations—not because of the eternal truth shadowed within, but because of the vanity that casts a shadow outwardly; for “that which is in part shall be done away.” Thus in the Gospel you have it said of those two who were going to Emmaus that they were talking and questioning with one another [Col. 0267D], perhaps because they were seeking and had not yet grasped, were wavering and did not stand firm in faith. Therefore they are said to have been seeking and discussing, walking and conversing; yet while they conversed, Jesus himself drew near and went with them (Luke 24:15).

3. You sweetly recall how often our heart burned within us concerning Jesus when we spoke of him on the way. For what we spoke concerning him, he himself had first spoken within us. Would that it happened to me more often, to seek, discuss, and converse wholly about him—about him, I say, and with you; and not so much to speak as to hear you speaking! Your speech is compressed, yet sufficiently expresses what you feel: few words, but full of meaning. You seem to me to call every single word to judgment; so carefully does none escape you without consideration. Thus your lips are “a dripping honeycomb.” For what you say comes forth with a certain delay and deliberation, as though weighed in a balance, so that you seem rather to distil than to pour forth.

Your words are refined, subtle, and evaporated; therefore they are dripping, secret, sweet, and bursting forth from inward depths; and for that reason they are like a honeycomb. This is what the following means: “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song 4:11). “Under your tongue,” it says, and not “on your tongue.” For greater is what lies hidden beneath it than what shines forth upon it. What if there is also something above the tongue? “Honey and milk under your tongue.” For it is not merely in speech, nor is it all in speech. Just as nothing in your mouth is feigned, so much is hidden in your heart. On the tongue are the things you speak openly; under the tongue are those you suggest secretly; above the tongue are those in whose exposition even the most eloquent person is tongue-tied, and speech is silence.

4. I remember, unless I am mistaken, that several times in the very course of prayer you compressed your speech: attentive and astonished at the light or joy breaking forth in your heart, you broke off a voice that was forming into words, so that it turned into a sigh.
