For although the tongue may suffice for clarity [variant: “for instruction”], nevertheless inward amazement, love, and admiration at the light shining from above turn the soul that is coming forth through words back upon itself, draw it into itself, and hold it within itself; and, spiritually, envelop it with Moses in a cloud (Exod. 24:15), putting “the cloud for his covering, and darkness for his hiding-place” [Col. 0268C], so that it becomes bewildered toward inward things and mute toward outward things.

Therefore there is honey under your tongue and sweetness beneath your voice—not as something lower, but as something inward; indeed, beneath your very mind, while it is not yet master of the sweetness conceived and cannot either fully express the joys springing up within or endure what it has experienced. It yields itself wholly to them, yet does not possess them wholly. “My eyes have failed for thy word,” says the Psalmist—not merely toward the word, but into the word: into thy word, by desiring it; toward thy word, by conceiving it; into thy word, insofar as it is enkindled; toward thy word, because it is exceedingly enkindled: “For thy word is exceedingly enkindled” (Ps. 118:123, 140).

Therefore, “my soul melted when my beloved spoke. I sought him” (Song 5:6). My soul melted, unable to contain what it hears; and, made more eager by the sweetness of what it hears, it does not cease to desire it. Therefore it adds: “I sought him.” The ear is not satisfied with hearing; yet the ear is insufficient for hearing.

5. Therefore “my eyes have failed for thy word,” and “my soul melted,” despising itself and striving toward and gazing upon him, admiring and loving him, and moving about him; unable either to direct itself toward him as much as it desires or to retain as much as it has received. How then should the spirit of one speaking not be interrupted where the inward faculty of one meditating is absorbed? For just as solid and more bodily material receives the force of fire into itself with greater difficulty, while material that is subtle, dried out, and thin is more quickly both kindled and consumed by devouring flame, so spiritual and refined meditations receive more quickly the sweet violence of enkindled love and do not bear it long.

“Your spirit,” says the prophet, “shall devour you like fire” (Isa. 33:11). I would indeed regard meditation as the material and love as the flame. “In my meditation a fire shall burn”; and if it burns with a more vehement blaze, it turns and consumes within itself every intention of the soul, so that what had been meditation becomes wholly affection. Reason can no longer be master of itself—reason whose task it is to draw out hidden things, judge ambiguities, review and recollect what it knows devoutly—when it has been absorbed by the force of love. “I was silent from good things, and my sorrow was renewed; my heart grew hot within me” (Ps. 38:3–4). “I was silent,” he says, “I grieved, I grew hot.” I grew hot from some perception of inward good; I grieved because of imperfection, and therefore I was silent. Divided, torn, and absorbed by this twofold passion, I “was silent from good things.” But from what goods? Perhaps from those of which he says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13).

6. Rightly, then, I was silent also concerning those things that are not yet seen. But if he is silent from prayers for these things, he is not silent from entreaties against them. Therefore it follows: “Make known to me, Lord, my end, and what is the number of my days, that I may know what is lacking to me.” What, then, is lacking? Rather, what is present? Hear what is added: “My substance is as nothing before thee. Yet every living man is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38:5–6). What then is present, when everything is either nothing or at least vain? What then? Are faith itself and the virtues vain? Or is this inward life of a human being called vanity—the life which is also called death? For “you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ” (Col. 3:3).

But if this is vanity because it is in part—for “that which is in part shall be done away” (1 Cor. 13:10)—then faith will pass away; for the righteous lives by faith, and the end for which he hoped is not in faith. Is the righteousness that comes by faith also to pass away? How then does charity, which alone is truly righteousness, never fail? What if we say that all things presently existing are vain when not referred to that future good, or when compared with it? Thus everything is vanity: through useless employment, through swift passing, or in the sight of the future.

7. If necessity is vanity, what is superfluity? If that truth which exists in the present is vanity, how great is vanity itself? “Every living man is altogether vanity.” Nor merely vanity, but adversity: “for he is troubled in vain.” In vain he rejoices and in vain he is troubled: in either case there is vanity, whether because the cause is useless or because its continuance is not lasting. “And now, amid these evil and vain things, what is my expectation? Is it not the Lord? And my substance is with thee” (Ps. 38:18). “My substance is as nothing before thee”; yet my substance is substance with thee. “Make known to me, Lord, my end, that I may know what is lacking to me.”

Human vanity is sufficiently known to me from its own defect; but let it become fully known through the taste of good itself. When, Lord, shall our desire be filled with good things—with the good things of thy house? When, I say, shall we be filled with thy truth, so that no taste or odour of vanity remains in us, as is written of Moab that “his taste remained in him, and his flavour was not changed” (Jer. 48:11)? There we shall not be silent from good things; rather, we shall be like storehouses—not empty but full, overflowing and pouring forth from one thing into another.

8. I have poured forth to thee certain things concerning our emptiness. Would that I might deserve to have something distilled to me from your fullness, from the dew of heaven and from the deep beneath—though not yet fully breaking forth—from that deep of future glory which shall be revealed in us! It is therefore now within us, yet not revealed; rather, hidden, stored up as seed, enclosed in certain veins of faith, and shut in by doors both of carnal affections and bodily imaginations.

By such doors the sea was shut in, when it was bursting out, as though proceeding from a womb. A good sea, of which we read: “The earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as waters covering the sea” (Isa. 11:9). A good sea, but a heavy door. Thus the first Adam himself restrained this sea by a certain barrier of disobedience and held down in unrighteousness the truth of God as it came forth and burst forth through itself. The first man removed us by the door of unrighteousness; the second removed that door, becoming himself the door for us, and “if anyone enters through him, he shall be saved and shall find pasture” (John 10:9).

Unrighteousness has been destroyed, but a heavy door still remains: the evil of this day. The habit of imaginative thought and the anxiety of necessary sustenance are a very cloudy door. To apply the mind to such matters is truly to dig in the earth—to dig a broken cistern and a well that cannot hold water. Yet how they quarrel, how they dispute, what charges the Philistines contrive against us over wells of this kind—for the waters not, I say, of passing pleasure, but of passing necessity! Happy is he who, with the patriarch Jacob [read: Isaac], leaves wells of this sort, who leaves occasions for dispute and material for enmity, in order to dig in the torrent-bed and find a vein of living water (Gen. 26:14–22), provided that he does not shut it in with the doors mentioned above.

I should think these things more accessible to you, and your access to inward things more familiar and frequent, so that you may not stand only outside, looking through the window and listening through the door. I shall now, then, “set a door upon my mouth,” so that, according to the proverb, the pipe may be fitted to you while I take breath.

## TREATISE V. He undertakes to explain that passage of the Apostle, “Every best gift and every perfect gift,” etc.; but the more important part of the letter or treatise seems to be missing.

1. You urgently demand what I myself had rashly promised, having given too little thought to the difficulty of the subject. A twofold burden also arises here: insufficient account seems to have been taken both of time and of comparison. If other causes have snatched away the time, I prudently decline comparison with others who have treated this subject, a comparison which I seemed to have rashly undertaken with too little consideration. Yet I shall approach the question, to whose solution I remain bound.

Your part now will be to obtain for me beforehand what you ask from me, so that, through the merit of your prayer, there may be poured down upon us from above that which we may pour back to you more abundantly. “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). What then? Are things that are not perfect, that are not best, not from him? Whence then are they, if not from him? “What have you that you did not receive?” Nor are only the best things from him and lesser goods from elsewhere; rather, as the Apostle says, “All things are from God” (Rom. 11:36).

Or perhaps nothing is excluded in these words, because, since all things are from him, all things are perfect and best? If so, then through the words “best” and “perfect” a distinction is not made between greater and lesser goods; rather, goodness is expressed. But how is every good best and perfect, since everything is from above? What is “from above”? “Coming down,” he says, “from the Father of lights.” How can anything imperfect be understood to exist with the Father of lights? Or perhaps every best gift and every perfect gift comes down from there, but was not there? For how could that which was in him—that is, in the Father of lights—come down from and depart from him? For descent seems to indicate not a local migration but rather a diminution of power.

2. The Lord himself also seems to distinguish between the perfect and the less perfect: “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke 10:28). “But if you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). And the Apostle: “Each has his own gift from God, one indeed in this way, another in that” (1 Cor. 7:7); likewise: “I gave you milk to drink as to little children in Christ, not solid food” (1 Cor. 3:1–2); but “we speak wisdom among the perfect” (ibid. 2:6).

On what principle, then, does he specifically say that every perfect gift is from above, when neither is every gift perfect nor is there anything that is not from above? Or, if every gift is best and every donation perfect because it is from above, why should not “gift” and “donation” be said to be one and the same rather than “every”? For whatever is with the Father of lights must be judged simple and uniform, not multiple. What if it is both best and perfect with the Father of lights, but, descending to us from the Father of lights, becomes less good and less perfect? But this would subject that immutable reality to the condition of mutable things; for to be diminished is in a sense to be changed.

On what principle, then, can what is in itself descend from itself? But again, how can what is not in it be said to descend from it? Or, if it descends from it, how is it not perfect? And since the authority of Scripture also maintains that some things are more perfect and others less perfect, what does it mean that only the best and perfect gift is said to descend from above, when it seems that every gift should rather be so called? Then what does the phrase “gift and donation,” “best and perfect,” mean? Some distinction is suggested by these names. Or are they said only for emphasis and commendation?

3. These difficulties are brought to birth in me by the words of this chapter; but now let us return to its sequence, praying God that he may deign to unlock what is closed in it and grant us to speak worthily concerning his gifts. “Every best gift,” etc. In the first place, a distinction of this kind seems to me possible between *datum* (“what is given”) and *donum* (“gift”). A *datum* is what you do not have from yourself; a *donum* is what is not from merit. It is a *datum* while you receive it; a *donum* while through it you merit something further. It is a *datum* while you have it for use; a *donum* while you possess it for fruit.

The rest is missing in the manuscript codex.

## TREATISE VI. On the mysteries of human redemption, written to a friend.

[Col. 0272B]

1. You wrote me a rather brief letter, but, as I think, with a warmly inclined affection. I rejoiced indeed in the favour you show me, but I took little delight in the praise with which you extol me. It belongs to an ingenuous person to blush at praises that he does not recognize as his own. To confess the truth, your judgment concerning me has wandered astray through a friendly kind of credulity; faith, when it is not informed by pious affection, is slower to believe. Hence you easily believed what you embrace with so great a favour.

Three things, accordingly, shine out to me in the countenance of your little letter: first, that you wish to abound toward me; second, that you are restrained with regard to me; third, that you turn away from me, yet are not diminished in yourself. These are affection, faith, and zeal: willing affection, favourable faith, and a pious zeal for learning the word of God. I receive the affection, correct the faith, and urge on the zeal. Increase your love, lessen your favour, and direct your zeal elsewhere. You will find far less in me than you are persuaded exists. Perhaps in speaking with you I shall become a barbarian, though in silence I had been a philosopher.

2. Therefore I commend in you the zeal for learning, but I transfer from myself the office of teaching. “I am not a physician, and there is no bread in my house” (Isa. 3:7). I have nothing by which either to heal the sick or sustain the needy. But you are neither sick nor needy, so as to require that you be healed by our skill or satisfied with our bread. Indeed, you ask neither of these things; rather, you seek—I know not what—drops of a more hidden wisdom, subtle and sweet, delicate and delightful.

Do I seem to you to be one of those mountains that “drop sweetness,” and do you suppose me to be, as it were, one of the mountains made into curds? Would that I were even a hill! For “the hills shall flow with milk.” Although flowing suggests abundance, the word “milk” nevertheless lessens the grace, for milk is for little children. By contrast, distillation appears to signify something small, but unqualified sweetness nourishes us unto immensity. For when something is expressed without qualification, what is expressed but the infinite? It surpasses every sweetness that is defined, by as much as it lacks every limiting determination of property. “The mountains shall drop sweetness, and the hills shall flow with milk” (Joel 3:18).

Milk is sweet, but it is not sweetness. Sweetness, however, is both sweet and sweetness itself, and from it come all things that are sweet, whether differing by kind or excelling by degree. Things sweet through participation in it nevertheless are not sweet in comparison with it. Therefore “sweetness” is not stated as this or that sweetness but simply, so that the immensity of the thing may be inferred from the manner of the word. The prophet understood something exceedingly infinite and inward; wishing to make it known but unable to explain it, he said: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from thee, what thou hast prepared for those awaiting thee” (Isa. 64:4).

3. That immense ocean of divine majesty eludes the narrowness of the human heart and mouth, and scarcely anything from it distils to us through tiny cracks. For how can what is not attained by understanding be enclosed in speech? Though we read that in certain persons the Spirit searches even all the depths of God, it does not follow that it penetrates them. It is not within our leisure or our capacity to reach that inward reality, penetrate the immense, immerse our heads in that abyss of hidden light, and sprinkle you with something from it in drops upon dripping locks—not drops of night, but of light; for, as the prophet says, “the dew of light” is that dew (Isa. 26:19).

Such drops you ask of me: small in quantity, certainly, but excellent in quality; and you ask wisely enough. For you know that almost everywhere in the Scriptures the subtle is preferred to the flowing, the sprinkled to the poured out, the crushed to the substantial. Thus the law of sacrifices commands the blood of animals to be poured out, but that of birds to be dripped. By this blood the altar outside and its base are drenched; but the altar within and the veil are either touched lightly or sprinkled seven times (Lev. 4 and 16). Manna likewise is said to be small (Exod. 16), and incense is reduced to powder, so that whatever you find in Scripture slight or refined you may attribute to spiritual and mystical meanings.

4. These, then, are the things toward which your more ardent thirst burns. It is a good thirst; but would that, as it is written, “the drunken man might take up the thirsty” (Deut. 29:29)—that drunken man who is said to be full of grace and truth; he of whose fullness we have all received (John 1:14, 16); he who is at once drunk and makes others drunk, who is the server and the cup, the vessel and the wine, wine both unmixed and mixed. For Wisdom “has mixed wine in the bowl” (Prov. 9:2).

“O how excellent you are, intoxicating bowl!” Truly excellent: radiant with truth and intoxicating with delight. For in him are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God (Col. 2:3). A good mixture, where grace is mingled with truth, knowledge with wisdom, human things with divine. The things of the Godhead are altogether unmixed, where nothing is joined by parts, subject materially, or affected formally; and therefore there is no diversity in them either simultaneously or successively. Rather, everything that differs among us and through us in name and notion converges and is indiscriminately mingled in one undifferentiated and essential simplicity.

These things, then, are unmixed and simple; but they have been mingled with human things in the unity of person through the mystery of the Incarnation. In Christ Jesus behold how there is unity of person and Trinity of essence: outwardly body, inwardly spirit, in the inmost place God. In him eternity began, immensity grows, power failed, abundance was emptied, wisdom does not know, speech is silent: “He shall not cry,” says the prophet, “nor shall his voice be heard outside” (Isa. 42:2).

5. What is this, good Jesus—what is this which we read: “Wisdom cries aloud outside; in the streets she gives her voice” (Prov. 1:20)? Are you not Wisdom, who came forth from the mouth of the Most High? How then does she cry outside while you do not cry? Your voice is not heard outside, while she gives hers in the streets. Are you not that Wisdom of which the Apostle speaks: “Christ was made for us wisdom from God” (1 Cor. 1:30)? Made for us, indeed, but born in himself; made for us—rather, we are made in him. For we are created in Christ Jesus, both in good works and in devout dispositions. Indeed, both we are in him and he in us. “My little children, whom I travail over again until Christ be formed in you” (Gal. 4:19).

He is formed in us unto life; he is formed unto truth. “I live,” he says, “yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). Why could he not consequently also say: “I am wise, yet not I, but Christ is wise in me”? Everything is in me: in me redemption, in me holiness, in me wisdom. Nothing is wise in me, Lord, except you; but you are not wise in me except as yourself, provided that in you I savour the things above. For glory is in the confusion of those who savour earthly things. Rightly the prophet says: “Let him who glories glory in this: to know and understand thee” (Jer. 9:24).

Since therefore you are Wisdom from God and Wisdom is God—wisdom in yourself and wisdom in us, wisdom known and wisdom knowing, wisdom outside and wisdom within, working outside and breathing within, appearing in the work and opening in the heart—what, I ask, does it mean that Wisdom cries outside while you do not cry? Your voice is not heard outside, while she gives hers in the street. Perhaps you cry through an evident manifestation to the unlearned [*perperis*], but are not yet heard unto full knowledge. You cry outside when you speak to us through indications of what you are; and likewise you do not cry when you remain hidden in truth as what you are in yourself. You cry outside by displaying benefits; and likewise you do not cry by concealing your essence.

Happy is the ear that can perceive the veins of that whisper. They are veins because they are vital, hidden, and closed; and what from them lightly evaporates to us is nearer to a whisper—indeed, to silence—than to a cry.

6. The essence of that majesty is exceedingly wonderful, inward, and subtler than can be comprehended by a gross heart; every created heart is certainly gross for apprehending it. Therefore it is thickened and made dense by a manifold enigma, tempered by a certain mixture of shadows and works, and finally clothed in the garb of the Incarnation, so that it may be more easily apprehended by us, recalled more frequently, held more long, and reconsidered more devoutly.

For everything that concerns Jesus is found, if examined, to be subtle; if observed, useful; pleasant in the mouth, fruitful in action, sweet in meditation—though some things may be somewhat hard in imitation. Even this outward affliction is bedewed and sprinkled with inward grace of heart, so that it is gently harsh, sweetly bitter, rich and dry; as though roasted on the grill of the cross, yet sprinkled with the oil of good hope, as it is written: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12).

Likewise in the Song of Songs: “I drank my wine with my milk” (Song 5:1), where the bride’s breasts are also compared to clusters of grapes (Song 7:7–8). Good is that cluster which was pressed in the winepress of the cross, so that the myrrh-scented and bitter wine of his Passion might grow sweet for us as nourishment of milk, and wounds might pass into breasts. To one who contemplates, they are breasts; to one engaged in action, wines; to one who meditates, sweet things; to one who imitates, somewhat bitter things. In the breasts, by tasting beforehand, we savour the things to come; in the clusters, by a certain intoxication, we lull the motions of the flesh. In the breasts we are planted together unto life; in the clusters we are buried with Christ unto death.

They are breasts to us while, through the merit of the Lord’s Passion and the gift of grace, we hope for eternal goods; they are clusters to us while, through zeal to emulate that same Passion, we separate the mind from the sensations of the flesh. In the breasts we are partly re-formed into what we shall be; in the clusters we are gradually transformed away from what we are, until we are fully conformed to the image for which we were created. “For when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2).

7. For truly now we know in part. Until, then, he fully reveals what he has beneficially withheld from our knowledge, let us devoutly reconsider both the good things he bestowed and the evil things he endured, contemplating not only the Lord’s delights but also his tribulations. There will be a time when delight will occupy everything, and death will be swallowed up in victory. This is what follows: “I will climb the palm tree and grasp its fruits.” Truly one climbs the palm when death, the last enemy, is destroyed. The palm is suited to victorious crowns. “Your stature is like a palm tree” (Song 7:8, 7).

“We stand by faith”; in faith we triumph, for “this is the victory that conquers the world, our faith” (1 John 5:4). Good is the victory that conquers the world; better is that which conquers death. By faith we conquer the world; by faith we conquer death. “You have,” says the Apostle, “your fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6:22); for “this is eternal life, that we may know the true God” (John 17:3). Thus knowledge is the end and faith the beginning; in faith we stand, and at the end we ascend. In faith we stand always upright and firm, neither bent by this world’s flatteries nor broken by its threats; in faith we ascend, stripped of burdensome corruptibility, neither needing the world’s service nor suffering its punishment.

8. Nor should the distinction be passed over: first it is said that the stature is likened to the palm, while later it is said that one climbs into the palm. In the latter expression likeness is not suggested but union expressed. For “he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6:17); and he is wholly spirit, suffused and infused with spiritual light and joy, losing himself altogether and grasping him alone. He does not lose himself through medicinal affliction, as in: “He who loses his life for my sake shall find it” (Matt. 10:38); but in a happier manner: neither vainly stretched beyond and below himself through curiosity, nor distracted around himself through necessary anxiety, nor content within himself by private enjoyment.

There, occupied and absorbed by divine contemplations, the mind is calmed with the most perfect security, irradiated with serenity, and intoxicated with sweetness: security without danger, serenity without cloud, sweetness with ineffable rejoicing.

9. But these things belong to those who, already weaned from milk, feast from the threshold of glory: “These things are too high for us; we cannot attain them.” Therefore, excluded from these feasts, let us return to the breasts—from the feasts of contemplation to the breasts of consolation, to breasts and to clusters; from that unmixed and festal simplicity to this tempered cup, which Wisdom mixed for us in that bowl “in whom dwells all the fullness of divinity” (Col. 2:9). Of this it is also said: “Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups” (Song 7:2).

Let, therefore, the navel of your soul be like a rounded bowl, thinned and polished by a certain iron of discipline and correction, made subtle and capacious, so that you may be abundantly filled and made drunk, and so that this may deservedly fit you: “Your navel is a rounded bowl, never lacking cups.” Thus it is said also to the fornicating woman: “Your navel was not cut on the day of your birth” (Ezek. 16:4). How many today cut the navel on the day of their birth and in the first season of conversion, only to draw on a foreskin afterwards—beginning in the Spirit but being completed in the flesh! Let your navel, then, be not merely cut but circumcised and rounded with enduring regularity, so that, with every corruption—indeed, every grossness—removed, it may overflow continually with the spiritual cup like a well of living waters, and henceforth you may not come here to draw water.

## TREATISE VII. TO ROGER, ABBOT.

This treatise has two parts. In the first he rebukes the ambitious and presumptuous; in the second he commends Roger for the gifts fitting him for prelacy and exhorts him to persevere.

### PART ONE.

1. You ask, my Roger, to be persuaded that you ought to retain what you hold, and that, by our arguments, the fear attending a dangerous authority should be mitigated. You certainly bid me add oil to the fire (Horace, *Satires* II.iii.321), and, on the occasion of yourself alone, to inflame with the breath of my discourse the desires of many which are already kindled of themselves. But why do I say “with breath”? A light breath, as it is written, will make coals of this sort burn (Job 41:12). Whoever speaks in this matter will be accounted eloquent enough, and will persuade easily: toward that end almost everyone’s heart is irrevocably set; we all readily persuade one another of anything suitable to it. But when one comes to what is fitting, there is the labour, and words must be poured out in vain. Indeed the prophet reproaches and mocks this very thing in himself: “Speak pleasant things to us; show us errors; do not speak what is right” (Isa. 30:10). It is a good cause that itself performs the part of an orator, and without the assistance of art attracts and softens its hearers’ minds.

This persuasion will be superfluous and seeks nothing else than to make the covetous wicked and to remove the slight barrier of shame, which alone seems to stand in ambition’s way and confines its boiling impulses, like the waters of the sea, in the vessel of the heart. This would be to open not a window but a door, and to bring the vents of bellows to an already kindled furnace. Ambition is a sufficiently luxuriant shrub; and man, as though in rich soil, does not so much bear fruit as run to excess.

2. This is the root of bitterness which, springing upward, hinders; through it many are defiled, and it cannot be uprooted. And do you ask that it be watered? The renewed plantation shoots up in the hands of those who wish it, and do you request that it be cultivated by a certain carefulness of exhortations? For though this perverse root dies in you, it springs up all around you; and though a word of exhortation addressed to you might be useful, it may perhaps fall ruinously upon others. This plantation is everywhere, like tamarisks in the wilderness. Nor do I know where it grows more luxuriantly than in a land of drought and salt.

Look at those whose skin is dried up, whose faces are pale from fasts, whose hard-working hands are covered with callus; who withdraw and remain in solitude, who devote themselves to sackcloth, and whose skin is foul with dirt. Look, I say, whether the roots of ambition do not grow abundantly precisely in the land of their squalor and solitude. Indeed, among the life-giving trees and pleasant shoots of paradise, where man had no folds of garments in which to hide his sins, a perverse offshoot sprang forth in the best soil. For God created all things very good.

3. But why do I rehearse paradise? That heavenly solitude and those angelic mountains, surpassingly deserted in respect of human condition and manner of life, proved in some degree unhappily fertile for this aforesaid shoot. Their fall bears witness to the perverse ascent which they were preparing. Hear what their prince says: “I will set my throne above the stars of heaven; I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High.” He said this not with his voice but with his desire; not, “Among the stars,” he says, “and among the clouds,” but, “Above the stars and above the height of the clouds.”

Thus, though he was created among the morning stars and was one of the sons of God, not content with the lot of the others, he wished alone to possess by inheritance the sanctuary of God and to sit on the mountain of the covenant, in the dignity of inheritance; for inheritance is conferred by a testament of paternal right: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant.” Where does wicked rashness rush headlong? What do you usurp for yourself that belongs to the Only-begotten? He himself is Son, he himself is only-begotten, he himself is the image of the invisible God, the radiance of glory and the imprint of substance—and do you say, “I will be like the Most High”? If you will be like him, then you are not yet so; but the Only-begotten always is, and is equal in likeness. In this he is not adopted but begotten; and he did not receive the rights of paternal authority through grace, but possesses them by nature.

The covenant of the divine essence is firm, immovable, and eternal: an undifferentiated unity. And do you presume for yourself the mountain of the covenant? “I will ascend above the stars and above the height of the clouds.” It should have been enough for rashness to extend itself thus far: not to be content with fellowship with the others. Here you might have set the limit of pride and fixed the step of ascent. “I will be like the Most High.” You rise above the height of the clouds and compare yourself to the Most High? You set yourself over creatures made with you [perhaps: “you presume to rule them”], and compare yourself with the Creator? These are disordered steps; you have usurped an undue step. Therefore you were cast down from your rank and your station; “your pride was brought down to hell” (Isa. 14:11–15).

The Lord planted you as a chosen vine, all true seed (Isa. 5:1–2; Jer. 2:21); but on the very day of your planting you became a wild vine, and before harvest you were wholly in bloom. Truly you bloomed: your flowers were emptied out and were not preserved for harvest, were not brought to maturity; but, as follows, “an unripe perfection sprouted” (Isa. 18:5). Therefore your little branches were cut off—sterile and fruitless branches, cut off by the sickles of the divine sentence. And you yourself, according to the taunt of the same prophet, were cast out from your place of rest and glory “like a useless shoot” (Isa. 14:19); and your dwelling became amid deceit and amid pain.

The shoot of pride could spring up in paradise, but it could not endure. For every plant which the heavenly Father has not planted shall be rooted up (Matt. 15:13). You wished to plant yourself in an improper place; therefore, like a bastard plantation, you did not put down a deep root. Indeed, “no one takes honour to himself, but he who is called by God”; but you assumed what was not due, and therefore consumed what had been given.

[Col. 0278C]

4. Alas for me! How no place is safe from this shrub, no region exempt! This root, the root of covetousness, grows and bears fruit almost everywhere, occupying the face of the earth and, as though remembering where it first arose, especially among those who bear the image of the heavenly one. When, Lord, will you uproot this faithless plantation, this alien shoot? When will that spoken through the prophet be fulfilled: “The vineyard of Sabama has been made desolate; the lords of the nations have cut down its shoots” (Isa. 16:8)?

*Sabama* is said to mean “lifting up height.” What is lifting up height except magnifying one’s merits? “I am not,” says the Pharisee, “like the rest of men” (Luke 18:11). Christ taught us otherwise: “When,” he says, “you have done all things, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17:10). He taught me not to raise high the greatness of virtues and works, but to diminish it; he taught and acted, as it is written: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1:1). For though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself and became like the rest of men. He bent down his height, and do you raise yours?

What then is understood by the vineyard of Sabama but the drunken disposition of the mind: the disposition raising itself against the mind of God; the disposition of which the Apostle says, “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus,” etc. (Phil. 2:6–7, 5); and again, “Do not set your minds on high things, but agree with the lowly” (Rom. 12:16)? Hear a mind thinking lofty things, exalting itself, and vanishing like smoke in its own thought: “I will visit,” says the Lord, “the fruit of the proud heart of the king of Assyria, and the height of his eyes. For he said: ‘By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom I have understood’” (Isa. 10:10, 12–13). And elsewhere: “Is not this great Babylon which I myself have made?” (Dan. 4:27).

5. You have heard the mind—the proud mind exalting itself; you have understood what the vineyard of Sabama is: a vineyard which I wish were desolate and had no cultivator. Now hear the Apostle; hear the lord and teacher of the nations: “The lords of the nations have cut down its shoots.” Hear how he himself cuts down the shoots of Sabama: “Do not think high things, but fear” (Rom. 11:20). “Command the rich not to think proudly” (1 Tim. 6:17).

“They cut down the shoots,” he says; they could not cut down the root. They cut down what stood out; they could not cut down what was hidden. Covetousness itself is the root; honour and exalted rank are the shoot. Desire is like the root; worldly concerns are like the shoots. Observe how pointedly he speaks. We consider high positions delights; the prophet calls them lashes. Truly they lash and strip the mind’s skin; they wound its tenderness and the affection fixed upon Christ. Thoroughly unhappy is one who has become so hardened in outward things that he does not feel these to be lashes, but joys: “They struck me, and I did not feel it” (Prov. 23:35).

The vineyard of Sabama was made desolate. Truly it was made desolate by our fathers, who knew how to cultivate not possessions but piety, to attend not to things but to religion. O times! O manners! Now almost all cultivate within themselves the mind of the world; they rejoice in possessing the spirit of this world, the wisdom of this world—which is foolishness before God, which does not know, indeed cannot be subject to, the law of God. For covetousness cannot serve charity; it does not know how to bear others’ burdens, but rather to impose its own upon others.

They are most eager gatherers and most sparing distributors, so that Saul may truly be seen in them as born from Cis. For *Cis* means “hard,” and *Saul* “request”: that is, avidity from avarice, wickedness from parsimony. The north wind is hard; by it waters are frozen. The south wind is gentle; at its breath the spices of mercy and charity flow. Cis is a hard father; gentle is he of whom Jesus Christ says: “That you may be children of your Father, who makes his sun rise upon good and evil” (Matt. 5:45).

6. How unlike are their judgments of things in buying and conducting business—not works, but merchandise! How cleverly they bring forth double weights from the purse of their mouth! They seem born and educated not in monastic life but in the marketplace. They abound in this kind of understanding, while knowing Christ scantily, thinly, and dryly. Therefore the prophet says: “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? And he grew up as a little shoot before him, and as a root from thirsty ground” (Isa. 53:1–2). Nothing strong, nothing lofty, but weak and humble; beyond the root of simple faith, they scarcely touch anything of higher and divine wisdom.

Paul says: “Bearing fruit and increasing in the knowledge of God” (Col. 1:10). These men, on the contrary, not content with their own ignorance, despise the learning of others; as jealous judges, they interpret the pursuit of wisdom as folly and blacken sober subtlety with the charge of madness or ostentation. They themselves work for food that perishes, not for that which remains unto eternal life. And if they should return home from the field, they are indignant at the music and dancing, and snarl at the joys of the younger brother (Luke 15:25–32).

That younger brother is good, of whom the Apostle says: “Put on the new man, who according to God has been created” (Eph. 4:24). The younger brother is good, of whom he likewise says: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away, and all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17). Foolish is that elder brother, who knows labour but does not know joy. He is rightly the elder, who persists in oldness and cares for the things of the old man; who makes provision for the flesh, if not in indulgences, then at least in desires—desires for possessing abundantly, even if not for using intemperately. “Those who wish,” he says, “not to become luxurious, but to become rich, fall into many useless and harmful desires” (1 Tim. 6:9). Desire is useless and harmful where, even if necessity is the issue, excess is in the concern.

The burning thirst to possess is evil. This, therefore, is the thirsty land from which the root of piety and faith rises weakly and humbly, scarcely lifting itself a little from the depths. It cannot but languish where worldly desires run riot and vain branches spread out. Happy is the person who has cut these away from himself, in whom the vineyard of Sabama has been left desolate and neglected: that vineyard, namely, which raises its own height, raising the height of conversion to the rank of prelacy. For Sabama is also said to mean “some conversion”; for those who seem to have reached, even in some degree, the beginnings of conversion—these, I say, are especially tossed by the wind of ambition, as by the highest shoots.

This plantation luxuriates enough by itself; it arises where it is not sown and comes up while it is being cut down. Therefore it needs not to be planted but pruned; not cultivated but cut down.

7. But let these things now suffice for showing why it is not expedient, on account of others, to give the exhortation which you request. Yet since we have already said something about ambition, it will be appropriate not to pass wholly over presumption in silence. We have partly refuted those who are borne upward by private covetousness; let us confound—or rather admonish—also those who boast that they are held fast by the pretext of fraternal necessity. Their heavy occupation is indeed praiseworthy, and rest is pleasing; yet they are moved by an empty—indeed insolent and swollen—fear, if they should leave the rank of leadership, that no one may remain to whom they can rightly entrust it.

They are wise in their own eyes and prudent before themselves; not content with this degree of vanity, they think themselves, with Elijah, left alone (1 Kings 18:22; 19:10). They regard themselves as a Moses, but above Moses. For he says, “Lord, provide another whom you may send” (Exod. 4:13); these say, “There is no other, Lord, whom you may send.” Isaiah says: “A man will lay hold of his brother, one of his father’s household: ‘You have a garment; be our ruler.’” What does he answer? “I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor garment. Do not appoint me ruler” (Isa. 3:6–7).

As though he said: It is not enough that I have a garment, unless I have abundance so as to share it with others. It is not enough, in order that I may hold rule, to possess the garment of discipline, the garment of outward conduct and observance—to have the outward man composed, which I use like a garment in every act and gesture. For it is not enough for me, much less enough for others. What is commended in me is too slight; greater things must be sought. It is too little that I myself am sound unless I can heal others also. Therefore he says: “Do not appoint me ruler; I am not a physician, and in my house there is neither bread nor garment.”

“I am not a physician”; but this man says, “I alone am a physician.” Wherever he looks about, he meets incompetence, impurity, deceit, or negligence, so that he may be the sole prudent and faithful servant. And therefore he says in his thought: “Do not appoint another ruler, lest perhaps a child be made ruler and effeminate persons rule.” Such men do not need the persuasion you request. Though they do not delight in a higher rank, they nevertheless console themselves with the gains of their labours; they answer toil with the desire for rest and peace, yet on the other hand rejoice in the rich fruits of their works.

Here I shorten a discourse that was running on, because you are already drawn to other things—or perhaps, as commonly happens, distracted by many things.

## Second Part of the Treatise

Roger is commended as furnished with gifts suited to prelacy and is commanded to persevere; first, however, the difficulties and burdens of prelacy are set forth.

1. In the preceding discourse we undertook to restrain the presumptuous together with the ambitious; in this one, to encourage those who are more fearful than is right. Good God, what an interval has intervened between this and that! What a violent storm of secular accusations has knocked the pen from my fingers and carried both hand and mind far away from the subject! Truly I have come into the depth of the sea, and the tempest has overwhelmed me. When, good Jesus, will you save me from the storm? If not yet from the storm, at least from faintness of spirit?

The storm grows and increases on every side, and I am weak in spirit and narrow in heart. Nor can I calm the assaults of whirlwinds and the fury of winds by the breeze of meditation. I cannot mingle spiritual joy in the cup of my heart amid forensic disputes. “The bed is narrowed,” as the prophet says, “so that one falls off; and the covering is too short to cover both” (Isa. 28:20). Holy Jacob alternated the embraces of his wives; and, unable to hold both at once, he passed with difficulty from one woman’s chamber into the rights of the other. Happy, indeed, in his own judgment, if he had yielded wholly to the possession of Rachel alone.

Our mind might have grown callous, worn by frequent injury and rendered harder against adversities by usage itself. And indeed it is often covered with callus and hardened by adverse things pressing upon it. O how often I consider myself firm to endure the storms of the world! There is now no reason why I should wish to hide myself or, as it is written, “hide myself from the wind and conceal myself from the tempest” (Isa. 32:2). But whenever the mind grows soft amid Rachel’s tender embraces, I am immediately restored to my accustomed tenderness and made untrained and unaccustomed to bearing tribulations. Indeed, I judge nothing better than humbly to avoid by a change of place the injuries that rush upon us, and to enter the caves of the rocks from the face of this terror.

2. Woe to those who are pregnant and nursing, especially in these days! Blessed indeed are breasts which have not given milk. For one who needs the nourishment of milk is a little child and has a mind too weak to bear poverty and the plundering of goods. Such are those on whose behalf quarrels must be undertaken, councils attended, rulers flattered, plunderers repelled, litigants answered, judges bought off, and those who lived with Paul in heaven conformed to the world.

There were times when we were accustomed to suck the milk of nations and to be nursed at the breast of kings; and now they urgently demand back what perhaps we sucked somewhat too intemperately. But while they press dry breasts more violently and, along with the milk of temporal goods, draw out their subjects’ blood—not the blood of the flesh, but that blood of the soul, that vital and inward blood which is contained in the spiritual veins of the mind, that blood of which the prophet says, “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, his holy name” (Ps. 103:1)—that blood, I say, they absorb and drink up by excessive disturbance.

Alas, how all things change by turns! In war we have peace; in peace, war. In peace there is most bitter bitterness—but for us who are bound to the affairs of the world, whom that Egyptian cloak of prelacy holds wrapped up, and whom the necessity of providing for others binds; who are still animal persons, to whom the Apostle says: “Let every soul be subject to higher powers” (Rom. 13:1). But “the spiritual person judges all things and is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2:15).

3. But to what end is this? Is it so that you may leave in the hand of the office you have undertaken the Egyptian cloak? Leave it, I say, and flee from it with Joseph as from something dangerous (Gen. 39:12); or lay it aside with David as something burdensome (2 Sam. 6:14–20). Indeed, so that he might often give himself freely to leaping, he stripped off and laid aside the cloak in which he was covered. For the body has enough burden in its own sluggishness, and its own weight sufficiently weighs it down.

Do I then wish you also to strip yourself of the covering of your office? But that would be contrary to my purpose. For I have undertaken to persuade you not to cast aside the pastoral burden, which you both assumed rightly and administer with sound judgment. Since you accepted it with little inclination, you are always willing to remove it, whether through fear of danger or under the pretext of rest. Yet for one so disposed there was reason to fear that, while the mind wavered in a kind of suspense, some negligence might creep into the administration. But how shall I try to persuade you of what I have almost persuaded myself against? The case is very different. I, an unskilled workman, find it difficult to labour over difficult material; with you, all things concur according to desire and answer according to expectation.

4. You cannot conceal what the evidence of things cries aloud. If you look to outward matters, they are both ample and secure: no poverty constrains you in them; nor does even injury disturb you. The place is secluded, planted, watered, fertile; and in springtime the wooded valley echoes with the sweet song of birds, so that it can revive a deadened spirit, wipe away the weariness of a delicate mind, and soften the hardness of a mind without devotion.

Indeed, these things either portray for you pledges of future delight or present some remaining traces of that first delight which the integrity of human nature enjoyed among the pleasant places of paradise. But you will say that no merit of virtue is placed in such things. I cannot deny it, since they are means; but although they are nothing for acquiring merit, they are by no means unhelpful for bestowing rest.

Nor do we so differ from the ancients, who handed down to us the experiments of their manner of life, whose authority is more ancient and whose purity greater, that we proclaim as instruments of virtue what they judged obstacles to perfection. They defined fertile and pleasant places as impediments for a stronger mind; we may call them a support for the weaker person, for one who cannot yet say: “My soul refused to be comforted; I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. 76:3–4); “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” (Phil. 4:13).

The ancient fathers sought terrible, dry places, so that they might have material for practicing abstinence and might have no reason for stretching out their minds in cares. They devoted themselves more freely to bodily labour in order both to possess freedom of heart and to avoid the restless lightness of roaming about, together with the wickedness of acquisition. In short, they sustained life more by the craft of their hands than by tilling fields, lightening the straits of a small—indeed almost nonexistent—substance by the gain of peace; for they were content with little, whether for afflicting the body or refreshing the mind.

For the heart is anxiously and miserably stretched and distracted when it is burdened by the necessity of providing much and providing far ahead. They served their own age; let us serve ours. This age of ours, declining for the worse, has introduced other habits. Abundance must now be provided for residents and delicacies for visitors. Nor do I mean by “visitors” secular persons—for what have I to do with judging those who are outside? Although even among them the customary strictness is not maintained, they endure poverty with difficulty where they reckon every kind of abundance to be available. But why mention those whose god is their belly? (Phil. 3:19.) The very professors and preachers of abstinence, the very leaders of the Order—how fastidious they are in others’ houses! How exquisitely and elaborately prepared are the dishes they artfully demand! How they draw their brows together, wrinkle their nostrils, and turn away their eyes if anything less elegant or festive is served!

5. But since the wickedness of this time is so constituted, your resources suffice for both purposes: they can serve display and use alike, the need of the poor and the vanity of the rich. What follows? What colleagues have you in office: how energetic, industrious, attentive, and—what is first—faithful! It is scarcely necessary that the entire burden of administering outward property be brought to you. You almost never leave the tabernacle of the Lord. In councils, gatherings, and the chief places of the streets, where the stones of the sanctuary are now scattered—though yours are occasionally among them—you are very rarely seen. This is a great sign that disturbance does not please you and that the necessity of going abroad is remote.

Neither your hand, nor your eye, nor your foot causes you to stumble; otherwise, however painful it might be, the member ought rather to be cut off and separated from the head than the head from the body. Therefore you have in these matters no ground for abandoning your office. Perhaps I seem unfair and to offer consolations too soft, unworthy of a learned and practiced mind. For what if poverty presses, or injuries, accusations, shortage of private—indeed common—resources, or even the plundering of that shortage; what if danger breaks forth at one’s side among false brethren? Must a strong and faithful man succumb? Must he yield his place and, contrary to Paul’s admonition, abandon the assembly? (Heb. 10:25.) Rather, it must be held and guarded all the more as the day threatening it becomes more dangerous.

Indeed, you have passed through almost all these kinds of trials. You who have run amid hardships—will your steps be poured out upon level ground? Or you who learned to lack—will you not know how to abound, hungry with Paul, but [supplied: “not knowing how”] to be filled with Paul? (Phil. 4:12). In both conditions you have furnished proofs of a mind well trained, pursuing the undertaken course of life with the unbroken thread of an uninterrupted tenor. But I have passed over these stronger grounds and wished to proceed by a middle way, recalling those things that removed from you causes of disturbance; for we have always heard that, in the deepest poverty, you rested quietly, relying more on faith and labour than on shameful begging or disgraceful trading.

6. But since we have said much about the ease of administration, it follows that we should not pass over skill in administering. Shall I call it skill or grace? Rather, both skill and grace. Even the most suitable material will be useless in the hands of an unskilled craftsman; skill itself, moreover, will be either harmful or ineffective if it lacks directing grace. For “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labour in vain” (Ps. 127:1).

Perhaps you will conceal the gifts bestowed upon you; but what humility conceals, usefulness proclaims. Why should I now mention estates, money, vessels, garments, buildings, people—people—and all things, both produced and increased under your hand, whether outward goods or matters of religious life, from the time when the Lord bound you to plough in his place and to break after him the clods of the valleys? How great a harvest of pious souls has arisen! How your valleys abound with grain—the grain of which it is said: “What is his goodness, or what is his beauty, except the chosen grain and wine causing virgins to spring up?” (Zech. 9:17).

You cannot administer without grace what has thus increased through you in glory. Glorious things have indeed been accomplished in your city, but through your hand. For whereas it was abandoned and held in contempt, and there was no one who passed by it, behold how it has been made into the pride of ages—though shaken by poverty and storm, without any consolation. How now have your stones been laid in order, and how have you been founded upon sapphires? If founded upon sapphires, in what have you been completed? “You have been founded upon sapphires.”

Foundation denotes humility; sapphire, purity: humility of conscience and purity of knowledge; humility of conduct and purity of contemplation. You have been founded, I say, upon sapphires. Therefore it is said: “Your Nazarites were whiter than snow, brighter than milk, more ruddy than ancient ivory, more beautiful than sapphires” (Lam. 4:7). In the first, they are contrite; in the second, nourished; in the third, strengthened; in the fourth, purified. In the first, penitents; in the second, innocent; in the third, lovers; in the fourth, contemplatives. In the first, mortified; in the second, made alive; in the third, inflamed; in the fourth, illuminated. And all this because you have been founded upon sapphires.

You yourself perform the office of a foundation through example and providence; you show yourself a sapphire through word and wisdom. Indeed, your voice is sweet and your face beautiful: the voice of teaching and the face of example; the voice of preaching and the face of conduct. Therefore the young women love you exceedingly. If you should depart, to whom else could they say: “Show us your face; let your voice sound in our ears”? Upon whose examples could they rely and whose judgments could they attend to? Who is like you, to call, proclaim, and expound the Order? What other such foundation could be laid as that which has been laid, Abbot Roger?

“Your sons are like new plantations; your daughters adorned and arranged like the likeness of a temple; your storehouses are full; your sheep fruitful, abundant in their offspring.” How shall we not call blessed, how shall we not call holy, the man to whom these things belong? How shall we not call the Lord his God whose riches are such? (Ps. 143:12–15).

7. These, therefore, are the things which give manifest signs that the Lord has chosen you in your ministry and has not rejected you. They persuade you to retain what you retain so profitably. When you console yourself in the consciousness of such great works, in what respect will our persuasion appear necessary to you? Your domestic virtues persuade you to retain the office, lest another take the place; your own familiar industry persuades you, as does another’s negligence; prosperous success, and a bad successor.

I know your mind, I know your pursuits, I know your habits, whether bestowed by nature or acquired by effort. I know how readily you would be free of this burden if someone were found to whom you could worthily confer it. Affection and reason contend with each other: the affection of humility and the reason of usefulness. You would count it welcome to be free for yourself and for God; but likewise grievous to leave your place empty. Empty indeed: for who will fill it? Who will give us another Jacob, who crossed the Jordan with his staff and now returns with many companies? (Gen. 32:10.)

Who, I ask, will provide us such a man, who knows how to move with moderation between Leah and Rachel, compensating the one’s ugliness by fruitfulness and covering the other’s barrenness with the grace of beautiful appearance? (Gen. 29.) There is none like you: one so caught up in contemplation as not to become remiss in action; one who does not abandon the business of providence for the leisure of wisdom; one who, under the pretext of usefulness, does not pass into the claims of idleness; one who does not commend Leah in such a way as to condemn—or even despise—Rachel; for whom Leah is not barren and Rachel not ugly.

You are one who is scorched by heat in the day and frost at night, anxious lest the flock suffer loss; more anxious, if any loss occurs, to restore it from your own resources—restoring it with tears, fasts, compassion, prayer, and exhortation. In your return you know no idols of avarice. Even if you have them in your company, you do not have them in worship; if you have them among your baggage, you do not have them among sacred things. You serve piety, not money, though it is written, “All things obey money” (Eccl. 10:19). Indeed, “avarice is the service of idols” (Col. 3:5).

You know neither avarice in outward occupation nor the bodily images—which are, as it were, idols—of eternal forms in contemplation; rather, in both respects your intention and perception are pure and prudent. You will see many people with tender affection toward God, a noble countenance, and a face pure and beautiful like Rachel, whether in conduct or thought; yet with counsel still weak and womanish, needing to be governed by the will of another Jacob. Indeed, when Rachel did not refer her actions to Jacob, she secretly stole her father Laban’s idols (Gen. 31:19). She took, I say, Laban’s idols: certain images of worldly respectability, worldly favour, worldly whitening. For *Laban* means “whitening.”

[Col. 0286C]

8. Do there not seem to you to be certain persons who have carried Laban’s idols on the journey, together with images of secular vanity—those who introduce into religious life certain superfluous refinements, I know not what; who temper the rules of ancient observance with novel dispensations and mix their wine with water; who transfer the laborious vineyard of the Fathers into soft gardens of vegetables and the austerity of monks into the delights of the world? For just as it is written, “whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19), so it may likewise be said: whose god is vanity. And so with each particular form of secular whitening and pleasure.

How greatly I fear that, returning from Mesopotamia of Syria, we carry with us many idols of this kind, no longer secretly but openly; not with Jacob unaware, but plainly consenting. Rachel carried off certain idols of her father, which she eagerly took and cautiously covered, holding them with a womanly and soft affection, veiling and excusing them under the pretext of weakness. But what Laban worshipped, Rachel concealed, and Jacob did not know (Gen. 31:34, 32): what was held in honour with Laban, in affection with Rachel, was, once known, held in horror by Jacob. Therefore, what he worshipped openly, she concealed temporarily in danger; Jacob buried forever. He buried them, I say, and dug down the foreign gods beneath the terebinth tree (Gen. 35:4): beneath the tree of faith, the remembrance of vain ambition and secular display.

9. Finally, after temptation, it is said to the faithful soul in the promise: “It shall be in manifestation like a terebinth, and like an oak that spreads out its branches” (Isa. 6:13)—beneath the terebinth which is beyond the city of the Shechemites (Gen. 35:4). *Sichima* means “shoulders.” Good are those shoulders of which it is written: “The hind part of his back is in the brightness of gold” (Ps. 67:14). Good is the shoulder of Christ Jesus: “For government has been made upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9:6). Beyond this Sichima the terebinth is set; it is planted in Christ’s passion and faith.

Happy is one who, in this tree, triumphs over all principalities and powers and buries beneath its root every image of vanity; for “their image is wind and emptiness” (Isa. 41:29). Thus the pomp of the world is rightly compared to images. This is not the work of a weak, womanly, fragile soul, but of a wrestler and supplanter. It belongs not to Rachel but to Jacob. For though there are many Rachels, there are not many Jacobs. Rare is the person who knows how to supplant Esau, deceive Laban, and bury his gods: to bury, I say, and put to death the old man, the image of the world, conformity to this age, so that he may no longer be conformed to this age but be reformed in the newness of a devout mind, made planted together with the likeness of Christ’s death so that he may likewise share in his resurrection.

For this is to condemn, erase, and bury Laban’s idols: that the image of the old and earthly man which we have borne may be made hidden away, and that of the new and heavenly man made manifest, like the terebinth.

10. I make these distinctions so carefully precisely lest perhaps the man be put under authority and the woman set over him; lest the strong man be idle and the frail woman conduct affairs; lest Jacob depart and Rachel succeed him. Yet these recent arrivals, who have begun to emerge in our times—well arranged, polished, and whitewashed, a certain progeny of Laban, who is called “Whitewashed”—do not even equal Rachel in modesty in this respect: she covered and excused the form of worldly vanity’s weakness with a veil; but they paint over and cloak the business of worldliness and excess with a color of humanity, not purging out the old leaven, but rather displaying to strangers festive preparations of food and a lavish, commendable array of banquets. It would take long if I wished to run through the many kinds of vanity and weave a catalogue of boastfulness. These are the men whom you see as swaggerers in manner, tavern-keepers at feasts, parasites in abuse; these are they who wish to appear Catos in chapters, Ciceros in lawsuits, Virgils in verse; in short, in conversation they are actors, not monks. They flow copiously with the witty salts of words—not with that salt of which the Apostle says, “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt” (Col. 4:6), but rather with that of which the Lord says, “But if salt has become tasteless and lost its savour, with what shall it be salted?” (Matt. 5:13).

11. Therefore, on account of such men, it seems to me that you should be carefully retained and not replaced; and so should any others in whom traces of the ancient, as they call it, rusticity remain. Otherwise, if we cast away good salt, we may receive what is tasteless, and that prophetic saying may come to pass: “In drought its harvests shall be broken; women shall come and teach it” (Isa. 27:11). I could ascribe to you individually the Patriarch’s virtues, and, in praise, draw out a fuller likeness in the name Jacob; but I refrain, lest, while I bless my friend in a loud voice, I seem like one who curses. Yet you, unless I know you altogether wrongly, though you ponder these things with yourself from time to time, do not credit them to yourself. Let this suffice, then, concerning the ease of administration, the abundance of graces, and the scarcity of persons fit to replace you. What if you can both easily and suitably perform the office entrusted to you—and I do not know whether any modern man performs it more suitably? I now see nothing that hinders, unless perhaps in a lower rank you promise yourself a more abundant grace of merits: to yourself indeed, but not to others; to yourself, but not to Christ’s Church, and therefore not even to yourself. For Christ cannot compensate in you alone what he would lose in many. But if this seems right, let us reserve it for another time: for now we have buried our dear one, and our discourse must change to our psalms.

## SERMON ON THE SEED OF THE WORD OF GOD

1. To misuse among you the Apostle’s words which you have just heard: “You gladly tolerate a fool, being yourselves wise” (2 Cor. 11:19). Paul said this as a reproach; I say it as praise. I commend your eagerness, and I commend your humility: for you ardently desire to hear the word of God, and you deign reverently to hear it from me, though I am little suited to this task. Thus, as it is written, although you yourselves are drunk, you nevertheless receive one who is thirsty (Deut. 29:19). Therefore I said, “You gladly tolerate a fool, being yourselves wise”: though in truth you do not so much tolerate me as force a word from me. From you I have received the command; from you the subject-matter—as though I could find veins of living water in every soil and sow beside all waters, and as though words might flow forth to my desire at a moment’s notice. Would that it might then be done to me according to your faith; would that all my limbs might be loosened into a tongue, and that with the prophet I might say: “All my bones shall say, Lord, who is like unto thee?” (Ps. 34:10).

2. Yet I shall strive as far as the occasion permits, and I shall not restrain my lips. Only take care lest the word of the Lord return empty to me—or rather, to himself. For it will not return empty, provided that it does not fall beside the way, upon the rock, or among thorns (Matt. 13:3–8, 18–23). Guard yourselves, I say, against these: against ways, rocks, and thorns. The cause of the first hindrance is the enemy’s cunning; of the second, the doubleness of our heart; of the third, the multiplicity of cares. In the first, we guard ourselves unwisely; in the second, we cultivate ourselves sluggishly; in the third, we take excessive care of what belongs to others. In the first, we resist feebly; in the second, we abandon what we began; in the third, we apply ourselves anxiously to superfluous matters. In the first, our thought is soft; in the second, unstable; in the third, burdensome. Indeed, in this third it is at once soft, unstable, and burdensome: soft in pleasures, unstable in passing riches and possessions, burdensome in anxious and troubled desires. For the cares and desires for transient things are anxious and troublesome, since their acquisition is difficult, their passing swift, and their fruit empty—not to say dishonourable.

[Col. 0289]

## LETTERS OF THE SAME GILLEBERT

### LETTER I. TO BROTHER RICHARD

He commends Richard, apparently offended by a rebuke or by some sharper word, but now reconciled once more.

[Col. 0289A]

1. You make use, my Richard, of a proverb as true as it is old: “Everything should be deliberated with a friend, but concerning the friend himself first.” “Do not trust a friend,” says the prophet, “and put no confidence in a leader. From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth” (Mic. 7:5). Pretended friendships bring true ones under suspicion, and the rarity of this virtue causes its reality to be doubted. Happy is he who does not err in either direction: showing himself prudent in forming friendships, yet not excessive in his caution. For it is useless to entrust seeds to sand; much more wretched not to sow at all, while looking to winds and clouds. We are anxious proprietors in the most worthless matters; in the most precious kind of possession—I mean friendships—we are altogether useless. Who is there, almost, that will raise up a friend when he falls, when everyone props up a house that is collapsing? I have said these things so that the rarity of this virtue itself may commend it to you, and that it may stand out more clearly when contrasted with the multitude of those who neglect it.

2. Having considered the face of your letter, I immediately recalled that philosophical saying: “Even after a bad crop, one must sow” (Seneca, *Letters to Lucilius*). You seem to burn with such eagerness for the commerce of friendships that, where a little while ago you suffered shipwreck, you repair it by embarking again. Quite prudently: perhaps the happier outcome of a single hour will compensate for the disadvantages of a long time. And, to introduce something from our domestic philosophy, I experience in you that apostolic saying: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8). You rebuke the error of a friend with such modesty that you seem to offer pardon rather than press a complaint. In short, you gnaw at me with such friendly sharpness that I feel myself gently rubbed with that salt which may not be absent from the Lord’s sacrifices (Lev. 2:13). You have flown to me as one of the Seraphim, ablaze and wholly fiery; and with the burning coal which you took from the altar, you cleanse the lapse of my lips (Isa. 6:6–7). The graver my fault, the more welcome the rebuke. I find you truly other than I had supposed. At last you have given me some taste of your prudence, for a wise man is recognized in patience (Prov. 19:11). I admire and revere your patience. You overlook injuries; you restore to favour one who provokes you; you smooth down one who exasperates you, and reward one undeserving—indeed, one ill-deserving.

Your gifts are welcome gifts to me: welcome because of their giver and welcome in their use. They both make you present to me and instruct me. The gifts of a wise man do not know how to be mute. For what do you signify to me by the staff, except that I should be upright and firm, lest I be of reed-like flexibility and fragility, according to that saying of the prophet: “Egypt is a broken reed for a staff; whoever leans on it will have his hand pierced” (4 Kings 18:21; Isa. 36:6). Such you found me; and the splinters of my brokenness could have made your hands bloody—except that your hands are stronger and blunt the opposing points. Blessed hands, which do not know how to break a bruised reed but rather consider [perhaps: strengthen] it, nor to quench smoking flax. “Those who work flax, combing and weaving fine fabrics, shall be confounded,” says the prophet (Isa. 19:9). Therefore I have been clothed with confusion, because beneath the wool of your simplicity I wove the flax of my own pretence. Perhaps, in reproach of this doubleness, you sent me a double cup. “Weight and weight, measure and measure: both are abominable” (Prov. 20:23). “Woe to him who gives drink to his friend, pouring out his gall and making him drunk, that he may look upon his nakedness: he shall be filled with shame instead of glory” (Hab. 2:15–16).

3. Why these things, brother, except that I may commend your gentleness and condemn my own wrongdoing? But since it would take long to run through each point, I give you a word made short and complete. I spoke foolishly, like one of the foolish women. I acknowledge my offence; do you forgive it. Asked, you will not refuse the pardon which you freely offer. I could put forward excuses, lessen the enormity of my guilt, lay the weight of the sin upon another, and brandish the sword against the head of him who struck me and by whom I was wounded. But I refrain, turning rather to prayer and supplication. For I do not wish, while repairing what has been torn, to tear apart again what has somehow been stitched; nor, in order to protect my own side, to wound another’s.

Yet I do not pass this over in silence. Your house is not well compacted; with the scales pressing one another, one does not adhere firmly to another, and the spirit of dissension, not of peace, passes through them all too easily (Job 41:6–7). As for the rest—why I prolonged the day, why I was unwilling for so long, why I act slowly, why I said you would be a burden to me—I answer briefly. We say many things in conversation to test another’s disposition rather than to disclose our own. For I shall speak openly with you, according to my heart’s judgment: I desired and desire your companionship; but I delayed so that it might happen more suitably, presuming that you would be a consolation to me rather than a burden, perhaps because of similarity in character and pursuits. Would that I might receive you more for eternity than for a time; to remain, not to return. Farewell.

### LETTER II. TO A CERTAIN ADAM

He exhorts Adam, that, at last mindful of his purpose, he may embrace the religious state.

1. How greatly I desire you in the bowels of Christ Jesus, my Adam—would that you yourself knew it, since my speech cannot adequately unfold it to you. I had long wished this, but a certain despair restrained my desire. Now, however, my longing has grown and increased more abundantly than usual, and has blazed into desire for your conversion, now that hope has been conceived—though a very slender hope—from your words. Yet I feared, if I may say so with your leave, that those words had slipped from you under some light and momentary impulse of mind. But say them as you will: whether they escaped from too ready and sudden an affection, or were uttered with prudent deliberation, I cannot but hope well of you, instructed by a familiar example. And would that our examples may move you—or rather, remind you; and that, taking up the dove’s wings, you may outstrip me with happy speed into the place of rest, though you began later! What a broad and open window for imitation you will have afforded, soon to become an example to others—and, to insert something from our own writings, a great door onto the path of virtue! Indeed, I seem to hear that passage from the Song of Songs sung concerning you: “Draw us after thee; we will run in the fragrance of thy ointments” (Song 1:3).

2. Truly happy, and twice happy, if you make your conversion an occasion of salvation for others: if you draw to life and truth those who now run after you. I was going to say, “in vanity,” but I feared that perhaps I might grieve an affection still tender and only now being born in Christ. Not that I disparage education in the arts, or ready memory for liberal disciplines, or clear understanding, in which the completeness of learning consists. Knowledge of the arts is good, but only if one uses them lawfully—that is, as a step and a track, not as something upon which one stands and clings, but as something to be used for higher, holier, and more inward mysteries of wisdom: for its hidden and pleasant recesses, and for that inaccessible light in which God dwells.

This I would call the art of all arts: law, form, rule, reason, and universal, uniform, unchangeable exemplar. Beyond it we cannot advance; but short of it we ought not to halt. In comparison with it, every other wisdom, whatever and however great it may be, is not merely vain if it does not equal this, but even wicked if it does not direct itself toward it—if it so occupies and entices our study toward itself that it keeps and deceives our delight within itself, and the exhausted mind comes to rest at that end, turned back from proceeding to more secret things; fed on emptiness and, as it were, painted feasts, so that it never hungers and never tastes how sweet the Lord is. For what is sweet except the Lord? [Perhaps: “For what is sweet but the Lord?”] This slight and uncertain knowledge of natures and reasons, reached only with difficulty by a long circuit and winding turns, greatly delights you and has seized and drawn your mind and love to itself. What then of creative Wisdom itself, by which all these things are both established in being and illumined so as to be known? Will not the apprehension of it commend itself to you much more eagerly, and more gently pour its sweetness into senses made serene, calling forth in unprecedented affections an inexhaustible desire for itself? “For those who eat me,” it says, “shall yet hunger; for my spirit is sweeter than honey” (Ecclus. 24:29, 27).

3. You possess, my friend, capacious receptacles for this very honey: I mean a keen and trained intellect, and knowledge of many subtle things. Yet I should regard these as cells capable of receiving favours, but still empty. Come, then, that you may be filled and your receptacles be filled; that they may overflow, run over, and be poured back upon us, so that we may rightly applaud you in the words of the Song: “Thy lips are a dripping honeycomb” (Song 4:11). Oh, if someday I may hear you disputing in the house of the Lord, unfolding its secret and consecrated senses, touching upon and delicately distilling for us something concerning the majesty of the divine essence—its eternity, immensity, simplicity. There nothing is small, because it is simple; nor manifold, because it is immense; but the whole is infinite, not through temporal succession nor through local bulk and extension, but through essential power and force. It is wholly everywhere, but wholly in itself, since its whole power, truth, and will are neither exhausted nor expressed in anything.
