Here there can be certain stages of discourse and, according to us, distinct significations of names; but the reality is one and inseparable. All is full of wonder, worthy of reverence, and delightful to investigate. In short, as it is written: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing” (Eccl. 1:8). I would gladly hear you prophesying of such matters; and when, as a curious investigator, you have immersed yourself in the boundless depth of this sea, sprinkling those not capable of fuller things with the sweet dew of life-giving wisdom. But when you turn to God’s benefits, then I would hear you unfolding more generously and explaining more abundantly what you have understood concerning pardon, grace, glory—concerning what the Lord has given, restored, or added; and all that he endured for us and bestowed upon us. Set before us Christ’s preceding sufferings and future glories, patience in tribulations and expectation of recompense, the elements of faith and the principles of conduct; and run through every stage of renewal and progress. This is indeed abundant material and a desirable undertaking; nor is there any field in which an ardent or learned intellect can exercise itself more fruitfully and more productively.

4. I have said these things so that you may not excuse yourself by devotion to empty letters, pursuing a shadow while deprived of light; nor, distorted by Aristotelian subtleties, make our silence and simplicity a pretext. For in these matters opportunity is especially furnished that, “beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, we may be transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). Does our silence seem idle and inert to you, though this work is carried on within it? Within it is taught and practised an art, as it were, of proceeding in a straight line toward God; of transforming and changing oneself into the new man, the new Adam; and of attaining to the mind of Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of God’s wisdom (Col. 2:3). Here are everlasting and almost readily available veins of shining metal, if only one prefers to dig deep rather than beg outside.

5. I am not now rehearsing to you the divine benefits bestowed upon you, the Lord’s graces, and your ingratitude—indeed, the evil return rendered for the best gift. Nor do I minimize in words, as far as I can, the destructive pleasures of the world, into which men rush with ardent zeal, turning their backs upon the Lord and not their faces. I do not explain present medicinal pains; I do not threaten future punishments and set forth glory; nor do I send your fear or expectation into the distant future. I persuade you only concerning the present pledge [perhaps: “the present”], not a future reward; concerning firstfruits, not fullness. It is beyond my ability to pursue this matter with words; nor is it fitting that the majesty of so great a subject should be compressed into the narrowness of my mouth. Only be willing to experience it, and you will know that the Lord’s statutes are songs even in this place of pilgrimage (Ps. 118:54), and that the harvests at the end of the age are sown in the first joys. Do not put off sweet things [variant: doubtful things] until next year. Do not resist the grace which freely presents itself to you. Woe to me if you cast away from yourself her whom I have found with you! Follow with eager and untiring foot where her first enticements call you. You commanded me to send to you; and would that I may find you there where I left you—in the very gates, I mean, and almost on the threshold, on the point of leaving worldly life! If I seem necessary to you in any way, I shall spend my whole self, because I owe my whole self. I await your presence rather than a letter. Farewell.

### LETTER III. TO BROTHER WILLIAM

He dissuades him from a dangerous journey to the court and commends another, spiritual journey.

To his beloved brother WILLIAM, Brother G., greeting in the Lord.

1. Our most dearly desired brother R. greatly gladdened us by his arrival; and, announcing your welfare, he flooded us with fuller joy, bringing the services of your greeting and asking in return the support of prayers. Would that our hand may be more sufficient than usual for this service, and that I may discharge it so much the more fully as you have decided to spare us in other respects! For I heard that you had quite frequently, in repeated and significant words, urged that I should devote prayers to you more diligently, and that henceforth I might be at ease. Excellent, brother—wholly excellent, and worthy of a man of virtue. For what else is there that anyone should ask more willingly, or that a monk may request more freely?

Be ashamed at the impudence of certain men who, although they ought to hope for all necessary things from the father of the monastery, beg supports from every quarter and then purchase certain refined and exquisite skins, extravagant garments and foreign little cloaks, and other things too numerous to list—incitements to pleasure in scents, colours, and flavours, instruments of vanity. In short, men who ought to be restrained even from things permitted for use may be seen shamelessly employing them for display. That blemish is far from your conduct, as that saying of yours, repeated so often, declares; it wipes from you the hue of this leprosy, so widely spread abroad. I am harsh and inhuman; though in other respects I am handsome, as they themselves say, in this particular our face is blackened beyond coals, because I do not know how to give except what I am accustomed to ask. Let them speak against me as much as they wish; let them make our avarice out of their own shamelessness, and forge my harshness from their softness. I have set my face as the hardest stone; and their hammer being shattered, I hope that I shall not be put to shame. Let me be less accommodating; let me be more tenacious. I shall gladly allow myself to be disfigured by this blemish, provided that dogs—indeed, these delicate and tender little puppies—do not eat the bread of the children; that they do not turn the squalor of Christ’s poor into other people’s superfluous finery; and that I do not seek for myself an empty name and false favour from a brother’s growling stomach.

2. But, leaving myself aside, to return to you and remind you that something must be sought from us: you asked for prayers, and I turn beyond this to exhortation, for I am zealous for you with God’s zeal. Yet I fear lest your thoughts be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ; lest prayers be poured out for you in vain, while you of your own accord rush toward a fall; and lest you ask in vain to be delivered while deliberately hurrying into the snare. You are about to set out, as I hear, for the court; and you are going where you suspect that you will be hindered. You are going to renew old ties with the Duke, to awaken buried—indeed, sleeping—desires, to raise on high wings long compressed and folded, when you have received the time, according to that parable of the ostrich (Job 39:18). Yet the stork and the swallow know the day of their visitation (Jer. 8:7), when the warmer breeze begins to blow.

I speak plainly to you of things which perhaps others say about you in secret. You are going to court, and I do not know whether you have been summoned. But what will you do there? Will you share the care of your soul with the Duke, cooling the heat of your heart by conversation with him? Perhaps so, but with that coldness of which it is written: “The charity of many shall grow cold” (Matt. 24:12). Hear, then, the prophet reproaching such persons: “What shall I do unto thee, Ephraim? What shall I do unto thee, Judah? Your righteousness is as a morning cloud, and as the dew which passes away in the morning” (Hos. 6:4). Morning indeed—rather, momentary; for scarcely have they begun in the spirit than they are immediately brought to completion in the flesh.

The Bridegroom in the Song complains that he has endured many such persons: “My head is full of dew, and my locks of the drops of the night” (Song 5:2). For when, because of the loftiness of their life, they have risen as it were to the Lord’s head, they cling in the hair; and, rendered insensible by greater preoccupation with outward things alien to the life-giving Spirit, they do not know how to savour the things of God. Therefore, having nowhere among such people to lay his head, if he finds anyone within, he asks that the door be opened to him.

3. Would that you too may dwell within; and, receiving Jesus as a guest in the lodging of your heart as soon as he knocks at the door, may glory and say: “My secret is for me; my secret is for me” (Isa. 24:16). In return, you will receive that welcome voice of praise: “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). Sealed indeed with the seal of light and joy of heart, with the seal of the sevenfold Spirit, which no one can unseal except he alone who uniquely enters the eastern gate, closed against strangers, according to the prophet’s saying: “Strangers shall no longer pass through Jerusalem” (Ezek. 44). Enclosed in such a paradise of delight—or rather, yourself like a watered field and a fountain of gardens whose waters do not fail—you will become deaf to the voice of strangers. If worldly ambition disturbs you, if an occasion for dignities calls you, and flattering ruin invites you—some hope of honours—you will immediately answer in the Bride’s words: “I have put off my garment; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song 5:3).

4. You surely see, brother, what it is that I wish to suggest to you in half-uttered words and shadow-like hints, more veiling than pressing the matter, knowing that I speak with a wise man. You see, I say, the whole point: that I may call you back from this dangerous journey and, with the sickle of my admonition, cut off the occasions of a swift fall; making smooth for you, according to the prophet’s command, the way free of stumbling and removing stones from the road (Isa. 62:10). My concern for you is great; my confidence in you is great. Otherwise I would rather our long-standing ties be weakened for a time than suppress in silence what I believe concerns your salvation; rather lose familiarity than endanger the humility in you which is still tender and growing.

You were running well. Take care lest the fascination of trifles darken your good things (Wis. 4:12), and lest, though conscience remains undefiled, even your reputation be brought into danger. You were running well, I say: where are you now hastening so eagerly? You were running well—but what if you do not finish? Being about to be finished in a short time, do you wish to consume much time, so that Paul may now reproach you: “Have you suffered so many things in vain?—if indeed in vain” (Gal. 3:4).

5. Would that I were present now, and could, by some vigorous hand of living speech laid upon you, lead you with Abraham into the land of Canaan—that is, into “Change.” For “those who trust in the Lord shall change their strength” (Isa. 40:31). It is a good change of which the same prophet speaks: “There shall be five cities in the land of Egypt speaking the language of Canaan; one shall be called the city of the sun” (Isa. 19:18). It is good indeed to be led out of Egypt’s darkness into light, and after Pharaoh’s house to be dedicated in the city of the Sun of righteousness. Good, I say, is this change, where dark things are transformed into light and many things into one. For in plurality there is disturbance, while “one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:41–42). It is a good change in which Leah’s bleared eyesight and Martha’s anxiety are turned into Rachel’s brightness and Mary’s tranquillity. This is why cities that belonged to Egypt—that is, to darkness—are called cities of the Sun; and why, in place of the number five, mention is made of one only.

He who speaks in the Psalm knew himself to have been changed: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his recompenses: who forgives all thy iniquities, who heals all thy infirmities; who redeems thy life from destruction, who crowns thee with mercy and compassions” (Ps. 102:2–4). He speaks the language of Canaan who recalls in himself so many transformations: forgiveness out of iniquity, healing out of infirmity, eternity out of destruction; and at each stage gives thanks to the author. By the signs of devout progress, as if in a certain language of transformation, he says with the Psalmist: “Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76:11). And, that we may reap apostolic fruits from prophetic seed: what Isaiah closes, Paul explains. “You were once darkness,” he says, “but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). We have heard of transformation; he reminds us of completion: “Walk,” he says, “as children of light.” He who walks in the day does not stumble. Let your light increase unto the perfect day; and when you have reached completion, seem only to have begun. Hear how Paul himself ran and grew, not merely from darkness to light but from light to light: “We all, beholding the glory of the Lord with unveiled face, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory” (2 Cor. 3:18).

6. When you see some who have renounced the world prospering in the world, let not your steps be poured out. But while they stumble as blind men at noon, do you glory and say: “I have not wearied thee, O Lord, by following thee.” For those who hope in the Lord shall renew their strength; they shall fly and not labour; they shall walk and not fail (Isa. 40:31). It would take long if I wished to lead you through every renewal of virtues, as through certain stations of the land of Canaan.

And indeed, first, following the devout patriarch, one must come to Shechem (Gen. 12:6), where, with shoulders humbled and bowed down—for *Sichem* means “shoulders”—one may receive Christ’s very light burden. “For it is good for a man when he has borne the Lord’s yoke from his youth. He shall give his cheek to him that strikes him; he shall be filled with reproaches” (Lam. 3:27, 30). And observe, at the word “filled,” not merely some slight tolerance that tastes what is bitter only with the lips and rejects it when perceived, but an insatiable appetite for enduring adversities.

Then, after happy affliction and medicinal pain, passing through Gerar, and with the old wall of enmities broken down, having escaped in free flight from the holes of the rock and clefts of caverns at the Bridegroom’s invitation, one may reach the streams of Beersheba. From Shechem, I say—that is, from humiliation and prayer—let one come to Beersheba, to the well of seven lambs, or rather of every grace. For “God gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). And because by another interpretation it is called “the well of satiety” (Gen. 20, 21, and 26), in accordance with the inviting voice, “Come to me, you who are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11:28), after affliction one hastens to refreshment. Drawn into still greater hunger by a draught of the sweetest liquor, let him experience in himself that true proclamation of Wisdom: “Those who eat me shall yet hunger” (Ecclus. 24:29).

I have decided to be silent now, because perhaps you have long begun to be weary of my chattering. Farewell; and please seek out Jerome on Isaiah for me, so that when I send for it, you may have it ready.

### LETTER IV. TO A CERTAIN FRIEND

In a brief letter he signifies that he cannot comply with the requests made.

With your leave, I say it: your excess makes me obstinate; indeed, the greater importunity of those whose intercessor you make yourself somewhat diminishes with me the weight of your own merits. I wonder that they did not also bring the lord of Fontibus against us, to overwhelm me again with the cloud of weighty intercessors. Yet, that I may satisfy you with a brief answer: this matter which you request I wished to refuse more by silence than by speech. Modestly indeed, according to my custom, as I do other things which I have decided by no means to do. Yet I defer rather than determine my answer, until shortly we may confer together. Farewell.

## [LETTER OR TREATISE OF GUIGO, FIFTH PRIOR OF THE CHARTREUSE, TO THE BRETHREN]

[Col. 0297]

## DOM MABILLON’S NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING LETTER

1. The authorship of the following Letter began long ago to be doubted; but it is established that it should be attributed to William, or Guillaume, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Theodoric near Reims.

2. An old manuscript belonging to the most learned and humane Leonor Foy, canon of Beauvais, written about four hundred years ago, expresses this doubt. In it the letter bears the following heading: “Here begins the Letter to the Carthusians, which, although entitled in the name of Abbot William, is nevertheless ascribed by many to Bernard.” Indeed, this very letter was cited under Bernard’s name by John Gerson, Chancellor of Paris, in his sermon on the Lord’s Supper; and at the same period by John of Ragusa, in Henri Canisius, vol. III of *Antiquae Lectiones*, p. 240, and by others here and there after them. Not a few manuscripts supported that opinion. Yet nothing from this letter was excerpted into the *Bernardine*, or the *Book of Flowers from Bernard*.

3. The occasion for doubting the author arose chiefly from the fault of copyists, who shortened, or even wholly erased, the name of the genuine author—William—placed at the beginning of the letter; indeed, they also removed a large part of the preface, in which the author compiled a catalogue of his works, all of which are known to belong to Abbot William. Bertrand Tissier, a religious and devout man, was the first to publish this preface in full from ancient manuscripts and restore it to its author, in vol. IV of the *Cistercian Library*.

Besides the manuscripts cited by him that attribute this letter to William—namely those of Signy, Charle-Locus, Longpont, and Foucarmont—we have found further witnesses testifying to the same: the Flavigny manuscript, now in the Royal Library; the Thou manuscript, now in the Colbert Library; and that of St Emmeram at Regensburg. In all these the letter bears this heading: “To the lords and brothers, H., Prior, etc.; W., delicate sabbath.” Here you see William’s name represented only by its first letter, as also that of Haimo, the Prior then presiding over the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu.

The Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu is in the diocese of Reims, under the jurisdiction of Mouzon. It was founded in 1136 by Odo, abbot of St Remigius, with Geoffrey as first Prior; Haimo succeeded him in 1144. Haimo was succeeded in the third place by Gervase—whose name, though suppressed, is mentioned in Bernard’s Letter 290—and Gervase in turn had Simon as his successor in the fourth place, as we formerly learned from the venerable Father Francis Ganeron. Moreover, that this letter was written at the very beginning of the foundation of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu is understood from the fact that its first inhabitants are designated by the term “novelty” in no. 3.

4. Whether William wrote this letter as abbot, or after becoming a monk of Signy from being abbot, is not so certain. The latter opinion is supported by the fact that he was already of advanced age when he wrote this letter. Further, nearly four hundred years ago, the letter was cited under the title “William of Clairvaux, *On the Solitary Life*” by a certain regular canon of St Saviour at Bologna, namely in book I, chapter 23, of his *Sermons to Hermits*. On this author, see our *Italian Journey*, p. 197.

5. From these considerations is refuted the conjecture—otherwise not implausible—of the learned translator of this same letter, who thought that it might be attributed to Peter of Celle. For, besides the fact that William’s name prefixed to the letter, the enumeration of William’s works in the preface, and the difference of style prove the contrary, the author himself in that same preface calls himself “old” and “failing.” This suits Abbot William, but not Peter of Celle, who was in the vigor of manhood when Haimo was prior, to whom the letter is addressed, and had scarcely then reached thirty years of age, as could readily be proved if the matter required it.

6. Therefore no doubt remains that this letter must be restored to Abbot William as its genuine author. Indeed, in an old manuscript of Saint-Theodoric near Reims it stands first in the recension of William’s works, in Marlot, vol. II of the *Metropolis Remensis*, p. 287, in these words: “The reverend Father William, abbot of Saint-Theodoric, composed many devout little works, which he sent to the brothers of Mont-Dieu: namely, *On the Solitary Life*, *The Mirror and Enigma of Faith*, *On the Contemplation of God*, *On the Dignity of Love*, etc.”

7. Finally, in the brief compendium of his life which we possess from an old parchment of the monastery of Radoul, the same [Col. 0299] letter is claimed for the same author together with the others. It will not be tiresome to reproduce the words of the parchment here.

“Moreover, he left behind not inconsiderable monuments of his talent and learning, of which I shall note only those which I have tested by sight and reading. Having undertaken to write the Life of Saint Bernard, he could not complete the work; nevertheless, he finished one book—the first—and it is of no small size. Against Master Peter Abelard, who had inserted into his works certain things discordant with the faith, he published one book, elegant in expression, Catholic in faith, vigorous in reasoning. He also made two little books, one of which he called *The Enigma of Faith*, the other *The Mirror of Faith*, in which he briefly and plainly shows what ought to be believed. He composed a moral exposition on the Song of Songs, a work which he mentions in the Life of Saint Bernard. There is another book of his, *On the Nature and Dignity of Love*, which, from its subject matter, we may call an *Anti-Ovid*. For in it he instructs the true philosopher by what stages and methods he can and ought to advance in the love of God.

“He also addressed one little book to the brothers of the Carthusian Order living at Mont-Dieu. Although it speaks specifically to them, it is useful to all who desire to be perfected in the religious life. He produced a brief compilation on physics—that is, on the nature of body and soul—in order that he might instruct simple readers in at least an initial knowledge of themselves; for, since to know oneself is the chief fruit of discourse, this accords with that saying which came down from heaven, *Gnōthi seauton* [‘Know thyself’].

“There is also a little book of his entitled *On the Contemplation of God*, in which, without doubt for the edification of readers, he speaks of his own contemplation in these words: ‘And sometimes, Lord, while I gape toward you as though with closed eyes, you put into the mouth of my heart something which I am not permitted to know what it is. For I perceive a sweet taste, so strengthening that, if it were perfected in me, I would seek nothing further.’

“He also composed a treatise of no small size bearing the title *Meditative Prayers*, in which he does not employ a single subject matter, but discusses diverse chapters; and in most of them, addressing God, he examines his own manifold conscience. In this work especially appears not merely this man’s love for God, but his ardor. And indeed, I think that whoever reads it devoutly and soberly, however religious and learned he may be, will nevertheless advance in the fear of the Lord, in greater knowledge and lower estimation of himself. I do not doubt that he fashioned other little works; but apart from these I have so far been unable to find any.”

8. Thus far the old parchment, at the beginning of which “William, born of distinguished family at Liège,” is said to have had a brother Simon. With him he went to Reims and, in the abbey of Saint-Nicaise—where there was then “the fragrance of a good reputation”—assumed “the habit of the sacred religious life.” In the course of time Simon became abbot of Saint-Nicholas-in-the-Wood, where, after he had long and religiously presided over the brothers, “full of days and perfected in virtue, he rested in a blessed end.” But Lord William “was chosen as abbot of Saint-Theodoric, which overlooks the lake near the city of Reims,” namely in 1120; sixteen years after becoming a Cistercian monk at Signy, as is explained more fully in the Notes on Bernard’s Letter 85, vol. I, col. 860.

8. From all this it appears that not only the letter to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, but also the treatises *On the Contemplation of God* and *On the Nature and Dignity of Love*, which had been falsely ascribed to Bernard, belong to William himself. It therefore seemed proper to restore them to him and to place them after the said letter in this edition. Other little works of the same William, indicated above, appear in vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*.

Now the Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu is to be presented. Those who excel in this form of life regard it as a kind of most complete model of monastic life; although John Gerson, in his sermon on the Lord’s Supper, warns the reader “to read Bernard’s second book to the brothers of Mont-Dieu cautiously on this subject”—namely, on the union of the perfected with God—here no. 62. You see from this that the letter was at some time divided into two books.

[Col. 0299]

## Admonition of Dom Massuet on the Following Letter, Which Is Asserted to Belong to Guigo or Wigo, Fifth Prior of the Grande Chartreuse

[Col. 0299] 1. Doubt concerning the author of the following Letter or Treatise began long ago. Some attributed it to Bernard and cited it under his name, such as John Gerson, chancellor of Paris, in his sermon on the Lord’s Supper; John of Ragusa, at the same period, in Henry Canisius, vol. III of *Antiquae Lectiones*, p. 240; and an author much older than these, who wrote in praise of the Carthusians about four hundred years ago, whose manuscript work exists at the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu. Not a few written manuscripts support this opinion, such as the old manuscript of Saint-Arnoul at Metz, and another from Mont-Dieu, in which the author’s name was erased and Bernard’s substituted.

The occasion of the error was the incompetence of copyists. Seeing this treatise attached to Bernard’s genuine works without an author’s name, they supposed it to be Bernard’s, rashly prefixed his name, attributed it to him, and afterward misled others. But once the error was exposed—both by the dissimilarity of style, by the fact that nothing from this treatise was excerpted in the *Bernardine* or in the *Book of Flowers from Bernard*, and finally by other arguments—almost everyone agreed that it belonged to William or Guillaume, formerly abbot of Saint-Theodoric near Reims and later a monk of Signy. One alone dissented: the learned translator of this same letter, who thought that it might be attributed to Peter of Celle; but both style and manuscript codices oppose him.

2. Indeed, the old manuscript of the most distinguished Leonor Foy, canon of Beauvais, written about four hundred years ago, seemed to Mabillon of blessed memory to express the doubt sufficiently. It gives this heading to the letter: “Here begins the letter to the Carthusians, which, although entitled with the name of Abbot William, is nevertheless ascribed by many to Bernard.” There was also the preface which Bertrand Tissier—a religious and devout man—first published whole, as he believed, from ancient codices, in vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*. In it the author sets out a catalogue of his works, all of which are certainly Abbot William’s.

A certain regular canon of Saint-Saviour at Bologna also cited the same letter, under the name of William of Clairvaux, as *On the Solitary Life*, nearly four hundred years ago, namely in book I of his *Sermons to Hermits*, chapter 23. On this author see Mabillon’s *Italian Journey*, p. 197. Thereafter, all manuscripts seemed to support this opinion: those that have the author’s name at the beginning of the letter abbreviated thus, “W.”—such as the Flavigny manuscript, now in the Royal Library; the Thouaneus manuscript, now in the Colbertine Library; and that of Saint-Emmeram at Regensburg. In all these the letter bears the heading: “To the lords and brothers, H., Prior, etc., W. [wishes] a delightful Sabbath.” Other manuscripts give the name in full, [Col. 0301] such as those of Signy, Charlelieu, Longpont, Foulquemont, and others cited by Tissier; finally, there are also those in which the name has been wholly erased.

3. But when Mabillon adopted that opinion, he had not seen the oldest and most authoritative of all, the Pontigny manuscript, elegantly written in 1156. Dom Edmond Martène, our diligent investigator of antiquities, happily found it while searching the library of that monastery in order to correct and embellish the new edition of *Gallia Christiana*, now under the press. This manuscript gives the name of Guigo, Prior of the Charterhouse, not abbreviated but in full, and in more than one place. For at the very beginning of the letter or treatise one reads: “Here begins the prologue to the book of Guigo, Prior of the Charterhouse, addressed to H., Prior of Mont-Dieu. To the lords and brothers H., Prior, and H., Guigo, [wishes] a delightful Sabbath.” Then, after the preface: “Here begins the book of the same Guigo.” Finally, at the end: “End of the third and final book of Guigo.” The same hand notes below the year in which the manuscript was written, namely 1156.

No one can readily persuade himself that, only a few years after the circulation of the Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu, and fewer years still after the deaths of Guigo and William, such a gross error in the author’s name could have occurred that the offspring of one should be attributed to the other—especially in the monastery where the memory was still fresh both of William, who had embraced Cistercian observance in another monastery not far away, and of his undisputed works, the praise of which the Cistercians would not have wished to transfer to an outsider.

4. A second manuscript of almost the same antiquity, preserved in the Cistercian monastery of Charlelieu, agrees exceedingly well with the Pontigny manuscript; its handwriting appears to be at least five hundred years old. We likewise owe knowledge of it to the tireless efforts of our Martène. In this manuscript the name of Guigo was indeed attacked for erasure by the envious and unlearned hand of some more recent pedant, in order to attribute the work to Bernard; yet not so completely that it does not still appear sound and intact. For the work’s title reads: “Here begins the prologue to the book of Guigo, Prior of the Carthusians, addressed to H., Prior of Mont-Dieu. To the lords and brothers H., Prior, and H., Guigo, [wishes] a delightful Sabbath.” After the prologue follows: “Here begins the book of the same Guigo.”

Then follow three books, as in the Pontigny manuscript. After the first one reads: “Book I ends; Book II begins.” After the second, something had been written in red, which is now entirely erased; but in its place a very recent hand has added: “The little work to the brothers of Mont-Dieu ends. The little book of Archbishop Anselm on True Blessedness begins.”

5. On the authority of these two manuscripts, the entire dispute concerning the author of the letter or treatise *On the Solitary Life* addressed to the brothers of Mont-Dieu must be considered settled. Nor, I think, will anyone henceforth wish to deprive Guigo the Carthusian of the credit for so distinguished a work. Certainly, the largest part of the manuscript tradition preserves it whole for its author; these manuscripts represent Guigo by the first elements of his name, thus: “W.” Those acquainted with the usages of the eleventh century know how ready the interchange of *Gu* and *W* was, and conversely. Thus one commonly finds *Willelmus* written for *Guillelmus*, *Wido* for *Guido*, and *Wigo* for *Guigo*, and conversely.

Hence, when some persons found the letter to the brothers of Mont-Dieu copied among the works of Abbot William, with the author’s name denoted only by its first elements, “W.,” in one and the same manuscript, they were deceived by the similarity of these initials. Thinking it William’s own offspring, they copied and cited it under his name, thereby giving later writers an occasion for error.

6. Yet the letter contains a good many things which, if weighed more attentively, would at once have been recognized as suitable to Guigo or Wigo alone, Prior of the Charterhouse, and certainly not to William, a monk of another observance. At the beginning of the work itself, in the very prologue, the author writes that, ever since he had departed from the Carthusians who cultivated Mont-Dieu, he had always been concerned for Brother Stephen and his companions, the younger brothers, and the novices coming to that new house:

“From the time,” he says, “when I departed from you until now, I have resolved to dedicate whatever daily labor of mine there may be, not to you, who have no need of it, but to Brother Stephen and his companions, the younger brothers, and the novices coming to you, whose sole teacher is God: that they may have and read, should they perhaps find there anything useful to them for the consolation of their solitude,” etc.

But it is wholly uncertain whether William ever even saw those new inhabitants of Mont-Dieu. Shortly after the foundation of the monastery at Signy, he withdrew there in 1134, as will be shown in vol. VI of the *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*. In that very year the foundations of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu were first laid, through the action of Odo, abbot of Saint-Remi at Reims. Although two years earlier, at the urging of Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, Odo had conceived a plan to establish a Carthusian house in the diocese of Reims, he could not carry it into execution before 1134. Returning that year from the Council of Pisa, he summoned a colony of solitaries from the Grande Chartreuse, sent to him by Prior Guigo, and himself led it to Mont-Dieu—then called Mont-Boson—in the territory of Reims, two leagues from the town of Mouzon, on the river Bar. He granted it sufficient land and revenues for building a monastery.

These matters, which we touch upon here briefly, will be explained more fully in the said volume of the *Annals*. But it is sufficiently clear from this that William could scarcely have seen, before his withdrawal, those first inhabitants of Mont-Dieu, who perhaps had not yet even arrived there. Entirely intent as he was upon his own withdrawal, and soon afterward harassed by grave temptations, as the author of his Life reports, he had to direct all his concerns toward himself and could scarcely attend to outsiders. Nor do we read anywhere that, after professing among the monks of Signy, he ever left the place in order to visit the Carthusians of Mont-Dieu.

7. But if, as is proper, we assign the said letter to Guigo, Prior of the Grande Chartreuse, no difficulty at all remains; everything fits perfectly. He is a devout teacher who, after departing from the disciples whom he had left, was always concerned for their salvation and resolved to dedicate his daily labor, such as it was, to them, in order to alleviate the weariness of solitude by holier counsels and exhortations, to strengthen the younger in their purpose, or to kindle them toward monastic profession. Thus he treats the loftiness of their profession, explains the virtues proper to Carthusians, gives precepts appropriate to beginners, and teaches how one should spend time in the cell. He sets out the proper measure of sacred reading, prayer, bodily exercise, food, sleep, manual labor, and so forth.

He writes in a manner that clearly bears and displays the character of a Carthusian writing to disciples of the same observance. Therefore he often speaks in the plural, to show himself bound by the same laws:

“Let both our labor and our leisure,” he says, book I, chapter 8, “effect this in every way: that we may never be idle; and let this always be our business, that what the Apostle says may be perfectly accomplished in us,” etc.

And in chapter 10, treating the offices and exercises of solitaries in the cell: “In our vigils,” he says, “in which we rise at midnight to confess the name of the Lord, the prophet, setting out the order of this very confession, says: ‘In the day of my tribulation I sought God; with my hands at night toward him, and I was not deceived’ [Ps. 76:3]. For at these hours above all we ought to place ourselves before God, as though face to face,” etc.

In the following chapter, prescribing the measure of food: “As for seasonings, I beg that they suffice to make our food edible, not also desirable or delectable.”

And in chapter 13, exhorting solitaries in the Apostle’s words to eat their own bread while working in silence (2 Thess. 3:12), he adds: “At least let us eat our bread according to Adam’s punishment, if we cannot do so in the sweat of our brow, then in the sorrow of our heart; in tears of sorrow, if not in the sweat of labor. Let piety and the devotion of a humble conscience make good this great loss of our profession.”

Nothing is clearer than the words “our profession,” by which he openly indicates the Carthusian observance, whose fathers—those ancient hermits dwelling in the Thebaid, as he explains at the beginning of the chapter—worked with their hands and fed the poor from their labor. These, I say, he calls his fathers: not Benedict, Bernard, Basil, or any other founder of a cenobitic order, but those who, “in Egypt and the Thebaid, most ardent imitators of this holy life, dwelling in the deserts … built cells for themselves, in which, sheltered and protected from wind and rain, they lived; and, abounding in the delights of hermit frugality, though needy themselves they enriched many.” Behold, then, a hermit speaking to hermits, an imitator of his hermit fathers dwelling in the deserts of Egypt and the Thebaid, and in poor huts: consequently Guigo the Carthusian, certainly not Abbot William, to whom these things do not at all apply.

8. But if anyone still had any doubt, it would be wholly removed by what the author writes in chapter 12 of the same book. Having learned that the new Carthusians of Mont-Dieu were building cells somewhat more costly than was fitting and than the laws of their observance allowed, he does everything possible to dissuade them from this plan and to recall them to the former simplicity and poverty of their fathers:

“Already there has entered among us the costly construction of cells on borrowed money, and—so far as shame scarcely permits one to say it—ambitious construction; and, abandoning holy simplicity and rusticity … we create for ourselves certain supposedly religious refinements of dwellings, in which so much has been granted to the animal nature that almost all of us have thereby become animal. Alienating from ourselves and from our cells the form of poverty and the appearance of holy simplicity, left to you by our fathers as a rightful inheritance—the true beauty of God’s house—we build for ourselves, through the hands of skilled craftsmen, cells not so much hermit-like as aromatic, each bearing a price-tag of one hundred solidi: the desires of our eyes purchased from the alms of the poor. Cut away, Lord, the reproach of one hundred solidi from the cells of your poor. Why not rather one hundred denarii? Why not rather none at all? Why do not the children of grace themselves build freely?”

In these words everyone must recognize, not William, not Bernard, nor any other monk living the cenobitic life—for individual cells, much less hermit cells, did not yet exist at that time for them, since they all slept in a common dormitory, not yet divided into cells—but a Carthusian hermit, the general father of hermits. He grieves that his sons, already fallen away from ancestral hermit simplicity, are arranging to build cells for themselves, not such as befitted hermits, but prouder than the observance of hermits permitted. Following their forebears’ example, they ought themselves to have built humble huts.

Hence he adds: “Therefore, I beg you, in the pilgrimage of this world, in this warfare upon earth, let us build for ourselves not houses to dwell in, but tents to leave behind … Is it not easy for a solitary man, sufficient for nature and useful for conscience, to weave a cell for himself out of branches, shape it out of mud, cover it somehow or other, and inhabit it most becomingly? And what more need be sought? … Therefore I beg that those more luxurious cells remain as they have been made, but that their number not increase; and let them serve as infirmaries for animal and weaker brothers until they recover … Let them remain as an example to our descendants, because you had such things and despised them.”

By what right, I ask, could William have given these commands to outsiders, whose care did not concern him at all? Why would he have intruded into Carthusian discipline? Why would he have labored to reform the customs of men not subject to him? They were governed by their own superiors, to whom it belonged to correct whatever had been done contrary to the discipline of the order.

Finally the author concludes, at the beginning of the following chapter, by recalling to his own hearers the examples of their common fathers—that is, the ancient hermits: “But you who are spiritual, like the Hebrews—that is, those who pass over—having here no lasting city but seeking the city to come, build for yourselves, as you have begun, huts in which you may dwell. For our fathers dwelt in huts.” Which fathers? “Our fathers,” he adds, “in Egypt and the Thebaid, most ardent imitators of this most holy life, dwelling in the deserts … built cells for themselves, in which, sheltered and protected from wind and rain, they lived; and, abounding in the delights of hermit frugality, though needy themselves they enriched many.” [Note: [Col. 0303] Book II, chapter 13, no. 38.]

By these words the author sufficiently reveals his own observance, wholly different from William’s, since he neither lived in the manner of hermits nor dwelt in a separate cell.

9. What has been said so far suffices to establish the Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu for Guigo, Prior of the Charterhouse, and to restore to its author the noble work of whose credit the incompetence of copyists had deprived him. Only three objections could be raised with some plausibility; lest they deceive the unwary, we shall consider them briefly.

The first and principal objection is taken from the preface which Bertrand Tissier first published whole, as he believed, in vol. IV of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*. In it the author enumerates other works published by himself, all of which are known to be by Abbot William. If it were equally certain that the whole preface, as Tissier presented it, belonged to one and the same author, this difficulty would not easily be resolved. But so far is this from being certain that it rather appears plainly that the section by which Tissier enlarged the preface is a mere interpolation, wrongly added through the fault of scribes.

For, as we have said, when scribes found the Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu copied in one and the same manuscript with Abbot William’s genuine works, they supposed everything to be by one and the same author. They rashly prefixed a preface common to all, poorly pieced together from that which Guigo had prefixed to his letter and that which William had written to introduce his own studies. Guigo had written in his preface that he thought fit to dedicate to his brothers what he composed for the consolation of those troubled, by a more conscientious piety, over everything that seemed in the slightest degree contrary to faith—as though it were some work other than the letter. Yet what he discusses so carefully in book II concerning the soul and its faculties and activities, and so on, seems to have been written in order to remove scruples from the minds of those less instructed brothers.

The scribes wrongly imagined these to be the little works William wrote, one entitled *The Mirror of Faith* and the other *The Enigma of Faith*. What the latter had prefaced concerning both works, they immediately and badly stitched onto Guigo’s words, altering them somewhat. And lest we seem to conjecture rashly, nearly all extant manuscripts and printed editions prove the truth of our conjecture: they lack the interpolation which we here reproduce.

“But that little work is divided into two booklets. The first, because it is plain and easy, I resolved to call *The Mirror of Faith*; the other, because it appears briefly to contain the reasons and form of faith according to the sayings and understanding of the Catholic Fathers, and is somewhat more obscure, I resolved to call *The Enigma of Faith*. In such study I was fleeing the idleness that is the enemy of the soul—since old age and illness have released me from common labor, not as a veteran, certainly, but as lazy and useless—more than I was pursuing other matters, which truly are not fitting in a sinner’s mouth and become only those who confirm by life what they plant by speech. In the first, the untrained hearer is taught what he ought to approach; in the second, with what caution he should proceed. For the Lord also says to his disciples in this order: ‘You know where I am going, and you know the way’ [John 14:4]. Hence also the prophet says: ‘The riches of salvation are wisdom and knowledge’ [Isa. 33:6]. For in the Psalm first ‘day pours forth speech to day’; afterward, truly, ‘night declares knowledge to night’ [Ps. 18:3].

“There are besides other little works of ours: two treatises, the first *On the Contemplation of God*, the other *On the Nature and Dignity of Love*; a little book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*; *Meditations* for forming the spirits of novices in prayer, not altogether useless; and [an exposition] on the Song of Songs down to the passage: ‘When I had passed a little beyond them, [Col. 0305] I found him whom my soul loves’ [Song 3:4]. For Peter Abelard prevented me from finishing the aforementioned work. I did not think it proper for me to enjoy such delicate inward leisure while he, outside, was cruelly ravaging—as it were with an unsheathed sword—the boundaries of our faith. What I wrote against him, therefore, since I drew from the fountains of the holy Fathers what I said, as in the Epistle to the Romans and the other works of which I shall speak below, in which I have said either nothing at all or not much of my own, it would be better, if this pleases you, that it be left among anonymous works with my name suppressed, than that I appear, as I said before, to gather together works I did not produce.

“For I excerpted from the books of Saint Ambrose everything that he discussed in them on the Song of Songs, a great and distinguished work. Likewise from blessed Gregory, though more diffusely than Bede did; for Bede, as you know, made this very excerpt the last among his other books. The statements on faith which I extracted especially from the books of blessed Augustine, if you wish to copy them, are surely strong and weighty, and better fit the aforesaid little work which I decided should be called *The Enigma of Faith*. There is also another little work of ours, *On the Nature of the Soul*, written under the name of John to Theophilus. Since it seemed fitting to touch upon something concerning the whole human being, I prefixed something also concerning the nature of the body, excerpting the former from the books of those who treat bodies, but the latter from the books of those who devote their attention to the cure of souls.

“Therefore read everything, and, if not first, then, if it seems good, at least last; lest, if these works fall into the hands of those who themselves do nothing and gnaw at everything done by others, I too—old and failing, as is said of Isaac [Gen. 27:1], failing, I mean, not in gait but in understanding—may not be able to escape uninjured. Finally, if they are found useless, I think it better that the avenging fire consume them by the counsel, rather than the judgment, of friends, than that the envy of detractors, rushing upon them, should assail them. For God has called us in peace, and good things must be provided not only before him but also before human beings, so that, if possible, as far as depends on us, we may have peace with all [Rom. 12:17–18]. For the same Apostle earnestly instructs us to judge in this way, lest we place a stumbling block or an occasion of offense before a brother [Rom. 14].

“Nevertheless, whoever reads with a brotherly spirit, even if he receives no consolation or edification from these writings, will find in them nothing on account of which he ought to be scandalized or offended, as though by a presumptuous author. And, not to speak of edification, anyone who is a friend will bear with whatever foolishness there may be in me even in this; nor will he interpret my simplicity with an evil eye. This is especially so for the reason I stated above: namely, that I am altogether ignorant of public affairs and am now broken not only by age but also by infirmity. Unless under the protection of this study, I would by no means have been able to escape the dominion of idleness, which, according to the testimony of Scripture, ‘has taught many evils’ [Sirach 33:29].”

For this interpolation is absent from all editions published before Tissier; it is absent from the oldest manuscripts of all, nearly contemporary with the author—the Pontigny and Charlelieu manuscripts; likewise from that of Saint-Arnoul at Metz; from an old French translation of the same work, made four hundred years ago and still preserved at the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu; in a word, from almost all manuscripts, except the Signy manuscript, which Tissier used especially. For we know of no other in which it occurs.

Moreover, in this Signy manuscript, which our Martène carefully examined in his customary manner, the addition itself openly betrays itself as a spurious insertion made by some later pedant. It is written neither in the same hand nor in one nearly so old, but in a hand at least one hundred years later; moreover, it is written on shorter paper, not of the same size as the rest of the manuscript. Everyone can see that this was improperly done by that later pedant in order to secure the letter for William, whereas the manuscript, to his dissatisfaction—or rather not at all—attributed it to William. For at the beginning it bears this title: “This volume contains certain little works of Lord William, abbot of Saint-Theodoric, later monk of Signy.”

Then the Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu appears with this beginning: “To the lords and brothers H., Prior, etc., W. [wishes] a delightful Sabbath.” And at the end of book II: “The little work of Lord W. to the brothers of Mont-Dieu ends.” There follows the little book beginning, “It should be noted that there are two blessednesses,” etc., which is Guigo’s third book to the brothers of Mont-Dieu—although in the manuscript margin another, later hand has written, “Sermon of Lord Anselm.”

Here you see that the author’s name is abbreviated to its first letters only, whereas William’s is not so abbreviated: his full name is prefixed to the following little works. “Book of William, monk of Signy, called *The Mirror of Faith*.” “Excerpts from the meditations of Lord William.” “Book of Lord William called *The Enigma of Faith*.” “Exposition of Lord William on the Song of Songs.” Even this specimen clearly shows what we have said: the abbreviated name of Wigo, and the mixture of his letter with William’s genuine works, proved a stumbling block over which careless copyists fell.

10. Nor should it here be omitted that in another manuscript of the monastery of Charlelieu, about five hundred years old and different from the one praised above, the Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu occurs under the name of Saint Bernard but without any preface; whereas the third book is attributed in the same hand to Archbishop Anselm. The preface itself, with its interpolation, as Tissier and, after him, Mabillon published it, is placed after the letter, with this heading: “Here begins the prologue to the following little books of Lord William, sent to the brothers of Mont-Dieu. To the lords and brothers H., Prior,” and “H., brother W.” Then follow the two little books of Abbot William, namely *The Mirror of Faith* and *The Enigma of Faith*.

Thus the copyist was convinced that the whole Tisserian preface did not suit the letter and its author. Perhaps he had found the whole thing in the manuscript he was copying, but could not distinguish its spurious part from the genuine. Falling, therefore, into the opposite error, he preferred to attach it whole to William’s undisputed works, to which it partly corresponded, rather than prefix it to the letter.

11. One might also object the manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Theodoric near Reims, which Marlot saw, in which the works of Abbot William are listed and, among them, the little works which he sent to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, *On the Solitary Life*. But the manuscript is recent: according to Martène’s judgment, its handwriting is scarcely three hundred years old. It therefore has no authority sufficient to weaken the testimony of the older Pontigny and Charlelieu manuscripts. The same judgment must be passed on the Life of the same William in the Radoul manuscript, in which the Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu is attributed to him; but its author is not contemporary, indeed is much later.

12. A third difficulty, finally, arises from the succession of Priors of Mont-Dieu, compiled by the venerable Father François Gagneron, a monk of that same Charterhouse. He places Geoffrey first as Prior, and thinks that Haimo succeeded him—the Haimo to whom the letter is addressed—and that Gervase succeeded Haimo, and so on. Now, since Guigo died in 1137, he could not have written this letter to Haimo, who became Prior only in 1144. But the received opinion, which ascribes the letter to Abbot William, will suffer from precisely the same difficulty, if it is a difficulty at all. For the very reading of chapter 12 of the first book makes it plainly evident that it was written at the very beginnings of the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu, when those Carthusians, insufficiently mindful of the model they had seen on the mountain of the Greater Charterhouse—to which the author plainly alludes—were arranging for cells to be built for themselves somewhat more costly than eremitical simplicity allowed. It was therefore written about the year 1135, certainly before 1137, in which year we read that a charter was issued by Odo, abbot of Saint-Remigius, in which he says not only that he founded and endowed the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu, but also that he built it: “We have built a monastery . . . in the place now called Mont-Dieu . . . We have gladly given the aforesaid monastery, and whatever our church possesses within the precinct of that same monastery . . . free from every rent and exaction.”

Thus the monastery had already been built and completed, with cells sufficient for the number of monks. Yet in that year Haimo was not yet Prior, if any credit is to be given to Gagneron’s catalogue. He indeed connects the beginning of that Prior’s tenure with the year 1144, but offers no argument for this opinion; nor is there any record at the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu which can support it, as the Carthusians themselves admitted when questioned by Martène. In the necrology of the same monastery, written only about a hundred years ago, Geoffrey is called the first Prior. But, apart from the weak authority of so recent a manuscript, Geoffrey may have presided for a few months, and, upon his death, Haimo may immediately have been substituted for him. Certainly the Pontigny manuscript, written in 1156—that is, only a few years after Guigo’s death—and bearing the full names both of Guigo himself and of Haimo, ought to outweigh by far Gagneron’s unsupported opinion.

13. Let the letter to the brethren of Mont-Dieu, then, remain restored and vindicated as Guigo’s—the fifth Prior of the Greater Charterhouse. Since, as we have said, it was written while the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu was being built, and before Guigo’s death in 1137, it must have been written about 1135 or the following year. We here publish it as the manuscript codices present it: divided into three books, and carefully collated and corrected chiefly according to the Pontigny manuscript.

The third book has not yet appeared in print, although it is also found in the Signy manuscript. But after the addition to the preface mentioned above had been made, someone read there that this little work was divided into two booklets; misled by those words, he supposed that Guigo’s work ended with two books. Hence, after the end of the second book, another hand, in different ink, has rashly written in the small space lying between the second and third books: “The little work of Lord W. to the brethren of Mont-Dieu ends.” And in the margin of the third book: “A discourse of Lord Anselm.” Yet it has neither Anselm’s character nor his style, nor has it ever been counted among his works by anyone. Consequently, manuscripts copied afterwards from the Signy manuscript omitted the third book as though it were by another author. Yet it will be clear to every sober reader, both from the manuscripts cited above and from the reading of the book itself—its connection with what precedes, the sequence of its composition, and its style—that it is by one and the same author.

14. Although this letter is regarded by those outstanding in the same kind of life as a kind of most complete model of monastic life, John Gerson nevertheless warns the reader, in his sermon on the Lord’s Supper, “that Bernard’s work to the brethren of Mont-Dieu, book two,” here chapter 3, section 16, should “be read cautiously on this subject”—namely, the union of the perfect with God. There you see that the letter was then read as divided into at least two books.

[Col. 0307]

# THE LETTER OR TREATISE OF GUIGO, FIFTH PRIOR OF THE GREATER CHARTERHOUSE, TO THE BRETHREN OF MONT-DIEU. (G)*

## PREFACE

To his dearest brethren and lords, HAIMO, Prior, and the rest: GUIGO, a delightful Sabbath.

[Col. 0307A]

1. Almost shamelessly, and more freely than was fitting, my mouth opens to you, dearest brethren in Christ. I cannot be silent; God knows it. Forgive me, for my heart has been enlarged. Be enlarged yourselves also, I beseech you, in your affections, and receive us; for I am wholly yours in him in whose affections we desire one another.

Therefore, from the time I departed from you until now, I have determined to dedicate whatever daily labour of mine there may be, not to you, who have no need of it, but to Brother Stephen and his companions, the younger brethren, and to the novices coming to you, whose teacher is God alone: that they may possess and read it, if perhaps they find in it something useful to them for the consolation of their solitude and an incentive to their holy purpose [Col. 0307B]. I offer what I can: good will; and I ask this same thing back from you, with its fruits. David pleased God by dancing (2 Kings 6:14–23), not because of the dance, but because of his devotion. Likewise the woman who anointed the Lord’s feet was praised by Christ [Col. 0308A], not because she anointed them, but because she loved (Luke 7:37–48); and because she did what she had, she was justified in that act.

2. Next, I thought that I should dedicate to you as well [Note: [Col. 0307B] The printed editions add: “another little work.”] that which a necessity, more anxious than perilous, on the part of certain brethren compelled me to compose for their consolation and for the aid of their faith. Their sorrow is usually a great cause of joy to me—except that I cannot bear to see them sorrowful. For, because of the greatness not only of their faith but also of their love, they so detest whatever seems contrary to faith that, if they are assailed or struck even slightly on this point, whether by a spirit of blasphemy or by the very prompting of the flesh, they judge the purity of their conscience to be altogether wounded within themselves, as though by hearing or contact alone [Col. 0308B], and they lament themselves miserably as though reprobate concerning the faith.

This also happens to those who come from the darkness of the world to the disciplines of a purer life, as commonly happens to persons suddenly emerging into light after prolonged darkness: just as in such persons the very light by which other things are to be seen, when it first bursts upon them, becomes troublesome to weak eyes, so these men too, at their first encounter with the light of faith, see dimly and cannot endure the unfamiliar rays of a new light [Col. 0310A], until they become accustomed to them through love of that light itself.

# BOOK ONE

[Col. 0309]

## CHAPTER I. Rejoicing at the renewal of the fervour of ancient religious life.

[Col. 0309A]

1. To the brethren of Mont-Dieu, who bring the eastern light and that ancient Egyptian fervour in religious life into western darkness and Gallic cold; who offer an example of solitary life and a pattern of heavenly conduct [Col. 0309B]: my soul exults to meet and join you in the joy of the Holy Spirit, in the heart’s laughter of fervent devotion, and in every service of devoted will.

And why should it not? For we ought to feast and rejoice in the Lord, because the fairest portion of Christian devotion and religious life—seeming to touch heaven more nearly—was dead and has come to life again; it had perished from the world and has been found. We had heard with the hearing of the ear, yet did not believe. We read in books and marvelled at the ancient glory of solitary life and at God’s great grace within it; when suddenly we found it in the fields of the forest, upon the mountain of God, the rich mountain. There already the beautiful places of the wilderness grow fat from it, and the hills gird themselves with exultation.

For there through you it offers itself to all, displays itself in you, and—hitherto unknown—makes itself known in a few simple men, through him who instils it into you, who formerly subjected the whole world to himself in a few simple men, while the world marvelled [Col. 0309C]. For though the miracles which the Lord performed on earth were great and plainly divine, this one nevertheless shone out above all others and illuminated all the rest: as was said, he subjected the whole world and all the height of its wisdom to himself in a few simple men. This he has now begun to do in you. Yes, Father, yes: for so it has pleased you. For you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent of this world and revealed them to little ones (Matthew 11:26, 25). Therefore do not fear, little flock, says the Lord, but have complete confidence, because it has pleased God the Father to give you the kingdom (Luke 12:32).

[Col. 0309D]

2. See, my brethren, see your calling. Where is the wise man among you? Where the scribe? Where the inquirer of this age? (1 Corinthians 1:26, 20.) For even if there are some wise persons among you, yet through simple wise persons he has gathered you together—he who formerly subjected to himself the kings and philosophers of this world through fishermen.

Allow, then, allow the wise of this world—swollen with the spirit of this world, thinking lofty thoughts and licking the earth—to descend wisely into hell. But while a pit is being dug for the sinner, you, as you have begun, having become foolish for God’s sake, with Christ as your leader—through the foolishness of God, which is wiser than all men—take hold of the humble discipline by which one ascends to heaven.

For your simplicity already provokes many to emulation; your entirely sufficient and lofty poverty already confounds the greed of many; your seclusion already inspires in many a dread of things which cause, or appear to cause, disturbance [Col. 0310A]. Therefore, if there is any consolation in Christ, any comfort of love, any fellowship of the Spirit, any tenderness [Col. 0310B] of mercy, fulfil the joy not only of myself, but of all who love the Lord’s name: so that, amid the variety of the gold-embroidered garment of the queen standing at the bridegroom’s right hand—the gold being God’s wisdom—by your zeal and persistence, to God’s glory, to your great crown, and to the joy of all good people, this ornament of holy newness may be renewed.

3. I call it “newness,” however, on account of malicious tongues—may God hide you from their contradiction in the hiding-place of his countenance—among ungodly people. Since they cannot obscure the manifest light of truth, they scoff at the name of newness alone: old men themselves, and with an old mind incapable of contemplating new things, old wineskins unable to receive new wine, which, if it were poured into them, would burst them.

But this newness is not novel vanity [Col. 0310C]. It is a matter of ancient religion, of devotion perfectly founded in Christ, an ancient inheritance of God’s Church, foreshown from the time of the Prophets. When the sun of new grace had already arisen, it was restored and born anew in John the Baptist; it was practiced most intimately by the Lord himself, and desired by his disciples while he was present. When those who were with him on the holy mountain saw the glory of his transfiguration, Peter at once—rapt, indeed, away from himself and not knowing what he said, because, upon seeing God’s majesty, he seemed to have enclosed the common good within his own private possession; yet wholly present to himself and knowing very well what he said, because, having tasted its sweetness, he judged it best always to remain there—desired this life in the companionship of God and the citizens of heaven whom he had seen with him [Col. 0310D], saying: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, let us make three tents here: one for you, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matthew 17:4). If he had been heard in this, without doubt he would afterwards have made three more: one for himself, one for James, and one for John.

4. After the Lord’s Passion, while the fresh memory of his shed blood still burned in the hearts of the faithful, the deserts were filled with those choosing this solitary life, pursuing poverty of spirit, and striving with one another for the rich leisure of spiritual exercises and contemplation of God. From among them we read of Pauls, Macarii, Anthonys, Arseniuses [Col. 0311A], and many others: consular men in the commonwealth of this holy way of life; outstanding names in the city of God; bearing noble and triumphant titles for victory over this world, the prince of this world, and their own bodies, through the cultivation of their minds and devotion to the Lord their God.

Let those, then, who judge light while in darkness and accuse you of novelty out of an abundance of ill will, be silent. They themselves should rather be accused of antiquatedness and vanity. Yet you will always have both admirers and detractors, as the Lord did. Pass over the admirers; and love in them the good which they love in you. Ignore the detractors, and pray for them. Forgetting what lies behind, and setting aside the stumbling-blocks placed beside your path on right and left, stretch yourselves toward what lies before you. For if you wish either to answer each admirer [Col. 0311B] or to quarrel with detractors, you waste time, whose loss is no small matter in a holy purpose. One who hastens from earth to heaven is greatly harmed by whoever delays him, even if he does not detain him.

## CHAPTER II. How arduous and lofty their profession is.

5. Therefore do not neglect it; do not betray it. For a great journey remains before you. Your profession is most lofty. It passes beyond the heavens; it is equal to angels and akin to angelic purity. For you have vowed not merely all holiness, but the perfection of all holiness and the end of every consummation. It is not for you to languish around common commandments, or merely to consider what God commands; rather, you are to discern what he wills, proving what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God [Col. 0311C] (Romans 12:2).

It belongs to others to serve God; to you, to cleave to him. It belongs to others to believe, know, love, and reverence God; to you, to taste, understand, recognize, and enjoy him. This is great; this is arduous. But God is omnipotent and good: in you he is a gracious promiser, a faithful fulfiller, and an untiring helper. To those who, through great love of him, profess great things; who, in faith and hope of his grace, undertake things greater than their strength, he gives both will and desire for that very end. And he who bestowed the grace of willing also adds the strength needed for success. When a person has faithfully done what he could, God himself, despite the accusation of the accuser, will mercifully judge the case and cause of his poor servant [Col. 0311D], because he did what he had.

6. Yet let every exalted thought be far from your self-estimation in conscience, from your lowliness and humility, and from your mouth. For to think lofty thoughts is death; and it is easy for one looking at himself on high to grow dizzy and to endanger his life. Give your profession another name; inscribe another title upon your order. Consider and call yourselves rather untamed wild creatures and beasts not yet shut in a pen—such as could not otherwise be tamed by the ordinary manner of men—looking far above yourselves to the virtue of those men and admiring the glory of those mighty men skilled with both hands, like Ehud, that most valiant judge of Israel, who used either hand as his right hand (Judges 3:15). So long as they are permitted, they most devoutly love to remain at leisure within, for the love of contemplating truth [Col. 0312A]; and when necessity calls or duty draws them, they most readily lend themselves outwardly—not give themselves—for truth’s sake, to fulfil love.

Take care also, servant of God, lest you appear to condemn any whom you do not wish to imitate. I want you, in your sickness, to do what he did when he was most sound, who said: “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first” (1 Timothy 1:15). Paul said this not with the rashness of lying, but from the disposition of his judgment. For one who understands himself through perfect self-examination judges no one’s sin equal to his own, because he does not understand another’s sin as he understands his own.

Therefore I do not want you to suppose that the common sun shines nowhere but in your cell, that nowhere is serene except with you [Col. 0312B], or that God’s grace works nowhere except in your conscience. Is God the God of solitaries only? Indeed, he is God of all. For God has mercy on all, and hates none of the things he has made (Wisdom 11:25). I would rather have you think that everywhere is serene except with you, and think worse of yourself than of anyone else.

## CHAPTER III. Virtue must be diligently cultivated as an example for posterity.

7. Rather work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. Consider not what others are, but what, so far as lies within you, may be made from among you: not only those who are now present, but also those yet to come, whom you will have as imitators in this holy purpose. For upon you, your example, and your authority depends throughout this region the entire future of this holy order of yours [Col. 0312C]. In it you will be called fathers and founders by your successors, with the due reverence of imitation.

Whatever is established by you, whatever, while you retain and observe it, is admitted into custom, must be held and observed by your descendants without any reconsideration; nor will it be lawful to alter anything. For their attitude toward you will be like ours toward the immutable laws of highest and eternal truth: it benefits all to examine and know them, but no one may pass judgment on them.

But thanks be to God that this will neither be unworthy of you nor useless to posterity, if you yourselves hold fast faithfully and courageously, and they in turn faithfully imitate in you what you now maintain. And if you ought still to think otherwise on any point, God will reveal this also to you. For, while preserving in every respect the due holiness of the Charterhouse, and its reverence, which should be extolled with every praise, many things are necessary amid those harsh and continuous Alpine cold regions which do not appear so necessary in these regions to people pursuing frugal sufficiency and voluntary poverty [Col. 0312D].

8. You understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding. For I rejoice in you; though absent in body, I am present in spirit. Seeing your order, the fervour of your spirit, the abundance of your peace, the grace of your simplicity, strictness in purpose, in mutual love the very sweetness of the Holy Spirit, and in your entire manner of life a full form of godliness [Col. 0313A], I wholly exult at the remembrance of Mont-Dieu and devoutly adore the firstfruits of the Holy Spirit and the pledge of grace in the hope of the religious life growing there.

For the very name “Mont-Dieu” bears an omen of good hope: namely, that, as the Psalmist says of God’s mountain, there shall dwell upon it the generation of those who seek the Lord, who seek the face of the God of Jacob—those innocent in hands and clean in heart, who have not received their soul in vain (Psalm 23:6, 4). This is your profession: to seek the God of Jacob, not in the common fashion of human beings, but to seek the face of God—which Jacob saw when he said: “I have seen the Lord face to face, and my life has been preserved” (Genesis 32:30).

To seek God’s face—that is, his knowledge—face to face, as Jacob saw it, concerning which the Apostle also said, “Then I shall know as I also am known; now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12); “we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2): godliness itself teaches us always to seek this in this life through innocence of hands and purity of heart. As Job says, according to the Septuagint, this is the worship of God (Job 28:28). Whoever does not possess it has received his soul in vain; that is, he lives fruitlessly, or does not truly live at all, since he does not live the life for which he received his soul, in order to live it.

## CHAPTER IV. What true godliness is; what solitude is; and what enclosure in a cell befits religious persons.

9. This godliness is the unceasing remembrance of God, the continuous activity of the mind directed toward understanding him, and untiring affection for loving him: so that no day—not even an hour—ever finds the servant of God except either at the labour of spiritual exercise and the pursuit of progress, or in the sweetness of experience and the joy of enjoyment [Col. 0313C].

This is the godliness about which the Apostle admonishes his beloved disciple, saying: “Train yourself in godliness. Bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for every good work, holding the promise of the life which now is and of that which is to come” (1 Timothy 4:7–8). For your habit promises, and your purpose requires, not merely the form of godliness, but its truth, in all things and before all things. For, as the same Apostle says, “There are some who have the form of godliness but deny its power” [Col. 0313D] (2 Timothy 3:5).

Whoever among you does not possess this in conscience, display it in life, and exercise it in the cell, ought to be called not solitary but alone; and for him the cell is not a cell but confinement and prison. For he is truly alone with whom God is not; he is truly confined who is not free in God. Solitude and confinement are names of misery; but a cell should by no means be the compulsory confinement of necessity, but the dwelling-place of peace: a closed door, not a hiding-place, but a place of secrecy.

10. For the person with whom God is is never less alone than when alone. Then he freely enjoys his joy; then he belongs to himself, to enjoy God in himself and himself in God. Then, in the light of truth and the serenity of a pure heart, his pure conscience freely lies open to him, and an affectionate remembrance of God freely pours itself out within him. Either his understanding is enlightened and his affection enjoys its good; or he freely weeps over the failures of human frailty.

For this reason, in accordance with the form of your purpose, dwelling rather in heaven than in cells, having excluded the whole world from yourselves, you have enclosed your whole selves with God. The dwelling of the cell and that of heaven are kindred, because, just as *coelum* (“heaven”) and *cella* (“cell”) seem to have a certain kinship in name, so too in godliness. For heaven and cell seem to derive their names from concealment (*celare*); and what is hidden in heaven is hidden also in cells; what is done in heaven is done also in cells. What is this? To be at leisure for God; to enjoy God.

When this is devoutly and faithfully practiced in cells according to due order [Col. 0314B], I dare to say that God’s holy angels regard cells as heavens and delight in cells as much as in heaven. For when heavenly things are constantly enacted in a cell, heaven is made near to the cell by likeness of mystery, by the affection of godliness, and by the love of similar work. Thus the praying spirit—or even the spirit departing from the body—finds no long or difficult road from cell to heaven.

From the cell one often ascends to heaven; but one scarcely ever descends from the cell to hell, except as the Psalmist says: “Let them go down alive into hell” (Psalm 54:16)—that is, lest they go down when dead. In this manner, indeed, inhabitants of cells often descend into hell. For just as they love continually to revisit heavenly joys by contemplation, that they may desire them more ardently, so they revisit the pains of hell, that they may dread and shun them [Col. 0314C]. And this is what they pray against their enemies: that they may go down alive into hell.

But scarcely or never does anyone descend from a cell to hell when dying, because scarcely anyone perseveres in it until death unless he is predestined for heaven.

11. For the cell cherishes, nourishes, embraces, and leads to the fullness of perfection the child of grace, the fruit of its womb; it makes him worthy of converse with God. But it quickly disowns and casts out one who is alien or substituted. Hence the Lord says to Moses: “Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5).

A corpse of dead affections, or a person dead in heart, is not long tolerated by a holy place or holy ground. The cell is holy ground and a holy place [Col. 0314D], in which the Lord and his servant often converse as a man with his friend.
