There the faithful soul is frequently joined to the Word of God; bride is united to bridegroom; heavenly things to earthly, divine things to human. For, just as the temple of God is holy, so is the cell of God’s servant.

Divine things are handled both in the temple and in the cell, but more frequently in the cell. In the temple the mysteries of Christian godliness are at times dispensed visibly and figuratively; but in cells, as in heaven, the very reality of all the mysteries of our faith is constantly celebrated in its own truth and order, though not yet in the very majesty of purity or the security of eternity.

Therefore, as was said, the cell quickly casts out the alien who is not a son, like an untimely birth; it vomits him out like useless and harmful food [Col. 0315A]. The workshop of godliness cannot long endure such a person in its womb. The foot of pride comes and the hand of the sinner carries him away and moves him; expelled, he cannot stand, but flees wretched, naked, and trembling, like Cain from the face of the Lord, exposed to vices and demons, so that whoever first finds him may kill him by the death of the soul.

Or if he remains there for some time, it is not through constancy of virtue but through stubborn misery; the cell is for him like a prison, or like a burial-place for one alive. But “when a pestilent man is scourged, the wise man will become wiser” (Proverbs 19:25), and “the righteous will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Psalm 57:11).

Therefore, as the prophet says: “If you return, O Israel, return to me” (Jeremiah 4:1); that is, attain the summit of perfect conversion. No one is permitted to remain long in the same state. The servant of God must either always advance or decline: he either strives upward or is pressed downward.

Yet perfection is required of all of you, though not in a uniform manner. But if you begin, begin perfectly; if you are already advancing, do even that perfectly; if you have attained anything of perfection, measure yourself within yourself and say with the Apostle: “Not that I have already attained, or am already perfect; but I pursue, if perhaps I may grasp that for which I too have been grasped. But one thing: forgetting what lies behind and stretching myself toward what lies ahead, I press toward the goal, toward the prize of the upward calling in Christ Jesus.” Then he adds: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this” (Philippians 3:12–15).

In this the Apostle’s teaching plainly declares that perfect forgetfulness of what lies behind and perfect stretching toward what lies before is the perfection of the righteous person in this life; and the perfection of this perfection will be there, where the prize of the heavenly calling is perfectly attained.

## CHAPTER V. The threefold state of religious life: the animal, rational, and spiritual; or, respectively, that of beginners, those advancing, and the perfect.

12. In this way, as star differs from star in glory, so cell differs from cell in manner of life: namely, those of beginners, those advancing, and the perfect. The state of beginners may be called animal; that of those advancing, rational; that of the perfect, spiritual. In some things, at times, allowance must be made for persons who are still animal, in which allowance ought not to be made for those already regarded as rational [Col. 0315D]. Again, rational persons are excused in certain things in which spiritual persons are not excused, since all things in the latter ought to be perfect and worthy rather of imitation and praise than of rebuke.

Since the whole state of religious life consists of these three classes of persons, distinguished by their proper names and also recognized by the distinctive quality of their pursuits, all God’s children who are in the day ought always to consider diligently what they lack; whence they have come; how far they have reached; and in what stage of progress their own judgment finds them on each day or hour.

There are animal persons who are neither guided by reason nor drawn by affection of themselves [Col. 0316A]. Yet, moved by authority, admonished by teaching, or stirred by example, they approve the good wherever they find it and, like blind persons led by the hand, follow—that is, imitate. There are rational persons who, through the judgment of reason and the discernment of natural knowledge, possess both knowledge and desire of the good, but do not yet possess affection. There are perfect persons, who are led by the Spirit and more fully enlightened by the Holy Spirit. Because the good toward which they are drawn by affection is savoury to them, they are called wise. And because the Holy Spirit, by whose affection they are drawn, clothes them—as Scripture once says of Gideon that the Spirit clothed him—they are called spiritual.

The first state concerns the body; the second exercises itself concerning the soul; the third has rest only in God [Col. 0316B]. Each, as it has a definite method of progress, so has within its kind a definite measure of its own perfection.

The beginning of good in an animal mode of life is perfect obedience; its progress is to subject one’s body and reduce it to servitude; its perfection is, through practice of the good, to transform habit into delight. The beginning of the rational person is to understand what is set before him in the teaching of faith; his progress, to prepare such things as are set before him; his perfection, when the judgment of reason passes into the affection of the mind. The perfection of the rational person is the beginning of the spiritual person; his progress is to behold the glory of God with unveiled face; his perfection, to be transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord.

13. To proceed first, then, with the first state, namely the animal: animality is a manner of life serving the senses of the body. It is present when the soul, as if outside itself, is affected through bodily senses by the pleasures of beloved bodies, and by enjoying them feeds or nourishes its sensuality. Or it is present when the soul returns within itself; unable to carry with itself into the place of incorporeal nature the bodies to which it has adhered by the strong glue of love and habit, it draws their images there with it and amicably associates with them there.

Accustomed to such things, it thinks nothing exists except what it left outside or what it has taken in within itself; and therefore, as long as it may, it finds pleasure in living according to the body’s delights [Col. 0316C]. But when it is overthrown from them, it knows no way of thinking except by imagining bodily things. When it raises itself to think of spiritual or divine things, it can form no estimate of them other than in terms of bodies or bodily things.

Turned away from God, this becomes folly when it is too much abandoned within itself and grows so brutish that it either will not or cannot be ruled. But when through pride it is excessively carried away from itself, it becomes the prudence of the flesh; and it seems to itself to be wisdom, though it is folly, as the Apostle says: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1:22).

But turned toward God, it becomes holy simplicity: that is, a will always directed toward the same object, as it was in Job, who was called a simple and upright man, fearing God (Job 1:1). Properly speaking, simplicity is a will perfectly converted to God, asking one thing from the Lord and seeking it, not desiring to be multiplied in the world [Col. 0317A]. Or simplicity is true humility in one’s manner of life: embracing consciousness of virtue rather than reputation, so that the simple person does not shrink from seeming foolish in the world in order to be wise in God. Or simplicity is a will turned toward God alone, but not yet formed by reason so as to be love—that is, formed will—not yet illumined so as to be charity, that is, the delight of love.

14. Simplicity, therefore, possessing within itself some beginning of God’s creature—that is, a simple and good will, like the unformed material of the future good person—at the outset of its conversion offers that will to its Author to be formed. For, already possessing with a good will the beginning of wisdom, that is, the fear of the Lord, it gathers from this very fact that it can neither be formed by itself [Col. 0317B] nor that anything is so expedient for the foolish as to serve the wise. Thus, submitting itself to a human being for God’s sake, it entrusts to him that very good will, to be formed in God in a humble mind and spirit. Now the fear of God begins to work in it the whole fullness of virtues: through justice it yields to one greater; through prudence it does not trust itself to itself; through temperance it declines to make distinctions; through fortitude it subjects its whole self to obedience—not obedience that judges, but obedience that fulfils.

For this is the wife to whom the Lord says: “Your turning shall be toward your husband” (Gen. III, 16). Her husband is her own reason or spirit, or that of another. A simple and upright man rightly obeys this husband within himself; but often he obeys more rightly and more safely in another than in himself. Therefore, by God’s command and by the very order of nature, [Col. 0317C] the wife must have toward her husband, animality toward its spirit or toward some spiritual man, a lawful turning—that is, perfect obedience. Perfect obedience, especially in one beginning, is undiscriminating: that is, it does not distinguish what is commanded or why it is commanded, but strives only that what a superior commands may be done faithfully and humbly.

For the tree of the knowledge of good and evil in paradise is the authority of discernment in religious life, belonging to the spiritual father, who judges all things, while he himself is judged by no one. It belongs to him to discern; it belongs to others to obey. Adam tasted, to his own harm, of the forbidden tree, instructed by him who suggested: “Why did God command you not to eat of the tree?” Behold discernment of why the command was given. And he adds: [Col. 0317D] “For he knew that on the day when you eat, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods” (ibid., 1, 5). Behold the purpose for which the command was given—namely, that it might prevent them from becoming gods. He made a distinction, ate, became disobedient, and was expelled from paradise.

Likewise, it is impossible for the discerning animal man, the prudent novice, the wise beginner, to remain long in his cell or to endure in the community. Let him become foolish, that he may be wise; and let this be all his discernment: that in this matter he has no discernment. Let this be all his wisdom: that in this respect he has none.

## CHAPTER VI. God gave man an intellect capable of diverse arts and sciences; some use it badly, others well.

[Col. 0318A]

15. At the boundary where animality and reason meet within themselves, the good Creator left in the nature of the human soul intellect and natural ability; and in ability, art. By these God set man over the works of His hands and subjected all these worldly things beneath his feet: to the proud animal man, as testimony to his natural dignity and to the likeness of God which he has lost; but to the simple and humble man, as an aid toward recovering that dignity and preserving that likeness.

“In them that which is known of God is manifest” (Rom. I, 19). By this the Creator is judged from the creature. [Col. 0318B] By this the justice of God is known: that those who do well are worthy of life, while those who act otherwise are worthy of death. By this the creature, which willingly serves man, is subjected and adapted to nature, so that it may serve the necessity arising from sin, as well as will and pleasure. Hence it is plain to everyone how many and how great are the things made and being made—necessary for this life, useful to good and evil alike, beautiful in their kind, and produced by both good and evil persons.

For from this source, in letters, crafts, and buildings, through the innumerably manifold inventions of human beings, there have arisen so many forms of study, so many kinds of professions, refinements, carefully developed branches of knowledge, arts, eloquences, varieties of ranks and offices, and countless acquisitions of this world. [Col. 0318C] The men called wise in this world use them together with the simple and the children of God, alike for need and utility. But the former misuse them for curiosity, pleasure, and pride; the latter use them from necessity, having their delight elsewhere.

Therefore the fruits of their flesh follow those who are slaves of their own senses and bodies: fornication, impurity, pride, luxury, enmities, strife, jealousies, angers, quarrels, dissensions, envies, revelries, drunkenness, and things like these. Those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God. But these are the fruits of the Spirit: charity, joy, peace, patience, kindness, long-suffering, goodness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity (Gal. V, 19–23), [Col. 0318D] and godliness, which has the promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come (I Tim. IV, 8).

16. While both sorts are engaged in action, human beings see similar actions, but God distinguishes wills and intentions. When each returns to his own interior, his own conscience feeds each one on the fruits of his intention. Yet one does not return equally to conscience from both paths, since no one loves to return to it after acting if he did not proceed from it to action with a right intention.

Nevertheless, the person who returns to conscience, if he has not yet conquered his desire, finds there either pleasant delights from that desire or grievous gnawings because of it; and from this he multiplies thoughts. But one who has already conquered desire, [Col. 0319A] so long as a greater desire or a greater delight in the true good has not taken possession of his mind, suffers—with a kind of hateful pleasure—the images of things done, seen, or heard. Thus in both cases “the loins” are filled with delusions of pleasures, and for thinking on divine or spiritual things “the light of their eyes—it also is not with them.” He who fights against desires suffers hardships, because he is not yet fully able to conquer his affections. But he who already aspires to freedom cannot shake from himself the images of affections and the harmful, distracting, or idle thoughts which arise from them on every side.

Hence, at the time of psalmody, prayer, and the other spiritual exercises, images turn over in the heart of God’s servant, even when he is unwilling [Col. 0319B] and resisting, and phantasms of thoughts move about. Like unclean birds settling upon or circling around him, they either snatch the sacrifice of devotion entirely from the hand that holds it, or often defile it even to the tears of the one offering it.

Then there arises a pitiable and wrongful division within the wretched soul. Spirit and reason defend the heart’s will, its intention, and the body’s ready obedience to themselves; while animal perversity seizes for itself affection and intellect, and the mind often remains fruitless. Hence, in weaker souls, and in those in whom the desires of flesh and world have not yet been perfectly mortified, the vices of curiosity boil up everywhere. Hence come disordered consolations of solitude and silence, hostile to one’s purpose; secret bypaths of one’s own will upon the royal road of common observances; weariness with accustomed things and presumption in novelties. [Col. 0319C] These seem, as though by scratching, to ease for an hour the itching and weariness of a sick mind; but they heat and inflame it, making it afterwards burn more wickedly and itch more intensely.

Hence new occupations arise every day, new inventions of actions and labors, and varied readings—not to build up the soul, but to deceive the weariness of the slow-moving day. Thus, when the solitary has condemned everything old and familiar, and novelty has failed him, nothing remains but hatred of the cell and a premature flight.

17. For this reason devout simplicity—and the new man in the profession of religion and solitude, who has neither reason to guide him, nor affection to draw him, nor discernment to moderate him, but uses a certain force upon himself as a thing fashioned by the potter—must be made and formed, as it were by foreign hands, according to a law of God’s commandments, in all patience, on the wheel of turning obedience, and in the fire of his testing. [Col. 0319D] He must be subjected to the will and judgment of his maker and fashioner.

For even if he is skilled in natural ability, vigorous in art, or eminent in intellect, these are instruments of vices as well as virtues. Therefore let him not refuse to be taught to use for good that which he can use also for evil; for this is the proper work of virtue. Let natural ability adapt the body, art give form to nature, and intellect make the soul teachable rather than proud. For natural ability, art, intellect, and things of this sort are possessed gratuitously; virtue is otherwise. [Col. 0320A] Virtue wishes to be taught with humility, sought with labor, and possessed with love. For it is worthy of all these; nor can it otherwise be taught, sought, or possessed.

## CHAPTER VII. What a religious novice, or an untrained hermit, must first be taught.

18. Therefore the inexperienced inhabitant of the wilderness must first be taught, according to the apostolic instruction of Paul, to present his body as “a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God, his reasonable service.” Paul also, restraining in the novice fervor the animal man, who does not yet perceive the things of God, from premature and curious inquiry into spiritual and divine things, added: “For I say, through the grace [Col. 0320B] of God given to me, to all who are among you: do not be wise beyond what it is fitting to be wise, but be wise unto sobriety” (Rom. XII, 1, 3).

Since all, or especially the principal, training of the animal man concerns the body and the ordering of the outward man, he must be taught reasonably to mortify his body and his members that are upon the earth; and, between flesh and spirit, which continually desire against one another, to make a just judgment of reason and discernment, accepting the person of neither in judgment. He must be taught to regard his body as an entrusted sick person: even when it strongly desires something, useless things must be denied it, while useful things must be imposed even against its will.

He must deal with it as with something not his own, but belonging to Him by whom we were bought at a great price, so that we may glorify [Col. 0320C] Him in our body (I Cor. VI, 20). Again, he must be taught to beware of what the Lord reproaches the sinful people for through the prophet: “You have cast me,” He says, “behind your back” (I Reg. X, 19). He must take great care lest, for this life’s necessities or conveniences, he allow his spirit to decline in any respect from the uprightness of its purpose or the dignity of its nature into love or honor of its own body.

Therefore the body must be treated more harshly, lest it rebel or grow insolent—yet so that it remains capable of serving, because it was given to serve the spirit. It must not be treated as though we lived for its sake, but as something without which we cannot live. For the covenant that we have with the body cannot be broken whenever we wish; rather, we must patiently await its lawful dissolution [Col. 0320D] and meanwhile observe what belongs to the lawful covenant.

19. Thus we must live with it, or come to terms with it, as though we were not to remain with it long; and in such a way that, should it turn out otherwise, we are not compelled to depart. This would require much anxious labor and would often entail dangerous error, unless the law of obedience and the cell, once and for all delivering a complete form of common observance, made the entering brother obedient, patient, quiet, and henceforth cautious and secure concerning food and clothing, work and rest, silence and solitude, and everything pertaining to the discipline or necessity of the outward man.

In these matters everything has once for all been cut away and superfluities removed; everything necessary has been bounded within the limits of suitable sufficiency and general restraint. [Col. 0321A] Thus there is what the strong may desire and the weak need not reject; the quantity of things permitted can no longer in any way harm the conscience of those who use them with thanksgiving; nor should what has been removed be able in any measure to tempt the sufficiency of the body in God’s servant, when that body is well disciplined and rightly trained.

In these things, as Solomon says: “He who walks simply walks securely; but he who is hard of mind shall fall into evil” (Prov. X, 9). For although necessity is so ordered that no place remains for complaint and every superfluity has been cut away, if anything is to be added or diminished, publicly or privately, this rests in the Prior’s judgment, [Col. 0321B] without any scruple or danger to obedient subjects.

20. The new hermit must therefore be trained, according to the rule of common observance, continually to subdue the desires of his flesh through penance for past sins, and, in despising all else, to arrive at contempt for himself. He must be continually fortified against temptations, which rage more fiercely against the solitary novice. For vices do not cease to solicit God’s servant, who serves God gratuitously, with the reward of offered pleasure: the devil suggesting, the flesh desiring, and the world presenting desirable things.

For the Lord our God tests us whether we love Him or not—not that He Himself, as though ignorant, may learn it, but that it may become more fully known to us in the temptation itself. [Col. 0321C] Those temptations, however, are easily overcome and reason easily meets them which are either suspect or plainly known at first sight to be evil. But those which present themselves under the appearance of good are more difficult to discern and more dangerously admitted. For just as moderation is held most difficultly in what is believed to be good, so not every desire for good is always safe.

## CHAPTER VIII. How greatly idleness must be avoided by every religious person, especially the solitary; and which occupations are suitable for him.

21. The cesspool of all temptations and evil and useless thoughts is idleness. For the highest wickedness of the mind is inert idleness. Let God’s servant never be idle, even though God has granted him leisure. [Col. 0321D] So suspect, empty, and soft a name ought not to be applied to a matter so certain, holy, and severe. To devote oneself to God is not idleness; indeed, it is the business of all businesses.

Whoever does not faithfully and fervently perform this in his cell, whatever else he does which he does not do for this purpose—namely, that God may be served—is idle in what he does. It is ridiculous to pursue idle things in order to avoid idleness. But idleness is that which has no usefulness or intention of usefulness. One must not merely act so that the day may pass with some pleasure or without great nausea of idleness; rather, something from the completed day must always remain in the conscience for the soul’s advancement, and something must be gathered daily into the treasury of the heart. Nor should a good dweller in a cell reckon that he has lived well on a day [Col. 0322A] in which he remembers having done none of those things for which one lives in a cell.

22. Do you ask what you should do, or with what you should occupy yourself? First, besides the daily sacrifice of prayers and the study of reading, a part of each day must be set apart for examining one’s conscience, amendment, and the ordering of one’s conduct. Then something should be done with the hands, as commanded—not so much something that holds the mind for an hour by delighting it, as something that preserves and nourishes delight in spiritual studies. Let the mind be relaxed for an hour in it, not dissipated; so that, when it sees that it must return to itself, it may readily disengage itself, without conflict from a restraining will, without contagion from a pleasure acquired or from an imagining memory.

“For the man is not for the woman, but the woman for the man” (I Cor. XI, 9). Bodily exercises do not exist for spiritual exercises; bodily exercises exist for spiritual ones. Therefore, just as when the man was created, a helper like himself was given or joined to him from human substance itself, so bodily exercises are necessary as assistance to spiritual study. [Col. 0322B] Yet not all bodily exercises seem equally suitable for this purpose at all times, but rather those which appear to have a closer likeness and affinity with spiritual exercises—for example, meditating upon what is to be written, or writing what is read.

Outdoor exercises and work, just as they distract the senses, often also exhaust the spirit, unless the heavier labor of rural work brings greater contrition of body, even unto contrition and humiliation of heart. For the pressure of more vehement fatigue often expresses an affection of devotion. It is evident that this frequently happens also in the labor of fasts, vigils, and all practices involving bodily affliction.

23. Yet the serious and prudent mind prepares itself for every labor; it is not dissolved in labor, but is instead gathered more fully into itself through it. Keeping before its eyes not so much what it does as the end at which it aims in doing it, it attends to the end of every undertaking. In proportion as it relies more truly upon that end, it works more fervently with faithful hands, subjecting to itself the service of its whole body. The senses are compelled together under the discipline of good will; under the weight of labor they have no leisure for wantonness; subdued and [Col. 0322D] humbled into service of the spirit, they are taught to conform to it both in sharing its labor and in awaiting consolation.

For nature, disordered by sin and turned aside from the rectitude of its condition, if it is turned toward God, quickly recovers, in proportion to its fear and love of God, whatever it lost by turning away. And when the spirit begins to be re-formed in the image of its Creator, the flesh too, flowering anew of its own accord, immediately begins to conform to the re-formed spirit. For, even contrary to its former inclination, it begins to delight in whatever delights its spirit. Moreover, because of its manifold deficiency arising from the punishment of sin, thirsting in many ways for God, it sometimes even strives to precede its ruler.

For we do not lose pleasures, but change them [Col. 0323A] from body to soul, from the senses to conscience. Bran bread, plain water, vegetables, and simple legumes are by no means delightful things; yet, in Christ’s love and in desire for inward delight, to be able gladly to satisfy a well-disciplined belly with these things is greatly delightful. How many thousands of poor people pleasantly satisfy nature with these, or with some one of them? Indeed, with the seasoning of God’s love added, it would be most easy and delightful to live according to nature, if our madness allowed us to do so. Once that madness is cured, nature at once smiles upon natural things.

The same is true of labor. The farmer has hard sinews and strong arms: exercise produces this. Let him become idle, and he grows soft. Will produces use, use produces exercise, and exercise supplies strength for every [Col. 0323B] labor.

24. But let us return to our subject. Let both our labor and our leisure achieve this by every means: that we may never be idle. And let this always be our business: that there may be perfectly fulfilled in us what the Apostle says to animal and beginning persons: “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For as you presented your members to serve impurity and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. VI, 19).

Let the animal man, hitherto the slave and friend of his body, hear this; he now begins to subject his body to the spirit and adapt himself to perceiving the things of God, and he must gird himself to cast off, through faith, the necessity of slavery and the ruling habit of [Col. 0323C] his flesh. Let him make necessity for himself against necessity, habit against habit, and form affection against affection, until he deserves more fully to receive delight against delight. Thus, according to the Apostle’s counsel, let deprivation of fleshly and worldly pleasures delight him at least as much as their possession once delighted him; and let service of the members of his body to righteousness unto sanctification delight him as much as service to impurity and iniquity unto iniquity previously delighted him.

This is the perfection of the animal man in his state, or of the beginning novice. When he has completed this animal or human stage, if he does not look back but faithfully stretches himself toward the things before him, he will soon arrive at that divine stage: he will begin to apprehend as he has been apprehended, and to know as he has been known. But this work is not accomplished in one moment of conversion; it is not the work of one day, but of much time, much labor, and much sweat, according to the grace of the merciful God and the effort of the human being who wills and runs.

## CHAPTER IX. Stability in the cell is commended, and guardians are appointed.

25. The workshop of all these goods is the cell and stable perseverance in it. Whoever is well content there with his poverty is rich; and whoever has a good will has with him everything necessary for living well. Yet it is not always expedient to trust good will: it must be checked and governed, especially in the beginner. Let the rule of holy obedience govern good will, and let good will govern the body, teaching it to remain in one place, endure the cell, and dwell with itself. This is the beginning of a good disposition in one making progress, and a sure token of good hope. [Col. 0324A]

For it is impossible for a person faithfully to fix his mind upon one thing if he has not first persistently fixed his body to some place. One who endeavors to escape a sickness of the mind by moving from place to place is like one fleeing the shadow of his own body. He flees himself and carries himself about; he changes place, not mind. He finds himself the same everywhere, except that mobility itself makes him worse, just as shaking a sick person by carrying him about tends to harm him.

Let him know that he is sick, and attend to the causal aspects of his illness. If his rest is not interrupted, continuous remedies will quickly succeed; and his healed mind, released from its estrangements, captivities, and temptations, will become wholly God’s own. Nature needs care—not slight care—not because it is defiled, but because it is infected. Therefore let him apply himself immovably to his infirmary—for physicians commonly call it the workshop for curing illnesses—and continue the use of the remedy he has undertaken until he experiences health. [Col. 0324B]

26. Your infirmary, sick and languishing man, is your cell; the remedy by which you began to be cured is obedience—true obedience. But know that remedies changed frequently do harm: they disturb nature and wear out the sick person. A traveler who keeps to one certain road quickly arrives where he is going and brings both journey and labor to an end. But if he takes many roads, he wanders and never brings his labor to an end, because error has no end.

Therefore do not change the remedy or take one in place of another. Use the remedy of healing obedience until the boundary of perfect health. Nor, once made well, cast it away in ingratitude; yet thereafter you will be permitted to use it in another manner. If, then, you hasten toward health, take care not to presume to do anything—or even a little—on your own without consulting the physician. If you expect his healing work, you must not be ashamed continually to uncover your wound to him.

Be ashamed, but reveal everything; hide nothing. For some, in confessing, relate the history [Col. 0324C] of their sins as though it were a story; they enumerate the illnesses of their soul without shame, and almost without penitence or feeling of grief. He readily finds tears and breaks forth into groaning who has a sense of pain. But if a more hopeless numbness comes upon a grievous sickness, then, in not feeling pain, one appears nearer to health precisely insofar as one becomes farther from it.

If the physician is overly gentle and wishes to cure everything with milder ointments and plasters, act for yourself: eager for a stronger and swifter remedy, seek the iron of health; demand the cautery. The physician is always at hand for you; he is ready.

27. So that your solitude may not be dreadful to you, and that you may dwell more safely in your cell, three guardians have been assigned to you: [Col. 0325A] namely, God, conscience, and a spiritual father. You owe devotion to God, to whom you should devote your whole self; honor to your conscience, before which you should be ashamed to sin; and charitable obedience to your spiritual father, to whom you should have recourse in all things.

Moreover, that you may hold me in grateful regard, I shall add a fourth. While you are still a little child, until you learn more fully to think upon the divine presence, I shall provide you with a tutor. Choose for yourself, on my advice, a person whose example of life has so entered your heart and whose reverence has so clung to it that, whenever you remember him, you rise in reverence for the one remembered and order and compose yourself. Let that thought, as though he were present, correct in you, through the affection of mutual charity, everything that needs correction; yet let your solitude suffer no loss of its privacy.

[Col. 0325B] Let him be present to you whenever you wish; let him often come to mind even when you do not wish it. His holy severity, brought to mind, will set before you his rebukes; his devotion and kindness, his consolations; the sincerity of his holy life, his example. For when you think that all your thoughts are seen by him, you will be compelled to correct them as though he sees and reproves them.

Thus, according to the Apostle’s command, “keep yourself diligently” (I Tim. V, 22); and so that you may always inspect yourself, always turn your eyes away from all others. The eye is an excellent instrument of the body—if, like the other members, it could also see itself. Since this has been granted to the inward eye, if, neglecting itself after the pattern of the outward eye, it busies itself with other things, then even when it wishes, it is unable sufficiently to return to itself. Attend to yourself: you yourself are abundant material for your own concern. [Col. 0325C] Exclude from your outward eyes what you have ceased to see; from your inward eyes, what you have ceased to love. For nothing returns so easily as love, especially in souls still tender and recent.

## CHAPTER X. The offices and exercises of the dweller in a cell.

28. Dare also at times to be wise, to desire the better gifts, and to become yourself a parable of edification. One cell of yours is outward; another is inward. The outward cell is the house in which your soul dwells with your body; the inward cell is your conscience, which God—the most inward of all your inward parts—ought to inhabit with your spirit.

The door of the outer enclosure [Col. 0325D] is a sign of the door of inward watchfulness: just as the bodily senses are not permitted to wander abroad through the outer enclosure, so the inward senses must always be restrained toward their own inward place. Love, therefore, your inner cell; love your outer cell; and give each its proper care. Let the outer one cover you, not conceal you—not so that you may sin more secretly, but so that you may live more safely.

For you do not know, inexperienced inhabitant, what you owe to the cell unless you consider how in it you are not only cured of your own vices, but also spared the need to contend with others’ vices. Nor do you know what honor you owe to your conscience if you do not experience in it the grace of the Holy Spirit and the sweetness of inward delight. Therefore give each cell its due honor, and claim your own primacy for yourself within it. Learn there, according to [Col. 0326A] the laws of common observance, to preside over yourself, order your life, compose your conduct, judge yourself, accuse yourself before yourself, often even condemn yourself, and not let yourself go unpunished. Let justice sit as judge; let conscience stand as defendant and accuse itself. No one loves you more; no one will judge you more faithfully.

29. In the morning, exact from yourself an account of the night that has passed, and impose upon yourself a rule of caution for the coming day. In the evening, require an account of the day that has passed, and make your rule for the approaching night. If you are thus strict, you will never have leisure for self-indulgence. According to the canon of common observance, assign its exercises to each hour: spiritual matters to the spiritual hour, bodily matters to the bodily one. In these, let every debt be paid: the spirit to God, the body to the spirit. Thus, if anything has been omitted or left incomplete, it must not pass without punishment or recompense in its own manner, place, and time. [Col. 0326B]

Besides those hours of which the Prophet says, “Seven times in the day I have praised you” (Ps. CXVIII, 164), the morning sacrifice, evening sacrifice, and midnight observance must be especially maintained. For the Prophet does not say without purpose, “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Ps. V, 5): then we are still fasting from outward cares. And: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight; the lifting up of my hands, the evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL, 2): then we are, in a sense, already digested from such impediments.

In our nocturnal vigils too—when we rise at midnight to confess the Lord’s name—the same Prophet, weaving together the order of this confession, says: “In the day of my affliction I sought God; my hands were raised to him by night, and I was not deceived” (Ps. LXXVI, 3). [Col. 0326C] At these hours especially we ought to place ourselves before God as though face to face; in the light of His countenance to perceive affliction and pain in ourselves arising from ourselves; and to call upon God’s name, sweeping our spirit until it grows warm, passing to the remembrance of the abundance of His sweetness until He Himself becomes sweet in our hearts.

But then above all we must do what the Apostle said: “I prefer to speak five words in the church with my understanding than ten thousand words without understanding”; and: “I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind. I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV, 19, 15). [Col. 0326D] For then the mind and spirit must gather their fruits, so that thereafter we may be released into the rest of night in the abundance of God’s blessing; or, when we rise for God’s praises, the entire course of our work may thereafter be shaped and enlivened in His praises.

For this reason, at the beginning of the nocturnal vigils it is not expedient to overwhelm the understanding, exhaust the spirit, or extinguish it with a multitude of psalms. Rather, while it remains sober, it must be moved to devotion and directed on its course toward God, until, with heart enlarged, it begins to run as far as the end of God’s work. Thereafter it will retain the measure or tenor of its fervor, unless great negligence intervenes or voluntary misery causes it to be abandoned.

[Col. 0327A] 30. Anyone who has the mind of Christ also knows how expedient this is for Christian devotion, and how fitting and useful it is for God’s servant, the servant of Christ’s redemption, to recollect more attentively, at least during one hour of the day, the benefits of His passion and redemption: to enjoy them sweetly in conscience and store them faithfully in memory. This is spiritually to eat Christ’s body and drink His blood in remembrance of Him, who commanded all who believe in Him: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII, 19).

How impious it is, because of the sin of disobedience, for a human being to be forgetful of so great a divine mercy is evident to all; for it would be wicked to forget the commended remembrance of a departing friend, under whatever sign it was entrusted. Certainly, the mystery of this holy [Col. 0327B] and venerable commemoration may lawfully be celebrated, in its proper manner, time, and place, only by the few persons to whom that mystery has been entrusted. But the reality of the sacrament or mystery may be performed, treated, and received for salvation at every time and in every place of God’s dominion, in the manner in which it has been handed down—that is, with the affection of due devotion—by all to whom it is said: “But you are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession, that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you from darkness into his marvelous light” (I Pet. II, 9).

For as the worthy person receives the sacrament unto life, so the unworthy receives it unto his own death and judgment. But no one receives the reality of the sacrament unless worthy and fit. For the sacrament without the reality of the sacrament is death to its recipient; but the reality of the sacrament, even apart from the sacrament, is eternal life to its recipient. [Col. 0327C] If you wish—and truly wish—this is available to you in your cell at every hour, both day and night. Whenever, in remembrance of Him who suffered for you, you are devoutly and faithfully moved by this deed of His, you eat His body and drink His blood. So long as you remain in Him through love, and He in you through the working of holiness and righteousness, you are counted among His body and His members.

31. Moreover, at fixed hours one should devote oneself to a fixed reading. For random and varied reading, found as it were by chance, does not build one up; rather, it makes the mind unstable, and what is lightly admitted departs still more lightly from memory. [Col. 0327D] But one must linger over particular authors, and the mind must be trained by habit. For Scripture desires to be read in the same Spirit in which it was written; it must also be understood by that Spirit. You will never enter into Paul’s meaning until, through the practice of good intention in reading him and through the study of continual meditation, you have absorbed his spirit. You will never understand David until by experience itself you have put on the very affections of the Psalms. And so with the rest. In every writing, study differs from reading as much as friendship differs from hospitality, or a social affection from a chance greeting.

Something from the daily reading should also each day be sent down into the stomach of memory, there to be digested more faithfully and, when recalled upward, more frequently ruminated upon: something suited to one’s purpose, advancing one’s intention, and holding the mind fast, [Col. 0328A] so that it has no wish to think of alien things. One should often draw an affection from the course of reading and shape a prayer that interrupts the reading—not so much hindering it by interruption as continually restoring the mind, purified, to an understanding of the reading.

Reading serves intention. If the reader truly seeks God in reading, everything that he reads works together for his good, captivates the reader’s understanding, and reduces every interpretation of the reading into service to Christ. If the reader’s mind turns aside elsewhere, it drags everything after itself; and it finds nothing so holy or pious in the Scriptures that, whether through vainglory, distorted sense, or perverse understanding, it does not apply either to malice or to vanity. In reading all Scriptures, therefore, the beginning must be the fear [Col. 0328B] of the Lord, so that the reader’s intention may first be established firmly in it, and from it the understanding and sense of the whole reading may arise and be ordered.

## CHAPTER XI. He sets forth the measure of bodily exercises, and likewise of food and sleep.

32. From spiritual exercises one should never go far away, nor depart from them altogether, into bodily ones; rather, the mind should be accustomed easily to return to them, and, while it occupies itself with the latter, to remain always attached to the former. For, as was said above, “man was not made for woman, but woman for man” (1 Cor. 11:9); nor are spiritual things for the sake of carnal things, but carnal things for the sake of spiritual things.

By bodily exercises we now mean those performed bodily through manual work. There are also [Col. 0328C] other bodily exercises in which the body must labour, such as vigils, fasts, and the like. These do not hinder spiritual things but assist them, provided that they are undertaken with the discernment of reason. But if, through the fault of indiscretion, they are conducted in such a manner that spiritual things are impeded, either because the spirit fails or because the body grows weak: whoever behaves thus has taken from his body the effect of good work, from his spirit its affection, from his neighbour an example, and from God honour; he is sacrilegious and guilty before God in respect of all these things.

This is not to say—according to the Apostle’s meaning—that it would be inhuman, unfitting, improper, or unjust for the head sometimes to ache in God’s service, when once it often laboured to the point of pain in the vanity of the world; or for the belly to hunger [Col. 0328D] to the point of rumbling, when it has often been filled, even to vomiting. But measure must be maintained in everything. The body should sometimes be afflicted, but not crushed. For “bodily exercise is profitable for a little, but godliness is useful for all things” (1 Tim. 4:8). Therefore care for the flesh must be undertaken also to a limited extent—that is, not in its desires, yet still care must be given to it.

Such care must be exercised soberly and with a certain spiritual discipline, so that neither in its manner, its quality, nor its quantity may anything appear unbecoming to a servant of God. “We ought to bestow more abundant honour upon those members of ours which are unseemly; but our comely members have no need” (1 Cor. 12:23–24). Yet not only in this matter: our whole life, though hidden from human beings, ought to be presented [Col. 0329A] to God as holy and honourable, and our whole manner of life should be conducted so as to be visible and pleasing to the holy angels, though enclosed within domestic walls. “Let all things among you,” says the Apostle, “be done honourably” (1 Cor. 11:40). Honourableness is pleasing to God and dear to the holy angels. For this reason the Apostle also commands women to be veiled because of the angels. Since they are undoubtedly with you in your cells both by day and by night, guarding you, rejoicing with you in your endeavours, and cooperating with you, it pleases them that, even when no person sees, all things among you should be done honourably.

33. Therefore, whether you eat, drink, or do anything else, do all things in the Lord, piously, holily, and religiously. If you eat, let your sobriety richly adorn your table, already sufficiently moderate in itself. And when you eat, do not eat wholly; rather, while your body obtains its refreshment, let your mind not neglect its own. By meditating—or at least by remembering and considering within itself—something from the memory of the sweetness of the Lord or from the Scriptures, let it chew over and digest what may nourish it.

Nor should this necessity itself be satisfied in a worldly or carnal manner, but as befits a monk and as is appropriate to a servant of God. Even with regard to bodily health, the more honourably and orderly food is taken and received, the more readily and wholesomely it is digested. Therefore the manner and time of taking food, and its quantity and quality, must be observed; superfluous and artificial seasonings must be avoided. The manner of taking food, I say, must be observed, so that the eater does not pour out his whole soul upon every [Col. 0329C] food; the time, so that he does not eat before the hour; the quality, so that he uses what the community of brothers uses, except where clear necessity requires otherwise.

As to seasonings, I beg, let it suffice that our foods become edible, not also objects of desire or pleasure. For desire has sufficient evil of its own. Since it can scarcely, or in no way, reach the end of satisfying necessity except by passing through some path of pleasure, if it begins to receive incentives from those who have undertaken perpetual warfare against its delights, then two are ranged against one, and continence is endangered.

34. Next, what has been said of food applies also to sleep. Take care, as far as you can, servant of God, that you never sleep wholly, lest your sleep be not the repose [Col. 0329D] of one wearied, but the burial of a suffocated body; not the restoration, but the extinction, of your spirit. Sleep is a suspect thing and in large measure like drunkenness. For apart from the vices which arise in sleep—when, as the body sleeps, there is no reasoning faculty to oppose them—nothing in our life is lost so completely, as regards the obligation of continual progress, as the time assigned to sleep.

Therefore, when going to sleep, always carry with you in memory or thought something in which you may peacefully fall asleep, something that may sometimes also help you dream, and which, welcoming you when you awaken, may restore you to the state of yesterday’s intention. Thus night will be illumined for you like day, and “your night shall be illumination in your delights” (Ps. 138:12, 11). You will fall asleep peacefully, rest in peace, [Col. 0330A] awaken easily; and when you rise, you will be ready and agile to return to that from which you did not wholly depart. For a sober sleep follows sober food and a sober mind.

But carnal, brutish sleep—“lethaean,” as it is called—is abominable to a servant of God. Yet sleep from which, after suitable rest, it is easy to summon the powers of body and mind, and, like the servants of a household, to rouse and send them forth to works necessary to the spirit—such sleep is not to be despised in its proper time and measure.

Thus a prudent mind devoted to God ought to conduct itself in its cell and in its conscience as a prudent householder does in his house. Let it not have, as Solomon says, in its house a contentious woman (Prov. 21:19)—that is, its own flesh—but let the flesh be disciplined unto sobriety, habituated [Col. 0330B] to obedience, ready for work, trained everywhere both to hunger and to be satisfied, to abound and to suffer want. Let it have the outward senses not as leaders but as servants; the inner senses sober and effective. Let it have the entire household, or family, of its thoughts so arranged and disciplined that it may say to one, “Go,” and he goes; to another, “Come,” and he comes; and to its servant, the body, “Do this,” and it does it without contradiction.

Whoever thus orders and governs himself in his conscience may most safely be entrusted and committed to himself in his cell. But this belongs to the perfect, or to those already beginning to be perfected. We have therefore set it before beginners and novices, so that they may know what they lack and toward what they should direct the intention of their effort.

## CHAPTER XII. Who are suitable inhabitants of the cell; costly buildings are condemned.

[Col. 0330C]

35. It must be understood that, when we discuss carnal or animal perception, rational knowledge, or spiritual wisdom, we describe one human being in whom, according to different stages and fruits of progress and dispositions of intention, all these things may be found at different times; and we describe three classes of persons, each serving in the cells under the religious profession in accordance with the characteristics of these states. Yet the dignity of the cell, the hiddenness of holy solitude, and the title of a solitary profession seem fitting only for the perfect, whose food, as the Apostle says, is solid, and who through habit [Col. 0330D] have their senses exercised for the discernment of good and evil (Heb. 5:14). Although the rational person, who is nearest to the wise, might somehow seem tolerable in this condition, the animal person—who does not perceive the things of God—would certainly be thought wholly to be excluded.

But the Apostle Peter meets this objection, saying concerning some: “If they received the Holy Spirit just as we did, who was I that I could forbid God?” (Acts 11:17). For the Holy Spirit is good will. One whose good will bears witness to the indwelling and drawing Holy Spirit ought not, without great scruple of mind, to be excluded from any height of religious profession.

Indeed, the inhabitants of cells must be supplied from two classes of persons: namely, from the simple, if they appear fervent and humble both in understanding and will for attaining religious prudence; or from the prudent, if they are known to be emulators of religious and holy simplicity. But foolish pride or proud foolishness must always be far from the dwelling of the righteous. Every pride is foolish, though not every foolishness is proud. For foolishness without pride is sometimes found to be simplicity; and if it is ignorant, perhaps it is teachable, and if it cannot be taught, perhaps it is manageable. Religious community is a particular city of refuge for simplicity—unless it is of such a kind that it refuses to be humbled, or is so brutish that it cannot be governed or managed.

Still, good will, even if very brutish, is not to be abandoned, but should be directed by salutary counsel toward a laborious and active life. But the proud person, however prudent he may seem to himself, must be left to himself [Col. 0331B] and driven away. For if a proud man is admitted, on the first day when he enters to dwell, he begins to make laws; while one who is excessively foolish cannot learn the laws that he finds.

Therefore one must carefully and prudently weigh whom one admits to dwell with oneself. For one who dwells with himself has with him no one but himself, such as he himself is. An evil person never dwells safely with himself, because he dwells with an evil person; and no one is more troublesome to him than he is to himself. For the insane and utterly deranged, and those who for whatever reason are not sufficiently masters of their minds, are customarily watched and are not left or entrusted to themselves, lest they misuse their solitude.

Therefore let animal persons who are poor in spirit be admitted to share the life of the cells; but let it be so that they themselves may become rational and spiritual, not so that those who have already merited to be this should turn back and become animal. Let them be received with every goodwill of charity; let them be borne with every patience of kindness. But those who have compassion on them must not conform to them, nor seek their progress in such a way that they are compelled on their account to incur a slackening of the rigor of their religious purpose.

36. For from this source costly—and, insofar as shame scarcely permits the word, ambitious—construction of cells, already entered into on borrowed money, has crept in. Holy simplicity and rustic plainness, “created by the Most High,” as Solomon says (Ecclus. 7:16), have been cast aside, and we create for ourselves certain supposedly religious refinements of dwelling. In these so much indulgence has been granted to animal persons that nearly all of us have become animal in this respect. For, alienating from ourselves and our cells the form of poverty and the appearance of holy simplicity—the true beauty of God’s house—bequeathed to us by our fathers as a hereditary right, we build for ourselves, by the hands of skilled craftsmen, cells not so much hermitages as perfumeries: each bearing the price-tag of a hundred solidi, objects of our eyes’ desire purchased from the alms of the poor.

Cut off, O Lord, the reproach of a hundred solidi from the cells of your poor. Why not rather a hundred denarii? Why not none at all? Why do not the sons of grace themselves build freely for themselves? What answer was given to Moses when he completed the tabernacle? “See,” God said, “that you make all things according to the pattern shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40). It is not fitting for the tabernacle of God among human beings to be made by worldly [Col. 0332A] people. Let those to whom the pattern of the true beauty of God’s house is shown in the height of their minds build for themselves. Let those whose concern for their inner life enjoins contempt and neglect of all outward things build for themselves the form of poverty, the appearance of holy simplicity, and the outlines of ancestral frugality. No skill of craftsmen can adapt these things as well as their own lack of concern can.

37. Therefore, I beg you, in the pilgrimage of this world, in this warfare upon earth, build for yourselves not houses to live in but tents to leave behind, since you will soon be called from them and depart for your homeland and city, the house of our eternity. For we are in camp; we serve in a foreign land; we labour in a foreign land. Whatever is natural is easy. Is it not easy for a solitary person—and sufficient for nature and useful for conscience—to weave a cell for himself out of branches, form it from mud, cover it in whatever way, and inhabit it most fittingly? What more is required?

Believe me, brothers—and may you never have occasion to learn this by experience—these refinements and fashionable elegances soon weaken a manly purpose and effeminate a masculine mind. Even though their pleasures are often lulled by habitual use, and even though there may be some who use such things as though not using them, nevertheless such affections are more successfully uprooted and overcome by contempt than by use. Our outer things also contribute no little to our inner things when they are fitted and arranged in likeness to the mind and answer in their manner to its good purpose. A poorer manner of life restrains desire in some; in others it disposes the conscience toward love of poverty.

Furthermore, a mind intent upon its interior life is better suited by all things outward being uncultivated and neglected; by these things the mind itself [variant addition: “the inhabitant of the house”] is recognized as more often dwelling elsewhere, and holy intention declares itself more occupied elsewhere. Such outward neglect effectively reconciles inner things to a good conscience, since it proclaims that all outer things have become cheap in its eyes. I therefore beg that those more luxurious cells remain as they have been made, but that their number not increase. Let them serve as infirmaries for animal and weaker brothers until they recover—that is, until they begin to desire not [Col. 0332D] infirmaries for the sick but the tents of soldiers in the camp of God. Let them remain as an example to your descendants that you possessed such dwellings and despised them.

## CHAPTER XIII. By the example of ancient monks and hermits—indeed, of Christ, the Apostles, and the first believers—he exhorts to moderation, avoidance of idleness, and love of poverty.

38. But you who are spiritual, like the Hebrews—that is, “those who pass over”—having no abiding city here but seeking the one to come, build for yourselves, as you have begun, little huts in which to dwell. For our fathers lived in huts while dwelling in the land of promise as in a foreign land, together with the fellow-heirs of the promise, awaiting the city that has foundations, [Col. 0333A] whose architect and builder is God; not having received the promises, but seeing and greeting them from afar, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth. For those who say such things make plain that they seek a better homeland, that is, a heavenly one (Heb. 11:9–10, 13–14, 16).

For this reason our fathers in Egypt and the Thebaid, most ardent emulators of this holy life, lived in deserts, distressed and afflicted, persons of whom the world was not worthy. They built cells for themselves, in which they merely sheltered and enclosed themselves from wind and rain. There, abounding in the delights of hermit frugality, though themselves needy they enriched many. I do not know by what name I should more worthily call them: heavenly human beings or earthly angels, dwelling on earth but having their citizenship in heaven. They laboured with their hands and fed the poor from their labour. Though hungry themselves, out of the wilderness’s barrenness they supplied the prisons of cities and the sick, and sustained those placed in whatever necessities, living from their own labour and dwelling in the labour of their hands.

39. What shall we say in comparison with these things—we, not animal persons but earthly animals, clinging to the earth and to the perceptions of our flesh, walking in the perception of our flesh, and dependent on other people’s hands? Yet in this respect we are in some measure consoled by him who, though rich, became poor for us (2 Cor. 8:9); and he who gave the command of voluntary poverty himself deigned to show us in his own person the pattern of that poverty. So that evangelical poor might know what they should do, he himself was willing to be fed by believers—and sometimes even by unbelievers; yet, in order to make them believers, he did not refuse to receive the necessities of life.

Likewise, in the primitive Church, the holy poor who had suffered the plundering of their goods for Christ, or who, following the counsel of perfection, had left and sold everything and made it common property with their believing brethren, were provided for by the faithful through the holy Apostles’ concern—with how great concern, with how great piety! Both the book of the Acts of the Apostles and Paul in his Epistles plainly show this. And although this is granted more freely, since the Lord himself commanded and ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel, nevertheless apostolic authority does not deny it even to those living evangelically, as to those holy poor then in Jerusalem. These are called holy poor also because they had enrolled themselves in the profession of holiness and common life, and had voluntarily made themselves poor for this very purpose (Luke 18:22; Acts 2:44–45; 4:34–35; Rom. 15; 1 Cor. 9; 2 Cor. 8).

For what the Apostle announces with the utmost severity to certain persons—“if anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat”—he immediately explains concerning whom he was speaking, adding: “For we hear that some among you walk disorderly, doing no work but busying themselves with curiosities. Now we command and exhort such persons in the Lord Jesus Christ that, working quietly, they eat their own bread” [Col. 0334A] (2 Thess. 3:10–12). “Their own,” that is, bread gained and acquired by their own labour. Yet lest he should seem to have cast aside and rejected those who, though disorderly, doing no work, and meddling in curiosities, nevertheless had the name of the Lord invoked over themselves, he immediately adds: “But you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good in Christ Jesus our Lord” (ibid., v. 13). It is as though he said: “Even if they persist in their malice or negligence, do not yourselves fail in beneficence toward their support.”

40. Therefore, although above he announced most severely that those unwilling to work ought not to eat, and afterward showed himself somewhat more merciful toward those willing to work but doing nothing, we could say, according to the wording of his text—and it would not wholly depart from the truth—that this severity is directed at those unwilling though able, while this indulgence is for those willing but unable. Yet even when he commands and exhorts these persons in the Lord Jesus Christ to eat their own bread quietly, they appear not to eat bread that is their own unless, by working as much as they can before the witness of God and their own conscience, they make it their own. [Col. 0334B]

Forgive, Lord, forgive us: we make excuses, we evade; but no one can hide from the light of your truth, which illuminates those who turn toward it just as it strikes those who turn away. For our frame is not hidden from you, which you made in the hidden place of human beings. But we make it hidden from ourselves, because there is scarcely anyone, in matters pertaining to you, who is willing to test what he can do, and to do what he can most readily do at some time according to flesh or world, whether fear impels him or desire draws him. And even if we deceive human beings who do not know, do not permit us, as though wishing to deceive you, to deceive ourselves. We do not labour because either we cannot, or we think that we cannot, or by the habit of our idleness and comforts we make ourselves unable.

41. Therefore let us always worship, fall down, and weep before you who made us and who, in this manifest sin of ours, formed us by your hidden judgment, so that perhaps, because we do not greatly will this, we cannot; or because we were unwilling when we could, when we will, we cannot. Let us at least eat our bread according to Adam’s punishment, if we cannot do so in the sweat of our face, then in the sorrow of our heart; in tears of sorrow, if not in the sweat of labour. Let the piety and devotion of a humble conscience make up this great loss to our profession.

Let our tears be our bread day and night, so long as it is said to our soul, “Where is your God?”—that is, so long as it is on pilgrimage from the Lord our God and from the light of his countenance. One thing indeed was necessary. But if we are fixed in neither the one nor exercised in the many, in what rank shall we be counted? Would that we might be counted with him of whom the Apostle says: “To one who does not work, but believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned for righteousness according to [Col. 0335A] the purpose of God’s grace” (Rom. 4:5). Would that we might be counted with the sinful woman, to whom much was forgiven because she loved much (Luke 7:47), and that the blessed soul might merit to be justified before God by this judgment—the judgment of those who love the name of the Lord—so that, abandoning every righteousness of works and confidence in merits, it may be justified in this alone: that it loved much. For in loving you, God, the love itself is a great reward to the loving conscience, and then eternal life.

Thus, brothers, I beg you: let us not excuse ourselves, but accuse ourselves and confess. And though we wear before human beings the shadow of a great name and a certain personal fiction of perfection, let us, knowing before God the poverty of our conscience, not depart altogether from truth; and truth will set us free.

## CHAPTER XIV. How the animal beginner, or novice in religion, should be taught to draw near to God through love and prayer.

[Col. 0335B]

42. Next, the animal beginner and recruit of Christ must be taught to draw near to God, so that God may also draw near to him. For thus the prophet admonishes: “Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you” (Jas. 4:8). A human being must not only be made and formed, but also made alive. First God formed the human being; then he breathed into his face the breath of life, and the human being became a living soul (Gen. 2:7). The formation of the human being is moral instruction; his life is love of God. Faith conceives this love, hope gives birth to it; love itself forms and brings itself to life.

For the love of God—or God the Holy Spirit, who is love—pouring himself into human love, disposes it toward himself. And God, loving himself from the human being, makes that person one with himself, together with the person’s spirit and love. For just as the body has no source of life except its own spirit, so the human affection called love does not live—that is, does not love God—except from the Holy Spirit.

The love of God, born in a person from grace, is nursed by reading, fed by meditation, strengthened and illumined by prayer. But for an animal person, new in Christ, the outward things of our Redeemer are more suitably and safely set forth for reading and meditation, to exercise the person’s inner faculties. In these are shown the example of humility, the prompting of charity, and the affection of piety; and from the holy Scriptures and the holy Fathers’ treatises, whatever is moral and plainer. [Col. 0335D] The deeds and sufferings of the saints should be placed before such a person, where the level ground of history requires no labour, and something always occurs to rouse the novice’s mind to the love of God and contempt of self.

Other histories, by contrast, may delight when read, but do not build up; indeed, they rather infect the mind and, at the time of prayer or spiritual meditation, cause useless or harmful things to spring from memory. Meditation commonly follows the character of reading. Reading difficult Scriptures also tires rather than refreshes the more tender mind; it breaks intention and dulls perception or intelligence.

43. In prayer too, such a person must be taught to lift the heart upward, to pray spiritually, and, when thinking of God, to withdraw as far as possible from bodies or images of bodies. He must be admonished to attend with the utmost purity of heart to him to whom he offers the sacrifice of his prayer; to attend to himself who offers it, and understand what he offers. For insofar as he sees or understands the one to whom he offers, so much is he disposed toward him in affection; and for him love itself is understanding. And insofar as he is disposed toward him in affection, so much does he perceive whether what he offers is worthy of God; and in this he is well.

For a person of this kind, praying or meditating, the image of the Lord’s humanity—his Nativity, Passion, and Resurrection—is set forth more suitably and safely, as has already been said, so that the weak mind, which knows how to think only of bodies and bodily things, may have something toward which it may be disposed, something to which it may cling, according to the measure of its own piety, with a devout gaze. For in the form of the Mediator there is that of which Job says, “a person visiting his own form does not sin” (Job 5:24): that is, when one directs the gaze of one’s attention toward him by thinking of the human form in God, one does not wholly depart from truth; and, while faith does not separate God from the human being, one learns at times to apprehend God in the human being.

Accordingly, among the poor in spirit and the simpler children of God, the affection is initially usually sweeter in proportion as it is nearer to human nature. But afterward, as faith passes into affection, embracing Christ Jesus at the centre of their hearts in the sweet embrace of love—whole human being assumed for the sake of man, whole God for the sake of the God who assumes—they begin no longer [Col. 0336C] to know him according to the flesh, though they are not yet able fully to think of him according to God. Sanctifying him in their hearts, they lovingly offer him the vows their lips have distinguished: supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings, suited to the time and the occasion.

44. Some prayers are brief and simple, shaped by the will or necessity of the one praying according to the circumstance that occurs. Others are more extended and reasoned, as when people seek, ask, and knock in inquiry into truth, until they receive, find, and it is opened to them. Others are eager, spiritual, and fruitful, arising from the affection of one enjoying God and from the joy of illuminating grace. These are the very kinds that the Apostle enumerates in a different order: supplications, prayers, petitions, thanksgivings (1 Tim. [Col. 0336D] 2:1).

For petition, which we placed first, concerns obtaining temporal things and certain necessities of this life. In it, God approves the petitioner’s good will, yet himself does what he judges better and willingly gives the petitioner what is rightly requested [variant: “follows the one who prays rightly”]. This is the prayer of which the Psalmist says: “For still my prayer is in their good pleasures” (Ps. 140:5). It is also the prayer of impious people, since the desire for peace and tranquillity, bodily health, temperate weather, and other things pertaining to the use and necessity of this life—and to the pleasure of those who misuse them—is common to everyone, but especially to the children of this age. Those who petition faithfully for such things, though they request them only for necessity, nevertheless in this very matter always subject their own will to the will of God.

Supplication, however, is an anxious persistence toward God in spiritual exercises, in which, before relieving grace comes, “he who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccles. 1:18). Prayer is the affection of a person cleaving to God: a certain familiar and pious converse, and the standing of an illumined mind in enjoyment, for as long as this is permitted. Thanksgiving, on the other hand, is, in the understanding and knowledge of God’s grace, an unfailing and untiring attention of good will toward God, even if at times either the outward act or inward affection is absent or grows dull. For this is what the Apostle means when he says: “The will lies near at hand for me, but I do not find the accomplishing of good” (Rom. 7:18). It is as if he said: “The will is indeed always present, but sometimes lies down—that is, it is ineffective—because I seek to accomplish a good work but do not find it.”

This is charity that never fails. It is the unceasing prayer, or thanksgiving, of which the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks always” (1 Thess. 5:17–18). For it is a certain continual goodness of mind and well-ordered disposition, and in the children of God a certain likeness to the goodness of God the Father: always praying for all and giving thanks in all things; continually pouring itself out toward God in prayer or thanksgiving in as many ways as the devout affection finds grounds for this in its own needs or consolations, and also in compassion or rejoicing with a neighbour. [Col. 0337C] Such a disposition is continually in thanksgiving, because whoever is so disposed is always in the joy of the Holy Spirit.

45. Therefore, petitions should be made piously and faithfully, but one must not cling to them obstinately; for we do not know, but the heavenly Father knows what we need among these temporal things. Supplications, however, must be persisted in, with all humility and patience, because they bear fruit only in patience. For sometimes, when grace does not quickly come to aid, heaven becomes bronze to the supplicant and his earth iron. And when the hardness of the human heart is left to itself and does not deserve to be heard according to its desire, the anxiety of the one who longs judges everything delayed to be denied. And, like that Canaanite woman, it groans that it is passed by and despised (Matt. 15:22–28), imagining that its past sins, like an uncleanness of flesh, are being charged against it or reproached to it.

At other times, however, with no little labour, the petitioner receives, the seeker finds, and to the one knocking it is opened; the labour of supplication at last merits to find the consolations and sweetnesses of prayer.

46. Sometimes the affection of pure prayer and that good sweetness of prayer is not found, but as it were finds one: when grace anticipates a person who neither asks, seeks, nor knocks, and who is as though unaware. Thus, as it were, the race of servants is received at the children’s table, when the still crude and beginning mind is assumed into that affection of prayer which is usually granted, as the reward of holiness, to the merits of the perfect. When this occurs, it comes about either that the negligent person is not permitted, to his condemnation, to remain ignorant of what he neglects [variant: “Whatever it may be, it comes about either that the negligent person is not permitted, to his condemnation, not to know what he neglects”], or that charity’s invitation kindles love in him when it freely offers itself.

Here, alas, very many are deceived. Because they are fed with the bread of children, they suppose that they are already children. Failing in the very matter through which they ought to advance, they vanish from awareness of themselves through the visitation of grace, imagining that they are something when they are nothing. They are not corrected by God’s gifts but hardened, and become those of whom the Psalmist says: “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him, and their time shall be for ages. And he fed them with the fat of wheat, and satisfied them with honey from the rock” (Ps. 80:16–17). For servants are sometimes fed by God the Father from the more precious substance of grace so that they may desire to be sons; but they themselves, abusing the grace of God, become enemies. Thus, even in their sins or desires, in order that they may misuse the holy Scriptures, when they return to them in prayers they say to themselves what Manoah’s wife said: “If the Lord had wished to kill us, he would not have received the sacrifice from our hands” (Judg. 13:23).

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0337]

## CHAPTER I. How useful the cell’s seclusion is for novices and the perfect.

[Col. 0337D]

1. How beloved are your tabernacles, O Lord of hosts, in which the sparrow finds a home for itself, and the turtledove a nest in which to place her young! (Ps. 83:2, 4.) The sparrow, I say, is by nature a faulty creature: restless, flighty, troublesome, chattering, and prone to lust. The turtledove is a friend of mourning, a familiar inhabitant of shaded solitude, an image of simplicity, an example of chastity. The former finds in them for itself a dwelling of rest and security; the latter, a nest for herself, in which to place her young. What are these but the naturally hot blood and fervent spirit of young people, their unstable age and restless curiosity; and mature manhood, a grave disposition, chaste and sober, weary, so far as it can be, of outward things, and withdrawing into itself?

The one, in the tabernacles of the Lord of hosts—in the discipline of cells—finds rest from all vices, a support of stability, and a secure dwelling; the other finds, in the secrecy of the cell, a yet more secret retreat of conscience, in which to place and nourish the fruits of its holy affections and of spiritual contemplative perception. The solitary sparrow upon the roof—that is, at the height of contemplation—loves to trample underfoot the habitation of carnal life.
