The turtledove is fruitful in lower places and rejoices in the fruits of humility. [Col. 0339A] For all who are perfect and spiritual, signified by the name of the turtledove, when through the virtue of obedience and subjection they attain the firmness and strength of their virtue, continually press and cast themselves down into that which belongs to beginners. From the very place in which they descend beneath themselves, they ascend above themselves; and by humbling themselves they make greater progress, because of the fruits of solitude—frequent and lofty transports of contemplation. Nor do they judge the conscience of voluntary subjection, the practice of common life, and the sweetness of brotherly charity to be neglected.

2. Therefore the spiritual man, using even his body spiritually, deserves to receive its servitude—which the animal man has by a force imposed upon him, but the rational man by a habit brought under control—as though it were a natural inclination. [Col. 0339B] Where obedience is for the former a necessity, the latter possesses it as charity. Where the former has virtues full of labor, the latter has them transformed into settled habits.

But those sparrows of God, striving upward toward what belongs to the perfect, not through presumptuous pride but through the love of devotion, exalted in the poverty of their spirit, are not rejected as proud but received as devout. At times they deserve to experience that which spiritual persons enjoy; and they always seek to imitate the active life of those whose contemplative consolation they desire. Thus, walking in one spirit though not with one step, the spiritual advance equally in humility and beginners in what is lofty.

Such are the holy exchanges of well-ordered cells: venerable pursuits, busy leisure, laborious rest, ordered charity; conversing mutually in silence, [Col. 0339C] enjoying one another more in one another’s absence, and advancing through one another. When they do not see one another, they see in another what ought to be imitated, and in themselves only what ought to be mourned. But I, as Jeremiah says, “a man who sees my poverty” (Lam. 3:1), when I reckon up the riches of others, blush within myself and sigh, because I would rather experience in myself what I consider in another. Of two evils, it is more bearable not to see what one loves than to see it and not possess it—though this is not so with the goods of the Lord. For to see the Lord’s goods is to love them; and to love them is to possess them. Therefore let us strive, as far as we can, that we may see; by seeing, understand; by understanding, love; and by loving, possess. “Lord, before you is all my desire, [Col. 0339D] and my groaning is not hidden from you.”

## CHAPTER II. On the second state of religious life, that is, the rational state

3. Passing from the animal state to the rational, so that from the rational state we may pass to the spiritual—by treating it, and—would that it might be so—by making progress—we must first know that Wisdom, as is read in the book bearing her name, “anticipates those who desire her, meets them, and cheerfully shows herself to them in her ways” (Wis. 6:14). Thus she is present not only in advancing but also in meditation and exposition, “reaching everywhere because of her purity” (Wis. 7:24). For God helps with his countenance the person who looks upon him; he moves, advances, and draws one contemplating the beauty of the highest good.

And when reason rises upward through progress into love, grace descends to the loving and desiring person. Reason and love, which produce those two states, often become one; and so too do what arises from them, namely knowledge and wisdom. Things that are now one, and belong to one operation and power, can no longer be treated or conceived separately—whether in the understanding of the knower or in the joy of the one who enjoys. Although, therefore, one must be distinguished from the other, when the matter presents itself in this way, each must be conceived and treated together with, and in, the other.

Since, then, as was said above (Book I, nn. 14, 19), in the progress of religious life the animal state watches over the body and the ordering of the outward person, fitting that person by the pursuit of virtue, [Col. 0340B] so the rational state must concern itself with the mind: making it, if it does not exist, or cultivating and ordering it, if it does. First we must consider who or what the mind itself is, which reason makes rational; and what reason itself is, which by making a mortal animal rational perfects it as a human being. But first we must speak of the soul.

4. The soul is an incorporeal thing capable of reason, suited to a body by giving it life. This is what makes human beings animal, when they are wise in the things of the flesh and adhere to the senses of the body. But when it begins to be not only capable of perfect reason but its ruler, it immediately puts off the name of the feminine gender and becomes *animus*, a participant in reason, suited to rule the body—or a spirit possessing itself.

For as long as it is *anima*, it quickly becomes effeminate in what is carnal; but *animus* or spirit meditates only upon what is manly and spiritual. Spirit was created in human beings with a subtle and effective nature for the desire of good; in the art of creative Wisdom it is superior to every body, and brighter and worthier than every bodily light because of the image of its Creator and its capacity for reason. Yet, entangled by the fault of carnal origin, it became a slave of sin and captive under the law of sin which is in the members. It nevertheless did not altogether lose free choice—that is, reason’s judgment in judging and discerning—although it lost its freedom in willing and acting.

> **Note:** [Col. 0339D] Thus all manuscripts. In one manuscript of Mont-Dieu: “although it lost its own [freedom] in willing and acting,” which amounts to the same thing. Our free choice is said to have lost its freedom in choosing and acting, not indeed the freedom [Col. 0340D] of nature, which it can never entirely lose, but the freedom of grace. This is restored when, through liberating grace, the will has been set free and the spirit begins to be guided by free reason, etc.

For, as a penalty for sin and a testimony to lost natural dignity, free choice was set within it as a sign—but as a captive sign. Even before the conversion and liberation of the will, it can never be wholly lost through any turning away of the will itself. Even when it abuses this faculty by choosing evil instead of good, it remains better and worthier than every bodily creature, both in itself and in the creative art [variant: “citadel”] of truth.

The will is liberated when it becomes charity, when “the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who is given to us” (Rom. 5:5). [Col. 0341A] Then reason truly exists: that is, a disposition of mind wholly in accord with truth. For when, through liberating grace, the will has been set free and the spirit begins to be guided by free reason, then it belongs to itself—that is, by freely using itself it becomes *animus*, and a good *animus*.

It is *animus* insofar as it gives good life to, and perfects, its animal nature through the addition of free reason. It is good insofar as it now loves its own good, by which it becomes good and without which it could be neither good nor *animus*. The *animus* becomes good and rational by loving the Lord its God with its whole heart, whole soul, whole mind, and all its strength; and by loving itself only in him, and its neighbor as itself. The good *animus* fears God and keeps his commandments: “for this is the whole human being” (Eccl. 12:13).

Reason is defined by those who define, or described by those who describe it, as follows: it is the sight of the mind by which, through itself and not through the body, it beholds truth; or it is contemplation of truth itself; or the truth itself which it beholds; or rational life, or rational service, by which it is conformed to the truth contemplated. Reasoning is reason’s inquiry: that is, the movement of its sight through the things to be viewed. Reasoning seeks; reason finds. When this sight is directed upon some thing and sees it, it is knowledge; when it cannot do so, it is human ignorance. Thus reason is both the instrument through which it works and the work which it performs. It always loves to be exercised in what is useful [Col. 0341C] and honorable, advancing by exercise but withering in itself through idleness.

5. For a person who possesses reason, no exercise is worthier or more useful than exercising it upon that which is best within that person, and by which one surpasses other animals and all one’s other parts: namely, the mind or *animus* itself. For the mind or *animus*, to which the rest of the human being is subjected for governance, nothing is worthier to seek, sweeter to find, or more useful to possess than that which alone surpasses the mind itself: God alone. Nor is he far from any one of us, “for in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:27–28).

And it is not as in this air that we live in the Lord our God; rather, in him we live through faith, move and advance [Col. 0341D] through hope, and are fixed through love. For the rational *animus* was created from him and for him, so that its conversion may be toward him and he may be its good. It is good from that good, created in his image and likeness, so that as long as one lives here, it may approach him as closely as possible through likeness—since one departs from him only through unlikeness. Thus it may be holy as he is holy, and in the future blessed as he is blessed.

In short, this alone is great and good: when the great and good *animus* looks upward, marvels at, and desires that which is above it, and, as a devout image, hastens to cling to its likeness. For it is the image of God. And because it is God’s image, it can understand that it is able and ought to cleave to him whose image it is. Therefore, though on earth it governs the body committed to it, yet by its better part—memory, understanding, and love—it always delights to dwell there from which it knows that it has received whatever it is and whatever it possesses; and where it may hope to remain forever, attaining, in the full vision of God, the full likeness of God, so far as a human being may hope for this, if that person does not neglect to conform life to good hope.

There it looks; from there it hangs. It dwells among human beings more in order to give them life through the life of God, for the seeking and receiving of divine things, than to animate them with this mortal and human life. For just as the body which it animates is raised by its natural condition toward heaven, which surpasses all places and bodies in nature, place, and dignity, so the spirit itself, by nature, [Col. 0342B] always loves to raise itself to what excels among spiritual things—that is, to God and divine things—not by thinking proudly, but by loving devoutly and living soberly, justly, and piously. The higher that to which it strives, the more it must be exercised by strenuous practices—practices which do not merely wash over it, but immerse it, so affect it as to perfect it.

6. Although these pursuits are sometimes helped by, and make use of, letters, they are not literary pursuits—not quibbling, disputatious, or talkative, but spiritual, peaceable, and humble, agreeing with the humble. Even if they are practiced outwardly, they are carried on chiefly within, in the spirit of the mind, where the human being is renewed day by day, putting on the new human being, created according to God in holiness and the righteousness of truth.

There [Col. 0342C] the *animus* is made; there good understanding is made for all who practice it, when, according to the rule given by the Apostle, “in all things we commend ourselves as ministers of God”: in great patience, tribulations, necessities, distresses, labors, vigils, the imprisonment of the cell, fasts, chastity, knowledge, long-suffering, gentleness, the Holy Spirit, unfeigned charity, the word of truth, and the power of God; by the weapons of righteousness on the right hand and on the left; through glory and dishonor, ill repute and good repute; as deceivers and yet truthful; as unknown and yet known; as dying, and behold, we live; as chastened but not killed; as sorrowful yet always rejoicing; as needy yet enriching many; as having nothing yet possessing everything (2 Cor. 6:4–10); in labor and hardship, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness (2 Cor. 11:27).

These and such things are holy pursuits, apostolic exercises, in which the *animus* examines, finds, and corrects itself, cleansing itself from every defilement of flesh and spirit and perfecting holiness in the fear of God. These pursuits love silence; they desire quietness of heart amid bodily labor, poverty of spirit, peace amid outward pressures, and a good conscience in all purity of heart and body. They make the *animus*, because they possess the means of making it. But vain, trifling, wordy, contentious, curious, and ambitious pursuits scatter and corrupt even a holy or already perfected *animus*. These pursuits search out the roots of the virtues rather than their flowers, [Col. 0343A] not in order to shine but in order to exist; not in order to be known but in order to be possessed.

7. They fear in themselves the appetite of vices more than their assault from others; contagion more than malice. For just as virtues are sometimes drawn, through great labor and persistent study, into good affection and mind, so vices, through the slightest opportunity of more relaxed license, pass into a mixture and become as though natural. Yet no vice is natural; every virtue, however, is natural to the human being. Nevertheless, the habit either of a corrupted will or of ingrained negligence often makes very many vices, as it were, natural in a neglected conscience. For habit, as philosophers commonly say, is a second nature.

Every evil *animus*, [Col. 0343B] before it becomes hardened, can have its wickedness softened; but even after it has become hardened, it must not be despaired of. For this is Adam’s curse: that in the soil of our labor and in the field of our heart or body, harmful or useless things spring up freely, everywhere and indiscriminately; while useful, necessary, and healthful things arise with labor. Yet because virtue is a thing of nature, when it sometimes enters the *animus*, it does not enter without labor; but it comes into its own place, sits faithfully, and agrees well with nature, since no reward is preferable to it than the consciousness of itself in God.

But vice, though believed to be nothing else than the privation of virtue, is sometimes felt to have such desolation and deformity that it overwhelms and crushes; such foulness that it defiles and infects; and such tenacious adherence through habit [Col. 0343C] that nature scarcely shakes it off. For the stream of every vice is dried up in vain unless its source has been stopped. For example, a lax will produces lightness of mind, from which proceed instability of mind, inconsistency of conduct, vain merriment often reaching to fleshly wantonness, vain sadness sometimes reaching to bodily sickness, and many other things arising, through the vice of levity, in the negligence or transgression of one’s purpose.

Likewise, a will made proud by habit often makes the *animus* swollen amid great poverty of heart. From this proceed vainglory, self-confidence, neglect of God, boasting, disobedience, contempt, presumption, and the other plagues of the mind that commonly flow from the swelling and practice of pride. In this way, every kind of vice derives its originating mother-source from some affection of an evil will or from the practice of an evil habit. The longer this has become ingrained in the mind, the more firmly it clings, and the stronger remedies and more diligent care it requires.

Such plagues of vice pursue the solitary person even into the remotest solitude. And just as virtue, well consolidated and faithfully dwelling in the *animus*, does not abandon its possessor amid any crowd, so a vice possessed through habit does not allow its possessor to be free in any solitude. Unless habit has been overcome by persistent study and prudent effort, it may be softened but can scarcely be conquered. Whatever order the *animus* may assume, and whatever solitude it may inhabit, habit does not allow it to have the secret place or silence of the heart. [Col. 0344A] The more deeply the practice of habit and will has come to dwell in someone, the more wicked and rebellious it is found there—not so much a spiritual evil as a kind of complex accumulation and hard corporeal necessity that must, as it were, be driven out by force of hands.

8. But let us return to the praise of virtue. What is virtue? The daughter of reason, but more truly of grace. It is a certain power by nature; but that it may be virtue, it has this from grace. It is power from the judgment of approving reason; but virtue arises from the appetite of the enlightened will. For virtue is a voluntary assent to the good. Virtue is a certain equality of life, wholly consonant with reason. Virtue is the exercise of free will in accordance with reason’s judgment. Humility is a virtue; patience is a virtue; obedience is a virtue. The virtues are prudence, temperance, fortitude, justice, and very many others. In each of these, virtue is nothing other than, as has been said, the exercise of free will in accordance with reason’s judgment.

For a good will in the *animus* is the origin of all goods and mother of all virtues. Conversely, an evil will is the origin of all evils and vices. Therefore the guardian of his own soul must be very careful in guarding his will, so that he may prudently understand and discern what he wills altogether, or ought to will, such as the love of God; and what he wills for the sake of that, such as love of neighbor. For while every lack of distinction is safe in the former, love in the latter must always be cautious and prudent according to the rules of obedience. For in the love of God there is no other rule or discretion than that, as he “having loved us, loved us unto the end,” so we should love him, if possible, unto infinity—as does the blessed man “who greatly delights in his commandments” (Ps. 111:1).

9. But although the devotion of one who loves ought to have no end or limit, the action of one who acts must have its own bounds, limits, and rules. So that excessive will may not at any time wander astray, guarding truth must always be present through the mediation of obedience. For nothing suits a person advancing toward God more than will and truth. These are the two which, as the Lord says, if they agree as one, whatever they ask shall be done for them by God the Father (Matt. 18:19).

If these two are perfectly united, they contain in themselves the whole fullness [Col. 0344D] of virtues, with no vice intervening. They can do all things in the person who is weak; they have and possess all things in the person who has nothing. They give, lend, bestow, and benefit the person who rests with them. Glory and riches are in the conscience of that holy man, from the fruits of his good will. Outwardly, the shield of God’s truth surrounds him—not on one side only, like the shield of this world, but on every side. For good will always makes him cheerful and joyful inwardly; while truth makes him serious and weighty, safe and secure in outward action. Thus that person, having passed beyond what is human, is always in serenity—like the air, men say, which lies above the sphere of the moon.

10. Will is a certain natural appetite of the *animus*: one kind directed toward God and its own inward things; another directed toward the body and external, bodily things. When it tends upward, like fire toward its own place—that is, when it is joined to truth and moved toward higher things—it is love (*amor*). When it advances and is nourished by grace, it is devoted love (*dilectio*). When it grasps, holds, and enjoys, it is charity (*caritas*), unity of spirit, God: for “God is charity” (1 John 4:16). But when a human being has attained completion in these things, then that person begins (Sir. 8:6), because none of them has complete perfection in this life.

When, however, the will declines toward things of the flesh, it is the lust of the flesh. When it declines toward the curiosity of the world, it is the lust of the eyes. When it declines toward ambition for glory or honor, it is the pride of life. Yet as long as it serves the utility or necessity of nature in such matters, it is nature, or nature’s appetite. But when it exposes itself to superfluous or harmful things, it is a vice of nature, or of itself.

From its first impulse or approach in these matters you may draw this conclusion about yourself. When, in things pertaining to the body, the will sets a limit to its first appetite in necessary matters, it is a natural appetite of the *animus*. But when in desiring it always advances to further things, it reveals itself: it is now not so much will as a vice of the will—avarice, greed, or something of that sort. For in such things the will is quickly satisfied, but its vices are never satisfied.

11. In spiritual matters and in things that concern God, when the will wills what it can, it is to be praised; when it wills what it cannot, and more than it can, it is to be governed; when it does not will what it can, it is to be stirred and urged on. For if it is not restrained, it often rushes forward and is driven headlong. If it is not stirred, it often sleeps, delays, forgets its goal, and easily turns aside, as if sideways, into the bonds [variant: “turnings aside”] of offered pleasure.

Therefore, as often happens with the body—for another sees a human body better than it sees itself—so in such matters another’s eye often sees us better than our own; and another person, who does not share equally in the fervor of the same will, is often a more upright judge of action. For through negligence or private self-love we often err concerning ourselves. Obedience, therefore, whether of command or counsel, subjection or charity alone, is a good guardian of the will.

For, as the Apostle Peter teaches, the children of obedience often purify their hearts more purely and sweetly in the obedience of charity toward their equals or even their inferiors than they subject themselves to their superiors through the obedience of necessity (1 Pet. 1:22; 5:2–3). [Col. 0345D] In the former, charity alone commands, counsels, and obeys; in the latter, imperious authority and fearful necessity fear or threaten punishment. And in the former, greater glory is often owed to the obedient; in the latter, greater punishment is always threatened to the disobedient.

Therefore, in one whose heart is set on things above, it is evident to all how necessary this guardianship is to the will for regulating, moderating, and ordering outward matters—and still more for inward matters. For when the *animus* thinks upon itself or God, the will itself is chief in every thought; and the whole course of thought necessarily follows the beginning supplied by the will.

12. There are three things that make thought: will, memory, and understanding. The will compels memory to bring forth material; it also compels the understanding to form what is brought forth, applying the understanding to memory in order that it may be formed from it; and it applies understanding, the sight of the thinker, in order that thought may arise from it. Because the will compels these things into one and joins them by a certain easy nod, thought (*cogitatio*) seems to have received its name from compelling (*cogere*).

From this arise all thoughts: some good, holy, and worthy of God; others evil and perverse, which separate from God; others idle and vain, from which God withdraws himself. [Col. 0346B] Thus it is said that perverse thoughts separate from God, and that the Holy Spirit withdraws himself from thoughts that are without understanding (Wis. 1:3, 5). In these words it should be observed that no thought whatsoever can occur without understanding, and no thought is wholly devoid of understanding. But one kind of understanding derives from the power of natural reason, another from the virtue of the rational mind.

Understanding itself is one and the same: wherever it is applied, whether to good or evil, it is naturally active. Yet one kind is found left to itself, another enlightened by grace. The former does not refuse itself to the serious and trifling affairs of the world; the latter applies itself only to worthy matters and to those like itself. The former often acts as one left to itself and infected by vice, through the vice of reason and of a corrupted will, weaving perverse thoughts by which the thinker willingly separates himself from God. The latter, always acting as enlightened and drawn toward virtue, performs piety, which joins the thinker to God.

13. The thoughts placed second—thoughts without understanding—are those vain and idle thoughts which, through the intention of the thinker, apply themselves to neither kind of understanding. They do not destroy suddenly, but corrupt gradually and little by little: occupying time, hindering necessary things, and infecting the *animus*. They are not so much thoughts as certain images of thoughts arising from real or imaginary recollections, or the recollections themselves spontaneously and repeatedly bubbling up from memory.

In these, an affection or passivity of the will rather than an action seems to be present, because there is no intention of the thinker in them. What spontaneously boils up from memory offers itself to be formed by the unconcerned understanding; and whatever takes place seems to take place more in the dream of a sleeping person than in the attentive gaze of one thinking. Although it is not the thinker’s purpose thereby to repel the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, through the fault of negligence, the spirit of discipline rightly withdraws from undisciplined thoughts. Though these are produced through a certain hidden force of reason, they are not produced from reason in such a manner that the understanding is drawn into them, because there is no assent in them from one who understands.

But when serious matters are considered seriously and well, the will, by free choice, calls forth from memory whatever material it requires; it applies a forming understanding to memory; and it applies whatever has been formed to the attentive sight of the thinker. Thus the business of thought is accomplished.

## CHAPTER III. He explains the third state of religious life, that is, the spiritual state

14. When thought concerns things which are of God or directed toward God, and the will advances until it becomes love, the Holy Spirit—the spirit of life—immediately pours himself in by the way of love. He gives life to everything, helping the weakness of the thinker in prayer, meditation, or exposition. Memory immediately becomes wisdom when the goods of God taste sweet to it; and it supplies to the understanding, to be formed in affection, what has been thought from those goods. The understanding of the thinker becomes the contemplation of the lover; and, forming this into certain experiences of spiritual [Col. 0347B] or divine sweetness, it affects the thinker’s attentive sight through them. That in turn becomes the joy of the one enjoying.

Then God is thought of well according to the human mode—if, indeed, it should be called thought where nothing is thought or compelled, but one simply exults and rejoices in remembrance of the abundance of God’s sweetness, and the one who has sought him in simplicity of heart truly perceives him in goodness. But this mode of thinking about God is not in the choice of the thinker but in the grace of the Giver: namely, when the Holy Spirit, who breathes where he wills, when he wills, how he wills, and upon whom he wills, inspires this.

It belongs to the human being continually to prepare the heart: freeing the will from alien affections, reason or understanding from cares, memory from idle and busy—sometimes even necessary—occupations. Thus, on the Lord’s favorable day and in the hour of his good pleasure, when one hears the voice of the Spirit breathing, the elements which make thought may immediately and freely come together, cooperate for good, and as it were make a common contribution to the thinker’s joy: the will presenting pure affection for the joy of the Lord; memory, faithful material; and understanding, the sweetness of experience.

15. Thus a neglected will produces idle thoughts, unworthy of God; a corrupt will, perverse thoughts, which separate from God; a right will, thoughts necessary for the use of this life; and a devout will, thoughts effective for the fruit of the Spirit and for enjoying God. The fruits of the Spirit are, as the Apostle says, charity, peace, joy, patience, long-suffering, goodness, kindness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, and chastity (Gal. 5:22–23).

In every kind of thought, all that occurs to the thinker is conformed to the intention of the will, through the mercy and judgment of God at work in these things, “that the righteous may still be justified, and the person who is filthy may still be made filthy” (Rev. 22:11). Therefore a person who wishes to love God, or already loves him, must always consult his own *animus* and examine his conscience: what it is that he wills altogether, and why he wills it; whatever else the spirit wills or hates; and whatever the flesh desires against this.

Thoughts that occur as though from outside and depart, and passing desires by which one now wills and now does not will, must be counted not among acts of will but almost among idle [Col. 0348A] thoughts. Even if they sometimes proceed as far as delighting the *animus*, the self-possessed *animus* soon shakes itself free from them. But concerning what it wills altogether, it must first consider what that thing is which it so wills; then how much it wills it, and how it wills it.

If what it wills altogether is God, it must examine how much and in what manner it wills God, and whether it does so even to the contempt of itself and of all things that are or can be. This must be examined not only by reason’s judgment but also by the affection of the mind, so that the will may become more than will: that it may be love, devoted love, charity, unity of spirit. For in this way God must be loved. A great will toward God is love; devoted love is adherence or union; charity is enjoyment.

But unity of spirit with God is the perfection of a will advancing toward God in one whose heart is set on things above. It is attained when one not only wills what God wills, but is so affected—and perfected in that affection—that one cannot will except what God wills. To will what God wills is already to be like God; not to be able to will except what God wills is already to be what God is, for in him willing and being are the same thing.

Hence it is rightly said that we shall then see him fully as he is when we are like him (1 John 3:2): that is, we shall be what he is. Those to whom power has been given to become children of God have been given power—not, indeed, to be God, but nevertheless to be what God is: to be holy, and to be fully blessed hereafter, as God is. For they are holy here, and will be blessed there, from no other source than God, who is both their holiness and their blessedness.

16. And this is the perfection of the human being: likeness to God. But to be unwilling to be perfect is to sin. Therefore the will must always be nourished toward this perfection, love prepared, and the will restrained lest it be squandered upon what is alien; love must be guarded lest it be defiled. For this alone were we created and do we live: that we may be like God, since we were created in God’s image. There is indeed a certain likeness of God which no living person loses except when he puts off life; the Creator of all human beings left it to every person as a testimony to the lost, better, and more worthy likeness. It is possessed alike by the willing and the unwilling, by one who can reflect upon it and by one so dull as to be unable to do so: namely, that just as God is everywhere, and everywhere wholly present in his creation, so every living soul is wholly present in its body. And just as God, ever unlike none of himself, works things unlike one another in creation in an unvarying manner, so the human soul, although it gives life to the whole body by an undiffering life, nevertheless continually performs unlike things in the bodily senses and in the thoughts of the heart in an undiffering manner. This likeness of God in the human being, as regards merit, has no weight before God, since it belongs to nature, not to one’s will or labour. But there is another likeness, nearer to God because voluntary, which consists in virtues: in it the mind, by the greatness of virtue, eagerly seeks as it were to imitate the greatness of the highest good; and, by steadfast perseverance in good, the unchangeableness of his eternity. Above this, moreover, there is yet another likeness of God. This is that of which something has already been said: so peculiarly proper that it is no longer called likeness, but unity of spirit, when a human being becomes one with God, one spirit—not merely by the unity of willing the same thing, but by a more fully expressed unity of virtue, as has already been said, being unable to will anything else.

This is called unity of spirit not merely because the Holy Spirit brings it about, or disposes the human spirit toward it, but because the Holy Spirit himself is it: God who is charity. Through him who is the love of Father and Son, their unity, sweetness, goodness, kiss, embrace, and whatever can be common to both in that supreme unity of truth and truth of unity, there comes about in a human being, in that person’s own measure, the same relation to God as the Son has to the Father, or the Father to the Son in their substantial unity. In the embrace and kiss of Father and Son, blessed consciousness finds itself, as it were, in the middle; and in an ineffable and inconceivable manner a human being is granted to become God—not God by nature, but nevertheless what God is by nature, the human being being so by grace.

17. Hence, in his catalogue of spiritual exercises, the Apostle wisely inserted the Holy Spirit among them, saying: “In chastity, in knowledge, in long-suffering, in kindness, in the Holy Spirit, in unfeigned charity, in the word of truth, in the power of God” (2 Cor. 6:6–7). Observe how he places the Holy Spirit, as accomplishing, ordering, and giving life to all things, in the midst of good virtues, as the heart is in the midst of the body. For he is the almighty craftsman who creates in a human being a good will toward God, makes God propitious toward the human being, forms affection, gives strength, aids action, accomplishes all things mightily, and orders all things sweetly. He gives life to the human spirit and holds it together in unity, just as he gives life to and holds together his own body. Human beings may teach one to seek God; angels, to worship him: he alone teaches one to find, possess, and enjoy him. For he is the earnestness of the one who seeks well; the devotion of the one who worships in spirit and truth; the wisdom of the one who finds; the love of the one who possesses; and the joy of the one who enjoys.

Whatever, however, is granted here to believers concerning the vision and knowledge of God is mirror and enigma; it is as far removed from the future vision and knowledge as faith is from truth, or time from eternity—unless at times there occurs what is written of him in the book of Job:

> “He hides light in his hands, and commands it to rise again;  
> and he announces concerning it to his beloved that it is his possession  
> and that he can attain it”  
> (Job 36:32–33).

18. For to God’s chosen and beloved person there is sometimes shown in return a certain light of God’s countenance—just as light enclosed in hands is revealed or concealed at the holder’s will—so that, through what is permitted to be seen as if in passing or in an instant, the mind may be set aflame for the full possession of eternal light and for the inheritance of the full vision of God. In order that what is lacking to that person may become known to some extent, grace sometimes, as it were passing by, strikes the sense of the lover, snatches the person away from himself, and carries him into the day that is, from the tumult of things into the joys of silence, showing him for his own measure, for a moment and an instant, that very reality to be seen as it is. Meanwhile it also makes him himself into that same reality, so that in his own manner he may be as that reality is.

When he has learned there the difference between the clean and the unclean, he is restored to himself and sent back to cleanse his heart for vision and to fit his mind for likeness. Thus, if he is again admitted at some time, he may be still purer for seeing and steadier for enjoying. Nowhere does the measure of human imperfection disclose itself better than in the light of God’s countenance, in the mirror of divine vision. There, in the day that is, seeing ever more clearly what he lacks, he corrects day by day through likeness whatever he has failed through unlikeness: approaching through likeness him from whom he has become far distant through unlikeness. And so a fuller likeness is always accompanied by a fuller vision.

For it is impossible for the highest good to be seen and not loved; nor can it fail to be loved as much as it is granted to be seen, until love advances into some likeness of that love which made God like humanity through the humiliation of the human condition, in order to make humanity like God through the glorification of participation in the divine. Then it is sweet for a human being to be humbled with the supreme Majesty, to become poor with the Son of God, to be conformed to divine wisdom, having in oneself the same mind that was also in Christ Jesus our Lord.

19. This, then, is wisdom with piety, love with fear, exultation with trembling: when God is considered and understood as humbled unto death—indeed, death on a cross—in order to raise humanity up to likeness with divinity. From this flows the rushing stream that makes glad the city of God: the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness in understanding and contemplating the good things he has done for us. When the things lovable in God, considered or even contemplated—his power, virtues, glory, majesty, goodness, and blessedness—readily lead a person to love God, shining in themselves within the affection of the contemplator, what especially carries the lover away into the Beloved is that he himself is in himself whatever is lovable in him: he who is all that he is, if indeed “all” can be where there is no part.

Toward this good, the devout affection directs itself by love of the good itself, and does not draw itself away until it is made one spirit, or one, with him. When this has been perfected in it, it is separated from, and delayed from, the Holy of Holies and that supreme heavenly blessedness only by the veil of this mortality. Yet, since in faith and hope it already enjoys in conscience him whom it loves, it awaits the remainder of this life with a more bearable patience.

20. This is the goal of the solitary’s contest, its end, its reward, the rest from labours, and consolation amid sorrows. It is itself the perfection and true wisdom of the human being, embracing and containing within itself all virtues—not gathered from elsewhere, but as though naturally implanted in it—in likeness to that God who is whatever he is. For just as God is what he is, so, in regard to the good of virtue, the settled disposition of good will and affection is so strengthened in the good mind that, through its most ardent attachment to the immutable good, it seems no longer capable of being changed from what it is.

For when that assumption by the Lord and Holy One of Israel, our King, takes place concerning the human being, the wise and devout mind, through illuminating and assisting grace, contemplates in the vision of the highest good also the rules of unchangeable truth, insofar as it deserves to attain them by the understanding of love. From them it forms for itself a pattern of heavenly conduct and a form of holiness. It contemplates the highest truth and the things true from it; the highest good and the things good from it; the highest eternity and the things that are from it. Conforming itself to that truth, that charity, and that eternity, it orders itself in these matters—not soaring over those realities in judgment, but looking up to them in desire or cleaving to them in love. It looks to these things and adapts and conforms itself to them, not without the judgment of discernment, not without rational examination and the judgment of reason.

From this holy virtues are conceived and arise; the image of God is re-formed in the human being; that life of God is ordered, from which, as the Apostle laments, some human beings have been alienated (Eph. 4:18); strength in virtue is gathered; and those two elements are attained in which the perfection of the contemplative and active life consists. Of these, according to those ancient translators, it is read in Job: “Behold, piety is wisdom; but to abstain from evil is knowledge” (Job 28:28, according to the Septuagint).

For wisdom is piety—that is, the worship of God, the love by which we desire to see him, and by which, seeing him in a mirror and in an enigma, we believe and hope; and in this we advance so as to see him in manifestation. But abstaining from evils is knowledge of temporal things, among which we are placed: in them we abstain from evils insofar as we strive after goods.

21. To this knowledge and abstinence belong, first of all, the exercises of all virtues; then, the discipline of all the arts of this present life in which we are occupied. Of these, the former—that is, the pursuit of virtues—seems rather to look toward higher things, displaying virtue through the preeminence of higher wisdom and sweetness through its fragrance. The latter, consisting in bodily exercises, unless bound by the religious bond of faith, runs down into the vanity of lower things.

In these matters, knowledge is something grasped either by reason or by bodily senses and committed to memory. If the matter is properly weighed, what we apprehend by the senses is wholly to be reckoned as knowledge. But what reason itself apprehends in such things is already that in which knowledge and wisdom meet at their boundary. Whatever is learned from elsewhere—namely, [or: “if”] through the senses of the body—is introduced into the mind as something foreign and accidental. But what comes spontaneously into the mind, whether from reason’s own force or from a natural understanding of the unchangeable laws of unchangeable truth—by which even the most impious people are sometimes found to judge quite rightly—belongs to reason in such a way that it is reason itself. It is not so much entrusted to reason by some teaching so as to become knowledge as, whether prompted by another or reminded by itself, reason understands that it naturally belongs to it.

Chief among such things is this: that what is known of God, God naturally revealing it, becomes manifest to a human being, even an impious one. Next is the natural affection for virtues, concerning which the pagan poet could say:

> “The good hate to sin from love of virtue.”  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 16, line 52.

Next comes every discernment of rational matters through the inquiry of reasonings. The lowest and downward-leaning part of knowledge is the animal experience of sensible things, which comes through the five bodily senses, through concupiscence, and through the experience of the flesh—whether of the eyes or of the pride of this life.

22. Therefore, when reason, conformed to wisdom, forms its conscience and orders life, it adapts to itself in the lower realm of knowledge the service and sufficiency of nature; in reasonings and rational matters, the order of life; and in the pursuit of virtues, the form of conscience. Thus advanced from below and aided from above, proceeding toward what is right, it hastens to break forth into the liberty and unity of the spirit through the judgment of reason, the assent of the will, the affection of the mind, and the effect of action. Thus, as has often been said, the faithful person is made one spirit with God. This is the life of God of which we spoke shortly before: not so much a progress of reason as the affection of perfection now in wisdom. For because these things now have savour for the wise person, that person is wise; because he has been made one spirit with God, he is spiritual. And this is the perfection of the human being in this life.

23. For one who until now was solitary or alone is made one, and the body’s solitude is turned into unity of mind. There is fulfilled in that person what the Lord prayed for his disciples as the consummation of all perfection: “Father, I will that, as you and I are one, they also may be one in us” (John 17:11, 21). This unity of the human being with God, or likeness to God, in proportion as it approaches God, conforms to itself that person’s lower element, making the lowest subject to it. Thus spirit, soul, and body are to be conceived as ordered in their own manner, assigned to their proper places, assessed according to their respective merits, and distinguished by their own properties, so that a person may begin perfectly to know himself and, advancing through self-knowledge, rise to the knowledge of God.

When the advancing affection first begins to rise and breathe toward this, one must take great care, in thinking upon this likeness, against the error of unlikeness: namely, that in comparing spiritual things with spiritual and divine things with divine, one should conceive of them only according to what each reality is. Therefore, in considering the likeness of God and oneself, the mind must first shape and adapt its thought so as to avoid altogether thinking of itself according to the body; and to avoid thinking of God not only according to body, as localized, but even according to spirit, as mutable. For spiritual things differ from the quality and nature of bodies to the same extent that they are removed from every local circumscription. But divine things surpass all bodily and spiritual things to the same extent that, free from every law of place or time and from every suggestion of mutability, they remain unchangeable and eternal in the blessedness of their own immutability and eternity.

Just as the mind discerns bodily things through the senses of the body, so it cannot discern rational or spiritual things except through itself. But let the understanding seek or await from God alone the things that belong to God. It is indeed lawful and possible for a person endowed with reason sometimes to think and inquire concerning certain matters pertaining to God—for example, the sweetness of his goodness, the power of his might, and similar things. But that which is itself what it is, the very “that which is,” cannot be thought at all, except insofar as it can be touched by the sense of illumined love.

24. Yet God must be believed—and, insofar as the Holy Spirit assists, conceived—as a certain eternal life: living and life-giving; unchangeable, making all mutable things unchangeably; understanding, and creating every intellect and every intelligent being; by wisdom making every wise person; fixed truth, standing and undeviating, from which all things that are true are true, and in which eternally exist the reasons of all things that occur in time. To it life itself is essence and nature; it is living life unto itself. It is divinity itself, eternity, greatness, goodness, and power existing and subsisting in itself; surpassing every place by the power of its non-local nature, and every time which can be comprehended either by reason or opinion through its eternity. It is far more truly and excellently than it is perceived by any kind of perception; yet it is attained more certainly by the sense of humble and illumined love than by any thought of reason. It is always better than it is thought, though it is thought better than it is spoken.

For it is the highest essence, from which all being proceeds; it is the highest substance, not subject to the categories of words, but the subsisting causal principle of all things. In it our being does not die, our understanding does not err, and love does not stumble. It is always sought that it may be found more sweetly; it is found most sweetly that it may be sought more diligently.

25. Therefore whoever wishes to see this ineffable reality—which can be seen only ineffably—must cleanse the heart; for it can be neither seen nor apprehended by any bodily likeness in sleep, by any bodily appearance while awake, or by any investigation of reason, but only by a pure heart that loves humbly. This is the face of the Lord which no one can see and yet live to the world; this is the form for contemplating which everyone longs who seeks to love the Lord his God with all the heart, all the soul, all the mind, and all the strength. Whoever loves a neighbour as oneself likewise does not cease to stir that neighbour toward it.

When one is at some time admitted to this, one sees beyond doubt, in the very light of truth, prevenient grace; when one is repelled from it, one understands in one’s own blindness that one’s impurity is unfit for its purity. And if one loves, it is sweet to weep, and one is compelled, not without much groaning, to return to one’s own conscience. We are altogether unequal to thinking upon this; but he whom we love—and of whom we rightly confess ourselves unable either to speak or to think—pardons us. Yet we are provoked and drawn to speak and think by love for him, or by love for his love.

Therefore it belongs to the one who thinks upon these things, in all things, to humble oneself and glorify in oneself the Lord one’s God; to become lowly in one’s own eyes in the contemplation of God; to be subject, in love for the Creator, to every human creature; to present one’s body as “a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God,” one’s rational service. Above all, one must not think more highly than one ought to think, but think unto sobriety; and, according to the measure of faith given by God (Rom. 12:1, 3), not set one’s good things before human mouths, but conceal them in one’s cell and store them in one’s conscience, always holding, as it were, this inscription both upon the brow of conscience and upon the brow of the cell: “My secret is for myself; my secret is for myself” (Isa. 24:16).

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0353]

## CHAPTER I. Nothing is more excellent than heavenly blessedness.

1. It should be noted that there are two blessednesses and two miseries. One blessedness is that which Adam possessed in paradise and lost; the other is in heaven, possessed by the holy angels whom the Lord has taken to himself. One misery is upon earth, which we suffer every hour; the other is in the prison-house of hell, which the lost suffer after death. The blessedness which Adam possessed in paradise was therefore temporal; but the other is heavenly, and for its sake he was made eternal. Likewise, the misery or tribulation which we suffer at present has an end; but that which is in hell lacks every end and is also called the second death.

2. The blessedness promised to the saints is so great and wonderful that neither eye has seen it, nor ear heard it, nor has it entered into the human heart. Since, therefore, we cannot see it because of its greatness, let us consider what naturally delights us in the present life, what seems good or honourable, in case something may perhaps be found by which that wondrous reality, “which eye has not seen and ear has not heard,” may appear more clearly to us and have a more pleasing taste. For all that is promised to the elect is contained in very few words; and because it is so hidden, so enclosed, and so far removed from weak minds, let us endeavour to say something of such excellent grace and, by dividing it into more parts, set it forth more clearly.

For if a large apple were offered to an infant to bite and chew, the child’s mouth, because of its extreme tenderness, could not bite or eat it; but if it were cut into small pieces, the child would be nourished and refreshed by it. What the child could not previously know—the taste of it while it remained whole—would now be eaten after division into pieces. Therefore, preserving that unseen promise of God until we come to where we shall see it as it is, let us attentively investigate what befits our bodies and our souls, what they may desire and in what they may delight freely and without offence; holding firmly that no honour or good of any kind will be lacking to all those who are granted to be in that blessedness.

## CHAPTER II. The endowments of blessed bodies are enumerated and explained.

3. There appear to be seven qualities which can fittingly be assigned to bodies; they are most becoming and wholly sufficient for the blessedness and advantage of those bodies. They are beauty, swiftness, strength, freedom, health, pleasure, and duration. If, indeed, any of these are things that holy people flee rather than desire, such as bodily beauty and pleasure, it should be understood that they are not to be avoided because they are not goods in themselves, but lest by occasion of them people somehow fall into the fault of sin. For if, in embracing them, they knew that they were not hindered from goodness or displeasing to God, they certainly would not wish to lack them. Nor, in the future, will the delight of holy sweetness in these things be slight, where there will be no fear of offence.

To holy souls, however, the following seem fittingly applicable: wisdom, friendship, concord, power, honour, security, and joy. There is no doubt that God’s elect will possess these in that blessed kingdom, since he dwells in them and presides over them—from whom comes whatever good exists anywhere, and who is ineffably powerful and glorious above all things.

4. But now let us return to what we began, and briefly say something by investigation concerning each item proposed. Do you ask about beauty? Hear what is written: “The righteous shall shine as the sun” (Matt. 13:43), “and the sun sevenfold, as the light of seven days” (Isa. 30:26). If, therefore, our bodies shall shine like the sun, which will possess the multiplied light of seven days, that glorious beauty will be incomparably great. Hear also another saying: “We await the Saviour,” says the Apostle, “our Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21).

Certainly, when the Lord was transfigured upon the mountain before his disciples, his face shone like the sun. Blessed Peter, delighted by the beauty of that brightness, said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:2, 4). The appearance also of the angel seated at the Lord’s tomb appeared shining like lightning (Matt. 28:3). If such was here the brilliance of a single angel, how glorious, how magnificent, do you suppose the beauty will be when countless thousands of saints, made like the bright body of our Lord Jesus Christ, appear with him? Holy David contemplated this blessedness, this beautiful and blessed beauty, when he said: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. 26:4). Much concerning this beauty, which is truly great blessedness, is found in sacred Scripture.

5. Swiftness is attendant upon this beauty. Those who are with God will possess swiftness as great as that of a sunbeam or of the eye of a person seeing clearly. When the sun comes over the earth in the east, it immediately extends its ray to the west. Likewise, the ray of the eye, when the eyelid is opened, is directed far away to heaven or to any other place, if no obstacle intervenes. So, without doubt, when our bodies have become spiritual and no longer feel weight and heaviness, after the manner of angels, they will move with the greatest ease wherever they wish.

For even in the resurrection of bodies, the individual parts of each person will be joined together. If someone’s hand or foot, or any other limb, has been buried in the east or devoured by beasts, while the rest of the body lies in the west or north, or has been scattered among the divided regions of the world, the whole body will be assembled as swiftly as an eye is shut or opened. For a great distance separates Babylon from Judaea; yet in an instant the angel carried the prophet Habakkuk from Judaea to Babylon and placed him over the lions’ den, where he offered Daniel a meal. When this was done, Habakkuk was immediately restored to his own place (Dan. 14:32–38). He could surely have wondered where he had been when he found himself again in his own place so quickly. Whoever, therefore, possesses such agility will undoubtedly obtain a great gift of great felicity.

6. Yet this blessed person will not be content with this blessedness alone. Strength follows, and every one of the blessed will possess it in a measure which no one can possess in the present life. For the measure of that same strength will be as great as the one who is to possess it chooses. If one wishes to move the entire mass of the whole earth with a single finger, one will certainly be able to do so with the greatest ease. For the devil, God’s enemy, by the strength of his nature moves the air, stirs up wind and storms, sometimes causes earthquakes, and does many other quite remarkable things. Hence he is called “the strong man armed” (Luke 11:21). And will God not give his elect either equal strength, or indeed strength far better and greater? Far be it that anyone who thinks soundly as a human being should suppose this.

For “the Lord will fulfil the desire of those who fear him” (Ps. 144:19), and, as is said elsewhere, “they shall lack nothing” (Ps. 22:1). If they lack nothing, they will not lack strength; therefore strength will be present, and no small measure of it.

7. But because neither strength, nor swiftness, nor beauty is so highly valued by one who is not free, there is no doubt that that blessed multitude will be free. For no wall, fire, water, or any other material whatever will be able to prevent them from entering or departing wherever they wish to enter or depart. For the Lord freely came forth from the closed tomb, freely despoiled hell, and freely entered among the disciples when the doors were shut. God’s saints, if they wish, will freely enter hell; freely pass through fire and burning pitch; freely remain there as long as they wish without injury to themselves. For in that hellish flame nothing will burn except sins alone; and because that holy company will have been cleansed from every defilement of sin, it will pass unharmed through cold and heat, through various punishments and steaming pools. Again, the sight—or contemplation—of those same places will lie within the choice of the blessed; and, to the confusion of the reprobate, their freedom will be as great as their will to possess it.

8. Most welcome health will accompany blessed freedom and so free a blessedness. This health will be great, because “God shall wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints, and there shall be no more mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21:4). Whoever considers carefully will see that none of us possesses perfect health in the present age. If any part of our limbs is at some time struck too hard, we suffer pain and immediately complain of injury. Why is this, except because we are weak and infirm everywhere? But no injury can come upon God’s elect: neither iron nor fire nor water nor the mention of any evil will harm them. No remembrance of anything suffered by any one of them will harm that person, because there will be such an abundance of joy there that no disturbance of mind can arise in them from the recollection of things past.

Moreover, when it is said, “The righteous shall stand in great steadfastness against those who afflicted them” (Wis. 5:1), they will not do this for revenge for their own injury, but rather for God’s justice, in which they will then appear strong and steadfast. For God’s justice itself, just as it will be sweet and a firm steadfastness to the good, will be bitter and sorrowful confusion to the wicked. Let the person who desires to please God therefore see to it that he commits the vengeance for his whole injury to God, since God says: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Deut. 32:35; Rom. 12:19). But if one begins to avenge oneself, one will by no means have God as avenger of that same injury, because one has presumptuously undertaken it oneself. The Lord will say: “Because you preferred to avenge yourself rather than wait for me, you ought no longer to appeal to me for vengeance.” But if, following God’s counsel, one defers vengeance, one will be blessed: for there will be no offence, no need, and no weakness, but sound felicity and most felicitous health.

9. These things that have been mentioned are very good; but if they have no savour, they are as if wholly fruitless. If they did have savour, they would be incomparably good. Therefore pleasure must necessarily be present, to give those blessed persons savour, that they may taste and understand how beloved and delightful are the tabernacles of the Lord, and how one day in the courts of Jerusalem is better than thousands. Pleasure, therefore, will be supreme and will intoxicate all with the immensity of its delight. For the prophet cries: “They shall be intoxicated from the abundance of your house, and you shall give them drink from the torrent of your pleasure, because with you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:9–10).

Truly wondrous is that intoxication, wondrous that abundance, wondrous that house. For a torrent flows downward in a rushing course. Thus God Almighty will fill us with the wondrous sweetness of his house. Since we cannot find an adequate example of so great a pleasantness, sweetness, or goodness, let us consider the bitterest pain which the reprobate will suffer, in contrast to the most delightful sweetness which the upright and truly blessed will possess. If someone pierced my pupil with red-hot iron, I would suffer no small pain; if that person pierced the other eye with a like torment, I would endure a much greater pain. If the same punishment were inflicted upon me throughout all my limbs and the same pain held me everywhere, what, do you suppose, would become of me? Would I not be driven mad by so great a pain? Would I not become altogether of another mind? When flame licked and burned me on every side, what mental state would remain to my soul?

In the same manner, according to our measure, we shall be filled with joy from the face of God; we shall be satisfied from the abundance of God’s house; we shall be intoxicated from the torrent of pleasure or sweetness of the Lord himself. A temporary delight or passing pleasure is felt only in some particular part of the body; but that delight will be felt throughout the whole, as fire is. Thus it will be felt through every part of body and soul. As if the whole body were a throat, it will delight in that holy joy. For if the wicked suffer ill in all their parts because they refused to act well, far more justly will the good fare well in every part of soul and body because they acted well.

10. Therefore the saints will possess this blessed pleasure, which is truly delightful and a great blessedness. Yet it is a small thing to possess this and the other qualities mentioned above unless they can retain them without failure. Let duration therefore be added, knowing no boundary of any end, because “the righteous shall live for ever” (Wis. 5:16). This duration knows no end, because blessedness, beauty, swiftness, strength, freedom, health, and pleasure shall have no end. Whoever possesses these things will sing with joyful mouth: “Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion: for he has strengthened the bars of your gates; he has blessed your children within you” (Ps. 147:12–13); for one who is blessed with such a blessing will rejoice greatly.

## CHAPTER III. The endowments of blessed souls are explained.

11. Having thus briefly indicated the elements of blessedness that seem to belong to the body, let us also, with the Lord’s help, consider those elements which we said above belong to the soul. The first of these elements is wisdom. Blessed men will possess it fully, so that nothing will be lacking to them of all that they may wish to know. For they will know all things past, present, and future; nor will anything be withheld from their knowledge which the Creator created to be known. Nor will anyone need to ask who his great-grandfather was, from what stock he sprang, or who this or that person is. They will also possess knowledge of every language, every creature, and every art, and they will see one another. Whatever I have done or do in the present life, all of them will plainly see; and whatever any of them has done, I too shall see, if I am there. Yet no one will blush on that account, if in this life he has made satisfaction to God through repentance. Thus, so that you may always have reason to show gratitude to your Creator, not only for yourself but also for those who will be with you, you will keep before your eyes the greatness of the misery from which he has drawn us—not for shame, indeed, but for a fuller glorification in joy. For mutual exultation in knowledge will be greater in proportion as the knowledge of those dwelling together is more manifest. We all know that the apostle Peter denied God, and that Mary Magdalene was a sinner; nor are they unaware that we know it. Yet they are no more ashamed than a man now fully healed would be ashamed that he had once been grievously wounded in battle. Why is this, brothers? Surely because they repented of what they had done and found pardon. So too we, if we have obtained forgiveness for our offences, shall not be ashamed of the faults we committed. For if someone reproached us in this age with what we did in childhood, we should scarcely be troubled, because that time and age have passed away. For when we were children, we thought as children, we reasoned and acted as children; but when we became men, we put away the things of childhood (1 Cor. 13:11). Therefore in that life there will be no shame when one sees another’s deeds, if, by satisfaction here, he has reached that place through God’s gift. For what God has cleansed, no one will judge unclean; no one will think it deserves reproach. Rather, he will praise God without ceasing for himself and for those with whom he has been joined.

Moreover, if an angel judged you unworthy of his fellowship because of your sins, you would have a reasonable answer to give him. If he were to rebuke you, saying: “You, though you are a human being, dust and ashes, swelled with pride and neglected God’s command, corrupt in sins—by what right or merit do you wish to be made equal to us, whom you see living in the service of the Creator?” you would reply: “Since I am dust and ashes, it is no wonder if, driven by the wind of temptation, I sometimes fell. But when I came to know my Creator, I corrected by repentance whatever I had done wickedly. Therefore tribulation, fasting, vigils, blows, and reproaches were welcome to me as satisfaction to him. But which of you ever endured anything of this sort for him? And that you did not sin was his gift. Furthermore, by whose grace you are so great that you did not sin, by his blood I was redeemed from the stain of sin—he who also willed to become man, in order to make me a sharer in his kingdom. Since, then, his death is a sufficient cause of my salvation, each of you ought rightly to rejoice that I am made a participant in your blessedness.”

12. In this holy fellowship there will likewise be unfailing and perfect friendship. For each one individually, and all together, will love their Lord God incomparably more than themselves; and each will hold every other person dear as himself. If someone says that he wishes to love his father or parents more than the rest, let him examine what he feels. Whoever you are who desire this, you wish all to love your parent, whom you yourself love with true and ardent affection, and to love him with no less love than you do. I feel, will, and desire the same concerning my friend; and all others do the same concerning their friends. Therefore, so that the fullness of holy love may be complete in every respect, and everyone there may possess what he wills, you must necessarily love all others as yourself, so that all may love you as themselves. When this comes to pass, there will be great and perfect friendship, because in each person individually and in all persons together there will be the affection of perfect love.

13. Blessed, therefore, is the friendship which joins so many blessed spirits in eternal glory. From it will arise loving harmony, which, like the harmony of the bodily members, will remain perpetually inviolate. It will be so great that no one will will anything other than what it is established that you will. For as we shall be one bride, one Church, one body, so there will be no less harmony than now exists among the members of one body. Our members, for example the eyes, possess such harmony with one another that one in no way wishes to do anything without the other. If one wishes to look upward or downward, to the right or left, it does not need to tell the other to look with it, because by nature it does not wish to see apart from the inseparable seeing of the other. Such is their harmony that whatever one wills, the other wills also.

The other members too are joined in great mutual harmony. The hands work for the feet and the whole body; the eye watches over the hands and the whole body; and the foot walks for the eye and the whole body, sometimes even with bare soles. Nor does it say, though it may sometimes be grievously bloodied by the prick of thorns, that it no longer wishes to go anywhere. Nor does the hand, however wounded, say that it no longer wishes to work. And if it happens that the hand, *siromaste*, that is, with a spear-point, pierces its own foot, the foot itself is moved by no anger against the hand. For they are united by such a harmony of love that they cannot disagree for any reason or upon any occasion; indeed, whatever is bestowed upon one pleases all, as though it were bestowed upon themselves. All serve the head and expose themselves to dangers for it. Hence it is clear that all truly love the head more than themselves; and it is beyond doubt that the head in every way accords with the wishes of all.

So also in the heavenly homeland you will love God ineffably; and you will find that all, even God himself, will will with you whatever you will. For as you do not differ from God’s will, so he will in every respect agree with your will; for the head cannot disagree with its body.

14. But perhaps someone will say: “If God and all the elect will what I will, when I am there I wish to be among the greater ones.” I think the answer is that he will be among the greater in glory, but he will be unable to wish to be some other one of the greater persons who is there, unless he wishes not to be himself—which cannot happen. Nor, if he is unequal in merits, will he be able to wish to become equal in glory to the greater, since the most beautiful ordering of that body would then appear to be violated; and he could in no way agree with this, given both love itself and the beauty of that ordering. For just as in the human body the hand does not perform the office of the foot, the eye does not seek to be a nose, hearing does not seek to be smell, and the little finger does not wish to be the middle finger or the thumb, so in that glorious ordering of the city of God no one will wish to exchange his own rank for a higher station. Each will love what is his own so completely because it will be sufficient for him.

For if one placed in that blessedness desired to have something greater than he had received, he would thereby be miserable, because he did not yet have what he desired. For to the degree that something rightly desired is lacking to anyone, to that degree he is judged miserable; for misery is the absence, against one’s will, of some good. But there is no misery there; rather, there is a sufficient harmony, a harmonious sufficiency. Therefore you will be all-powerful with respect to your will, when you have the Almighty agreeing with you in all things.

15. The blessed will have as much power as each of them wishes to possess. For whatever any one of them commands, whether in heaven, on earth, in the sea, or in the depths of hell, will happen without any contradiction or delay. What we say may perhaps seem astonishing; but if one carefully considers where we shall then be placed, whose head’s members we shall then be, and that nothing will be lacking to those who love God, what we affirm will by no means seem incredible. The saints of God will have this power, for they will truly possess all things with the Son of God. They will therefore be omnipotent with respect to their will. This power will be eternal power and will therefore be no small blessedness to those who possess it. Great also will be their honor, because “your friends, O God, are exceedingly honored” (Ps. 138:17).

16. This honor will be so great that human understanding cannot comprehend it. Yet let us take an example: suppose some servant is honored by his master. Certainly, if an emperor or king found his servant in severe illness, rescued him from sickness, and honored him by freeing him from servitude and placing him among his own soldiers, that man would become greatly indebted to and a friend of his lord. If he placed him among his chief men and raised him to royal dignity, with what joy, do you think, would he exult? With what love would he rightly burn for his lord? All would show him favor for his lord’s sake; all would serve him, lest they incur the anger of the lord who honored him. But if that master loved him so greatly still further as to adopt him as his son and appoint him his heir, then beyond doubt the servant’s exultation would be greater.

From this one may infer how marvelous is the honor given in eternal life by the Creator of life itself and of humankind. He will make those who serve him not merely live forever in eternal peace and be called and truly be his friends, but will establish them as gods, sons of God, heirs of God and fellow-heirs of Christ, citizens of the heavenly homeland, as it is written: “I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). The gracious God excluded none of the righteous from this divinity. But let us attempt, by an example, to see how a human being may be deified through participation in divinity.

Let there be one fire into which materials of different kinds are placed. All are set ablaze, but one more, another less. Yet each retains its own nature; and, according to ordinary speech, because it is ignited, it is called fire. Thus, indeed, though in a certain higher manner, all the blessed are also deified by participating in deity. Although some more and some less, all who are deified will nevertheless be called gods by the same name. What honor, then, will he receive from every creature whom the God of all creation will count as a friend, call brother, and regard as a son? For every creature will bow before him—an honor great and incomparable.

17. These gifts of God are sufficiently great and glorious; but if they lasted for a year, or indeed for an entire lifetime, do you think you would rejoice? Would you pay a price for them? “Gladly,” you say. Therefore they must possess security, so that they may always retain what they have. Their security, then, will be sufficient, since there will be no further mourning or pain of any kind. I shall never be able to lose so wonderful a blessedness unless I wish to, or unless God wishes to take it from me, or unless someone stronger than he invades his kingdom and takes it away. But I am secure: if I attain it, I shall not wish to lose it. I am secure also because God, “with whom there is no change nor shadow of alteration,” will not take it from me once he has given it. I am secure, and shall be secure, because no one stronger than he can arise. Therefore, since this is so, there can be no doubt that there will be complete security there.

18. Finally, there will be joy, immeasurable because of all these things, wholly surpassing the understanding of all. For who can conceive the joy each person will have in himself when he possesses such beauty, swiftness, strength, freedom, health, delight, duration, wisdom, friendship, harmony, power, honor, and security? Certainly no one can say how great this joy is or will be, because no one has experienced it in the present life. Yet if the Almighty gave that same joy to one of your friends—you, whoever you are who will come there—what would you think? Would you not rejoice greatly? And if he gave it to two or three, or indeed to more, even to those whom you loved no less than yourself, what would you say? Truly you would have great joy and would exult beyond all expression.

This gift, then, will in no way be absent if the Lord gives that same joy to our dearest friends and relatives, who by God’s mercy will be there with us, so that we may rejoice in him who is above and exult in ourselves and our neighbors. Indeed, that joy is and will be so great that it contains all within itself: it will overflow for all, surround all, and be theirs in every respect. For as fish in the sea have the sea surrounding them on every side, so the saints of God will have that magnificent sweetness of joy around them everywhere—the joy of which it is said to the good servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21, 23).

19. Having thus briefly considered the fourteen elements of blessedness, or of happiness, perhaps someone may ask what benefit or purpose so much beauty, swiftness, and several other elements can have, since merely to live blessedly and possess those things without which life cannot exist might seem entirely sufficient. But it must be known that God has need of nothing; and as he is sufficient in all things, so his friends and servants will possess every sufficiency in all things. For if any one of them felt himself powerless in any respect, he would not rejoice as fully as he will when he knows himself truly omnipotent with respect to his will. Therefore, that our joy may be full, nothing will be lacking to those who fear—indeed, who love—God.

## CHAPTER IV. The Supreme Misery of the Damned

29. Since such great blessedness belongs to God’s friends, what will belong to his enemies? Certainly, “not so the wicked, not so” (Ps. 1:4).
