In contrast to the saints, who will be most beautiful, I think that they will be most hideous, and that they will not be changed for the better in the resurrection. Rather, as the good will be glorified on the day of the Lord’s revelation, so they, cast down into eternal damnation, will be dishonored. The blessed and holy will be most swift in whatever they wish; the unhappy and evil will be most sluggish. In contrast to the greatest strength of the blessed, the wretched will have the greatest weakness. The righteous will have the freedom to go wherever they wish; but the unrighteous, condemned to eternal confinement, will be able to go nowhere. God’s elect will enjoy unbroken health; the damned will be tormented by perpetual sickness. The good will be satisfied with the delight of God’s house; and the evil will be filled with the most bitter cup of the devil’s house. The good will have enduring continuance in good things; the evil will never lack an end to their evils. The upright will be endowed with the greatest wisdom; the wicked will be confounded in their folly as wretches. God’s friends will possess the highest friendship with one another; his enemies, the greatest enmity among themselves. The blessed will be united in perpetual peace; the wretched will be discordant in continual dissension. The righteous will possess royal power to command; the unrighteous will lack even the power to move themselves anywhere. God’s saints will be raised high in great honor; the damned will be crushed by much disgrace. The good will be secure that their good will never perish; the evil will be tortured by fear without end. Mourning and desolation to those who have despised the Lord Christ; joy and delight to those who have loved and love him—to whom be honor, glory, and dominion for ages of ages. Amen.

## [Treatises of William, Abbot of Saint-Theoderic]

### Prefatory Notice to the Following Treatises

1. Like the *Letter to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*, the treatises *On Contemplating God* and *On the Nature and Dignity of Love* were attributed to Bernard. It seemed right to restore the former to its author Guigo, and the latter to William, abbot of Saint-Theoderic near Rheims and later monk of Signy, and to include them in this edition. For, besides the fact that in most and in the better-known manuscript codices these two treatises bear William’s name, William himself claims them in the short preface published by Tissier, which he wrote to be prefixed to his works and which, as we have shown, was improperly attached to Guigo’s preface to his letter. In the brief summary of his Life which we possess from a parchment of the monastery of Radol, the same treatises, along with others, are assigned to the same author. It will not be tiresome to quote the parchment’s words here:

> “Moreover, he left behind not inconsiderable monuments of his talent and study, of which I shall record only those that I have verified by sight and reading. He undertook to write the Life of Saint Bernard, but could not complete the work; nevertheless, he finished one book, the first, and one of no small size. Against Master Peter Abelard, who had inserted into his works certain matters discordant with the faith, he published one book, elegant in expression, Catholic in faith, forceful in reasoning. He also made two small books, one of which he called *The Enigma of Faith*, the other *The Mirror of Faith*; in them he briefly and plainly showed what ought to be believed. He composed a moral exposition on the Song of Songs; he mentions this work in the Life of Saint Bernard. There is another book by him, *On the Nature and Dignity of Love*, which, in accordance with its subject matter, we may call an *Anti-Ovid*. For in it he instructs the true philosopher by what stages and methods he can and ought to advance in the love of God. [lacuna]
>
> “On physics—that is, the nature of body and soul—he made a brief compilation, so that, because self-knowledge is the chief fruit of learning, in accordance with that saying which came down from heaven, ‘Know thyself’ (*Γνῶθι σεαυτόν*), he might instruct simple readers in at least an initial knowledge of themselves. There is also a little book of his entitled *On Contemplating God*, in which, undoubtedly for the edification of readers, he speaks of his own contemplation in these words: ‘And sometimes, Lord, as though with closed eyes gaping toward you, you send into the mouth of my heart something which I am not permitted to know what it is. For I perceive a sweetness so strengthening that, if it were perfected in me, I would seek nothing further.’
>
> “He also composed a substantial treatise whose title is *Meditative Prayers*. In it he does not employ one subject matter, but discusses diverse chapters; and in most of them, addressing God, he examines his own manifold conscience. In this work there appears especially not merely this man’s love for God, but his ardor. And truly, I think that whoever reads it devoutly and soberly, however devout and somewhat learned he may be, will nevertheless advance in the fear of the Lord, in greater knowledge and lower estimation of himself. I do not doubt that he produced other small works; but up to this point I have been able to discover none besides these.”

2. Thus far the parchment of Radol, at the beginning of which it is reported that William was born at Liège to a distinguished family and had a brother Simon. He went with him to Rheims and took the habit of holy religion at the abbey of Saint Nicasius, where there was then a reputation for good observance. In time Simon became abbot of Saint Nicholas of the Wood; after presiding long and religiously over the brothers there, full of days and perfected in virtue, he rested in a blessed end. Lord William, however, was made abbot of Saint-Theoderic, a place overlooking the city of Rheims, namely in the year 1120. Fourteen years later he became a monk at Signy, of the Cistercian Order, as was said in the notes on Bernard’s Letter 85.

3. From all this it is clear that the treatises *On Contemplating God* and *On the Nature and Dignity of Love*, wrongly ascribed to Bernard, are William’s own. It is therefore worthwhile to restore them to him and publish them here. Other small works of this same William, indicated above, are found in volume four of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*.

## Treatise of William, Abbot of Saint-Theoderic near Rheims, Later Monk of Signy, on Contemplating God

[Note: In certain manuscripts: *The Book of the Soliloquies of Saint Bernard*.]

### Prologue

1. Now almost rotted away in the pit of misery and in the mud of filth, fixed in the mire of the deep where there is no firm ground, from the depths of my sorrows I cry to you, Lord: “Lord, hear my voice.” For, in punishment for your form—by which, good Creator, you had conformed me to yourself, creating me in your image and likeness—which I neglected and lost, you have disfigured me into the form of this misery in which I am wretched; and, weighed down by sin, I am fixed ever lower in the mire of sin. You have laid upon me the hand of your just and hidden judgment, pressing upon me so that I may not rise. In neither pit, mud, nor mire, Lord, do I find firm ground upon which I may lean in order to emerge, something I may grasp in order to be drawn out. The pit of hell has no bottom except the depth of despair. The mud of filth has the corruption of nature, into which I am always sinking; it has nothing through which I may rise again—indeed, it obstructs and entangles me. The mire of the deep, the love of the flesh, ever seeking the lowest things and the abyss of insatiability, holds me fast by your just judgment.

2. But, O Lord, “deep calls to deep”: the abyss of my most profound misery calls upon the abyss of your most exalted mercy. Seeking a firm ground on which to lean, something to grasp, I find nowhere anything except you, who are truly certain and solid being, subsisting from yourself alone, from whom all things that are have their being. But what am I saying—“I find”? If I had already found you, I would stand firmly. I seek where I may find him whom my soul loves. I go about the streets of this great city, of this world. People live for themselves who, as the Apostle says, are alienated from the life of God (Eph. 4:18). I go about its squares, the broad ways of the world; and all things within me and outside me call me back with loud cries, that is, with certain reasons, to my inward parts, testifying from you that the kingdom of God is within me, so that I may seek you inwardly in the chamber of my heart, since, going outside, I do not find you.

Behold, I am within. Tell me, all my inward faculties, have you seen him whom my soul loves? And my memory answers me: “He is with me.” “Where?” I ask. “For you are the great sea; in you are creeping things without number, small living creatures with great” (Ps. 103:25). It does not say “with creeping things,” nor that you should seek him in a human being. “Where, then?” “In love. There is his dwelling-place; there is his chamber. The affection of love is naturally in you. If he whom you seek is in your love, he is in you; if he is not there, he is not in you. But you would not seek him whom you seek unless you loved. Therefore you possess him whom you seek, and he is with you. But you do not enjoy him unless I am wholly present with you.”

3. Therefore do not divide and scatter me among alien things; gather me wholly to yourself, into him. Then you will have the capacity for enjoyment; you will pour forth the remembrance of the abundance of his sweetness and exult in his righteousness. Indeed, let us enter wholly, O my memory, and all my affections; let us enter. And through remembering, understanding, and seeing, let us enjoy the highest good and all his goods. He is truly with me: I find him in my love, because with assured conscience I love him, and I love and desire to love him more and more perfectly. Therefore let us be borne toward him in complete embraces and press close in kisses.

O beloved, awe-inspiring, worshipful, sweet and gentle one, abounding in mercy: deign to receive my embrace, you who deigned to take my nature; deign to kiss me with your charity, you who deigned to unite your nature to my nature. Our embrace toward you is the striving and stretching forth of affections and works in order to enjoy you. Our kiss is when we offer you the pure affection of a pure mind. Your embrace toward us is the gracious condescension of your visitation and consolation. Your kiss is the revelation and infusion of your grace. Let not your left hand, Lord—your temporal consolation—be absent, but let it be under my head for my support. But may your right hand, your spiritual consolation concerning spiritual and eternal things, wholly embrace me for enjoyment. And in the embrace of your charity, in the kisses of your sweetness, may my soul sleep and rest in the peace of complete unity, because you, Lord, “have made me dwell in hope alone” (Ps. 4:9–10).

## CHAPTER I. The Soul That Loves God Asks to Be Raised Upward, Purified from Earthly Things and Vices

1. “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob, and he will teach us his ways” (Isa. 2:3). My intentions, thoughts, wills, affections, and all my inward faculties, come: let us ascend the mountain, or place, where the Lord sees or is seen. Cares, concerns, anxieties, labors, punishments, servitudes: wait for me here with the ass, this body, until I, with the boy—that is, reason with understanding—hasten there and, after we have worshiped, return to you (Gen. 22:5). For we shall return—and alas, return very soon. The charity of truth draws us away from you, but the truth of charity does not permit us, because of the brothers, to renounce and abjure you. Yet though your necessity draws us back, that sweetness must not for your sake be wholly abandoned.

Lord God of hosts, turn us again; show your face, and we shall be saved (Ps. 79:20). But alas, alas, Lord God! How premature, rash, disorderly, presumptuous, and contrary to the rule of the word of truth and of your wisdom it is to wish to see God with an impure heart! Yet, O highest goodness, highest good, life of hearts, light of inward eyes: because of your goodness, Lord, have mercy. For this is my cleansing, this my confidence, this my righteousness: the contemplation of your goodness, good Lord. Therefore, O Lord my God, who say to my soul, in the way you know, “I am your salvation” (Ps. 34:3): Rabboni, highest master, sole teacher in seeing what I desire to see, say to your blind beggar, “What do you want me to do for you?” (Luke 18:41). And you know—you who already grant this very thing—how, having withdrawn from every recess of its being and cast far away all the heights, beauties, delights of this world, and whatever can or usually does stir the desire of the flesh, the eyes, or the ambitious spirit, my heart says to you: “My face has sought you; your face, Lord, I shall seek. Do not turn your face away from me; do not turn aside in anger from your servant” (Ps. 26:8–9).

2. For I am shameless and wicked, O my ancient helper and unfailing protector. But see that I do this out of love for your love. [For since by the gift of your grace, Lord, I do not turn the face of my heart toward things of the flesh, but you have set them beneath me; and have set beneath me the world and all that is in it—what is it, I ask, that, while searching for you with all my heart, when I rejoice that I have grasped your face, which alone my face desires, I suddenly find myself apart from it? Why do you hide it? Do you think me your enemy? Do you wish to consume me for the sins of my youth? Am I not turned toward you, or are you still turned away from me? If I am not turned, O God of hosts, turn me; if you are turned away, O God of hosts, turn back. You said: “If you return, Israel, return” (Jer. 4:1); and again: “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you” (Zech. 1:3). You know the dwelling of your grace in the heart of your poor servant: “My heart is ready, O God; my heart is ready.” Command what you will; make me understand what you command; grant ability, you who granted the will, and whatever you will shall be done in me or through me. God of hosts, turn us again; show your face, and we shall be saved.]

[Note: The words enclosed in brackets are absent from the edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*.]

3. For within my soul and mind the voice of your testimony answers me, tumultuous within me and shaking all my inward faculties. And my inner eyes grow dim from the splendor of your truth, impressing upon me that no human being can see you and remain alive. For I, still wholly in sins, have not yet been able to die to myself so as to live to you. Yet by your command and gift I stand upon the rock of my faith, the Christian faith, in the place that is truly with you. There, as I can, I bear patiently for the time being, embrace, and kiss again and again your right hand that covers and protects me. Sometimes, contemplating and longing to see the back of the one who sees me, I survey the path of the human dispensation of Christ your Son.

But when I long to draw near to him—or, like the woman with the issue of blood, when I, sick and wretched in soul, long as it were to steal healing by the saving touch even of his hem (Matt. 9:20–22); or, like that Thomas, a man of desires, when I desire to see and touch him wholly, and not only this, but to approach the most holy wound in his side, the door of the ark made in its side, so that I may put in not merely a finger or my whole hand, but enter wholly to the very heart of Jesus, into the Holy of Holies, into the ark of the covenant, to the golden urn, the soul of our humanity containing within itself the manna of divinity—alas, I am told: “Do not touch me” (John 20:25, 17), and that saying from Revelation: “Dogs are outside” (Rev. 22:15). Thus, driven out and repelled with the deserved blows of my conscience, I am compelled to pay the penalties of my shamelessness and presumption.

Then, returning again to my rock, which is a refuge for hedgehogs (Ps. 103:18), filled with the thorns of sins, I embrace and kiss again and again your right hand that covers and protects me. And from what I have even lightly felt or seen, with desire more inflamed, I can scarcely wait patiently until you remove from me the hand that covers me and pour in illuminating grace, so that at last, in accordance with the answer of your truth, dead to myself and living to you, with unveiled face I may begin to see your very face and be affected by you through the sight of your face.

4. And, O face, face most blessed, worthy, by seeing you, to be affected by you: it builds in its heart a tabernacle for the God of Jacob and does everything according to the pattern shown to it on the mountain. Here, indeed, it fittingly sings: “My heart said to you: My face has sought you; your face, Lord, I shall seek!” (Ps. 26:8). Thus, as I said, through the gift of your grace, considering every corner and boundary of my conscience, I desire you alone and uniquely, so that all the borders of my land may see the salvation of the Lord their God; so that I may love, when I see, him to love whom is truly to live.

For in the sickness of my desire I say to myself: “Who loves what he does not see? How can that which is in no way visible be lovable?” Yet, to one who desires you, your lovable things come forth. From heaven and earth and every creature of yours they freely offer and present themselves to me, O Lord, worshipful and lovable in all things. And the more clearly and truly they proclaim and prove you lovable, the more ardently they make you desirable to me. But alas—not unto the perfect sweetness and joy of enjoying you, but unto the torment of striving [variant: “and intensification”] and deprivation, though not without some sweetness. For as the things I offer do not please you perfectly unless I myself accompany them, so contemplation of your goods refreshes us sweetly indeed, but does not perfectly satisfy without you.

## CHAPTER II. The Soul Desiring God Complains That It Is Weighed Down by the Burden of the Body

5. This is my soul’s continual exercise. By this I continually direct my spirit toward its mark; and, leaning upon your goods and lovable things as upon feet and hands, and with all my strength, I stretch upward toward you—in you, highest love, highest good. But the more forcefully I strive upward, the more harshly I am thrust down into the earth, into myself, beneath myself. Thus, looking back, discerning, and judging myself, I have become to myself, from myself, a laborious and wearisome question. Yet, Lord, I am certain through your grace that I have in all my heart and soul the desire for your desire and the love for your love. By your action I have advanced this far: I desire to desire you, and I love to love you. Yet in loving this, I do not know what I love. For what is it to love love, to desire desire? By love we love whatever we love; by desire we desire whatever we desire.

But perhaps, when I love love, I do not love the love by which I love what I wish to love, and by which I love whatever I love; rather, I love myself as loving—when in the Lord my soul is praised and loved by me, a soul which I would without doubt detest and hate if I found it elsewhere than in the Lord and in his love. But what shall we say also about desire? If I say, “I desire to be desiring,” I already find myself desiring; but do I desire desire for you, as though I did not possess it, or a desire greater than that which I possess?

6. Therefore, since in this way the inner eyes of my soul fail, grow dim, and become half-blind, I pray that they may quickly be opened by you—not as Adam’s bodily eyes were opened, so that he saw his own shame (Gen. 3:7), but so that I may see your glory, Lord: that, forgetting my littleness and poverty, I may rise wholly and rush into the embraces of your love, seeing him whom I shall have loved, and loving [Col. 0370A] him whom I shall have seen; and, dying in myself, may begin to live in you; and may fare well in you, in whom one fares worst when one is in oneself. But hasten, Lord; do not delay.

For the grace of your wisdom, Lord—or the wisdom of your grace—has its own shortcuts. And he to whom it is given, faithfully seeking and faithfully knocking, often suddenly finds himself there: at the torrent of your delight, at the full joy of your love, to which one ascends not by any arguments or discussions of reason or reasoning, as by certain ladders. But, Lord, if ever—how rare this is—I find myself in some share of this joy, I cry out and shout: “Lord, it is good for us to be here; let us make here three tents” (Matt. 17:4): one for faith, one for hope, one for love. Do I not know what I say when I say, “It is good [Col. 0370B] for us to be here”? Yet suddenly I fall to the ground as though dead; looking about, I see nothing, and find myself where I was before: namely, in pain of heart and affliction of spirit.

“How long, Lord? How long? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, sorrow in my heart day after day?” (Ps. 12:1–2). How long will the spirit not remain in human beings, because they are flesh (Gen. 6:3)? Yet it comes and goes, and breathes where it wills (John 3:8). But when the Lord restores the captivity of Zion, we shall be like those who are comforted. Then our mouth shall be filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation (Ps. 125:1–2). Meanwhile, alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged: I have dwelt among the dwellers of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner (Ps. 119:5–6). But within my heart the truth [Col. 0370C] of your consolation answers me, and the consolation of your truth.

## CHAPTER III. Whether and how inequality of love is given among the blessed

7. There is a love of desire, and there is a love of enjoyment. The love of desire at some time merits vision; vision, enjoyment; enjoyment, the perfection of love. I give thanks to your grace, which deigns to speak to the heart of your servant and to answer, in some measure, his anxious questions. I receive and embrace this earnest of your Spirit, and joyfully await in this earnest your promise.

Therefore I desire to love you, and I love to desire you; and in this way I run, that I may lay hold of that for which I was laid hold of: namely, that someday I may love you perfectly, because you first loved us, Lord, worthy of love and beloved. But is this perfection of your love, this consummation of blessedness in your love, ever or anywhere such that the soul thirsting for God, the living fountain, is satisfied and filled so as to say, “It is enough”? I wonder whether anyone, wherever he may be, does not fail if he says, “It is enough.” But where there is failure in such sufficiency, what perfection can there be? Therefore perfection is nowhere and never.

But, Lord, will the unrighteous possess your kingdom? And unrighteous is the person who neither desires nor feels and understands himself to be your debtor for loving you as much as it is possible for any rational creature to love you. It is also certain that those blessed Seraphim, who are both called and are “Burning Ones” from the nearness of your presence and the brightness of your vision, love you more than anyone lesser in the kingdom [Col. 0371A] of heaven. If such a one is in the kingdom of heaven—not, I say, the least, but certainly one of its members—he desires to love you as much as either you can be loved or ought to be loved by anyone; and perhaps he is one “into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1:12). Therefore that blessed lesser one, whoever he is, desires to love you as much as any person who loves you more than he does—not with jealous rivalry, but with devout and pious imitation.

But if he also progresses in love, then the more sweetly the eye illumined advances into the inner things, the more sweetly he perceives and understands—if he is not ungrateful and unrighteous—that you can be loved more, and that he is bound to love you more, even as the Cherubim and Seraphim love you. But one who desires what he cannot attain is miserable. Misery, however, is wholly alien to the kingdom of blessedness. Therefore whoever desires anything there attains what he desires.

8. What shall we say to these things? What, I say, shall we say? Speak, I beseech you, Lord, for your servant hears. Are all, both great and small, who are in the kingdom of God each in his own order loving and desiring to love, while the unity of love does not allow diversity to exist? For the one to whom it is given loves more ardently; while the lesser in love, without envy, loves the good wherever he sees it, which he desires for himself; and he surely has, however great or small it may be, the love that he has and loves in the one who loves.

Assuredly, love itself is what is loved. From the great abundance and nature of its goodness it fills lovers and fellow-lovers, those rejoicing and those rejoicing with them, with equal grace, though in unequal measure. And the more abundantly [Col. 0371C] it pours itself into the perceptions of those who love, the more capable of itself it makes them, producing satisfaction but without weariness; not diminishing desire from that very satisfaction, but increasing it, with every misery of anxiety removed.

For love, as has been said, is what is loved; and from the torrent of its delight it drives away from its lover every misery—whether the weariness of satiation, the anxiety of desire, or envy in jealousy. It illumines them, as the Apostle says, “from glory to glory” (2 Cor. 3:18), so that in light they may see light and in love conceive love. For this is the fountain of life which always flows and is never exhausted. This is the glory; these are the riches in the house of your blessed lover: that what he desires and loves is at hand for one who desires and loves.

Therefore one who desires always loves to desire, and one who loves always desires to love; and you, Lord, so make what the desiring and loving person desires and loves abound, that neither anxiety afflicts the one who desires nor weariness the one who abounds. And is this, I beseech you, Lord, eternal life, of which the Psalm sings: “See whether there be a way of iniquity in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Ps. 138:24)? This is the disposition; this is perfection: always to go in this way is to arrive. Hence your Apostle, who shortly before had said, “Not that I have already received it or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if I may lay hold of that for which I was laid hold of in Christ Jesus. One thing: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I press toward the goal for the prize [Col. 0372A] of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus,” adds, “Therefore, let all of us who are perfect think this” (Phil. 3:12–15).

## CHAPTER IV. God must be loved for his own sake; everything else only for God’s sake

9. And this is your loving, by which you love those who love you: from the sweetness of your goodness which you have toward your creature, good Creator, to inspire in them the desire to love you, and the love by which they desire and love you. For when you love us, you are not affected toward us or by us; but you are he who is always the same, for whom to be is to be good. Good is in you for yourself and for every one of your creatures in you.

But when we love you, we are affected from you, toward you, and in you; for we can in some miserable way exist and not love you—that is, exist and exist badly. But to you, who are always the same, nothing is added if through loving we advance toward you, and nothing is diminished if we fail away from you. When you love us, you love us only for your own sake, since the most true rule of supreme justice allows even us to love nothing outside you.

And surely it is possible for the love of one who loves God, where great grace is present, to advance so far that, loving neither you nor himself for his own sake, he loves both you and himself for your sake alone. Through this he is re-formed to the image in which you created him. For, by the truth of your most excellent nature and by the nature of your truth, you can love neither yourself except for yourself, nor angel nor human being except for yourself.

[Col. 0372C] 10. O happy—most happy—soul that deserves to be thus affected by God toward God: so that through the unity of the Spirit it loves in God God alone; loves no private possession of its own; and loves itself only in God. And God in it loves or approves what God ought to love or approve: that is, himself; indeed, what alone ought to be loved, both by God the Creator and by God’s creature.

For neither the name nor the affection of love belongs or is owed to anyone but you alone, O true Love and Lord worthy of love. And this is the will of your Son in us; this is his prayer for us to you, God his Father: “I will that, as I and you are one, so they also may be one in us” (John 17:11, 21). This is the end; this is the consummation; this is perfection. This is [Col. 0372D] peace; this is the joy of the Lord; this is joy in the Holy Spirit; this is silence in heaven.

For as long as we are in this life, the affections sometimes enjoy this silence of most blessed peace in heaven—that is, in the soul of the righteous, which is the seat of wisdom. But it lasts for half an hour, or as it were half an hour; while intention, from the remnants of thought, keeps a perpetual feast before you. But in that blessed and eternal life of which it is said, “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21, 23), there will be only perfect and eternal enjoyment; and it will be happier insofar as, with everything that seems able to delay or impede it now removed, the eternity of that love will be indissoluble, its perfection unassailable, and its blessedness incorruptible.

## CHAPTER V. Nothing must be loved above God, beyond whom nothing can be desired

[Col. 0373A]

11. O Love, come into us; take possession of us. Let every name of foulness perish from before your face within us—those names which grow upon this affection from the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, like certain spurious offspring. I mean that affection which is called love in us and is often corrupted by the diseases of the soul created by you and for you. This affection, created only for you, joined to you, resisting and protesting against the law of nature, is forced to be called gluttony, lust, avarice, and the like; whereas, uncorrupted and abiding in its own nature, it belongs to you alone, Lord, to whom alone love is due.

For love in the rational soul is, as one of your servants said, a movement, or a resting station, or an end beyond which the appetite of the will desires nothing or judges that nothing should be desired. But one who seeks anything beyond you or above you, as though it were better than you, seeks nothing; for nothing is better or sweeter than you. Therefore, in departing from you, who alone are truly to be loved, nothing is accomplished; one commits fornication and indulges in lust through alien affections, which bear alien names, as I have said. For love, as has been said and must often be said, belongs to you alone, Lord, in whom alone is whatever truly is, where there is a quiet and secure resting-place; because to fear God with the chaste fear of love and to keep his commandments—this is the whole human being.

## CHAPTER VI. God first loved us and stirred us to love through the Son

[Col. 0373C]

12. Therefore let every injustice depart from my soul, that I may love you, the Lord my God, with my whole heart, with my whole soul, and with all my strength. Let every jealousy depart, lest I love with you anything that I do not love for your sake, O truly unique Love and truly Lord. But when I love something for your sake, I do not love that thing, but you, for whose sake I love what I love.

For you alone are truly Lord: for you to rule over us is to save us; while for us to serve you is nothing other than to be saved by you. For what is your salvation, Lord—yours whose is salvation, and whose blessing is upon your people—except that we have received from you both to love you and to be loved by you? Therefore, Lord, you willed that the son of your right hand, the man whom you strengthened for yourself, should be called Jesus, that is, Savior: “For he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21), and “there is no other in whom salvation is found” (Acts 4:12).

He taught us to love him, since he himself first loved us even to the death of the cross, and washed us by loving and cherishing us, raising us up so that we might love him who first loved us to the end. This is the justice of human children: “Love me, because I love you.” But rare is the one who can say: “I love you in order that you may love me.” You did this, [Col. 0374A] because, as the servant of your love cries out and proclaims, you first loved us (1 John 4:19). And so indeed it is. You loved us first, that we might love you—not because you needed to be loved by us, but because we could not be what you made us to be except by loving you.

Therefore, in many portions and in many ways God spoke of old to the fathers through the prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us in the Son (Heb. 1:1–2), in your Word by which the heavens were established and all their host by the spirit of his mouth. Your speaking in your Son was nothing other than setting your tent in the sun—that is, in what is manifest.

13. How greatly and in what manner you loved us: you “did not spare your own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32); he too “loved us and gave himself for us” (Gal. 2:20). This is your Word to us, Lord: this almighty Word, who, while all things held the midst of silence—the deep, namely, of error—came from royal thrones, a stern conqueror of errors and a sweet commender of love [Col. 0374B] (Wis. 18:14–16).

And whatever he did, whatever he said on earth, even to insults, spittle, and blows, even to the cross and the tomb, was nothing but your speaking to us in the Son, provoking and stirring our love toward you by your love. For you knew, God, Creator of souls, that this affection could not be compelled in the souls of human children, but had to be invited forth; and also that where there is compulsion, there is no longer freedom, and where there is no freedom, there is no justice.

But you, righteous Lord, wished to save us; and you save or condemn no one except justly. You yourself formed our judgment and cause, sitting upon the throne and judging justice—but justice which you made (Ps. 9:5)—so that every mouth might be stopped and the whole world made subject to God (Rom. 3:19), when you have mercy on whom you have mercy and grant mercy to whom you will have mercy (Rom. 9:15). You therefore willed that we should love you: for we could neither rightly be saved unless we loved you, nor love you unless love came forth from you. Therefore, Lord, as the Apostle who loved you says—and as we have already said—you first loved us; you love before all your lovers.

## CHAPTER VII. With what love God loves us

14. But we, Lord, love you with the affection of love implanted in us by you. Yet you, Creator of all things, of good affections, and of souls capable of affection—do you love those whom you love with an affection of love that befalls or comes upon you? Are you in any way affected by anything, you who make all persons and all things? Far be it! It is absurd, far from faith, alien to the Creator of all.

How then do you love us, if you do not love us with love? But your love is your goodness, O highest Good and supreme good: the Holy Spirit proceeding from Father and Son, who from the beginning of creation is borne over the waters (Gen. 1:2), that is, over the fluctuating minds of human children. Offering himself to all, he draws all things to himself, inspiring and breathing upon them, warding off what is harmful and providing what is useful, uniting God to us and us to God.

For your Holy Spirit, who is called the love of Father and Son, their unity and will, dwells in us by his grace, commends God’s charity in us, and through that charity reconciles himself to us; by the good will inspired in us he unites us to God. [Col. 0375A] The intensity of this good will is called love in us: by it we love what we ought to love, namely, you. For love is nothing other than a strong and well-ordered will.

Therefore you love yourself, O Lord worthy of love, in yourself, when the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: the Father’s love for the Son and the Son’s love for the Father. And the love is so great that it is unity; the unity so great that it is *homoousion*, that is, the same substance of the Father and the Son.

You also love yourself in us, sending the Spirit of your Son into our hearts, crying out from the sweetness of love and the strength of the good will inspired in us by you, “Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6). Thus you make us your lovers—or rather, you thus love yourself in us—so that we who first hoped because we knew your name, Lord, and gloried in you, who loved the name of the Lord in you, O Lord, may now, through the grace inspiring us and through your Spirit of adoption, confidently believing that all things belonging to the Father are ours, invoke you by the very name which your only-begotten Son has by nature, through the grace of adoption.

240. 15. But because all this is from you, whose loving is doing good, and from whom comes every good gift and every perfect present, supreme Father of lights (Jas. 1:17): you love yourself in us and us in you, when we love you through you and are united to you insofar as we deserve to love you. Thus, as has been said, we are made participants in that prayer of Christ, your Son: “I will that, as I and you are one, so they also may be one in us” (John 17:11–21).

For we are your race, Lord: God’s race, as your Apostle says, transferring a pagan saying from an evil vessel into a good vessel, so that it may convey nothing but itself and a good vessel. We are, I say, God’s race (Acts 17:29), and “gods, all sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6), claiming through a certain spiritual kinship a great affinity with you. Through the Spirit of adoption your Son does not disdain to share one name with us; and, warned with saving precepts and formed by divine instruction with him and through him, we dare to say: “Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9).

Therefore you love us insofar as you make us your lovers; and we love you insofar as we receive from you your Spirit, who is your love. He takes possession of and holds all the recesses of our affections, perfectly converting them into the purity of your truth and the truth of your purity, into full consent to your love. [Col. 0375D] And so great a union, attachment, and enjoyment of your sweetness comes about that it is called unity by our Lord himself, your Son, when he says, “That they may be one in us”; of such dignity and glory that he continues and says, “As I and you are one.” O joy, O glory, O riches, O pride! For wisdom too possesses a pride of its own kind, saying: “With me are riches and glory, proud resources and justice” (Prov. 8:18).

## CHAPTER VIII. Through love we become one with God

16. But what could be more absurd than to be united to God in love and not in blessedness? For those are truly, uniquely, singularly, and perfectly blessed who truly and perfectly love you. “Blessed,” they have called, “the people to whom these things belong”; but they lie, because he alone is blessed whose Lord is his God (Ps. 143:15).

For what is it to be blessed except to will only the good and to have everything one wills? Therefore to will you, and to will you intensely—which is to love—and to love in a singular manner, you who do not deign to be loved together with anything whatever, whether bodily or spiritual, earthly or heavenly, unless it is loved for your sake: this at last is to will only the good; this is to have all things whatsoever one wills. For one possesses you insofar as one loves you.

Therefore, united to God both by love and by blessedness, we understand that “salvation truly belongs to the Lord, and your blessing is upon your people” (Ps. 3:9). And therefore we continually offer you our prayers, vows, sacrifices, and all that is ours, Father, through our Lord Jesus Christ your Son, believing and understanding that from you, through you, and unto you, through him, comes whatever is well with us—he from whom we have existence itself.

17. We believe and understand all these things through the ministry of your Holy Spirit dwelling in us, so far as it is lawful to understand. As has been said, he confirms our spirit to himself and unites it to himself, breathing in us when he wills, how he wills, and as much as he wills. We are his workmanship, created for good works; he is our sanctification, our justification, our love. For he himself is our love, through which we reach you and embrace you.

Otherwise, O incomprehensible Majesty, you seem comprehensible to the soul that loves you. For though no perception of any soul or spirit comprehends you, nevertheless the love of one who loves comprehends you wholly, as great as you are, because it loves you wholly, as great as you are—if indeed there is wholeness where there is no partiality; quantity where there is no magnitude; or comprehensibility where none of these exists.

But when we love you, our spirit is affected toward your Holy Spirit, through whom, dwelling in us, we have the charity of God poured out in our hearts. And since your love—the Father’s love for the Son and the Son’s love for the Father—is the Holy Spirit dwelling in us and is toward you what he is, namely love, converting and sanctifying in himself all the captivity of Zion—that is, every affection of our soul—[Col. 0376D] we love you, or you love yourself in us: we by affection, you by effect. You make us one in you through your unity, that is, your Holy Spirit whom you gave us.

Thus, just as for the Father to know the Son is nothing other than to be what the Son is, and for the Son to know the Father is nothing other than to be what the Father is—whence in the Gospel: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father” (Matt. 11:27)—and just as for the Holy Spirit to know or comprehend the Father and the Son is nothing other than to be what the Father and Son are: so for us, who were made in your image, made old from that image through Adam, and through Christ are renewed toward it day by day, may it be nothing other than to love and fear God and keep his commandments, when we love God, than to be and to be one spirit with God. For “to fear God and keep his commandments, this is the whole human being” (Eccles. 12:13).

You whom we must adore, fear, and bless, give him to us. “Send forth your Spirit, and they shall be created, and you shall renew the face of the earth” (Ps. 103:30). For they shall not draw near to God “in a flood of many waters”—that is, in the disturbance and confusion of so many and such diverse affections. This deluge, the punishment of Adam’s children, has endured long enough, Lord. Bring the Spirit over the earth; let the sea withdraw, let the salt bitterness of ancient condemnation withdraw, and let the dry land appear, thirsting for the fountain of life.

Let the dove, the Holy Spirit, come, after the foulest bird, brooding over its corpses, has been driven out. Let the dove come, I say, with an olive branch—that is, a branch of refreshment and light—announcing peace [Col. 0377B] (Gen. 8). May your holiness and sanctification sanctify us; may your unity unite us, so that through the name of charity we may be joined to God, who is charity, as though by a certain kindred affinity, and through the power of that name be made one.

18. Yet, Lord, it matters how one loves you. For many, as one enlightened by you has said, love truth when it shines but do not love it when it rebukes (St Augustine, *Confessions*, book 10, ch. 23, §34). And many honour justice in affection while being far from it in practice: they approve and love it in itself but do not practise it in themselves. Do these truly love you, O God who are true justice? Do these truly love you?

The philosophers of this world once cultivated justice both in loving affection and in the effect of action, so that it was said of them by one of them:

> The good hate to sin from love of virtue.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.16.52

Yet they are convicted of not having loved justice because they did not love you, from whom are the fountain and origin and to whom are the end and return of true justice, and without whom all human justices are like the cloth of a menstruating woman. For they did not have faith working through love, although they had a certain affected love and certain works of honourableness. Since these did not proceed from the fountain of true justice or go toward the end of true justice, they wandered all the more hopelessly the more vigorously they ran outside the way. For the way, Father, is your Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

## CHAPTER IX. Love consists in keeping the commandments

19. Therefore your truth—or the life to which one goes—describes for us, through the way by which one goes, the true and simple pattern of divine and true philosophy. It says to its disciples: “As the Father has loved me, I also have loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you shall abide in my love, as I too have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love” (John 15:9–10).

Behold, the Beloved of the beloved, as is read in the Psalm (Ps. 67:13), loves the Son with the Father, and the Son abides in the Father’s love unto the full keeping of his commandments. Again, the beloved of the Beloved—the beloved disciple—loves Christ the teacher unto the keeping of all his commandments; and even to the necessity of death he does not lose this will. In the illumination of his truth and love, he makes good use, for good, of all things suitable for good, inclined toward evil, and intermediate between the two. This is proper to Christian virtue.

For virtue, as has already been said before our time, is the good use of free will; and the work of virtue is the good use of those things of which we can also make bad use. Hence, lest charity be maimed, we are taught to love our neighbour according to the pure law of charity: so that, just as God loves in us only himself and we say that we love God alone, we may likewise begin to love our neighbour as ourselves, loving in him only God, [Col. 0378B] as in ourselves.

20. But why, Lord, so many words? My poor soul is naked, cold, and freezing, Lord, and desires to be warmed by the heat of your love. Therefore, having no garment, I draw together and sew up these little scraps, gathered from wherever they may be, to cover my nakedness. Not like that wise woman of Zarephath, gathering two sticks, but these tiny twigs from the wasteness of my desert, from the wide emptiness of my heart, so that someday I may enter into the tabernacle of my house and make for myself from a handful of flour and a jar of oil, eat, and die—or perhaps not die so soon (3 Kings [1 Kings] 17:10–16). Indeed, Lord, I shall not die, but live and declare the works of the Lord (Ps. 117:17).

Standing therefore in the house of solitude like a solitary wild ass, having my dwelling in the land of saltiness and drawing in the wind of my love (Jer. 2:24), I open my mouth to you, Lord, and draw in the spirit. And sometimes, Lord, when I gape toward you as if with closed eyes, you send into the mouth of my heart something which I am not permitted to know what it is. I do indeed perceive its taste, so sweet, so delightful, and so strengthening that, if it were brought to perfection in me, I would seek nothing further. But when I receive it, you do not allow me, through any sight of the body, perception of the soul, or understanding of the spirit, to discern what it is.

When I have received it, I wish to hold it, chew it over, and distinguish its flavour; but it immediately passes away. I swallow it, whatever it may be, into the hope of eternal life. Yet by long chewing I longed to pour the power of its operation, like some vital juice, through all the veins and marrow of my soul, so that it might lose taste for all other affections and taste that alone, always; but it hastens to pass away.

21. And when, from investigating, receiving, or using it, I strive to imprint upon memory certain formed outlines more firmly, or even to assist my wavering memory by writing, experience itself compels me to learn what that is which you say in the Gospel about the Spirit: “And you do not know whence he comes or whither he goes.” For whatever I have taken care to entrust to memory, as though by certain pictured outlines, so that by returning to them I might, whenever I wished, recollect myself there and thereby have it at my disposal whenever I wished—I hear from the Lord, “The Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3:8), and feel even in myself that he breathes not when I will, but when he himself wills. Thus I find all those things dead and tasteless, and find that my eyes must be lifted to you alone, fountain of life, so that in your light alone I may see light.

Therefore, Lord, my eyes are and may be toward you, toward you; in you and from you may all the advances of my soul advance; and when my strength—which is none—fails, may all its failures pant after you. But meanwhile, how long do you delay me? How long do you draw out my wretched, anxious soul, panting after you? Hide me, I beseech you, in the hiding-place of your face from the disturbance of men, and protect me in your tent from the contradiction of tongues (Ps. 30:21). But now the donkey calls me back, and the children make a noise.

## CHAPTER X. Profession of worship and love toward God

22. Now therefore, Lord, in full faith I worship you as God: you, the one principle of all things and the wisdom by which every wise soul is wise; you, the good itself by which all who are blessed are blessed. You alone I worship, adore, and bless as God; with my whole heart, my whole mind, and all [Col. 0380A] my strength, I either love you or desire to love you.

Whoever among angels or good spirits loves you, I know loves me also, loving himself in you. Whoever abides in you and can perceive human prayers or affections, I know hears me in you; and in you I too rejoice with them in their glory. Whoever has you as his good helps me in you and cannot envy me participation in you. For it belongs to the apostate spirit alone to make our misery his joy and our good his loss, since, fallen from the common good of all and from true blessedness, he is not subject to truth: delighting in his private good and hating the common good of all.

Therefore we worship and bless you: God the Father, by whose creative power we live; the Wisdom of the Father, through whom, re-formed, we live wisely; the Holy Spirit, whom and in whom, by loving, we live blessedly and shall live most blessedly; Trinity of one substance, one God, from whom we are, through whom we are, in whom we are; from whom we depart by sinning; to whom we have become unlike; by whom we have not been permitted to perish; the beginning to which we return, the form which we follow, the grace by which we are reconciled. To you be glory for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0379]

# THE SAME WILLIAM’S TREATISE ON THE NATURE AND DIGNITY OF LOVE

## CHAPTER ONE. Love, naturally implanted in humankind, has degenerated through the fault of the flesh and been corrupted

[Col. 0379C]

1. Love is the art of arts; nature itself, and God the author of nature, have reserved its teaching for themselves. For love itself, implanted by the Creator, teaches itself, unless its native ingenuousness has been impeded by certain adulterous affections. Those teachable by love are teachable by God (John 6:45).

For love is a power of the soul which, by a certain natural weight, carries it toward its proper place or end. Every creature, whether spiritual or bodily, has both a definite place toward which it is naturally carried and a certain natural weight by which it is carried. For, as one truly philosophical writer says, weight does not always carry things downward: fire upward, water downward, and so with the rest. A person too is moved by his or her weight, which naturally carries the spirit upward and the body downward, each to its proper place or end.

For what is the body’s place? “You are earth,” he says, “and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). But concerning the spirit, the book of Wisdom says: “The spirit shall return to him who created it” (Eccles. 12:7). See the person dissolved, how the whole person is borne by his own weight [Col. 0380C] to his proper place. When things proceed well and in their proper order, the spirit returns to God who created it; the body to the earth—and not to earth alone, but to the elements from which it had been composed and formed.

For since earth claims one part in it, water another, and air another, and since the dissolution of natural composition is natural, each thing returns by its own weight to its own element. The dissolution is complete when all these have been restored to their proper place. Whether this ought better to be called corruption or putrefaction, rather than, as has been said, dissolution, let whoever wishes judge.

And though none of these departs from the course of its nature, the wretched soul alone and the degenerate spirit, though of itself it naturally tends thither, does not know—or learns only with difficulty, corrupted by the fault of sin—how to return [Col. 0380D] to its own principle. Yet by its natural weight it is always driven toward that end: when it desires blessedness, it dreams of blessedness and seeks only to be blessed. But blessed is that person, and no other, whose Lord is his God (Ps. 143:15).

Yet, seeking blessedness outside its own country and outside its own way, it strays far from its natural intention. Therefore, having lost its natural instruction, it now needs a human teacher, who may teach it concerning the blessedness naturally sought through loving: reminding it where, toward what, in what country, and by what way it should be sought.

2. Love, therefore, as has been said, has been naturally implanted in the human soul by the Author of nature; but after it lost the law of God, it must be taught by man. It must not be taught in order that it may exist, as though it did not exist; rather, it must be taught how it may be purified and how it may make progress; how it may be strengthened and made firm. For even base carnal love once had teachers of its own baseness—men so perceptive and effective in the very matters in which they were corrupt and corrupted others—that the teacher of the art of love was compelled by lovers and companions of that very baseness to recant what he had sung too intemperately, and to write a remedy for love after having written of the conflagration of carnal love: he who had poured out all his genius either upon the old incitements of love, detestable, as it were, through a certain itch, or upon discovering new ones. [Note: [Col. 0381D] Ovid.]

That man did not seem to teach the ardor of carnal love, for he burned, both in his teaching and in the subject he taught, with a kind of natural fire untempered by any restraint of reason. Rather, by certain undisciplined lessons he trained its natural force into a kind of wantonness, and by superfluous stimulants of luxury drove it into a kind of madness. For in those wicked and depraved men, through the overflowing vice of carnal lust, the whole order of nature had perished. Since, according to the due order of nature, [Col. 0381C] their spirit ought by its natural weight, by its love, to be borne upward to God who created it, humbled by the enticements of the flesh, it did not understand; and, being compared to senseless beasts, it became like them (Ps. 48:13, 21). Thus they became those of whom it might be said: “My spirit shall not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3); in whose person it is said: “My heart has become like melting wax in the midst of my belly” (Ps. 21:15).

For the heart, placed within the narrow region of the body—where, as though in a central citadel of the higher faculties and of the lower body, like a kind of commonwealth of the humbler people, it might govern and administer the whole surrounding realm of thoughts and actions—melting in a degenerate softness before the fire of carnal desire, [Col. 0381D] flowed wholly down into the belly, into the midst of the belly. That is, it understood nothing except what belonged to the belly; and from the belly into its lower parts it confused everything, degraded everything, adulterated everything, perverting love’s natural affection into a brutish appetite of the flesh. It desired not only what is forbidden, to the disgrace of the body in passions of dishonor; it also so forgot its ancient nobility that it, which had been created for God alone, was judged by its corrupt and corrupting masters to be rather the natural dwelling-place of lust and a brothel of every vice. Unhappy are those who, while nature herself protested, became so vile that they made the place of their soul—which [Col. 0382A] properly belonged to God their Creator and could be shared with no creature—the seat of Satan, the seat of filth, and of every uncleanness.

## Chapter II. On the origin and progress of love

3. Therefore, intending to treat of love, insofar as he whose love is the object of this work’s striving may grant it, let us begin, as it were, the sequence of our account from love’s very beginnings, and trace the course of its advance through its successive ages, even to a fruitful old age—not one full of senile pain, but full of abundant mercy. For just as, according to the increase or decline of ages, a boy changes into a young man, a young man into an adult man, and an adult man into an old man—changing even the names of the ages according to changes in their qualities—[Col. 0382B] so, according to the progress of virtues, the will grows into love, love into charity, and charity into wisdom.

Nor should it be unknown, concerning the love of which we speak, from what birth it arose, by what line of nobility it is distinguished, or from what place it comes. The first place of its birth, then, is God. There it was born, there nourished, there advanced; there it is a citizen, not a stranger but a native. For love is given by God alone and remains in him, because it is owed to none but him and for his sake.

Moreover, if its lineage is considered: when the Trinity, who is God, created man in his image, he formed in him a certain likeness of the Trinity, in which the image of the creating Trinity might shine forth; and through which this new inhabitant of the world, the like naturally returning to the like, might cling inseparably, if he wished, to his beginning, his Creator—lest that created trinity, enticed, drawn away, and distracted by the manifold variety of creatures, should fall away from the unity of the supreme and creating Trinity. For when he breathed into the face of the new human being the breath of life, a spiritual power—that is, an intellectual power, which is conveyed by *spiratio* and *spiraculum*, “breathing” and “breath”—and a vital power, that is, an animal power, which is conveyed by the name “life”; when he breathed this into him, he created it. In this being’s citadel, as it were, he placed the power of memory, so that it might always remember the power and goodness of the Creator. Immediately, and without any interval of delay, memory begot reason from itself; and memory and reason brought forth [Col. 0382D] will from themselves. Memory possesses and contains the goal toward which one must tend; reason, that one ought to tend toward it; will tends toward it. These three are one thing, yet three operations; just as in the supreme Trinity there is one substance and three persons. In that Trinity, as the Father is begetter, the Son begotten, and the Holy Spirit from both, so reason is begotten from memory, and will proceeds from memory and reason. Therefore, that the rational soul created in man might cleave to God, the Father claims memory for himself; the Son claims reason; and the Holy Spirit, proceeding from both, claims the will that proceeds from both.

4. See from what parentage will has arisen: of what birth, what adoption, what rank, what nobility. When, through prevenient and cooperating [Col. 0383A] grace, it begins by its good assent to cleave to the Holy Spirit himself, who is the love and will of Father and Son; and begins vehemently to will what God wills, and what memory and reason suggest ought to be willed—then, by willing vehemently, it becomes love. For love is nothing other than a vehement will toward the good.

Will in itself is a simple affection, implanted in the rational soul so that it may be capable of both good and evil: it is filled with good when aided by grace; with evil when, left to itself, it fails in itself. So that nothing might be lacking to the human soul from its Creator, a will free toward either side was given to it. When this agrees with assisting grace, it receives the progress and name of virtue and becomes love. When left to itself it wishes to enjoy itself according to itself, it suffers its own failure in itself; and it acquires as many names of vices as it has vices: covetousness, avarice, lust, and others of this kind.

5. Thus, at its first advance, will is set free as though at the fork of the Pythagorean letter. If it is raised, in accordance with the dignity of its natural endowments, into love, then according to the natural order of its virtues it progresses, as has been said, from love into charity and from charity into wisdom. But if, without any order of its own, though by the just ordering of God, it is driven headlong in ruin, it is buried in the hell of vices beneath the darkness of confusion, unless grace soon comes to its aid.

But if, having abandoned the way of hell, it begins to lift its steps upward, and, following grace as it leads and nourishes it, has matured into love, then, established in the strength of youth, [Col. 0383C] it begins to advance from the spirit of fear—by which it had hitherto, like a child, feared punishment—to the spirit of devotion. In God, from whom it now begins to taste new grace, it begins devoutly to love and worship God, of whom it is written: “Devotion is his worship” (Job 28:28, according to the Septuagint).

Here, then, this young man—not in age but in virtue—must exercise the natural strength and power of youth, and must not lose youth’s natural incentives, though reason forbids their corruption. If those who corrupt them rage, who “pass away in an image,” whose spirit is like the spirit of beasts or cattle, whose flesh, according to the prophet, is like the flesh of asses (Ezek. 23:20), then much more may those who are in the truth of love and are impelled by its spiritual incentives be permitted, in the ardor of spiritual youth, to rage in their own way. For it is a grave reproach against nature if its corrupters can make greater progress toward evil than true lovers can toward good.

## Chapter III. On a certain holy madness required in the truly religious person

6. Hear of holy madness: “Whether,” says the Apostle, “we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13). Do you wish to hear madness still further? “If you forgive them their sin,” he says, “forgive it; but if not, blot me out from the book which you have written” (Exod. 32:31–32). Do you want another example? Hear the Apostle himself: “I wished,” he says, “to be anathema from Christ for my brethren” (Rom. 9:3).

Does it not seem a certain sound madness of a well-disposed mind to hold firmly in affection what cannot be accomplished in effect—to wish, for Christ’s sake, to be separated from Christ? Such was the drunkenness of the apostles at the coming of the Holy Spirit; such was Paul’s madness when Festus said to him, “You are mad, Paul” (Acts 26:24). Was it surprising that he should be declared mad, when, in the very danger of death, he strove to convert to Christ the very judges by whom he was being judged for Christ? It was not much learning that caused this madness in him, as the king said—understanding the truth but concealing it—but, as has been said, the drunkenness of the Holy Spirit, in which he longed to make those who judged him like himself, both small and great. And, to omit other instances, what madness could be greater or more unexpected than that a man who has left the world, desiring and burning to cling to Christ, should for Christ’s sake again, by the necessity of obedience and brotherly charity, cling to the world; that one tending toward heaven should plunge himself into mud?

This is the youthful Benjamin, who in the ecstasy of his mind (Ps. 67:28) perceives neither himself nor anything belonging to himself, but him alone into whom he has wholly passed. With this madness the martyrs were mad, smiling amid their torments. Why should I not say here what the wanton poet said in the heat of his own wantonness: “I delight in being mad”? [Note: [Col. 0383D] Virgil, *Eclogues* 3.36.]

7. Here, then, although youthful ardor and an ardent course of religious life may stand out, it nevertheless submits to reason’s bridle, though at this stage it neither has nor ought to have full discretion. [Col. 0384C] The merciful acts of discretion toward oneself, the management of such discretion, and easy indulgences according to one’s own judgment do not teach the fervor of novices; yet such indulgences are not to be rejected when they come from another. Toward oneself there ought to be a stern judgment and strict severity; but toward one’s superior or adviser, a gentle and obedient humility in all things, joined with paternal or fraternal charity and devotion.

If either is lacking, then in the sluggish and lukewarm person I do not hope for perseverance in the course, while in the headlong person I fear a fall. Therefore the novice’s whole discretion ought to be to make himself a fool in all things for Christ and to depend upon another’s judgment—especially if he has an elder of whom it is certain that he learns from God what he is to teach a human being. Yet the person who is making progress and obeying ought not readily presume the liberty of judging, so long as nothing plainly contrary to God is commanded, until long and patient experience gives understanding in these matters to hearing. Above all, he should always strive to practise that obedience of which it is written: “Purifying your hearts in obedience to charity” (1 Pet. 1:22); for this is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.

8. To acquire and preserve these things, one must continually seek the aids of diligent and long-suffering prayer. In it let faith be so great that it hopes all things; devotion so great that it seems to compel God; love so great that, in prayer itself, it feels it has obtained everything it asks; humility so gracious that in all things it prefers that not its own will but God’s will be done in it.

Such a person should also strive for and embrace purity of heart, cleanliness of body, silence or well-ordered speech; steady eyes, not raised high; ears not itching for novelty; moderate food and sleep, such as support rather than hinder the regimen of good work; restrained hands and a gentle gait. Let him not betray the wantonness of his heart by laughter, but by a gentle smile show graciousness. Let him have spiritual and continual meditations, suitable reading that is not curious; subjection to superiors, reverence for elders, love for younger persons. Let him not desire to rule, but love to be subject; let him wish to benefit all those with whom he lives. Let him be neither overwhelmed by severity nor emptied by leniency; let his countenance have serenity, his heart sweetness toward all, and his work grace.

This also is the place and time for cutting off pleasures, uprooting every vice, and breaking self-wills; so that, after other “wills”—which are not really wills but only semblances of will—have been cut off and pruned away like adulterous, self-growing shoots, hope of progress may increase for the natural and true will. For they are not so much wills as appetites of the soul: namely, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and worldly ambition (1 John 2:16).

## Chapter IV. On effort and striving toward love’s progress or perfection

[Col. 0385C]

9. Here the one who loves more must run more. Here is labor; here is work: labor of many sweats, work of many toils. This is especially so while love is still blind: it does what it does, but does not yet know whence it comes or where it goes. It acts through such affections as a blind person acts with his hands: he works indeed with his hands, but sees neither the hands with which he works nor the work that he performs.

For just as, if a seeing person instructs one who does not see in some task, he draws the pupil, bends him, raises him, and arranges him, directing him toward a certain practical use rather than into the art of the undertaking; so through all the things mentioned above blind love is externally formed into a certain uprightness of life and conduct. But when the substance of the inner person, softened by long practice of discipline, can be fully impressed and formed in their likeness, then it will produce the most peaceable fruit of salvation; then it will perceive in reality, not merely in appearance, the usefulness of all these things and others like them.

For whatever observances we have set forth are not yet in the affection, but in desire and in the instruction of reason; and concerning all these things it still humbly sings to God: “I have longed to desire your justifications” (Ps. 118:20). Yet, as I said concerning the blind person, although the eye does not yet see, the hand must not cease from work. Thus whoever wishes to make progress in great things must be faithful in small things; and in that sphere in which, by the generosity of the Creator, he already has the prerogative and right of power—namely, in his own body—he must render the service of good will. Let him do what the Apostle says: [Col. 0386A] “I speak in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented your members as slaves to uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members as slaves to righteousness unto sanctification” (Rom. 6:19).

It is as though he said: When love has passed into charity, when the soul has attained its perfect purity, then I shall tell or show you something far different and divine. But for the present receive this human instruction: that, just as in the time of former negligence and sin you were free from righteousness—rendering the service of your members to righteousness in nothing, but to sin in all things, and that unto iniquity—so henceforth present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification. If he proves faithful in this, as was said, he will begin to experience in himself what David said: “In your name I shall lift up my hands. Let my soul be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. 62:5–6). For if by the Spirit he puts to death the deeds of the flesh (Rom. 8:13), if he glorifies God in his work, then the soul, filled with the rich grace and abundance of the Holy Spirit, begins to be renewed in the spirit of its mind and to put on the new human being, created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. 4:23–24).

10. From this point a new appearance of things begins to show itself to him; the better gifts, for the pursuit of which he has labored thus far, begin to disclose themselves to him more familiarly; the body, humbled by holy disciplines, passes by now-good habit into the willing service of the spirit; the inner face of the new human being is renewed day by day and revealed unto the contemplation of God’s goods. [Col. 0386C] Frequent and unexpected manifestations of God, and the splendors of the saints, begin to refresh and enlighten the soul that continually labors in desire. For wisdom, meeting one cheerfully in the ways, as Job says, “hides light in the hands and commands it to come again, and announces concerning it to his friend that it is his possession and that he can ascend to it” (Job 36:32–33).

Thereupon the soul, long laboring, begins to gather certain unusual and sweet little affections. When they are present, it rests while holding them; when they are withdrawn and do not return as it desires, it is tormented. For like one raised in the country and accustomed to rustic food, when it has begun to taste these affections of which we have spoken, as it were at the first entrance of a royal court, it is sometimes shamefully driven away, forcibly expelled into the house of its poverty, and scarcely consents to return again of its own accord. [Alternative reading: *iterum ultro*, incorrectly.] It repeatedly runs back to the door; importunate, shameless, anxious, like a needy person, like a beggar, it looks hopefully and sighing upward to see whether something may be handed to it, whether the door may at last be opened. At times, by its shameless persistence and importunity, it so overcomes and passes every obstacle that, leaping in headlong desire as far as Wisdom’s inner table, it sits down as an uninvited guest, though immediately to be expelled again, and hears: “Eat, friends, and be drunk, beloved ones” (Song 5:1).

From this there now arises love of holy poverty, a desire to remain hidden, hatred of worldly distractions, the practice of prayer, and frequent psalmody.

## Chapter V. On the dangers and harms of neglected grace, and the praises of true charity

[Col. 0387A]

11. But, unless it is prevented, there comes a serious obstacle of temptation, which either greatly delays the hitherto prosperous and most happy course of many, or sometimes turns it back into a kind of sluggish lukewarmness. What one receives from the compassionate Father on the way lest one fail, one begins to possess as though it were sufficient; and, setting here the limit of progress, where one ceases to advance one begins to decline. Indeed, trampling upon God’s grace and fashioning from it, against it, a vain confidence for oneself, one boasts aloud or in one’s heart that one has not been entirely abandoned by God. One thus eats and drinks judgment upon oneself as often as one receives from God the grace of visitation and consolation, and from it ventures confidence not for carrying out the Lord’s will but one’s own wills.

“The enemies of the Lord,” says the Psalmist, “lied to him, and their time shall be for ages. And he fed them with the fat of wheat, and from the rock he satisfied them with honey” (Ps. 80:16–17). Hear that they were fed, and hear that they were enemies; hear that they were satisfied, and hear that they lied. Hear not merely wheat but the fat of wheat; not merely rock but honey from the rock: that is, the hidden and divine grace of the sacraments, with which those proved to be enemies are reported to have been satisfied. If they had not been enemies, they could not so quickly have become satisfied. For the person who is satisfied asks no more than he receives, because he is full, and what he has is enough for him.

This is what the Apostle describes: after the first illumination, after tasting the heavenly gift, after sharing in the Holy Spirit, after likewise tasting God’s good word and the powers of the age to come, voluntarily sinning after receiving the knowledge of truth; crucifying and trampling underfoot the Son of God again for oneself, treating as unclean the blood of the covenant by which they were sanctified, and insulting the Spirit of grace. For what else is it to crucify the Son of God for oneself than to do evil so that good may come, to sin confidently, and to lay upon Christ’s cross whatever one sins? Oh, that they might hear what follows: “The earth which drinks the rain often coming upon it, and produces a useful crop for those by whom it is cultivated, receives blessing from God; but if it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, and its end is for burning.” But let us return, as the Apostle himself says, [Col. 0387D] to better things and things nearer to salvation (Heb. 6:4–9; 10:26, 29).

12. Thus the youth of good hope, whose youth God begins to make glad, begins to grow into a perfect man, into the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness (Eph. 4:13). For love now begins to be strengthened and enlightened, and to pass into the affection and name of a greater virtue and ampler dignity. Enlightened love is charity; love from God, in God, and toward God is charity. And charity is God: “God,” he says, “is charity” (1 John 4:16). The praise is brief, but it encompasses everything. Whatever may be said of God may also be said of charity, provided that, when the natures of gift and giver are considered, in the giver the name denotes substance, in the gift quality. Yet by emphasis even the gift of charity is called God, because above all virtues the virtue of charity cleaves to and is made like God.

What shall we say of charity? We have heard its report; we do not know it, we have not seen it. The Apostle knew it; calling it a more excellent way, he poured out his whole self in its praise, saying: “And I show you a still more excellent way. If I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels but do not have charity, I have become sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith so as to remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and deliver my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing. Charity is patient; it is kind. Charity is not jealous, does not behave improperly, is not ambitious, does not seek its own things, is not puffed up, is not provoked, thinks no evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things. Charity never fails: whether prophecies are abolished, tongues cease, or knowledge is destroyed. But now faith, hope, and charity remain, these three; and the greatest of these is charity” (1 Cor. 12:31; 13).

This is the Lord’s sweet yoke and light burden: a burden which bears its bearer and makes him light; the light burden of the Gospel, sweet to those to whom the Lord himself says, “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15:15). The one who formerly could not bear the commandments of the Law afterward finds the commandments of the Gospel light through cooperating grace. The one who at first could not fulfill “You shall not kill” (1 John 3:16) afterward finds it light to lay down his life for his brethren; and likewise with the rest. As when a heavy load is put upon a beast and it recoils as though it were unbearable, a swift chariot is brought up—that is, the Gospel, speeding through the whole world—and the burden which it first recoiled from as heavy it afterward draws, doubled, without effort.
