So too, a little bird without feathers and wings cannot carry itself; once the weight of feathers and wings is added, it flies without effort. Likewise, hard bread that cannot pass down by itself becomes swallowable in the throat when milk or another liquid is added.

13. Love, therefore, first had striving and a certain affection; charity has accomplishment. The hand of charity now works so much more easily as the enlightened eye assists it. At first we work with the hand; afterward with the hand we wipe the eye. Hence he says: “From your commandments I have understood” (Ps. 118:104). Now one begins to understand one’s works and discern one’s affections. One is now so affected by virtues that, just as for God to be is to be good, so for the just and holy soul it is no longer possible to be otherwise than holy, just, and devout: holy in itself, just toward all, devout toward God.

For through the increase of God’s grace a just affection so possesses the just soul that in no part of itself—whether thoughts, affections, or acts—does it know or can it be anything but just, being wholly, in everything that it is, fully and indissolubly devoted to righteousness. Hence the Apostle says: “Charity never fails.” The effects of affection or action indeed sometimes falter or go astray, so long as charity in this life can see only in part and through a mirror in an enigma; yet its affection remains always whole and sound in its own power.

## Chapter VI. Love is preserved even while a person, as though unwillingly, serves the law of flesh and sin

14. Affection (*affectus*) is one thing; a particular emotion (*affectio*) another. *Affectus* is that which possesses the mind with a certain general capacity and enduring, firm, stable power, which it has obtained through grace. *Affectiones*, however, are the various emotions brought by changing events of things and times.

For weakness of the flesh, through the fault of the first origin, often offends, often falls, often wounds grievously; and it is wounded while the mind grieves inwardly, enduring rather than doing what is wrongly done outwardly. Yet it does not lose charity, but out of charity groans and cries to God: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” Hence the Apostle says: “I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin”; and again: “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:24–25, 17).

Therefore, whoever that person may be, as blessed John says, in respect of that which is born of God—that is, according to the reason of the inner human being—does not sin insofar as he hates rather than approves the sin which the body of death performs outwardly, the seed of spiritual birth by which he was born of God preserving him inwardly. Even if in the meantime he is sometimes wounded and crushed by an onslaught of sin, the root of charity, fixed deep, does not perish. Rather, it immediately grows stronger, more fruitful and more alive in hope of good fruit, and rises again. For blessed John says: “Everyone born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born of God” (1 John 3:9).

The force of the words must be noted. “He does not commit sin,” he says: the one born of God rather endures than performs the sin. And “he cannot sin,” that is, he cannot persist in sin, while he hastens also to subject to the law of God, which he serves with his mind, the flesh that [Col. 0389D] seemed, when temptation and sin assaulted, to serve the law of sin.

Peter, when he sinned, did not lose charity [Note: [Col. 0389D] What the author says here concerning Peter’s sin was long ago raised as an objection by St Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II–II, question 24, article 12, reply to objection 2, citing this passage as though drawn from St Bernard. From this you may see that this treatise was not first attributed to the Holy Doctor today. He answers that charity is lost in two ways: first, directly, through actual contempt; and in this way Peter did not lose charity; second, indirectly, when something contrary to charity is committed through a passion of desire or fear; and in this way Peter, acting against charity, lost charity, but quickly recovered it.

This answer, however, does not wholly please Duvallius, who gives another explanation of this passage in II–II, question 2, “On Charity,” article 7: namely, that the author is not here treating of supernatural and theological charity, which is lost through every mortal sin, but of a certain acquired charity and human benevolence by which Peter was moved toward Christ. It is certain that this was not wholly extinguished through sin, but only in some way put to sleep; and the same must be said of David.

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that St Thomas’s solution is sufficiently in accordance with the author’s intention, who indicates that Peter did not lose charity by sinning because, he says, “he sinned rather against truth than against charity.” It may also be said that this passage is expressed in the rhetorical manner in which we say that things are not lost when they are quickly recovered. And just as this same author says that one born of God does not sin because he does not persist in sin, so he could say that Peter and David did not lose charity by sinning—that is, by remaining in that deprivation to the end. Gilbert, abbot, aptly says in the forty-seventh sermon on the *Song of Songs*, no. 3: “The stain of sin is not imputed while it is not lingered over . . . . . A lapse is, as it were, no lapse where there is a swift return.”]: for he sinned rather against truth than against charity, when with his mouth he falsely denied belonging to him to whom he belonged wholly in his heart. Therefore the truth of charity immediately washed the denial of falsehood with tears (Matt. 26:69–75).

Likewise David, when he sinned (2 Sam. 11), did not lose charity; rather, charity in him was, as it were, stunned by the violent blow of temptation. Charity was by no means abolished in him, but underwent a kind of sleep; and as soon as it awoke at the rebuking voice of the prophet, it immediately burst into that confession of most ardent charity: “I have sinned against the Lord.” And immediately he deserved to hear: “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” [Col. 0390B] (ibid. 12:13).

15. Still in praise of charity: love is in faith and hope; charity is in itself and through itself. Faith and hope may also exist without charity; but charity cannot fail to contain faith and hope within itself. For faith declares that what is loved exists; hope promises it. Thus one who loves in faith and hope loves as one can love what is merely believed and hoped for. Charity already possesses, already holds, already embraces what is believed and hoped for.

Therefore love belonging to faith and hope desires to see God because it loves; charity loves because it sees. Charity itself is the eye by which God is seen. For the soul too has its senses; it has its sight, or eye, by which it sees God. Just as the body has [Col. 0390C] its five senses, through which it is joined to the soul by means of life, so the soul has its five senses, through which it is joined to God by means of charity. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not be conformed to this age, but be renewed in the newness of your sense, so that you may prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Rom. 12:2).

Here it is shown that through the bodily senses we grow old and are conformed to this age; but through the sense of the mind we are renewed in the knowledge of God, in newness of life, according to God’s will and good pleasure. For there are five animal or bodily senses through which the soul gives sensation to its body—beginning from the lowest: touch, taste, smell, hearing, and sight. Likewise, there are five spiritual senses through which charity gives life to the soul: namely, carnal love of parents, social love, natural love, spiritual love, and love of God. Through the five bodily senses, by means of life, the body is joined to the soul; through the five spiritual senses, by means of charity, the soul is united with God.

## Chapter VII. The aforesaid five loves are compared with the five senses

16. Love of parents is compared with touch, because this affection, ready for all and in some manner coarse and tangible, offers and presses itself upon everyone with a kind of natural encounter, so that you cannot escape it even if you wish to do so. For touch is a wholly bodily sense, produced by the contact of any bodies whatsoever, provided that one or both of them are alive, so that touch may exist. Just as, wherever you turn, [Col. 0391B] your body cannot be without touch, so neither can your soul be without this affection. Therefore this love is not greatly commended in Scripture; indeed, lest it become excessive, it is restrained, as the Lord says: “If anyone does not hate his father or mother, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26).

17. Secondly, social love, brotherly love, the love of the holy and catholic Church, is compared with taste. Of it it is written: “Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity!” For just as through taste the life of the body is sustained, so “there the Lord commanded the blessing and life” [alternative addition: “unto the age”]. Although taste is exercised bodily, it nevertheless produces inwardly a flavor by which the soul is affected. Therefore this sense is chiefly bodily, yet is also shown in some respect to be animal.

So too social love, because it is bound together by bodily dwelling together, similarity of professions, equality of pursuits, and other such causes, and is nourished by mutual services, seems chiefly animal. Yet it is also in large part spiritual, because, as flavor belongs to taste, so the affection of brotherly charity burns [alternative reading: *fragrat*, “is fragrant”] in the affection of which it is written: “Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, Aaron’s beard; which descends to the hem of his garment, like the dew of Hermon which descends upon Mount Zion” (Ps. 132).

18. Third, natural love is compared to smell, [Col. 0391D] which, from the natural likeness and fellowship of nature itself, loves every human being without any hope of recompense. Coming forth from the hidden recesses of nature and entering the soul, it suffers nothing human to be alien to it. This sense, namely smell, seems more animal than bodily, because in producing it inwardly the body does nothing except make a slight drawing-in through its instrument, the nostrils; and although the breath is taken in through the body, it affects the soul, not the body. So too natural love seems more spiritual than animal; for, apart from the mere consideration of shared human nature, neither blood relationship, fellowship, nor any bond of that sort whatever is taken into account in it.

19. Fourth, spiritual love—the love of enemies—is compared to hearing. [Col. 0392A] For hearing accomplishes nothing inwardly, that is, within the body, but in a sense acts outwardly, striking upon the ears and calling the soul forth to listen. Thus no force of nature and no affection arising from any bond arouses the love of enemies in the heart, but obedience alone, which is signified through hearing. Therefore this love is called spiritual. It is so also because it advances one toward likeness to the Son of God and the dignity of the children of God, as the Lord says: “Do good to those who hate you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:44–45), and the rest.

20. Fifth, divine love is compared to sight. For sight is the principal sense, just as divine love holds primacy among all affections. The other senses are said to “see” by analogy with the sight of the eyes, although the eye alone sees. [Col. 0392B] For we say, “Touch and see,” “Taste and see,” and likewise of the rest. In the same way, the other things which are rightly loved are said to be loved by divine love, although it is clearer than light that nothing ought to be loved except for God’s sake; nor is a thing loved which is loved for the sake of something else, but rather that for whose sake it is loved. Hence: “From whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. 3:15).

Sight is a pure, powerful, and unalloyed faculty of the soul. So too divine love is powerful, because it performs great things; yet it is pure, because, as he says, “nothing defiled enters into it” (St Augustine, *Confessions* and elsewhere). For God does not deign to be loved together with anything else that is not loved for his sake. Sight, moreover, set in the lofty citadel of the body and in the distinguished place of the head, has beneath it—both in the body’s structure and in rank and power—the instruments of all the other senses and the senses themselves: those which are, so to speak, more animal are nearer; those more bodily, more remote. [Col. 0392C] For touch, the lowest and basest of all, though it appears common to the whole body, properly belongs to the hands.

So the mind, which is the head of the soul and its ruling part, ought to be the seat of love for God, so that it may have beneath itself, rule, and illuminate the other loves; and there should be nothing in them that hides itself from its warmth and light. The more spiritual loves it holds nearer; the more animal or fleshly loves, farther off—when we have loved the Lord our God with all our heart, [Col. 0392D] with all our soul, and with all our strength, and our neighbour as ourselves.

As we have said, sight, having its seat in the worthier part of the body, seems even to accomplish something beyond the faculty of animal life. So far as is permitted, it strives to imitate the power of mind or memory: in a single moment of time it flies across the middle of heaven; in a single instant it traverses countless stadia of lands. Thus the illuminated love of God, occupying its seat in the Christian soul, raises it into a certain likeness of divine power: it makes every creature appear narrow and fleeting—indeed, nothing—in comparison with God; it trusts that all things belonging to the Father are its own; all things work together for its good (Rom. 8:28); and whether Paul, Cephas, death, life, [Col. 0393A] or all things whatsoever, they are its own (1 Cor. 3:22); and the whole world is the wealth of the faithful person.

> [Note: [Col. 0393D] The Seventy Interpreters give this saying in Proverbs 17, after verse 4, although it is absent from the Hebrew, Chaldee, and Latin, in this form: “The whole world is the wealth of the faithful man; but for the unfaithful man, not even an obol.” The same saying is read frequently among the holy Fathers: Jerome, Letter 103 to Paulinus: “To the believer the whole world is wealth; the unbeliever lacks even an obol”; Augustine, *Confessions*, book 5, chapter 4, and Letter 54 to Macedonius, no. 26: “Indeed,” he says, “if we consider wisely what is written, ‘The whole world is the wealth of the faithful man,’” etc. Cassian explains the same saying in *Conferences* 24, chapter 26. Bernard also uses it in the *Life of St Malachy*, chapter 28, no. 63: though poor in money, yet rich in trust in God, he lacked no resources for building large monasteries.]

## Chapter VIII. How reason and love make a person indifferent to all things, and strong and fearless in whatever is difficult

21. Sight, then, the natural light of the soul created by the Author of nature for seeing God, is charity. In this sight there are two eyes, ever quivering with a certain natural yearning to behold the light which God is: love and reason. When either strives without the other, it does not progress so much [variant: *so greatly*]; when they assist one another, they can do much—namely, when they become one eye, of which the Bridegroom says in the Song: “You have wounded my heart, O my friend, with one of your eyes” (Song 4:9).

[Col. 0393B] Yet in this each labours greatly in its own way. Reason cannot see God except in that which he is not; love, however, refuses to rest except in that which he is. What, indeed, can reason grasp or discover by all its effort, of which it dare say, “This is my God”? It can discover what he is only insofar as it discovers what he is not. Reason also has certain sure tracks and straight paths on which it proceeds; love, however, advances more by its failure and grasps more by its own ignorance. Thus reason seems to progress through that which is not toward that which is; love, setting aside that which is not, gladly fails in that which is. For it came forth from there and naturally breathes toward its own source. Reason has greater sobriety; [Col. 0393C] love, greater blessedness.

Yet when, as I have said, they aid one another—when reason teaches love and love enlightens reason; when reason yields to love’s affection and love accepts being restrained within the bounds of reason—they can accomplish something great. But what can they accomplish? Just as one who is progressing cannot make progress in this or learn it except by experience, so neither can he communicate it to one without experience; for, as Wisdom says, “No stranger shall share in its joy” (Prov. 14:10).

22. Thereafter love, strong as death, enters the soul, hitherto tenderly nourished by the sweetness and delights of love and at times worn down by the disciplines of paternal mercy. This love slays it from love and attachment to the world with the sweet sword of love, [Col. 0393D] utterly killing and destroying it just as death destroys the body. So completely does it do this that what is said of Enoch may be said of it: namely, that it is not found among the world’s deeds, because God has taken it away (Gen. 5:24).

But by its death the body is deprived of all its senses; the soul, by its death, makes greater progress, is made alive, and is strengthened in its own faculties. It now walks strongly, steadfastly, and wisely in its paths and in every step, and ventures to set the foot of good assent wherever it had previously scarcely dared to go through ignorance, [Col. 0394A] doubt, and groping. “The strength of the upright is the way of the Lord” (Prov. 10:29).

It therefore mortifies itself to the deeds and affections of the world, as the apostle Paul says: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). For since neither cared for the other, bound by their own affections, they could not and did not care to approach one another: Paul and the world were crucified to each other. Yet, although Paul’s whole manner of life was in heaven (Phil. 3:20), he did not refuse to be on earth whenever people needed him. Thus he said with a groan: “I desire to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better” (Phil. 1:23).

And how much better it is to be with Christ! For Christ’s being with Paul, as he himself said, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” [Col. 0394B] (Matt. 28:20), was Paul’s great security. But Paul’s being with Christ—here through contemplation or there through the presence of blessedness—was Paul’s blessed and glorious happiness. Therefore the charity of God raised him upward, whereas charity toward his neighbour weighed upon him below, as though hanging from his neck. Hence he continues: “But to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:24).

23. The affection of charity, then, clinging inseparably to God and gathering all its judgments from his countenance, acts and orders outward things as the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God dictates inwardly. It finds sweetness in always fixing its gaze upon that countenance; [Col. 0394C] and, as in the book of life, in reading there the laws by which it should live and understand, in enlightening faith, strengthening hope, and stirring charity. For now the Spirit of knowledge [variant: the Holy Spirit] plainly teaches the holy soul what should be done and how; the Spirit of strength supplies the powers or virtues for doing it; the Spirit of counsel orders it.

When that soul is free to cling to God, it is made like God through the devotion of piety and unity of will. But when it is compelled to return to people and human affairs, it brings back to them, from the law of God’s countenance and with its face made glad by the oil of God’s charity, both in deeds and words, and even with a certain glory and grace of the outward person. By a certain disposition of goodness and grace [Col. 0394D] it claims, or brings about, reverence for itself among them, so that it has at hand their obedience in whatever it wishes.

For even if, coming forth at times from that hidden place to confront the vices of sinners and the corrupt morals of those who wander, the truth and severity of the judgments of God’s countenance make it appear, as it were, horned and terrible (Exod. 34:29–30), when those who must be corrected see that everything is done and ordered according to the unbreakable law of truth in weight and measure (Wis. 11:21), one yields to charity [variant: credence is given to charity], and that wrath of charity is understood as discipline.

Therefore the wheels in which is the spirit of life always go to accomplish the will of the Lord; they do not turn back to perform their own. If they are commanded to preside, they preside with diligence; if to be subject, with humility; if to live with others, with charity. If they are superiors, they are like fathers to children; if subjects, like children to their fathers; if living together, they make themselves servants of all. Their affection is kindly toward everyone; their agreement in what is good is sweet; [Col. 0395A] their meeting is cheerful, their common life gracious, their departure an expression of charity. Toward inferiors, their disposition is gentle in every way and in deed; toward fathers, love reaches to submission; toward superiors, reverence reaches to service. They seek not what is their own, but what belongs to all. If possible, amid adversities they often make their own what belongs to all.

> [Note: [Col. 0395] The words “If possible . . . what belongs to all” are absent in other witnesses.]

And for all these things, whatever that highest law has ordained, they readily lend both the members of the body and their good will, having received the earnest and pledge of the Holy Spirit: knowing that this servitude of creation and of their own members will shortly pass into the adoption and revelation of the children of God.

## Chapter IX. He depicts the common life of religious people as a kind of school of love

24. But let us come to what the Apostle calls “the fellowship of the Spirit” (Phil. 2:1), and to the praise of discipline: to that good and pleasant thing, [Col. 0395C] the dwelling together of brothers in unity, where the Lord commands blessing and life (Ps. 132:3); concerning which the Lord says, “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32).

The praise of this discipline began with the Apostles. As they had learned from the Lord, or from the Holy Spirit, by whose power they had recently been clothed from on high, they established for themselves such a manner of living together that the multitude had one heart and one soul, all things were common, and they were always unanimously in the Temple (Acts 2:44–47; 4:34–35). Some, emulating this form of apostolic institution, have no houses or lodgings except the house of God, the house of prayer. Whatever they do, they do in the name of the Lord. They dwell together under one rule, live under one law, possess nothing [Col. 0395D] as their own, and have neither their bodies nor their wills in their own power. They sleep together, rise together, pray together, chant psalms together, and read together. Their firm and immovable purpose is to obey their superiors and to be subject to them.

Those superiors, keeping watch over them as persons who must render an account for their souls, preach to them in deed what Gedaliah is read in Jeremiah to have preached to the people of Israel: “I will answer to the Chaldeans who come to you. But gather grain, wine, and oil into your vessels, and dwell securely in your cities” (Jer. 40:10). Daily offering to God for them the laughter of their heart and the joy of Isaac—the son of the free woman, the son of promise—they preserve and keep Ishmael, [Col. 0396A] the son of servitude. For their sake they neglect the fruit of the Spirit and, serving the others’ salvation through works of service, set aside every concern for their own advancement. But to those others they preach a perpetual Sabbath, keeping them apart from worldly cares and the anxieties of necessities.

For when necessities are compressed into a small compass, one lives on little. Their clothing is plain, their food restrained, and all else is bounded by the limits of a prescribed rule, so that no one has more than is permitted, yet all have enough; nor does anyone desire to have more, if he has what it is permitted to have.

25. Is not this a paradise—not earthly but heavenly? Yet in this paradise only the superiors are permitted continually to eat from the tree [Col. 0396B] of the knowledge of good and evil; that is, to administer the dispensations of discernment. But for subjects, whose role is to obey rather than to judge, if anyone touches it, he shall die. All continually cultivate silence of the mouth, while speaking to one another by the affection of the heart. The frequent exhortations of those who preside add oil to the furnace, although they themselves more often stir one another up by example. They eagerly anticipate one another in honour and service (Rom. 12:10), and, according to the Apostle, provoke one another to charity by mutual encouragement (Heb. 10:24), receiving one another.

They permit no one among them to be solitary, lest Solomon say of him: “Woe to the one who is alone!” (Eccl. 4:10). They deem solitary the person who does not wish, through confession, to have a companion in his conscience, or who disturbs [Col. 0396C] the fellowship of the brothers by his own novel and solitary inventions. When a matter requires it, gentle conversation about matters necessary for soul or body is permitted; otherwise, gentler silence prevails everywhere.

Their devotion to prayer is everywhere so great and so continual that every place is a place of prayer, as though it were a place of divine dominion. Their melody of psalms is so devout, harmonious, and fervent that it seems composed according to the rules of life, conduct, and good affections—not of music but of charity—and by a certain likeness of harmony seems to present and offer a sacrifice to God. In their common exercises of piety, and even in a certain grace of faces, bodies, and bearing toward one another, seeing within themselves the presence of divine goodness, they embrace one another with such affection that, like the seraphim, one burns for the love of God from another (Isa. 6:3); [Col. 0396D] nor can the service rendered by one to another ever be enough.

26. This is the special school of charity. Here its studies are cultivated, its discussions conducted, and its solutions settled not so much by reasoning alone as by reason and the very truth and experience of things. Here, one who has failed in making progress, if he remains with the baggage which he still drags along from his own burdens and those of his fellow residents and their necessities, is compelled by the rule neither to die, nor to go back, nor to proceed farther. And if, remaining faithfully here, he guards the baggage, he will be little unlike in the triumph of victory from one who has advanced further (1 Sam. 30).

Is this not the place of baggage, where we endure those who oppress us by power, [Col. 0397A] as though trampling down our head and making enemies ride upon our back; children clinging as though in embraces at the heart’s centre [variant: grievously wounding]; conflicts without, fears within; the daily—indeed continual—care of all? Yet he still has a “Jeduthun” by which to leap over; a great road still remains for one ascending the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob. Yet it is not lawful to proceed farther with baggage; and reverence is owed to one’s old age. For from this point old age begins—not an old age measured by the number of years, but venerable, measured by the number of virtues, breathing the maturity of wisdom and rest from labours, like the reward of a completed military service.

27. For wisdom, taking up the journey of advancement to bring it to completion, does not cast off or abandon charity, but advances it. Yet it is so weary, as has been said, of carrying its baggage that, turning now to other concerns, it strives to prepare and fit itself for entering into the joy of its Lord. Therefore it hates every care; even when it undertakes some labours, it does not love the anxieties of labours. Its strength does not fail for carrying, but it avoids hindrance.

Therefore the Lord, arousing one at this stage of progress and summoning the holy soul, as has been said, to enter into his joy, says: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind” (Deut. 6:5).

## Chapter X. That taste and savour of divine things are imparted to us through Christ

[Col. 0397C]

28. Four whole affections are required from us and directed toward God. In saying, “With all your heart,” he claims for himself the whole will; in “with all your soul,” the whole love; in “with all your strength,” he signifies the power of charity; in “with all your mind,” the enjoyment of wisdom. First, the will moves the soul toward God; love advances it; charity contemplates; [255] wisdom enjoys. Wisdom, moreover, is fittingly established in the mind. Since *mens* (“mind”) is so called either because it remembers or because it stands pre-eminent in the soul, it is rightly ascribed to that faculty which stands above all the soul’s faculties. For mind is a certain power of the soul by which we cling to God and enjoy him; and this enjoyment consists in a certain divine savour, [Col. 0397D] whence *sapientia* (“wisdom”) also derives from *sapor* (“savour”). This savour is found in a certain taste.

No one can fittingly describe this taste except one who deserves to taste it: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9). By this taste, according to the Apostle, the word of God is tasted; the riches of the age to come are also tasted (Heb. 6:5). We must therefore inquire more subtly into this taste which possesses that savour in which wisdom finds savour.

First, it must be said that although the one who ascends comes by stages to the citadel of wisdom, nevertheless, unless wisdom at every stage, even to the last—as she herself says in the book bearing her name—had sought those who seek her and met them on the ways, showing herself cheerfully (Wis. 6:17), the will would not have moved them, love would not have advanced them, contemplation would not have come to charity, nor enjoyment to wisdom. [Col. 0398A] Therefore, as we began, let us continue concerning taste.

29. The whole Church, of both the Old and New Testaments, is the body of Christ. In the head of this body—that is, in its first, more ancient, and higher portion, which is the primitive Church—there are four senses: sight, hearing, smell, and touch. The eyes are the angels, because of the subtlety of contemplation; the ears, the patriarchs, because of the virtue of obedience; the nostrils or smell, the prophets, because of their knowledge of absent things; while touch is the common sense.

All these senses were in the head before the coming of the Mediator, but they languished because the lower body was dead through the absence of one sense, namely taste. Without taste’s assistance, the body could neither live nor could the senses possess the force of their own vitality. [Col. 0398B] Whatever nourishment belongs to the whole body, place it before, beneath, or around all the senses and the entire body: if taste alone is absent, what good will it do? Pour it into the ears, force it through the nostrils, or introduce it by any other part: it can harm, but it cannot benefit.

Taste, however, is followed by a certain sweetness of savour. Feeling this in its interior, the soul, by a singular mode inaccessible to the other senses, discerns and judges all that it receives; and it invigorates and confirms itself and all the senses. Taste, then, placed at the boundary of head and body—that is, in the throat—joins, as it were, the two. It signifies him who by the condition of flesh was made a little lower than the angels, [Col. 0398C] Moses, Elijah, and the other patriarchs and prophets; yet by displaying patience and humility he made himself in a sense lower and humbler, whereas they overthrew God’s enemies and their own through mighty power, but he taught his disciples: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. 5:39).

30. For he, coming after the prophets and patriarchs, is a kind of boundary of Law and Grace, of head and body. Through the mysteries of his humanity, passion, and resurrection, Christ the man tastes, that is, understands, as though with his own mouth, whatever in the Law, the Prophets, the Psalms, and the hymns is health-giving, vital, or useful to the body; and he conveys it through himself for the body to understand. By an inward savour of his divinity—by which Christ became for us wisdom from God [Col. 0398D] (1 Cor. 1:30)—he finds these things savoury and makes them savoury and useful to us.

Living in himself and giving life and conformity through himself to the whole body, he gives joy to himself and to the angels over the body’s completion; joy to the patriarchs and prophets over the vision of his day, as he himself says: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he should see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56); and joy and life to the whole body. Thus, made alive and strengthened by that universal spiritual touch, we cry out in a certain exultation of mind: “What we have seen and heard, and what our hands have handled concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1).

Therefore in all our prayers we add, “Through Christ our Lord”: either because through him, as our mediator, we direct all our prayers and sacrifices to God the Father; or because whatever we hope for from the Father of lights—every good gift and every perfect donation (Jas. 1:17)—we ask that it be poured, not through ear or nostrils, but through him into [Col. 0399A] our mouth, taste, and wisdom, so that it may benefit the one receiving it.

31. This is the taste which the spirit of understanding gives us in Christ: namely, understanding of the Scriptures and of God’s sacraments. Therefore, when the Lord appeared to the disciples after his resurrection, “Then,” says the Evangelist, “he opened their understanding, that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45).

For when we begin not only to understand the inner sense of the Scriptures and the power of God’s mysteries and sacraments, but even, so to speak, to touch and handle them with the hand of experience—which happens only through a certain awareness of conscience and the training of an understanding made experienced; indeed, to say more, through one inwardly reading within itself and feeling the goodness of God and the power which the work of grace itself exercises in the children of grace with mighty goodness and effective power—then at last wisdom performs what belongs to it. [Col. 0399B] Then it teaches those whom it judges worthy, by its anointing, concerning all things. Then, having applied the seal of God’s goodness, it stamps and forms all that is ours, pacified and softened by that anointing; and if it finds anything pure or rigid, it presses upon and breaks it, until, having received the saving joy of God and been strengthened by the princely spirit of wisdom, the holy soul sings joyfully to God: “The light of your countenance, Lord, is marked upon us; you have given joy in my heart” (Ps. 4:7).

Thus too the Lord says: “This is eternal life: [Col. 0399C] that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Blessed knowledge, in which eternal life is contained. This life comes from that taste, because to taste is to understand. By this taste, through this savour, in this wisdom, that least of the Apostles was satisfied, made glad, and strengthened: “To me,” he says, “the least of all the saints, this grace has been given: to preach among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ, and to enlighten all as to what is the dispensation of the mystery hidden from ages in God, who created all things; so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God may be made known to principalities and powers in the heavenly places, according to the eternal purpose in Christ Jesus our Lord, in whom we have boldness and access in confidence [Col. 0399D] through faith in him.” And a little later: “For this reason,” he says, “I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may give us, according to the riches of his glory, power to be strengthened through his Spirit in the inner person, that Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts, being rooted and founded in charity, so that you may be able to comprehend what is the breadth, length, height, and depth” (Eph. 3:8–18). Here it is pleasing to observe whether perhaps we may penetrate in some measure into the meaning of apostolic wisdom.

## Chapter XI. What we owe to God, and the necessity of a mediator

32. We owe two things in response to God’s four attributes. In God there are four: power, wisdom, charity, and truth [Col. 0400A] or eternity, which are one. For nothing truly is except what is unchangeable. We ought to respond to these in two ways. To power, which can punish us, and wisdom, from which nothing can be hidden, we owe true fear: that is, fear which neither the numbness of complacency nor the refuge of pretence impedes. Pretence is either when we feign difficulty in obeying a command, or when we feign an irrational mercy in God.

To charity and truth we owe true love: that is, love which neither lukewarmness of affection nor the scruple of suspicion impedes. For what is owed to charity except charity? The truth of charity and the charity of truth remove every scruple of suspicion. By suspicion I mean the fear that charity may not love, truth may deceive, or eternity may fail away.

[Col. 0400B] Hence Paul says: “That you may be able to comprehend with all the saints what is the length, breadth, height, and depth” (Eph. 3:18). In the height recognize power; in the depth, wisdom; in the breadth, charity; in the length, eternity or truth. And this is the cross of Christ. Elsewhere the same Apostle expresses more clearly the power of highest wisdom in us: “Therefore I also, hearing of your faith which is toward God and of your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you, making remembrance of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation [257] in the knowledge of him, enlightening the eyes of your heart, that you may know what is the hope of his calling among the saints, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance [Col. 0400C] in the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to the working of the might of his power, which he worked in Christ, raising him from the dead” (Eph. 1:15–20).

33. Therefore, when, as the Apostle prays and God hears, the spirit of wisdom and revelation is given to us for the knowledge of him—that is, so that we may know him and find him savoury, or that he himself may have savour in us—when our eyes are enlightened to see the good and understand the good things of the Good, to which the hope of his calling draws us, namely the riches of the glory of his eternity among the saints: in all these things the goodness or kindness of the one who enlightens and calls appears to us. But when, so that we may follow the one who calls, strength too is added, then through the very experience of the spirit of wisdom there is revealed to us what, or how surpassingly great, is the magnitude of his truth toward us.

[Col. 0400D] From this point, therefore, the person so constituted, with the palate of the heart healed by the taste of divine contemplation, discerns all things and judges all things. In Christ, the author of all good things, he first finds savour in his own conversion toward God; then in the remission of sins; afterward, in the manifold increase of grace in place of the wrath whose children we were. And all these things are only through our Lord Jesus Christ. For he is our mediator and our wisdom, whose foolishness is wiser than human beings (1 Cor. 1:25).

34. For though the goodness of God abounded in such gifts and was offered to all, there was no one to receive it, to know how to receive it, or to teach others how to receive it; nor was there anyone able [Col. 0401A] to ascend where these good things are distributed, or to bring down to us what was there. A mediator was needed between us and God, through whom what is ours might draw near to God and God’s good things might draw near to us.

Therefore the whole Trinity entered into counsel—that counsel of which the Prophet says: “Let your ancient true counsel come to pass” (Ps. 32 according to the Septuagint). For the Lord saw that, as regards humanity, all things were confused and disturbed; nothing stood in its own place, nothing proceeded in its proper order. He saw that humanity had gone into the region of unlikeness so far away that it neither knew nor could return by itself. For the angel had presumptuously claimed likeness to God, saying: “I will set my seat in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). Likewise, man desired to be God, having been persuaded that he would be like the gods (Gen. 3:5).

[Col. 0401B] “Then,” says God the Father, “shall my Son, the brightness of my glory and the image of my substance” (Heb. 1:3), “have in the very likeness of me so many rivals, equals, and companions?” Both were cast down. Seeing the angel and the human being, made for the Image itself—that is, for the image of God—perish through their disordered desire for that image and likeness, God the Son, the Image of God, says: “Alas! Misery alone is free from envy; but aid must be given to one whom justice does not forbid us to aid. Therefore I present myself as a good man, despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness” (Isa. 53:3), “so that he may emulate and imitate in me the humility by which he may attain the glory to which he hastens prematurely; so that he may hear from me: ‘Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you shall find rest [Col. 0401C] for your souls’” (Matt. 11:29).

## Chapter XII. The counsel and progress of human redemption are set forth

35. Therefore the Son of God girds himself, as it were, and undertakes through humility to recover the one who could be recovered, who had perished through pride. Thus, making himself the middle between God and humanity—humanity which, departing from God, had been taken captive and bound by the devil—he assumed both the person and office of the good mediator in this way.

He became human: “A rod came forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower rose from his root. And the Spirit of the Lord rested upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and [Col. 0401D] piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isa. 11:1–3). Understand here our most mighty contest-master, as though entering the field of the world to be anointed for the contest with the oil of the Holy Spirit; and the giant rejoicing to run the course of the dispensation of humanity (Ps. 18:6).

Observe, moreover, that the prophet began from the higher gifts and descended to the lower, because he was proclaiming the descent of the mediator. But we, through the same graces of the Holy Spirit, investigating both the progress of this mediator’s work and its return to higher things, begin from the lower, namely fear. Christ, then, had fear toward the Father—but just fear, filial fear—by which he gave honour to him in all things, saying: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven” (John [Col. 0402A] 4:34); and in the Psalm, “Let my heart rejoice, that it may fear your name” (Ps. 85:11), and many other things of this kind. By this fear he seemed also to cast aside, humble, and disregard himself, so that he might restore and return to the Father the work which the Father had made through him but which had perished.

36. Thus our mediator had fear directed, as it were, upward toward the Father; piety directed, as it were, downward toward the wretched person to be reconciled; and knowledge toward both, knowing what was to be afforded to each. But, in order to fulfil his ministry of mediation, although he possessed from above the Father’s good will, he possessed nothing from the wretched person lying below; and yet the rationale and order of mediation required that he receive something from him. Therefore he required faith from him. But he required faith by first bestowing piety [Col. 0402B]. No demand could have been more compelling, since it was not difficult for the wretched man to entrust himself to one by whose piety he saw himself anticipated.

And since he could not entrust himself to one in whom he had no hope—for who would entrust himself to one in whom he had no hope?—he offered hope together with faith, adding fear also to hope, without which hope could not exist: namely, lest he should be abandoned by so merciful a mediator. Therefore, having received from his accused party so great a pledge of salvation, the mediator returns to the Father—when, that is, he went up alone onto the mountain to pray, or when, having entered into agony, he prayed more intensely with a bloody sweat: “Father,” he says, “glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you” (John 17:1). “See what I offer you; see what I offer him. See what I have from you; see what I have from him. For I am mediator [Col. 0402C], and now the grounds of my mediation seem to converge upon his salvation. But he has been captured and bound. The strong man has bound him; and unless one stronger than he comes upon him, he will not plunder his goods. But stretch forth your hand from on high, and I shall rescue him from his most powerful enemies, in the spirit of might: your might and your power. For I know what I shall do. I shall die innocent for the guilty; and my goodness will be incomparably more powerful than hostile malice, the punishment of my innocence more powerful than the punishment of human disobedience.”

37. And the Father says: “I have glorified [him], and I will glorify [him]” (John 12:28). The most strong mediator now needs the spirit of counsel, because, “if the ruler of this world had understood, he would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). Therefore, concealing from him in every respect the power of his divinity [Col. 0402D], and presenting to him only the weakness of the flesh, Christ aroused the envy of hostile wickedness through the righteousness of his life. Through the weakness of his flesh he gave the enemy hope of victory, while miracles accompanied this inducement to envy—miracles by which he strengthened faith in himself for their reconciliation.

The ancient deceiver was deceived: he inflicted the penalty of sin, namely the most cruel death, upon one who was liable to no sin. The righteous man, unjustly slain for righteousness, obtained a new justice from the enemy: namely, the justice arising from the death unjustly inflicted upon him. Since this death was, as it were, unnecessary for him because he was without sin, he shared it with sinful humanity and absolved the guilty by the punishment of his innocence. Placing his body and blood in the hand of that man, he says: “Eat this and drink; live from this.” And presenting humanity to the Father [Col. 0403A], he says: “Behold, Father, the price of my blood. If you require an account of this person’s sin, behold my blood for him. Lord Father, you have bestowed kindness, and the earth of my body has yielded its fruit; now righteousness shall walk before you, and you shall set your feet in the way of human salvation” (Ps. 84:13–14). “And so that one who was justly lost may now be justly saved, you, Lord, have made ordinances; you have executed judgment and righteousness in Jacob” (Ps. 98:4).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the true wisdom of those who love God, or of God’s children

38. Therefore, satisfied by the fruit of this work, a human being, through the mediation of God’s wisdom, is not merely reconciled but is also made wise. For what he eats has savour for him. He eats and drinks the body and blood of his Redeemer [Col. 0403B]: heavenly manna, bread of angels, bread of wisdom; and by eating he is transformed into the nature of the food which he eats. For to eat Christ’s body is nothing other than to become Christ’s body and a temple of the Holy Spirit.

When this temple has been adorned by the establishment of the virtues described above, and consecrated in the aforesaid order of dedication, it can thereafter accept no alien claims of ownership and no inhabitant except the God who formed and created it. Therefore that holy soul loves or cares for nothing further that is earthly, material, or perishable, once it has returned from the place of burdens. If it sometimes uses any such thing as though while passing through, it disdains to enjoy it. If some prosperity of this sort occurs [Col. 0403C], it passes by; it is not disturbed if adversity happens. Whatever it receives, it savours wholly; and nothing can fail to have savour for the lover if it touches him like saliva descending from Christ’s head. Whatever pertains to the body, whether good or evil, is outside; it cannot reach one who is within.

Thus the Apostle, lying amid bodily squalor and chains, crowned—insofar as the body was concerned—with tribulation and misery, wrote to his disciples: “I shall send Timothy to you, that you may know the things concerning me” (Phil. 2:23). “The things concerning me,” he says: that is, those in the outward person, in the outward garment of flesh, which do not reach me who am within.

39. This is the wisdom of which the Apostle says, “We speak wisdom among the perfect.” We speak of it as those who have heard but have not seen: as we might speak of a city which we have not seen but of which we have heard very much; whereas one who had seen it would speak far differently and more exactly. Yet this wisdom has set against it another wisdom, wisdom of an unhappy name—which the Apostle calls the wisdom “of the rulers of this world” [1 Cor. 2:6]—as black is opposed to white and darkness to light. Of it Scripture says: “Wisdom overcomes malice” (Wis. 7:30). For malice is the taste of evil, whence *sapientia* (“wisdom”) also derives from *sapor* (“taste”). Therefore, when evil has savour, and there is no lack of cunning or will to carry it out, the wisdom of the rulers of this world is in every respect contrary to heavenly wisdom. This indeed is the malice that wisdom hates. For there is there a taste of good in itself; here there is a taste of evil in itself [Col. 0404A]. There prudence is ready for execution; here, as has been said, cunning is not lacking.

40. But between these two wisdoms there is a certain intermediate wisdom, coloured as it were with a middle colour between black and white. Whether it tends downward or upward, it stands in such a relation to either side that its outcome follows the intention and endeavour of the one who uses it. This is the wisdom which the Apostle calls “of this world,” and which he places between the wisdom of God and the wisdom of the rulers of this world (1 Cor. 2:6–7). It is entirely occupied with the useful and the honourable, and is ordered by a certain studied prudence. It consists almost wholly in knowledge: namely, in knowing how to distinguish prudently and judge between the useful and useless, the honourable and dishonourable, even if this knowledge is not suited to one’s life and character. “Knowledge puffs up, but charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1) [Col. 0404B]. Some labour in investigating such matters merely in order to know, which serves curiosity alone; or in order that they may be seen—or known—to know, which serves vanity. And this pursuit can advance and raise itself on high only as far as reason can go without love.

## CHAPTER XIV. Antithesis of true and false wisdom: on the power and excellence of true wisdom

41. This philosophy is divided into the knowledge of human and divine things. So long as it concerns human things, it remains, for the time being, itself. But when it raises itself to divine things, the higher it ascends, the lower it falls; and in it is fulfilled: “In lifting me up, you dashed me down” (Ps. 101:11). For by the effort of natural ability it is sometimes advanced so far that, as the Apostle says, what may be known of God—that is, as much concerning God as reason can comprehend—is known to them, and known within them, that is, within themselves. For God revealed it to them, because he created them so that they should possess within themselves that by which they might know God.

They rise from their ethical discipline to a kind of natural philosophy, and perceive by understanding, through the things that have been made, the invisible things of God, even his everlasting power and divinity, so that they are without excuse. For they refuse to proceed or advance further, although they can do so, into true theology. Though they knew God, they neither glorified him as God nor gave thanks; instead they became futile in their thoughts [Col. 0404D], and their foolish heart was darkened. “Claiming to be wise, they became fools.” And those who foolishly lost theology fall miserably even from natural philosophy when they exchange the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, birds, four-footed animals, and reptiles. Therefore neither are they permitted to remain in our ethical discipline: God gives them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity, so that they dishonour their bodies in themselves; he gives them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting (Rom. 1:19–28).

But wisdom always overcomes malice. Dwelling with God, it knows always how to advance and never to fail; it “reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1), acting wisely in divine matters [Col. 0405A], cautiously in natural matters, and prudently in moral matters.

42. Therefore the wise soul, cleansed, as written above, of every alien affection, savouring God alone, puts off the human being in the human being. Entirely and in all things directed toward God, it regards every creature beneath God just as God regards it, arranging and ordering all things in the light and power of wisdom. Thus it acts, thus it judges concerning them, as is fitting for one who exists and lives, exercising judgment and righteousness from him from whom it exists and lives.

For the wisdom of God, as Wisdom herself says, is “a brightness of eternal light and an unstained mirror of God’s majesty” (Wis. 7:26), and “a pure emanation of the glory of almighty God” and “a vapour of his power.” Therefore, just as the wise soul bears within itself the brightness of eternal light and the mirror of God’s majesty [Note: At [Col. 0405D] some editions omit the words “and emanation . . . majesty.”], so, when it turns itself toward creation [Col. 0405B], it expresses and displays the image of God’s goodness and righteousness. And just as it is inwardly suffused with the vapour of God’s power, so it pours outward the emanation of God’s glory and love.

Hence Solomon says elsewhere: “A person’s wisdom shines in his face” (Eccl. 8:1); and elsewhere: “The eyes of the wise,” he says, “are in his head” (Eccl. 2:14), because they pour themselves forth outwardly from nothing other than the natural and inward power of their brain—that is, wisdom—and do not depart from the head. Solomon says: “A multitude of the wise is the health of the world” (Wis. 6:26). O how happy human affairs would be if the foolish everywhere served the wise! And human affairs would also be happy, says a certain philosopher [Note: At [Col. 0405D]: Plato.], if either the wise alone ruled or all rulers practised philosophy. But while the wise wisely avoid ruling over the foolish, the foolish also foolishly avoid being under the wise: all things become senseless, confused, and disturbed. The wise hide and conceal themselves; children rule and govern; and those who eat in the morning become princes—and woe to that land! (Eccl. 10:16). But let us return to the subject.

43. Therefore the soul illuminated by the spirit of wisdom, because it loves righteousness and hates iniquity, is on that account anointed by God with the oil of gladness with which Christ was anointed above his fellows (Ps. 44:8), and is flooded with grace. It pleases everyone and is loved by everyone. Even those who stand opposed, when they see such a soul, fear and reverence it. Though hardened wickedness refuses to imitate goodness in the good person, nature cannot conceal it [Col. 0405D].

Among themselves the wise possess a certain private grace and a kind of angelic language, in which they speak to one another through mutual affections, by a certain spiritual grace, while their outward looks contribute to this same communication. No one knows this language except the King of Angels, his angels, those who belong to the race of Israel, and the citizens of Jerusalem. No Egyptian knows it; no Canaanite. For just as they seem in this life already to taste in advance and receive initiation into the blessedness of the life to come—through holiness of life, the glorification of the inward person, contemplation, and enjoyment of divinity—so too in this life they receive something of the glorification of their bodies, which they will receive fully there.

Apart from that grace already mentioned, by which, dwelling together as one, they enjoy themselves in God and God in themselves, they feel that all the conflicts of the flesh have so vanished [variant: *convenisse*, “have come together”] that the whole substance of the flesh is to them only an instrument of good work [Col. 0406A]. For though they waste away through its sufferings and weaknesses, by this very means they grow stronger in the inward person. “For when I am weak,” says the Apostle, “then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. 12:10). The senses themselves receive a certain new grace, almost spiritual: the eyes become simple and the ears restrained. At times, in the fervour of prayer, there breathes so great a fragrance of some unknown odour, such sweetness of taste even without tasting, and so great an incentive of spiritual love through reciprocal touch, that they seem to carry within themselves a paradise of spiritual delight.

Through their countenance and the bearing of the whole body, through the beauty of life, morals, and actions, and through mutual service—whether in devout ministries or charitable hospitality—they meet and unite with one another in the delight of a certain grace, so that they are truly one heart and one soul [Col. 0406B]. Clearly, from purity of conscience and the grace of mutual fellowship, they already begin here the future glorification of their bodies, which they will possess perfectly in the future and everlasting life.

## CHAPTER XV. On the blessed consummation of wisdom unto attainment of the blessed end and highest good

44. For just as now all living things are suffused with the brightness of the sun [Col. 0406C], and seem mutually to be suffused by one another; and just as we see one another living here, yet do not see the life by which we live [Note: At [Col. 0406D] some editions omit: “yet do not see the life by which we live”]: so in that life God will be seen by each in all things and by all in each thing. This does not mean that divinity will be seen with bodily eyes; rather, the glorification of bodies will manifest the presence of divinity through a certain evident grace of itself.

The religious use of bodily sacraments also has this purpose in this life. Since, while we pass through an image, we scarcely understand anything except bodies and bodily things, we are bound by bodily sacraments lest we depart from God; thus *religio* (“religion”) is also said to derive from *religare* (“to bind”). But when the faithful soul, taught by such things, begins no longer to need them, and passes from bodily things to spiritual things, and from spiritual things to the Creator of spiritual and bodily things, this will truly be to depart from burdens.

Therefore, leaving the body and every bodily care and hindrance behind, it forgets everything other than God; attending to nothing but God, it considers that only itself and God exist: “My beloved is mine, and I am his” (Song 2:16). “What have I in heaven? And what have I desired from you upon earth? My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart and my portion for ever” (Ps. 72:25–26). Then comes death. The unhappy unbelievers call this passage into life death; but what do the faithful call it except Passover? In bodily death, therefore, the soul dies perfectly to the world in order to live perfectly to God. It enters “the place of the wonderful tabernacle,” entering even to the house of God (Ps. 41:5). And, when all things have preceded well and in due order, as we said at the beginning, each thing bears its own weight to its own place: the body to the earth from which it was taken, to be raised and glorified in its time; the spirit to God who created it [Col. 0407A].

45. But when this passage to God takes place, all bonds having been broken and all obstacles overcome, with perfect blessedness and everlasting love, the truly holy soul from then on cleaves perfectly to God—or rather is truly united with God on earth—so as to become one of those to whom he said: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6). This is the end of those who set Jerusalem at the beginning of their joy (Ps. 136:6); whom the anointing of the Holy Spirit teaches concerning all things (1 John 2:27); who wisely arrange ascents in their heart, from strength to strength, until the God of gods is seen in Zion (Ps. 83:6, 8) [Col. 0407B–0408A]: the God of gods, blessedness of the blessed, joy of those who rejoice well—finally, the one good, the highest of all goods.

From the end of good purpose, at the beginning of the ascent, to the end of all consummation, wisdom reaches mightily, preserving the strength of the one ascending to it lest he fail in the ascent; “ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1), both adversity and prosperity, shaping and arranging all things for his good, until it restores the soul to its beginning and hides it in the hidden place of God’s face.

Every wise ascender should know, however, that the steps of this ascent are not like the rungs of a ladder, such that these individual affections are necessary only in their respective periods and at no other time. Each affection indeed has its own time and place in the order of ascent, in which, with the other affections cooperating, it may more diligently fulfil its part. Yet all converge and cooperate, precede and follow one another; and often the first become last and the last first [Col. 0408B].

[Col. 0407]

## A BRIEF COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST TWO CHAPTERS OF THE SONG OF SONGS, COMPILED FROM ST BERNARD’S SERMONS, CONCERNING THE THREEFOLD STATE OF LOVE. (G)*

262

## NOTICE

[Col. 0407] The following exposition on the first two chapters of the Song of Songs was published by us from the Dunensis manuscript in the earlier edition and appended to Bernard’s Sermons on the Song as his genuine offspring, which William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, had indicated in Book I, chapter 12, of his *Life* of Bernard, in these words:

> “Accordingly, he then discoursed to me on the Song of Songs, as much as the period of my illness allowed me, only in a moral sense, omitting the mysteries of that Scripture, because this was my wish and because I had requested it of him. And every day I committed to writing whatever I heard on this subject, lest it escape me, insofar as God granted and memory assisted me.”

At that time we thought that these words indicated this very exposition. But, upon more careful consideration, we judge it to be nothing other than a brief compendium of Bernard’s first fifty-one Sermons on the Song, compiled by some diligent and devout person. The work indicated by William seems rather to be that which was published under his name in volume IV of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis*. There one should note these words of the Preface:

> “But we do not attempt those deeper mysteries contained in it concerning Christ and the Church; rather, restraining ourselves within ourselves . . . we touch only upon a certain moral sense.”

These words fittingly accord with the preceding passage from Bernard’s *Life*, where William says that he requested from Bernard an exposition of the Song “only in a moral sense, omitting the mysteries of that Scripture.” This consideration moved us to place the following exposition among the collections made from Bernard’s works, and indeed after William’s preceding two books, to which it is appended under Saint Bernard’s name in the Dunensis manuscript. If anyone should wish to attribute the following commentary also to William, we shall not object—especially since its style approaches William’s style closely enough.

[Col. 0407C] 263

1. There are three states of the love of God in the Christian soul. The first is sensory or animal; the second rational; the third spiritual or intellectual. The Lord speaks of them in the Gospel: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37). The first is signified in the heart, that is, in the weak part of the flesh, on account of its devout affection toward the Saviour’s humanity. The second is signified in the soul, by which that first love is now animated and made alive, when it humbly and devoutly investigates the mysteries of faith and the power of the sacraments. The third is signified in all one’s strength, because at this stage, however much you have advanced, you can say: “And I said: Now I have begun” (Ps. 76:12).

The first delights so greatly in contemplating the sweetness of Christ’s humanity that Christ rightly says to such persons: “It is expedient for you that I go away” (John 16:7). The second already has a burning heart, but its eyes are still held, while Christ speaks to it on the road and opens the Scriptures to it (Luke 24:15–32). The third now says in complete confidence: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). The first cannot say this at all, and the second can scarcely say it.

For what the apostles experienced in the bodily presence of the Lord, these persons experience in a certain devout imagination of their mind, concerning the sweetest recollection of Christ’s humanity, his conduct and works, his passion, resurrection, and ascension, and the benefits bestowed upon us through these. They assume that affectionate love by which Peter, wishing to hold God as a human being holds another human being, urged him—when he foretold the course of his passion—“Far be it from you, Lord; be gracious to yourself; this shall not happen to you” (Matt. 16:22) [Col. 0409A].

But the third stage is wholly outside and above the human being; wholly in God. It loves God for God’s sake, the just for the sake of the just, and the good for the sake of the good—not because he is good to us, but because he is good in himself. It is so affected by God, goodness, and justice that it would prefer not to exist rather than not to exist good and just in God. This is love “strong as death” (Song 8:6); this is the power from on high that clothed the apostles (Luke 24:49). For the holy soul, made one spirit with God, can no more endure even a slight deflection from righteousness than righteousness itself can endure ceasing to be righteousness [Col. 0409B].

2. The rational state, placed between this highest and the lower state, governs and enlightens the lower state. But when it sometimes attempts to reach the higher with the hand of devout desire, it soon retreats into itself and, like David, strikes its own heart because it has presumed to lay a hand upon the Lord’s Christ. “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned” (Heb. 12:20); and when a voice comes above the firmament over the heads of the living creatures, they stand still, do not proceed, and lower the wings of their efforts. For rational discipline does nothing there, where everything consists in the experience of love, understanding, and affection.

That higher state is as it were a firmament of heaven in which God dwells, and it is not supported by lower reason. Yet it sometimes creates for itself reasons of its own kind; returning in some fashion from the hidden place of God’s face to its lower companions, it restrains them by the light of heavenly brightness. But just as it is said in the Apocalypse, “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1), so, delighting them with a momentary consolation, it seems to say to them: “Run, that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9:24). But only day utters this word to day.

These reasons are not entangled in the perplexities of reasoners, but are pure and simple from pure and simple truth; joyful from the oil of God’s gladness, honeyed from the honey of heaven. They do not puff up their discoverer with knowledge but build him up with charity; they are very accessible to the poor in spirit, incomprehensible to those wise in lofty matters. They are so effective that the saying seems to refer to them: “The Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. 2:10); so solid in themselves and needing nothing external that the saying may be understood of them: “The judgments of the Lord are true, justified in themselves” (Ps. 18:10) [Col. 0409C–D].

All three of these loves, or states of love, often converge and cooperate. In a certain mutual and friendly generosity, each gives and receives from the others what it possesses in abundance. For the highest often delights and rejoices in the delights of the lower, and the lower is sometimes suffused and affected by the joy of the higher, while the middle moves alternately between both and rejoices with each.

[Col. 0410A] 3. But it is pleasant to contemplate more closely the riches in which each abounds. The first is against temptations; the second against heresies; the third sings: “In peace, in the selfsame, I shall sleep and rest” (Ps. 4:9). In the first are forgiveness of sins and cleansing from vices; in the second, the exercise of virtues; in the third, the perfection of virtues and attachment to, or enjoyment of, the highest good. In the first is the use of sacraments; in the second, of mysteries; in the third, the reality of sacraments or mysteries.

The first is humble in sinful Mary, fervent in Peter, devout and sweet in John. The second sleeps with regard to worldly things, watches in spiritual matters, and languishes when its soul fails for God’s salvation: seeing but not seeing fully, and languishing through love and desire to see fully. The third hears ineffable words—silence, namely that peace of God which surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4:7) [Col. 0410B].

The first drives its sheep—that is, the weak affections of sensuality—into the inner part of the wilderness, that is, the inward retreats of contemplation. Considering the bush that burned but was not consumed, that is, the mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation, and wishing to draw nearer through understanding, it hears from the Lord: “Do not come near here; take off the sandals from your feet, for the place where you stand is holy ground” (Exod. 3:1–5). The second goes up onto the mountain and hears from the Lord: “But you, stand here with me, and I shall teach you the laws and commandments which you shall set before the children of Israel” (Deut. 5:31). It sees the model of the eternal tabernacle, which God made and not man, and hears from the Lord: “See that you make all things according to the model shown you on the mountain” (Exod. 25:40) [Col. 0410C].

The third is buried by the Lord on the mountain—that is, hidden in the hidden place of his face—and no human being, that is, no human wisdom, knows its tomb to this day (Deut. 34:6). The first hears from people, and daily it is said to it: “Where is your God?” The second remembers and pours out its soul within itself; the third passes into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God (Ps. 41:4–5). The first serves faith, the second hope, the third charity. And just as faith begets us to God, hope nourishes us, and charity brings us to perfection, so the first state consecrates human affection in us to God; the second puts off the old human being with his deeds and puts on the new human being [Col. 0410D], created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth (Eph. 4:22, 24); the third perfects and conforms us to God in purity of mind and holiness of life.

Whether prophecies, tongues, faith, hope, or all other charisms, they will cease; but charity never fails (1 Cor. 13:8). Sometimes, moreover, that higher state, as though repaying its guardians, tutors, and stewards, pours into them a divine affection, or at times one more than human, so that in a wonderful and unknown way they are often astonished to find themselves carried above themselves. It leads and nourishes them to the point at which the Lord’s prayer is fulfilled in them: “Father, I will that, as I and you are one, they also may be one in us” (John 17:11–21).

[Col. 0411A] 4. According to these three states, in the Song of Songs the young women, companions, bridegroom, and bride each speak in their own manner. Thus the bride says of the bridegroom: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). But there are tongues of angels and tongues of human beings. By the tongue of human beings—that is, in the customary manner of human beings—the Holy Spirit makes known his secrets to people through certain parables, since their weakness could not otherwise understand them. Hence the Lord also spoke in parables.

Indeed, God himself became human for all, so that those who did not know how to think of God might gradually be taught by him, through the one whom they knew—namely, a human being—to raise the rational understanding of their mind toward thinking and understanding God. For this reason he not only spoke to people in parables; his whole life on earth was for them a kind of remarkable parable, so that his invisible things might be perceived by understanding through his visible things.

For in every carnal affection nothing is sweeter or ordinarily more desirable than the union of bride and bridegroom; but in spiritual affection, nothing is sweeter than the union of created spirit with uncreated Spirit. There, one flesh is made from two; here, one spirit is made from two. Therefore, drawing the comparison from carnal to spiritual things and from human to divine, the bridegroom and bride are here described as Christ and the Church, or any holy soul which, having to some extent experienced the first two degrees of love, now pants after the third and longs to pour itself wholly beyond itself into the bridegroom’s love and sweetness. Already desiring the embrace of his love and the kiss of his knowledge, it says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” [Col. 0411B–C].

A kiss is a sign of peace. And if our sins, as Scripture says, separate us from God, when we make satisfaction for them in order to be reconciled, we seek, as it were, the kiss of peace.

5. For according to the three states of love, there are also three kisses of the lover. The first is propitiatory or reconciling; the second meritorious; the third contemplative. The first is at the feet; the second at the hand; the third at the mouth. The first occurs when the sinner, stained in the dust of penitence, kisses the Lord’s two feet and, with the sinful woman, receives forgiveness of sins.

The Lord’s two feet are mercy and judgment, by which he traverses the whole world and walks upon the waves of the sea. With these he continually circles and traverses spiritual minds, “rejoicing as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6), provided they are such that he may rightly say of them: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (2 Cor. 6:16). The one who adapts himself to these feet kisses them, singing mercy and judgment to the Lord [Col. 0411D].

Then one rises to the hand, so as to offer the second kiss, when the faithful soul, now walking in newness of life, rises from the humility of the penitent to the hand of the giver, giving thanks for receiving the affections and effects of good works, which are signified by the hand. For in the splendour of good works it does not kiss its own hand—which, as Job says, is “the greatest iniquity” and a denial of God Most High (Job 31:27–28) [Col. 0412A]—but kisses the giver’s hand, to whose grace it ascribes all that it is, with sweet thanksgiving signified by the kiss.

The third is the kiss of contemplation, or contemplative kiss. Having been cheered by the first two and gathered confidence, the bride desires to be marked by it, now to be united with the bridegroom by knowledge and love, and to become in some measure privy to his secrets. This is the kiss of his own mouth and is far unlike the preceding kisses. “Let him kiss me,” she says, “with the kiss of his mouth.” We must consider what this kiss is, what that mouth of his is, and what are the lips of the one impressing it and of the one receiving it.

6. In God, being and knowing are not different things; nor does the Father have knowledge from the Son, lest He be thought to receive both knowledge and being—which would be absurd. The Father therefore has from Himself both being and knowledge; and if the Son has being from the Father, He also has knowledge from the Father. Thus the subsistences—which the Greeks call *hypostases*—are complete; neither is supported by the other so as to subsist, or to be what it is through the other. Rather, as we have said, they are, according to the Greeks, complete hypostases subsisting in themselves, or, according to the Latins, persons, sounding forth in themselves; although God is one perfect Trinity.

Let no one be disturbed, nor let the names substance, subsistence, or person cast darkness upon anyone. They are names belonging to our poverty: they do not express the essence of divinity, but, through their own inadequacy, bear witness to its incomprehensibility. The name “subsistences” attempts to express the distinct property of the persons; the name “substance,” the simplicity and unity of that highest essence.
