There is a certain turning of the Father toward the Son and of the Son toward the Father; but the Father’s turning toward the Son is first, because the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son. It is first not in time, but in a certain relation, as the Father is related to the Son.

This turning is in a kiss and an embrace. The kiss is their mutual knowledge of one another; the embrace is their mutual love. Hence the Son says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and no one knows the Son except the Father.” The kiss and embrace of Father and Son, therefore, is the Holy Spirit proceeding from both: the Father’s love for the Son and the Son’s love for the Father. Of Him it is further said: “And to whomsoever the Son wills to reveal him” [Matt. 11:27]. For this will is Himself the Holy Spirit, the will of Father and Son, who reveals to us the unity of Father and Son, Himself one God with the Father and the Son.

For it belongs properly to the Father to reveal the Son, as in the Gospel the Son says: “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” [Matt. 16:17]. It is the Son’s due to glorify the Father, as there: “I glorify my Father who is in heaven” [John 8:49]. The office of the Holy Spirit is to reveal both, as the Apostle says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him—but to us He has revealed it through the Holy Spirit” [1 Cor. 2:9–10].

Therefore, when the Son reveals someone through the Spirit, God is not to be said to kiss that person with His mouth, but with the kiss of His mouth. For we do not touch the mouth; rather, we are touched by the kiss. We are touched by the kiss when love and knowledge are poured into us. We do not touch the mouth—that is, that mutual understanding—for, as was said, “No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son.” But we are touched by the kiss when the Son wills to reveal. We do not touch the mouth, because “eye has not seen, nor ear heard”; we are touched by the kiss because God has revealed to us through the Holy Spirit. For He reveals to no one except through the Holy Spirit.

He, then, is the kiss. He touches us when He pours His twofold grace into us: namely, knowledge and love of the truth. These are not God’s lips themselves, but the trace of the lips—or rather, if it may lawfully be said, of the lip. For what is twofold in us is single in God, to whom knowing and loving are the same thing. This trace is impressed, in the holy kiss, upon the bride’s two lips: namely, the will and reason—love upon the will, knowledge upon reason. Yet these two, knowledge and love, because, as we have said, they are one in God, are expressed by the beautiful singularity of the mouth in the words: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

Or: let the Son kiss me with that kiss by which He kisses His own mouth, that is, the Father, who is called His mouth because the Son is the Father’s Word. Thus in Wisdom: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High” [Ecclus. 24:5]. Or: let God the Father kiss me with the kiss of His mouth, that is, of His Son or Word—for a word comes forth from the mouth, and this is figurative speech—that is, let Him pour into me that utterance by which the Father knows the Son and the Son knows the Father. Or: let the Father Himself kiss me with the kiss of His mouth; that is, let Him send into my heart the Spirit of His Son, so that we may love the Son as He Himself loves Him.

But why “Let him kiss,” rather than “Kiss me”? For a carnal bride and bridegroom customarily anticipate one another with a certain mutual reverence. Hence this bride, like Rebecca, covering her face, as it were, with a veil of modesty when she went to meet her new bridegroom [Gen. 24:65], does not speak in the imperative, but in the desiring or optative mood: “Would that at last, sometime, he might kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

7. There is another kiss also: the one which He who “spoke in many and various ways formerly to the fathers through the prophets” promised to His Church, and who “in these last days has spoken to us in the Son” [Heb. 1:1–2]. For the statement, “He has spoken to us in the Son,” is itself the kiss. The union of Word and hearer, of divinity and humanity, is a kind of kiss of love.

Foreseeing this in the Spirit, Isaiah said: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root; and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” [Isa. 11:1–3]. These are the seven gifts, or seven charisms, of the Holy Spirit, which shone forth especially in the Lord Jesus, just as the Holy Spirit rested especially upon Him.

Humility is designated in fear; mercy in piety; knowledge of earthly things in knowledge; patience in strength; usefulness in counsel; union with divinity in understanding; moderation of power in wisdom. Through the first five Christ joined Himself to humanity in assuming human substance; through the last two the person of Christ was always united to divinity. For, as a good physician, He humbly bent down to the sick person, mercifully treated the wounds, cared for the creature known to Him, patiently bore with the madman, and applied what was useful to each illness. Remaining indivisibly one with the Father, He uniquely understood God in the very truth of humanity, because no one knows the Father except the Son; and through that wisdom which He Himself is—the wisdom of the Father—reaching mightily from end to end, He ordered all things moderately and sweetly.

This union, therefore, of the divine and human natures is a kind of kiss of bridegroom and bride, and desiring it the Church says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” There are also three other kisses by which the bride is united to the bridegroom: the kiss of nature, the kiss of teaching, and the kiss of grace. Since much has already been said concerning kisses, these are left for the reader’s meditation.

8. “Because your breasts are better than wine” [Song 1:1]. It is written: “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; your ear has heard the preparation of their heart” [Ps. 10:17]. Since desire, therefore, usually precedes confidence, the bridegroom answers, gives confidence to the desiring bride, and also supplies the ground of confidence: “Because,” he says, “your breasts are better than wine.”

I seem to see here the trembling Esther, as though fearfully approaching the king’s throne and scarcely daring to raise her eyes to the radiance of his face; while the king extends to her the sceptre of mercy and says: “What do you desire, Esther? What is your petition?” [Esther 5:1–3]. So too the bridegroom says to the bride: “Why do you fear to ask what you desire? You have already received many things from me which ought to give you confidence to dare greater things. From receiving former gifts there may be a firm expectation of future ones. You desire contemplation; already, in the active life, you have received from my gift perfection. For your breasts are better than wine.”

A grape, once pressed, pours out all its contents at once; so too secular wisdom, or the carnal understanding of the Law. But the more the bride’s breasts are pressed, the more abundantly they overflow. Your breasts, through my grace, are better than wine—that is, more effective than the love and wisdom of the world. These intoxicate, and those intoxicate; but your breasts much more abundantly intoxicate toward good than they toward evil. For simple, milky Christian and apostolic teaching dissolves all the arguments of dialecticians.

Moreover, just as the Apostles were filled and intoxicated with the new wine of the Holy Spirit, so the blessed poor in spirit, the children of grace and children of the New Testament, were filled, so that they embraced the love of God even to contempt for themselves, and regarded all things as dung so that they might gain Christ. Therefore the bride’s breasts are better than wine.

These two breasts of the bride are compassion and shared rejoicing. From the breast of compassion is drawn the milk of consolation; from the breast of shared rejoicing, the milk of exhortation. That these breasts may be better than wine, they are fragrant with the finest ointments, because the best ointment—that is, surpassing love—works effectiveness in them. The bride’s breasts are thus anointed: softened by the bridegroom’s touch through anointing; spread far and wide like a good fragrance by the sweetness of good example; or raised to the bridegroom’s own fragrance through the sacrifice of devout intention and holy desire.

9. “Fragrant with the finest ointments” [Song 1:2]. There are three ointments: that of compunction, from remembrance of sins; that of devotion, from remembrance of benefits; and that of piety, from remembrance of the miserable. With the first the Lord’s feet are anointed; with the second, His head; with the third, His whole body.

Of the first it is said: “Mary anointed the feet of Jesus and wiped them with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment” [Luke 7:37–38; John 12:3]. Of the second: “A woman brought an alabaster jar of costly spikenard and poured it upon the head of him reclining” [Mark 14:3]. Of the third: “Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome went and bought spices, that they might come and anoint Jesus” [Mark 16:1].

Observe the order of progress from lower things to higher, as above concerning the state and kiss of love. Thus Mary Magdalene, who had been a sinner, anointed Jesus’ feet. Nor indeed is this a trivial ointment, of which it is written: “The house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment.” Nor is this surprising, since the fragrance of such ointment is perceived even in heaven, Truth Himself bearing witness that “there is great joy among the angels of God over one sinner doing penance” [Luke 15:10].

Yet however precious this ointment may seem, in comparison with that called devotion, which is compounded from the remembrance of divine benefits and with which the Lord’s head is anointed, it is reckoned cheap and of no value. For of the former it is said: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” [Ps. 50:19]; but of the latter: “The sacrifice of praise shall honour me” [Ps. 49:23].

You anoint the head with it when you give thanks to God for His gifts; for the head of Christ is God. Thus divinity in Christ is touched whenever, in praise of Him, we remember His benefits within us; whereas humanity, rather than divinity, must necessarily be considered when we remember not His gifts but our own sins. For in assuming flesh He is known to have received those two feet for this purpose—mercy and judgment—so that the sinner, who had no access to the head, that is, divinity, might approach the feet, that is, humanity.

For unless the foot which we called mercy belonged to the assumed human being, the Apostle Paul would not say of Him: “Therefore He had to be made like his brethren in every respect, that He might become merciful” [Heb. 2:17]. And unless judgment likewise belonged to the human being, the God-man Himself would not have said of Himself: “He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man” [John 5:27]. Therefore, to these feet of the man who, according to the prophet, was “a man of sorrows and acquainted with weakness” [Isa. 53:3], the sinner now approaches without hesitation and speaks confidently: “Now, therefore, we approach with confidence the throne of his grace. For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses” [Heb. 4:15–16]. The sinful woman, therefore, approaches the feet; the righteous woman, to anoint the head.

10. The ointment for the head should be reckoned as much more precious than the other applied to the feet as the spices from which it is made are more precious than those from which the other is made. The latter we find easily and without labour—for they are in our own land: all of us, indeed, are sinners. But the former we receive only with difficulty and from very far away, as though brought from the paradise of God. For “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” [James 1:17].

What, finally, is more excellent than this sort of ointment? Even the Apostles seem to have murmured at its pouring out, saying: “Why this waste? For it could have been sold for much and given to the poor.” And even now, when someone perhaps seems to devote himself to God and to possess such devotion and grace that he may deservedly be believed to anoint Christ’s head—persisting continually in holy quiet, thanksgiving, and the delight of divine contemplation—there are people who call it waste and complain, with what seems to them righteous indignation, that one who might benefit many should remain at rest for himself. This is not because they envy holiness, but because they are concerned for love.

Yet charity itself, which is God, often spares such a soul, seeing it delight in spiritual pursuits—especially if He knows it to be still, through faint-heartedness or weakness of spirit, a woman and not yet advanced into the perfect man. Certainly He who looks upon the heart discerns this better than people who see only the face and judge only according to appearance. They do not sufficiently consider that devout rest and fruitful activity are not equally easy; humble subjection and useful authority; being ruled without complaint and ruling without fault; willing obedience and prudent command; in short, being good among good people and being good among evil people; indeed, being peaceful among children of peace and showing oneself peaceable to those who hate peace.

Jesus, therefore, knowing who are truly unfit to become entangled in ecclesiastical cares and burdens, answers on behalf of such a delicate soul—whom, because of her still tender condition, He sees as less adequate for managing affairs—against those who think otherwise and accuse her repose as unfruitful, with good zeal indeed but not according to knowledge: “Why do you trouble this woman?” [Matt. 26:8–10]. For although, as must be admitted, that to which you try to draw her is better, still “she has done a good work to me.” Allow her meanwhile to do the good she can, while she is not yet able to do what is better; for I know that she is still a woman.

But when, through “the change of the right hand of the Most High,” a woman has become a man—and when that will be, if it ever is, cannot be hidden from me—then, because she will advance at my call and will be kept fast by my protection, “the wickedness of a man will be better than a beneficent woman” [Ecclus. 42:14]. Yet I hope for that better thing as well; meanwhile I do not despise this good thing, nor do I regard the outpouring of this ointment as waste. In it both the woman’s devotion is signified and my burial is foreshadowed. Moreover, it diffuses its fragrance so widely on every side that, wherever this Gospel is preached throughout the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.

11. Let us now approach the third ointment. Certainly, in comparing either of the two previously mentioned ointments, the latter is recognized, without any ambiguity, as better and far more excellent than the former. But it seems remarkable if a third can be found which should rightly be preferred to both, in accordance with the bride’s boast that her breasts are fragrant with the finest ointments. Otherwise they are not finest if they do not surpass those which are better; just as things are not truly called better unless they surpass good things.

Now the second ointment, which anoints the head, has been found to be of such excellence that scarcely any riches, I do not say can be preferred to it, but can even seem comparable with it. Perhaps, if we search the Gospel, we shall find that the figure of this third ointment also came first: “Mary Magdalene, Mary of James, and Salome bought spices, that they might come and anoint Jesus” [Mark 16:1].

Do you see, at the very outset of the chapter quoted, how highly even this material ointment ought to be valued, when neither one nor two women were sufficient to purchase its spices? One woman brought the first ointment, and one the second; but for purchasing this one, three came together, so that they might jointly buy what each could not buy separately and, coming, anoint Jesus. Not merely His feet or merely His head, but, “that they might come,” it says, “and anoint Jesus”—that is, His whole body.

But note that Christ would not allow, as it were, this ointment to be wasted. When they did not find the body, they carried it back intact; and they were commanded to offer to the living One what they had prepared for the dead. This they did when, immediately after the joyful announcement of the resurrection, they took care to soothe the sad hearts of the disciples, who were beyond doubt Christ’s members and living members. Unless Christ loved these members more than that crucified body, He would not have delivered that body to crucifixion for their sake.

It is clear, therefore, that this last ointment surpasses the two former by as much as Christ’s body to which it is offered—that is, the Church, which He willed to be anointed through them and for whose redemption He willed it to be delivered up—is more beloved by Him. The bride’s breasts, then, are fragrant not merely with good and better ointments, but with the finest. Her two breasts of compassion and shared rejoicing, arising from piety and consideration for the miserable, abound in the milk of consolation and exhortation. Healed by the first ointment, purified by the second, and sanctified by the third, she has breasts fragrant with the finest ointments.

12. Or these may also be the bride’s words, as if she were plainly saying: “What I seek, the kiss of contemplation, is presumptuous; but confidence is given by consciousness of good action, because my breasts—mine, because given to me by you; yours, because filled by you and serving you—are better than wine.”

Alternatively, this may be the voice of the companions, that is, the angels, urging the bride, greedy for contemplation, toward the labour of action by considering the progress of those subject to her. They say, therefore: “You will indeed not be deprived of the kiss when you arrive; but when you see the fruit of your labour, do not fail because you are delayed. For behold, your breasts—that is, your gentler teaching—are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.”

Here we see three things in the bride’s breasts: touch, smell, and taste. Touch is in the gentleness of the anointing; smell, in the fragrance of the ointment; taste, in the wine. Touch belongs to those present through the word; smell, to those absent through example; taste, to the bridegroom, through which a good intention of mind is signified.

13. What follows—“Your name is oil poured out”—must be connected in two ways with the three interpretations. If they are the bridegroom’s words, we must understand that here the bridegroom, having comforted the bride’s desire, shown grace, and given confidence, gave her the kiss. Having received the kiss, and with the kiss the oil—that is, through inward inspiration having received in some measure knowledge of the bridegroom, and together with knowledge, love and joy—the bride cried out: “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the maidens loved you” [Song 1:2].

“If we are beside ourselves,” says the Apostle, “it is for God; if we are sober-minded, it is for you” [2 Cor. 5:13]. “Your name is oil poured out” are words of one beside herself for God; “therefore the maidens loved you” are words of sobriety for her neighbour. For after she was beside herself for God, she became sober-minded for the maidens through the abundance of oil received from God. For the bridegroom’s love compelled her.

At the bridegroom’s name—that is, knowledge of the bridegroom—from Him from whose fullness we have all received, such an outpouring of oil, that is, love, took place that the bride, filled for her own part, cried: “Your name is oil poured out”; and, pouring back from her fullness upon the maidens, said: “Therefore the maidens loved you.” For outpouring denotes abundance. This is an outpouring in faith or hope, but only in the fullness of love.

Or, according to the preceding two interpretations, the bride says: “I said that your breasts are better than wine—that is, filled by you and serving you—but by the grace of God I am what I am, because your name is oil poured out. Yet the grace of God in me was not empty; therefore the maidens loved you.”

According to the anagogical sense, oil and name—that is, knowledge and love of God—before they were poured out and abounded among all nations, were infused, not poured out, because God was known only in Judea. But when the outpouring occurred from the infusion, maidens became churches from the Gentiles: not maidens, but brides, because they loved. For she who first becomes a maiden, or handmaid, through faith begins to be a bride when she begins to love. Therefore, because your name is oil poured out, the maidens loved you.

14. In the moral sense, when oil is infused into us by grace, we must beware lest its outpouring be disordered. For something is infused into us that belongs to ourselves, and something that belongs to our neighbour. What belongs to ourselves is that without which we are not saved; the rest belongs to our neighbour. If we pour out what is ours, we are foolish and empty; if we retain what belongs to another, we are deceitful.

What belongs to us is faith, hope, and love. Faith makes servants; hope, hirelings; love, children. Faith makes a female servant or handmaid; hope, a concubine; love, a bride. Faith says, “It is so”; hope, “You shall have”; love, “Give glory to God.” Faith is knowledge of evils or goods; hope is confidence in avoiding or obtaining them; and love is thanksgiving for both, when one, secure concerning each, gives thanks.

Since these things are ours, therefore, they must not be poured out—that is, lost for the sake of others. Rather, we must act so that they work in us what belongs to them: that we may be healed, kept safe, and saved. We are healed through bodily labour, kept safe through reading and meditation, and saved through prayer. Idleness lies in wait for labour; restlessness or idleness for reading; excessive security for prayer.

Therefore we sin if we pour out what is ours, as has been said: that is, if we neglect labour through idleness, reading through restlessness or idleness, and prayer through excessive security. But what is not ours, but another’s, is whatever we possess without which we are saved: such as the word of wisdom, the word of knowledge, gifts of healing, and the other things which can be possessed apart from love, in which alone we are saved.

If we retain these when it is time to pour them out, we are deceitful. When the matter requires that they be poured out, we must beware lest they be withheld lukewarmly, fearfully, or enviously: lukewarmly, through distrust of the hearers; fearfully, through irrational fear; enviously, through failure to love a brother. In the first is found a defect of faith, in the second of hope, and in the third of love.

When they are poured out, we must beware lest they be poured out carelessly, rashly, or ambitiously: carelessly, lest one give what is holy to dogs; rashly, lest the speaker exceed the rule of faith; ambitiously, lest one seek one’s own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ. We must also beware lest this be done unseasonably, presumptuously, or fruitlessly: unseasonably, before the maturity of soul and body; presumptuously, without office; fruitlessly, without grace.

In all these matters, if the outpouring is good where this oil has been infused, the oil performs its three powers. For oil nourishes, gives light, and anoints; love likewise nourishes itself, gives light to its neighbour, and anoints God.

15. “Draw me after you; we will run in the fragrance of your ointments.” The bride condescends to the maidens from that height in which she had been beside herself for God. After she had poured back upon the maidens that outpouring of oil infused into her, while she laboured among them, she remembered the kiss, the oil, and the bridegroom; and, sighing for Him from whom concern for her neighbour drew her unwillingly away, she says: “Draw me after you.”

For when she is beside herself in mind, she is for God; when sober-minded, she is for her neighbour. When she is beside herself, she is shown how greatly God loves her; when sober-minded, she shows in concern for her neighbour how greatly she loves God. The love of truth draws her upward; the truth of love draws her downward. But although this necessity holds her here, that sweetness cannot depart from her soul. Therefore, “Draw me,” she says, “O bridegroom.”

There are four things that draw us away from God: the flesh through enticements, the devil through deceits, the world through cares, and the neighbour through affection. The bride, drawn unwillingly away from God by these things, or by some of them, longs and prays to be drawn by God to God. For one kind of drawing is voluntary, another compelled: compelled, as into prison; voluntary, as for the weary or blind. The bride who prays to be drawn wishes to be drawn; and because she wishes it, this is on account of blindness, weakness, or both.

She was suffering exhaustion from the world or devil; moreover, her mind’s sight was disturbed in the care of her neighbour. Against all these things she desires to be drawn from them to God, by God and through God’s power. For this drawing is in power. It is, according to the Apostle, “as from the Spirit of the Lord,” when we are transformed from glory to glory [2 Cor. 3:18].

Or thus: “And because the maidens, through my work in making them love not me but you, love you and no longer need me, draw me after you—that is, take me out of the body.” But the maidens cry out: “After you, we will run in the fragrance of your ointments”—that is, we too shall come with you.

16. Or: “Draw me”—that is, make me spiritual—“after you,” that is, in imitation of you; because “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his steps” [1 Pet. 2:21]. For when the Bridegroom came forth from the virgin bridal chamber, He rejoiced like a giant to run His course through the whole dispensation of His life, laying out and ordering for us a way of life. Along this way He might guide us after Himself by examples, as by footprints, and draw us by love. Thus He says in the Gospel to Peter and Andrew: “Come after me” [Matt. 4:19].

If we consider His conception or birth, our spiritual conception is the direction of devout will. This occurs in a virgin soul, because it desires to please God alone. The Lord’s birth is the beginning in us of a good work; and so with the remaining things. Circumcision, which may not be performed by one’s own hands, is the discernment of teachers concerning the works of disciples. In that circumcision Jesus receives His name, because the work of the subject receives the name of virtue or salvation from the teacher’s discernment.

The Lord’s manifestation, moreover, is the manifestation of a work by God’s command, not by itself. At the manifestation the Virgin Mother is always found by both Magi and shepherds, because continual modesty always accompanies true virtue among both wise and foolish persons. The purification of forty days is the exercise of a good work until its end. The presentation of the child in the temple is the offering of a perfect work after the end of life.

But the presentation in the temple occurs through two kinds of persons—persecutors and hypocrites. While these remain outside, the parents, that is, the performers of the good work, introduce it into God’s temple. Aged Simeon is the Ancient of Days, almighty God; the child in His arms is the weighing in God’s hand of every work or merit. For conception must be pure, birth voluntary, circumcision discerning, manifestation modest, purification continual, and offering holy. Whoever faithfully imitates these and similar things from the Lord runs strongly after Him.

17. Or: “Draw me after you,” that is, by love of yourself alone. “Turn away my eyes, lest they behold vanity.” Nor do I wish to be drawn alone, because the maidens and I will run in the fragrance of your ointments.

There are three things that make one run: fear, desire, and love—fear by fleeing, desire by seeking, love by loving one’s neighbour. There are also four things that hinder this running: cold, heat, a laborious road, and the excessive speed of the runner. Under other names, these are distrust, concupiscence, impatience with hardship, and excessive confidence; or the numbness of distrust, carnal desires, the harshness of observances, and the impetuosity of one advancing or reaching perfection.

Against numbness, a relaxing ointment of composition is necessary, compounded from remembrance of Christ’s miracles and testimonies; against heat, a cooling ointment from the elements of Christ’s life and instruction; against the sorrow of the labourer, a healing ointment from remembrance of Christ’s sufferings and promises; against the impetuosity of those advancing, a soothing ointment from remembrance of Christ’s gentleness and mercies. Yet all these ointments are useless unless compounded from the bridegroom’s oil.

In the fragrance of these ointments run the maidens whose course is not impeded. But the bride does not merely smell all these things: she touches them, because she displays all these things in herself, yet for others rather than herself. She displays the glory of miracles, the example of conduct, and the instruction of admonition. She also bears about the marks of Christ’s sufferings; and she both preaches and displays gentleness and mercies to all.

18. “The king brought me into his storehouses” [Song 1:3]. Hearing the maidens’ promise, “We will run in the fragrance of your ointments,” the bride replies: “You will run rightly, and you ought to run. Believe one who has experienced it: the king brought me into his storehouses, from which He sent me back full and filled to overflowing. The king brought me in, I say—He who guides my steps in truth. He brought me into His storehouses through His liberality; I did not burst in through my presumption.”

For when the bridegroom heard the vows of the bride praying, “Draw me after you,” He drew her, as it were, away from the flesh and after Himself into a hidden place of His contemplation, and showed her His secrets. There, after she had been beside herself for God, she again became sober-minded for her neighbour and returned to the maidens. And, appearing wonderful and terrible from her vision and conversation with God, as though displaying the two horns of contemplation—reason and love—she said: “The king brought me into his storehouses.”

Blessed is the director of souls who deserves to be admitted into that secret place concerning all that he desires, worries about, or doubts, so that he may do all things according to what has been shown him on the mountain. “The king brought me into his storehouses.” Since we are soon to discuss the wine-cellar, let us defer discussion of the king’s storehouses until that place.

“We will exult and rejoice in you.” Hearing the bride commend the bridegroom’s liberality, the maidens speak as did the children of Israel, who could not ascend the mountain with Moses: “Speak to us, and let not the Lord speak to us” [Exod. 20:19]. “For the present, you are enough for us: we will exult and rejoice in you”—that is, in your teaching and imitation. “We will exult” when we work bodily; “and rejoice” while we enjoy spiritual delight, remembering your breasts [Song 1:3], which meanwhile suffice for us.

For the milk of consolation and exhortation which we have drawn from them makes us sing, with a certain glad exultation of mind: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous; praise befits the upright” [Ps. 32:1]. Hence there follows:

19. The upright love you. There are those who lie prostrate, those who stand erect, those who are crooked, and those who are upright. Those lying prostrate neither fear nor love; the crooked fear but do not love; the upright love. The bride therefore prays for the young women, that those whom she still sees bent over in fear she may see made upright in love for the bridegroom—as though she said: “I see these women bent over; but make them upright, because the upright love you.” Or otherwise: seeing the young women applaud her, the bride, while commending them, fears for others—while these rejoice, those others are envious—as though she said: “These are upright, and therefore they love you; and if they love me, they love me only in you. For I have taught them to love not me, but you.” For, seeing herself overwhelmed by their goodwill, the bride turns to the bridegroom and prays for them: “The upright love you.” But what are we to do about the envious? Turning to them, and taking thought for those who had sometimes insulted her because of her former manner of life, she says: “I am dark, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” And observe the order of charity. When she speaks of the bridegroom’s love, she in some manner wholly melts into him; when she speaks of the young women, she is moved by compassion and becomes, as it were, one of them; when she speaks of her enemies, she burns for them with the full zeal of charity. “I am dark, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem.” O daughters of Jerusalem, daughters of peace: have peace with me, who have peace with you. This of yours is reproach, not compassion. I am indeed dark because of my former conduct, but beautiful because of pure confession and right intention. For there are two things that make one dark and two that make one beautiful. Evil conduct and distorted intention make one dark; innocent conduct and right intention make one beautiful. In the soul these correspond to a lovely complexion and a well-proportioned form in the body. But she who has not had an innocent manner of life, after putting on confession and directing her intention toward what is better, confidently says, “I am dark, but beautiful,” because confession covers her past sins. For confession is the beauty of memory, and right intention the harmonious ordering of the will. The truth of confession covers the first; the justice of right intention gives form to the second. Hence she says:

20. “Like the tents of Kedar,” that is, darkness. I am not the tents of Kedar, but like the tents of Kedar; and if I was a tent, or like a tent of Kedar—that is, a dwelling-place of darkness—I was a tent, not a permanent house. For we were once darkness, but now light in the Lord. “Like the skins of Solomon.” For I live—yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me; that is, faith in Christ covers my former darkness. It is rightly called Solomon’s skin, because, drawn from Christ’s death and putting us to death, it is laid over the tent of Kedar—that is, over the dark conscience—and makes it a worthy dwelling for the true Solomon.

Mary, the Mother of the Lord, could have said to the daughters of Jerusalem who wondered at her: “I am dark through Adam’s nature, but beautiful through faith—that is, through Solomon’s skin.” Or, otherwise, she says this to the same women when she sees herself despised by some on account of the sobriety by which she had become all things to all, in order to gain all: “I am dark,” she says, “by this outward abasement, but beautiful by the beauty of my intention.” For all the glory of the king’s daughter is within. Like Kedar’s tents, I am outwardly dark; but inwardly I am beautiful with a skin—not my own, but Solomon’s.

Or, to the young women who rejoice in her rather than insult her: “Because,” she says, “you rejoice in me and run after me, do not attend to the fact that I am dark—that is, sober—toward you; or that I am dark amid the humiliation and pressures of the world, since I am beautiful in the bridegroom’s eyes, because the sun has darkened my colour.” Colour appears in the body’s skin. The bride’s skin is her intention; its colour is her action. The skin is therefore darkened when concern for one’s neighbour obscures an intention directed toward God by its actions. “Do not therefore,” she says, “look at me because I am swarthy, because the sun—that is, the love of God—has darkened my colour” (Song of Songs 1:3–5), having made me dark through the occupations of your activity. But what is darkened by the sun soon returns to its natural colour; so too shall I return to my own beauty. Yet the skin is darkened, not the inward mouth with which I constantly sing to the bridegroom: “My substance was not hidden from you, when I was made in secret” (Psalm 138:15). That is, the inward love of the heart suffers no injury.

274. 21. “My mother’s sons fought against me” (Song of Songs 1:5). Alas, what a change! She who shortly before was rejoicing in that secret peace of God which surpasses all understanding now suffers the accusations that arise amid human quarrels. David, contemplating in the Spirit such fluctuations of prelates, says: “Those who go down into the sea of this age in ships”—that is, in the governance of churches—“doing their work in great waters, these have seen the works of the Lord and his wonders in the deep. He spoke, and a stormy wind arose, and its waves were lifted up. They went up to the heavens and down to the depths; their soul melted away in evils. They were troubled and reeled like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up. My mother’s sons fought against me” (Psalm 106:23–27).

It is no wonder that the sun darkened my colour, when the conflict I suffer is severe, when even my mother’s sons—the sons of the Church—have fought against me by their depraved conduct. While I fought against them by arguing, entreating, and rebuking them, “they made me a keeper in their vineyards” (Song of Songs 1:5); that is, they entrusted themselves to my keeping. Some did so through strife and envy, in order, as the Apostle says, to raise affliction for my tribulations (Philippians 1:17); others, from good will. “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7); the vine is Christ; the branch put forth is the converted sinner; the fruit is fruits worthy of repentance. While I contend against them and afterwards keep watch over them, while, like Jacob, I suffer heat by day and frost by night, it is no wonder that the sun has darkened my colour.

But though I have been set as keeper in vineyards and labour in those belonging to others, I have not kept my own vineyard. Keep it, you who keep Israel, for whose sake I neglected it, for whose sake I have been darkened. And that I may know what I owe to my own vineyard and what to another’s: “Tell me, O you whom my soul loves, at noon”—that is, in the heat of so great wickedness, in which even my mother’s sons fought against me—“where I may rest while attending to myself, where I may feed those entrusted to me.” What she says is this: “Tell me where, while I rest, you rest with me, and while I feed, you feed with me, so that I may do nothing against you or without you, but may do everything with you, and you with me.” This, then, is what she prays for: that she may know what and when she owes to herself, and what and when to others.

Or otherwise: noon is the heat of wickedness, the noonday demon, when Satan’s angel transforms himself into an angel of light. “That I may not fall into him, tell me where you feed, where you rest at noon” (Song of Songs 1:6).

Or otherwise: there are four days, two good and two evil, concerning which the Psalm says: “At evening, morning, and noon I shall relate and proclaim” (Psalm 54:18). The first day begins in the morning and ends in the evening of night and eternal death: this is the evil angel. The second begins in the morning of creation and proceeds to the noon and fervour of perfection; its feet do not depart from there: this is the good angel. The third begins in the evening of sin and proceeds into the night of eternal ruin: these are the reprobate. The fourth day is the day of our Lord Jesus Christ, which begins at the evening of the Sabbath and dawns on the first day of the week. That is, it begins at the evening of our sin and, after the very brief intervening space of fear, as if of night, leads the children of light to the morning of hope and thence to the noon of angelic perfection and love; nor does it thereafter allow them to be removed from it.

The bride therefore prays to him whom her soul, not her flesh, loves—that is, whom she loves spiritually—that he may place her in the noon of angelic perfection, so that, freed from all the darkness of ignorance, she may begin, without any contrary doubt, to see what is expedient for herself or for the flock; lest, being left uncertain whether to rest or labour, she begin to wander after the flocks of the bridegroom’s companions—that is, after those who make themselves equal to him or seek their own interests.

22. “After the flocks.” For whoever leaves the perfection of truth for the byway of error does not merely go with the wandering flocks, but goes after the flocks, because he is found worse than all of them. But it must not be passed over that the Lord’s flock is fed by its shepherds in three ways: by example, word, and prayer. By example, against the concupiscence of the flesh; by word, against the concupiscence of the eyes; by prayer, against worldly ambition.

“If you do not know yourself, O beautiful among women.” The bride was seeking the bridegroom at noon, that is, in the manifest light of truth, lest one thing present itself to her in place of another. She sought where he might rest at noon, that is, in what affection of noonday perfection, so that she might see what affection should be chosen at what time, where the bridegroom might rest with her and she with the bridegroom. The bridegroom therefore answered: “O beautiful among women”—namely, between Mary and Martha—because I do not wish you to choose one of these, but to hold both: the contemplative life and the active life. “O beautiful among women, if you wish to know me, do not be ignorant of yourself.” This is the answer of Delphic Apollo: “Know yourself.”

Two things make us ignorant of ourselves: excessive rashness concerning ourselves, or excessive timidity of self-abasement. In accordance with these two things the bridegroom answers the bride, either recalling her from rashness to humility through experience of herself, or from timidity to confidence through her perception of past gifts. For there are two forms of self-ignorance: when a person estimates himself either more or less highly than he ought; and there are two things that produce this, presumption and faint-heartedness; and two causes of these effects, pride and insufficient experience of oneself. But experience of oneself produces humility, and humility self-knowledge.

Thus the bridegroom, reproving her rashness, says: “You desire the noon of angelic blessedness too hastily and impatiently, because you must first do much and labour in the morning of virtue. Therefore, if you do not know yourself, go out from me, or from the good of your conscience; do not remain with me, but go after the tracks of the flocks and feed your kids”—that is, the wicked motions of the flesh, or lost hearers, who will stand at the left—“beside the tents of the shepherds”; that is, having followed the teachings of reprobate teachers, not in the Church but in the tents of their conventicles, where they teach wickedly. But by saying, “Go out,” he permits rather than commands; indeed, he does not seem to permit it altogether, but recalls her to labour.

23. “I have compared you, my friend, to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots” (Song of Songs 1:8). O my friend, although I reprove you as rash, although I recall you to labour, you are no less my friend for that. You already wish to sit with me in my kingdom. I should be indignant at presumption, but I pardon love. O friend, it is not yet time for you to reign, but to fight; for I have compared you to my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots. You have been placed in the midst of Pharaoh’s chariots. You must not merely escape yourself; you must lead my people out of the land of slavery.

Or, to raise her faint heart: “You shall not perish, O my friend, because among Pharaoh’s chariots I have made you like my cavalry”—that is, I have made you like the cavalry of the angels, so that, just as they possess charity, chastity, humility, and order, so may you, placed in the midst of Pharaoh’s chariots. For as long as we are here in battle array and our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places, the two armies—the chariots of God and the chariots of Pharaoh—are, as in war, intermingled. For as Pharaoh’s chariots, that is, the devil’s, are many, so God’s chariots are “ten thousandfold” numerous.

It is pleasing to describe more closely the chariots both of God and of the devil, and to show more clearly who serve God or the devil. The devil has three chariots, in which he traverses the whole world: luxury, pride, and malice. The chariot of luxury has two wheels, gluttony and softness; the impulse of the flesh, like an unbroken horse, draws them. Self-love rides it on the saddle of pleasure, holding want as its bridle and the goad of lust as its spur. The chariot of pride has two wheels, presumption of oneself and rashness. The horse which draws it is the desire for vain glory; love of the world rides it on the saddle of flattery, holding avarice as its bridle and envy’s goad as its spur. The chariot of malice has two wheels, pretence and concealment. Its drawing horse is ill will; delight in evil rides it on the saddle of fraud, holding evasiveness as its bridle and anger’s goad as its spur.

Against these three chariots are three chariots of God. The chariot of continence has two wheels, prayer and bodily discipline. Devotion draws it; the soldier of God rides it, with self-contempt on the saddle of purity, holding discipline as a bridle and the goad of the fear of the Lord as a spur. The chariot of innocence has two wheels: the humility that does not wish to rule and the meekness that wishes to be subject. The horse that draws them is love of peace. Contempt of the world rides it on the saddle of goodwill, holding zeal for truth as its bridle and the goad of love for God and neighbour as its spur. The chariot of wisdom has two wheels, prudence and simplicity; its horse is fortitude; its rider, love of God; its saddle, watchfulness lest it fall; its bridle, moderation, that it may govern; its spur, zeal for justice.

Therefore, friend, although you have chariots like Pharaoh’s and I have made you like my cavalry among Pharaoh’s chariots, you must now strive for victory, not for the prize of victory. What you seek is too great and too hasty. You shall not yet see my face, but you shall see my back. Although you do not now receive the noon which you ask for, you nevertheless receive many things from me in the meantime, for which you are deservedly praised.

24. For already, by my grace, “your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove”; that is, great are both the outward and inward gifts with which I have enriched you. What you have received inwardly is shown outwardly by the propriety and maturity of your conduct. These are the two cheeks of the turtledove—that is, of the soul—which mourns in the bridegroom’s absence, receives no consolation, and dwells alone. Just as the condition of the outward person is detected in the pallor or flush of the cheeks, so the sincerity of a well-ordered mind is displayed in propriety and maturity of conduct.

And not only this, but “your neck [is] like necklaces.” As I said, propriety and maturity of conduct commend to people the purity of your soul; but before God, the rectitude of your intention does so. For your intention, which, like a neck, joins the whole body of your work to Christ the head, is like a necklace when it becomes manifest to all that it serves God and neighbour. For this is signified by a necklace, the ornament of the neck: outwardly it has gold, but inwardly a jewel; that is, intention is stirred by love of God and love of neighbour. When the bridegroom reveals this to people, he adorns the bride’s neck with a necklace—or rather, makes it to be like necklaces.

When, says the bridegroom, I have given you all these things, I shall add another ornament: “We shall make for you golden earrings.” This is indeed so; it is usually so. When the bride seeks glory in this world, she does not obtain it, or, if she does obtain it, it is useless. But when she seeks glory in the bridegroom alone, she incurs glory even without knowing it—and glory that is useful. Just as glory offered itself in the ornament of the neck through example, so gold appears in the ornament through word. Glory ought to seek you, not you it. If you seek it, it flees; if you flee it, it comes upon you; if you seek and find it, it is harmful or useless.

25. “We shall make you golden earrings,” he says, “inlaid with silver” (Song of Songs 1:6–10). Earrings are ornaments of the ears, given by the bridegroom to the bride when her preaching receives a favourable hearing. “Inlaid with silver,” that is, distinguished by eloquence, because to one is given the word of wisdom, signified by gold, and to another the word of knowledge (1 Corinthians 12:8), signified by silver. The bridegroom therefore promises that he will glorify her inwardly and outwardly.

“We shall make them,” he says: I, the Father, and the Spirit—myself as wisdom, the Father as efficacy, the Holy Spirit supplying kindness. We shall make them from nothing, that is, from no preceding merit; for this is what the name *making* signifies. Hence it is said there also: “Let us make man” (Genesis 1:26). Or, “we shall make”: I, my angels, and my teachers—I by inspiring, angels by suggesting, human beings by teaching. For God sees intention, the angel sees affection, and the human being sees the deed. An angel does not see intention, but sees affection. Therefore the evil angel does not see the good God, because God is identical with his affection and will; for he is not acted upon emotionally.

The suggestions of angels are themselves their languages, of which the Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of angels” (1 Corinthians 13:1). These are certain hidden spiritual signs unknown to us, by which they speak to one another and make their wills known—not only to one another, but also to some people who lead an angelic life. Thus one understands the language of angels who understands their suggestions. One speaks their language who, like Nicholas and Benedict, suggests what he wishes in dreams, or by certain other hidden means, either to sleeping persons or to persons far away. Or, “we shall make you golden earrings inlaid with silver”: that is, speech of grace seasoned with salt.

277. 26. Hearing the bridegroom’s kindly promise, the bride gladly returns to the young women. It is indeed a consolation of human life to have someone to whom you may entrust your heart, someone whom you make a sharer in your joy and also in your sorrow. Therefore, whenever the bride receives an outpouring of oil from the bridegroom, she is filled to overflowing. Since she must pour it out, she returns, in the overflow of charity’s fullness, to the young women, for whom she desires the same thing that she desires for herself. Happy friendship and blessed fellowship, where one who hears immediately says, “Come.”

Returning to them, she says: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” This means: “I thought myself worthless and rejected in the bridegroom’s sight, because, when I sought noon, I suffered a rebuff. But the Lord is the one who judges me. For while my king and Lord was at his table”—that is, in the secret of his judgments, ordering all things at the discretion of his judgments according to the good counsel of his will—“my nard,” that is, my humility arising from my former conduct or from the world’s pressures, “gave forth its fragrance” in his sight, according to the quality of its sweetness. Nard is a low-growing, warm, fragrant herb, by which is figured humility, fervent with charity and acceptable to God through purity of intention.

And truly my nard gave forth its fragrance, for “my beloved is to me a little bundle of myrrh” (Song of Songs 1:11–12). That is, love for my beloved—which is the cause to me in this world of tribulation and bitterness, concerning which I groaned to him when my mother’s sons fought against me—has become for me myrrh: bitter indeed, but preserving me, lest I rot in the torpor of security and negligence. Yet it is not a bundle of myrrh for me, but a little bundle, because it will not endure long; or because it is small to me in comparison with his love; or small in comparison with consideration of my former evils.

“But let Zion rejoice, and let the daughters of Judah exult because of your judgments, O Lord” (Psalm 47:12). For however bitter the myrrh, however heavy the little bundle, it “shall dwell between my breasts”: amid my prosperity and adversity, amid my rejoicing with others and my compassion with them. There it shall dwell and shall never be removed. For I shall rejoice only in the Lord, and grieve only in the Lord. And he himself, whether he consoles me by prosperity or exercises me in adversity, shall not be moved from between my breasts—that is, from the midst of my heart. Whether I must rejoice with others in their good things or suffer compassionately with them in their evils, I do so only in the Lord.

27. “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.” Above, her zeal had caused the bride to waste away, because her enemies had forgotten the words of the Lord—whether those who insulted her darkness, or her mother’s sons who fought against her and made her keeper in the vineyards. While she watched over them to the neglect of her own vineyard, and had nearly despaired of them, and was growing dim in concern and anxiety for them, she sought the bridegroom’s noon. Gently restrained by him and again made glad by consolation—not such as she wished, but such as was expedient—she suddenly, through grace working where she had not hoped, finds fruit: namely, a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi. And she cries out for joy: “My beloved has become for me a cluster of Cyprus.”

Cyprus is an island famous for the fertility of its good vineyards. Engaddi is interpreted “Spring of the Kid.” Cyprus, abounding in wine, signifies the Church, shaken on every side by the waves of the age, yet overflowing in abundance of graces. The Spring of the Kid signifies the font of baptism, into which kids enter but from which newly born lambs come forth, as is said later: “Like a flock of shorn sheep which have come up from the washing, all bearing twin offspring.” The bride therefore marvels that in the vineyards of a new way of life she finds the fruit of perfection, and a fruit none other than Christ himself. For when Christ is the cause in all our actions or endeavours, our fruit is Christ. Conscious of the labour which she had undergone among them, the bride claims this suddenly found fruit for herself with devout exultation: “My beloved is for me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi.”

Or otherwise, to return briefly to what was said above: after the bride deserved to be adorned by the bridegroom, she immediately burst forth in his praise and in proclamation of his works, saying: “While the king was at his table, my nard gave forth its fragrance.” While the King reclined—that is, humbled himself in the Virgin’s womb—my nard, that is, the humility of my Lord, gave forth its fragrance, when, because of the exceeding charity with which he loved us, he deigned to be made from a virgin under the Law. Then he deigned to become not a bundle but a little bundle of myrrh, when he suffered the bitterness of death, cross, and tomb for the space of only three days. Soon afterwards, in the resurrection, he appeared as a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi, when he distributed spiritual goods to the faithful.

28. It follows: “Behold, you are beautiful, my friend; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are those of doves.” Seeing the bride’s devotion, and that she gave him a place to dwell between her breasts, the bridegroom says: “Behold”—that is, in this state of yours, in this confession and knowledge of yourself—you are beautiful, because the very source of your beauty is the source of my being not beautiful and having neither form nor comeliness. You, he says, are beautiful. And again: “Behold, you are beautiful”: beautiful inwardly and beautiful outwardly; beautiful in intention and beautiful in action.

“My friend.” Friendship is made by two things: mutual knowledge and the same will. The friendship of bridegroom and bride is made by a certain mutual knowledge and sameness of will, when the Lord reveals his good secrets to the bride, and the bride makes her evils known to him through pure and humble confession. You are beautiful, I say, and I do not fear that you will vanish away, because “your eyes are those of doves”; that is, they are simple, looking neither to yourself nor to others except in God.

Moreover, the bride’s two eyes are the mystical and the active—or the contemplative and the moral. Yet it is pleasing to examine the eye more closely. In order to see clearly, an eye needs these things: a strong and pure ray proceeding from the pupil; pure and bright air, which does not impede its passage; an object upon which it may be cast; reason, to which it may report; and memory, which reason may consult. If any of these is lacking, sight will not be perfect.

Likewise, for the love of God to be true, it needs: pure affection, by which one loves God only for God’s sake, and loves nothing together with God except in God and for God’s sake; purity of life and conscience, which does not obstruct love; discernment of spirits, which does not allow the purity of the contemplative person to err, but teaches him to understand God, and not something else in place of God; reason, which judges concerning discernment; and faith, which reason consults concerning all its judgments and which, restraining and defining reason by its rules and limits, does not allow it to err. This is the dove-like eye.

29. “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved.” Understanding that she had in some measure pleased the bridegroom in his eyes, the bride longs for embraces. Therefore, rising to praise his beauty, she invites him to her embrace. “You proclaim me beautiful,” she says, “but, O my beloved, behold”—that is, in the delightful manifestation of your grace—“you are more beautiful, from whom comes all beauty: beautiful in humanity, comely in divinity. And if you are beautiful and I beautiful, if you are beloved and I beloved, what remains except the little bed?”

As we said concerning the little bundle, “little bed” is an endearing expression. “Behold, the little bed of conscience—not mine or yours, but ours: mine by confession, yours by grace and illumination. It is flowering,” that is, in the purpose of virtues it blooms with the flowers of good thoughts. “Do not send me back to domestic care, as when I sought your noon you sent me back to the cavalry of your chariots, or drove me to keep the flocks. For now, through your grace and my care, the household of young women entrusted to me is so strengthened and adorned that they need not fear storm and rain, while for the present I enjoy, on the bed of a pure conscience, union with your sweetness.”

How blessed is the soul which on this bed becomes one spirit with God, enjoys the kiss of understanding God, clasps and is clasped by the embrace of his love, and thus sleeps and rests in peace, in that very unity.

30. “The beams of our houses are cedar.” Truly the house is defended, because “you have commanded your angels concerning it, that they may guard it.” Cedar drives away serpents with its shadow. The cedar beams, therefore, are angels who protect God’s house and, by their power, drive away demons like housebreakers. They bear the saints’ merits—the roof of prayers—fixed with the nails of the fear of God. “The panelling is of cypress”; the house is secured outwardly by a roof, but inwardly it is adorned and ordered.

For within it are panels which, in order that the house or its ornament may be enduring, are of cypress and are well interwoven. When panelling is interwoven, it opens one thing and binds another, so that one is caught by another. This is to love and be loved. Where these things are, all is well ordered. For where all both love one another and make themselves lovable to one another, the union is so great that it ought properly to be called fraternal unity rather than a gathering.

“I am a flower of the field.” Hearing and approving the bride’s desire, the bridegroom delays in order to increase it; he humbles her in order to exalt her. “I am the flower of the field, the flower of the world, because just as a flower in a field, so I alone blossomed in the world from the Virgin’s womb. Therefore the little bed is flowering not from you but from me. And I am a lily,” namely, an example of chastity and purity: not of the proud, but “of the valleys.” For proud chastity is not chastity, but a brothel—the devil’s ornament. “As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among daughters” (Song of Songs 1:12; 2:2).

It is as though he said what Solomon says: “If you have daughters, do not show them a cheerful face” (Ecclesiasticus 7:26). Therefore beware of the young women concerning whom you consider yourself secure; but, “as a lily among thorns,” so be, O my friend, among the daughters. If you are thus among them, then you will be my friend. I am a lily; you too are like a lily, beautiful indeed but tender. Your daughters are thorns: whichever of them you bend toward, you will be wounded. Therefore remain upright in their midst, offering yourself as an example to all.

Hearing that she was being humbled by the bridegroom, the bride humbles herself and exalts him. “I am,” she says, “like a lily—beautiful but fragile—among thorns; but you are an apple tree among the trees of the forest,” that is, among the angels, as among sons. Therefore you are strong to sustain the frail; beautiful to behold, to strengthen faith; fragrant, to confirm hope; and wholesome in taste, to nourish charity.

31. Again the bridegroom withdraws from the bride and hides in the secret of his heaven, though he had seemed to be held in the bed of conscience. Therefore, returning as usual to the young women, while retaining in her heart the tenor of thought with which she had addressed the bridegroom, comparing him to an apple tree among the trees of the forest, she says: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired I sat, and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song of Songs 2:3).

The body of Christ is the shadow between Christ’s divinity and us. Under it the bride sits when she modestly and humbly contemplates the mystery of his Incarnation. His fruit is sweet to her throat because it does not reach her stomach—that is, fullness of satisfaction—as in Job: “You do not allow me to swallow my spittle” (Job 7:19). For scarcely anyone can be satisfied with the sacrament of God’s Word. We can taste, but we cannot be satisfied; for the sounder the taste, the stronger the appetite. “His fruit,” therefore, says the bride, “is sweet to my throat,” showing me by the sweetness of his example how much I must suffer for his name. “For this reason I return to you; for this reason I do not abandon you. Indeed, the king has brought me into the wine-cellar, where I learned what the wise of the world do not know: namely, to preside in charity.”

For the bridegroom has, as it were, three treasuries of his riches: the garden or paradise of delight, the cellar, and the house or chamber. The garden contains pleasant and useful things. The pleasant things remain in the garden; the useful are carried into the cellar; from the cellar the king is served with them in the house or chamber. The garden contains the historical sense; the cellar, the moral sense; the house, the mystical sense. The garden contains the histories of the New and Old Testaments, of the present and future age; the cellar, Christ’s moral instruction; the house, the glory of eternal reward. In the garden is the creation of all things that exist; in the cellar, the reconciliation of all human beings who are saved; in the house, the confirmation and glorification of all who are reconciled.

The garden is divided into three periods; the cellar into three merits; the house into three rewards. The garden has three periods: planting, maturity, and gathering. The time of planting is as in Genesis, the Prophets, and the writings of the Old Testament, concerning the creation of heaven and earth and the beginnings of the world. The time of maturity is when the maturity of human conduct appeared in Christ and the Gospel, so that it is no longer said, “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Deuteronomy 19:21), but: “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the left as well” (Matthew 5:38–39), together with many other things which, although they must be understood simply and in a manner like historical narrative, nevertheless pertain to the maturity of life. The time of gathering is the time of the age to come, concerning which we declare simply and as it were historically: “Whoever has done good shall go into eternal life; but whoever has done evil, into eternal death” (Matthew 25:46; John 5:29).

In the garden, walking is the overshadowing of examples. But the garden’s fruit is carried into the cellar. In this garden, as was said above, the bride sat beneath the apple tree while she humbly contemplated the historical sequence of Christ’s humanity; but its fruit would not have been sweet to her throat had she not entered the cellar. Therefore the text immediately continues there:

32. “The king has brought me into the wine-cellar” (Song of Songs 2:4). For, as has been said, the fruit of the garden is carried into the cellar: its charm remains in the garden, but its usefulness must be sought elsewhere; if you wish to find it, enter the cellar. It has three merits, as though three chambers of moral life: one’s disposition toward superiors, which is discipline; one’s disposition toward equals, which is justice or friendship; and one’s disposition toward subjects, which is charity. To put this more briefly and clearly [Col. 0432C], it is that one should know how to be subject, how to live with others, and how to preside. The first chamber is full of fragrances; the second, of flavours; the third, of grace. For the first is advanced chiefly by examples; the second by moral or mystical studies; the third by the charisms of the Holy Spirit. This, indeed, is the wine-cellar. Here friends drink, and the beloved are made drunk.

For before God none is higher than the order of prelates: filled with God’s wisdom and taking his place among their subjects, they “reach mightily from one end to the other” of possibility to the end of impossibility, and “order all things sweetly” between those two. According to the Apostle, these wish to be “anathema from Christ” for their brothers’ sake (Rom. 9:3)—from Christ as blessedness, not from Christ as justice. For Christ is both to us, [Col. 0432D] blessedness and justice; yet they acquire blessedness all the more gloriously insofar as, for the sake of blessedness, they refuse to abandon justice. These words of the Apostle express an affection, not an accomplished fact.

This intoxication, by which the beloved are made drunk when, through love of God and of their brothers, one casts forth his inmost self—this is the wine-cellar into which the bride deserved to be brought when she learned to preside in charity. This cellar lies beside the king’s house. Therefore from it she often enters the king’s house and the secrecy of his chamber, serving the Lord Bridegroom, both herself and through her subjects, with the good things of the garden and cellar entrusted to her. Whether one is prelate or subject, whoever has put on this disposition of charity has free access here.

Hence, when above the bride desired to be drawn after the Bridegroom and herself to draw the young women after her, saying, “We shall run after you in the fragrance of your ointments,” [Col. 0433A] the king, as she herself declares, immediately brought her into these cellars, so that she might receive there what would restore them, lest they fail in the course; and might lead them in due order from the garden to the cellar, and from the cellar to the king’s chamber—now through the disposition of contemplation and love, but afterwards through the fulfilment of blessedness.

Moreover, the house has the one reward of the Lord, except insofar as it is divided through this into three rewards, so that we may know what God is, how great he is, and how he is to be found: namely, what he is—body or spirit; how great—created or uncreated; and how he is to be found.

33. “The king has brought me,” then, says the bride, “into the wine-cellar,” that is, into the fullness of charity; and lest, [Col. 0433B] intoxicated with the new wine of the Holy Spirit, I should do something improperly when I returned to my subjects, “he ordered charity within me” (Song of Songs 2:4).

Charity has two elements: affection and action. Of affection: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole mind, and with all your strength” (Matt. 22:37); in which every kind of affection is comprehended. Affection, therefore, is owed principally to God and secondarily to one’s neighbour, whom we ought to love in God as ourselves. We come first, because primacy is granted us, so that we first love ourselves and then our neighbours as ourselves.

A certain purgative—that is, cleansing—action is owed to the charity of God, cleansing us for the vision of God: such as vigils, fasts, meditations, readings, and compunctions. Action is also owed to one’s neighbour, such as [Col. 0433C] works of mercy and the other things required by the needs of active and social life. Yet we ought always to prefer affection for God to affection for our neighbour, though we should not always prefer action for God to action for our neighbour. And even in ourselves, we must often prefer the bodily action of charity to the action of charity toward the soul, and the action of charity toward the soul to the action of charity toward God—that is, contemplation. Yet all these things apply when necessity requires it, for necessity has no law.

For there is a law of charity, and there is a necessity of charity. The law of charity commands that the action of charity toward God be preferred to the action toward the soul, and the action toward the soul to the action toward the body. The necessity of charity often commands everything contrary to these. Hence many say, but few understand: “Necessity has no law.”

The order and rule of charity proceeds thus: it commands that one love one’s own body and another’s body less than one’s own soul and another’s soul; and that one love one’s own soul and another’s soul more than one’s own body or another’s. One is not to love one’s own soul more than another’s, but another’s as one’s own. This concerns the affection of charity. But the action of charity itself is often ordered otherwise. For in action, as has been said, the body is often preferred to the soul, and the soul to God.

If you first assist your brother, who is in the same necessity as yourself and of equal merit and usefulness, you abound in charity; if you assist yourself, you do not sin. For in the words “as yourself” (Matt. 22:39), primacy is granted to you. But if he is of unequal merit, the better person must be assisted. And although we ought to love all equally, we nevertheless offer particular prayers for particular persons not without cause: not because we do not wish to benefit all, but because we believe our prayers benefit especially those who entrust themselves to us, or because our hearts are more strongly stirred for them. Thus the Bridegroom ordered charity within me.

34. And since the charity of Christ presses us toward you: “Support me with the flowers” of your affections; “surround me with apples” of your works, because I languish from love of the absent one. There is a pious love, a fervent love, and a languishing love. Pious love seeks the pardon of sins; fervent love is active in the performance of works; languishing love occurs when the soul faints for God’s salvation—that is, in the gaze of contemplation.

As the bride languished while saying these things, she again sensed the Bridegroom present: his left hand under her head and his right hand embracing her. Therefore, taking breath, [Col. 0434B] she says: “Behold, the Bridegroom again: ‘His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me.’” The bride therefore lays down her head to rest not upon, but in, the Bridegroom’s left hand, when she is affected by the mysteries of Christ’s humanity; but the Bridegroom’s right hand embraces her when, with her eyes enlightened, love and understanding of the Divinity possess her wholly. In this most pious embrace the bride fell asleep and rested together in unity.

The Bridegroom too, rejoicing in the embrace of her charity, adjures the daughters of Jerusalem—that is, he inspires in them a certain reverence toward the bride. He adjures them by the gazelles and stags of the field when he displays to them the agility and cheerful readiness of good works. “I adjure you,” he says, “daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and stags of the field, that you do not rouse the bride through the occasions of [Col. 0434C] your necessities, nor cause her to awaken through the pressure of your evils, until she herself wishes”; that is, satisfied with contemplation of my grace, she herself will return to you from the impetus of love conceived.

The bride, hearing the Bridegroom’s words amid the sleep of consolation and contemplation—that is, perceiving the disposition of his grace, because the young women would neither rouse nor awaken her, but would exercise themselves like the gazelles and stags of the field in the cheerful performance of good works, and would judge it unlawful to disturb her in the repose of contemplation—rises to praise the Bridegroom. “The voice,” she says, “of my beloved” (Song of Songs 2:5–8). This is the voice of my beloved; this is his will; this is his work; this is his power in their conversion; [Col. 0434D] this is his sweetness in my love.

See how, when charity has been ordered, all things are ordered, including sins; and “his place is made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3), when the bride rests in the Bridegroom’s embrace, when the Bridegroom cherishes and protects her, and when the daughters neither rouse her nor make her awaken, but rather make her glad and joyful by their good pursuits.

35. This was signified by that woman who cried to Elisha when her husband, his servant, had died: she represents the bride calling upon God the Father through the death of her husband, his Son. “Your servant,” she says, “my husband, is dead; and behold, the creditor has come to take my two sons to serve him.” So too the bride had begotten two sons, one by word and the other by example, and had taken them from the hand of [Col. 0435A] the devil. When, with charity ordered, she devoted herself to God and neglected her sons, preferring the action toward God to action toward them, there came a famine of God’s word: “The little ones asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them.” The devil-creditor began to return, and now demanded them back to serve him, not as a destroyer but as a creditor.

But because the mother did not wish to occupy herself with the labour of good pursuits and deeds, believing that she would act by prayer alone, she began to cry to God. And what answer did the divine response give her? “What,” he says, “do you have in your house?”—that is, in your conscience? But she says: “As the Lord lives, I, your servant, have nothing in my house except a little oil in a vessel”—that is, devotion in the mind, with which I may be anointed. Notice the luxury: she does not need to be fed but desires to be anointed.

But he says: “Go and borrow many empty vessels”—that is, the hearts of hearers—“and pour into all those vessels the oil of devotion in which you abound; and when they have been filled, return to me.” For you do not have, as you say, only a little oil, since in a time of famine you presume that you are to be not only fed, but anointed. Hearing this, the bride reordered charity: as she had been sent, she poured the oil of the Holy Spirit into the minds of her hearers, [Col. 0436A] and God filled the empty vessels.

When this had been done, he says: “Go, sell the oil, and free yourself from the creditor”; that is, for the outpouring of your devotion, await the rewards of eternal life. “But you and your sons live from what remains” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 4:1–7): for as great as the outpouring of this oil from you to others shall be, so great shall be my infusion into you. But he says, “Live,” not, “Be anointed”: you and your sons must strive to live; I shall provide in its proper time for the anointing of your delights.

[Col. 0435]

# DECLAMATIONS OF ABBOT GEOFFREY ON THE CONVERSATION OF SIMON WITH JESUS, COLLECTED FROM THE SERMONS OF ST BERNARD. TO HENRY, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH. (G)*

## NOTICE

[Col. 0435] 282

1. The author of this little work is Geoffrey, Bernard’s disciple, who wove it together from various sermons of the holy Father, as he himself states at the beginning of the following prologue. For where the printed editions read, “from many sermons of the Fathers,” all manuscripts have, “from many sermons of our Father”; the Cheminion manuscript reads, “from many sermons of blessed Bernard, our Father.” In this codex the title of the book reads: “Here begins the little work of Lord Geoffrey, on the sayings of blessed Bernard, addressed to Henry, then subdeacon of the Roman Church, afterwards a monk of Clairvaux, and then cardinal, on ‘Simon Peter said to Jesus.’”

The Aquicinctum codex, written four hundred years ago, has: “A book on the Gospel reading, ‘Behold, we have left all things,’ collected from the sayings of Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.” In Vatican codex no. 658, written for Nicholas V, it occurs under this title: “On the conversation of Simon and Jesus, addressed to Henry, subdeacon of the Roman Church, who afterwards became a monk of Clairvaux and then abbot of the monastery of Saint Anastasius at Rome”; and at the end: “Here ends the book of blessed Bernard.” The older Vallis-Lucentis manuscript has: “Here begin the chapters of the little work made by the abbot of Igny for Henry,” etc. Finally, the Clairvaux and Royal Navarre manuscripts give Geoffrey’s name, not Bernard’s.
