From these and other manuscripts it is understood that this book was formerly attributed by some to Geoffrey and by others to Bernard. One of the latter is William, monk of Tournai, who in his *Bernardinus*, or *Book of Flowers from Bernard*, frequently cites the book “On the Conversation of Simon and Jesus” under Bernard’s name.

Both are true: this little work belongs to Bernard as author, and to Geoffrey as collector, since Geoffrey fused into one the various sermons of Bernard, delivered from the speaker’s mouth concerning Simon’s conversation with Jesus. Certainly it was customary at that time to take down sermons from the speaker’s mouth, not only Bernard’s—as is clear from the Sermons on the Song of Songs and others—but also those of others, as we shall see in the case of the sermons of Abbot Guerric.

2. Geoffrey, therefore, must be acknowledged not as the author of this little work but as its collector. Yet there were several monks of Clairvaux bearing that name. The Vallis-Lucentis manuscript calls him abbot of Igny. He is therefore the Geoffrey who was first Bernard’s secretary, then, after Guerric, abbot of Igny, and afterwards, following Fastred, abbot of Clairvaux; he composed two books on Bernard’s life and a sermon about him. Henry, to whom this little work is dedicated, is the same man whom this Geoffrey praises in the Acts of the Council of Rheims against Gilbert of Poitiers in these words: “Lord Henry of Pisa, then subdeacon of the Roman Church, afterwards to become a monk of Clairvaux, and, from being abbot of Saint Anastasius, cardinal-priest of Saints Nereus and Achilleus,” etc.

3. In 1501 this book was published in print at Speyer, under the title *Declamations* and Bernard’s name, without division into sections. The word *Declamations*, together with Bernard’s name, passed into subsequent editions, not contrary to the author’s intention, since he says that he composed this booklet “after the manner of a certain copious declamatory discourse.” But since the author testifies at the end of the prologue that he divided the reading of this book into brief sentences, and the manuscripts commonly divide it into sixty sections, it seemed right to preserve this division in accordance with the author’s intention. Certainly, in the White-Mantled manuscript at Paris this treatise is entitled: “Sentences excerpted from the little works of the venerable Abbot of Clairvaux.”

# PROLOGUE OF THE COLLECTOR

[Col. 0437A]

283–284

That I should send you these present pages of exhortation, which charity does not allow to remain idle, was persuaded by charity itself, which assuredly believes all things and hopes all things. Yet do not suppose that I have handed down to you anything of my own, nor receive it as ours; rather, know that from the many sermons of our holy Father—whose praise is richly deserved in the Church—I have gathered those sayings which seemed suited to this undertaking, and have issued this little book for your Love, reducing them, however imperfectly, to a single form, after the manner of a certain copious declamatory discourse.

I judged this kind of writing more effective for persuasion, because it ordinarily moves the reader more deeply, presenting living voices rather than mute letters. But since my own ignorance and my own forgetfulness are suspect to me, [Col. 0437B] I exhort and urge you: if you discover anything deserving rebuke, either endeavour to correct it yourself, or, if perhaps you shrink from doing so out of gentleness and humility, at least do not fail to inform me amicably of whatever troubles you.

This I say regarding the thought. As for the words, perhaps there may be some who, if these reach their ears, will mock them, saying: “Who is this that wraps up counsels in unlearned words?” (Job 38:2). Yet I do not think that anything of the sort need be feared from your learning. For charity free from suspicion casts out both this fear and shame. A friend, I think, will weigh the affection in these pages more than the words, especially since I have intended to publish a page not for display but for edification, wishing rather, if it seemed possible, to imprint these things upon your heart even without words. May he do this who works invisibly in the hearts of the elect, and, in his merciful condescension, reckoning this voice to be his own, grant it a voice of power and efficacy.

For industrious love does what it can, being urgent in season and perhaps out of season. No material more fitting or worthy presents itself for the work than the Gospel reading in which is contained that most blessed conversation of Simon and Jesus. I have therefore chosen to take it up, for exhortation rather than exposition, so that an occasion for discourse might be drawn from it. And I have sought to divide the reading into brief sayings, so that the division itself may not permit weariness.

# I. On the Praise of Obedience and the Power of Christ’s Words

[Col. 0437D]

1. Simon Peter said to Jesus: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19:27). Faithful is the saying, and worthy of all acceptance, in the conversation of Simon Peter and Jesus. For obedience is familiar and friendly to salvation—yet obedience firm and steadfast, founded upon the rock. “Obedience is better than sacrifice,” and refusal to submit is “as the sin of divination” (1 Sam. 15:22–23). Hence the Saviour himself preferred this virtue even to life, choosing rather to lay down his soul than to fail in obedience. Finally, even the very name of Jesus, which is above every name, at which every knee bends, is, as the Apostle testifies, the reward of obedience [Col. 0438A] (Phil. 2:8–10).

It delights me, therefore, to be present at this most sacred conversation and to receive with the inward ear of the heart the things said. For I judge that the words of this reading are those concerning which the Church cries to the immortal Bridegroom from the ends of the earth: “Because of the words of your lips, I have kept hard ways” (Ps. 16:4). These indeed are the words that have persuaded people throughout the whole world to despise the world and embrace voluntary poverty. These are the words that fill monasteries for monks and deserts for anchorites. These, I say, are the words that despoil Egypt and plunder all its best things (Exod. 12:35–36). This word is living and effective, turning souls by a blessed emulation of holiness and by the faithful promise of truth.

# II. On Leaving All Things

[Col. 0438B]

2. For Simon Peter said to Jesus: “Behold, we have left all things.” Well—excellently—and not foolishly on your part. For the world passes away, and its desire; and it is more expedient to leave these things than to be left by them. “Behold,” he says, “we have left all things and followed you.” Surely because he “rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6), and you could not follow while burdened as he ran. Nor is it an unprofitable exchange to leave all things for him who is above all things. For all things are given together with him, and when you have grasped him, he alone will be all things in all persons to those who have left all things for his sake.

By “all things” I mean not only possessions, but desires also—and especially desires. For the desire of the world harms more than its substance. The chief reason why riches are to be fled is that they can scarcely, if ever, be possessed without love. For our substance, not only external but internal, seems exceedingly muddy and adhesive; and the human heart easily clings to everything with which it is occupied.

# III. On Him Who Bought Five Yokes of Oxen

[Col. 0438C]

3. Therefore, you who intend to leave all things, remember to number yourself among the things to be left. Indeed, deny yourself chiefly and principally, if you intend to follow him who emptied himself for your sake. Lay down the heaviest burden; lay down the millstone of an ass, the earthly mass; lay down those five yokes, clearly not of human beings but of oxen, which you foolishly purchased. Otherwise, oppressed and weighed down by this fivefold bodily sensuality, you cannot follow the Bridegroom or come to the spiritual wedding-feast. Even if at last you arrive and knock, it most certainly will not be opened to you; but you will be answered from within that God has no concern for oxen, asses, and the other beasts of burden.

Can anyone doubt that a person who has bought himself yokes of beasts of burden has become comparable to them? Indeed, he is convicted of being more stupid than those beasts and shown to be more bestial than beasts, because he voluntarily undertook the yokes which necessity lays upon them. What is nature to them is guilt to him, while he, like one of the creatures devoid of reason, lives without reason and likewise bends himself beneath bodily senses. But why do we accuse him of having accepted yokes? Let us rather charge him with having bought them. The first is pitiable stupidity; the second is extreme madness.

“The labourer is worthy of his wage”; but for someone to give wages for labour is unheard of. Finally, on this word the Lord speaks through the prophet, rebuking under the figure of a prostitute the crimes of Israel: “Wages are given to all prostitutes; but you gave wages to all your lovers and gave them gifts that they might come in to you from every side for prostitution. And in you it was the contrary of women’s custom in your prostitutions, and after you there shall be no prostitution. For in that you gave wages and did not receive them, the contrary has come about in you” (Ezek. 16:33–34). Clearly, in the person who buys yokes the contrary is likewise manifestly done.

For why does he buy yokes—yokes of oxen—when a pleasant yoke is offered him for nothing? Christ’s yoke is a human yoke, since Christ too is human. It is not merely given freely: those who take it also receive abundant reward, so that it may be not only purchased by no one, but even freely endured by everyone. Why, miserable man, do you sell your soul for a yoke of oxen, when by accepting Christ’s yoke you might buy the kingdom of God, gain eternal life, and win Christ?

For meanwhile you cannot be without a yoke, being human and “born for labour” (Job 5:7). But “a heavy yoke is upon all the children of Adam” (Ecclus. 40:1)—namely, those who follow him. Over those who follow Christ it is light and pleasant (Matt. 11:30). Finally, to omit other considerations, since they cannot be without a yoke, what a thing it is to choose five rather than one! Who can serve five masters, much less five tyrants, five robbers? [Col. 0439C] For “my eye plunders my soul” (Lam. 3:51). Does not gluttony often demand one thing while the itch of the ears calls to another? Thus smell and touch also sometimes command diverse, perhaps opposing, things, as each appetite seeks to snatch for itself the common servant and draws him in its own direction. You see the excuse of the person who does not follow Christ and excuses himself from the wedding-feast because he has bought five yokes of oxen (Luke 14:19).

# IV. On the Multiple Dominion of Vices

4. What if you consider their toil and pain, if you count the yokes of those who serve various moral vices rather than bodily senses? You will certainly find people who are much less subject to human toil, yet endure punishments far more alien to humanity. You will find persons purchasing not merely five but more than fifty-five yokes—not indeed of beasts of burden, but of demons.

Ambition and pride of heart contend: one prepares a nest, the other a pit. One commands a person to fly, the other counsels him to crawl, although neither is truly human. “Who are you,” says the latter, “and who is this man or that man, or what is their father’s house, that you should yield to them in anything, show them reverence, or flatter them at all?” But ambition says: “A good word finds a good place, and sometimes even someone who cannot be helpful can be harmful. Therefore dissemble: set out the good wine first, until your hour comes.”

Avarice and the desire for praise likewise oppose each other: what the former gathers, the latter scatters. No less contrary are the things which pretence and faint-heartedness suggest to the cries of shamelessness and impatience; and both are toil, pain, and affliction of spirit.

# V. On the Two Daughters of the Leech

5. All these evils, whether similar or dissimilar, spring from one root: one’s own will. This leech has two insatiable daughters, crying, “Bring, bring” (Prov. 30:15). For neither the mind with vanity nor the body with pleasure is ever satisfied, as it is written: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing” (Eccl. 1:8). Flee this leech, and you have left all things. For it draws all things to itself. Lay it down, and you have cast off a yoke as intolerable as it is manifold.

There is no cruel master equal to it; there is no impious and inhuman tyrant so urgent with his little slave and so unsparing. It presses harder on one already exhausted and drives the weary person onward. It is an unquiet evil, always brooding over the spirit and devising unimaginable things. “O guardian of men, why have you set me against you, and made me burdensome to myself?” (Job 7:20). No burden is more intolerable to me, no load heavier. “I have become a talent of lead,” and wickedness sits upon it (Zech. 5:7).

But let me hear the voice of consolation; let me hear what the Angel of great counsel says. “Come to me,” he says, “all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:28–29). But these matters belong elsewhere; perhaps they will find a place at the end. Meanwhile, it is surely clear that those who have been unburdened and follow the Lord unencumbered are blessed. For a very narrow opening awaits us. If we follow someone, we wish to overtake him; we must strive to enter through the narrow gate. What are you doing, camel, lifting your hump? What are you doing, rich man, taking up the traitor’s money-bags? You will not enter thus, impious man; you will not enter thus. The eye of the needle admits no such burdens.

# VI. On the Riches of the Patriarchs of the Old Testament

6. But perhaps some excuse themselves, saying: “Do we not read that Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the other saints possessed earthly riches? It is enough for us to be as they were; for we are not better than the Patriarchs. If possession of riches were blameworthy, they would never have obtained such great grace from the Lord amid riches; or, having obtained so great grace, would nevertheless not have possessed riches.”

What shall we answer to these new imitators of the ancient saints? Let them certainly lay calves upon the altar of the Lord, slaughter rams, and offer goats, because Abraham too did this and this was the rite of the Patriarchs, than whom we are not merely not better but not even worthy to loosen the strap of their sandals. “But,” they say, “these things no longer obtain: when truth was revealed, they passed away.” What if we say that the temporal riches of the saints themselves were likewise a shadow of things to come? For we read that all things happened to them in figure (1 Cor. 10:11).

Why indeed should holy and perfect men not openly possess earthly riches when only earthly things were still openly promised by God? For as with those sacrifices, so with riches, divine dispensation accommodated itself to peoples still carnal, so that like little children they might gradually withdraw from the custom of the Gentiles, offering to the Lord the same things that the Gentiles offered to demons, and expecting those same things from the Lord rather than from demons. Once the heavenly promise sounded forth, spiritual things necessarily had to be compared with spiritual people, and the sacrifice changed when hope was changed.

All who were perfect even in that age knew these things, but they adhered to the people in charity, so that outwardly they appeared both to do the same things and seek the same things. Or does what we say about shadow and signification seem a forced interpretation? Another once wrote on this subject as follows:

> “Let no one set before me the gold of the Jewish Temple. That existed at the time when blood was offered, and all of it was a figure. Therefore let us reject gold along with the other superstitions of the Jews; or, if gold pleases, let the Jews also please.”  
> —St Jerome, *Letter 2 to Nepotian*

Finally, I recall having read of few who were not either grievously afflicted or grievously tempted—and perhaps endangered—in the very prosperity of this world.

# VII. How the Jew Is among the Waters, Peter upon the Waters

7. Clearly, it is one thing to make one’s way through the mud of many waters, with the sea-bed divided, by lawfully possessing earthly things; another to tread the wave itself with new steps by leaving all things. But this prerogative was due to the time of grace: a new path, and the type of a new path, was reserved for Peter.

In the days of the ancient Patriarchs, while the Lord of majesty had not yet been seen upon earth and had not yet conversed among human beings, there was no evangelical form of perfection; rather, they followed God, who is spirit, with the spirit alone for the time being. But when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), there was then handed down to us in him an image of life and an example of conduct which we must imitate also bodily, so that, following with both feet, we may no longer limp on one thigh with the patriarch Jacob (Gen. 32:31).

For where do we hear that it was said to the ancients: “Unless anyone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:33)? Or again: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21)? We do not say this as though someone could not be saved even now if he acted otherwise, but so that he may recognize his own rank and the place of perfection, and not usurp the office of discipleship.

# VIII. On the Remedy for the Imperfect

8. The Gospels contain both the counsel of perfection and the remedy for weakness. “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth” (Matt. 6:19): this is perfection. For the Son of Man had nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58); Peter and John had neither silver nor gold (Acts 3:6); and Paul, content with simple food and clothing (1 Tim. 6:8), acquired even these by the labour of his hands (2 Thess. 3:8).

But not everyone receives this word, just as not everyone receives the counsel of chastity. What is said to the people? “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). These are the Lord’s words, and what he says is such as this: The judgment that those who wish to become rich in this world fall into temptation and the devil’s snare remains firm and immovable (1 Tim. 6:9); but because “I have compassion on the crowd,” and can lead even a camel through the eye of a needle—which human beings cannot do—you who do not at all avoid the hunters’ snare must at least beware of the harsh word. Clothe the naked, feed the needy, visit the sick, lest perhaps you should hear the hard saying, the harsh word, the grievous sentence: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41).

“Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.” It is as though he said more plainly: “Woe to you rich, for you have your consolation” (Luke 6:24). Yet one thing now seems to remain. Share it with the poor, whose is the kingdom of God, so that when their hour comes they may remember you and receive you, when you fail, into their eternal dwellings; and may mercifully share with the desolate their consolation—which they now prudently await while receiving yours. For they shall give “a good measure, pressed down and overflowing” into their bosoms (ibid., v. 38); and there shall not be that short cloak which cannot cover two, nor that narrow bed from which one falls (Isa. 28:20).

# IX. On the Danger of Clerics

[Col. 0442C]

9. Hence we see churches endowed and enriched by the powerful and rich of this world, who, rich in good works in accordance with the Gospel’s admonition, have sought to make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they might be received by them into eternal dwellings. Why should they not hope to be received by those who seem to possess the keys?

But alas! Their very provision has been made an occasion for the flesh; and those who ought to prepare eternal dwellings in heaven, both for themselves and for others, join house to house and field to field upon the earth! Who has snatched from the mouth of the Apostles the word of grace for this age, the confident saying: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you”? For “as with the people, so with the priest” (Isa. 24:2). They likewise wish to become rich in this world; likewise—indeed, more abundantly—they seize their consolation here beforehand. They too require friends, that they may at least be received into others’ dwellings, having none of their own. For “blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3).

But whether persons who occupy the place of perfection, are powerful in dignity, pre-eminent in authority, and discharge an office may hope for even the remedy of weakness and imperfection—which they so strongly repudiate—let them themselves be judges even in this matter; let them, I say, judge whether it is permitted. For that it is by no means fitting is manifest. Let us at least be permitted to hear him who says: “If salt has lost its savour, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing any longer but to be cast out and trampled underfoot” (Matt. 5:13).

And let the Presbyter, whom perhaps they will fear to disparage because he is holy, be permitted his customary freedom of spirit: to flatter no one, stroke no one, but plainly utter naked truth. “The cleric,” he says, “who has a portion upon earth shall not have a portion in heaven.” Again: “If a cleric possesses anything besides the Lord, the Lord will not be his portion—for example, gold, silver, possessions, or various household goods. With these things the Lord does not deign to become his portion.”  
—St Jerome, *Letter 2 to Nepotian*

# X. How Clerics Appropriate from Each Class of People Whatever Delights Them
[Col. 0443B] 10. Holy David too seems to brand certain persons with a severe cautery; let those whom this parable touches see to themselves. “They are not in the toil of men, nor are they scourged with men; therefore pride has possessed them” (Ps. 72:5–6). For every class of people has some labor and some pleasure. Yet one may observe the cleverness of certain people, and marvel how, by a new artifice, distinguishing and separating these things from one another, they choose and embrace everything pleasant, while fleeing and avoiding whatever is burdensome.

Thus, like soldiers, they cultivate prideful arrogance, a large household, noble display, trappings for horses, hawks, dice, and every such pursuit. Some perhaps borrow from women the dyed skins of mice hanging from their necks, decorated chambers, baths, [Col. 0443C] and every softness and glory of clothing; while carefully avoiding the weight of armor, sleepless nights in camp, the uncertain hazards of battle, womanly modesty and discipline too, or whatever labor that sex is thought [variant: is seen] to have. Farmers sweat; vine-growers prune and dig. Yet those who lie idle amid all this, when the season of fruits arrives, order their granaries to be replenished for them, and their storehouses to be full—would that this were not in preference to those farmers; would that it were at least alongside them. They live on wheat and drink the unmixed blood of the grape; this is too little—they grow fat and expand upon the fat of the grain. Wines borrow an exotic flavor from the juices of herbs, and oil is added to the furnace.

11. Consider merchants also. They traverse [Col. 0443D] sea and land, gathering riches that will perish, through bodily labor and peril to life. These things are hard; let our prudent persons beware of them. Meanwhile, let them enjoy sweet sleep—or rather, let them revel in their beds. Yet on a feast day you may find the hands of servants weighed down with gold and silver vessels, satchels filled with varied wealth, poles laden with burdens, and in chests so many little compartments that, if tables were set out, you would think them money-changers. Why need I enumerate smiths, masons, and other workers of that kind? They seek their livelihood by great labor; these men, idle, drip with luxury and abound in resources. Does not the poet rightly mock such people?

> Lest, when someday the flock of birds comes to reclaim its feathers,  
> the little crow, stripped of its stolen colors,  
> provoke laughter.  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 3, vv. 18–20.)

But still more should that great prophet, and more than a prophet, rebuke them terribly, saying: “Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the wrath to come?” (Luke 3:7). For where are the fruits of repentance? When human beings begin to rise again, each in his own order, where, do you suppose, will this generation be placed? If they should turn perhaps to the soldiers, the latter will blow them away with scorn because they bore none of their labor or dangers. So too the farmers; so too merchants; and every order of people will likewise exclude them from its bounds, because they were not in the toil of men. What then remains, except that those whom every order alike rejects [Col. 0444B] and accuses should receive the place where no order dwells, but everlasting horror?

## XI.—On the office of clerics

12. Or will they dare to aspire to election into the clergy? For theirs is indeed a great place in the kingdom of God; and those who have served well acquire a good rank for themselves (1 Tim. 3:13). Yet they too seem to have their own, and no small, labor; and he who labored more than all said: “Whoever does not work shall not eat” (2 Thess. 3:10). And Peter was told: “Simon, son of John, do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17). The same was repeated a third time; three times he was told, “Feed,” and not once was “Milk” or “Shear” added. Therefore let him hope for the place of a disciple, the rank of a minister, who endeavors to feed rather than shear the Lord’s flock; and to feed [Col. 0444C] in three ways—by the example of his conduct, by the word of preaching, and by the fruit of prayer. Let him feed according to Christ’s command, “that no one may take this honor upon himself, but only one called by God, as Aaron was” (Heb. 5:4). For if anyone enters through him, he shall be saved and shall find pasture. But if he climbs up by another way, he is plainly a thief and a robber (John 10:9, 1). And would that, even now, among stewards it were sought that someone faithful be found.

## XII.—An apology for speaking only of matters that are manifest

13. Yet let no one be angry with us or take what is said ill. If he is holy and knows himself least of all guilty of these things, we congratulate him; let him also grieve with us that these evils are found in so many. For we are not now revealing hidden shameful deeds, nor digging through a wall [Col. 0444D] so that a greater abomination may appear (Ezek. 12). We have not yet said a word about fornication, although this too reigns extensively and in many ways among those who, serving the author of purity with impure heart and body, do not fear to stand before the angel of the Lord, “who cuts them in two and destroys them” (Dan. 13:55). Yet they dare to touch the sacred flesh of the spotless Lamb and dip in the Savior’s blood their impious hands—hands which a little earlier, alas, had handled the flesh of prostitutes; thus to go about the altars, thus to frequent the psalms, although praise of this kind is abominable and prayer becomes sin (Ps. 108:7).

Nor do we recount the sacrileges of those who love gifts, pursue rewards, sell sacraments, [Col. 0445A] and betray justice; whose throats have not yet drawn them to the noose, whose jaws have not yet been choked by the blasphemous word, the sacrilegious voice, the wicked speech: “What will you give me, and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. 26:15). We see all these things, yet in a manner do not see them, since we have neither the scourge nor that zeal which consumes. We speak of manifest matters, matters of which scarcely anyone is ashamed. Finally, we too have been among the clergy; let it be permitted to examine even our own case.

## XIII.—How clerics enter upon ecclesiastical benefices

14. “Consider your calling,” says the Apostle who was called (1 Cor. 1:26). Let us too consider whether we came by a call—and by a call from God, whose call this surely is. I do not mean merely the common calling by which, according to the same Apostle, “those whom he predestined, them he also called” (Rom. 8:30); rather, I would have the conscience of each person consider who called us to the honor of the clergy, so that I may speak, according to the Lord’s command, to the heart of Jerusalem (Isa. 40:2).

For provident parental concern was already securing ecclesiastical benefices for this child still small, perhaps not yet even born. “We,” it says, “will entrust this one to such-and-such a bishop, with whom we have influence, or whom perhaps we have served, so that he may be enriched from the Lord’s goods and our inheritance may not be divided among so many children.” Another is raised by a provost or dean, with more than maternal affection, to succeed him; he is nurtured amid luxuries and sins. Another is worthy of an archdeaconry because he is the son of a prince; still more so if he is [Col. 0445C] the bishop’s cousin, in whom, surely, resides the whole progeny of the episcopate. Another goes everywhere as a busy seeker, flatters, obliges, pretends and conceals; nor is he ashamed to beg for wretched support for himself, crawling on hands and feet if only somehow, at last, he may force his way into the inheritance of the Crucified One and the goods of the Lord, which alone today are found left exposed. Surely he has gone abroad, but perhaps at the full moon he will return to demand strictly what is his.

15. Who seeks ecclesiastical ranks and the ministries of the sanctuary with this intention—or rather, who is sought for them (for he ought to be sought rather than seek them himself): that, free from worldly anxieties, he may approach the Lord to be enlightened in holiness of heart and body, and may work for his own salvation and that of his neighbors, devoted to the study of prayer and to the word of preaching? For if he seeks or holds these things with the intention and purpose of obtaining the necessities of this life, he preaches the Gospel in order to eat, and in a perversely inverted order trades heavenly things for earthly. How much more worthy and reasonable it would be for him, in exchange for bodily food, to pursue bodily work and business, instead of overturning the proper order of things and dishonoring spiritual ministry. But nature is content with little, and not many seek in these things necessities alone, which can readily be obtained with less danger. They want to go about honored; they strive to please people, to indulge themselves and be proud, and in every respect to conform to this world.

Hear the Lord’s complaint; hear what the patient requiter says concerning so great human rashness—one who desires repentance rather than vengeance: “They have reigned, but not through me; princes have arisen, and I did not call them” (Hos. 8:4). For all who, in ecclesiastical ranks and in the other offices belonging to the sanctuary, seek their own honor, wealth, bodily pleasure, or finally what is their own rather than what belongs to Jesus Christ, are plainly and beyond doubt introduced not by God, who is love, but by that which is alien from God and the root of all evils: covetousness (1 Tim. 6:10). What rashness is this—indeed, what madness? Where is the fear of God, the remembrance of death, the dread of hell, and that terrible expectation of judgment? The bride does not presume to enter the bedchamber or inner room unless the king brings her in; [Col. 0446B] do you rush in irreverently, neither called nor introduced? “Draw me after you; we shall run after the fragrance of your ointments,” she says (Song 1:3). But now each person is drawn by his own pleasure; and pursuing the scent of shameful profit, they “suppose gain to be godliness” (1 Tim. 6:5). Their condemnation is certain.

## XIV.—On Judas’s money-bags

16. Yet even if one’s entrance seems irreproachable and one’s intention pure, is there nothing further to fear? There is indeed much to fear. Not everyone who begins in the Spirit also finishes in the Spirit; some finish in the flesh (Gal. 3:3). Thus Saul was established as prince by the Lord (1 Sam. 9:16), and Judas too is recorded as having been chosen as an apostle by no other. “Did I not choose you twelve,” he says, “and one of you is a devil?” (John 6:71).

Would that among twelve one Peter might today be found: one who has left everything, one who has no money-bags. “One of you,” he says, “is a devil.” *Diabolus* is so called, certainly, from two *boli* [a wordplay of uncertain force]; and Judas has not a little bag [variant: place], but bags. Would that you understood, wretch, and perceived that with a treasure of money you are likewise heaping up a treasure of wrath; would that, looking to the last things, you noticed that it is not heaps of riches but heaps of sins that will easily pass through the eye of a needle. “For we brought nothing into this world; without doubt neither can we carry anything out” (1 Tim. 6:7). Silver and gold are certainly not nothing; the world keeps both for itself. It has appointed an inexorable gatekeeper: the opening is narrow, and none of these things may be carried away. But sin, because it is nothing, cannot be held back by the narrowness of the opening. This alone follows you wherever you go; wherever you enter, you will not lay aside this skin.

“And the things you prepared, fool, whose will they be?” Woe, woe! In God’s house we behold dreadful things. Why should we not see idolaters serving there? I lie if covetousness is not slavery to idols (Col. 3:5), if for some even their belly has become their god (Phil. 3:19). For whatever each person honors above all else, that he is proved to have made his god. How many, indeed, do we see who love gifts and pursue recompense? How many who do not serve Christ the Lord, but their own belly?

## XV.—On the four virtues

[Col. 0447A]

17. Who, do you suppose, is “the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has appointed over his household, to give them food at the proper time?” (Matt. 24:45). Perhaps you ask what food. “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:34). Surely, “life is in his will” (Ps. 29:6). No one can either feed upon that will himself or feed others with it unless he is faithful and prudent, so as both to understand and to love it; and let him love it strongly and fervently. For when can ignorance excuse a man who professes himself a teacher of infants and an instructor of the foolish? “The ignorant person shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14:38); indeed, he will cause many to be ignorant and to be ignored.

For what danger there is when the shepherd finds no pasture, the guide does not know the road, and the steward does not know his lord’s will, the Church daily experiences in manifold and miserable ways. God’s will is as most sacred as it is most hidden, and is an utterly secret counsel, concerning which the Apostle himself boasts: “I think,” he says, “that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 7:40). Hence Truth itself says: “No one knows what is in a man except the spirit of the man that is in him. So also no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God who is in him” (1 Cor. 2:11). Reading is therefore useful, learning is useful, but anointing is much more necessary, since it alone teaches concerning all things (1 John 2:27).

How, then, will a man appear to know what the good, acceptable, and perfect will of God is, if he is not accustomed to knock, seek, and ask; if, until he took upon himself the care of other souls, he never cared for his own, but seemed to have received it in vain? [Col. 0447C] And would that he cared for his own even then, so that one might hope that he would afterward care for mine as well; and that he first removed the splinter from his own eye, before undertaking to remove the beam from mine (Matt. 7:5).

As for those who perhaps understand the Lord’s will, and where it is found, but nevertheless neglect it and oppose it as far as they can; who have given their hands to death and entered into a covenant with hell, so that, hating good and cleaving to evil, they are ready to consent freely to sin, nurture wickedness, and favor iniquity: since they are plainly hateful to God and detestable to the world, it is better to be silent about them than to speak.

18. Certainly no one becomes utterly vile all at once; scarcely anyone passes into this disposition of wickedness except through evil habit. There are weak and lukewarm lovers of righteousness, who lack either strength or fervor, or perhaps both; although both are especially necessary for one living amid prosperity and adversity. For just as it is recognized as the part of strength not to yield to tribulation, but profitably to endure persecution for righteousness’ sake, so it seems to belong to fervor that one be captured by no pleasures and weakened by no enticements. These are necessary for all the people, but especially and particularly for leaders of the people, lest they happen to go astray to the ruin of all. For what does it matter by what occasion they depart from the way of truth: whether they are led astray unknowingly, follow willingly, are compelled unwillingly, or are drawn by enticement? What difference does it make, provided that they go [Col. 0448A] to destruction?

Thus prudence failed Eve, temperance Adam, righteousness Cain altogether, and fortitude Peter. This ministry of which we speak wholly demands the perfection of this fourfold virtue and the throne of holiness; one who lacks this endowment flatters himself in vain that he has entered through Christ. For it is said of the ignorant person: “If the blind lead the blind, will not both fall into the pit?” (Matt. 15:14). Again: “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ and those who hold the law did not know me” (Jer. 2:8). “The prophets and shepherds themselves went into a land which they did not know” (Jer. 14:18). To the wicked person it is said: “The thief comes only to kill and destroy” (John 10:10), and also: “You loved wickedness more than goodness” (Ps. 51:5). To the faint-hearted it is said: “The hired man, who is not a shepherd, sees the wolf coming and flees, because he has no care for the sheep” (John 10:12–13). To the one who follows his own desires it is said: “Death is set beside the entrance of pleasure” (St. Benedict, *Rule*, ch. 7); and likewise: “All seek what is their own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ” (Phil. 2:21). But enough of this.

## XVI.—How clerics should serve in return for what they receive from churches

19. Now let one who seems to have entered through Christ into the allotted share of this ministry carefully examine within himself how henceforth he serves him, ministers to him, and feeds, as we said, the Lord’s flock in three ways. For he is proved unworthy of milk and wool if he does not feed the sheep. If he does not keep watch over the flock’s care, he eats and clothes himself to his own judgment. Woe, woe to you, cleric: “Death is in the pot” (2 Kings [4 Kings] 4:40). Death is in pots of meat; death is in luxuries of this kind. Not only because death is known to be set beside the entrance of pleasure, but especially because what you eat is established to be the sins of the people (Hos. 4:8).

Do you think you receive church revenues for nothing? As they say, goods seem to come to you merely by singing; but it would have been better to dig, or even to beg. For you eat the sins of the people, as though your own did not seem enough for you. Be anxious, as one who must render an account, to pour out fitting groans for them and produce fitting fruits of repentance. Otherwise, know that those sins which you now eat amid luxuries, disdain, and overlook as though they had nothing to do with you are charged to your account. O profound abyss of God’s judgments! O God terrible in counsels over the children of men! (Ps. 65:3). In vain will the wretched then begin to say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” (Luke 23:30). They will come, they will come before Christ’s tribunal; the peoples’ grave complaint will be heard, their harsh accusation—those upon whose wages these men lived, without washing away their sins, and to whom they became blind guides and deceitful mediators. What sweetness, fool, do you find in pleasure? Why do those riches delight your blind eyes, by which you purchase so severe a judgment and bind yourself to so harsh an accounting? For everything will be exacted from you down to the last farthing.

## XVII.—How they should expend those same revenues

[Col. 0449A]

20. But let a man be diligent and work fruitfully. “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (1 Tim. 5:18); and one who serves the altar should live by the altar (1 Cor. 9:13). Let him live, I say, by the altar, so that, according to the same Apostle, having food and clothing, he may be content with these (1 Tim. 6:8). For this is the third danger. “Let him live by the altar,” he says; let him not be proud, indulge in luxury, or become rich. In accordance with the judgment of a saint, surely worthy of all acceptance, “let him not become richer through clerical office” [Note: [Col. 0449D] The manuscripts add, “or glorious from being low-born.”] (Jerome, to Nepotian).

Let him not build for himself vast palaces out of the Church’s goods, changing square things into round; nor gather money-bags from them [variant: bags of Judas]; nor squander them on vanity or superfluity; let him not exalt his relatives by means of the Church’s resources, or give nieces—lest I say daughters—in marriage. Not to give the goods of the poor to the poor is recognized as a crime equal to sacrilege. Church resources are surely the patrimonies of the poor; and whatever minister-stewards, who are certainly not lords or possessors, take beyond food and clothing is sacrilegiously stolen from them in cruelty. For God did not ordain that those who serve the Gospel should seek luxuries or adornment from the Gospel, but should “live,” Paul says, “by it” (1 Cor. 9:14): that is, they should be content with bodily sustenance, receiving not provocatives to gluttony or stimulants to lust, and receiving what covers them, not what adorns them.

Indeed, one who has not entered faithfully or through Christ will act unfaithfully and against Christ. The fruit will undoubtedly make the tree known, the branch the root, and the deed the intention. He will do that for which he came: namely, kill and destroy. For when can a man of this kind serve at the altar—and serve in spirit and truth? The Father seeks worshipers of that kind (John 4:23). Otherwise his ministry is a ministry of death, unto judgment and condemnation. Or how can one be content with necessities if he entered with the intention of collecting, storing, and spending the clergy’s revenues for pleasure, curiosity, and vanity? Therefore a threefold cord, which is not easily broken, draws the wretched man to destruction: he enters impurely, ministers unworthily, and abuses even the temporal benefit itself.

## XVIII.—On the rod and staff

21. What if he flourishes in this world and prospers in his path? He shall swiftly wither; the flower of grass will quickly fall, and the vapor that appears for a little while. The rod is spared, because “his iniquity is found unto hatred” (Ps. 35:3), not unto wrath. “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Ps. 22:4). For he has a rod, but he also has a staff. It is a consolation that the one struck by the rod is supported by the staff. Or certainly the shepherd carries rod and staff: the former for the sheep, the latter for the wolf, but all things are for the elect.

For the rod comforts them against the stings of conscience, when in this way they feel their sins forgiven, as the Lord says: “I am he, I am he himself who blot out your iniquities” (Isa. 43:25). And the staff helps them endure the rod, since by comparison with it the rod becomes lighter. But to the hardened it is said: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. 3:3); and he adds: “My zeal has departed from you; I will no longer be angry with you” (Ezek. 16:42). For whom he loves, he rebukes and scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6). It is therefore clear that those who are not in the toil of men and are not scourged with the children of men (Ps. 72:5) are neither loved nor received by God. Do you perhaps think that those whom you see flourishing in the world are loved by the maker of the world? Hear what Scripture says about this.

## XIX.—Who is a friend of the world

22. “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4). And elsewhere: “Beloved, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.” These are the words of apostles: first, indeed, of James; secondly, of the disciple whom Jesus loved, who could not have been ignorant of his master’s mind [variant: friends]. But do you wish to know who loves the world? You are not commanded to hate God’s creatures, but are forbidden to love those things which are not from God. John himself explains what these things are, adding: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and worldly ambition; these,” he says, “are not from the Father, but from the world” (1 John 2:15–16).

Let each person here consider to what spirit he belongs, what he loves, desires, and pursues. For behold the mirror of truth: only let no one look upon the face of his conscience and pass on, forgetting what he was like. Ambition, curiosity, and pleasure are not from the Father but from the world. Or rather, since many manuscripts have not “worldly ambition” but “pride of life,” understand in “the lust of the flesh” the whole delight of bodily senses, from which curiosity itself is not free; then understand “the lust of the eyes” as whatever pertains to the human day—which the prophet did not desire (Jer. 17:16)—to worldly glory, and to external vanity. Further, understand in “pride of life” the exaltation of heart. Whoever loves these three things loves the world and is made an enemy of God. Let such a person undertake the office of reconciliation, not that of mediator, since by the crime of betrayal he has added to his enmities; so that he is rightly judged no longer as an enemy, but as a traitor—like Judas, certainly, not like Saul.

## XX.—On shamelessness

23. For when shamelessness and brazenness have hardened the heart so that it neither fears, recoils, nor trembles, that is at last despair. What then? A man conscious of these things does not fear to present himself before the divine countenance as though he had done righteousness; as though he were a member of the household, he comes and goes, greets the master, bends his knees, and kisses with a sacrilegious mouth. He acts deceitfully, but in God’s sight, so that “his iniquity is found unto hatred” (Ps. 35:3).

Brazenness is plainly hateful to God, and shamelessness detestable. For why has the wicked person provoked God? Why has the sinner exasperated the Lord, so that, according to the multitude of his wrath, he does not seek? (Ps. 9:4, 13). Is it on account of fornications, incest, or sacrileges? The Prophet mentions none of these, but that the man said in his heart, “He will not seek.” The speech of the heart is its disposition; and to say, “He will not seek,” is not to fear that he will seek. This is the impiety toward which God, according to the multitude of his wrath, shows mercy [variant, apparently corrupt: “does not show mercy”]; neither seeks nor rebukes nor scourges nor takes vengeance upon their devices, as we read of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, to whom he was indeed propitious (Ps. 98:8).

## XXI.—On cruel mercy

24. But let us hear explicitly and emphatically whose impiety this is. “Let us show mercy to the wicked,” says the Lord (Isa. 26:10), as though deliberating in the council and assembly of angels. Nor was it hidden from them that the Judge was contemplating a mercy more cruel than all indignation: a mercy by which a person does not learn to do righteousness, but, miserable and slumbering, says, “God has forgotten; he has turned away his face” (Ps. 9:11), lives out his days in prosperity, only to descend to hell in a moment (Job 21:13); and when he says, “Peace and security,” sudden destruction comes upon him (1 Thess. 5:3), and he does not escape. “And he will not learn to do righteousness,” they say. “In the land of the saints he has acted wickedly,” says the Lord (Isa. 26:10), as though he said: I do not wish him to learn righteousness; his iniquity is found unto hatred.

Is it still necessary to ask who this wicked person is? “In the land of the saints,” he says, “he has acted wickedly”: in ecclesiastical possessions, which had been assigned for the needs of the saints; in God’s house, which holiness befits. Paul, carefully exhorting his disciple concerning this house, says: “That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of truth” (1 Tim. 3:15). When a man acts wickedly among the clergy as though in heaven, of what can he be judged except of his ministry? He holds a heavenly office; he has become an angel of the Lord of hosts (Mal. 2:7). Like an angel, he is either chosen or rejected. For perversity found in angels must necessarily be judged more strictly and more inexorably [Col. 0451D] than perversity found in human beings.

25. Come then: since judgment is severe for those in authority, and “the mighty shall suffer mighty torments” (Wis. 6:6–7), let your pride always ascend; follow your king. Let your eyes behold every lofty thing. Hurry to multiply prebends; from there fly up to archdeaconries, and finally aspire to a bishopric—where you will not find rest either, because thus one goes to the stars. Where are you going, wretch? Is it so that the fall may be more severe from a higher rank? You will not fall gradually in this manner, but, like lightning in its violent rush, like another Satan you will be suddenly cast down.

“They are not in the toil of men, nor are they scourged with men; therefore pride has possessed them” (Ps. 72:5–6)—the devil’s sin, by which those who work iniquity fell. This is what does not accept correction, refuses to be healed, and cannot endure a remedy: a most grievous ulcer, which does not suffer itself to be touched even by the tips of the fingers. I too fear its indignation in speaking of these matters, and the severe judgment. Why should I not fear its bites, knowing this spiritual madness and frenzy of souls? But these are the Lord’s words which I repeat; they too read and understand them alike, for they know the law. “In the land of the saints he acted wickedly, and he shall not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26:10). This is a hard saying and a most terrible threat: “He shall not see the glory of the Lord.” What advantage, then, is there in having seen other things? Is this the whole end of mercy? I do not want this mercy; let compassion so cruel be far from me, lest my soul enter into their company.

## XXII.—On exchanging human punishment for diabolical punishment

26. For who has shown you, wretches, how to flee from the wrath to come? Why do you flee the present wrath so greatly, fear the scourge, and avoid the rod? Yet this is your day, tending toward your peace—if only you had recognized it. By making an exchange, you do not escape repentance, for evil cannot go unpunished. What is not punished here by one’s own will will be punished elsewhere without end. A wretched exchange, full of the utmost madness: to avoid human labor and choose the everlasting gnashing prepared for the devil!

Consider and see: that fire is prepared not for human beings but for the devil and his angels. He is the enemy and the wolf; but we are his people and the sheep of his pasture. For him the axe and hammer are due; for us the scourge and rod. His iniquity is found unto hatred; he has his own prison, where there is no redemption and from which there is no possibility of relief. But for me a prison more tolerable in suffering and shorter in duration is appointed, where, when the Lord is angry, he remembers mercy, sending abundant redemption to his people. Finally, he has set a limit of time for me: he says to me, “until”; for the devil he prepares eternal fire. “In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken” (Gen. 3:19). That most evil angel was not taken from earth and will never return to earth. Therefore he has no “until”; eternal fire is prepared for him.

It is therefore by no means advantageous, in the wisdom of this world, to suppose that we may frustrate the judgment of the world’s maker and wish to evade his sentence by avoiding human toil and sweat, as though what was said to Adam did not touch us at all; or as though we had not received the sentence of labor in that in which we all sinned without exception; or as though the punishment ought not likewise to be common where the guilt is common.

## XXIII.—On Abraham’s judgment

27. Perhaps some will say: “What sin do we commit? Every creature of God is good; we lawfully possess what is ours and use our own resources, abstaining from robbery and theft.” Yet you will not feed ravens on the cross. For I hear that rich man whom the Savior mentions in the Gospel accused of none of these things. He was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day; but he is charged with cruelty because, possessing this world’s goods and seeing his brother in need, he shut his heart against him. When is this lacking in a rich man? How many Lazaruses do you yourselves see—hungry, naked, sick—and yet you think more about your beasts and their trappings than about these people’s miseries.

But let us come to Abraham’s dreadful judgment. It is not Abraham’s judgment, but the judgment of Abraham’s God. “Remember, son,” he says, “that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things.” Both statements are true and cannot at all be denied. Accept the sentence, because the whole sum of the matter is expressed in few words: he received good things, and this man evil things. What now? “But now,” he says, “this man is comforted, while you are tormented” (Luke 16:19–25). Awake, you drunkards, and weep. For God is terrible in judgments over the children of men.

Is this the whole reason for torments: that one received good things in this age? Precisely this. For the divine punishment does not seem to have expelled us from the paradise of pleasure so that human ingenuity might make another paradise for itself here. Man is born for labor. If he flees labor, he does not do that for which he was born, that for which he came into the world. What will he answer the one who sent him, who appointed him to work? “Remember,” he says, “that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things; but now this man is comforted, while you are tormented.” What shall we say to these things? If such is the end and such the judgment, that grief occupies the place of final joy, should not evils in this world be preferred to good things? For it is clear that those are not true goods, nor these true evils. Solomon’s judgment is truer: “It is better to go to the house of mourning than to the house of feasting” (Eccl. 7:3).

28. But if those who receive good things in their life are to be tormented in this way, and everlasting woe is reserved for those who have present consolation (Luke 6:24), while earlier there have been found some who, in the wisdom of the flesh, know how in all things and through all things to reject evil and choose good—what end can await them, if, according to the multitude of their consolations, pains seize the souls of the wretched? It seems to follow that those who receive every good thing and all the consolation of this age will nevertheless have the whole woe and suffer all torments.

Or should it equally be inferred from this same judgment of Abraham that those led by the contrary spirit, who reject all the good things of the present life and choose evils, will also possess all the Lord’s good things and every consolation? Perhaps this was what Peter wished to hear when, with such confidence and freedom, he addressed the Lord: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you; what then shall there be for us?” (Matt. 19:27).

## XXIV.—How he who had scarcely anything of everything left everything
29. A well-known question is how Peter, though he is known to have possessed scarcely anything at all, could so confidently boast that he had left everything. Hence one of the saints says: “He has left much who has relinquished the desire to possess.” And shortly afterwards: “Therefore those who follow have left behind as much as those who do not follow might have desired.” (St Gregory, Homily 5 on the Gospels.) It is a faithful saying, yet perhaps it too is obscure. Does the desire to possess embrace so much that abandoning it [Col. 0454B] amounts to leaving everything? What human being could desire [variant: aspire to] everything, much less this poor and insignificant fisherman? But if one examines more carefully what might suffice for each person, it is easy to find someone who desires everything. For no limit can be set to desire until it appears fulfilled, until it has acquired what can make it content. Moreover, the lover of money will never say, “It is enough”; nor will the lustful man be satisfied with pleasure. Thus every cruel person continually thirsts for blood; and the ambitious man, or one greedy for human praise, having obtained titles of rank or favour, finds in these no remedy whatever, but burns with still greater desire. Yet the one who desires to please himself and his own circle, and who glories in the foolish testimony he gives concerning himself, saying, “My hand is exalted” [Col. 0454C] (Deut. 32:27), and so forth—thinking himself to be something when he is nothing—finds still less rest.

## XXV.—On unnatural and insatiable hunger

30. I once saw five men—why should I not have judged them mad? The first, with swollen cheeks, was chewing sea-sand. The second stood beside a sulphurous lake and eagerly wished to inhale the most foul and loathsome vapour it exhaled. A third, bending over a fiercely blazing furnace, delighted in receiving glittering sparks into his gaping throat. The fourth, seated atop a pinnacle of the Temple, drew the breath of the gentler breeze in through his open mouth; and, if it seemed to flow in too little, he himself stirred up the wind with a fan, as though he hoped to swallow the whole air. [Col. 0454D] The fifth, standing apart, laughed at the rest—himself laughable too, and most of all. For with incredible zeal he laboured to suck his own flesh, now applying his hand, now his arm, now other parts to his mouth.

> [Note: [Col. 0453D] By these verbal coverings—or rather, by this parabolic discourse—he signifies various kinds of sinners wasting away with hunger. For he means the world to be an assembly of hungry people, pursuing temporal and perishing goods with insatiable hunger, while at the same time suffering nausea toward heavenly goods. They eat nothing [Col. 0454D] that can satisfy them; and therefore all are tormented by hunger and perish. Thus the first represents the avaricious, the second the luxurious, the third the wrathful, the fourth the proud and ambitious, and finally the fifth, sucking their own flesh, represents either the envious or people pleased with themselves and presumptuous about themselves.]

Moved with pity for these people, and asking each in turn the cause of his misery, I found it to be one and the same in all: an exceedingly strong hunger. Then, as I looked upon their emaciated faces, I remembered the prophet lamenting miserably and saying: “My heart has withered, [Col. 0455A] because I forgot to eat my bread” (Ps. 101:5). “What good are these things to you?” I said. “They are not natural foods: they provoke hunger rather than extinguish it. For righteousness is the bread of the soul; and only those who hunger for it are blessed, because they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6). Certainly, the rational soul, made in the image of God, can be occupied with all other things, but can never be filled by them. Whatever is less than God will not fill that which is capable of God.

## XXVI.—On the circuit of the wicked

31. This is why everyone is shown by natural desire to seek the highest good, and to have no rest unless he attains it. Yet miserable people wander because they do not find the way; and, as it is written, “the wicked walk in a circuit” (Ps. 11:9), while, seeking each lesser good, [Col. 0455B] they always desire what they do not yet seem to have attained and what is nearer to them. Indeed, would that, if it were possible, one person had obtained everything else: he would undoubtedly seek with desire that one thing alone which he saw was lacking to him—the highest good—just as he always seeks other things that he has not obtained. But these things are innumerable, and are likewise sought by others. Each person draws to his own side whatever he can; and this circuit can never be traversed. Do you wish to get ahead? Begin by leaping over it. Otherwise, miserable man, you will be swept away in the desire for earthly things, and you will find yourself farther from the highest good in proportion as you give yourself more fully to seeking perishable and transitory things. For you walk in a circuit; and that which was near you, in [Col. 0455C] your heart and in your mouth, if you believed in your heart and confessed with your mouth, you turn your back on and decline from, and become distant from it. Hence he cries out: “Turn back, O children of men” (Ps. 89:3); and likewise: “Return, return, O Shulammite; return, return, that we may look upon you” (Song 6:12). For the road is winding and impassable; and you will arrive more easily by despising all things than by acquiring them.

## XXVII.—On hastening conversion

32. “Behold, we have left everything and followed you: what then shall we have?” A saying altogether worthy of apostolic faith and devotion. You have already left everything; you have already followed the Lord, Peter; and only now do you ask what you are to receive. Truly Simon, truly obedient in the hearing of the ear, without negotiating an agreement. For at the sound of a single command Peter and Andrew left everything and followed the Redeemer (Matt. 4:20). If this perhaps seems foolish to the carnal man, let him hear: “What is foolish in God is wiser than men”; and that “God was pleased through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe,” since the world did not know him through wisdom (1 Cor. 1:21, 25). For how many does the accursed wisdom of the world overthrow, extinguishing within them the spirit whom the Lord had wished to kindle intensely? “Do not act rashly,” it says; “consider for a long time, examine more carefully. What you propose is a great matter and needs much deliberation. Test what you can do; consult friends, lest you happen to repent afterwards.”

33. This wisdom of the world is earthly, animal, diabolical, [Col. 0456A] hostile to salvation, a strangler of life, the mother of that lukewarmness which commonly provokes God to vomit. “Beware,” it says. Why? When you do not doubt that the word is from God, what need is there for deliberation? The Angel of Great Counsel calls you: why wait for alien counsels? For who is more faithful or wiser than he? “Deceive me, Lord, and I shall be deceived; be stronger than I, and prevail.” I know what things must be done quickly. Shall I be rescued from the mouth of the pit of Gehenna, and then seek a delay, linger, and hesitate to leave, in case something should happen meanwhile? I have hidden a fire in my bosom; and now that my side is burned, my entrails laid bare, and matter flowing out—must I deliberate long whether to awaken, shake it off, or cast it away? Great indeed is what is offered; but for that very reason it should be received all the more willingly and quickly, [Col. 0456B] seized with eager hands, fervour, and joy. Let him test himself who relies upon his own strength; but the divine gift has been tested in every way. Let him consult friends who has not read: “A man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. 7:6).

## XXVIII.—On the Lord’s three answers to those who promised to follow him

34. Why does a man constantly read the Gospel if he does not obey the Gospel? Yet in it we certainly read that to one who promised to follow the Lord, but wished first to bury his deceased father, the Lord answered that he should allow the dead to bury their own dead (Matt. 8:22). To another, who wished only to bid farewell to those in his home, he said: “No one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke [Col. 0456C] 9:62). But what had the first heard? “Master,” he said, “I will follow you wherever you go.” The Lord answered him: “Foxes have dens, and birds of heaven nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:19–20). In the fox’s den he censures the prudence of the flesh; in the bird’s nest, the pride of heart.

For one may sometimes see people who, having left all things and intending to renounce the world, wish to offer rightly but do not wish to divide rightly. Fearing to commit themselves wholly to the divine will through human shrewdness, they retain some leaven—I know not what—to corrupt the whole lump (1 Cor. 5:6); and this has often been found true of many. Another, thinking that he can easily undertake spiritual striving without a guide and teacher, [Col. 0456D] walks amid things great and wonderful beyond him; as the common saying has it: “Leaping before he sees, he will fall before he ought.” Peter, casting his thought upon the Lord and throwing all his care upon him, certain that the Lord would care for him, left everything and followed the Lord. He did not even ask concerning the reward until the danger of riches, which the Saviour was explaining, gave him occasion to inquire:

## XXIX.—On the second regeneration

35. “What then shall we have?” Jesus said to him: “Amen, I say to you.” A word of confirmation is placed first: understand that what follows is great. “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit” (Matt. 19:27–28), and so forth. [Col. 0457A] What does he mean when he says “in the regeneration”? Or what is this new regeneration? For we already know that a human being must be born again, not of bloods nor of the will of man, but of water and the Holy Spirit (John 3:3–5). But since this promise cannot in any way pertain to that regeneration, perhaps another regeneration is needed; and a person must be born not only again, but even a third time. Unhappy am I, and wretched is my condition, for whom one regeneration does not suffice, for whom a twofold regeneration is necessary. Since I consist of body and soul, I fell wholly at once; yet I cannot rise wholly at once. Or is it not fitting that the portion which seems greater and prior should be restored first? And no one of sound mind is ignorant that this is the soul itself. [Col. 0457B] Therefore let that which fell first be restored first; especially since the punishment of the other arose from its fault, and its corruption was also the cause of bodily corruption. Hence the Saviour first came to souls, to take away the sins of the world, not the sufferings of the flesh. This he taught still more clearly in himself, exposing his body to every punishment while preserving his soul altogether free from sin.

## XXX.—That the body should await the time of its regeneration

36. The children of men are not so today—not so. They neglect care for the soul, but fulfil care for the flesh in every desire. They do not fear sinning, but being punished; and labour is not given to virtue of heart, but to bodily health—indeed, even to pleasure. They learned this in the school of Hippocrates [Col. 0457C] and Epicurus; for Christ taught none of this to his disciples. Rather, he said: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29). Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood? (Ps. 4:3). This time is assigned to souls, not bodies: it is a day of salvation, certainly, not of pleasure. “Everything has its time” (Eccl. 3:1): now it is necessary to devote attention to souls. For whoever sows in the flesh will reap from it only corruption (Gal. 6:8). “But,” they say, “no one ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:29). True; but one who has zeal without knowledge, while he hastens to help, is found [Col. 0457D] to harm.

Since the judgment of the flesh depends upon the soul, nothing can be more useful to the flesh than to provide for the salvation of the soul, so that the flesh may be regarded in its proper time and, as companion in suffering, may deserve a share in happiness as well. Hence the Apostle says: “We await the Saviour, our Lord Jesus Christ, who will refashion the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory” (Phil. 3:20–21). Rest in this hope, miserable flesh: he who came for the sake of the soul will come also for your sake; he who refashioned it will not forget you to the end. Meanwhile let the soul be regenerated; and, as foreknown and predestined by the Lord, let it be conformed to the image of his Son in meekness and humility of heart. For by his merit know that you too will someday be regenerated [Col. 0458A] and conformed in glory and splendour to his body.

## XXXI.—That we should not sit down on the way

37. “In the regeneration,” he says, “when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit” (Matt. 19:28), and so forth. You shall attain him whom you follow: when he sits, you too shall sit with him. For when did he sit down in the world? When did he stand still? When did he lay down his head? “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6); “he went about doing good” (Acts 10:38). Indeed, he had neither nest nor den nor lodging-place, until at last, having completed the work he had undertaken, he deserved to receive the command to sit, and the Lord said to my Lord: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1).

[Col. 0458B] Fool that you are, choosing to preside rather than to sit with others, seeking resting-places on the journey. He came to minister, not to be ministered to (Matt. 20:28); and do you, above your master and greater than the Lord—indeed neither disciple nor servant—already hurry to recline? “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands” (Prov. 6:10). He leaps upon the mountains, he skips over the hills. Cry to him, my soul: “Draw me after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). Otherwise, how do you hope to catch him by delaying, growing lukewarm, and pausing? “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course.” Without doubt he loves a cheerful follower. You have not yet reached the prize; you have not yet grasped the goal. A great road still remains: do not halt your step; do not sit down midway on the journey. “In the sweat of [Col. 0458C] your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken” (Gen. 3:19). Then indeed will be the time of rest, when the Spirit himself says that you may rest from your labours. Yet even then peace will not be complete, rest not perfect, and finally the sitting-down not full.

## XXXII.—How in no respect do we sit now

38. “In the regeneration,” he says, “when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit.” Happy regeneration! When shall I be reborn to sit, I who was born a miserable man for labour? Oh, if ever I may sit wholly, when now not even the smallest part of me sits—when nothing in me is tranquil, nothing at rest, nothing settled, nothing ever remaining in the same state! [Col. 0458D] “You also shall sit.” O sitting! Who will grant me to express in fitting words what I conceive in my heart’s affection concerning this sitting? Or rather, who will grant me to enjoy the undisturbed rest of this sitting, which I desire, seek, and long for? For behold, as I said, nothing in me sits, but all things are in motion; everything sways, everything fluctuates. Finally, while flesh still desires against spirit and spirit against flesh, what part of the human being appears to sit? Nor does desire alone now disturb peace, prevent sitting, and forbid settledness; but a twofold affliction of the body also harasses the miserable human being: the pain felt in the present, and fear of future death. Since it is both capable of suffering and mortal, a twofold concern nonetheless seems to agitate the soul—[Col. 0459A] hope and fear. Between these it continually fluctuates as long as it inhabits the body of sin, ascending to heaven and again descending to the abyss; wasting away amid evils, yet nonetheless burning for good things.

## XXXIII.—On imperfect sitting

39. But when it departs from this dwelling of clay, it will indeed be wholly freed from fear, but not yet from expectation. From that time there will no longer be fear within our borders; but, established uniquely in hope, each of us will sing with mind and spirit, as one had in some manner anticipated when he said: “Return, my soul, to your rest, because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you; because he has delivered my soul from death, my eyes from tears, and my feet from falling” (Ps. 114:7–8). But concerning expectation, the same man says: “The righteous await me until you repay me” (Ps. 141:8). They await not merely the completion of the number of their brothers, but also the restoration of the body in its own regeneration. Indeed, they long for it with desire, crying aloud to God beneath his altar; as one who was worthy to hear was also able to testify (Rev. 6:9–10). For who could say that the body is sitting at that time, while it flows away and is reduced to decay and dust? [Col. 0459B]

## XXXIV.—On perfect sitting

40. “In the regeneration,” he says, “you also shall sit.” For “the body is sown animal; it shall rise spiritual. It is sown in dishonour; it shall rise in glory” (1 Cor. 15:44–45). Then where, O death, is your victory? For you too, the last enemy, shall be destroyed. The body of the resurrection [Col. 0459C] no longer dies; death shall no longer have dominion over it (Rom. 6:9). Every pain and groaning will also depart, because God will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints; and there will no longer be mourning, crying, or any pain, because the former things have passed away (Rev. 21:4). Happy tears, which the gracious hand of the Creator will wipe away; and blessed eyes, which chose to melt in such weeping rather than be lifted up in pride, rather than behold every lofty thing, or serve avarice and wantonness.

The body, then, will sit, endowed with the twofold happiness of immortality and impassibility: free from every necessity, secure from every corruption, foreign and immune to every desire, full of glory, and finally [Col. 0459D] conformed to the splendour of Christ’s body. The soul too will sit, as fearing nothing and desiring nothing further: enjoying complete blessedness and secure fullness, sensing no surges of thoughts, no conflicts of temptations, no movements of affections; but wholly immersed in that eternal unchangeability and cleaving to God in such a way that it has become one spirit with him.

## XXXV.—On the Lord’s sitting

41. But when will these things be, and for whom? “You,” he says, “who have followed me, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit.” The Son of Man now sits on the throne of majesty, for having ascended into heaven he sits at God’s right hand. Yet it was said, “when he shall sit”: that is, when he appears seated, as the Apostle says: “When Christ, [Col. 0460A] your life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4). Or shall we rather dare to say that he too in some way still stands, since his sitting does not yet seem complete, because the footstool promised by the Father has not yet been placed beneath his feet? Not that anything is lacking to that fullness, but that the head awaits the members. Let the one who deserved to behold it dare to testify to this. “Behold,” Stephen says, “I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of the power of God” (Acts 7:55). Paul likewise writes: “Christ, standing forth as high priest of the good things to come, entered once into the Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9:11–12).

But in the regeneration of bodies, he will sit on the throne of majesty—he who, for the regeneration of souls, stood [variant: sat] [Col. 0460B] in the shameful punishment of the cross, questioned amid both insults and torments, condemned not only to the harshest death but also to the most disgraceful. For because he became obedient to the Father unto death—even death on a cross—therefore God exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend (Phil. 2:8, 10). I have said these things, brothers, so that you may know what are the two sides of the ladder set before those who wish to follow the Lord and must be climbed; what are its bases, what its capitals, and what steps, upon whose summit God rests.

## XXXVI.—On the sides of the ladder

42. We must tame the flesh and tread down the world, so that, avoiding bodily pleasure, we may also beware [Col. 0460C] the vanity of the age. These are the abominations of the Egyptians which we sacrifice to the Lord our God (Exod. 8:26). Everything that deters the children of this age from the way of life and discipline, and everything that meanwhile exercises the servants of God, is contained in these two things which the prophet commends in one verse: “See,” he says, “my lowliness and my labour” (Ps. 24:18). Let these, then, be the sides of the ladder: lowliness and hardship. Into them let the steps of inward virtue and grace thereafter be firmly joined.

For one sees people who despise worldly glory, trample popular favour underfoot, and do not desire the human day; yet they are not so strong in bearing bodily discomfort, do not so reject softness, and do not so overcome the allurements of the flesh.
