What shall I call such people except those who do not hold the other side? But the ascent of one who leans upon one side only is exceedingly dangerous and near to ruin.

43. And if the person who seems too weak regarding the flesh is in danger, though he rejects worldly glory and is unmoved by insults, then surely the danger is far more dreadful and much less excusable if someone, although he chastises his body manfully and does not spare its affliction [variant: affection], is nevertheless found less resistant to the desire for glory, less patient under injuries, and less free from the vanity of the world. What have you, unhappy man, to do with these trifles and calamities, with this ostentation and vanity, which [Col. 0461A] profit neither soul nor body? Why are you provoked? Why are you inflamed by the breath of a word, which neither wounds the flesh nor defiles the mind? Nothing is so alien to nature, nothing so contrary to reason. For I cannot similarly say, “What have you to do with food and clothing?” or “Why are you disturbed by cold or hunger?” Since the soul is personally united not to this world but to the body, it can hate the flesh far less than the world, because it owes much to the one and nothing to the other. I say this not to excuse pleasure equally, but so that vanity and impurity may before all things be fled.

## XXXVII.—On the steps of the ladder

44. Once you have thus settled and strengthened in your heart your acceptance of the hardship of bodily abstinence and labour, and your contentment with all lowliness and extremity, [Col. 0461B] the sides are good. Now safely insert the steps of spiritual practice, so that you may expend in the pursuit of piety all that you withdraw from the world and the flesh. Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forth toward what lies before (Phil. 3:13), arrange ascents and advance from virtue to virtue, that you may deserve to see the God of gods in Zion (Ps. 83:8). First you will ascend through the wilderness of your own heart and the valley of weeping like a wisp of smoke; then, having passed into something more serene, you will also ascend from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon your beloved (Song 8:5), led from brightness to brightness as by the Spirit of the Lord—indeed, that Spirit who searches even the deep things of God. And in these steps you will find no few degrees of manifold grace. But these are spiritual things, to be compared with spiritual things.

Now, however, the discourse is directed rather to beginners; its whole purpose is to recall transgressors to their heart. Those who are advancing, however, have a little work published long ago, occasioned by a sermon, on the twelve Steps of Humility.

> [Note: [Col. 0461D] That is, St Bernard’s treatise *On the Steps of Humility*.]

These are the steps which that man, Benedict—truly blessed in every respect, filled with the spirit of all the righteous—set forth in his Rule (chapter 7).

## XXXVIII.—On the eastern way which proceeded from the cell of Blessed Benedict

45. For he raised for us the spiritual ladder whose summit touches heaven. We read this commended in an evident miracle at his glorious passing, Pope St Gregory writing thus: “Supported by the hands of his disciples as his limbs grew weak, he stood with hands lifted toward heaven and breathed out his last breath amid words of prayer. On that very day a revelation of one and the same vision appeared to two brothers, one situated at a distance and the other dwelling in the cell. They saw a road paved with coverings and shining with innumerable lamps, extending straight eastward from his cell up to heaven. A man of venerable appearance, shining from above, stood beside it and asked whose was the road that they saw. They declared that they did not know. He said to them: ‘This is the way by which Benedict, beloved of the Lord, ascended to heaven’” (St Gregory, *Dialogues*, book II, chapter 37).

For what is the way proceeding from [Col. 0462A] his cell except the Order which this blessed man established, and the pattern of life which took its beginning from him? By this way the beloved of the Lord ascended, because “the holy man could not teach otherwise than as he lived” (*ibid.*). This indeed is the chief confidence of those who strive, however imperfectly, to adhere to his footsteps: they follow him as teacher and guide. For there can be no doubt whatever that the manner of life by which this truly blessed Benedict obtained so great a grace of holiness in life and so great a glory of blessedness after death is holy, formed more by divine inspiration and counsel than by human prudence or invention.

46. But enough of this, lest anyone perhaps accuse us—as may it always be far [Col. 0462B] from our hearts!—of wishing rather to disparage those who have devised various modes of religious life, according to what each thought proper, than to console and encourage others. Yet let each person ask himself, and not pretend not to confront his own conscience on this point, from which saint the form of clergy we see in churches today—lest I call it an unformed life—derives; who, I ask, in either the New or the Old Testament lived thus or taught people to live thus. For how many followers do we see of ways that indeed seem good to people, but whose end descends into the depth of hell? (Prov. 14:12). How many climbers of a ladder whose summit does not touch heaven, but which is altogether contrary to it: its sides are the lust of the flesh [Col. 0462C] and the lust of the eyes, and its steps the pride of life—things which are from the world, not from the Father?

47. But the steps and sides of the ladder which we wish to commend to you are indeed from the Father, not from the world—the ladder upon which he appeared to rest. “Let us live soberly,” says the Apostle, “and piously and justly in this age” (Titus 2:12). Sobriety attacks the pleasure of the flesh; justice, the vanity of the world, since by rendering to each what is his own, it grieves over the flatterer and has compassion on the angry person. Finally, the Saviour himself, when he bowed that lofty head beneath the Baptist’s hands, said: “Thus it is fitting for us to fulfil all justice” (Matt. 3:15), reckoning humility alone as justice. Let sobriety therefore be displayed toward ourselves, justice toward our neighbour, piety toward God. [Col. 0462D] For piety is the worship of God.

And as pleasure and vanity are known to foster pride of heart, so sobriety and justice foster piety; so that, advancing between these sides from faith to faith with hope as intermediary, one may at length attain the surpassing excellence of charity.

## XXXIX.—On the bases of the ladder

48. These sides rest upon the bases which Wisdom the craftsman has set beneath them—perhaps the two timbers of the cross. For where he is punished by death and disgraced on the cross, which of his followers could endure, much less dare seek, pleasures or glory? Christ is scourged and smeared with spittle; he carries his cross for himself; he is made a mockery with a derisive robe, a reed sceptre, and a crown of thorns; he is pierced with nails, numbered among criminals, stretched out upon the wood, and wounded even when dead. And the person who is called a Christian, looking upon these things, is not at all ashamed to indulge his own pleasures and wish to flourish in [Col. 0463A] the world!

But if everyone who says that he abides in Christ ought himself to walk as Christ walked (1 John 2:6), much more is the person without excuse who says that he abides for Christ, performs an embassy for him, and ministers to him, if he does not follow him. Certainly, unless he denies himself and takes up his cross, he cannot follow him at all (Matt. 16:24). And what is taking up the cross except embracing labour and humility? As it is written: “I chose to be cast down in the house of God” (Ps. 83:11).

## XL.—On the capitals

[Col. 0463B]

49. But perhaps these still seem insufficiently firmly established if they are supported only by bases and are not also joined together above by capitals. Hence the Saviour, not content with his own examples, also promises rewards, so that the desire for recompense may draw one whom the invitation of the one who goes before does not perhaps move. If he is pleasure-loving, let him thirst for that torrent of delight; if greedy for glory, let him aspire to that height of judicial authority. “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28). It is as if he said: “For your twofold shame and disgrace your portion shall be praised. Therefore in your land you shall possess double [Col. 0463C] and everlasting joy shall be yours” (Isa. 61:7). In exile you have a double affliction: namely, humility and labour. But be comforted and do not fail, for in your land—the land of the living—a twofold recompense nevertheless awaits you: exaltation and delight. For in thrones undisturbed rest is signified, and in judgment the eminence of dignity.

## XLI.—On judgment

50. What worldly honour can be imagined that would not become utterly cheap in comparison with so great an exaltation? For they are to preside with Christ as judges not of one city, people, or region, but of the whole world. They will judge not only human beings but even angels themselves (1 Cor. 6:3): those who, scorning and spurning their parent for the slight vapour of present glory, prefer the reproach of Christ to every title of dignity. “Do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom” (Luke 12:32). The counsel has been determined and will not be annulled; the unchangeable purpose endures. Indeed, the Lord has sworn, and he will not repent: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man shall sit on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit, judging.”

What could be more glorious? Let the sons of pride judge and prejudge now; let them sit with their king, who chose for himself the sides of the north. Let them be exalted and raised like the cedars of Lebanon. We shall pass by, and behold, they will not be. Let them oppress [Col. 0464A] whom they can now; let them blaspheme; let them heap curses upon us; let the reproaches of those who reproach Christ come upon us, because our reward is abundant in heaven. Let them have the glory that comes from one another—vain and false indeed—for the children of men are vain, the children of men false. The glory which is from God alone, true and enduring glory, they do not want, because he is truth and he is the One Who Is.

## XLII.—On the early figs

51. Most unhappy indeed is ambition that cannot aspire to great things, seeking to grow from a little thing and to diminish from the greatest. For they love the chief seats, which, like early figs (*grossi*) of fig trees, will quickly fall. Early figs are certain first figs, wholly useless, having only the appearance of figs and not the flavour; [Col. 0464B] they are not so much fruits as signs of fruits to come, and they must fall so that other figs fit for human use and eating may succeed them. Hence the Bride says in the Song of Songs: “Winter has passed; the rain is gone and departed”; and shortly afterwards: “The fig tree has put forth its early figs” (Song 2:11, 13). That is, when persecution had ceased, the Church became illustrious and was set amid the pride of the ages. This height and excellence of dignities he quite fittingly calls early figs, to warn us to think rather of the future in them than the present. For things seen are temporal; things unseen are eternal.

Let those, then, who love the chief seats beware lest they come to lack the second; and let those who now choose the first places at table begin, in shame, to occupy the last place. “You shall sit,” he says, [Col. 0464C] “upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel.” These will now be figs, not early figs. He who said of the heavenly city, “There thrones sat for judgment, thrones over the house of David” (Ps. 121:5), had foreseen these thrones. There indeed, not here. For how can the seats that we see here be said to sit, when they so often sway, so often totter, and so often are overthrown? They are surely early figs, cast down and scattered by a light breeze.

But what does it mean that he promises they shall judge the twelve tribes of Israel, in which the world itself is also understood to be judged? Is it because God is still known only in Judea, and he wished to designate the whole body of believers by the name of the twelve tribes, remembering them as though they alone were to be judged because of the saying: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged”? [Col. 0464D] (John 3:18). For this is the distinctive glory of the perfect: to stand out even among the faithful themselves, and to excel in judicial authority over others who are also to be saved, so that, in accordance with the Psalm’s saying, they may sit over the house of David. What misery is this, that at the word of so great a promise human negligence sleeps?

## XLIII.—The Saviour’s complaint
52. “My people,” says the Lord, “what ought I to have done for you that I did not do?” (Isa. 5:4). What reason is there that you prefer to serve my enemy—and yours—rather than me? For he did not create you; indeed, he does not even feed you or order your times. If these things seem small to the ungrateful: it was not he but I who redeemed you. But [Col. 0465A] at what price? Certainly not with perishable gold and silver, not with the sun or moon, nor even with any angel; I redeemed you with my own blood. Yet if, despite so many claims, I cannot draw from you the service owed to me, setting all these aside, at least agree with me for the daily wage. Let him have done you no harm, and let me seem to have done you no good. Obey him who promises you more and greater things, with whom recompense is surer and more abundant; let me even, in my most gracious mercy, pass over that I—having no need of your goods—seek only your welfare, lest you refuse the gifts of grace I now offer, promising that these same gifts shall be crowned by the rewards of future glory.

XLIV.—On the Excuses of Worldly People

[Col. 0465B] 53. What can human conscience answer to this? When these things begin to be reproached to them on the day of judgment, how will the wretched endure it? What excuse can they offer for sin? Will they then begin to say, “Presently—yes, presently; wait a little”? For thus these unhappy people now evade the matter: “Presently, presently,” and “presently” has no limit; and “wait a little” stretches on indefinitely. “God,” they say, “is good, and helps at hand.” The divine promise is indeed great; but the delay is far too long, and the waiting burdensome. To abandon one’s earthly lot and not yet obtain the heavenly is unbearable affliction and inconsolable grief. Why need one hasten, only to prolong misery?

A truly miserable and deceptive thought. For this is a new complaint: until now the children of men did not complain that life was too long. Human days seem short until conscience stings them and they are admonished about repentance and conversion, either inwardly by the Spirit or outwardly by another person. Then, indeed, a new weariness with long life is conceived, and a new confidence arises that death may be deferred.

54. But suppose much of your course of years remains. You are young; you will live into old age and senility. Why must you lose so much time and waste such great gains? Nothing is more precious than time; yet, alas, nothing today is valued more cheaply. The days of salvation pass by, and no one reflects; no one laments for himself that irrecoverable moments have perished. Do you suppose, O man, that the work of only two or three years can be recompensed by the Almighty? Has the Lord’s hand become so shortened [Col. 0465D] that it cannot reward the labor of a hundred years? 305 Sit down and calculate what you can gain each day, being assured that with God no good at all shall go unrewarded; and that, as no hair from the body, so no moment of time shall be lost.

Why should I press upon you the counsel of the Wise Man: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord” (Ecclus. 5:8)? You do not know what the coming day will bring forth (Prov. 27:1). Why should I reproach the madness of one who so rashly presumes upon the future—as though the Father had placed times and seasons in your will rather than, more truly, in his own? Finally, why should I speak of an uncertain end, the certainly brief duration of labor, and the eternity of recompense? The Lord knows our frame; [Col. 0466A] he makes provision for our faint-heartedness, meets human thought, drives away anxiety, and forestalls trembling.

XLV.—On the Twofold Promise

55. For he continues: “And everyone who has left father, or mother, or house, or field for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:20). What more will you say, children of men, when such great promises are made to you even in this world: that you may sleep between the two portions concerning which you complained a little earlier, and, on leaving your earthly lot, may immediately receive a more abundant consolation—so that you await not merely patiently but even joyfully the lot of the saints promised in the regeneration? For the expectation of the righteous itself is joy. “He shall receive,” he says, “a hundredfold, [Col. 0466B] and shall possess eternal life.” You have, children of Adam, the promise of the life that now is together with that which is to come, so that every mouth speaking iniquity may be stopped and all who work iniquity in vain may be confounded (Ps. 24:4).

Does not the man utterly work iniquity in vain who could serve God not only more profitably but also more delightfully, not only more beneficially but also more sweetly, than he could serve the world? Observe that the Lord answered Peter only concerning the future; for Peter could neither doubt nor need to ask about what he was presently experiencing. Thus he did not say, “What do we have?” but “What shall we have?” (Matt. 19:29, 27).

56. Can anyone doubt that the promise of the hundredfold belongs to the present time? The very sequence [Col. 0466C] of the words clearly proves it, where we are said to be about to receive the hundredfold and to possess eternal life. But lest any room remain for shameless obstinacy, I refer you to the Gospel according to Mark, where the same promise is set out more plainly. For the Lord says: “There is no one who has left father, or mother, or children, or fields, or house for my sake and for the Gospel, who shall not receive a hundred times as much now, in this present time” (Mark 10:29–30).

And, so that the carnal mind—which does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit but considers them folly—may be all the more astonished, he significantly adds: “with persecutions.” For perhaps, upon hearing that a hundredfold was promised “in this time,” it might suppose that temporal things were also being bestowed; but the added word “persecutions” forestalls this interpretation. What earthly consolation is there that earthly persecution cannot readily take away? What earthly thing did the holy martyrs receive amid persecutions, when even the earth containing the blessed bodies was delivered into the hands of impious men?

XLVI.—On Unbelief

57. Yet, wherever this hundredfold may be received from, provided that it is a hundredfold—provided that it has a hundredfold power to please, console, delight, and be loved—what madness it is that people hesitate to leave the single for the hundredfold! Where is the greedy man, where the ambitious man, where the seeker after this world? Why has human avarice grown lukewarm and fallen asleep before this trustworthy transaction and most profitable exchange? To what Jew would you deny this, O man who have received the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in vain? To what sacrilegious person would you hesitate to give all you possess in return for a hundredfold? Yet the Lord’s hand is accursed in your eyes, so that you consent to receive no exchange from him and to have no dealings with him at all in the reckoning of what is given and received.

Or perhaps you refuse, not from hatred, but from unbelief? For I confess that this seems more believable to me. No one would prefer to perish for the sake of even the smallest consolation rather than be saved with the greatest exultation. But faith is not possessed by all—not even by all who are believers merely in name. I could certainly offer you many examples, produce many witnesses, who assuredly think as they have believed and experience as they have heard. Every nation, every region, and every language—wherever there is a gathering of saints—abounds in such testimonies and such consoling embers. But how shall one who does not believe Truth when it promises believe human experiences? I judge it even more astonishing that you seem more believing in the greater matter than in the lesser. Is it difficult for him to give a hundredfold in the present, when he will give eternal life in the future? He who will give what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart—can he not give a hundredfold?

XLVII.—On Contrived Labor

58. “But how,” you ask, “can these things happen? By what reasoning does one who has left himself nothing from all things receive a hundredfold?” This is precisely what he mentioned a little earlier: “Take my yoke upon you, and you shall find rest” (Matt. 11:29). A wonderful novelty—but the novelty of him who makes all things new. Taking up a yoke, one finds rest; leaving all things, one possesses a hundredfold.

That man according to God’s heart also knew this, when he spoke to him in the Psalm: “Can the throne of iniquity cling to you, which devises toil in commandment?” (Ps. 93:20). Is not toil contrived by a commandment a light burden, a sweet yoke, an anointed cross? The mystery of this is that, at the dedication of churches, the bishop anoints with holy oil the crosses painted on the wall.

So also of old, when Abraham was told, “Take your son Isaac, whom you love, and offer him to me as a holocaust” [Col. 0467D] (Gen. 22:2), labor in the commandment was only apparent. Isaac was offered, indeed, but sanctified, not slain. Therefore, if you hear the Lord’s voice within your mind and are told to offer your Isaac, whatever joy is yours, sacrifice it to God—for Isaac means “Joy” or “Laughter”—obey faithfully and steadfastly. Do not fear. Even if the prophet tells you some great thing, you must do it and obey him in all things, even should Isaac himself have to be sacrificed.

But now, whatever self-love may judge, be secure: Isaac will not die, but the ram; your joy will not perish, but your stubbornness—whose horns, indeed, are caught in thorns and which cannot exist without the pricks of anxiety. For the Lord your God tests you. Isaac will not be slain, as you suppose: he will live and keep on living, but [Col. 0468A] elevated upon the wood, so that you may rejoice on high; and you may glory not in your own flesh but in the cross of the Lord, through whom you yourself are crucified—crucified to the world, for to him you live.

XLVIII.—On the Bride’s Blackness and Beauty

59. This, indeed, is the manner of life of the perfect, the life of the saints, spiritual grace. Thus they say: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; as having nothing, and possessing all things; as dying, and behold, we live” (2 Cor. 6:10, 9). “Those who saw me outside fled from me” (Ps. 30:12), says also the king’s daughter—she, of course, whose whole glory is within. Hence in the Song of Songs she cries out, recalling the young women whom she sees frightened by her outward lack of adornment: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon. Do not look upon me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me” (Song 1:4–5).

It is as though some spiritual person, exhorting tender and weak minds, were plainly saying: Why do you so diligently enumerate every laborious and humble feature of our way of life? They are hair shirts and reddened rams’ skins, beneath which that inward splendor and interior glory are covered, so that they may be preserved unharmed from the injury of dust and rain. Do not look upon me because I am dark; do not be afraid, do not wonder. For this outward neglect and external blackness do not arise from sadness or necessity, but from hidden splendor and inward exultation. “The sun,” she says, “has discolored me”: the inward light cannot endure the outward. It is fire, indeed, and admits no empty leaves. Otherwise the leaves must either be burned up or, if they prevail, extinguish the fire. The Apostle teaches that this must altogether be avoided: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. 5:19). Rather, Christ forbids it, desiring that it be kindled intensely (Luke 12:49).

Thus the bride is black, but beautiful; the Apostles are as sorrowful, yet always rejoicing; and Christ himself, if viewed with Jewish eyes, had neither form nor beauty. On the contrary, Truth compares others to whitewashed tombs: outwardly splendid and gleaming, inwardly filthy and foul-smelling. For they walk in robes and, as has been said, love the first seats, glorious, honored, and great in the eyes [Col. 0468D] of men; but inwardly, where God sees, they are full of avarice, envy, ambition, pride, and perhaps some of them lust (Matt. 23:5–7, 27–28). For when is that precious gift of continence given to such people, unless perhaps for judgment and condemnation, lest they should one day fear, come to their senses, and turn from their pursuits, but instead fall asleep in sins and perish more grievously through their very irreverence and false security?

XLIX.—How Inner Poverty Drives One Outward

60. Just as contempt for outward things is a clear sign of spiritual discipline and care for the heart, so concern for them is likewise a sure sign of an uncultivated mind. For it is written: “Every idle person lives among desires” (Prov. 21:25); and again: “The sluggard shall be stoned with the dung of oxen” (Ecclus. 22:2). Woe, woe to the wretched man! While he is being covered with dung, he imagines that he is being adorned.

Paul was an ox, treading out grain on the Lord’s threshing floor and acknowledging his owner; hence he said: “For Christ I have counted all things as loss, and I count them as dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3:8). He embraces this dung, even if he was once brought up in scarlet garments (Lam. 4:5). The sluggard is stoned with this dung: neglecting to gain Christ, he is compelled by an empty and deserted heart to wander outward. Thus the patriarch Jacob was compelled by famine to go down into Egypt (Gen. 46:6); and that prodigal son, forced by want, was made to serve swine and to hunger for husks (Luke 15:15–16).

L.—On the Worm That Does Not Die

61. But what does Scripture say? “To him who has, it shall be given, and he shall abound; but from him who does not have, even that which he seems to have shall be taken from him” (Matt. 13:22). The grass shall wither and the flower fall; the windows themselves will also be shut, so that they can draw in no further earthly consolation. Finally, the Lord says: “I will reprove you and set you before your own face” (Ps. 49:21).

What confusion, misery, and pain there will be when the leaves are scattered and dispersed, every disgrace is laid bare, shame is uncovered, and the corruption appears; when that inward worm of conscience, now made immortal, will gnaw the unhappy soul with its whole malice but not consume it; and when there will be no place at all for concealment and no hope of consolation. For why is it that even now they cannot bear the stings of conscience to any extent, but turn away the eyes of their heart and turn to miserable consolations, or deceive themselves by some pretenses, so that iniquity lies to itself? Is it not because that torment is intolerable—even though hope still flatters them and greatly diminishes the pain—while they measure out time for themselves as they please and rashly assure themselves that all they do may easily be washed away, and that what they seek may be abandoned? Yet through habit and negligence, dull and senseless in heart, they scarcely feel anything. All these things, however, will be far removed when what is written comes to pass: “I will reprove you and set you before your own face.”

LI.—That Bodily Things Touch Our Spirit Differently from Spiritual Things

[Col. 0469D] 62. The nearer and more dearly bound by natural kinship the soul is to its own flesh, the more sharply it must grieve and the more painfully bear injury to itself than bodily injury, once it has been awakened from this numbness and insensibility. Conversely, when it has experienced its own goods, spiritual delights, and inward pleasure of mind, it must embrace and enjoy them all the more delightfully, because they touch it more closely and directly and are not begged from without.

No one can take delight in the refreshment of his beast in the same way as in the refreshment of his own body. The former does indeed please him, but the latter has a very different taste and is felt differently. But if you acknowledge that the body is the soul’s beast, the same principle must surely be observed in the body itself. Do not therefore err or be deceived [Col. 0470A] into believing that the spirit can be more delighted by bodily than by spiritual things. Consult even human reason, if faith has entirely fallen asleep within you.

LII.—On the Three in Prison and the Three on the Cross

63. We read that there were once three in prison and three on the cross. Joseph, indeed, was committed to prison custody with the king’s cupbearer and baker; Christ, the true Joseph, was counted with two criminals. Those in prison saw dreams and heard their interpretation; those on the cross spoke words, and one received a promise.

Of the former, one served drink to the king and heard, “You shall be restored to your former rank.” The other fed birds [or: ravens] and received the answer of death (Gen. 40). These are, indeed, the swine fed by that prodigal young man (Luke 15:15). For the filthy and the proud are fittingly denoted by the names of swine and birds.

But of those crucified with the Savior, to the one who confessed was said: “Today you shall be with me in paradise”; while the blasphemer received his answer not from the Lord—for at that time he was judging no one—but from his companion: “Do you not fear God, since you are under the same condemnation?” What then do we suppose could have troubled those two to whom it was said respectively, “You shall be restored after three days,” and “Today you shall be with me in paradise,” except the delay itself in the meantime? But what could please the man to whom it was said: “After three days, when your head has been cut off, you shall be hanged and become food for birds”?

Indeed, all of us are in this condition: no one is outside prison, and meanwhile no one is without a cross [variant: an inward cross]. Since not even the innocent is found exempt, when should the sinner hope for rest? But if someone bears it willingly and says, “We indeed justly” (Luke 23:39–43), he will have his reward. But if unwillingly, blaspheming and denying God by his deeds, he suffers a double crushing. If anyone has the testimony of salvation, even his flesh rests in hope; and the prophet’s flour seasons and sweetens the pottage, so that in the pot there is now not death but life (4 Kgs. 4:41).

LIII.—That the Hundredfold Is Promised Without Exception

64. Finally, let no sound-minded person believe that delight in vices is greater than delight in virtues, especially since God is the God of virtues, the source of all true pleasure, and the origin of joy and exultation. For to serve not the flesh, the world, or the evil ruler, but Christ, is truly to reign. Hear a man give faithful testimony to Truth from his own experience: “In the way of your testimonies I have delighted as in all riches” (Ps. 118:14). What will there be in the homeland, if such abundance of delight is found on the way? Thus the Apostle taught us to glory not only in hope but also in tribulation (Rom. 5:2–3).

“He may indeed be so,” says the friend of this world, the enemy of the world’s Creator; “he may indeed be so, but perhaps I am not. I am soft; I am a sinful man; I cannot endure so great a labor without much grace, and I cannot merit grace itself.” As though grace were not grace but the reward of works; as though not all had sinned or not all stood in need of God’s grace. Do you think, O man, that there is respect of persons with God, and that he does not console all who leave all things equally abundantly? Do not be unbelieving; submit at least to Truth, whose testimony no faithful person may doubt: “And everyone,” he says, “who has left father, or mother, or house, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold” (Matt. 19:20).

Christ excepts no one. Wretched, therefore, are those who say, “Except us,” who exclude themselves and make themselves exceptions to the universal benefit. Clearly, they judge themselves still more unworthy of eternal life, since they do not even hope for the hundredfold. But because God who promises is true, the human being who distrusts is a liar.

LIV.—On Those Who Seem to Have Left All Things Yet Do Not Have the Hundredfold

[Col. 0471B]

65. “And everyone who has left father, or mother, or house, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life.” I could easily endure the contradiction of tongues if I spoke this from myself, since the carnal man does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit, but they seem foolish to him (1 Cor. 2:14). But now it is spoken by him whose words will not pass away even when heaven and earth pass away (Luke 21:33).

“But I have heard,” says a person seeking an occasion for his own perdition and, as the common saying goes, “a straw with which to gouge out his own eye”; “I have heard of this man and that who had left all things and returned to their vomit. How did they receive the hundredfold?” Arise, Lord; judge your own cause. For the slander of such persons, and the murmuring of those who perhaps seemed to have left all things but nevertheless did not receive the hundredfold, is directed not against us but against you, who said: “Everyone who leaves father,” and so forth, “shall receive a hundredfold.”

But what shall we say? Can anyone be rejected from the company of disciples unless he possesses moneybags? There are moneybags not only of money but of one’s own will. Therefore let one who complains that the promised grace of the hundredfold is absent from him search his own ways and pursuits. Without doubt, he will find a corner, a hiding-place, and a resting-place—not for the Son of Man, indeed, but either a fox’s den or a bird’s nest.

Rather, I beg him to leave all things more perfectly and follow Christ alone, casting his care upon him, to be nourished by him, and he will undoubtedly receive the hundredfold. For Scripture cannot be broken: resting upon such certain truth, it promises this to all without exception. Let him retain nothing for himself and nothing for his own, lest a little leaven corrupt the whole lump (1 Cor. 5:6).

For there are those who retain something for themselves, forgetting the Lord’s word that he came not to do his own will. Even among communities of saints, they cling too insistently to their own desire or perhaps to their own judgment; they make themselves self-styled wise persons, retaining something of themselves for themselves, when they ought utterly to have denied themselves and entrusted themselves to divine providence, to obedience to their fathers, and also to the counsels of spiritual men. There are those who retain for relatives [Col. 0472A] and friends what they cast away from themselves, burning with utterly vain and worldly concern for their present prosperity. They are cruel, certainly, because they do not love their neighbors as themselves—cruel, I say, either toward themselves or toward their own; rather, as is truer, toward both. Therefore no one who sees that he has not left all things should wonder that he has not received the hundredfold.

LV.—That Those Ready to Return to Earthly Things Deprive Themselves of Heavenly Consolation

66. Divine consolation is precious, indeed, and is not granted at all to those who admit another consolation. Unhappy Esau, who said: “Have you only one blessing, father?” (Gen. 27:38). How much better you would have said with the Prophet: “One thing have I asked of the Lord; this will I seek” (Ps. 26:4). For he is shown unworthy of heavenly blessing who seeks it with a doubtful affection and asks with a divided intention, preparing another refuge for himself should he fail to obtain it.

“The first fratricide says, “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for.” What then? Let your soul refuse consolation if it does not merit forgiveness. Lament this alone, weep for this alone; do not even think of anything else. But now, he says, “Everyone who finds Cain will kill me” (Gen. 4:13–14). A grave loss, surely, a great disaster, if the body is destroyed when the soul has perished! Yet the unhappy man complained that he would be killed, as though it would be a great benefit if he were prevented from dying. And this came to pass: he obtained the miserable consolation he sought [Col. 0472C] and forgot the greatest desolation [variant: wrongly, “evil consolation”], for which he ought far more earnestly to have prayed and sought a remedy.

You have read something similar about Saul. After sparing the king of the Amalekites, he first seemed to entreat the holy Samuel for pardon; yet, when Samuel persisted in his sentence, he said: “Now honor me before the people.” Is this what you meant when you said, “I have sinned; pray to the Lord for me”? (1 Sam. 15:24–30). Rightly, 310, he who looked upon the heart did not spare him and had no pity on his feigned humility.

David, however, even after greater crimes, did not find God inexorable. Indeed, David had scarcely yet said, “I have sinned,” when the answer came to him: “The Lord has taken away your sin from you” (2 Sam. 12:13).

67. Thus indeed, beloved, even to this day, whoever’s mind longs after other consolations and does not utterly refuse consolation in perishable and transient things thereby surely withdraws from himself the grace of heavenly consolation. If he strove to ask, seek, and knock for it with worthy devotion, whole-hearted affection, and ardent desire, he would without doubt receive when asking, find when seeking, and have the door opened when knocking.

Otherwise, if he should perhaps—God forbid—venture upon that shameful leap of apostasy, it will be an altogether certain testimony to those who receive it that either he never left all things, or that he afterward abandoned the hundredfold which he had received. For some begin in the Spirit and, alas, are afterward consummated in the flesh. But if it is madness not to receive the hundredfold, it is rightly judged more than madness to wish to abandon it. Do you think that a man is to be pitied who, drawn away and enticed by his own desire, leaves it of his own accord, casts it away gladly, and voluntarily deserts it; who, though brought up in scarlet garments, embraces dung? Such a person has no basis for complaint, as though in his case the Lord’s word appeared void or the promise annulled. For while he left all things, he unquestionably possessed the promised blessing of the hundredfold. He argues without cause. We do not believe him more than Christ, nor do we at all consent to make a liar of him who promised.

LVI.—On the Hundredfold and Eternal Life

68. “He shall receive a hundredfold,” he says, “and shall possess eternal life.” The former is on the way; the latter is in the homeland—or rather, the latter is the homeland, and the former the way. The former is consolation in present labor; the latter the consummation of future blessedness. Thus workers in this world are accustomed to receive food while working and wages at the end; soldiers receive pay for the needs of the time, and at last a greater bounty is distributed according to the measure of their labor.

Thus too the children of Israel lacked no manna in the desert until they entered the promised land; and the Church, having sought the coming of the kingdom of heaven, asks daily for daily bread in the prayer instituted by the Savior himself. You have this twofold promise plainly expressed also in the prophet, where he says: “God will render a reward for the labors of his saints, and will lead them in a wonderful way” (Wis. 10:17). For this is the way of the Lord’s testimonies, in which another prophet testifies that he delighted as in all riches (Ps. 118:14). Why, then, children of men, will you die in unbelief?

LVII.—That This Hundredfold Is Spiritual

69. But perhaps some worldly person still says to this: “Show me the hundredfold you promise, and I will gladly leave everything.” Why should I show it? “Faith has no merit when human reasoning furnishes proof by experience” (St Gregory, Homily 26 on the Gospels). Or would you rather believe a man showing it than Truth promising it? You fail in searching with scrutiny: unless you believe, you shall not understand.

It is the hidden manna promised to the conqueror in John’s Apocalypse (Rev. 2:17). It is a new name which no one knows except the one who receives it. Some perhaps think that the present communion of saints, of possessions and likewise of wills, is here denoted by the name of the hundredfold. This itself is indeed a great consolation; but it is not so universal that it can apply to all without exception. For how many saints do we know who lacked human consolation because they voluntarily abandoned it—as anchorites—or because the violence of persecution drove them into exile—as martyrs? This hundredfold is an excellent gift, descending from above, from the Father of lights.

LVIII.—What This Hundredfold Is

70. Does not he possess all things for whom all things work together for good? Does not he have the hundredfold of all things who is filled with the Holy Spirit, who has Christ in his breast? Except that the visitation of the Paraclete Spirit and the presence of Christ are far more than a hundredfold.

“How great,” he says, “is the abundance of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you, and accomplished for those who hope in you!” (Ps. 30:20). Do you see how the holy soul pours forth remembrance of this abundance of sweetness? How, yearning to express it, it multiplies words? “How great,” it says, “is the abundance!” This hundredfold, therefore, is adoption as children, freedom and the firstfruits of the Spirit, the delights of charity, the glory of conscience, the kingdom of God that is within us—not food and drink, indeed, but righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. 14:17).

It is joy, certainly, not merely in hope of glory but also in tribulations. This is the fire which Christ desired to be intensely kindled (Luke 12:49). This is the power from on high which made Andrew embrace [variant: desire] the cross; Lawrence laugh at the executioner; and Stephen, in death, bend his knees in prayer for those stoning him. This is that peace which Christ left to his own when he gave them his peace. For “gift and peace [are] for God’s elect” (Wis. 3:9): peace, indeed, of the present [variant: wrongly, “of the present”], and the gift of the future. That peace surpasses every understanding; yet with this present gift nothing that pleases under the sun or is desired in the world can be compared. This is the grace of devotion and the anointing that teaches concerning all things: the experienced know it; the inexperienced do not know it, because no one knows except the one who receives.

LIX.—A Brief Exhortation

71. Would that the desire of the children of men might awaken here; would that even curiosity might be stirred, so that they would say in their hearts: “This saying does not seem a human invention, since the testimonies of Scripture agree with it so unanimously. If this is so, then beyond doubt we are grievously mistaken. We desire to test whether these things are so, to taste what this hidden manna tastes like, to experience what this hundredfold is, what joy in the Holy Spirit is like.”

Tomorrow his own righteousness shall answer the man who diligently seeks it. As soon as he tastes, he will see that the Lord is sweet, that he is good not merely to the soul which possesses him but also to the soul which seeks and hopes in him (Lam. 3:25). Otherwise, “Come and refute me,” says the Lord (Isa. 1:18), if everyone who leaves father, or mother, or house, or field for my name’s sake does not receive a hundredfold now in this time—and that is too little—and possess eternal life.

LX.—On Eternal Life

72. But if speech fails in commending the present hundredfold, and the narrowness of the mouth, from the abundance of the heart, closes it up, why should not even thought itself acknowledge its inadequacy before the promise of eternal life? If even one who has experienced that which is partial cannot express it, how should one who has not experienced it attempt to stammer about perfection? “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you.” For it is peace surpassing every understanding: peace beyond peace, unfailing exultation, a torrent of divine delight, a river of joy, fullness of joy.

Think whatever you will; desire whatever you can: that felicity, that eternity, that blessedness exceeds every thought and surpasses every desire. May he, who comes that we may have life and have it more abundantly, Jesus Christ our Lord, bring us to it in his mercy: he who goes before us in the blessing of sweetness and unfailingly grants us meanwhile the promised grace of the hundredfold, as consolation and remedy for this labor, lest we fail on the way, and so that, through the bestowal of present gifts, our expectation of future ones may be firm; he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through infinite ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0475]

# THE LADDER OF MONKS, OR A TREATISE ON THE MANNER OF PRAYING. (G)*

[NOTE]

This treatise is found among the works of St Augustine (now in volume VI) under the title “The Ladder of Paradise,” together with this censure of the Doctors of Louvain: “This little work is also ascribed among the works of St Bernard, although it does not seem to be his either.” In a manuscript of the Charterhouse of Cologne, however, it is attributed to Guigo (perhaps the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse?). Another little work on the same subject appears in Chifflet’s *Manual of Solitaries*, “On the Fourfold Exercise of the Cell,” under the name of another Guigo, addressed to the prior and the Carthusians of Witteham. There the four exercises of the cell are explained: the first three are the same as here—namely reading, meditation, and prayer—but the fourth is action in place of contemplation, which is preferred in the present treatise, whose title appears thus in the Cologne manuscript:

**THE LETTER OF LORD GUIGO THE CARTHUSIAN TO BROTHER GERVASE, ON THE CONTEMPLATIVE LIFE.**

[Col. 0475B]

To his beloved brother GERVASE, brother GUIGO: may you delight in the Lord.

I am bound to love you because you began to love me first; and I am compelled to reply to you because you first invited me to write by your letter. I have therefore resolved to send you some thoughts which I had devised concerning the spiritual discipline of monks, so that you—who have learned such matters better by experience than I have by treating of them—may be the judge and corrector of my thoughts.

And rightly I offer you first these beginnings of our labor, that you may gather the first fruits of a new planting. For, by laudably stealing yourself from Pharaoh’s servitude through a choice solitude, you placed yourself in the ordered battle-line of a camp; wisely grafting into an olive tree a branch skillfully cut from a wild olive.

# CHAPTER ONE. Description of the Four Stages of Spiritual Exercises.

I. Once, while I was occupied with the bodily labour of my hands, I began to think about the exercise of the spiritual person. Four spiritual steps at once presented themselves to my mind as it reflected: namely reading, meditation, prayer, and contemplation. These are the Ladder of Monks, by which they are lifted from earth to heaven: distinguished indeed by few steps, yet of immeasurable and incredible height. Its lower end rests upon the earth; its upper part [Col. 0475D] pierces the clouds and searches out the secrets of heaven. These steps are distinct both in name and number, and likewise in order and function. Whoever carefully considers their respective characteristics and offices, what each accomplishes in us, and how they differ from and excel one another, will count whatever labour or study he expends upon them brief and easy in comparison with the greatness of their usefulness and sweetness.

Reading is diligent examination of the Scriptures with concentrated attention of mind. Meditation is the studious activity of the mind, investigating, under the guidance of its own reason, knowledge of hidden truth. Prayer is the devout direction of the heart toward God, for the removal of evils and the obtaining of goods. Contemplation is the elevation of a mind held aloft toward God, tasting the joys of eternal sweetness.

## CHAPTER II. Description of the functions of the four steps.

[Col. 0476C]

2. Having therefore set forth the descriptions of the four steps, it remains to consider their functions. Reading seeks the sweetness of the blessed life; meditation finds it; prayer asks for it; contemplation tastes it. Thus the Lord himself says: “Seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). Seek by reading, and you shall find by meditation; knock by prayer, and it shall be opened to you by contemplation.

Reading places, as it were, solid food before the mouth; meditation chews and breaks it; prayer acquires its flavour; contemplation is the sweetness itself, which delights and refreshes. Reading is concerned with the bark; meditation with the fat beneath it; prayer with the petition of desire; contemplation with delight in the sweetness attained.

That this may be seen more clearly, I shall offer [Col. 0476D] one example out of many. In reading I hear: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). Behold a brief saying, yet full of sweet and manifold meaning. It has served to the soul’s nourishment, as it were, a grape; and after the soul has carefully examined it, it says within itself: “There may be some good here. I shall return to my heart and try whether perhaps I may understand and discover this purity.” For this is a precious and desirable thing, whose possessors are called blessed, to whom the vision of God—which is eternal life—is promised, and which is praised by so many testimonies of Holy Scripture.

Desiring to have this more fully explained to itself, the soul begins to chew and break apart this one saying, and places it, as it were, in a winepress. Then it rouses reason to inquire what this purity, so precious and desirable, is and how it may be possessed.

## CHAPTER III. The function of meditation.

[Col. 0477B]

3. Diligent meditation approaches, therefore; it does not remain outside or cling to the surface, but sets its foot further within. It penetrates the inner places and searches every point. It attentively considers that the saying did not declare, “Blessed are the pure in body,” but, “in heart”: for it is not enough to have hands innocent of evil deeds unless we are cleansed in mind from depraved thoughts. This is confirmed by the authority of the prophet, who says: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord? Or who shall stand in his holy place? He who is innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. 23:3–4).

It likewise considers how greatly this same prophet desired purity of heart, when he prayed: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps. 50:12); and again: “If I have looked upon iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me” (Ps. 65:18). It reflects how watchful blessed Job was in this guard, when he said: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I should not even think of a virgin” (Job 31:1). See how strictly that holy man restrained himself: he shut his eyes lest he should see vanity, lest unwittingly he should look upon what later he would unwillingly desire.

After considering these and similar matters concerning purity of heart, it begins to consider its reward: how glorious and delightful it is to behold the longed-for face of the Lord, “beautiful in form beyond the children of men”; no longer abject and lowly, without the comeliness with which his mother, the Synagogue, clothed him, but arrayed in the robe of immortality and crowned with the diadem with which his Father crowned him on the day of resurrection and glory—the day which the Lord has made. It reflects that in that vision there will be the fullness of which the prophet says: “I shall be satisfied when thy glory shall appear” [Col. 0477D] (Ps. 16:15).

Do you see how much liquid has flowed from so small a grape, how great a fire has arisen from this spark, how greatly this small lump—“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8)—has been stretched upon the anvil of meditation? Yet how much further might it be extended if one experienced in such things were to approach! For I perceive that the well is deep; but I am still an untrained beginner, and have scarcely found where to draw these few things from it.

4. Inflamed by these torches and stirred by these desires, the soul, after the alabaster jar has been broken, begins to sense the fragrance of the ointment—not yet by tasting it, but as it were by the scent of the nostrils. From this it gathers how sweet it would be to experience that purity whose meditation [Col. 0478A] it knows to be so delightful. But what shall it do? It burns with desire to possess it, yet does not find in itself how it can possess it; and the more it searches, the more it thirsts. As it applies meditation, it applies pain as well: for it thirsts for the sweetness which meditation shows to exist in purity of heart, yet it does not taste it beforehand.

For it does not belong to the reader or meditator to feel this sweetness unless it is given from above. Reading and meditation are common to the good and the evil alike. Even the philosophers of the nations discovered by the guidance of reason in what the highest true good consisted. Yet because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God (Rom. 1:21), and because they relied on their own powers, saying, “We shall magnify our tongue; our lips are our own: who is lord over us?” (Ps. 11:5), [Col. 0478B] they did not deserve to receive what they were able to see. “They became vain in their thoughts” (Rom. 1:21), and all their wisdom was swallowed up (Ps. 106:27)—the wisdom bestowed upon them by the pursuit of human learning, not by the Spirit of wisdom, who alone gives true wisdom: namely, savoury knowledge, which delights and refreshes the soul to which it clings with inestimable sweetness. Of this it is said: “Wisdom shall not enter into a malicious soul” (Wis. 1:4).

But this comes from God alone. For the Lord granted the office of baptizing to many, but reserved to himself alone the power and authority to forgive sins in baptism. Hence John said of him, distinctively and by way of special designation: “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33). So we may say of him: “This is he who gives the taste of wisdom and makes the soul savoury.” Speech, indeed, is given to many, but wisdom to few; and the Lord distributes it to whom he wills and as he wills.

## CHAPTER IV. The function of prayer.

5. But when the soul sees that it cannot by itself attain the desired sweetness of knowledge and experience, and that the more it approaches the lofty heart, the more God is exalted (Ps. 63:7–8), it humbles itself and flees to prayer, saying:

“Lord, who art seen only by the pure in heart, I have searched through reading; by meditation I have sought how true purity of heart may be possessed, so that through it I might know thee, if only in some small degree. I sought thy face, O Lord; I sought again thy face [Col. 0478D] (Ps. 26:8). Long have I meditated in my heart, and in my meditation a fire was kindled, together with a greater desire to know thee” (Ps. 38:4).

“While thou breakest for me the bread of Holy Scripture, there is great knowledge in the breaking of bread” (Luke 24:30–31); “and the more I know thee, the more I desire to know thee: no longer in the bark of the letter, but in the meaning of experience. Nor do I ask this, Lord, because of my merits, but because of thy mercy. For I confess that I am unworthy and sinful; yet ‘the little dogs also eat of the crumbs which fall from their masters’ table’” (Matt. 15:27). “Give me, Lord, the pledge of the inheritance to come—at least a drop of heavenly rain, by which I may cool my thirst; for I burn with love.”

## CHAPTER V. The function of contemplation.

[Col. 0479A]

6. By these and similar fiery utterances the soul kindles its desire; thus it displays its affection. By such incantations it calls its bridegroom. But the Lord—whose eyes are upon the righteous, and whose ears not only attend to their prayers (Ps. 33:16), but do not wait even for the prayers themselves until they have finished speaking—interrupts the course of prayer midway. He hastens to make himself present and hastens to meet the desiring soul, surrounded by the heavenly dew of sweetness and anointed with the choicest perfumes. He restores the weary soul, refreshes the hungry, enriches the dry; and causes it to forget earthly things, wonderfully strengthening, enlivening, inebriating, and making it sober through remembrance of himself.

And just as in certain carnal acts the soul is so overcome by bodily desire that it loses every use of reason and the human being becomes, as it were, wholly carnal, so, fittingly, in this heavenly contemplation carnal motions are so consumed and absorbed by the soul that in no respect does the flesh resist the spirit, and the human being becomes, as it were, wholly spiritual.

## CHAPTER VI. Signs of the Holy Spirit’s coming to the soul.

7. But, O Lord, how shall we know when thou dost these things, and what is the sign of thy coming? Are sighs and tears the witnesses and messengers of this consolation and joy? If so, this is a new antiphrasis, an unprecedented use of meaning. For what agreement has consolation with sighs, or joy with tears? Unless, indeed, these ought to be called not tears, but rather an overflowing abundance of inward dew poured down from above, and an outward cleansing of the outer person as a sign of the washing of the inner person: so that, just as in the baptism of children an outward washing signifies and represents the inward washing of the soul, so here, conversely, inward purification precedes outward washing.

O happy tears, through which inner stains are cleansed, through which the fires of sins are extinguished! “Blessed are you who mourn thus, for you shall laugh” (Matt. 5:5). In these tears, O soul, recognize thy bridegroom; embrace thy beloved. Now make thyself drunk from the torrent of his delight; suck milk and honey from the breast of his consolation. These are the wondrous little gifts and comforts which thy bridegroom has given thee: namely, groans and tears. [Col. 0479D] In these tears he gives thee drink by measure. These tears are thy bread by day and by night—bread indeed strengthening the human heart, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.

O Lord Jesus, if the tears stirred by remembrance and desire of thee are so sweet, how sweet will be the joy received from the manifest vision of thee! If it is so sweet to weep for thee, how sweet will it be to rejoice in thee! But why do we bring such secret conversations into public? Why do we attempt to express ineffable and unutterable affections in ordinary words? Those without experience do not understand such things unless they read them more clearly in the book of experience, where the anointing itself may teach them. Otherwise, the outward letter profits its reader nothing. The reading of the outward letter has little savour [Col. 0480A] unless it receives its gloss and inward meaning from the heart.

## CHAPTER VII. On the concealment of grace.

8. O soul, we have prolonged our discourse for a long time. For it was good for us to be here, with Peter and John, contemplating the bridegroom’s glory and remaining long with him; if he wished, there might be made here not two or three tents (Matt. 17:1, 4), but one, in which we might be together and delight together. But now the bridegroom says: “Let me go, for dawn has now risen; thou hast now received the light of grace and the visitation which thou didst desire.”

Therefore, once the blessing has been given, the sinew of the thigh mortified, and the name changed from Jacob to Israel (Gen. 32:25, 31), the long-desired bridegroom withdraws for a little while, swiftly gone. [Col. 0480B] He withdraws himself both from the vision described above and from the sweetness of contemplation, though he remains present in respect of governance.

## CHAPTER VIII. How the temporary concealment of grace works for our good.

9. But do not fear, O bride; do not despair; do not suppose that thou art despised if the bridegroom withdraws his face from thee for a little while. All these things work together for thy good, and thou gainest profit both from his coming and his departure. He comes to thee, and he also withdraws from thee. He comes for consolation; he withdraws for caution, lest the greatness of consolation exalt thee; lest, if the bridegroom were always with thee, thou shouldst begin to despise thy companions and attribute this continual visitation no longer to grace but to nature.

The bridegroom grants this grace to whom he wills and when he wills; it is not possessed as though by hereditary right. It is a common proverb that excessive familiarity breeds contempt. Therefore he withdraws, lest perhaps, by being too constantly present, he be despised; so that, when absent, he may be desired the more; when desired, sought the more eagerly; and when long sought, found at last with greater gratitude.

Moreover, if this consolation—which, compared with the glory to be revealed in us, is enigmatic and partial—never failed us, perhaps we would think that we had here an abiding city [Col. 0480C] and would seek the future one less earnestly. Thus we are not to reckon exile as our homeland, nor the pledge as the full price.

The bridegroom comes and withdraws in turn: now bringing consolation, now changing all our bed into infirmity. He allows us for a little while to taste how sweet he is, and before we fully feel it he withdraws himself. Thus, hovering above us as though with wings outspread, he provokes us to fly. He seems to say: “Behold, you taste a little how sweet and delightful I am; but if you wish to be fully filled with this sweetness, run after me in the fragrance of my ointments, having your hearts on high, where I am at the right hand of God the Father. There you shall see me, not through a mirror in an enigma, but face to face; and your heart shall rejoice fully, and no one shall take your joy from you.”

## CHAPTER IX. How cautiously the soul ought to conduct itself after a visitation of grace.

10. But take heed, O bride. When [Col. 0481A] the bridegroom makes himself absent, he will not go far; and though thou dost not see him, he nevertheless always sees thee, full of eyes before and behind. Thou canst never be hidden from him. He also has his messengers about thee, spirits like most shrewd spies, to see how thou conductest thyself while the bridegroom is absent, and to accuse thee before him if they discover in thee any signs of wantonness or buffoonery.

This bridegroom is jealous. If perhaps thou admit another lover, if thou strive more to please others, he will immediately depart from thee and attach himself to other young maidens. This bridegroom is fastidious; he is noble and rich, beautiful in form beyond the children of men; and therefore he deigns to have no bride but one who is beautiful. If he sees a spot or wrinkle in thee, he immediately turns away his eyes. For he can endure no uncleanness. Therefore be chaste, [Col. 0481B] be modest and humble, that thou mayest thus deserve to be visited often by thy bridegroom.

I fear that this discourse has detained us too long; but a subject both fruitful and sweet compelled me to it. I did not lengthen it of my own choice; I was drawn unwillingly by I know not what sweetness of it.

## CHAPTER X. Recapitulation of what has been said.

11. Therefore, that what has been said more diffusely may be better seen when brought together, let us gather the substance of the foregoing in a recapitulation. As was indicated in the examples above, it may be seen how the steps mentioned are joined together and precede one another not only in time but also in causation.

Reading, as it were, first presents itself as the foundation and, having supplied material, sends us on to meditation. Meditation more diligently investigates what ought to be sought and, as though digging out a treasure, finds and displays it. But because it cannot obtain it by itself, it sends us on to prayer. Prayer, raising itself to the Lord with all its strength, obtains the desirable treasure: the sweetness of contemplation. When contemplation comes, it rewards the labour of the preceding three, inebriating the thirsty soul with the heavenly dew of sweetness.

Reading, therefore, belongs to outward exercise; meditation to inward understanding; prayer to desire; contemplation surpasses every sense. The first step belongs to beginners, the second to those making progress, the third to the devout, and the fourth to the blessed.

## CHAPTER XI. Neither reading without meditation nor meditation without prayer is profitable.

[Col. 0481D]

12. These steps are so linked together and serve one another by reciprocal aid that the preceding steps, without those which follow, are of little or no benefit; while the following steps can rarely or never be attained without those which precede. What benefit is there in spending one’s time continually in reading, running through the deeds and writings of the saints, unless we also, by chewing and ruminating them, draw out their juice and, by swallowing them, convey it into the inmost parts of the heart, so that from them we may carefully consider our own condition and strive to perform the works of those whose deeds we desire to read?

But how shall we think upon these things, or how shall we be able to avoid passing, in meditation upon certain false or empty things, beyond the bounds established by the holy Fathers, unless we have first been instructed concerning such matters by reading or hearing? For hearing in some way belongs to reading. Therefore we are accustomed to say that we have read not only the books which we ourselves read, whether to ourselves or to others, but also those which we heard from teachers.

Likewise, what benefit is it to a person, if through meditation he sees what must be done, unless, by the help of prayer and the grace of God, he is strengthened to attain it? For “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17), without whom we can do nothing. Yet he performs the works in us, but not altogether without us. For “we are God’s fellow-workers,” as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 3:9). God wishes us to assist him, to open the bosom of our will to him when he comes and waits at the door, and to consent to him.

He demanded this consent from the Samaritan woman when he said: “Call thy husband” (John 4:16). It was as though he said: “I wish to pour grace into thee; do thou apply free will.” He demanded prayer from her when he said: “If thou knewest the gift of God, and who it is that saith to thee, ‘Give me to drink,’ perhaps thou wouldst have asked of him living water” (John 4:10). Hearing this, the woman, as though instructed by reading, reflected in her heart that it would be good and useful for her to have this water. Thus kindled by the desire to possess it, she turned to prayer, saying: “Lord, give me this water, that I may not thirst any more, nor come here to draw water” [Col. 0482C] (John 4:15).

Behold: hearing the Lord’s word and subsequent meditation upon it prompted her to pray. For how could she have been eager to ask unless meditation had first kindled her? Or what would preceding meditation have conferred upon her, unless the prayer which followed had obtained what meditation showed should be desired? Therefore, if meditation is to be fruitful, the devotion of prayer must follow it; contemplation’s sweetness is, as it were, the effect of this devotion.

## CHAPTER XII. How the steps aforesaid are linked to one another.

13. From these things we may gather that reading without meditation is dry; meditation without reading is erroneous; prayer without meditation is lukewarm; meditation without prayer is unfruitful; prayer with devotion obtains contemplation; and the attainment of contemplation without prayer is either rare or miraculous.

God, whose power has neither number nor limit and whose mercy is over all his works, sometimes raises up children of Abraham from stones, when he compels the hard and unwilling to consent, so that they may will; and thus, as though prodigal—as the common saying goes—he “draws an ox by its horn,” when he pours himself in unbidden. Although we read that this has sometimes happened to some, such as Paul and certain others, we nevertheless ought not, as though testing God, presumptuously to expect divine intervention. Rather, we ought to do what belongs to us: namely, read and meditate upon the law of God; pray to him that he may help our weakness and see our imperfection. He himself teaches us to do this, saying: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). For now “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12).

Behold: from the distinctions already indicated, the characteristics of the aforesaid steps may be perceived—how they are joined together and what each accomplishes in us.

14. Blessed is the person whose mind, free from other business, always desires to occupy itself with these four steps; who, selling all that he has, buys that field in which the desirable treasure lies hidden: namely, leisure and the seeing of how sweet the Lord is. Having practised in the first step, watchful in the second, devout in the third, and raised above himself in the fourth, he shall ascend by these ascents, which he has arranged in his heart, [Col. 0483B] from virtue to virtue until he sees the God of gods in Zion.

Blessed is the one to whom it is granted to remain, even for a short time, upon this highest step, who can truly say: “Behold, I feel the Lord’s grace; behold, with Peter and John I contemplate his glory upon the mountain; behold, with Jacob I am often delighted by Rachel’s embraces.” But let such a person take heed lest, after this contemplation by which he has been raised to the heavens, he fall by disordered collapse into the abyss; and lest after the vision of God he turn back to the wanton acts of the world and the enticements of the flesh.

When, however, the weak vision of the human mind cannot bear for longer the illumination of true light, let it gently and orderly descend to one of the three steps by which it had ascended; and let it remain alternately now in one, now in another, according to the measure of free will and as place and time require—now so much nearer to God as it is farther from the first step.

But alas for fragile and miserable human nature! By the guidance of reason and testimonies of Scripture, we clearly see that the perfection of a good life is contained in these four steps, and that the exercise of the spiritual person ought to be occupied with them. Yet who is there who holds to this path of life? Who is this person? “And we shall praise him.” Many have the will close at hand, but few the accomplishment. Would that we were among those few.

## CHAPTER XIII. Four causes which draw us away from these four steps.

[Col. 0483D]

15. There are four causes which commonly draw us away from these steps: unavoidable necessity, the usefulness of honourable activity, human weakness, and worldly vanity. The first is excusable; the second tolerable; the third pitiable; the fourth culpable. For those whom this last cause draws away from a holy purpose, it would have been better not to know the glory of God than, after knowing it, to turn back.

What excuse, indeed, will such a person have for sin? May not the Lord justly say to him: “What ought I to have done for thee, and have not done?” (Isa. 5:4). “Thou wast not, and I created thee. Thou didst sin and make thyself the devil’s slave, and I redeemed thee. Thou didst run with the ungodly in the course of the world, and I chose thee. I had given thee grace in my sight and wished to make my dwelling with thee; but thou hast despised me. Thou hast cast not only my words but my very self behind thee, and hast walked after thy lusts.”

But, O good God, gentle and mild, sweet friend, wise counsellor, mighty helper: how inhuman and rash is one who rejects thee, who drives so humble and gentle a guest from his heart! O how unhappy and ruinous an exchange: to reject one’s Creator and receive depraved and harmful thoughts! To hand over to unclean thoughts and sins, for their trampling, that secret chamber of the Holy Spirit—the secret place of the heart—which only a little before had been intent upon heavenly joys!

The bridegroom’s footprints still burn in the heart, and adulterous desires are already admitted! It is ill-fitting and shameful that ears which lately heard words that it is not lawful for a human being to speak should so quickly bend to hear tales and slanders; that eyes lately baptized with sacred tears should suddenly turn to behold vanities; that the tongue which lately sang the sweet wedding-song, which by its fiery and persuasive utterances reconciled the bride with the bridegroom and brought her into the wine-cellar, should again turn to empty speech, buffooneries, contriving deceits, and slanders.

Far be it from us, Lord! But if perhaps through human weakness we slip into such things, let us not therefore despair; rather, let us again have recourse to the merciful Physician, who “raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dunghill” (Ps. 112:7), and who does not will the death of the sinner. He will again cure and heal us.

16. It is now time to bring the letter to an end. Let us therefore pray to God that in the present life he may mitigate for us the hindrances which draw us away from his contemplation, and in the life to come may wholly remove them; that through the steps described above he may lead us from virtue to virtue, until we see the God of gods in Zion. There the elect will receive the sweetness of divine contemplation not drop by drop nor intermittently, but, filled without ceasing by the torrent of delight, [Col. 0484D] will possess joy which no one shall take from them, and unchangeable peace—peace in perfect unity.

Therefore, my brother Gervase [Note: [Col. 0483] The manuscript reads thus, not “Godfrey,” as it has hitherto been read.], if it is ever granted thee from above to ascend to the height of the steps described, remember me; and pray for me when all is well with thee, so that curtain may draw curtain, and he who hears may say: “Come.”

[Col. 0485]

# MOST DEVOUT MEDITATIONS ON KNOWLEDGE OF THE HUMAN CONDITION. (G)

[NOTE.]

319 In almost all manuscripts these are attributed to Bernard, and indeed are often entitled “On the Inner Person.” Nevertheless, they are found in Hugh of St Victor under the title “Book Four on the Soul,” although they do not appear to be his either. In the Dunensis manuscript they bear this heading: “A useful treatise from the words of Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and other Fathers, On the Inner Person and how it finds God.”

Certainly, sayings of Ambrose, Augustine, and Boethius—not to mention Seneca—are several times cited in these Meditations. They are more than once praised under Bernard’s name in the *Bernardinus*, or the very ancient book *Flowers from Bernard*, namely in book 5, chapters 10, 11, 13, 17, 44, and 48. Yet few passages from Bernard’s commonly received works are adduced in these Meditations. They are neither unworthy of Bernard nor, in our view, his: both because of the difference of style and because of the citations of poems, unfamiliar in Bernard; to say nothing of that confession of sins, beginning at chapter 9, which is very different from that found in Bernard’s treatise *On the Steps of Humility*, chapter 18.

## CHAPTER I. On the dignity of the human being.

[Col. 0485A]

1. Many know many things and do not know themselves. They examine others and abandon themselves. They seek God through outward things, abandoning their own inward parts, where God is more inward than they are. Therefore let me return from outward things to inward, and ascend from lower things to higher, so that I may know whence I come or whither I go; what I am and from what I am; and thus, through knowledge of myself, may be able to attain knowledge of God. For the more I advance in knowledge of myself, the more nearly I approach knowledge of God.

According to the inner person, I find three things in my mind through which I remember, behold, and desire God. These three are memory, understanding, and will or love. By memory I recollect; by understanding I contemplate; by will I embrace. When I remember God, I find him in my memory, and in it I delight concerning him and in him, according as he deigns to grant this to me.

By understanding I contemplate what God is in himself; what he is in angels, in saints, in creatures, and in human beings. In himself he is incomprehensible, because he is beginning and end: beginning without a beginning, end without an end. From myself I understand how incomprehensible God is, since I cannot understand even myself, whom he made. In angels he is desirable, because they desire to look upon him. In saints he is delightful, because the blessed rejoice continually in him. In creatures he is wonderful, because he creates all things powerfully, governs them wisely, and orders them graciously. [Col. 0485C] In human beings he is lovable, because he is their God and they are his people. He dwells in them as in his temple, and they are his temple. He does not disdain individuals or the whole body. Whoever remembers, understands, and loves him is with him.

2. We ought to love him because he first loved us and made us in his image and likeness, a gift which he did not will to bestow upon any other creature. We were made in God’s image—that is, for understanding and knowledge of the Son, through whom we understand and know the Father and have access to him.
