So great is the kinship between us and the Son of God that he himself is the image of God, while we were made in his image. The likeness itself bears witness to this kinship, since we were made not only in his image but also in his likeness.

Therefore that which is in the image must accord with the image and must not share the name of image in vain. Let us then represent his image in ourselves in the desire for peace, the contemplation of truth, and the love of charity. Let us keep him in memory, bear him in conscience, and venerate him as present everywhere. For our mind is his image precisely because it is capable of him [Col. 0486B] and can partake of him. It is not his image because the mind remembers, understands, and loves itself, but because it can remember, understand, and love him by whom it was made. When it does this, it itself becomes wise.

For nothing resembles that highest Wisdom so much as the rational mind, which consists in that ineffable Trinity through memory, understanding, and will. But it cannot abide in that Trinity unless it remembers, understands, and loves him. Let it therefore remember God, in whose image it was made; let it understand, love, and worship him, with whom it can always be blessed.

Blessed is the soul with whom God finds rest and in whose tabernacle he rests. Blessed is she who can say: “He who created me rested in my tabernacle” (Ecclus. 24:12). For he will not be able to deny her the rest of heaven.

3. Why, then, do we abandon ourselves and seek God in these outward things, when he is with us, if we are willing to be with him? Truly, he is with us and within us, but still through faith, until we deserve to see through direct vision. “Christ dwells through faith in our hearts,” says the Apostle (Eph. 3:17): for Christ is in faith, faith in the mind, mind in the heart, and heart in the breast.

Therefore through faith I remember God as Creator; I worship him as Redeemer; I await him as Saviour. I believe that I shall see him in all creatures and possess him in myself; and, what is ineffably more joyful and blessed than all these, know him in himself. For to know the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit is eternal life, perfect blessedness, and supreme delight. Eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the human heart how great is the brightness, sweetness, and delight awaiting us in that vision, when we shall see God face to face: he who is the light of those enlightened, the rest of those who labour, the homeland of those returning, the life of the living, and the crown of those who conquer.

Thus I find in my mind a certain image of that highest Trinity. To remember, behold, and love that supreme Trinity—so that I may remember it, delight in it, embrace it, and contemplate it—I ought to direct all that I live toward it. The mind is the image of God, in which are these three things: memory, understanding, and will. To memory we attribute everything we know, even when we are not thinking about it. To understanding we attribute everything true that we discover by thought, which we also commit to memory. To the will we attribute everything which, once known and understood, we desire as good and true.

Through memory we are like the Father; through understanding, the Son; through will, the Holy Spirit. Nothing in us is so like the Holy Spirit as the will, or love, or charity—which is the higher form of will. For charity is God’s gift, such that no gift of God is more excellent. For charity which is from God, and is God, is properly called the Holy Spirit, through whom “the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts” [Col. 0487C] (Rom. 5:5), and through whom the whole Trinity dwells within us.

## CHAPTER II. On the misery of the human being, the horror of death, and the severity of the supreme Judge.

4. According to the outward man, I come from those parents who made me condemned before they made me born. Sinners begot a sinner in their sin and nourished him from sin. Wretches brought a wretch into this misery of light. From them I have nothing but misery and sin, and this corruptible body which I bear. Yet I hasten toward those who have departed hence through death of the body. When I look upon their tombs, [Col. 0487D] I find in them nothing but ash and worms, stench and horror. What I am, they were; and what they are, I shall be. What am I? A human being made from liquid moisture. For at the moment of conception I was conceived from human seed; then that foam, coagulating and growing a little, became flesh. Afterwards, weeping and wailing, I was delivered over to the exile of this world; and behold, now I die full of iniquities and abominations. Soon, very soon, I shall be presented before the strict Judge, to render an account of my deeds. Woe to wretched me when that day of judgment comes and the books are opened in which all my acts and thoughts will be recited, to be presented to the Lord! Then, with head bowed in shame at my evil conscience, I shall stand trembling and anxious before the Lord in judgment, [Col. 0488A] recalling the crimes I have committed. And when it is said of me, “Behold the man and his works,” I shall bring before my eyes all my offences and sins. For by a certain divine power it will come about that each person’s good or evil deeds are recalled to memory and seen with wondrous swiftness by the mind’s gaze, so that knowledge may accuse or excuse conscience, and thus both each individual and all together may be judged.

> Each shall pass judgment on his own deeds,  
> And all the secret things of all shall lie open to all.

For what we are now ashamed to confess will then be made known to everyone; and whatever we now conceal by flattery or pretence, the avenging flame will there burn up entirely.

> Fierce fire everywhere will reign with its reins unbroken.

And the longer God waits for us to amend ourselves, [Col. 0488B] the more strictly he will judge us if we neglect to do so.

5. Why, then, do we so greatly desire this life, in which the longer we live, the more we sin? The longer life is, the more numerous is guilt. For evils increase daily, and good things are taken away. A person is continually changed by prosperity and adversity, and does not know when he will die. For just as a glittering star races swiftly through heaven and suddenly fails; and just as a spark of fire is suddenly extinguished and reduced to ash:

> So this life is seen to be brought swiftly to its end.

For while a person willingly and most pleasantly lingers in the world, and thinks that he will live long,

> And makes many arrangements for deeds to be done over a long time,

[Col. 0488C] he is suddenly snatched away into death, and his soul is unexpectedly taken from the body. Yet the soul is separated from the body with great fear and great pains. For angels come to take it, to lead it before the tribunal of the fearful Judge; and then, remembering its evil and most wicked deeds, which it performed day and night, it trembles and seeks to flee them, asking for a delay and saying: “Give me even the space of one hour.” Then the deeds, as if speaking together, will say: “You performed us; we are your works. We shall not leave you, but shall always be with you; we shall go with you to judgment.” The vices also will accuse it of many and manifold crimes, and will produce many false testimonies against it, although true testimonies [Col. 0488D] would sufficiently serve for its condemnation. The demons, moreover, will terrify it with dreadful faces and a horrible appearance. They will pursue and seize it in immense fury, seeking, most terribly and horribly, to hold and possess it—unless there is one who rescues it. Then the soul, finding the eyes, mouth, and other bodily senses closed, through which it was accustomed to go out and take delight in external things, will return into itself. Seeing itself alone and naked, shaken by immense horror, it will fail within itself in despair and collapse beneath itself; and because through love of the world and 322 pleasure of the flesh it had abandoned the love of God, miserable as it is, it will be abandoned by God at the hour of such great necessity and handed over to demons to be tormented in hell.

8. Thus the sinner’s soul, on a day it does not know and [Col. 0489A] at an hour it does not know, is seized by death and separated from the body; and it goes forth full of miseries, trembling and grieving. Since it has no excuse that it can offer for its sins, it wastes away and is terrified to appear before God. It is shaken by immense horror and driven about by manifold storms of thought when the dissolution of the flesh presses upon it and, all other things having been removed from its midst, it considers itself and the end it is approaching; and after a little while it finds that which can never be changed for eternity. It plainly considers how strict the eternal Judge comes, and what account it can render of its life before the severity of such justice. For even if it has avoided all the deeds it was able to recognize, it nevertheless fears more greatly, when it is to come before the strict Judge, those things which it does not recognize within itself. [Col. 0489B] Its dread increases when it considers that it could in no way pass through the course of this life without fault; nor even is that which it lived commendably free of some guilt, if it is judged apart from mercy. For who can consider how many evils we commit in the moments of time, and how many good things we neglect to do? For just as sin is the perpetration of evil, so offence is the abandonment of good. It is indeed a grave loss when we neither do good nor think good thoughts, but permit our heart to wander through empty and useless things. Yet it is exceedingly difficult to restrain the heart and guard it against unlawful thought. It is also exceedingly difficult to manage earthly occupations without sins. Therefore no one can judge and comprehend himself perfectly; but, occupied by many thoughts, [Col. 0489C] one remains in some way unknown even to oneself, so as not to know at all what one endures. Therefore, as departure presses near, one is frightened by a more searching fear: for even if one remembers never having neglected the things one knew, one nevertheless fears the things one does not know.

## Chapter III. On the dignity of the soul and the worthlessness of the body

7. O soul, marked with the image of God, adorned with his likeness, betrothed by faith, endowed with the Spirit, redeemed by blood, numbered with the angels, capable of blessedness, heir of goodness, participant in reason: what have you to do with the flesh, from which you suffer these things? Because of the flesh, other people’s sins are charged to you, and your acts of righteousness are reckoned as a menstrual cloth (Isa. 64:6); and you [Col. 0489D] yourself are reduced to nothing and counted as though nothing and emptiness. For the flesh, with which you have such great fellowship, is nothing else than foam made into flesh and clothed in fragile beauty; but it will become a wretched and decaying corpse, food for worms. For however much it is cultivated, it is always flesh. If you carefully consider what proceeds from its mouth and nostrils and its other bodily passages, you have never seen anything viler than a dung heap. If you wished to enumerate its individual miseries—how laden it is with sins, entangled in vices, itching with desires, occupied with passions, polluted with delusions, always prone to evil and inclined toward every vice—you would find it full of every shame and disgrace. Because of the flesh, man has become like vanity (Ps. 143:4), because from it he has drawn the vice of concupiscence, [Col. 0490A] by which he is held captive and bent down so that he may love vanity and work iniquity.

8. Consider, human being, what you were before birth, what you are from birth until death, and what you will be after this life. Certainly there was a time when you did not exist. Afterwards, formed from vile matter and wrapped in a most worthless cloth, you were nourished in your mother’s womb by menstrual blood, and your garment was the placental membrane [variant: a fur garment].

> Thus clothed and adorned, you came forth among us;  
> Yet you do not remember how vile your origin is.
>
> Beauty, popular favor, the ardor of youth, and wealth  
> Have stolen from you the knowledge of what a human being is.

A human being is nothing but foul semen, a sack [Col. 0490B] of excrement, food for worms.

> After the human being comes the worm; after the worm, stench and horror.  
> Thus every human being is turned into a non-human being.

323 Why then are you proud, human being, when you consider that you were vile seed and clotted blood in the womb; then exposed to the miseries and sin of this life; and afterwards destined to be a worm and food for worms in the tomb? Why are you proud, dust and ash, whose conception is guilt, whose birth is misery, whose life is punishment, and whose death is anguish?

> Why is a human being proud, whose conception is guilt,  
> Whose birth is punishment, whose life is toil, and who must die?

Why do you fatten and adorn your flesh with costly things, though worms will devour it in the tomb after a few days; while you do not adorn your soul with good [Col. 0490C] works, though it is to be presented in heaven before God and his angels? Why do you despise your soul and set the flesh before it? For the mistress to serve as a slave and the slave to rule as mistress is a great perversion. Indeed, this whole world cannot be valued at the price of a single soul. For God did not choose to give his own soul for the whole world, as he gave it for the human soul. Therefore the soul’s price is higher, since it could be redeemed only by Christ’s blood. What exchange, then, will you give for your soul, you who give it away for nothing? Did not the Son of God, while he was in the Father’s bosom, descend from royal seats for its sake, in order to free it from the devil’s power? When he saw it entangled in the cords of sins and on the very point of being handed over to demons for condemnation to everlasting death, he wept over it, [Col. 0490D] though it did not know how to weep for itself. Nor did he merely weep: he even allowed himself to be killed, that he might redeem it at the precious price of his blood.

> Look, mortal: such a victim is given for you.

9. Recognize, human being, how noble your soul is and how grievous were its wounds, for which it was necessary that Christ the Lord should be wounded. If these were not unto death, and everlasting death, the Son of God would never die to remedy them. Do not, then, despise your soul’s suffering, for you see such great compassion shown to it by such great Majesty. He shed tears for you; wash your bed also every night with compunction of heart and constant tears. He shed his blood; [Col. 0491A] shed yours as well by daily affliction of the body. If you cannot lay it down once for Christ, at least lay it down in a certain gentler but longer martyrdom. Do not attend to what the flesh wants, but to what the spirit demands. For it will then be glorious when it returns to its God—provided, however, that it carries with it no sin from the body and has washed away every defilement. But if you say, “This saying is hard; I cannot despise the world and hate my flesh,” tell me: where are the lovers of the world who were with us a short time ago? Nothing of them remains except ashes and worms. Consider carefully what they are or what they were. They were human beings like you: they ate, drank, laughed, passed their days in prosperity, and in a moment went down to hell (Job 21:13). Here [Col. 0491B] their flesh is assigned to worms, and there their soul to fires, until they are again bound together in an unhappy union and wrapped in everlasting flames—those who were companions in vices. For one punishment binds those whom one love has bound in sin. What did empty glory, brief joy, worldly power, fleshly pleasure, false riches, a great household, and evil desire profit them? Where are laughter, jesting, boastfulness, and arrogance? From so great a joy, what grief! After so slight a pleasure, what grievous misery! From that exultation they fell into great misery, a great ruin, and great torments.

10. Whatever happened to them can happen to you, because you are human: a human from earth, mud from mud. You are from the earth, you live from the earth, and you will return to the earth [Col. 0491C] when that last day comes—which will come suddenly, and perhaps will be today. It is certain that you will die; but it is uncertain when, how, or where. Since death awaits you everywhere, you too, if you are wise, will await it everywhere. If you follow the flesh, you will be punished in the flesh; if you delight in the flesh, you will be tormented in the flesh. If you seek luxurious clothing, then in place of your clothing’s adornment moths will be spread beneath you and worms will be your covering (Isa. 14:11). For God’s justice can judge nothing other than what our deeds deserve. Whoever loves the world more than God, the age more than the cloister, gluttony more than abstinence, lust more than chastity, follows the devil and will go with him into eternal 324 punishment. [Col. 0491D] What mourning, do you suppose, what lamentation and sorrow there will be when the wicked are separated from the company of the saints and from the vision of God, and, handed over to the power of demons, go with them into eternal fire, where they will always remain without end in lamentation and groaning! Exiled far from the blessed homeland of paradise, they will be tormented in everlasting Gehenna, never to see light and never to obtain relief, but to be tortured in hell through thousands upon thousands of years, never to be freed from there—where neither the one who torments ever grows weary nor the one tormented ever dies. For the fire there consumes in such a way as always to preserve; the torments are inflicted in such a way as always to be renewed. Each person will bear the punishment of Gehenna in proportion to the quality of his guilt, and those guilty of like sins will be joined with their like [Col. 0492A] to be tormented. Nothing else will be heard there but weeping and lamentation, groaning and howling, sorrows and gnashing of teeth; nor will anything else be seen there but worms, the ghostly faces of tormentors, and the most hideous monsters of demons.

> Cruel worms will bite the inmost parts of the heart:  
> Here pain, there terror, groaning, stupefaction, and dreadful fear.

And the wretched will burn in eternal fire for ever and beyond. They will be tortured in the flesh by fire, in the spirit by the worm of conscience. There will be intolerable pain, horrible fear, incomparable stench, and death of soul and body without hope of pardon or mercy. Yet they will die so as always to live, and live so as always to die. Thus the sinner’s soul is either tormented in hell for sins [Col. 0492B] or placed in paradise for good merits. Let us now therefore choose one of two things: either to be always tormented with the wicked or to rejoice perpetually with the saints. For good and evil, life and death, are set before us, so that we may stretch out our hand to whichever we wish. If torments do not frighten us, let rewards at least invite us.

## Chapter IV. On the reward of the heavenly homeland

11. The reward is to see God, to live with God, to live from God, to be with God, to be in God, who will be all in all; to possess God, who is the highest good. And where the highest good is, there are highest happiness, highest delight, true liberty, perfect [Col. 0492C] love, eternal security, and secure eternity; there are true joy, full knowledge, every beauty, and every blessedness.

> There are peace, devotion, goodness, light, virtue, honor,  
> Joys, gladness, sweetness, everlasting life,  
> Glory, praise, rest, love, and sweet concord.

Thus a human being will be blessed with God, in whose conscience no sin has been found. He will see God according to his desire, possess him for delight, and enjoy him in joy. He will flourish in eternity, shine in truth, and rejoice in goodness. As he will possess the eternity of abiding, so will he possess ease of knowing and the happiness of rest. For he will be a citizen of that holy city, whose citizens are angels, whose temple is God the Father, whose splendor is his Son, and whose love is the Holy Spirit. O [Col. 0492D] heavenly city: secure dwelling, fertile and spacious homeland, containing everything delightful; a people without complaint, peaceful inhabitants, people lacking nothing! How glorious are the things said of you, city of God! “The dwelling of all who rejoice is in you” (Ps. 86:3, 7). All rejoice in joy and exultation; all delight in God, whose appearance is beautiful, whose countenance is lovely, whose speech is sweet. He is delightful to behold, pleasant to possess, sweet to enjoy. He is pleasing through himself and sufficient through himself: sufficient for merit and sufficient for reward. Nothing outside him is sought, because in him is found everything that is desired. It is always pleasing to behold him, always to possess him, always to delight in him and enjoy him. In him the intellect is made bright and the [Col. 0493A] affection purified, for knowing and loving truth. And this is the whole good of human beings: namely, to know and love their Creator.

12. What madness, then, drives us to thirst for the wormwood of vices, pursue the shipwreck of this world, suffer the misfortune of a slipping life, endure the dominion of impious tyranny, rather than hasten to the blessedness of the saints, the fellowship of 325 angels, the festival of heavenly joy, and the delight of the contemplative life, so that we may enter into the powers of the Lord and see those overflowing riches of goodness? There we shall have leisure and see how sweet the Lord is, and how great is the abundance of his sweetness. We shall see the beauty of glory, the splendor of the saints, and the honor of royal power. We shall know [Col. 0493B] the power of the Father, the wisdom of the Son, and the most gracious mercy of the Holy Spirit; and so we shall have knowledge of that highest Trinity. Now we see bodies by means of the body, and we behold images even of bodies through the spirit; but then we shall see the Trinity itself by the pure gaze of the mind. O blessed vision: to see God in himself, to see him in us, and ourselves in him, in blessed delight and delightful blessedness! Whatever we desire, we shall possess entirely, desiring nothing more; and whatever we see, we shall love, blessed by that very love—blessed by the sweetness of love and the pleasantness of contemplation. This will be the summit of that contemplation; this will be the summit of that happiness: sincere divinity will be understood in its pure being, and the incomprehensible Trinity will be comprehended in it. The mysteries of divinity will lie open; [Col. 0493C] God will be seen and loved; and this vision and delight, filling and satisfying the whole human heart, will be the complete fulfillment of blessedness. All will have one tongue: unwearied jubilation; one affection: eternal love. Truth will be made manifest, love will be fulfilled, and there will be an integral fellowship [perhaps: satiety, “full satisfaction”] of body and soul. Glorified humanity will shine like the sun; the fellowship of flesh and spirit will be peaceful and harmonious. Angels and human beings will share one joy, one conversation, one banquet. Love will not grow weak, nor affection melt away. With every good thing present, there will be no distress of delay, because the beatifying presence of the divine Majesty will be all things to all, and will be the common omnipotence, wisdom, [Col. 0493D] peace, justice, and understanding of all. In that peace there will be no diversity of languages, but a peaceful and harmonious concord of character and affection. In the torrent of that delight, full satisfaction will desire nothing further; so great will be the happiness. For there will be a fullness of happiness: surpassing glory and overflowing joy.

13. But who is fit for these things? Certainly: the true penitent, the good and obedient person, the lovable companion, the faithful servant. The true penitent is always in labor and sorrow: he grieves for the past and labors to guard against the future. For true repentance is to grieve for sins without interruption of time. Thus he laments what he has done, so that he does not commit deeds to be lamented. He is a mocker, not a true penitent, who still does what requires repentance. If, therefore, you wish to be a true penitent, cease from sin and [Col. 0494A] do not sin further; for repentance is empty when subsequent guilt defiles it. Every good and obedient person surrenders both his willing and his unwilling, so that he may say: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 107:2): ready to do whatever you command, ready to obey your nod without delay, ready to devote itself to you, to serve neighbors, to guard myself, and to rest in contemplation of heavenly things. The lovable companion is helpful to everyone and burdensome to no one. He is helpful to all because he is devout toward God, kind toward his neighbor, and sober toward the world: servant of the Lord, companion of his neighbor, master of the world. He has higher things for joy, equals for fellowship, and lower things for service. He burdens no one, but brings lower things into service of the middle things and to the honor of [Col. 0494B] the higher: following the higher, drawing the lower; possessed by the former, possessing the latter. The faithful servant is faithful in contemplating God and guarding himself. Apply, then, first every diligence to your own guarding. Next, understanding that by your own effort you can never suffice to guard yourself, implore divine clemency. Likewise, in order to contemplate within yourself the good, pleasing, and perfect will of your Creator, pray for angelic protection, and ask the patronage over you of all those reigning with Christ. Run to each one, supplicate each one, and cry to all together, saying: “Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends” (Job 19:21). Receive your fugitive—yet your brother, yet your kinsman through the blood of the Redeemer. Behold, a poor man stands at [Col. 0494C] the door, crying out and knocking. Open to the one knocking, and lead him to the King, so that, prostrate before him, I may set forth 326 to him all the miseries and necessities that I suffer. Finally, entrust your heart, with all its offspring, wholly to your superior. Let no sin remain in it that is not erased by pure confession. Set Jesus Christ also over your heart like a seal. For when Christ guards the door of the heart and is its doorkeeper, so that all the households of the heart enter and depart through him, then thousands upon thousands of angels stand watch at the gates of the external senses; and no foreigner dares to break through those terrible ranks, because of reverence for the doorkeeper and the angels’ guardianship.

## Chapter V. On daily examination of oneself

[Col. 0494D]

14. As a searching investigator of your integrity, examine your life in daily scrutiny. Consider carefully how much you advance or how much you fall short; what kind of person you are in conduct and what in affections; how like or unlike God you are; how near or how far—not by intervals of place, but by dispositions of character. Strive to know yourself. How much better and more praiseworthy you are if you know yourself than if, neglecting yourself, you knew the courses of the stars, the powers of herbs, human constitutions, the natures of animals, and possessed all knowledge of heavenly and earthly things. Restore yourself, then, to yourself; and if not always, at least often; if not often, at least [Col. 0495A] sometimes. Rule your affections, direct your actions, correct your steps. Let nothing remain undisciplined within you. Set all your transgressions before your eyes. Place yourself before yourself as before another person; and thus lament yourself. Weep for the iniquities and sins by which you offended God. Tell him your miseries; show him the wickedness of your adversaries. And when you have worn yourself away before him in tears, I beg you, remember me.

15. For ever since I came to know you, I have loved you in Christ; and I carry remembrance of you to that place where even an unlawful thought merits punishment, and an honorable one earns reward. For when I stand, a sinner though a priest, at God’s altar, memory of you accompanies me. You in turn will repay me if you love me and make me a participant in your prayers. There I desire to be present with you in remembrance, where you pour out devout prayers before God for yourself and those close to you. [Col. 0495B] Do not wonder that I said “present.” For if you love me, and love me because I am the image of God, I am as present to you as you are to yourself. For whatever you are substantially, I am. Every rational soul is the image of God. Therefore whoever seeks God’s image in himself seeks his neighbor as much as himself; and whoever finds it by seeking it in himself recognizes it in every human being. For the sight of the soul is understanding. If, therefore, you see yourself, you see me, who am nothing other than you. And if you love God, you love me as God’s image; and I, by loving God, love you. Thus, while we seek one thing and tend toward one thing, we are always present to one another—but in God, in whom [Col. 0495C] we love one another.

## Chapter VI. On the attention to be maintained during prayer

16. When you enter church to pray or chant psalms, leave outside the tumult of your shifting thoughts, and forget entirely the care of outward things, so that you may attend to God alone. For it cannot happen that a person speaks with God while, even in silence, he converses with the whole world. Attend, then, to him who attends to you; hear him speaking to you, so that he may hear you speaking to him. This will happen if you stand to perform divine praises with due reverence and attentiveness, carefully attending to every word of Holy Scripture. I say this not because I do these things, but because I would wish to do them, repent that I have not done them, and am grieved that I do not do them. But you, to whom greater grace has been granted, bend the Lord’s merciful ears toward yourself through vows and devout prayers; plead with him mercifully through tears and sighs for your transgressions; and in spiritual songs praise and glorify him in all his works. For nothing is more pleasing for the heavenly citizens to behold; nothing is offered more joyfully to the highest King, as he himself testifies: “A sacrifice of praise will honor me” (Ps. 49:23). O how happy you would be if, with spiritual eyes, [Col. 0495D] 327 you could once behold how the princes go before, joined to those who sing psalms amid maidens playing tambourines! (Ps. 67:26.) You would undoubtedly see with what care and with what rejoicing they take part with those who sing, stand by those who pray, are present to those who meditate, preside over [Col. 0496A] those who rest, foresee, and make provision. For the heavenly powers love their fellow citizens, and for those who receive the inheritance of salvation they rejoice diligently, strengthen, instruct, protect, and provide for everything. They all desire our coming, because they expect from us the restoration of the ruins of their city. They carefully seek and gladly hear good news about us. They eagerly move to and fro as mediators between us and God, faithfully carrying our groans to him and most devoutly bringing his grace back to us. They will not disdain to be our companions, since they have already become our ministers. We made them rejoice when we were converted to repentance. Let us hasten, then, to fill up their joy concerning us. Woe to you, whoever [Col. 0496B] you are, who desire to return to vomit and go back to mud. Do you think that you will have them appeased in judgment, when you wish to deprive them of so great and so hoped-for a joy? They rejoiced when we came to the religious life, as over persons whom they saw called back from the very gate of hell. But what will it be then if they see returning from the very door of paradise and going backward those who already had one foot in heaven? For though their bodies are below, their hearts are above.

17. Let us run, therefore, not with bodily steps, but with the affections of the mind, with desires, with sighs; because not only angels but the Creator of angels awaits us. God the Father awaits us as children and heirs, to establish us over all his good things. The Son of God awaits us as brothers and co-heirs, [Col. 0496C] to offer to God the Father the fruit of his birth and the price of his blood. The Holy Spirit awaits us; for he is the love and kindness in which we were predestined from eternity, and there is no doubt that he wishes his predestination to be fulfilled. Therefore, since the entire heavenly court awaits and desires us, let us desire it with all the desire we can. Whoever does not strongly desire to see it will come to it with great shame and embarrassment. But whoever lives in it through continual prayer and constant thought will depart hence in security and be received into it with great joy. Wherever you are, pray within yourself. If you are far from an oratory, do not seek a place, for you yourself are the place. If you are in bed or elsewhere, pray, and there is the temple. Pray frequently, and with the body bent, let the mind be raised to God. For just as there is no moment in which a person does not use or enjoy God’s goodness and mercy, so there should be no moment in which he does not hold God present in memory.

18. But you say: “I pray every day and see no fruit from my prayer; I return just as I approached it. No one answers me, no one speaks, no one gives me anything; I seem to have labored in vain.” Thus speaks human foolishness, failing to heed what Truth promises concerning this matter, saying: “Amen I say to you: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you receive it, and it will be yours” (Matt. 21:22; Mark 11:24). [Col. 0497A] Do not, then, despise your prayer, because he to whom you pray does not despise it; rather, before it leaves your mouth, he commands it to be written in his book. And we must without doubt hope for one of two things: either that he will give us what we ask or what he knows to be more useful for us. Think, therefore, the best things you can of God, and the worst things you can of yourself. You ought to believe more concerning him than you can think. Count every time in which you do not think of God as lost. For every other thing is alien to us; time alone is ours. Therefore be at leisure, and wherever you are, be your own. Do not give yourself over to things, but lend yourself to them. Wherever you stand, cast your thoughts toward God and turn over something salutary in your mind. [Col. 0497B] Every place, indeed, is suitable for meditation.

19. Therefore, gathering your mind with all your power, dwell freely with yourself; and, walking in the spaciousness of your heart, provide there a great furnished upper room for Christ. For the wise person’s mind is always with God. We must always 328 have before our eyes him through whom we exist, live, and understand. For we have him as author in order that we may exist; we ought also to have him as teacher in order that we may be wise; and as giver of inward sweetness in order that we may be blessed. In this we recognize his image—that is, the image of the highest Trinity—in ourselves. For as he exists and is wise and good, so too, according to our measure, we exist, know that we exist, and love both to exist and to know. [Col. 0497C] Use yourself, therefore, as God’s temple, because of that in you which is like God. For the highest honor given to God is to reverence and imitate him. You imitate him if you are devout. For a devout mind is God’s holy temple, and its heart is the best altar. You reverence him if you are merciful, just as he is merciful to all. For a sacrifice acceptable to God is to do good to all for God’s sake. Do everything as a son of God, so that you may be worthy of him who deemed you worthy to be called a son. In all that you do, recognize that God is present. Take care, then, that neither your sight nor your thought lingers on that which gives evil pleasure. Do not say or do what is unlawful, even if it pleases you; and do not offend God by any act or gesture, for he is present everywhere and sees whatever [Col. 0497D] you do. You need great vigilance, because you live before the eyes of the Judge who sees all things. Yet you are always safe with him, if you make yourself such that he deigns to be with you. If he is not with you through grace, he is present through vengeance. But woe to you if he is with you in that way. Indeed, woe to you if he is not present with you in that way. For God is angry with the person whom he does not chastise while sinning; for the person whom he does not correct by chastisement, he condemns in the future.

## Chapter VII. On guarding the heart and the practice of prayer

20. It is certain that death threatens you everywhere. The devil lies in wait to seize your soul when it departs from the body. But do not fear, because God, who dwells in you—if indeed he dwells in you—[Col. 0498A] will rescue you from both death and the devil. For he is a faithful companion and does not abandon those who hope in him, unless he himself is first abandoned. He is abandoned when the heart, with a wandering mind, runs about through perverse and useless thoughts. Therefore you must guard and hold it with all care and vigilance, so that God may be able to rest in it. For in all creation occupied beneath the sun with worldly vanities, nothing is found higher than the human heart, nothing nobler, nothing more like God. Therefore he seeks nothing else from you but your heart. Cleanse it by pure confession and constant prayer, so that with a clean heart you may see God through continual watchfulness toward God. In every place be subject and attentive to him, and compose your conduct so that you may be at peace within yourself. Love all human beings, [Col. 0498B] and show yourself lovable to all, so that you may be peaceable and a child of God. Thus you will be a good monk, holy, humble, and upright; and when you are such, remember me.

21. Woe is me, who say these things and do not do them; and if I do them at some time, I do not persevere long. I retain these things in memory, but do not keep them in life; I have them in my words, but not in my conduct. All day long I chew over the law in heart and mouth, yet I act contrary to the law. I read in it about religious devotion, and I love reading more than prayer. Yet divine Scripture teaches me nothing else than to love religious devotion, preserve unity, and possess charity. But I, wretched and pitiable, run more quickly to reading than to prayer; I prefer reading to hearing Masses. Someone waits for me, wishing to speak to me of his need [Col. 0498C]; but I take up some book which this or that person would like to have. I read in it, and by reading I lose the fruits of charity, the affections of piety, tears of compunction, the benefit of Masses, and contemplation of heavenly things. Yet in this life nothing is felt more sweetly, nothing received more eagerly, nothing so separates the mind from love of the world, nothing so strengthens the soul against temptations, nothing so arouses and assists a person toward every good work and every labor, as the grace of contemplation.

329 CHAPTER VIII. On abhorring carelessness or negligence during prayer.

22. Have mercy on me, O God, because there I sin most where I ought to correct my sins. For in the monastery [Col. 0498D], while praying, I often do not attend to what I say. I pray indeed with my mouth, but, while my mind wanders outside, I am deprived of the fruit of prayer. I am within in body, but outside in heart; and thus I lose what I say. For it profits little to sing with the voice alone, without the heart’s attention. Therefore it is great perversity—indeed, great madness—when we presume to speak with the Lord of majesty in prayer, yet senselessly turn away the ear and turn the heart toward I know not what trifles. It is likewise great madness, and deserving of severe punishment, when the most worthless dust deigns not to listen to the Creator of the universe speaking to it. But ineffable is the condescension of divine goodness, which daily beholds us unhappy creatures turning away our ears and hardening our hearts, and nevertheless cries out to us, saying: “Return to your heart, O transgressors” (Isa. XLVI.8). [Col. 0499A] “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. XLV.11).

God speaks to me in the Psalm, and I to him; yet when I recite the Psalm, I do not attend to whose Psalm it is. Therefore I do God a great injury when I ask him to hear my prayer, though I myself, who pour it forth, do not hear it. I entreat him to attend to me; but I attend neither to myself nor to him. Worse still, while turning over impure and useless things in my heart, I offer up a horrible stench before his eyes.

CHAPTER IX. On the instability of the human heart.

23. Nothing within me is more fleeting than my heart; whenever it deserts me and runs off through depraved thoughts, it offends God. My heart is a vain, wandering, unstable heart: while it is guided by its own judgment and lacks divine [Col. 0499B] counsel, it cannot stand fast even within itself. Rather, more changeable than every movable thing, it is distracted through endless things and runs here and there through innumerable objects. While it seeks rest among diverse things, it does not find it; but, miserable in its labor, it remains empty of rest. It does not agree with itself; it is at variance with itself; it recoils from itself; it changes its wishes, alters its plans, builds new things, destroys old ones, rebuilds what it has destroyed, and again and again changes and arranges the same things in one way and another, because it wills and does not will, and never remains in the same state.

For just as a mill turns swiftly and rejects nothing but grinds whatever is put upon it—yet, if nothing is added, wears itself away—so my heart is always in motion and never rests. Whether I sleep or wake, it dreams and thinks upon whatever [Col. 0499C] comes before it. And as a mill, if sand is put on it, destroys it; pitch defiles it; straw clogs it: so my heart is disturbed by bitter thought, stained by impure thought, and unsettled and wearied by vain thought. Thus, because my heart does not heed future joy or seek divine help, it is removed from the love of heavenly things and occupied in love of earthly things. And when it slips away from those things and is entangled in these, vanity receives it, curiosity leads it away, covetousness entices it, pleasure seduces it, lust defiles it, envy torments it, anger disturbs it, sadness afflicts it. Thus it is submerged in miserable falls through every vice, because it has abandoned the one God who could have sufficed for it.

24. It is scattered among many things and seeks here and there where it may rest, yet finds nothing sufficient for it [Col. 0499D] until it returns to him himself. It is led from thought to thought and altered through varied occupations and affections, so that it may at least be filled by the variety of things whose nature cannot satisfy it. Thus the misery of the heart slips away when divine grace is withdrawn. And when it returns to itself and examines what it has thought, it finds nothing; for it was not a work, but an importunate thought, which makes much out of nothing. Thus imagination deceives it in the end—an illusion fashioned by demons.

God commands me to offer him my heart; and because I am neither obedient nor subject to the commanding God, I am rebellious and contrary to myself. Therefore I shall not be able to subdue myself until I have been subject to him; and unwillingly I shall serve myself, since I refuse willingly to serve him. Therefore [Col. 0500A] my heart devises more in one moment than all people could accomplish in one year. I am not united with God, and therefore I am divided within myself. But I cannot be united with him except through charity, nor subject to him except through humility, nor truly humble except through truth.

25. It is therefore fitting that I examine myself in truth and recognize how base, how frail, and how unstable I am. Then, when I have known all my miseries, I must cling to him through whom I exist, without whom I am nothing and can do nothing. And because I departed from God by sinning, I cannot return to him except through true confession. Therefore I must confess what must be confessed; for I have never confessed my sins in the manner or with the intention in which I sinned, nor [Col. 0500B] have I remembered them all, whether because of their age or their multitude. And if I have confessed, I have not confessed purely, because of shame. I also divided my confession, so that I might disclose different things to different priests; and so I was deprived of the pardon which I thought I could attain piecemeal. For it is an abominable pretense to divide sin and scrape it merely on the surface rather than uproot it inwardly. Confession is of no use unless it be in truth of mouth and purity of heart. And since there are three who bear witness for us in heaven—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—let us add priests as witnesses to our heart and mouth, so that every word may stand by the mouth of two or three witnesses.

26. But you say: “It is enough for me to confess to God alone, because a priest cannot absolve me from sins without him.” [Col. 0500C] To this, not I but blessed James replies, saying: “Confess your sins to one another” (James V.16). For it is altogether fitting that we who were disobedient to God by sinning should be humble suppliants to priests and his ministers in penitence, so that the person who needed no human mediator to preserve grace may now recover it only through a human mediator. Let him groan and sigh; let him fear and tremble anxiously because of sin; let him go about in concern, seeking helpers and intercessors; let him humbly prostrate himself before the person, since he refused humbly to stand before the Creator. For this also is most salutary: that a person repent in heart and confess his offense with the mouth, so that God, who graciously is present through grace, may pierce the heart with compunction unto repentance, and then be present to grant forgiveness of sins to the one confessing [Col. 0500D].

But if perhaps the sinner truly repents, yet because an emergency intervenes cannot come to confession, we ought confidently to believe that the supreme Priest accomplishes in him what a mortal could not. And it is already certain before God that the person truly wished, though was unable, to fulfill it; for confession was excluded not by contempt but prevented by necessity.

CHAPTER X. On impatience under correction, and the accusation of one’s own defects and vices.

27. In chapter, where I ought to have corrected my sins, I added sins to sins. When I was accused of them, [Col. 0501A] I either excused myself somehow, or denied them altogether; or, worse still, defended them and answered impatiently—although there is no sin by which I have not been defiled or by which I cannot be defiled. It is therefore right that, putting aside every excuse, I promise amendment whenever and by whomever I am accused, so that I may thus be freed from sin already committed or yet to be committed.

Fearing the multitude of my own iniquities, I was afraid to rebuke the transgressions of others and thus became an agent of death, because I did not expel the poison which I could have driven out by crying aloud. I grew indignant against others who reproved me for my vices, and hated those whom I ought to have loved. I wished that things which harmed or displeased me did not exist. Yet I knew that in their own nature they were good [Col. 0501B] and made by a good Maker; but they harmed me because I was evil and used them badly. Nothing is contrary to me except myself. Whatever can harm me is with me, and I myself am a burden to myself.

28. I even wished that God did not know my sins, or did not wish, or could not, punish them; and thus I wished God to be ignorant, unjust, and powerless—which, if he were so, he would not be God. There is no pride greater than my pride; therefore, “the words of my offenses are far from my salvation.” Pride is surely suspect and hateful to God, and it cannot return with him into grace. Their dwelling places are different; they do not dwell in the same mind, since they were not permitted to dwell together in heaven. Pride was born in heaven; but, as though forgetful by what path it fell from there, it could not afterward return there.

When the air was disturbed by rain, excessive cold, or heat, I wickedly murmured against God. For we turn all things received for the use of life into the use of sin. Therefore it is just that we who sinned in all things should be struck in all things. Often at the sacred Mystery I strained my voice in order to sing more sweetly; I delighted more in the modulation of my voice than in compunction of heart. But God, from whom nothing unlawfully done is hidden, seeks not sweetness of voice but purity of heart. For while the singer soothes the people with his voice, he provokes God by depraved conduct. I often extracted permission to speak or do something from my prelates by excessive importunity [Col. 0501D] or cunning, not attending, wretch that I am, to the fact that the one who secretly or openly strives to have his spiritual Father command him to do what he himself desires deceives himself.

29. I often desired a needle, a little knife, or some useful object too much, and did not confess it, because I did not reckon it a sin on account of the object’s worthlessness. Yet it makes little difference whether one seeks a worthless or a precious possession, when the affection is equally corrupt. For the knife is not a vice, but craving for the knife; nor is gold a vice, but greed for gold.

In labor I did not work as much as I ought or as much as I could. In silence too I was idle, which is a very great sin. For in silence no one should be so idle as not to think, even in that idleness, of the benefit of his neighbor; nor so active as not to seek contemplation of God [Col. 0502A]. For one who does not benefit another when able makes little progress. I often boasted of my vices, imagining a badge of virtue where there was a fall into sin. I also made vices out of virtues. For justice, when it exceeds its measure, produces the vice of cruelty; and excessive pity gives birth to a relaxation of discipline. Thus what is thought a virtue is often a vice. Thus lax sluggishness is reckoned gentleness, and the vice of idleness imitates the virtue of repose.

I pretended to be what I was not; I said that I wanted what I did not want, or did not want what I did want. I said one thing with my mouth and turned another over in my heart; and thus beneath a sheep’s skin I preserved a fox-like conscience. A fox-like conscience indeed is lukewarm conversion, animal-minded thought, feigned confession, brief and rare compunction; obedience without devotion, prayer without attention, reading without edification, speech without circumspection [Col. 0502B].

30. O how harsh are these things that I say to myself, because in speaking I strike myself! Yet because I do not deny that I am a sinner, but acknowledge my sin, perhaps that very acknowledgment of guilt will obtain pardon from God, the merciful judge. Therefore I shall speak—I shall speak my misery—if perhaps his mercy may move him. I shall speak my sin, because knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation.

I wear a large tonsure and a round garment; I keep the rule of fasts; I chant at the appointed hours, but my heart is far from my God. Looking at the outward surface [or, cleansing it], [Col. 0502C] I judge all things safe for me, not perceiving the inward worm which corrodes the inner parts. Hence Hosea says: “Strangers devoured my strength, and I did not know it” (Hosea VII.9). And so, proceeding wholly among outward things and ignorant of my inward state, I was poured out like water and reduced to nothing: forgetting the past, neglecting the present, and not foreseeing the future. I am ungrateful for benefits, prone to evils, and slow to good.

31. If I do not examine myself, I do not know myself; but if I examine myself, I cannot endure myself. For I find so many things in myself worthy of rebuke and shame; and the more subtly and frequently I examine myself, the more abominations I find in the corners of my heart [Col. 0502D]. For ever since I began to sin, I have never been able to pass even one day without sin; nor have I yet ceased sinning. Instead, day by day I add sins to sins; I examine the things before my eyes and do not groan; I see shameful things and do not blush; I behold things to be lamented and do not grieve. This is a sign of death and an indication of damnation. For a limb that feels no pain is dead, and an insensible disease is incurable.

I am frivolous and undisciplined, and do not correct myself; rather, I return daily to sins which I have confessed. Nor do I avoid the pit into which I, miserable man, fell, or into which I caused others to fall, or saw them fall. And though I ought to weep and pray for the evils I have done and the goods I have neglected, alas, the opposite has happened to me. For I became lukewarm and cold from the fervor of prayer [Col. 0503A], and now remain cold without feeling; and therefore I cannot weep for myself, because the grace of tears has departed from me.

CHAPTER XI. On the inseparable companionship of conscience, which everywhere reproaches us.

32. I cannot conceal my sins, because wherever I go my conscience is with me, carrying with it whatever I have placed in it, whether good or evil. It keeps safe while I live, and when I am dead it will restore the deposit it received to keep. If I do evil, it is present; if I seem to do good and become proud because of it, it is present. It is present while I live and follows me dead. Everywhere glory or shame, according to the character of the deposit, is inseparable from me [Col. 0503B].

Thus, in my own house and from my own household I have accusers, witnesses, judges, and torturers. Conscience accuses me; memory is witness; reason is judge; pleasure is prison; fear is torturer; delight is torment. For as many evil delights as there have been, so many dreadful torments will there be in punishment: for we are punished by the very things in which we take delight.

CHAPTER XII. On the three enemies of man: the flesh, the world, and the devil.

33. Help me, O Lord my God, because my enemies have surrounded my soul: namely, the body, the world, and the devil. I cannot flee from the body, nor drive it away from myself. I must carry it about, because it is bound to me; I am not permitted to destroy it, and I am compelled to sustain it. When I fatten it, I nourish my enemy against myself. For if I eat enough and it becomes strong, its health and strength oppose me [Col. 0503C].

The world surrounds and besieges me on every side, and through five gates—namely, the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch—it wounds me with its arrows; and death enters through my windows into my soul. The eye looks and turns aside the mind’s awareness. The ear hears and bends the heart’s attention. Smell hinders thought. The mouth speaks and deceives. Through touch the heat of lust is aroused by some small occasion; and unless it is immediately rejected, it suddenly takes possession of the whole body, burns, and sets it ablaze. First it lightly tickles the flesh by thought [Col. 0503D]; then it stains the mind with shameful delight; and finally, through consent to wickedness, it subjects the mind to itself.

Moreover, the devil, whom I cannot see and against whom I therefore guard myself less, has bent his bow and prepared his arrows on it, to wound me suddenly. He told how he had hidden his snares, and said: “Who will see them?” (Ps. LXIII.6). He set a snare in gold and silver, and in all things which we misuse when we delight in them badly and are ensnared by them. Nor did he set only a snare, but also birdlime. The birdlime is love of possessions, attachment to relatives, desire for honor, and pleasure of the flesh; by these the soul is made sticky and entangled, lest it fly on the wings of contemplation through the streets of the heavenly Zion. The devil’s arrows are anger, envy [Col. 0504A], lust, and the other things by which the soul is wounded. And who is able to extinguish his fiery darts?

> Alas! the faithful are often overcome by these weapons.  
> Woe is me! How many battles I see prepared for me!

34. From every side weapons fly, from every side temptations, from every side dangers. Wherever I turn, there is no safety. I fear all things, both those which soothe and those which grieve or trouble: hunger and refreshment, sleep and vigils, labor and rest fight against me. Jest is no less suspect to me than anger, for by joking I have scandalized many. Nor do I fear prosperity less than adversity. For prosperity makes me careless by its sweetness and deceives me. But adversity, because it has something bitter in it, makes me wary and fearful, like bitter draughts [Col. 0504B].

I fear the evil I do secretly more than that which I do openly. For evil which no one sees no one rebukes; and where a rebuker is not feared, the tempter comes securely, and iniquity is more easily committed. Assuredly there is battle on both sides, danger on both sides, cause for fear on both sides; and just as those living in hostile territory must look around in every direction and turn their neck at every sound.

The flesh suggests soft things to me, the world vain things, the devil bitter things. For whenever a carnal thought importunately beats upon my mind concerning food and drink, sleep, and other such things belonging to the care of the flesh, it is the flesh speaking to me. When a vain thought concerning worldly ambition, boasting, or arrogance turns over in my heart, it is from the world. But when I am provoked to anger and wrath [Col. 0504C] and bitterness of spirit, it is a diabolical suggestion. It must be resisted no otherwise than the devil himself, and guarded against no otherwise than damnation itself. The office of demons is to introduce evil suggestions; ours is not to consent to them. For whenever we resist, we overcome the devil, gladden the angels, and honor God. For he himself exhorts us to fight, assists us to conquer, watches us as we contend in battle, lifts us when we fail, and crowns us when we conquer.

CHAPTER XIII. On the assault of the said three enemies.

35. My flesh is from mud, and therefore from it I have muddy and pleasure-seeking thoughts; vain and curious thoughts from the world [Col. 0504D]; evil and malicious ones from the devil. These three enemies attack and persecute me, sometimes openly, sometimes secretly, but always maliciously. For the devil places greater confidence in the assistance of the flesh, because a domestic enemy harms more. The flesh has made an alliance with him for my overthrow, since it was born from sin and nourished in sin, corrupted by vices from its very origin and made much more vicious by wicked habit.

Hence it so fiercely desires against the spirit; hence it continually murmurs and is impatient of discipline; hence it suggests unlawful things, obeys neither reason nor any restraint of fear. That crooked serpent, the enemy of the human race, joins himself to it, helps it, and uses it. He has no other desire, no business, no pursuit [Col. 0505A], except to destroy our souls. He continually devises evil, speaks shrewdly, suggests artfully, and deceives cunningly. He breathes in unlawful impulses, inflames poisoned thoughts; he stirs up wars, nourishes hatreds, incites gluttony, excites lust, urges desires of the flesh, prepares occasions for sin, and never ceases to strike at human hearts with a thousand arts of harm.

Thus he beats us with our own staff and binds our hands with our own belt, so that the flesh given us for help may become our ruin and stumbling block. It is a grievous struggle and great danger to fight against a domestic enemy, especially since we are foreigners and it is a citizen. It inhabits its own country; we are exiles and pilgrims. It is also a great hazard to endure such frequent—indeed, continual—conflicts against the cunning of diabolical deceit [Col. 0505B], which is made crafty both by a subtle nature and by long practice in this malice.

CHAPTER XIV. On longing for the heavenly homeland and its supreme happiness.

36. Deliver me from my enemies, O my God, and from those who hate me, because they have grown strong against me. But I, who until this day have lived against myself, shall now at last, through your grace, begin to live for myself. For we ought so to live in this world that, when the body begins to be devoured by worms in the grave, the soul may rejoice with the saints in heaven. The spirit must be directed where it is going; we must hasten where we shall live always and shall no longer fear death [Col. 0505C].

If we so love this unstable and perishable life, in which we live with such great labor, in which by eating, drinking, and sleeping we scarcely satisfy the needs of the flesh, much more ought we to love eternal life, where we shall endure no labor, where there are always supreme joy, supreme happiness, blessed freedom, and blessed beatitude; where human beings will be like God’s angels, and the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father (Matt. XIII.43). What, do you suppose, will then be the splendor of souls when the light of bodies possesses the splendor of the sun? There will be no sadness there, no distress, no pain, no fear, no labor, no death; but perpetual health will endure there forever.

[Col. 0505D] 37. There wickedness does not arise, nor misery of the flesh. There is no sickness there, no need whatsoever; there is no hunger, no thirst, no cold, no heat, no weariness from fasting, no temptation of the enemy, no will to sin, no power to transgress; rather, all is joy, all is exultation. Human beings joined with angels will remain forever without any weakness of the flesh. There will be infinite delight, everlasting beatitude, in which whoever is received once is held forever. There is rest from labors, peace from enemies, loveliness from newness, security from eternity, sweetness and delight from the vision of God.

And who would not ardently desire to dwell there, for the sake of peace, loveliness, eternity, and the vision of God? No one is a stranger there; rather, all who deserve to come there will dwell securely in their own homeland [Col. 0506A], always joyful and always satisfied by the vision of God. And the more obedient any person has been to God here, the greater the reward he will receive from him there; and the more he loves God, the more closely he will see him whom he longs to behold.

CHAPTER XV. On the characteristics and affections of the old man, and his mortification and transformation through Christ.

38. The days of a human being are like a shadow upon the earth, and there is no delay; and then he is properly nothing when he appears to stand. Why, then, does a person store up treasure on earth, when both what is gathered and the one who gathers it pass away without delay? And you, O human being, what fruit do you expect in a world whose fruit is ruin and whose end [Col. 0506B] is death? Would that you were wise and understood, and prudently foresaw your last things!

I know someone who has lived intimately with you for many years, sat at your table, received food from your hand, slept in your bosom, and conversed with you whenever he wished. By hereditary right he is your slave. But because from earliest age you have brought him up delicately and spared the rod, he has become obstinate: he has lifted his heel over your head, reduced you to slavery, and cruelly rules over you.

39. But perhaps you will say, “Who is this?” It is your old man, who tramples your spirit, who accounts the desirable land as nothing, who has his mind only on the things of the flesh. This man is blind, deaf, and mute from birth [Col. 0506C]; made old by evil days, rebellious against virtue and truth, an enemy of Christ’s cross. He mocks the innocent and the one who passes by simply; he walks in great and marvelous things above himself. His arrogance exceeds his strength. He reveres no one. In his folly he says, “There is no God.” He wastes away at good things and feeds upon others’ evils. He feeds upon impure thoughts and will not tire in transgressing to the end. He scatters and dissipates his own goods like a prodigal; he desires and seizes others’ goods like a miser; he gathers shame and dishonor for himself; as a pretender and a cunning man, he provokes God’s anger.

This man was born wholly in sins and thus nourished: a friend of iniquity, a son of death, a vessel of wrath for dishonor, fit for destruction. Though such as he is, he recounts the righteousnesses [Col. 0506D] of God and takes God’s covenant upon his lips. He hates discipline and casts his Lord behind his back. When he sees a thief, he runs with him and puts his portion with adulterers. He sets a stumbling block against his mother’s son (Ps. XLIX.16–20). He also stores up wrath upon the earth for the day of wrath.

He wishes to take your inheritance from you and remove you from the earth above; and you do not avenge so great an injury, but overlook it. You speak to him no harsh word and show no angry face, but smile upon him when he flatters you? You play with a mocker. Do you not know that it is Ishmael who plays with you? (Gen. XXI.9.) This play is not of childhood, simplicity, or innocence; it is deception of the soul, persecution, death. Already he has cast you into the pit he made [Col. 0507A]; already you have become effeminate; already, pressed beneath the yoke of most miserable slavery, you are wretchedly and basely trampled beneath his feet.

40. O wretched and pitiable human being! Who will free you from the bond of this disgrace? Let God arise, and let this armed man fall; let the enemy-man be struck down and crushed—the despiser of God, worshiper of himself, lover of the world, slave of the devil. What do you think? If you judge rightly, you will say with me: “He is guilty of death; let him be crucified.” Therefore do not overlook it, do not delay, do not spare him; but quickly, boldly, urgently crucify this man—yet with the cross of Christ, in which are salvation and life. If you cry to him from the heart, your Crucified One will hear you, graciously answering: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII.43).

O mercy of Christ! O unlooked-for salvation for the wretched! So gratuitous and proven is God’s love, so wondrous its sweetness, so unexpected its condescension, so unconquerable its gentleness, that whoever cries to him [Col. 0507B] he hears, because he is merciful. O how great is God’s mercy! How ineffable is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High! Yesterday you were in darkness; today, in the splendor of light. Yesterday, in the lion’s mouth; today, in the hand of the Mediator. Yesterday, at the gate of hell; today, amid the delights of paradise.

But what use are these letters of admonition unless you erase from the book of your conscience the letters of death? What use are these writings, read and understood, unless you read and understand yourself? Apply yourself, therefore, to inward reading, that you may read, examine, and know yourself: read, so that you may love God, fight and overcome the world and every enemy; so that labor may be changed into rest, mourning into joy, and after the darkness of this life you may see the dawning of the rising morning light. May you also see the noonday Sun of righteousness, in whom [Col. 0508B] you will behold the Bridegroom with the bride, the one and same Lord of glory, who lives and reigns for endless ages. Amen.

[Note: In a Cistercian manuscript and several others, certain chapters are appended in a single sequence, the first entitled “On the Soul and Its Piety,” etc., and beginning thus: “The soul is a certain substance sharing in reason.” But they are not continuations of the foregoing; indeed, in Hugh of Saint-Victor they constitute the second book, *On the Soul*; while in Augustine, volume six, they constitute the book *On the Spirit and the Soul*. Moreover, in the manuscript of the distinguished Claude Joly, canon and cantor of Paris, another chapter is appended to the foregoing, beginning with the words: “The most perfect and complete righteousness is to love God with one’s whole heart,” etc. These words are taken from the beginning of Paulinus of Aquileia’s treatise *On Salutary Precepts*, in the appendix to volume VI of the works of St Augustine. Therefore, here we bring the foregoing *Meditations* to an end.]

[Col. 0507]

336 TREATISE ON THE INNER HOUSE, OR ON BUILDING THE CONSCIENCE. (G)

[NOTE]

This treatise is listed among the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor and is counted as the third in the sequence of the four books *On the Soul*. It nevertheless seems to be the work of a monk professing the Rule of St Benedict: for in chapter 20, no. 40, he mentions the cowl; and, unless I am mistaken, it is by some Cistercian contemporary of Bernard, as it is permissible to infer from the character of the diet described in chapter 30. Whoever its author may be, it is not Bernard’s. It is nevertheless devout and useful, though without order or method; especially from chapter 24 onward it heaps together varied precepts, repeatedly returning to earlier subjects and borrowing much from the preceding book of *Meditations*. The division of chapters found in Hugh’s works seemed more suitable to us, and we shall largely follow it, though altering the chapter summaries here and there.

PREFACE.

[Col. 0507C]

This house in which we dwell threatens us on every side with ruin. Therefore, because it will shortly fall, another must be built for us. Let us then return to ourselves and examine our conscience. For just as our body is called a tabernacle in which we serve as soldiers, so our conscience is called a house in which we rest after military service; and one serves rightly as a soldier who, through the service he performs in the body, builds the house of conscience. “Cultivate your field carefully,” says the Wise Man, “that afterward you may build your house” (Prov. XXIV.27).

This field is our body, when we rightly use its senses and impulses, bending them to the use of virtue by subjecting them to the command of the soul [Col. 0508C], while the body is continually subjected to the soul and the soul wholly to God. By these means the inward conscience is built; it is made good, indeed, by worthy satisfaction for past evils and by cautious, provident avoidance of evils presently at hand. Worthy satisfaction is to correct evil deeds and not repeat what has been corrected.

Conscience is perpetual, for it never ends, just as the soul does not. Since the soul is immortal, just as it cannot cease to be a soul, so it can never be without conscience. For conscience is each person’s inseparable [Col. 0509A] glory or shame, according to the quality of the deposit.

CHAPTER ONE. On cleansing and pacifying conscience before building it.

1. Therefore this conscience, in which the soul will dwell forever, must be built, but first it must be cleansed. And who will cleanse it? Certainly God and the human being: the human being through thoughts and affections; God through mercy and grace. Thoughts and affections are necessary in cleansing conscience: thoughts in the investigation of truth, affections in the practice of virtue. Mercy at one time blots out sin; at another gives the virtue to resist sin; now removes the occasion of sinning; now sends bitterness; and very often heals the affection. Grace assists toward good, defends against evil, and instructs one to discern both.

Therefore, stirred by truth, a person confesses his sins; but God, moved by mercy, has mercy upon the one confessing. For every hope of pardon and mercy lies in confession, and no one can be justified from sin unless he has first confessed the sin. For each person begins to be righteous from the time when he has become his own accuser.

2. Happy is the conscience in which mercy and truth have met one another, justice and peace have kissed (Ps. 84:11). The truth of the one confessing and the mercy [Col. 0509C] of the one showing mercy have met, because mercy cannot fail one who knows himself in truth. The kiss of justice is to love one’s enemies, to leave parents and all one’s own possessions for God’s sake, patiently to endure an injury inflicted, and everywhere to decline glory when it is offered. The kiss of peace is to invite those who hate to peace, to recall the discordant to harmony, peacefully to bear with opponents, lovingly and kindly to teach those who err, gently to comfort the sorrowful, and to have peace with everyone. Blessed is the soul founded in Christ’s peace and made firm in God’s love: though it suffers wars outwardly, its inward peace is not disturbed. Whatever troubles may noisily assail it from without, they do not break through to disturb the silence of its inward rest. For, touched by the taste of inward sweetness, it is gathered within by [Col. 0509D] desire; nor is it now extravagantly dissipated outwardly in pleasures of the flesh, because it possesses wholly within [337] itself that in which it delights; and thus, made peaceful within itself, since there is nothing it desires outwardly, it rests wholly inwardly through love. And when it is wholly gathered to inward joy, it is reshaped into the image of God which it venerates within itself. Angels and Archangels frequently visit such a soul and honor it as God’s temple and the dwelling-place of the Holy Spirit. Therefore be God’s temple, and God Most High will dwell in you. For the soul that has God within itself is God’s temple, in which the divine mysteries are celebrated.

3. But the soul that does not strive to remain within itself or to fix its desire in the love of God goes out through the eyes, ears, [Col. 0510A] and other bodily senses, and delights in these outward things. But when it finds these gates closed, then, returning to itself and seeing itself naked and desolate, it will be shaken by inestimable shame and horror. And because it sought the world’s consolation, it will not have that consolation which God gives inwardly in the conscience. God will not merely disdain to visit it; rather, being conscious of evil, it will not even be able to endure itself. It will be unable to have rest within itself, because it has abandoned him with whom it ought to dwell and rest.

Therefore, while you are now placed in the company of others, consider that you cannot always remain with them. Meanwhile choose for yourself that companion who, when all these things have been taken away from you, will keep faith with you—the one who keeps faith with those who love him and does not depart in a [Col. 0510B] time of distress. That is your God, whom you ought to choose.

4. Therefore gather together all distractions of the heart and fluctuations of the mind, and fix all your desire in God alone. Let your heart be where your desirable and greatly lovable treasure is. For he frequently visits and gladly inhabits the tranquility of the heart and the leisure of a peaceful mind, because he is peace, and “his dwelling-place is made in peace” (Ps. 75:3). Therefore prepare yourself so that God may be with you: let him be in your mouth and in your heart; let him always go with you and return with you; let him not depart from you. He will never leave you unless you first leave him. Wherever you are, you can never be alone if God is with you. [Col. 0510C] Therefore cleanse your conscience and always be ready, so that at whatever hour the Lord comes and wishes to dwell with you, he may find within you a dwelling prepared for himself. For he himself said: “Make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in your midst” (Exod. 25:8).

5. Let us therefore strive to build a temple for God within ourselves: first, so that he may dwell in each of us individually, and then in all of us together; for he will disdain neither individuals nor all together. Let each person first take care not to be divided against himself, because “every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste, and house will fall upon house” (Luke 11:17). Christ will not enter where the walls have leaned over and the fences have been cast down. The soul wishes the house of its body [Col. 0510D] to remain whole, and it must leave it if its members are scattered from one another. Let it therefore see—if it desires Christ to dwell by faith in its heart, that is, in itself—and diligently beware lest its members be at variance with one another: namely, reason, will, and memory. That person prepares a worthy dwelling for God whose reason is not deceived, whose will is not perverse, and whose memory is not defiled. Happy is the soul which strives so to cleanse the house of its heart from the filth of sins and fill it with holy and righteous works that not only angels, but even the Lord of angels, delights to dwell in it. Once the house has been cleansed and every evil excluded from it, let it be filled with every good, so that we need not seek anything outside, having abandoned all outward things.

## Chapter II. On raising the seven columns for building the house of conscience; and first, on good will, which is the first column

[Col. 0511A]

6. Therefore let Wisdom build herself a house; let her raise seven columns upon which the entire structure may rest. The house is conscience; the columns are good will; memory—that is, remembrance of God’s benefits; a pure heart; a free mind; a right spirit; a devout mind; and enlightened reason. Let the first column, then, be raised first. For among all God’s gifts that seem to pertain to human salvation, [338] good will is recognized as the first and chief good, through which the image of God’s likeness is restored in us. It is first because every good begins from good will. [Col. 0511B] It is chief because nothing more useful is given to human beings than good will. Whatever a person does cannot be good unless it proceeds from good will. Without good will no one at all can be saved; with good will no one can perish. Good will can neither be given to one unwilling nor taken away except from one willing. Human will is God’s power. It is human will because willing lies within human will; and therefore all merit lies in the will. As much as you will, so much do you merit. As your good will grows, so your merit grows. Therefore make your good will great, if you wish to have great merit. Thus God, as a most loving and merciful Father, has placed our redemption in that in which no one can be lacking unless he wills it.
