For rich and poor alike can love [Col. 0511C] equally, even though they cannot give money equally. Yet good will is not good if it does not do what it can.

## Chapter III. On the second column, which is remembrance of God’s benefits

7. Let us therefore remember God’s mercies, so that we may thus be kindled in his love. Let us call back to mind the good things he has bestowed on us: how he has often mercifully rescued us when placed in dangers; how our sins have never been able to overcome him so as to prevent his showing mercy; how he reminded those forgetful of him concerning himself; recalled those turned away from him; kindly received those coming to him; pardoned the penitent; guarded those who persevered; upheld those standing; [Col. 0511D] raised those who had fallen; turned evil pleasures into bitterness; and again granted his consolations to those beneficially embittered. Finally, after they were cleansed through tribulation, he restored perfect rest and peace—he who was never lacking even to sinners, in order to correct them, nor to the righteous, in order to guard them.

Let us consider how many good things God did for us when we neither asked nor desired them, indeed when we refused them; how many sins he forgave us; and from how many dangers God our Deliverer set us free. How great was the condescension of his loving-kindness: although ungrateful and in many ways opposed to him, we were kept by God’s grace from so many sins into which we could have fallen, just as we fell into many others. Therefore, just as there is no moment in which we do not use or enjoy God’s [Col. 0512A] goodness and mercy, so there ought to be no moment in which we do not hold him present in our memory.

## Chapter IV. On the third column, which is a pure heart

8. It follows that we should love with our whole heart him from whom we have received such great benefits: that is, with all thought and all affection, without falling away. Let the heart be upright, so that it may please God in all things. Let it be upright through rectitude of intention, the exclusion of perverse thought, and constancy in contemplation. Let it be ready to follow God’s will in whatever direction it recognizes that will to incline. Let it be raised on high, to contemplate and desire heavenly and divine things alone. Let it be pure, so that it permits no evil to linger within it; nor judges even a slight [Col. 0512B] stumbling-block tolerable, whether in its own conscience or another’s. Let it be gentle in sweet response, pleasant admonition, kindly rebuke, and moderate correction. Let it be clean, so that, rejecting the defilements of every impurity, it may mourn the sins of thought as well as action. Let it weep for its own misery and that of others; let it grieve not only for its own offences but also for others’; let it be pierced with compunction for evils it has committed and goods it has neglected.

## Chapter V. On the free mind, the fourth column

9. Let the mind be free from worldly cares, pleasures of the flesh, and perverse thoughts, so that it can, when it wishes, either attend to itself, minister to the good of the brethren, or rest in the contemplation of heavenly things. [Col. 0512C] Let it be firm, so that no sudden disturbance may shake it; [339] let it not be ensnared by allurements or broken by troubles. Let no anger and no impatience be able to disturb the mind’s peace and rest, because Christ is peace, and the lover of peace rests in peace; he cannot dwell in a disturbed mind. Let it be made perfect in God’s love. For this is to love God: to occupy the mind with him, conceive a desire for enjoying his vision, have hatred of sin and contempt for the world, and love one’s neighbor, whom he himself judged worthy of love.

## Chapter VI. On the right spirit, the fifth column

10. Let the spirit be upright, wholly turned away from all earthly and present things, and inseparably [Col. 0512D] joined and united to God. Let it ascend in devout devotion and visit the dwellings above, and the many mansions in the Father’s house, humbly prostrating itself before the throne of God and of the Lamb. Let it run through the streets of heavenly Zion; let it hear that melody of the angels and reverently make supplication to every order of blessed spirits, commending itself to each separately and to all together.

Yet a mind which has not long been exercised and fully instructed in self-knowledge does not deserve to receive so great a grace. For one who is not yet fit to see himself raises the eye of his heart in vain to see God. You must first know the invisible things of your own spirit before you can be fit to know the invisible things of God. And if [Col. 0513A] you cannot know yourself, do not presume to grasp what is above you.

11. The chief and principal mirror for seeing God is the rational mind finding itself. For if “the invisible things of God are perceived through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20), where, I ask, are the traces of his knowledge found more expressly impressed than in his image? Therefore let whoever thirsts to see his God wipe his mirror clean; let him cleanse his spirit. “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). The true penitent does not cease daily to inspect, wipe, maintain, and guard this mirror: to inspect it, in order to discover in it anything displeasing to God; to wipe away not only sins of action but also sins of thought, [Col. 0513B] so that nothing remains in it which offends God; to maintain it, lest, falling downward, it adhere to the earth through love, and lest it be dirtied by the dust of empty thoughts; and to guard it, so that he whose tabernacle is with human beings, whose delight is to be with the children of men, and who stands at the door and knocks, may, whenever he wishes to enter, find a clean lodging. For God, who loves cleanliness, cannot dwell in a polluted heart.

12. Therefore, once the mirror has been wiped clean and long and carefully examined, a certain brightness of divine light begins to shine through it, and an immense ray of an unfamiliar vision appears to the eyes of the heart. Inflamed by the sight of this light, the mind begins, with the clear gaze of a pure heart, to behold things above and within; to love God and [Col. 0513C] cling to God. It regards everything present as though it were not; it renounces all its affections, and wholly devotes itself to love alone, knowing that only the one who loves God is blessed.

But the mind never attains such grace by its own exertion. It is God’s gift, not human merit. Yet undoubtedly such great grace is received by one who abandons the care of the age and takes up care of himself: one who strives often to consider himself and diligently to know what he himself is. Therefore return to your heart and carefully examine yourself. Consider where you come from, where you are going, how you live, what you do, what you lose, how much you advance each day or how much you fall back; by which thoughts you are more often assailed; by which affections [Col. 0513D] you are more frequently touched; and by what stains of temptation you are more fiercely attacked by the evil spirit. When you have fully learned, insofar as possible, the condition and disposition of the inward and outward person, and not only what you are but also what you ought to have been, you can rise from self-knowledge to contemplation of God. For as much as you advance daily in knowledge, so much do you always strive toward higher things.

But perhaps you have already ascended, have already returned to your heart, and have learned to stand there. Let even this not suffice you. Learn to dwell there and make your home there; [340] and whenever some wandering of mind has drawn you away, hasten always to return there. Undoubtedly, by much practice it will at last become a delight to you, so much so that you can remain there continually without any difficulty of [Col. 0514A] labor; indeed, it will be a punishment to you rather to spend any time elsewhere than there.

## Chapter VII. On the devout mind, the sixth column

13. Therefore, if you perceive that your desires are attracted by outward pleasures and your thoughts are continually occupied with them, constrain them with great vigilance and do not permit them to enter your heart. Rather, return to your heart and strive in every way to enter and dwell there. For the mind that does not raise itself to consideration of itself, but is still scattered among various desires and stretched this way and that by diverse thoughts, cannot gather itself into unity, because it does not yet know how to enter into itself, but is still lowly in thought and manner of life. [Col. 0514B] Therefore it cannot fly on the wing of contemplation to things above itself.

Let it learn to gather the dispersions of the heart; let it become accustomed to linger in its inward places; let it strive to restrain the wanderings of the mind and forget everything external. Let the one who longs for contemplation of heavenly things and yearns for knowledge of divine things learn to love inward goods alone and think of them more frequently. And when, by diligently attending to itself and searching long, it has finally discovered what it is, it remains for it, by divine revelation, to know what it ought to be, what kind of edifice of mind it should prepare for God, and by what services it ought to please him.

14. Whoever thus gathers the wanderings of the mind into one and fixes all the movements of the heart upon the single desire for eternity [Col. 0514C] has surely already returned to his heart; he now gladly remains there and is wonderfully delighted. And when, because of joy, he can no longer contain himself, he is led above himself and raised to the heights through an ecstasy of mind. Thus through himself above himself, through knowledge of himself he ascends to knowledge of God, so that he may learn to love God alone, think of him unceasingly, and rest delightfully in him.

When Christ’s love has absorbed a person’s whole affection so that, heedless and forgetful of himself, he perceives nothing except Jesus Christ and what belongs to Jesus Christ, then at last, I think, love is perfect in him. For one so affected, poverty is not burdensome; such a person does not feel injuries; he laughs at insults, [Col. 0514D] despises losses, and reckons death gain. Indeed, he does not think that he dies, because he knows that he passes through death rather to life. Whomever God’s love holds thus bound inwardly cannot go out even for a little while; rather, he burns inwardly with desire for God, all the more as this desire is more intimate, and more vehemently as it is more frequent.

Whoever is continually delighted in God’s love frequently undergoes ecstasies of mind. Carried away from all present and earthly things, he is brought before God; and while he beholds God’s beauty, astonished at its greatness, he is wholly suspended in wonder at him. He wonders at the glory of the King, the magnificence of the kingdom, the nobility of the heavenly city, and the happiness of its citizens. He also contemplates the beauty of glory, God’s goodness, the sweetness of inward [Col. 0515A] delight, and the tranquility of eternal rest. He meditates upon the Father’s power, the Son’s wisdom, the Holy Spirit’s kindness, and the blessedness of angelic nature. He delights from God into God, while he marvels at God’s loving-kindness and contemplates his beauty.

Oh, how delightful it would be to perceive this, if he were not carried away for so brief a time! He is carried away while contemplating heavenly things alone and delights in contemplating them. But when he tries to remain there longer, he suddenly falls; and, returning to himself, he can tell no one what he saw above himself. Yet, drawn by awareness of sweetness, he marvels inwardly at the pleasantness of the sweetness he has tasted and at that heavenly infusion of spiritual joy. In silent thought he also turns over in his heart the brightness of incorporeal light, the savor of inward fullness, the secret of inward rest, [Col. 0515B] and the mystery of highest tranquility. In this contemplation and in the sweetness of contemplation, the mind is delightfully affected and wonderfully delighted. Therefore let it will and not grow weary. Let it will until it comes before the King; and there let it weep and sigh and offer itself in tears. Let it beg forgiveness, ask for grace, and not depart from there until it feels that the God whom it has grievously offended has been appeased, and receives consolation from him.

## Chapter VIII. On enlightened reason, the seventh column

15. Finally, reason, raised through ecstasy of mind to contemplation of sublime things and carried into the hidden mystery of divine contemplation, and there enlightened [Col. 0515C] to knowledge of truth and of the true light, and inflamed with desire for goodness, gathers together all illicit pleasures, affections, wandering thoughts of memory, dispersions of heart, fluctuations of the mind, wanderings of the spirit, and distractions of mind, and fixes all its desire in that fountain of blessedness. Let reason always hold the higher place, and let no movement rebel against it; rather, let all obey it, just as it obeys God. But if it perceives any impulse moving toward what it ought not, or moving as it ought not, let it not consent but immediately resist. For consent alone makes us guilty, even if something prevents the acts from following. For then, as it is written, the soul is said to die when reason itself bends to sin through [Col. 0515D] consent: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:20). Therefore let it resist, lest it die; let it fight, that it may be crowned. The struggle is painful but fruitful, because if it entails suffering, it will also have a crown. Sensation does no harm where consent is absent; indeed, what wearies one who resists crowns one who conquers.

## Chapter IX. On the marks and characteristics of a well-built conscience

16. Thus, surely thus, a good conscience is built. A good conscience is one that punishes past sins and recoils from committing sins that deserve punishment; if it senses sin, it does not consent to sin; if thought defiles it, reason washes it. A right conscience is one to which its own sin is displeasing and which does not consent to another’s sin; yet it does not on that account abandon the sinner or conceal his [Col. 0516A] sin; and when it rebukes, it does not insult. It is tranquil because it is gentle to everyone and burdensome to no one: using a friend for favor, an enemy for patience, everyone for goodwill, and, so far as it can, for beneficence. By such means the house of the soul is built.

But if perhaps, as often happens, a thief should arrive—one who comes only “to steal, slaughter, and destroy”—if, I say, the thief comes, whether as an inwardly rising exaltation of heart, an outwardly arriving desire for human praise, or any other plague seeking to break through this house, then let the anger of reason, like a dog guarding a treasure, wake up, bark, bite, and kill. Let it rush upon its enemies, spare no one, allow no one to enter, but cry out and rouse those dwelling within to take up arms. From whatever quarter a vice may try to harm, secretly or openly, let it drive that vice far away, so that the conscience may be secure. [Col. 0516B] It is secure when it suffers no accusation, whether in a time of good or through expectation of evil. It is clean and of good conscience when it is neither justly accused regarding the past nor unjustly delighted regarding the present. It is pure when God imputes to it neither its own sins, because it did not commit them; nor others’ sins, because it did not approve them; nor negligence, because it did not keep silent; nor pride, because it remained in humility.

## Chapter X. On preferring care for conscience to knowledge

17. Many seek knowledge, but few seek conscience. Yet if conscience were sought with as much zeal and care as worldly and vain [Col. 0516C] knowledge is sought, it would be attained more quickly and retained more profitably. For reflecting upon conscience is perfected understanding, and one who keeps it will always be secure. With all due reverence for wisdom, it is more useful to run to conscience than to wisdom—unless that wisdom is the kind that builds conscience. For the soul understands itself when conscience is illumined; [342] the heart is filled with good conscience when the created image has received within itself God, and itself in God, through a reciprocal turning. The Creator’s image in the created image is nothing other than wisdom in the soul, glory in the conscience, and sanctification in the ark.

Oh, how ineffable is God’s loving-kindness, which bends such majesty down to such lowliness! He who created us is created in us; and as though it were too little for us to have God as Father, he also wishes us to become his brother and mother. “Whoever,” he says, “does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that person is my brother and mother” (Matt. 12:50). Brother by obedience; mother by giving birth; brother through sharing in the inheritance; mother through instructing others. O faithful soul, spread wide your bosom, enlarge your affections, lest you be too narrow in your inward parts to conceive him whom the whole world could not contain, until the Blessed Virgin conceived him by faith. For Christ is conceived by faith, born through the preaching of the word, nourished by devotion, and held by love. Therefore let conscience be pure, so that it may bring God as a guest into our lodging; let it be attentive in faithful service, lest such majesty refuse the heart’s [Col. 0517A] bosom; let it be devout, so that it may please God alone, attend to God alone, and not depart from him. Such a conscience gladdens the soul, shows itself pleasing to God, worthy of reverence to human beings and angels, and remains reconciled and at rest within itself.

## Chapter XI. On the benefits and fruits of a good conscience

18. Conscience is the heart’s knowledge, understood in two ways: either as that which knows itself through itself, or as that which, beyond itself, knows other things through itself. For the heart knows both itself by its conscience and many other things. When it knows itself, it is called *conscientia* (“conscience”); when it knows things besides itself, it is called *scientia* (“knowledge”). A good conscience is the badge of religion, Solomon’s temple, a field of blessing, a garden of delights, a golden couch, [Col. 0517B] the joy of angels, the ark of the covenant, the King’s treasure, God’s court, the Holy Spirit’s dwelling-place, a sealed and closed book to be opened on the day of judgment. Nothing is more pleasant, safer, or richer than a good conscience. Let the body be oppressed, the world drag it along, and the devil terrify it: it will remain secure. A good conscience will be secure when the body dies; secure when the soul is presented before God; secure when both are set before the dreadful tribunal of the just Judge on the day of judgment. No remedy is more useful, and no testimony more certain, for future blessedness than a good conscience. Though the world rolls round in all its instability, weeps, laughs, perishes, and passes away, a good conscience never withers. Let the body be subjected to punishment, worn down in fasts, torn by lashes, stretched on the rack, [Col. 0517C] slaughtered by the sword, and afflicted by the punishment of the cross: the conscience will remain secure.

19. In the mirror of conscience, the condition of the outward and inward person is known. For the soul knows itself and is without a mirror. A good conscience is the clean, bright, and pure mirror of all religious life. As a woman wishing to please her husband or friend arranges the charm and beauty of her face by looking into a mirror which reflects the image set before it, so the soul rereads and understands in conscience the respects in which it departs from the image of truth, or the respects in which it receives the traces of the Creator’s image. We did not without reason compare conscience to a mirror, because in it, as in a mirror, the eye of reason can grasp in itself, with clear sight, both what is becoming and what is [Col. 0517D] unbecoming.

## Chapter XII. On the guarding and restraining of the heart necessary for a good conscience

20. No one’s life is known except in conscience; nor does one arrive at a good conscience except through guarding the heart. For the heart, left to its own judgment, turns itself either toward life or toward death. To will to sin is evil; to sin is worse; to persevere in sin is worst; to refuse repentance is deadly. Therefore whatever the heart thinks which in no way pertains to its own good or that of its neighbors must be rejected. From the various regions of the world in which the wandering and deep heart is held or vainly occupied, [Col. 0518A] let it return to itself and examine itself; when it discovers guilt, let it fear punishment. But in seeking guilt, let it find it nowhere except in itself. When guilt and the cause of punishment have been found, let it set itself before itself by punishing itself, and judge itself as though another: itself accused, itself afflicted before itself; itself guilty, itself a stern judge before itself; itself ungodly, itself returned to piety before itself. Let it set itself before itself; let it determine what it must do with itself; let it justly inflict just punishments upon its unjust self.

Let it also speak thus to itself: “Because you abandoned peace with the Lord your God and incurred war within yourself, you suffer division, so that you are condemned by yourself. Because you broke the covenant of peace, you will what you do not will, and do not will what you will: you will be condemned by yourself. You will what ought not to be [Col. 0518B] willed; you do not will what ought to be willed. Behold, from your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant.” Therefore afflict yourself and set yourself before your own face, that you may behold your ugliness and reconsider your folly. Thus in its miseries the heart returns to itself, and heart is set against heart.

There is a certain force which works thus upon the heart and restrains the flowing and vain heart, lest it flow out into the abyss of destruction. This force, or violence, seizes the kingdom of heaven. The Lord says, “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11:12). Whoever possesses his own heart possesses a noble kingdom. One does not reign who, enslaved in his heart to the vices, rules over cities and crowds of people. Only that person reigns who, having laid aside the heart’s own rule, orders the whole household of inward and outward movements according to the laws of reason. [Col. 0518C] If leonine rage rises up, it is subdued through patience; if the wantonness of a goat, through abstinence; if the fierceness of a boar, through gentleness; if the pride of a unicorn, through humility.

## Chapter XIII. On restraining the heart’s mobility through consideration of the divine majesty and power

21. Among the other liberal arts there is no art more liberal than this art by which the heart is restrained—a thing more mobile than every moving thing and more slippery than every slippery thing. Naturally unstable through mobility, it refuses to remain fixed even for a moment; its life is in movement, and movement is its life. This tiny vital movement in the heart moves the mass of the entire human body; and by what art can it be restrained, [Col. 0518D] so that, while moving other things, it may itself not be moved? Perhaps if a millstone were hung about its neck, it would not move. No: rather, it would be driven all the more violently with the millstone.

Therefore one must deal with it in this way: let it go around the earth and walk through it, if perhaps it can find something swifter and more mobile than itself. If it finds nothing like itself upon the earth, let it go around even the circuit of heaven and bring the wheels of God’s chariot into competition with its course. What then will it do in relation to those who walk upon the wings of the winds? Perhaps it can compete even with them. Or will it run alongside that power which “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8:1)? Will it also overtake that of which it is said, “Wisdom is more mobile than all moving things” (Wis. 7:24)?

At least, when it sees [Col. 0519A] the power of its Creator leaping over such vast bounds, let it stop and fold its wings. Holding itself back, and gathering and restraining itself by the reins of comparison with God, let it not transgress its bounds. Thus the holy living creatures in Ezekiel’s vision, when there came a voice above the firmament that was over their heads, stood still and lowered their wings (Ezek. 1:25). This is plainly what the saints do when, having surveyed the works and wonders of God and the hidden mysteries beyond understanding, they find that they know nothing and weigh all their works in the balance’s moment. Then the heart understands that it is not moved by itself, because by itself it would remain motionless, unless he who moves all things also moved it among all things. Therefore, recognizing that it has borrowed its movement from God, [Col. 0519B] it must no longer claim it as its own but regard it as a loan. For the borrower must use the borrowed thing according to the will of the lender; otherwise, the borrower commits theft in the borrowed thing.

[344]

## Chapter XIV. On divine admonitions by which the human heart is repeatedly moved to use creatures cautiously and govern itself rightly

22. Therefore, when God moves you, or wishes to move you, O human heart, be moved; do not otherwise be moved, because that would not be movement, but agitation. But when does God move you? When he admonishes you. And he admonishes thus:

“You are vainly occupied, O wise heart, surpassing all things in every prerogative, with things that are vanities of vanities. It does not befit you to be subject to these things, but to rule over them. [Col. 0519C] These things need you in order that they may subsist better and more fittingly; you need them neither for blessedness nor for immortality. They indeed prepare provisions for your beast of burden on the way, but they must be taken according to measure, not unto excess. For from an excess of food beasts are sometimes bloated and dissolved into an excessive discharge of the belly, so that they fail through refreshment. So too your body, O prince and lord of the body: if it exceeds the rules of necessity and opens its mouth to the abyss of desire, it digs for itself a pit of perdition in the lodging of restoration; from a remedy it procures destruction, from a vehicle shipwreck. What then? Excess takes away what is necessary. Remove what is superfluous, and the necessities will be lacking to no one, because from the overflowing abundance of some arises the grievous want of others [Col. 0519D].”

23. It is yours to correct evil deeds; yours to arrange in order and duty the household of the body’s members and the soul’s movements; yours to assign the business of each according to what is fitting. Let there be no one in the kingdom of your body who may violate the laws and rights of your ordinances with impunity—not eye, hand, foot, ear, or throat. What need I say of the baser and common members? If they dare even to attempt rebellion, let them be overwhelmed with stones, pierced with the darts of rebukes, and know that King Solomon sits upon the king’s mule—that is, reason upon the body’s sensuality.

But what if those shameful members, which modest and chaste lips always call by a veiled name, [Col. 0520A] infest the commonwealth with disordered motion? Certainly let them be cut off—not by iron, but by fasting; not by mutilation, but by mortification. “I wish,” says the Apostle, “that those who trouble you would cut themselves off” (Gal. 5:12). By these persuasions the unbridled heart, rushing headlong in its course, can be restrained, so that there may be a good conscience. It is good if it has purity in the heart, truth in the mouth, and rectitude in action. For by these it will merit the vision of the Trinity. O blessed vision, in which God will be so known and manifest that he will be seen by each of us in each of us; seen in himself; seen in the new heaven and the new earth, and in every creature that will then exist!

## Chapter XV. On correcting the book of conscience
[Col. 0520B] 24. Human conscience is the Lord’s vineyard, which ought to be cultivated by confession of sins, satisfaction for them, the performance of good works, and the keeping of those works. Each person’s conscience is his book; and all other books were devised for examining and correcting this book. When the soul leaves the body, it will be able to carry with it no book other than that of its conscience; and in it it will learn where it ought to go and what it ought to receive. We shall be judged from what has been written in our books; and therefore they ought to be written according to the pattern of the book of life. If they have not been so written, they must at least be corrected. Let us therefore compare our books with the book of life; and if they contain anything otherwise, let them be corrected, lest in that final comparison, if they are found to contain anything [Col. 0520C] differently, they be cast aside.

Blessed is the person who can know and despise himself, approve and disapprove himself. For one who displeases himself pleases God; and one who is lowly in his own eyes is dear to God. There are many kinds of human knowledge, but none is better than that by which a person knows himself. Therefore let me return to my heart, and accustom myself to remain there, so that I may examine my whole life and know myself. I shall pour out all my miseries before God, in the hope that his great compassion may perhaps move him. I shall confess my sins to him, to whom all things are naked and open; whom I cannot deceive, because he is wisdom; nor escape, because he is everywhere.

## CHAPTER XVI. A man laments before God his miseries, the unrest of his heart, and its inclination toward evil.

[Col. 0520D]

25. Hear, therefore, most merciful God, my confession; look upon your compassion, and deal with me according to your mercy. Hear how often the rushing multitude of innumerable thoughts has driven you from my memory—thoughts which, like a crowd streaming to some spectacle, are accustomed to pour into my heart. When I wish to pray or chant in the monastery, I know not what foolish thought seizes my heart and leads it through various places. When I call it back to myself, I cannot hold it: it immediately slips away, scatters here and there, and pours itself out through countless things. Thus the frequent enticement of earthly desires and the overflow of vanities so occupy my heart that I think about and turn over in my mind precisely what I strive to avoid.

[Col. 0521A] For my heart and my thoughts are not in my power: unexpectedly poured forth, they confuse my mind and spirit and drag them elsewhere than I had intended. They call me back to worldly matters, introduce secular concerns, inject pleasures, and weave alluring things together; and at the very time when I prepare to raise my mind to you, infected by empty thoughts, I am often cast down to earthly things. Every day I wish to drive this uproar of clamorous thoughts from my heart, yet I cannot. Things seen and heard, words spoken and deeds done, return to memory and clamor there with great importunity. I think what must be thought; I rethink what has been thought; and I do not cease to repeat the same things again and again. And after I have thought long and much about whatever I can, I cannot be without thoughts: [Col. 0521B] they enter and leave, and some introduce and exclude others.

I endure these things unwillingly; yet often I consent, as I run aimlessly through things I have seen or done, without profit and without discernment. Thus my mind, always mobile and never steady, always wandering and as though drunk, is distracted in various directions. I sin grievously when I abandon my heart, for grievous is the loss that occurs through negligence. I suffer violence when it abandons me. Strengthen my heart, O God, for when it strives to stand within itself, even without knowing how it is somehow drawn away from itself. Thus, through the habit of sinning, I sin even when I do not know it; and my heart, a vain heart, is led through endless things and divided among many desires.

26. At night, when I wish to sleep, I see with closed eyes [Col. 0521C] images and phantasms of many things, and endure them unwillingly. The more I strive to turn the gaze of my mind away from them, the more they thrust themselves upon me and stain my heart with the vexation of shameful thoughts. From this often arose the deadly pleasure which has harmed me—a pleasure accustomed to arise from the recollection of past sins, but especially from the recollection of lust. For the more familiar this pestilence is to me than other vices, the more prone it is to harm and the harder to repel. When I wish to repel it, it intrudes itself upon me against my will: sweetly burdensome, pleasing while displeasing, and displeasing while pleasing.

I have never been able to flee the lust of the flesh; it always pursues me, and whenever it can seize me by some thought of pleasure or by a fixed [Col. 0521D] look, it allows me no rest by day or night. It enters subtly and occupies the mind; unless it is immediately repelled, it entices and inflames, and like the poison of a pestilence gradually diffuses itself throughout the whole body. It multiplies evil thoughts, produces evil affections, infects the mind with unlawful pleasure, bends the spirit toward consent to perversity, and corrupts every virtue of the soul. When I am held bound by this plague, I can scarcely tear myself away from it, because I either do not know how to confess its stings or am ashamed to do so: so subtle and shameful are they. Truly, it is difficult to extinguish the fires of lust. It pricks the immature, inflames the young, enervates men, and wearies the old and decrepit. It does not disdain hovels; it does not reverence palaces. Would that it fled monasteries alone.

[Col. 0522A] Help me, Lord my God, that I may be able to resist so pestilential and deadly a vice. For I know that what wearies one who resists crowns one who conquers. I know also that if I pollute my mind with an unclean thought, I cannot please you, who are the author of purity.

## CHAPTER XVII. He continues to accuse and lament his miseries concerning bitter thoughts, the misuse of the members, and external things serving the necessities of life.

27. Create in me a clean heart, O God, for not only does vain thought occupy it and foul thought defile it, but bitter thought also scatters it. For when I am stirred by some injury, I am oppressed in my heart by dense tumults of thoughts. Anxious and blind on every side, I search for an opportunity of revenge for the injury received; [Col. 0522B] I multiply schemes, and enact in my heart nothing but quarrels that are absent outwardly. I do not see those who are present; I argue with the absent; within myself I utter and receive insults, and answer the received insults more harshly. Since no one is present to oppose me, I compose disputes in my heart, consider the snares of those who envy me, and weigh what they may be able to bring against the quarrels. I seek what I may answer; and though I have no case at all, I labor as an empty litigant. Thus I turn the day into idleness and the night into thought. I grow sluggish in useful work because I am wearied by unlawful thought. Thus the mind fights within when no one fights against the mind.

At times I turn over afterward in my mind, with importunate thought, what I did in the body; and often I am more grievously tortured [Col. 0522C] in remembering than I was formerly captured in committing the deed. I often reconsider things that I never did, nor even intended, as though I regretted not having done them. Cleanse me from my hidden faults, O Lord; for when I do nothing outwardly, I sin grievously within. For in my heart I keep images of what I have seen and done. Therefore I do not cease to turn over in my heart the tumult of temporal affairs even when I am at leisure. In thought I eat when I fast; I speak when I am silent; I am angry while I am calm; the body rests, while the spirit runs here and there.

28. Thus I have never been able to pass through this life without guilt; nor indeed is even that which I have lived commendably without some liability, if it is examined apart from mercy. [Col. 0522D] Deliver me from my necessities, O Lord. For while I frequently strive to meet the debts of necessity, I serve the vice of pleasure; beneath the covering of necessity, I fall into the snare of pleasure. Very often I ate and drank not for necessity but for pleasure; and what was enough for necessity was too little for pleasure. I also thought about food and drink when I ought not, where I ought not, and more than I ought. Thinking about food, I ruminated upon feasts in thought all day long.

When I seek clothing to cover my limbs, I seek not only what covers but also what exalts. Against the numbness of cold, I seek not only things that protect by their thickness, but also things that soothe by their softness; not only things that, by softness, soothe the touch, but also things that by their color seduce the eyes. [Col. 0523A] When for some necessity I had permission to speak to someone, I spoke not only of necessary matters, but also of unnecessary ones: of things that did not concern me and concerning which I had no permission. I immersed myself in people’s conversations. There I spoke not for edification but for destruction; not what was fitting but what pleased me: vain words and words suited to laughter, idle and useless words. Serving verbosity and pursuing detraction, I defiled my mouth with lying and detraction. My tongue is full of every deceit and has harmed me more than all my other members. For what I heard or saw I can never report exactly as it was said or done: I assert one thing in place of another, often add many superfluities, and so, whether praising too much or blaming, I [Col. 0523B] lie almost whenever I speak.

29. My throat burns with insatiable gluttony; my appetite cannot be satisfied with diverse flavors. I have never been able to cleanse by pure confession my perverse heart, full of deceit and malice. My hands were ready for wicked work and slow to perform good. My stomach and intestines have often been distended by excessive food and drink, and are therefore full of pain. For from what gluttony delights in, the belly is swollen, the body weakened, and death often follows. Through the pleasure of gluttony I fell into the greediness of the belly; and from that from which I ought to have procured health for myself, I contracted destruction by eating too much. My feet carried me more swiftly to look at some curiosity than to church. My eyes corrupted me by an evil gaze [Col. 0523C] and drew every movement of my body toward unclean desires. I opened my ears more readily to idle and vain words than to holy ones. My sense of smell delighted in vain fragrances; taste in the differing flavors of different things; likewise every other individual sense in this and that, according as its own appetite carried it. Thus, my God, I exceeded the measure of nature in all my members. All my members, as if by a conspiracy, delivered dominion over me to my enemy; they entered into a covenant with death and made a pact with hell.

## CHAPTER XVIII. A further accusation of his own wickedness, especially concerning the vice of envy, hatred, boasting, and so forth.

30. Deliver me, Lord, from the evil man—that is, from myself, from whom I cannot withdraw. [Col. 0523D] For wherever I turn, my vices follow me; wherever I go, my conscience does not leave me, but stands present and writes down whatever I do. Therefore, although I may evade human judgments, I cannot escape the judgment of my own conscience. Even if I conceal from others what I have done, I cannot conceal it from myself, who know the evil I have committed. Consciousness of my own guilt does not permit me to rest, but torments me vehemently day by day and terrifies me still more concerning the day of judgment. For on that day, when the Lord comes for judgment, each person’s conscience will be brought forward as testimony; and when the book of conscience is opened, every fault will be brought again before the eyes. Thus, conscience compelling him, each person will be his own accuser and judge.

[Col. 0524A] Therefore I shall set myself before myself and judge myself, that I may escape the judgment of that final and dreadful day. My conscience condemns me, although divine judgment has not yet condemned me. It accuses me of murder: if I have not committed it in deed, I have often committed it in will and desire. It accuses me of adultery, and I give the same answer. It accuses me of envy; and I too confess that envy has very often torn my heart to pieces. For through envy I made the merits of those living holily into sins of my own. The good things which I heard done or said by them I did not believe to be true at all; I distorted deeds well done into evil by perversely interpreting them. Every evil that lying rumor alleged about them I believed at once, as though I had seen it myself. I [Col. 0524B] imagined every evil about my rivals and languished at their advancement. These hatreds I concealed within myself and nourished for my own torments. I envied those who advanced, favored those who sinned, rejoiced in their evils, and grieved at their advancement.

31. I burned with unprovoked enmities, and feared that this malice of my breast might be discovered. I was always bitter toward another and never trustworthy; thus I was a friend of the devil and an enemy of myself. Among friends I sowed discord; I confirmed the discordant in their dissension; I blackened their reputations with lies. In spiritual persons I praised fleshly things, so as to persuade them that spiritual goods were lacking to them. I feigned friendships so that I might deceive, by whatever art I could, those who carelessly entrusted themselves to me. [Col. 0524C] By perverse suspicions I piled up occasions for hatred; and thus I made glad the demons whose deeds I followed. To many I was like a friend in service, an enemy in soul, polished in speech, base in deed. I was a betrayer of secrets, tenacious of evil suspicions, perverse in both respects. And thus “the enemy pursued my soul; he humbled my life to the ground” (Ps. 142:3).

Most merciful Lord, how can I be good, who was so evil in what was good? I sinned, and you overlooked it; I prolonged my wickedness for a long time, and you prolonged your compassion, because you were considering repentance and pardon. Grant, then, mercy to a wretch, you who so long spared a criminal. For I believe that whatever you decree to forgive me will be as though it had never been.

[Col. 0524D] 32. Not only did envy afflict my heart, but vanity also involved my languishing soul in various pleasures. For through vanity I shamefully boasted of works of which I was not conscious. I also rejoiced to teach what I did not know. I wanted lofty things to be believed about me; I preferred pleasant things to serious ones; I denounced in word what I desired in mind; I gave my vices the names of virtues, and thus deceived myself and misled those favorable to me. I was quick to make honorable promises, false in fulfilling them; changeable from good, tenacious of evil; solemn in speech, base in mind, deceitful everywhere; cheerful in prosperity, weak in adversity; puffed up by services done for me, anxious at reproaches, unrestrained in joys, easily inclined to human concerns, [Col. 0525A] difficult toward honorable ones.

Most merciful Lord, thus my days failed in vanity—days in which I ought to have wept for committed iniquity, roused my slackened will, sighed for my lost inheritance, aspired to promised blessedness, hastened toward the society of angels, and sought anew the favor of your majesty.

## CHAPTER XIX. He still groans and laments before God over his miseries and vices.

33. My whole life terrifies me, my God, because when carefully examined it appears to me either sinful or barren; and if any fruit seems to be in it, it is either feigned, imperfect, or in some way corrupt, so that it may either fail to please you or displease you. [Col. 0525B] And though the matter is truly so, it is to me as if it were not so—which is misery upon misery. Thus I eat, drink, and sleep secure, as if I had already passed the day of death and escaped the day of judgment and the torments of hell. Thus I play and laugh as if I already reigned with you in your kingdom.

Therefore, trembling at the multitude of my iniquities yet trusting in your mercy, I confess to you, my Creator and Redeemer, who promised that after guilt pardon and forgiveness may be obtained through pure and tearful confession: I was conceived in sins and nourished in sins, and throughout the whole course of my life until this day I have lived in sins. I find no sin by which I have not in some manner been defiled. Through pride I transgressed your commands [Col. 0525C] and those of my elders. I did not keep silence and quietness, as the Rule teaches. What was not permitted me, I possessed, gave, and received. I did not willingly or mercifully hear the cries of the poor and wretched, nor did I visit them in their infirmities. I consented to those persuading me to evil. I think much more readily about many things below than one thing above; I rebuke others’ vices more readily than my own, and am not ashamed to do what I rebuke in others. I attend more readily to each person’s vices than to their virtues. When I see others’ offenses, I do not look at my own. I am lenient in my own offenses but wish to maintain severity in those of others. I am strong in inflicting insults, weak in enduring them; slow to obey, but troublesome in provoking others; [Col. 0525D] sluggish toward the things that I both ought and can do, but ready toward the things that I neither ought nor can do. Thus my soul has been filled with evils, as my sins deserved.

34. In church I find myself worse: before the sacred altars I do not make supplication devoutly; I do not handle sacred vessels reverently; in choir I am present in body but occupied in some business in mind. Now I remain inside, now I go outside: so great is the fickleness both of body and mind. I sing one thing and think another. I utter the words of psalmody and do not attend to the meaning of the psalmody; wandering in mind, careless in bearing, staring with my eyes and looking this way and that, I survey and observe whatever is being done there. Woe is me, because I sin there where I ought to correct sins.

[Col. 0526A] At times, indeed, even in the good things that I do I draw nearer to worse things; for while they produce joy in the mind and generate a certain security, my mind is made self-secure and relaxes into sluggishness. I often praised myself and the works I had done, and wished to be praised by others. Often human praise, though I did not seek it, pleased me when offered; and when I was heedlessly lifted up by it, many things that I had done immediately came to mind, so that I might be raised still higher in self-exaltation. Rehearsing these subtly and heaping them all together, I began, increasingly deceived, to swell more and more. And while I was fixed in admiration of myself, giving glory to myself and not to God from whom I had received everything, I lost all the fruit; and thus I learned that those who praised me were swearing against me. For the more anyone [Col. 0526B] glories in himself, the more he is separated from the love of God.

35. Thus, my God, my life has drawn near to hell. If you deliver me, I shall have cause to give you thanks; if you do not deliver me from it, I have no cause to reproach you, because you are just. Alas for me! How I have lived! How many evils I have done and spoken! I am ashamed that I have lived so and that I was born. I would rather not be than be such a person. I was good, and made myself evil; certainly, since I freely made myself wretched, it is just that I should always be wretched. My conscience deserves condemnation; my repentance does not suffice for satisfaction. But it is certain that your mercy blots out every offense. Blot out, therefore, gracious Lord, my iniquity in the multitude of your mercies. And I, who have lived without purpose until this [Col. 0526C] day, do not wish henceforth to live without purpose.

36. But alas, wretch that I am! So often have I made this very confession: rising and falling, I am exhausted; sinning again so many times and confessing so many times. I often promised to reform myself, and never kept the promise; instead I always returned to sin and joined new and worse crimes to former ones. I never changed my habits for the better as I ought, nor withdrew from evil deeds. By ruining myself, I also made very many others sin, and became the cause of evil to many; some have been overthrown by the examples of my life. Behold, most merciful God, I do not hide my sins but show them; I [Col. 0526D] accuse myself, not excuse myself, because I know my iniquity. Yet I am not therefore righteous, since if another accused me as I accuse myself, I could not endure it patiently.

Indeed, I might have despaired because of my excessive sins and vices, faults and infinite negligences, which I have committed and commit daily without ceasing in heart, mouth, deed, and every way in which human frailty can sin, had not your Word, O God, become flesh and dwelt among us. But now I do not dare to despair, because he who was obedient to you unto death—even death on a cross—took the written bond of our sins; and fastening it to the cross, he crucified sin and death. I give you thanks, Lord my God, because you visited me and showed me my sins. Now, through your inspiration, I have for the first time learned to return to my heart and know myself. Therefore I shall summon one of your friends and lay all my offenses before him, as [Col. 0527A] you commanded me, so that through his counsel and help I may be freed from all my iniquities and reconciled to you.

## CHAPTER XX. Confession before a superior.

37. Hear, therefore, Father, a wretched sinner; hear the voice of one weeping and repenting; consider how grievously I have sinned and offended my Creator. At God’s command I returned to my heart; and, having excluded from it everything but the Lord God and myself, I examined my whole life the more carefully because more intimately. And, to confess the truth, I found there nothing but a place of horror and vast desolation: namely, a conscience long neglected, wholly uncultivated, overgrown with thorns and briars, and full of every horror.

[Col. 0527B] For I find no vice from which I have not contracted some contagion. Anger disturbed me, envy tore me to pieces, pride puffed me up. From these I contracted instability of mind, buffoonery of speech, insults against neighbors, the crimes of detraction, and unbridled speech. I did not keep, but judged, the commands of my elders. When rebuked for my negligences, I was either rebellious or murmured. I shamelessly desired to be preferred to better persons. I mockingly ridiculed the simplicity of spiritual brothers and insolently boasted of my own opinions. I disdained services offered to me and sought those denied me; in my pride I despised those younger than myself. I did not observe reverence in service, moderation in speech, or discipline in conduct. I had obstinacy in intention, hardness in heart, and boasting in conversation. I was deceitful in humility, persistent in hatred, biting in jest.

[Col. 0527C] Impatient of subjection, a seeker of power, lazy in good work, harsh toward unity, hard in service; quick to speak of things I did not know, ready to trip others up, inhuman toward the fellowship of brothers. Rash in judging, loud in speaking, disdainful in listening, presumptuous in teaching, shamefully unrestrained in loud laughter; burdensome to friends, hostile to peace, ungrateful toward benefactors, puffed up by services rendered to me, and domineering over those subject to me. I often boasted that I had done what I had not done, seen what I had not seen, and said what I had not said. I also pretended that I had not done what I had done; denied that I had said what I had said; denied having [Col. 0527D] seen and heard what I had seen and heard. Thus I am guilty on every side: guilty in the world, guilty in the cloister—there through ignorance, here through negligence; and both terrify me.

38. Yet what terrifies me far more is that in the monastery, before the sight of God, I find myself worse. God placed me in a place of delight, in a house of abundance, in a paradise of pleasures; but I, wretched and miserable, perish from hunger amid the tables of those feasting, thirst beside a fountain, freeze before a fire—and I do not wish to stretch out my hand to either, so lazy and slothful am I. Thus I waste the time which God in his mercy granted me for doing penance, obtaining pardon, acquiring grace, and meriting glory.

[Col. 0528A] I stand like some monster among the children of God, having the habit of a monk but not his manner of life. In a great tonsure and broad cowl, I suppose all is safe for me. Like a barren tree I occupy the ground, and like a worthless beast I consume more than I benefit. I hold a place higher than another’s and fulfill no one’s office; I am like a trunk without leaves or fruit. Others feed me from the labor of their hands, as their prebendary. But I, like a poor and wretched man, perform the part of neither cleric nor layman. For I cannot sing or read; I do not know how to labor. I am the reproach of men, meaner than cattle, worse than a corpse. For a rotting dog stinks less intolerably to human beings than a sinful soul to God.

Therefore I am weary of living; I am ashamed to live because I make little progress. I fear to die because I am not [Col. 0528B] prepared. Yet I prefer to die and commit and commend myself to God’s mercy, because “he is gracious and merciful” (Joel 2:13), rather than cause someone scandal by my evil way of life. For all day long my shame is before me, and “the confusion of my face has covered me” (Ps. 43:16), when I see myself sleepy at vigils, late for the canonical hours, and idle at manual work. But I see others attending the divine praises so vigorously and devoutly; others standing before God so reverently and eagerly and praising him. Yet I cannot be moved to tears of compunction: so great is my heart’s hardness. I have no desire to sing; prayer gives no delight; I find no holy meditations. So great is the barrenness of my soul and the lack of devotion that I endure.

39. Alas for me! The Lord visits everyone around me, but does not draw near to me. For I see one person of singular abstinence, another of admirable patience, another of highest humility and gentleness, another of great mercy and compassion; one frequently carried beyond himself in contemplation, another knocking at and penetrating the heavens by persistence in prayer, and still others excelling in other virtues. I observe and behold them all fervent, all devout, all of one mind in Christ, all abounding in heavenly gifts and grace: truly spiritual persons, whom God visits and in whom he dwells. But in myself I find none of these things, because in anger the Lord has turned away from his servant.

[Col. 0528D] Hence, while others keep watch, I sleep; when others chant in the monastery, I run here and there; when others withdraw into some secret place from human conversation in order to speak there with the King of angels, I seek human conversation. When others devote themselves to reading, I devote myself to tales and idle words; when others examine and judge themselves, I judge others. Others delight in common life, common discipline, and common study; but I delight in corners and side-paths. Thus, thus, from the time I was able to sin, I have never ceased from sins and evil works. I have always heaped sins upon sins; and the sins which at some time I could not fulfill in deeds, I have never ceased to complete in evil wills and evil desires.

40. [Col. 0529A] Above all evils, the pleasure of the flesh, which has grown with me from my very cradle, has always clung to me. Even now, though my limbs fail from old age, it does not leave me. In many and varied ways it has stained, dissolved, enslaved my unhappy soul, and, stripping it of every virtue, has made it empty and weak. I confess that I have often been stirred and inflamed by unclean recollections of this shameful deed and have endured considerable and dishonorable fires. Nor have only the evil memory and foolish recollections of my own pleasures harmed me: evil deeds of others, reported to me and brought back to mind through foul recollections, have also stained my heart with no slight poison of iniquity. And in this I am miserably most wretched: I do not grieve as much as I know that I ought to grieve, but lie sluggishly secure, as though I did not [Col. 0529B] know what I suffer.

41. But this is more miserable to me than every other misery: being so perverse in deed, polluted in speech, and unclean in heart, I approach the altar and do not tremble to handle Christ’s body with my hands. I approach the humble One in pride, the gentle One in anger, the merciful One in cruelty; yet the humble One bears with the proud, the gentle One with the angry, the merciful One with the cruel. I approach the Lord as a servant, not in love but in fear, not in devotion but from habit. I approach the Lord whose servant I struck. I approach the Father whose son I killed: I struck by word and killed by example. Yet I neither tremble before the Lord nor reverence the Father.

[Col. 0529C] Remaining among the company of brothers, troubling some and troubled by another, I sometimes approach the Peacemaker. Such as I am, I also draw near to the kiss of peace, though I ought first to have been reconciled before approaching the kiss of the troubled brother. My iniquity proves me guilty and God’s enemy; my sin has often separated me from God. Therefore I beseech you, Father, to instruct me how I may either always stand with my God or return when, because my sins demand it, I have been removed from him.

## CHAPTER XXI. The spiritual father’s response and instruction to the penitent.

42. Your confession, son, has moved me to tears, both on my own account and on yours. I weep on my own account because I find in myself nearly the same or similar things as those you have said about yourself, and you have brought back to memory many things that I had forgotten. I rejoice on your account because “the Dayspring from on high” has visited you. For you are not far from the kingdom of God. Knowledge of sin is the beginning of salvation.

I trust in the Lord that whatever is lacking in you in fervor and good work will be supplied by the humility of pure confession. [Col. 0530A] For at whatever hour the sinner, having turned, groans, he shall be saved (Ezek. 18:21, 27), because God “will not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50:19). Indeed, it seems to God longer to have granted pardon to the sinner than it does for the sinner to have received it. For the merciful God hastens to release the guilty person from the torment of his conscience as though compassion for the wretch tormented merciful God more than the wretch’s compassion for himself tormented the wretch. Whoever truly repents and genuinely grieves will undoubtedly receive forgiveness without delay. And the more often and more intensely a person is affected by inward sorrow for his guilt, the more certain and secure he becomes concerning the pardon of forgiveness.

Thus the Paraclete Spirit consoles the soul afflicted by tears of repentance as often as gladly. He visits it often, strengthens it gladly, and wholly restores to confidence in pardon the soul which he sees, by weeping, condemn its crimes, and by condemning them, weep. From that point a certain familiarity begins between God and the soul, because the soul feels itself more often visited by him and, at his coming, not merely consoled, but sometimes filled with an ineffable joy.

43. But who is fit for these things? Certainly the person who truly repents. [Col. 0530B] For all things are washed in confession: conscience is cleansed, bitterness removed, sin put to flight, tranquility returns, hope revives, and the spirit is gladdened. After baptism, no other remedy has been appointed for us than recourse to confession. Let there therefore be devout compunction of heart, true confession of mouth, prudent mortification of flesh, swift uprooting of vices, and joyful performance of good works. Do not be ashamed to confess to God, from whom you cannot hide. For he knows the secrets of hearts; all things are naked and open to him, and all our sins are written before his sight. But what transgression writes there, confession erases here.

Do not then be ashamed to say what you were not ashamed to do. But if you are perhaps ashamed to disclose your sins to me alone, a sinner, what [Col. 0530C] will you do on the day of judgment, when your conscience will appear exposed to all? If you were compelled to pass before a multitude with your body naked, you could not help being ashamed. Why, then, are you less confounded when an unclean thought stains your mind? Why are you less ashamed of the shameful parts of the heart than of the shameful parts of the flesh? Why do you fear human faces more than the faces of angels? Such shame separates from God.

All hope of pardon and mercy lies in true confession. For feigned confession is not confession, but a double shame. Pretending to be miserable excludes God’s compassion; nor is there room for divine condescension where there has been presumptuous self-importance. But humble confession of misery calls forth compassion. For no guilt is so grave that it does not have pardon through pure confession. [Col. 0530D] Therefore immediately disclose the vices of your heart and your evil thoughts. A sin brought to light is quickly healed, but a crime is enlarged by silence. If a vice is exposed, it becomes small from being great; if concealed, it becomes great from being small. For prompt confession quickly brings healing. It is better to avoid a vice than to correct it, lest perhaps, once you have fallen into it, you may be unable to return.

## CHAPTER XXII. He proposes effective remedies against evil thoughts: remembrance of Christ’s Passion and of the last things.

44. Whenever you feel yourself assailed by shameful thoughts and enticed toward unlawful pleasure, set before the eyes of your mind how Christ was crucified on the cross [Col. 0531A] for you. Consider how Judas hands him over to the Jews, how shamefully he is treated, blasphemed and struck, judged and condemned, stripped and scourged; and finally, afflicted with insults and reproaches, suspended between two thieves: fixed to the cross by nails, mocked with spittle, crowned with thorns, pierced by a lance. Blood flows from every part, and, bowing his head, he gives up the spirit. Thus your Redeemer dies for you—and you stain your mind with some foul thought, I know not what! This reflection could suffice to exclude every unlawful thought. But behold, let us proceed to other matters.

45. Consider how you will die: when, harassed by some grave illness and brought to the last extremity, cast down there upon the ground, amid long sighs and difficult sobs, amid various pains and fears, you will breathe out your soul. Then the body will come to pallor and horror, to corruption and stench; it will be a worm and food for worms. But those ghostly faces which await the soul at its departure will immediately seize and snatch it away; and terrible and frightful demons will terrify it on every side. Consider who will defend it from those roaring, prepared for prey; who will console it when it sees those utterly hideous monstrous demons rushing upon it in troops; or who will lead it through an unknown region. Consider also how suddenly the last day comes: suddenly it comes, and perhaps it will be today. It is already at hand; you will already be presented before the dreadful Judge. You will be accused of many and great offences; [Col. 0531C] not of one crime, nor of a few, but of countless crimes; not small, but immense; not doubtful, but certain; not by a brief accusation, but one as long as your whole life; not by one accuser, but by as many as your offences are. The Judge himself will be your strict accuser. All good and evil spirits likewise will accuse you before God with him: the good, because they owe justice to God; the evil, because they preserve your iniquity. You will stand before as many judges and peoples as have preceded you in good works. You will be put to shame by as many accusers as have given you examples of good living. You will be convicted by as many witnesses as have admonished you through good words and righteous actions. Before all peoples your iniquities will be exposed, and before all hosts all your crimes will be laid open—not only deeds, but also thoughts and words.

46. Many sins, which you do not now see, will then rush unexpectedly upon you as if from ambush—perhaps more numerous and more terrible than those you now see. On every side there will be distress for you. Here will be sins accusing you; there, justice terrifying you; beneath, the gaping, dreadful abyss of hell; above, the angry Judge; within, the burning conscience; without, the world ablaze. If the righteous man is scarcely saved, into what quarter will the sinner, thus caught, press himself? To hide will be impossible; to appear, intolerable. In so great a crisis your conscience, conscious of evil against itself, will torment you; the secrets of your heart will torture you. Your conscience compelling you, you yourself will be your own accuser [Col. 0532A] and judge. Convicted by the testimony of your own conscience and by the witnessing eyes of the Judge himself, you will not be able to flee; but trembling and anxious, you will stand suspended before the most grievous sentence, in narrow peril and perilous constraint, as though immediately about to receive that which you will be unable to lose forever. The Judge will then be vehemently angry and terribly strict; once pronounced, his sentence will be unchangeable. Horrible torturers, who never show mercy, will stand ready, so that, once sentence has been given, they may drag you, condemned, to torments. The torments will be without interval and without relief. Fear will throw you into confusion when the earth opens before you and you plunge and fall into the lake of burning, stinking sulphur. Fire will burn your flesh outwardly; the worm will gnaw your conscience inwardly. [Col. 0532B] There you will be without end, without hope of pardon or mercy. Yet all the punishments of Gehenna will be surpassed by not seeing God and by lacking those goods which it was in your power to obtain.

47. If you wish to drive all evil thoughts from your heart, think often upon these things. For your thought is where your affection is; your heart is where your desire is, since we turn most often in thought to that by whose love we are most moved. Each person falls or stands in his thought. If you think good things, your holy thought guards you. If you think evil things, “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful, and will withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom 1:5); and the temple of God will become a den of the devil, for whom God abandons the devil seizes. The Holy Spirit [Col. 0532C] suggests things good and sweet; the evil spirit, things evil and bitter, vain, useless, and unclean. Therefore, at whatever hour an evil thought touches your heart, do not consent to it; do not allow it to remain in your heart, but immediately repel it. Resist an iniquitous thought at its beginning, and it will flee from you.

For our thoughts do not fly empty before God’s eyes, and no moments of time pass into the mind without an appointed recompense. An evil thought produces pleasure; pleasure, consent; consent, action; action, habit; habit, necessity; necessity, death. As a viper is killed when torn apart by the young placed within her womb, so thoughts nourished within us kill us. It belongs to demons to suggest evil thoughts; it is ours immediately to drive them out. For allowing them to lie in our mind belongs to our own will and is reckoned as our own fault. For by his own will he who falls falls, and by God’s will he who stands stands. Yet an unclean thought does not defile the mind when it attacks, unless it subjugates the mind to itself through pleasure.

## Chapter XXIII. On the harms of the sins of pride, envy, and detraction

48. As pride is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of all virtues. It is first in sin and last in conflict. At the outset it casts down the mind through sin; or at the end it throws it down from its virtues. Therefore it is the worst of all sins, because it destroys the human [Col. 0533A] mind both through virtues and through vices. Other vices attack only those virtues by which they themselves are destroyed: lust, for example, attacks chastity; anger, patience. Pride alone raises itself against all the virtues of the soul and, like a general and deadly disease, corrupts them all. Therefore, unless humility precedes all our works, accompanies and follows them—set before us that we may look upon it, placed beside us that we may cling to it, set between us and pride that we may be restrained by it—pride wrests everything from our hand. However great the justice of an action may be before the inward Judge, it is nothing if the swelling of the mind exalts it. Truly, everything that is done perishes unless it is carefully guarded in humility.

These are the signs of pride: shouting in speech; bitterness in silence; license in merriment; rage in sadness; seemliness [Col. 0533B] in appearance; unseemliness in conduct; rancour under reproof.

49. Envy is the moth of the soul. It consumes understanding, burns the breast, afflicts the mind; like a certain plague it devours the human heart and consumes every good thing with pestilential heat. The envious person makes another’s good his own sin by envying it. When we see any sinners, let us not readily judge them, but rather mourn for them; for in like things we have either fallen or may fall. If you wish to correct an offender, rebuke him openly and do not bite him in secret. For what benefit is there if, without my knowing it, you report my evils to others? Woe to one who refuses to correct his own life and does not cease to disparage another’s. If you wish to disparage, turn your own sins back upon yourself; behold not the offences of others, but your own. For you will never disparage others [Col. 0533C] if you examine yourself properly. Do not defile your mouth with another’s evil; do not disparage the sinner, but sympathize, for detraction is a grave sin. Those who disparage and those who listen are held under equal guilt. As you are angry with another when he disparages you, so be angry with yourself when you disparage another. Detraction bites more sharply than a true rebuke of the heart.

## Chapter XXIV. Various admonitions on avoiding curiosity, lying, idle speech, and the pursuit of vengeance

50. Curiosity deceives many. So long as anyone curiously considers the sins of others, he remains ignorant of his own. Whoever looks at himself does not seek what he may frequently condemn in others, but what he may mourn in himself. Never desire to know what people say among themselves. Flee every kind of lie with utmost care. Speak falsehood neither by chance nor deliberately, “for a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11). Do not preserve anyone’s life by any deceit. Flee shameful words; reject speech that does not edify its hearers. For idle speech quickly pollutes the mind, and what is gladly heard is easily done. Idle speech is an index of a vain conscience. The tongue reveals a person’s character, and as the speech is shown to be, so the mind is proved to be; for “the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matt. 12:34). Idle speech will not be without judgment, because those who slip away through vain words fall from every state of uprightness. [Col. 0534A] Whoever does not seek praise does not feel insult. Distinguish yourself by your own judgment, not another’s. No one can know better who you are than you yourself, who are conscious to yourself. What benefit is it, while you are evil, if you are called good? Be such as you wish to be considered.

If you are wise, you will always remain the same person. Strive to say not whatever you please, but what is fitting. Whoever does not restrain an idle word quickly proceeds to harmful ones. It is a great virtue not to injure one by whom you have been injured; it is great glory to spare one whom you were able to harm.

A noble kind of vengeance is to forgive one who has been defeated. Whatever adversity befalls you happens to you because of your sin. Restrain, therefore, your grief and say: “In proportion to my offences, a small punishment is given.” Overcome the evils of others by your own goodness. Conquer malice with goodness; by overlooking them, trample down the errors of those who disparage you. Do not be faithless in peace or fickle in friendship. Invite those who hate you to peace; recall those at discord to concord.

## Chapter XXV. He sets forth various and notable moral precepts

51. Human conscience is a many-fold abyss. For just as an abyss cannot be drained, so the human heart cannot be emptied of its thoughts; rather, they roll about within it in continual motion. “The sea is great and broad of hands; there are creeping things without number” (Ps. 103:25). For as a creeping thing creeps secretly and travels here and there through winding turns, so poisonous thoughts enter and leave a person’s conscience, so that the person does not know whence they come [Col. 0534C] or whither they go. He understood this well who said: “The heart of man is perverse and unsearchable; who shall know it?” (Jer. 17:9)—a heart which admits neither investigation nor knowledge.

52. No punishment is heavier than an evil conscience. An evil conscience is driven by its own goads. If public reputation does not condemn you, your own conscience condemns you, for no one can flee himself. Do you wish never to be sad? Live well. A good life always has joy; the conscience of a guilty person is always under punishment. Be as merciful in the offences of others as in your own, and judge no one more strictly than yourself. Judge others as you wish to be judged yourself. Your own law binds you. The judgment you impose upon others, you yourself will bear. [Col. 0534D] Condemn no one before judgment: examine first, and then judge. For it is not the person accused, but the person convicted, who is guilty. It is very dangerous to judge anyone on suspicion. In doubtful matters reserve judgment for God’s judgment. Do not choose whom you will show mercy to, lest perhaps you pass over the one who deserves to receive. Give yourself, if you can, to all who ask you [Note: “[Col. 0533D] The words ‘to those who ask’ appear to be lacking”], for it is uncertain on whose behalf you may please God more. Let your goodwill be greater than what is given, for your work will be such as your intention has been. Whoever extends his hand with sadness loses the fruit of recompense. There is no mercy where there is no goodwill. Do not take from one in order to give to another, for it profits nothing if you feed one person from that [Col. 0535A] by which you leave another empty. Cast away from yourself whatever can hinder your good purpose; while living, despise what you cannot possess after death.

53. It is difficult—indeed impossible—for anyone to enjoy present goods and future ones: to fill the belly here and the mind there; to pass from pleasures to pleasures; to appear glorious on earth and in heaven. If you wish to live with gladness of mind, do not possess much. When each person ends this life, he can possess after it only what he has merited in it. For the more we delight in what is below, the more we are separated from love above. Let there be no misfortune which your reflection has not anticipated; let there be no misfortune that finds you unprepared. Set before yourself that there is nothing which cannot happen to you. Avoid the pit into which you see another fall before you. [Col. 0535B] Let another’s ruin be your warning. While we do not know, death comes suddenly. For we do not know what may happen to us today, and we do not know whether the condition of death may demand our soul this night. Every day we move toward life’s end and hurry toward death. Therefore we ought every hour to think whither we hasten at every moment.

Hence the Lord says through the prophet: “Your destruction, O Israel, is from yourself; only in me is your help” (Hos. 13:9). It is as though he said: “That you perish, attribute to your own desert; that you are saved, to my help.” A penitent ought never to have security concerning sins. For security breeds negligence and often leads the unwary back to sins already passed. Not only grave sins but slight ones must be avoided. For many slight sins make one great sin, just as immense rivers commonly grow from small and tiny drops. There is no doubt that those who persevere chaste and virginal are made equal to God’s angels.

## Chapter XXVI. On the importunity of the belly and the devil’s cunning

54. No exacter is so importunate to a person as the belly, which presses you daily with the demand of hunger. With other vices, although we are sometimes born with them, yet sometimes we do not die with them; but with this one we are born, and with it we die. My father left me indebted to many creditors, but I have been freed from them all. One, however, remains, from whom I cannot be freed: namely, the belly. The belly does not hear commands; it demands, it calls out. Yet it is not [Col. 0535D] an immoderate creditor: it is dismissed with little, provided only that you give it what you owe, not what you are able to give. Foreknowing that some may sin, God chastises them, for their salvation, with bodily sickness, lest they sin; so that it is more beneficial for them to be broken by sicknesses unto salvation than to remain sound unto damnation. Health is ruinous when it leads to disobedience; sickness too is salutary when, through divine correction, it breaks and humbles a mind hardened in obstinacy.

55. When the devil attempts to deceive anyone, he first studies each person’s disposition; then he adapts himself by the way in which he sees that person to be suited to sin. To gentle and mild minds he offers lust or vain glory; to harsh minds, anger, pride, or cruelty. When our adversary sees himself excluded from outward sensuality, he attacks and enters the inner parts with gathered strength.
