But the spiritual person, who judges all things, does not fail to recognize his cunning. He restrains what he can; what he cannot, he endures. For although he endures a dog’s barking, he does not fear its bite. The devil bites when he draws one to consent; he barks when he suggests. Then he does not wound but crowns, since, although he tires one who resists, he binds only one who consents.

## Chapter XXVII. On prayer and the right manner of praying

56. Prayer is the devotion of the mind; that is, turning to God through a devout and humble affection: humble from awareness of one’s own weakness, devout from consideration of divine mercy. By no other means is God more quickly bent toward mercy than when the soul of the petitioner turns to him with the whole affection of devotion. Nothing embraces God as does a pure affection of mind. Therefore, when you wish to pray, enter alone into the solitude of your heart; gather your spirit; with a whole mind, empty of cares, enter the house of prayer. Standing before God, before one of the altars, let the urgency of prayer pierce heaven; and, presented before the choirs of heavenly beings, lament pitiably in their presence the miseries and calamities that you suffer. Declare your need; ask their compassion; and I trust in him who said, “Ask, and you shall receive” (Luke 11:9), because, if you persevere in knocking, you will not depart from there empty-handed. Pray thus when you pray: as though you had been taken up and presented before [Col. 0536C] the face of Majesty upon the exalted throne, where “thousands of thousands minister to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stand before him” (Dan. 7:10). Then we pray truly when we think of nothing else. “We must pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17). For just as there is no moment in which a person does not enjoy or make use of God’s goodness and mercy, so there ought to be no moment in which he does not hold God present in memory. Blessed is the soul that strives to gather every wandering of the mind into one and to fix its desire in that fountain of true blessedness.

When we pray, we call the Holy Spirit to ourselves. Prayer belongs to the heart, not to the lips. For God does not attend to the words of the petitioner; he looks upon the heart of the person praying. Do you wish to increase your virtues? Do not disclose them. Preserve in silence what you can lose by revealing it. For to some it is granted only to act well and not to have the fruit of their good work, because they themselves take it away through the pursuit of human self-display. As ice is melted by heat, so virtue is melted by the mouth of one who praises.

57. When I wish to return to my heart, crowds of carnal desires and the tumult of vices disperse my thought by their temptations and disturb my heart’s attention in prayer. And while I strive to turn to God after committing vices, and seek to entreat him against the very vices that I have committed, images of the sins I have done occur to my heart; they strike back the gaze of my mind, confuse my soul, and suppress the voice of my prayer. [Col. 0537A] Thus the evils I have done, impressed upon my thought in their images, trouble me in my very prayer. Yet the more heavily I am oppressed by the tumult of carnal thoughts, the more fervently I ought to persist in prayer. And as much as I commonly endure phantasms of my sins in prayer, so much must the attention of my heart, the more harshly it is repelled, persist more strongly in prayer, so that it may overcome the tumult of unlawful thought and, by the excess of its importunity, break through to the merciful ears of the Lord until it drives evil thoughts from the eyes of the heart with the hand of holy desire. This is true tranquillity: when the whole mind is gathered into itself and fixed immovably in the single desire of eternity. It ought, therefore, to restrain the fluctuation of the heart and gather the movements of thoughts and affections toward desire for the one true joy.

## Chapter XXVIII. On the vices and abuses of the tongue, singing, swearing, and so forth

58. To speak much is folly, for “in much speaking sin cannot be absent” (Prov. 10:19). It is called *lingua* (“tongue”) because it licks. It licks by flattering, bites by disparaging, kills by lying. It binds, and cannot be bound; it is slippery and cannot be held, but slips and deceives. It slips like an eel and pierces like an arrow; it removes friends, multiplies enemies, stirs quarrels, and sows discord. With one blow it strikes and kills many. It is bland and deceitful, broad and ready to exhaust [Col. 0537C] goods and mingle evils. “He who guards his tongue guards his soul” (Prov. 21:23), for “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21). Whoever cannot guard his tongue and his belly is not a monk. Whoever follows another’s sin must necessarily follow that person’s punishment. The fall of each person is a crime so much the greater as his virtue had been greater before he fell. By the things through which you sinned, by those same things you will be tormented. You followed the flesh; you will be scourged in the flesh. The crime lies not in things themselves, but in the use made by the agent. Often an excessively long reading, because of its length, erases the reader’s memory.

59. There are some undisciplined in voice who glory in the modulation of their voices; they do not merely rejoice in the gift of grace, but despise others as well. Swollen with self-exaltation, they sing something other than what the books contain—so great, perhaps, is the levity of their voice and of their mind. They sing to please the people rather than God. If you sing in order to seek praise from others, you sell your voice and make it not yours, but theirs. You have authority over your voice; have authority over your mind also. You break your voice; break your will too. You preserve harmony of voices; preserve harmony of conduct as well: that by example you may be in harmony with your neighbour, by will with God, and by obedience with your master. Take care that, as you delight in the height of your voice, you do not delight in the exaltation of your mind. Nor do riches harm a rich person if he uses them well; nor does poverty make a poor person praiseworthy if, amid want, he does not avoid the filth of sin.

60. [Col. 0538A] By whatever verbal device anyone swears, God, who is witness of the conscience, understands it as the person to whom it is sworn understands it. But one who swears with a double meaning becomes guilty in a double way, because he both takes the Lord’s name in vain and ensnares his neighbour by deceit. God often permits those whom he prepares for everlasting salvation to be punished here. Joy of heart is a person’s life; a perverse heart brings sadness. Sadness is an impediment to every good. Humility neither becomes angry itself nor allows others to become angry. Humility means that, whenever your brother sins against you, you forgive him before he repents of having sinned. Each person will receive from God such forgiveness as he himself has given to his neighbour who sins against him. In vain does one seek to make God propitious to oneself who neglects quickly to be reconciled to one’s neighbour. In your sickness do not despise yourself, but pray to God, and he will heal you. God often does not hear many according to their will in order to hear them according to salvation. Prayer is hindered from obtaining what is asked in two ways: if a person either commits evil or does not forgive the debt of one who has sinned against him.

61. True confession and true repentance occur when a person so repents of having sinned that he does not repeat the offence. Nothing is worse than to recognize one’s fault and not mourn it. If you see your persecutor at some time raging excessively, know that he is being driven on by the demon riding him. Every person who persecutes another in the body is first known to suffer persecution in the heart. The perfection of humility rests securely upon three things: that a person consider what he was before birth, [Col. 0538C] what he is from birth until death, and what he will be after this life. For why should a person be proud, remembering that he was vile seed and coagulated blood in the womb; then exposed to miseries and sin in the wilderness of this life; and finally destined to become ashes and food for worms in the tomb?

> Why is man proud, whose conception is guilt,  
> Birth punishment, life toil, and death necessity?  
> When, how, or where—he does not know.

## Chapter XXIX. The penitent’s confession concerning the instability of the heart, and the response of the spiritual father

62. Alone I enter the solitude of my heart, and for a little while converse with my heart, asking it about itself [Col. 0538D] and about the things surrounding it. My heart—perverse, vain, and wandering, more changeable than all changefulness—passes in wandering course from one thing to another, seeking rest where it is not. For in all visible things I have sought rest and could not find true rest in them. Then, returning to myself, I cannot remain within myself, because my mind is very light and exceedingly unstable, wandering and fugitive; it changes itself everywhere and fluctuates from every direction. For, sluggishly both willing and unwilling, it changes its plans and alternates its desires, like a leaf moved and carried about by the wind. Hence my vain and importunate thoughts draw and lead me now to the market-place, now to the disputes of litigants, now to the banquets of the rich, now to the unclean things of lusts. Now the flesh is inflamed by a filthy [Col. 0539A] tickling; now the soul is defiled by a foul thought. And when I wish to escape the darkness of my shame, I cannot. Thus—yes, thus—when I examine myself closely, I cannot endure myself. For there is no hour of the day nor moment of time in which I do not in some way offend my Creator and in some way obscure his image in me. When I carefully examine my life, I cannot confess by daily confession the most evil shoots of vices which sprout anew in me daily. Behold, Father, you have heard my evil and most evil abominations; yet know that much worse and more wicked things remain hidden in the corners of my heart, things which I am ashamed to bring to the light of true confession. Nevertheless, if you possess God’s counsel, advise what ought to be done.

63. When with wandering mind you run about through perverse and foolish thoughts, you open within yourself a way for deceiving spirits to tempt you. Thus you separate yourself from God, because “perverse thoughts separate from God, and the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee the deceitful and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wisdom 1:3, 5). But the unstable and restless mind, while always striving to grasp what it desires, is whirled about by its desires and never rests. Therefore it must be fixed immovably in the single desire of eternity. Do not be ashamed, however, to confess your sins, for all things are washed in confession, and no sin is forgiven unless it is first confessed. Go on, therefore; and if you desire to attain [Col. 0539C] perfect health, do not delay to vomit out, by the vomit of pure confession, everything that weighs upon the stomach of conscience. For unless the poison of vices is promptly expelled, it first corrupts the inner parts; then, boiling over outwardly, it occupies and defiles the whole body.

## Chapter XXX. The penitent continues to disclose his conscience and the state of his soul before the spiritual father

64. Since you do not abhor your Egyptian, but cherish and instruct him, I shall reveal to you not only sins of deeds, but also those of thoughts. Hear, therefore, my misery. Countless thoughts often come into my mind, many desires rise up, and they trouble me about care of the body and suggest many things concerning the uses of necessity. They gather there to deliberate, but in truth to deceive; many counsellors assemble, and they are vain advisers—indeed, real deceivers. They gather as though into one council and as though to seek good counsel; many counsels are proposed in common, but they are useless and vain, because it is a counsel of vanity and all their counsel concerns vanity. They urge me to have blood drawn so that I may rest and eat richer foods; to abstain from vigils so that I may sleep enough. They advise restoring the body lest it fail, cherishing the flesh lest it waste away, relaxing abstinence a little, and indulging in rest for a short time. Thus a superfluous care is exercised concerning the body, a vain question is debated concerning vanity, and often an hour is consumed [Col. 0540A] over such a useless matter.

65. Whoever does not resist the desires of his flesh and neglects to guard the movements of his heart becomes at last so bound by evil habit that afterward, even if he wishes to resist them, he cannot. Therefore, whenever you perceive counsellors of this sort, wicked and giving wicked counsel, assembling together, do not consent to them. Instead, immediately shake yourself free—now to prayer, then to work, and often to meditation—and do not cease until they vanish. Behold how Christ stood upon the cross; consider how you will die, where, and when; set yourself before the terrifying tribunal of the dreadful Judge; descend to the lowest hell, and there see how souls are punished for their sins. Such reflection is indeed the most tested remedy against shameful thoughts.

## Chapter XXXI. The penitent’s confession concerning care for the flesh and the vices of gluttony

66. Since you do not disdain to hear the words of my offences but listen patiently, I must confess what remains to be confessed. When I yield to the aforesaid wicked counsellors, who counsel wicked things, and gladly receive their counsels, evil thoughts suddenly appear; perverse desires rise, very anxious but little discerning, concerning how I may cherish my flesh most luxuriously—though, however sweetly it may be nourished, flesh is always flesh. They offer me the infirmary; but because it is shameful to remain in it long, they seek and find an occasion for riding. Without delay, horses are prepared, casks are filled, lodgings are chosen, and the necessities for the journey are tied up and made ready. I am summoned, and, being summoned, I come. That obedience is enjoined upon me; but I, fearing to become contemptible through my own desire, refuse with my mouth what I desire with my heart. I yield as though compelled; and so I mount gladly and set out on the journey. Alas! Religious observance is abandoned and silence is broken; here and there vain and useless, perhaps even disparaging, words fly about. Thus, in conversation, an entire day is often consumed. I come to the lodging and sit down at table; white bread and good wine are set before me, fish and cheese, eggs, and so forth. Meanwhile my mind returns to the brothers in the convent, and it grieves me that I am refreshed differently from them—[Col. 0540D] that I feast splendidly while they take dry refreshment. My conscience reproaches me if, instead of beans, I take fish; instead of onion or millet, cheese; instead of a morsel, a little cake for my meal; if I drink wine while the brothers drink water.

67. But gluttony, impatient of waiting, invites and urges me to eat and drink. It says: “You ought not to be burdensome to one who has received you charitably; rather, you ought in every respect to conform yourself to his wish, gladly obey his admonitions, and receive benefits bestowed with thanksgiving, because nothing offered with charity ought to be refused. It belongs to charity that you take, with him and on equal terms, what he sets before you, lest he be scandalized if he sees you eating something other than what he eats.” Therefore do as is fitting: [Col. 0541A] share and partake with your host, as it is written: “Eating and drinking what they have” (Luke 10:7). But conquered by these persuasions, I share and partake with the host for the host’s sake. And because the food is supplied from another’s property and not my own, I begin to indulge myself more freely and to be more liberal with my hand. I pursue the purpose for which I came to the table. For I eat and drink profusely, as is customary; dishes and cups multiply until both the belly is weighed down and the brain confused. The excess is not reproved, because hospitality excuses it. Thus—yes, thus—forgetful of myself, while I follow the appetite of gluttony, I soon begin to forget what the brothers do in the refectory; beans, cabbage, hard bread, and the drinking of water fall from my memory. My life is like a tale. I fear also that, by thus telling tales, I myself may become a tale if I am found without good works. Tell me, then, what I ought to do and how I may restrain gluttony, lest I become the slave of so small a bailiff.”

68. Gluttony is always at war and at fault. Whether you eat or drink, it is present to wage war with you. If you do not fight well, you will certainly be conquered by it; it fights with many and is overcome by few. Therefore overcome it so much more vigorously as you recognize more plainly that it must be overcome. And because you cannot attain knowledge of God except through knowledge of yourself, examine yourself again and again, lest perhaps something lie hidden in you that displeases God. For you cannot see God except with a clean heart; nor will the heart become joyful unless it first becomes clean [Col. 0541C] from every defilement.

## Chapter XXXII. The penitent accuses himself concerning the faults of confession and envy

69. I still have much to tell you, but I am ashamed to confess it. Nevertheless, because I cannot otherwise see God, I shall open my heart to you. I confess that I neglected to review my sins, and therefore consigned many to forgetfulness. Nor have I confessed all those I knew, because of their multitude. Those which I did confess, I did not confess purely because of shamefulness, or I concealed them altogether. Those which I confessed, whether well or badly, I did not mourn worthily, because of their long standing and inveterate habit. I confessed to one to whom I ought not to have confessed; and from one to whom I ought to have confessed I concealed my sins. What is worse, I sought vain glory from confession. I excused manifest sins when I was convicted of them, or, worse still, defended them. Through the shame of embarrassment I covered my fault. Thus—yes, thus—I always heap sins upon sins, and I resolve to correct my life daily; yet I always defer it from day to day, and while I propose that this be done in the future, it comes about that that future is always still future—indeed perhaps never to come. “O Lord my God, how long shall I lay up plans in my soul?” (Ps. 12:2). “What profit is there in my blood, when I descend into corruption?” (Ps. 29:10). There is no vice to which I have not in some manner been a servant. For all contend over me, to see whose servant I may chiefly appear. [Col. 0542A] Yet above all vices envy persecutes me. This plague torments me everywhere. Give me counsel, therefore, how I may escape it.

## Chapter XXXIII. The spiritual father’s response concerning envy

70.

> Nothing is sadder [variant: “more just”] than envy, which [immediately itself …]

It torments and racks its own author. Therefore it must be altogether shunned and abhorred, since in it God is offended, one’s neighbor is harmed, and the mind is afflicted. For envy always torments the mind of the person who possesses it, even though it may often be unable to harm the neighbor against whom it rages. But although every envy is evil, the worst form of this evil is that which commits its injuries under the appearance of holiness. [Col. 0542B] For often, when it rages against a neighbor through the vice of anger or the poison of envy, the mind pretends to itself that it acts from zeal for justice. Anyone who has been injured by his neighbor can no longer easily look upon him with a single, simple eye. Whatever he sees that person do displeases him. At almost every hour he silently accuses him within himself. Countless grounds arise daily that show the other to be culpable; many arguments occur that prove him guilty and deserving of punishment. Indeed, the evil often grows to such an extent that he believes himself guilty before God unless he rebukes the other more severely and reproves him for his perversity.

For such a malicious thought speaks within him: “How long shall I tolerate him in this state? I am shown to consent to him if I do not rebuke him; and by consenting [Col. 0542C] I offend God. Therefore I shall rebuke him, lest I offend God. For I do all this, not to avenge an injury done to myself, but an injury done to God.” Indeed, I shall thus restore him to himself: for to rebuke and chastise one’s neighbor is not to wish to harm one’s neighbor, but to wish him good. Thus malicious thought often speaks within itself; for its own malice has blinded it. It thinks its hatred to be love, and its injustice to be an exercise of justice. Such malicious thoughts therefore assemble from every side in the mind and pretend that they gather in God’s service, rather than wishing to exercise their own hatred.

Therefore examine yourself still more often; consider intensely; investigate your conscience diligently, so that you may know what you ought to correct, and also what you ought to give thanks for. For it is very useful and altogether necessary to know what you lack, what you want, what you desire, and what you wish to possess.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. The accusation of oneself concerning various, wandering, and idle thoughts, and the response of the spiritual father

**71.** I could more easily count the atoms of the world than the motions of my heart. The speed of animals and birds cannot be compared with my movements. There is no one able to comprehend my thoughts. My desires have no limit. Now I think and desire one thing, now another; yet I can possess neither this nor that. While my body is inactive, I wander in thought through diverse places. At no hour, at no instant of time, do I rest; but in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, ranging through many regions, I create new creatures [Col. 0543A] and again with equal ease destroy them, or vary them repeatedly in one fashion and another. I desire to possess this or that; I wish to be such or such a person—as though God did not know how, or could not, give me that thing or make me such.

**72.** O keeper of the heart, how petty and covetous a heart you have! It is small, yet desires great things. It could scarcely suffice to feed one kite, yet the whole world does not suffice for it. With your heart alone, in restless motion, you range through the whole world. You run without feet, work without hands, have no wings, and yet never cease from flying. Each day you gather riches and cannot be satisfied; you prepare feasts for refreshment and do not eat from them. You think of these things and those things—and what you think is false. Hear how this is so, that henceforth you may guard yourself.

Perhaps [Col. 0543B] you are now thinking about the sun, or some friend of yours, or yourself. If the sun is one, then the sun you fashion in your thought is false, because the real one performs its course in fixed places and times, whereas you place this one wherever you wish. If that friend of yours is one person, then the one you fashion in thought is false, because you do not know where he is, whereas you imagine him wherever you wish. Moreover, you perceive yourself to be in this place; nevertheless, by the invention of thought you go wherever you wish and speak with whomever you wish. Yet this is not true, because you are not there now. Since these things are false, therefore do not henceforth think such things; but cast your thought upon the Lord, who made you and remade you, chose you and called you, will judge you and save you.

**73.** O how many and how great are those who at this hour converse with him and embrace him within themselves! But you delight in things that perish and pass away, and cannot remain with you. Consider how many are dying now. If the present hour for doing penance, which has been granted to you, were granted to them, how they would hasten to the altars, and with what urgency; and there, with bent knees—or indeed with their whole bodies prostrate on the ground—how long they would sigh, weep, and pray, until they deserved to obtain from God the fullest pardon for their sins! But you, by eating, drinking, jesting, and laughing, waste in idle living the time God granted you for acquiring grace and earning glory.

Consider also how many souls are now tormented in hell without hope of pardon or mercy. If the love of God cannot hold you, let at least the fear of judgment hold and terrify you: fear of Gehenna, the snares of death, the pains of hell, burning fire, the gnawing worm, fetid sulphur, Tartarean flame, and every evil. Examine yourself yet further, so that you may know what you lack, lest in that final examination [Col. 0543D] you be put to shame before all, if iniquity is found in you.

## CHAPTER XXXV. He continues to confess his varied and unstable feelings and disturbances

**74.** I cannot duly weigh or sufficiently assess what is this so manifold volatility of my thoughts, this restless and tireless swiftness that makes me range through so many, so varied, so innumerable things. At no hour and at no instant of time can I rest; rather, with astonishing haste I pass through limitless expanses [Col. 0544A] of places and stretches of time. A ready passage and agile course lies open to me from every direction: from heights to depths, from depths to heights; from first things to last, from last things to first.

I cannot adequately express what modes of alternation I assume in momentary changes, how variously I customarily vary through the motions of alternating vicissitudes, and by what disturbances I am affected each day. Now I raise myself to confidence; now I fall into distrust. Now I am fixed by steadfastness; now I am shaken by sudden terror. At one time anger troubles me; at another immense rage agitates me. Nor is it so remarkable that I am affected every moment by diverse qualities and different disturbances; rather, what is astonishing beyond measure is that at almost the same instant I am often touched by contrary feelings: now I am led by hatred, now by love; now I am drawn by joy, now by sorrow. How often, amid the wondrous festivities of my rejoicing, does some suddenly arising cause of sadness shake and cast me down violently, abruptly turning all the festivity of my exultant mind into grief! Things long and deeply loved I afterward pursue with excessive hatred; things intensely approved and desired I suddenly detest. But who could enumerate the kinds of all my feelings? Who could adequately explain every mode of my variation? Almost as many as are the differences among things are the varieties of my feelings.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. The response of the spiritual father: how useful and necessary self-knowledge is

[Col. 0544C]

**75.** Since among all living creatures humankind is found to be more worthy both in nobler form and in nobler power, no knowledge is better than that by which a person knows himself. Therefore leave other things and examine yourself. Run through yourself, and remain within yourself. Let your thought begin from yourself and end in yourself; do not fruitlessly scatter yourself among other things while neglecting yourself. Think of nothing apart from your salvation, because in gaining your salvation no one is more closely related or nearer to you than yourself.

But if anything presents itself to your thought which in no way concerns your own salvation, immediately reject and spit it out, so that you may always be able to inspect yourself and [Col. 0544D] come from knowledge of yourself to knowledge of God. A person ought to know to what good things he is naturally more inclined, or to what evils more prone; in what pursuits he ought to labor more earnestly, against what evils he ought to keep more vigilant watch; by what exercises he may advance more profitably, by what vices he may be more easily corrupted; to what faults he is subject or in what merits he excels; and what punishment or reward he ought to expect for these; how much he advances or falls back daily; with what industry of mind he strives to mourn past evils, avoid present ones, and forestall future ones; with what constancy of mind he endeavors to recover lost goods and preserve and multiply those possessed. O how necessary an examination, and how wonderful a scrutiny: to keep before one’s eyes so many virtues of the mind, so many of its exercises, so many of its pursuits or merits, and to remain long devoted to such contemplation!

**76.** Therefore withdraw your mind from love of lower things, lest perhaps, cast down from higher things and drawn away and enticed from the place of delight by your own desire, it follow your desires and become a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth. Finally, if you wish to fulfill the Lord’s command, “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. 4:23). For one who does not first reflect upon his own spirit does not know what he ought to think concerning the angelic spirit or the divine Spirit. One who does not know himself judges nothing rightly. One who does not weigh the dignity of his own condition does not know that all worldly glory lies beneath his feet.

O keeper of the heart, if you are not yet fit to enter into yourself, how will you be fit to investigate those things which are within you or above you? If you are not yet worthy to enter the first tabernacle, with what face do you presume to enter the second tabernacle—that is, the Holy of Holies? If you cannot yet undertake lofty steps, so as to ascend the high mountain with the Lord Jesus, or at least with Moses, by what presumption do you suppose you can fly into heaven? Return to yourself before you presume to investigate what is above you. The sun first illuminates the boundaries of its rising before it climbs to higher places.

Therefore the first thing is that you return to yourself, enter into your heart, and learn to assess your spirit. Examine what you are, what you have been, what you ought to be, and what you can be: what you have been by nature; what you now are through fault; [Col. 0545C] what you ought to be through diligence; what you can still be through grace. Learn from your own spirit to know what you ought to judge concerning other spirits. This is the gate, this the ladder, this the entrance, this the ascent: by this one enters the inmost places; by this one is lifted to the highest. Do you see how much a full knowledge of oneself can accomplish for a person? By it he advances to knowledge of all heavenly, earthly, and infernal things.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. The penitent’s purpose: distrusting himself and yearning for intimacy with God

**77.** I would like to know what I myself am like, but I can scarcely discern the truth about myself. For the private love I have for myself takes away my true judgment about myself. Therefore I trust myself little concerning myself, as one who is a liar, fearing that, if I judge myself, “iniquity may lie to itself” (Ps. 26:12). Let him judge me, then, to whom all things are naked and open; whom I cannot deceive, because he is wisdom; nor escape, because he is everywhere; nor corrupt, because he is justice. Let him come to me whose delight is to be with the children of men (Prov. 8:31), who stands at the door and knocks, ready to enter if I open to him (Rev. 3). Let him enter and sanctify a sanctuary for himself, because he is holy, and holiness befits his house. Let him uproot vices, order thoughts, heal affections, and compose my conduct. Let no one resist him in anything, that “his place may be in peace” (Ps. 75:3).

Would that no human being were outwardly with me, so that inwardly I might speak more intimately with him. [Col. 0546A] For he seeks secrecy and loves a solitary place. Therefore I shall flee the consolations and conversations of people, so that I may have God dwelling in the secret place of my heart. Yet it is very difficult to recall the mind from outward things to inward ones and remain there. Nor is it less difficult to penetrate from visible things to invisible and remain in them for a long time. These things are hard and very laborious, but very fruitful.

Therefore I shall accustom myself to think only inward things, love only interior things, and remain in them, so that I may hear what the Lord my God says within me. Behold, I am here, most merciful Lord: I am with you; I am within. So long as I was occupied with outward things, I could not hear your voice within me. But now, having returned to myself, I have entered in to you, that I may hear you and speak to you. Speak, therefore, most merciful one, for your servant hears. Speak, for I am prepared to obey. Whatever you command, I will gladly and devotedly fulfill according to my ability.

**78.** O my soul, the King of Angels comes to us and has lodged with us. Let us therefore rejoice with a perfect heart over so great a guest. Let us give him glory and honor, because he has deigned to visit his servants. Let us feast and rejoice with him in gladness and exultation. Let us delight in him because of him; and let no one be troublesome to him in any respect, lest in anger he depart from us and bring upon us a curse instead of a blessing. Let us offer him every service of love, asking and entreating that he may deign to remain with us. If we cannot render all that we owe, [Col. 0546C] at least let us humbly submit ourselves to his whole will.

Let this be a solemn day, on which we gladly received our Savior as a guest in our dwelling. Let no member, no faculty, be excluded from this joy. Let all thoughts and feelings therefore come together as one, celebrating the feast day in all purity and holiness. Let no alien thought insert itself and disturb the joys of this solemnity. Let my eyes be always toward the Lord, through whom I am, live, and understand; nor let them cease to water his feet with tears. Let my ears hear and understand what displeases him in us and what pleases him; what he condemns and what he approves. Let the sense of smell delight in that most sweet fragrance of his sweetness. His fragrance is the fragrance of eternal life, the fragrance of all sweetness and delight. Let my mouth be filled with praise, that I may sing your glory, most high Lord (Ps. 71:8). Let the meditation of my heart always be in your sight (Ps. 18:15), so that I may see you through faith and contemplation until I deserve to see you face to face. Most merciful Father, let nothing in us cease from your praise. “Bless the Lord, O my soul; and all that is within me, his holy name” (Ps. 103:1). Bless him and say:

> Glory, praise, and honor be to you, O Christ the King, Redeemer.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The analogy and likeness of the soul with God

**79.** O my soul, if you wish to be loved by God, restore his image in yourself, and he will love you; renew his likeness in yourself, [Col. 0547A] and he will desire you. For by the counsel of the Holy Trinity your Creator created you in his image and likeness—a gift he granted to no other creature—so that you might love him all the more ardently as you understand yourself to have been more wonderfully made by him.

Consider, therefore, your nobility. Just as God is wholly everywhere, giving life to, moving, and governing all things, so you are wholly present everywhere in your body, giving it life, moving it, and governing it. And just as God is, lives, and knows, so you, according to your measure, are, live, and know. And just as in God there are three persons—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—so you have three powers: understanding, memory, and will. And just as the Son is begotten from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from them both, so [Col. 0547B] will is generated from understanding, and memory proceeds from both of these. And just as God is Father, God is Son, and God is Holy Spirit—yet not three gods but one God and three persons—so the soul is understanding, the soul is will, and the soul is memory—yet not three souls, but one soul and three powers.

By these powers of the soul, as though by its higher faculties, we are commanded to love God: that we may love him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind—that is, with all understanding, all will, and all memory; with all affection, without failure, guided by discerning attention. Understanding concerning God alone does not suffice for blessedness unless the will is present in love of him. Indeed, these two do not suffice unless memory is added, by which God may remain always in the mind of the person who understands and wills; so that, just as there can be no moment in which a person does not use or enjoy God’s goodness or mercy, so there may be no moment in which he does not hold him present in memory.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the soul’s dignity, in that it can spiritually give birth to Christ

**80.** Understand your dignity, noble creature: not only are you marked with God’s image, but you are also adorned with his likeness. For just as your Creator, who created you in his likeness, is love, good and just, gentle and mild, patient and merciful, and possesses the other attributes read of him, so you were created to possess love and to be pure and holy, beautiful and fair, gentle and humble. [Col. 0547D] The more you have these virtues within you, the nearer you will be to God and the greater a likeness to your Creator you will bear.

What greater thing could your maker do for you than create you in his likeness and adorn you with the same garments of virtue with which he himself is adorned? Attend, therefore, diligently to the excellence of your first creation, and recognize in yourself the venerable image of the Holy Trinity. Strive to possess the honor of the divine likeness in which you were created through nobility of conduct, the exercise of virtues, and the dignity of rewards, so that when he appears as he is, you may then be able to appear like him. For like seeks like; and as you prepare yourself for God, so God must appear to you.

If, therefore, [Col. 0548A] you restore your natural beauty within yourself, “the king will desire your beauty, for he is your God” (Ps. 45:12). He is friend and bridegroom, brother and son. For he himself said: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, that one is my brother and sister and mother” (Matt. 12:50). Hear how this is so. The Father’s virtue and wisdom is the Father’s Son. The Father’s Word is the Father’s will. A human being’s will is nothing other than a certain offspring of the mind. If, therefore, your will and the Father’s will are the same, your son and the Father’s Son are the same. Truth, wisdom, and will are conceived in the heart and generated from the heart.

**81.** If, therefore, you will and know the same thing as the Father, you have the same Son as the Father. It lies within you whether you are father or mother, or rather both father and mother—not by your own merit, but by God’s gift. For you can give birth to him in your own heart and in another’s heart. You can conceive him from your own heart and from another’s mouth. He is begotten by understanding, conceived by consent, born through affection, and nourished through action. When you understand truth, or cause another to understand it, you give birth to Christ. Do you know God’s will? Consent to it, and you have conceived. When you beget, you are father; when you conceive, you are mother. In loving, you give birth; in acting, you nourish.

Thus—yes, thus—it is left to the power of each person whether that person becomes the mother of such great offspring. Cursed, therefore, is the barren woman who does not give birth, though by God’s grace she could have such a son in fulfillment of her desire. Why is the man who does not beget not likewise cursed? Because it does not lie equally within our power to understand truth [Col. 0548C] and to consent to truth. For I do not always understand truth when I wish; but once it is understood, I always consent to it. Yet I cannot will unless God’s grace is with me. For no human effort exists without God’s grace.

Since the first human being sinned, we have lost the good of nature and likewise the strength of free choice, though not choice itself, lest the correction of sin not belong to us. For within us remains freedom of choice for seeking salvation—that is, rational will—but only when God first admonishes and invites us to salvation, so that we may choose or follow. It lies within our power to assent to divine inspiration and to choose and follow what pertains to our salvation; but it is the gift of God that we may attain what we desire to obtain by following. It is through our own power and sloth that we fall; but it is through our own vigilance together with heavenly assistance that we do not fall. Happy is the person who walks wisely in this way, so as not to fall; or, if he falls, to rise at once. Happier is the one who never fell; but happiest is the one who already reigns with God.

## CHAPTER XL. On the soul’s readiness to receive Christ and on the inmost recess of divine love

**82.** Happy is the person who, whenever he wishes, has the Son who is God ready at hand. O how great is human dignity—to have God as Son! And how great is the humility of the Almighty—to have a human being as father! And how great is the soul’s nobility—to have Christ Jesus as bridegroom! [Col. 0549A]

Therefore a holy soul, friend of the true bridegroom, ought always to long with supreme desire for the coming of her beloved, and to be ready and unencumbered, so that she may receive her knocking friend without the injury of any delay and hasten with every eagerness to meet him when he calls, lest he arrive suddenly and unexpectedly and find her insufficiently ready and adorned; or lest, long excluded, he endure some distress from lengthy waiting.

But it is one thing to enter with him, another to go out to him. In the former, the soul returns to itself and enters with its beloved into the innermost chambers of its heart. In the latter, it is led out beyond itself and raised to contemplate sublime things. What is its entering, then, if not gathering its whole self into itself? And what is its going out, if not pouring its whole self out beyond itself? Therefore the soul’s entering the chamber with its beloved, abiding alone with the alone, and enjoying his sweetness means nothing other than forgetting all outward things and delighting supremely and intimately in his love.

It sees itself alone with the beloved when, having forgotten all outward things, it presses its desire onward from self-consideration into love of its beloved; when, from what it considers in its inmost self, it inflames its mind with such affection; and when, from consideration both of its goods and of its evils, it rises to thanksgiving and offers sacrifices of inward devotion, now for grace bestowed, now for pardon granted. It is led into the beloved’s inmost place and set in the highest good when it loves from the inmost affection of the heart and above all [Col. 0549C] things.

**83.** Consider what in your life you have loved most ardently, desired anxiously, what affected you most pleasantly and delighted you more deeply than all other things. Consider, then, whether you feel the same force of affection and abundance of delight when you burn with longing for the supreme Beloved and rest in his love. Who could doubt that he does not yet occupy the innermost chamber of your affection if the sting of deepest love penetrates and stirs your soul less intensely in divine affections than it once customarily penetrated or stirred it in alien affections?

But if you perceive within yourself concerning divine things a force of love or delight altogether as great—or perhaps stronger—than any you have ever experienced elsewhere, consider further whether there is perhaps anything else in which you can take delight or consolation. Certainly, as long as I can conceive consolation or pleasure from any other thing whatsoever, I do not yet dare say that our beloved occupies the innermost chamber of most fervent love. Therefore strive and hasten, whatever kind of soul you may be, to draw him yet farther into the inner and secret chambers of your heart. For who would deny that the innermost chamber of the human heart can possess such recesses that, when the force of supreme and singular love has fastened something there by affection, it cannot be torn away by any alien delight? Certainly, if you seek or receive some alien consolation, you do not yet love your God, though perhaps supremely, yet not uniquely. [Col. 0550A] He has not yet, then, been brought into the inmost place or established there. If, therefore, you do not strive to lead him into your inmost parts, how can I believe that you either wish or are able to follow him into his sublime places?

**84.** Therefore let this be a sure sign to you, whatever soul you may be, that you love your beloved less, or are loved by him less, if you are not yet called to those contemplative ecstasies, or have not yet deserved to follow when he calls. For how do you love perfectly or receive perfect love if, in longing for the highest things, you are not carried up to the things above and do not pass into those contemplative and anagogical endeavors through an alienation of mind? Do you wish to know that the sublimity of divine revelations is a clear indication of divine love? “I shall no longer call you servants,” he says, [Col. 0550B] “but friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John 15:15). Therefore strive to love your God intimately and supremely, and at every hour long with supreme desire for the joy of divine contemplation. Gather yourself into yourself and rest in the desire for divinity alone.

## CHAPTER XLI. The soul is stirred to contemplate sublime and divine things

**85.** For the perfect soul, devoted constantly to contemplation of the highest things, ought at every hour to await with supreme desire the end of its pilgrimage and departure from this prison, and to direct its mind toward that spectacle of divine contemplation which we hope for in the life to come, longing ardently in this expectation, so that it may deserve to see face to face what for the present it sees “through a mirror, in an enigma.” [Col. 0550C]

It is therefore necessary to ascend to the lofty heart and, through divine revelation and ecstasy of mind, learn what that thing is to which one ought to aspire or devote oneself, and what disposition of sublimity the mind ought to adopt and grow accustomed to. For if someone has once been admitted to that light-bearing glory of angelic sublimity and deserved to enter that spectacle of divine rays, with what intimate desires, what deep sighs, what inexpressible groans, do we suppose that person persists; with what continual recollection, with what joyful wonder, do we believe that person recalls and turns over in the mind the splendor he has seen—desiring it, sighing for it, contemplating it—until at last he is transformed into that same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord? (2 Cor. 3:18)

**86.** Yet when we return from that state of sublimity to ourselves, we are utterly unable to recall to memory, in the truth or clarity in which we first perceived them, those things that we saw above ourselves. And although we retain something of them in memory and see as though through a veil set between, and as though amid a mist, we cannot sufficiently comprehend or remember either the manner of life or the quality of the vision. In a wondrous way, remembering, we do not remember; and not remembering, [Col. 0551A] we remember: seeing, we do not see through; looking, we do not perceive clearly; attending, we do not penetrate—until we rise again by meditation into contemplation, by contemplation into wonder, by wonder into alienation of mind.

Contemplation of truth is begun in this life but celebrated in unbroken perpetuity in the life to come. Through contemplation of truth, a person is instructed unto justice and perfected unto glory. The grace of contemplation not only cleanses the heart of every worldly love but sanctifies it, and inflames the mind with love for heavenly things. One advanced by divine inspiration and revelation to the grace of contemplation receives certain earnest-money pledges of that future fullness, where he will cleave perpetually to everlasting contemplation.

But anyone who wishes to devote himself to contemplation of truth must learn to rest not only from evil works but also from superfluous thoughts. For many, though they know how to be inactive in body, are by no means able to be at rest in heart, because they do not know how to make “sabbath from sabbath”; and therefore they cannot fulfill what is said in the Psalm: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Ps. 45:11). For those who rest in body but wander everywhere in heart do not deserve to see how sweet the Lord is and how good the God of Israel is to those who are upright in heart (Ps. 73:1). Thus their enemies mock their sabbaths (Lam. 1:7): that is, they stretch out the leisure of their rest into useless thoughts, and roam everywhere, here and there, by every byway in wandering course, without regard for arriving anywhere. Their minds are carried in different directions, and by running now to one side, now to another, are driven with remarkable swiftness into contrary places.

**87.** Thus, thus, as long as we live under the impoverished elements of this world, we extend our desires beyond our joys, because the things we desire are infinitely more numerous than those we can attain in this life. But that blessed multitude of heavenly spirits does not extend its desires beyond the fullness of its joys, since it is wholly unable to comprehend the infinity or immensity of its blessedness.

Their joy arises not only from contemplating the Creator but also from contemplating [Col. 0552A] his creatures. For while they find God wonderful in all his works, what wonder is it if, marveling everywhere, they venerate; and venerating, marvel at the great deeds of him whom they love? Thus they find, not only in incorporeal creatures but also in bodily creatures, grounds for wonder and for worthy veneration of their Creator. They contemplate all these things unceasingly; contemplating, they marvel; marveling, they rejoice. They rejoice in divine contemplation, exult in one another’s vision, and marvel in the observation of bodily things.

**88.** Let us too learn, in contemplating, to marvel, and in marveling, to contemplate: how the citizens of that heavenly blessedness unceasingly behold all things beneath them and understand the reason and order of everything they see from on high; how they rejoice without end in mutual fellowship and indissoluble love; how they burn insatiably for that vision of divine brightness. Nothing is more pleasant, nothing more profitable, than the grace of contemplation. The more abundantly you delight in the contemplation of heavenly things and marvel in delighting, the more willingly you remain there, the more diligently you search, and the more deeply you are enlightened. There you will always find what to marvel at and what to delight in. Nowhere is there a richer material for wonder, and nowhere a more useful cause for delight. Let your wonder and delight, therefore, always be in these things. You will have no need to seek one thing in place of another and range here and there through the vain wandering of thoughts. For to know God is the fullness of knowledge; [Col. 0552C] the fullness of this knowledge is the fullness of glory; and the consummation of grace is the perpetuity of life.

Yet for the fullness of this knowledge, inward compunction is more necessary than profound investigation; sighs more than arguments; frequent lamentations more than abundant disputation; tears more than maxims; prayer more than reading; the grace of tears more than knowledge of letters; contemplation of heavenly things more than occupation with earthly things.

Here, in more recent editions, another little treatise *On Conscience* followed; but Horstius rightly deleted it, as being a mere repetition of what precedes.

[Col. 0551]

# TREATISE ON CONSCIENCE, ADDRESSED TO A CERTAIN RELIGIOUS OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER. (G)

[Note.]

This treatise is not unworthy of Bernard, although it does not appear to be his. At the end, the author wishes his name to remain unmentioned, whereas Bernard does not customarily do so.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0551D]

You ask of me, my beloved friend, what is above me—indeed, what is against me—namely, the light of knowledge and purity of conscience. In both matters you are mistaken, though you do not believe yourself mistaken, so strongly are you moved either by affection for me or by your opinion of me. What am I, and what can I do? For I am a sinner, and a sinner sinning beyond measure; nor has any liveliness of intellect a place in me. Added to this is a multitude of affairs, which in a person of talent either smothers or drives away the seeds of all learning, according to the Wise Man: “Wisdom is to be written in the time of leisure, and one who is less occupied with action shall attain it” (Ecclus. 38:25).

Nevertheless, although not because you are my friend, yet because you are importunate, I shall rise in accordance with the Lord’s command (Luke 11:8) and give, not what is necessary for you, but what is at hand for me. May the Lord grant you according to your heart. For he is the one who gives to his voice a voice of power; who in his sweetness makes provision for the poor; who fills your desire with good things. [Col. 0553B]

## CHAPTER ONE. How obscure and impenetrable a thing conscience is
1. Human conscience is a deep abyss. For just as the depth of an abyss cannot be drained, so the human heart cannot be emptied of its thoughts. Human conscience is like the great and wide sea, “where are creeping things without number” (Ps. 103:25). How aptly he said, “creeping things”! For as a creeping thing crawls secretly and wanders hither and thither through winding turns, so poisonous thoughts gently enter and leave a person’s conscience, so that one does not know whence they come or whither they go. He knew this well who said: “The heart of man is perverse and unsearchable; and who,” he says, “shall know it?” [Col. 0553C] (Jer. 17:9). He does not say “who?” as though it were difficult, but as though it were impossible: for what admits no investigation admits no knowledge.

See that great Apostle—I mean Paul—the unique investigator of his own conscience. “It is of very little account to me,” he says, “that I should be judged by you, or by a human day.” See how he had escaped human judgment, having no concern about those who are outside. “But neither,” he says, “do I judge myself” (1 Cor. 4:3). And where, O Apostle, is that holy saying of your own: “If we judged ourselves, we should certainly not be judged” (ibid. 11:31)? Why do you either conceal from us, or deny, that you judge yourself? Hear why: “I am conscious,” he says, “of nothing.” Blessed is the conscience that is conscious of nothing in itself, which fears neither its own judgment nor that of another. Do you see how, by so exalted a manner of life, he feared neither another’s judgment nor his own?

Yet a snare and a great pit still lie hidden, O vessel of election; but they cannot escape that most watchful eye of yours. For he added: “But I am not thereby justified”; and he went on: “He who judges me is the Lord” (1 Cor. 4:4). This is the third judgment, God’s judgment, which even that most purified conscience does not comprehend. For, according to Scripture, it does not know whether it is worthy of love or hatred, since all things are reserved for it as uncertain in the future (Eccl. 9:1–2). Shaken and struck by fear of this judgment, he groaned and said: “For I do not understand what I do” (Rom. 7:15). Even if I escape the judgment of the world and the judgment of myself, there remains the judgment [Col. 0554A] of God, which does not permit me to understand what I do, because I do not know whether He accepts what I do. For He knows me better than I know myself: He searches reins and hearts, knows hidden things, and reaches “to the dividing of soul and spirit” (Heb. 4:12); He alone knows all things and the reasons for all things.

2. O singular instrument of the Holy Spirit: if you do not understand what you do, why do you say elsewhere, “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12), calling your conscience your glory? But he understands in part and does not understand in part. He certainly understands because he has risen above his own judgment and that of others; but he is held back before the judgment of God, where beyond doubt he does not know what he does. For he is not justified by those two judgments, but will be justified by the third, which, just as it cannot be known, cannot be comprehended.

Nevertheless, the exclusion of the two judgments—that is, present justification—is in some measure a sure indication of eternal predestination, in which God foresaw that we should be made conformed to the image of His Son; and of future glorification, when we shall be in Him and He in us, when He shall be all in all. Therefore he spoke elsewhere with as much confidence as sincerity: “I am certain,” he says, “that neither death, nor life,” and many other things—indeed almost all those enumerated there—“will be able to separate me from the love of Christ” (Rom. 8:38–39). But when he had said so many and such great things, he passed over one thing: namely, his own will, which is the cause of salvation and damnation.

Observe how this man filled with God called [Col. 0554C] his conscience his glory, as though fully understanding it and himself within it. Yet he had said that he did not understand what he did, making his conscience captive not now to glory but to ignorance. Thus the Apostle, investigating his conscience by searching, fails; and, when he thought that he had reached its bottom by setting aside both another’s judgment and his own, he encounters the depth—namely, the judgment of God—which he cannot penetrate. Thus, now convinced or convicted, he cries out: “Your judgments, O Lord, are not merely an abyss, but a deep abyss” (Ps. 35:7).

What then shall we wretched and pitiable people do, if he who “laboured more abundantly than they all” (1 Cor. 15:10), to whom even the Keeper of the keys of the kingdom, together with John and James, seemed to have contributed nothing (Gal. 2:6–9), [Col. 0554D] who was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2), thinks and speaks thus of himself? But now, that I may disclose to your purity in plain and unadorned words all that I think concerning conscience, I have decided to set before you four kinds of distinction, so that what has been divided into parts may be read more pleasantly and retained more easily.

370

## CHAPTER II. Four kinds of conscience

3. One conscience, then, is good and tranquil; another good and troubled; another evil and tranquil; another evil and troubled. But let us first consider the first. A good conscience is one which both punishes past sins and shrinks from committing sins that deserve punishment; which, though it feels sin, does not consent to sin. “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin,” says the holy man (Ps. 31:2). He did not say, “Who has committed no sin”; for there is no such person except one, namely the Son of God, “who committed no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22). Therefore, whatever He has determined not to impute to me is as though it had not been. Blessed, then, are not those in whom no sins have been found, but those “whose iniquities have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered” (Ps. 31:1). He did not say, “whose sins do not exist,” but “whose sins have been covered,” so that by some covering they may in a manner be hidden from the eyes of God.

Happy is the soul which, though feeling sin, does not consent to it; which, though thought defiles it, is washed by reason as it struggles and resists the law of sin. The struggle is painful, but fruitful; for although it brings suffering, it also brings a crown—or rather, what wears out one who feels it crowns one who conquers it. For in this conflict, where there is sensation but no consent, there is “no condemnation,” according to the Apostle, “for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:1).

Moreover, one who has the will not to sin and to guard his feet from falling; who both bewails and punishes the deeds of former time; who repels evil thoughts coming to his heart by dashing them against Christ—such a person, bound and constrained as if by a threefold cord, has a conscience both cleansed and pure. I would call it tranquil when the Spirit Himself now bears witness to that person’s spirit that he is a son of God; when such a person is sweet to all and burdensome to none, making use of a friend for kindness, an enemy for patience, everyone for goodwill, and, where possible, for beneficence. Such a conscience is a rare bird upon earth; but the rarer it is, the dearer it is to God.

## CHAPTER III. On a good and troubled conscience

4. A conscience is good but troubled when it admits nothing soft or lax, but, so far as it can, scrubs itself more rigorously clean of the world’s defilement—not, however, amid sweetness, but amid much bitterness. For the straight path seems hard to it, and the austere life severe. Everywhere it sees what displeases the flesh; yet it holds itself with the bridle of the fear of God, and in every storm of its heart fastens itself to this anchor. For, according to the Prophet, “he was troubled and did not speak” (Ps. 76:5).

But I have heard what the Lord says concerning such a person: “I am with him,” He says, “in tribulation.” For what purpose? “I will deliver him and glorify him” (Ps. 90:15). I will deliver him from bitterness and glorify him in delight: what he previously did from fear, he will do with love. This conscience speaks to God in the Psalm and says: “You have shaken the earth, O Lord, and troubled it; heal its breaches, for it has been shaken.” The earth is shaken when the sinner confesses and repents; it is troubled when, in the religious life, one endures bitterness. But to heal these wounds belongs to Him alone who heals all our infirmities. Hear, however, what follows: “You have shown Your people hard things.” What hard things? “You have given us wine of compunction to drink” (Ps. 59:4–5), not the milk of anointing.

[Col. 0556A]

5. It should be noted that some living the religious life are given milk to drink, and others wine; yet both are divine. Those drink milk to whom vigils seem short, food pleasant, labours welcome, and garments soft; to whom even what is great in the exercises of holy life seems too little. For milk is drunk pleasantly, flows down sweetly, without injury and without bitterness. So too such persons proceed sweetly in their holy purpose and run gladly, without injury to their own conscience and without bitterness toward another’s.

One who drinks such milk has this characteristic: that his own sin displeases him; that he does not consent to another’s sin; that nevertheless he does not abandon the sinner on account of it; that, insofar as lies in his power, he does not pass over the sinner’s fault in silence; [Col. 0556B] and that, after correcting the sinner, he does not insult him. This is concerning the drinking of milk; hear concerning the drinking of wine.

Wine, indeed, is harsh and unpleasant. Those drink wine who, having undertaken and entered upon the ways of life, are tormented alike by bodily and spiritual tribulations, but do not yield or withdraw in tribulation. These are they to whom the Lord Himself declares and foretells with His own mouth: “You are they who have remained with me in my temptations” (Luke 17:28). But which of these seems to you happier: the one who runs the way of God’s commandments amid sweetness, or the one who runs it amid harshness? The first seems happier; the second stronger. Yet both are righteous, both devout, each having his own gift from God, “one indeed in this manner, another in that” [1 Cor. 7:7].

Would you know that in both there is what pleases God? “I have drunk my wine with my milk,” He says (Song 5:1). For He first delivers one from temptation; He strengthens the second in temptation. Thus one experiences that the Lord is sweet, while the other that the Lord is strong—indeed strong and mighty in battle, in which, in the multitude of His mercies, He permits His servant to be pressed but not crushed. “Come,” says the prophet, “buy wine and milk without money” (Isa. 55:1). Every God-fearing conscience that comes to God buys from Him either milk or wine, according to what has been said and explained. Note that in both instances wine was put first, because the one who perseveringly endures greater tribulation for God receives a greater reward. [Col. 0556D] Let this suffice concerning the difference between a good and tranquil conscience and a good and troubled conscience.

## CHAPTER IV. On an evil and tranquil conscience

6. There follows the evil and tranquil conscience, than which nothing is worse, just as nothing is more unhappy. Do you ask what it is? It is the conscience which neither fears God nor respects a human being; which, “when it comes into the depths of evils, despises” (Prov. 18:3). Observe its fall—indeed, its collapse—and how an evil conscience declines from God little by little and step by step, and so descends into the deep that the pit presses its mouth over it.

At first, when a person accustomed to good deeds commits a grave sin, it seems so unbearable that he seems to descend alive into hell. In the course of time it comes to seem not unbearable, yet still grave; and there is no small descent between unbearable and grave. A little later he judges it light; and though struck by repeated blows, he does not feel the wounds or notice the blows. Of such people Scripture speaks plainly: “They struck me, and I did not suffer; they dragged me, and I did not feel it” (ibid. 23:35). Within a short time, he not only does not feel it, but it pleases him; what was bitter becomes sweet, and what was harsh is turned into pleasure. He is then led into habit, so that it not only pleases him, but pleases him continually, and he cannot restrain himself. Finally, he cannot be torn away, because habit is turned into nature; and what had formerly been impossible to do becomes impossible to refrain from doing.

Thus one descends—indeed, falls—from Jerusalem to Jericho; thus one goes into turning away and hardness of heart. Here the sinner stinks; here he has been dead four days; here the stone set over the cave (John 11:38–39) admits none of those merciful rays of divine light. Here, according to Scripture, “confession perishes from the dead, as from one who is not” (Ecclus. 17:26), unless perhaps God in His mercy should at some time turn the heart of stone into a heart of flesh.

7. This is the evil conscience which rushes, falls, and collapses upon itself through such dangers—indeed, such precipices. How is it tranquil? When the prosperity of this world plays about it and deceives it; when the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the wicked person is blessed; when the favour of sinners, and the fear of those unwilling to sin, smile upon it despite themselves and against their will; when there is no one [Col. 0557C] to rebuke it, or even one among all those around it who dares rebuke the sinner. Thus is fulfilled in it what is written: “The prosperity of fools shall destroy them” (Prov. 1:32).

Nothing equally exasperates the majesty of that dreadful Judge as to sin, to sin securely, and to glory in vices as though they were virtues. “Have no mercy, O Lord,” says the righteous man, “upon all who work iniquity” (Ps. 58:6). This is the iniquity on which God has no mercy: when a person defends what God hates and asserts that sin is righteousness, so that the person resists the Almighty and the Almighty resists that person. This is the pride of which it is written: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6).

Understand what he says: “resists.” For resistance is between equals. But one proposes to resist God as an equal who, insofar as lies in him, destroys what God establishes, calling evil good and good evil, bitter sweet and sweet bitter, light darkness and darkness light (Isa. 5:20). This tranquility, moreover, is nourished by impunity: the mother of security and negligence, the stepmother of virtues, the poison of religious life, the moth of holiness.

## CHAPTER V. On an evil and troubled conscience

8. An evil conscience, however, is troubled when it is caught and seized in the act of its sins. For while it thinks it is feeding upon pleasures, it yields to human anxieties, beaten back by shame and confusion, as it is written: “The sinner has been caught in the works of his hands” (Ps. 9:17). For example, someone seeks adultery for pleasure, but is caught there for anxiety; and anxiety is much greater than pleasure, considering every shame and distress of one who both lives and thinks as a human being.

Although some are converted to the Lord in the very moment of being caught, yet the number of those who remain in sin amid that very confusion is greater than that of those who leave sin because of the shame of sin. Of those who leave it, it is written: “Fill their faces with shame, and they shall seek Your name, O Lord” (Ps. 82:17). Of those who do not leave it, Jeremiah the prophet says: “You struck them, O Lord, and they did not grieve; You crushed them, and they refused to receive correction” (Jer. 5:3).

These are the four streams of consciences running from the fountain of the will: in them the righteous are purified and the unrighteous are defiled, so that what is written may come about: “Let the one who is filthy become filthier still, and let the righteous be justified still” (Rev. 22:11). Since the thoughts of people, whether good or evil, are rolled about in continual motion, I have resolved, according to my measure, to show you the many kinds of thoughts and the directions in which they turn, so that you may better understand how far we are from Him who always remains in the same state, our Lord Jesus Christ.

## CHAPTER VI. On the various kinds of thoughts

9. Of thoughts, some are burdensome, some affectionate, some obscene, some idle, some curious, some suspicious, and some distracting. Understand burdensome thoughts in the soul of a righteous person as those which he wishes to resist yet cannot; whether he wishes it or not, the plague of Egyptian flies rushes upon the eyes of his mind and frogs make a din in the inner chambers of his heart. A person often thinks fearful things concerning faith, horrible things concerning divinity; and, carried along through phantasms of bodily images, he feels things which even a sinner weighed down with guilt shudders to vomit forth in confession. And the more strictly he does not present his members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, the more severely he is shaken and assailed by such a spirit.

For when that insatiable murderer sees himself excluded from external sensuality, he attacks the inward parts with forces gathered together. But the spiritual person, who judges all things, is not ignorant of his wiles. What he can, he restrains; what he cannot restrain, he endures, because though he bears the barking of a dog, he does not fear its bite. The dog barks when it suggests; it bites when it draws one into consent. But when one does not entertain what has been suggested, it does not wound but crowns; for though it torments the one who feels it, it does not bind the one who does not consent.

Thoughts are also burdensome when a person, undertaking Martha’s office, is anxiously troubled over many matters on behalf of many people, so that they may have the means to be sustained in the divine office.

10. Thoughts are affectionate when one is occupied with care for one’s flesh, as in food and clothing. A person is also often touched by affection for relatives according to the flesh. Thoughts are obscene when carnal pleasure tickles and stings; but these, like most filthy dregs, must be driven away at the very outset. Thoughts are idle when one neither takes pleasure in nor is emotionally moved by them—for example, when one thinks of a horse running or a bird flying. In this state one almost stands between vice [Col. 0559A] and virtue, neither descending to the former nor ascending to the latter.

Thoughts are curious when one proposes to investigate the secrets of one’s neighbours; and, though one ought inquisitively to examine oneself, forgetting oneself one attends to others’ affairs—now wandering within, now without, restless and talkative, impatient of quiet. Thoughts are suspicious when, possessing no certain evidence, one suspects evil of a neighbour and interprets in the worse sense matters that may incline either way. Thoughts are distracting when one makes plans and deliberates about distant affairs, kingdoms, and regions; when one is stretched out in the questions and reasonings of this world—“that most grievous occupation,” according to Solomon, which God has given to the children of men “to be exercised in it” (Eccl. 1:13).

11. Again, thoughts are known to have manifold varieties. Some puff up the heart; some lift it up; some trouble it; some scatter it; some confound it; some stretch it out; some bind it; some defile it; some contract it; some corrupt it. They puff up, as proud thoughts do; lift up, as vain thoughts do; trouble, as envious thoughts do; scatter, as angry thoughts do; confound, as slothful thoughts do; stretch out, as ambitious thoughts do; bind, as gluttonous thoughts do; defile, as lustful thoughts do; contract, as fearful thoughts do; corrupt, as malicious thoughts do.

When these have been excluded, the mind is purified if it is continually exercised in holy thoughts, as it is written: “A holy thought shall guard you.” There are, moreover, good and holy thoughts. We ought to think about God, so that we may delight in Him; about the passion of our Redeemer, which He endured for us upon the gibbet of the cross, so that we too may be ready gladly to endure tribulations and distresses for Him; about the hour of our passing, that we may always be prepared; about the day of judgment, because there we must render an account of our deeds; about hell, that we may fear its punishments, since there is no redemption from it; about paradise, that we may desire the crowns which we shall possess in the future; and about the commandments of the Lord and the sacraments of our redemption, that we may persevere in the way of righteousness through the grace of God. Amen.

## CHAPTER VII. On the four spirits speaking in human hearts

[Col. 0559D]

12. Four spirits speak continually in all these thoughts of human hearts [Col. 0560A]: the spirit of the world, the spirit of the flesh, the spirit of the devil, and the Spirit of God. The spirit of the world speaks vain things; it speaks to our heart when we love vanity, rejoice in vanity, and delight in vanity. The spirit of the flesh speaks when we seek things soft and pleasant for the flesh and its senses, when we provide for it in its desires and pleasures. The spirit of the devil speaks when we think bitter things and utter harsh things, when we are sorrowful within ourselves, angry with others, ungrateful, envious, without natural affection, without fidelity. The Spirit of God speaks when we meditate and speak sweet things, cheerful toward ourselves and our neighbours, in all sweetness and goodness, “careful to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3).

These consciences, these thoughts of consciences, these spirits speaking in our thoughts—your conscience, sweetest brother, sees and distinguishes them better than my page does. I have become foolish; you compelled me. Yet I preferred to display my own ignorance rather than put your face to shame. If anything has been well said, attribute it to yourself, for whose faith the Son of God gave both thought and word. If anything has been said wrongly, attribute it to yourself, because you commanded it. Yet pardon my haste also, because nothing is so contrary and so discordant in writing as acceleration and speed. For to discover worthily what you seek, to clothe fittingly in words what you have discovered, requires a suitable place, leisure time, a lively mind, and a practised pen.

Nevertheless, conceal this letter—or book, if you prefer to call it so; or, if you decide to make it public, keep silent concerning the author’s name. The Author of salvation, to whom alone be honour and glory, knows how much I love the salvation of your soul and the honour of your person. He is our Lord Jesus Christ, who both gives Himself to you and crowns you in mercy and compassion. Farewell, and pray for me.

In other editions you will find some matters ineptly stitched onto what precedes, drawn from the treatise *On the Interior House*. But we do not think it worthwhile to fill pages by idly repeating material, especially since the epilogue of the present treatise itself omits this addition.

[Col. 0559]

# TREATISE ON THE ORDER OF LIFE AND THE FORMATION OF CHARACTER

[Note: [Col. 0559] In certain manuscripts it is entitled *On the Instruction of Boys*; elsewhere, *On the Modesty of Young Men*.] (G)*

[NOTE.]

374 Although this Treatise is not by Bernard, it is nevertheless by a certain Benedictine, as appears from chapter 5, no. 16, and is woven from sayings of the Fathers, especially Ambrose. It is divided into four parts: the first, chapters 1–5, concerns the virtues of young people; the second, chapter 6, the virtues of those making progress; the third, chapters 7–8, the virtues of the perfect; the fourth, chapters 9–12, vices.

## CHAPTER I. The very great importance of good formation in early life

[Col. 0561A]

1. Brotherly love indeed urges the timid inexperience of my mind to speak briefly about the order of life and the formation of character. But since the time has come for me to undertake the work, with the help of Him who inspired it, I have judged it necessary to take my beginning from that praiseworthy virtue called modesty. Although it is fitting for every age, person, time, and place, it especially becomes adolescents and youthful minds. For three virtues are particularly suited to boys and adolescents: modesty, silence, and obedience. There is no doubt that, if they strive to possess these, they can, under Christ’s guidance, ascend to the summit and perfection of the virtues.

For we undoubtedly see the marks of good character and the ornaments of virtues in those old men who, from the very apprenticeship of their earliest years until mature adulthood, have been trained in heavenly disciplines and have run boldly in the Lord’s way. Their wisdom is vigorous and shining in proportion as old age itself becomes more learned through years, more assured through experience, and more prudent through the passage of time.
