Such old age produces the sweetest fruits of former studies and refreshes others. But many old men, long-lived and making no progress, because they gathered no riches for themselves at the proper time, themselves destitute of every virtue infect young minds with the disease of a reprobate life.

For just as holy religion is destroyed by an old man who is vicious and foolish, so it is destroyed by an adolescent who is shameless and reckless. After unlearned and wicked prelates, no plague more powerful for harming the weak is found in the holy Church. Indeed, alas, these times of which the Apostle foretold (1 Tim. 3:1) produce persons of this kind without number, when we see nearly everything good and holy being ruined and brought to shame. Since it is most difficult for old men to be changed for the better from their ingrained habit of vice, we ought to lend a hand to adolescents. If they are willing to apply themselves, then, all lukewarmness being expelled, they can certainly by Christ’s grace correct their lives, order their morals, and improve all their actions.

2. For this reason I have long desired, for the salvation of younger people—especially those with whom I live—to gather by selecting a few flowers from the little works of the Fathers, things that seem especially suited to advise their tender age. For I confess that I have great sorrow and continual grief over the blindness of their hearts: although they have learned in Christ’s school how they should repel vices and labour at holy virtues, yet, alas, armed with a spirit of rebellion, they run with such headlong force through the precipices of vices toward death that the charioteer set over them cannot restrain them by any bridle of discipline.

Surely they ought in the house of God to shine, for the worship of divine honour, beyond every adornment, like a golden vessel. Why, then, were they brought up from the earliest rudiments of childhood with such care and labour, unless it was that, made strong in battle, they might fight manfully against [Col. 0562A] the world and its desires, against the flesh and its cravings, and against the devil and his many temptations? Yet what is astonishing and grievous is that the rule of discipline seems harsher and more austere to them than to others. Why is this, except because they love worldly life more?

Certainly, either no one or scarcely anyone among them is found who willingly follows the institutions of the ancient Fathers and loves the life of the elders: whether because labour frightens him, or because abstinence is more difficult at an unstable age, or because life seems darker to vigorous youth. They therefore turn to pursuits which they judge more attractive. For many prefer present things to future things; but they ought to remember that we serve not present things but future things. Hence, the more excellent the cause, the more attentive the care ought to be.

Unhappy is the person who casts aside the law of life and discipline and refuses to be governed by the teaching of the elders. Such a person lives not according to God but according to himself. If able, he remains with whom he wishes; goes where he wishes and for as long as he wishes; laughs and jokes among whom, where, and when he wishes; finally, he practises and follows whatever is pleasant to the brethren, agreeable to touch, delightful to the eyes, or pleasing to the other senses of his flesh. But the person who lives according to God does not do what carnally pleases him, but what spiritually edifies him; and whatever he desires or does, he does not wish it to proceed from his own will but from God’s will and the command of his elders.

Nevertheless, let no one placed upon the slippery ground of adolescence or intemperance despair of conversion. For the wild olive, grafted into the olive tree, loses its bitterness and becomes fruitful. If agriculture changes the nature of plants, can not the pursuit of learning and the constancy of discipline soften whatever passions of the soul’s sickness there may be?

## CHAPTER II. Modesty as the chief virtue adorning adolescents, and where it is especially to be practised

3. But lest childish life be spoiled by various falls, tender minds must diligently be committed to the virtues mentioned above, so that good habit may grow together with age. Therefore, that it may become clearer how great and what sort of virtue modesty is, let us set down in large part the thoughts and words of Father Ambrose, lest, if they perhaps despise me, a foolish little man, they should not dare to despise great Ambrose—or rather, Christ in Ambrose. For thus says that master of moral formation (*On Duties*, book I, chapters 2, 3, 17–20):

“It belongs to good adolescents to have the fear of God, to render honour to their fathers, to guard chastity, not to despise humility, and to love gentleness and modesty, which are ornaments of younger age. For just as dignity recommends old men and liveliness young men, so modesty recommends boys and adolescents as a kind of natural dowry. What a beautiful virtue modesty is, and what a sweet grace: it is seen not only in deeds but also in speech itself, lest you go beyond measure in speaking or your speech utter anything unbecoming. For the mirror of the mind often shines out in words.

“Let modesty regulate even the sound of the voice, lest an uncontrolled voice offend someone’s ear. Indeed, in the very manner of singing, modesty is the first discipline; rather, in every use of speech, one should begin gradually, whether in chanting, reading, or finally speaking, so that modest beginnings may commend what follows. There is also modesty in the eyes, by which the chaste soul of a good adolescent is forbidden to gaze upon or address women—not in order to abhor the sex, but in order to flee vice. The guarding of the eyes greatly contributes to the protection of chastity. Many, indeed, have perished because of bodily beauty. Hence the Lord says: ‘Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart’” (Matt. 5:28).

376

4. Adolescents of good disposition living in a monastery should preserve themselves with every care so that they may not stain their youth with any filth of lust, but may approach Christ’s altar as a virgin comes forth from the bridal chamber. Their minds should be so pure that, out of excessive modesty, they do not even wish to hear an indecent conversation or be in an indecent place. And lest they be overcome by natural incentives, their unruly flesh must be subdued by frequent fasts. It is better for their stomach to hurt than their mind. Blessed indeed is the adolescent who perseveres chaste in body and mind. For such a one, the flesh and blood of our Redeemer undoubtedly become salvation and life.

There are also those who, because of human embarrassment and without regard for the fear of God, being full of filth, boldly thrust themselves into such great mysteries. [Col. 0563C] Let them hear what is written: “Man sees what is before the face, but God sees the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7). Yet they fear human beings more than God. O blind recklessness! O wondrous patience of God! Did those whom fire consumed, or whom the earth swallowed up, commit so great a sin? (Num. 16:31–35). Was the crime of Aaron’s sons, offering strange fire (Lev. 10:1–2), such a crime as that of these persons who receive such terrible sacraments to their own death?

For one must live in such a manner as always to be able to receive that supersubstantial Bread; for woe to one who has made oneself a stranger to it, and great woe to one who approaches it defiled and unclean. There is great danger on both sides. Therefore, there is a pressing need that we not be found unworthy. For this reason modesty must be maintained in all things, as the companion of chastity; by its companionship chastity itself will be safer. For modest shame is a good companion in governing chastity: if it repels the first dangers, it does not allow chastity to be wounded.

Indeed, a lustful mind is disclosed by shameless eyes and wanton speech, and the life of the inner person is shown through the outer person. Adolescence endures many harsh bodily conflicts; inflamed by the heat of the blood, it needs every safeguard in order to escape. The more numerous the things which assail chastity, the greater the rewards; for where labour is greater, there the recompense will be more abundant.

5. Let lovers of modesty take their example from the Mother of the Lord, who, though she was most gentle, did not return the angel’s greeting because of modesty (Luke 1:28–29). Modesty is especially pleasing in our prayer and wins much grace with our Lord. Did it not prefer and commend the Publican, who did not even dare lift his eyes to heaven? Therefore he is justified by the Lord’s judgment more than that Pharisee whom presumption disfigured (Luke 18:10–14).

Let us also pray, insofar as we can, in the incorruptibility of a quiet and modest spirit, which is rich before God. Paul likewise, when he commands that prayer be offered with modesty and sobriety (1 Tim. 2:8–9), intends this to be the first and, as it were, preliminary condition of the prayer that follows: so that the sinner’s prayer may not boast, but, as though covered with the colour of shame, may deserve fuller grace in proportion as modesty offers more from the remembrance of sin.

6. Modesty must also be maintained in one’s movement, bearing, and walk. For the disposition of the mind is discerned in the posture of the body. From this the hidden person of our heart is judged to be either light, boastful, or disturbed—or, conversely, serious, steadfast, pure, and mature. Thus bodily movement is a kind of voice of the soul. For a person’s character is often disclosed by the way he walks. In some people’s gait there plainly shines an image of frivolity, a sort of likeness to running buffoons. There are those who, walking slowly, imitate theatrical gestures, as though they were processional platforms or the motions of swaying statues, so that whenever they take a step they seem to observe particular rhythms.

7. Nor do I think it honorable to walk hurriedly, [Col. 0564C] unless the reason be some danger or a just necessity. For we often see those who are hurrying twist their faces as they pant; and, if they lack a necessary cause for haste, this becomes a blemish worthy of reproach. But I do not speak of those whose occasional haste arises from a cause, but of those in whom continual and unremitting haste becomes habitual. Therefore I approve neither the former as images of statues, nor the latter as the ruinous rush of runners [AMBROS.: “of those shaken about”]. There is a commendable gait in which there is an appearance of authority, the weight of seriousness, and a trace of tranquillity: 377—provided, however, that there is no studiedness or affectation, but that the movement is natural and simple. For nothing artificial pleases.

Let nature shape one’s movement. If, indeed, there is any defect [Col. 0564D] in nature, let diligence correct it, so that where natural art is lacking, correction may not be lacking. But if such matters are observed in walking [AMBROS.: “are regarded more deeply”], how much more must we beware lest anything shameful proceed from the mouth? For this grievously defiles a person. It is not food that defiles, but unjust slander and obscene speech. Even among ordinary people these are matters of shame. [Col. 0564D]

In the practice of our religion, let no word that falls indecently provoke shame. We ought not merely to say nothing unbecoming ourselves, but not even lend an ear to such speech; for the person who takes pleasure in hearing it encourages another to speak it. To hear what is shameful is itself a very great disgrace; but if something of this kind happens accidentally to be seen, what horror it causes! Can what displeases in others fail to displease in oneself? [Col. 0565A]

Nature itself teaches us no differently. It has fully arranged all the parts of our body both to provide for necessity and to adorn it with grace. Yet those parts which were to be pleasing to behold—where the summit of beauty was placed, as it were, upon a height, where loveliness of form and the appearance of the face stand out, and where the use required for action was more ready—it left exposed and open. But those in which lay the natural service of necessity, lest they present an unsightly spectacle of themselves, it in part placed and concealed within the body [variant: “placed in the lower part”], and in part taught and urged us to cover. Does not nature itself, then, become the teacher of modesty? Following its example, modesty has covered and clothed what it found added in this structure of our body. [Col. 0565B]

Thus the maker of nature took such care for our modesty, and so preserved what is becoming and honorable in our body, that he relegated certain channels and outlets of our passages to the rear and turned them from our sight, lest the evacuation of the belly offend the eyes. Concerning this the Apostle speaks well: “Those members of our body which seem to be weaker are more necessary; and those members of the body which we think less honorable, we surround with more abundant honor; and our unseemly members have more abundant comeliness” (1 Cor. 12:22–23).

Indeed, human ingenuity, imitating nature, has increased this grace: we not only hide such things from the eyes, but also judge it improper to call by their own names the signs and functions [Col. 0565C] of those members which we understand should be concealed. Finally, if these parts are accidentally exposed, modesty is confounded; if deliberately exposed, it is judged shamelessness.

[Col. 0565D]

8. Since, therefore, in certain human members there is such unseemliness that it is a great shame even to name them, alas—how vile and shameless are those who not only look with desire upon these secret parts of the body, but even deliberately touch them! I am ashamed and grieved to recount the deeds of those in whom Sodomite lust reigns. God was so angry with them, and they were so given over by his just judgment to a reprobate mind, that a male commits shamefulness with a male. Have they not become worse than brute animals, which have no understanding? For if Ham, who saw his father naked and laughed, was cursed in his son, with what curse are these struck, who, in their desire to sin, are not ashamed to uncover the shamefulness of themselves and of others? Would that they saw how greatly they offend God by such crimes!

9. There are also those who love, praise, admire, and honor handsome people while despising the unattractive. But those whose eyes are sound love and reverence in a person only the beauty of the soul. What sort of beauty is that which a slight fever destroys, and wrinkled old age so dissolves that it seems never to have existed? Yet there are people who exalt themselves because they possess it; and though empty of virtues, they suppose themselves glorious on this account alone. [Col. 0566A]

We certainly do not assign virtue a place in physical beauty; nevertheless, we do not exclude grace, because modesty commonly suffuses even the face with blushes and renders it more pleasing. As an artisan commonly works better with more suitable material, so modesty stands out more brightly even in bodily beauty—provided, however, that bodily beauty itself is not affected, but natural, simple, more neglected than sought after; 378 not aided by costly and gleaming-white garments, but by ordinary ones, so that nothing is lacking for decency or necessity and nothing is added for display. [Col. 0566A]

The voice itself should not be relaxed or broken, nor sound in any way feminine—such as many are accustomed to feign under an appearance of gravity—but should retain a certain form, rule, and vigor appropriate to a man. For this is to maintain beauty in one’s manner of life: to render what is fitting to each sex and person. This is the best ordering of gestures; this is an adornment suited to every action. [Col. 0566B]

But while I do not approve an effeminate and affected tone of voice or bodily gesture, neither do I judge that a boorish and rustic manner should be imitated. The pattern of this discipline is the image of uprightness. Let the devout young man imitate the footsteps of Isaac and Joseph. Let him be modest, chaste, simple, and sober; humble, obedient, patient, and forgiving of injury. Let him do as Daniel and the three youths did: let him apply himself to wisdom, and not give himself to the enticements of gluttony.

“A fat belly does not produce a subtle mind.” [Note: [Col. 0565] A Greek proverb, according to Jerome, Letter 2 to Nepotian, chapter 14.]

Let him flee drunkenness as poison. If he wishes to be devout and wise, let him never smell of wine, lest he hear [Col. 0566C] that saying of the philosopher: “This is not offering a kiss, but serving wine” (Jerome, Letter 2 to Nepotian, ch. 14). Let him love the knowledge of the holy Scriptures, lest his mind be open to wanton thoughts. Blessed is the person who, while reading the divine Scriptures, turns words into deeds.

Let him refrain from anger and flee quarrels, so that he may prove by this evidence that he possesses good morals. Let him conduct himself so that the elders among whom he lives, while admiring his life, are not permitted to despise his age. Among his brothers of the same age, let him be first in work and last in rank; and let him devote himself so thoroughly to every virtue that he is found second to none of them.

## CHAPTER III. Association of young people with elders is conducive to progress in virtue

[Col. 0566D]

10. I still delight to linger over the aspects of modesty, because I am speaking to those who as yet do not recognize its benefits from themselves or know its losses. A rule of life must indeed be maintained. Its first foundations should be drawn from modesty, which is a companion and familiar friend of a tranquil mind. It flees insolence, is remote from every alien luxury, loves sobriety, cherishes honorableness, and seeks nothing ostentatious.

Let the choice of companionship follow, so that young people may be joined to elders of proven worth. For as the company of equals is sweeter, so that of old men is safer: by a kind of instruction and guidance they color the morals of young people and dye them, as it were, with the purple of integrity. [Col. 0567A] If people unfamiliar with a region seek to set out on a journey with skilled guides of roads, how much more should young people undertake an unfamiliar journey with elders, so that they may be less able to wander or depart from the true path of virtue! Nothing is more beautiful than for them to have elders both as teachers of life and as witnesses.

Beautiful, therefore, is the union of elders and young people. Some provide testimony, others consolation; some delight, others honor. We read that Barnabas took Mark with him (Acts 15:37), and Paul took Silas (ibid., v. 40), Timothy (Acts 16:3), and Titus (Gal. 2:1), so that the elders might prevail by counsel and the younger by service. For it is clear that no art is learned without a teacher. If animals, wild beasts, birds, and bees have leaders and follow their chiefs, how much more can human beings not exist without teacher and guide? [Col. 0567B]

Accordingly, care must be taken that younger persons and children do not enter without a guide a road which they have never travelled; otherwise, by turning aside in one direction or another, they suffer errors—walking either more or less than is necessary, becoming weary through running, or falling asleep while delaying. Often those equal in virtue though unequal in age delight in each other’s company, as Peter and John delighted in it. For we read that John was a young man [Note: [Col. 0567D] According to many authorities, Mark 14:51. See Chrysostom on Psalm 13; Ambrose on Psalm 36; Gregory, *Morals*, book 14, chapter 23; Baronius and others.], although in virtue he was second to none of the elders. For in him there was a venerable old age of morals and the gray-haired wisdom of every virtue.

It is a great consolation in this life to have someone to whom you may open your breast; with whom you may share hidden things; to whom you may entrust the secrets of your heart; [Col. 0567C] whom you may love and follow; who, with a father’s affection, may sympathize with you in troubles, encourage you in persecutions, and rejoice with you in prosperity. Happy is such companionship and such friendship; nothing in human affairs is more beautiful. Let us therefore maintain modesty, or rather that moderation which raises us to the adornment of the whole of life. 379

[Col. 0567D]

11. Great, moreover, is moderation, the inseparable companion of modesty. Though more yielding in asserting its own rights, claiming nothing and vindicating nothing, and in a sense restraining itself within its own powers, it is rich before God. Modest moderation and moderate modesty are that which lays snares for no one, is not angry when injured, looks simply upon all, and suspects nothing sinister of anyone.

Let us hold to this, children; let us love it. And, that we may always possess it, we must flee familiarity and conversation with those who live shamefully and without discipline. Their number is indeed countless. Modesty has its own reefs—not ones which it brings upon itself, but ones into which it often runs if we fall into the company of intemperate people, who under the appearance of pleasantness pour poison into the good. If such people are frequent companions, especially at banquets, in games, laughter, and jesting, they weaken that manly seriousness, corrupt youthful minds, and accustom them to their own evils.

Let us therefore beware lest, while we wish to relax the mind, we dissolve the whole harmony, [Col. 0568A] as though it were a certain concord of good works. Habit quickly bends nature. How many people does the company of fools deceive? What have we to do with tales, laughter, and joking? For although decent jokes may sometimes be pleasant, they depart from the ecclesiastical rule; since what we do not find in the holy Scriptures, how can we presume to use? Everything capable of bending the seriousness of our purpose and profession must be avoided.

“Woe to you who laugh, for you shall weep,” says the Lord (Luke 6:25). Do we seek matter for laughter so that, laughing here, we may there be brought low? For we read that the Lord himself wept (ibid. 19:41). I judge that not only immoderate but every kind of jest should be avoided—unless perhaps speech wholly full of seriousness and grace is unbecoming. [Col. 0568B] [Note: [Col. 0568D] This period is read differently in Ambrose, but seems capable of correction from this passage.]

We must rather groan continually and, setting security aside, mourn, lest we be abandoned by God because of pride and negligence and left in the power of demons. Truly, those whom God abandons demons receive, and having received them, make them partners in their own destruction. “God is terrible in his counsels over the children of men” (Ps. 65:5). From the same lump the potter makes one vessel for honor, another for dishonor. There are vessels of mercy and vessels of wrath (Rom. 9:21–23). The last are first and the first last. Many are called, but few chosen (Matt. 20:16). Therefore let each of us work out his own salvation, as the Apostle says, with fear and trembling (Phil. 2:12).

Let him turn away from vanity and despise the love of the world. Let him embrace mourning and quietness, and pursue, as far as he can, modesty and tranquil gentleness, which makes a person live peaceably among others and blush at everything dishonorable. [Col. 0568C]

## CHAPTER IV. Silence and reticence are especially fitting for young people

12. The virtue of modesty is worthy of praise because, possessing the eyes, ears, and tongue of those under its influence, it does not permit them to play or laugh shamefully, but makes them serious and gentle. Conversely, the shamelessness of the young is a great vice; by its wicked boldness and licentiousness it disturbs fathers and brothers. For, as it is written, it reveres neither God nor human beings (Luke 18:4), but rejoices [Col. 0568D] when it has done evil and exults in the worst things (Prov. 2:14). “She has acquired the brow of a harlot, because she cannot blush” (Jer. 3:3). Where the tongue is bold and the forehead shameless, a person does not care what he says or does.

When good and gentle young people reverence their elders by keeping silent, however, let no one think that this praise belongs to silence alone; for silence itself, in which the other virtues have repose, is the greatest act of modesty. For if silence is natural, it is attributed to infancy; if it arises from pride, it is treated as a reproach; if from modesty, it is reckoned as praise.

Susanna was silent in dangers (Dan. 13:42–43), and thought the loss of modesty [Col. 0569A] graver than the loss of life; she spoke only to him to whom chaste modesty could speak. Beautiful Joseph also fled, leaving his garment in the hands of the adulteress; and he departed swiftly in silence (Gen. 39:12), because, hearing what was unsuitable to his modesty, he could not remain long. Moses (Exod. 3:11; 4:10) and Jeremiah (Jer. 1:6), through modesty, excused themselves from what they were able to do by 380 grace.

For it is safer to learn than to teach, safer to be silent than to speak. What good can modesty offer more than that young age should be obliged rather to learn than to speak? Pythagoras indeed imposed a law of silence on his disciples, so that by remaining silent for five years they might learn to speak; and do you refuse to be silent, though the virtue of silence is especially your own? Young man, why do you hasten to incur danger by speaking, [Col. 0569B] when by silence you can be safer? I have seen very many fall into sin through speaking; scarcely anyone through silence. Therefore, to know how to be silent is more difficult than to know how to speak. I know many who speak because they do not know how to be silent. Rare is the person who keeps silent when speaking offers him no advantage. Therefore wise is the person who knows how to be silent.

Bind your speech, I urge you, lest it run wild, become wanton, and gather sins for itself through much talking. Let it be more restrained and held within its own banks. A river that overflows quickly gathers mud.

13. Let there be seriousness in your walk, weight in your speech, and measure in your words. If you keep these things, you will be gentle, meek, and moderate. Guard your heart and restrain your tongue. For a good mind is a good possession. [Col. 0569C] Therefore fence in this possession and fortify it on every side, lest the irrational passions of the body break into it and carry it captive. Guard your inner person as far as you can. Do not neglect or despise it as something worthless, for it is a precious possession, and deservedly precious: its fruit is not perishable and temporary, but stable and of eternal salvation.

If you wish to guard it well, first be silent and listen, and do not sin with your tongue. It is a grave evil for someone to be condemned by his own mouth. For if everyone must render an account on the day of judgment for an idle word, how much more for a word of impurity, shamefulness, or impiety? Let us also take care not to render an account for idle silence. For there is a fruitful and active silence. By being silent before people, we speak better to God. Many contemplations wonderfully nourish the soul devoted to God in silence.

The prophet David taught us to walk about in our heart as though in a spacious house, and to converse with it as with a good companion, so that he said to himself and spoke with himself: “I said, I will guard my ways” (Ps. 38:2). Moses spoke in silence (Exod. 14:21) and worked in repose (ibid. 16). [Col. 0569D]

14. When, then, is the righteous person alone, who is always with God? How is he solitary, who is never separated from Christ? When is he free from work, who is never free from the merit through which his work is brought to completion? Within what places is he confined, for whom the whole world is a possession of riches? By what estimation is he limited, whom not even operation can comprehend? [Col. 0570A]

Now he thinks of God and his holy angels, and of the unfading glory of eternal blessedness; now of the wiles of the devil, his own sins, the hour of death, the punishments of hell, and the day of dreadful judgment; now of the depth of the divine Scriptures, the nature of virtues, and the formation of good morals. How glorious is such silence, in which the utterances of the Lord are pure utterances!

There is, therefore, a measure for silence and for speech. A good and modest mind considers many things before speaking: what it should say, to whom it should say it, in what place, and at what time. Rightly is that person called wise who knows the time for speaking. Thus Scripture aptly says: “A wise man will be silent until the proper time” (Ecclus. 20:7).

Therefore the holy servants of the Lord, knowing that human speech is generally joined with sin and that a person’s speech is the beginning of human error, loved silence. Thus holy David says: “I have set a guard upon my mouth” (Ps. 38:2). The prophet kept guard, and will you not keep guard? You can guard it if you do not speak quickly. [Col. 0570B]

## CHAPTER V. Prompt obedience is commended to the young

15. The Law says: “Hear, Israel,” and so forth. It says “hear,” not “speak.” For it belongs to your age to be silent and obey, not to judge the opinion of one older than yourself. Again it is written: “Hear, Israel” (Deut. 6:3–4), and be silent. Isaac rendered honor to his father and, obedient to his will, did not refuse to die (Gen. 22:6–10).

Joshua son of Nun reverently honored Moses with diligent service; and, being obedient in all things, 381 earned such favor with God that he was chosen as Moses’ successor to govern God’s people (Deut. 31:7). Elisha, leaving the plough and slaughtering the oxen, followed Elijah when called (3 Kgs. 19:19–21); through true and gentle obedience he rose to such moral eminence that the spirit of so exalted a master rested doubly upon the good disciple (4 Kgs. 2:9–15). [Col. 0570C]

That faithful old man Abraham, at the Lord’s command, left the land of his birth; and although in many places he endured frequent injuries and severe labors, he never repented of his obedience once begun. Indeed, through obedience and faith he so pleased God that the promise concerning Christ was first made to him (Gen. 12–22).

Finally, our Lord Jesus Christ teaches us much about obedience in his deeds and words. True submission for God’s sake is the mortification of one’s own will: it accounts itself lowly and unworthy, and makes ready obedience acceptable to God and gracious to human beings.

For self-will, arising from the presumption of free choice, turns even good things into sin for the obstinate and disobedient. A good person should endeavor to possess obedience along with all his good works. For it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen is better than to offer the fat of rams; because resistance is as the sin of divination, and unwillingness to submit as the crime of idolatry” (1 Sam. 15:22–23).

You see how great and what kind of evil disobedience is, since it is compared with idolatry and magical arts. Young people filled with such an evil disdain to submit to their elders; they do not heed their deeds or words, but judge them with inflated words and an erect neck; they do not exalt them through reverence but mock them through contempt. [Col. 0570D]

16. Yet not with impunity. For they plainly fail at the very point where, unhappy as they are, they ought to have advanced. God wills that a person be taught through a person and that the lesser be subject to the greater. For if angel commands angel, and perfect harmony always remains between the one commanding and the one obeying, let that person see how grievously he sins who does not care to render due reverence to his elders.

Much might be said concerning the destruction of those who are disobedient and despise their elders and patrons, had I not, mindful of promised brevity, deliberately passed it over. [Col. 0571A]

Why say more? One saying is sufficient for both obedient and disobedient persons, spoken by Truth itself: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). Therefore let those rejoice with great joy who hold their elders in reverence and honor for Christ’s sake.

Many have written much concerning the virtue of obedience. Among them our holy father Benedict spoke of it so terribly (St Benedict, *Rule*, chapters 5, 68, 71) that even the hearts of brethren who obey well may be shaken by excessive fear. That highest Gregory, of honey-flowing speech, also wonderfully exalts and magnifies it. Wishing to show how great is the merit of obedience, the eloquent man says:

> “Obedience alone is the virtue which implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves them when implanted. Hence the first human being received a command to observe; if he had wished to subject himself obediently to it, he would have come to eternal blessedness without labor.”

Then the same teacher, explaining the words spoken above by the Holy Spirit through Samuel, says:

> “Obedience is rightly preferred to sacrifices, because in sacrifices another’s flesh, but through obedience one’s own will, is slain. The more quickly anyone pleases God, the more he sacrifices himself before God’s eyes through the sword of the command, having repressed the pride of self-will. Conversely, disobedience is called the sin of divination, in order that the greatness of obedience’s virtue may be shown. For by its opposite, what is thought of its praise is better made known. If resistance is as the sin of divination and refusal to submit as the crime of idolatry, obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it anyone is proved unbelieving, even if he appears to be faithful.”

17. “Hence Solomon says, in displaying obedience: ‘An obedient man will speak of victory’ (Prov. 21:28). The obedient person speaks of victories because, when we humbly submit to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in the heart.

“Hence Truth said in the Gospel: ‘The one who comes to me I will not cast out, because I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’ (John 6:37–38). What then? If he did his own will, would he have rejected those who 382 come to him? Who, however, does not know that the will of the Son does not differ from the will of the Father?

“But because the first human being departed from the joys of paradise because he wished to do his own will, the second, coming for humanity’s redemption, taught us to remain within by showing that he did the Father’s will and not his own. Therefore, when he does not his own will but the Father’s will, he does not cast out those who come to him; because, by subjecting us to obedience through his example, he closes to us the way of departure.

“Again he says: ‘I can do nothing of myself; as I hear, I judge’ (John 5:30). We too are commanded to preserve obedience unto death. But he judges as he hears; even when he comes as judge, he then obeys.

“Therefore, lest obedience appear laborious only until the end of the present life, our Redeemer shows that he preserves it even when he comes as judge. What wonder, then, if sinful man subjects himself to obedience during the short span of this present life, when the Mediator of God and human beings does not abandon it even when he rewards those who obey? [Col. 0572B]

18. “It must truly be understood that evil must never be done through obedience; but that sometimes a good work being done must be interrupted through obedience. The tree in paradise which God forbade man to touch was not evil; but, in order that the human being, well created, might grow more excellently through the merit of obedience, it was fitting that God should prohibit him from something good, so that what he did might be virtue all the more truly insofar as, abstaining even from a good thing, he showed himself more humbly subject to his Creator.

“But because sometimes the prosperities of this world, sometimes adversities, are commanded us, we must understand above all that obedience is at times nonexistent if it has anything of its own; and at times minimal if it has nothing of its own.

“For when success in this world is commanded, when a higher position is imposed, the person who obeys in receiving these things empties obedience of its virtue if he longs for them from personal desire. For he is not guided by his obedience who, in receiving the prosperities of this life, serves the desire of his own ambition.

“Again, when contempt for the world is commanded, when one is ordered to receive reproaches and insults, the person who does not seek them himself diminishes for himself the merit of obedience, descending unwillingly and reluctantly to those things despised in this life. Obedience is brought to loss when one’s own desires do not in some degree accompany the mind in accepting the reproaches of this age.

“Therefore obedience ought to have something of its own in adversities, and again to have nothing of its own in prosperities: so that in adversities it may be more glorious insofar as it is joined to the divine order by desire, and in prosperities more genuine insofar as the mind is utterly separated from the present glory which it receives from God” (Gregory, *Morals*, book 35, chapter 10). [Col. 0572D]

19. Moses and Paul undoubtedly bear witness in their deeds to these most clear assertions of so great a teacher. Seek out and read what each of them did. Nevertheless, amid these matters we must know that the virtue of obedience is always joined to innocent minds, as the Lord testifies when he says: “My sheep hear me, and I know them, and they follow me” (John 10:3, 4, 14). [Col. 0573A]

Therefore one who is not innocent does not obey his Redeemer; and one who scorns obedience cannot be innocent. Yet obedience itself must be rendered not from servile fear but from the affection of charity; not from dread of punishment but from love of righteousness. For there is no innocence and no true obedience unless charity shines in them, charity which surpasses all virtues.

False obedience is often cloaked under the appearance of fear. Therefore, if you see a young man slow to obey and quick to speak, do not doubt that he suffers from various passions of mind, especially from the plague of pride. For disobedience follows pride, its mother, as you have it: “An untamed horse will become stubborn, and an indulgently reared son will become headlong” (Ecclus. 30:8). As the pride of an untamed horse tends toward a precipitate fall, so the wantonness of an undisciplined young man is close to the ruin of sin.

You who are older, speak: it befits you. Young man, speak only in your own cause and scarcely when necessary. If you are questioned twice, let your answer contain the substance. In many matters be as though ignorant, and listen while at once remaining silent and asking questions. Do not presume to speak among the great; and where elders are present, do not speak much.

Before hail comes lightning, and favor precedes modesty, and in return for reverence good favor will come (Ecclus. 32:4, 10, 14). From these words of Wisdom you may understand how greatly the virtues stated above adorn younger age. 383

## CHAPTER VI. On chastity, humility, and patience

[Col. 0573C]

20. Children are so called from purity (*puritas*), and it is fitting that simplicity, innocence, and purity—that is, virginity—should reign in them. Let them grow with these and persevere in them, so that they may deserve to follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

Young people, according to the interpretation of this name, should grow day by day in good works, love modesty, and be exceedingly fervent in obedience. We have placed these virtues first, as certain beginnings of good works, so that through them they may be able to arrive by a straight path at chastity, humility, and patience, which occupy the second place.

Chastity, therefore—because both sexes suffer from the vice of lust—easily falls unless supported by the aid of other virtues. It must accordingly be guarded with the utmost care, because once lost it cannot be restored. The eyes are the first weapons; words are the second. For every idle person is in desires, and “desires kill the slothful” (Prov. 11:25).

Therefore modesty greatly aids chastity, since it guards the eyes; silence, since it restrains the tongue; and obedience, since it occupies the mind and wearies the body by fasts, vigils, prayers, and manual work. But above all it has need of humility, by which things acquired are preserved until the end. For many have fallen through pride into lust even in old age. On this account one must fear and beware lest a sudden heat overcome a long period of time and wantonness condemn shameless old men.

Humility, the guardian of chastity and mother of patience, must therefore always be maintained. For without it, one labors in vain who gathers virtues. True patience, however, is neither acquired nor retained except through profound humility.

Whoever truly possesses it needs neither the benefit of a cell nor the refuge of solitude; and if some adversity happens to him, he is not distressed, but “all things work together for good to one who loves God” (Rom. 8:28). Such a person fears in prosperity and rejoices in adversity. He loves and helps his persecutors, because patience and kindness accompany him as inseparable companions. [Col. 0574A]

21. Therefore, if anyone possesses a virginal soul and loves chastity, he ought not to be content with mediocre things, which quickly wither and dry up when the heat rises; rather, let him pursue perfect virtues, so that he may have everlasting light. For the person who strives to advance always finds room for growth and becomes better than himself every day.

Young man, make progress. You have been devoted to the service of Christ, and you have begun to do great things and imitate lofty ones: let your heart be strengthened, and act manfully. Great glory will be given you after victory. Although the path on which you walk is slippery, nevertheless, trusting in the Lord’s help, leave low things behind as far as you can and seek the heights.

Do not fail or grow lukewarm, so that you may be able to ascend to the degree of perfection, which is reached only through many labors. Well done now, well done, good brother: pass beyond beginnings and stretch toward higher things, so that you may sing to God, with a voice of exultation, the Song of Ascents.

For you, hastening from root to summit, the way of entry lies open to those four principal virtues, which are begun in adolescents, increased in young adults, and perfected in elders; for mature age, trained by many labors, now knows through experience what it learned through knowledge.

## CHAPTER VII. The four cardinal virtues and their offices are described. Likewise, concerning the theological virtues.

22. Therefore we now rightly place prudence, fortitude, justice, and temperance in the third rank, because it is chiefly through them that character is formed and the art of living well is taught. Of these, prudence delights in the knowledge of truth; justice preserves love of God and neighbour; fortitude despises the fear of death; temperance moderates the inclination of the flesh. The first, indeed, understands; the second lives rightly; the third restrains appetite; the fourth sets a limit. The former three accomplish what is honourable; this fourth makes graceful that which proceeds from the root of honourableness. For prudence is the knowledge of the true faith and acquaintance with the Scriptures, in which one must perceive that threefold kind of understanding: the first is historical, the second allegorical, and the third that higher understanding which they call anagoge. Justice, moreover, is to fear God, revere religion, render honour to parents, love one’s country; benefit all, harm no one, maintain the bond of brotherly love, undertake others’ dangers, bring aid to the wretched, repay good turns, and preserve equity in judgments.

[Col. 0575A] Fortitude is greatness of spirit and contempt for honours or riches. In adversities it either yields patiently or resists bravely. It is subdued by no enticements, broken by evils and adversities, nor lifted up by prosperity; unconquered in labours and strong amid dangers. It disregards money, flees avarice, prepares the mind against every danger, yields to no troubles, and avoids the desire for glory. Yet among these, temperance must always be embraced. For it is moderation in every word and work. It is the companion of sobriety and modesty, which is also called *modestia* [self-restraint]. It keeps the rule of humility, preserves tranquillity of mind, loves continence and chastity, cherishes propriety and honourableness, restrains appetite by reason, despises anger, and does not repay insult.

23. By these wounds, O man of God, shut up heaven; with these weapons, warrior of Christ, gird, protect, and adorn yourself. This fiery chariot will carry you, a valiant soldier, when your course is completed, to the palace of heaven, that you may stand before your King, for whom you fought the good fight and kept the faith. Govern well this four-horsed chariot of virtues, and sit firmly in it, that by this vehicle you may be borne higher and led into the house with three chambers, set upon the summit of the mountain. By this I mean firm faith, unshaken hope, and perfect charity, which casts out every slavish fear, where one runs with an enlarged heart in the way of God’s commandments. Hence the soul of the righteous, made the seat of wisdom, bears God its rider with an even and measured pace.

[Col. 0575C] For such a one, Christ is life and death is gain. The discerning and contemplative man passes daily onward and beholds a marvellous vision; he is drawn by God and runs after him in ardent desire. But if you dwell upon this lofty mountain and in this beautiful house, you too will be able most often to behold that land of promise, the land flowing with milk and honey, where the true Israel dwells and is eternally fed with the nourishment of truth.

24. But you say to me: “Why have you not placed faith first, since in the Christian soul it is the foundation of all virtues?” I certainly would have done so, if faith did not grow. But if faith did not grow, the Apostles would never have said to the Lord: “Increase our faith” (Luke 17:5). For through the continual exercise of virtues and constant meditation upon the holy Scriptures faith is instructed; being instructed, it is enlightened; being enlightened, it increases; increasing, it is perfected; and being perfected, it is established.

[Col. 0575D] Thus it is not moved from the state of its uprightness by any storm of heresy or persecution. Therefore, before a person knows his Creator through faith, ignorance—the mother of all vices—possesses his soul. Ignorance, then, is night; faith is day. As day grows through the hours, so faith grows through the illumination of divine grace and through the teaching of mother Church. First, therefore, the sincere root of holy faith is planted in the soil of the human heart. Into it is grafted that little branch of the holy tree, namely the fear of the Lord, which is called the beginning of wisdom (Psalm 110:10).

[Col. 0576A] It begins with faith and rises with it unto the fullness of light. When faith has become fully mature, like a great tree bearing diverse fruits within itself, from which the soul filled with God is refreshed, then there cleaves to it that chaste and holy fear of eternal charity, which endures for ever and ever (Psalm 18:10). For this is the faith that works through love, so that a person may become a new creation: the most prudent and unconquerable faith, which cannot be overcome amid contentious words, in a time of persecution, or on the day of necessity. Accordingly, firm faith and full charity, faithful companions and inseparable sisters, containing within themselves every kind of virtue, make a perfect man, insofar as he can be perfected in this life, full of miseries and errors.

[Col. 0576B] Such a man can truly say the Apostle’s words: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword? For I am certain that neither death nor life, nor angels nor principalities nor powers nor virtues, nor things present nor things to come, nor strength, nor depth, nor height, nor any other creature shall be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:35, 38–39).

## CHAPTER VIII. One must walk cautiously between the boundaries of virtues and vices.

25. This, then, is the discipline of the good life and the right sequence of virtues. This is the royal road, trodden by the feet of the fathers who went before. Walk in it, O flock of young men, and do not turn aside from it either to the right or to the left (Proverbs 4:27). He turns to the left who entangles himself in manifest vices. But he turns to the right who does not earnestly avoid vices that lie concealed beneath the appearance of virtues. For many are deceived by these, and do not know that they have been deceived. Thus the soul is guilty in two ways: both if it does not do the good by which it may live spiritually, and if this very failure remains hidden from it.

[Col. 0576C] The proud man wishes to be thought steadfast; the prodigal, generous; the avaricious, diligent; the rash, brave; the inhuman, sparing; the gluttonous, humane. Shamelessness appropriates to itself the name of steadfastness. Insolence assumes the designation of freedom. Wordiness pretends to eloquence, and the evil of curiosity lurks under the guise of spiritual study. For sometimes cruelty is practised under the pretext of justice, and what is plainly a vice is thought to be a virtue: just as lax sloth is believed to be gentleness, and what torpid negligence does is thought to be done by the mercy of compassion. Likewise, fear hides beneath the appearance of obedience, and that which is in fact the vice of fear is called the virtue of humility.

[Col. 0576D] Further, the vice of restlessness wishes to be called the virtue of concern; the ease of precipitancy is considered zeal for a good undertaking; and slowness in doing good appears to be the delay of deliberation—although the latter is a virtue and the former a vice. Although these may be distinguished by human judgment, yet, as it seems to me, without the gift of God virtues can neither be possessed nor sought, nor can their likenesses—the vices that imitate virtues—be avoided.

26. But you must know that some virtues are supreme, while others are intermediate. The supreme virtues are hope, faith, and charity. For those who possess them truly possess them. Learning, fasting, chastity, knowledge, and other things like these are intermediate virtues, because they can be possessed either for benefit or for ruin. Truth cannot coexist with falsehood, modesty with wantonness, faith with perfidy, or chastity with lust. Against the assaults of vices one must fight with their contrary virtues. Against lust, let purity of heart be employed; against hatred, love; against anger, patience; against fear, the virtue of confidence; against sloth, zeal for a good work.

[Col. 0577B] Let joy be opposed to sadness; fortitude to *acedia* [spiritual listlessness]; generosity to avarice; humility to pride.

## CHAPTER IX. Pride and avarice are detestable vices, hostile even to religious persons.

27. Pride is the queen and mother of the seven principal vices. The worse it is than all the others, the lower it lies even as it raises itself on high. The seven principal vices bear many vices from themselves, joined to one another by a kind of kinship, so that one springs from another. As pride is the origin of all crimes, so it is the ruin of all virtues. It is first in sin and last in conflict. From pride is born arrogance, which must be guarded against alike in deeds and words. Woe to him who strives to please himself more than God.

[Col. 0577C] Above all through *cenodoxia* [vain glory] the devil subjects the monk to himself, because through it he is cast down from the summit of humility. Humility, therefore, is the monk’s highest virtue; pride is his greatest vice. By pride, contention, quarrelling, murmuring, detraction, whispering, negligence, contempt, and doing their own wills, countless monks of the present day incur faults. Hence it is that among the great multitude of those who leave the world, very few are found who strive, after putting their vices to death, to rise to the perfection of virtues.

These things are signified by the six hundred thousand armed men brought out of the land of Egypt. Yet only two men, Joshua and Caleb, out of all those people entered the land of promise; while those wishing to return to Egypt fell in the wilderness and perished by diverse kinds of death. Understand Egypt as the world; Pharaoh as the devil, who is king over all the children of pride (Job 41:25); the Red Sea as the washing away of all sins; and the Egyptians who died in it as the sins themselves, which are Pharaoh’s army.

[Col. 0577D] You, indeed, have already left Egypt, fled Pharaoh, and, washed from your filth, have sung to the Lord a song of joy after the chariots were submerged. At last you have entered the wilderness and come to Mount Sinai, where the commandments of life and the ordinances of heavenly discipline were given you, which you promised before God and his saints to observe. Yet even if you have done everything, do not be secure. Many dangers are found in the very wilderness through which you walk.

[Col. 0578A] There indeed are fiery serpents, which strike and kill murmurers. There is leprosy, which infects and disfigures detractors and whisperers. There is the cruel sword which devours the makers and worshippers of an idol: namely, those monks who pursue avarice, which is the service of idols (Colossians 3:5). The Apostle calls it the root of all evils (1 Timothy 6:10). Know, however, that this vice attacks only the most lukewarm monks. Take care that you have, or wish to have, nothing beyond food and clothing. Detest pride; flee contention. Love the rulers of the monastery as parents; fear them as masters; believe that what they prescribe is salutary.

28. But you will not be able to keep these things unless you first make yourself foolish in order to become wise: that is, making no distinction and passing no judgment concerning what has been commanded you, but always rendering obedience in complete simplicity and faith; judging only that to be holy, useful, and wise which either the law of God or the judgment of an elder has prescribed for you.

[Col. 0578B] Let the example of those who rebelled against Moses terrify you: some of them heavenly fire consumed, while hell received others alive (Numbers 16:31–35). Time would fail me if I wished to set forth everything in order.

29. I see that this must be impressed upon you: while we live, we run among snares. Nowhere is peace secure—alas!—nowhere is rest secure; everywhere are wars, on every side enemies. For Pharaoh, with his Egyptians, holds back the one departing; in the middle of the journey are very many disasters that greatly hinder the traveller; and at the far end before you are dread and mighty enemies who wish to resist, lest you enter the land of promise: Amalek, Sihon, Og, Moab, the children of Ammon, and the robbers of Mount Seir.

[Col. 0578C] But if perhaps, after overcoming these, you enter that excellent land through many labours, you will see that even there you cannot be secure. For Philistines remain, and other peoples are left round about you, through whom God may test whether you love him, and so that you may always look to his hand, lest, after you have eaten and been satisfied, you forget him.

## CHAPTER X. The capital vices are explained together with their species.

[Col. 0578D]

30. Therefore, by the seven peoples expelled from that land understand the seven capital vices. Two of them are carnal, namely gluttony (*gastrimargia*) and fornication; the rest are spiritual, and are distinguished in their members as follows.

The desire of gluttony is divided into five modes. First, if someone seeks food before the proper time. Second, if he seeks more luxurious foods. Third, if someone takes excessive care in preparing even ordinary foods. Fourth, if someone consumes too much even of cheap food. Fifth, if a person takes whatever he takes merely from desire.

Fornication has a threefold form. The first is when sexual union is consummated through the luxury of pleasure. The second is when the lust of the flesh is stirred to uncleanness by touch alone. The third is when one is polluted by a nocturnal illusion through the intention of shameful thoughts.

[Col. 0579A] There is also, according to Scripture, a fourth kind: namely idolatry and avarice. Indeed, every unclean defilement is called fornication.

*Philargyria* [love of money] is divided into two members: the desire to increase one’s possessions and the fear of losing them. There is also a third form of this plague: when a monk desires to have more than is necessary even of the necessities without which he cannot live; or when we wish to possess in monasteries things which, if we were in the world, we would by no means be able to have.

There are three kinds of anger. One burns outwardly; another bursts forth into words without taking effect in action; the third, unlike the first, does not dissipate its heat in an hour but stores it up for days and periods of time. From the former arise heat and indignation; from the latter, hatred. All these must be condemned by us with equal abhorrence.

[Col. 0579B] The vice of sadness is divided into three parts. The first is restrained and rational, arising from repentance for sins. The second is disturbed and irrational, arising from anxious fear or despair concerning sins. The third proceeds from anger, from an injury inflicted, or from frustrated desire.

There are two kinds of *acedia*. One compels the monk to be sluggish and sleepy in the work of God. The other makes him wander here and there and urges him to flee the society of the brethren with whom he lives.

31. These six vices are joined together by a kind of kinship, so that the excess of the preceding becomes the beginning of the following. From the first comes the second, from the second the third, and so with the rest. Therefore one must fight against them in the opposite direction, in the same way and by the same principle: for when the first has been conquered, another is more easily overcome.

[Col. 0579C] Although these vices are interconnected in the manner described, they must more particularly be divided into three pairings. Fornication is joined to gluttony, anger to avarice, and *acedia* to sadness by a special association. But after these have been overcome, a greater struggle remains for you, and one so much more severe as these have been more fully conquered. With all your strength, you must undertake an unceasing contest against the most cruel three-formed beast: pride, vain glory, and envy. It has three heads in one body, and in those heads iron teeth crushing everything.

[Col. 0579D] Oh, how many men this most monstrous beast has bitten, cast down, and trampled under its feet! Therefore put on strong armour, that you may be able to stand against such wickedness. Put on the breastplate of charity, gird yourself with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; take the shield of faith, place the helmet of salvation and hope upon your head, and let your feet be shod in readiness for the gospel of peace, so that no place in you may lie open to the snares of the mighty adversary (Ephesians 6:11–17).

The head of pride is like the head of a viper, its fury like the fury of a dragon, and its breath deadly, like the incurable breath of the basilisk. More distinguished than the others, it sends forth from its viperous mouth three venomous tongues to strike. The first strikes those who, through the fault of transgression, hold God’s commandments in contempt. The second strikes those who, through keeping the commandments, exalt themselves in the pride of virtues.

[Col. 0580A] The third strikes those who, through obstinacy of mind, disdain to be subject to the commands of their superiors. Some are proud on carnal grounds, others on spiritual grounds; but pride is one under diverse colouring.

32. The second head, that of *cenodoxia* [vain glory], is a many-formed monster and a manifold evil. In four ways it breathes out dreadful voices and terrible roars more loudly from its swollen throat. For there are those who have gifts yet do not know the Giver. There are those who say that they have received gifts because of their preceding merits, rather than by the grace of the One who bestows them. Again, some imagine in their swelling pride that they possess what they do not possess. Others, despising everyone else, think that they possess something singularly. But this exaltation, arising from boastfulness about singularity, is more destructive than the rest.

[Col. 0580B] Yet although this dire plague raises itself on high and fills the ears with its cries, it does not have strength and power corresponding to the height to which it exalts itself. Envy itself likewise spews forth twofold flames. This third head sometimes burns one who envies a better man for what he himself is not; at other times it afflicts one who grieves that any equal should be his equal. So that you may distinguish these three, I give you these signs: pride blushes, vain glory turns white, envy grows pale. In the proud there is fiery rage from indignation; in hypocrites whiteness from pretence; in the envious pallor from excessive grief.

When these matters have thus been arranged, it seems to me that the seven criminal vices are more correctly marked out than counted. For just as the devil, prince of the seven vices, subjects us to their powers, so Christ our God, filled with the Spirit’s sevenfold grace, delivers us from their domination and makes us subject to himself.

[Col. 0580C]

33. But you must know that these vices have different origins and unlike modes of decline. Gluttony and fornication are carnal, because they can be fulfilled only through the body; therefore they require bodily affliction and, at the same time, more secluded places, that they may be cured more swiftly. Avarice and anger, although not of one nature—for the former is contrary to nature, whereas the latter seems original, since man is an irascible animal—nevertheless arise in a similar manner, since they conceive the causes of agitation inwardly. Sadness and *acedia* are accustomed to arise without any external provocation. Pride, vain glory, and envy are consummated without bodily agency.

[Col. 0580D] For curing those called spiritual vices, human companionship is of great benefit, especially if you live among good and prudent men who always rebuke them.

## CHAPTER XI. Not everyone is assailed most severely by the same vices, but some by some and others by others.

34. But amid these matters it must be known that in some people the greed of the belly, in others fornication, occupies the chief place. In some pride, in others vain glory, holds the citadel. In some anger, in others avarice or sadness, or another of these, claims tyranny for itself. Therefore each of us must undertake the fight according to the character of the war by which he is chiefly harassed. Thus one person must make his first conflict against the vice placed third; another against the fourth or fifth. According as the vices hold mastery in us, and as the mode of assault requires, so we too must order our battles.

[Col. 0581A] And let us fight bravely against that one vice, yet not neglecting the others by which we are less assailed. Let us labour with all our strength, trusting not in our own labours but in God’s help. In this way, with Christ’s aid, we shall be able to attain purity of heart and the fullness of virtues.

35. I also wish you to know this no less: in all persons there are diverse mixtures of dispositions. Hence some vices are akin to quiet and gentle dispositions, while others are akin to hard and harsh ones. Often what pleases the latter displeases the former. When the devil seeks to deceive anyone, he first observes each person’s nature; then he adapts himself from the point at which he sees the person suited to sin. For the devil tempts a person on the side on which, because of an excessive humour, he sees him readily inclined to vices; he applies temptation according to the mixture of the humours.

[Col. 0581B] Therefore let no one think lightly of the fault he suffers because of his own disposition; rather, as far as he can, let him fight against what he endures. For if he yields to his disposition, he does not resist temptation or vice at all. Therefore steadfast and hard dispositions should continually resist together pride, anger, and cruelty. But cheerful and gentle dispositions should never cease especially to fight against vain glory, hypocrisy, and false piety. For this sort of people are more easily captured by the love of praise. They wish to displease no one; they seem to bear everyone with equanimity; they deceive and are deceived. And the more they please men, the more hateful they become to God, as it is written: “The crafty and dissemblers provoke God’s wrath” (Job 36:13).

[Col. 0581C] Good men who fear God shrink from appearing to be what they have deserved to become. Certainly human praise torments the good and delights the wicked.

36. Hypocrites are condemned in two ways: both for hidden iniquity and for open pretence. For hypocrites are not always concealed. Everything sincere endures; for what is feigned cannot last long. Hypocrites are white outside and filthy within. The lover of vain glory never ceases doing whatever may gain him praise. Some, through the false opinion of arrogance, suppose themselves perfect when they are not; they become known when temptations arise. The nearer a man becomes to truth, the farther from it he considers himself to be. There is a humility of fear and ignorance which is not worthy of praise.

[Col. 0581D] The hypocrite has the words of saints but not their life; boastfulness always closes for him the eyes by which God can be seen.

37. The devil has greater dominion over the proud and the lustful. Lust once indulged always leaves behind repentance for itself. It is never satisfied, and when extinguished it is rekindled. Woe to him whose lust came to an end only when his life did! Wine acts against its drinker, because after he rises, neither foot nor hand keeps to its office, and all his exhilaration turns into ruin.

[Col. 0582A] A proud man will neither be adorned nor bring his own will to its end. The conscience of God’s humble servant ought always to be humble and sorrowful: humble, that he may not be proud; sorrowful with a useful grief, that his heart may not dissolve into wantonness. God’s servant ought without interruption to read, pray, and work, lest vices seize beforehand a mind given over to idleness. A mind dedicated to God should guard against lesser vices as against greater ones, because those who plunge into the greatest begin with the smallest. He treats himself very delicately who wishes, without great labour and continual diligence, either to overcome vices or acquire virtues. As the soul, weighed down by the mass of the flesh, rises with difficulty toward virtues, so it falls easily into vices, because the latter lie below while the former stand upon the highest citadel.

38. Finally, some do not care to labour because they renounce the world not out of love for God. Would that our leaving the world were a matter of will rather than necessity. For those who pursue the monastic profession without rigorous purpose, the more loosely they seek the aim of heavenly love, the more readily they are drawn back again to love of the world. Some of these seek bodily pleasure, others honour.

[Col. 0582B] But one who puts on the appearance of a holy way of life in order to desire someday to preside over others is not a disciple of Christ but a follower of perversity. For to bear the cross and not die is characteristic of hypocrites. But he who gives himself for God to the hardships of monks ought to be constant in prayers, offer his tears to God rather than men, and moderate fasts, like a charioteer, according to the weariness and strength of his body.

## CHAPTER XII. An exhortation to the young religious to undertake vigorously the path of virtue.

39. Therefore, good brother, do not shrink from applying yourself, as far as you can, to holy deeds, that you may someday receive the fruit of your labour. Attend only to this: you have become a monk, and therefore do what belongs to a monk. Among those with whom you live, follow the better men. In every rank and order the worst are mingled with the best.

[Col. 0582D] Do not imitate the high-spirited and obstinate old men whom you see abounding in these perilous times. Flee their habits and manner of life, lest they become for you a snare and a ruin. Oh, how many old men and judges of Israel, shamefully neglecting their lives, the king of Babylon possesses in the land of captivity and confusion; and how many young men, fervent in spirit and serving the Lord, do violence to heaven and seize it for themselves with all their strength! Would that our old men imitated the praises of such young men, so that aged old age might render what tender youth freely brings forth! If you wish to make progress, do not look at what evil others do, but at what good you yourself ought to do.

Do you not see merchants and soldiers enduring many dangers in order to attain uncertain honours and perishing riches?

[Col. 0583A] Indeed, at the peril of their souls they guard things which they acquire with many tribulations.

40. What then, tell me, I ask, ought you to do—you who seek the precious pearl after selling everything, and who have bought the field in which the treasure lies hidden, which no thief can take away? You must diligently guard against every snare, lest, if you suffer ruin, you receive disgrace in place of glory. Although you are in safety, do not be secure. Often, in the midst of tranquillity, the unwary and sluggish are overwhelmed by the quicksands of vices. How many creatures, alas, does the wilderness of this world nourish, creatures which feed upon negligent monks with cruel bites!

And because I believe that you can make more progress by prayer than by this exhortation of ours, I shall add a form of prayer, so that by reading and praying you may provide a twofold refreshment for your hungry soul and may more readily obtain from God what you desire.

[Col. 0584A] For compelled by the great desire I have for your salvation, I have undertaken this task beyond my powers: to gather, in the bonds of my words, the sayings of the Fathers for your instruction. Meditate on these things; write them on the tablets of your heart. And so that you may know by what path you ought to walk, and may accomplish in deed what you learn by reading, cry out to God, without whom no good is done; cry out, I entreat you, with a great cry from your whole heart, and, sorrowful and suppliant, pray.

[Col. 0583]

# BOOK, OR TREATISE, ON CHARITY. (G)

[NOTE.]

[Col. 0583] This Treatise was compiled by an anonymous writer, first from Richard of Saint Victor—namely, the first five chapters from the Treatise on the Degrees of Charity; then from Peter of Blois—from the ninth chapter to the end—being excerpted word for word from his two books *On Love of God and Neighbour*, with a few omissions here and there. Moreover, whatever lies between the fifth and ninth chapters is woven together from various passages of St Bernard, especially from the Sermons on the Song of Songs. It was first published by Gretser at Ingolstadt in 1617, from the Library of the Carthusians of Erfurt.

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0583B]

The insistence of your charity, most beloved to me, compels me to write something to you concerning charity, and to presume beyond myself and beyond the measure of my littleness—or rather, as it seems to me, to give from emptiness and to give what I do not possess. I tell you, my mind reluctantly consents to say anything about charity, feeling that neither heart nor tongue is sufficient to treat it. For how can one who does not love, who does not feel the power of love, speak about love? On other matters abundant material occurs in books; but this matter is wholly within, or nowhere at all, because it does not pass from outward things to the inward secrets of sweetness, but proceeds from inward things to outward expression. Therefore only he speaks worthily of it who frames outward words according to what the heart inwardly dictates.

[Col. 0583C] Do not wonder, then, if I would rather hear another speak of this subject than speak of it myself. I would hear, I say, one who dipped the pen of his tongue in the blood of his heart, for teaching is then true and venerable when what the tongue speaks is dictated by conscience and prompted by charity. You are mistaken if you think me such a person—or rather, I am mistaken. For it is devout in you, in that charity which believes all things, to think of me more highly than what is in me; but it is hard for me to have attributed to me a good which I do not possess. Even if I possessed it, perhaps it would be better to be unaware of it.

When what does not exist is loved, neither the lover nor love is anything, but only that which is loved. O great power of charity, which calls things that are not as though they were! At once transferring the virtues and vices of all into the increase of your merit, you merit in each person more than each person merits for himself. O strong virtue, which robs no one and yet seizes everything! You make everything your own and take from no one what is his; the good which you love in another you make your own.

[Col. 0584B] And indeed, it may happen that you perform in vain the good which you do; but it is altogether impossible that I should love in vain.

## CHAPTER I. On the strength of love.

1. Behold, at hand is the strength of love which we seek, and no one can resist it. It subjects all things to itself and compels all things to serve its progress. By loving, it overcomes enemies and makes them friends, even against their will. For though it may have rivals, it has no enemies at all. One who knows how to be an enemy to no one can have no enemy. For just as friendship exists only between two friends, so enmity exists only between two enemies. The person who hates one who loves him should be called not so much an enemy as unjust.

[Col. 0584C] Charity alone does not fail in adversities, because it is patient; does not repay injuries, because it is kind; is not tormented by another’s prosperity, because it does not envy; is not stung by an evil conscience, because it does nothing wrongly; is not exalted in honour, because it is not puffed up; is not confounded in humiliation, because it is not ambitious; is not constrained by covetousness, because it does not seek its own; is not provoked by insults, because it is not irritated;

[Col. 0585A] is not polluted by sinister suspicions, because it thinks no evil; is not made glad by others’ evils, because it does not rejoice in iniquity; is not blinded by errors, because it rejoices together with truth; is not broken by persecutions, because it bears all things; is not hardened by faithlessness, because it believes all things; is not swallowed up by despair, because it hopes all things; and is not cut short by the separation of death, because it never fails (1 Corinthians 13:4–8).

2. What wonder if it is not conquered by death, since it is strong as death (Song of Songs 8:6)—indeed, stronger than death, since in the death of the Redeemer it compelled death itself to die? O unconquerable power, charity! You overcame even the One who is unconquerable, and in some manner subjected to all men him to whom all things are subject: for God, conquered by love, humbled himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7–8), becoming not only man but “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21:7).

[Col. 0585B] Because of the exceeding charity with which he loved us (Ephesians 2:4), he could no longer restrain his mercies in his anger (Psalm 76:10), but exposed his beloved soul to enemies for his friends, in order to take away from his friends alike the fear and the force of death. And if charity was strong against God, how much more will it prevail against men?

From this comes thereafter that fearless constancy of heart among the faithful, by which, despising torments and trampling death underfoot, they joyfully return to their homeland through the very jaws of death. Dying, they exult and taunt death, saying: “Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55). Now you are no longer a sting but a shout of joy, since through your midst you open a broad and glad passage, the way to the kingdom.

[Col. 0585C] Charity therefore makes them not fear but desire to die for him and in him, since they see themselves loved by him in such a way that, lest they themselves should die, he was willing to be condemned to a most shameful death. For admiring and embracing in Christ that excess of love by which, “for the joy set before him, he endured the cross, despising human shame” (Hebrews 12:2), they are ashamed not to return love in kind. Spurred on by the mockeries of his passion as by certain goads, they are borne without restraint into the abyss of love and the depth of charity, seeking wholly and solely this: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Psalm 115:12).

[Col. 0585D] Carried away by a kind of perceptive and holy madness of mind, they judge themselves to love too little though so loved. The vehement force of love is not restrained by reason, because, as the Apostle testifies, it surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19); it is not frightened by majesty, because it casts out fear (1 John 4:18); it is not checked by miseries, because it is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). It is truly an omnipotent power, making miseries themselves powerful by turning into help what was prepared to harm.

Supported by it, Christ’s holy soldiers, fearless and certain of victory, walk in the midst of dangers in complete safety, fearing neither demon nor man.

3. Hence Paul, after enumerating the many perils in which he had triumphed gloriously, adds the cause of his triumph: “In all these things we overcome through him who loved us” (Rom. VIII, 37). Secure amid the flashing spears and whizzing darts of enemies raging on every side, he sleeps in charity, which alone is able to quench the fiery darts of the wicked one (Eph. VI, 16). For it covers a multitude of sins (I Pet. IV, 18), and prevails against the flies of temptations.
