It prevails also over that Jebusite people, and makes the rest of the Canaanite race serve under tribute (Deut. XX, 11). And in the field where virtue is exercised, it is certainly a greater power to cast down an enemy who stands erect than to restrain one who is merely attempting to rise. It is charity’s particular work not to destroy temptations before they arise, but, once they have arisen, to lay them low so that they do not advance. Therefore it should be called not so much a powerful virtue as the power of virtues, because all other virtues receive from it the power by which they are truly virtues. This is the life of faith, the strength of hope, and the inmost force and marrow of all virtues. This is what orders life, kindles the affections, gives form to the affections, corrects excesses, and shapes conduct; it is effective for all things and prevails over all things, even in some manner rendering omnipotence itself powerless.

4. Is this not what, in Moses, resisting divine justice and power, prevailed in strength? “Let me alone,” he says, “that my wrath may burn against this people.” Hear: “Let me alone”; and do not doubt that the Lord is held fast—and by nothing other than the strength of love. You ask whose love? Surely that of the faithful servant who refused to become greater and more glorious through the destruction of the people; not overcome by a carnal affection, as commonly happens, but lest the poisoned darts of blasphemers should strike against God’s glory. “No, I beg you,” he says, “let not the Egyptians say: ‘He craftily brought them out in order to kill them in the mountains’” (Exod. XXXII, 10, 12), “and he was unable to bring them into the land which he promised” (Num. XIV, 16). Why should justice not yield, why should power not yield, where charity from a pure heart was not so much asking as urgently pressing? This power, Lord, you who endure it also bring about—at once mighty and merciful.

Oh, what a lack we suffer of such men, who would set themselves before the Lord on account of our sins, appease wrath, and restrain vengeance! “There is none,” says the prophet, “who calls upon your name, who rises up and holds you fast” (Isa. LXIV, 7). Love alone is the power capable of holding the Lord, and by it alone he permits himself to be held. Yet he mercifully complains through the prophet that he is not held: “I sought among them for a man who would put up a hedge and stand in opposition before me, so that I should not destroy it; and I found none” (Ezek. XXII, 30). God seeks someone to oppose him in his anger—he whose proper work is mercy, while vengeance is foreign to him. “His work,” he says, “is foreign to him” (Isa. XXVIII, 21). What work? Surely the work of vengeance and wrath.

5. Thus charity, by its strength, restrains God’s outstretched hand from striking; it crushes Satan underfoot and heaps burning coals upon the heads of enemies (Rom. XII, 20). It is powerful not merely against flesh and blood, but against the principalities and powers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavens (Eph. VI, 12). Strong in adversity, it is stronger still in prosperity. For Christ’s love alone despises and spits upon the impure blandishments of fortune, whether smiling or mocking, delighting in a sweeter savor; in comparison with it every sweetness is bitter, every pleasure sorrowful, every beautiful thing ugly, every agreeable thing burdensome.

Let this suffice concerning its invincibility—if not for the abundance of material contained in the text, at least for your present occupation.

## CHAPTER II. On the Insatiability of Love

6. Let us now approach its insatiability. Indeed, that sweetness which it feels produces love’s strength: with the slightest taste of it, the soul, easily seeing God, despises all things. For he cannot be loved except through contempt for this world; the soul knows that it cannot first find the Beloved unless it has passed beyond the figure of this passing world with a certain disdain. Therefore, drawing itself wholly into itself, it does not merely employ steps or paces of ascent; rather, it is borne by unexpected raptures and ecstasies, flying rather than walking into those sublime and hidden regions of heaven. Hence Paul reports not that he ascended to the third heaven, but that he was caught up (II Cor. XII, 2). There he is affected as though by fire from the altar: intoxicated with divine love, the mind forgets everything and proceeds wholly into God, tasting that which no one knows except the one who receives it (Apoc. II, 17). But whenever it receives that happiness, it must be unaware of this misery; for the two cannot coexist.

7. Yet although mortals are sometimes granted access to this degree of love, the soul is forbidden to remain there long, until, having put off its corruptible garments, it has freely escaped into the freedom of the glory of the children of God (Rom. VIII, 21). It strives and is drawn by desire for that countenance which, according to the prophet, the Father set like a diamond (Ezek. III, 9), so that it might draw even hearts of iron. This drawing, though it has a certain sweet violence, nevertheless marks more clearly the incapacity of mortality: weighed down grievously by it, the wretched soul is often compelled to fall from its flight and fail in its effort.

Thus loving spirits, stretched out by the body’s corruption, have frequent joy from God’s visitation, but no abundance of it: they are permitted neither to be full nor to linger. Hence Wisdom seems, as it were, to play for a time in a pleasant jest with the children of men (Prov. VIII, 31). While she is thought to be held by them, she slips from their hands; she allows herself to be pursued and caught, then vanishes and is not seen again, until she returns when summoned afresh by tears and prayers. Thus, though the visitation delights, the alternation is painful.

But with what stupor, do you suppose, is the soul overwhelmed when that sweetness is withdrawn and it is dragged back captive into these snares of the senses? Is it not as though, driven from the homeland of spirits into the valley of bodies, it had fallen into another age unknown to itself, far unlike the former—an age in which charity grows cold, sensuality reigns, the mind’s eye is darkened, and bodily sense flourishes? Then it mourns, drawing sighs from on high; it is made wretched from the very source from which it was made blessed. For the more pleasing the things it had experienced, the more painfully it bears their removal. The withdrawal of a beloved thing is an increase of desire; and the more ardently you desire a thing, the more painfully you lack it. This lovesickness is nothing other than the weariness of impatient longing, which must deeply affect the mind of one who loves intensely when the beloved is absent.

8. In vain, unless I am mistaken, does anyone attempt to soothe the pain and moderate the grief of such a languishing soul by outward consolation, when the sweet wound of love must be healed from within. The sacred bitterness of secret sorrow is softened by no human comfort; when the inward taste of sweetness has been removed, outward consoling is of no use. Indeed, according to blessed Job’s judgment, the soul regards all comforters as burdensome (Job XVI, 2). He experienced this who said: “My soul refused to be comforted; I remembered God and was delighted” (Ps. LXXVI, 3–4).

Blessed is the sadness conceived not from the creature but from the Creator, which does not mourn any hardship of the present life. It is fitting indeed that the soul which refuses consolation amid any abundance of passing things should have God, the consolation of all, as its comforter. There is no grace apart from God from which it can take comfort, for it has learned to love nothing besides him. Let others have their vain consolations, to whom it is said: “Woe to you who are rich, for you have your consolations” (Luke VI, 24). He alone is its comforter who is also its indweller: God, who is charity. Although he never fails the righteous as regards merit, he is often absent as regards consolation. The former is more useful; the latter more pleasant. Thus he is possessed, yet hidden: the sweetness that is possessed but concealed does not touch the feeling of the heart.

9. When the one whom it desires delays, the soul no longer dozes or sleeps with the foolish virgins (Matt. XXV, 5). Inflamed by frequent sighs and awakened by groans, it can no longer conceal its sorrow or hide the fire that burns its grieving breast. It no longer deliberates, consults reason, or feels shame; it knows neither measure nor order, its mind wholly and solely intent upon the return of the sweetness once made present, and it considers any haste, however great, to be delay.

This, dearest friend, is what you once asked: what Augustine means when he says, “The love of God does not find consolation in impossibility.” Every desire is ordinarily moderated by reason when the desired object cannot be possessed. But the violence of love is restrained by no impossibility. For although it is clearly altogether impossible for any human being, while the soul is weighed down by earthly habitation and immersed in mire, to enjoy that happiness in its fullness, this impossibility gives no consolation to one who loves in this way, so as to prevent burning and yearning to possess what he desires. Yet although this desire exceeds reason, it does not offend God, who seems to have intimated something similar in the command: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart, with your whole soul, and with your whole mind” (Matt. XXII, 37). That this cannot be fulfilled by anyone in this mortal life—or, rather, this living death—

> [Note: Col. 0587. That is, according to all its perfection. See St Bernard’s treatise *On Loving God*, ch. 10, no. 29, and the notes.]

—is established both by arguments and by authorities. Yet no one doubts that every person ought to desire it. Hence the description of the righteous says: “He will delight exceedingly in his commandments” (Ps. CXI, 1). To will exceedingly is to will more than one is able. In this sense I also understand the saying: “The young maidens loved you exceedingly” (Song I, 2). For what does “exceedingly” mean except beyond one’s power and strength? God, toward whom their love tends, is infinite and immeasurable; therefore there can be no end or measure to their love. Thus the loving soul loves, though beyond its power, yet less than its will; it finds no consolation in this impossibility, but rather an increase of desire. “My soul,” says one, “has longed to desire your justifications” (Ps. CXVIII, 20). He who longed to desire things unseen could not be satisfied by desire. For hunger of the soul is desire. Thus the soul that truly loves the Lord is not sated with love, because God is love, and whoever loves him loves love. But to love love makes a circle, so that love has no end.

10. You see, then, how charity is invincible, overcoming all things; so too it is insatiable, devouring all things, and from abundance producing want, since even from delights already tasted it burns ever more intensely in longing. Though such delights are given unto fullness, they are never given unto satiety. “Those who eat me,” she says, “will still hunger” (Ecclus. XXIV, 29). O good God, whom to love is to eat: how do you refresh those who love you in such a way that they hunger more, unless you are at once food and hunger? Whoever has not tasted you does not know at all how to hunger for you. Therefore you feed in order to make them hunger. “He has filled the hungry,” says she who is full, “with good things” (Luke I, 53). With what good things? Do not ask me what are the good things of charity. I judge them surely to be those of which it is said: “No eye has seen, O God, apart from you, what you have hidden for those who fear you” (Isa. LXII, 4); and elsewhere: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II, 9). You hear that these things are prepared for those who love, so that you need not doubt that they are the goods of love. In love are stored the delights of eternity and every heavenly sweetness. In it are peace, patience, long-suffering, and joy in the Holy Spirit (Rom. XIV, 17), and whatever pleasant thing can be conceived in the mind—and beyond it. This, I say, you have prepared for those who love you; but you have hidden it from those who fear you, until charity casts out the veil of fear (I John IV, 28), so that they may see how great is the abundance of your sweetness (Ps. XXX, 20), which, though it fills, never satiates. Therefore I dare to call such persons, if any there are, clothed in the second robe.

11. Perhaps you object: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI, 15); and the Jerusalem above “is satisfied with the fat of wheat” (Ps. CXLVII, 14). But you should understand that satisfaction there signifies an abundance of the desired thing, not the end of desire. “The end of desire,” says someone, “is satiety.” But those who always hunger plainly are not sated. Yet blessed indeed is the hunger which hungers only for what it possesses, and possesses only what it hungers for. Let your charity therefore be persuaded of this: no one can be sated with the sweetness of divine love in the life to come, and no one can be filled with it in the present life. Let your consolation in this impossibility be that you have no consolation. I wish you patience; but in this matter it is more fitting that you should be impatient.

## CHAPTER III. On the Unceasingness of Love

12. Having touched on these two matters, however imperfectly, let the pen proceed to investigate the rest, insofar as God in his sweetness deigns to open to the poor an entrance into things so worthy. Yet in these matters entrance is usually more easily opened to those who knock devoutly than to those who investigate subtly. He knocks who desires, who prays; and to those who knock it is opened (Matt. VII, 7). For there can be no doubt that he gladly opens to one who knocks, since he urges one who has not yet knocked to knock. Thus God first wills that even what he promises should be sought from him. And so he promises beforehand what he intends to give, that he may provide boldness to ask and that devout prayer may earn what he was going to give freely. In this way, while he goes before us by granting us what we may return, he draws merits from us for ourselves, acting so that he may not give gratuitously.

Clearly he is worthy to be loved in return, since he so precedes us in loving. “In this,” says John, “is charity: not that we loved God, but that he first loved us” (I John IV, 10). His love therefore goes before ours, more generous indeed; but ours is reckoned more just. For he freely loves those still ungrateful; whereas we plainly love by his gift, not by anything due to us. He gives that by which, and causes the reason why, he is loved—so that he may be loved both from what is his and for what is his. I pass over pursuing that gift, since it is ineffable. Although a few spiritual persons may experience it, no one can express it. Only he who gives and he who receives know it (Apoc. II, 17); everyone else is excluded. Even to those who receive and possess it, that hidden bestowal is questionable and uncertain—and beneficially so, lest they presume.

13. But now, I beg you, turn your eyes back to these lower things, which many see without seeing; and consider whether all things which either serve us in prosperity or rage against us in adversity are not certain spurs of charity, in some way urging us onward in love’s course. For all things direct their course toward this end: to meet human needs and pleasures, or at least to assist human deficiencies. This heaven, earth, sea, and air; this cycle of time, renewing the old through recurrent births, remaking what has fallen apart, restoring what has been consumed—never ceases to accomplish this. Thus, just as no one can reject these continual and common benefits, so no one ought not to love so great a benefactor.

Perhaps you agree concerning prosperity; but you wish to know how adversities teach or demand love. Since human ingratitude often proudly claims the Creator’s gifts as its own, the Creator of humankind wills, by a lofty and salutary counsel, that human beings should be exercised by tribulations, so that when the human being fails and God comes to the rescue, God may rightly be loved by the human being. This is what he says: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation; I will deliver you, and you will glorify me” (Ps. XLIX, 15). From the occasion of frequent needs, God must necessarily be approached frequently by human beings through repeated entreaties; by frequent approach he is tasted, and by tasting it is proved how sweet God is. Thus the iron heart, which could not be softened by benefits, melts into gratitude for its deliverer when trained by scourges; it learns to love God, if not for his goodness, at least for its own advantage. This is the first degree of love for those beginning to love. But for those already loving, it is the lowest degree: when we love God not even for his own sake, but for our own.

It is clear, then, how adversities instruct and in some manner compel to God’s love the person who loves merely carnally and loves carnal things.

14. Yet even for those inflamed with love, prosperity is sometimes withdrawn and adversities imposed, by no inferior counsel: so that if flattering prosperity has perhaps stolen some portion of love for itself—as is difficult to avoid—its successor, adversity, may take it away. For adversity alone, according to John’s teaching, truly teaches us not to love the world or the things that are in the world (I John II, 15). Thus the Israelites are compelled by the Egyptians to leave Egypt. For, as blessed Gregory testifies, when the world strikes the mind with calamities, it proclaims nothing other than that it should not be loved.

Therefore love alone is what God requires from us, whether he overwhelms us with benefits, corrects us with scourges, teaches us by counsels, or binds us by commandments. “Charity is the fullness of the law” (Rom. XIII, 10), and it contains both law and prophets. For whatever divine law commands or forbids is reduced to love alone. Pay the tribute of love, and you will know that the Lord has been satisfied.

15. “What good, then,” someone says, “does such great austerity in our food, lowliness in clothing, and constant severity in vigils and disciplines do us?” Receive the answer in a few words. Certain works are services of charity, pleasing and propitiatory if done in charity; but without charity they profit nothing. For charity is the virtue in which no work, however small, is rejected, and without which no work, however great, is accepted. Not preaching, even if it be done in the tongues of angels. Not faith, even if it removes mountains. Not almsgiving, even if one distributes all one’s possessions as food for the poor. Not affliction of the body, even if the body is handed over to be burned (I Cor. XIII, 1–3). Not the solemnities of Masses, since one is forbidden to offer a gift before reconciliation with one’s brother (Matt. V, 24).

For God himself is the love of human beings, and every creature rightly acknowledges and says to him: “You have no need of my goods” (Ps. XV, 2). Yet he requires from every person this one thing alone, which is plainly difficult for none. “Love alone,” as Augustine says, “does not know the name of difficulty.” When it has expended much on a friend, it judges that it has expended little or nothing. Hence Jacob’s many years seemed few days because of the greatness of his love (Gen. XXIX, 20). For a true lover scarcely feels whatever he suffers for his friend, since he is so wholly intent upon love that he is not allowed fully to think of anything besides the beloved, whom he bears as a seal upon his heart and upon his arm (Song VIII, 6).

16. Finally, by what route could forgetfulness of him creep in, when, besides those rays of unbounded light and those streams of incorruptible sweetness with which he ineffably pours himself into the soul, he does not cease to show himself to the lover even in visible things? The whole lover of God, wherever he turns, has with him a familiar reminder of love. He uses these things as mirrors; in everything he sees the memory of his love resounds. He looks upon all things, and upon him who made them and the end for which he made them. In them he feels him to be not so much admirable as lovable; and from the earnest of love which God has given beforehand, he wisely judges how great a dowry God has reserved.

Love is surely a chaste and dove-like eye. It is fixed with no lust upon things granted for human use, but contemplates the eternal in transient things. This is the eye that is not closed, because it lacks the eyelid of carnality. It is troubled by no intrusion, because it admits nothing external. It is blinded by no darkness, because it has no beams within it. It is weighed down by no sleep, as he testifies who says: “I sleep, but my heart keeps watch” (Song V, 2). It is an upright eye, a truly right eye, which no leftward intention turns downward and no earthly affection bends downward. It is a truly simple and prudent eye, shaken by no uncertain suspicion and held back by no curious anxiety, gazing unceasingly upon him into whom angels desire to look (I Pet. I, 12). For, as Augustine says, vehement love cannot fail to see the one it loves: love is an eye, and to love is to see.

He who says, “You have wounded my heart with one of your eyes” (Song IV, 9), confesses himself wounded by this eye. The soul has, indeed, two eyes: one by which it understands, the other by which it seeks. “The Lord,” says the Psalm, “looked down upon the children of men, to see whether there is one who understands or seeks God” (Ps. LII, 3). Of these two, love is the right eye, which wounds by seeking. For the one leaping upon the mountains and skipping over the hills (Song II, 8)—that is, surpassing every understanding, human and angelic—cannot be grasped except through the wound of love.

17. You ask what it is for God to be wounded. And I answer: for that omnipotence mercifully to condescend to our weakness is, as it were, through a certain opening of a wound, to disclose the secrets of inward sweetness. Thus he can be wounded who, though impassible, is nevertheless capable of compassion. This wound is inflicted without anger and felt without pain.

The king of the Ammonites plots to tear out this wounding eye by means of the shameful covenant proposed to the unhappy people. “On this condition,” he says, “will I make a covenant with you: that I may put out the right eyes of you all” (I Kings XI, 2). For once love—the right eye—has been taken away, understanding alone remains for error; and this we have called the left eye. For theirs was an error of understanding without loving: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God, but became vain in their thoughts” (Rom. I, 21). How many who seem to pursue errors are blinded by this error, than which perhaps none worse can be found!

18. Therefore God is seen by lovers with both eyes, but he is wounded by one: where understanding is darkened, love penetrates; where the former is repelled, the latter is admitted. For we are forbidden to scrutinize and to be wise beyond what is fitting (Rom. XII, 3), but commanded to love even beyond what we can. Nor can the eye of love be so darkened that it cannot see the one it loves—though not “as he is” (I John III, 2), which, John testifies, is reserved as a reward, but as a traveler sees him, which is granted in the present life for consolation.

Each lover sees according to the manner in which he loves: one in this way, another in that, according to the variety of affections by which they are borne toward him. Some long more ardently for the mysteries of divinity; others contemplate more securely the mysteries of humanity, admiring God’s most lofty counsel concerning the salvation of humankind. Yet whatever the eye of love beholds is wholly safe; it alone now sees for merit and will one day see for reward, when, the cloud of corruption removed, it shall, as written, “see that countenance in joy” (Job XXXIII, 26).

Much could be added here, useful to those who hunger, though not to the fastidious; but lest I burden you with a longer discourse, I restrain my pen, although I confess that it desires much more.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Inseparability of Love

19. Let us now come to the middle—that final part of your request, especially the matter which you urgently ask to have explained, most devout man [Richard adds: Severinus]. It is to be unfolded indeed by my lips, but certainly through your merits, in which I have no small trust, not only in my studies but in all my necessities. But so that our discourse may proceed in its proper course through the matters proposed, let what has been said be recalled in a brief catalogue [Richard: epilogue]. You have in the foregoing that charity fights invincibly, tastes insatiably, sees unceasingly; it remains to add that it clings inseparably.

For the glue of love is so tender that it is called not so much a joining as a uniting. It is truly a good glue, binding the person of virtue in three ways, so that he may be harmonized and joined in truth with himself, with his neighbor, and with God. In himself, a person is made one through love: gathering himself within himself and drawing his affections back from all the places where they are held captive, he loves one thing alone unchangeably and is no longer altered into diverse things. For one divided by love among many things is never found to be one and the same within himself, but is always unlike himself, because he must change as often as what he loves changes. Whoever leans upon that which is falling must fall with it.

A person is also united with the neighbor through charity, when, not merely by living blamelessly, he strives to become one with all and to share in everyone’s success; to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. XII, 15), to be weak with the weak and burn with those who are scandalized (II Cor. XI, 29), according to what is written: a companion in tribulation and kingdom (II Cor. I, 7; Apoc. I, 9). Thus the multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul (Acts IV, 32), when neither diversity of wills nor private ownership of things divided their minds; rather, charity bound them firmly and sweetly restrained them in the unity of the Spirit and the bond of peace (Eph. IV, 3).

Alas, I say, we have fallen into a lower age—we upon whom the ends, indeed the dregs, of the ages have come (I Cor. X, 11). For, to say nothing of worldly people, whom ambition has blinded, even the very choice of religious life in our miserable time is scattered by such great division that scarcely one person agrees with another as one, unless perhaps against the Lord and against his Christ (Ps. II, 2). Everywhere the breaches in David’s tower of charity appear; they now gape so widely that they utterly threaten its impending collapse. Beneath one tunic and a similar garment there is kept a vain and utterly dissimilar heart, so that scarcely the signs of ancient religious life remain. Those who come to the Lord’s tomb—that is, the cloister—and seek Christ find only the linen cloths exposed: that is, the outward form of the habit. I confess, I am weary of being here; let us leave this place, for it is not our purpose here to speak of vices.

20. Charity unites God to a human being and a human being to God—not only by that ineffable union in which our nature is united with the eternal Word in unity of person, a union effected by that charity with which he loved us before the foundation of the world (Eph. I, 4), but also by the union of which the Apostle says: “He who clings to God is one spirit” (I Cor. VI, 17). This unity is surely that of love, because the person is united to God, conformed with all the depths of the heart and all desires to the heavenly and eternal will, by a glue that shall not be dissolved.

For charity is “the bond of perfection” (Col. III, 14), through which the minds of the faithful, joined in the closest embrace, cling to one another and are connected through all their joints to their head in one body, in the mutual sharing of all goods. Thus each may confidently say: “I am a companion of all who fear you and keep your commandments” (Ps. CXVIII, 63). I think this is what is meant by: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Eccles. IV, 12). It is called threefold because, as I said before, it binds in three ways.

Would you have the Apostle describe the threefold cord? “The end of the commandment,” he says, “is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I, 5). A pure heart alone does not know how to overflow. What is laid open is easily defiled; charity alone keeps it from being exposed in vain. Further, according to the Apostle, the person who loves the neighbor’s good as his own has “a good conscience toward all” (Heb. XIII, 18); otherwise he is convicted of not having that charity which “does not seek its own” (I Cor. XIII, 5). Unfeigned faith is faith which works through love. Otherwise James does not hesitate to call it not merely feigned, but dead (James II, 20).

And truly this threefold cord is not easily broken. Bound by it, Paul fervently says: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or hunger, or nakedness?” (Rom. VIII, 35). It is a powerful bond, against which no violence prevails, holding the lover inseparably with the beloved.

21. Yet let no one suppose that I think with—or rather, think foolishly with—those who maintain that charity once possessed can never afterward be lost. For if everyone who possessed charity also possessed perseverance, the Lord would have warned his disciples in vain: “Remain in my love” (John XV, 9). But I also hold without hesitation that charity can be freely abandoned, though it cannot be forcibly taken away. It is offered to everyone and taken from no one, so that no one lacks it except through his own fault.

But for the affections of lovers to meet in one through this mutual power, the heart of the loving soul must melt, so that it can be poured into and transformed into the one whom it loves, and changed into another person. So a drop of water poured into much wine seems wholly to cease being itself as it takes on another’s flavor and color. Hence come those frequent failures—or rather, advances—of pious lovers, while they perceive nothing of themselves in themselves except what they are in Christ Jesus. You know what I mean; no one knows it better than you. Only what is liquid conforms to every shape; and this especially suits the lover’s heart. “My heart,” says the Psalmist, “has become like melting wax” (Ps. XXI, 15).

22. A thing is softened, expanded, and purified by melting. Now consider this threefold effect in love, which is truly a divine fire, dissolving hearts, purifying them, and fusing them into a mass of unity, just as different metals, melted by fire, flow together into one. At its touch, that hateful hardness softens and yields—the insensibility of heart by which a person neither feels himself nor another; is moved neither by pity nor by prayers; is not led by examples nor frightened by threats; is hardened by benefits and not instructed by scourges; is brazen toward shameful acts, prone to what is unlawful, and knows neither how to bend nor submit except when unable to resist. In all things, let hardness of heart be your example.

23. But a softened heart, according to Paul’s teaching, is enlarged (II Cor. VI, 11): it spreads everywhere to the right and the left, aiding enemies and friends alike, and with a certain grateful and spontaneous impulse meets all, rejoicing in neighbors’ advancement and grieving with them over their failures. Thus it flows, but does not flow out; for it is so directed toward others that it does not entirely depart from itself.

Consider whether perhaps the Prophet meant the same thing when, after comparing his heart to melting wax, he immediately added: “In the midst of my belly” (Ps. XXI, 15). It was liquid, but did not flow out. Only the one who so attends to others as not to attend to himself flows out. “Take heed,” says the Apostle, “lest perhaps you flow away” (Heb. II, 1). Nor is it necessary that in those ecstasies in which human spirits are torn from muddy bodily senses, they should be said to be outside themselves, since Paul, in his rapture, declares that he wholly does not know whether he was in the body or outside the body (II Cor. XII, 2–3). “Where then are they?” you ask. In what is inwarder than themselves. The heart of a human being is deep and inscrutable (Jer. XVII, 9), and one is so hidden from oneself that one does not know oneself inwardly.

Therefore spirits are not led out, but led in, into that inner chamber, however great it may be, so that, with the doors of the senses shut apart, they may meet more securely, more secretly, and in a most chaste embrace with the beloved. There they are better with themselves when they do not know where they are; they are safer when they have thus lost themselves.

24. Moreover, what has melted must be purified and refined to purity, if it has any dross. This is done by love itself, which is a consuming fire, purging away the chaff of ignorance and the sins of youth, making the soul most pure and worthy of divine marriage, “without spot or wrinkle.” Hear the devouring flame: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 47). Finally, “all things work together for good to those who love God” (Rom. VIII, 28), and nothing is imputed unto death. Whatever he himself does not impute is as though it had not been. “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord will not impute sin” (Ps. XXXI, 2). For no one is without it except he alone who is “free among the dead” (Ps. LXXXVII, 6).

Thus a heart warmed and melted is easily pierced and bubbles over at every word of the beloved, experiencing what is sung: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song V, 6); and what is read in the Gospel: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way?” (Luke XXIV, 32). O sweet converse of God in the soul and with the soul, formed without the noise of tongue and lips, received without the ear and in silence! Only the one who speaks and the one to whom he speaks hears it; every outsider is excluded.

25. These words, then, are like streams from a heavenly spring, watering hearts made dry by the abundance and longing of love. They are an account of the delights [Richard: “whose sweet”] of the city of God—its peace and abundance, the glory of its citizens, and the beauty of its most radiant dwelling-place. They drive weariness from the heart [Col. 0596C] and fatigue from the body, announcing to the beloved that it is his possession and that he may ascend to it. Nor did he who said, “My soul has slumbered through weariness; strengthen me in your words” (Ps. 118:28), ask or endure anything else.

Words of truth are likewise present to our thoughts; yet no one is so observant that he can readily distinguish what the heart produces, except one who attends to the Lord speaking: “Why do you think evil in your hearts?” (Matt. 9:4); and, “Evil thoughts come forth from the heart” (Matt. 15:19); and, “Everyone who speaks a lie speaks from his own resources” (John 8:44); and the Apostle’s words: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves” (2 Cor. 3:5). We call those things evil in the heart in accordance with: “The fool said in his heart, ‘There is no God’” (Ps. 13:1). But we have heard good things. Hence: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9). And to this hearing there will indeed be given joy and gladness: “This word shall not return empty, but shall accomplish whatever purpose for which I sent it” (Isa. 55:11), watering and making fruitful the inner chambers of the heart.

Those taught by such words are taught by God, and the anointing teaches them concerning all things (1 John 2:27). It alone teaches all truth and, with swift instruction, speaks certain mysteries of God which it is not lawful for a human being to utter; and, even if it were lawful to hear them, they are such as are never heard among the teachers of this world. Through their power and hearing hearts melt; by melting and failing they are perfected, as they come together into that unity [Col. 0597A] which the Savior prays and desires for his own in the Gospel: “That they may be one,” he says, “as we also are one” (John 17:11, 21). John recalls this in his Epistle, saying: “As he is, so are we in this world” (1 John 4:17). Thus, just as that blessed and beatifying Trinity of persons is held together by eternal love without confusion—so that the number of the persons, which does not multiply the essence, does not disturb the unity, nor does unity reduce the Trinity to the singularity of one person—so they too may be united and ordered in charity: not indeed by equality, but by some likeness. Nor should it be thought absurd that I said God is held together by love, since I said that he is held together by none other than himself, and that he loves himself from among all others.

[Col. 0597B] Therefore God loves, and loves from his whole self; for the whole Trinity loves—if indeed “whole” may be said of the infinite and incomprehensible, or at least of the simple. How, O soul, will you return love to the gratuitous giver of your life, the most generous provider, the merciful comforter, the watchful governor, the abundant redeemer, the eternal preserver, enrichener, and glorifier?

## Chapter V. On the dignity and pre-eminence of charity

26. Charity is plainly an incomparable and most desirable gift. For what do we think can be compared with it, when it is preferred even to martyrdom and to faith that removes mountains? Through charity, moreover, a human being is in God and God in a human being. For what is so characteristic of God [Col. 0597C] as charity? Indeed, God is charity. Charity grants freedom and drives out fear (1 John 4:16, 18); it does not feel labor, does not consider merit, does not demand rewards; yet it impels more than all else. No terror so urges, no rewards so invite, no justice so requires. Charity does not seek its own interests. Charity is not provoked, is not hasty, never fails, does not fall into the pit, and heaps up good in return for evil received.

O patient charity—and compassionate as well! Charity is patient: that is enough. It is kind (1 Cor. 13:4, 5, 8): that is abundance. Patient charity overlooks, waits for, and bears with the offender; but kind charity draws, brings near, and causes conversion from error. Kind charity loves even those whom it tolerates, and loves them fervently. For charity weeps, but from love, not sorrow; it weeps from longing; it weeps with those who weep (Rom. 12:15).

27. O good mother Charity, whether she cherishes the weak, exercises the advanced, or rebukes the restless, offering different things to different persons, she loves them all as children. When she rebukes, she is gentle; when she caresses, she is guileless. She is wont to be severe mercifully and to soothe without deceit; she knows how to be angry patiently and indignant humbly. When injured, she is not provoked; when despised, she calls back. She is the mother both of human beings and of angels. She has reconciled not only things on earth but also things in heaven (Col. 1:20). She is the one who, making God favorable to humankind, reconciled humankind to God.

Surely, scandals against the little ones are injuries to charity. For charity neither offends nor despises charity when it perceives an offense [Col. 0598A]. It cannot deny itself, nor is it divided within itself. Rather, it knows how to unite things divided in itself; it does not know how to divide things once united. It loves peace and rejoices together in unity. For it alone begets, gathers, binds together, and preserves unity wherever unity is known to be preserved in the bond of peace.

With complete confidence charity knocks at the door of a friend, never supposing that it will suffer rejection, since it knows itself to be the mother of friendships. Nor does it fear to disturb, for a little while, the most secluded repose for its own business. For that is true and sincere charity by which the good of one’s neighbor is loved as one’s own. Whoever loves his own good more—or loves it alone—is shown not to love good chastely, since he loves it for his own sake, not for the good’s sake [Col. 0598B].

Let us love and be loved: in the one case providing for ourselves in others, and in the other for our own through others. For in those whom we love, we surely rest; while for those by whom we are loved, we prepare rest for them in ourselves. To love in God is to possess charity; to seek to be loved for God’s sake is to serve charity. I embrace both loves—the love of God and the love of neighbor—when I love you, Lord Jesus, who are my neighbor because you are human and have shown me mercy, and who nevertheless are God above all, blessed forever.

## Chapter VI. On the nature, character, and power of true love, both human love for God and God’s love for humankind

28. Burning and vehement love, especially divine love, when it cannot contain itself within itself, pays no attention to the order, rule, sequence, or brevity of the words in which it overflows, provided that it suffers no loss of itself thereby. Sometimes it requires neither words nor any voice at all, being content for this purpose with sighs alone.

O headlong, vehement, burning love, which violently permits me to think of nothing but you! I disdain everything else; I despise all things besides you; I am content with you. You confuse order, disregard custom, and know no measure. Whatever seems to belong to expediency, reason, modesty, counsel, or judgment, you triumph over in yourself and reduce to captivity.

In vain does one who does not love approach to hear or read the speech of love; for a cold breast cannot receive fiery speech [Col. 0598D]. Just as one who does not know Greek does not understand a speaker of Greek, nor one who is not Latin understands a speaker of Latin—and similarly in other cases—so the language of love will be barbarous to one who does not love; it will be like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal (1 Cor. 13:1).

Love knows no reverence, for love is named from loving, not from honoring. Let one honor who trembles, is astonished, fears, or marvels. All these things are absent in the lover; therefore one who loves love knows nothing else. He who is worthy of honor, merit, astonishment, and wonder nevertheless prefers to be loved. God requires that he be feared as Lord, honored as Father, and loved as Bridegroom. Which of these excels or stands highest? Surely not fear—far be it! Fear has punishment (1 John 4:18) [Col. 0599A], honor has no grace, and honor not proceeding from love is not honor but flattery. To God alone indeed belong honor and glory (1 Tim. 1:17); yet God will accept neither unless they are seasoned with the honey of love.

Love is sufficient in itself; it pleases in itself and for its own sake; it is its own merit and its own reward. Love seeks no cause or fruit beyond itself: its fruit is its exercise. I love because I love; I love in order to love. Where love is, there is no labor but savor, because nothing is difficult to one who loves. Love knows no master: it is sufficiently subject of itself, obeys willingly, complies without payment, and is held freely.

29. God too loves, and does not possess this from another source. He himself is the source from which he loves, and he loves the more vehemently because he does not so much possess love as himself is this very thing. Love looks down on no one, nor indeed despises anyone. It looks equally upon all who perfectly love themselves, and in itself harmonizes the high and the low; it makes them not merely equal but one.

Love is a great thing. For when God loves, he wills nothing other than to be loved; indeed, he loves for no other reason than that he may be loved, knowing that those who love him are blessed through love. O sweetness! O grace! O power of love! The highest of all became the lowest of all. Who accomplished this? Love, ignorant of rank, rich in condescension, mighty in affection, effective in persuasion. What is more powerful? Love triumphs over God, so that we may know that it was love by which fullness was poured out, height made equal, and singularity joined in fellowship. God is not merely loving but is love, and he requires only love returned and faithfulness.

[Col. 0599C] 50. Why should love not be loved? And what is so much the life of hearts as my God Jesus? He truly is both loving and lovable, and everything that belongs to him truly is, since he himself is nothing other than truth itself. What love of the soul is faithful and true except that by which truth is dearly loved? I possess reason; I am capable of truth. Yet I wish that I were not, if love were lacking in me. I am not safe from the axe if I am found without it. I must indeed love greatly the one through whom I live, exist, and understand, unless I am ungrateful and unworthy.

He is plainly worthy of death who refuses to live for you, Lord Jesus; and such a person is dead. Whoever has no relish for you is foolish; whoever takes thought to exist not for your sake is accounted as nothing and is nothing. “For your own sake, O God, you made all things” (Prov. 16:4); and one who wishes to exist for himself and not for you begins to be nothing among all things. For these reasons, therefore, I love you as much as I can. Yet there is something that moves, urges, and inflames me still more. Above all, I say, the cup that you drank—the work of our redemption—makes you lovable to me, good Jesus [Col. 0599D]. This readily claims my whole love for itself. This is what both attracts our devotion more gently, demands it more justly, binds it more closely, and moves it more forcefully.

## Chapter VII. On the two languages: that of the Word and that of the soul

31. The Word is spirit, and the soul is spirit; and they have their own languages, by which they speak to one another and reveal their presence. The Word’s language is the favor of condescension; the soul’s is the fervor of devotion. The soul that does not have this is speechless and infant-like, and it can have no conversation at all with the Word. Therefore, when the Word moves this language of his, wishing to speak to the soul, the soul cannot fail to perceive it. “The word of God is living and effective, and more penetrating than any two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. 4:12).

Again, when the soul moves its own language, it is far less possible for the Word to remain hidden, not only because he is present everywhere, but especially because the language of devotion cannot be moved to speech unless he himself prompts it. Thus, for the Word to say to the soul, “You are beautiful,” and to call her friend, is to pour into her that by which she both loves and presumes herself to be loved. For the soul, in return, to call the Word beloved and to confess beautiful the one whom she loves and by whom she is loved (Song 1:14–15), is to ascribe this to him without pretense or deceit, to marvel at his condescension, and to be astonished at grace. Thus the Word’s speech is the infusion of a gift, and the soul’s answer is admiration with thanksgiving.

32. [Note: “[Col. 0599] The following words seem in no way to accord with the preceding purpose.” —Editors of the *Patrologia*.]

When what is loved is present, love flourishes; when it is absent, love languishes. This is nothing other than the weariness of impatient longing, by which the mind of one who loves intensely must necessarily be affected when the beloved is absent. Suspended wholly in expectation, such a person considers even the greatest haste to be delay. For deprivation of the thing you love increases desire, and the more ardently you desire it, the more painfully you lack it.

## Chapter VIII. On the active and contemplative life

[Col. 0600C]

33. Perhaps you seek the repose of contemplation? You do well. Therefore let holy leisure be preceded by diligent exercise in the virtues. Otherwise, if you seek repose without training, you will wish merely to sleep in luxurious idleness, neglecting Leah’s fruitfulness and desiring only to delight in Rachel’s embraces. It is also a perverse order to demand reward before merit and to take food before labor.

Do not suppose, therefore, that acts of holy obedience or the traditions of the elders may in any way be prejudiced by your private love of repose. Otherwise the Lord will not approve the empty idleness of your contemplation; because of it he will not hear your prayers, and, when summoned, will not come. For so great a lover of obedience—who preferred to die rather than not to obey—will not grant the disobedient person possession of himself [Col. 0600D].

A mind accustomed to repose receives consolation from good works whenever, as often happens, the light of contemplation is withdrawn from it. For who, I do not say continually but even for long, while remaining in this body, enjoys the light of contemplation? Yet whenever it falls from the contemplative life, it returns to the active life, from which, as from a neighboring dwelling, it will return more familiarly to contemplation itself; for these two are companions dwelling together and inhabit the same house. Martha is Mary’s sister. Even if the mind falls from the light of contemplation, it nevertheless does not permit itself to fall into the darkness of sin or the sloth of idleness, but keeps itself in the light of good activity.

[Col. 0601A] 34. I speak to you from an experience I have undergone. Whenever I have found some among us to have profited from my counsels, then, I confess, I did not regret preferring the care of preaching to my own leisure and repose. I patiently tear myself away from the barren embraces of Rachel, so that the fruits of your progress may abound for me. For charity, which “does not seek its own interests” (1 Cor. 13:5), long ago readily persuaded me to prefer none of my desires to your benefit. Prayer, reading, writing, meditation, and whatever other gains belong to spiritual study—I have judged these losses for your sake.

For true and chaste contemplation has this characteristic: it so fills the mind, which it has vehemently kindled with divine fire, with zeal and longing to win for God persons who may love him likewise, that it most willingly interrupts contemplative leisure for the work of preaching. And when it has gained you to some extent in this respect, it returns to contemplation itself all the more ardently because it remembers having interrupted it more fruitfully; and, having again tasted contemplation, it returns with stronger vigor and its customary eagerness to seek further gains.

But amid these alternations the mind often fluctuates, fearing and being greatly troubled lest, drawn in different directions by its affections, it cling more than is fitting to either of these pursuits and so deviate, even briefly, in one or the other from the divine will. The one remedy or refuge in such matters is prayer and frequent groaning to the Lord, that he may continually deign to show us what, when, and to what extent [Col. 0601C] he wills us to do.

## Chapter IX. On the various effects and praises of charity

35. Friendship is not true unless it has a firm foundation in God. Therefore, since friendship is God’s gift, it is right that one who loves from God’s gift should love nothing apart from God, and that rivers should flow back to the place from which they flow (Eccl. 1:7); nor should the stream degenerate from its source when it flows from the fullness of abundant grace.

We profess that friendship to be uniquely and singularly true and perfect by which God deigned to call us his friends, if we keep his commandments. “You are my friends,” he says, “if you do what I command you” (John 15:14). This friendship of God [Col. 0601D] is charity, by which he loved us before the foundation of the world and chose us in his beloved Son (Eph. 1:4–5). It is the source of every good and every gift that comes to us from heavenly generosity. From it every legitimate love receives its order and form; nor can any affection of the mind be ordered unless it derives from charity its cause, measure, and order.

36. Of this most constant charity, Wisdom says in the book bearing her name: “I was ordered from eternity” (Prov. 8:23). Ordered by God, it orders angels in their ministries. It directs the pursuits and exercises of the righteous in their callings. Through it the law was ordained through angels by the hand of the Mediator (Gal. 3:19). Without it, friendship among human beings cannot be ordered. For since the Apostle says, “Let all things be done among you according to order” (1 Cor. 14:40), and again, “Let all your things be done in charity” (1 Cor. 16:14), it is clear that things not done in charity have no order.

Charity is the way and life of virtues; it is the more excellent way, and the path on which God’s salvation is shown (Ps. 49:23). Hence the Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Cor. 12:31); and likewise: “That you may know the charity of God which surpasses knowledge” (Eph. 3:19). This is the way of which Isaiah says: “Those liberated and redeemed by the Lord shall walk on this way; they shall come to Zion with praise; sorrow and groaning shall flee away. Everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain joy and gladness” (Isa. 51:10–11).

[Col. 0602B] Charity is the radiant commandment of the Lord, enlightening the eyes (Ps. 18:9). It is the light of the heart, clarifying and brightening all the human being’s senses and affections, so that one may learn where the light of the eyes and peace are.

37. Charity is oil that floats above every liquid, that heals and illumines, and that gladdens all harshness by its own sweetness. Anointed with this oil, apostles and martyrs regarded the bitterness of death and the immense cruelty of torments as most sweet. For Christ was anointed by God with this oil above his companions (Ps. 44:8), and with it he anointed his own, causing the yoke of the oppressor to rot away because of the oil (Isa. 10:27). “The Spirit of the Lord,” he says, “is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. 61:1).

Charity not only sweetens the bitterness of death and punishments; it also, most powerfully, puts death itself to death by death. Was not Christ’s charity the destroyer of death, when he himself, the leader of life and destroyer of death, threatened and said: “I will be your death, O death” (Hos. 13:14)? Indeed, it is stronger. For death takes away temporal life, but charity brings us into eternal life. Death casts us down from transient life; charity restores us to life and glory without end.

Charity is the Beautiful Gate which, when Jerusalem was overthrown and all the other gates utterly destroyed, remained whole and untouched. “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8). It is the beautiful Shunammite woman who warmed David in his virginity because he could not be warmed by the skins of dead animals (3 Kings 1:1–4). Those who occupy themselves with dead works, after charity has grown cold, are warmed anew by meditating on Christ’s sufferings.

This is the little cloud that, at Elijah’s prayers, grew into a great rain. For when someone begins to love God with the whole heart, that person immediately pours out not only droplets of goodwill but streams of grace upon neighbors and even enemies. Nor is this surprising. Charity is the widow’s oil, which received continual increase through distribution. For the woman among the wives of the prophets, Obadiah’s wife, cried to Elisha: “My husband is dead, and behold, the creditors are taking my two sons to serve them” (4 Kings 4:1–7). At the prophet’s command, she filled vessels with the oil by which she was to be anointed.

The sons are fear and love, which offer no small vessels, into which the mother of grace pours the oil of goodwill [Col. 0603A] and devotion. Yet she shut the door of conscience against the favor of human praise, lest she be reckoned among the foolish virgins without oil. The creditors are importunate exactors, malicious spirits, who demand eternal torments in return for transient pleasure. The neighbors from whom vessels are borrowed are angelic powers and the souls of saints, who teach us by counsel and example to pour the oil of mercy upon our neighbors, knowing that the oil will not cease while such vessels remain, and that charity bestowed upon more persons will receive a more abundant increase.

38. The tongues of angels and human beings, support for the poor and martyrs, are nothing without charity. Prophecy foretells, knowledge comprehends, faith believes; but neither prophecy nor knowledge nor faith, even if it removes mountains, can avail anything without charity (1 Cor. 13:2). Without charity nothing can profit; with charity nothing can harm. When charity’s benefit intervenes, sins do no harm, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

Charity is the law of life, discipline of morals, peace among those living together, glory of those in concord, abolition of crimes, fulfillment of the law, compendium of sacred Scripture, completion of God’s commandments, virtue of virtues, and fulfillment of good merits. All commands of life and all works of righteousness are directed to it. From it the commendation of works and devoted prayers receive their effect; and from it, like fruit from a tree or a branch from a vine, hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:40). Just as fruit receives nourishment from the branch until it reaches maturity, so the fruit of good work, holy devotion, and everything done piously receive their beginning and progress from charity.

## Chapter X. On God and his attributes

39. It must be understood that, by as much as the earth is lower than the height of heaven, so much more excellent, exalted, and incomparably sweeter than love of neighbor is love of God. And so that, when speaking of the love of God, the field of our undertaken subject may open itself more desirably and freely to understanding, let us briefly touch upon a few matters concerning him, as though tasting them, so that it may appear with what ineffable grace and incomparable condescension the God of glory, through the benefit of charity [Col. 0603D], descends to humankind.

God, therefore, is to be believed and conceived as a kind of everlasting life, living in himself and giving life to all things; understanding all things and creating every intelligence; wise and wisdom itself; fixed truth, unwavering justice, highest power, perfect goodness, divinity, eternity, greatness, immensity, highest essence—from which all being comes—supreme and eternal substance, not subject to the categories of words or of things conceivable, but the causal, efficient, and superessential principle of all things.

God is to be conceived as simple, pure, whole, and perfect, having nothing that passes into number and drawing nothing from time or place. He is in every place in such a way that he is neither enclosed nor excluded by place. God is to be conceived as without visible form, bodily appearance [Col. 0604A], composition of parts, or distinction of limbs; from whom all things are causally, not materially; in whom all things are, not spatially but by power. He is good without quality, great without quantity, presiding without position, containing without possession, and ordering all things. For he orders as wisdom, works as power, loves as charity, reveals as light, has mercy as loving-kindness, knows as truth, judges as equity, and rules as majesty.

40. You do not comprehend his height unless you become lowly in your own eyes through contemplating him. Nor do you comprehend his greatness unless you become small in your own eyes, subjecting yourself to every creature for his sake. “God is charity” (John 4:16). The Holy Spirit is designated in a special manner by the name of charity. He is the love of the Father and the Son, their sweetness and unity, their kiss and embrace, and whatever can be common to them both.

Since through the grace of the Holy Spirit the human soul is wonderfully united with God, it must be understood that in that union the same Spirit is both giver and gift. For the Spirit gives life to the human spirit and instructs and forms it to love God, seek him and find him, hold him and enjoy him. He is the earnest concern of those who seek the Lord in humility; the piety that exhorts in spirit and truth. He is the wisdom of one who finds, the love of one who possesses, and the joy of one who fully enjoys.

## Chapter XI. That stable happiness is not found in created things

41. Some choose for their own enjoyment things destructive of salvation. Infected by the poison of desire, they set the goal of their intention in this world’s wickedness, deceptive riches, transitory honors, fleshly pleasures, and worldly favor; and in things that are occasions of eternal damnation they portray their happiness by a false opinion, as though dreaming.

But where greater abundance of riches overflows, there the heavier trouble of anxieties, disturbing all repose, grows hot. Thus, although the rational soul longs for supreme blessedness, it is drawn away by other things, and some false image of happiness deceives it, or the semblance of true misery frightens it. Who, indeed, would not regard poverty, persecution, sickness, grief, and hunger as a great share of misery? Yet by these both true misery is avoided [Col. 0604D] and true blessedness acquired. Nor is this surprising. Poverty obtains the kingdom of heaven. “Blessed are the poor, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are those who mourn, who hunger, and who suffer persecution, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:3, 5, 6): the former shall receive consolation, and the latter have already obtained the heavenly kingdom, not merely to possess it but to confer it upon others.

How deceptive and delusive is that destructive happiness which many place in fleshly pleasure is continually read in the book of experience: in the act of impurity, what delights soon passes away, while what torments remains without end. I judge that such persons are more to be lamented than discussed. What, then, is more unworthy of a human being than to subordinate one’s soul, for which Christ died, to the baser part of one’s body and to make oneself like brute and irrational creatures? It is utterly clear how destructive are love of the flesh and the practice of lust, for the detestation of which God says to the avenging angels concerning the harlot clothed in purple: “As much as she exalted herself in delights, so much give her torment and mourning” (Rev. 18:7).

42. It remains to pursue the point that blessedness or repose is not found in the pleasure of eyes, ears, and the other senses, nor in things pertaining to the delights of this life, ambitious honor, or the rule of power. Let, then, the richest, most powerful, wisest, and most pleasure-loving king—Solomon, that is—come forward, and let us hear his judgment concerning the end of such things.

“I said in my heart,” he says, “I will go and abound in delights and enjoy good things.” And below: “I built houses, planted vineyards, made gardens and orchards, and planted them with every kind of tree.” Continuing, he adds many similar things: “I possessed male and female servants and a very great household; I heaped up for myself gold and silver, the wealth of kings and provinces.” And adding concerning the pleasure of hearing: “I made for myself singers, male and female.” Then he adds: “Whatever my eyes desired I did not deny them, nor did I restrain my heart from enjoying every pleasure and delighting in the things I had prepared.” What, I ask, could be more luxurious or more delightful?

Solomon continues and adds: “When I turned myself to all the works which I had wrought with labor, I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing endures under the sun” (Eccl. 2:1–11) [Col. 0605C]. He had already given the general judgment, saying: “I saw all things done under the sun; and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (Eccl. 1:14).

## Chapter XII. That true repose lies beneath Christ’s yoke

43. You have, as noted above, vanity and affliction of spirit from the words of the Wise Man. Truth adds a third: slavery. “Everyone who commits sin,” he says, “is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). Let these three, then, be joined together: vanity, slavery, and affliction of spirit. Where, then, is repose? Where is the sabbath? Is not this the word of the law: “You shall do no sinful work on it”? Who is there who has not sinned? King David said: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50:7).

Who, then, will free us from the old yoke and the slavery of sin? He of whom Truth says in the Gospel: “If the Son sets you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8:36). He invites us to the sabbath: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.” Behold refreshment, as though the preparation of the sabbath. Let us hear the sabbath also: “Take my yoke upon yourselves and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls.” Behold the sabbath; behold peaceful tranquility. “For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (Matt. 11:28–30).

This yoke does not press down but raises up; it has wings by which one may fly, not wings by which it weighs anyone down. That yoke is love of God and love of neighbor; here one rests [Col. 0606A], here one keeps sabbath, here one is free from every servile work. Certainly charity “does not act improperly” and “does not think evil” (1 Cor. 13:4–5), and love of neighbor “does no evil” (Rom. 13:10). Do you see, O Jew, where the sabbath is? Hence, even if some intrusion of sin occurs through some weakness, the sabbath observance is not lost, because “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8).

44. We see some who, although they ought to breathe sweetly beneath so sweet and light a yoke and burden, labor and complain beneath both. Their boiling with anxieties, burning with hatreds, and torture by envy certainly belong to the yoke of the world. This is the yoke of covetousness and the heavy burden of the age. But the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light.

What is sweeter or more delightful for a human being than to despise the world, consider oneself above the age, stand on the summit of a good conscience, have the world beneath one’s feet, see nothing in it to desire, no one to envy or fear, and no evil that anyone can inflict? What is sweeter or more delightful than, by fixing one’s eyes upon the inheritance “incorruptible, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven” (1 Pet. 1:4), to trample deceptive riches, ruinous honors, and condemnable pleasures?

What, I ask, is more desirable or more tranquil than so to establish one’s soul that it is stirred by no movements of fleshly desire, but compels the flesh, growing lukewarm under the dew of chastity, to serve as a handmaid, so as to have it a most ready helper in the exercise of spiritual warfare? [Col. 0606C] What, further, bears so much the image of divine tranquility as the soul that so strengthens itself for bearing every injury that insults do not move it, and no engines of threats or wrongs cast its mind down from its state? To look with the same eye upon friend and enemy—is this not like him “who makes his sun rise upon the just and unjust, and rains upon the good and evil” (Matt. 5:45)? And when all things around such a person change, there is no change in that person’s heart.

## Chapter XIII. That charity brings one to true repose and the festival of the spiritual sabbath

45. It is truly true that the sabbath is in charity. For while the other virtues serve as a vehicle or provision for attaining repose, all rest in charity. This is worthy of wonder: without charity no virtue is anything, while charity itself enables each virtue to be a virtue.

Faith, which now works these things unto life, will no longer be faith in the vision of God, but truth. There faith will be absorbed when that which is loved above all things is seen. There will be no need to believe what we shall be permitted to apprehend in full knowledge. Nor thereafter will there be a place for hope: enjoying God, we shall have nothing left to hope for. Here temperance fights against lusts, prudence against errors, fortitude against adversities, and justice against injustices. But in charity chastity is perfect; therefore there is no lust for temperance to oppose. In charity [Col. 0607A] knowledge is perfect; therefore there is no error there for prudence to eliminate. In charity is true blessedness; therefore there is no adversity for fortitude to overcome. In charity all things are tranquil and equal; therefore there is no inequality there requiring rectification.

Finally, faith is not a virtue [Note: “[Col. 0607] That is, it is not a formed virtue conducive to eternal blessedness.”] without love; nor is hope a virtue unless that which is hoped for is loved. What is temperance but love which no pleasure entices? What are the other virtues but love distributing to each what is its own?

46. Just as charity is truly the repose of the human mind and its perfect sabbath, so also the six virtues mentioned above—faith, hope, temperance, prudence, fortitude, and justice—are, as it were, days of labour; while charity is a luminous, most luminous day [Col. 0607B] of rest, tranquillity, and peace. “And now what is my expectation, but thee, O Lord?” If perhaps your ear may hear the desire of the poor, so that for a little while I may rest with kings and consuls, 407 “who build solitudes for themselves and fill their houses with silver” (Job 3:13–15). Yet scarcely for a moment is repose permitted me from Pharaoh’s taskmasters, so that I am not allowed to keep sabbath even for half an hour. Would that I might be granted leisure, and see that Jesus is himself God. He is the sabbath of the soul that seeks him, preparing for those who love him a tranquil and unchangeable sabbath-rest. O how blessed are those who enter “the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God,” and [Col. 0607C] dance and exult with the voice of rejoicing and confession, mindful of your breasts, sweet Jesus, singing with the prophet Habakkuk: “But I will rejoice in the Lord, and exult in God Jesus my God” (Hab. 3:18).

47. The Jew keeps sabbath because he reads that God worked for six days and, as though wearied by the labour of his work, rested on the seventh day (Gen. 1; 2:3). This is not to think of God, but to fashion an idol in insult to God. Certainly the Creator did not labour in working: “He spoke, and all things were made according to his good pleasure” (Ps. 148:5). God, the supreme and eternal essence, needing no one, fully sufficient to himself, remaining unchangeably and immovably in his supremely tranquil charity and working wonders, rests [Col. 0607D] in himself: life living in itself, the peace and unfailing repose of good things. Therefore, just as the mutability of the creature is signified by the succession of days, alternately varying through morning and evening, so in God—to whom nothing comes, passes away, or succeeds—is indicated his eternal tranquillity and peaceful eternity.

48. It should be noted, moreover, that the number six is assigned to the works of God, while the number seven is ascribed to the divine rest. For six is a perfect number, consisting of its own parts. If you add together one, two, and three, you have the perfect number six, which is especially assigned to God’s works, so that in the whole universe you find nothing superfluous and nothing imperfect. Great indeed [Col. 0608A] is the excellence of the day on which God divided the upper waters from the lower by means of the firmament. Nor do I think less dignity belongs to the day on which, after the waters had been gathered together into one, the dry land was clothed by God with herbs, adorned with trees, made lovely with flowers, and made fruitful with fruits. Nor is the day to be reckoned inferior on which God adorned heaven with its luminaries. Nor is that day without praise on which God placed one part of living creatures in the waters and another in the air. The sixth day does not fall short of their eminence and privilege, on which God created man in his own image and, breathing life into him, set him over the whole multitude of living creatures. But the pre-eminence of the seventh day surpasses them all: on it no thing was created, but the perfection of all creatures [Col. 0608B] and God’s rest are commended. Of each individual day it is written: “Evening came and morning came, one day,” or “a second day,” and so on (Gen. 1). But for the seventh day neither morning nor evening, neither beginning nor end, is described. For the day of Christ’s rest is unchangeable and eternal. The mutual love of Father and Son, the most delightful embrace of both—that is, the charity by which the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father (John 10:38)—is itself the most joyful repose, indivisible unity, undisturbed peace, eternal tranquillity: the Holy Spirit, who proceeds from both. Indicating this, the Son of God says: “I have kept my Father’s commandments, and abide in his love” (John 15:10); and again: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). And the Father says likewise concerning the Son: “This is my beloved Son, [Col. 0608C] in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17), etc.

## Chapter XIV. The spiritual Hexaemeron, or work of the six days, is expounded.

49. Thus, having set forth an apt comparison, we are exercised, as by six days, so by six virtues, in order that after the successive changes of sacred actions we may breathe freely in the tranquillity of charity, as in the true sabbath of the mind. Accordingly, we make faith the first day, on which the faithful are separated from unbelievers as light from darkness. Let hope likewise hold the place of the second day, through which those whose citizenship is in heaven are distinguished from others who set their minds on earthly things. Let temperance [Col. 0608D] shine forth as the third day, on which, mortifying our members upon the earth, we restrain the flow of fleshly desire, as though it were most bitter water, within the fixed boundaries of continence, 408 so that dry land may appear in the soil of our heart and, thirsting for the fountain of life, may produce the flowers and fruits of virtues. Let prudence act as the fourth day, and let the light of knowledge break forth; distinguishing between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, let it divide day from night, so that the light of wisdom may shine like the radiance of the sun, while the light of spiritual knowledge—which fails in some—may appear as the lesser light of the moon. Fortitude is the fifth day, by which, in this great and wide sea, we endure the stormy masses of waves like [Col. 0609A] spiritual fishes; we restrain the slipperiness of the tongue under the discipline of silence; and, like winged birds, we are now raised to heavenly things, while now, descending to works of mercy, we render the fruits of good works under God’s blessing. Finally, let justice be established as the sixth day, by which, remade in the divine image and ruling over bestial desires and creeping vices, we subject body to spirit and spirit to God, and thus give to each what is its own.

50. And it should be observed that the Lord blesses all creatures, but all things are subjected to man. But to those who bear God’s image within themselves are subjected beasts of burden—that is, bodies—and beasts—that is, spiritual wickednesses, concerning which the prophet prays: “Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you” (Ps. 73:19). And the Lord says through another prophet: “I will remove evil beasts from your land, and will make you sleep securely” (Lev. 26:6; Hos. 2:18). This is sleep and the most tranquil rest of the seventh day. The seventh day is charity: the sabbath day, the day of rest, joy, and peace, through which a person securely—indeed, most securely—says: “In peace I will lie down and rest” (Ps. 4:9). It is the consummation of all virtues, the sweet refreshment of holy souls, the mind’s most tranquil holiday. It is the seventh day on which heavenly manna refreshes us. It is the seventh month in which, after the flood of onrushing temptations, the ark of the heart rests most sweetly. It is that sabbath [Col. 0609C] following sabbath, that month following month; and after the seventh year seven times repeated, the year of jubilee begins—the year acceptable to the Lord (Isa. 61:2)—in which each receives back his inheritance, complete joy, the ancient possession, and eternal liberty.

Lord God, how long will the jubilee be deferred? When will your mercy come beforehand, so that my portion may be in the land of the living? (Ps. 141:6). “For you are the portion of my inheritance and of my cup; you are he who will restore my inheritance to me” (Ps. 15:5). The joy by which I shall be satisfied when your glory appears is indeed delayed, but not taken away (Ps. 16:15). Meanwhile I shall eat my bread in the sweat of my face and with tears by measure, until wine is given to mourners and strong drink to those of bitter spirit [Col. 0609D] (Prov. 31:6), and my whole soul is absorbed in those delights whose firstfruits I already taste.

## Chapter XV. On the threefold sabbath, or the threefold love: of oneself, of one’s neighbour, and of God.

51. “There shall be month after month, and sabbath after sabbath,” he says (Isa. 66:23). In the Old Testament a threefold distinction of sabbaths is assigned. The first sabbath is called the seventh day; the second, the seventh year; the third, the year following the seventh year seven times repeated—that is, the fiftieth year. Thus the first is the sabbath of days; the second, of years; the third, the sabbath of sabbaths, so that all is brought to completion in unity. And it should be noted that this threefold sabbath is found in charity, if you will observe carefully. In the Law two commandments of love are expressly given: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your mind and with all your strength; and your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22:37, 39). These two commandments imply two objects to be loved; for no one can love his neighbour as himself unless he loves himself. The first sabbath of man is self-love; the second, love of neighbour; the sabbath of sabbaths, love of God.

## Chapter XVI. On the first sabbath, or self-love.

52. Therefore, when a person loves himself in Christ, love of God begins; when he loves his neighbour, a broader capacity of affection is opened. Yet when that divine fire, warming to the marrow, draws all other loves—as certain sparks of itself—into its own fullness, it absorbs every motion of the soul into desire for that sublime and ineffable good.
