Thus neither a person loves himself nor his neighbour except insofar as the whole affection of the soul, failing away from itself, is transferred into God. For by an ineffable artifice of providence it comes about that, although these three loves are always present, they are not always felt equally. At one time that delightful sweetness of the mind proceeds from the purity of one’s own conscience; at another, it receives the affection of rejoicing from a neighbour’s good; at another, contemplating in longing and exultation, it aspires to him. Just as someone entering various storerooms of spices is delighted now by the fragrance of these kinds, now by those [Col. 0610C], so the soul of one who loves is now suffused with an inestimable sweetness through the contemplation of itself, now of God, or of its neighbour.

53. Therefore, one who formerly recalled his lost days in bitterness of soul, after he has given a bill of divorce to concupiscence and, having obtained the cancellation of his sins, has recognized that he has received himself as a pledge and earnest of heavenly grace—when he reads nothing in the book of his conscience that accuses him or ought to displease God—“the remnants of thoughts shall keep festival for him” (Ps. 75:11). For when, free from outward tumult, he has withdrawn himself into the secret places of contemplation; when he has shut the door of his mind against the crowds of clamorous anxieties; when he has examined inwardly the treasures of conscience and found nothing disordered, unsuitable, or opposed to reason, but sees all things peaceful and delightful, and the multitude of thoughts, words, and deeds obeying him, as a well-disciplined household obeys its master, and all his inward parts rising to him in a certain humility: from all this there bursts forth a wonderful security; from security, wonderful tranquillity; and from this an ineffable jubilation of heart, the more devout in Christ’s praise as he more clearly understands that all this comes from Christ’s grace. This is the festive solemnity of the seventh day, preceded by six days—that is, by six works of mercy. For the righteous person proves this in their exercise; and, breathing freely in the bosom of holy conscience and in the testimony of good works, happily keeps sabbath in the grace given to him by God [Col. 0611A]. This is the final joy of the first sabbath, in which servile works—that is, sins, which make slaves—are forbidden; in which neither the fire of concupiscence is kindled nor burdens—that is, thoughts of ungodliness—are carried without transgressing the law.

## Chapter XVII. On the second sabbath, or love of neighbour.

54. But if, from this purer bridal chamber of the heart, which he dedicated in the first sabbath, he passes into that lodging where he is accustomed to rejoice with those who rejoice, to be weak with the weak, to burn with those who are scandalized, and feels his soul united to his brethren by the indissoluble glue of charity—so that neither malicious suspicion, nor a movement of envy, nor the heat of anger or sorrow can creep in upon any occasion, but, embracing and cherishing them with the arms of most sincere love, he bears his own and others’ concerns upon one and the same shoulder—then, with every clamour of vices silenced, he is dissolved into the delights of such sweetness with inestimable joy, and in the sweetness of love becomes free leisure within, released from all harmful things. For that fraternal charity permits absolutely no vice to remain in the repose of this sabbath is attested by the Apostle, a continual celebrant of this second sabbath, who says: “You shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; and if there be any other commandment, it is fulfilled in this saying: You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Rom. 13:9). David, moved by the sweetness of this delight, bursting into a cry of jubilation from such union of minds, says: [Col. 0611C] “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity” (Ps. 132:1).

55. Observe, moreover, that just as in the first sabbath only one day is dedicated—because it is singular and consists in the tranquillity of one’s own conscience—so here, not without reason, a whole year is consecrated. For as a year is made up of many days, so one heart and one soul are fused from many souls in the fire of charity. The six years preceding this sabbath may be understood as six classes of people, among whose love we linger or toward whom we are exercised by the obligation of the commandment. And just as a year contains many days, so in each class of people many souls are joined to us in unity.

56. First of all, true love should by natural order extend to the members of our own household and blood, whom, as we are necessarily bound to love by nature, it is exceedingly inhuman to drive from the sanctuary of our love. For the Apostle testifies: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has transgressed the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8). Hence this love proceeding from nature holds the first place, by God’s command, among the commandments concerning love of neighbour: “Honour,” he says, “your father and your mother” (Exod. 20:12). From there our love, going forth to those who are especially joined to us by reciprocal friendship or duty, is relaxed into a somewhat wider embrace. Nevertheless, this love does not surpass the righteousness of the Pharisees, to whom it was said: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy.” Indeed, though affection for parents and friends is to be maintained, it gains little reward: natural law leads us to the former, mutual services urge us to the latter. Yet if either is neglected, it brings an accumulation of condemnation. Truth says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the Gentiles do the same?” (Matt. 5:43, 46). Therefore, that our love may extend to a greater breadth, let it embrace also those who serve God alongside us and are duly joined to us, through the profession of the same life, in the bond of peace and the Spirit. God is indeed the effective cause of this love, while spiritual anointing flows from the head down upon Aaron’s beard and even to the hem of his garment [Col. 0612B] (Ps. 132:2), so that those anointed by the Anointed One, called Christians from Christ, may all embrace one another in the fellowship of Jesus’ name through the common bond of charity.

57. Two further classes of people remain. If we gather them into the net of our love, nothing remains except that we enjoy the repose of that true sabbath. For we must grieve over the ignorance of those outside—that is, Gentiles and Jews, schismatics and heretics—have compassion for their weakness, and bewail their hardness with the devout affection of compassion, coming to their aid by the support of prayers, so that they too may run in the fragrance of our ointments in Christ Jesus our Lord.

58. Charity stretches out its tent still further, and so broadens and extends the cloak which, in the time of the old Law, was short, that it suffices to cover two, joining its enemy to its own soul by the new union of the Holy Spirit. By this love a human being is made a son of God; by this the image of divine goodness is most fully restored. “Love your enemies,” says the Lord; “do good to those who hate you; and pray for those who persecute and slander you, that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:44–45). This love, when it looks upon an enemy with a simple eye, can say in complete security: “Forgive us, as we also forgive” (Matt. 6:12). Thus the one who forgives is forgiven; thus he becomes a son of God, and thus an heir of God and co-heir with Christ (Rom. 8:17). Consider, therefore, how secure, how sweet, [Col. 0612D] how delightful it is to have compassion on enemies, not to be moved by injuries, to love for Christ’s sake one by whom I feel myself unloved, and to bear toward that person the affection which a most indulgent father shows toward a dearly beloved son suffering from frenzy: the greater the injuries inflicted by him, the more fervently does the father burn toward him with charity.

## Chapter XVIII. On the joy and solemnity of the third sabbath, or on love of God.

59. The third sabbath has six preparatory days, on which we gather heavenly manna, so that in that splendid solemnity to be celebrated in the love of God we may suck milk from the breasts of his consolation and, between the two portions, between the bridegroom’s breasts, between left hand [Col. 0613A] and right, rest most blessedly through the tender mercies of our God. These six days are Christ’s Conception, Nativity, Preaching, Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension. On these six days the Lord “worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. 73:12); and, resting from every work which he had accomplished and sitting in the glory of God the Father, he mercifully invites us to that sabbath which is most solemnly celebrated in his love.

O good Jesus, O gracious one, O lovable one, O gentle one, O sweet one, O God who is love: what is sweeter, gentler, or more lovable than to have leisure and see how greatly you have loved us? How devoutly and mercifully you deigned, in your conception and birth, to empty yourself even to the weaknesses of infant nature! How graciously and diligently you taught us the way of life by word and example! With what condescension you offered yourself to death for us! How, rising into your glory, you restored human nature; and, ascending into heaven, placed it gloriously upon the throne of your majesty! What is happier, what more delightful, than the sabbath of that soul which, embracing the Lord in contemplation and love and forming within itself certain experiences of divine sweetness, is moved by the inestimable joy of holy fruition, while, estranged from itself, it already dwells in heaven and exults and rejoices in remembrance of the abundance of God’s sweetness? O peaceful repose, O delightful sabbath, O sweetness of charity, which carries the soul that loves God to his loftiest mighty works, and, once carried there, makes it rest amid eternal delights! In the holiday of this sabbath [Col. 0613C] the whole inner person rejoices, understanding is made serene, affections are sweetened, and holy desires are dissolved in God through a certain most blessed fruition. O morning, O day, which is better in the courts of the Lord than thousands! (Ps. 83:11). O splendour of light and ardour of charity, which inflames angels and illuminates the inward parts of the saints! O splendid solemnity and delightful repose, and delightful sabbath! O glorious sabbath!

60. And what glory can be more delightful or desirable than to cling to God from the marrow, to cast upon him all one’s thoughts and affections, and to gather from love of him fruits of such certainty that one need in no way hesitate concerning the salvation of one’s soul, the fellowship of angels, and that unending exultation prepared [Col. 0613D] for those who love God? Therefore the Apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council (Acts 5:41); Andrew ran to the cross glorying and exulting; Paul, suffused with the sweetness of such great joy, said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). Secure, he says: “I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that neither death, nor sword, nor angel, nor powers, nor any other creature will be able to separate me from the charity of God which is in Christ Jesus” (2 Tim. 1:12; Rom. 8:38–39). Moses, relying upon such firm charity, chose rather to be blotted out of the book which the Lord had written than to endure the destruction, by divine indignation, of the people entrusted to him (Exod. 32:32). Fortified by this impregnable citadel, Ezekiel went down into Chaldea; Jeremiah into Egypt, trusting in its protection. Through it Job was made a brother of dragons without fear of danger (Job 30:29). Under its shadow David does not fear to walk through the shadow of death. For since “God is charity” (1 John 4:16), he knows that where charity is, there God is. “Though I walk,” he says, “in the midst of the shadow of death, I will fear no evils, for you are with me” (Ps. 22:4).

61. Unhappy that I am, I have hitherto loved the world; I have set aside your love, O God, in favour of worldly love. Now, on the contrary, according to the riches of your mercy, you bring it about that I love you and despise the world and all that is in it in comparison with your love; that in longing for you, O God, my soul may disdain heaven and earth [Col. 0614B] and all that is in them. “For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired upon earth apart from you? God of my heart, and God my portion for ever” (Ps. 72:25–26). Let my soul fail and melt away in your love, so that, as my spirit fails from myself (Ps. 141:4), I may sing and chant to you the delights of love and the riches of charity itself, by which those are made drunk from the torrent of eternal pleasure (Ps. 35:9) whose affection has been utterly absorbed by your love. For just as heated iron passes into a kind of substance of fire; just as a drop of water poured into a cask of wine, laying aside its own tastelessness, takes on the substance of the better liquid; and just as air suffused with solar radiance becomes entirely brightness: so the human spirit moved by divine love becomes entirely love. Therefore, whoever loves God [Col. 0614C] is dead to himself and lives for God alone, and in some manner—so to speak—becomes consubstantial with the beloved. For if David’s soul was joined to Jonathan’s soul (1 Sam. 18:1), or if the one who clings to God becomes one spirit with him (1 Cor. 6:17), then by a similar principle of union the whole affection passes into God through a kind of co-essencing, being wholly gathered into itself and transferred to God, who is the fullness of all desirable things, without any exception of another desire. Yet the soul will love more perfectly when it is brought into the joy of its Lord (Matt. 25:21–23), into the bridegroom’s embrace; and through the fellowship of charity it will make the blessedness of all the righteous its own, by whose benefit God will be all things in us.

## Chapter XIX. Christ’s passion and death ought to be meditated upon continually.

62. “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth” (Isa. 1:2), how greatly God has magnified his mercy toward us. And who has considered the abyss of such ineffable grace, who has tasted from the fountain of such sweetness, and not loved? “Will you not be subject to God, my soul?” (Ps. 61:2). Why do you not pour out upon God the affections that you direct toward vanities and false madnesses? (Ps. 39:5). “Why are you sad, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. 41:6). Have you no counsellor or saviour? “Is there no balm in Gilead, or is there no physician there?” (Jer. 8:22). “Return, return, O Shulammite, return” [Col. 0615A] (Song 6:12) to the Lord your God—you who are torn apart, my mangled one, my lost one, yet at last raised again by Christ’s death and redeemed by Christ’s passion. Why, I ask, do you love anything besides him who so graciously, so mercifully redeemed you from so many miseries? With unceasing inquiry and continual meditation turn over again how the Only-Begotten of God the Father, though he was the splendour and image of his substance (Heb. 1:3), after emptying himself even to the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), after hunger, thirst, weariness, tears, bonds, scourges, gall, vinegar, a crown of thorns, nails, and a lance, once hung upon the cross between two thieves for your salvation. Truly, “horns were in his hands” upon the cross (Hab. 3:4), and from them that merciful Samaritan poured oil and wine into [Col. 0615B] your wounds (Luke 10:34). Yet there his strength was hidden (Hab. 3:4), and in the bitterness of death was his sweetness. “O how great is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Ps. 30:20). In Isaiah’s testimony: “Truly you are a hidden God, the God of Israel, the Saviour” (Isa. 45:15).

63. Your Saviour was dying, my soul, that he might give you life; he was fastened to the cross so that he might fasten your iniquities to the cross with his own hands. He raised his hands to the Father in the evening sacrifice, that he might invite you to the embraces of friendship; and he offered his life, which was liable to death for no one, to death for you, so that when the righteous one was unjustly killed by the prince of darkness, the latter—having been convicted of usurping what was not his—might be deprived of the power he had over you. In so overflowing a benefit, in so great a accumulation of graces, by which divine generosity has, as it were, overwhelmed and confounded you, take care that you are not ungrateful. For ingratitude is destructive of salvation: it is the breath of an asp, the poison of the soul, the scorching of virtues, a pestilential wind and corrupting breeze, drying up the drops of piety, the dew of grace, and the streams of mercy [Col. 0615C].

## Chapter XX. On the benefit of redemption, and others.

64. I say still more: for nothing has been said enough which must always be spoken and repeated in continual remembrance. You were bound to that most grievous creditor—I mean the angel of Satan, that most savage taskmaster—by the bond of a written obligation, with as many debts as sins, and you were unable to pay. But the Son of God paid for you not what he had taken, but what you had taken; and, what was a more generous condescension and richer grace, he did not appoint another debtor, but gave his own life for the cause of your salvation. When that renegade and deserter angel sought to reduce you to detestable slavery, Christ made his own the suit brought against you. After he had produced various witnesses—laws, oracles, prophets, signs—and finally alleged his own blood, that plea obtained for you the verdict of liberty. Upon the judicial decree were written the letters on the scroll above the crucified head; and they were confirmed by mercy and truth, peace and justice, which have met together from everlasting. Finally [Col. 0616A] the seal was impressed: namely, the wound in his side, which he continually presents before the Father’s eyes as the price of our redemption and perpetual propitiation.

65. The title of the document, inscribed in memory of such great charity, still remains; and know that if he finds you ungrateful and unwilling to make use of so great a benefit, he will most strictly demand his death from you. I fear that at some time he may say to you in deepest indignation: “Put forth your hand and put it into my right side; put your fingers into the nail-marks” (John 20:27), and see how much I have suffered for you. O ungrateful and cruel impiety! Do you not think that God repents of the benefits conferred on you if he sees them lost through ingratitude? For this reason our prayer is often rejected. And I judge that this happens by a merciful dispensation, lest we who have been ungrateful for benefits already received should be burdened with the graver guilt of ingratitude through a new bestowal of heavenly gifts. Since God counts a benefit lost when thanksgiving does not follow it, it is better for us not to be heard than, to the increase of our condemnation, to obtain what we ask as material for ingratitude. With what presumption, then, will you fail to love him who loved you when you did not love him, who did not despise you when you were a sinner? Consider, I ask, with what recompense, with what merit, you can answer the supreme and eternal Trinity [Col. 0616B].

66. For you the Father delivered his Only-Begotten to death. The Son likewise delivered himself to death for your salvation. Finally, the Holy Spirit was given, as the Apostle testifies: “Because the charity of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” [Col. 0616C] (Rom. 5:5). Thus the Father loves us, the Son loves us, the Holy Spirit loves us; the whole holy Trinity loves us: the eternal, almighty, immeasurable God, “of whose greatness there is no end” (Ps. 144:3), “whose wisdom has no number” (Ps. 146:5), whose peace surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4:7), from whom and in whom are all things, visible and invisible, heavenly and earthly. If you love him, you do this from obligation; if he loves you, he does it freely. Consider the height of heaven, the vastness of the firmament, and a little mud in marshy places. Yet the disproportion between you and God is still immeasurably greater than that between mud and heaven. And what comparison is there between you and the ineffable, incomparable, incomprehensible One? You could render him nothing commensurate with his due, even if, in recompense for what he suffered for you, you were tormented a thousand thousand years even in the fire of Gehenna [Col. 0616D].

## Chapter XXI. On the benefit of creation.

67. All things that are in God are immeasurably more excellent than those that are ours. For he loves as charity; judges as equity; orders as wisdom; reveals as light; has mercy as piety; knows as truth; works as power; presides as majesty. But setting aside all that pertains to the dispensation of his incarnation, attend carefully to the fact that the whole universe obeys you by command, and all nature serves your needs; heaven, air, earth, sea, and all that is in them alike minister to your necessities and delights [Col. 0617A]. The annual cycle restores the flowers and fruits of trees and herbs through a renewed rebirth; and the cycles of time continually provide you with God’s gifts as the natures of plants put forth shoots and bloom again with the renewal of their former growth.

Recognize, soul, that once you did not exist, and that you were made by him. You gave him nothing in order that he might make you, for you could give nothing when you did not exist. But since it was better to exist than not to exist, he freely granted you existence, preferring you to all those things which he could have brought from non-being into being but did not bring forth. He added beauty to you; and although your essence came forth from nothing by the Creator’s grace, he marked you with his own image and likeness, and joined life to beauty. Whence came such great, gratuitous, and unheard-of condescension—that you should be made in his image and likeness [Col. 0617B] (Gen. 1:27)—unless it was that you might love your likeness and, through reciprocal love, be conformed to him who first loved you freely?

68. Therefore offer the heart and the innermost parts of your being to love him who deigned to love you, though he found nothing in you worthy of love. Love your seal and your image; and, that the form of your Creator may appear more distinctly in you, conform yourself by faith and charity to him who is charity, and by continual meditation make his benefits material for thanksgiving. Your lover invited you to this by prophetic exhortation: “Set me,” he says, “as a seal upon your heart and upon your right arm” (Song 8:6). It is as though he said: Set me as your memorial [Col. 0617C] in heart and arm—that is, in thought and deed—so that, having laid aside the image of the earthly man, you may bear the image of the heavenly man (1 Cor. 15:49), considering the proofs of divine love which cannot be refuted. Set me upon your heart as the seal of faith and the example of love.

Before his transgression, the apostate angel bore such a seal within himself, as Ezekiel testifies when he says: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty” (Ezek. 28:12). In his creation the angel was joined to God in such conformity that he was rather a seal of likeness than something similar or sealed. For from a seal such likeness is expressed representationally as the seal itself possesses essentially; and this belongs to humankind. But by reason of his subtle nature the angel adhered to God in a more exact likeness, because he was wholly and only spirit. We, however, enclosed in a prison of clay and weighed down by earthly habitation, are restored by charity to the rank of angelic dignity. And although “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15), nevertheless the new commandment of loving God remakes us, deformed by sin, in the likeness of God [Col. 0617D].

69. God has multiplied his gifts in you. To your beauty he added life, sensation, and discernment; and in all that his generosity bestowed upon you, your need received his grace—it was not preceded by any claim of your merit. He betrothed you by faith; outwardly he adorned you [Col. 0618A] with the senses, as with certain gleaming jewels; inwardly he distinguished you with wisdom, as with a natural beauty. He knew what adornment was more fitting for you; and therefore he gave what became you—and so greatly that, for this very reason, he who gave it might himself love you.

You are indeed mad if you love only moderately him who anticipated you with so great a love, who, having bestowed gifts so numerous and so precious, promises still greater things to one who loves him—things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, and whose valuation has not entered into the human heart (I Cor. II, 9). From his gift you are bound to reckon how greatly he must be loved who loves so greatly, so that you should judge it not merely rash but even wicked not only not to love one who loves you, but not to embrace with all your inmost being and every inward affection [Col. 0618B] the love of one so great, so powerful, so surpassing.

The Bridegroom is the fairest of all, made beautiful above the sons of men. Love the Bridegroom; love the King in his beauty, the King of powers, full of grace and truth, crowned with glory and honor, the Lord of majesty.

70. The King has desired your beauty, and the gifts with which he has deigned to adorn you have inclined his affection toward love of you. He loves you in his gifts. For if you possess any good, you ought to understand that it is his gift [variant: “you ought”]. The Apostle’s word is: “What have you that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7). If you boast of something as though you had received it from yourself rather than from God, you steal from God what is his; you seize another’s honor for yourself; and, presumptuously intruding [Col. 0618C] into another’s glory, you indeed have glory, but not before God (Rom. IV, 2), because you wickedly usurp another’s glory against God.

Take care lest the mark of ingratitude ever steal upon you. Recollect unceasingly that you were ruined by your own iniquity, and restored by his mercy.

## Chapter XXII. The soul, more worthy than other created things, ought not to love anything above God

71. Endeavor to please him in every way you can, who deigned to make you such that you might please him, might know yourself, and might recognize the grace of your Creator in contemplating your own beauty. The eye, moreover, which sees all things does not see itself. Therefore sometimes contemplate the face [Col. 0618D] of your heart in the mirror of your own reason, lest you do injury to your dignity. You surely do this if you wish to prefer things more abject than yourself to yourself, and to make equal with yourself—who are most beautiful in truth—those things whose beauty is imaginary and shadowy.

You cast yourself down from your dignity most monstrously and shamefully if you seek and admire transitory and empty beauties. The world, certainly, was made for your sake; therefore do not love the world, because the world is not worthy of you, since you are far worthier than it, than the sun and moon, and than all creatures. For all temporal things acknowledge the failing of their beauty; but you, in the future, do not fail through toil, nor grow pale through sickness, nor wither through old age, nor waste away through death.

Accordingly, if you love anything in this world, which is wholly [Col. 0619A] subject to you, it is the height of rashness—unless you wish to love such things as serving you, as the Bridegroom’s gifts, as a friend’s presents, as the Lord’s benefits. Do not love these things alongside him; rather, love them for his sake, and love him above them. You will indeed descend into the love of harlots if you love the giver’s gifts more than the affection of the lover. You do injury to the giver; indeed, you dishonor yourself with harlot-like shame if you receive gifts and do not return love in exchange.

Therefore love him for his own sake, and his gifts for his sake. Love yourself for him, and him for yourself. Love him so that you may enjoy him, place your affections in him, and, when you have loved more fervently, may be loved more affectionately. This love is holy, containing nothing foul or impure; sweetest in the remembrance of God, surpassing all the world’s delights [Col. 0619B] and, in a sense, eternal by the very nature of its stability.

72. Keep this also in continual remembrance: inasmuch as his pre-eminent essence differs from human frailty, so much more sweetly, incomparably more sweetly and delightfully, does he love and is loved than angel, human being, gold, silver, precious stone, charity, freedom, or anything else by which human hearts are drawn apart.

Nor should you suppose that you are loved less by him because he shares with certain earthly living creatures, together with you, the benefit of the sun and moon and the other gifts of his grace. Do not doubt that whatever has been bestowed on them has been bestowed for your sake. For in order that all things may serve you, they receive from divine goodness the goods necessary to them, without which they cannot exist or serve.

Would his love for you seem more intense if he had bestowed everything upon you alone? Would you be happier if you lived alone in the world and possessed all that is in it, without any consolation of shared life? Even if you complain of association with evil people, know beyond doubt that, just as other things serve both you and evil people, so divine providence makes the life of evil people serve your progress in the struggle. For by association with the wicked, those who are good are exercised toward better things: they are taught both to seek virtues and to seek the other gifts of God which the wicked lack and which are far better than all things possessed together with unjust people.

73. Finally, when they see the wicked rushing into destruction, [Col. 0619D] their expectation of salvation increases their love for God; and from divine gifts, in which there is no fellowship with the ungodly, follows a more devout offering of thanksgiving. Therefore, since all things cooperate for your good, so that the wicked become an exercise for you and the good a consolation, do not suppose that you are loved less because he does not love you exclusively—he who nevertheless loves you with a certain singularity of love, inasmuch as he turns both good and evil persons toward the use of your benefit.

And since, by the very right and obligation of charity, you desire all others with you to share in eternal blessedness, your good will makes another’s good your own; and through the communion of the Holy Spirit, the blessedness of each individual grows through the blessedness of all. Thus love becomes singular through this very communion [Col. 0620A]: nothing is diminished through the participation of many, and, though poured out upon all, it is found whole in each. He therefore loves you singularly who, loving nothing apart from you, loves other things for your sake. For although love is distributed among many, it is whole in each, so that he who loves all uniquely is uniquely loved by all.

For this reason this love is unique, not private; solitary, not lonely; common, not divided; neither failing through use nor diminishing through time or participation. Therefore lay up in the treasury of memory, and continually recollect, the things God has bestowed on you, so that neither may you presume upon what you have received nor ever grow sluggish in thanksgiving for his received benefits.

## Chapter XXIII. God’s wondrous love toward us in turn demands from us the most ardent love

4. As divinity surpasses humanity, so the love which the Lord and Savior has for us is sweeter, firmer, deeper, more compelling, more penetrating, more compassionate, more fervent, and gentler than that love which we have for him or for our neighbor. The love he has for us surpasses with inestimable charity every maternal affection and every harmony of brothers and spouses.

He himself, expressing in himself the grace of fatherly gentleness, addresses the faithful soul, saying: “Henceforth call me: You are my Father; you are the guide of my virginity”; and again: “You will call me Father, and you will not cease to follow after me” (Jer. III, 4, 19). He himself, anticipating us with maternal kindness, says: “As a mother comforts her children, so I will comfort you” (Isa. LXVI, 13); and again: “Can a mother forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? And even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you” (ibid., XLIX, 15).

He takes upon himself the manner of brotherly love and so speaks to the faithful soul: “A garden enclosed,” he says, “my sister, my bride” (Cant. IV, 12). He is a friend when he says to the faithful soul, “You are beautiful, my friend” (ibid., I, 14); and she herself says of him, “Such is my beloved, and he is my friend” (ibid., V, 16). He is a bridegroom when it is said of him: “The bridegroom will rejoice over the bride, and your God will rejoice over you” (Isa. LXII, 5).

Let us therefore have in ourselves what is in Christ Jesus (Phil. II, 5), who, stretching out his hands [Col. 0620D] toward his disciples, calls them brothers; and, what is more, calls father, mother, and sister everyone who holily and humbly, chastely and sociably, does his or his neighbor’s will (Matt. XII, 49–50).

75. If you carefully recount the abundant and unwearied magnificence and generosity of God’s grace toward you, although he is the universal dispenser of all things, you will nevertheless see him as if wholly and singularly occupied with your welfare. Wherever you turn, a concerned and loving provider attends you: in intentions, meditations, words, counsels, works, adversities, prosperity, outwardly and inwardly, his grace follows and precedes you. In every tribulation he provides you a remedy. He heals the weak soul, brings back the wandering one, [Col. 0621A] corrects the delinquent, consoles the afflicted, raises the fallen, gladdens the sad, and does not permit one who is failing to waver for long.

My soul, I offer you this counsel as to my own soul [perhaps: “my friend”], just as I recall having advised myself elsewhere: attend to the first fruits of your creation; turn over in continual examination and careful meditation the fact that he made you beautiful, that he added the endowments of manifold grace, and that, when afterward you had through your own doing become foul and fetid, he who is compassionate and merciful, pitying your turning away by his free kindness, loved you when you did not exist in order to create you, and likewise restored you by his grace when created but lost.

76. The Lord, the fountain of mercy, speaks in Jeremiah, saying: “It is commonly said: If a woman has slept with an adulterous man, will she return to her former husband? But you have prostituted yourself with many lovers; nevertheless, return to me and I will receive you, says the Lord” (Jer. III, 1).

He who had created you undefiled and whole had bestowed upon you the bridal gifts of manifold grace. But you, clinging to alien lovers, gave your Bridegroom a bill of divorce; you exposed your integrity to corrupters; and, desiring illicit embraces, spread your legs to unclean spirits. At last you became more vile than all harlots: you refused to be ashamed, but with an unbridled spirit rushing into forbidden acts, you cast yourself down into the abyss of eternal condemnation.

Yet he—so exalted, so wondrous, so powerful, so eminent—after a fall so condemnable, looked upon you with the eye of mercy. In order to raise you from the mire of foulness, he descended from the majesty [Col. 0621C] of his glory; in order to abolish the shame of your corruption, he endured harsh and shameful things for you; and, to compress much into few words, in order to free you from death, he offered himself to a most condemned death. He could not have shown more expressly, faithfully, sweetly, or kindly how great was the affection of charity with which he loved you.

77. Even now, forgetting your transgression, he pours back upon you the grace you had lost; he renews the love you had corrupted; and he reproaches you neither with his benefits nor with your offenses. Indeed, if you deign humbly and faithfully to cleave to him, he will heap grace upon grace, so that you may become more beautiful and purer than ever; and you may know how great his love toward you is from the restoration after your fall. You will know how fruitful it is to love him who is so ineffably good and incomparably gentle—something you perhaps would never have learned without the experience of so great a danger—feeling yourself made strong from weakness, stable from falling, cautious from danger, and happy from misery.

Accordingly, again and yet again, even to weariness, I shall repeat that you should continually consider how much so great a one endured for you, so small and so lost: he set his blood and his death as your price, although his blood is beyond price and his death admits no measure of valuation.

78. Above all, you must also take care not presumptuously to rely upon his abundant generosity, but continually recall how he washed with his blood, loved, and restored to integrity you who had been prostituted in the disgrace of a brothel [Col. 0622A] amid uncleannesses. For his love is accustomed to restore violated integrity, not to violate intact integrity.

Although you do not see his face, do not doubt that he is present to you. Take care, then, lest by some unbecoming act of yours you offend the eyes of him who is present; and know beyond doubt that he who loved you while ugly loves you more fully when beautiful. Put on, therefore, I beg you, the garment of innocence; adorn yourself, as with an embroidered garment, with the variety of virtues; and let him who pledged you with the ring of faith delight to smell in you the fragrant spices of graces.

I beg you, love with your whole soul the Lord your God—your Bridegroom, your life, your consolation, your counsel, your help and refuge. In short, love him who is for you whatever can be lovable or desirable. Love him chastely, devoutly, and holily, not in word or [Col. 0622B] tongue but in deed and truth. In your love seek not what is yours, but what belongs to Jesus Christ (Phil. II, 21). For thus the prophet taught us to love, when he said: “Give thanks to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever” (Ps. CVI, 1). But of one who seeks what is his own it is written: “He will praise you when you have done good to him” (Ps. XLVIII, 19).

79. Thus cast your whole self upon him; thus, by loving, pass wholly into the Beloved, so that, forgetful of yourself and made in your own estimation like a lost vessel, you may live in him and fail away from yourself, and may say with the prophet: “My flesh and my heart have failed; God is the God of my heart and my portion forever” (Ps. LXXII, 26). “O Lord God, my heart said to you: My face has sought you” (Ps. XXVI, 8).

But when will this be, O God? When will you come, my soul, and appear before the face of God? (Ps. XLI, 3). When will the left hand be turned into the right? When will the Bridegroom present you without spot or wrinkle? (Eph. V, 27). When the rushing of the river makes glad the city of God (Ps. XLV, 5); when the holy temple, which you are (I Cor. III, 17), will be adorned with golden curtains (II Chron. IV); when the whole earth will be filled with majesty (Ps. LXXI, 19); when he will serve you as you exult before God and delight in joy (Ps. LXVII, 4), passing by (Luke XII, 37)—I mean, passing from that bodily form which he showed his Apostles to that form of glory in which he is coequal, coeternal, and co-omnipotent with God the Father.

Therefore continually exercise yourself, in hope and exultation in future things, with vows and desires; and let thanksgiving and a voice of praise always be with you for the reception of present things (Isa. XII, 3).

## Chapter XXIV. How greatly the soul must beware of being ungrateful toward God who so loves it

80. How long will you sleep, my soul? How long will you slumber, so that even a brief idle hour may steal upon you in which you have no remembrance of the Son of God, crucified for your misery and for his mercy? Anyone would think it most grievous if he had rendered great service to his equal and found him ungrateful for the benefit bestowed. What then will the Lord of majesty do if he finds us, who are ashes and dust, ungrateful for so great a mercy?

“As a father has compassion on his children,” he has had compassion on us (Ps. CII, 13). For if he hardens, judges, and condemns anyone, this does not come from him but from us. Although “he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills” (Rom. IX, 18), yet he, whose own property is always to have mercy and to spare, crowns us with his mercies and punishes our wickedness. Indeed, the Father of mercies himself speaks through the prophet: “Is the death of the wicked my will, and not rather that he should turn and live?” (Ezek. XVIII, 23).

81. Recollect, recollect, that God, God’s only-begotten Son, bent the heavens and came down for your salvation (Ps. XVII, 10); and in order to draw you out of the mire of dregs, by an ineffable art, while remaining what he was, he lowered himself from his majesty even to the bruises and wounds of the Passion.

Moses indeed took an Ethiopian woman as wife (Num. XII, 1), but he did not change the blackness of her skin in her. Christ Jesus, the Son of God, found you blackened by the manifold ugliness of sins; at last he washed you with his tears, his baptism, and the flood of his blood, and presented you to himself glorious (Eph. V, 27). You know, nor should you doubt, how far you are inferior to your Bridegroom in birth, beauty, and dignity.

Whence, then, comes to you so great and ineffable an honor: that God has deigned to choose you as his bride—he through whom all things were made (John I, 3), who has power over your life and death, King of heaven and earth, splendor and image of the Father’s substance, into whom angels desire to look (I Pet. I, 12), whose beauty sun and moon marvel at, Creator and Governor of the universe, desire of angels and archangels, God of glory and Lord of majesty? Whence comes this to you, that he receives you as a companion of glory, a partner of the kingdom, a sharer in the bridal chamber? When you touch him, you are chaste; when you know him, you are learned; when you see him, blessed; when you can enjoy him, glorious.

Act, therefore, so that the heart of your husband may trust in you (Prov. XXXI, 11). Forget your people (Ps. XLIV, 11), and do not turn your mind away from him even for a moment. The angel of the Lord stands ready to cut you in two (Dan. XIII, 55) if you receive another lover, if your love toward him grows cold, or if you show yourself even slightly undevout or ungrateful toward him. Recollect how much God has done for you: he drew you to himself, intending to bring you to the house of his glory, though you did not dare to think of his footstool or of pardon.

## Chapter XXV. How God is to be loved

82. How affectionately, sincerely, gently, and sweetly you are bound to love God, the Lord teaches through Moses, saying: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. VI, 5). This commandment of God contains within itself the strictest necessity of observance. Someone may excuse himself on the ground that he is unable to keep watch and labor. But no one can excuse himself on the ground that he cannot love.

Concerning virginity, counsel is given, not commandment. “He who can receive it,” says the Lord, “let him receive it” (Matt. XIX, 12); and the Apostle says, “Concerning virgins I have no commandment, but I give counsel” (I Cor. VII, 25). [Col. 0624A] But charity is commanded by God strongly and insistently, and is enjoined upon human hearts under threat of punishment.

The Lord indeed commanded this commandment to be kept most strictly; and, in order to drive it into our hearts more deeply than a nail, he repeatedly impressed it upon us as with frequent blows: first, that we should love with all our heart; then he adds, with all our soul; finally, he adds, with all our strength. This commandment is truly a nail or goad. For, as Solomon says, “The words of the wise are goads, and like nails driven deeply” (Eccl. XII, 11). Is not the living and effective word of God, more penetrating than every two-edged sword, more than a goad or nail? (Heb. IV, 12).

Certainly the hardness of our heart required this insistence of repetition, so that this commandment might pass into the inmost parts [Col. 0624B] of our hearts, just as a nail is driven into a hard log by repeated blows until it is forced inward. It was therefore expedient for us, whose hearts worldly love had infected and whose souls’ inner hiding places it occupied, that it should be cast out from every marrow of the heart; that the prince of this world also should be cast out (John XII, 31), banished from our heart, so that it might abide in God and God in it (I John IV, 16).

But who can be confident of possessing his whole heart, when the prophet complains of his own heart and says: “They are multiplied above the hairs of my head, and my heart has forsaken me”? (Ps. XXXIX, 13). And again, rejoicing in the restoration of his heart: “Your servant,” he says, “has found his heart, to pray this prayer to you” (II Kings VII, 27).

83. We often read in the book of experience how we are forsaken by our heart. Now it is with us; now elsewhere. Now it flies away; now it returns. Remaining only in instability, it never stands in any firmness of its own. How then shall I love with my whole heart, when I am cut off from my whole heart [variant: “am cut off”]? Or how can I possess my whole heart, unless God makes it mine? I shall possess nothing of my heart except so much as God makes mine of it.

But if, with God’s help, I directed all the affections, intentions, and motions of my heart toward him, held it fixed in him with unwavering devotion, and if that heavenly fire kindled also the marrow of my soul—the fire of which the prophet speaks: “The Lord sent fire into my bones and instructed me” (Lam. I, 13)—then perhaps it would be possible [Col. 0624D] for me to love with my whole heart. But now let my eyes see my imperfection (Ps. CXXXVIII, 16), so that, if we are not granted to love as much as we ought, at least we may love as much as we can.

If we recollect God’s benefits—not only those by which the Dayspring from on high visited us through the dispensation of the flesh, but also the daily and almost continual benefits by which the Father of mercies continually comforts us when we are placed in distress and affliction of spirit—who could answer or repay him one thing for a thousand? He presses and heaps mercy upon mercy, performs great things with us in all things, and overwhelms and confounds us by such frequent generosity.

Therefore, in order to draw our entire heart into the grace of his love and wholly tear us away from love of the world—for whoever is a friend of the world is his enemy [Col. 0625A] (Jas. IV, 4)—and because sacred teaching instructs us thus, he invites our heart to his love with fatherly gentleness. For to be commanded to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our mind is the same as God instructing us to love him sweetly, wisely, and strongly.

## Chapter XXVI. Christ is especially to be loved because of his Passion

84. And what is sweeter than continual recollection of his dispensation, through which the goodness and loving-kindness of God our Savior appeared? (Titus III, 4). Above all things, Christ Jesus, your Passion makes you lovable to us: it has made propitiation for all our iniquities (Ps. CII, 3). For by the shedding of guiltless blood, the bonds recording all sins have been erased.

Thanks be to your cross, Jesus: it empties all our torments. Let us give thanks for the nails and for the lance, which opened for us the depths of mercy of our God, in which the Dayspring from on high visited us (Luke I, 78). O how dreadful and insatiable is the wound of our transgression, for which the Son of God had to endure so many harsh reproaches, so many and such grievous wounds!

Abel’s blood cried from the earth for vengeance. Naboth’s blood cried. The blood of all the righteous which had been shed upon the earth cried (Matt. XXIII, 35), saying: “Avenge, Lord, our blood which has been shed upon the earth” (Rev. VI, 10). Christ’s blood alone cried for reconciliation and redemption for his people. His death cried to the dead, for life; to sinners, for pardon; to captives, for liberation; to the lost, [Col. 0625C] for salvation. He continually intercedes with the Father, that the price of his blood and the reward of obedience which he rendered to the Father may be applied for sinners toward the redemption of penitents.

For the Apostle testifies that God set forth his Son as a propitiator through faith in his blood (Rom. III, 25). The Apostle inserted this qualification, “through faith,” with the greatest care. For if you cast your faith and trust upon the bruises and wounds of the Crucified One, and apply remembrance of the Lord’s Passion to the benefit of your salvation, his blood will be the price of your redemption; his death will become life for you; his pain, your joy; his distresses, your delights; his reproaches, your honor. And so, with the grace of your fervor increased, you will obtain the salvation which he wrought in the midst of the earth; his temporal suffering will yield for you eternal joys.

85. O Jesus, fountain of mercy, whom would not this move to love you: that amid the reproaches of those reviling you, amid the agonies of death, forgetful of your sufferings but mindful of your mercies, you intercede so piously and so fittingly with the Father for those who crucified you? For in the stretching out and piercing of your body, when your appearance had already been turned into hatred; at that hour of sacrifice, when the power of the burnt offering had already opened heaven, shaken the earth, and despoiled hell, you, the high priest, entering with blood into the holy of holies (Heb. IX, 12), crying aloud to be heard because of your reverence (ibid. V, 7), said: “Father, forgive [Col. 0626A] them, for they do not know what they do” (Luke XXIII, 34).

How sweet he will be to those who love him, when he anticipates those who hate and kill him with such great, so undeserved, so free, and so wondrous a kindness!

## Chapter XXVII. Love ought to be prudent and steadfast

86. Yet because the love of the heart is wholly in affection, lest it be excessively headlong, it should be governed by wisdom and discernment. We are therefore commanded to love God with our whole soul—that is, wisely. For the soul is the seat of wisdom.

Peter loved the Lord sweetly, but not wisely, because he loved carnally. The love of the heart approaches carnal affections most readily; therefore he sought to prevent him from dying. He loved not wisely but sweetly, not discerningly but rashly. [Col. 0626B] And because the disciples loved sweetly but imprudently, it was said to them: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28). It was as if he said: If you loved me wisely, my ascent to the Father would be desirable to you, because I carry with me your human nature, to be placed in the Father’s glory.

87. The third love is strengthened by the zeal of faith and a certain fervor of affection, when a person establishes his mind with all inward strength upon loving God, and makes himself steadfast and strong in enduring harsh and dreadful things for Christ, through the desire for heavenly things and contempt for temporal things.

Because Peter did not love thus wisely as he ought, although he loved affectionately, he was rebuked by the Lord and called Satan, because he opposed the redemption of all, which Christ was arranging in the Passion of his body (Mark VIII, 31–33). In this it is also clear that he then loved imprudently, when, led merely by carnal affection, he hindered his own salvation and Christ’s glory. Nor did he love sweetly, wisely, or strongly when he denied him at a maidservant’s voice—he who had promised that he would not deny him even to avoid the danger of death.

In order that this threefold love might be purified and strengthened in Peter, he was, as we believe, questioned three times by Christ: “Peter, do you love me?” (John XXI, 15–17), so that he who had been found deficient in this threefold love might redeem and supply his imperfection by a threefold confession.

Thus, in the ministry of his dispensation, he is to be loved sweetly; and, lest we presume too greatly upon the benefit [Col. 0626D] of our redemption or lose confidence in any respect, he is to be loved wisely. But when we consider the power and glory of the resurrection, through which he powerfully snatched us from the dominion of darkness and opened to us the gates of glory, he is to be loved strongly and steadfastly.

## Chapter XXVIII. God must also be loved in his promises

88. Finally, as God is to be loved with the whole heart in his benefits, as we set out above, so likewise we are bound to love him with the whole soul in his promises. He who is truth, who wills, knows, and is able to save us, promises us rest from labor, security from fear, joy instead of sorrow, resurrection instead of death, eternal life instead of the passing away of this life. He promises the kingdom of heaven and refreshment at the Father’s table. He promises what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, as he has prepared for those who love him (I Cor. II, 9). Moreover, he promises himself: he swore to Abraham our father that he would give himself to us (Luke I, 73).

Let us run with all the capacity of our soul toward all promises which surpass every desire. Although human desire for these things ought to be without measure, it nevertheless receives a measure from human deficiency. But if desire, despite this deficiency, exceeds measure concerning God’s promises, this excess has no excess; and such impatience is praiseworthy, when delayed hope afflicts the soul (Prov. XIII, 12).

Love receives continual increase from desire. David, bearing this delay most impatiently, says: “As the stag desires the springs of waters, so my soul desires you, O God” (Ps. XLI, 2). The Apostle too, impatient even of patience, says: “I am constrained between two things, having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. I, 23–24). The Bride likewise, ardently and impatiently burning with desire for the Bridegroom, and commending her affections to the prayers of the heavenly powers and saints, says: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love” (Cant. V, 8).

And it should be noted that the love proceeding from desire for the promises belongs properly to the soul. For in the desires of the saints this affection of the soul is often expressed, as in: “My soul longs for and fails away in the courts of the Lord” (Ps. LXXXIII, 3); likewise: “My soul has thirsted for you, O God” (Ps. XLI, 3); and elsewhere the prophet says: “Your name, O Lord, and your memorial are in the desire of the soul. My soul has desired you in the night, and also my spirit within me” (Isa. XXVI, 8–9).

## Chapter XXIX. God is to be loved in his judgments

89. As affection proceeds from God’s benefits, by which we love God with our whole heart, and desire arises from God’s promises, through which we desire God with our whole soul, so from God’s judgments love has its ground and discernment, by which we love God with all our strength [Col. 0627D] and all our powers—that is, strongly and steadfastly.

Now there is a desirable judgment of God, according to the words: “Look upon me and have mercy on me, according to the judgment of those who love your name” (Ps. CXVIII, 132). And there is a dreadful judgment, of which it is said: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, O Lord” (Ps. CXLII, 2). From this dreadful judgment no one loves either God or himself.

Therefore, by his most just judgment, God has mercy upon some here, though he will not have mercy upon them in the future; while he chastises others as though angry, so that his wrath and scourges may be turned to glory for those who are afflicted. He gives them up according to the desires of their hearts, that they may go in their own contrivances (Ps. LXXX, 13), may add iniquity to iniquity (Ps. LXVIII, 28), and may become more filthy who are already in filth (Rev. XXII, 11).

Of this mercy and wrath the prophet speaks, saying: “Who is wise, and will keep these things and understand the mercies of the Lord?” (Ps. CVI, 43); and again: “Who knows the power of your wrath, or who can number your anger because of your fear?” (Ps. LXXXIX, 11–12). “O God, how magnified are your works! Your thoughts have become exceedingly deep. A foolish man will not know, and a fool will not understand these things” (Ps. XCI, 6–7). Therefore the prosperity of fools will destroy them (Prov. I, 32).

90. But if they are corrected by God, they are neither cleansed nor reformed; rather, their cleansing becomes an occasion of their destruction, according to the words: “You destroyed them because of cleansing” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 45). These people murmur and blaspheme amid God’s scourges, and pile Gehenna’s punishments upon their present punishments.

But the saints of the Lord, amid scourges, love even his scourges for God’s sake. They also give thanks to God for his judgments, accuse themselves, and say with the prophet: “All that you have done to us, O Lord, you have done in true judgment, because we have sinned against you; but give glory to your name” (Dan. III and Jer. XIV). To such persons belongs the prophetic saying: “The children of Judah rejoiced because of your judgments, O Lord” (Ps. XCVI, 8).

There are some who not only endure God’s judgments patiently, but judge themselves: they assist the hand that scourges them; they accuse themselves, bear witness against themselves, judge themselves, and execute their own sentence.

91. God’s judgment produces patience in the afflicted. “Tribulation produces patience; patience, testing; testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint” [Col. 0628C] (Rom. 5:3–5). For when could there be disappointment where there is that which surpasses every hope and every confidence—namely, certainty of eternal glory? Under this expectation the prophet said, “Lord, in your judgments I have hoped beyond hope” (Ps. 118:43); and likewise: “The judgments of the Lord are true, more desirable than gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Ps. 18:10–11). Why then should I fear in the evil day? (Ps. 48:6). It is wiser to be punished here, burned here, and tortured here by accusing and judging ourselves, than to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10:31) and, on the dreadful day, await the punishment of eternal condemnation from a terrible and inexorable judge.

## Chapter XXX. God ought to be loved in his commandments

[Col. 0628D]

92. God is to be loved with the whole mind in his commandments. For God wills that the whole human mind should so incline itself to obedience as to devote all its senses and affections to keeping the heavenly commandments. To obey God, indeed, is to consent in all things to his will and thus to live in obedience, because “life is in his will” (Ps. 29:6). Since God’s will is expressed in his commandments, and no one can love God unless he loves his will, it follows that no one can love God unless he loves his commandments. Finally, love is proven through God’s commandments: if we meditate upon them, act in accordance with them, and occupy ourselves in their practice. Indicating this, the prophet says: “I will meditate [Col. 0629A] on your commandments, which I have loved.” Behold, attentive meditation. “And I lifted up my hands to your commandments, which I have loved.” Behold, loving action. “And I shall exercise myself in your statutes” (Ps. 118:47–48). Behold, an exercise that makes righteous.

Of meditation it is written: “Always consider the things God has commanded you” (Ecclus. 3:22). Let God’s commandments therefore be considered: how holy, how honorable, how sweet and health-giving, how pleasant, how trustworthy, and how “established for ever and ever” (Ps. 110:8). In the lifting up of hands, holy action is signified, to which the righteous person gladly applies himself. For he is certain that eternal recompense will answer his merits with overflowing abundance. Continual exercise, however, has struggle joined to it and unceasing labor. But the righteous person fights in order to be crowned, to receive from him rest after labor, who “fashions toil into a commandment” (Ps. 93:20).

93. Therefore, whether charity is genuine is proven if a person loves God’s commandments; if he serves him—whom to serve is to reign—by meditation and action [or: prayer], and by the exercise of works. For obedience to the commandments has no merit unless it proceeds from charity. Since obedience and charity are joined together, whoever does not love does not keep the commandments. Hear him who is Truth: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word” (John 14:23). And he adds this, plainly indicating that whoever loves obeys, and whoever does not obey does not love. True obedience, indeed, is true observance of God’s commandments. Therefore obedience always adheres inseparably to charity, on account of what is written: “Whoever offends in one point has become guilty of all” [Col. 0629C] (James 2:10).

This may briefly be explained through one commandment, so that a similar judgment may be made concerning similar cases. Under the commandment, “You shall not kill” (Exod. 20:13), a person who does not love yet does not kill fulfills the commandment according to the letter, but does not fulfill it according to the merit of the commandment, because he does not love. To fulfill the law is not outwardly to follow the words of the law, but obediently to carry them out in mind and intention. Since, therefore, obedience that does not arise from true love is not sincere obedience, a person who does not love is not said to obey, even though he does not kill, because he keeps the law merely in outward act and not with pure intention.

For charity “is patient, is kind,” in which qualities obedience is commended. “It does not act improperly,” because it does nothing against its own conscience. “It is not puffed up” by God’s benefits. “It is not ambitious,” because it rejects every dominion. “It does not seek its own,” but the things of Christ or of its neighbor; indeed, it does not even demand back what has been taken away. “It is not provoked”—understand, *to anger*. “It does not think evil,” so as to repay evil for evil. “It does not rejoice in iniquity”—understand, *another’s*, for it has no iniquity of its own. It patiently bears all things; it believes all things and hopes all things said or promised by God. It “endures all things” [Col. 0629D] (1 Cor. 13:4–7), humbly obeying.

94. Therefore, whoever obeys out of charity fulfills the law of God’s commandments, which no one can fulfill at all without charity. Thus charity itself is “the end of the law” (1 Tim. 1:5), the fulfillment of the commandments, and the boundary [Col. 0630A] of perfect completion. “I have seen an end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96). This is the testimony of our conscience. This is the glory that comes to us from the Spirit of truth: for the Spirit of truth bears witness to our spirit that we are children of God (Rom. 8:16), reborn into the hope of life through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead (1 Pet. 1:3).

John the Evangelist, indicating this rebirth, says: “We know that whoever is born of God does not sin, because the heavenly generation—that is, the renewal of charity—preserves him” (1 John 5:9), through which God foresaw that he would be made conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:29). For although David added adultery and murder to treachery; although Mary Magdalene suffered from seven demons; although Peter incurred the guilt of apostasy: nevertheless, there was no one who could snatch them from the Lord’s hand. Charity is the renewal of life, through which the old human being in us—earthly, animal, and carnal—is crucified and destroyed. Thus ambitions and desires, evil works and perverse longings, vanish away, since charity makes all things new. “But now, if anyone is a new creature, in that person the old things have passed away” [Col. 0630B] (2 Cor. 5:17).

## Chapter XXXI. By what signs God’s presence in the soul may be detected

95. Let the rational soul therefore exercise itself in these affections with prudent watchfulness; let it “think of the Lord in goodness, and in simplicity of its heart” (Wis. 1:1). Let it endeavor with such vigilance to make itself a wine-cellar and a receptacle of divine fire that, on the Lord’s favorable day [Col. 0630C] and in the hour of his good pleasure, when it hears the Spirit’s voice and the sacred whisper like the murmur of a gentle breeze, it may offer pure affection and faithful understanding, deserving to gather spiritual fruits as though from the tree of life.

Now the fruits of the Spirit, according to the Apostle, are charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, kindness, self-control, goodness, gentleness, faith, modesty, and chastity (Gal. 5:22–23). O happy soul, if you are permitted to experience by sure signs his benevolence, the inspiration of heavenly grace, and his presence with you. For in the remembrance of him a certain sweetness will touch you, affecting you with a new and untried delight, so that, as if drawn out of yourself and wholly estranged from yourself, you exult in a certain heavenly pleasantness.

The following, however, establish the reality of his presence: all your senses become joyful, your understanding is made serene, your desires grow warm; you rejoice and breathe eagerly for the embraces of him whom you feel yourself holding, and fear lest he slip away. Therefore, not as much as you wish, but as much as you can, you bind him with a delightful bond of inward charity [Col. 0630D].

96. This is, O soul, your beloved, coming invisibly and incomprehensibly, mercifully and graciously: that he may awaken you, breathe himself into you, insinuate himself into the bosom of your love, kindle your desire, illuminate your inward eyes, and inflame your affection. Thus he offers you the first-fruits, not the fullness, of his love—not for satiety but for tasting—so that by such experience you may prove how sweet, how gentle, how pleasant, how delightful he will show himself to you when his glory appears; when you see him with unveiled face, crowned with the diadem of his Father, whom you now worship crowned with the diadem of his mother, the glorious Virgin Mary.

This is the only sober intoxication. Hence the Apostle: “Whether we live or whether we die” (Rom. 14:8), we are sober unto God. This sober intoxication is produced by the wine of charity, as the bridegroom in the Song of Love intimates, saying: “Eat, friends; drink and be intoxicated, beloved ones” (Song 5:1). In this life, the soul that serves God first eats the bread of tears in the sweat of its face; after departing this life, it is not fed with the bread of sorrow, because “there shall be no more sorrow or mourning, for the former things have passed away” [Col. 0631A] (Rev. 21:4). Rather, it will be refreshed and intoxicated by the cup of love, according to the words: “My intoxicating cup—how splendid it is!” (Ps. 22:5).

Of this cup, I believe, Isaiah also spoke: “To you also, daughter of Edom, the cup shall come, and you shall be intoxicated” (Lam. 4:21). Therefore it is intoxicated “with the abundance of God’s house” (Ps. 35:9), drinking pure and new wine in the kingdom of Christ’s Father. Meanwhile it drinks its wine with tears in measure, until the King brings it into the wine-cellar, makes it itself his cellar, and orders charity within it (Song 2:4). For she now loves, but does not yet receive the fruit of love; exercising herself solely in affections, she says: “I am wounded by charity,” and speaks to the angels and saints, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, tell him that I languish with love” [Col. 0631B] (ibid. 5:8).

## Chapter XXXII. Why love is languor

[Col. 0631C]

97. Yet it is remarkable how love or charity can be the languor of the bride or the soul, since charity “covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8), and since Mary Magdalene, because she loved much, was healed from the assault of seven demons—that is, from the languor of the seven deadly sins (Luke 7:47). Love, however, is languor when the lover is tormented by the delay of desire, when she sighs for the bridegroom’s embraces.

But he “who heals all your infirmities” (Ps. 102:3), O my soul, will cure your languor through the enjoyment of himself, when he grants himself to you for possession, sight, and enjoyment with unveiled face; and thereafter you shall never be separated [Col. 0631D] from his kiss and embrace. Indeed, the bridegroom shall rejoice over the bride, and your God shall rejoice over you (Isa. 62:5). Then the fruit of love will shut out the distress of languor. For languor shall pass away, but not love, because “charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:8). Therefore love is now languor while it is tortured by the desire to live; but it will be satiety when it delights in the possession of its desire. For the desire to possess differs from the possession of desire as appetite differs from the fullness of satisfaction, and hunger from satiety.

98. Meanwhile, then, she is gravely sick and afflicted with languor, while he brings her aid upon the bed of her sorrow. The voice of one languishing and weeping is: “Support me with apples; strengthen me with flowers, for I languish with love” (Song 2:5). The beginnings of virtues, indeed, are flowers, and their fruits are honor and uprightness [Col. 0632A] (Ecclus. 24:23). Apples, however, are the riper exercises and examples of patience.

The soul is therefore supported with apples when it receives the fruits of time past, turning to its own benefit Christ’s scourges, reproaches, pains, and everything else that he suffered, even to the ignominy of the cross. And all these things have passed away: for Christ “dies no more” (Rom. 6:9). Yet we gather daily fruit from his Passion. The bride is strengthened with flowers, which the renewal of human nature produced from Christ’s resurrection. For “winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed; flowers have appeared in our land.” He, certainly, who says, “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 1:11–12, 1), by rising from the dead caused the earth of our flesh—which under the ancient curse brought forth thorns and thistles [Col. 0632B] (Gen. 3:18)—to blossom anew, and restored us to the infancy of a new rebirth.

With these apples and these flowers she must be supported and strengthened, lest the affection which she has toward the Lord grow dull, until, received into the bridegroom’s embraces, she says: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand shall embrace me” (Song 2:6). For whatever she now receives from the bridegroom’s left hand at his first coming, in comparison with the glory that she is to receive in the embrace of his right hand, she will reckon little, as it is written: “In his left hand are riches and glory, and in his right hand length of life” (Prov. 3:16).

## Chapter XXXIII. The dimensions of charity

99. Indeed, just as God is now known imperfectly and in part [Col. 0632C], so he is loved imperfectly. For the knowledge which we now have of God, when compared with the knowledge of the homeland, when we shall see God with unveiled face, when he shall be seen in his glory, when he shall show his face, is like the entrance of morning light through the thinnest crack compared with the noonday splendor, when the sun shines in its strength. So too is the love of God possessed in this pilgrimage: it is like a tiny spark of fire compared with that great fire of love by which the righteous, with the Seraphim in the heavenly Jerusalem, shall burn in the fire of charity. For now there is “a fire in Zion”; then there shall be “a furnace in Jerusalem” (Isa. 31:9).

But although, as the Apostle testifies, there are length, breadth, height, and depth in God’s love toward us [Col. 0632D] (Eph. 3:18), human love does not correspond to divine charity with a proportionate measure, because of its inadequacy. God certainly does not love us superficially, falsely, or moderately, but fully, sincerely, and from the depths of his being; so that we too may comprehend with all the saints what are the height, breadth, and depth of so great a charity.

Its height is the excellence of the glory that God has prepared for those who love him, whose value has not entered into the human heart. Its depth is the abasement of majesty from equality with the Father, the emptying of the Son even to the form of a servant, even to death and the ignominy of crucifixion. Its length is without beginning and without end. For his love neither begins nor ends: he chose us before the foundation of the world in his beloved Son (Eph. 1:4); and, as it is written, “His mercy is from eternity and unto eternity upon those who fear him” [Col. 0633A] (Ps. 102:17). Its breadth is broad, extended, and poured forth in every mode of benevolence. For he wills all people to be saved through him (1 Tim. 2:4). He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all; and, in giving him to us, as the Apostle testifies, gave us all things in him (Rom. 8:32).

100. In the same way, by reciprocal correspondence, human charity conforms itself to divine charity in a corresponding fourfold division. It is high when it contemplates eternal and heavenly things. It is deep when a person embraces lowliness and abjection for God’s sake. It is long when it perseveres to the end. For faith, hope, knowledge, and the rest shall be brought to nothing; but charity shall never fail [Col. 0633B] (1 Cor. 13:8). It is broad because it is joyful, when the human heart is enlarged in delight in righteousness. It is broad when it extends itself not only to God and neighbor, but also embraces an enemy with devout love. It is broad, whose commandment is broad, as the prophet says: “I have seen an end of every perfection; your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. 118:96).

O broad and enlarging charity, how great is your house and how vast the place of your possession! (Bar. 3:24). The saints comprehend its breadth and length, height and depth, so that we also may alike be caught in the same net of charity. Charity therefore enlarges its tent among the saints, so that, if we love God and neighbor, we may be received into the saints’ common exultation.

[Col. 0633C] 101. Therefore let us not be straitened in our inward parts, nor confined within the limits of whatever little joy is ours. Let us believe in the Holy Spirit, the holy catholic Church, and the communion of saints, that your eyes, O Jesus, may see our imperfection (Ps. 138:16), and that in your good pleasure, in the communion of saints, our insufficiency may be supplied. For if we love God in the saints, they too, in proportion to the merits belonging to them, will share with us their blessedness before God.

For where God, all in all, sits in the midst of those who love him, it is necessary that common affection be accompanied by a communion of joys. Therefore not only the blessedness of our neighbor, but Christ’s whole blessedness, shall be ours through a communion of love and exultation and through participation in another’s joy. Whatever less of blessedness I shall possess in myself, I shall make up from another’s blessedness. For the good which I love in God or in my neighbor, by loving I shall make my own, so that the perfection of another’s joy may supply my deficiency.

Do you wish me to establish the truth of this by a familiar example? A mother sees her son, whom she loves above all things, distinguished by royal anointing, an imperial diadem, sceptre, and augustal fillets. As great as the mother’s love is, so great is her exultation; and the mother appropriates to herself her son’s honor and joy, the applause of the people, and everyone’s congratulations. Thus, in the land of the living, every person by the benefit of charity rejoices together with the blessedness of all.

102. O communion of charity, O sweetness of love, O security, O rest, O delightful Sabbath, O entrance into eternal happiness, which charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith produces as more precious than all treasures, more desirable than all riches, more excellent than all kingdoms! [Col. 0634A] (1 Tim. 1:3). Who will grant me to be intoxicated with this cup of love, to be put to sleep in this lethargy, so that, wholly dead to my own heart and wholly carried out of myself into love of God and neighbor, between these two lots I may “sleep and rest in peace in the selfsame place”? (Ps. 4:9).

Who will enroll me in that holy communion, where the joy of the angels is poured into all and by all poured back into God, and where God shall be all in all (1 Cor. 15:28), so that he may be for all who love him love, life, peace, joy, rest, brightness, security, jubilation, [Col. 0634B] the satisfaction of every desire, and the eternal, complete blessedness of glory? Amen.

## Chapter XXXIV. The unceasing sighs of the soul that loves and longs for God

103. Jeremiah speaks in the person of the soul which loves, sighs, and desires: “My eye has brought down streams of waters” (Lam. 3:48). There are principally two kinds of compunction, because the soul thirsting for God is first pierced by fear and afterwards by love. At first it afflicts itself in tears, because, when it considers the multitude of its evils, it fears that it will suffer eternal punishments for them. But when it has been worn away by a long sorrow of grief, a certain security born of confidence in pardon arises, and the mind is inflamed with love of heavenly joys. Then the soul which formerly wept lest it be led to punishment afterwards weeps most bitterly because it sees its sojourn in this life prolonged [Col. 0634C].

Is this not “the change of the right hand of the Most High”? (Ps. 76:11).
