And certainly it is no wonder that it weeps and grieves at being in this exile when it contemplates the nature and quality of the most beautiful choirs of angels; that fellowship of good spirits; the joy of God’s eternal vision; and the seven other things which complete and make blessed that sweet banquet: the loveliness of the place, the dignity of the attendants, the beauty of those reclining at table, the multitude of dishes, the security of the guests, the constancy of jubilation, and the eternity of the feast. Considering these things, it weeps, grieves, and laments more because it lacks such great goods than it previously wept while fearing eternal torments. Thus perfect compunction of fear draws it toward compunction of love. When it has reached this point, it can cry out from ardent desire and say:

“Grant, Lord Jesus Christ, my bridegroom, that through love I may taste what I taste a little through knowledge. My wretched soul languishes with hunger for your love; refresh it, Jesus, and let your love heal it, let your affection enrich it, let your honey-sweet love fill and intoxicate it. Alas—woe to the soul that does not seek and love you! Woe, Lord, to those who love your creatures instead of you! The soul that loves the world serves sin, and apart from you will never be quiet or secure. Hence Augustine says: ‘You have made me, Lord, for yourself, and my heart is restless until [Col. 0635A] it rests in you.’

“O sweetest Jesus, when shall I see you? When shall I appear before your face? (Ps. 41:3). When shall I be satisfied with your beauty, into which angels desire to look? (1 Pet. 1:12). O how exalted you are, who are higher than heaven! And yet you deigned so greatly to humble yourself that you chose humble souls as your dwelling-place. Therefore holiness befits your house (Ps. 92:5). We may thus consider the benefit of this so glorious and beloved guest: he awakens the sluggishness of the mind he inhabits, because he is a cock; restrains its restlessness, because he is a master; kindles what is cold, because he is fire; moderates what is kindled, because he is ointment; softens what is rigid, because he is reason; tightens what is loose, because he is medicine.

“It is therefore clear that your love is not idle, because whoever loves you does not grow lukewarm. Grant me, therefore, best Jesus, to love you and to meditate upon you without ceasing. Your fragrance, merciful Lord Christ and most loving bridegroom, raises the dead and heals the sick. Grant me, therefore, dearest Lord Jesus Christ, always to hold these things in my memory, and to remember the bitterness of vinegar and gall which you, eternal sweetness, tasted for us in death.”

104. Take comfort, you who are nourished under the cloak of voluntary poverty, you who reject beds covered with silk, because God is with you in poverty. He does not lie upon the delights of a splendid bed. He “is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly” [Col. 0635B] (Job 28:13). Truly, a bride would be excessively delicate—indeed, foolish and dishonorable—if she saw her wise, most beautiful, and delicate bridegroom reclining in a low place upon hay, and, while he watched, fled and established herself in a luxurious place. What could the bridegroom believe about such a woman except that she wished to seek a divorce from him?

Do not seek separation, my soul, but say: “It is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28). And nowhere is there salvation, nowhere delight, nor perfect rest for me except in you, Jesus Christ, most faithful bridegroom [Col. 0636A]. If you wish me to depart from you, give me another you, so that I may flee from you to you; otherwise I shall not depart from you. Poor with you, lowly with you, and abject with you, I desire this far more than “to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 83:11). It is pleasing to me to be separated from you for a time for your sake; but it is exceedingly difficult to be without you for any length of time, although in these miseries I lack you—yet without you I cannot be.

105. I shall arise and go about every place that I can. I shall give no sleep to my eyes nor rest to my feet until I find him whom my soul loves. Pour forth tears, my eyes; weep, do not fail, and do not rest until you find him. But what shall I do to find him? Where shall I turn? To whom shall I go? From whom shall I seek counsel? Whom shall I ask? Who will pity me? Who will console me? Who will show me him whom my soul loves, that it may rest?

I look around to see whether I might see him, and I do not see him. I would find him, but I do not find him. Wretched me! What shall I do? For where has my beloved gone? “I sought him and did not find him; I called, and he did not answer me.” Alas, alas! Where has my joy gone? Where is my love hidden? Where is my sweetness? Why have you forsaken me, my salvation? Alas for me, Lord, alas! Have mercy on my soul! You have departed, comforter of my life, and have not said farewell to me. What shall I do? Where shall I seek you, my only good? And when shall I, wretched as I am, find you? “My soul refused to be comforted” [Col. 0636B] (Ps. 76:3), except in you, my holy sweetness.

O my Savior, I beg that the time may come when, with unveiled eyes, I may behold him whom I now cry out to from afar; when I may seize him whom I desire and embrace him, wholly absorbed in the abyss of your love. I beg you, let nothing delight me apart from you, and let nothing precious please me. But grant me, good Jesus, to live in you and to die for love of you, who deigned to undergo the torment of bitter death for me. Amen.

[Col. 0635]

# The Mystical Vine, or Treatise on the Passion of the Lord, on “I Am the True Vine” (G)*

[Note.]

This treatise is not by St Bernard, but by some other devout author, neither unlearned nor inelegant, who composed short sermons, beginning with no. 53.

## Prologue

[Col. 0635D]

Kind Jesus, true vine, tree of life, set in the midst of paradise; Lord Jesus Christ, whose leaves are for healing and whose fruit is for eternal life; blessed flower and fruit of the most chaste Virgin Mother, without whom no one is wise, because you are the Wisdom of the eternal Father: deign to refresh my weak and dry mind with the bread of understanding and the water of saving wisdom, so that, as you, O key of David, open, hidden things may be unlocked for me; and as you, O true light, shine, dark things may be revealed. Thus, through me your humble servant, while you yourself make things manifest and illumine them, may we who speak and hear together possess eternal life. Amen.

## Chapter I. That Christ Jesus is the true vine

1. “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). With the help of the Lord Jesus Christ himself, let us consider certain properties of the earthly vine, in which we may also identify properties of that heavenly vine. Nor should we consider merely the things outwardly applied to its cultivation.

First, a vine is usually planted in the ground, not sown, being transplanted from its own vine. This seems to me to pertain to Jesus’ conception. For the vine first born from the vine is God begotten from God, the Son from the Father, coeternal and consubstantial [Col. 0637B] with him from whom he is begotten. But in order to bear greater fruit, he was planted in the earth—that is, conceived in the Virgin Mary—becoming what he was not while remaining what he was.

Blessed is this earth, bringing forth the blessing of all nations. Truly blessed, since, with God granting graciousness, it brought forth such a blessed fruit. This is the earth of which it is written: “No one cultivated the earth, but it was watered by a fountain rising from paradise” (Gen. 2:5–6). For this earth received no human cultivation in order that the Son of God might be conceived in it; rather, it was watered by the water of the Holy Spirit. Thus you read: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 1:35).

Again, it is written of this earth: “Let the earth be opened, and it shall bring forth the Savior” (Isa. 45:8). It was opened through faith, believing and obeying the angel; and it brought forth saving life, our Savior, who bestows the rewards of eternal life. Thus, after our vine had been brought forth into the light, certain practices belonging to the cultivation of vines were applied.

## Chapter II. On pruning the vine, or on the various mysteries relating to Christ’s state of self-emptying

2. For a fruitful vine is usually pruned. This may be understood both literally and figuratively. Jesus was circumcised, not because he needed this circumcision—which, in the ancient Fathers, removed original sin just as baptism does in us. For he owed nothing to original sin contracted through the defect of concupiscence [Col. 0637D], because he had been conceived without all carnal concupiscence—but lest he appear to abolish the law which he himself had given.

Morally, however, he teaches us that we ought not to bear it bitterly if at times we suffer penalties for sins which we do not recognize in ourselves, since he, the purifier of sins, did not disdain, for our sakes, to undergo the remedy for sins. Let us therefore console our pains, we who are by no means without sin, with the pains of him who suffered and was wounded not for himself but for us—not for himself, but in order to heal our wounds. See how eagerly he hastened to receive pains, how ready and willing he was to shed his blood. He was circumcised for us on the eighth day after his birth (Luke 2:21).

Would that at least in our eighth year we might suffer something for the Lord. Yet what are we saying, when we find many people who, after being planted for eight years, or after eighty years, when their labor and pain are naturally due, neither turn even their will toward the Lord nor amend a life subjected to vanity for so long, mindful of neither the precious blood so promptly poured out? What could be more miserable? Christ scarcely waits for the eighth day from his birth to begin to shed his blood for you; and you, not after eight days, but not even after eighty months—indeed, not even after eighty years—return to him even your will alone? He, scarcely born, sheds his blood for you; and you, already about to die, do not give back your will?

Certainly Jesus is good, for he receives even the servant who comes in the fourth watch as a penitent. You have given the strength of your youthful years to Christ’s enemy. At least give your weak will to Christ, who mercifully waits; and do not doubt that he will receive it. For “a child is born to us” [Col. 0638B] (Isa. 9:6), so that he may console little ones with small gifts, because small things suit the small. But if what you offer is not small—that is, humble—you cannot by that very fact enter in to the humble one, who says of himself, “I am the door” (John 10:9), and elsewhere: “Come to me, all of you; and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:28–29).

3. We may understand the pruning of our vine in another way: let us say that everything was pruned away from him which he lacked in this life, though he could have possessed it. Let us understand this pruning from the Apostle’s words: “Though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Col. 0638C] (Phil. 2:6–7). This emptying itself is a kind of pruning. Just as a vine is diminished when it is pruned, so Christ, the true vine, was made lower than the angels by his incarnation—indeed, humbled beneath all human beings.

How glory was cut away from him by the knife of ignominy; power by the knife of abasement; pleasure by the knife of pain; riches by the knife of poverty! See now how greatly he was pruned. He whom all the glory of heaven serves—indeed, he who alone is true glory—seems to cast glory away. Clothed with a servant’s garment, he bears ignominies and is covered with disgrace, in order to redeem you from disgrace and recall you to your former glory. He to whose mighty command all things infernal, earthly, and heavenly are subject becomes so abject that he was reckoned “the last of men” (Isa. 53:3). He is subjected to hunger, thirst, heat, cold, pains, and infirmities; and after all these things he does not escape the punishment of death.

He who “dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16), into whom angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1:12), whose fragrance alone so intoxicates the minds of the saints that, forgetting both the present world and themselves, they run after him with all their strength, is subjected to such pain that in him there is truly known to have been fulfilled what he had previously said through the prophets: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow!” [Col. 0638D] (Lam. 1:12).

He in whom are hidden all the treasures of God’s wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2:3), King of kings, rich toward all, alone in need of no one, becomes so poor that, by his own testimony, he is found poorer even than the foxes of the earth and the birds of heaven, when he says: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Matt. 8:20). Poor at his birth, poorer in life, poorest on the cross. At birth, he has virgin’s milk for food and cheap swaddling-clothes for covering. In life, if he had clothing, he often lacked food. In death you will find him both naked and thirsty—unless perhaps, as a remedy for his thirst, you would offer him vinegar mixed with myrrh and gall [Col. 0639A] (John 19:29).

4. Finally, by the knife of fear all friends and neighbors were cut away from him, so that among all those dear to him there was no one to console him. For he trod the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with him (Isa. 63:3); and when his heart endured reproach and misery, he waited for one who would grieve with him, and there was none; and he found none to console him either (Ps. 68:21). See now how greatly our Vine was cut back. What vine was ever cut back so severely? Yet what consolation is there in this pruning? Much fruit. For he endured a great and incomparable pruning.

Yet the saying seems deliberately phrased: “And of the nations there is no man with me,” as though it should be understood that women alone remained with him. For while men, of the stronger sex, fled in fear, female weakness did not flee; they did not abandon him as he bore his cross, nor when he died upon it (Luke 23:27; John 19:25), as blessed Job speaks in the person of the complaining Christ: “Only my lips around my teeth have been left” (Job 19:20). By “lips,” which are softer than the other members, the gentle and weak female sex is understood and represented—the sex which alone remained attached to Christ when the disciples fled. For the Lord chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong (1 Cor. 1:27).

But if we understand a mental flight, neither man nor woman remained with him, except she who alone is blessed among women; she alone stood firm in faith throughout that sorrowful Sabbath, and the Church was preserved in her alone.

> [Note: That the Church remained in the Blessed Virgin alone during the three days of Christ’s death is likewise maintained by Alexander of Hales, Durandus in the *Rationale of the Divine Offices*, and others cited and followed by Turrecremata, book I, *On the Church*, ch. 31. But this opinion is commonly rejected. For, Melchior Canus says in book IV of *On Theological Places*, final chapter, since the name “Church” is collective, if only one person believed, the Church would not believe, since a congregation must consist of at least three persons.  
>  
> The foundation which the aforementioned authors offer for their view is that candle which, in the office of Holy Week, remains lighted alone when the others have been extinguished, as though the extinguished candles signified the extinguished faith of the apostles, and the lighted one the unimpaired faith of the Blessed Virgin. If this proves anything, it establishes only that the apostles failed in the confession of faith, or even in that living faith which works through love, says Canus in the same work, ch. 5. Rupert, however, in book V of *On the Divine Offices*, ch. 26, maintains that the extinguished candles denote the earlier prophets killed by the Jews, while the lighted candle denotes Christ himself. See Duvallius, on 2–2, Treatise on Faith, q. I, art. 2.]

For this reason the whole Church most fittingly observes the Sabbath day, throughout the yearly cycle, in praise and glory of that same Virgin. Truly and uniquely blessed was the branch which no fear could cut away from its Vine. Cut away were the men who said: “But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). Cut away were the women who, though devoutly hastening to render to the dead body the service due to human nature (ibid. 23:56), nevertheless did not at all believe that he would rise again. And perhaps for this reason—though I say it without asserting it, lest I seem to introduce new claims—that Mother, who had greater devotion, did not come with the others to anoint Christ’s buried body, because she thought it futile to anoint one whom she knew would rise again. Truly this woman was strong, and, after her Son, worthy of honor above all others. Truly she may be called a heroic woman (*virago*), for she was not separated from the man Christ by the strength of love [or: of spirit]; but she believed that he whom she saw dying and dead had been exalted to the glory of immortality.

## Chapter III. On digging around the Vine: that is, on the plots of the Jews and the wounds of Christ

[Col. 0640B]

5. The Vine is dug around. This digging signifies the deceit of plotters. For one who devises a scheme to deceive someone is, as it were, digging a pit. Hence he says in complaint: “They dug a pit before my face” (Ps. 56:7). Yet no deception could be hidden from him who sees before and behind, and who beholds past and future as though present. For all things are naked and open to his eyes (Heb. 4:13).

Let us show by an example one such deceitful digging. The Gospel says that they brought to the Lord Jesus a woman taken in adultery, saying that Moses commanded in the Law that persons of this kind should be stoned: “But what do you say?” (John 8:3, 5). See the pit with which those most wicked husbandmen dug around our blessed Vine—not in order to make it sprout, but rather to make it wither. Yet their intention turned out contrariwise: the Vine, dug around, became more fruitful and distilled the moisture of mercy.

Let us examine their pits. They said among themselves: “If he says, in accordance with the Law, that the woman must be stoned, he will fall into the pit of cruelty—he who says of himself, ‘I am meek and humble of heart’ (Matt. 11:29), and again, ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’ (Hos. 6:6). But if he says she is to be absolved, he will not escape the pit of transgression; and he will rightly be condemned as a transgressor of the Law.” Thus they lay snares for the soul of the righteous (Ps. 93:21); sinners watch the righteous and gnash their teeth (Ps. 36:12), not knowing that “a net is cast in vain before the eyes of winged creatures” (Prov. 1:17), and that “he who digs a pit will fall into it” (ibid. 26:27).

But our Ibex lightly leapt over these pits and cast the diggers themselves into them. For he said: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her” (John 8:7), as though saying: “I do not contradict my Law; I do not abandon my mercy. She indeed deserved to be stoned; but she will not be stoned, because no one is found who can justly cast a stone at her.”

6. Do you wish to see still more pits? “Is it lawful,” they say, “to pay tribute to Caesar, or not?” For they had said among themselves: “If he says, ‘It is lawful,’ he will be held guilty as a destroyer of our liberty; for payment of tribute is a sign of servitude. If he says, ‘It is not lawful,’ he will be guilty of treason.” O fools! A fool habitually judges others by himself, and thinks that every wise person is as ignorant as he is of what he himself does not know.

But what does Wisdom say? “I do not diminish liberty; I do not offend majesty; I do not fall into your pits. Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:17, 21). For the righteous God is not offended when he wills each person to receive what is his own. If you render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, Caesar is not offended. If you render to God what he has justly created, you do what is right. Therefore render Caesar the denarius, which bears Caesar’s image; render God the soul, which he created in his own image and likeness—and behold, you will be righteous.

It would be far too long to set forth all the pits which these malicious men dug for our true Vine, since they strove to slander all his words and deeds.

7. But when they saw that their digging around did the Vine no harm, and indeed that while digging they themselves had fallen into the very pits, they labored to dig into and pierce the Vine itself, so that it might at least, after the manner of other trees, incur everlasting dryness. Thus they dug into and pierced not only his hands and feet, but also his side; and with a furious lance they pierced the inmost depths of his most holy heart, which had long before been wounded by the lance of love.

The Bridegroom of love says in the Song of Songs: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart” (Song 4:9). Your bride, your beloved, your sister, wounds your heart, Lord Jesus. What need was there that enemies should wound it further? What are you doing, enemies? If the sweet Jesus’ heart has been wounded—indeed, because it has been wounded—why do you add a second wound? Do you not know that a heart struck by a single wound dies and becomes insensible? The heart of the Lord Jesus is dead because it is wounded. The wound of love has taken possession of the bridegroom Jesus’ heart; the death of love has taken possession of it. How shall another death enter?

“Love is strong as death”—indeed, stronger than death (Song 8:6). For the first death cannot be expelled: that is, love, the slayer of evil deaths, cannot be driven from the dwelling of the heart, which it has acquired for itself by its own wound with inviolable right. If two equally strong persons contend, one inside a house and the other outside, who doubts that the one within will gain the victory? See, then, how great is the power of love which possesses the house of the heart and sweetly kills through its wound—not only in the Lord Jesus, but also in his servants.

8. Let us turn to the martyrs. Though martyrs are terrified, they laugh; they are struck, and rejoice; they are killed, and behold, they triumph. Why? Because, having long been dead through the death of love within their hearts—dead to sins, dead to the world—they became as insensible persons, unable to feel threats, tortures, or death. What wonder? They were dead. “For you are dead,” says the Apostle (Col. 3:3).

A certain fool wisely desired such a death when he said: “May my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my last end be like theirs” (Num. 23:10). A good death, despising death; a good death, conferring eternal life. Thus the heart of Jesus, mortified for us, “accounted as a sheep for the slaughter all day long” (Ps. 43:22), had long before been wounded and was dead. Then bodily death also came, and prevailed for a time, in order to be conquered eternally. It was conquered, because he rose from the dead, and death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6:9).

But since we have once come to the most sweet heart of Jesus, and it is good for us to be here, let us not permit ourselves easily to be torn away from him, of whom it is written: “Those who depart from you shall be written in the earth” (Jer. 17:13). But what of those who draw near? Teach us yourself. You said to those drawing near to you: “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). Let us reconcile these sayings: if those persons are written in heaven, what then of those written on earth? They will surely mourn. But who would not wish to rejoice?

Let us therefore draw near to you, and we shall exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your heart. O how good and delightful it is to dwell in this heart! Your heart, good Jesus, is a good treasure, a good pearl, which we find by digging in the field of your body. Who would cast aside this pearl? Rather, I will give all things, exchange every thought and affection of my mind, and purchase it for myself, casting every thought of mine into the heart of the Lord Jesus; and without deception it will nourish me.

9. At this temple, these Holies of Holies, this ark of the covenant, I shall adore and praise the name of the Lord, saying with David: “I have found my heart, that I may pray to my God” (2 Sam. 7:27). And I have found the heart of the king, brother, and gracious friend, Jesus. Shall I not then adore? Surely I shall pray. For his heart is with me—boldly I say it—if, indeed because, Christ is my head. How can that which belongs to my head not be mine? Just as the eyes of my bodily head are truly my eyes, so too the spiritual heart is my heart. Therefore it is well with me. With Jesus I possess my heart.

And what wonder is this, when the multitude of believers had one heart? (Acts 4:32.) Therefore, having found this heart of yours and mine, most sweet Jesus, I shall pray to you, my God. Only admit my prayers into the sanctuary of your hearing; rather, draw my whole self into your heart. Although the crookedness of my sins hinders me, yet because that heart has been enlarged and expanded by incomprehensible love, and because you alone can make clean what is conceived from unclean seed, so that, having laid aside the burden of my hump, I may pass through the eye of a needle—O Jesus, most beautiful among all beauty—wash me yet more from my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin. Thus purified by you, may I draw near to you, the altogether pure One, and deserve to dwell in your heart all the days of my life, and always both behold and do your will.

10. For this purpose your side was pierced: that an entrance might lie open to us. For this purpose your heart was wounded: that in it, and in you, we might dwell free from outward disturbances. No less, moreover, was it wounded so that through the visible wound we might see the invisible wound of love. How could this burning love be shown more clearly than by his permitting not only his body, but even his very heart, to be wounded by a lance? The bodily wound, therefore, displays the spiritual wound.

Perhaps this is also indicated by the authority cited above, in which “You have wounded” occurs twice. For the sister and bride herself is the cause of each wound—as though the Bridegroom plainly said: “Because you wounded me with the zeal of your love, I was also wounded by a soldier’s lance. For who would permit your heart to be wounded by a stake, unless it had first received that wound of love?” Therefore he says: “You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride; you have wounded my heart” (Song 4:9).

But why “sister and bride”? Could the designation of sister alone, or of bride alone, not sufficiently express the affection of a loving bridegroom? Or why “bride,” rather than “wife,” when the Church—or any faithful soul—ought daily to bear offspring of good works for Christ her bridegroom? I will say it briefly: brides not yet bound by the marriage bond are usually loved more ardently than they are afterward, for with the passing of time love itself settles down. Therefore our Bridegroom, to indicate the greatness of his love, which does not lessen with time, calls his beloved his bride, because his love is ever new.

11. But since brides are also loved carnally, he calls his bride his sister, so that you may perceive nothing carnal in the love of our Bridegroom; for sisters are no longer loved carnally. Thus he says, “You have wounded my heart,” and the rest, as though saying: “Because I love you supremely, as a bride, and chastely, as a sister, my heart has been wounded for you.” Who would not love that wounded heart? Who would not return the love of one who loves so greatly? Who would not embrace one so chaste?

She surely loves him wounded who, wounded by the excess of his love, cries out: “I am wounded by love.” Does she not return the love of her loving Bridegroom, she who says: “Tell my beloved that I languish with love” (Song 5:8)? She embraces him as one whom she loves with fraternal love, who says: “Who will give you to me as a brother, nursing at my mother’s breasts, so that I may find you outside, embrace you, and kiss you, and no one may any longer mock [or: despise] me?” (ibid. 8:1).

But who is “outside”? I think it means outside the body. “While we are in this body, we are away from the Lord.” Who can patiently endure this pilgrimage? It is full of grief for things past, toil in things present, and fear of things to come. Although the Bridegroom sometimes grants himself through the grace of consolation, he nevertheless stands far off, as though behind a wall, this body of sin separating us from him. Nor does he readily offer himself to be touched and kissed, except to that soul which has advanced to such a height of merits that he says to it: “Arise, my beloved, my dove, my beautiful one” (Song 2:13–14). She alone, though rarely, in some manner deeming herself to have grasped him, cries out: “I found him whom my soul loves; I held him, and I will not let him go” (ibid. 3:4).

But one does not easily ascend to this degree. Therefore, while we still remain within—that is, in the body—let us, as much as we can, love, return the love of, and embrace our Wounded One, whose hands and feet, side and heart, the wicked husbandmen dug into. Let us stand firm, that he may deem it worthy to bind our still hard and unrepentant heart by the bond of his love and to wound it with his dart.

## Chapter IV. On the bonds of our Vine: that is, the various bonds and punishments of Christ

12. The Vine is bound. Who does not see the bonds of our Vine? Yet let us consider this binding. First, there was obedience. For he obeyed the Father unto death, even death on a cross (Phil. 2:8). He obeyed his Mother and Joseph, according to the text: “He came to Nazareth with them and was subject to them” (Luke 2:51). He also obeyed earthly authorities by paying the didrachma tax (Matt. 17:23–26).

The second bond was the Virgin’s womb, of which we sing: “Because him whom the heavens could not contain, you bore in your holy womb” (*Responsory for the Nativity of the Lord*). The third was in the manger, according to the words: “The infant cries, shut within narrow mangers; the Virgin Mother binds his limbs in swaddling clothes, tightly girding feet, hands, and legs with bands” (*Hymn of the Office of the Passion*).

The fourth bond was the rope by which he was bound when he was seized; for this is what you have: “Then”—that is, when he had been betrayed—“they laid hands on Jesus and bound him” (Matt. 26:50; Mark 14:46). O King of kings and Lord of lords, what have you to do with bonds? Vines are bound so that, if they lie upon the ground, they may not be diminished or their fruit spoiled. But his fruit was, and is, incorruptible. Why, then, is he bound?

A certain noble king, when he had been struck by a human arrow and was urged to allow himself to be bound until the arrow could be cut out—though the slightest movement might bring on death—said: “It is not fitting that a king be bound.”

> [Note: A similar saying of Alexander is found in Quintus Curtius, book IX, ch. 11; likewise of Gaius Marius in Plutarch, *Roman Apophthegms*.]

Let a king’s power be free and ever unharmed. O God of gods, how greatly, then, was your freedom and power diminished! You are bound with so many bonds, though you alone possess the power of binding and loosing. Yet you were bound because of your mercy, that you might free us from our miseries. O how cruel were the bonds of those most cruel men, by which they bound the gentlest Lamb!

With the eyes of my mind I see you, Lord Jesus, constrained by such hard cords, drawn like a thief to the judgment of the chief priest; and then I see you brought to Pilate. I shudder, marvel, and would fail in my wonder, did I not clearly recognize that you had first been bound in your heart by the bonds of love; these enabled you lightly to submit to more grievous bonds. Thanks be to your bonds, good Jesus, which so powerfully burst ours.

13. The fifth bond was that by which he was tied to the column when he was scourged. Indeed, the scourges themselves, which encircled his body, may not unfittingly be called bonds. Though savage, hard, and unjust, I love the bonds of those scourges which were permitted to touch your most sacred body, and which, O good Jesus, were abundantly soaked in your most pure blood. For if your blood was poured out so copiously in the scourging that the column, still sprinkled with its drops, is said to preserve red traces, how much blood should I believe clung to the very scourges as they tore your most gentle body? The Lord was scourged so harshly that his blood sprang upward into the air.

See, moreover, how fittingly the fact that a vine is tied to a stake corresponds with this binding. For what else is meant by the stake but the column to which the Lord Jesus is understood to have been bound? As the vine is tied to the stake, so Christ is tied to the column.

14. The sixth bond was that crown of thorns which, enclosing that lovable head with great bitterness and leaving in it the marks of many sharp points, drew out drops of blood and, I think, sent them down over the venerable face, scarcely yet dried from the spittle of the Jews. This bond was cruel; besides the sufferings he endured on the wood, it possessed much honor and adornment.

O Lord Jesus Christ, King of glory, crown of all who confess you, follow you, fight for you, live for you, and abide in you: who consigned you to so bitter a bond of shame? Behold, shame covers your head and your lovely face. A mockery of honor in the form of a crown is pressed upon you by a perverse and bitter generation; but pain and shame contend against you through the thorns’ sharp points. I do not know by which you are punished more severely. The crown brings mockery; the thorns bring piercing pain.

“Go forth, daughters of Zion, and see King Solomon in the diadem with which his mother crowned him on the day of his betrothal and on the day of his heart’s joy” (Song 3:11). Let every soul which confesses itself a daughter of Zion—that is, of the Church—go forth from worldly cares and vain thoughts, and behold by inward contemplation King Solomon, that is, Christ Jesus, who is our peace, destroying enmities and restoring friendship between God and humankind.

15. See him, happy soul, in the diadem with which his mother—that is, the synagogue, the people of the Jews—crowned him. O bitter mother! What has this good son of yours done, that he should even be bound with bonds? He is the one who frees prisoners, raises up the crushed, receives strangers, and consoles orphans and widows; and did he deserve to be bound? Is this the dowry, these the little gifts, which you confer upon his marriage?

For this day is the day of his betrothal: a day of indignation and blasphemy, a day of tribulation and misery, a day of blows and pain, a day of bonds and death—this is the day of his betrothal. By this pledge, faithful soul, your precious Bridegroom has pledged himself to you; and today he went forth crowned as a bridegroom. Crowned, I say, not with gold or jewels, but with thorns. Nor was the purple of the mocking garment lacking. For they put around him a scarlet cloak, although he himself dyed the garment of his body far more nobly by the outpouring of his most precious blood. Purple is dyed no more than twice; but he dyed the purple garment of his body not merely twice, but a third time in a torrent of blood. Behold, O bride, your Bridegroom is reddened in sweat, in scourging, and in crucifixion.

Raise the eyes of your mind and see whether this is your Bridegroom’s tunic or not. Behold, a most savage beast has condemned your son, your brother, your Bridegroom. Who could restrain groans and tears here? Who would not grieve here? For as it is devout to rejoice for Jesus, so it is devout to weep for the devout Jesus.

16. The seventh bond by which he was bound upon the cross was iron. This bond was much more savage than the others, for it not only separated the joints of his most holy hands and feet, but also separated that most pure soul from the most spotless lodging of its body.

Now also, daughters of Zion, go forth and behold our peaceable one, fighting for our freedom, dying in battle. Behold the author of our life entering the gates of life for us, that he may call us back to the way of life. Behold the most cruel bonds, the iron nails, cruelly piercing the feet and hands which worked our salvation in the midst of the earth. Behold the wood of the cross set into our bread—the whitest bread, the delicate bread, the bread of angels, who came down from heaven to give himself to us as food and to refresh our souls, continually subject to toil, with himself, not with food from another. By incorporating himself into us, he refashions not himself into our flesh, but us into his Spirit.

Behold how the righteous one is bound, how our freest and best Bridegroom is reckoned among the wicked. Our life dies, not for his own needs, but for ours. Shed streams of tears for him dying in such bonds, since he himself first wept. Be still, and see how bitterly, how shamefully, he is condemned to death. For he still endures and carefully looks to see whether there is anyone who will grieve with him; whether he may find one to wipe away the streams of blood, to wrap him when taken down from the cross in a clean linen—not of cloth, but of heart—and to follow him weeping to the tomb with the blessed women who weep.

17. Whatever soul does these things continually, I hope will one day deserve to be refreshed by the most joyful gladness of the resurrection. “For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him” (2 Tim. 2:12). The bride in the Song of love shows this well, first saying: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts,” and then adding: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus” (Song 1:12–13).

What is a bundle of myrrh? Myrrh, being bitter, signifies the bitterness of the Passion; while a bundle shows the gathering together of many sufferings. Thus the Bridegroom becomes a bundle of myrrh to his bride when she calls to mind his affliction by manifold injuries—some of which have already been enumerated and others are yet to be enumerated.

But what are the bride’s breasts, between which she says that he will dwell? The bride’s two breasts are prosperity and adversity. She is nourished by these as by breasts, being comforted by adversity lest she be lifted up in prosperity. She places her beloved between these breasts when she remembers him both in adversity and in prosperity. The result is that he who had just been a bundle of myrrh—that is, who had made the bride’s mind bitter with the bitterness of his sufferings—suddenly becomes a cluster of Cyprus, containing in himself the wine of gladness and joy. This occurs when she sees in the glory and honor of his resurrection triumph the Bridegroom whom she had seen oppressed by so many injuries and condemned to a most shameful death; when she sees him seated at the Father’s right hand together with the humanity which he assumed; and when she confidently trusts that she herself will most certainly enter, through various tribulations, into that same joy of her Lord.

18. Let us therefore also go forth, according to the admonitions of Paul the Apostle, with our good Bridegroom Jesus outside the camp—that is, outside the desires of this present world—bearing with him the reproach of the cross and the harshness of his bonds (Heb. 13:13). For it is not fitting that a delicate member should be under a crucified head; nor does that member show itself to belong to the body of the head which has not suffered with the head.

Let us therefore be bound by the bonds of the Passion of good Jesus, that we may also be able to be bound with him by the bonds of love. For he, bound by the bonds of love, was drawn from heaven to earth in order to undergo the bonds of the Passion. Conversely, we who desire to be drawn from earth to heaven must first bind the bond of the Passion to our head, so that through it, belonging to the bonds of love, we may become one with him, according to his prayer to the Father: “I ask, Father, that those whom you have given me, established in love, may be one in us, as you and I are one” (John 17:11, 20–21).

What is more glorious than this unity? What more could you desire or possess? You shall be one with the Bridegroom. O happy, happier—indeed, happiest of all—unity! The Apostle felt himself united to Christ by this unity when he said: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or famine? Or persecution? Or danger? Or nakedness? Or the sword? I am certain that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers, neither height nor depth nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love which is in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8:35, 38–39).

Let us desire with all our longings to be joined by these bonds of love to our Bridegroom and Lord, so that, following in his footsteps, we may arrive where he is, he who said: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John 12:26).

## Chapter V. On the cultivation and beauty of our Vine: that is, on the inner and outer beauty of Christ

[Col. 0648A]

19. Having seen in part the things externally applied for the cultivation of a vine, let us now turn our mind to the vine itself, so that through certain resemblances of it we may contemplate our Vine more properly and more closely. The whole trunk of the vine is found more misshapen than other trees and shrubs, and seems almost entirely useless and contemptible, neither pleasing in appearance nor agreeable to behold.

What shall we say here? What should the body of our Vine, the Lord Jesus, signify, unless something that seems greatly at odds with this ugliness and the beauty of him of whom it is written: “You are fairer in form than the children of men” (Ps. 44:3)? There are some who refer these words not to the outer but to the inner person—that is, to the soul or to the divinity—in which he surpassed not only the children of men but also the children of God, namely the angelic spirits themselves. For “he was made so much better than the angels as he inherited a more excellent name than they” (Heb. 1:4).

Lest we seem to contradict this view, authorities are readily available to us. Yet I know that many who have not become altogether spiritual think otherwise, imagining some spiritual [perhaps: special] beauty in the Lord’s body. If they hear that the Lord himself was contemptible in appearance, they cannot bear it patiently; and, even if their tongues are silent, they contradict it with resentment and inward agitation, failing to attend to what is written: “It is the Spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:64).

They do not hear Isaiah—or hear him unwillingly—saying of him: “Behold, we saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty; his appearance was not in him, and we desired him, despised and the lowest of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity; his face was as though hidden and despised. Therefore we did not esteem him. And we accounted him as though he were a leper, stricken by God and humbled” (Isa. 53:2–4). Behold how the Prophet describes him. What could be clearer? And indeed he was such in the eyes of unbelieving and fleshly people, who knew only how to look upon flesh.

20. This we can also establish by clear arguments: first, through the affection of compassion; then, through the wasting caused by the Passion. Since he truly took on our affections, let us see how people are commonly affected regarding those whom they love, that we may come from what is known to what is unknown. Who does not know that a person, moved by such affection and grief for a friend in danger, often suffers injury to his own body? If one human does this for another human being, how much do you think the God-man Jesus did for humankind? If through compassion you incur bodily danger for one person, what do you think the Lord Jesus endured for all people? For all were his own, and all were mortally sick.

Certainly we know that the Apostle Paul said of himself: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29). And truly he was weakened to such an extent that, as he himself admits, his bodily presence was contemptible (ibid. 10:10); and, as he says, “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6:14). The world was crucified to him because he regarded all that belonged to the world as dead. But he too was crucified to the world, because, worn down and wasted in body by the repeated weaknesses both of compassion and suffering, the world abhorred him, finding nothing in him that belonged to itself.

If, then, Paul became weak with the weak, being a fellow servant and brother among fellow servants and brothers, what did gracious Jesus, Lord and Father, do for his creatures and children? Paul burned as though set ablaze by a ray of the sun: how greatly, then, do you think the Sun himself blazed? If one who possessed a spark of love was inflamed by compassionate affection even to such weakness, what should be thought of Love itself, from whose fullness all have received?

21. There can be no doubt that he endured an incomparable weakness and wasting of body, he who came even to endure the cross; and that he was more exhausted than others in proportion as the affection of compassion was greater in him, who observed not only deeds but even thoughts. The Lord’s own saying supports these arguments: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, how often I wished to gather your children together as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23:37).

Let us see why the Lord chose to compare himself to a hen rather than another animal. According to the understanding of the holy Fathers, this was done to express his incomparable loving compassion. For no animal is moved with such compassion toward its young as a hen. Its whole body becomes bristling, its voice hoarse; it burns wholly in spirit, becomes weak in all its members, and reaches the point of utter exhaustion. If a hen, an irrational animal, thus suffers with its chicks, how much do you think the most good Jesus suffered with the human race? To what exhaustion and weakness do you think he came? How greatly do you think he was worn down by emaciation, he who is known to have grieved for all? Hence Isaiah says: “Truly he bore our weaknesses and carried our sins” (Isa. 53:4).

22. But now let us turn to the wasting of the Passion. By “Passion” we do not mean merely that one day on which he died, but his whole life. For Christ’s entire life was cross and martyrdom. Let us therefore speak briefly, but linger longer in meditation, over how great was his restraint in fasting; how prolonged his vigils; how frequent his prayers; how constant he was in labor and the sweat of his brow, as he went about villages and towns everywhere, preaching the Gospel and healing; and how often he endured hunger and thirst—he, the living Bread, the Fountain of water springing up into eternal life.

Let us consider that other fast of forty days and forty nights, after which he hungered. Let us meet him as he returns from the wilderness to people, and contemplate that lovable face afflicted by such fasting. The Evangelist fittingly adds after the fast, “He hungered” (Matt. 4:2), so that you may know that Jesus fasted not by the power of his divinity, but according to the nature of his humanity. For what great thing would it have been had he fasted forty days in the strength of his divinity, in which he never hungered?

23. But let us now come to that agony of the final day, and we shall be unable to overlook the causes of the disfigured body. Let our meditation therefore begin at the very place where, as he himself testified, when he began to be afraid and to be distressed, his soul was sorrowful even unto death (Mark 14:33–34). The bloody sweat of him who prayed and agonized copiously drenched his limbs, so that it did not merely trickle down, but ran in drops to the ground (Luke 22:43–44). Let us proceed now and review the afflictions of that night [Col. 0650B]: how he was seized, bound, dragged, beaten, spat upon, struck with fists and slaps, crowned with thorns, his head beaten with a reed, torn by most cruel scourges, burdened with his own cross—first carrying that which was soon afterwards to carry him. Behold Jesus thus. What place of delight is this? What beauty of appearance is here? Who would seek beauty of form in a body so slaughtered?

24. But let us come to the end. Jesus is stripped naked. Why? So that you may be able to behold the disfigurement of his most pure body. Therefore good Jesus is stripped. Alas for me! He who clothed the heavens with diverse stars, stripped before the cross, naked as he was, livid, is fastened to the cross. Alas! The brightness of eternal light grows dark in the flesh, for the salvation of flesh; and the face which Cherubim and Seraphim [Col. 0650C] desire to behold was swollen with tears. The Lord is stripped, who, reigning before the ages, put on beauty and strength, to whom we sing: “You have put on confession and beauty; clothed with light as with a garment” (Ps. 103:1–2).

437 He is made a spectacle and a reproach to the world and to men; he is made as a portent to many, and our Head, our joy, our honour, good Jesus, becomes a shaking of the head among the peoples. But why do I delay? When he is raised upon the cross, the hands and feet of that most good and gracious man Jesus are pierced. Blood is poured out, if any yet remained. Our Mediator stands before the sight of his Father in brokenness, so that he may turn away his wrath, lest he destroy us. Truly he does not lose heart: he stands steadfast even in the constancy of good will. O [Col. 0650D] how I behold you, sweet Jesus! O sweetest and most loving Jesus, who consigned you to a death so bitter and so hateful? O sole Saviour of our ancient wounds, who drew you on to endure wounds so not only dreadful but shameful? O sweetest Vine, good Jesus, does your vineyard, which you transplanted from Egypt, render you this fruit? You had waited patiently until this day of your marriage that it might bear grapes; but it bore thorns. For it crowned you with thorns and surrounded you with the thorns of its sins. Behold into what bitterness the vine has been changed: no longer yours, but another’s. For it denied you, saying and crying, “We have no king but Caesar!” (John 14:15).

25. Therefore, having cast you outside the vineyard of the city and [Col. 0651A] of your fellowship, the sacrilegious husbandmen killed you—not swiftly, but after you had been worn down by the prolonged torment of the cross, and tortured alike by the many wounds of scourges and nails. O how many are your assailants, Lord Jesus! Your Father strikes you, who “did not spare his own Son,” that is, you, “but gave you up for us all” (Rom. 8:32). You strike yourself: for you deliver your soul unto death, which no one can take from you apart from you (John 10:18). The impious disciple strikes you by betrayal and a false kiss. The Jew strikes you with fists and slaps. The Gentiles strike you with scourges and nails. Behold how greatly you are struck and humiliated. O how many are your assailants, and how many your betrayers! Your heavenly Father gave you up, because, as has been said, he gave you up for us all. Thus one of [Col. 0651B] your servants says joyfully concerning you: “Who loved us and gave himself up for us” (Eph. 5:2). O truly wonderful exchange! The king gave himself for the servant, God for man, the Creator for the creature, the innocent for the guilty.

You therefore gave yourself into the hands of that betrayer, the false disciple. He gave you up to the Jews, and those most wicked betrayers gave you up to the Gentiles to be mocked, spat upon, scourged, and crucified. You spoke and foretold these things (Mark 10:33–34), and behold, they have come to pass. For when all things had been completed, behold, you were crucified. Nor was it enough that you were wounded: over and above the pain of your wounds they added this also, giving you, thirsty as you were, wine mixed with myrrh and gall to drink.

26. I grieve over you, my Lord, king, teacher, and [Col. 0651C] father—indeed, also brother—my Lord Jesus Christ, exceedingly beloved beyond the love of women, whose arrow never turned backward (2 Sam. 1:26, 22). For your arrows, that is, your teaching, are sharp, because your word is living and effective, and more piercing than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. 4:12). Nor does your shield turn aside in battle. For you have crowned us with the shield of your good will. The spear of your prayers was not turned away, because you even prayed for transgressors that they might not perish; how much more for those whom you loved? You are stronger than the lion. For you, the lion of the tribe of Judah, overcame that lion which goes about roaring and seeking whom it may devour (Rev. 5:5). You are swifter than the eagle. For you rejoiced as a giant to run [Col. 0651D] the way (Ps. 18:6), to fulfil the mystery of your incarnation, until, like an eagle provoking its young, you spread the wings of your arms upon the cross; and, flying over us, you took us up and bore us upon your shoulders, in your strength, to your holy dwelling-place, to the house of your intimacy and glory. There, concerning the lost and found sheep and drachma, you made a feast for your neighbours and friends, your most blessed spirits, joyfully inviting them to share your rejoicing, making joy in heaven over a sinner who repents. And though you are such and so great, you are condemned to a most shameful death; and, commending your spirit into the hands of the Father, with bowed head you expire.

27. Come, I beseech you, and mourn with him, all you who desire to rejoice in the Lord. Consider our mighty one [Col. 0652A], how he has been crushed; our beloved, how he has been 438 miserably disfigured; our peacemaker, how he has been slain in battle. Where is the rosy hue? Where the youthful brightness? Where will you find beauty in a body so broken? Behold, our days have failed like the day of the Lord Jesus, who alone is the day without darkness, and his bones have dried up like a firebrand. He was struck like grass, and his heart withered; he was lifted up and grievously cast down. Yet in his outward beauty he retained at once true inward beauty and glory.

Do not therefore lose heart on his account in your tribulations, because all who looked only at outward things saw upon the cross him who was beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, and saw him as having neither appearance nor beauty; but his face [Col. 0652B] was despised as though disfigured. Yet from this disfigurement of our Redeemer flowed the price of our beauty—but of inward beauty. For “all the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14). She perceived this, who cries out in the Song of Solomon: “I am black, but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the skins of Solomon” (Song 1:14). Unless the body of the Lord Jesus had been disfigured—of whose blackness we have above spoken in part—who could recount his inward beauty, since in him is all the fullness of divinity? Let us therefore be disfigured outwardly in body with disfigured Jesus, that inwardly in soul we may be re-formed with beautiful Jesus. Let us be conformed in our body to the body of our Vine, so that he may re-form the body of our humanity, configured to the body of his glory. Let us be imitators [Col. 0652C] of the Apostle Paul, as he was of Christ (1 Cor. 11:1), who says of himself, “I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. 2:19); and elsewhere, “I always bear the marks of Jesus Christ in my body” (ibid. 6:17). Well did he bear in his body the imprint of the passion of Jesus Christ, to whom the world was dead, and he to the world. He was made dark, because the sun of Christ’s passion and love had changed his colour.

Yet it should be understood that what we have said concerning the disfigurement of the beautiful body has been said not of a natural but of an accidental disfigurement of the Lord: we do not accuse him of a defect of nature, but commend the love shown in his passion.

## CHAPTER VI. On the leaves of the vine generally; that is, on Christ’s various sayings which pertain to the commendation of the virtues.

[Col. 0652D]

28. The leaves of the vine are superior to the leaves of almost all trees. What, then, is commended in the leaves but the words of our true Vine, most gracious Jesus? The vine excels in its leaves; the Lord Jesus excels in his words. This was perceived by the officers of the Jews, who, having been sent to bring Jesus, returned and, when reproved, said: “Never has a man spoken thus” (John 7:46). Seeing the beauty of the leaves, they did not accuse the weakness of the trunk; indeed, through the leaves they perceived that something other than what appeared to sight lay hidden in the weak body. Peter also perceived it. When many were withdrawing from the Lord Jesus and he asked the twelve [Col. 0653A] Apostles, “Do you also wish to depart?” he replied: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (ibid. 6:68–69); and to whom shall we go? Far be it from us. As if he said: You have most beautiful leaves, which protect us from every heat. Give us, therefore, another more beautiful—that is, better—than yourself, and we shall go away from you to him. Since you, who can do all things, cannot give such a one, to whom shall we go if we leave you?

She also perceived the power of these leaves, that is, of the words of gracious Jesus, who, while he was speaking to the crowds, delighted in the singular beauty of the leaves, did not merely think it silently, but raised her voice and said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you, and the breasts which you sucked” (Luke 11:27). Truly blessed—indeed, most blessed—was the earth which bore such a vine: the Virgin Mary, mother of Jesus. Truly you also are blessed, [Col. 0653B] who, considering the beauty of the leaves, alone among so many snares of slanderers boldly bore witness to the truth. But I believe that even now you have a great reward, and will have a greater one, for this confession: Truth itself, to which you bore witness, now confesses you before his Father, and will nevertheless confess this when he says to his slanderers: “I do not know you. Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” But to those known to him he will say: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:12, 41, 34).

Peter, John, and Matthew saw the greenness of the leaves of the true Vine; at one summons, the former left their nets and the latter his tax-office. Who could sufficiently enumerate the power of gracious Jesus’ words? What power of words is there which is not commended by his words? None at all [Col. 0653C].

439 29. Do you wish to hear briefly those words which, like leaves, grant us refreshment from the heat of vices? In commendation of humility, he says: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be your servant”; and: “The Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his soul as a ransom for many” (ibid. 20:26, 28); and likewise: “Whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (ibid. 23:12 and 11:29).

In commendation of meekness against anger: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart”; and likewise: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.”

In commendation of love against envy: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you and slander you, [Col. 0653D] that you may be children of your Father, who makes his sun rise upon good and evil, and rains upon just and unjust” (ibid. 5:4, 44–45).

In commendation of readiness for spiritual exercises against sloth, he says to the disciples: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (ibid. 26:41); and elsewhere: “One ought always to pray and never to fail” (Luke 18:1). Here it is understood that prayer is not only of the voice, but of devotion. For we cannot always cry out by the movement of our lips; but we can always burn with good desire. The Lord showed this when he spoke to silent Moses: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. 14:15). He calls the desire of a holy man a cry, because his tongue was certainly silent. Hence the Lord says in the Psalm: “The Lord heard the desire of the poor; [Col. 0654A] your ear heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. 9:17).

In commendation of generosity against avarice: “Give alms, and all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41); and: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). From the riches of iniquity—that is, inequality, namely, those things which abound to us while others lack them—we make friends for ourselves when we distribute them to the poor; so that, if we are now merciful to them, through them we may obtain mercy after this life. For “blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7).

But in commendation of abstinence against gluttony: “Take heed,” he says, “lest your hearts be weighed down by feasting and drunkenness, and the sudden day come upon you” [Col. 0654B] (Luke 21:34). And he added the parable of the rich man who feasted splendidly every day and who, when dead, while in torments sought a drop of water from Lazarus, at rest after death, but could not obtain it, receiving everlasting evils for a transient pleasure now past (ibid. 16:19, 26).

In commendation of chastity against lust: “You have heard,” he says, “that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:27–28). Let our eyes be covered by the leaf of this word, lest, if perhaps they are opened with insufficient caution, what Jeremiah says should happen: “Death has ascended through our windows” (Jer. 11:21). The windows of our soul are indeed the openings of our senses—[Col. 0654C] namely, of the eyes, ears, nostrils, and mouth. Through these, as through certain windows, death ascends whenever they are opened to desire any criminal things. By these and many other words, as by the shade of certain leaves, we are refreshed from the heat of vices through our Vine, gracious Jesus, and revived in the temperate air of the virtues.

## CHAPTER VII. On the shade of the vine’s leaves; that is, on the words uttered by Christ when raised upon the cross.

30. But since the shade of vine leaves is usually more pleasant when the vine itself is raised and stretched this way and that over a framework of wood, let us see whether our true Vine was ever raised and stretched out, and [Col. 0654D] let us contemplate whether he then put forth any leaves of sweet words for our protection. That our Vine was raised up, he himself testifies concerning himself, saying: “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John 12:32); likewise: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (ibid. 3:14). Therefore he was raised up because he was exalted. It is manifest that this exaltation was said of the cross.

See how suitably the framework of wood over which vines are usually raised signifies the cross. For the timbers are latticed, that is, arranged crosswise, and so the raised vine is more fittingly stretched over them. The timbers of the cross are latticed; upon it our Vine, good Jesus, is raised and stretched out by his arms and his whole body. For he was stretched out upon the cross [Col. 0655A] so greatly that all his limbs could be counted. Thus he said through the prophet: “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:17–18). How greatly he was pierced has been said above; but how greatly he was stretched out is now added: “They counted all my bones.” As if he said: I was stretched so far to right and left, and from top to bottom, that, with my body stretched out like the skin of a drum, all my bones could easily be counted.

Look upon the face of your Christ, O Christian soul; lift your eyes to his torments, not without tears, and your contrite heart, not without groaning; and see how great a tribulation and pain he found while seeking you, in order to find you. Open your eyes, therefore, that you may look upon the face [Col. 0655B] of your Christ. Listen with attentive ears to the word which he utters amid such great pain, and, once heard, store it away as a most precious treasure in the chamber of your heart. Behold, he is placed upon the cruel bed of his death—I mean the cross. Keep the final commands of your bridegroom, if you wish to obtain an inheritance undefiled and unfading. Nor are the words he spoke while dying many; they will be easily kept by Christ’s willing bride.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the vine’s leaves in particular, or on the first word of Christ hanging on the cross: “Father, forgive them,” etc. Luke, chapter 23, v. 34.

31. There are seven little words which our Vine, when raised upon the cross [Col. 0655C], put forth like seven ever-green leaves. Your bridegroom became a lyre to you: the cross had the form of wood, while his body supplied the role of strings stretched across the flat surface of the wood. For unless he had been fastened to the wood, stretched out, he would by no means have produced the sound of words as one playing a lyre, by which you might take still greater delight. Observe more carefully. A lyre has seven strings. It sings to you, plays for you, invites you to listen—you who ought rather to have invited him to speak. Therefore behold the leaves of your Vine, and remember to commit them indelibly to memory. These seven are arranged in different ways, and their order cannot easily be discovered, since they were not arranged by one Evangelist. We therefore arrange them according to what we have been able to ascertain.

[Col. 0655D]

32. We learn from Luke that, when Jesus had been crucified, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” O green leaf! O word fitting for the Word of the highest Father! The good teacher does what he commanded. He prays not only for those persecuting and slandering him, but even for those killing him. Store this leaf in the treasury of your heart, so that whenever you encounter enemies, you may be able to pour forth the memory of the abundance of Jesus’ sweetness, always setting the leaf before you like a shield against the assaults of enemies. Christ prays for those who kill him: will you not pray for slanderers?

33. But let us examine the prayer itself more carefully. “Father,” he says. Why does he use the name Father? Children who wish to make some request more affectionately are accustomed to name their father, so that they may call to mind his natural love and more easily obtain the effect of their petition. So too our Redeemer, compassionate and merciful, patient and abounding in mercy, patient and abounding in mercy, and gracious in all things—even though he knew himself always heard by the Father—nevertheless, to commend to us with what affection one ought to pray for enemies, used the name of love [Col. 0656A]. As though he said: By the fatherly love through which we are one, I beseech you to hear me by forgiving these my killers. Acknowledge your Son’s friendship, so that you may forgive his enemies.

And he adds why forgiveness should be granted: “For they do not know what they are doing.” What shall we say here? Did they not know that they were crucifying him whom they crucified? By no means; but they did not know who he was whom they were killing. For “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8). They did not know what they were doing, because they did not know how greatly they sinned.

This is how you must think, this is how you must pray, you who desire to be called the bride of the Lord. When enemies rage against you, speak against you, threaten you, inflict losses upon you, strike you in the face, indeed even kill you, remember the leaf [Col. 0656B] of your Vine; recall the sound of your lyre; follow—that is, imitate—your bridegroom, and say from your whole heart: “O bridegroom, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”; that is, they do not know how greatly they sin. For if they knew how great a blessedness they lose and how great an unhappiness they incur by sinning, they certainly would not sin. For what incites all men to sin except ignorance of the good that is lost and of the evil incurred by sinning? By sinning, the supreme good, God, is lost; the punishment of Gehenna is acquired. No one desires this exchange unless utterly mad. And truly, whoever knowingly lose the delights of heaven by sinning and plunge into the punishments of hell are mad: therefore they do not know what they are doing.

Thus such persons must be forgiven, both for our salvation and for their ignorance, and prayer must be offered for them with great confidence, because prayers of this kind forcefully break into the Lord’s ears. Certainly he hears others, he in whom he willed himself to be heard. And he was heard when, at Peter’s preaching, three thousand on one day and [Col. 0656C] four thousand on another day of those who had shouted for the Lord’s death were converted (Acts 2:41; 4:4). What joy there is in heaven when one who has been killed, or any injured person, leads his killer or assailant to heaven by his prayers! O how great was Stephen’s rejoicing at Paul’s conversion! Converted to the faith through Stephen’s prayers, Paul was afterwards stoned for Christ’s faith as he himself had stoned Stephen, and endured for Christ many evils which he had formerly inflicted upon the saints. Let us therefore also follow this course by praying for enemies, so that together with them we may deserve to obtain eternal salvation.

## CHAPTER IX. On the second leaf of the vine, or on Christ’s second word on the cross: “Today you shall be with me in paradise.” Luke, chapter 23, v. 43.

[Col. 0657A]

34. The second leaf of our Vine, and the second string of our lyre, is the second word of the crucified Lord, which he said to the thief who confessed him and sought fellowship with the crucified one: “Amen, I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise.” How green is this leaf! O what sweetness this string resounds! How suddenly an enemy became a friend, an outsider a member of the household, a stranger a neighbour, a thief a confessor! O what confidence the thief possessed! Conscious to himself of every evil and of no good, a transgressor of the law, a robber of another’s life and goods, set at the gates [Col. 0657B] of death, at the end of life, despairing of the present life, he does not fear to seek and conceive the hope of the future life, which he had so often forfeited and had never deserved. Who could despair while the thief hopes?

But it is worthwhile carefully to consider what this thief was like, lest, if we do not know the basis of his hope, we fall into the vice of presumption. All friends, neighbours, and acquaintances—brothers also, indeed the very disciples, unanimous and chosen from the world by the Lord Jesus Christ—amid the distress of so many pressures, such confusion, and such reproaches, when the shepherd was struck, were scattered like wandering sheep. The disciple whom Jesus loved had also fled. That ardent disciple followed from afar, forgetful of the divine signs which they had so often seen the Saviour perform—indeed, which they themselves had performed in his name [Col. 0657C]. And now the thief, amid so many reproaches and miseries, indeed amid so many torments of cross and death, confesses one whom he had not previously known, and confidently seeks help from one who seemed to need help. Which of the disciples was inflamed with such boldness? All fled from him whom they had confessed while he lived; but this man, who had denied him living, confesses him dying.

35. He prays in faith, hope, and love, saying: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom.” He surely believes in him whom he calls Lord and King. Who asks for what he does not hope for? And he loves him to whom he desires to be joined. What would that good Father deny such a petitioner, he who had prompted him [Col. 0657D] to ask, especially as he sat upon the bridal seat on his wedding day? The bridal seat was the cross, upon which the true bridegroom joined his bride, the Church, to himself, giving her the earnest of his own sacred blood poured out. Therefore Christ heard the soul, now no longer of a thief but of his confessor—his bride—and strengthened her prayer with a fitting answer: “Amen, I say to you”—“truly I say to you”—“today you shall be with me in paradise.”

To whom is this “you” addressed? To you who confessed me upon the cross of torments: you shall be with me in the paradise of delights. “With me,” he says. Wondrous graciousness! He does not say merely, “You shall be in paradise,” or “You shall be with the angels,” but “You shall be with me.” You shall be satisfied with him whom you desire; you shall see in majesty him whom you confess placed in weakness. Nor do I defer what I promise, for today [Col. 0658A] you shall be with me. But good and sweet Jesus hears quickly, promises quickly, gives quickly. Who could despair of one so pious in hearing, so swift in promising, so ready in rendering? We have hoped in you, who know your sweet name, because you do not forsake those who seek you. Therefore we come to you, O good Jesus, with such mind as we can, seated upon the throne of majesty, praying that by you and to you we may deserve to be brought in where your thief entered after confessing you upon the throne of the cross.

## CHAPTER X. On the third leaf of the vine; that is, Christ’s third word on the cross: “Woman, behold your son,” etc. John, chapter 19, vv. 26–27.

36. Let us now prepare both the sight and hearing of our heart to see the third leaf of our Vine. “Woman,” he says, “behold your son. Behold your mother.” A good and sweet word, a wonderful word, containing a great affection of pious love! Certainly we read that the Lord Jesus, especially once he had reached mature age, remained in more familiar closeness with his most beloved Mother, ate with her more frequently, and addressed her more gently than others. But with what great affection of love he had been toward his Mother, when he was about to depart bodily, he disclosed in brief words.

And, leaving aside the passion of his cross, how greatly do you think his most gentle heart was affected by mutual compassion for his blessed Mother, when he knew perfectly that it was pierced through by so powerful a sword of his own suffering? Maternal compassion increased the suffering of his wounds. With a most broken heart, clasped hands, eyes flowing with a torrent [Col. 0658C] of tears, a drawn face, a plaintive voice, and all the strength of her heart exhausted, she saw him courageously as she stood by while he hung there. How often do you think she lifted her modest eyes toward those cruel things?—if indeed she ever turned them away, or could behold them through such an overwhelming flood of tears. How often do you think that, because of virginal modesty and the immensity of her pain, she stood, as I suppose, with covered head, groaning as she mourned her son and saying, “Jesus, my son; Jesus, my son! Who will grant that I may die with you and for you, my sweet son Jesus?” How often do you believe she could have fainted from the immensity of grief—she whom I greatly marvel was not actually dead? Living, she was dying; by living, she endured a pain crueler than death [Col. 0658D].

But lest she fail by dying, she was strengthened by her Son for that very mortality. She was strengthened inwardly, and outwardly piously consoled both by words and by deeds. How did his Mother stand beside the cross of Jesus? Truly she stood beside the cross, because, more than the others, the Mother bore her Son’s cross with greater pain. Others also stood there, but she was the nearest.

37. Therefore, when Jesus saw his Mother and the disciple whom he loved standing there, he said to his Mother: “Woman, behold your son.” But to the disciple: “Behold your mother.” As if he said: You are deprived of me bodily as a son; therefore I give you as a son this friend beloved above all others, whose presence may console you meanwhile, while I am absent. But you are deprived of me as a father; therefore I give you this Mother most dear to me as your mother. Preserve the rights [Col. 0659A] of mutual love toward one another, you having him as your son, and you her as your mother.

O how generous you became at your marriage, king and bridegroom, good Jesus! How lavishly you gave away everything that you possessed! Behold, to your very crucifiers you gave the affection of prayer; to the thief, paradise; to your Mother, a son; to the son, a mother; to the dead, life; to the hands of the Father, your soul; to the whole world, signs of your power. To redeem the servant, you poured out not a part but all your blood from many wide openings. To your betrayer you gave the punishment due to his guilt; to the earth you gave your body, not to undergo corruption, but only for a time.

38. But this moves me: when he had said, “Woman, behold your son,” he added, “Behold your mother”; although, even if he had not added this, it would necessarily have followed that she was the mother 443 of him who had been given to her as a son [Col. 0659B]. Yet this seems to commend to me the affection of mutual love. For there are some who wish to be loved by everyone, but embrace no one with reciprocal affection. They wish their labours and pains to be relieved; and while many bear them, they themselves are unwilling to bear anyone’s burdens, and so forth. For Christ neither taught nor did this. He bore your burdens, inviting you to bear his also—that is, to imitate his sufferings. For Christ suffered, leaving us an example, that we might follow in his steps (1 Pet. 2:21).

This too he taught when he mutually entrusted the Mother to the disciple and the disciple to the Mother: clearly, not wishing spiritual love to remain cold on one side, but that, sleeping together—that is, resting together in true and pure love—they might warm one another; that is, might mutually inflame each other to the exercises of love [Col. 0659C]. For this is an effective sign of true and pure love: those who are spiritually joined through pure love inflame one another to spiritual exercises, so that they may delight to pray more devoutly, kneel more often, and receive bodily discipline more frequently.
