Especially, each loving person should neither envy nor fail to rejoice if a third or fourth person, or more, join themselves in love to the one whom they love—provided that they are such persons as are not suspect in familiarity—and in all these things and similar matters they should preserve perseverance in the fervour of love. For a stream of love that sometimes diminishes does not appear to have had a good fountainhead.

Let us therefore also love one another and approve the effectiveness of love by works, because such love is from God: it is the end of the commandment, and fulfils the law.

## CHAPTER XI. On the three kinds of love commended by the first three words.

39. But in the three little words discussed, three kinds of love seem to me to be commended. One is that which is directed even toward enemies unwilling to be reconciled, of which John says: “Let us love the Lord, who loved us” (1 John 4:19), when we were still enemies; and this is the highest and more admirable love. For to love enemies is more divine than human.

The second is directed toward those who were once enemies but, having sought reconciliation, have been received into favour [Col. 0660A]; hence Paul says: “We were reconciled to God through his blood” (Rom. 5:9–10).

The third is directed toward those who have never been enemies; of this the same Apostle says: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Gal. 6:10).

The first kind of love is commended to us in the first word, where the Lord Jesus prays for his enemies. The second, where he promises paradise to the thief who asks. The third, where he entrusts his chief friends to one another. Let us therefore be sheltered by the shade of these leaves. Let us hear and heed these sounds of our lyre, most sweetly playing; and, with the aid of the Lord who is true love, let us moderate ourselves against the fervour of all envy, hatred, anger, and every bitterness of detraction, flattery, and pretence, being imitators in spirit [Col. 0660B] and in works in every kind of love.

## CHAPTER XII. On the fourth leaf of the vine, or Christ’s fourth word on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Matthew, chapter 27, v. 46.

49. But now, to behold the fourth leaf and hear the fourth string, let us direct together the eye and ear of the heart. This leaf requires keen eyes; this string, ears well purified. Indeed, it can itself purify and sharpen ears and eyes, because the Lord Jesus now says this word not simply as he says the others, but, as the Evangelist testifies, at about the ninth hour Jesus cried out in a loud voice: “Heli, Heli, lamma sabacthani?”—which is interpreted, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” What eyes do not see this leaf [Col. 0660C]? What ears do not hear this string? Why then did he cry out, except that he might be heard more strongly? How great, do you suppose, was the pain of this most bitter cry, when the Lord Jesus, stretched out in his whole body, cried it out?

But beware lest, because of the cry, you suppose that the Lord Jesus fell into impatience. For when he was in the utmost bitterness of the cross, nothing came forth from his heart but sweetness. For he retained patience in his most bitter passion, as we shall show in the following leaf and string; and he showed the greatness of his pain, as was first shown in the blessed Job, whose name means “Suffering,” both by his words and deeds. When he heard the words of the messengers, he outwardly displayed the bitterness of his mind in words. For, having torn his garments and shaved the hair of his head [Col. 0660D], he fell to the ground. Behold the greatness of grief. Afterwards he said: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done: blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21). Behold the strength of patience. If Job patiently endured his miseries, how much more patiently, do you suppose, did the Lord Jesus endure his cross, for the endurance of which he had come?

41. That he spoke these words in the person of the assumed man—who formed one person with God the Son—is clear from his saying, “Lord, my God.” Certainly he who is one God with the Father would not say this unless he had assumed a man. But what does he mean when he says, “Why have you forsaken me?” Could the Father forsake his only Son? Far be it. Rather, he speaks this for his whole body—that is, for himself and for the whole Church. [Col. 0661A] For our head, the Lord Jesus, wishing to commend unity and the love which he bears for the Church, his bride, showed that he too would suffer with all his members. For he now endured the Passion in the head, that is, in his own body which he assumed from the Virgin. He cries that he has been forsaken, though he could not be forsaken, because many of his members were to undergo tribulation so great that they would appear utterly abandoned by God. He bore the person of those of whom it is said: “Those who watched for my life took counsel together, saying: ‘God has forsaken him; pursue and seize him, for there is none to deliver him’” (Ps. 70:10–11). This too was flung as a reproach at gracious Jesus in the torment of the cross: “If you are the Son of God, save yourself” (Matt. 27:40).

42. It may also be understood thus: the Lord, foreseeing some—indeed, very many—in his body who would withdraw from the unity of his Church through heresies or other criminal sins, took their person upon himself and cried, “Why have you forsaken me?” As though he said: “Why has one of them turned back, to perish outside the unity of my body, though they are united to me at such cost of suffering?” Hence it is said in the person of the martyrs in the Psalm: “Our belly clung to the earth” (Ps. 43:25). By the belly, the softer and weaker part of a human being, are signified those who lack patience and steadfast perseverance and who, failing amid the bitterness of torments, clung to the earth—that is, consented to earthly counsels and actions. [Col. 0661C] But we, who still live amid daily tribulations, who have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to human beings, and “as the filth of this world and the offscouring of all things until now” (1 Cor. 4:9, 13), should draw ineffable confidence of spirit especially from this: the Lord himself, the consoler of all afflictions, is joined to us in such unity of spirit and love that he deigned, in words so manifest, to take upon himself the person of our weakness. Even now before the Father he intercedes for us by displaying his wounds, praying that he may not be forsaken in his lower members, though he could in no way be forsaken in himself as the head. And how could members perish when they know that their salvation rests in the will of their head? [Col. 0661D] Is there any member in our mortal body with whose suffering our head does not suffer? If foot or hand is afflicted, the head immediately cries out through the tongue: “Why am I afflicted?” The Lord cried to Saul, who raged against his members: “Why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4), although he himself remained secure in heaven. Blessed be the Lord Jesus, who first deigned to suffer tribulation for us in himself, and now also with us and in us, reckoning as his own the tribulation which we suffer as justice requires, and crying: “I am with him in tribulation” (Ps. 90:15), so that we may trust more securely.

445

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Fifth Leaf of the Vine, or the Fifth Word of Christ on the Cross: “I Thirst.” John 19:28.

[Col. 0662A]

43. The fifth leaf, or fifth string, seems short indeed; yet, if it is examined and considered more carefully, it may be found most powerful as an indication of love. For the Evangelist says: “Jesus, seeing that all things had been accomplished, that the Scriptures which had to be fulfilled might be fulfilled”—namely, those which say, “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22). The Evangelist then adds: “A vessel, therefore, full of vinegar was set there; and one ran, filled a sponge with vinegar, put it round hyssop, and gave it to him to drink” (John 19:28–29). Another Evangelist, explaining more fully how the Scripture was fulfilled, also mentions the gall, saying: “They gave him myrrhed wine to drink, mixed with gall” (Matt. 27:34; Mark 15:23). When all his limbs had been broken, sweet Jesus wished even his tongue to be punished. Thus that alien vine, turned to bitterness, gave him from its fruit a bitter drink—not a drink to be swallowed, but rather tasted; for, as punishment for the tongue, it was enough to have tasted the vinegar.

44. Yet although these things were truly done for the fulfilment of Scripture, something else seems to be signified by this word, “I thirst.” For I think that by it he plainly wished to commend to us the immensity of his most burning love, because drink is desired far more ardently by a thirsty person than food by a hungry one. [Col. 0662C] Therefore, by showing in himself the desire for that which is most ardently longed for, the Lord Jesus showed that the ardour of his love was figured by it. We may also truly understand that he thirsted, since, drained throughout his whole body by the shedding of his sacred blood, his bones were dried out like a *cremium* [meaning uncertain]. But it is not sufficiently credible that he spoke of bodily thirst in order to ask for a bodily drink, when he knew that he was at that moment about to die bodily. Rather, we believe that he thirsted with the most burning desire for our salvation.

But something moves us to wonder: when the hour of his final Passion was imminent, the Lord Jesus went forth to pray, fell upon his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Luke 22:42); and he did this not only once, [Col. 0662D] but a second and a third time. By the cup which he was to drink he undoubtedly signified the Passion which he was to suffer. Yet now, having already drained that same cup of suffering, he says, “I thirst.” What is this? Before tasting it, O good Jesus, you ask that the cup be removed altogether; and after you have drained it, you thirst. As I see it, you are a marvellous drinker. Was your cup filled with the wine of delight, rather than with the wine of compunction and utmost bitterness? Indeed, it was full of most bitter compunction, such as ought to produce not thirst but rather a loathing for drinking.

45. But, as I think, before the Passion you prayed that the Father’s cup might be removed from you, not in order to avoid the Passion for which you had come and which had to be suffered, without which salvation would not come to humankind; but so that no one might suppose that, because of the union with glory, you did not feel bitterness as a true human being. By asking once, twice, and a third time that the cup be removed, you showed the supreme severity of your Passion to those who doubted it. [Col. 0663A] You also prescribed for us, who follow you, a pattern of teaching and example: when dangers are imminent, even if they contribute to our good, we may and ought repeatedly to entreat the Lord to deign to turn away from us the scourges of his wrath. Nevertheless, if they are not removed, they must be borne, after the example of your Passion, gratefully, patiently, manfully, and with every perseverance.

But when you had drained the cup of suffering which you had earlier asked to be removed, you said, “I thirst.” You commended the greatness of your love for us, as though you said: “Although my Passion was so bitter that, so far as human feeling was concerned, I might have wished to avoid it, yet, O human being, your love conquering me and overcoming even the torments of the cross, I still thirst, if need be, to undergo yet more and greater torments. For there is nothing that I refuse to suffer for you, for whose ransom I lay down my life.” Therefore let every faithful soul imitate her sweet bridegroom Jesus, thirsting for and at the same time drinking the cup of such bitterness 446 for her sake. And as she herself drinks it for him amid present adversities, so let her also thirst for her most sweet bridegroom. [Col. 0663C] She will be able to perceive his sweetness better through present bitter experiences; and, when evils have been drained for his sake, she will be able more confidently to thirst for him and say with the prophet: “My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41:3); and again: “My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly my flesh has thirsted for you” (Ps. 68:22).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Sixth Leaf of the Vine, that is, the Sixth Word of Christ on the Cross: “It Is Accomplished.” John 19:30.

46. In the sixth leaf of the vine, or the sixth string of our lyre, the virtue of perseverance is commended to us. For the Evangelist says that, when sweet Jesus had received the bitterness of the vinegar, he said: “It is accomplished.” What is this? It was said above that, seeing [Col. 0663D] that all things had been accomplished, so that the Scriptures might be fulfilled, the Lord said, “I thirst”; and, after he had tasted the vinegar offered to him, he added, “It is accomplished.” For the testimony of Scripture was accomplished—that is, perfected—which says: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22). And through this all Scripture concerning him received its fulfilment.

Therefore, as our head, enduring the bitterness of the Passion for our sins, persevered patiently unto accomplishment—that is, unto the fulfilment of all the Scriptures concerning him—so we too, if we wish to be members of this head, should preserve the virtue of perseverance in all our adversities. Thus, arriving at the end of all our sufferings with gracious Jesus himself as our guide, [Col. 0664A] we may confidently say with him: “It is accomplished.” That is: “By your help, not by my own strength, I have fought the good fight, finished the course, and kept the faith. Therefore render what, by your promise, is laid up for those who contend lawfully in the contest: namely, the crown of righteousness, which you, the righteous judge, will render on your day—that day which has no cloud; that day which will be better in your courts than thousands of days; that day in which you alone—that is, uniquely—will be the sun, O Sun of righteousness, gracious Jesus Christ, shining in your power and giving yourself as the everlasting reward to all who have persevered in the contest of the struggle.” For they will receive from you everlasting brightness, in which they rejoice happily without end.

[Col. 0664B] 47. Yet no one can attain this brightness unless he has persevered to the end. For perseverance is assuredly the strength of a good work; to it alone is the crown of righteousness rendered. What profit is there in being good, wise, or powerful if you do not persevere to the end? Saul was good, and excellent; for Scripture teaches that there was no better man than he among the people of Israel. But what did he become? He fell and was made reprobate: so that he did not obey the voice of the Lord, despised the prophet, was tormented by an evil spirit, persecuted an innocent man unto death, and finally consulted a witch and perished miserably at the hands of a foreigner.

Who was wiser than Solomon? Yet, failing in the Lord’s commandments and joined to Gentile women, he built temples for their gods—indeed, for their demons—so that he himself worshipped idols with them. He became foolish and fallen in proportion as he had formerly been exalted in wisdom. How many men do we read of in the *Lives of the Fathers*, powerful in vigils, fasts, and labours beyond human measure, even shining in miracles, who fell because they did not persevere to the end? “He who perseveres to the end,” says the Lord, “shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). The end, not the struggle, crowns. Praise the good fortune of one sailing—but when he has reached the harbour. Hence:

> You began better than you end; the last things  
> yield to the first; here are a man and a boy unlike each other.  
> (Ovid, *Heroides*, epistle 9, verses 23–24.)

[Col. 0664D] How rightly this will instil in you humility and fear, when you observe that the chief of the angels fell in heaven with a great multitude of his followers; that the first-formed human being was cast out of paradise with his wife; and that so many good, wise, and powerful people have perished in our world because 447 they did not reach the completion of good works! For one person is more righteous than another, and no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred. Why? Because one does not know whether one will persevere or be crowned.

48. But there is an effective remedy to apply to this fear: namely, let us place our confidence, hope, and strength in him of whom the Psalm sings: “My helper, I will sing to you; for you are God my protector, my God, my mercy” (Ps. [Col. 0665A] 58:18); and of whom Isaiah says: “Behold, God is my saviour; I shall act confidently and shall not fear, because the Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Isa. 12:2). For all who fell undoubtedly fell because they trusted more in themselves than in God. They built the house of their purpose upon sand. Therefore, when the storm of temptations came, the rivers flowed—that is, transient desires persuading appetite—and the winds of pride and vainglory blew; and their house fell, and all their works were destroyed, because they built upon sand—that is, upon themselves (Matt. 7:26–27), trusting, of course, in their own powers.

But let us lay a much better foundation: namely, him of whom the Apostle says, “No one can lay another foundation than that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Cor. 3:11). Let us safely build good works upon it; so long as they cling to that foundation, they cannot fall, until, with the help of him who began, they are brought to their due completion.

## CHAPTER XV. On the Seventh Leaf of the Vine, or the Last Word of Christ on the Cross: “Father, into Your Hands I Commend My Spirit.” Luke 23:46.

49. Now let us consider the final leaf of our Vine, or the final string of our lyre, so that we may entrust it to indelible memory—indeed, so that we may continually chew it over with unwearied mouth. “Father,” says that good Jesus, “into your hands I commend my spirit.” The wording is plain. But why did the Son, coeternal and consubstantial with the Father, so openly commend his soul into the Father’s hands, when it would no less have been commended even if he had not said this?

[Col. 0665C] In the Gospel of John we read that, when the Lord Jesus was about to raise Lazarus, he said: “Father, I give you thanks because you always hear me; but I said it because of those standing by, that they may believe that you sent me” (John 11:41–42). It is surely the same now. Although he knew that his most holy soul was commended to the hands of the Father—he who had said shortly before, “The ruler of this world comes,” that is, Satan, “and has nothing in me” (John 14:30)—yet he did this to instruct us, who are earth and ashes, to learn to commend our spirit to the hands of the eternal Father. Thus, when it has departed from the body, it may not be seized by the ruler of this world, who will find in us—alas!—not a few things belonging to himself. Though Christ himself owed nothing to sin, and indeed had come to take away sins, he commended to the hands of his Father his most pure spirit, about to depart from his most pure body, not from necessity but for the sake of an example.

[Col. 0665D] We too shall be able to do this in hope of grace and mercy if we have sheltered under the shadow of the preceding leaves; if we have heard with the ears of the heart the sounds of the strings of our lyre: namely, if we pray for enemies; if from the whole heart we forgive those who repent of sins against us; if we render reciprocal love to our neighbours; if in all our tribulations we hope in him who became human for our sake, so that, united to our nature, he might be with us; if with ardent desire we long for the salvation of our neighbours; and finally, if we persevere in good works unto completion. To the extent that we do these things, we may confidently say to the eternal Father with the Lord Jesus: “Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.” Let us always pray while we live that he may deign to grant that we too may breathe out our spirit in these words in which he breathed out his own, and effectively commend it to his hands.

50. Behold, according to what we could do—not what we ought, nor according to what we wished—we have shown to your love the seven leaves of our Vine extended from above. It is not enough merely to look upon them; [Col. 0666B] rather, we must approach, 448 and sit under their shadow, so that with the bride we may truly say: “Under the shadow of him whom I desired, I sat” (Song 2:3). Whose shadow? Surely that of the bridegroom whose leaves have a shade so much broader because he himself, the Word of the highest Father, has words more lovable in their virtues, nearer to salvation, better suited to piety, and more accessible to every understanding. For though that good Jesus spoke in all the Prophets and Apostles, you will nevertheless find no one’s words at all so suited both to the strong and the weak—that is, to learned and unlearned, wise and foolish persons—as the words of the most learned Word, the Lord Jesus. For, as someone says:

> Waters are drunk more sweetly [more agreeably] from their very source.  
> (Ovid, *Epistles from Pontus*, book III, epistle 5, verse 8.)

[Col. 0666C] It should be understood that one must meditate day and night in the shadow of these leaves, that is, in the words of the Lord. We are indeed sheltered by their shadow whenever, being tempted by vices or the devil, we bring forward through interpreters some word from the Gospel Scriptures, by whose admonitions and authority we resist the vices rushing upon us. For example, if you are tempted by pride—namely, if you wish to rule and do not wish to be subject—there immediately comes to you the word of the Lord saying: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be the servant of all; for as everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled, so everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. 20:27; 23:11–12). If the heat of anger assails you, you immediately have a leaf of our Vine to set against that fervour: namely, the saying that everyone who is angry with his brother without cause is liable to judgment (Matt. 5:22). Thus, against each temptation you will find words by which you may be defended from the heat of vices and may foster the virtue appropriate to the occasion, with gracious Jesus himself, the Vine, granting us aid.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Delightfulness of the Flowers of the Vine, That Is, the Virtues of Christ.

51. Next let us incline our minds to the delightfulness of the flowers—or rather, truly lifting them up, let us see how our Vine flowered. For it flowered, and did so more abundantly and delightfully than all others, because it is itself better than all others: its magnificence is exalted above the heavens; [Col. 0667A] all things are subject beneath its feet; yet, bound by our love, it was for a time made a little lower than the angels. For this reason it emptied itself, taking the form of a servant; it was planted in our earth and took on the deformity of our body. It put forth leaves, flowered, and bore many fruits, so that through its union with our humanity it might unite us to its divinity.

But because fruit is not reached without flower, gracious Jesus flowered. What are his flowers but virtues? This Vine flowered wonderfully, very singularly, and excellently: not with one kind of flower, as other vines and trees do, but containing in itself the appearance of every flower. Among other saints, one is chaster than another, another more patient, another more fervent in love; [Col. 0667B] but this Vine surpassed all angels and human beings in kindness, patience, chastity, love, and every other virtue. This true Vine therefore had the appearance not of one flower but of all: the violet of humility, the lily of chastity, the rose of patience and love, and the flower of abstinence, which we call the crocus. How delightful, do you suppose, will be the fruit of our Vine, flowering with such delightfulness?

52. But now, with his assent, let us say something about each of these flowers of our Vine. First, however, it should be noted that flowers are chiefly considered for the pleasure of sight and the sweetness of scent; they are not usually eaten, except that bees draw sweet food by sucking it from certain flowers. We have said that no flower—that is, no virtue represented by any flower—is absent from our Vine. For what virtue could be absent from the Lord of virtues?

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Flower of Humility, Which Is the Violet.

53. First, then, let us consider the flower of humility, that is, the violet. Why the violet flower signifies humility is shown by its size, position, scent, colour, and power. Its size—that is, its extent—is small. 449 [Col. 0667C] What flower is smaller than this little flower? For the humble are small in their own eyes. Thus the Apostle, who had laboured more than all the others, says of himself: “I am the least of all the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:9). You see how small this great man was in his own eyes? And it comes about in a wonderful way that those whose conscience is secure, who are conscious of nothing against themselves, are inclined to think so humbly of themselves.

The position of this flower is close to the earth, and rightly so. For you have the Apostle teaching: “Do not be high-minded, but consent to the lowly” (Rom. 12:16). Those who consider themselves better than others, or wish to appear better than others, do not possess this characteristic of the flower, even though they are small in their own estimation. For there are some who judge themselves subject in their own consciences, yet outwardly wish to appear better than others. Such persons possess the size of this flower, since inwardly in mind they count themselves small; but they do not possess its position, because they wish outwardly to be raised above others. Of such persons Solomon says: “Measure and measure, weight and weight, are an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. 20:10). [Col. 0668A] And in the law of Moses it is forbidden to have a double weight (Deut. 25:13–16). One has a double weight who, conscious of evils in himself, judges himself evil, but wishes outwardly to seem good to others and better than they. In his own judgment he is close to the earth, yet he wishes to appear exalted to others. All such people are driven by the vice of hypocrisy, concerning whom we spoke more fully in the sermon which we wrote on little things.

54. The scent of the violet is sweet and health-giving, because even among the proud the praise of humility is extolled. Its praiseworthy reputation itself is the sweetness of its scent, and is truly salutary; sometimes hearers are corrected by praise of the humble, even though they are of such a kind that they lose this scent, although they consider carefully. Its colour, as is evident, is lowly, especially to those who do not know the power of the little flower; but to those who recognize the flower’s power, even the flower’s very despised appearance becomes commendable and beloved. [Col. 0668B] We shall readily recognize this in gracious Jesus himself, the master of humility, according to the Apostle’s saying: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling block, and to the Gentiles foolishness; but to those called, the saints, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–24). Certainly Christ crucified is a violet, for on the cross he was made most humble. To Jews and Gentiles who looked only at the colour in this humility, that colour appeared vile; but to us, who acknowledge the power of the Passion, even that despised humility—the humility of Christ—is pleasing, and is especially commended through humility. Therefore let the hidden inward power of the flower be joined to the despised colour, so that by its inward power what appears outwardly vile may not be despised, but rather loved more greatly.

55. Let us therefore now look with a more perfect and purer eye at how greatly that singular flower blossomed, of whom it is written: “A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isa. 11:1–2). A good flower, upon whom the Holy Spirit of the Lord rests. And although this flower, our Lord Jesus, who says of himself, “I am the flower of the field” (Song 2:1), possessed in himself without any diminution the power and beauty of every flower, nevertheless no flower is more fitting than the violet for the Holy Spirit to rest upon him. [Col. 0668D] Nor do I affirm this on my own authority, but he himself says: “Upon whom shall my spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet person, and one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2). What could be clearer? Could he not have set forth the rose of patience and love, the lily of chastity, or the crocus of abstinence, when he wished to show the resting-place of the Holy Spirit? Passing these over, he set forth the violet of humility, whose attendants are quietness and fear, mentioned afterward. For violets—that is, the humble—cannot be moved by the wind of pride, which always seeks lofty hearts to shake, as someone says:

> Envy aims at the heights; the winds blow through the loftiest things.  
> (Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, v. 369.)

For when humble persons are found, they cannot be moved. Therefore they are quiet, and they do not shake off the Spirit resting upon them, since they are moved neither by the wind of pride nor by that of envy. [Col. 0669A] There is also a fear—not any fear of losing money or transitory goods, but fear of the Lord’s sayings, the attendant of humility—because the humble person presumes nothing from personal strength and, attending to the Lord’s sayings for consolation, always fears failing to fulfil the commandments or offending the commanding Father by transgression. 450 This, then, is a good flower, generating quietness and fear, fear being indeed the parent of security; for it is written: “Whoever fears God will do good” (Ecclus. 15:1). And what reward will be given for such deeds except everlasting security?

56. The violet is indeed a good flower: by the wondrous sweetness of its scent it drew the heavenly flower, the Word of the eternal Father, into the womb of the earthly flower, the most blessed Virgin. She herself testifies to this when she says: “My spirit has rejoiced in God my Saviour, because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid.” What do you say? Do you not have other flowers? “I do,” she says. “For I flower altogether, lacking no flower, because I lack no virtue, since I am altogether beautiful and there is no stain in me. I have the lily of chastity, because I was the first to vow to the Lord a vow of preserving virginity. I have the rose of love, for if I had not loved the Lord so greatly, whence would I have had such confidence, such boldness, to undertake something new—a young and modest girl, still placed under parental authority and under the commandments of the law? [Col. 0669C] But, to confess the truth, love made me bold: the burning rose, devouring servile fear, compelled me to make a new vow and to possess a singular lily, so that I might someday say to my beloved: ‘I am white and ruddy, as you too are white and ruddy.’

“I have whatever other flowers there may be, but the Lord did not deign to regard any of these in me with such prerogative as the flower of my violet: ‘For he has regarded the humility of his handmaid.’ And do you all wish to see from whom I borrowed my flowers, and how much I have obtained from this flower? ‘For behold, from this all generations shall call me blessed’” (Luke 1:47–48). “From this,” I say, “because I was regarded by the Lord. The flower of my violet is my nard, which gave its fragrance”—and nard signifies the same thing as the violet, namely, the virtue of humility. Delighted by its fragrance, the King, the Son of the King, God the Son of God, while he was “at his table” (Song 1:11), that is, in the bosom of the Father, [Col. 0669D] was drawn into me, as by a certain force, by so delightful a scent; and he willed that flower should be conceived in flower within flower—that is, within Nazareth, which is interpreted “Flower”—so that he might become the flowering flower, that is, the Nazarene. Everything agrees with the flower. The abiding flower is conceived in flower, that is, in Nazareth. Thus the violet flower is wholly good, and best: by the fragrance of its scent, as by a delightful bond, it bent the flower of heaven into the womb of our flower, the humble Virgin.

57. Let all learn—and above all the flowers of the world, that is, virgins, who excel throughout the whole Church of God as flowers among grass—that the Virgin of virgins, the first, holiest, and most chaste of consecrated virgins, places her highest glory in the violet of humility, although in her the lily [Col. 0670A] of chastity shines singularly and the rose of love glows red. Do not boast, virgins, of bodily chastity, though it is a praiseworthy virtue. But the greater you are, the more humble yourselves in all things, so that you may find grace before God. For the Lord did not regard the chastity, but the humility, of his handmaid. If you wish to be regarded by the Lord with the eye of mercy, the eye of grace, be humble. For, Scripture says, “He gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6), because “he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Matt. 25:1–12). If you wish your lamps to be filled with oil when the bridegroom comes to the wedding—that is, if you wish to have an untroubled and joyful conscience, for oil in the lamp is spiritual joy in the heart—do not think highly because of the height of your lily, that is, because of the purity of your chastity. Do not seek outward praise, [Col. 0670B] lest, when the door of the kingdom of heaven has been shut, the bridegroom say to you, “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you,” and exclude you from himself—he who regarded the humility of his handmaid. For many virgins will be excluded, because no proud person shall enter; but no humble person, whether married, virgin, or widow, will deserve to be cast out. Narrow is the gate of the kingdom of heaven, and it receives only the little ones. The swollen are repelled—indeed, they cannot approach at all—whatever their sex, condition, or age. And, to say it briefly: no virtue gains entrance unless it has inclined itself to the violet of humility.

For the Master of humility himself says and teaches this, when, calling a little child, he set him in the midst of the disciples and said: “Unless you are converted and become like this little child, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 18:1–3). Did he set before the disciples as an example John, the lily of chastity, or Peter, the rose of love, who were then present? The former, it is asserted, was called and chosen by the Lord from the wedding itself; [Col. 0670C] the latter, 451 by a threefold confession to gracious Jesus, whom he could not lie to, testified to the affection of perfect love. For just as John is commended for the special prerogative of chastity, so Peter is commended for more fervent love. Yet he did not set these before those who were to enter the gate of heaven as an example, but a little child exalted by the virtue of humility.

58. Let us see, then, how greatly the Lord, the Lord of all virtues, commended this virtue in himself. First, attend to his words, where he says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. 11:29). What is this, good master, best Jesus? Have all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in you come to this: that you should teach this singularly, that you are meek and humble of heart? You do not teach how heavens are to be made, miracles performed, the dead raised, and other things of this kind; but: “Because I am meek and humble of heart.” Is something small so great? Certainly, because through it rest is found for souls. For what other cause is there for all our labour and struggle except that we may find rest for our souls? A brief teaching, a brief way, has been shown. Learn this from the Lord Jesus, who is meek and humble of heart: that is, see [Col. 0671A] how greatly and why he was humbled who is the Lord exalted above all nations and whose glory is above the heavens; and learn also that you are mud and ashes. Thus you will find rest for your soul.

But note that he says, “humble of heart.” He who is humble of heart is not pleased by feigned humility, but by true humility. He delights in humility of heart, he who looks upon the heart, because he rests in humble hearts. He seeks humble hearts to raise up, not swollen hearts from which he recoils.

59. But since we have set forth two matters for our consideration—how greatly and why our Vine, the Lord Jesus, was humbled—let us now explain both, because they are desired by your love. Human understanding fails and reason yields when considering how greatly the Lord was humbled in his earthly life. For how can you know the abasement of humility unless you also recognize the excellence of his lordship? Speak, then. What can you do? Can you attain the measure of his glory, power, and beauty? Neither angels nor cherubim nor seraphim have attained this. For no creature knows God as fully and perfectly as he is; much less does a human being, or a son of man, a worm. Yet, though he was so great that there was no end to his greatness, he stooped so far as to become a son of man, a worm. O what humility! The incomprehensible God wills to be comprehended; the highest to be humbled; the most powerful to be despised; the most beautiful to be made deformed; the wisest to become as a beast; the immortal to die; and, to state it briefly, God wills to become a little worm! [Col. 0671C] What is higher than God? What is lower than a little worm? “I am a worm and not a man,” he says (Ps. 21:7). Why a worm? Because he is the Son of Man. For thus you have it in Job: “The stars are not pure in his sight; how much less is man, rottenness, and the son of man, a worm?” (Job 25:5–6).

60. If, then, the Son of Man is a worm, surely he himself is also a worm, since, by his own testimony, he is the Son of Man. “Whom do men say that the Son of Man is?” he says (Matt. 16:13). See what a distinction he makes between “man” and “Son of Man.” He calls “men” those who descend through corruption from the first man, Adam. Hence Job also says: “How much more is man rottenness?”—because corruption is in rottenness. [Col. 0671D] But Christ the Lord alone is pure, because he was born of the Virgin Mother without corruption; he does not call himself “man,” who is indeed rottenness, but “Son of Man,” who is a worm. For as a worm is generated from earth alone, so Jesus Christ is generated from the Virgin alone. O how humble a little worm is Jesus Christ, who became “the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Ps. 21:7), despised by men without cause and trampled without retaliation like a worm! “When he was reviled, he did not revile; when he suffered, he did not threaten” (1 Pet. 2:23). He humbled himself so as to become man, so as to be subject to human beings—to his blessed Mother and to Joseph, who nourished him; to Simeon, who awaited him (Luke 2:51, 28); and not only to the good, but even to evil earthly authorities, paying with Peter the [Col. 0672A] didrachma found in the mouth of the fish (Matt. 17:23–26). He subjected himself in his baptism to John, who rather ought to have been baptized by him (ibid. 3:13–15). The good and gracious Jesus humbled himself even to the washing of his disciples’ feet (John 13:5). Finally, he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross. Beyond this, where can we go? He died not by just any death, but was condemned to death on the cross, a most shameful death. Do you see, then, how greatly this violet flower blossomed in our Vine, gracious Jesus? Many have humbled themselves unto death; but they have by no means descended to such contempt, because they never attained to such exaltation. For which of all the good who die could claim for himself [Col. 0672B] what was said of Christ Jesus: “Though he was in the form of God, he did not count equality with God a thing to be seized” (Phil. 2:6–8)? Certainly none, because no human being other than he was God. Therefore he was humbled most of all, who alone, though in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, and came to such abasement that he was now reckoned by human beings not as a man but as a little worm.

61. But what is the cause of such great humiliation in gracious Jesus? For the Son and Wisdom of the Father, who does nothing without cause, was not so humbled without reasonable necessity and just cause. Why delay over many words? He became man in order to redeem man; he became weak in order to heal our weaknesses; he became poor in order to enrich us by his poverty [Col. 0672C]; he was humbled in order to exalt us; he was delivered over to death—indeed, he died—in order to give us life. Who of sound mind despises being humbled for the sake of one so humbled for us? And although there are many causes which compel us to humility—namely, a shameful beginning, a painful life, a fearful end, fear of Gehenna, hope of heavenly things, and other causes, if there are any—yet, even if all these causes were absent, the humility of our king and redeemer, our sweetest and best Father, Jesus, ought not merely to urge us but forcibly to compel us to the virtue of humility. Therefore let us humble ourselves, both for the reasons mentioned above and in order to repay in some measure the Lord Jesus, humbled for our sake, offering the violet of his humility, by which he, our Vine, blossomed so [Col. 0672D] excellently, and tasting it in our heart. May he recognize in us this flower of his own, which he especially chose to commend in himself; and may he deign, at the time of his visitation, to exalt us with himself, who is exalted above every name.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the flower of chastity, which is the lily.

62. The flower of the shining lily, the eminent emblem of chastity, could not be absent from our flourishing Vine. Among all virtues, chastity deserved, by a certain special prerogative, to be called a flower, and it is figured by the lily. But by the name of chastity in this treatise, understand not every sort of chastity, but that which is called virginity. For there is also the chastity of the continent, or of widows; and there is marital chastity. But these are by no means now called [Col. 0673A] flowers, because they have lost the lily-flower of virginity. Therefore we now wish to call those who have not been deflowered—that is, virgins—by the name of the lily flower; nor in saying this do we wrong to the continent and the married. For when we praise John’s chastity, we do not blame Abraham’s marriage; nor, in commending Mary’s virginity, do we reject Anna’s widowhood. Rather, each has its own merits, though distinguished by no small difference of dignity. Who indeed does not praise the thirtyfold fruit in the married and the sixtyfold in widows, although the hundredfold fruit of virginity is excellently preferred to these (Matt. 13:23)?

63. Since we are about to speak of this grace of the lily in which our Vine blossomed, let us see, with the true light illuminating us, why so great a virtue is figured by the lily. And [Col. 0673B] the answer plainly occurs: because of the purity of whiteness by which that flower is preferred to other flowers. Accordingly, virginal purity is rightly figured by the type of the lily. Moreover, no other flower displays so much charm by its very appearance as this one alone; therefore virginity, most pure and gracious to all the devout, is rightly figured by this flower. By what praises, then, shall I extol you, O virginal brightness? Truly, I do not know. Yet let that unique Lily teach my ignorance: the uncreated wisdom of God, the Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of the Father and the unique son of the singular lily—that is, of his most chaste Virgin Mother—who, on the boundary between the two laws, consecrated a vow of perpetual and most unblemished virginity. Let him teach me, I say, how, by considering the material lily, I may discern the characteristics of the virginal [Col. 0673C] lily. Therefore, because of the properties already set forth, let us diligently investigate this material lily in its root and stalk, its leaves, and those other small flowers enclosed within it. We hope that, by considering all these features particularly, we may discover an encomium of perfect virginity.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the root of the lily, that is, thoughts hidden in the heart.

64. The root of the lily is commended in three respects: it is white, shining, and pliant. What is figured by the root hidden in the earth, except a thought hidden in the heart [Col. 0673D]? By the whiteness of the root, therefore, we understand purity of thought. What is bodily purity without purity of thought? Concerning this the Lord commands: “Wash yourselves; be clean.” And lest you should understand only outward cleanliness, he adds: “Put away the evil of your thoughts from before my eyes” (Isa. 1:16). For perverse thoughts separate from God; and, as Truth himself testifies, “From the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, blasphemies,” and the rest which defile a person (Matt. 15:19–20). Now black or defiled thoughts are, namely, diabolical, worldly, and carnal thoughts. When someone considers himself better than another; when he wishes to appear equal to one greater than himself; or when he does not wish to be subject to one set over him—these are diabolical [Col. 0674A] thoughts, invented by the devil and more familiarly practiced by him than by others, so that pride is properly said to be the devil’s distinctive mark. Worldly thoughts are those which ensnare the mind in desires for possessions: they are excessively intent on acquiring them and take excessive pleasure in what has been acquired; they do not distribute these goods to their neighbors’ needs, and thus become strangers to the love of God, because it is written: “Whoever has the substance of this world and sees his brother suffering need, and closes his compassion against him—how does the love of God abide in him?” (1 John 3:17). Carnal thoughts are those that draw people toward the lust of the flesh, as when men think about women, or women about men, with disordered affection and pleasure. Foolish people presume to call this love, though it could more truly be called hatred. [Col. 0674B] There is also the indulgence of food and drink, when richer and more delicate things are sought merely for taste, not for the recovery of health. One might use delicacies with moderation; yet this is difficult to observe. The same judgment applies to those who desire to use fine clothing.

65. The lily loses its characteristic, and virginity its beauty, if the root lacks whiteness and the thought lacks virginal purity. For if the body is clean outwardly while thought is defiled inwardly, it must no longer be called virtue but hypocrisy. Yet we should know, according to the testimony of Gregory (*Morals*, book 21, ch. 23), that however impure a thought may be, it does not defile the mind when reason does not consent to it. For who can restrain thoughts so completely [Col. 0674C] that no impurity whatever ever provokes them? But the assaults of such thoughts must immediately be repressed, so that the enemy departs more thoroughly defeated precisely by that through which he hoped to conquer. This happens whenever, drawn by wicked and impure thoughts, we immediately have recourse to the sign of the cross, remembrance of the Lord’s Passion, and the aid of tears; and, made strong in battle by his own weapon, we strike the enemy.

66. The root of the lily is not merely white, but bright or shining. By brightness or radiance, however, cheerfulness of mind appears to be signified. There are some who indeed perform good works through compulsion, necessity, or habit, but are moved by no eagerness to do them; this vice is properly called acedia. [Col. 0674D] Religious persons are especially afflicted by this vice. For exceedingly few secular persons notice it, even if it is a vice. Bound to the world, they can scarcely grasp the name of a spiritual vice, although this vice is numbered among the seven principal sins. Let us now, therefore, speak to spiritual persons, who can understand this vice. The vice of acedia produces a certain numbness in the mind, so that all spiritual exercises seem tasteless and turn into a heavy weariness. Of this weariness the Psalm says: “My soul slumbered from weariness” (Ps. 118); and elsewhere: “Their soul loathed every food, and they drew near to the gates of death” (Ps. 106:18). For at times the soul of good persons is so afflicted by this vice [Col. 0675A] that it loathes every food—that is, every spiritual exercise—so that it has no desire to pray, read, meditate, or perform manual work. Indeed, they even draw near to the gates of death: that is, being weary even of life itself, they desire to be ended by death, saying with holy Job, “My soul is weary of my life” (Job 10:1). This grave vice is healed by joy, signified by the brightness of the lily’s root. It restores the sick and dejected mind, incites it to spiritual meditation, and restores the desire to labor, pray, and read; so that it may “rejoice as a giant to run his course,” and say with the Psalmist: “I ran in the way of your commandments when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118:32). For the way of God’s commandments is run when the heart is enlarged—that is, opened by spiritual joy. It is naturally said that the heart is closed by fear and sadness, but opened by confidence and gladness. How fitting, do you think, is this virtue of cheerfulness for consecrated virgins, who have despised the joy of this world and every worldly adornment for love of their Lord Jesus Christ, so that what is lacking outwardly may be fulfilled inwardly? Rejoice, therefore, always in the Lord, because you have cast out vain joys. Again I say, rejoice, because you have merited to cleave to true joy and always to possess the radiance of cheerfulness in the thought of your heart. For God loves a cheerful giver—the singular giver of true cheerfulness.

67. The lily’s root is also pliant; by this we ought to understand the virtue of gentleness. For we know [Col. 0675C] that very many excel in the virtue of chastity, yet are accustomed to be provoked by a slight cause—indeed, by no cause at all—so that they become excessively burdensome both to themselves and to those against whom they are angered, carrying an exasperated mind in response to everything they take in by sight or hearing. This does not become a virgin of Christ, who says and teaches: “Learn of me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29); and who promises blessedness to the gentle, saying: “Blessed are the gentle, for they shall possess the earth” (ibid. 5:4). What, then, of the ungentle? They will be exiles from the land. From which land? From that of which it is written: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114:9). What good is chastity to those exiled from that land? Certainly they are not lilies to which this characteristic is lacking; hence they do not belong to that most perfect lily, gracious Jesus, who says of himself: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys.” What lilies belong to him? Hear: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song 2:1–2). The lily is pliant and soft; thorns are piercing and hard. The lily does not lose its gentleness although it endures the harshness of thorns. O how wicked are daughters through their common faith, yet thorns through the bitterness of their conduct! Therefore, if you wish to be a true lily, if you wish to be praised by your most sweet bridegroom, be a lily among daughters—among souls of the same faith and profession as yourself. And even if they pierce you by the bitterness of their conduct and harshness of speech, be gentle and pliant among such people. Do not be exasperated at every [Col. 0676A] word, but be patient, so that you too may deserve to hear: “As a lily among thorns,” and so forth.

68. Yet we do not say this so that every perversity may pass unchallenged, or so that the restless should not be rebuked and the proud restrained. On the contrary, such people ought to be reproved, lest, while you wish to be a lily, the pliancy of your root be lost. But, according to the Apostle, “rebuke, entreat, reprove; be urgent in season and out of season, in all gentleness and patience” (2 Tim. 4:2). It is as though he said: Exercise the zeal of discipline so strongly that you do not inwardly lose gentleness of mind, lest, in recalling the perverse person, you yourself also become perverted. At times the vices of the wicked must be rebuked; at times they must be silently endured, according as you judge it expedient for the good of each person concerned, because not all sick persons are healed by one kind of medicine. [Col. 0676B]

## CHAPTER XX. On the stalk of the lily, or the good resolution that rises from the root of good thought.

69. Next we must consider the stalk of the lily, in which three things are observed: straightness, strength, and length. Therefore, the stalk of the lily arising from the root is a good resolution arising from a good thought. For when you have thought good thoughts, and they grow strong within you like a root in the earth, necessity requires that you resolve to bring what pleases the thought into the affection of good action. Thus you at once have the lily’s stalk—that is, a good resolution proceeding from a good root and thought.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the straightness of the lily, that is, right intention.

[Col. 0676C]

70. Straightness is necessary to this stalk of good resolution: that is, we must resolve to do good with right intention, seeking neither earthly riches, human favor, nor the eminence of passing honor. For when that crafty serpent, Satan, cannot resist the beginning of a good thought, he lays snares in the way by which he may overthrow the intention of a good resolution, and through a crooked stalk make even the root of good thought bitter. The Psalm complains of these snares: “In this way in which I walked, the proud hid a snare for me” (Ps. 141 and 129:6). [Col. 0676D] O how many have been caught and deceived by these snares! They began good things well indeed, but later, as outward thoughts arose, abandoned the straightness of their resolution and became wholly perverse. Having once obtained riches, honors, or earthly pleasures through their good works, they forgot their first intention; and, seeking something other than God, they became idolaters, changing the glory of the incorruptible God—who alone is glorious and alone ought to be sought—into the likeness of birds, beasts, and serpents (Rom. 1:23). How do they change God’s glory into the likeness of birds? Because the good works that they previously intended to do for God’s glory, after changing the straightness of their intention, they labor to do for the [Col. 0677A] vain glory of the world. For birds—light, unstable, and seeking the heights—figure vanities. They change God’s glory into the likeness of beasts when they perform good works, through which they had previously intended God’s glory, for the fulfillment of bodily pleasure. For beasts, which pursue only things of the flesh, signify pleasure. They change God’s glory into the likeness of serpents when they perform good works—which ought to be done only to acquire heavenly riches and God’s glory—in order thereby to obtain earthly riches. For serpents, which eat the earth, signify the greedy, who pursue only earthly gains and desire to fill the belly of their soul.

71. These are the stumbling blocks which the devil conceals for those walking in the way of right intention [Col. 0677B], so that he may twist the lily’s stalk—that is, good resolution—from its straightness. Alas, alas, Lord God, who will escape these snares? Leaving secular people aside, how many and how great prelates of various Orders do we see, whom we know beyond doubt to have followed Christ, naked, while themselves naked, with a good intention! Yet, though they are drawn unwillingly into prelacies, before long—indeed, immediately—they corrupt their intention, spoil the stalk, and alter their resolution. They willingly cling to the offices to which they came unwillingly, desiring to rule rather than to be useful; they serve richer and more exquisite dishes for the pleasure of the belly rather than for utility or the divine will. They are even sometimes said to gather money, not in order to supply necessities to their spiritual children, [Col. 0677C] but to bestow something superfluous on their carnal little nephews and friends! O Lord Jesus, would that I were lying; would that I were lying—so that, if I alone were lying, all might remain in uprightness and truth.

72. But for you, O virgins of Christ, we judge that the virtue of humility, which we have often commended to your charity, is sufficient in great part for preserving the straightness of your resolution. For as you ascend to so lofty a height of chastity, your adversary Satan labors to bend you away from it. He cries out to us often—indeed, always suggests to us—that voice: “Bend down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51:23). What does “Bend down” mean? Bend your intention toward earthly things, though you raised it toward heavenly things, so that a passage through you may be open to us [Col. 0677D], that we may trample you. Do not consent to your enemy, O chaste soul, virgin of Christ, friend of your bridegroom and bride of your friend; do not consent, lest you be bent down. That is: seek nothing earthly—not human praise, not honors, not earthly riches. For if you turn aside to these things, that liar will pass over you; he will trample, press, and crush you, and set upon you the unbearable yoke of his iniquity, if you cast off Christ’s light and sweet yoke. O how senseless are those who so bend the straightness of their intention as to receive that most foul and wicked Satan as their rider, casting aside that most beautiful and best first ruler, the Lord Jesus, whose yoke, as he himself declares, is most sweet and whose burden most light (Matt. 11:30).

## CHAPTER XXII. On the strength of the stalk, or constancy in good resolution.

[Col. 0678A]

73. The strength of the stalk expresses the virtue called fortitude. Fortitude, as we take it here, is a virtue that endures the attacks of every temptation, not merely troublesome temptations but also prosperous ones. This virtue is fitting for the stalk of our lily, the resolution to do good, and especially for the vow of virginity: for the more praiseworthy a vow is, the more deceitfully and forcefully the devil presses to prevent its being well completed [variant: “brought to an end”], when he could not prevent its good beginning. Such a stalk must truly be strong against cold. For the source of temptation to a good resolution is acedia, by which the elect are sometimes tempted so severely, as we said above [Col. 0678B], that they have no desire to pray, read, meditate, or do anything else that serves as nourishment for the soul. For the soul’s strength is restored, preserved, and increased by prayer, reading, meditation, and even outward bodily labor; once these are removed, the soul must languish and dissolve into deadly cold. Then lust immediately enters, claims a seat in the cold soul, and warms it most wickedly with its own fire. But our lily, the virgin of Christ, must pray, read, meditate, or perform some outward work without interruption, lest the stalk of good resolution be corrupted within her. For these things, as blessed Augustine says, if done with discretion so that bodily health is not harmed, are transformed into spiritual delights.

[Col. 0678C] 74. The heat by which the stalk of good resolution is corrupted is worldly prosperity, in which the enemies’ snares lie deeply hidden. For we find many who resist adversity, because in adversity temptation is manifest. The body is sound; the adversities that weaken the mind are absent, and temptations are quieted. What remains but security? Beware, beware: woe to this security, woe to this peace, of which Truth himself says: “When the strong man armed guards his court, the things he possesses are in peace” (Luke 11:21). Therefore, fear when everything is prosperous and tranquil, lest that strong armed one, Satan, possess you without resistance. Do not say within yourself what that rich man said whose field produced abundant crops: “My soul, you have many goods stored up for many years; eat, drink, feast” (Luke 12:19). [Col. 0678D] For “when they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, and they shall not escape” (1 Thess. 5:3). But if you wish to have true peace and security, see that you are never secure, knowing certainly that nothing is so much to be feared as present peace, which without doubt produces everlasting fear. For you are not better than all the saints, who were tested and perfected in temptations. Who was better than blessed Job, to whom the Lord himself bore witness that he was a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil, and that none like him was on earth? (Job 1:1, 8). See the same in all who fear God—in the Apostles and martyrs. How great were the torments they suffered in order that they might safely attain [Col. 0679A] the palm of the kingdom, they who “became strong in battle” (Heb. 11:34), not in prosperity.

75. The storms assailing the stalk of our lily are manifest adversities. In them there must be sought the one unique remedy: that best physician; the guide who does not lead astray; the king who raises up his own; the strongest athlete, fighting and conquering in his people and for his people, and then crowning them as victors—Lord Jesus. What do you seek that you cannot find in him? If you are sick, he is physician. If you are in exile, he is guide. If you are desolate, he is king. If you are attacked, he is champion. If you thirst, he is drink. If you are cold, he is clothing. If you are sad, he is joy. If you are in darkness, he is light. If you are an orphan, he is father. He is bridegroom, friend, brother—the highest, best, most merciful, strongest, [Col. 0679B] most beautiful, and wisest, governing all things without end. Why do I labor on? The Lord Jesus Christ is everything that you can and ought to desire. Desire him; seek him. For he is that one precious pearl, to purchase which all that is yours must be sold; possessing him, you will fear no tempestuous storm. Let him be the end of your resolution; let your strength be placed in him, not in your own powers, and you will by no means be broken, because he—and no other—is the truest and best comforter in adversities and afflictions.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the worms that gnaw the stalk, that is, evil suggestions corrupting good resolution.

76. The worms that corrupt the stalk of good resolution are inward temptations, [Col. 0679C] which are all the more near because they are more familiar, often corrupting good resolution under the appearance of good. There is someone who, from the root of good thought, has put forth the stalk of good resolution. He resolves to leave everything worldly behind, in order to follow naked Christ while himself naked; but inwardly a worm of wicked suggestion arises, saying: “You have a sister without a dowry, a poor little mother; perhaps brothers, children, or any other friends suffer want of family resources. They depend on you alone; they look to you alone. If you leave them, they will either beg shamefully, to the disgrace of your family, or surely steal or violently seize another’s property, and thus perish in both body and soul. But if you, who could assist them by remaining [Col. 0679D] in your possessions, seem to have left them in certain danger and closed your compassion against them, how does the love of God remain in you? Therefore, in order to remain in charity, remain with them; for without charity nothing that you do will profit you. And even if it should profit you, it would still be better for you to save many with yourself than yourself alone. Has the Lord anywhere commanded that everyone must leave the world entirely? Indeed, rather, the elect who are to be saved will be commended for works of mercy on the day of the last judgment. What, then, do you seek outside the world that you could possess better and more safely in the world?” Other deadly worms are added to these: the difficulty of monastic observances; the fact that the higher the rank, the greater the fall; scant food; fasts [Col. 0680A]; vigils; unbearable labor without rest; hard beds; continual toil; and, above all, renunciation of one’s own will, together with the danger of false brethren and the harshness of superiors. Who could enumerate everything? Countless are these worms of most wicked suggestions, grievously gnawing the stalk of good resolution. They must be resisted altogether, altogether; and they must be killed by the arguments of Holy Scripture.

77. Therefore, the worm that so indiscreetly urges charity and compassionate mercy must be killed with the ointment of the Lord’s saying: “If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother, wife and children, brothers and sisters, and even his own soul, he is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:26). We are taught how they are to be loved and how hated by the cows drawing the cart with the ark of the Lord. While their calves were shut up at home, the cows bore the ark and went straight on their way to Beth-shemesh. When they heard the voices of their calves, they indeed gave a lowing, which was a sign of natural affection; nevertheless, they did not turn aside from the path once taken (1 Sam. 6:10–12). But if you already bear the Lord’s yoke—whether by open and solemn profession or by secret resolution—that is, whatever Rule was established by the Fathers through the Holy Spirit; if the suggestions of the aforesaid worms begin to gnaw at you, [Col. 0680B] imitate the Philistine cows carrying the ark of the Lord. Give a lowing—that is, a sign of affection: grieve with, sympathize with, and console those joined to you by natural love. Yet [Col. 0680C] nonetheless keep the path you have begun: that is, fulfill your good resolution by directing your feet toward Beth-shemesh, toward the House of the Sun, that is, the heavenly homeland, where is the supreme and spiritual dwelling of our Sun, the Lord Jesus, who is the Sun of righteousness, who shines in power in that house, dwelling in inaccessible light. Friends are thus to be hated: the affection of love toward them is to be preserved. And they are thus to be loved: their love must by no means be preferred to the love of God. Indeed, we ought not even to prefer our own soul’s comfort to his love; rather, we should in a sense hate our souls by afflicting them with fasts, vigils, and disciplines, so that we may teach them to obey the Lord’s commands. Those too whose poverty we could relieve by remaining in the world we shall commend for preservation to him who is King of kings and rich toward all who call upon him, praying that he may govern their condition as he knows to be expedient for their salvation.

[Col. 0680D] 78. Moreover, the worms that suggest the austerity of regular life will quickly be killed if we have taken care to anoint our mind with myrrh—that is, with the bitterness of the Lord’s Passion—compared with which whatever we may be able to suffer can be reckoned little or nothing. These worms are especially troublesome to the virginal resolution, because Beelzebub, master of worms, who at first easily tripped up Eve while she was a virgin, now rightly grieves that he is so often tripped up by young virgins of both sexes. Therefore see, foresee, and beware of the worms lying in ambush for you, virgin of Christ. [Col. 0681A] For whenever you think that you have either already attained, or will easily attain, the perfect stature of the chaste lily, shake off and drive away from yourself these worms of harmful suggestions, which threaten both the stalk and root of your lily and say to you by their suggestion: “What are you doing? Why are you turning aside? Do you wish to extinguish the flower of your youth? Will you not experience the sweetness of marital union? Will you not have most beloved sons and daughters, the solace and survivors of your life? Will you lack the service of faithful attendants? The path upon which you are embarking is foolish. Imitate your parents who begot you. Bear children too, and enjoy marriage according to the Lord’s institution, who gave no command concerning virgins.”

[Col. 0681B] 79. These are deceitful worms, O virgin of Christ, in whose face you must spit. If you take care to escape them, look more carefully at who Jesus Christ is, O virginal soul: whether he is virgin or married; to whom he entrusted his Virgin Mother; whom he loved more intimately. Why use many words? Christ Jesus is a virgin, born of a Virgin, whom he entrusted to a virgin most pure—namely, blessed John—whom the special prerogative of chastity had made worthy of a fuller love. This Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, is one whom you should follow rather than your parents, if you wish to preserve the youthful flower of your soul, which never grows old. For virginity never falls away. And if you wish to speak of bodily bloom, do not virgins flourish more in mind and body alike than [Col. 0681C] those who are corrupted? Indeed, virgins truly flourish both in body and soul: singular lilies of the singular Lily. I firmly hope that, even in this mortal life, he pours forth upon his lilies the abundance of his sweetness more abundantly than upon others, because in them he sees his likeness more distinctly expressed. For wherever Christ goes, virgins follow; and they become fruitful, conceiving from his Spirit a good resolution and bringing forth good works which never die. Earthly generation, by contrast, is conceived in sin, born in sorrow, nourished in anxiety, and at last lost or abandoned with grief. Your children will not be such, O virgin of Christ—not so. For they will never die, never be lost; indeed, whether you are dying or living, they will always follow you, [Col. 0681D] protect you, and lead you into eternal life. Therefore the abandoned woman—that is, the virgin of Christ, who seems for the present to be abandoned—has many children, and much better children, than she who has a carnal husband. If you frequently bring these and similar things back to mind, the worms of evil suggestions will undoubtedly die within you; and, with your bridegroom protecting you, they will by no means prevail in gnawing the stalk of your good resolution.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the length of the stalk, or the virtue of long-suffering and perseverance in good resolution.

80. The length of the lily’s stalk, raised upright on high, signifies the virtue of long-suffering, which is especially necessary to those who wish to persevere [Col. 0682A]. But because we have spoken more fully above, in the discussion of the sixth leaf, concerning the virtue of perseverance, we shall say something more briefly here. This virtue seems especially worthy of commendation in virgins, particularly of the female sex, in whose minds and bodies a certain weakness and frailty naturally implanted is contrary to long-suffering or perseverance. But blessed be God, who even in the present day has chosen the weak things of the world to confound the strong, and offers himself as defender to the most tender minds of young virgins, in order to crush the head of that first and strongest corrupter—the ancient serpent, I mean—who lies in ambush for Christ’s most humble virgins. Who of sound mind would not leap for joy when he now sees our times crowned with so many lilies of virgins [Col. 0682B], fighting manfully with strength not their own but their bridegroom’s against the rage of the hostile dragon, and deserving the crown of triumph?

81. I indeed rejoice that now these lilies are lacking neither in villages nor in cities nor in cloisters; indeed, that many deserts and pathless places are filled with virginal cloisters, so that it may truly be said that the fields of the wilderness put forth shoots, a shoot with the fragrance of the Lord. For young virgins ascend from the wilderness, abounding in the delights of virtues, leaning not on themselves but on their beloved, and patiently awaiting their bridegroom’s coming; so that, when the cry has been raised, they may trim their lamps and enter with him into the everlasting wedding feast, where joy and exultation shall be stored up for them, and the Lord our God shall make them inherit an eternal name [Col. 0682C]. Therefore, O virgins of Christ, do not grow faint in waiting for Christ. For your bridegroom will be present very soon; and he delays his coming for this reason: that, together with your other good works, he may also grant a crown to your waiting. I know, though I have not experienced it, how you groan, how you are pierced with compunction in that most pure chamber of your hearts. Do not fail in your good resolution, so that you may attain the completion of the good work and perseverance, through which you may deserve an everlasting crown.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the leaves of the lily around its stem; that is, on the devout and fruitful words of virgins.

[Col. 0682D]

82. Let us now consider the leaves that are around the stem. The leaves, then, as we said above concerning the leaves of the vine (chap. VI, no. 28), represent words. Regarding these leaves, one should observe that they are always green below; that near the ground they are larger and more numerous than in the upper part; and that, when laid upon abscesses, they break and soften them. The words of virgins ought assuredly to resemble these leaves. The greenness of the leaves therefore signifies the virtue of words: namely, that no word should proceed from the mouth of a virgin of Christ which contains no virtue within it. Here there must be cut away not only foul, buffoonish, jocular, lustful, proud, angry, slanderous, and flattering words, but also superfluous words. For a superfluous word—that is, an idle word—is a dry leaf. [Col. 0683A] But a dry leaf is not a lily leaf. Therefore, if you wish to be a lily, have virtuous words, green leaves, of which it is written: “Its leaf shall not fall” (Ps. 1:3). Do you wish to see that an idle word is a dry leaf? Hear Truth himself, the Lord Jesus: “Every idle word which people speak, they shall render account for it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). O what great terror! The most wise Judge, who counts every drop of rain, the discerner of every thought of every human being from the first Adam to the last who shall be at the end of the age, wishes to hear an account of all idle words when he sits upon the throne of the majesty of his judgment, where mercy will no longer be sung to the Lord, but judgment. What then shall we wretched and pitiable ones do? [Col. 0683B] You are most wise, Lord: you cannot be deceived; you are most just: you cannot be corrupted. The time for showing mercy will then have passed, because you will judge the world in equity and judge peoples in justice—you who previously spared through mercy. What then shall I say? Have mercy, I pray, while it is the time for mercy, Father of mercies, so that you may not judge me in the time of judging. Set a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips, so that I may turn aside not only from cursed and shameful speech, but may also avoid idle words; lest I have to render an account of them on the day of judgment, when an account must be rendered not of the good and green leaves of words but of the evil, dry ones.

83. But what is an idle word? According to Gregory’s testimony, an idle word is one lacking the ground of just necessity [Col. 0683C] or the purpose of pious usefulness (*Morals*, book VII, chap. 18). Therefore, whatever you say, unless you intend to benefit someone, is idle. Who can render an account for all such things? Let every person therefore moderate the tongue, but especially virgins of Christ, so that they may know when and what kind of speech to utter. For it does not become a mouth that sings a new song to its bridegroom to let proceed any word contrary to that song. What then is the new song? The song of charity. Why new? Because at the beginning of the world there was among the first creatures an old song, a song contrary to charity. Do you wish to know it? The angel destined to perish sang in heaven the song of pride, saying: “I will place my throne in the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14). He afterward sang [Col. 0683D] the song of slander in paradise when, approaching the woman, he said: “Why did God forbid you to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?”—as though he were saying, “He forbade it with an evil intention.” The woman sang the song of doubt, saying: “Let us not eat, lest perhaps we die.” O “perhaps,” how much weakness you have brought upon us! But when the devil saw the woman doubting, he burst forth into the song of falsehood, saying: “You shall by no means die” (Gen. 3:1–4). O wicked one, O wicked one, where now is your “by no means”? Behold, those whom you said would by no means die have died a twofold death. “You shall by no means die,” he says. This word contrary to truth is an evil and old song. For God had said: “On whatever day you eat, you shall die by death” [“you shall surely die”] [Col. 0684A] (Gen. 2:17): namely, the death of the soul; or, as others explain it: “You shall die,” that is, “you shall become mortal,” so that you will then have the necessity of dying, whereas now you can avoid death. For had they remained in obedience, they would not have died. Adam too sang the song of excuse in sin when he said: “The woman whom you gave me as a companion gave to me, and I ate” (Gen. 3:12); as if he were saying: “You ought rather to be accused, since you joined to me such a woman as would induce me to sin.”

84. Beloved, these are old songs: the song of pride, the song of slander, the song of doubt, the song of falsehood, and the song of excuse. These songs must be avoided—and avoided in every way—O virgins of Christ, if you wish [Col. 0684B] to sing the new song. Nor should you open your ears to such songs, you who desire to hear Christ’s voice more especially and intimately. That malignant serpent still lives, and beneath a virginal appearance—that is, beneath the semblance of good conversation—he distils the poisons of his malice.
