He still sings the song of pride in the hearts of his hearers when he secretly suggests that they should aspire to honors, dignities, and prelacies, whether because of nobility, learning, or even their own goodness. Indeed, he himself was deceived by these things when he saw himself set above other choirs of angels in nobility of beauty, wisdom, and virtues; and he burst forth into the song of pride, through which he fell and causes all to fall who presume to sing that same song with him.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the new song to be sung by virgins.

[Col. 0684C]

85. The mother of Christ, imitator of the new song, did not sing in this manner, but was a true lily crowned with truly green leaves. Do you wish to see her leaves? Do you wish to hear her song? Exalted beyond all that can be spoken or conceived, set above the whole world and the heavens, she did not rise above herself, but sang the song of humility, which is also the song of charity, because charity is not puffed up. From her heart made drunk she poured forth a good and sweet word, a new song for virgins to sing. And what did she say? “My soul magnifies the Lord” (Luke 1:46). See how contrary this song is to the song of the angel about to fall. He began on high and therefore did not descend to the depths, but fell headlong. Mary began from the low place in order to be raised on high. She magnifies the Lord, not herself; though exalted beyond measure, she observed what is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3:20). Hence she deserved to be raised above all the choirs of angels. He magnified himself above the Lord, and therefore deserved to be cast down beneath everything that exists. The humble Mary’s spirit rejoiced in her Lord Jesus; therefore she deserved to be anointed with the oil of gladness above her companions. That foolish angel rejoiced in himself; therefore he deserved perpetual condemnation to mourning. She glories that her humility has been regarded; therefore she will bear fruit in the regard shown to holy souls. He gloried in the abundance [Col. 0685A] of his power; therefore he incurred perpetual contempt.

86. Therefore, O virgins of Christ, be green in your leaves—in words of charity, humility, and patience. Follow that preeminent lily, the Mother of the highest lily, good Jesus, so that, magnifying him alone who alone is great, you may deserve to be magnified in him, through him, and with him. Likewise beware the song of slander, which began in paradise: an old song that leads into the oldness of sin. See how utterly contrary it is to the new song of charity, since it is necessary not to love the person against whom slander is spoken. For charity is accustomed neither to speak against another nor to slander, but rather to excuse another’s sins; or, if correction is perhaps necessary, it does so [Col. 0685B] not with the intention of maligning but of correcting. Beware also the song of doubt: do not doubt the Lord’s mercy, but boldly cast all your care upon him, because he has care for you. For he is not cruel, so as to allow you to fall if you cast yourselves upon him—he who urges you to do this, and who knows that for his sake you have voluntarily deprived yourselves of every earthly consolation. Nor doubt that punishment will be inflicted upon the wicked according to their deserts, lest you fall into the vice of presumption; nor doubt that reward will be bestowed upon the just, lest perhaps you incur the peril of despair. Beware lest at any time the song of falsehood proceed from your mouth, by which you disdain spiritually to praise your bridegroom, who is Truth. A virgin’s mouth destroys her virginity whenever she knowingly speaks in a malicious spirit lies contrary to truth. Likewise beware the song of excuse in sins, always holding in mind that testimony of the blessed virgin John, who bears witness to truth [variant: “virginity”]. [Col. 0685C] “Little children,” he says, “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just: he forgives us our sins and cleanses us from all iniquity” (1 John 1:8–9). Therefore let no one think that he is without sins; nor, when he has recognized them, let him excuse himself, as fools are accustomed still today to repeat Adam’s excuse and say: “The woman whom God gave me deceived me. Why did God give me such a woman as would deceive me?” This woman who deceives the man is the flesh, leading our spirit [Col. 0685D] to consent to sins. Because of her, fools daily accuse God while wallowing in their sins and saying that they cannot resist the allurements of the flesh, which they received from God. It is a very great sin to accuse the supremely good God, who made all things very good for your sake, and especially adorned humanity above the other creatures. The good God, who made all things good—indeed, very good—for your sake, undoubtedly made you good. For he would not be good if he had made you evil, you for whose sake he made all things, and made all things very good for your sake. God therefore made you good, and very good. You yourself, though good, make yourself truly evil. If you remove from yourself what you yourself make, you will discover that you are very good among the creatures [Col. 0686A] which he himself made. He first made you according to himself, and afterward was made according to you. He first made you in his image and likeness, and afterward he himself was made human in your likeness. For “the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14). Let us therefore praise God, who made us according to himself. Let us love God, who for our sake was made according to us. Let us pray to him that he may deign mercifully to restore his image wherever it has been disfigured in our soul; and likewise that he may deign to preserve immaculate his body, which he took according to our likeness and nature. And let us bring forth green leaves—that is, words containing virtues—if we wish to be true lilies, which do not possess the words of the old songs but are known to accord with the new song, that is, [Col. 0686B] with charity, hope, humility, and the other virtues.

87. Let us put forth leaves—and you especially, O virgins of Christ, who take your name from greenness—that are green, and that, laid upon abscesses, may break them, relieve them, and heal them when the pus has been expelled. This happens whenever by good words consonant with truth we lead the unchaste person to chastity, the proud to humility, the angry to gentleness, the avaricious to generosity, the gluttonous to sobriety, the envious to charity, and the slothful to earnestness. These vices weigh down the soul like ulcers, containing within themselves the poison of impurity and evil habit. Since we remember that, in the treatise on the leaves of the vine, we gave examples concerning each of them, we judge that for brevity’s sake they should here be passed over [Col. 0686C]. We say only this: each person’s particular affliction must be considered, so that according to the magnitude and character of the ailment we may administer the medicine of words; and likewise with the other vices, as was set forth above. For this must be understood: one should not always pursue silence, although silence must be kept with great care; rather, we ought sometimes to close and sometimes to open the door of our mouth, so that evils may be silenced without also silencing good and useful things together with them. The Prophet likewise intimates this in his petition when he said: “Set, Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140:3). A door is neither always open nor always shut; but in the house of the wise person [Col. 0686D] it stands open for sending out wise messengers and is shut for keeping fools inside. So too our mouth is the door of our heart, through which words go forth as certain messengers, reporting what takes place inwardly in the heart. It must be opened at the proper time to prudent and useful words; but it must constantly be closed to evil words that arise from the heart’s bad impulses. “There is a time to speak and a time to keep silence.” Nor does one who withholds a word at a fitting time sin less than one who, by speaking wickedly, causes others to stumble. For a person seems exceedingly miserly and envious if he neglects to dispense to his neighbors, for their benefit, words received freely. When do you suppose he will give his own substance to a needy neighbor—substance which is diminished by division—if he does not give words that never fail? Let the Lord therefore set a guard upon our mouth, so that we may know when and what kind of speech we ought to utter; and a door of restraint around our lips, so that it may be not only opened but also shut at the proper time, lest we offend in either respect. But let our words, laid upon the abscesses of sick souls like lily leaves, with the Lord’s help cast out the pus of vices and be able to implant the strengths of virtues in their hearers [Col. 0687A].

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the lower and upper leaves of the lily; or, on abundance and restraint in speech.

88. What does it mean that the leaves near the ground are larger [Col. 0687B] and more numerous, while those above are fewer and smaller, except that just people, and especially virgins, the higher they ascend to the summit of virtues, leaving earthly thoughts and desires below, ought to be so much the more disciplined and restrained in their words? For the diminution of the leaves in the upper part signifies discipline in speech, because disciplined persons, as it were, prune and make their words slender, lest anything contrary to modesty or discipline be found in them; whereas undisciplined and base persons pour forth swollen and inflated words, devoid of all decency. By the fewness of the leaves, moreover, is fittingly understood a scarcity of words, to which all good people apply themselves more diligently the nearer they stand to the cultivation of virtues. Hence it is read of one brother [Col. 0687C] who wished to learn and, as it were, acquire the practice of correcting his tongue, that he carried a stone in his mouth for three years; and of another, that he had not spoken anything for thirty years. We see many people who, at the beginning of a good resolution and still, as it were, close to the earth, led by former habit, are unable to observe either moderation or fewness of words; their words are represented by the lily’s leaves near the ground. But as time goes on and grace is added, they moderate their speech according to their progress and strive for silence, so as to avoid not only wicked but even idle words.

89. To what good state, however, does discipline and fewness of speech better belong than to a virgin [Col. 0687D] of Christ? For if every Christian is commanded that neither foul speech nor buffoonery should proceed from their mouth, but rather thanksgiving (Eph. 5:4), how much more ought a virgin who consecrates chastity to her Lord to abstain from all these things at all times? She who has undoubtedly not violated her chastity ought to render to the Lord thanksgiving so much the greater as the grace she has received is greater. For to be good virgins is the highest good and the highest grace, because they alone follow the Lamb wherever he goes (Rev. 14:4). Who cannot see how much she also ought to abstain from an abundance of words, since all talkativeness is a sign of immodesty, which can in no way coexist with virginal modesty? Therefore let chaste virgins especially avoid the vice of talkativeness [Col. 0688A], if they wish to preserve the virtue of chastity. For it is evident that “in much speaking sin will not be lacking” (Prov. 10:19); rather, one proceeds little by little from idle words to slanders, until at last one bursts forth into open insults. The apostle James rebukes talkativeness in these words: “If anyone thinks himself religious, while not restraining his tongue but deceiving his heart, that person’s religion is vain” (Jas. 1:26). Let no one therefore flatter himself concerning the religious habit who has not yet learned to bind his tongue. Bind your tongue if you wish to be religious, for without the binding of the tongue religion is vain. Hence the most holy Fathers who founded religious orders, and their most wise followers, taught as they had been taught by the Spirit of wisdom [Col. 0688B], strictly ordained the observance of silence, not being ignorant that, “as a city lying open and without the circuit of walls, so is a man who cannot restrain his spirit in speaking” (Prov. 25:28). And, as the Psalm says: “A man of tongue shall not be established on the earth” (Ps. 140:12). Spiritual persons also know, through experience, how much the frequent unloosing of the tongue removes devotion inwardly and brings laxity. For as a furnace whose mouth is always open cannot retain heat within itself, so neither can a heart retain within itself the grace of devotion if its mouth is not closed by the door of silence. Therefore let us close our mouth, so that with the ardor of devotion we may preserve Christ, the giver of devotion, in the fervent affection of our heart.

[Col. 0688C]

90. But you especially, O virgins, brides of Christ, enter the chamber of your heart; and, with the door of your mouth shut, pray intimately, humbly, tearfully, joyfully, sweetly, and confidently to your bridegroom, your king, your father, and your comforter. Pour out before him—who beholds all hearts—your hearts; converse with him in remembrance of him; pour out your souls over yourselves; and, leaving earthly and bodily things behind, rise on the spiritual wings of charity. Pass into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, unto the house of God, where you may hear with the ears not of the body but of the heart the voice of rejoicing and the sound of confession, celebrating a feast day. There, refreshed by inward consolation, when the moment of storm and need [Col. 0688D], temptation and flesh comes upon you, you may be able to remember heavenly refreshment and say: “Why are you sad, O my soul? And why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall yet praise him: the salvation of my countenance and my God” (Ps. 42:5). Remember the supremely good Lord God; remember and delight yourselves, and let the spirit of your flesh fail, so that you may be refreshed by his Spirit, who is sweeter than honey, and learn to despise outward conversations after you have tasted the sweetness of inward conversation. O how good and pleasant—O how good and pleasant it is—to dwell together with you, O sweetest Jesus; to converse with you; to reveal to you the cause of our soul; and to enjoy the answer of your consolation! O how good it is [Col. 0689A] to approach, led by charity, you who dwell in inaccessible light—whom, if charity alone is our guide, nothing inaccessible can remain! Your heart, O sweet Jesus, wounded by the lance of charity, knows how to make a way for charity, to whom it shall never be shut.

91. Therefore approach him through him with the steps of charity, and be enlightened; taste that he is sweet. Those who have experienced it know—and know well, those who have tasted God’s good gift from another side—how bitter and wearisome it is, after they have at some time been brought by our true vine into the wine-cellar, to be separated from the sweetness of that contemplation’s inward presence and brought back to outward bodily sights or sounds. For when good Jesus, insofar as is permitted in the present life, has wished to lead his familiar disciples apart from the other brethren onto the mountain of contemplation [Col. 0689B], to be transfigured before them, to appear in a white garment of his sweetness and goodness to their astonishment, and to intoxicate with steadfast charity those whom he had previously visited by fear of judgment or through the violence of salutary temptations—for God sometimes presents himself to the hearts of his own through scourges—when therefore, as we have said, he has at some time deigned to be transfigured in the hearts of his own so that sorrow may be turned into joy, if meanwhile, while these things are taking place in some manner I cannot explain, someone seeking an outward presence is so affected as to compel him to descend from the mountain of beloved contemplation: do you suppose that he would patiently endure such an outward compulsion, rather than cry out with Peter, “Lord, [Col. 0689C] it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17:1–4), and with Paul, “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24). O how bitter it is for those who have known how to be satisfied with such inward refreshment to be drawn back again to outward things! They seem to themselves to die, because it is indeed a kind of death to be torn away again from the contemplation of life, from the contemplation of white-clad Jesus, from the contemplation of his countenance shining like the sun, into these shadows; and to be recalled from Mary’s sweetness to Martha’s service.

92. In short, I say that whoever knows how to occupy the eyes of the mind with inward contemplations and to open the tongue of the soul for divine conversation not only takes no delight in outward sights or conversations, but is greatly wearied by them. [Col. 0689D] But those who are inwardly blind and mute, and do not know how to occupy themselves with divine contemplation and devout prayers, seek the support of outward senses and strive to spend the length of time that burdens them in useless talk. For wishing to be occupied with outward conversations is the surest sign of an idle soul, which is not raised by any devotion at all to divine conversation. Certainly those who do not know, or refuse, to restrain their tongue from an abundance of words have not yet reached the summit of the lily. And each person knows that he has climbed so much higher through the degrees of virtue as he takes less delight in human conversation—unless, perhaps, it is with persons of such a kind that God himself speaks in them [Col. 0690A] and through whom God’s word is heard. Such persons are heard not for their own sake, but for God’s, who both dwells and speaks in them. By conversing with such people, the Lord often cooperating, we are freed from our doubts, drawn away from evil, and strengthened in our good resolution. Yet in all things the spirit of discernment must be desired and implored from the Lord, so that by his revelation we may know which spirit is to be believed, to whom the thought of our simple hearts is to be revealed, and from whom a word of salvation is to be heard; lest our simplicity be caught by the deceit of the crafty serpent, who is accustomed very often to mingle evil with good, falsehood with truth, and error with what is right.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On contemplating in the lily—that is, the beauty and excellence of true virginity.

[Col. 0690B]

93. Let us now come to contemplate the lily flower itself. See, O virgin of Christ, how greatly this flower of yours—signifying your own flower—surpasses other flowers in beauty. See what special grace it obtains above all flowers on earth. See what praise it deserves from your Bridegroom himself above every flower. “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow. Amen, I say to you, not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed as one of these” (Luke 12:27). Therefore read, O virgin, read through, and read again and again this saying of your Bridegroom; and understand how, in commending this flower, he commended your glory. That wisest Creator and Maker of all things covered all the world’s glory with your single little flower; indeed, he did not set glory beneath the little flower, but preferred this little flower to all glory. In Solomon, of whom it is written that he was magnified above all the kings of the whole earth in riches and honor (1 Kings 10; 2 Chron. 9), you must understand all worldly glories. In the flower of your lily, which bears the figure of your own virginity and that of all Christ’s virgins, contemplate the glory of virginity. If, then, the beauty of your lily is so highly commended by Truth himself that all the glory of Solomon is rightly set beneath it—Solomon, who beyond doubt was magnificently clothed in proportion to the greatness of his glory—how greatly, do you suppose, must the incorrupt lily of your virginity itself be commended, which no stain shall ever corrupt, when even its shadow and figure deserved such honor? If all the raiment of all Solomon’s glory cannot be compared with the beauty of one material little lily, what beauty can be compared with your flowering virginity, which is your true and special lily? None, I say; for no earthly beauty can surpass the splendor and loftiness of your beauty, because not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.

94. Therefore do not sing sadly: “I have despised the kingdom of the world and all the adornment of the age for love of our Lord Jesus Christ” (*Responsory in the Church Office for Holy Virgins*). For he has given you even in this present life a beauty greater than every worldly beauty: by preserving for himself the lily of your integrity, dedicating it to himself particularly above the other beauties of virtues, and binding it to himself with special love. You will see this clearly in the Song of Love, where, with almost all other flowers passed over, he repeatedly names your flower, continually repeating the name of the lily: “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters” (Song 2:2); and likewise, “My beloved went up to the bed of spices, to gather lilies”; and again, “My beloved is mine and I am his, who feeds among the lilies” (Song 6:1–2). A praiseworthy lily, the bridegroom’s beloved; a lovely lily, gathered by the bridegroom. For, as I judge, it is not gathered in order to wither thereafter, but to be placed upon the golden altar that is before the eyes of the Lord—that is, placed in the heavenly sanctuary, so that this lily may be an ornament to the other saints. Truly a delicate lily, in which the bridegroom feeds: not because he delights in this alone, [Col. 0691B] but because by a certain special prerogative of love he delights in it more than in others. Nor without reason. For virgins possess a twofold good which in other saints, who are not virgins, is single. Since the whole Church is a virgin in soul, having neither spot nor wrinkle and remaining incorrupt in faith, hope, and charity—on account of which she is called a virgin and deserves praise from the bridegroom—how great, do you think, is the praise due to our lilies, which here possess in both body and soul what the whole Church possesses only in soul? For virgins of Christ are, as it were, the fat and marrow of the Church; and by a certain singular excellence they cling more intimately than other flowers to the bridegroom’s embraces.

95. This, however, must be considered with the utmost care by virgins who delight in the beauty of the lily: the lily flower is white both within and without. What is signified by the flower’s white outer part except bodily purity, or by its inner part except the purity of the virginal mind? It would be shameful—indeed, it would not be a lily—to lack the purity of either its inward or outward whiteness. So also shameful is the virgin—indeed, she is not a virgin—who does not possess both, namely, chastity of mind and body. Here I do not doubt that many of either sex have died virgins in body and will be saved, yet will by no means deserve the virginal reward. For they died while physically incorrupt but mentally corrupt; yet their mental corruption did not itself require eternal death, because they awaited lawful marriages and, apart from them, did not wish to commit any unlawful unions. [Col. 0691D] For if, as the Apostle says, “a virgin marries, she has not sinned” (1 Cor. 7:28), even she who marries solely from desire has nevertheless already corrupted in her mind the flower of virginity. Blessed Augustine agrees with this judgment, saying that a virgin aspiring to marriage is by no means better than a woman who has obtained marriage: for she who has already married is content with one husband, whereas she who is about to marry, seeking throughout the whole people someone to whom she may attach herself, must commit fornication in mind with many (*On Holy Virginity*, chap. 11). [Col. 0692A] For one man pleases her today, another tomorrow, then a third and a fourth, and perhaps more; and if such a woman dies, how will she obtain the merit of uncorrupted virginity?

96. But whether those virgins who are violated by force after a vow of virginity and never consent at any time to the corruption; or those who before their vow at some time firmly aspired to marriage, though afterward moved by repentance they bound themselves by a vow of chastity; or again those who, after the vow, at some time withdrew from the vow of continence in will alone but returned once more to steadfastness in the vow and persevered until the end—whether, I say, such virgins ought to be crowned with the reward, I confess that I do not know from authority. I think this should be left to more learned persons, or rather to divine judgment itself. [Col. 0692B] Concerning the first group, those who suffer violence, I speak more by conjecture than by definition: if they never consent to their corruption either in will or in pleasure, they should not be deprived of the blessed virginal reward. [Note: [Col. 0691D] See Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chaps. 16–20.] This seems capable of confirmation from Lucy’s words, if indeed they are authentic. [Note: [Col. 0691D] For she answered Paschasius: “The body is never defiled except by consent of the mind. If you cause me to be violated against my will [Col. 0692D], my chastity will be doubled for my crown.” In Surius, 13 December.] If virginal chastity is lost even through violence and without the consent of those who lose it, I hope that such a loss of chastity turns to the good of those who suffer it. For perhaps benign Jesus permitted them to be deprived of such a good because he foreknew that they would not use it well. Indeed, it would be beneficial for a woman who, because of the merit of virginity, would be destined for pride [Note: [Col. 0692D] See Augustine, *City of God*, book I, chap. 28.] to lose her virginity and thereby attain the virtue of humility.

97. But virgins must with the greatest care avoid places and occasions favorable to seducers [Col. 0692C], lest, if through their own foolishness they furnish an occasion for their own corruption, they seem rightly to have harmed themselves and be deprived of their crown. For if Bathsheba had not bathed herself immodestly or incautiously on the roof, and Susanna in the orchard, where they could in some degree be seen, the former would not have fallen into adultery nor the latter into danger of death. Let virgins be cautious, as they are chaste. Let them learn to bar the windows of their eyes and ears and to hide their faces, lest through seeing or hearing what perhaps is unfitting they bring death upon themselves; lest, while they are heedlessly seen and heard by others, they kill those others, though unknowingly. We know that this has often happened, through the prompting and snares of him of whom it is written: “He sits in ambush with the rich in secret places, that he may kill the innocent” (Ps. 10:8). [Col. 0692D] But concerning others who have fallen at some time in will alone, whether before the vow or after it, it seems to me—without prejudice to anyone’s better opinion—that they do not lose the crown of virginity, provided that they soon returned to the vow and remained faithful in it. Yet I think that the merit of the crown should be diminished in some measure according to the change of will: thus, if someone persisted for a long time, or with firm resolve, in the intention of breaking her vow of virginity, she has so much less merit in the crown [Col. 0693A]. But I judge that those who have striven from their earliest years to vow and preserve virginity for their bridegroom, the Lord Jesus, will possess a wholly undiminished crown.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That the lily flower, bent toward the earth, teaches humility.

98. Nor should it be passed over that the flower of the lily itself, though so tall, so white, so delightful, always bends down toward the earth. What else is commended to us by this but humility? For to bend one’s head toward the earth is to incline our mind toward earthly generation and the frailty contracted from the earth, lest we dare to presume anything whatever concerning ourselves, when we reflect that we are mud and ashes. [Col. 0693B] Now this virtue is necessary to no one so much as to virgins, lest they fall into the depth of pride while considering the excellence of their merits.

For Christ’s virgins, while still living on earth, lead the life of angels, since they are such as the Lord said human beings would be after the resurrection: “For then they shall neither marry nor be given in marriage, but shall be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. XXII, 30). Yet Christ’s virgins do not merely await the incorruption of the resurrection; even in the present they live incorruptibly, undoubtedly emulating an angelic life. Therefore, lest from so exalted a rank—which they have courageously ascended not at anyone’s command, but by their own will—they fall shamefully through pride, let them bend toward the earth like the lily flower. [Col. 0693C] Let them remember that they are dust, and that their days are like grass; nor let them yet suppose that they have risen to the blessedness of immortality, but that they are still enclosed by that fleshly wall which separates them from their beloved Jesus.

Let them beware of that crafty serpent, who lies in wait for them in many ways, lest he seduce them into presuming something concerning themselves: so that they may think that the good they possess is not from God but from their own strength; or believe that it has been bestowed on them for their own merits; or, because of what they have received from God, believe themselves uniquely better than others; or suppose that they possess what they do not possess. These are the four kinds of boasting by which that most wicked serpent not infrequently deceives even good people.

99. Those deceived by the first kind—who do not think [Col. 0693D] that they have received from God what they possess—fall into the greatest of all crimes, that of ingratitude. For what is worse than not to acknowledge God as the giver of every good? How will one who does not acknowledge this give thanks to him, from whom he thinks that he has received nothing? Certainly there are not a few such people, whom you can recognize from their own words. For what do they say? “Why,” they ask, “have you not preserved your chastity? Why do you not possess the virtue of humility and patience? Why do you not have devotion in prayer and streams of tears?” What do you suppose those who say this think, except that they themselves have these things from themselves, and that anyone may have them from herself?

Do not think thus, O virgin of Christ; rather, know that from yourself you have nothing except sins. All other [Col. 0694A] good things are gifts of the grace of your bridegroom. Rejoice therefore—that is, be glad and give thanks—to him from whom you have both being and well-being. And love your beloved all the more, the more numerous and greater the goods by which he proves his love toward you. Indeed, love the gifts of virtues themselves more, and preserve them more carefully, because you have deserved to receive them from one so beloved and so worthy of love, rather than because you had attained them through your own powers. By carefully retaining what has been given, show your love for your beloved bridegroom who gave it; for so precious a giver ought not to give cheap gifts.

100. Those of the second kind, who believe that they have indeed received from God what they possess, but nevertheless on account of their own merits, wish to strip the gracious Lord Jesus of his grace. Why do you think that you have received virtue on account of your merits? Tell me: who gave you the ability to merit? “For what have you that you did not receive? Why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7). Yet if you wish to know how you received it, hear the same apostle: “By the grace of God,” he says, “we have been saved.” But when we are saved according to our works, we are not saved by our own righteous deeds; rather, grace is given for grace. For by God’s grace we are what we are, whether in possessing virtues or in attaining heavenly things.

101. Those of the third kind, who from a spiritual gift think themselves better than others and despise others as inferior to themselves, are oppressed by the plague of that Pharisee who, even while giving thanks for virtues received, sinned because he despised the Publican (Luke XVIII, 11). But since very many suffer from this plague, let us attempt, with the Lord’s help, to apply some remedy to them.

This, I think, must be considered: someone lacks a certain spiritual virtue; perhaps that person has another virtue like it, or one greater than it. Hence Jerome says: “Virginity and the virtue of chastity are splendid, provided they are not weakened by falls into other stains.” For the greater the one whom we must please, the greater must be our effort to please him. If you are a virgin, it is still uncertain to you to what degree of virginal dignity you have ascended. For all virgins are not of equal merit. What holy man can be counted equal to John in chastity and praise? What woman among virgins has attained to the height of the dignity of the most exalted Virgin Mary? Therefore do not [Col. 0694D] exalt yourself above anyone whose mind you do not know, lest you fall beneath all.

Likewise, even if you perhaps hold the lowest place in the dignity of virginity, how will you dare to compare yourself with one who has perhaps ascended near the highest degree in humility, charity, or obedience? What if the person whom you dare to prefer yourself over has attained such perfection that he does not doubt—indeed, with God as witness, to whom his conscience is known—that with all his mind he burns to drain the cup of suffering for the Lord? But perhaps you say here that, with your conscience also bearing witness, you are prepared to endure suffering. To this we answer that no one can truthfully recognize in himself the steadfastness of this virtue unless he has learned it in actuality, with experience as his teacher. [Col. 0695A] For how many, do you think, failed amid the bitterness of tortures who thought that they would persevere courageously unto death?

Therefore do not judge yourself, since you do not know yourself. For Paul, most perfect of all, says: “But neither do I judge myself; he who judges me is the Lord.” You ought much less to judge others, because he adds in the same place: “Therefore judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will also bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (I Cor. IV, 3–5). There, without doubt, many people will be preferred, contrary to human opinion, by the judgment of the Lord who sees all things; and those thought falsely worthy of preference will be placed after them. There is also a further strong reason which should draw you away from this kind of boasting. Hold it thus: one person may be more righteous than another, another more holy than another; nevertheless, that same person does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or of love.

102. Let all who are best exercise their minds in this matter; and, constrained by fear and humility, they will bend toward the earth after the example of the lily, when they remember that they do not know whether they are worthy of love or hatred. And truly they do not know, nor do they know what the coming day—indeed, not even the coming hour—will bring forth. How much less do they know what their end will be, or the end of those who are now evil?

If you had seen Judas the traitor while he was still a disciple and among the foremost, casting out demons in the name of gracious Jesus, and had seen the Thief afterwards crucified with Christ, who until then had persisted in robbery and murder, I do not doubt that you would have preferred the Disciple to the Thief. Yet we all know [Col. 0695C] which of the two was preferred at the end. Therefore, even if you have already attained such perfection of life that you work miracles, fear lest in the end you be found rejected together with Judas himself. But if you see someone else laboring at most wicked deeds, do not prefer yourself to that person, since you do not know whether, after the example of the Thief, he may be converted at the last, as it is written: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not imputed sin” (Ps. XXXI, 2). This is commonly understood of those who, after their crimes, are turned to the Lord by the Lord, who considers the manner in which each person dies.

Therefore do not dare to judge anyone; nor, even if you are excellent, prefer yourself to any other person, however evil, because you do not know what your own end, or that person’s, will be. To bend to the earth with the flower of the lily, then, means: consider [Col. 0695D] your own frailty in yourself, because you are earth and ashes; and the greater you are, humble yourself in all things, bowing the purity of the flesh by the virtue of humility.

103. But what is more vain than those who think that they possess what they do not possess? Yet almost the whole human race suffers from this plague. For who is there who knows himself perfectly, except one to whom this has been granted by the Father of lights, by the true light that enlightens every person? From heaven came, “Γνῶθι σεαυτόν” [Know yourself]. For in the Song of Songs, the Bride herself, who panted for the embraces of the Bridegroom and had sensed the fragrance of his ointments, was in a manner rebuked for ignorance of herself, when the Bridegroom said: “If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, depart from [Col. 0696A] me” (Song I, 7).

See, therefore, how great an evil every ignorance of oneself is, on account of which one deserves to be rejected by the most loving Bridegroom. Let us therefore return to self-knowledge—that is, to our own earth—if we wish to be true lilies and to be admitted to the Bridegroom’s presence. Let us continually examine ourselves within, ceaselessly crying to the true and gracious Jesus that he may deign to enlighten the eyes of our minds for knowing ourselves.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the number of leaves of our lily, or the three disadvantages of the present life which virgins escape, and the equal number of advantages of the future life which await them

104. Let us now turn our attention to the number of leaves of the flower itself, our most gracious Jesus, the whitest of flowers, enlightening [Col. 0696B] us. In perfect lilies the white flower itself consists for the most part of six leaves. By these six we understand six reasons which ought to stir the minds of virgins toward the purity of virginity: three concern the present life, and three the future.

There are three disadvantages in the present life for married persons, on account of which virginal chastity is to be sought. There are likewise three benefits of future glory, on account of which vowed virginity is to be acquired and preserved. We have two disadvantages of the present life from the curse inflicted upon our first parent Eve after the transgression of sin. For the serpent was subjected to three curses, Eve to two, and Adam to one. To the serpent the Lord said: “Upon your breast you shall go; you shall eat earth; and the woman shall tread upon your head.” [Col. 0696C] But to Eve God said: “In sorrow you shall bear children, and you shall be under the power of your husband.” And to Adam he said: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread” (Gen. III, 14, 15, 16, 19).

105. The curses of Eve, and through her of all married women, are two that are expressed in the present passage: namely, that they bear children in pain and are under the power of their husbands. No human being knows how great the pain of women in childbirth is, except those who have experienced it. In the Scriptures, however, we frequently find testimony concerning this pain, because when we wish to express the magnitude of some grief, we customarily compare it to a woman in labor. For the Lord himself, who knows all griefs, when he saw that his disciples were exceedingly distressed at his death, wished to compare their sorrow with the sorrow of a woman in labor, saying: “A woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow because her hour has come; so you also now indeed have sorrow” (John XVI, 21–22).

Likewise, blessed Paul, wishing to show the pain of those who will be found unprepared on the day of final judgment, says: “When they say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them, like pain upon a woman with child, and they shall not escape” (I Thess. V, 3). Many examples of the magnitude of this pain are also found repeatedly in the Prophets and other Scriptures. But because living women who have known it from experience furnish more abundant testimony, it seems unnecessary to dwell longer on the matter.

[Col. 0697A] But blessed and truly prudent are the virgins who, apart even from temporal advantages, have chosen more closely to be joined to the Lord in spirit, producing spiritual offspring—that is, good works—for their immortal bridegroom Jesus far better, more abundantly, and more securely, not at intervals of years but every day. They love him into whose most chaste bridal chamber they entered with chastity as their guide—or rather, whom they received into the bridal chamber of their own heart. They heard his harmonious voice in his commandments and promises of heavenly rewards; and as their Bridegroom spoke, they answered him through obedience. His love makes chastity; his touch makes purity; his marriage makes and preserves virgins.

O truly blessed women, who have consecrated to such a husband purity not only of mind but also of body! By fellowship with him they are made so fruitful [Col. 0697B] in mind that they become mothers of every virtue. The children of these virtues dwell eternally in the heavenly house, and the seed of their works shall be established before their Bridegroom forever.

106. Christ’s virgins likewise escape the second curse of our mother Eve—and through her, of all married women—namely, that they are not under the power of a mortal husband. Consider more carefully how great a good you find in this, and how great an evil you escape. Let us hear the judgment of the apostle Paul concerning this: “The virgin who is unmarried thinks of the things of God, that she may be holy in body and spirit. But she who is married thinks of the things of the world, how she may please her husband” (I Cor. X, 34).

What is gained? A considerable evil is escaped: worldly anxiety about how to please one’s husband. [Col. 0697C] How greatly, do you think, is devotion increased in virginal minds because, without any care hindering them, they can freely devote themselves to prayers and other spiritual exercises whenever they wish and whenever they ought? How many troubles do married women have, even when they are religious and wish to give themselves to God, when they are prevented by their own husbands, to whom they must be subject? This is a great burden of marriage when women are joined to husbands who are at odds with their good morals and good manner of life.

How many married women, do you think, would wish to purchase with torments the freedom, released from the power of evil men, to offer free service to the Lord? Blessed, therefore, are the virgins who, receiving Christ as their Bridegroom, have subjected themselves to him alone, whose yoke is sweet and whose burden light; and who desire with their whole and undivided [Col. 0697D] mind to please him alone, who is indeed beautiful beyond the children of men. They do not divide their minds so as partly to desire and anxiously seek to please God, and partly to please a husband; rather, they give themselves whole and entire to him from whom they received that they might exist, and received that they might exist well; and beyond this, they received him himself as their Bridegroom by a free gift.

What can you repay worthily to your giver? He gave you to yourself when he created you, so that you might exist; he restored you to yourself when he re-created you, so that you might exist well; as provision for your journey, lest you fail on the way, he gave you his Body and Blood—himself, true God and true human being. And what will you repay? If you cannot repay him in return for what he gave you when he created you, what, finally, will you repay for the fact that he gave himself to you? Certainly, even if you could repay yourself a thousand times, what would you be in comparison with God?

Yet repay as much as you can: repay yourself wholly to him who both gave you wholly to yourself and restored you wholly to yourself; and, not content with this, gave his whole self also to you. Love him who so greatly loves you, and love your unique Beloved with all your soul, with all your heart, and with all your strength, because he himself gave you both a heart of good will, a rational soul, and strength for accomplishing good things. Let your soul bless the Lord, and do not forget all his benefits. Bind yourself with the bonds of his love, so that you may more freely give yourself to him and see how sweet the Lord is. If you taste him rightly, then, as he himself draws you, you will no longer be brought under another’s power. For every wise person [Col. 0698B] would refuse to be released from the service of him for whom to serve is to reign. Who, moreover, would not wish to reign? Do you wish to reign happily? Serve gracious Jesus, and you shall reign, because to serve him is to reign. Thus it is written of the saints that they shall reign with Christ forever (Rev. XXII, 5).

What does “they shall reign” mean? They shall be kings. For the Apostle also says: “They shall indeed be heirs of God, but co-heirs of Christ” (Rom. VIII, 17). Therefore they shall truly be kings: heirs of God’s kingdom and co-heirs of the King. Most blessed, therefore, are the virgins subject to the yoke of him alone, who changes his servants into kings, whose kingdom shall not be changed forever.

107. The third reason for seeking virginity is freedom from the manifold anxieties that attend, beyond description, the rearing of children. Only parents know how great this anxiety is. For the magnitude of their concern extends according to the love they feel toward their children; and no one except parents knows that love. Truly did he say:

> Only parents know what the love of offspring is.

Hence, it sometimes happens that this concern grows so extensive that it occupies all the powers of the mind, and, setting everything else aside, parents think only of their children. The mind runs about and wanders, traversing sea and land; it leaves nothing untried. The bodies of wretched parents are also worn down by much and varied labor so that money and property may be acquired for their children. Nor, even after acquiring more than necessity requires, do they rest, because greed enters under the pretext of love for their children, and so forth.

[Col. 0698D]

> Love of money grows as money itself grows.  
> —Juvenal, *Satires* IV, line 139.

And one desires it less when one does not possess it; consequently they die in miseries. They cannot suffer with others and do not wish to show mercy; and these most wretched parents make themselves unworthy of obtaining mercy. By now, I think, you see how great an evil the concern felt for children produces, and to what end it tends.

But how much anxiety, do you think, is added even to good parents, and especially to mothers, who are customarily moved by greater affection toward their children, when they see their children’s lives wandering into the byways of vices, having abandoned the path of virtues; when they see them afflicted by various bodily illnesses; and finally when they see them come at last to the destruction of death? What place remains, amid such miseries, for divine contemplation? How can the heart be held aloft toward the Lord when oppressed by such heavy burdens?

O how blessed are virgins whose Bridegroom can die no more, whose children—that is, their virtues—always live, indeed even lead them to life; whose minds do not descend toward diverse earthly things, forgetful of what lies behind! Blessed virgins already bear heaven and its joys in their minds, as far as is permitted to a human being—heaven which will moreover bear them. Already they range through heavenly joys, pass in singular fashion through the choirs of most blessed spirits, discern with the living keenness of their spiritual mind the distinct offices of each choir, and with the untrammeled eagerness of their minds taste beforehand the joys of the individual virgins prepared for them by their King and Bridegroom, [Col. 0699B] delayed by no anxiety over earthly children.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the three benefits of the future life which virgins shall obtain

108. Let us follow, and continue to pursue, the three benefits of the future life which will belong especially to Christ’s virgins, in our treatment of the proposed subject. In his Apocalypse, the most blessed John the Evangelist saw twelve times twelve thousand holy harpists, possessing unstained virginity in body and inviolable freshness in heart, following the Lamb, the Bridegroom of virgins, wherever he goes (Rev. XIV, 1–4). Behold the special reward of virgins, by which the fourth leaf of the lily flower is signified: that they follow the Lamb wherever he goes.

Where do we think this Lamb goes, where no one may dare or be able to follow him except you? Where, I ask, do we think he goes? Into what glades? Into what meadows? I believe that he goes where true joys are found: not the vain, mad, deceitful joys of this world; nor even such joys as are granted to others in the kingdom of God itself; but joys of Christ’s virgins, distinct by their lot from those of others—joys concerning Christ, with Christ, after Christ, through Christ; joys proper to Christ’s virgins.

The joys of non-virgins—that is, of those who are not virgins, though they belong to Christ—are not the same. There are different joys for different persons, but none like these. They follow the Lamb wherever he goes because the flesh of the Lamb is itself virginal. For while he was in the body, he retained in himself what he did not take away from his Mother. [Col. 0699D] For he was conceived, a virgin, from a Virgin; born a Virgin from a Virgin; and after his birth remained a Virgin with his virgin Mother: the Lord Jesus Christ, author, guardian, lover of virginity, and most generous rewarder of it.

Rightly, therefore, they follow him wherever he goes in this life also, through virginity of heart and body. For what is following except imitating? Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, as the apostle Peter says, “that you may follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II, 21). Each person follows him in that respect in which he imitates him, in those matters in which he is presented to all as greatly to be imitated; but bodily virginity is not proposed to all. For they cannot make themselves virgins. Therefore let the other faithful who have lost bodily virginity follow the Lamb, not wherever he goes, but wherever they themselves can.

They can follow him in all virtues, except when he proceeds in the beauty of virginity. For how can those who have lost here what they can by no means recover afterwards follow him along the virginal way? You therefore, O his virgins, go after him; since for this reason you follow him wherever he goes, persevere in what you have vowed and eagerly do what you can, lest the good of virginity perish for you. Once it has been lost, you can do nothing to make it return.

O with how much amazement and joy will the rest of the multitude of saints see [Col. 0700A] you, though they cannot follow the Lamb in these matters! They will see and not envy; and, rejoicing with you, they will possess in you what they do not possess in themselves. For that Lamb whom you follow wherever he goes will not abandon those who are unable to follow him where you can. We speak of the almighty Lamb, who will go before you and will not depart from them, when God shall be all in all. Those who have less than you will not be distressed, for where there is no envy, difference is harmonious.

Therefore presume, be confident, be strengthened, and remain in what you have vowed. Render to the Lord your God your vows of perpetual continence, not only to avoid the miseries of the present age, but far more for the singular delights of the age to come, which our Lamb, Christ, as he passes among us, will minister to us spiritually.

109. But let Christ’s virgins beware of understanding this childishly, so as to believe that virginity alone is sufficient for them to follow the Lamb of God wherever [Col. 0700C] he goes, since the Lamb himself walks not only the path of virginity but also the way of every virtue. Therefore a virgin of Christ must imitate the most gentle Lamb in the path of every virtue even in this life, if she wishes to come to that place where she will follow him without end wherever he goes.

For how could a proud virgin follow the Lamb walking on the way of humility, whom she will by no means approach? How could an angry woman follow the gentlest one? How could an envious woman follow one fervent in charity? How could an avaricious woman follow the most generous one? How could a drunken woman follow the sober one? The Lamb walks in every path of all virtues; let the virgin who desires to imitate the Lamb walk thus also. Let her be gentle, humble, fervent in charity, generous, joyful, sober; and she will imitate the Lamb wherever he goes. Finally, she will deserve to hear from her Bridegroom himself: “How beautiful are your steps in your sandals, daughter of the prince!” (Song VII, 1).

The virginal soul will be the special daughter of God the Prince and lady of the kings of the whole earth, whose steps are commended in sandals. By sandals we understand the examples of the dead, because sandals are made from dead animals. Therefore the steps of virgins in sandals are beautiful when they follow directly along the path of every virtue Christ the Lamb, who died for them; when they are themselves ready, for the Lamb, to follow the Lamb even unto death and through death, if necessary; when in every deed they fortify the feet of their affections with the examples of the best Lamb, Jesus Christ, against the serpent lying in wait for the virginal heel, [Col. 0701A] while the serpent’s head is trampled by the virginal foot with the Lamb’s own help.

110. The fifth leaf of the lily flower signifies the fifth reason why virginity should be sought: namely, that virgins will sing a new song before the throne of God and of the Lamb, which no one except virgins can sing. O blessed virgins, and virgins happier than the rest, who bring to those eternal nuptials of the Lamb the new song which you will sing upon your harps: not indeed a song such as the whole earth sings, as it is said, “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. XCV, 1), but such a song as no one except you can sing.

Yet the whole multitude of the faithful will hear and delight in your own gift, so excellent. But you, who will both sing it and hear it because it will be sung by you, will exult more happily and reign more joyfully. Who could explain this happiness? Indeed, who could conceive in the human mind the jubilation of such exultation? Now if all virgins will sing this song, will not that Virgin, the chief among virgins, sing it? She certainly will sing, and all the more joyfully because she is chaster than the rest. She will offer the whole choir an example in singing, she who by her example stirred them to the love of virginity.

Therefore in that festal gladness the virgins will sing their song into the heart of the Lamb, their virgin Bridegroom, from whom they received the capacity to sing such a song. But what then? Will not the Lamb himself—surpassing not only the assembly of other virgins but even his Virgin Mother, and the one from whom they have received not only that [Col. 0701C] they are virgins but also that they exist—will not, I say, the Bridegroom of virgins, himself a virgin and the best of virgins, also sing? Indeed, he himself will sing; and that most delightful voice of the Word of the eternal Father will be heard with all, before all, and in all.

O most blessed song! O most delightful celebration, without comparison or end! Who would not long for it? Who would disdain to labor to come where he may hear the new song of so many virgins; where he may perceive the voice of the Lamb’s Mother, wonderfully overflowing beyond that of the other virgins; where he may hear the most merciful Lamb himself singing his utterly honey-sweet melody? For if, in the testimony of the Psalmist, the words of the Lord are so sweet to any person even while he remains in this body of death that they surpass honey and the honeycomb (Ps. CXVIII, 103), how abundantly must they surpass in sweetness where all mortality, all fear, and all pain have passed far away; where no place remains for bitterness, but all shall be made drunk with the torrent of divine delight, intoxicated with the abundance of his house? Great is the happiness of all who hear the Lamb’s most sweet virginal song; yet more abundant for Christ’s virgins, who sing with the Lamb himself.

111. With how great care ought virgins rightly to keep their mouths, that they may sing the song to be sung only by virgins and preserve them in all purity—not only from every defiling act, but from every lustful, shameful, coarse, jesting, and even idle word! [Col. 0702A] And, as it is said in the Bride’s song, the lips of virgins shall be like a scarlet ribbon and their speech sweet (Song IV, 3). For lips are like a scarlet ribbon when they always abound in words of burning charity, by which carnal movements and thoughts are restrained. For by the scarlet color charity is understood; by the ribbon, with which hair is bound, the restraint of carnal thoughts is understood, these thoughts being signified by hair.

Therefore the lips of the Lamb’s brides—that is, Christ’s virgins—should especially be like a scarlet ribbon, so that their speech may always burn with charity and be reddened by the passion of the Lamb and Bridegroom. Fair and ruddy, sweet Jesus should always be in their hearts and always on their lips. Nor do I fear deceit from such persons, because they do not wish to lie at all when they speak of most sweet Jesus, the truth. But coarse, shameful, jesting, and idle words cannot accord with words concerning the Passion. What indeed is more useful, more bitter, or more fitting than the Passion of Jesus Christ?

112. O sweetest and most loving Jesus, spotless Lamb, white through innocence and red through the blood of your Passion: how delightful it is to think of you, how health-giving to speak of you! For when people speak of you, you are present; you sweetly kindle the mind, shape words, and draw the affections of all who speak of you. They run in the fragrance of your ointments until you, King of kings, lead them into your wine-cellars; there they drink the wine of your most sweet consolation in the gladness of their hearts, hear your most sweet voice saying, “Drink and be intoxicated, beloved ones” [Col. 0702C] (Song II, 1), and perceive that they, though unworthy, are loved by you freely, most loving and most welcome Jesus.

Do you see, then, to what the words of charity and of the Passion of gracious Jesus tend? His name, which is above every name, ought to be named by none more than by sacred virgins, his brides, and tasted by none more sweetly than by them, so that the name of sweetest Jesus may never depart from their mouths. In him they alone will sing the new song to the Lamb of the heavenly Father. Therefore begin, as far as is permitted, O virgins, to enjoy your Bridegroom. Always bearing him on your lips and in your hearts, let your lips become for him like a scarlet ribbon and your speech sweet, so that afterward you may be considered worthy to be kissed by the kiss of his mouth and to be led by him into the heavenly bridal chamber.

113. The sixth and final reason why virginity should be sought is signified by the sixth leaf of the lily flower. This reason is shown to us by the testimony of Isaiah, who says: “To eunuchs—that is, to my virgins—I will give in my house and within my wall a named place far better than that of sons and daughters; I will give them an eternal name, which shall never fail” (Isa. LVI, 5).

O sublime merit of virgins! O surpassing glory, O spiritual reward! Let all virgins read, understand, and commit this saying—this good and sweet saying—to memory. Let boys and girls alike rejoice, and let those who have already vowed continence run perseveringly until they attain it. Let those who have not yet vowed hear and delight in the loftiness of the rewards, so that they also may vow [Col. 0703A] a vow of chastity to most chaste Jesus, take hold of the most exalted and narrow path of virginity, and, walking along it, deserve to receive the prize of an everlasting name and to dwell in a place far better than those who have begotten sons and daughters from themselves.

What is signified by this name which the Lord promises to give his virgins? Surely it signifies a glory proper to them and surpassing, which the virgins will not share with many others, although they are established in the same kingdom. Perhaps it is called a “name” because it distinguishes those to whom it is given from others, just as people are distinguished by their individual names. For although all predestined to eternal life will remain in one kingdom and enjoy one God, nevertheless, as the Apostle says, “as star differs from star in glory, so also is the resurrection of the dead” (I Cor. XV, 41–42): such are the differing merits of the saints.

For just as it is common to all heavenly bodies that they are in heaven, yet the glory of the sun is one thing, that of the moon another, and that of the stars another, so in eternal life itself the lights of merits will shine distinctly. In the house of the eternal Father there are many dwelling places (John XIV, 2), where one person will not live longer than another, because all will have eternal life. But in the many dwellings one is honored more gloriously than another.

How great, do you think, will be the glory in which Christ’s virgins shine there, following Christ in purity alike of heart and mind? What choir of saints is more fittingly compared with the moon than virgins? They alone will follow Christ, the sun of righteousness, as the Lamb of the Father, wherever he goes; hence they alone are like him and most like him. [Col. 0703C] Therefore, in the same kingdom, they will be honored above the rest with a surpassing splendor, just as we see the moon preeminent above the other stars. And in the house of the Lord they will possess a place far better than that of other sons and daughters who are not distinguished by the merit of virginity.

114. Go forward, therefore, holy boys and girls of God, men and women, celibate men and unmarried women; go forward perseveringly unto the end. Praise the Lord more sweetly, whom you contemplate more abundantly; hope more happily in him whom you serve more diligently; love more ardently him whom you please more attentively. Let there be in you no incitements to vice; but consecrate and preserve your whole person together for your spouse, “beautiful in form beyond the children of men.” Let there not be seen in your virgin body [Col. 0703D] a wicked expression, wandering eyes, an unbridled tongue, wanton laughter, a buffoonish jest, improper dress, or a proud or loose gait. No longer render evil for evil, or curse for curse. Finally, now attain that measure of love by which, in imitation of your spouse, you lay down your life for your brothers. For these things, added to virginity, display an angelic life among human beings and the manners of heaven upon earth. But the greater you are, the more humble yourselves in all things, that you may find grace before God, who resists the proud, humbles those who exalt themselves, and does not convey the puffed-up through the narrow gate. Let there be no superfluous anxiety: where charity burns, let humility not be lacking.

[Col. 0704A] 115. If, therefore, you have despised marriages with the sons of men, by which you might bear children of men, love all the more in your heart the Son of Man, beautiful in form beyond the children of men. Behold the beauty of your lover; and behold, by inward lights, how beautiful is that very thing in him which the proud deride. Behold the wounds of the one hanging, the scars of the one rising again, the blood of the one dying—the price and exchange of the Redeemer. Consider what these are worth; weigh them in the balance of charity; and whatever love you would have bestowed upon your marriages, repay to him who seeks not a beautiful body but your inward beauty, who gave you power to become children of God. See, moreover, with how great a security you love him: you need not fear that you displease him through false suspicions. Husband and wife love one another because they plainly see in one another signs of affection; yet they often suspect one another of some evil, because they do not behold one another’s hidden things. It is not so with your most sweet and desirable love, Jesus, in whom you will find nothing that you can reproach; nor need you fear that he falsely suspects any evil of you, he who beholds the reins and hearts. If, then, you owed great love to spouses, how greatly ought you to love him for whose sake you did not wish to have spouses? Let him be wholly fixed in your heart, who was wholly fixed upon the cross for you; 475 always keeping in mind how great a charity he showed you. He who preserved you inviolate for himself both in body and in soul—how great and how special a glory [Col. 0704C] has he prepared for you, whom he has so exalted?

A special glory, I say; a special crown has he given you in heaven, which our forebears call the *aureola*, the “little golden crown.” I judge it to be named from gold so that the very name of the crown to be bestowed upon you as the reward of virginity may suggest the excellence of virginal glory. What, I say, shall be given to Christ’s sacred virgins? That they may surpass the other saints, as gold surpasses other metals. For Isaiah says: “On that day the Lord shall be a crown of glory and a garland of exultation to the remnant of his people” (Isa. 28:5). Observe that a crown is made of gold and precious stones; a garland, of flowers—such as roses, violets, and the like. Observe how great a thing it is to have God himself as one’s crown! Virgins will not only have God as their crown [Col. 0704D]—which is common to all who are glorified—but will have, as a flowering adornment of exultation, the prerogative of spiritual excellence which will appear in virgins in the heavenly homeland. But what is that place far better than that of the children of God? What is that eternal name? What is the *aureola*? It is very great, and inexplicable to those who have not experienced it. Therefore those who will be able to experience it by enjoying it alone must run with great eagerness and persevere with great courage.

But because, by recalling the special grace freely granted to virgins by their spouse, and likewise the special glory prepared for virgins in heaven by him, we seek to stir the souls of virginal purity to a special love of their kindly heavenly spouse Jesus—as he himself, author of virginity and love, has deigned to bestow it—let us, following the order of our subject, add a few remarks concerning love of neighbour, without which love of God does not endure; for “on these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40).

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the six little yellow flowers in the middle of the lily: that is, on love of neighbour and the six works of mercy

116. The six little flowers of golden colour which stand in the middle of the white flower in the lily signify the charity to be held toward one’s neighbour. This consists in six works of charity, which are also called works of mercy. Charity, therefore, since it cannot be idle, shows itself in works wherever it is. [Col. 0705B] As blessed Gregory says, “The proof of love is the performance of a work” (*Homily 30 on the Gospels*). And John, the Lord’s specially beloved disciple, says: “Whoever has the resources of this world, and sees his brother suffering need, and closes his compassion against him, how does the charity of God remain in him?” (1 John 3:17). For if he does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? (1 John 4:20).

Truth itself took care to set forth the works of mercy by which the charity of God is demonstrated, showing that on the day of final judgment he will praise only the righteous for these works and condemn the reprobate for their lack of them. He says: “When the Son of Man comes and sits upon the throne of his majesty, and sets the righteous at his right hand and the reprobate at his left, the King himself will say to those at his [Col. 0705C] right hand: ‘Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you. For I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was a stranger, and you took me in; naked, and you covered me; sick and in prison, and you visited me. For what you did to one of my least ones, you did to me.’ Then he will say to those on the left: ‘Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink; I was a stranger, and you did not take me in; sick and in prison, and you did not visit me. For what you did not do to one of my least ones, neither did you do to me’” (Matt. 25:31–45).

Behold the works of mercy proceeding from the root of charity. We must therefore consider how great is their dignity: they alone deserve to be praised in the strict examination, [Col. 0705D] and their dignity is signified by the golden colour of the lily’s little flowers. The purity of the white flower—that is, virginal purity—is of no value without works of charity.

117. But what shall we say of those who, through lack of 476 earthly means, cannot fulfil these works, whether they still remain in the world or, having renounced the world and all that they possessed, have followed the naked Christ in nakedness? Will all those who cannot minister to Christ through works of mercy be reprobate? Far from it! For it is not those who are unable, but those who are unwilling, who will be condemned. For one does not close one’s *viscera*—that is, one’s compassion—against a neighbour suffering need if, were one able, one would wish to help. And for the Lord, who looks upon the heart, it suffices if the will alone is present; for he reckons the will itself as the deed.

Therefore no one will be able to excuse himself from giving to everyone who asks, either by deed or by will. Let not those who cannot give, then, excuse themselves. Those afflicted by poverty no less than those constrained by voluntary poverty are bound to give their will. Let each person examine whether he has this will. When you see a poor person, a sick person, or a traveller, and pass by such people without being moved by any compassion, pouring out neither prayer nor sigh for them, do you have the will to give? By no means. For if you do not share the affection of charity with your neighbour in need, it is as though you did not have compassion upon one who suffers. If you do not grieve with one who grieves, how would you divide your outward substance? [Col. 0706B] If you do not give the affection of compassion—which grows more abundant the more it is given—how would you give earthly substance, which is diminished when divided?

Whenever, therefore, we see anyone in need, let us recognize Christ in that person; for one who is needy is also a member of Christ. Let us not close the compassion of our hearts against that person; and by this we shall know that the charity of Christ remains in us. Above all, let Christ’s virgins have within the white flowers of virginal purity these golden little flowers of charity, without which no purity of chastity, no labour of suffering, no fullness of knowledge enters through the gate of eternal life.

118. Yet one must likewise—indeed, much more—have compassion upon the wretched who have strayed from the way of right faith or of works of faith and lie in the filth of sins, whether they themselves recognize their sins or not. For them that heavenly bread of angels, sweet Jesus, must be broken—that is, bent toward mercy by our prayers and tears. Likewise, those to whom the Lord has given understanding should break and set before such persons the bread of sacred Scripture, praying the Lord to deign to open their eyes, that they may recognize him, heal the palate of their heart, and taste and see that the Lord is altogether sweet; and that they may recognize him in the breaking of bread—that is, in sacred Scripture—whose eyes of understanding were previously held so that they might not know him, being covered over by the filth of sins.

The bread of consolation must be broken for those set amid afflictions, whether in bodily sicknesses, under the burden of poverty, or in troubles affecting themselves [Col. 0706D] or their friends; so that, according to the counsel of the Wise Man, strong drink may be given to the sorrowful, and wine of sweet consolation to those who are bitter in spirit (Prov. 31:6). Have a will rich toward all: not only toward friends and members of the household of faith, but also toward enemies, that we may be children of our Father who is in heaven, “who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the righteous and the unrighteous” (Matt. 5:45).

But perhaps someone will say: “What does my God lose by bestowing his sun and his rain upon bad people as well as good?” Nothing, I say; indeed, it is beneficial, because the wicked are often overcome by the abundance of God’s goodness and benefits, and turn from their crooked paths. And you, tell me: what do you lose if you share your charity—which, like the sun, illumines the other virtues—and the rain of your tears even with enemies, praying and weeping for them, that at some time they may return to their heart, acknowledge their errors, and receive the unity of charity? O, if you knew the goodness of the best God, and how good is he who bids you pray for those who persecute and slander you, and how great a reward he prepares for those who pray thus! Surely you would long ago have asked him, and he would have given you the sun of such charity and the rain of such tears. He gives to all abundantly and does not reproach; with him is the fountain of life, and in his light light shall be seen—the true light that enlightens every person, sweet Jesus.

Following his example, divide your charity and divide your tears both [Col. 0707B] with your enemies and with your friends, that you may be a child of your heavenly Father, and a brother and imitator of the Lord Jesus, who wept over the sinful city and prayed for his killers that they might not perish.

119. But now let us come to the end of this flower. The little flower standing above the golden little flowers in their midst, longer than all the rest, signifies the Divinity, who is God above all, blessed for ever. Amen. This little flower has one triangular head, by which the Trinity itself is signified. Its one head represents the unity of the divine substance; its three projecting and mutually distinct angles signify the persons of the Trinity.

This little flower is highest in the virginal lily, because the virgin of the Lord ought to refer all her thoughts, all her will, all her words, all her deeds, and all the purity of her body and heart to the honour of her heavenly Spouse. For if she seeks her own glory, she will not have a lamp—that is, a pure body—but will lack the oil of spiritual gladness and the fire of charity. We know what terrible word, terrible not only to hear but even to think, the spouse will say to those virgins who have lamps without oil: “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). O harsh saying! Deliver us, Lord Jesus, while there is still time to deliver us poor sinners, from the snare of the hunters, lest afterwards we hear that harsh saying.

We know that our adversary, that most cunning serpent, spreads before us innumerable and most subtle snares, so that those whom he cannot turn away from good works [Col. 0707D] he may at least make to glory in good works through wicked suggestions. And how, do you suppose, he rages and gnashes his teeth when he sees tender young virgins, from the first rudiments of their childhood, despising the kingdom of the world and all worldly adornment, and ascending the lofty path of virginity? How many snares, do you suppose, does he lay now for the root, now for the stem, now for the white leaves, now for the golden little flowers of the lily of virginity, in order to induce them to seek their own glory in some good work, lest they reach the highest summit of virginity?

But let the virgin of Christ always look upon the face of her spouse, so that she may do all things for his sake, refer all things to him, and seek him in all things, saying with him: [Col. 0708A] “I do not seek my own glory” (John 8:50); but I honour my Lord, and he will honour me, for he alone is my protector and my glory, who will lift up my head—sweet Jesus. If any virgin speaks and acts thus, she shall be a perfect lily and shall flower forever before the Lord, and in her Lord and spouse; and her Lord and spouse shall flower in her, he who came down into the garden of his Church to gather such lilies.

120. We have taken pains to treat at greater length, by a certain digression, of the flower of the spiritual lily with which our Vine and Life, the Lord Jesus, especially flowers. We have done so for the benefit of virgins, to whose attention we believe this treatise will come, so that here they may find the matter briefly stated and commit it more readily to memory: they may read it with greater eagerness because what other holy Fathers have treated more diffusely, and burdened with many difficult disputations, is too difficult to be understood by the simple understanding of simple virgins.

Nor do we fear the tongues of detractors, who may say that we have not maintained unity of subject because we have fallen from a treatise on the Vine into a treatise on the Lily. For we are certainly confident that we shall be excused by the charity and kindness of Christ, indeed the spouse of virgins, to whom in this treatise we confess that we have rendered service according to our understanding.
