In his hand are both we and our words. As we firmly hope, we have followed him in treating this subject, seeking not the glory of teachers but the profit of learners.

Yet, as far as I understand, our Vine does not flower with any other flower [Col. 0708C] or draw the fragrance of any other flower as strongly as it does of this lily—that is, the virtue of virginity. Drawn by love of it, so many young women run so freely after the fragrance of the spouse’s ointments, crying out in word and deed together: “Draw us after you; we shall run in the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3). For what do so many thousands of virgins, despising the world’s enticements, love? What, I say, do they so love in their spouse, by delight in what virtue are they drawn, if not by the fragrance of the lily—that is, by love of virginity? Let it therefore be permitted us especially to commend this flower in our Vine, for none is more precious or more beautiful in the vine itself. But now let us pass on to treat the others more briefly.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the flower of charity, or the red and burning rose

[Col. 0708D]

121. In our Vine, kindly Jesus, there likewise flowers a rose, red and burning: red with the blood of the Passion, burning with the fire of charity, dewy with the outpouring of the tears of sweetest Jesus. For the Lord Jesus—my joy, indeed the joy of the angels—wept and was sorrowful because of me. As the Apostle says, “In the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears to him who was able to save him from death, he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5:7).

Do you hear this, heart not of flesh but of stone: that great and best Jesus, in the days [Col. 0709A] of his flesh, which he had assumed to redeem me, was moistened with tears, while you remain dry? O hard heart! Do you hear that he who stands forever and shall not be moved was moved to tears for me, and are you still not moved to tears? I shall add both the fire of charity and the blood of the Passion, perhaps you may be warmed and softened, so that you may at least repay sweetest Jesus with tears alone for his tears and the shedding of his blood. I shall add also a heavy hammer and strike iron wedges into you, that you may be split open.

For if you, heart, had dried out like land without water, surely you could be softened, even slightly, when drenched with the tears of weeping Jesus. But if you have been hardened into the rigidity of stone by the coldness of iniquities, I add powerful instruments: the hammer of the cross and the wedges of iron nails, that, struck into you, they may split you open and you may pour forth a health-giving fountain of tears.

122. Since even thus you are still not moved, O hard and unrepentant heart, you are harder than the rock which, struck twice by Moses’ rod in the wilderness, sent forth most abundant waters (Num. 20:11). This is especially so because the hammer of the Lord’s cross is more powerful to strike than Moses’ rod, and the three iron nails struck into you ought to be more effective for drawing forth the water of tears than the doubled blow of Moses’ rod. But if you still remain unmoved because you have been changed into the hardness of adamant, which can be softened only by a goat’s blood, I bring you the abundant blood alike of the goat and of the spotless Lamb, best Jesus, burning with the heat of incomparable [Col. 0709C] charity. By its strength it utterly crushed and dissolved that adamantine wall of enmity set between God and man.

This wall had endured for so many thousands of years and had not been in any way crushed, though the Law and the Prophets struck it with the hammers of diverse commands, admonitions, and threats. But when the blood of our goat and Lamb, kindly Jesus, came, it was not only pierced but destroyed. Good Jesus, though most pure, is also called a goat—an unclean animal—because he bore our flesh, full in us of the impurities of sins, though in him it had nothing of the kind. Yet because of his supreme purity he is the Lamb, who not only has no sins but bore the sins of the whole world.

123. Therefore, O adamantine heart, anoint and immerse yourself in the abundant blood of this goat and Lamb; lie in it, that you may be warmed; being warmed, that you may be softened; and being softened, that you may pour forth a fountain of tears. Abundant water is needed to refresh my people and my cattle. My people are the rational movements of my soul, seeking those things that suit my spirit alone. I also have cattle: namely, the other thoughts that are occupied with the flesh and are bound to render service to the soul as beasts of burden. Both kinds of thought ought to be refreshed by the fountain of tears, lest they fail on the way of this life or turn aside from the straight path; that what is good in them may be strengthened [Col. 0710A] and what is filthy washed away. Both powers are found in tears.

Therefore I shall seek for myself, and would that I might find, a fountain of tears in the tears, the cross, the nails, and finally in the blood of ruddy Jesus. I shall therefore read and understand, as far as he himself grants, the redness in the flesh and soul 479 of the beloved, most loving Jesus. For he was ruddy in both—that is, in body as well as soul: in the flesh by nature, since all flesh is naturally red; and no less by the blood of the Passion, with which, compelled by love for us, he drenched his flesh so often and so abundantly. We have frequently recalled in the preceding pages that we explained these outpourings of his most sacred blood. Therefore we need not linger over them, lest the reader grow weary.

[Col. 0710B] 124. But who, unless wholly flesh and blood and possessing nothing spiritual within himself, would grow weary of this blood? Who, wishing to free himself from contracted blood-guilt, would not desire this most pure and health-giving blood of most pure Jesus? Who, once intoxicated with this sweetest blood, which God in his sweetness prepared for the poor, would not thirst for it more and more, hearing the true voice of God’s Wisdom, the Father’s Only-Begotten, best Jesus, saying: “Those who eat me will still hunger, and those who drink me will still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29)?

If it is true—indeed, because it is true—that human blood naturally possesses such sweetness above all others that, once tasted by any beast, it thereafter always desires to taste it, so that, putting other animals aside, beasts lie in wait for human blood and rush to their death to obtain it: how much sweetness do you believe the blood of Jesus Christ, the Son of Man, contains in itself? Behold, irrational beasts thirst for human blood, and shall I not thirst for the blood of the Son of God? The more beasts taste, the more they thirst for human blood; and shall I grow weary of the blood of God and man, kindly Jesus? Beasts rush to their death, drawn by the sweetness of human blood; shall I not hasten to my life, to the blood of ruddy and white Jesus? Indeed, I shall hasten: I shall buy and drink.

I shall buy, without silver and without any exchange, wine and honey, which the Wisdom of the Most High Father has most kindly mixed for us in the cup of his heart—namely, his blood, the price of our life. Hasten with me, you who love the Lord: buy, not with corruptible gold and silver, but by the exchange of your conduct and manner of life, wine and milk—I mean that most pure and precious blood. It intoxicates the perfect like wine; like milk, it nourishes the little ones. If you are perfect and strong, this blood, most unmixed blood, is wine for you. If you are still weak and need milk, it is milk to nourish you. Drink, therefore, this most unmixed blood through faith, remembrance, and spiritual contemplation.

Behold, in brief, I bring before you again the manifold shedding of the most generous Jesus’ blood, by which he reddened the rose of his Passion and charity. The human intellect cannot comprehend the ardour of that charity except insofar as it apprehends it from his Passion, which was manifest to all.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the rose of charity

125. Yet let us first consider the rose of charity, and then the rose of Passion. We shall weigh the ardour of the rose of charity if we carefully consider who the merciful and wondrous lover was, what he was like, how greatly, and why he loved. Our lover is he than whom nothing is greater, richer, or stronger; to whom every spirit confesses: “You are my God, for you have no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2). In this brief verse is comprehended who our lover is—God—and why he loved is drawn from the following expression: namely, he did not love us in order to receive anything of ours, since [Col. 0711B] he has no need of our goods, but by his freely bestowed grace. And even if there were something good in us that he desired, we would possess it not from ourselves but from him.

But how our lover loved us is explained by him who says: “While we were still enemies, we were reconciled to God” (Rom. 5:10). For the righteous one loved the unrighteous; the one alone good and merciful loved sinners and the ungodly. O what condescension! Now let us consider how greatly he loved. Who can state this sufficiently?

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the rose of the Passion

126. Behold, in explaining this matter we must join the rose of the Passion to the rose of charity, so that the rose of charity may redden in the Passion, and the rose of the Passion may burn with the fire of charity. For our lover loved us so greatly that, compelled by the ardour of charity, he underwent the redness of the Passion and gave his soul over to death—death upon the cross—not a death that passed swiftly, but one enduring from the beginning of his birth until the end of his most harsh death.

For, as we have commended to your charity above, the cross of best Jesus Christ was not only of one day: his whole life was cross and martyrdom. Therefore everything which the Lord suffered in the days of his flesh belongs to the redness of the Passion, to the rose of the Passion, although it was especially reddened by the frequent outpourings of his most sacred blood. But because we cannot enumerate all that he suffered, let it not weary us to repeat the saving outpourings of blood, so that things which must be continually remembered may be impressed more firmly upon a tenacious memory.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the seven outpourings of blood of our Vine, Jesus Christ

127. We read of the first shedding of blood at the circumcision, when his name was called Jesus. Even then the mystery signified that through the shedding of his blood he would be for us the true Jesus—that is, Saviour. Let tender boys and girls hear and understand, and let the mature martyrdom of innocent Jesus be frequently impressed upon their minds. Thus Isaiah, speaking of the birth of this same Jesus Christ, says: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us; and dominion is upon his shoulder” (Isa. 9:6). [Col. 0712A] He immediately joins the cross, which he signified by the name of dominion, to the birth, because indeed the Passion of the cross arose together with the beginning of his birth.

For it contributes not a little to commending the ruddy Passion that our Saviour was born in a strange place, in midwinter, in the middle of the night, in the stable of an inn, from a poor little mother. His blood was not shed there, but this followed after so brief an interval, namely, seven days. O what charity! O what a commendation of charity! Hardly is sweet Jesus born—the glory, riches, and delight of heaven—and behold, to his fresh birth are joined the ignominy, pain, and poverty of the cross. Yet he redeemed the wretchedness of the cross by the true name of kingship. For by the cross strong Jesus subjected at once the whole world and the underworld, he who reigned from the tree. Because of the cross, to which he humbled himself, becoming obedient, God the Father exalted him and gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2:8–10). Thus this name Jesus was fittingly given to him at the first shedding of the most pure Lamb’s blood, because even then he began to pour out his blood for our salvation, he who in completing our salvation was to be wholly poured out.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the second shedding of blood

128. The second shedding of Jesus Christ’s blood, by which the rose of the Passion is coloured, is found in the bloody sweat of kindly Jesus praying and struggling in agony. For the evangelist says: “Being in agony, he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like drops of blood running down upon the earth.” Even if all the other outpourings of his most pure blood fell silent, could not this alone sufficiently redden our rose? Truly it can tear apart my wretched heart and moisten it with bloody tears, for behold, my Creator is drenched in a bloody sweat for me—and not a slight sweat, but one running down to the earth. Woe to my wretched heart, which is not moistened by being drenched with such a great sweat!

Look upon the affliction of that most gentle heart, by which he was distressed [Col. 0712D] when bloody sweat flowed from his whole body on every side. For the body could not outwardly flow with so great and such a sweat unless the heart inwardly were broken by the distress of some pain. “My heart is broken within me,” says the prophet (Jer. 23:9). Therefore, when the heart was split inwardly, the skin of our Solomon was split outwardly also, and bloody sweat was poured upon the earth. The rose of the Passion and charity of ruddy Jesus Christ was reddened. Behold how ruddy he is, and how wholly ruddy. Nor is this general outpouring of Jesus’ blood without mystery.

For he sweated blood with his whole body, he who had come to remove from our flesh the infirmities contracted from flesh and blood, so that for the restoration and healing of the whole spiritual body—that is, the Church—the bloody sweat poured out from every part of the body of our head, the Lord Jesus Christ, might suffice. We have therefore been freed from blood-guilt. Thanks be to God, to the author of our salvation, kindly Jesus, who most generously poured out his blood for us. Or certainly the bloody sweat poured out from the whole body of our head signified this: that in his whole spiritual body, which is the Church, the blood of martyrs was to be shed and the Church reddened.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the third shedding of blood

129. The third shedding of blood was in the plucking of the cheeks. We have testimony to this in the prophet, speaking in the person of the crucified one: “I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them” (Isa. 50:6). Some explain this as a tearing of the jaws by the nails of the wicked Jews; [Col. 0713B] others, as the plucking out of the Lord’s beard. Both may have been true. I believe this was not done without some shedding of blood.

Thus I see the sacrilegious hands of that most wicked people not satisfied with blows of the fist and open-handed slaps, and with spitting upon Christ’s desirable face; but also inflamed to pluck his cheeks, drawing blood even from that most sweet face so as to redden our rose. I see the admirable and imitable patience of that spotless Lamb, through which he offered his most chaste cheeks, with all gentleness, to be torn by the nails of the most shameless. Thus may we patiently endure if our face is ever covered with shame for his sake—indeed, even if anyone strikes us in the face by words and deeds because of sweet Jesus.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the fourth shedding of blood

[Col. 0713C]

130. We can find the fourth outpouring of most pure blood in the crown—in the crown of thorns, not lightly placed but forcefully pressed upon the most sweet head of my sweet Jesus. For it accords sufficiently with the truth that those who hated truth sought not only his reproach but also his punishment. Nor do I think that streams of blood were absent here, flowing from the head of sweet Jesus, crowned in mockery and envy, down upon his neck and face. For had they not wished to inflict punishment as well as mockery on the crowned one, they could more easily have woven a crown from other branches or twigs of some tree. But to display the prickles of their own dispositions, they then crowned with the prickles of thorns the most gentle Lamb, sweet Jesus, who is now crowned with glory and honour.

And although they crown him in mockery, unknowingly and mockingly they confess that the crowned one is king, since it belongs to kings to be crowned. Thus he is shown to be king by those who do not know it. But in the thorns the malice of those who crown him is revealed. Morally, we are taught to imitate our head, king, and leader, sweet Jesus. If we are pricked and mocked by the perversity of any wicked persons, then, when we behold our head so pierced and so mocked, let us not murmur or kick against it. Let us endure with all evenness of mind and patience the few things inflicted on us in this present and brief life, that we may be worthy to be members of our head [Col. 0714A] and good soldiers, following the footsteps of our standard-bearer.

## CHAPTER XL. On the fifth shedding of blood
131. The fifth reddening of the rose is found in the cruel scourging of the gentlest rose-like Lamb, Jesus. Oh, how great an abundance of that most holy blood do you suppose dripped to the ground from his torn and scourged body! Oh, what cruelty of the raging wicked, with what raging fury do you suppose sweet Jesus was scourged—he who had come to free us from eternal scourges! “Without cause,” he says, “they struck me with scourges.” (Responsory of the Church’s Office for the Passion.) Truly without cause—unless perhaps those most wretched and perverse persons judged your good works worthy of punishments, they who held your truth in falsehood. [Col. 0714B]

But here too we are morally instructed to learn to bear with equanimity the scourges of our most gracious Father, since sweet Jesus so patiently endured the scourges of the worst men for us who are unworthy. For what human being would not endure scourges: a man prepared for scourging, born for toil, nourished and conversant in sins, yet destined for the inheritance of the heavenly court, which receives none but the clean—when he sees the King of kings and Lord of lords, sweet Jesus, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found, crushed by such grievous scourging? Hear, foolish and senseless man; take instruction; and do not merely fail to reject discipline, but even embrace it, lest perhaps at some time you perish from the righteous way while the Lord is angry with you—he who did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up to be scourged for your sake (Rom. VIII, 32). [Col. 0714C]

He did not spare his natural Son, consubstantial and coeternal with himself, and incapable of suffering, but for your salvation caused him to be born in time and to become capable of suffering; and he crushed him with scourges, as it is written: “The Lord willed to crush him in infirmity” (Isa. LIII, 10). And how will he spare you, an adopted son, when your inclinations are prone to evil? Rather, they will constrain your jaws with bit and bridle, so that at least affliction may give you understanding, and you may be compelled to draw near to him who, though painfully, nevertheless salutarily scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. XII, 6).

## CHAPTER XLI. On the sixth and seventh effusions of blood.

[Col. 0714D]

132. The sixth effusion of blood, which reddened the rose of the Passion, is found most abundantly in the driving in of the nails. Who could doubt that an abundance of sacred blood flowed from the pierced—indeed, transfixed—hands and feet of innocent Jesus? In torrents of this blood our rose was made purple; for here truly are found most burning charity and most ruddy Passion. In the greatness of the Passion, let the greatness of charity be considered: consider the burning heat of the rose of charity and the redness of the Passion. Who ever suffered things so grievous, so shameful? It is God who suffers, and in no respect does he lighten for himself the harsh winepress of the Passion—he who is accustomed either wholly to remove from his servants, or to lessen, or to shorten, the force of their torments. [Col. 0715A]

He who knows how to spare his own did not spare himself. You see evidence of this in the Gospel of John, where, when those who had come to seize him told him that they sought him, he added: “I am he whom you seek. If therefore you seek me, let these go away” (John XVIII, 8). O burning heat of truest charity! Charity itself reveals and gives itself over to raging enemies, sparing not itself, and asks for its own people that they be spared.

Thus, after very many mockeries, both from Jews and from Gentiles, after several effusions of blood, our Savior, the gentlest Jesus, is pierced through hands and feet with cruel nails and fastened to the wood of the cross. Look upon and behold the blood-red rose of the Passion, how it is red as a sign of most burning charity. Passion and charity strive together: the one, that it may burn the more; the other, that it may grow the redder. Yet wonderfully, through charity’s burning heat the Passion is made red, because if he had not loved, he would not have suffered; and in the redness of the Passion the greatest and incomparable charity is displayed. [Col. 0715B]

For as a rose, closed by the cold of night, is wholly opened when the heat of the rising sun comes forth, and, spreading its petals, reveals in its redness a delightful warmth, so the delightful flower of heaven, best Jesus Christ, who from the sin of the first man had for a long time been, as it were, shut up in the cold of night from sinners, not yet bestowing fullness, was at length, when the fullness of time arrived, opened in every part of his body by the rays—that is, the burning rays—of charity; and the heat of the rose of charity shone forth in the redness of his shed blood.

See, then, how our best Vine blossomed with this flower of the rose—ruddy Jesus. Look over the whole body to see whether you find anywhere no flower of the blood-red rose. Examine one hand and the other: do you find the rose-flower in each? Examine one foot and the other: are they not rose-red? [Col. 0715C]

133. Examine the opening of his side, for it too is not without a rose, although it is itself somewhat reddish because of the mixture of water; for, as the Evangelist relates: “When one of the soldiers pierced his side with a lance, blood and water came out” (John XIX, 34). For he is the one who came through water—not through water only, but through water and blood—best Jesus Christ.

O sweetest Lord of all and good Savior Jesus, what fitting thanksgivings can I render to you, who from the beginning of your birth until your most harsh death—indeed, even after death—poured out your most precious blood for me, and took care to manifest the ardor of your supreme charity by such frequent effusions of your blood? Oh, with how great a number of petals your rose has been multiplied and adorned! Who can number them all? Number the drops of blood shed from the most sweet body of sweetest Jesus, and you will have numbered the petals of charitable Passion. For each drop of his blood is a petal of the blood-red rose of his Passion. [Col. 0715D]

But let us pass on to other matters, because we have already briefly spoken of the seventh effusion of the Lord’s blood when we taught concerning the opening of his side, from which blood and water came forth, through which we received the sacrament of Baptism.

## CHAPTER XLII. On the saffron of abstinence in our Vine.

[Col. 0716A]

134. We also perceive the saffron of abstinence to have blossomed in our Vine, sweetest Jesus Christ. He was abstinent not in order to chastise his own body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps he should become reprobate, but in order to give us a pattern and instruction in abstinence—just as in circumcision and baptism, which he underwent not for his own cleansing, for he was always most pure and the cleanser of all, but in order to give us a pattern of obedience and righteousness.

Without doubt he possessed the virtue of abstinence: the King of virtues, mortifying himself more excellently than all saints past and future, not from necessity but voluntarily. But the saying of the Lord Savior himself concerning himself is objected to us: “John the Baptist came to the Jews neither eating nor drinking, and you said, ‘He has a demon’; likewise, the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and you say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners’” (Matt. XI, 18–19). [Col. 0716B]

Here is the testimony of Truth: John neither ate nor drank, while Jesus himself both ate and drank. Does John therefore excel our beloved Jesus in the virtue of abstinence? By no means.

135. But it should be noted that the virtue of abstinence is twofold. One form is inward, in the mind; the other outward, in action. That which is in the mind ought always to be maintained; but that which is in action must be displayed according to the nature of things and times. John, being a mere man, rightly practised abstinence both in mind and body, lest perhaps he be defiled. But our true man, Jesus, who could not be defiled, used food and drink according to the occasion, in order to draw those who ate with him toward the virtue of abstinence and the other virtues. [Col. 0716C]

Nor should you suppose in any way that it is a greater virtue wholly to abstain from food than to use foods themselves moderately. For it is exceedingly difficult to preserve complete moderation in foods: so that nothing may be taken beyond what can suffice for nature, and nothing necessary be withheld from nature itself. If, then, someone happens to possess the virtue of abstinence with John—that is, to practise it in mind and deed—let him not condemn one who practises abstinence with the most perfect Jesus; that is, one who, as times and persons require, now applies and now relaxes abstinence for the good either of his own body or of his neighbor, yet observes in all things everything that must be observed concerning the virtue of abstinence, so as always to avoid the fault of the vice opposed to abstinence, namely gluttony. [Col. 0716D]

The abuses of this vice are noted in the following verse:

> Too soon, luxuriously, too much, eagerly, and too attentively.

For those eat and drink too soon who anticipate the time of eating, compelled by pleasure alone rather than necessity. We read in the *Lives of the Fathers* of holy Fathers who, bound by charity toward spiritual guests, anticipated their customary mealtime; yet, because they ate in charity, they judged that they had in no way broken their fast. Indeed, some, after such a light refreshment, did not fear to celebrate the solemnities of Mass. Although it does not suit us to take this as an example in order to do the same, since we are far too distant from their perfection, we nevertheless trust that they did such things without sin—things which they would never have done unless the Holy Spirit had truly revealed this to them. [Col. 0717A]

Those eat luxuriously who use delicate foods drawn by pleasure alone: for them the natural taste of meats or fish, which the Creator assigned them, is not enough. Disdaining nature’s ways, they seek artificial flavors of pepper and varied sauces, in order to stimulate their appetite for eating. They do not fear to disparage the best Creator of humanity in his creatures, when they themselves impose tastes on them other than those which the Creator of their nature bestowed. Oh, how greatly a Christian ought to avoid such foreign flavors, if he considered that his sweetest and wisest Lord made all things very good, and that no one but an evil person is accustomed to alter creatures that are truly good! I say “is accustomed,” because sometimes there is no fault, or only a slight one, in using richer foods to repel bodily illness, when the palate is not indulging food but rather resisting it. [Col. 0717B]

136. Therefore, for the shame of those whose god, as the Apostle says, is their belly and whose glory is in their shame (Phil. III, 19, 18), whom he also tearfully declares to be enemies of Christ’s cross; and for the shame of the imitators of that poorest and most wretched rich man, who feasted splendidly every day, not at times for a remedy to restore health but for pleasure, and for that reason, when buried in hell, did not deserve to obtain even a drop of water to cool his tongue, certainly burning in the flame (Luke XVI, 19–26)—a tongue always delighted with foreign and superfluous flavors, nor deserving to be refreshed by the natural coolness of water because he had adulterated nature’s taste in his pleasures—for the shame of such persons, I shall not hesitate to recall the judgment of a pagan writer. Let one who is Christian in name blush when he is taught by one better than himself though ignorant of himself: one who neither knew how to honor creatures through their Creator nor knew how to suffer harsh flavors for Christ, whom he either did not know or did not believe drank wine mingled with myrrh and gall for him on the gibbet of the cross. Yet, agreeing with nature alone, he cries out against voluptuaries:

> O extravagance, wasteful of resources,  
> Never content with modest provision;  
> O ambitious hunger, seeker of foods  
> Obtained from land and sea, and glory of the lavish table!  
> Learn with how little life may be sustained,  
> And how little nature requires. No noble wine,  
> Poured out beneath an unknown consul, raises up the sick;  
> They do not drink from gold and gems. Rather, from pure water  
> Life returns: for peoples, a river and Ceres are enough.

(Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book IV, verses 373–381), that is, water and bread. This accords well enough with that familiar and true saying: “Bread and water are the life of man” (Ecclus. XXIX, 28). [Col. 0718A]

Yet the hardened brows of gluttons are not even now broken by this rebuke—though struck by the rebuke and instruction of Truth itself, most true Jesus, and of his Apostles, indeed even of a pagan writer. They say, “We are Christians,” but they do not receive the voice of Christ speaking and warning in the Apostle: “Make not provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. XIII, 14). Hence it frequently happens that, while their food is still in their mouths, the wrath of God rises against them (Ps. LXXVII, 30–31); and those who have spent their days in evil circumstances descend in a moment into hell, where the worm that devours them does not die and the fire is not quenched—receiving eternal evils in return for brief delights.

[Col. 0718B] 137. What it is to eat too much is known to all. For a person eats too much who takes more nourishment than may suffice to sustain his nature, especially if he does this knowingly. It happens not infrequently that a person, considering his labors, takes more simple food in order to endure the work, and, compelled by fear of failing, exceeds the measure of refreshment. I scarcely think anyone is free from this sin. But sins of this sort must, as soon as they are recognized, be cleansed by frequent confessions mingled with voluntary abstinences.

In no kind of food, however, is that vice of superfluity in food and drink excused. For we read that the sin of Sodom was abundance of bread (Ezek. XVI, 49), and that the devil, when about to tempt the Lord, tempted him concerning nothing other than bread (Matt. IV, 3), undoubtedly knowing that sin is not absent from excessive consumption of bread—he who deceived the first parents, and through them all human beings, by the eating of a single apple. Although the measure is not so easily exceeded in plain food, where taste does not deceive, as in richly prepared food and altered flavors. [Col. 0718C]

138. To eat eagerly is to take food or drink with excessive desire; this can occur with simple as well as delicate foods. We have an example of this in Esau, who, drawn by pleasure in a simple food, willingly sold his birthright. For Genesis says that, when Esau came from the field, he saw his brother Jacob cooking lentils and said to him: “Give me some of this red stew, for I am exceedingly weary.” And, after making an agreement with Jacob concerning the sale of his birthright, he ate the much-desired stew greedily and lost the dignity of his birthright. For, because he desired lentils too eagerly, he said: “Behold, I am dying; what good will the birthright do me?” (Gen. XXV, 29–32). [Col. 0718D]

There is no doubt that he ate eagerly what he had desired so eagerly. Have mercy, most merciful Lord Jesus, on me, a most wretched sinner, who feel that no day passes for me without a sin of this kind; lest through such excess I deserve to lose the dignity of that faith by which I have been begotten for you. Conversely, we have received that the most holy Elijah and John the Baptist used no meat whatever, and by the sobriety of temperance lost no merit at all on that account. [Col. 0719A]

139. To eat attentively is to linger too long over food or drink. We speak of this as persons with experience—and would that we had not been experienced, nor ever would be. It frequently happens that, after foods have been taken which, according to custom, could and ought to suffice for the eater’s need, some new pleasure arises. It makes a person heedless and unwary of the devil’s snares cling with such attention to that food as though he had eaten nothing before, or would take no food for many days afterward.

But those who discern this form of gluttony in themselves can, with God’s help, easily resist it, because its impulse lasts no longer than until they rise from the table and the memory of that which they so eagerly desire is withdrawn. Yet very many neither regard such attentiveness in eating as a sin nor credit anyone who suggests that it is sinful. They maintain the condemnable habit of resisting no desire that can receive some defense from nature; nor do they set any limit to the desire to eat until, exhausted, they fail for want of time. [Col. 0719B]

But the Christian eats in order to live; he does not live in order to eat, as someone has said. Therefore this too is well said of the useless and gluttonous:

> We are but a number, born to consume the fruits.

(Horace, *Epistles*, book I, epistle 2, verse 27.)

But the Christian is not so. Rather, he should always rise from the table while he still has an appetite to take more, and offer to the Lord Jesus as a grateful gift the appetite which would still be filled by food—he who often willed to hunger and thirst for our salvation. By these and other similar reasons, someone may be led to mortify himself with such abstinence that, consumed by excessive hunger, he falls into prolonged illnesses, so that he is wholly unable to benefit either himself or others; indeed, he becomes a burden to everyone, whereas, if they were burdened, he ought rather to relieve them. [Col. 0719C]

Who teaches this? What wise person would do this? Such persons do not know that:

> Virtue is a mean between vices, equally removed from each.

(Horace, *ibid.*, epistle 18, verse 9.)

For there is a certain mean between eating too much and abstaining too much, and that mean is virtue: namely, to take enough nourishment that nature is not excessively weakened, but not so much that vices are nourished. If one cannot preserve such a mean altogether, one may nevertheless avoid withdrawing too far from it: that is, let one who eats less than he ought not abstain excessively; and let one who exceeds the measure of eating not exceed it excessively, so that the body may not be nourished for vices but preserved for virtues. [Col. 0719D]

140. The reason why the saffron flower signifies abstinence is shown by its color: abstinence makes its cultivators saffron-colored, like the saffron flower. For a face cannot be ruddy when the stomach is marked by abstinence. The multitude of saffron flowers, however, signifies many kinds of abstinence. Abstinence is not merely from food and drink, [Col. 0720A] but also from sleep and wantonness, from clothing, and from all other conveniences whatever that are superfluously granted to the body; likewise from baths, ointments, musical instruments, songs, and other such things that corrupt the human senses and overthrow the mind.

That some of the petals are red in color signifies that charity ought always to be mingled with works of abstinence; for if someone gives over his body so that it burns, without charity it profits him nothing (I Cor. XIII, 3). For that some mortify themselves by abstinence not for God’s charity but for vainglory is shown by Truth itself, the Lord Jesus, saying to his disciples: “When you fast, do not become sad like the hypocrites, who disfigure their faces in order to appear to men to be fasting. Amen I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 16). [Col. 0720B]

Why? Because they are not true saffron: they lack the red petals of charity, without which no work is perfect. For charity is the virtue of which it is said: “Whoever has one has all; and from him who does not have it, even that which he has shall be taken away.”

## CHAPTER XLIII. On the fragrance of the flowers of the Vine.

141. Let us now approach the fragrance of the flowers of our Vine, asking sweetest Jesus himself to deign to breathe the fragrance of his sweetest scent upon our hearts, so that we may be able to think and speak sweetly concerning him. But what can we say of this fragrance? This fragrance of our Vine is marvelous, beyond what can be believed or imagined, inestimable. Other holy branches also blossomed, and in them he himself certainly blossomed; but those most sure persons cried out to our one head, best Jesus—namely that spiritual bride: [Col. 0720C]

> Your breasts are better than wine, fragrant with the finest ointments.  
> Your name is oil poured out; therefore young maidens have loved you.  
> Draw me after you; we will run after the fragrance of your ointments.

(Song of Songs I, 1–3.)

It is no wonder that the fragrance flowing from this flourishing Vine of ours is altogether inestimable, if we attend more carefully to his names: Jesus, Christ, Nazarene. Jesus, as you know, is interpreted as “saving” or “Savior”; concerning him the Psalm says: “Restore us, O God our Savior” (Ps. LXXXIV, 3), and again: “You saved us from those afflicting us” (Ps. XLIII, 8). Who, placed in affliction, would not wish to be saved? [Col. 0720D]

If you wish to be saved and drawn by the fragrance of this saving name, which has been poured out like oil, begin to delight in sweetest Jesus, and confidently seek salvation in the true Savior. Do not imitate those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Prov. II, 14), in which they think their salvation consists. Rather imitate her whose spirit “rejoiced in God her Savior” (Luke I, 47), and who had drawn in the fragrance of this saving name all the more sweetly and perceived it more perfectly because she was nearer to him in faith, hope, and charity: namely, she who bore him from her own womb, the true and perfect God and man, saving Jesus.

For she was not ignorant how he had been conceived without all carnal desire, how he had been born of her without all pain, how he had been proclaimed by shepherds, adored by Magi, nourished with her virginal milk, and commended by Simeon and Anna. [Col. 0721A] That most faithful Virgin knew all these things, I say, and many more; and with most perfect faith she followed the fragrance of the true Savior’s salvation. Nor could she fail to hope in him whom she knew by most perfect faith both able, knowing, and willing to save all who desire salvation. For as much as a person believes, so much he hopes; and as much as he hopes, so much he loves. Therefore, the more perfect this best Mother was in faith, the stronger she was in hope and the more fervent in charity, casting all her care upon him.

142. “Your name is oil poured out.” Why? Because the weak are nourished by oil, the hungry are fed, and lamps are replenished. For who is so weak that he would not be healed by this saving oil, namely the name of saving Jesus, provided that he wishes to be healed? For the Savior himself says to a certain sick man lying beside the sheep-pool: “Do you wish to be made whole?” And he replies: “Lord, I have no man to put me into the pool when the water has been stirred” (John V, 6–7). [Col. 0721B]

Foolish man, behold the saving oil of saving Jesus, whose name is like oil poured out. What have you to do with water? If you wish to receive salvation, behold the fountain of the oil of mercy, in which no one prevents you from being baptized. His name is poured-out oil—that is, made known to all nations; and the sick who are anointed with this oil are healed. When you hear and understand the surpassing mercy of best Jesus—who descended from the Father’s bosom to earth in order to redeem you, and redeemed you by his most merciful Passion—how can a certain hope not arise in you that he will not wish to lose one redeemed at so great a price, whom he came from heaven to redeem? Therefore, when you think and hope in this manner, the oil of Jesus’ name has been poured out for you. Anoint yourself in order to be healed: that is, hope in the mercy of the Savior, who saves all those hoping in him. [Col. 0721C]

143. Moreover, this oil also feeds you, if you are hungry—if you hunger, it is the Word. In this Word of God, best Jesus, you find that which will satisfy you, if you are willing to incline the ear of your heart to his sayings and deeds. For everything that sweet Jesus said or did heals the hungry soul. If you hunger and thirst for righteousness, the word of his mouth will heal you—he who said: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. V, 6). [Col. 0721D]

He will also add fire to oil, which is most fitting for this name Jesus, because by the power of this name faith is strengthened and charity burns brightly. For few possessed faith before this oil was poured out, that is, before the preaching of your name, O good Jesus; few burned with even a little spark of charity. But behold: through that pouring-out, how many were enlightened in faith! How many were set ablaze with charity! The poured-out oil of your name—the oil of Jesus—gave fragrance, that is, good fame, and it became clear that you are also Christ, that is, the Anointed One. For the Psalm says of you: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8). Therefore oil is also ointment, because ointment is made from oil and spices. What wonder, then, that this Vine gave an admirable fragrance, since it is both anointed and flowering? For “Nazarene” is interpreted “flowering.” [Col. 0722A]

144. Our Vine, Jesus Christ the Nazarene—that is, saving, anointed, and flowering—would not draw all those who desire salvation, glory, riches, or delights? All will come to this Vine. For Jesus will give salvation because he is saving; Christ will give the kingdom in which glory is possessed with riches, because he is anointed, which properly pertains to kings; and the Nazarene will give delights because he is flowering. What is more pleasant than a flower? But many—indeed, all—the flowers of every virtue are in our Nazarene, and by their delightful fragrance he drew the whole world after himself.

For those who come to him because of humility follow the scent of his violet; those because of chastity, that of his lily; those because of the charity of his Passion, that of his rose; and those because of abstinence, that of his saffron. [Col. 0722B] Thus, preachers everywhere, by these virtues of best Jesus Christ as by a certain precious ointment poured out, have drawn forth his fragrance; and young maidens, delighted with his wondrous scent, have run after anointed Jesus. And indeed they still run, crying with all their heart: “Draw me after you, that we may run in the fragrance of your ointments,” knowing that it depends neither on the one who wills nor on the one who runs, but on God alone who has mercy.

But surpassing all scents of all the virtues of anointed Jesus is the scent of the Crucified One, where perfection especially flourished and from the flowers of his wounds poured forth an inestimable fragrance. For when the alabaster vessel of the most pure virginal body of sweet Jesus was broken, the ointment of his most sacred blood was poured out. His soul also, in which undoubtedly the ointment of the sevenfold Spirit gave fragrance, was sent forth; and the scent of our flowering Vine spread and was dispersed not only throughout the earth but also through the underworld. The dead were raised—both to bodily life and to the life of the soul, as they are raised every day—because the house of Christ, that is, the Church, was filled with the fragrance of the ointment of our Vine, especially flowering in the Passion. [Col. 0722C]

The sack of the body of the Lord Jesus was torn; grains of bloody drops fell, which may still be gathered in the mind by believers and are gathered faithfully and devoutly by those who come to the cross. The drops of the blood of Jesus Christ are a most precious and incomparable treasure. [Col. 0722D]

145. Come here, faithful soul, and gather for yourself the remnants of your Bridegroom’s feast: most welcome crumbs, petals of roses. See in what abundance they drip from the hands and feet, and also from the side, of sweetest Christ Jesus crucified. There is no illness of the soul for which you cannot find a remedy in these flowers. Only gather the petals of the flowers of flowering Jesus, the drops of ruddy blood; and store them in the chamber of your heart like pills, without which I would not have you be. Their taste and fragrance will be for you a health-giving medicine, repelling any illnesses that may exist and guarding against those to come. See only that you never wish to be without them—things that truly bear the name expressed by every faithful person: “Without which I would not wish to be.”

Therefore draw in with the whole affection of your heart the fragrance of the true Vine, Jesus Christ the Nazarene, and delight in it, as the heavenly Father delighted in him, so that he might truly say: “Behold, the scent of my son is like the scent of a full field, which the Lord has blessed” (Gen. XXVII, 27). Truly full: in him dwells all the fullness of divinity, and in him all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Col. II, 9, 3). [Col. 0723A]

146. There is yet another reason why the Crucified One gave forth so great a fragrance. The body of any living animal has little or no smell; but when flesh is placed upon fire, no one is ignorant how sweet and delightful a fragrant scent comes forth from it. Let us therefore consider what fire, and how great, was applied to the body of our Vine. Crucified Jesus burned inwardly with the fire of immeasurable charity and outwardly with the heat of the Passion, a most true, most acceptable, and most health-giving holocaust upon the altar of the cross. [Col. 0723B]

What holocaust is like this? Truly none, because none is said to be consumed so wholly by fire. And if that was truly called a holocaust which burned wholly, though only the flesh burned there, how much more truly shall our victim be called a holocaust, which burned incomparably both inwardly and outwardly? Lawrence, Vincent, and very many others also burned wholly, but they are nothing compared with this. For who would dare compare any punishment to the burning heat of the furnace of the cross? We have mentioned many examples of it above.

Therefore an utterly inestimable fragrance proceeded from our crucified Jesus, the incomparably burning holocaust. The Lord God the Father smelled the odor of sweetness, blessed us, and turned the wrath of his indignation far from us, peace being wholly restored and the ruddy blood of Jesus being the pledge of eternal peace both for us and for him who shares it. [Col. 0723C]

Many others also, hastening from east and west, north and south, smelled this fragrance and gathered to the flowering body of sweetest scent in order to be satisfied from it, though it remained whole; they fulfilled the saying of sweetest Jesus himself: “Where the body is, there the eagles shall be gathered” (Luke XVII, 37). But this flesh is no longer eaten raw, since it has been excellently cooked by the twofold fire of charity and Passion. Thus, intoxicated by so delightful a fragrance, not only men, naturally stronger, but even most tender young maidens run with all their heart’s affection and all the powers of their soul toward the delights of the cross, to drink as much as is permitted in the present life of the delights of their heart from the ointments flowing abundantly from our holocaust burning with such mighty fires. [Col. 0723D]

147. The fragrance of spiritual ointments—that is, the bestowal of gratuitous gifts—which the Lord Jesus conferred upon the Apostles after his Passion, greatly increased the already delightful scent of his burning body. Before the Passion, the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified (John VII, 39). But when gracious Jesus had been humbled and exalted, the ointment of the Holy Spirit flowed down from the head—that is, from Christ, that is, the Anointed One—into the beard, that is, into those who acted manfully and were strengthened so as to conquer in the Lord. [Col. 0724A]

Nor was this ointment, melted by the fire of Christ’s Passion so as to give forth the fragrance of good repute throughout the whole earth, given only to Aaron’s beard—that is, only to Christ’s Apostles—but it “descended to the hem of the garment” (Ps. CXXXXII, 2), that is, to the lowest members of the Church, which is as Christ’s garment. This was fulfilled in such a way, and is still fulfilled, that the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured out even upon the nations (Acts X, 45), and they perceive Christ’s scent—the spiritual ointment flowing down from the supreme head of all—so that young maidens may be made pure, draw near to and love our Anointed One, and run in the fragrance of his ointments.

148. Nor is it surprising if they take intense delight in the twofold scent of our Vine: one proceeding from ointments, the other from flowers. For they scent and follow sweet-smelling Jesus, imitating a certain animal that delights so greatly in the smell of baked bread, still fresh, that, wherever it perceives it, it follows it even to destruction. Behold, as he himself testifies, he is the living bread that came down from heaven (John VI, 33, 41, 51), baked by the twofold fire of charity and Passion, scattering his fragrance far and wide. Who would not follow him? An irrational animal follows the scent of bread baked and to be consumed; will a rational human being not follow the scent of the twice-baked bread of angels? Indeed, one who does not understand and honor the scent of that fragrant bread is more foolish than an animal. [Col. 0724B]

But we cannot pass over the fact that those intending to cross the sea need twice-baked bread. Whoever, then, knows himself to be on this great sea of the present age—which cannot be crossed quickly because it is broad, and is dangerous because of the creeping things without number and because it rages with winds and storms—if he wishes to be safe, should have this most strong baked bread, Jesus, in the ship of his cross: to eat him, adore him, be refreshed by him, be consoled by him, and, in brief, be rescued by him from every danger. [Col. 0724C]

For if, as the Psalm says, “Ships pass through there” (Ps. CIII, 26)—that is, people follow Jesus upon their crosses—which ship passed through more fittingly than the ship of crucified Jesus? Therefore, according to Paul’s saying, “I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. II, 19), let us too be crucified with Christ; let us embrace his cross—indeed, himself upon the cross—with an unfailing affection of heart; let us delight in the life-giving fragrance of burning Jesus, who says of himself: “I, like a vine, have borne the sweetness of fragrance, and my flowers are the fruit of honor and uprightness; my spirit is sweeter than honey.”

Let us delight, I say, in his fragrance; let us be cherished by the ointments of his gifts; let us be strengthened by heavenly bread, that is, his most pure body; so that, eating his body and drinking unto our salvation the blood shed for our salvation, we may be able to taste and may be permitted to see, through a glass darkly, that the Lord is most sweet. Thus may his promise also be fulfilled in us, as far as is lawful in the present life—he who says: “Those who eat me shall still hunger, and those who drink me shall still thirst” (Ecclus. XXIV, 23, 27, 29).

## Chapter XLIV. That flowers are to be found in our Vine

[Col. 0725A]

149. Finally, let us observe that flowers delight both sight and smell. Although they are not usually eaten, they are sucked by bees, which from the liquid pressed out of flowers make for themselves the sweetest honey. Such bees, I think, are those who know and are able to rise on the wings of contemplation, to leave behind their own hives—that is, the care of the body—and to fly over to the garden of delights, where they find the riches of every flower and abundant delights. For this garden is Paradise. Thus you have it in the Song of Love: “Your shoots, O most fruitful Virgin Mary, are a paradise” (Song 4:13).

For this Paradise came forth from the virginal womb, filled with every flower and every [Col. 0725B] fruit, though its fruits were for the time being deferred. Let us see, gather, or rather suck the flowers of this Paradise. For it is fitting that we should now be such bees as know how to suck honey from the rock. For the garden and the Rock are the same: that is, Christ. If, therefore, flowers are to be sought, where could they be sought more fittingly, or found more readily, than in most sweet Christ? The flowers of his virtues and wounds are manifest. Behold, he stands with arms outstretched, body naked, hands and feet pierced, head bowed down.

Take courage now and rise up, my wretched and weak soul; strive with the wings of faith and hope toward this garden of charity. Gather into one the whole gaze of your mind, scattered among many things; and, imitating the industry of bees, 490 ascend to the Paradise of charity to prepare for yourself the honey of devotion, approaching [Col. 0725C] the lofty heart. For behold, he whom you seek has been exalted and humbled. He was not lifted up upon the cross in order to make himself difficult of access to those wishing to approach him, but rather so that he might be found more readily by all.

150. Therefore, approaching this Paradise confidently, recognize in the stretching out of his arms the affection ready to embrace you and inviting you into his embrace; and hear him, as it were, crying both pitifully and mercifully: “Return, return, that we may behold you” (Song 6:12). Return from evil will, evil deeds, obstinacy, and despair. Return, I say, to me, you who have turned away from me, that we may behold you with that gaze of grace with which I looked upon the sinful woman, [Col. 0725D] Peter, and the Thief.

Read me, the book of life written within and without, and understand what you read. Gather for yourself my bloody flowers, that you may be able to enter the gate of that Paradise, before whose doors the Cherub was stationed with a flaming and turning sword. For the knowledge which you can learn fully from me is able to remove the obstacle presented by the Cherub. Therefore let the flowers of my blood draw out the dreadful flames of the turning sword, flames fearful to you. Enter then, O soul, into the Paradise better than all paradises—now with such affection of thought as you can; that afterward, in soul and body, you may be able to enter both the earthly and the heavenly Paradise.

151. This Paradise is not to be embraced only briefly; rather, you must fly through each flower of this Paradise, [Col. 0726A] and suck the petals of every flower. Now toward the right, now toward the left, you must approach more closely and inwardly the little streams and drops of blood which it scatters. Devotion and the grace of tearful compunction must be sought from every side. Consider on both sides how harsh were the nail-piercings, how bitter the breaking of veins and bones in the hands of him who made heaven and earth, who “worked salvation in the midst of the earth”; and amid these reflections frequently repeat: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation” (Ps. 50:14). Do this in imitation of the bee, which always makes some sound while flying and does not fall silent until it has entered among the flowers, where it gathers and sucks out the sweetness of the desired honey.

O how happy you will be if, after you have been admitted among the bloody flowers of our flowering Paradise—I mean his wounds—you can be wholly freed, if only for half an hour, [Col. 0726B] from the noise of this world and the assaults of temptations, and, attending solely to him into whom you have entered, can taste and understand how good, how sweet the Lord is. In the same way his feet, no less full of blood, no less than his hands pierced and broken, flowing with bloody drops, must be contemplated.

152. At last one must approach the most humble heart of the most high Jesus through the gate of his side pierced by the lance. There, without doubt, lies hidden the ineffable treasure of desirable charity; there new devotion is found; from there the grace of tears is drawn forth; there are found gentleness, patience in adversities, and compassion for the afflicted. Above all, there is found a contrite [Col. 0726C] and humbled heart.

Jesus himself desires your embraces; being such as he is, he waits to embrace you. He inclines toward you his flowering head, pierced by many thorns, in order to invite you to the kiss of peace, as though saying to you: “See how I have been fashioned, how pierced, how slain, so that I may set you, my wandering sheep, upon my shoulders and lead you back to the pastures of Paradise. Return the favor: be moved with compassion over my wounds, and set me, such as you now see me, as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm” (Song 8:6), so that in every thought of your heart and every work of your arm you may be found like me, marked as you see me marked.

When I created you, I conformed [Col. 0726D] you to the image of my divinity; I was conformed to the image of your humanity in order to refashion you. Therefore, you who did not retain the form of my divinity impressed upon you in your creation, retain at least the form of your humanity impressed upon me in your re-creation. That is: if you do not retain the form in which I created you, retain at least the form in which I re-created you. If you do not comprehend how great were the riches of virtue I gave you in creating you, comprehend at least how great were the miseries I assumed in your humanity for your sake in re-creating you, 491 and in refashioning you unto delights greater than those for which I had created you.

For I became visible man so that I, who in my divinity was invisible, might be loved by you. Therefore give yourself as the reward of my incarnation and passion—you for whom, incarnate [Col. 0727A] and suffering together, I gave myself. O sweetest and most loving Jesus, Father of lights, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift, look mercifully upon those who humbly confess to you and truly feel that without you we can do nothing. You who gave yourself as the price for us, grant, though we are unworthy of so great a price, that we may be restored in such integrity by your grace that, conformed to the image of your passion, we may also be refashioned into that image of your divinity which we lost by sinning.

153. Nor should it be passed over that bees make a honeycomb from the liquid gathered from flowers—that is, wax containing honey within itself. What does this mean? By wax understand a tenacious memory, apt to receive the form of a seal and to nourish fire, provided that there is in it flax [variant: wood]; this wax contains within itself most sweet honey, cleansing and descending. But if we are truly spiritual bees, let us form for ourselves, from the flowers of our Paradise, the Nazarene—that is, the flowering garden of the most flower-filled Christ—a tenacious memory which is not dissolved by just any temptation. Let that memory be fit to receive the impression of the seal, that is, of crucified Jesus, so that we may always remember him who says: “Set me as a seal.”

For the royal seal is the Cross. If we bear it in the memory of our heart, we shall be able safely to pass into the kingdom of so great a King, whose end there is none. This seal bears the image of crucified Jesus, carved and impressed by many incisions upon the seal of the cross itself, just as the image of kings is impressed on seals by engraving. It also bears the superscription, the title written by Pilate: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews” (John 19:19).

[Col. 0727C] Whoever takes care to bear this seal of the Cross impressed upon a tenacious memory will attain the spiritual meaning of this superscription. He will possess Jesus—that is, salvation—which is the first word in the superscription. Now the salvation desired by everyone of sound mind consists in three things, as it is expressed in three words. In the word *Nazarenus*, “Flowering,” understand pleasure or delight, since the beauty of flowers delights. Hence in the Book of Wisdom the pleasure of the luxurious is expressed in these words: “Let no meadow escape our pleasure. Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither” (Wis. 2:8).

In the word *Rex*, “King,” riches are expressed, for kings are commonly rich beyond all whom they rule. In the word *Judaeorum*, “of the Jews,” glory is understood, because in one interpretation *Judaeus*, “Jew,” means “glorious.” Therefore the willing bearer of the seal of our king, crucified Jesus, will attain the fruit of the superscription: he will be saved—that is, he will attain everlasting delight, drinking from the torrent of the pleasure of the supreme King; he will store up eternal riches in the best Jesus, in whom are hidden all treasures of wisdom and knowledge; and he will glory in him without end, who is exalted above all nations and whose glory is above the heavens.

This seal also illuminates the house of our heart and fosters in it the fire of divine charity. Wax signifies tenacious memory [Col. 0728A] through wood; provided, however, that there is flax in it—that is, the exercise of spiritual labor, signified by flax, derived from the flax-plant, which is commonly worn down by much labor before it is brought to some use.

154. Therefore, if we have the labor of Christ’s passion in our memory, his charity [variant: propriety] can be kindled and burn in us: he who illumines the darkness of our ignorance and inflames the coldness of our sluggishness, so that we too may be ready to suffer for him and with him, who first suffered for us. In such wax of our memory there ought to be honey: that is, delight in the remembrance of the Cross, which is most sweet honey. What is so bitter that it cannot be sweetened by the remembrance of the life-giving passion?

Certainly we read that when the Hebrews had departed from Egypt, they came to most bitter water, which no one could drink; but when Moses cast wood into it, it was made sweet (Exod. 15:23–25), so that they drank it delightfully. What more plainly than the bitter water signifies the bitterness of every adversity? When the wood of the Cross is cast into it—that is, when the passion of sweet Jesus is contemplated—every human suffering must appear light in comparison with the Lord’s passion, which God and man, the mediator of God and men, the Lord Jesus, willed to undergo for human beings.

[Col. 0728B] There is also cleansing honey, for truly nothing so purifies our thought from every assault and contagion of vices, and preserves it in purity, as the continual remembrance of the Cross and passion of the Lord Jesus.

155. There is also descending honey, because, contrary to the natural behavior of other liquids, what is purest in honey descends to the bottom, while what is dreggy rises. What does such descending signify except the virtue of humility? This virtue is indeed acquired and preserved through remembrance of the Lord’s passion, for no one can fail to be humbled when he remembers the Lord of majesty humbled for his sake. It would be unworthy for a human being, mud and ashes, by exalting himself to ascend to the place where the angel most perfect in all knowledge and beauty could not remain because he lacked humility.

Therefore let us gather for ourselves, among the flowers of our Vine, the Lord Jesus, such memory and such delight that, continually retaining in memory the marks of our Crucified One, we may delight so in him, who alone is sweet, that through him we may overcome all the bitterness of this present life, be cleansed from every sin, and be continually preserved in good works through the safeguarding of humility.

## Chapter XLV. On the fragrance of the flowers of the Vine

156. It remains, with sweet Jesus helping us, to say what it means that by the fragrance of the flowers of the vine all poisonous things are especially put to flight. The explanation of this is more readily found if we recognize what serpents signify. What is said about serpents should also be understood of other poisonous creeping things. What, then, could we more suitably understand by serpents than diabolical suggestions? For, like serpents, they creep secretly through human minds; yet unless recognized, they suddenly inflict deadly bites upon the unwary. This we take as prefigured in the children of Israel, miserably slain by serpents in the wilderness (Num. 21:6).

The Apostle gives the cause of this destruction, saying: “Neither let us test God, as some of them tested him and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10:9). But what is it to test God? It is not to believe the Lord. For they were oppressed by the vice of unbelief, and for that reason were killed by serpents. And what is the wilderness in which they were slain but this world, in which we wander, passing through the Red Sea as it were by baptism, liberated by our lawgiver, the Lord Jesus, [Col. 0729B] from Egyptian slavery, under which we were oppressed before the grace of baptism?

157. If we consider more carefully, we shall find that almost all vices arise from the vice of unbelief. Who would seek the vain glory of the world if he perfectly believed that another, unfading glory was to come in heaven—one which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, and which is kept for the humble? Do you suppose that he would incline his mind toward this worldly glory, so uncertain and transient? By no means.

But the reason such people assert that they believe God is a kind of habit: they see and hear that almost the whole world holds such a faith. But if the number of unbelievers grew, and they could not confess Christ’s name without punishment or fear, you would sooner hear them disclose in speech what they carry in their hearts, and even renounce in words him whom they do not fear to deny by deeds.

The same is true of the greedy, who do not care for heavenly riches; of the envious, who do not attend to the praise and reward of charity; of the angry, who do not possess their souls in patience; of the slothful, who shrink from undergoing temporal labors for eternal benefit; of the lustful, who do not direct the eye of the mind toward heavenly pleasures; and of the gluttonous, who place their earthly feasts before that most delicious bread of angels. For if they truly believed the things promised for the future, they would never desire earthly things so ardently.

Therefore, because of their unbelief, they are handed over not only to be wounded by temptations [Col. 0729D] but also 493 to be killed by the infusion of poison by fiery serpents: that is, demons, ministers of that greatest and crooked serpent, the first corrupter. These demons corrupt together with themselves and consign to eternal fires those whom in this life they corrupt by the fire of their wicked suggestions.

158. But let us consider the remedy by which the vice of unbelief is corrected. The Lord said to Moses: “Make a bronze serpent and set it upon an upright pole; whoever looks upon it shall be healed from the bites of serpents” (Num. 21:8). The Lord Jesus himself undertook to explain the mystery of this serpent, saying: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish” (John 3:14–15).

Do you see where we are being led? Directly to kindly Jesus, raised upon the Cross, who is most aptly compared to the bronze serpent raised on high. The serpent is called deadly because death entered the world through the serpent’s suggestion. It is bronze because he was forged in the fires alike of charity and passion, reddened with the blood of his passion, and made hard like bronze in the resurrection, because he dies no more. The raising of the serpent signifies the raising up of crucified Jesus.

This is the serpent upon whom unbelievers wounded by evil spirits and turned toward cruelty are admonished to look if they wish to be saved. For this serpent was transformed from Moses’ rod. By the rod, which is a royal emblem, understand God; by the serpent, through whose suggestion our first parents died, understand mortal man. The rod was changed into a serpent when “the Word became flesh,” assuming what he was not—that is, humanity—while remaining what he was—that is, God.

Just as the serpent made from the rod devoured the serpents of the Egyptian magicians (Exod. 7:10, 12), so God made man nullified the suggestions of sins and deceits of hostile powers, especially when he was raised upon the Cross, displaying the flowers of his blood, pouring out the fragrance of the flowers—that is, of his virtues—throughout the world, and healing hearts wounded by whatever vices.

159. Therefore let us also look upon the face of the lifted bronze serpent, Christ, if we wish to be freed from the serpentine suggestions of wicked demons. To look is to direct oneself toward him in faith; and this is accomplished not by weak, but by strong and perfect faith. There are indeed those who confess with their mouths that they are Christians but deny it by their deeds. I do not think that they direct themselves in faith toward the merciful, crucified Jesus.

To illustrate this somewhat by an analogy: such faith is like wine which has merely the color of wine, but is devoid of the taste and strength of genuine wine. I do not think that wine of this kind is favorably received by God. Rather, it must be like the wine praised in the Song of Songs, where the bridegroom says to the bride: “Your throat is like the best wine.” And she immediately replies: “Worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his teeth to chew” (Song 7:9). And shortly afterward she says: “I will give you spiced wine, mixed with the pomegranates of my own” (Song [Col. 0730D] 8:2).

Behold what kind of wine will please the beloved and kindle him to love us. The best wine is perfect faith, when the judgment of the heart and confession of the mouth agree together. The further phrase, “I will give you spiced wine,” means faith seasoned and exercised by the good works of virtues. By such faith one is directed and fixed upon the merciful God, not by feigned faith lacking works, without which faith is dead.

Therefore let us give our beloved, merciful God the best wine of perfect faith, and wine savory with the diverse spices of virtues; and so let us look upon his face, he who for us was hung upon the Cross in the likeness of the bronze serpent. Whenever we recognize that we have been wounded by the bite of some serpentine temptation, let us run to the Cross and approach the throne of the Cross—once of ignominy, now of highest glory. Looking with faith, hope, and charity toward the most merciful Deliverer, through the death of our Serpent, who killed the death of the ancient serpent, we shall ask and be able to be freed from the bites of serpents.

## Chapter XLVI. On the fruit of our Vine, or Christ, who suffered and was crucified for us

160. Since, as I hope, kindly Jesus, the best guide and teacher, has together taught and led us, we have delivered a discourse on the flowers of our Vine much longer than we expected. Now, with the help of him who loves and guides his own unto the end, in whose hand are we and our words, let us turn our minds to the fruit of that Vine, to make up for the expenditure of words on flowers by the brevity of our treatment of fruits.

For knowledge of the fruit of this Vine of ours is well established, and the slowness of our little intellect cannot rise to it. Therefore, to cut short all digressions: if we seek the fruit, redemption was preeminently planted in the blessed earth, in Mary, Virgin of virgins. That true Vine, sweet Jesus, appeared at his birth, was cut at his circumcision, dug around by plots, pierced by nails, bound by many bonds, put forth leaves in virtues, bore fruit in his passion, and redeemed humankind, who could fittingly be redeemed in no other way.

But you say: How is he said to have borne fruit in the passion when shortly before he was said to have flowered in the birth [perhaps: “passion”]? Are flowers and fruits the same? Or did his fruit follow its flower so suddenly, with no interval of time? For we do not see this happen in the natures of things: flowers come first, and a long interval intervenes before fruit is brought to ripeness.

161. We admit that this is true; but the matters now before us are not merely human but divine. Therefore they do not in every respect follow the natures of things; rather, natures follow their own Creator. You will understand this more clearly if you look more carefully at every kind of tree: when fruit is born, the flower falls and dies. Likewise among human beings and almost all living creatures, the fruit cuts off the flower of virginity from the leaves. But it was not so in the birth of our Vine.

For his most blessed Mother indeed brought forth the blessed fruit without losing the flower of virginity; rather, she was more greatly adorned through a marvelous and most pure birth, in which the law and ordinances of nature were set aside. It is therefore no great matter if the most health-giving fruit followed, without an interval of time, the flowers of our Vine which did not perish. The most beautiful Mother bore him without the loss of her virginal flower; and he himself bore the fruit of our redemption without the withering of the flowers of his virtues.

Yet the accelerated ripening of the fruit is not without reason. It is plain that according to the increase or decrease of heat, the fruit’s ripening is hastened or delayed. See, then, the greatness of the heat—indeed, the fervor—in kindly Jesus as he suffered, and you will not wonder at the rapidity of his fruit. Within he burned with incomparable fire of charity, and without with the fire of passion, so that he might bring forth without delay the fruit of our redemption.

Thus was produced that cluster desired by all Patriarchs, Prophets, and other righteous persons: namely, our redemption. The Church, gathered justly not only from those who live in the time of grace but from the beginning of the world, rejoices that this fruit is sweet to her, saying of the bridegroom in the Song of Love: “Under his shadow, whom I desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2:3).

162. What wonder if the redemption of the righteous from diabolical tyranny, from darkness and the shadow of death, and from the infernal prison in which they were held confined—their return to Paradise—was assigned to the keeping of angels? What wonder if Christ’s presence was delightful and eagerly desired, he having been awaited and longed for during so great a time? For amid afflictions, the arrival of a deliverer is usually more welcome in proportion as the affliction has been more prolonged.

For how long had Abel, the first righteous man and first martyr, who by his passion first prefigured the Deliverer, awaited him? How long had Adam and Eve, our first parents, still recalling to one another in hell the joys of Paradise, thirsted for this redemption along with the other saints and righteous persons who hoped to be liberated? How greatly, do you suppose, did they exult in dancing when the Crucified One arrived, with angels going before and crying: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter” (Ps. 23:7, 9)?

How eagerly, do you suppose, did they sing together, leap forth with harmonious rejoicing into their common gladness, and say:

> “You have come, O Desired One, whom we awaited in darkness, that you might lead the bound out from their prisons. Our sighs called for you; our abundant laments sought you. You became hope for those who longed, great consolation for ever.”  
> (Office of Easter)

O how sweet was the fruit of redemption to those who had been placed in such great and bitter slavery! This is the fruit of which the bridegroom speaks in the Song of Love: “I said: I will climb the palm tree and seize its fruits” (Song 7:8). What means “the palm tree”? His Cross, one part of which is said to have been made from the palm tree.

163. For the Cross is reported to have been made from four kinds of trees: cypress, cedar, olive, and palm. The cypress is in the depth, the cedar in the length, the olive in the height, and the palm in the breadth. Hence the Apostle says: “That we may comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth” (Eph. 3:18).

The depth of the Cross is the wood fixed in the earth. Upon it stood the upright wood, against which the back of the crucified Lord was placed: this is the length of the Cross. The transverse wood placed upon it, to which the hands were fastened, is called the breadth of the Cross. That which Pilate placed above, on which the triumphal title was written, is called its height. Each of these woods has its own mystical meaning according to its nature.

For the cypress signifies fear or humility, where the root of the Cross is. By it not only its low position but its nature is expressed, since it is said to drive serpents away by its scent: that is, it puts demons to flight, whose characteristic pride is expelled by the virtue of humility. The cedar, a tree exceeding other trees in height, signifies the length of the Cross—that is, perseverance or patience. For by its natural power it is proved very durable and incapable by nature of decay.

The olive, a tree which yields oil, signifies charity, by which works of mercy are signified; and this tree fittingly supplies the breadth of the Cross, because charity is broad and is commanded to extend even to enemies. The palm, moreover, a tree signifying victory, most fittingly signifies the height of the Cross: hope which must be fixed on high things and not pressed down toward what is low.
