This tree has written upon it the triumphal title in which the fruit of the Cross is found. For its first word is “Jesus,” by which salvation is understood, the same as redemption. Behold the fruit of the Cross. Christ was crucified for this reason: to redeem humankind. And in saying, “I will climb the palm tree,” he signifies the whole Cross from one part of the Cross. And fittingly by the palm, on which is found the title, the sign of redemption which is the fruit of the Cross.

164. But someone may say: “You were going to speak of the fruit of the vine, and instead you speak of the fruit of the palm. What agreement is there between vine and palm?” To this I reply: the palm signifies the Cross, but the vine signifies the Crucified One. Tell me, then: is the fruit of the Cross different from that of the Crucified One? I think not. Therefore the fruit of the palm and of the vine is the same.

The vine climbed the palm and seized the fruit of the palm—not fruit which the palm had of itself, but fruit from the vine extended upon the palm. Why, then, does the Vine itself say, “I will seize its fruits,” rather than “my fruits,” when the palm has its fruit from the vine, not the vine from the palm? Christ did not have this fruit without the palm—indeed, he had it through the palm, that is, through the Cross—for if Christ had not been crucified, redemption would not have followed. Therefore Christ seized the fruit of the Cross: precisely that fruit which he himself had worked through the Cross.

165. But this cluster has many grapes: the fulfillment of Scripture, victory over the devil, the glory of the resurrection, the wondrous ascent of the ascension, and the sending of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The Lord himself bears witness concerning the fulfillment of Scripture, saying to Peter: “The cup which the Father has given me, do you not wish me to drink it?” (John 18:11). “How then shall the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must happen thus?” (Matt. 26:54). And elsewhere: “Was it not necessary that all things written concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms should be fulfilled?” (Luke 24:44).

Victory over the devil, even if it could have been achieved in another way, nevertheless ought not to have been accomplished otherwise. For he is greatly mistaken who thinks that the wisdom of God and of the Lord ordered anything other than what was most excellent. It was necessary that he who had conquered humankind by a tree should be conquered through a human being and through a tree, so that life might rise again from the place whence death arose, and he who conquered by the tree might also be conquered by the tree (Preface of the Mass of the Cross).

Why it was through a human being who was God, rather than through a mere human being, is sufficiently plain: all human beings were liable to sin, and no one who could not free himself was able to loose another’s bonds. But Christ the mighty one owed nothing to original sin, because by the singular privilege of his birth he was conceived without every fleshly desire. He alone is free among the dead; he alone was able to free the dead from death, as the Apostle says: “He had no need to offer sacrifice for himself, as the other priests do, both for their own and for the people’s ignorance” (Heb. 7:27).

166. But if it is asked why God wished to liberate humankind through himself rather than through some other creature, we may indeed ascribe this to his charity, which he commended to us by not only becoming incarnate but also dying for us. Through this he also gave the pattern of charity, that we may be ready, when necessity requires, to lay down our lives for our brothers, seeing that our King laid down his life for us.

There is also another reasonable cause why we were redeemed through the Lord: namely, that it was by no means fitting for us to be refashioned by anyone other than him by whom we had been formed. For refashioning moves us more strongly to charity than formation, as has often been said above. If we had been refashioned by someone other than him through whom we were formed, we would owe more to our refashioner than to our maker, and thus would love the creature more than the Creator—which would be unfitting. Therefore, in order to move us to love him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, the best God has bestowed upon us all that he owed in creating and refashioning us; no stranger shares in his benefits.

167. Therefore let us embrace with our whole desire the fruit of our redemption, and frequently—indeed, without ceasing—call to mind its hidden sweetness. Let us taste with the tongue of our understanding, and store in the vessel of our memory, the utterly pure blood of this grape, the blood, I say, of ruddy Jesus, because he was made redemption for us, because through him we have been saved and delivered.

With these flowers and this fruit, by which it has been redeemed from demonic tyranny, the faithful soul must continually be refreshed, lest it fail in this wearisome wilderness, where it labors without rest and without interruption, sighing for that land flowing with milk and honey, and crying out with the bride: “Support me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love” (Song 2:5).

She does not fail to know what and how great was the fruit of the Vine, the tree of life, Jesus Christ. For she had sometimes strewn the bed of her conscience with the flowers of the virtues and passion of her bridegroom; she who cries out to him in the same Song of Love: “Our bed is flowering” (Song 1:15)—not with strange flowers, but with yours, sweet Jesus. Come, then, and recognize your flowers; rest in the bed adorned with your flowers.

Thus the bride asks the companions [Col. 0735A] of the bridegroom, the proclaimers of God’s word, to support her with these flowers. For she knows well what power such flowers have, what effect they produce in her when recalled to memory by the minister of the word; how greatly they strengthen her amid the temptations and dangers of this present life, and how much they inflame her with desire for the heavenly homeland.

And I do not doubt that this same bride was at some time introduced into the garden of her bridegroom’s holy Scriptures, where without doubt she found the tree of life, the true Vine. She eagerly seized its fruit, turning it over and over in her mind and considering it carefully and keenly: what fruit she had obtained from the ardor of her beloved—indeed, from the beloved himself. She perceived unfailingly how much love she owed him, and how fittingly she ought to be strengthened to endure every danger, having tasted the most fruitful spirit which she received from the tree so beloved.

Therefore she desires that these flowers and this fruit be recalled to her memory often, because she prays to be supported by the former lest she fall, and surrounded by the latter lest she be moved in any way, knowing indeed what strength both the fragrance of those flowers and the savor of this fruit possess.

168. But when she adds, “For I am sick with love,” what is this except that the bride, inflamed with longing for the heavenly homeland, cannot bear a long delay? Hence elsewhere in the same book: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I am sick with love” (Song 5:8). What is this love, so powerful and yet inducing languor? Is it not the love of which it is written: “Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6)? What sort of strength is this which produces weakness? Let those answer who have read the solution to this question in the book of experience [Col. 0735C]. I said “experience.” And why not “wisdom,” which derives its name from taste? Let those, then, who have read in the book of wisdom—that is, who have experienced the inward taste—speak and teach us what this love is which, though strong as death, makes lovers languish unto death, because they are healed only in the death of this body, and not before.

Meanwhile, while they dwell in this mortal life—or this living death—they may indeed be consoled by the flowers and fruits of the beloved and desirable one, but not satisfied, until that day comes which they desire with the Prophet, saying: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15); and elsewhere: “You will fill me with gladness through your countenance; delights are at your right hand unto the end” [Col. 0735D] (Ps. 15:11). Of this right hand it is elsewhere read: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6).

See how well this authority agrees with what preceded: the left hand of the beloved is called the remembrance of that love than which none is greater, namely, that by which he laid down his life for his friends. But in the right hand are the blessed vision of God which he promised to his friends, and joy in the presence of the divine majesty. Rightly, then, that vision of God which makes divine, that inestimable love of the divine presence, is placed at the right hand, concerning which it is sweetly sung: “Delights are at your right hand unto the end.” Rightly too is placed at the left hand that commemorative love, ever to be remembered, so that until iniquity passes away the bride may rest and recline upon it.

[Col. 0736A] Thus the bridegroom’s left hand is rightly beneath the bride’s head, on which, bending down, she supports her head; that is, she bends the intention of her mind, lest it turn toward carnal and worldly desires. For “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks many things” (Wis. 9:15). Therefore the flowers and fruit of our Vine, and the left hand of the bridegroom himself, signify the same thing; but healing from languor is signified by his right hand.

169. Those, then, who ask to be supported by these flowers and by the fruit of our Vine do not boast of being sustained by an alien love, since they have placed neither their hope nor their confidence in perishable things. Rather, it is that soul alone which now languishes—indeed, dies—from love and longing for the beloved amid bodily and worldly cares, to which it is said: [Col. 0736B] “Who is this who comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5). For she comes up from the wilderness of this world who has joined her heart to the heart of the beloved in that love, seeking the things above, not those upon the earth. Hence she abounds in the delights of virtues, as though anointed with the perfume of diverse spices gathered from the beloved’s paradise, following him who suffered for her and left her his own example.

Thus it is rightly said, “Leaning upon her beloved,” not upon a human being; for “cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. 17:5), nor upon any earthly things, which she has counted all as dung in order that she might gain Christ. Such a soul [Col. 0736C], then, now supported by the flowers and fruit of the true Vine, her bridegroom, and now languishing unto death through love of him, saying with Job, “I despair; I shall live no longer” (Job 7:16)—such a bride, I say, will afterward deserve to be embraced ineffably by that sweetest right hand and to be satisfied with the fruit of eternal joy, her languor not only healed but increased.

For the unbearable languor of desire will be healed in the most joyful enjoyment of the beloved whom she desires; yet this desire will not be taken away—indeed, it will be increased. But then it will not be languor, but the banishment of weariness, when one who desires is most fully satisfied by the desired one, and, satisfied, learns in satisfaction to desire, by a reciprocal, endless, and inexplicable generation: desire generating satisfaction, and satisfaction giving birth to desire.

[Col. 0736D] But now let us return to the grape.

170. The third berry in the cluster of our redemption is the Lord’s resurrection. Who can explain how much sweetness it had and has? Yet let someone, if he can, set in his heart the ineffable greatness of that most blessed and most sorrowful Passion; let him see with what grief of despair the hearts of those who loved the suffering Jesus were struck; let him see the lamentations of those faithful women who did not abandon sweetest Jesus as he went to the place of suffering carrying his cross, nor when he breathed out his most sweet soul. Above all, let him see that little woman then looking on, but now Lady of the world, the Mother of the Lord, whose soul the sharp sword of sorrow pierced. Let him see the whole structure [Col. 0737A] of the world sympathizing with its Maker and wrapped in dreadful darkness. Let him see these things, I say, and join to such turmoil the serenity of the third day and the unexpected joy of that most joyous resurrection. Let him consider more intently with what exultation they received the Lord rising from the dead, whom they had watched die with immense sorrow.

See with what joy, in the resurrection, he repaid his disciples for that sorrow and for the most holy supper of his last meal, at which he said: “I shall not henceforth drink of the fruit of the vine until I drink it new with you” (Matt. 26:29). Behold, now the true Vine has risen in glory; and he ate and drank with those same disciples, undoubtedly with the greatest joy, and presented himself to some who doubted, to be both seen [Col. 0737B] and touched.

171. Let no one suppose that he rose for the joy of the disciples alone. Rather, he rose also for us and for the whole world, making blessed all who, though they do not see, nevertheless believe that he “was delivered up for our offenses and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4:25). By this we are taught that, if we are companions in his Passion, we shall also be companions in his resurrection; and that we need not doubt that our mortal bodies will be raised to the glory of resurrection, since we believe that our head, condemned to a most shameful death, rose again. For as all die in Adam, so all shall be made alive in Christ. “For Christ is the firstfruits of those who sleep; afterward, those who belong to Christ, at his coming” (1 Cor. 15:22–23); they shall rise, after the example of the risen Christ, to a glory in which they will die no more.

[Col. 0737C] 172. The Ascension too is a berry in the cluster of redemption accomplished through the Passion: a sweet berry indeed, containing in itself a great abundance of sweetness and bringing joy to heaven and earth. For who could doubt that great joy came upon the disciples when they saw him, as man, penetrating the heavenly realms? They stood with minds and hearts alike raised toward heaven, unable to contain their soul’s joy, but congratulating the departing Lord with shouts of jubilation.

Heaven too undoubtedly exulted: that is, all the choirs of angels came to meet their Lord, clad in the purple robe of our flesh, and with highest praise received their supreme victor. And if the whole choir of angels rejoices at the arrival of the soul of a single righteous person or martyr, how greatly, do you suppose, did the spirits of every order exult at the arrival of their unique Emperor? Therefore, since human understanding fails before the greatness of this praise and joy, let us too rejoice. Let us, by wonder and love, draw in the sweetness of this berry as something to be recalled, exulting in the Holy Spirit because a portion of our flesh, in our sweetest Lord, has been most exaltedly placed upon the supreme throne of the Trinity. Let us direct our minds, as far as we can, after him and into him, humbly beseeching him that he may deign to draw us after himself, so that, running in the fragrance of his ointments, we may deserve to be brought into those wine cellars, that supreme storehouse of spices, that inner Holy of Holies [Col. 0738A], where Christ our head has gone before us.

173. The fifth berry of our cluster is the sending of the Holy Spirit. Who can explain the most delightful wine of this berry? Wine, I say—or, if you prefer, new wine. For as soon as the Apostles and the others waiting with them received the Holy Spirit, they were intoxicated, poured forth a good word, and spoke in diverse tongues the mighty works of God. Formerly hidden by fear, they now ran out openly. No longer did they fear the water of the roaring people, being inflamed with the fire of love. Then they experienced with certainty the truth of what is written: “Many waters could not quench love, neither could floods overwhelm it” (Song 8:7).

For floods [Col. 0738B] of authorities rushed upon them; the waters of the populous multitude poured forth; the winds and storms of threatening words blew; yet the fire of love was not extinguished, but was even increased. For “the Apostles departed from the presence of the council rejoicing, because they were counted worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Christ” (Acts 5:41). The fire of love was increased because many were kindled through their preaching and inflamed with the same joy with which they themselves burned.

But what did the Jews, unbelievers in every good thing, say? “They are full of new wine” (Acts 2:13). In lying and in ignorance, they spoke the truth. For they were filled with that most noble new wine of God’s love—or rather, with God who is love—kindling them to love and strengthening them against fear. Just as new wine does not permit itself to be confined within a vessel unless there is an opening through which it may burst forth, so the new wine of the Holy Spirit manifested itself from their hearts through their mouths, as they spoke the mighty works of God with wondrous eloquence.

[Col. 0738C] For a draught of this new wine does not hinder the tongue, but assists it, so that that poetic saying proves true:

> “What man has not rich cups made eloquent?”  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, Book I, Epistle 5, line 19.

But the Lord’s fruitful and splendid cup had intoxicated them, because, as the Apostle says, “the love of God had been poured out in their hearts” (Rom. 5:5). Yet Peter’s words seem contrary to ours. Made bold by the draught of new wine, he now feared not only no woman’s words, as formerly, but not even the words [Col. 0738D] of rulers. Putting himself forward, therefore, he said that the disciples were not drunk with wine. But let us hear his words, carefully distinguished: “For these,” he says, “are not drunk, as you suppose” (Acts 2:15). They are not drunk with earthly new wine, as you think, but with the heavenly Spirit.

Let us, then, beloved, also drink from the most delightful wine of this berry. And if we lack that by which—or in which—we may drink, namely the vessel of understanding, let us run in full confidence to our unique and provident Maker, whose workmanship we are, and pray that he may form in our souls a vessel capable of receiving this sweetest new wine. Thus, having received our Comforter, the sevenfold Spirit of grace, may we escape the manifold snares of the tempter, our adversary, and cast the feet of our affections into the fetters of wisdom; [Col. 0739A] so that, bound to Wisdom herself by the bonds of love, we may run after her without ceasing and without weariness until we attain the fullness of her taste. There we shall no longer see through a mirror and in a riddle, but face to face behold our King in beauty, and know as we are known.

174. Here, I think, it should be observed that the fruit of our Vine is both eaten and drunk. The grape is chewed, but the wine contained in the grape is drunk; and in both there are use and enjoyment. But in wine both enjoyment and benefit endure longer. This seems to me to belong to the enjoyment of this cluster of which we have spoken.

For in the present life we chew this cluster when we examine with the teeth of our understanding the sweetness, delight, and benefit of our redemption; when, in the consideration of our heart, we turn over the power of the resurrection, the glory of the Ascension, and the benefit of the coming of the Holy Spirit, as grapes in the mouth. From these there sometimes arises some joy in our heart. But that joy will be complete after time—that is, the mutability of times—has ceased, when we shall no longer eat these things but drink them, having obtained from them an inestimable and everlasting joy.

For there is some labor in eating; but what is drunk is received without labor. Thus by eating is signified whatever delight, of whatever kind or however great, which in this life cannot be perceived apart from the body, but which always weighs down the soul. But by drink, received without labor, are signified the joys of that place and time where and when there shall be no more mourning, nor crying, [Col. 0739C] nor any pain, because all these things have passed away. And he himself, stable from eternity, who for our sake became passing, lest we should pass away like a shadow, will minister to us.

Then we shall no longer eat with the labor, fear, and hindrance of this body of death; rather, with great delight, we shall drink the wine of our redemption. And, contrary to the nature of noble wine, the more we drink, although we are satisfied, the more we shall thirst, endlessly and unceasingly admiring and praising the wonderful goodness of our Redeemer, which he willed to display toward us in the fruit of our redemption.

175. See whether this distinction between food and drink is not commended to us in the bridegroom’s words in the Song of Love [Col. 0739D], when he says: “Eat, friends, and drink; and be intoxicated, beloved ones” (Song 5:1). For he first commands eating, which certainly belongs to the present life, in which, as we have said, contemplation is mingled with the labor of action. In the life to come, freed from every action, we shall enjoy joy as from a cup. For we shall drink and be intoxicated from the abundance of God’s house, and be given drink from the torrent of his delight, then knowing with clarity that we are most beloved of our King and Bridegroom, when all the water of earthly toil and activity is changed into the wine of divine contemplation, and all the water jars are filled to the brim.

For all will be filled with the good things of the Lord’s house when the desirable marriage of the Bridegroom—that is, Christ—and the Bride—that is, the universal Church—is celebrated. Then, in the supreme joy of heart, all who cry to the Lord will drink and say: “You have kept the good wine until now” [Col. 0740A] (John 2:10). Yet we say that this joy is signified by food, since it is written, “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22:30), although the exposition of the preceding authority may also apply here. If, however, someone should maintain that it would be unworthy for so great a Vine, which has labored so much and is laboring, to produce only one cluster, he may, if he wishes, call the things which we call berries “clusters,” and assign to each a multitude of berries.

176. Nevertheless, we shall not without reason find innumerable clusters in the present Vine if we wish to consider all the churches, all the monasteries, all the communities which exist throughout the universal Church. For who produced these clusters except our Vine? For Christ and the Church are one Vine, just as they are one body; the individual communities are individual clusters; and the berries express the individuality of persons—not inappropriately, as it seems to me.

[Col. 0740B] For the outer skin of the berry or grape signifies the body; the seeds, the bones; and the juice signifies the soul, or the blood, which is the seat of the soul. At a person’s death, the soul is pressed from the body as wine from the grape; and, if found worthy, it is carried into the royal wine cellar of the heavenly paradise, that joy may be made for the heavenly King and his blessed guests, who are called and come to the marriage of the Lamb. For the Bridegroom himself drinks his own wine from his own vine and vineyard, namely the Church, of which he too is the head.

He himself drinks the purest blood of grapes, namely the souls of saints pressed out and separated from the grapes in the winepress of the cross: in labor and thirst, cold and nakedness, many vigils, and other spiritual exercises. He will drink them—that is, he will delightfully incorporate them into himself—causing them, having become one spirit with him, to rest henceforth with him and in him from all labors.

[Col. 0740C] Let those rotten berries beware and take heed for themselves—the false brethren, I mean, the perverse Christians—who contain not wine but poison, who refuse to be pressed in the winepress of the cross and are not among human labors. Let them beware, I say, while there is time, lest they be cast out to be devoured by swine, that is, by devils; for there is no way into the royal wine cellars except through the winepress of the cross.

177. It remained for us to speak of the second flowers of our Vine and their fruits, according to what is written, “And my flesh has blossomed again” (Ps. 27:7). No one doubts that this is said of the resurrection, whose fruit will be the glory of the second resurrection. But preferring to leave the reader thirsty rather than satiated to weariness, we here set an end to this discourse. We are ready to correct, remove, and alter anything that we may have said contrary to the faith and to the Holy Scriptures. In all things, we humbly give thanks to him who has taught us by his gratuitous grace, who opens the mouth of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent. To his name we consecrate both the new beginning and the end of this little work: to the best and sweetest Jesus. Amen.

[Col. 0741]

# MEDITATION ON THE PASSION AND RESURRECTION OF THE LORD. (G)

[NOTE.]

It appeared in the earlier edition from a manuscript belonging to the learned Leonorius Foy, distinguished canon of the church of Beauvais; in this manuscript, as also in the Parisian Victorine manuscript, Saint Bernard is named as author. Carolus Sacci, a Parisian doctor of the fifteenth century, attributes to Bernard a book *On the Passion and Resurrection of the Lord*, which appears to be none other than this work. Yet, among other considerations, its dissimilarity of style sufficiently proves that it is not Bernard’s.

501

# CHAPTER I. On Christ’s Triumphal Entry into Jerusalem

[Col. 0741A]

1. “Do not fear, daughter of Zion: behold, your King comes to you, meek, and sitting upon a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke” (John 12:15). Come, Lord Jesus, come, desire of all nations, for my soul has fallen asleep through weariness at your death, and my eyes have grown faint through lack of your light. Rise, beloved sun, so that a human being may go forth to his work and to his labor until evening, and may work not for food that perishes but for that which endures unto eternal life.

Do not fear, daughter of Zion. Fear belongs to the weak. Therefore you are still a daughter because you fear; that is, you are not yet Jerusalem, but daughter of Zion—that is, of the watchtower. Learn, therefore, to watch. Do not fear, because fear clouds the eye. A cheerful pupil looks out clearly. Faith [Col. 0741B] is the pupil of your eye. As the pupil of the eye is exceedingly delicate and, unless it is guarded alertly and carefully by the eyelids, is blurred by the touch of the slightest and finest dust, so the sharpness of faith, unless it always has vigilant protection, is disturbed more quickly than anything else.

But do not fear, daughter of Zion: behold, your King comes to you. The sun rises for you, who may guard and enlighten you and lead you where there is no dust. He comes to you meek. As he is, so he desires you to be. Become meek in bearing his yoke, so that he may sit upon you, his she-ass, and upon the colt, the foal of the yoked animal. And what is this she-ass? It is the same thing called flesh, woman, and *virago*, because she was taken from man. And who is her colt? The male human being. And how is he her colt? Because “not that which is spiritual comes first, but that which is natural; afterward that which is spiritual” [Col. 0741C] (1 Cor. 15:46).

The meek King first sits upon the she-ass and afterwards upon the colt. First the flesh is tamed so that it may be fitted to the yoke; then the colt is born, nourished, and strengthened so that it may bear its rider. And why is he the foal of a beast under the yoke? Because woman is subject to man, and man is the head of woman. Yet he is the foal of a beast under the yoke because man comes through woman, and she will give birth in pain. Let the meek King sit upon both, making peace, lest they oppose one another.

2. He comes to you, yet you do not go to him. Go forth from the land of your flesh, from the kindred of your mind, and from the house—that is, the memory—of your father. Your father is an Amorite and your mother a Hittite. Forget this father, and then the King will desire your beauty. Your beauty [Col. 0742A] is great if you hear, see, and incline your ear. You hear through obedience, see through understanding, and incline your ear through humility. This beauty, this whole glory, is within, amid golden fringes (Ps. 44:11, 12, 14); the meek King desires this beauty of yours.

Go forth, therefore, from the city, because, he says, “I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city” (Ps. 54:10). Go out with the Hebrew children, who pass over simply to meet the Lord. Spread olive branches in the way, so that you may set works of mercy beneath his feet. Take palm fronds so that you may triumph over the princes of darkness. Let nothing remain within you that does not come forth to meet him, for not even one hoof is to be left in Egypt for Pharaoh. Let hand, heart, and tongue sing together: “Hosanna in the highest” [Col. 0742B] (Matt. 21:9).

# CHAPTER II. On the Prayer and Sweat in the Garden, and the Sleep of the Disciples

3. You have indeed seen, Lord, the affliction of your people who are in Egypt, and you have bowed your heavens and descended to set us free. A little respite too, Lord, has been granted me from the harshest works of darkness, by which Pharaoh, the importunate taskmaster, grievously afflicted my mind; and preparation for your Sabbath has already made my soul glad. Yet I have not yet reached the mirror in which I may more fully perceive the pimples and blemishes that stain my face and are greatly displeasing in your eyes. For though I wash myself with nitre and multiply for myself the herb borith, I am stained with my iniquity.

And now, Lord, the days of your Passion ought to press us more urgently than Pharaoh’s overseers do, because in your works are righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. But we sleep while you, Lord, pray for us, because our eyes are weighed down by our lukewarmness. Awaken us, that we may watch and pray lest we enter into temptation, because tribulation is very near to us. How quickly the eye closes so as not to see you; how our foot slips into this great sea, broad in its expanse, where there are creeping things beyond number, [Col. 0742C] which mock the soul intent upon the phantasms of its dreams and draw it into the heart of the sea, whence return to the heights is not easy unless you send out your hand from on high and deliver us from many waters.

Awaken us, Lord, that we may watch and pray with you even one hour. But who is there who watches one hour with you? For you have been torn away from us as far as a stone’s throw, and you agonize at greater length, so that a drop of your blood runs down to the earth. Far, far from us you have been torn away, because the stone was cut from the mountain without hands, and the stone was thrown and struck Goliath on the forehead, and the statue on its feet.

4. This is your being cast far from us, because you entered even within the veil as our forerunner, where you ever intercede with the Father. But would that the drop of blood which runs down from your agony might run down even to our earth, that it might open its mouth and drink it, and cry to you, and with you to the Father, better than the blood of Abel.

But who, Lord, watches one hour with you? Even in heaven there was silence only for about half an hour; how much less shall we keep watch with you for one hour upon earth? How often and how often you return to us and find us sleeping! Yet you graciously awaken us, and again you go away a second and a third time, saying the same words. But as soon as you depart, sleep again takes possession of us, and we cannot keep watch except while you are with us and awaken us.

[Col. 0743B] You come in the second and third watch; but blessed is that servant whom you then find awake. No mention is made now of the first or fourth: for neither early age receives the capacity for wakefulness, nor does the last retain hope of a long sleep. And what is it, Lord, that on returning the third time you grant an opportunity for sleep? “Sleep now,” you say, “and rest.” Do you allow one sleep in which they may rest and forbid another in which the eyes are weighed down? It is so. For one who watches in you sleeps sweetly, is silent, and rests in his sleep; but one who sleeps apart from you is violently tossed, like a drunken person in the night who knows nothing.

“My soul is sorrowful unto death” [Col. 0743C] (Mark 14:41, 34). The soul is sorrowful that awaits the tribulation of death. For who knows whether it will go to the left or to the right? Who knows how it will answer one who accuses it, when the Judge will speak like a woman in labor? Therefore let the sorrowful soul become like the pelican of the wilderness, which hears the city and their assemblies concerning bloodshed, and grows pale with the emaciation of solitude; or like the night-raven among the ruins of Scripture, seeking food for itself all night, and let it fly into the watchful sparrow upon the roof, singing when the thief will come.

5. Or do you not see Judas, how he does not sleep? How wakeful are the eyes of avarice! How it ranges over the whole earth! Its hand does not cease, its foot does not cease, and it heaps up wrath for itself on the day of wrath. Yet Simon sleeps, James and John sleep. Why? Because they do not attend to what will happen shortly afterward. The greatness of danger drives sleep away. Did Peter sleep in the courtyard? Did those sleep who fled after abandoning him? Did the young man sleep when they seized him and he fled naked, leaving behind the linen cloth? Yet it was cold, because Peter stood and warmed himself. The greatness of danger makes one forget sleep, cold, and hunger.

Awaken at last, miserable soul, if not from love, at least from fear. Consider at least the torment which you will soon suffer in death. Certainly there is no cross harder than death. Death itself, I say, is the harshest cross prepared for you, toward which you hurry daily without noticing. See how death crucifies you. The body stiffens, the legs are stretched out, hands and arms fall limp, the breast gasps, the neck grows weak, the lips foam, the eyes become fixed, the face sweats, the expression becomes dreadful, and it grows pale like a potsherd. This cross awaits you.

[Col. 0744A] I do not know whether one dies more pleasantly in a soft bed or upon a rigid cross, except that the cross cuts off pain more quickly. The things we see and feel are slight in comparison with what the soul already tastes within. For sensation quickly withdraws from the body; but death ever accompanies the soul as its own.

# CHAPTER III. On Human Hardness toward Christ’s Passion

[Col. 0744B]

6. “When the living creatures moved, the wheels beside them moved also” (Ezek. 1:19). If our life made progress, the wheel of Holy Scripture would move along with us; but because we stumble as we walk on foot through marshes and rocks, the wheels scarcely follow us. The Lord’s Passion is celebrated, and we devote ourselves to pleasure. From the cross he cries to us: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow” (Lam. 1:12); and there is no one to hear, no one to console, no one to reply.

“I thirst,” he says [Col. 0744C] (John 19:28). Lord, for what do you thirst? Does thirst, then, torment you more than the cross? You are silent concerning the cross and cry out concerning thirst. “I thirst.” For what? For your faith, your salvation, your joy; concern for your souls possesses me more than the suffering of my body. “O all you who pass by, attend and see whether there is any sorrow like my sorrow.” Attend to my sorrow, so that in my sorrow you may see your own. My sorrow is an image of your sorrow. What you attend to in my body, attend to and see whether there is not a similar sorrow in your heart. You pass from yourselves to me; pass back from me into yourselves, and see whether there is not in you a sorrow like mine. “Do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves, daughters of Jerusalem” (Luke 23:28). That sorrow of yours, which you pass by and do not attend to, is more to be wept over than my sorrow. For I was struck because of your crime.

These things you cry out to us from your cross, kind Jesus, if not in words, then by the deed itself. What shall I answer you, what shall I say, or what shall I render in return? You have made your body a mirror of my soul. I did not know insults, terrors, and Satan endlessly striking me with blows, unless I saw your medical art healing like with like, and weighing in the balance your calamity on one side, my iniquity on the other. You gave your body to those who struck it, your cheeks to those who plucked them; you did not turn your face away from those who spat upon you, so that your blows might remove my blows, lashes atone for lashes, and the reproaches of those who reproached you might remove from me everlasting reproach.

These are the most spotless linens of your flesh with which you bound up my wounds [Col. 0745A], merciful Samaritan, that you might place me upon your beast and bring me to the inn; for truly you yourself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows, and by your bruise we have been healed.

504

# CHAPTER IV. On Christ Being Struck and Peter’s Denial

7. Christ is struck with blows in the house of the high priest, his face veiled, because the Christian is struck with blows in the house of conscience, his mind blinded. What Christ suffers publicly, I suffer secretly; and what he suffered outwardly from Caiaphas’s attendants, I suffer inwardly from Satan’s wickedness. For sinners have built upon my back; they have veiled my face, fixed my face to the earth, made my back their anvil, and built upon my back.

Yet I am still held within the house, where the girl both dies and is raised. For Peter also denied there. “I am not a man” [Col. 0745B] (Luke 22:58). I attend to man, not God; I fear man, not God, whose truth I deny. Does it not seem to you that Peter had a veiled face in these words? Thus he was struck a third time, because he denied a third time. Paul too asked God three times to remove from him Satan’s angel who struck him with blows (2 Cor. 12:8). Therefore each apostle was struck; each suffered shipwreck three times: Peter inwardly, Paul outwardly.

Satan would have wished, if it had been permitted him, to sift Peter by striking him like wheat until he had shaken from him every particle of faith. “But I,” he says, “Peter, have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail.” Hence Christ looked at him, and Peter went out and wept bitterly. Peter had his face veiled until Christ looked upon him. But did Christ not look upon him even earlier while he was denying him? Certainly; but Peter did not look back at Christ who looked upon him, because he had a veiled face. Hence another Evangelist rightly says: “And Peter remembered” [Col. 0745C] (Luke 22:32, 61, 62). Peter’s remembrance was Christ’s look. Therefore, when you remember your sin, you are seen by Christ; indeed, once the veil is removed, you see Christ.

“And he went out.” For that reason he denied him: because he wanted to remain inside. Yet when he denied him, he went outside. Outside from where? From Christ’s house, from the house of the faithful. But when he went outside from Caiaphas’s house, he was admitted into Christ’s house. How many today say, “We belong to Christ’s house; we belong to the Church’s house,” yet belong to Caiaphas’s house—that is, to hypocrisy! What Peter did by denying, these do by affirming. But unless they go out through confession and weep bitterly, they do not enter God’s Church. The bitterness of tears washes the veil from the eyes.

Therefore Christ is struck in Caiaphas’s house because Peter was struck in Caiaphas’s house; and what Peter suffered inwardly from Satan, Christ endured outwardly from Satan’s attendants. Attend, then, and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow. See who endured the more grievous reproaches: Christ outwardly in his body, or Peter inwardly in his breast. But now let us go to Pilate.

# CHAPTER V. On Pilate’s Examination, Christ’s Scourging, and the Soldiers’ Mockery

[Col. 0746A]

8. When morning came, he was led bound to Pilate. So long as guilt is concealed, it is night; but when it begins to become known, morning comes. Then he is bound by the chief priests and handed over to Pilate—that is, to the prince of darkness—as the Apostle also commands that such a person be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Cor. 5:5). The young man is brought out of the house to the gate of the city, to Pilate, where Pilate sits on the judgment seat. For judgment was customarily held at the gate.

Pilate, having seized him, scourged him. Often, when guilt is uncovered, the sinner becomes unrestrained through shamelessness. Crimes increase; blows are multiplied. For “many are the scourges of the sinner” [Col. 0746B] (Ps. 31:10). With these scourges Pharaoh also struck the children of Israel.

9. After this he is handed over to the soldiers to be mocked. This is the very wickedness of the spiritual soldiery. Observe the order of misery. He is handed over by the chief priests to the prince of darkness, who, having made him his slave by his scourges, exposes him to his soldiers for still deeper mockery, and afterwards finally to crucifixion. For after the cross no punishment remains, because sin is ended by death; but when death is already near, the sinner is tormented by the greater derision of demons. Stripping him of the garment of all Christian adornment, they put around him, as though for royal splendor, a scarlet cloak—that is, a garment mingled with blood—when, because of the bloody cruelty of his life, he is both honored and surrounded by many. Hence, too, they weave a crown of thorns and place it upon his head, when, heaping up for him thorny riches from the plunder of the poor, they raise his head toward a kingdom of pride. For money claims for itself what Wisdom is accustomed to say: “By me kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just” (Prov. 8:15). Where money is, there are king, law, and a multitude of dependents. Hence they also put a reed in his right hand. For the power and kingdom of the wicked are a reed shaken by the wind; but Christ’s kingdom is an iron rod. And fittingly the reed is put in the right hand, because “their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.” What follows is now clearer than light: bending the knee, such men mock him rather than serve him: “Hail, King of the Jews” (Matt. 27:29). And, spitting upon him with superfluous praises—“the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed” (Ps. 10:3)—they take the reed and strike his head. For from rulers of this kind their soldiers receive authority to harm and devour the poor; yet all this rebounds upon his head, under whose authority they shelter themselves. This is the third death, when he who stinks sits in the seat of pestilence. By these deaths the unhappy soul is afflicted before the final death of the cross; and, what is more pitiable, it delights in such insults as though they were great honors, and is daily led to the cross, itself carrying its own punishment.

10. But what does it mean that after the mockery he is stripped of the cloak and reclothed in his own garments, except that [Col. 0747A] proud Adam often, when through bodily pain he enters the borders of death, lays aside his exaltation and returns to consideration of his own corruption? There he either finds, through divine mercy, the fruit of repentance, or is crushed by a fearful judgment with a double breaking. Thus Herod, when, radiant in royal clothing, he was acclaimed by the people beyond what was fitting, was immediately struck by an angel; stripped of the cloak, he put on his own garment and, consumed by worms, expired. Was he not rightly mocked? “Hail, King of the Jews.” Why are you proud, earth and ashes? Why do you glory in splendid clothing? “The moth shall be spread beneath you, and worms shall be your covering” (Isa. 14:11). This is your garment. Those who wrapped you in the scarlet cloak mocked you. Thus Antiochus, and Herod, the enemy of the Lord’s birth, having put off alien garments, expired in their own garments—that is, in worms.

## Chapter VI. On the Thief’s Confession and the Praise of the Holy Cross

11. Return at last to your heart; return, old Adam. See where and how the new Adam sought you and found you. In his body he showed you the disgraces of your soul. It was not enough that, through blows, scourges, and new kinds of mockery, he ran after you as you fled, crying out and pitying you; he pursued you and found and seized you at the very last punishment of the cross, when you were already at the point of breathing your last. For who was that thief but Adam, who, from the time when he first committed the murder of himself in paradise, fled from Christ as a guilty man and hid himself, until, at the climax of the cross, finally spent and apprehended, he could flee and hide no longer? There, seized by you, good Jesus, he was converted; he confessed his guilt; he willingly embraced punishment. For you were warning him not to shrink from suffering what he saw you also suffering with him. He alone, one man out of this whole world, clung to you; and therefore he alone out of the whole world entered paradise with you. There he was firmly established, no longer as guardian of paradise but as a citizen and member of God’s household, so that he could fall from it no more.

O most blessed thief—indeed, no thief, but a martyr and confessor! For he changed necessity into willingness, punishment into glory, and the cross into triumph. In you, most blessed [Col. 0747D] confessor and martyr, Christ gathered the remnants of faith from the barrenness of the whole world. When the disciples fled and Peter denied him, you rejoiced to become his companion and fellow sufferer in the Passion. You were Peter upon the cross, and Peter in Caiaphas’s house was a thief; for Peter was a thief so long as, hiding within, he denied Christ without. Therefore you went before Peter into paradise, because your leader and guide, who embraced you on the cross, brought you in with himself that same day when he entered, as a faithful and glorious soldier.

12. I am needy and poor, Lord, and lame from my mother’s womb; and behold, I sit at the gate of your temple called Beautiful, unable and unwilling to enter. Rather, outside I beg, in want of your good things, for food for my flesh: the brazen and false images of men, with which I may heap up for myself a talent of iniquity—burdensome bundles. And behold, it is the ninth hour of prayer. Your apostles Peter and John go up to pray in your holy temple; but I cling to earth and mud, savoring earthly and empty things. While others enter, I remain outside, not seeking with them the things that are your Father’s, but the things which my first parents, who daily put me outside from here, wickedly desired. And behold, it is already the ninth hour of prayer. The day has declined; night is near. When I rise early in the morning, I shall find none of the things for which I now beg in my hands.

It is, I say, the ninth hour of prayer. For at this hour, hanging upon the cross, you prayed; with your head bowed, crying out [Col. 0748B] in a loud voice, you prayed and expired. You prayed with bowed head in the spirit of humility, crying aloud with the loftiest and most secret affection of paternal and our own love. In that mighty cry, Lord, you expired, and you carried with you the same compassionate disposition toward us which you then had; and I believe, Lord, that you still preserve it with you, because your love does not know how to grow cold. Now it was the ninth hour of prayer. And why the ninth? Because about the ninth hour darkness came to be (Matt. 27:45). The horror of darkness which had covered the whole earth had to be driven away; the gloom of the peoples, which had then begun to abound, had to be driven away, from the time when you began to walk in the afternoon breeze. From then on you have not ceased crying, “Where are you, Adam?” (Gen. 3:9), following behind one who fled and hid [Col. 0748C] himself, so far as lay in him. And he was cast out from the paradise of delight and came at last to the punishment deserved by his iniquity. “And we,” he says, “receive things worthy of our deeds; but what has this man done?” O Adam, how late you burst forth into these words! Only now have I found you. “Amen I say to you, today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:41, 43).

For this reason the ninth is the hour of prayer. At the ninth he prayed; at the eleventh he entered paradise. For this reason the lame man did not enter the temple, because he had not yet come as far as the tenth generation; but Peter said to him: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk” (Acts 3). Truly you are the mountains to which I lifted up my eyes, whence help shall come to me. But my help is from the Lord: “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk.” At Christ’s word you cast the net; at Christ’s word you raise the lame man; at Christ’s word his ankles and soles are made firm. What are his ankles? Faith and fear. And what are his soles? Hope and love. Therefore Peter and John fittingly went up together, one bearing the emblem of faith, the other of love. They went up to your temple, Lord, to pray with you, so that they too might enter together with you into the paradise of your sanctuary; for at your death the veil which was over Moses’ face was torn. But they do not wish to enter alone, because you too, Lord, did not enter paradise alone. You bring in the thief; they bring in the lame man. Yet the thief is no longer in paradise a thief, nor the lame man in the temple lame. For how is he lame who stands and walks, leaps, [Col. 0749A] and praises God? Or how is he a thief who is with Christ in paradise? “For evil does not dwell beside you” (Ps. 5:6). He was a thief when he hid before confession, but righteous after prayer. For what did he pray? “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

13. O great faith, O great hope, O great love! He prays for future things, not present ones. He does not wish to be taken down from the cross, but to be placed in Christ’s kingdom. For what else is this saying than, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ”? I do not know what Paul could have desired more than this thief. “Remember me.” O contrite and humbled heart! What lesser or humbler thing could be requested than that he should merely be remembered? “Remember me.” Whom do I mean by “me”? Me, I say: so unworthy, so sinful. [Col. 0749B] “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is before me; I am ashamed to lift my eyes to you. Against you alone have I sinned; you alone can cleanse me from my sin. I did evil before you when I wished to hide myself from you. I am the thief of my own soul: the murder I committed I wished to conceal, but I did evil before you. Remember me; have mercy on me. Deservedly I have come into this misery, since I abandoned your blessedness. I was rich, and behold how poor I have become. From every tree of paradise I could eat and delight myself, and behold, I am tormented and die upon this tree. Remember me. I had forgotten you, but when you are angry you will remember mercy. Have mercy on me according to your great mercy.”

I see in you a great mercy—and one that is yours, that is, fitting for you—which made you descend to a misery like mine. But I receive things worthy of my deeds; what, however, have you done? I see you like me in punishment, whom in conduct I see to be so unlike me. You could not pursue me farther. From where have you come? You came forth from the highest heaven. You proceeded from the Virgin’s womb, beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, and you hang with me upon the tree! Who brought you here? Mercy alone. According to this great mercy, have mercy on me, God. You are God, not merely man. You are God; I am man, your creature, whom you made in your image and likeness. Have mercy, God, on your image. But by what shall I recognize that you have mercy on me? By this: I see my image in you, suffering [Col. 0749D] a misery like mine and the same misery with me. What therefore remains but that I should hope? Who could ever despair in the face of such mercy? Therefore, “remember me when you come into your kingdom.” You are going to your kingdom; you have completed your business; for this you came: to bring me back with you. I desire to go with you; and for this I neither tremble at a most bitter death nor am ashamed. For how could I tremble when I saw you with me? “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evils, for you are with me.” And how could I be ashamed, when I saw that I bore you, the Lord of heaven? For whoever is ashamed of you and your words, him you will be ashamed of when you come in your majesty, and that of the Father, and of the holy angels. “Whoever does not carry his cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Luke 14:27): this is your word. Whoever is ashamed of this word, you will be ashamed of him. For whoever is ashamed of your cross is ashamed of your glory. But as for me, may it be far from me to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ.

Your cross is your glory; your cross is your dominion. Behold, your dominion is upon your shoulder: you carry your cross; you carry that which carries you. Whoever carries your cross carries your glory. Whoever carries your glory carries you. But you carry upon your shoulder the one carrying you, because your dominion is upon your shoulder. Therefore those who carry you are your dominion: for in them you reign, O greatest Emperor. But how, or where, do you carry your dominion? Upon your shoulder. Your shoulder is high; your shoulder is strong; your shoulder reaches as far as the Father’s seat, [Col. 0750B] above every principality and power and might. There you bring back the hundredth sheep; there you bring back Joseph’s sheep.

14. Go now in safety, Joseph’s sheep: Christ carries you upon his shoulder. His shoulder is strong; do not fear. It is high; do not look down toward the depths, because “no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:62). “A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth until the day of their return to the mother of all.” So long as I am a son of old Adam, I bear a heavy yoke; if I were a son of the new Adam, I would bear a light yoke. What is the heavy burden? A talent of lead. And what is the light burden? Christ’s cross. The former, as it is written, [Col. 0750C] “is sunk in mighty waters” (Exod. 15:10); the latter swims upon the waters. A marvelous thing. Nothing is more dreadful to a human being than suffering the cross. But why do people fear the cross? Because they are thieves. If they were not thieves, they would not fear the cross. Therefore, whoever fears it is a thief. “How,” you ask, “is he a thief?” Hear Christ: “But you have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. 21:13). “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). Therefore people make themselves a den of thieves. They slaughter men and drag them into their den. For what murder is greater than for a person to kill himself? Or what murder is more grievous: to kill the body or the spirit? O how often a person kills the spirit! How many murders he commits in himself! Whenever he deliberately and intentionally commits sin, what else does he do but cut his own throat? For “everyone who takes the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:52). The sword of the soul is sin; the death of the soul is sin. Whoever takes this sword in the hand of his own deliberation—that is, holds it as something accepted and welcome—first lays hands upon himself, first kills himself. “Let their sword enter into their own hearts” (Ps. 36:15). Nor is it enough to kill once and rest: a thousand times and a thousand times they turn cruel hands against themselves, and “their feet are swift to shed their own blood,” men of blood and deceit. How deceitful? Because they pile up the corpses of the dead in their den and cover them with a mound of earth, lest they themselves see them or be seen by others. [Col. 0751A] They do not wish to see them, lest the stench of decaying corpses bring horror or foulness before their faces; they do not wish to be seen, lest, perhaps discovered as thieves and murderers, they be dragged away to dreadful punishments.

But what punishment is as dreadful as the cross? Therefore thieves fear the cross, because the cross is the avenger of crimes; the cross is the punishment of the wicked; with an even balance it judges and rewards—on one side the guilty, on the other the innocent. Therefore the cross is dreadful to the wicked but, for the godly, more gracious than all the trees of paradise. Did Christ fear the cross? Did Peter? Did Andrew? On the contrary, he even desired it. “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6). And: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15). He ate the Passover with the disciples; he ate the Passover also when he suffered, when he passed from this world to the Father. “I have food to eat which you do not know; my food is to do the will of my Father” (John 4:32, 34), and the Father’s will is that I drink his cup.

15. Therefore upon the cross he ate and drank, became drunk and slept; and accursed Ham laughed at his nakedness. But the sons, turning back, covered with a cloak the mystery of that deepest sleep. For the Lord cast a sleep upon Adam, took one of his ribs, built it into a woman, and brought her to Adam. The matter is plain: Christ slumbered and slept; and from his side the Church is daily built, fed, nourished, and brought from the ends of the earth, so that the queen may stand at his right hand in golden clothing, surrounded by variety. Therefore upon the cross he ate the Passover, because he climbed the palm tree and gathered its fruit. “When I am lifted up, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). What are “all things”? Heaven, earth, and the lower regions. He drew the Father to himself, because his cry entered before him, into his ears; and the earth trembled, the rocks were split, and the tombs were opened because they heard the voice of the Son of God. Thus Christ Jesus, the man who is mediator between God and men, set between heaven and earth, was eating the Passover and gathering the fruit of the tree from every side, transferring it into his body, because all things flowed together to the tree of life which was in the midst of paradise. For the flaming sword which had blocked the way [Col. 0751D] was quenched.

Who, then, should any longer fear the cross? Truly, whoever fears the cross thereby testifies against himself that he is still a thief. For upon the cross hangs every fruit of life, because it is itself the tree of life in the midst of paradise; it is height and breadth, loftiness and depth; it gathers and rewards the good, destroys and condemns the evil; it is consolation for the sorrowful, refreshment for the hungry, and glorying for the perfect. I can travel about heaven and earth, sea and dry land, and find you nowhere except in the cross; there you sleep, there you feed, there you lie down at noon. For your cross is faith, whose breadth is love, length is long-suffering, height is hope, and depth is fear. In this cross whoever finds you finds you. Upon this cross the soul is suspended from the earth and plucks sweet apples from the tree of life. Clinging to its Lord upon this cross, it sweetly sings: “You are my protector, my glory, and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. 3:4). Therefore no one seeks you, no one finds you, unless crucified. O glorious cross, take root in me, that I may ascend into you.

## Chapter VII. On Judas’s Sin and Despair

16. But where did they crucify him? At the place of Calvary. Truly blessed is the place where the cross is fixed; good is the baldness clothed with such foliage. To this baldness Elisha was going up: “… Go up, baldhead; go up, baldhead” (4 Kgs. 2:23). See whether our Elisha too is not bald. “The Son of Man,” he says, “has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9:58). See how bald he is [Col. 0752B] who has nowhere to lay his head: he is bald because his kingdom is not of this world; our Elisha is bald because his disciples, leaving him, all fled. For what are disciples but the hairs of the head, all of which are numbered? Therefore at the place of Calvary the banner of the cross is raised. “Because the daughters of Zion walked with stretched-out necks and with signals of their eyes, the Lord shall make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion” (Isa. 3:16–17). May the Lord make bald the crown whose hairs wander about in their transgressions. May he, I say, make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion and make there a place of Calvary, so that Christ’s glorious cross may be fixed there where pride had established its seat. “Make your baldness broad as an eagle’s” (Mic. 1:16). A bald eagle enjoys the clear sun; so the more broadly the soul’s baldness spreads, the more purely true light pours itself into it. But those who grow hair for themselves acquire a condemnation of blindness and heaviness. Therefore Absalom lost the vision of this blessed light, because his long hair weighed him down; it was cut only once a year, and he weighed his hair at two hundred shekels by the public weight. By this same hair he was suspended from a tree and perished.

Absalom means “the Father’s peace”; he is Judas, and anyone who is most bitter bitterness to Christ under the guise of peace. “Hail, Rabbi” (Matt. 26:49): by voice and kiss he bore peace to the Father. “With their mouth they blessed, but with their heart they cursed.” “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread” (Ps. 40:10), and so forth. He is one, and they are many. Behold Absalom; behold Judas; behold the body of Satan. But how did he grow his hair? “He was a thief and had the money-box”: this was the hair weighing him down. And he was shorn once a year, when once he returned the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the temple; he weighed them at two hundred shekels—the number of the unclean—by the public weight, not by the sanctuary weight. For, moved by repentance, he weighed his sin very heavily: “I have sinned, betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4). Every word is full of weights, but by the public weight, not by the sanctuary weight; for he weighed his disgrace more than his conscience, and his own wickedness more than God’s mercy.

Hear the sanctuary weight: “I have sinned; I have done evil before you; blot out my iniquity. On the one hand, I acknowledge my iniquity; on the other, I consider your great mercy: Have mercy on me, God” (Ps. 50:1–6). Hear also the public weight: Cain says, “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. 4:13). Therefore he returned the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the temple. See how greatly he valued them. He did not throw them into a dungheap but into the temple; doubtless he had always devoted his temple to gods of this kind. For “covetousness is the service of idols,” and covetousness blinds the eyes of the wise.

17. See how the unhappy man was blinded: he preferred to lose himself rather than let the coins perish; he consigned the coins to the temple and himself to the noose. He loved his heirs, who would gather those same coins from there, and who still keep them in their *corbona* [temple treasury]. He threw them into the temple and, going away, hanged himself by a noose. Indeed, he had long since departed from Christ and hanged himself by the noose of avarice; but what he had done in secret became openly known to all. The character of the outward punishment revealed the manner of his torment, because “by the things through which a person sins, by these he is also punished.” Hanging, he burst open in the middle: his belly was full, and the vessel burst; he burst open in the middle, where Satan’s seat was. Thus the vessel of dishonor burst, because it was not among the potter’s vessels; he had no share in the burial-place of strangers, but, like a potsherd cracking apart in emptiness, he burst asunder. “And all his entrails were spilled” (Acts 1:18). Money is the entrails of the greedy: they are spilled and lost, but men of mercy are gathered up. Judas and Absalom still hang by the hair of their heads, and the mule on which they rode passes on. “Do not become like horse and mule,” because the world passes away and its desire. Absalom’s hair, by which he hangs, is avarice, the root of all evils: where this has taken root, a whole mass of every evil will abound. The mule, mixed from horse and ass, is the double-minded person who displays outwardly what he does not maintain inwardly. Such was Judas; such Absalom. Outwardly piety, inwardly malice: double is the iniquity. The horse openly swells with pride; the ass walks simply; the mule is wicked and deceitful, and brings down the unwary.

## Chapter VIII. On the Opening of Christ’s Side

18. Open to us, Lord, open to us the door of your side, which is in your ark, so that you may bring us in with the clean animals, seven and seven. For you are the true Noah, whom God your Father alone found righteous before himself. “This is my beloved Son,” he says, “in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3:17). You know your sheep, and they know you, because they are clean animals, seven and seven, who, having attained Sabbath from Sabbath through sevenfold grace and works of light, are now worthy to be enrolled in the eighth, the number alone saved in the ark. Bring us also to you through the door of your side, which is the faith of the Church; and shut the door from outside until iniquity passes away. When the flood has ceased, open to us again the door—not now the door of faith, but the door of hope, opposite the door shown to the prophet Ezekiel in the structure of the mountain (Ezek. [Col. 0754A] 40:13).

Meanwhile, however, you also have a window in the ark through which the Beloved puts forth his hand and awakens his dove: “Arise, my friend, my beautiful one, my dove, and come” (Song 2:13–14). And when she flies out after you to seize you, you flee and ascend above the cherubim and fly upon the wings of the winds, so that the foot of your dove may find nothing of you firm where it may rest, unless it returns again to the ark and you take it by the hand and again place it in its own little dwelling. For it is better meanwhile to await and rest in the harbor of faith than, by pursuing you too eagerly and vainly, to fall and drown in the impassable waters of the flood. For the waters flowing from the right side of the temple, measured for a thousand paces, reach to the ankles; after another thousand paces, to the knees; and again after another thousand they rise to the loins. But after another thousand paces the river grows and swells so greatly that it cannot be forded, and one must rather return to the firm ground of the bank. Therefore the holy animals went and returned; and the dove likewise, when it found nowhere for its foot to rest, returned to the ark. But the raven, once sent out, does not know how to return, because, pursuing the world not with a single eye, it is caught in the flood of vanity. And deservedly. For what has the dove to do with the raven? What has white with black? What has Judas with John? What has Christ with Belial? Yet Christ sits in the middle between Judas and John; he hangs in the middle between the chosen and rejected thief; and Noah stands between raven and dove. But the raven, once sent out, did not return, because Judas, going out into the air, was drowned.

19. But what is this, Lord, that one of the soldiers—[Note: [Col. 0753D] Something is missing here.]—unless perhaps he was the one who happened to receive your seamless garment? This indeed is the unity of the faithful, which serves as soldier to you alone; its lance of preaching opened your side. For “the word of God is living and effective, and more piercing than any two-edged sword” (Heb. 4:12). This is the lance which the prophet Habakkuk calls a flashing spear (Hab. 3:11). David took this spear together with the water jar from the head of Saul, his sleeping enemy, because from the proud, envious, and negligent the word of wisdom is withdrawn together with grace. But the son of Zeruiah wished to pierce the sleeping man once, so that there would be no need a second time, [Col. 0754D] had not David kindly forbidden him; because, unless the merciful and long-suffering patience of God sustained the lazy and contemptuous sinner, Satan’s sword would kill him once—that is, eternally. For wicked Satan wishes that he who sleeps should not further add to rise again.

But merciful David, from the distant summit, repeatedly cries aloud: “Will you not answer, Abner?” For you repay good for evil to the sinner, most gentle David, and you admonish and wait a long while, that he may answer you one thing for a thousand. But your voice seems hateful to them because you disturb their restless sleep. “Who are you,” he says, “that you cry out and disturb the king?” At your rebuke, Lord, “those who mounted horses fell asleep,” and their charioteer does not wish them to awaken until they plunge headlong into the deep. For the king of the wicked, pride, sleeps in shade, in the shelter of the reed, in damp places, and shadows protect his shadow. He is Abner, who protected Saul. “Why,” he says, “do you disturb the king?” Yet at times the proud heart is pricked by David’s voice, but not so as to amend. Proud Saul is bent by David’s most humble words, when David says: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog and a single flea, like a partridge in the mountains” (1 Sam. 26). Not without reason does David compare himself either to a dead dog or to a flea. A living dog, dead to the world, is better before God than a proud and rejected lion, dead to God and alive to the age. A flea is small, and it bites and leaps; so the humble righteous person boldly bites the vices of the flesh and leaps upon the mountains, where he has a most secure refuge, so that he need not fear the adulterous partridge that pursued Elijah and killed John the Baptist.

## Chapter IX. On the Lord’s Burial

20. Give me, Lord, a portion in the land of the living, in the burial-place of strangers, in the field *Hacheldemach* [Field of Blood], bought at the great price of your blood. For there all our fathers were buried, who were strangers and sojourners upon this earth. There Abraham buried his most beautiful wife Sarah in the double cave. But why did he neither wish to receive even the field itself freely, nor to bury his dead in their chosen tombs? Because he did not believe that, without the price of Christ’s blood, he could be saved freely through himself; nor did he judge it good for himself to dwell in the stinking tombs of the world. “Bury your dead,” they say, “in our chosen tombs” (Gen. 23:6). The world has chosen tombs: those, undoubtedly, whom the summit of pride or the laboriousness of superstition makes conspicuous. All Egypt is full of tombs, for there was no house in which a dead man did not lie. The children of Israel desired those tombs in the wilderness. “Were there no tombs in Egypt,” they say, “that our corpses should lie naked and unburied in the wilderness?” (Exod. 14:11). The most holy Patriarch did not wish to bury his dead in such tombs. But where? In the double cave, where hope of good works and contemplative love rest. There Leah too lies buried. Therefore Sarah and Leah are hidden in the double cave. The former, first barren and then old, bore only one son of joy; the latter, after six sons, ceased to bear, except that at the last she bore a daughter, the disgrace of a sacred stock. A marvelous thing! She who had six sons is said to have ceased bearing; she who had only one is not recorded as having ceased bearing. But the active life has an end; the contemplative always bears. The former labors in pain; the latter brings forth in joy. Yet both are buried in the same field. For Rachel was placed near Bethlehem beneath the oak of the cross; surely she sits at Jesus’ feet, that from the house of bread she may always bear fruitfully. Therefore Sarah and Rachel will never [Col. 0756A] cease bearing. Leah, however, after six sons either ceases altogether to bear, or bears a daughter. She is carnal pleasure, which sometimes creeps into the active life under the appearance of discernment. Yet if she is truly a widow, she shall be saved, not through the begetting of a daughter but through the begetting of sons. Thus the noble patriarchs, together with their wives, were buried in the double cave. For they lived in tents as strangers and sojourners upon the earth; therefore both they and all their descendants possess by inheritance the burial-place of strangers.

21. But why is Jacob, the aged patriarch, buried there by his son Joseph with greater magnificence, sweetness, and glory than the rest? By aged Jacob is expressed perfect love, in which the Father is buried by the Son—or rather, together with the Son—he himself saying that “if anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). This is the glorious and sweet burial of the Father, Ancient of Days, who buries with himself those who love him and hides them in the hiding-place of his face from the disturbance of men. There also Joseph’s bones, the memorial of our Savior, are daily brought out of Egypt by the children of Israel. For Joseph’s bones were not left in Egypt, because he detests stinking and whitewashed tombs. God buried Moses, but his tomb is not found by man to this day (Deut. 34:6). Finally, who can ascend there where he ascended through the midst of the cloud [Col. 0756C] upon the highest mountain, was there forty days and forty nights, and saw and examined the pattern of the wonderful tabernacle, which God established and not man? Therefore, to this day, while Moses is read, he has a veiled face, because his tomb is not found by mortal man. In the same field of blood the glorious line of kings also received its lot, those who were buried in the burial-place of their fathers in Jerusalem; there too the vision of the prophets and the warlike valor of the Maccabees are gloriously displayed.

22. Let that tower of Babel, once glorious among kingdoms and renowned for the pride of the Chaldeans, now be compared, if you please, with this burial of pilgrims. What likeness to our burial is found there? There one language is divided into many [Col. 0756D]; here the five cities of Egypt no longer speak either the Egyptian or the Canaanite tongue, but one is called the City of the Sun. For from that tower of Babel the harlot Jezebel was cast down—the mother of fornications, worshipper of idols, contriver of avarice. And when they wished to bury her, because she was the king’s daughter, they found nothing but her skull, the extremities of her hands, and a wall sprinkled with blood. This indeed is the burial of the ungodly; this is their fitting recompense: that scarcely the outermost extremities of their hands—that is, of their deeds—remain, and the skull, which had been the seat of pride, stripped of the glory of its hair. “I saw the wicked greatly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Ps. 36:35–36).

This is Jezebel’s skull, she who [Col. 0757A] had clothed herself in harlot’s finery and painted her eyes with antimony. The crown of pride has been made bald; there is now no one who deigns to look upon it, save one who wishes to abhor her wickedness, to wash his hands in the sinner’s blood, and, like a strong and swift horse, to pierce the cast-down harlot with his hoof, trample her, and pass on. For this reason too the bloodstained wall was left behind, to terrify bloody and deceitful men who, because of their avarice, stone humble Naboth. But the most shameless dogs, lovers of carrion, make the flesh of the harlot their own flesh; and consequently they lap her blood, because they shall share alike in lust and in vengeance.

There are, however, other dogs, those made from enemies by Him himself (Ps. 67:24): they suffer hunger for righteousness and go about [Col. 0757B] the city—not Babylon’s city, but that of the Church—and what they find there dead to vices they consume and bury with themselves. But woe to those whom birds flying through the void—that is, demons—devour when they are dead outside the city: such were Ahithophel and Absalom, Jezebel and Judas, who, having received their soul in vanity, also breathed it out in vanity.

23. But let us return to the field of Haceldama, that we may rather admire and emulate the glory of blessed dwellings. For “the memory of the wicked shall perish with a sound,” but the memory of the righteous shall live for ever and ever. Such were Joseph, who was a councillor, a just and good man; and Nicodemus, who, [Col. 0757C] once a minister of the night but now of the day, came to anoint the Lord’s body, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. Jesus loves such ministers of his burial—those who boldly rescue his body from the power of darkness and claim it for themselves, so that each may know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour, binding it with the laws of chastity and the linen bands of discipline, and preserving it from the decay of worms by a mixture of myrrh and aloes.

For these spices are bitter indeed, but they remove corruption. The chastening of the flesh is laborious indeed, yet otherwise neither the mind nor the flesh itself is kept incorruptible. “About a hundred pounds” (John 19:39). O good measure, pressed down! Truly a most subtle discernment must hold the balance between body and soul, so that each may rejoice in possessing its proper fullness, and peace and equality may arise between flesh and spirit, to the end that measure may be kept without perfection being forsaken. These are, as it were, the hundred pounds which keep Christ’s body whole [Col. 0757D] and sound in the tomb of the faithful.

Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s couch, all holding swords and most skilled in war. Your couch, Jesus Christ, greater than Solomon, is your burial, in which on the Sabbath you rested from every work that you had accomplished.
