Your tomb is new, in a garden, and hewn out of rock: for your beloved, the faithful soul, is “a garden enclosed” (Song 4:12), renewed daily in knowledge of you, and made firm upon the rock of your love, burying herself with you in the inner person, in [Col. 0758A] the secrecy of your chamber. There sixty mighty men from among Israel’s mightiest surround you: in them the works of the six days, works exceedingly good, are perfected, so that in six and ten they may preserve the image and likeness of your Law.

## Chapter X. On the soldiers’ guard at Christ’s tomb

24. These guard you better than the deceitful guard of the ungodly, for they are most skilled in war—not only in driving away the enticements of the flesh, but also aerial powers and terrors of the night. Those who, drunken as it were, besieged your tomb by night “trembled there with fear where no fear was,” because the power of darkness, unable to bear the light, became as dead men at the messenger’s announcement of life. Therefore it is not the sons of night who guard you, [Col. 0758B] but the sons of day. Your brightness strikes terror into the former, so that they flee from you; but it brings joy to the latter, so that they draw near to you.

“While we were asleep, his disciples came and stole him away” (Matt. 28:13), they say. O liars! You spoke truth, but falsehood and iniquity lied to themselves. Those asleep cannot guard Christ; but “those who watch for me in the morning shall find me.” And what appears to you while you sleep except dreams? Behold, you have abundant money in your hands: guard it, if you can, lest thieves dig through and steal it. For Christ’s disciples will guard their treasure. Each strives to preserve what he loves.

Certainly Michal loved David more than her father Saul; therefore she let him down through the window [Col. 0758C] and saved him. What does this mean? Michal, Saul’s daughter, daughter of former pride, after marrying the beautiful David, begins to hate her father. To her it is said in the Psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, forget your father’s house, and the king shall desire your beauty” (Ps. 44:11–12). Therefore she lets David down through the window. Understand that window through which the Beloved puts forth his hand. Through this window he is let down by his beloved to his beloved—that is, to himself—and is hidden in the inner person, where he may both live securely and remain concealed from the wicked.

For he hides himself and departs from the temple of faithlessness. While he plays the harp before Saul, so that the evil spirit of the Lord may depart from him, the ungodly man attempts to pin him to the wall with a spear. But when David turns aside, what does it mean that [Col. 0758D] the spear is fixed in the wall, except that, when Christ’s grace withdraws, the hardened mind is pierced by the weapon of its own malice? What does Saul, the king of darkness, hate so much even today as David, his son-in-law? Therefore, while David is absent, he takes away his daughter and gives her to another husband, an ignoble man. But when the strong hand returns and receives the kingdom, he claims her again for himself, because he had betrothed her to himself with two hundred Philistine foreskins (1 Sam. 18, 19, 25; 2 Sam. 3), cutting away from her the uncleanness not only of the flesh but also of the mind.

25. Woe to sinners, Lord, who besiege your tomb. For you truly turn aside from them, and they do not find you upon your sweet and flowery couch; rather, they stumble against the image of their own heart, wrapped in darkness, [Col. 0759A] with a goatskin at its head—the foul-smelling remembrance of their sins. Blessed, however, is the one who watches at your tomb in order to guard you, and wrestles in the morning with the Angel of the Resurrection, refusing to let him go until he hears something concerning his name, which is wonderful; so that Jacob’s name may be changed into Israel and, once the sword of the soul’s pain has passed through, the sun of righteousness may immediately rise for him.

## Chapter XI. On the rolling away of the stone, the appearance of angels, and Christ’s resurrection

26. “Who shall roll away the stone for us from the door of the tomb?” (Mark 16:3). The door of my mind is shut, Lord, and the stone of mortality presses upon my understanding, weighed down by the burden of my iniquity. [Col. 0759B] Human strength is utterly unable to remove it unless the almighty Word comes from the royal seats, the Angel of Counsel, to tear down the wall of enmity, open our understanding so that we may understand the Scriptures, and see the linen cloths laid before us—the truest testimonies to your humanity and resurrection.

Whoever, aided by you, is able to search you out in these will taste beforehand something of the glory of the resurrection which you have prepared for those who love you. Its firstfruits you have gathered into your bosom, continually offering them already before your Father’s presence, roasted by the fire of the Holy Spirit. And that angel, the herald of so great a joy, who rolled away the stone, terrified ungodly minds but gently forbade devout ones to fear—this angel, I say, bore witness to the blessed resurrection not only by word, but by countenance, dress, and action. He rolled away the stone and sat upon it: the stone, I say, which even now is rolled over us and weighs down our face. In the first resurrection, which is that of the soul, this undoubtedly occurs: the spirit, reversing the relation, subjects to itself the burden of corruption that had oppressed it, and, as judge and lord, takes up the governance of its inferior.

27. What is signified by the whiteness of snow and the appearance of the garments except the chaste, cool, and utterly pure condition of our body, which both bears witness to and obeys the angelic brightness presiding within it? But his inward appearance, where the light of your countenance is sealed, Lord, is like lightning—terrible [Col. 0759D] and bright: terrible, that it may divide and terrify the enemies of the soul; bright, that with righteousness it may always appear before you, the true Light.

Such was Moses’ face through fellowship with your Word: both luminous and terrible, because it was horned to scatter enemies and veiled because of a brilliance which fleshly eyes could not endure. And now, Lord, we know and rejoice that you have truly risen from the dead and are still far removed from us mortals, because you have ascended upon your fiery horses and fiery chariot, manifold with ten thousands. Yet your mantle has fallen from you to us and remains with us even to this day: it is the linen cloths of your body, through which we may experience the help of your power at a fitting time, so that your spirit may become double within [Col. 0760A] our inmost being, and in you we may love both God and our neighbour.

The pains of death have surrounded us, and torrents of iniquity have troubled us. The garment of our mortality, teeming with worms which continually devour me and do not sleep, has surrounded us. These are pains foretelling that greatest pain which comes upon us like an armed man and strives to overwhelm the unprepared. Yet who is so prepared as to be able to endure its terror? Nevertheless, whether we wish it or not, it must certainly be endured and passed through. But do not forget Elijah’s mantle; otherwise the torrent will not be divided for you without it.

There are also other torrents of iniquity—the sea of my sins—which trouble me. Would that they troubled me in such a way that I cried in sorrow: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” [Col. 0760B] (2 Kgs. 2). For the torrents of iniquity trouble me by taking away the light of my eyes, so that I cannot see most gracious Elijah when he is taken away from me. If I saw him, his spirit would surely become double within me, and I would cry, “My father, my father.” “God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts,” says the Apostle, “crying, Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6). The double spirit cries “My father, my father” twice over. My Father, my Creator; my Father, my Restorer; my Father, my Father. O affectionate cry! Chariot of Israel and its charioteer: you carry and rule, sustain and govern. Whom? Israel, believing in you and sighing for you.

Behold, you have been taken up; your Elisha will see you no more. Yet your mantle remains for him in remembrance of you, so that the presence of your absence [Col. 0760C] may always soothe his sorrow by increasing it, and increase it by soothing it.

28. “Do this,” he says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). This is the sacrament of your body, which we receive in remembrance of you until you come. Your mantle is your flesh, with which you came forth clothed to us. You concealed yourself from the faithless, but showed yourself to your faithful, just as you do even now. Beneath this mantle your greatest strength was hidden, O most strong Samson; and even from the beloved woman who did not love you, you did not conceal it to the end, so as to turn an enemy into a friend. You loved a woman who did not love you but persecuted you so greatly that, for love of her, your wisdom became foolishness and your strength became weakness.

But “the foolishness of God” became wiser than men, [Col. 0760D] and “the weakness of God” stronger than men. For voluntarily sacrificing yourself to the Father and dying by your own power, you shook the princes of darkness and crushed their kingdom. Thus your cross became “a stumbling-block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles, but to those who believe, the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–25).

## Chapter XII. On Christ’s appearance to the disciples going to Emmaus

29. So long as we are in this body, we are away from you, Lord. You indeed walk with those who love you and speak about you and grieve over you; yet your countenance is that of a stranger, and although you recognize them, you are not recognized by them. Truly you are that Joseph who spoke more harshly to his brothers as though they were strangers—not in indignation but in compassion—when you drew near to those two walking sadly on the road, teaching and rebuking them: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe!” (Luke 24:25).

Thus your brothers come to you as strangers, but you graciously draw near to them. They come to you with the asses of their foolishness and slowness, and with sacks empty from want; but you not only fill them with grain, you even return the money, bound in the mouth of the sack. “When one sack was opened,” he says, “to give fodder to the beast, he found the money in the mouth of the sack. ‘My money has been returned,’ he says; ‘behold, it is in my sack’” (Gen. 42:27–28). What then have you done for us, God? They come [Col. 0761B] to you empty and foolish, but you send them away laden and abundant in the grain of wisdom; moreover, you return to them the money of eloquence, bound by the authority of Scripture. For you make infants’ tongues eloquent, that they may give fodder and their measure of wheat in due season to beasts which do not yet understand you.

30. Walk with us now, Lord, lest we be left desolate and sorrowful on this road that we travel. For you yourself once went before the children of Israel in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night; at your command they set down their tents and raised them again. What is the cloud that goes before the true Israelites, except your most true and most holy body, which we receive at the altar? In it [Col. 0761C] the height of day—the immensity of your majesty—is veiled from us, whose heat and brightness mortal weakness could not endure unless a mediating cloud were interposed, tempering the burning from above and showing the safe way beneath.

The whole host follows this cloud, Lord, King of hosts. Whoever does not follow it is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going. For from this cloud shines the path leading to life: the path of humility and patience, of gentleness and mercy, and of whatever you deigned to reveal to the human race through the mystery of your incarnation. From this light there shines upon us the glory of Law and Prophecy, since Moses and Elijah appeared with you upon the mountain, but a bright cloud overshadowed them. For they themselves, like us, could not have been saved without your protection.

Yet for them, as friends and members of your household—indeed, chief among your household and friends—the cloud of your sacrament shone brightly; whereas for us, lying cast down from before your eyes, it is very dim. Yet your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book, because [Col. 0761D] beneath your cloud you nourish, perfect, and lead Joseph like a sheep. This is the pillar of cloud which went before the children of Israel by day. The pillar of fire by night is the Holy Spirit, who appeared over the Apostles in fiery tongues, who illumines and raises the darkness of our blindness so that we may savour the things above, not those upon earth.

Therefore: the cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night; because your flesh tempers for us the heat of divinity, and the Holy Spirit’s light illumines the darkness of our mind. Thus, while you spoke on the road with the two disciples walking with you, and a stranger’s cloud veiled your countenance, they said: “Was not our heart burning within us while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:32, 35). The pillar of fire was surely burning within, because the pillar of cloud spoke to them without.

31. But where at last did they recognize him? In the breaking of bread. And truly, Lord, you are not recognized except in the breaking of bread. The bread is your flesh. You broke your body with your own hands, because you had power to lay down your life and power to take it again. You broke the body which appeared outwardly and showed the marrow hidden within; for unless you suffered, you would not [Col. 0762B] be recognized. “There his strength is hidden,” it says (Hab. 3:4).

What is your strength except mercy, gentleness, humility, and patience? In the breaking of bread—that is, in your Passion—you showed us these most strong and sweet virtues. By these virtues our flesh, which we are, is gradually nourished, advances, and is perfected. First it is ground like grain between the two millstones of hope and fear, that it may become new dough. Then, when it has passed into the form of bread, it is baked in the oven of sufferings. Afterwards, when you have blessed it with every spiritual blessing and said, “It is finished” (John 19:30), you break even our body, which is in your hands and which we commend into your hands. There you are recognized, not in a stranger’s appearance but in your proper countenance: so that no longer may a lance open your side for us, but we may touch and see with a finger that you are, Lord, our God.

## Chapter XIII. A devout aspiration to Christ for obtaining an understanding of Holy Scripture

32. Father of orphans and judge of widows, do you not see this poor and desolate widow, my soul? She has neither brothers nor friends nor neighbours from whom she might borrow not a few empty vessels, which my sons might bring to me, and into which I might pour the little oil that remains to me from you (2 Kgs. 4), so that you may show the fullness of your blessing to all?

For I understand, Lord, that the empty vessels are certain literal and historical senses of your Scripture, [Col. 0762D] and they are not few, so that the whole world could not contain them. The Babylonian king—that is, the dominion of pride—carries away captive the vessels of your most holy temple and forces them to serve at his banquets, not to his glory but to his shame. He arrogates to himself the knowledge of your Law, drinks the wine of his prostitution from the vessels of the sanctuary, and defiles your gifts with the ointments of harlotry. Therefore, opposite the wall, a cruel but just sentence is written against them: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be desolated” (Luke 11:17); and it shall be given to the Medes and Persians (Dan. 5), who do not seek silver nor desire gold, but kill their little ones and foolish thoughts with poisoned and burning [Col. 0763A] arrows.

But you, Lord, will have mercy upon the poor and desolate widow, lest that most wicked and importunate creditor, who has lent me many talents of his iniquity at the interest of my destruction, take my two sons—the inner faculties of my soul—to serve him. Your good and saving counsel is that I should borrow not a few vessels and, with the blessing of overflowing oil, redeem my sins; and thereafter live with my sons. But because I have neither neighbours nor children from whom I may borrow an exercise for my mind, as soon as I relax my hands that shameless creditor attacks me and compels my two sons, namely understanding and affection, to serve idleness and his empty illusions.

Therefore you, merciful defender of widows, because you are exceedingly rich and give abundantly to all—you yourself, I say, lend to me both the vessels that you know to be useful for these purposes and the oil, so that all things may be yours and all may serve you. For I do not wish to carry your oil into Egypt and so sin against you, but only not to eat the bread of idleness; rather, may I exercise myself all day in your ordinances and live. And behold, whatever the son of my memory has offered me, as soon as it comes into my hands, I shall seize.

## Chapter XIV. On the three groups of fifty sent to Elijah, allegorically related to the catching of the one hundred and fifty-three fish

[Col. 0763C] 33. Elijah stood on the top of the mountain. The first captain of fifty sent to him was consumed by fire, and likewise the second; but the third was spared because of his humility and devotion. Behold a vessel, yet empty, because received in this way it rather resounds with cruelty. Let it be filled with oil, and its harsh sound will cease.

For who is Elijah standing on the mountain’s summit except you, Lord Jesus, who stand above with the Father? The first captain of fifty comes to you, sent by a world parched with excessive dryness, and cries: “Man of God, come down from the mountain” (2 Kgs. 1). The world knows that it cannot be saved without you. “Man of God” [variant: “God”] and God who became man: let the man whom you seek move you to condescend to humanity. Come down from the mountain. No one can approach you unless you approach him; no one can ascend to you unless you descend to him. Man of God, come down from the mountain. You are the mountain raised above the tops of the mountains: descend and have compassion on us in the valley of tears.

“If I am a man of God,” he says, “let fire come down from heaven,” and so forth. For “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12:49), and how I desire it to be kindled, to devour you and your fifty! I beseech you, Lord, let that fire descend upon me and devour in me the old man with his deeds. This is the first fifty, whom your fire devours in order to make him rest from every servile work. The second group of fifty is the active life itself, which likewise has an end: Sabbath after Sabbath. Your fire also consumes this as a whole burnt offering. In the first [Col. 0764A] group of fifty the goat is burned; in the second the ram is consumed by fire. But the third, which is that of resurrection or contemplation, has no end, but always lives with Elijah.

Hence the Gospel aptly speaks of one hundred and fifty-three large fish, all reduced into one fish, set upon coals, which the seven disciples saw and with which they breakfasted together with Jesus, who was the eighth (John 21:1–13).

34. This same number, namely one hundred and fifty—the three groups of fifty and the seven disciples—harmoniously signifies rest. As each group of fifty tends toward unity, so the seven disciples tend toward the eighth, that is, Christ; and all are consummated in one. Now as Christ and all the elect are one body, one bread, one man, or one fish, so the devil and all the reprobate are one body and one enemy.

For he is “a great eagle with great wings,” and so forth: an eagle because of the excessive keenness of his winged nature; great because of the height of his pride; the great wings, those cleaving to and exalting him, are the powers of evil spirits; the long extension of limbs, most wicked human beings, whose service he uses in fighting against the good. And fittingly long, because they still come daily and endure to the end of the age, following the leadership of pride; full of feathers, because of deceitful wiles; and variegated, because he changes the same arts into various forms for deception.

He shall come to Lebanon: the soul of the world, made white by the merit of life and faith. “He took the marrow of the cedar.” The incorruptible cedar is the height of hope; its marrow is love, which the devil especially strives to attack. “He plucked off the top of its branches,” that is, he tears the word of wisdom, which is most excellent, away from the love of God; and “carried it into the land of Shinar” (Ezek. 17:3–4), that is, into their stench, signifying vain glory.

## Chapter XV. On Mary Magdalene’s devotion in seeking Christ, and her vision of him

35. “On that day the Lord shall whistle for the fly which is at the farthest part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee which is in the land of Assyria” (Isa. 7:18). Whistle, Lord, also for this unclean fly, my sinful soul. May your good Spirit [Col. 0764D] lead her into the straight way, that I may go to the lofty and mountainous land of promise, watered from its upper regions and awaiting rain from heaven, unlike the land of Egypt, which a river bubbling from the earth entirely covers.

For no mountain stands in opposition, no obstacle hinders Egypt’s desires; rather, as they bubble up from an earthly mind, they run at once across the cast-down surface of the soul.

36. The river of Egypt has seven mouths, deriving from one head, namely pride. The farthest of these is understood as bodily lust, from which flies arise, ever lovers of uncleanness. Yet the abundance of grace does not despise even this fly, but whistles and calls it from the end of the rivers and joins it to the bee which was in [Col. 0765A] the land of Assyria, so that they may come and rest together in the torrents of valleys, in the caverns of rocks, in all the thickets, and in every hollow.

The bee is virginal; but so long as it remains in the land of Assyria, that is, in self-exaltation, it cannot produce honey. Only the land of promise flows with milk and honey. When grace whistles, therefore, the fly and bee meet and rest together in the torrents of valleys. In those torrents, the bee is cleansed from the filth of pride and the fly from that of lust. The torrents of valleys are disciplines of humility. Why torrents? Because any sorrow or severity involved in correcting vices passes quickly away. Hence “a woman, when she gives birth, has sorrow” (John 16:21), and so forth. For labour is changed into love, weariness into desire, bitterness into sweetness; and thus from the torrents of valleys they advance to the caverns of rocks.

The rocks are the Fathers, most firm and strong in faith. In their sufferings, as in their own exemplars, the fly and bee, nesting like doves, find rest. Therefore their hand does not cease, nor their foot; but, continually exercised in every thicket of good works, they finally attain the openings of contemplation.

37. These are your works, Lord Jesus, for they are exceedingly good. Thus you whistled for Mary Magdalene, from whom you cast out not one but seven rivers. See how she rested in the torrents of valleys. She entered among those reclining at a meal, ran to Jesus’ feet, and poured upon them torrents of tears. To wash her Lord’s footprints she brought no water but the streams [Col. 0765C] of her own eyes; she used her hair instead of linen cloths.

Then, when her emotion burned more vehemently and, like a coal sprinkled with the moisture of tears, blazed more fiercely, you would have seen her pressing innumerable and insatiable kisses upon those sacred feet; you would have seen the whole house filled with the sweetness of the poured-out anointing. What else, then, was she doing but resting in the torrents of valleys, she from whom so many and such great torrents of grace flowed? Thus, once her many sins had been forgiven because she had loved much, she was already seated like a dove washed with milk at Jesus’ feet beside most abundant streams, while her sister Martha was busy with much service.

Why should I mention the service of burial which she anticipated, ascending from the feet to the anointing of the head, while that foul-smelling tomb of avarice raged against her, unable to endure the fragrance of devotion? Such love could not die even when Christ died. When men—that is, the Apostles—fled and hid themselves, the undaunted woman stood weeping at the tomb. She did not have him living, and yet she burned wholly for the dead. The body had been removed, but she could not depart from the tomb. The more he was taken from her hands and eyes, the more ardently her soul pursued him. If it had been possible, to ransom the body she would have filled the tomb with tears.

“She stood weeping,” it says: that alone remained to her of you. The body had been taken away—but who could take away her weeping? Give free rein, lady, give free rein; hastening on, pour yourself out in untiring tears until you attain your Lord who has been taken away—indeed, who has risen again. Again and again bend down; look more and more often upon the empty [Col. 0766A] place where he had been laid. The place itself provokes you ever more to weeping, as it sets before you the absence of him whom you seek.

38. “She saw,” it says, “two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain.” “Woman,” they say, “why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” And surely, most gracious angels, you knew well what she wept for and whom she sought. Why do you stir her again to tears by calling it to mind? But the joy of an unlooked-for consolation was near; therefore let the whole force of sorrow and weeping run its course.

“Turning round, she saw Jesus standing, and did not know that it was Jesus.” O pious and delightful spectacle of loving devotion! He who is sought and desired both hides himself and manifests himself. He hides himself in order that he may be sought more ardently; sought, that he may be found with joy; found, that he may be held with solicitude; held, that he may not be released until he is brought into the chamber of his love, there to make a dwelling. By this art Wisdom plays in the world, and her delights are to be with the children of men.

“Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” You possess the one you seek and do not know it? You possess true and eternal joy, and you weep? You possess within the one whom you seek without. Truly you stand outside the tomb, weeping. Your mind is my tomb: there I rest, not dead, but living for ever. Your mind is my garden. You rightly supposed that I am the gardener. I am the second Adam; I cultivate and guard my paradise. Your weeping, your devotion, your desire: these are my work. You possess me within and do not know it; therefore you seek me without. Behold, I shall also appear without, in order to bring you back within and that you may find within the one whom you seek without.

“Mary, I know you by name; learn to know me by faith.” “Rabboni,” that is, Teacher. This is to say: Teach me to seek you; teach me to touch and anoint you. “Do not touch me,” he says, as a man, nor as you previously touched and anointed me when mortal. “I have not yet ascended to my Father” (John 20:1–17): you have not yet believed me equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father. Believe this, then, and you have touched me. You see a man and therefore do not believe, for what is seen is not believed. You do not see God: believe, and you shall see. By believing, you will touch me, just as that woman [Col. 0766D] touched the fringe of my garment and was immediately healed. Why? Because she touched me by her faith.

Touch me with this hand; seek me with these eyes; hasten running to me with these feet. I am not far from you. For I am God who draws near; I am the word in your mouth and in your heart. What is nearer to a human being than his own heart? There I am found by all who find me. For the things that are outside are seen: they are indeed my works, but they are passing and perishable. But I, their maker, dwell in the most hidden and most pure hearts.

## Chapter XVI. A devout aspiration to Christ for obtaining virtues

39. To you, Lord Jesus, has been given all power in heaven and on earth, great King, King of virtues, because [Col. 0767A] you became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Behold, your magnificence has been raised above the heavens, and all things have been subjected beneath your feet.

David first reigned at Hebron seven years over Judah; afterwards he was anointed over all Israel and reigned over it thirty-three years. But when you, most true David, were anointed over Judah alone at Hebron, Saul, the king of pride among them, was already dead. Otherwise, while he lived and sin ruled over them, they would not say to you: “We are your bone and your flesh.” For who can be a member of Christ and at the same time a member of a harlot? Or what fellowship has Christ with Belial?

“Behold,” they say, “we are your bone and flesh; and yesterday and the day before, while Saul was king over us” (2 Sam. 5:1–2), [Col. 0767B] you bore with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, and went out before us, provoking battle against vices, delivering and leading the unworthy out of the hand of sins. Therefore Judah, that is, Confession, first anoints you king over himself at Hebron. For when Saul has died, Judah remembers your benefits and, confessing his error, makes a passage from sins to you, King of righteousness.

You reign over Judah seven years at Hebron because you render to them sevenfold into their bosom and, having cleansed the seven vices over which proud Saul presided, restore them by your sevenfold virtue. Afterwards the passage of your kingdom is made at Jerusalem over all Israel, because through the work of confession, once the faculties have been enlightened, one comes to the vision of peace, in which your dwelling has been made. This also is [Col. 0767C] the mountain which you appointed for the disciples, that they should go into Galilee and there see and worship you after your resurrection, because God, your God, had anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions, that you might be the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth.

40. Moreover, you reign in Jerusalem for thirty-three years. Thirty has three decades; in the decade is the Law, which consists of ten commandments; and in the number three is understood the threefold progress of the soul, which keeps God’s Law by living, meditating, or loving. Of the first it is said, “I will praise my God in my life” (Ps. 145:2); of the second, “Your law is my meditation” (Ps. 118:77); of the third, “How I have loved your law, O Lord!” (ibid. 97). But the three above thirty indicate certain most eminent contemplatives [Col. 0767D], who by purity of conscience, fullness of wisdom, and perfection of charity draw near to the supreme Trinity. This too is the number of the mighty men in your army, O Most Mighty One; yet even their foremost do not attain to your wisdom and strength, “for who among the clouds shall be compared to the Lord, or be like God among the sons of God?” (Ps. 88:7).

You are like the tenderest little worm of wood, who, born of a virgin, pierce through every hardness by your humility and charity, slaying eight hundred, the commander of the host, by a single onset of your Spirit [Col. 0768A]. Who is so strong as you? Who so merciful, who wept over Jerusalem and made lamentation over the destruction of your enemies? And then you grieve over Saul and over Jonathan his son, who daily fall upon the mountains of Gilboa. For unless you grieved, you would not cry from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4). For whom does Saul signify, if not the proud prelates in your Church, who seem to themselves to rise above all the people from the shoulder upward? And whom does Jonathan signify, if not young men teachable and of refined ability, who, corrupted by the habits and conversation of their elders, cannot cultivate friendship with David except secretly, as though guarding against the snares of those who disparage and mock them?

[Col. 0768B] 41. Rightly, therefore, do you weep, O gracious David, over Saul and Jonathan his son (2 Sam. 1); for they would not deserve weeping if they had fallen well, but they fell upon the mountains of Gilboa, which run down into the deep, and upon which neither the dew of grace nor the rain of teaching shall come any more, because there the shield of the mighty, the shield of Saul, was cast away. The shield of the mighty is hope in divine protection, by which the fiery darts of the devil are repelled. Saul was grievously wounded by these darts from the archers, so grievously that in despair he killed himself (1 Sam. 31:4). But Saul’s shield is confidence in one’s own strength, which cannot withstand the arrows of the uncircumcised.

“Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclus. 2:16), that is, the shield of the mighty; and “cursed is the man who trusts in man,” which is Saul’s shield. For he shall be [Col. 0768C] “like a tamarisk in the wilderness” (Jer. 17:5–6), because neither dew nor rain shall come upon you, mountains of Gilboa. “How have the mighty fallen?” For if they were mighty, how did they fall? And if they fell, how were they mighty? But “let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength; but let him who glories glory in the Lord,” so that “he who stands may take heed lest he fall.” For though they be swifter than eagles, so as to outfly contemplatives by the swiftness of their understanding; and though they be stronger than lions, so as to surpass true preachers in the strength of their work: nevertheless, if, presuming upon themselves, they cast away the shield of salvation, they shall fall before their enemies. But he who trusts in the Lord, like Mount Zion, shall not be moved forever.

Yet Saul preferred to fall upon his own spear rather than lean [Col. 0768D] upon the Lord; therefore the reed-staff of Egypt pierced his hand. For his own spear—his own charioteer, who drove the chariot of his arrogance—killed him. “I knew,” he says, “that he could not live” (2 Sam. 1:10); for the obstinacy of the arrogant does not know how to humble itself so that it may live. Command, O most just King David, command your servant—that is, the spirit of pure discernment—to kill within me this Amalekite, Saul’s armour-bearer, who has dared even now, every day, to lay his hand upon the Lord’s Christ.

[Col. 0769]

# LAMENTATION ON THE PASSION OF CHRIST

[NOTE.]

521 First published at Ingolstadt in 1617 by Gretser, under Bernard’s name, from the library of the Carthusians of Erfurt.

[Col. 0769A] Who will console me, Lord Jesus Christ, who saw you hanging upon the cross, bruised by wounds, pale in death, and did not suffer compassionately with you crucified or attend you dead, so as at least to soothe those places of your wounds with my tears? How did you leave me without farewell, when, beautiful in your robe, O King of Glory, you received yourself into the heights of heaven? My soul altogether refuses consolation. Alas for me, one of Eve’s wretched children, estranged from God! What shall that distant exile do, O most high Lord? Alas, Lord, alas for my soul! You, the comforter of my soul, have departed and did not bid me farewell! What shall I say? What shall I do? Where shall I go? Where shall I seek you, my Lord? Where shall I find you? Whom shall I ask? Who will tell my beloved that I languish with love? My soul refuses consolation [Col. 0769B] unless I look upon you, my holy sweetness, and upon the kiss of your mouth.

O good Jesus! You did not shrink from the bloody beast, but gently placed the mouth in which no deceit was found against the mouth in which wickedness abounded. Who can hear without groaning how, at that hour, murderers laid hands upon you and, binding your innocent hands, O good Jesus, dragged you, the meek Lamb who uttered no protest, like a thief to slaughter? Yet even then, Christ, the honeycomb of your merciful sweetness did not cease to drip upon your enemies. For you healed, by touching it, the ear of your enemy which your disciple had cut off.

2. Consider, my soul, who this is who bears the semblance of a king and yet is filled with the humiliation of the most despised slave. He advances crowned, but his crown is torment to him, for it wounded his beautiful head with a thousand pricks. He is clothed in royal purple, but in it he is despised rather than honoured. He holds a sceptre in his hand, but with that very sceptre his venerable head is struck. They worship before him, bending their knees to the ground, and call him king; and immediately they rush to spit upon his lovely cheeks. They buffet his jaws with their palms and dishonour his honourable neck. Under the burden of the cross his back is forced to bend, and he is commanded to carry his own disgrace. Melt away, my soul, in the fire of compassion over the bruising of this beloved young man, whom you see afflicted by such great pains in such meekness. Who is this, for whom heaven and earth suffer with compassion? Know, my soul. This one, beautiful beyond the sons of men, indeed beyond thousands [Col. 0769D] of angels—how disfigured beyond the sons of men he has become! “For we saw him as the last of men, having neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2–3).

[Col. 0770A] Look, holy Father and Lord: for behold, the voice of the blood of my brother Jesus Christ cries to you from the earth—that is, from the cross. Behold your sweet Son stretched out in his whole body. See his innocent hands pouring forth blood, and remit the crimes which my hands have committed. Consider your Son’s side pierced by a cruel spear, and renew me in the holy fountain which I believe flowed forth from it. See the spotless footprints fastened with hard nails, and perfect my steps in your paths (Ps. 16). His bared breast shines white; his bloodied side is red. Look upon the punishment of the God-man, and relieve the misery of the created human being. I have sent your offspring between myself and you, God the mediator; I have sent, I say, an intercessor through whom I hope for pardon. For great indeed is what my impiety has deserved, [Col. 0770B] but far greater is what the Creator’s mercy demands. As much as God is above man, so much is my wickedness beneath his goodness. We have the Lord Jesus Christ as advocate; we do not have a harsh man or a cruel tyrant as judge, but a gracious Lord, who knows well how to have compassion upon my weaknesses. For I know that, if your Son were not coeternal with you, holy Father, sinful man would not dare to open polluted lips to you. Christ God gives confidence to speak, whom we have as priest in heaven 522 interceding for us. In such an advocate I trust; in his mercy I hope.

3. O most beloved Father, when shall I see you? When shall I appear before your face? (Ps. 41:3). When shall I be satisfied with your beauty? When shall I see [Col. 0770C] your desirable countenance, into which angels long to look, who fills all with joy, whom all the rich among the people entreat, whom they defiled with spittle, struck with hands, covered as though he were a mocker, and did not spare to tear the virginal flesh with bitter wounds? What have you done, most beloved boy, that you should be tortured thus? What have you done, most loving young man, that you should be judged thus? Certainly I am the cause of your pain, the cause of your guilt, and the occasion of your offence. O love wondrously ardent, laying aside, so to speak, its very height, weakening power, emptying majesty! To what end are all these things? Certainly, that from this poor harlot he might present a bride having neither spot nor wrinkle. The bride is the human soul, which has committed fornication with many gods, because as a harlot it lay down beneath every leafy tree with its lovers.

O harlot, what shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? [Col. 0771A] Woe to the soul that does not seek you and does not love you! If it loves the world, it serves sins, never at rest, never secure. I pray, let nothing be sweet to me without you; let nothing please me; let nothing beautiful, nothing precious apart from you smile upon me; let all things apart from you become vile. Let that which is opposed to you be burdensome to me; and let your good pleasure be my unfailing desire. I am weary of rejoicing without you; I delight to rejoice with you, to weep with you, and to be troubled for you. Let your name be my refreshment and your remembrance my consolation. If my sins prevent me, if my offences shut me out, [Supplement: “your goodness toward me”] [lacuna] does not reject [me]. O good Jesus! Your remembrance is sweeter than honey; meditation upon you is sweeter than every food; to speak of you is full refreshment; to know you is perfect consolation; to cling to you is eternal life; [Col. 0771B] to be separated from you is everlasting death. O how exalted you are, and how lowly of heart! Make me taste through love what I taste through knowledge. My soul languishes with hunger for your love: refresh it; let your love satisfy it, let your affection enrich it, let your charity fill it. For what could move me to frequent tears except the absence of Jesus Christ? O good Jesus! If it is so sweet to weep over you, how sweet it is to rejoice over you! I know that by nature you are gentle, meek and humble of heart, gracious in countenance, and indeed anointed with the oil of gladness above your companions. Whoever does not perceive your fragrance, Christ, is either foul-smelling or dead. The entire sweetness of earth is Christ’s humanity; the entire sweetness of heaven is Christ’s Spirit.

4. O how sweetly, Jesus Christ, you lived among human beings! How strongly you endured such unworthy and harsh things for them! And you, Lord, suffered for the unjust, dying on account of our offences—you who came freely to give life to the dead, make slaves brothers, captives co-heirs, and exiles kings. But, O good Jesus, what did you do that was greater, when there were more rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0771C] Something is missing here.] when you worked salvation in the midst of our earth, fastening our sins to the cross, condemning the devil, and saving the wretched? Truly, Lord, it was fitting and just that you should weep; and the same cause for weeping exists for us today over the children of Adam. For God wept, so that his Passion might suffice for the redemption of all, although it benefited the redemption of few.

[Col. 0772A] O sweet Lord, you offer your hands and feet to be pierced, so that the heavenly treasure hidden in them may come forth and there may be abundant redemption for us. O how great is the bitterness of my sins! Woe to me! For them the Lord had to be wounded. Certainly, good Jesus, if these did not lead to eternal death, it would by no means have been necessary for you to undergo death so that I might live. But what shall I do? Behold, you, Son of the Most High, die so that 523 I may live. From where came to you such condescension, such immeasurable charity? And what, good Jesus, shall I repay to you for such a death of yours and such life of mine? For you seem to love my life more than your own soul, which [Col. 0772B] you delivered into the hands of enemies for me, Jesus Christ, so that you might restore me to life, snatch me away from enemies so cruel, and free me from death. And who am I, for whose salvation you did so much, emptied yourself so utterly, loved me so greatly, and for whom you even descended into flesh, into suffering, into death—indeed, death on a cross?

Alas for me, a sinner, because of my excessive iniquity and impiety! O tears, where have you withdrawn? Where are you, fountains of tears? Moisten my cheeks, water my face, flow over my countenance. Alas for me! All creation suffers with Christ and is troubled at his death, but my wretched heart does not suffer with compassion for its Creator dying for it. Weep for me, heaven and earth; mourn for me, all creatures. It would have been better for me not to have been created than that my heart should remain so hardened [Col. 0772C] at such a death. O Lord, how greatly you humbled yourself! But by your death—to which my soul was so dear, O good Jesus—free me from my iniquities, and by your Passion put my impiety to flight. Therefore, by those bonds which so bitterly bound your holy hands, loose the bonds of my iniquity. May your holy and harsh Passion free my soul, so beloved by you, from eternal death. Amen.

[Col. 0771]

# INSTRUCTION FOR A PRIEST, OR A TREATISE ON THE CHIEF MYSTERIES OF OUR RELIGION. (G)*

[NOTE.]

524 This treatise was first published by Horst; it is indeed devout, but does not attain the genius of St Bernard, whose name the manuscripts nevertheless bear. In a Cistercian codex sent to us by the Reverend Father Jacques de Lannoy, it bears the title *The Jewel of the Crucified One*.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0771]

[Col. 0771D] To the reverend priest, Brother BERNARD, that servant both ancient and new, wishes him to walk in newness of life.

[Col. 0772D] It is more than sufficiently evident how eagerly you desire, with what burning intent your heart grows warm within you, and how, in your meditation, fire flames up in your bones [Col. 0773A]. In token of this, you charged me in person, wrote to me in my absence, and again, through a faithful messenger, repeatedly urged me to gather for you a few little sparks leaping forth from that great furnace of the charity [variant: brightness] of the incarnate Word. But who am I, that I should presume to set my mouth in heaven? For it is written: “The beast that touches the mountain shall be stoned” (Exod. 19:12–13; Heb. 12:10); and again: “Seek not things higher than yourself” (Ecclus. 3:22); and, “He who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27).

Thus I am constrained by two things: what you ask exceeds my powers, yet I fear to refuse anything you request. For I know him who said, “Let the good work be ours in intention, for its completion will come through divine help”; and charity [Col. 0773B] supplies the strength which incapacity denies. Receive, therefore, some syllables gathered here and there from the sacred Scriptures. If you taste in them any fragrance, sweetness, or inward savour for the palate of a devout heart, I do not wish you to attribute it to me, but to render glory to those noble spice-merchants, from whose shops it has been begged.

Your intention, unless I am mistaken, was this: that it should be explained to you by true authorities and fitting examples how Christ, though covered and veiled under the appearance of bread upon the altar, nevertheless remains in the splendour of unbounded and inestimable brightness. You must know that to know this is not for one on the way but for one who has attained; [Col. 0774A] not for an exile in the valley of weeping but for a citizen of the heavenly homeland; not for one engaged in battle but for one triumphant. It is not granted to those who run, but to those who arrive; it does not precede merit, but is added as a reward. For who is greater than or equal to him who, after being caught up to the height of the third heaven, after beholding heavenly mysteries which it is not lawful for a human being to speak, says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:12), and again, “Now I know in part; then I shall know even as I am known”? (ibid.). If the vessel of election had the eye of conscience darkened, who shall presume to see?

Yet meanwhile let us see with him through a mirror and in an enigma as far as we can. And if we are not yet able to behold with unveiled face the glory of the Lord, nor gaze upon the sun’s disk with direct sight [Col. 0774B], let us at least desire to be illuminated in some measure by its rays when a cloud intervenes. With these preliminaries concerning our purpose, let us, with God’s grace preceding us, carry out what we can. Since we are to say little, we divide the sequence of our subject beforehand into only three chapters, setting forth three gifts which the Wisdom of God foreordained from eternity to be bestowed upon us—or rather, one gift to be given by three works for three uses:

1. That the Son of God gave himself to us by dying for us.
2. That he gives himself to us in the Eucharist.
3. That he gives himself to us in eternal life.

# PART ONE. That the Son of God gave himself to us by dying for us

[Col. 0773]

## CHAPTER ONE. On humanity’s fall from the dignity of its original condition

[Col. 0773C]

1. “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change nor shadow of turning” (Jas. 1:17). Truly it is the best gift, because its giver is best. For, as Boethius says, that supreme craftsman is wholly good, and all envy is far removed from him. See, O human being, what he has bestowed upon you—indeed, what he has granted beforehand and bestowed beyond measure! He created you when you did not exist; he re-created you when you were lost. He created you so that you might share in his blessedness; he re-created you so that after your fall you might not remain deprived of your homeland and excluded from eternal happiness. He created you in his image and likeness: in the image, bestowing natural endowments [Col. 0773D] upon you; in the likeness, granting gratuitous gifts, so that you might excel in mind and surpass all irrational beings by reason.

> While all other creatures gaze downward at the earth,  
> he gave humankind an uplifted face  
> and commanded it to look upon heaven,  
> lifting its raised countenance to the stars.  
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, I.84–86)

Thus, always looking upward, you might keep your Creator in mind and incessantly call your origin to remembrance. For, as has been said, God made you in his image and likeness: in the image [Col. 0774C], so that you might possess memory, understanding, discernment, and the other natural faculties; in the likeness, so that you might possess innocence, righteousness, and the other gratuitous gifts. In the image, through knowledge of truth; in the likeness, through love of virtue. Or, rather, you were made in God’s image through all these things bestowed on you; in likeness to the divine essence, you were made immortal and indivisible.

Every creature was made for your sake: heaven, that it might be your homeland and that you might delight in beholding its beauty; earth, that it might bear for you delightful and beautiful fruits. He made the sun, moon, and all the other stars to give you light; he gave you dominion over the birds of heaven, the beasts of the field, and the fish of the sea, so that you might rule all these at your pleasure. Behold the best gift and the perfect gift coming down from above [Col. 0774D]. What more ought he to have done for you, and did not do?

2. After gifts so great and so many, you transgressed and went into a most wretched state: from life into death, from incorruption 525 into corruption, from freedom into slavery, from glory into punishment, from innocence into guilt, from homeland into exile, from joy into mourning, from blessedness into misery, from rest into affliction. You who had been a fellow citizen of the citizens above became subject to demons; and you who with unveiled face could continually enjoy the sight of the desirable countenance of divine brightness [Col. 0775A], into which angels long to look (1 Pet. 1:12), are compelled instead to behold shameful and disgraceful things. And, according to the prophet, you who ought to have been nourished in saffron-coloured garments embraced dung (Lam. 4:5).

Finally, banished from the place of delight, driven from the paradise of pleasantness into the valley of weeping, you became that wretched traveller—or rather, wanderer—who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell into the hands of robbers, at the mercy of evil spirits. They wounded him in his natural endowments, stripped him of his gratuitous gifts, and departed leaving him half alive—indeed, afflicted with the twofold death of body and soul. This is the time of your wandering. For the learned distinguish four periods for the human race according to four states: the time of wandering, [Col. 0775B] the time of recall, the time of reconciliation, and the time of pilgrimage.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the time of wandering

3. The time of wandering ran from the fall of the first parents to the time of Abraham, who received the command of circumcision as a sign of faith and was the first to hear from the Lord the promise of grace: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18). Hence the Apostle says: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ as though to many, but as though to one: ‘and to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16). And Luke, herald—indeed evangelist—of that same grace, says of the incarnation of the Word [Col. 0775C]: “The oath which he swore to Abraham our father, that he would give himself to us” (Luke 1:73).

It is called the time of wandering because almost all who lived in it wandered from the way of truth. They did not call upon God; “there was no fear of God before their eyes” (Ps. 13:3–5), except for a few: namely, Enoch, who was taken up lest wickedness should alter his understanding; and Noah, who was saved with eight souls in the ark, lest he should be swallowed up in the flood.

## CHAPTER THREE. On the time of recall

4. The time of recall extended from Abraham to the coming of the Redeemer. During that time faith in the Trinity flourished. It flowered already in the Patriarchs, [Col. 0775D] bore fruit in the Kings, and brought its fruit to ripeness in the Prophets, because the Dayspring from on high visited us. It was aptly called the time of recall, because God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, had already devised for the human race thoughts of peace and not of affliction (Jer. 29:11). He purposed to call back the sheep that had perished; he sent the Patriarchs, gave the Law, provided signs and wonders, aided humanity with innumerable benefits, and at last, because of the exceeding charity with which he loved us, sent his only-begotten Son in the likeness of flesh without sin, that he might wash all. This truly was the time of mercy and the year of gracious favour.

## CHAPTER FOUR. On the time of reconciliation

[Col. 0776A]

5. The time of reconciliation began then and continued until the mystery of our redemption was accomplished, when that saving sacrifice, once offered, reconciled us to God the Father. Of him it is truly written: “Behold the great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous, and in the time of wrath became reconciliation; none like him was found” (Ecclus. 44:17, 20; 50:1). And of him the Apostle says: “We act as ambassadors for Christ; we beseech you: be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5:20). And this name, reconciliation, truly arose from its effect.

526 ## CHAPTER FIVE. On the time of pilgrimage

[Col. 0776B] 6. The time of pilgrimage is from the coming of the Holy Spirit to the consummation of the age. From that time the faithful Church began to recognize its pilgrimage and to sigh for its homeland. Thus the vessel of election says with groaning: “So long as we are in this world, we are pilgrims away from the Lord” (ibid. 6). And David says: “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged!” (Ps. 119:5). Yet he also consoles himself, saying: “Your statutes were songs to me in the place of my pilgrimage” (Ps. 118:54). The reason why it is termed the time of pilgrimage is evident from these examples.

## CHAPTER SIX. The time of reconciliation further considered, and the whole work of human redemption briefly expounded

[Col. 0776C] 7. Having distinguished these four times and assigned the reasons for their names, consider, O human being, the time of your redemption; remember and behold how you have been redeemed. “You were bought,” says the Apostle, “at a great price; glorify and bear God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:20). Not merely at a great price, but at a very great one. You had been sold under sin for a cheap and contemptible price, the bite of one fruit; you were bought and redeemed at a great and inestimable price, the death of the Son of God. What price is more precious than this? What more beyond estimation?

He through whom all things were made, and without whom nothing was made—the only-begotten Son of the supreme Father, consubstantial and coeternal with that Father, equal in majesty, equal in glory, the same in essence, his very power and wisdom—he, being such and so great, though he was in the form of God, emptied himself, taking the form [Col. 0776D] of a servant. He descended from the Father’s bosom into the valley of our weeping; he confined himself in the womb of a maiden. And he who was in the beginning with God became “the shortened word” (John 1:1–3, 14). See how shortened, how immense a being was made small. He shut himself within a maiden’s womb; there, surrounded by bloody wrappings, he endured the weariness of nine months. Then, brought forth into the light, he wailed as an infant; he was wrapped in filthy cloths after the manner of our misery, bound in swaddling-bands, laid in a manger amid the breath of brute animals, and placed in a foul stable beside his mother’s poverty. What written text teaches, what tongue relates, what examples show that anyone born into the human race has endured the pressure of such poverty [Col. 0777A]? The nourisher of all is nourished with human milk; he lies filthy in swaddling-clothes so that you might not lie filthy in sins. He is circumcised in the flesh so that you may be circumcised in mind. He humbles himself beneath the hands of his servant John to be baptized in the Jordan—not to wash away any stain from himself, for he entered the world without stain, committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth—but in order to sanctify the waters for you and, by the touch of his most pure flesh, give the waters regenerative power to wash away your crimes.

8. Immediately after his baptism, in order to set before you an example of holiness and religious conduct, he goes out into the wilderness. He fasts forty days and forty nights, tasting no food at all—something utterly impossible for human weakness [Col. 0777B], which, unless it strives daily to repair the collapse of the stomach with sustenance, succumbs to the harm of exhaustion. Therefore God, hungry by the will of his power and by the necessity of the nature he had assumed, endured temptation by the devil. In the matter of disordered appetite for food, he conquered the tempter no less patiently than wisely and drove him back in confusion.

In this he bestowed three benefits upon you, O human being: an example of humility, a pattern of patience, and an imitation of caution. Humble yourself if you are tempted, because a servant is not greater than his master. The Lord was tempted; the servant must be tempted, because “the life of man upon earth is temptation” (Job 7:1). But because the temptations of demons are manifold and subtle, the Lord tells Peter: “Satan has demanded you, that he may sift you like wheat” (Luke 22:31). Bear it patiently [Col. 0777C] if you are tempted. For though the Lord could have cast his tempter by command into the depths of hell, he bore it patiently and overcame him by reason. Be cautious if you are tempted, lest the tempter 527, transforming himself into an angel of light, deceive you under the appearance of what is right, as he deceived Eve, to whom he said: “If you eat from the tree, you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil” (Gen. 3:5). Resist humbly; resist cautiously; resist patiently. “God is faithful,” Scripture says, “and will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but will also provide with the temptation a way out, so that you may be able to endure it” (1 Cor. 10:13). “To him who conquers,” he says, “I will make him a pillar in my temple” (Rev. 3:12); and again: “To him who conquers, I will give to eat from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God” [Col. 0777D] (Rev. 2:7). Sweet is the promise, and blessed the prize for one who runs well, the happy crown for one who conquers well.

9. Therefore, O human being, he was tempted for you, not for himself; he conquered for you, not for himself; for you he hungered, thirsted, and endured weariness. For you he was filled with reproaches and insults, and for you he accepted all his sufferings, which he had to and fittingly ought to accept. He excluded none of your deficiencies from himself except sin. For your sake he worked salvation in the midst of the earth in many ways: raising the dead, enlightening the blind, restoring hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, cleansing to lepers, and performing innumerable other miracles. He travelled through towns and fortresses, villages and streets, proclaiming the Gospel in words and examples, and showing by signs and wonders the way of life.

Further, to show you more examples of humility in himself, on the sixth day before he suffered he chose to enter Jerusalem humbly, on a humble and lowly ass [Col. 0778A], and to be greeted by the crowds, so that his every action might be your lesson and his whole life your teaching. He was betrayed by the faithless and lost Judas and sold as a worthless slave for thirty denarii, so that you, sold under sin, might receive redemption. As he sat at supper with his blessed Apostles on the day before he suffered, he gave his flesh to be eaten and his blood to be drunk, and left you this same mystery to perform in remembrance of him. Then, rising from supper, girded with a linen cloth, he poured water into a basin. The King of Angels bent down before the feet of his lowly servants; with his most pure hands he did not disdain to touch [Col. 0778B], wipe, and wash the uncleanness of their feet, which clung to them from the mud of the streets. And he left you the same example, saying: “If I, your Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14). Why then are you proud, earth and ashes, rot and worm? Why do you, a putrid member, raise yourself over the head before which the very angelic heights must stand in awe?

10. Then, while the Lord was at prayer, because of the anguish of his spirit, he was wholly drenched in a bloody sweat. There he was seized and held, then led before the judge’s tribunal. Though many false witnesses came forward against him and accused him in many lies, he, like an innocent lamb led to slaughter, kept silence; he did not open his mouth, like one who does not hear and has no reproofs in his mouth [Col. 0778C] (Ps. 37:14–15). There they spat upon the face of sweet Jesus; they beat him with fists, and the attendants zealously struck his head with blows from their palms. Then, bound again to the column, he was beaten with whips; his flesh rose in swellings beneath the knots of the scourges and turned to bruises, while blood ran drop by drop from the wounds to the ground. Then his head was bloodied everywhere by the punctures of thorns, and, for mockery, a reed was put in his hand; clothed in a scarlet cloak, he was derided as a fool.

I say little. Here, O human being, tremble wholly, grow stiff with trembling, rightly turn pale, strike your breast with your fists, pour out your whole soul in tears, and suffer compassionately with him who suffers. He is led to death [Col. 0778D] so that you may be brought out of death. Wicked executioners lead him; they lead the Lamb to be sacrificed, and compel him to carry his own cross upon his own shoulders and bear it to the place of his Passion. He does not cry out, grumble, or resist; he submits to his torturers.

11. Imagine here, O human being, by what price, what kind of price, and how great a price you were redeemed: you were not redeemed by corruptible gold or silver. The simple death of your Redeemer, Creator, and Maker does not suffice for your redemption. See the manner of death; consider the quality of his dying; consider what you owe to him who dies. Behold how the righteous one dies. He is stretched out upon the cross; his limbs are pulled apart; his back, still wounded by recent blows of the scourges, still dripping fresh blood from fresh wounds, is rubbed raw against the rigid timber of the cross. His hands 528 [Col. 0779A] and feet are pierced; nails are driven in with hammers; and the deeper the nails penetrate, the more they tear open the wounds by their thickness and intensify his suffering. Gall mixed with vinegar is poured into his thirsty mouth; myrrhed wine is added. The ministers of the devil shake their heads, mocking the pain of the one hanging there: “If he is the Son of God,” they say, “let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27:40, 42); as if to say: “He shall not rise again” (Ps. 40:9), so great are the shame and punishment binding him.

12. Then, most merciful Redeemer, you deliver your most holy soul unto death, that you might bring my wretched soul to life from death. Yet those most wicked executioners are not satisfied even with this: they still pierce your side with a lance and compel the stream of your blood, by which we are redeemed, to flow out in a flood. O soul, what are you doing? Who will give water to your head [Col. 0779B] and a fountain of tears to your eyes, so that you may sufficiently lament and weep for the slain one of your people? Let your beloved be to you this bundle of myrrh (Song 1:12), and not merely a bundle, but an immeasurable weight of bitterness. Suffer compassionately with the sufferer, that you may deserve redemption. Be a dove in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall (Song 2:14). Fly through the hands, fly through the feet, fly into the side; leave none of these unexamined; bathe each member in the bitterness of compassion. Behold the price of your redemption, O redeemed human being; behold what a sacrifice is offered for your fault, for your transgression.

13. But by what necessity did he endure these things? By what need did he shed his blood so often? For it is recorded that he was drenched five times in an outpouring of blood, which I have judged not useless to state here briefly:

> Five times and in five ways, O Christ, you are bloodied:

Circumcision, the bloody sweat, and the scourges, the thorns,

The five piercings—of the side, the hands, and the feet. He endured such wonders for the redemption of humankind, though by the most mighty command of his majesty alone he could have redeemed them. Hear, O human being, of your necessity, not his. The first-created man committed a sin requiring expiation by transgression, which could not be expiated without the offering of a victim. A mere human being could not offer a pure victim, since the contagion of sin had made him wholly unclean; neither God alone nor an angel ought to be sacrificed, since nature rendered the latter and grace the former incapable of suffering [Col. 0780A]; nor was an irrational creature sufficient for so great a matter. Therefore God and man had to become the victim: God, through the power to liberate; man, through the capacity to be sacrificed; God, through mercy; man, through need. Therefore he was offered, because with him is propitiation, and with him abundant redemption (Ps. 129:4, 7). He was offered because his inestimable love toward humankind so decreed. He was offered because he himself willed it (Isa. 53:7); he was offered because humanity so needed it.

14. O human being, what will you repay to the Lord for all that he has repaid to you? He demands love alone; love alone suffices him. Why do you not love the one who loves you? Let us love him, because he first loved us (1 John 4:10). Do you wish to hear the measure of his love [Col. 0780B], to know its effect? God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son (John 3:16). God did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all (Rom. 8:32). Hear the Son himself: “No one,” he says, “has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Therefore love, O human being, your lover; love him not only in word and speech, but in deed and truth (1 John 3:18). Love him with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your strength, and with all your mind (Matt. 22:37). Say: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength; O Lord, my firm foundation, my refuge, and my deliverer” (Ps. 18:1–2). Truly a deliverer, because you have delivered me, the poor, from the mighty, and the needy one who had no helper [Col. 0780C] (Ps. 72:12); and you have delivered my soul from destruction (Sir. 51:16). Behold the best gift, promised at the beginning of this chapter, of which Isaiah says: “A child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9:6); and elsewhere: “How will God not also, together with him, give us all things?” (Rom. 8:32). If he gave us him who is all in all, he undoubtedly gave us all things together with him. If, therefore, he has been given to us, let us use the gift as our own, lest we give to strangers our honor and our years to the cruel one (Prov. 5:9). Let what has been said for the present about the first part suffice.

## PART TWO. That Jesus, the Son of God, gives himself to us in the Eucharist

[Col. 0779]

529 CHAPTER VII. On the ineffable and perpetual radiance of the incarnate Word.

[Col. 0779D]

15. He who was first given to us as the price of redemption does not cease to give himself to us daily as Viaticum: at first capable of suffering and exposed to sufferings, now incapable of suffering and crowned with glory and honor; then a mortal man, now a man victorious over death; then made a little lower than the angels, now exalted above all angels. “Having become,” says the Apostle, [Col. 0780D] “so much better than the angels, as he has inherited a more excellent name than they. For to which of the angels did the Father ever say, ‘You are my Son; today I have begotten you’? And again, ‘I shall be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me’? And again, when he introduces the firstborn into the world, he says, ‘Let all the angels of God worship him’” (Heb. 1:4–6). In this place, beloved priest of God, it seems to me that the chief object of your desire lies especially in this: that you wish to be illuminated in some measure by that radiance [Col. 0781A] which the incarnate Word possessed after the glorification of his assumed humanity. I desire to satisfy your wish; the will is present to me, but I do not find in myself the power to accomplish it, unless he gives it who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach them (Jas. 1:5). Whatever, therefore, he deigns to give, it will not be burdensome for me to write, but necessary for you.

16. First observe what is written: “God dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16); and again: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. 4:24). Both statements are made concerning the divine essence, in which the Father is one with the Son and the Holy Spirit; for in that Trinity nothing is earlier or later, nothing greater or less, but all three persons are coeternal and coequal with one another (the Creed attributed to St. Athanasius). Hence the Son also says: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). If, therefore, they are one, they dwell in the same inaccessible light; they are the same consuming fire, the same radiance, the same power, the same wisdom, the same majesty, the same eternity. Thus the Son is from the Father: God from God, light from light, true God from true God. He is indeed the brightness of the Father’s glory. Hence the Apostle says: “Being the brightness of glory and the image of his substance” (Heb. 1:3)—without doubt, the Father’s. Therefore the Son shines equally with the Father; indeed, the Son and the Father are the same radiance. Are these testimonies concerning the Son’s radiance sufficient for you? Or perhaps you will say that you desire and delight more in his radiance insofar as he is God and man. Nor will testimonies be lacking in this respect either, with his grace assisting.

[Col. 0781C] 17. First I want you to be warned not to suppose that the radiance of the Word was obscured through the humanity assumed by God. Hear what is written: “God assumed human things; he did not relinquish divine things. He assumed what he was not, remaining what he was” (*In the Office of the Church*). The angel said to Mary: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:35). The meaning of this saying is that the Holy Spirit will effect in you the incarnation of the Word who was to be incarnate, separating from your flesh a small portion which will receive a soul and be joined to the divine essence in unity of person. But what was the reason for the overshadowing by the power of the Most High? Assuredly this was its chief purpose: unless the Virgin’s flesh had been overshadowed by some hidden operation, [Col. 0781D] it could in no way have borne the splendor of so great a majesty without being consumed. Hence the Lord said to Moses: “No human being upon earth shall see me and live”; as if he said: “Such is the radiance of my divine nature that a human being established in mortal flesh cannot see me without being consumed.” Hence, when Moses pleaded with the Lord with great steadfastness, saying, “Lord, show yourself to me,” he said: “Stand in the cleft of the rock, and when I have passed by, you shall see my back; but you shall not be able to see my face” (Exod. 33:18–23). By “face” he meant divinity, and by “back” humanity—yet Moses did not see even that with bodily sight, but left it to be seen by later generations. This is understood figuratively when the glorious flesh of Christ, which is consecrated at the altar [Col. 0782A] and distributed to the faithful as Viaticum, is made radiant by the fire of divine ardor. For just as the brightest purple dyes the whitest wool and compels it entirely to take on its own color; and just as the soul animates, sustains, and gives life to the whole body; so too fire, penetrating iron, makes it incandescent, imparting its brightness and heat and making it sparkle, flame, and burn contrary to its own nature: thus God deifies the human being united to himself and, exalting him above every creature, makes him radiant with himself through the omnipotence of purity and the prerogative of divinity. The Son bears witness concerning himself, saying: “I came as light into the world, and human beings loved darkness rather than light” (John 3:19); and again: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). John states the same thing expressly: “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). Before the Passion, the Son spoke to the Father in prayer, saying: “Father, glorify me beside yourself with the glory which I had before the world existed” (John 17:5); to whom the Father replied: “I have glorified, and I shall glorify” (John 12:28). What could be clearer, more manifest, or more evident?

18. Gather from the Gospel the radiance which the God-man, now glorified according to his humanity, possesses. As the time approached when he was to pass from this world to the Father, he took Peter, John, and James, ascended Mount Tabor, and was transfigured before them. His face became bright [Col. 0782C] as the sun, and his garments like snow, such as no fuller on earth can make. When Moses and Elijah appeared, the disciples, looking upon the radiance of his face, could not bear its brilliance; but, exceedingly afraid and overwhelmed in mind, they fell upon the ground as though lifeless (Luke 9:28–36). If, then, while his body was still subject to mortality and his limbs had not yet put off corruption, he deigned to appear with such a beam, such radiant splendor, such unbearable radiance to human eyes, how great a radiance must we believe belongs to the Son of God in the form of assumed humanity—now glorified, now exalted above the heavens of heavens, now possessing the name that is above every name, so that at his name every knee should bend, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth [Col. 0782D] (Phil. 2:9–10); now established on the day of his power, in the splendors of the saints, where the Father, storing up delight and exultation, says: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 110:3). There indeed he shines: in the day of his power, in the day of his eternity. No night interrupts this day; no darkness breaks it; no gloom separates it. There he is surrounded by an abyss of light because of the immeasurable sea of radiance. There Christ himself shines like the sun upon golden shields, and the mountains shine again from him. There the saints are illuminated by him. Hence the Prophet says: “You shine wondrously from the eternal mountains” (Ps. 76:4 [Vulg. 75:5]). And again it is written: “Around you, O Lord, there is a light which never fails; there the souls of the saints rest”; and again: “Holy is the true and wonderful [Col. 0783A] light, which supplies light to those who have persevered in the struggle of contest: they receive from Christ everlasting brightness, in which, blessed, they rejoice continually” (*In the Office for Martyrs*).

19. Behold how true and harmonious are these testimonies concerning that blessed and ineffable radiance in which Christ is—or rather, which Christ is. It cannot be diminished or increased, because it is immeasurable, eternal, surpasses every sense, exceeds every thought, and transcends every estimation. “Man approaches to a deep heart, and God shall be exalted incomprehensibly in his radiance” (Ps. 64:6–7 [Vulg. 63:7–8]). The radiance remains always the same: it gains no increase from any accession and suffers no loss from any departure. It was not diminished through the assumed humanity; nor did it become more excellent in God through glorified humanity. The Prophet makes this clear, saying: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 102:27 [Vulg. 101:28]). The prophet Habakkuk likewise, beholding this light, says: “His splendor shall be as light; horns are in his hands. There his strength is hidden; death shall go before his face” (Hab. 3:4–5). He plainly indicates that even when Christ’s hands were nailed to the cross, although the sun itself veiled its rays lest it see Christ dying on the cross, the light of divinity shone no less in Christ. Hence he had said beforehand: “His splendor shall be as light.” You, Jew, tauntingly said: “We saw him with neither form nor beauty” (Isa. 53:2). You saw with a bleary eye—indeed, with an altogether blinded eye, because then blindness fell upon Israel.
