But Habakkuk had clear [Col. 0783C] eyes; and the people of the nations, who walked in darkness, saw a great light: light arose for them in the region of the shadow of death.

20. Therefore Habakkuk’s testimony establishes that the Passion of Christ’s humanity did not diminish the light of his divinity. Indeed, he himself, dying, the conqueror of death, triumphed over death by death, and his death trampled your death. “There his strength is hidden.” A little body, lifeless, parched, and bloodless hangs on the cross; its head, with neck bent down, scarcely clings to its hanging body; its face is bruised, its eyes mourning in death and half shut; its hands are stretched out and fastened to the wood with nails. There his strength is hidden—hidden from the Jews and hidden also from the disciples. It was hidden from the Jews, who said: “Let us destroy him from the land of the living; let us condemn him to a most shameful death” [Col. 0783D] (Wis. 2:19–20). It was hidden from the disciples, who said: “But we had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:20). “His splendor shall be as light; horns are in his hands.” On the cross he withers; in the air he shines; he hangs upon the instrument of execution, he gleams in the highest heaven. O holy Habakkuk, how well the splendor of this light shone for you, since it shone upon you so many ages beforehand! The horns of the cross are in his hands, but his hands too are on the horns of the cross. There his strength is hidden, but not among those below. There he shattered iron bars; there he broke bronze gates; there he reveals his strength; there, himself stronger, he binds the strong man and plunders his goods, he who formerly guarded his courtyard in peace (Luke 11:21–22). There it is cried: “Who is this [Col. 0784A] king of glory?” There it is heard: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle, the Lord of hosts—he is the king of glory” (Ps. 24:8, 10 [Vulg. 23]). “Death shall go before his face.” “O death, I shall be your death; O hell, I shall be your bite. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting? Death has been swallowed up in victory” (Hos. 13:14; 1 Cor. 15:54–55). The victor returns in noble triumphal procession from hell. “The devil,” it says, “shall go forth before his feet” (Hab. 3:5). “Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the ruler of this world be cast out” (John 12:31). “His splendor shall be as light,” to give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death (Luke 1:79). Therefore the radiance of the incarnate Word remains in the glorified human being; it persists in him who is seated at the Father’s right hand. It does not decline with time, nor is it diminished by time; no event obscures it. He shines equally when he is on the altar and when he is in the heights of heaven; he radiates no less when he is in the priest’s hands than when he is in the bosom of God the Father.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the dignity of priests

21. Therefore always glory—but in the Lord—O priest of God Most High. Consider your dignity; behold your exalted rank with the eyes of the mind; reflect on your prerogative; see your allotted portion. Surely measuring-lines have fallen for you in splendid places, if you do not neglect your splendid inheritance (Ps. 16:6 [Vulg. 15:6]). Observe how greatly your God has raised you up, how much he has exalted you above all creatures. Let your prayer be pure, because a place is given to your voice in heaven when you duly stand at the sacred [Col. 0784C] altars and purpose to celebrate the most holy mystery of the heavenly sacrifice. At your uttered voice, at your life-giving word, at your saving petition, the supreme Father—at whose command all things subsist, whom angels praise without ceasing, to whom the morning stars raise songs of joy, whom Dominions adore, whom Powers fear; who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble (Ps. 104:32 [Vulg. 103:32]); who alone has wrought great wonders (Ps. 136:4 [Vulg. 135:4])—he, I say, so great and immeasurable, lowers his most sweet Son and places him in your hands; he sends him down from the highest heights and puts him into your fingers. There your burnt offering becomes rich, more so than thousands of fat lambs and rams.

22. Abel’s gift was greatly accepted, but not in this way; the sacrifice of Abraham the patriarch was greatly pleasing, but not to this degree; Melchizedek’s offering was greatly approved, but far less than this. Finally, what does the Prophet say? “Sacrifice and offering you did not desire; burnt offering and sin-offering you did not require. Then I said, ‘Behold, I come’” (Ps. 40:6–7 [Vulg. 39:7–8]). This was said by him who entered once into the Holy Place, having obtained eternal redemption, not through the blood of goats or calves but through his own blood (Heb. 9:12). All things happened to the ancients in figure. Here is truth; there, figure. There, shadow; here, light. There, cloud; here, radiance. There, the legal lamb; here, the innocent lamb who takes away the sins of the world. For the Son of God is truly he whom you, priest, sacrifice; whom you handle with your hands; whom you receive with your mouth; whom you convey into your body. Yet that majesty does not come to you alone. The Son comes to you, but not without the Father. “He who sent me,” he says, “is with me, and has not left me alone” (John 8:29). The Son comes to you, but not without the Holy Spirit. For what does [Col. 0785A] John say? “He upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is Christ” (John 1:33). The Holy Spirit descends upon others, but does not always remain; upon Christ, however, he descended to remain forever. Nevertheless the whole host of heavenly citizens is present. “Thousands of thousands,” it says, “ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. 7:10). For angels, although they are ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation, nevertheless always see the face [Col. 0785B] of the Father, continually stand before the countenance of majesty into which they desire to look. They enjoy it and do not tire of it; for the more they enjoy it, the more they thirst to enjoy it. How great a light, holy priest, do you believe surrounds you in the presence of so great a majesty, at so solemn an advent and assembly of the Trinity and the whole host of heaven? How great a radiance do you judge to be present in and belong to the entire heavenly court? It is assuredly so great that you could not bear it unless the power of the Most High overshadowed your weakness so that you might bear it.

## CHAPTER IX. That the priests’ power is greater than angelic dignity

23. Therefore attend, as I have said, and always keep in mind, retain in unceasing memory, the grace singularly bestowed upon you by God—a grace he has granted neither to angels nor to other human beings. For bread in your hands is transubstantiated into the body of the only-begotten Son of God; wine, by your blessing, is changed into the most holy blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. The Seraphim burn greatly, united with the Holy Trinity above all other spirits in rank and charity. Hence *Seraphim* is interpreted as “burning” or “kindling.” Each order is designated by the name of that thing which it has received more abundantly as its gift. Yet they do not excel in this privilege: to sanctify, in created things subject to them, the body or blood of our Redeemer. The Cherubim, in whom is fullness of knowledge—as their name also testifies, because they know the heavenly mysteries more familiarly than all others—wonder that priestly knowledge and power have been made wondrous beyond them, and that they cannot attain to them. The Thrones, of such dignity that the Lord sits in them and through them decrees his judgments, do not possess that power in which priests excel. The Dominions, though they have received lordship over the others from the Lord; the Principalities, although they rule the others subject to them; the Powers, although they excel in the loftiness of power; the Virtues of heaven, although by their strength they restrain the aerial powers from exercising all their wickedness upon humankind; the Archangels, although they are to announce the highest mysteries of the divine will to lower spirits and, by authority, send those lower spirits to human beings; [Col. 0786A] the Angels, although they always see the face of the Father who is in heaven—all these holy orders of blessed spirits, though they enjoy such blessedness that nothing is lacking to them from supreme felicity, nevertheless reverence the glory of the priest, marvel at his dignity, yield to his privilege, and honor his power.

24. O ecclesiastical race, royal priesthood, holy nation, people of acquisition: proclaim the mighty deeds of him who called you from darkness into his wonderful light (1 Pet. 2:9), and his ineffable mystery. You are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth (Matt. 5:13–14). To the Levites it is said: “Be cleansed, you who carry the vessels of the Lord” (Isa. 52:11); to you it must be said: “Be cleansed, you who are vessels of the Lord.” Glorify and bear God in your body (1 Cor. 6:20). God chose you as his inheritance. In you is buried that glorious and glorified body which was once buried in Jerusalem, lifeless and dead. Certainly that holy Joseph did not wish to bury it except in a new tomb, in which no one had yet been laid; he took care to wrap it in a clean shroud (Matt. 27:59–60; John 19:41). Woe to you if you do not also place it in a new—or at least renewed—tomb; that is, in a body wholly cleansed from sins, or, if you have sinned, cleansed through repentance and satisfaction. Woe to you if you do not place it in a clean shroud; that is, in a conscience wholly purified and freed from every defilement. Let there be no fellowship of Christ with Belial in your body; no agreement of God with idols; no partnership of light with darkness (2 Cor. 6:15–16). Let sin not reign in your mortal body [Col. 0786C] (Rom. 6:12), and thus you will dedicate a venerable tomb to Christ, a temple to the Holy Spirit. “The temple of the Lord,” says the Apostle, “is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17); and again: “Do you not know that our bodies are temples of the Lord, and that the Holy Spirit dwells in us?” (1 Cor. 6:19). If this is truly said of every person possessing charity, it should much more be said of a priest pleasing to God.

25. Consider and observe also, devout priest, with what care and watchfulness the holy angels guarded the place of the tomb, after the Lord’s body had been removed, restored to life and glorified; with what brightness and beauty of face and garments they appeared to the holy women visiting the tomb and seeking the body. [Col. 0786D] You ought undoubtedly to know that, if you worthily handle that same Lord’s body—now surpassingly glorious, reigning in heaven, and honored at the Father’s right hand—and prepare the clean and new tomb of your body, the frequent guardianship of the angels themselves will not be lacking to you. They will guard your soul, govern your body, and protect you amid all your vices; and they will say to you and those like you: “You shall be called priests of the Lord, ministers of our God” (Isa. 61:6). Take care, therefore, not to touch that sacrifice unless you are innocent in hands and clean in heart; otherwise he himself will say to you: “Do not touch me, because your touch is contagion.”

## CHAPTER X. On a priest’s meditation, or his preparation to celebrate so great a mystery worthily

[Col. 0787A]

26. Meditate, beloved priest of God, and let this always be the meditation of your heart: John the Baptist, the Lord’s forerunner, the Bridegroom’s friend, the bride’s attendant, prophet and more than prophet, sanctified in the womb and justified in the wilderness—he, so great, of such eminent merit, so singularly sanctified—trembles and does not dare to touch the holy head of God, but cries out trembling: “Sanctify me, Savior” (Matt. 3:14). Meditate that Peter, appointed by the Lord as key-bearer of the kingdom of heaven, established as shepherd of the sheep by his threefold confession of love, and prefigured as prince of the apostles—in peril of death, when shipwreck threatened, feared to approach the Lord who was near and wished in fear to withdraw from him, saying: “Depart from me, Lord, because I am a sinner” (Luke 5:8). That chosen and beloved disciple John, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at supper, to whom Christ on the cross entrusted the Virgin Mother to a virgin, and to whom, though still in mortal flesh, the secrets of heaven were revealed—he greatly gloried in merely hearing, outward sight, and touch of the Lord’s body, saying: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard and have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon, which our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1:1). If, then, these glorious princes of the earth, eminent nobles of the heavenly court, so greatly reverenced the outward touch of the Lord’s body, [Col. 0787C] not yet borne into glory in heaven, with what reverence, fear, and trembling, with what bodily chastity and purity of soul, ought the priest now to consecrate, touch, receive, and convey into his own body that glorious body—exalted above all things in the radiance of the Father’s glory?

27. Therefore, whatever priest you are, if you offer your gift at the altar, if you intend to celebrate that venerable and ineffable mystery, and remember that your brother has something against you—this great brother who is the Son of God by nature, who gave us power to become children of God (John 1:12) and his brothers by grace; who deigned to call us his brothers, saying through the Prophet: “I will declare [Col. 0787D] your name to my brothers” (Ps. 22:22 [Vulg. 21:23]), and again after the resurrection: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. 28:10), etc.—if that brother has anything against you; if you have offended that majesty in thought, word, or deed; if you have darkened the brightness of your innocence with some stain; if you have a conscience either grievously sick or insufficiently healed: leave your gift there, defer the mystery, and first go to be reconciled to your brother through devout contrition of heart, pure confession of the mouth, harsh bodily mortification in repentance, and fitting satisfaction. Wash your bed every night; for every sin cleanse 534 your conscience. Ascend the tribunal of your conscience; sit in the judge’s place; condemn yourself and pronounce yourself guilty. Let the memory [Col. 0788A] of sin come forward as accuser; let the act be witness; let consent and delight aggravate the sin or guilt. Let all things accuse you; let nothing excuse you. Let fear come as executioner and torturer, and torment the guilty person. Let it shed the blood of the heart, namely tears; and thus through your own judgment you will escape the punishment of divine judgment, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “If we judged ourselves, we would surely not be judged by the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:31). Then, when you come, you will offer your gift, and it will please God more than a calf putting forth horns and hoofs (Ps. 69:30–31 [Vulg. 68:32]).

## CHAPTER XI. From the rite of legal purification he teaches the pursuit of purity

28. By the rite also of the legal priest about to enter the Holy [Col. 0788B] of Holies, make for yourself a basin from the mirrors of the women who keep watch at the entrance of the tabernacle (Exod. 38:8), so that, when you wash yourself, if you discover a stain upon your body, you may wash it away. Understand the basin as sacred Scripture; understand the women keeping watch at the entrance of the tabernacle as holy souls watching at the entrance of the kingdom of heaven. Their mirrors are the examples of the saints or the testimonies of Scripture: in these, the souls of the righteous behold themselves as in a mirror, and correct whatever deformity they discover in themselves. Therefore devote yourself continually to sacred meditation upon the divine writings; delight in them as though divinely illumined; there behold your whole self in a shining mirror. If you discover anything crooked in yourself, correct it; retain what is right; set in order what is deformed; cultivate what is beautiful; preserve what is sound; strengthen what is weak. Read the Lord’s commandments untiringly, love them insatiably, fulfill them effectually; and through them, sufficiently instructed, recognize what you ought to avoid and what you ought to pursue.

29. Behold, you have a certain elementary pattern for avoiding evil and doing good. If you keep it, the lawgiver will give you a blessing, and, with him as your guide, you will go from strength to strength (Ps. 84:7 [Vulg. 83:8]); and he himself will be for you a protecting God and a place of refuge, to save you (Ps. 31:2 [Vulg. 30:3]); and he will say to you: “Behold, I am with you all the days of your life, even to the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20). He will truly be with you, because he will give himself as Viaticum, lest you fail [Col. 0788D] on the way, until he fully refreshes you in the homeland. Test yourself, therefore, in the manner stated, and so eat of that bread of the holy Eucharist and drink from the cup.

## CHAPTER XII. On the threefold reception of the Lord’s body and blood

30. A discerning priest ought not to be ignorant that there is a threefold reception of this most sacred bread and venerable cup—that is, of the life-giving body and blood of the Lord. One reception is sacramental and spiritual; it is true, holy, and sanctifying; blessed and beatifying; vital and life-giving. Another is spiritual only; nevertheless it confers grace, increases virtues, and accumulates merit. The third is sacramental only; it is condemnable and condemning, hateful to God and separating from him, and in no way beatifying. Sacramentally and spiritually receives the holy Eucharist every devout priest who, suitably clothed in the wedding garment—that is, charity—and subject to no mortal sin, enters the altar of God and duly celebrates the sacred mystery. In the same manner and with the same merit, every faithful person receives who accepts the sacrament itself from the priest’s hand. Yet the priest is marked out above others by a singular prerogative: every day, unless prevented by some fault or infirmity, he has the power to consecrate and receive the Eucharist; others, however, are permitted only at certain times to communicate from the priest’s hand. Spiritually only receives every faithful person who is a member of the Church and perseveres in charity; for, although such a person does not touch the Sacrament with the mouth, through faith and union with the Church he or she obtains the power of the Sacrament [Col. 0789B]—that is, the remission of sins and the infusion of spiritual grace. Sacramentally only receives the person who, persisting in mortal sin, presumes to communicate; such a person is a companion of Judas the betrayer, and it would have been better for that person not to have been born, unless he repents and makes worthy satisfaction to God.

31. Concerning the first reception, which is sacramental and spiritual, the Lord says: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him”; and again: “Whoever eats me will live because of me.” Concerning the second, which is spiritual only, the Lord himself again says: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the spirit that gives life” (John 6:57–58, 64); as though he said: [Col. 0789C] “If you understand only a carnal reception without grace, it profits nothing—indeed, it harms; but the spiritual reception without the carnal makes you alive.” Concerning the third, which is sacramental only, the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:29); that is to say, not distinguishing the Lord’s body from other foods. [Col. 0790A] This is the saving distinction of the Lord’s body from other foods: when we consume other foods, we incorporate them into our body; but when we receive the Lord’s body as food, if we act worthily, we are incorporated into the Lord—indeed, we are wholly transformed into God, because “whoever is joined to God is one spirit with him” (1 Cor. 6:17). Blessed is the traveler who is refreshed with such Viaticum, which safely leads him by the way and conveys him into the homeland.

32. Therefore the first reception belongs to priests themselves who honor their ministry by a worthy performance of its office; and only through them does the dispensing of reception belong to the other faithful. For they possess the keys of this Sacrament; they are the true mediators between God and human beings; they are the voice and instrument of holy Church; they offer God the prayers of the people [Col. 0790B] and bring back propitiations. O how faithful the promiser, how true the fulfiller, how generous the giver! You said, Lord Jesus: “Behold, I am with you until the end of the age” (Matt. 28:20). You truly said this. “The word,” Scripture says, “is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (Deut. 30:14). The Word who was in the beginning with God deigns to be with humankind at the end of the age: he is in the mouth; he is in the heart. What is nearer? What more inward? He is in your mouth; therefore let his praise always be in your mouth. He is in your heart; therefore confess to him with uprightness of heart, and do not forget all his benefits. What benefits? He propitiates all your iniquities; heals all your infirmities; redeems your life from destruction; crowns you in mercy [Col. 0790C] and compassions; fills your desire with good things, giving himself to you as Viaticum. “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. 103:2–5 [Vulg. 102]) in the resurrection of the righteous, when he will give himself anew as the reward. Concerning this reward, in this final chapter, we shall pursue in the service of the pen whatever he himself deigns to give.

## PART THREE. That Christ gives himself to us as a reward in heaven

[Col. 0789]

## CHAPTER XIII.

[Col. 0789D]

33. It is an Aristotelian maxim: “Everything perceptible which is placed outside perception is uncertain.” Divine is this: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man, [is that] which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Cor. 2:9); and this: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. 64:4); and John: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18). What then? If the rewards of life promised to us are invisible to eyes, unheard by ears, and inscrutable to hearts; if no one has ever seen God, who is the light and reward of the righteous, who would dare to speak of things unheard and utterly unknown? Who would presume to speak of things ineffable? This one thing I know: the more ineffable they are, the more desirable they are; and nothing that is desired can be compared with them. Yet because, according to the Apostle, we still walk by faith and not yet by sight (2 Cor. 5:7), and because “the invisible things of God, from the creation of the world, are perceived by the understanding through the things that have been made” (Rom. 1:20), let us attempt, however feebly, to say something, from the likeness of things subject to the senses, about the ineffable good promised to the faithful and blessed; presuming plainly nothing from our own heart, but drawing such testimonies as we can from the divine Scriptures. [Col. 0790D]

536. 34. Certainly no wise person doubts that after this life the souls of the righteous are in the hand of God (Matt. 8:12), while the souls of the reprobate fall into punishment, according to the saying: “Those who have done good will go into eternal life; but those who have done evil [will go] into eternal fire” (Athanasian Creed). [Col. 0791A] Thus for the elect there is a twofold cause of blessedness: one, escape from punishment; the other, attainment of glory. Something must be said briefly about the punishment of the wicked, so that, when it has been considered, the glory of the good may be valued more highly; for the worth of nothing is better shown than when the depravity of its opposite is not passed over in silence. “Virtue shines forth more beautifully from the opposite vice of ugliness,” says Isidore.

O human being, consider all the torments of the world and compare them with Gehenna: the whole will be light. Even purgatorial fire, which is not Gehenna, though it torments only for a little while, exceeds every earthly torture. Hence Augustine, on the Psalter: “O Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor correct me in your anger” (Ps. 37:2); that is, may I not be among those to whom you will say at judgment: “Depart, [Col. 0791B] accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41). “Correct me not in your indignation”; that is, may I have no need of the corrective fire, which is also called purgatorial. For it is more severe than anything a human being can suffer in this life, although many criminals pay for their crimes through widely differing tortures, and many have departed to the Lord through immense and exquisite torments (Exposition on Psalm 37, §3).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Punishments of Hell

35. Hell indeed has, as may be demonstrated from the authorities, nine notable punishments, besides the innumerable other evils which it contains; hence this verse:

> Hammer and stench, with worms, fire and cold,  
> Demonic sight, darkness, shame, fiery chains.

[Col. 0791C] There will be there unquenchable fire, incomparable cold, immortal worms, intolerable stench, hammers striking repeatedly, dense and palpable darkness—where there is no order, but everlasting horror dwells; where the crimes of all are wholly manifest to all; the sight of demons, whom they continually see sparkling with fire, than which nothing in the world is more horrible or terrifying; fiery chains binding every limb. [Col. 0792A] The heat there, I say, is so great that even all rivers gathered into one could not extinguish it.

Hence in Matthew: “There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. 8:12), because smoke stirred up by fire causes weeping of the eyes, and cold causes gnashing of the teeth. If a fiery mountain were cast in there, it would be turned into ice. The wretches assigned to these miseries wander about: now from heat into cold, now from cold into heat, seeking a remedy for contrary sufferings in contrary conditions, yet suffering no less. Thus blessed Job says: “They shall pass from snowy cold to excessive heat” (Job 24:19).

36. There are there immortal worms, serpents, and dragons, dreadful in appearance and hissing, which live in flame as fish live in water. They afflict the wretches [Col. 0792B] and especially roam through and gnaw those members which have especially served sin: the genitals of the lustful, the palate and throats of the gluttonous, and likewise the respective members of all the rest. Hence the saying of Wisdom: “By the things through which one sins, by these one is also tormented” (Wis. 11:17). Hence also Isaiah: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24).

From the fire there exhales a stench so severe that it tortures no less than the heat. Hence the same Isaiah: “Instead of a sweet fragrance there will be stench” (Isa. 3:24); and the Psalm: “Fire, sulphur, and a blast of storms are the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10:7). By “a blast of storms” he means the exhalation of smoke and stench, which blows from the fire violently like a tempest. They are struck incessantly with scourges as with hammers, while demons compel them to confess their crimes, so that those who [Col. 0792C] were here inciters of evils may there become their tormentors. Thus Solomon says: “Torments are prepared for mockers” (Prov. 19:29). For demons open their mouths wide over the wretches, laughing and saying: “Aha, aha, our eyes have seen it” (Ps. 24:21), because they neglected the fellowship of the nine orders of angels.

[Col. 0791]

## TREATISE ON THE STATE OF THE VIRTUES. (G)

**[NOTE.]**

537. The library of the Laetian Benedictine monastery, in the diocese of Cambrai, recently supplied us with this little work from an old manuscript, bearing this title: “Bernard, abbot, On the State of the Virtues.” It is not, however, by St Bernard, but by a certain Benedictine, as may be inferred from §14. It was composed for the benefit of novices and divided into three parts or sections: the first on Humility; the second on Obedience; the third on Charity.

## PREFACE

[Col. 0791D]

By the inspiring grace of him who breathes where he wills and when he wills, and makes the tongues of infants eloquent, I wish, if I can, to gather in simple speech certain things concerning the changeable state of the virtues—some which I have found through reading, some which I have heard from my teachers—adding also whatever may perhaps occur, provided it does not conflict with faith and is supported by reason. Therefore may the Paraclete, who precedes by his inspiration, accompany me throughout; [Col. 0792D] may he enlighten the heart, disclose obscure matters, and grant effectiveness, for his glory, for my benefit, and for the advancement of the novices who have descended from the mountain of pride into the valley of weeping, and who meditate upon the law of the Lord day and night. But because humility is the mother of virtues, and a human being’s humility is not from human beings but from above, let us begin with the humility of him who said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

## PART ONE. ON HUMILITY

[Col. 0793A]

1. Therefore Christ, though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). He emptied himself, I say, so as to become less than the Father, less than himself, less than an angel; to be subject to human beings—indeed, to Joseph himself as to a foster-father, and to holy Mary as to a mother—according to what is written: “And he was subject to them” (Luke 2:51).

He also emptied himself so that he became not only human but poor. He hungered, thirsted, and was weary, but because he willed it. Finally, he emptied himself even to mockery, reproaches, and scourges; “he was led as a sheep to slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth.” Behold, he who was beautiful in form beyond the children of men was without form or beauty; his face was, as it were, hidden and despised, so that he was not even reckoned among human beings, but numbered with the wicked, as though leprous, struck, and humbled by God. Yet he was wounded for our sins and crushed for our crimes; the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruising we have been healed (Isa. 53:2–7). [Col. 0793B]

O ineffable mercy of God, who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all: he was born for us, lived in the world for us, and died for us—poor and humble in his manner of life, poor and humble on the cross—sharing what was ours and so graciously dispensing what was his, so that our conduct might accord with his life and [Col. 0793C] our redemption be in his death.

2. Behold the incomparable humility of God, because it admits no worthy comparison; immeasurable, because it cannot be measured; ineffable, because it cannot be explained in words: that God and Lord of all should become a human being and servant of all; that the invisible should be seen; that the bread of angels should be fed; that the strength of heaven should be weakened; that life should die. But the cause of this mystery is God’s justice and mercy. Pride had cast humanity down; but neither the human being who ought to have made satisfaction nor the angel who ought not to have done so could make fitting satisfaction to God, nor was any other creature capable of this. Therefore God became man justly and mercifully: mercifully indeed with regard to God, who owed humanity nothing but punishment; justly with regard to [Col. 0793D] humanity, because humanity had sinned against God—so that his humility might humble the proud, and his wisdom enlighten the blinded and kindle the cold.

For he is the way, the truth, and the life (John 14:6): the way, certainly, of conduct; the truth of teaching; the life 538 of blessedness. He is the way without which one either does not go or goes wrongly; the truth without which one either does not learn or learns wrongly; the life in which one lives well, without which one lives altogether badly. For he is the power of God and the wisdom of God; and because he is God’s power, he grants his own the strength to pass through every adversity; and because he is God’s wisdom, he grants understanding.

3. But now it comes to mind that the angel fell from heaven through pride; he did not descend. He fell [Col. 0794A] to the ruin of himself and his followers; Christ descended for the exaltation of his elect. Pride made the angel into the devil; Christ’s humility made the devil’s children into children of God. The proud devil and his followers fell from heaven into hell; humble Christ and his followers, having returned from the lower regions, ascended into heaven.

You see, then, how great are, in the one person of Christ, the exaltation of humanity without human merit, the humility of God without divine obligation, charity without measure, and an example without equal. If, then, God is humbled on earth, why is the human being still proud—dust and ashes, a worm, corruption—who is exalted today and not found tomorrow? Whoever is proud on this earth, where Christ was found humble, sets himself above Christ. Yet even if pride should ascend to heaven and its head touch the clouds, in the end it will perish like dung; and the higher it rises before human beings, the more grievously it falls before God. [Col. 0794B] Humility, however, the lower it descends before human beings, the higher it rises before God.

The humble person is the friend of the humble God; and every friend of God ascends, according to what is written: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14:10). Thus every humble person undoubtedly ascends, and true humility can in no way experience a fall; for it is always at the bottom and despises its own eminence. For if humility and pride are opposites, and pride is love of one’s own excellence, humility is rightly contempt for one’s own excellence. Just as pride is the vice by which a blinded person is pleased with himself, although precisely in this he displeases God and human beings, so [Col. 0794C] humility is the virtue by which an enlightened person is displeased with himself, and precisely in this he pleases both God and human beings.

4. There is one humility which is beginning, another progressing, another perfect: beginning in novices, progressing in those who fight well, perfect in veterans. There is another that is sufficient, another abundant, another superabundant. That humility is sufficient by which a person submits to a superior and does not prefer himself to an equal. That is abundant by which a person submits to an equal and does not prefer himself even to an inferior [the third definition is supplied]. But the humility which is sufficient is rightly called the mother of virtues, by which a person begins, in repentance, to confess his sins and submit himself to a superior. Abundant and superabundant humility, however, both nourish virtues and preserve and increase them.

Humility is differentiated in seven ways. There is humility in laying aside temporal possessions. There follow six others: two in speech, two in the body, and two in the heart. There are two in speech because the humble person speaks peaceably in response to a word of impatience and humbly in response to a boastful word. There are two in the body because there is lowliness in dress and mortification in the flesh. There are two in the heart because one prefers common counsel to one’s own, and, setting aside one’s own will, submits oneself to another’s command. [Col. 0794D]

5. Humility is like a kind of underground pit in which the treasure of virtues is stored most safely, where neither the violence of robbers breaks in nor thieves dig through and steal. Humility is also an impenetrable shield by which we are spiritually protected; an unfailing two-edged sword, striking on both sides: for outward humility beneficially strikes outward enemies so that they repent, and inward humility strongly strikes invisible enemies so that they make no progress—indeed, so that they fail. Hence humility of heart is rightly called a wall against invisible temptations, and humility of body an outer wall against outward impediments. Humility is also called a tower of strength from the face of the enemy; for just as a tower in a city is both its beauty and its fortification, so humility is the beauty and fortification of the heart. [Col. 0795A]

6. There is also a useless humility by which a person withdraws even from good work and hides himself under silence because he fears becoming contemptible, should something perhaps be laid against him which his conscience fears. There is another humility which does not build up but destroys, when someone, at an unsuitable place or time, excessively abases himself in words or deeds, sometimes even in the presence of those who are easily scandalized. There is also the feigned humility of hypocrites, who display an appearance of humility in their dress and take pride in that very appearance; although they are proud in the hidden place of the heart, they wish to appear humble before human eyes, acting deceitfully like a fraudulent goldsmith who sells a gilded silver ring as a gold ring. [Col. 0795B]

7. It should be noted that one humility is simple and is not lifted up by human praise; another is enriched with virtues and yet is not honored by human beings; another is honored by human beings and yet is not enriched with virtues. A person is said to have simple humility when he is neither subject to vices nor supported by an abundance of virtues from which he might grow proud, and does not prefer himself to anyone in the matters in which he excels. But when humility is either honored or despised by human beings, it is severely assailed; for human praise, although not sought, nonetheless delights when offered, while reproach, although it is sometimes not feared when absent, nevertheless wounds the unwary when it is present. [Col. 0795C]

8. Nor do I think it should be passed over that the virtue of humility is called outstanding among the other virtues because the only Son of God especially displayed it in himself as an example to us, and by this virtue all the snares of the many-formed deceiver are avoided. When Antony saw all the snares of the enemy spread out against him and wondered who could escape them, he received this answer by a divine voice: “Humility alone.”

[Note: [Col. 0795D] In the *Lives of the Fathers*.]

Whoever you are, if you gather virtues without the virtue of humility, you are like someone carrying dust in the wind. But if you wish to display the height of virtue, do not think lofty thoughts, and then you will show that what you have done is more exalted. Do not think that you have accomplished anything when you have accomplished it, and you will have done all things most fully. Do not corrupt the fruits of your labors. Do not direct your course into emptiness, lest after a thousand circuits you lose the reward of your labor. For if you say that you deserve praise, you become blameworthy, even if previously praiseworthy; but if you confess yourself useless, you become useful, even if previously blameworthy. [Col. 0796A]

9. Therefore, if humility is present, it is necessary to preserve it; if it is absent, it is necessary to acquire it. Carefully consider not your good deeds but your evils, both hidden and public; attend also not to the evils but to the good deeds of others. And if these sometimes do not appear publicly, perhaps they are hidden privately—which it is charitable to suppose. Thus it usefully comes about that, by humbling yourself, you exalt another, just as, conversely, the proud person, considering his own goods, if he has any, and not his many evils, and also considering others’ evils rather than their good, both humbles others and exalts himself.

Therefore a certain forgetfulness of past virtues is necessary to us. I understand this to mean that we should never call any virtue of ours to mind. For the remembrance of virtues, when referred to the simple praise of God, is not merely not blameworthy but praiseworthy. Yet when your good deeds frequently become known to others, beware lest someone perhaps plunder them. This is what the Pharisee suffered in his speech, carrying his good deeds about, and therefore the devil seized them. For to praise God by reproaching others is not thanksgiving but merely the emptying of virtues. [Col. 0796B]

10. Let us therefore beware of saying anything boastful about ourselves, for this makes us hateful both to God and to human beings. Accordingly, the more good we have done, the more humbly we should speak of ourselves. When we have done any holy things, 540 we undoubtedly have God as our debtor; but when we judge that we have done nothing, we deserve still more by such a disposition than by the works which we have done. Thus the good of humility surpasses the merits of all virtues. If it is absent, those virtues cannot be praiseworthy; but if humility is present, the other virtues advance together with humility. This we show better if we add examples of the Fathers.

11. The centurion, humbling his heart before the Lord, said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. 8:8), and for that reason he became worthy. Likewise Paul says: “I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:9), and thus [Col. 0796D] he was found great before God and human beings.

Likewise the woman who humbly bent herself at the Lord’s feet was afterwards exalted by God, so that she was admitted both to anoint the Lord’s head and to be the herald of the Lord’s resurrection to the apostles, and therefore the apostle of the apostles. Likewise David, when he danced naked before the ark of the Lord and was despised by Michal, Saul’s daughter, displayed an appearance of humility in his clothing and preserved the virtue of humility in his heart. He made it known to us also by his humble words when he said: “I will play, and I will become more lowly than I have become, and I shall be humble in my own eyes” (2 Sam. 6:22).

But his humility appeared outstanding in this: though he was a most valiant soldier and was to be king, he did not compare himself to a soldier but to a flea and a dog—not a living one but a dead one—when he spoke thus to King Saul: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? One flea and a dead dog” (1 Sam. 24:15). [Col. 0797A] He was therefore transferred from servitude to kingship by the merit of his humility.

Likewise the tax collector, praying in the temple and condemned by the Pharisee, did not dare, while his accusing conscience reproached his heart, to raise his eyes to heaven; but striking his breast he said: “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13). Therefore he went down from the temple more justified than the Pharisee. Likewise Peter, though he was chief of the apostles, was the humblest of all. Thus he had such great merit before God that, when the shadow of his body fell upon them, the sick were healed (Acts [Col. 0797B] 5:15).

12. Likewise John the Baptist, though he had been announced by an angel and filled with the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb, and though before he was born he perceived the Lord’s coming in the office of forerunner; and though, when already a young man, he was a despiser of the world and dweller in the wilderness, rough in dress, singular in abstinence, an outstanding preacher, the Lord’s Baptist, red with martyrdom, white with virginity; and though, after the Virgin’s Son and the Virgin Mother, he was chosen from among thousands—so that the people even thought that he himself was Christ—yet, though he was such and so great, he chose to stand firmly within himself lest vain glory carry him away above himself.

For he confessed and did not deny; he confessed: “I am not the Christ” (John 1:20). But because he humbly confessed the truth, he rose to a still more perfect degree of humility. For he said: “One stronger than I comes after me, and I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Luke 3:16). If this is understood simply according to the letter, his humility appears sufficiently admirable. But according to the spiritual sense it is explained thus. By the Lord’s sandal the Lord’s incarnation is understood, just as the Lord says through the Psalmist: “I shall stretch out my sandal into Idumea” (Ps. 107:10); that is, “I shall appear incarnate in the world.” This came to pass, and thereby foreigners were made subject to him. [Col. 0797C]

John, moreover, confessed himself unworthy to loosen the strap of the Lord’s sandal—that is, to disclose the mysteries of his Incarnation. In this his humility is believed to have been so great that he placed himself below every priest, whose office it is to disclose to others the mysteries of the Incarnation. And because among those born of women none was found humbler than John, neither was any found greater. John therefore safely hid his manifold treasure of virtues in the pit of humility. [Col. 0797D]

13. Likewise Mary, whom we call the star of the sea, although born of royal lineage, the pattern of every virtue, both lady and mother of human beings, queen of angels, fruitful virgin of virgins, divinely endowed, and without an equal before or after—for she was the temple of the Lord and sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, chosen by the splendor of the Father’s glory—though she was such and so great, did not exalt herself because of heavenly gifts. Rather, she took care to show to human beings the humility which she had shown to the archangel Gabriel, when, carrying both Lord and man in her womb, she humbly rendered the service of a servant to her kinswoman Elizabeth, an elderly woman, as though she were a young virgin. [Col. 0798A]

Although she was humble and a virgin, the Lord is said to have regarded not her virginity but her humility. “My spirit has rejoiced,” she says, “in the Lord God my Savior, because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:47–48). O humility, by which a woman became the Mother of God; by which God descended from heaven to earth; by which souls were transferred from hell to heaven. This is the ladder set before you by God, by which one ascends from earth to heaven. By it our fathers ascended, and by it we too must ascend; otherwise we shall not ascend. [Col. 0798B]

14. But it must not be passed over how the degrees of humility are arranged in the Rule of St Benedict. He says that fear belongs to the first degree of humility; not loving one’s own will to the second; obedience to the third; patience in obedience to the fourth; revealing one’s thoughts to one’s father to the fifth; being content with every lowliness and extremity, and judging oneself an unworthy workman for all tasks imposed, to the sixth; not only declaring with the tongue but believing also in the heart that one is inferior and more contemptible than all, to the seventh; doing nothing except according to the common rule of the monastery and the examples of one’s elders, to the eighth; restraining the tongue in silence until questioned, to the ninth; not being ready to laugh, to the tenth; speaking, when one does speak, quietly and humbly, with seriousness, using few and reasonable words, to the eleventh; and, in the twelfth, not only being humble in heart but showing humility itself outwardly by suitable signs to those who see, as an example, in the plainness of clothing and simplicity of countenance (ch. 7). [Col. 0798C]

15. But though humility is distinguished in many ways, in my view humility is one; it grows in many ways according to inward and outward effects. Just as one and the same person passes through various ages, from infancy to childhood, from childhood to youth, and thence to old age—he is one person, not several people, but one—[Col. 0798D] so from one root of a tree proceed the trunk, from the trunk branches, from branches flowers and leaves, and then fruit. Thus from the one root of humility proceed good works, as branches; the garb of poverty and religious words, as flowers and leaves; then joy in the Holy Spirit, as the fruit of a good tree.

Therefore, if I judge rightly, the virtue of humility is in the heart, the appearance of humility in the mouth, the labor of humility in work, and the fruit of humility here and in its attainment. For God gives grace for grace: in the present the Lord rests upon the humble and quiet person; and the humbler each person is on this earth, the more glorious he will be established in the kingdom. We have said these things about humility for novices, so that they may know that humility is the foundation [Col. 0799A] upon which the other virtues must be built.

## PART TWO. ON OBEDIENCE

16. Therefore, because obedience, the sister of humility, inseparably accompanies it, let us say something about obedience. But the good of obedience is shown more clearly by the evil of disobedience: for as disobedience increases in evil, so obedience increases in good. Disobedience embraces every evil. Disobedience made an angel into the devil, expelled the first parents from paradise, and afterward handed innumerable persons over to hell; it empties out good things, multiplies evils, and fashions an idol in the heart. To refuse assent is the crime of idolatry.

But what sort of sin it is, and how great, may clearly be considered in the first parent. God, then, having placed the human being in the paradise of delight and granted him many and excellent fruits of various kinds for food, forbade only the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. [Col. 0799B] It is certain, however, that that tree was not harmful as food; for he who had made all things very good had not established anything evil in paradise. But in order that the human being, made good, might grow through the better merit of obedience, it was fitting that he be forbidden even something good, so that what he did might more truly be a virtue insofar as, abstaining even from a good thing, he submitted himself more humbly to his Creator, and obedience itself might be the virtue by which he deserved his Lord.

I can most truly say that this alone is the virtue of every rational creature living under God’s power; and that the first [Col. 0799C] and greatest vice leading to ruin is for a human being to wish to use his own power, the name of which vice is disobedience. There would have been no means by which he might think and perceive that he had the Lord as his Lord unless something were commanded him.

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil, from which Adam was forbidden to eat, signifies in us the middle part of the soul, that is, its ordered integrity. It is said to be planted as a tree in the middle of paradise and is called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil because, if the soul which ought to stretch itself toward the things before it—that is, toward God—and forget the things behind, should turn toward itself after abandoning God, and should wish to enjoy its own power without God, and if the punishment of its sin should follow, it will immediately learn by experience the difference between the good it abandoned and the evil into which it fell. This will be, for it, to have tasted of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. [Col. 0799D]

17. Adam’s sin, however, was most grave because, “although he was in honor, he did not understand” (Ps. 48:13, 21). That is, though he had been created in the image and likeness of God, he did not wish to remain obedient, but listened to the voice of his wife rather than to God’s. Having seen the sin of the apostate angel and the punishment of that same sin—namely, that an angel had been made into the devil—his heart blinded by pride, he too set his seat in the north so as to be like the Most High.

His place had indeed been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion; but because he willingly lost peace, he was compelled unwillingly to feel manifold pains. For he went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, [Col. 0800A] who also stripped him and, having inflicted wounds, went away leaving him half-dead. For he who abandoned the vision of peace learned by experience the decay of this world. The robbers, that is, evil spirits, stripped him of the garment of immortality. He was grievously wounded because he sinned grievously; but he was left half-dead, because in sinning he was, as it were, dead, and because he did not lose reason, life, as it were, remained.

His sin was most grave because neither necessity, nor his own weakness, nor ignorance of the good compelled him to sin. Ignorance did not compel him, since not many things but only one had been commanded him; and again, seeing God face to face, he could not fail in memory. Nor did weakness compel him, since he possessed free will—not weakened as it was afterward, but strengthened by the illumination of the Holy Spirit—and thus so confirmed by God’s grace that he would not sin if he did not wish to sin. [Col. 0800B] Nor again did want compel him, because he was afflicted neither by hunger nor thirst nor any other misery. If he wished to eat any fruit in order to forestall the troubles of suffering, there were various fruits in paradise which he was free to eat. One fruit met hunger, another thirst, another other sufferings. Although all these were set before him as though forbidden, he desired the fruit forbidden to him by the Lord’s word as though he had been commanded to eat it. Therefore, because by will alone he withdrew from his Creator, and all his descendants were killed by this plague, he sinned most grievously.

[Col. 0800C] 18. It should also be noted that, as blessed Augustine testifies in the *Enchiridion*, many criminal sins are comprised in this sin. In knowingly raising himself against God, Adam committed great pride; in desiring more than was sufficient for him, he committed avarice. For avarice concerns not money alone but also exaltation. In casting himself into death, he committed murder; in loving himself and thereby alienating himself from love of the heavenly bridegroom, he incurred the crime of adultery; in appropriating forbidden food, he committed theft; and in not believing God, he committed sacrilege (*Enchiridion*, ch. 45, §13). These and similar things are found in us also when we knowingly act against obedience.

19. O dreadful evil of disobedience! For everyone who, while his own conscience accuses him, acts against obedience, so far as he is concerned wishes to be subject neither to God nor to man, but, desiring likeness to God, commits robbery. Just as God’s will is unconquered and subject to no one, so such a person wishes to be conquered by no one and voluntarily subject to no one, because he is not subject even to God. [Col. 0800D] Therefore, since he does not wish to be subject to God and it is certain that he cannot be God, he wishes either to make himself equal to God or to rule over him: the former is evil, the latter worse; both are utterly foolish.

How grave the fault of disobedience is, not only in greater but also in lesser offenses, is easily understood. Because Jonathan, even without knowing his father’s command, tasted a little honey on the day when Saul had forbidden everyone to eat, divine grace was withdrawn by God, so that victory was then wholly interrupted. A penalty so severe followed that fault that Jonathan would have died without reprieve unless he had been delivered by the prayers of the entire people (1 Sam. 14). [Col. 0801A]

We also read that one of the prophets had received a command from God not to eat until he returned from the place to which he had been sent. But another prophet came to him, saying that the Lord had appeared to him and had shown that he ought to eat by the Lord’s command. Deceived by these words, the prophet believed and ate; and in the very matter in which he thought that he was obeying, he was disobedient. Such a punishment followed the fault of this disobedience that a lion killed him on the road. Yet in death the sin of disobedience was absolved, as is indicated by the fact that the lion which had slain the prophet afterward did not dare touch either his corpse or his donkey (3 Kings 13). [Col. 0801B] If, then, the offense is so grave when disobedience occurs through ignorance, how horribly does the person sin who, while conscience accuses him, despises obedience? Thus, as was said above, the greatness of obedience’s good is plainly understood through the evil of disobedience.

20. Let us now describe obedience simply, briefly adding its divisions, the things that hinder it, the things that assist it, its character, dignity, perfection, and merit. Obedience, then, is the virtue by which a person, setting aside his own will, embraces in mind the commands imposed upon him for fulfilment in action—unless an insuperable cause prevents it, [Col. 0801C] or the authority of the superior forbids the very thing it had commanded.

One kind of obedience is perfect, another imperfect. Imperfect obedience is that which does not reach the limit of death. Perfect obedience is not consumed by death, but brought to completion by it.

Again, one obedience is of great merit, another of little merit, and another of no merit, although it may appear to be obedience. It is of great merit when, as blessed Gregory explains (Morals, book XXXV, ch. 10), obedience has something of its own in adversities—that is, when it embraces adversities out of desire. It is of little merit when someone obeys unwillingly amid adversities. Obedience in prosperity has no merit when the obedient person’s mind longs for that same prosperity.

Again, one obedience is mercenary, another servile, another filial. [Col. 0801D] Mercenary obedience looks toward any temporal advantage or worldly glory. Servile obedience is done from any fear that is not chaste. Filial obedience looks to charity alone. Filial obedience is very good; servile obedience neither suffices for salvation nor is very evil; mercenary obedience is very evil—especially that by which a person fraudulently strives to attain the summit of prelacy, so that one who, while subject, displays signs of humility, when set over others maliciously displays the horns of pride.

Again, we who are subject ought to render obedience: first to God, then to superiors, and afterward to one another. To God, by necessity; to superiors, by authority, because we have voluntarily subjected ourselves to them; and to one another, by charity.

21. Again, obedience is our guide to the virtues, our guide [Col. 0802A] to wisdom, our guide to martyrdom, our guide to our homeland. It is a guide to the virtues, I say, according to Gregory’s words: “Obedience alone implants the other virtues in the mind, and preserves them once implanted” (ibid.). Elsewhere he says that obedience possesses the merit of faith, without which every person is proved unbelieving, even if he appears to be faithful.

It is a guide to wisdom, according to the saying: “Do you desire wisdom? Keep the commandments” (Ecclus. 1:33). It is a guide to martyrdom, because one who truly wishes to be perfectly obedient must endure the gravest sufferings of heart and body. Yet we have great consolation, because if we suffer with Christ, we shall reign with him; and because, according to the [544] multitude of our sorrows, God’s consolations will gladden our souls. And just as the sons of Jonadab, because of the obedience [Col. 0802B] which they had shown to their father—namely, by not drinking wine and by dwelling in tents—deserved a blessing from the Lord (Jer. 35), so all who show perfect obedience to their superiors deserve a blessing from the Lord, indeed a threefold one. The first is the blessing of virtues, according to the Psalmist: “You will multiply strength in my soul” (Ps. 137:3). The second is that the soul, on leaving the body, may immediately pass into rest. The third is that, in the resurrection of the righteous, every son of obedience may receive two robes, according to what is written: “In their land they shall possess double” (Isa. 61:7).

Moreover, true obedience is accompanied by charity, simplicity, and concord. This is figuratively suggested to us by the fact that, after Job recovered from his affliction, each of his friends offered him [Col. 0802C] one golden earring and one sheep (Job 42:11). But what is signified by the earring, a golden ornament, if not obedience? What by the sheep, if not simplicity? And why a golden earring, except because gold signifies charity, without which obedience ought not to exist? Why is one earring and one sheep mentioned, except because unity, by the bond of concord, is joined to charity and simplicity? For all our affairs ought to be governed by such concord that, through our fault, the scandal of division may not arise in the Church.

22. Moreover, love of the world and private love greatly hinder obedience; and obedience is greatly strengthened if a person despises the world and himself. These, however, are the characteristics of obedience: that the subject obey not fearfully, not lukewarmly, not with the speech of one unwilling; that he obey without delay and unto death. This is the perfection of obedience, on account of which perfection it is said: “Unto death.” For one person remains obedient as far as verbal insults, another as far as loss of possessions; another as far as bodily sufferings, another as far as death. This one alone attains the perfection of obedience.

And it should be noted that we are commanded to preserve obedience unto death. Therefore, lest obedience should seem burdensome to us until the end of this present life, our Redeemer became obedient unto death. What wonder, then, if sinful man subjects himself to obedience during this life’s brief span, when he who [Col. 0803A] rewards the obedient did not leave it aside? Nor should this be passed over: to our first parents it was said, “Eat of every tree of paradise; but do not touch the tree of the knowledge of good and evil” (Gen. 2:16–17). For one who forbids subjects one particular good must grant many things, lest the obedient mind perish altogether if it fasts after being repulsed from every good. He granted all the trees of paradise for food when he prohibited one, so that he might the more easily restrain from one his creature, whom he did not wish to destroy, the more broadly he granted access to all the rest.

23. What was said above (no. 20)—that the obedient person ought to endure adversities not only by command but also out of his own desire, whereas in prosperity he ought to have nothing at all of his own—we can truly affirm if we bring Moses and Paul forward as examples.

For Moses, when he was tending sheep in the wilderness, was called by the Lord speaking through an angel in fire, and commanded to preside over the whole multitude of Israelites. But because he was humble in his own mind, he immediately dreaded the glory of so great a rule which was offered to him, and quickly had recourse to the defence of his weakness, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither yesterday nor the day before yesterday, since you began to speak to your servant; I have become slow and impeded of tongue.” Setting himself aside, he asked for another, saying: “Send whom you will send” (Exod. 4:10, 13). Behold: he speaks with the author of speech, and, lest he undertake the authority of so great a government, pleads that he is without speech.

Paul, however, says: “I am prepared not only to be bound but also to die in [Col. 0803C] Jerusalem for the name of Jesus” (Acts 21:13); “nor do I make my life more precious than myself” (Acts 20:24). Thus, as he travels to Jerusalem, he recognizes adversities, and yet freely seeks them. He hears what he might fear, but longs for it more ardently. Moses, therefore, has nothing of his own in regard to prosperity, because he resists with prayers lest he be set over the Israelite people. Paul is brought [545] even to adversities by his own desire, because he receives knowledge of the evils threatening him, yet through the devotion of his spirit burns even for harsher things. The former wished, though the Lord commanded, to decline the glory of present authority; the latter, as the Lord disposed, strove through hardships and rough ways to hasten toward more grievous things.

By the example of these preceding men, therefore, we are profitably instructed that, if we truly strive to grasp the palm of obedience, we should serve amid this world’s prosperities from command alone, but amid adversities from devotion.

24. And it should be noted that, so far as can be gathered from human reasoning, just as no evils ought to be imposed by superiors under command, so neither ought all goods, but intermediate goods—those which are, as it were, given us by the Lord within our own power; for example, reading, writing, speaking, keeping silence, working, resting, and the like. Yet, as has been said, not all goods are to be commanded. For who would dare to command, by obedience, the abandonment of all things, a vow of virginity, remaining in virginity, loving an enemy, or dying for one’s neighbour? Although, if anyone has faith like a grain of mustard seed, he can and ought even to embrace things which seem impossible [Col. 0804A] according to human reasoning, if they are commanded him by a superior. For many saints, transcending human reasoning by faith, walked upon water and removed mountains from their places.

25. It remains now to show what is the dignity of obedience. The dignity of obedience is most like God. Whoever simply preserves charity in his conduct possesses the likeness of God. But whoever, together with charity, diligently applies himself to fasts, vigils, and the other labours of virtue is more like God. Yet whoever, together with all these things, binds himself under another’s authority by the bond of obedience, depends in every respect upon the will and command of his master, and keeps obedience unto death, is most like God.

The merit of obedience will be life in the kingdom; and there each person will be established the more highly, the more perfectly he has remained here in obedience. Those especially deserve to be exalted by God who preserve the virginity of obedience unto death. By the virginity of obedience we mean obedience’s incorruptibility: namely, when a person, from the time he has subjected himself to a master, has never at any hour been disobedient either in deed or in will. And just as, in the kingdom of life, all who remained virgins in body and spirit but did not preserve the virginity of obedience will sing a new song to the Lamb, though not the song of obedience’s virginity, so conversely all who remained in the virginity of obedience but did not preserve virginity of body and spirit, although they will not sing the song of virgins, will nevertheless sing the song of the virginity [Col. 0804C] of obedience before the Lord and the Lamb.

26. Great, then, is the virtue of obedience, which in some manner makes virgins out of the corrupt. This virtue leads Christ’s soldiers through fire and water, so that they may pass into refreshment; it tests them, makes those whom it has tested perfect, and, because perfect, victorious. “For an obedient man speaks victories” (Prov. 21:28). For whenever something harsh and difficult is commanded an obedient person, if he slays himself with the sword of command and sacrifices himself to the Lord, he speaks a great victory, because he conquers himself. For obedience is much better than sacrifices (Ecclus. 4:17), because in sacrifice another’s flesh is slain, whereas by obedience one’s own [Col. 0804D] will is slain.

The obedient man prays cheerfully and confidently, because, as blessed Augustine says: “One prayer of an obedient person is better than ten thousand prayers of one who despises obedience” (On the Work of Monks, ch. 17, no. 25). Obedience directs prayer to heaven; without obedience, prayer does not ascend to the Lord, just as a stone thrown toward heaven does not reach it.

The obedient man is confident like a lion. And just as the lion trusts not in the strength of others but in the strength of his own breast, nor fears an encounter with any beast, so the obedient man glories not in others’ prayer and life, but in his own conscience, according to the Apostle’s saying: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. 1:12); nor does he fear an encounter with evil beasts. For if the spirit of avarice, pride, [Col. 0805A] fornication, or any other evil spirit meets him and says, “Bow down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51:23), the virtue of obedience itself so strengthens him that he does not bend down, but passes on as victor.

Nor is this surprising. The virtue of obedience is the salvation of all the faithful; obedience [546] is the mother of all virtues; obedience is the discoverer of the kingdom of heaven; obedience opens heaven and raises man from the earth; obedience dwells with the angels; obedience is the food of all the saints. For by it the saints were weaned, and through it they came to perfection.

27. Again, there are other modes which seem to belong to obedience, although the truth of obedience is not in them. There are those who choose for themselves an unlearned master, not in order to obey him, but in order to be able to bend him according to their carnal [Col. 0805B] will; or they choose a learned man who lives carnally and carnally loves those who comply with him. Therefore, those who seem to obey in outward matters not in order to please the Lord but to nourish their own desires are rightly called Ishmaelites. For *Ishmaelite* is interpreted “obedient to himself.”

There is also an obedience arising from excessive simplicity, which we call foolishness, when someone strives to obey both in evil and in good, although it is written that evil should never be done through obedience, whereas good ought sometimes to be left undone. There is also an obedience which indiscreetly exceeds itself, when someone, deceived by excessive subtlety, decides which things his superior ought to command him and which he ought not. There is also a truncated obedience, when someone chooses a good thing for himself and asks that it be commanded him by his superior—which is plainly evil—but is broken by impatience when his superior refuses it. But if he humbly suggests to his superior the good which he desires and remains unmoved when it is refused, this is good.

Again, there is an obedience corrupted by the plague of pride and folly, descending from one’s own will, when someone considers within himself, concerning good things, which he would do if they were commanded him and which he would not. . . . And sometimes it happens that the superior never commands him to do those good things which he does not wish to do; nevertheless, because of the foolish deliberation and disobedience of his heart, he is held guilty of death before God.

This too should be noted: sometimes a master commands something discreetly, but the disciple does not assent in any way. Rather, as though about to give better counsel, he subjects his master’s will to his own will, whereas he ought to bend his own will and counsel beneath the will and command of his master. Thus he is led far from the path of obedience by a wandering error when he makes himself master and makes his master disciple.

28. Further, it should be observed that the subject ought to avoid his master’s errors in such a way as always to revere the master; lest he be so deceived either that, in revering the master, he imitates his errors, or that, in avoiding the errors, he disdains to be subject to the master. For while he examines his master’s acts or words with curious subtlety, he is deceived and does not know what sort of person he himself secretly is within. And while he refuses to consider his own evils, whether great or small, but considers his good qualities, if any; while he neither thinks well of his master’s hidden matters nor approves his evident goods, but gladly notices his evident evils, if any—while, I say, he does this, he both vainly exalts himself and maliciously depreciates his master.

Yet, considering his own sins, he confesses himself a sinner; nevertheless, he does not think that he has sinned so greatly as to deserve to be subject to such a master. As malice increases, he withholds a word of reply, and keeps silence more wickedly than he would speak wickedly. But this vice of disobedience is far from the children of obedience, whose endeavour is always to think humbly, speak humbly, obey humbly, and not reject the habit of humility.

We have set down these matters concerning obedience and its purpose simply, for the sake of simple children of obedience. [Col. 0806B] But since charity is the queen of humility and obedience, and all virtues ought to be directed to her rule, I wish, if I can, to give the novice brethren drink from the most abundant fountain of charity. But because fear introduces charity, entering in such a way as to go out, let us set forth some matters concerning fear.

[547] PART THREE: CONCERNING FEAR AND CHARITY

29. There is a certain natural fear, common to us with animals, arising from the nature of the flesh. For we fear things harmful to our bodies; we naturally avoid them and seek things conducive to health. Hence it is written: “No one ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it” (Eph. 5:29). This fear [Col. 0806C] is not sin, but the punishment of sin. It neither introduces charity nor expels charity once introduced, but is naturally in us whether we have charity or not.

Christ had this fear when he said: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26:38), in order thereby to show the reality of the manhood he had assumed and to strengthen by his example his elect, who would suffer the adversities of the world and death. And let no one wonder that one of the elect is shaken by fear, when Christ was sorrowful unto death.

30. But the fear which is the beginning of wisdom, and is called servile, is also believed to have been in Christ. Isaiah says of him: “He filled him with the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. 11). Hence the question rightly arises: since it is impious to deny that perfect charity, which casts out fear, was in Christ, how could perfect charity and servile fear coexist in him?

Various answers are given, though I do not know whether they are sufficient. It is said that he who, under no compelling necessity but voluntarily, assumed the other defects of our mortality also had this fear, since it is a gift of the Holy Spirit. Perfect charity, however, was in him: he had the one from his perfection, the other from our weakness.

Another explanation: when it is said, “He feared,” it should be understood as, “He neglected nothing”; the cause is put for the effect. For fear is the cause of this effect, that nothing be neglected. This exposition seems to agree with the words of blessed Gregory, who says: “To fear God is to omit none of the things that must be done” (*Morals*).

Another explanation: Christ truly feared, [Col. 0807A] but just as he is incomprehensible in himself, so he had an incomprehensible fear.

Another: Christ, who through his divinity knew all the torments of hell and beheld those who were being tortured in them and would be tortured, feared in his humanity and felt horror within himself; just as one of us, if he saw someone condemned to be tortured by a most severe punishment, would immediately shudder in the trembling of the flesh.

Another, according to Jerome: Christ had fear not in order to fear, but in order to give it; just as a healthy physician possesses medicine not in order to cure himself, since he is healthy, but to cure the sick.

31. Again, diverse fears arise in human beings. There is fear arising from a vice of the mind, when a person fears human beings more than God, lest he fail to obtain temporal things or lose things already gained. This fear does not introduce charity, but attacks it once introduced. There is also a blameworthy fear, when a person fears becoming contemptible—not in God’s sight, which is to be feared, but in human eyes, which is not to be feared. There is also a reprehensible fear, when death itself and bodily suffering are feared beyond measure. Therefore the Lord prayed three times, lest we succumb through the threefold temptation of fear.

Again, there is an evil fear concerned with hell alone, when a person fears neither God nor sinning, but burning; and withdraws for a time from the act of sinning, not from evil will, because he would wish to sin if he could do so without punishment. He does not love righteousness, but hates it. This fear is not called fear of the Lord, nor fear of correction, nor the beginning of wisdom.

32. [Col. 0807C] There is also another fear which looks to God: namely, when we fear the Lord himself because of his power, because he can cast soul and body into hell. The Lord commanded us to have this fear when he said: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather, fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell” (Matt. 10:28).

There is some force of charity in this fear, because it looks to the Lord and is God’s gift. But because it arises from his power, it has punishment and is called servile. Though it is good in its beginning, it is not perfect and does not suffice for salvation; nevertheless, through growing stages it is improved and so corrects a person that he has no desire to sin either in act [Col. 0807D] or in will, even if he is bound by invincible sins. This fear is called fear of the Lord, fear of correction, and wisdom.

From this fear, by means of virtues, we advance toward that fear which is said to remain for ever and ever (Ps. 18:10). And note that just as a woman has chaste fear—namely, lest her husband depart from her or she offend him in some respect—so fear of the Lord is called chaste when someone fears offending God and, through this, losing the grace he has received. Yet such chaste fear does not remain for ever and ever, since in the blessed life everyone will be certain that he neither will nor can offend God.

But the chaste fear which remains for ever and ever, if carefully considered, can be called love. For we love him for his own sake, looking not to punishments but beholding him, desiring him above all things, and adhering to him chastely. This chaste affection casts out fear. This is customarily understood not of the charity possessed in the present, but of the perfect charity that will be possessed in the future; and then fear is truly cast out—or, in the present, expelled through charity. For though natural fear is in a human being, when charity comes, one no longer serves from fear, as before, but for God himself.

33. Scripture commends the fear of the Lord in many ways.
