For example, it is written: “It shall be well with one who fears God at the end, and on the day of his death he shall be blessed”; “The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling peace and the fruit of salvation”; “The root [Col. 0808B] of wisdom is the fear of the Lord”; “The fear of the Lord is glorying, and a crown of rejoicing”; “The fear of the Lord will give joy in length of days”; and “The fear of the Lord expels and restrains vice, makes a person cautious and watchful; for one without fear cannot be justified, because where there is no fear, there is dissolution of life” (Ecclus. 1:11–29).

Elsewhere it is written: “Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts” (Ecclus. 2:20); “Fear the Lord [perhaps: serve the Lord] with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling” (Ps. 2:11); “Blessed is the person who is always fearful; but one who is hard of heart shall fall into evil” (Prov. 28:14); “Fear the Lord, all you his saints, for there is no want to those who fear him” (Ps. 33:10); “You who fear the Lord, wait for his mercy, and do not turn aside [Col. 0808C] from him, lest you fall”; “You who fear the Lord, love him, and your hearts shall be enlightened”; “You who fear the Lord, hope in him, and mercy shall come to you in delight”; “You who fear God, believe in him, and your reward shall not be made void” (Ecclus. 2:7–10); “No evils shall come upon one who fears the Lord, but in temptation he will preserve him from evils” (Ecclus. 33:1); “The spirit of those who fear God is sought, and in his regard it shall be blessed”; “One who fears the Lord will be troubled by nothing and will not be afraid, for he is his hope”; and “His capacity and strength have exalted his heart” (Ecclus. 34:14–20).

On this fear Ambrose says: “Let one who fears the Lord turn aside from error and direct his ways to the path of virtue.” Gregory says: “Unless a depraved mind is first overthrown through fear, it is not corrected from its habitual vices.” But amid these things it should be noted that God’s preceding grace sends us to a threefold reflection, arising from our transgressions: upon God’s future judgment and upon the fire of hell. This reflection, goading the mind by its timely importunity, sends us to fear, and fear in turn to charity.

These incidental remarks about fear have been made for charity’s sake. May charity itself teach us what should be thought concerning charity, what we are to set forth, and what its beginning, increase, and perfection are.

34. Let us say, then, that charity is spoken of in many senses. It is taken for a work of charity, as when people commonly say, “Giving alms is charity.” [Col. 0809A] This kind of charity, when it does not proceed from the affection of the mind, does not save. Charity also signifies God himself, as when it is said, “God is charity” (1 John 4:16). Charity also signifies the purified affection of the mind. Hence St Augustine gives this definition: “Charity is a movement of the mind to love oneself and one’s neighbour for God’s sake.”

It should be noted that when it is said, “Charity is a movement of the mind,” bodily movement is excluded. Although such movement may sometimes be a work of charity, it is not itself charity. And because the mind is moved to judge and to similar actions, “to love” is added; but because the mind is moved to [549] love the world, “God” is added. And lest anyone expect from the Lord a reward other than God himself, “for God’s sake” is rightly added. Again, because no one ought to love himself for his own sake, nor his neighbour for the neighbour’s sake, but for God’s sake, it is fittingly added: “oneself and one’s neighbour for God’s sake.”

Observe how rightly “for God’s sake” is specified. A human being does not exist through himself and is not good through himself; rather, he is from God and good through God. The same, I say, is true of an angel and of every creature. For God exists through himself and is good through himself. In him who exists through himself and is good through himself lies the end of our blessedness—therefore, in God alone. If a person loved himself for his own sake or his neighbour for the neighbour’s sake, he would establish the end of his blessedness not in God but in a creature, which would be impious. Thus beyond doubt a person would fall into misery, since neither he himself nor anything other than God could be his blessedness. Therefore everyone ought to love himself, not for his own sake but for God’s sake.

35. But because this charity cannot be evident or perfect unless proved by works—for the proof of love is the offering of a work—works done for God’s sake must follow. Hence it is said: “You shall love your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. 22:39), namely, for God’s sake: that is, so that God’s service may be fulfilled by him. Here “as” signifies likeness, not quantity: as you love yourself in order to serve God, so love your neighbour, that he may serve God and reign with God.

For I do not dare to judge it a sin if someone has less affection for another than for himself; but if it is equal, it is perfect. We also ought to provide those same neighbours with temporal and spiritual things: spiritual things, such as preaching and whatever is fitting for the spirit; bodily things, whatever we possess beyond necessity. We ought not to give our own goods to neighbours in a time of necessity; rather, we ought to share our necessities themselves. For blessed Gregory testifies thus: “He is proved to love his neighbour too little who, when necessity compels, does not share necessities.” And indeed charity prefers that two should be affected by tolerable want rather than that one should be tormented by intolerable misery. Nor is this surprising, because charity, which “does not seek its own,” gives help according to its means and wishes to do so beyond its means.

36. [Col. 0810A] It is customary to ask which comes first: love of God or love of neighbour. The matter is determined as follows. One love of God is beginning; another is nourished. A person indeed begins to love God before his neighbour; but because love of God cannot be perfected unless it is nourished and increased through love of neighbour, the neighbour must be loved. Thus love of God comes first as a beginning; it proceeds through love of neighbour, as being nourished by it.

This is the perfection of love of God: if a case of necessity arises, a person should die by whatever kind of death rather than transgress one of God’s least commandments. The perfection of love of neighbour is that a person love his enemy and lay down his life for his brethren. For thus it is written: “Love your enemies, do good [Col. 0810B] to those who hate you, pray for those who persecute and slander you” (Matt. 5:44); and elsewhere: “No one has greater charity than this, that one lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

37. Charity is therefore rightly called the mark by which the elect are distinguished from the reprobate. For they cannot be distinguished by faith, generosity in almsgiving, knowledge, devotion to fasts or vigils, or martyrdom; for these are common to elect and reprobate. Charity alone distinguishes the children of God from the children of hell, as the Lord says: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35).

Charity gathers the children of God and makes them dwell as one. “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132:1). [Col. 0810C] Elsewhere it is written: “Where charity and love are, there is the assembly of the saints. There is neither anger nor indignation, but firm charity for ever.” No virtue is strengthened without charity; indeed, it turns into sin. For the learned person without charity is foolish, while any unlearned person who has charity is very learned, as divine Scripture testifies. Whoever keeps charity in his conduct possesses both what is evident and what is hidden in the divine sayings.

Oh, what worthy account can I give of charity, which does not conceal knowledge from the ignorant, nor [550] fruit from those in need, nor deny medicine to the sick or protection to the healthy? By inward inspiration, charity calls the predestined, justifies those called, and glorifies the righteous. It rouses the slothful to fight, helps the fighter to conquer, and crowns the victor to reign. It touches the puffed-up learned person so that he may be humbled; it teaches the humble unlearned person so that he may be wise and exalted. It is gentle without flattery and severe without cruelty; it is weak with the weak and burns for those who are scandalized. It does great things and small things, so that it is never idle. It rejoices in confessors, delights in virgins, burns fervently in martyrs, and reigns in angels. In humble confessors it is fragrant like a violet; in devout virgins it buds like a lily; in holy martyrs it is red like roses; in blessed angels it shines like refined gold.

Oh, how sweet and health-giving is the bond of charity, in which, as blessed Augustine affirms, the poor person is rich, and without which the rich person is poor! Charity is temperate in prosperity, patient in adversity, most secure in temptation, most generous in hospitality, most joyful among true brethren, and most patient among false brethren. It is free in Paul to rebuke, humble in Peter to obey, humane in Christians to confess, divine in Christ to forgive.

38. Therefore charity, wondrous, beautiful, and best, teaches and acts. It teaches that what ought to be loved should always be loved; that what ought not to be loved should never be loved; that nothing which ought to be loved equally or less should be loved more in relation to this thing; that what ought to be loved less or more should not be loved equally; and that what ought to be loved equally or more should not be loved less.

Every person ought to love only four things: God, angels, himself, and other human beings. Other things, however, are not to be loved at all, but are to be used according to place and time; and in them the Creator is to be praised and admired according to their condition. [Col. 0811B] For example, God and one’s neighbour must always be loved, but sin must never be loved. Again, God is to be loved not less or equally in relation to anything else, but more. Neighbours are to be loved neither less nor more, but equally, although works of charity are not to be bestowed equally. Likewise, our bodies are to be loved neither more nor equally with our souls, but less.

39. Likewise, it teaches a person to rejoice with those who rejoice, to weep with those who weep, to abstain from what is unlawful, to rise above what is lawful, to give what is superfluous, to share what is necessary, to love an enemy, to die for one’s neighbor. Charity cleanses, enlightens, kindles, and strengthens the heart: it cleanses, I say, from the filth of sins; enlightens it for understanding; kindles it for love; strengthens it for action [Col. 0811C] and perseverance. Charity is the life of words and thoughts, the life of virtues and works; for if each of these does not spring from the root of charity, it does not live but is dead. Likewise, charity is the life of blessed souls and also the life of angels; for neither souls nor angels live except through the charity of God, by which they are nourished.

Likewise, charity is the death of crimes, the strength of combatants, the palm of victors; faith conceives it, hope runs toward it, and the advance of every good thing serves it. Charity is not whole unless brotherly love is maintained together with love of God; for one who is separated from the fellowship of brothers is deprived of participation in divine charity. Christ is God and man: therefore, one who hates man does not love the whole Christ [Col. 0811D]. Although some may appear to share in faith and good works, yet, because they lack brotherly love, they have no growth in virtue. For, as the Apostle says: “If I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but do not have charity, I have become like sounding brass or a tinkling cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries [Col. 0812A] and all knowledge, and have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions to feed the poor, and deliver my body so that I may be burned, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

For charity holds the primacy among all virtues, and is therefore called “the bond of perfection” (Col. 3:14), because all virtues are bound together by its bond. O how blessed is the virtue of charity, which embraces all, loves all, cherishes all; blots out sins, nourishes virtues; and, as it is written, restrains anger, excludes hatreds, drives out greed, restrains 551 quarrelling, and likewise puts every vice to flight! It is secure amid reproaches and pleasing amid anger; beneficent amid hatred, [Col. 0812B] steadfast in truth. It is not plundered by wicked assailants, stolen by thieves, burned by fire, or divided by heresy: it stands indivisible, remains unconquerable, perseveres unshaken, and rejoices incorruptibly.

Charity is the concord, merit, and fellowship of the elect. Charity is patient, because it is not broken in adversity; it is kind, because it bestows works of mercy upon friends and enemies. Charity is not jealous, because it loves another’s good as its own; it does not act perversely, because it is not led to a perverse deed; it is not puffed up, because no prosperity exalts it; it is not ambitious, because it does not wish to be preferred to others; it does not seek what is its own, because it prefers common things to private possessions, not private possessions to common things; it is not provoked, because [Col. 0812C] it is not stirred to anger, and not only does no harm in deed, but does not even think evil. It does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with truth; it bears all things in action for truth; believes all things that truth urges; hopes all things that truth promises; endures all things in the Head himself—that is, Christ. “Charity never fails” (1 Cor. 13:4–8), because, even if its works cease, charity itself nevertheless does not end either in this age or in the age to come. Or, charity does not fail in the elect because, even if an elect person sins grievously, charity nevertheless does not fail in him irreversibly.

Whoever preserves this virtue in his works receives a blessing, as Scripture affirms when it speaks thus to the people of Israel: “If you hear so as to do all his commandments, the Lord will make you higher [Col. 0812D] than all the nations that dwell upon the earth: blessed shall you be in the field, and blessed shall you be in the city; blessed shall be the fruit of your womb, and blessed the fruit of your land; the Lord shall send a blessing upon your storehouse and upon all the works of your hands” (Deut. 28:1–8).

[Col. 0811]

## EXPOSITION OF THE LORD’S PRAYER. (G)

[NOTE.]

552 It was published recently from the Library of Dunes. It is by the same author as the preceding Treatise, which is mentioned here in no. 3.

[Col. 0811D] 1. “Our Father.” There are seven petitions, just as there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit and seven virtues. Through [Col. 0812D] the petitions one comes to the gifts, through the gifts to the virtues, and through the virtues to the beatitudes. These petitions are distinguished [Col. 0813A] according to two lives, for one life is temporal and the other heavenly. One passes through the temporal to the heavenly, if the traveler uses temporal things well and rightly, so that he never clings to this world but is set free from it. The three lower petitions belong to temporal life, and the first three will be fulfilled in heavenly life. The middle one, however, although it concerns heavenly things, is fulfilled here, because spiritual bread is asked from God so that we may enjoy it in the present and be strengthened through it.

But before one comes to the petitions, an appeal for goodwill is placed first in the mouth of the person praying: “Our Father.” Each person is presented as praying together, not for himself but for the common salvation of humankind, so that the charity and unity of the Church may be signified, in which a brother desires his brother’s salvation as much as his own. He says, therefore, “Our [Col. 0813B] Father.” Since he calls him Father, he ought to be a son and not degenerate from so great a Father, who is Father in affection and goodwill. When we call him Father, we signify that we are no longer servants but sons; when we say “our,” we signify that he belongs to many, not to one alone. For he who naturally had one Son wished, through his grace, to add other sons by adoption as well.

Behold, he is the common Father of us all, by which we are admonished of brotherhood and of the same unanimity. Let not the rich man, nobleman, or lord applaud himself, since the poor, obscure, and enslaved man is likewise a son of God. Therefore we are all brothers. When it is said, “who art in heaven,” the one who is in the depths seems to pray that he may be able to ascend to his Father who is in heaven—that is, in immutability, eternity, and impassibility—[Col. 0813C] so that he may be with him immutable and impassible.

2. Having prefaced the appeal for goodwill, he comes to the petitions; but here they are ordered differently from the way in which they are fulfilled in human beings. For those petitions that will be fulfilled in the future are placed first, because they are more worthy; afterward come those pertaining to the present life, because they are less worthy. Thus Isaiah did, who set the more worthy gifts of the Holy Spirit first, descending to the lesser ones (Isa. 11:2–3); and Moses, who set the love of God before love of neighbor (Deut. 6:5), although the latter is later in time. Therefore, that we may better see their dignity and how one arises from another, let us first follow the natural order [Col. 0813D] in which they are fulfilled in us, and afterward return to this order.

3. The final petition is: “But deliver us from evil”; yet it is the first in us. For a person who wishes to ascend to heaven, seeing that he cannot otherwise ascend unless he is delivered from the evils of this world, cries out: “Deliver us from evil,” that is, from original and actual sin, and from desire for this world, so that I may be able to cast aside temporal things and myself, and become poor in spirit. All this comes about through the spirit of fear, as was explained more fully in the treatise *On the Virtues*.

“And lead us not into temptation.” Once all earthly things have been renounced, inward and outward temptations must press upon us. Gentleness is therefore necessary, so that a person may be gentle [Col. 0814A] and humble toward all who harm him, and be moved by no anger or resentment; this comes about through the spirit of piety. He does not pray that temptations may not occur, but that he may not be led into them. He is led into temptation who succumbs to temptation and is submerged in it.

“And forgive us our debts.” Although he has been delivered from evil, although he is not broken by temptations, he nevertheless cannot avoid offending God in many things; just as a ship passing through the sea takes in water through its cracks. Therefore mourning is necessary, by which sins are washed away. For those sins to be forgiven to him, he must forgive others and grieve over the miseries of this world; all this comes through the spirit of knowledge. Knowledge makes a person mourn when it makes him recognize how great is the misery of the present state; and, when sins have been recognized, it makes him cry out, [Col. 0814B] “Forgive us our debts,” that is, the sins for which we ought to mourn, “as we forgive our debtors.”

Debtors are those who owe us money and those who have done us some injury. If one owes money, forgive him if you are perfect; if you are imperfect, you may lawfully demand it back if he has the means to repay it; but if he does not, you must forgive it. If he has done an injury and humbled himself before you, forgive him; if he is unwilling, be ready to pardon and do what lies within your power. But what you do will profit him nothing unless he asks you; yet you have freed yourself.

4. “Give us today our daily bread.” The preceding three petitions belong to earthly life, because deliverance from evil, temptation, and mourning for [Col. 0814C] sins occur in the present, and this is called separation from the world. Now he passes to heavenly things, and first asks that heavenly bread may be given him, so that he may act well and be strengthened on the way, lest he fail. Bread is indeed sought from heaven, but so that it may be eaten here; thus this petition is the boundary from temporal to heavenly life, because a heavenly reality is requested to incline downward so that it may be possessed here in the present.

This bread is God, who feeds the angels. And just as bread eaten by a mother is turned into milk so that the child may enjoy it, so God, whom angels enjoy as he is, has been turned into milk for us, that we might be able to enjoy him. For he assumed a visible form in order to teach human beings, that at least in this manner we might recognize him. Therefore we always eat him under some form: in the sacrament of the altar, in the Scriptures, in the word of preaching, [Col. 0814D] and in all the ways by which he is revealed in us.

We also enjoy that bread when we feed upon earthly bread, so that, sustained, we may serve him more vigorously. Matthew calls this bread “supersubstantial” (Matt. 6:11), because it is above all substances; Luke calls it “daily” (Luke 11:3), because each day we eat it in one of the aforesaid 553 ways. “Today” denotes the present time. Through this bread we hunger and thirst for future righteousness; for present righteousness is imperfect and is, as it were, hunger. Of this hunger it is said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15); this is desire for heavenly righteousness, which is perfect. This bread is received through the gift of fortitude.

5. “May your will be done.” The three remaining petitions [Col. 0815A] cannot be fulfilled perfectly except in heaven. There are two wills in God. One is the will of mercy, which does not compel and takes nothing from free choice; by it he wills all human beings to be saved, although this lies in their free will. The other concerns the effects of things, of which it is said: “He has done all things whatsoever he willed” (Ps. 113:3). No one can resist this will: “For who has resisted his will?” (Rom. 9:19). This will always accords with providence; the other does not always do so.

For if, through mercy, he wills that someone wicked may become just and bestows his grace upon him, but that person resists through free choice and does not consent to God’s grace, the will of providence does not accord with this will; because, although God bestows it sweetly, he nevertheless knows that the person will not consent. [Col. 0815B] The will concerning effects, however, is of two kinds: one permitting, the other approving. The permitting will allows a person to do evil when he wishes; the approving will is that he does good when he wishes. Both are from justice. Thus human beings resist the will of justice with respect to its effects.

In Paul, however, God’s will seems compelling, but it is not; for although he was struck down, his will remained free to resist if he wished. In heaven all God’s wills are done, and no one there resists God’s will. But on earth many oppose God’s will, namely the will that springs from mercy; for although he would save even the wicked if they wished, they nevertheless oppose this will by their deeds. This person therefore prays that, just as God’s will is done in all the citizens of heaven, so he may make other earthly people such that they in no way [Col. 0815C] resist God’s will; and this is fulfilled in no one except in heavenly life.

Yet it is fulfilled in some manner in this life among the saints, though not in every respect, because no one can live without stain. “As in heaven and on earth” can be variously interpreted: “as in heaven,” that is, in Christ, in whom Deity dwells in the Lord’s human nature, and that man never opposed his will; “and on earth,” that is, in the Church, may it be done. Or: “as in heaven,” that is, among angels; so also “on earth,” that is, among human beings. Or: “as in heaven,” that is, in the soul of the righteous person; so also “on earth,” that is, in the flesh—so that the flesh may in no way oppose the spirit, but may agree with it in the same will. Or: “as in heaven,” that is, in holy men; so also “on earth,” that is, in sinners.

All this comes through the spirit of counsel, which gives us [Col. 0815D] good counsel by which we may attain this mercy, namely, that we may be merciful: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.”

6. “May your kingdom come.” After he has attained that mercy, so that he does not resist God’s will, he asks for the higher gift: namely, that he may see God clearly, with every cloud of phantasms removed. This will not be perfectly fulfilled except in the future. And although these things are not given in that order in heaven, they are nevertheless asked for according to the order of dignity; because, although they are not fully bestowed on earth, they are received in order by the saints on earth.

This petition is sixth because on the sixth day—that is, in the perfection signified by the number six—a human being was made in God’s image [Col. 0816A]; afterward that image was corrupted through sin. He now asks to be reformed into that same image, that is, into the same understanding, so that he may understand God openly. This image is called the kingdom of God, for to see the highest good 554 is the kingdom of heaven. The reformation of this image is the same as purity of heart; hence it is said: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:7–8). This is possessed to some extent in the present. This petition is fulfilled through the spirit of understanding.

7. “Hallowed be your name.” This is the seventh petition, beyond which there is none, and it fittingly follows the vision of God. For it would be little to see God unless one delighted in that vision. [Col. 0816B] This rest and delight were prefigured on the seventh day, on which God is said to have rested; hence it is also said: “He sanctified the Sabbath day” (Exod. 16:23), because in the future rest the faithful will truly be holy. This is the peace of which it is said: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9).

For when they are like God—immortal, impassible, incorruptible—moved by no disturbance but living in eternal peace, in which God is, then they will be sons of God, and indeed gods by participation. This person prays: “May your name be hallowed in us,” so that you may be called Father and we sons, and even gods; as though he said: Our holiness will not be ours, but yours in us; therefore may it be hallowed—that is, may your holiness come to be and appear in us, and may your holy name [Col. 0816C] appear in the dignity of your children.

This petition is fulfilled through the spirit of wisdom. Wisdom and understanding differ, as we can see among ourselves. Understanding among us is the very activity of investigating the Scriptures; wisdom, however, is the delight of knowledge, when we investigate nothing further, but already know, as it were, all things and delight in what is known. So in heaven, to understand is very much like seeing—not because there is any labor in heaven.

> [Note: [Col. 0815D] Something appears to be missing.]

Wisdom, however, is delighting in things known. Thus the person who is on earth ascends to heaven, and the seven petitions are fulfilled in this order. Now let us consider them according to the order in which they are arranged by descent.

8. Because the one who prays knew God to be Father reigning in heaven, he placed first [Col. 0816D] that petition which is nearest to that Father, concerning the peace by which human beings become sons of God. It is as though he said: “Our Father who art in heaven, grant that your name may be hallowed in us”; that is, grant that we may remain in heaven with you and become your sons. We cannot have that delight unless you reform in us the image that has been corrupted: “May your kingdom come.” Since that image and purity of heart cannot be restored until we consent to your will: “May your will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” And because we cannot obey God’s will in every respect unless we are strengthened by bread: “Give us today our daily bread.” And because we are unworthy of Christ’s body [Col. 0817A] as long as we are defiled by sins: therefore, “forgive us our debts,” and so forth.

But so that we may understand and be able to lament our sins, we must pray that the temptations of the enemy may not subject us to him; and therefore we must say: “And lead us not into temptation.” We cannot resist these temptations unless we renounce earthly things; therefore we must ask: “But deliver us from evil.” “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins; but if you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive your offenses [Col. 0818A] to you.”

Since he had set down a certain difficult condition—namely, “forgive us our debts, as we [forgive]” (Matt. 6:9–15), and so forth—he commends it, in order to invite us to it, as a medicine for our sins, saying that if we wish to forgive others the sins they have committed against us, God too will forgive ours; but if not, neither will he forgive ours. Note that he says “people,” and does not say “you people,” because those to whom forgiveness must be granted are sinners.

## VARIOUS SERMONS FOR CERTAIN FEASTS AND SUNDAYS OF THE YEAR

[Col. 0817]

555 AELRED, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX IN ENGLAND, OF THE CISTERCIAN ORDER: SERMON FOR THE ADVENT OF THE LORD, ON THE ELEVEN BURDENS OF ISAIAH

[Col. 0817B] 1. It is time, dearest brothers, that we sing mercy and judgment to the Lord. For it is the Advent of the Lord, of him who comes and who is to come, the Almighty (Rev. 1:8). But how will he come, or how does he come? Surely his voice says: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jer. 23:24). How then does he come to heaven or to earth, he who fills heaven and earth? Hear the Gospel: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him; and the world did not know him” (John 1:10). Thus he was both present and absent: present, because he was in the world; absent, because the world did not know him.

“He is not far from each one of us,” Paul says, “for in him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:27–28); and yet “salvation is far from sinners” (Ps. 118:155). Thus he is near in essence, far in grace. How is he not far off when he was neither recognized nor believed; neither feared nor loved? He was far from sinners: he neither called them back when wandering, nor raised them when fallen, nor redeemed them when captive, nor raised them when dead. He was far off, I say, when he did not give heavenly reward to the righteous or inflict eternal condemnation upon the wicked through manifest judgment.

Accordingly, he came so that he who was not recognized might be recognized; he who was not believed might be believed; he who was not feared might be feared; he who was not loved might be loved. Thus he who was essentially present came mercifully, so that his humanity might be recognized, his divinity believed, his power feared, and his kindness loved. His humanity appeared in his assumption of our weakness; his divinity in the working of miracles; his power in the overthrow of demons; his kindness in the reception of sinners. For it belonged to his humanity [Col. 0818B] that he hungered; to his divinity, that he satisfied five thousand men with five loaves. It belonged to his humanity that he slept on the sea; to his divinity, that he commanded the sea and the waves. It belonged to his humanity that he endured death; to his divinity, that he raised the dead. Likewise, it belonged to his power that he drove the Pharisees from the temple; to his kindness that he received tax collectors and sinners at a feast. It belonged to his power that he terrified demons; to his kindness that he absolved the adulterous woman. Finally, it belonged to his power that he struck to the ground those wishing to seize him; to his kindness that he restored his persecutor’s severed ear at once both to its place and to health. Since all these things belong to the first Advent, we say that they are to be ascribed to mercy.

2. Consider, then, what God is; and see what it is that laid aside such majesty, emptied such power, weakened such strength, humbled such height, and made such wisdom foolish. Was it human righteousness? Far from it! For “all have turned aside; together they have become useless; there is none who does good” (Ps. 13:3). What, then? Was it any need of his? Not at all, for “the earth and its fullness are his” (Ps. 23:1). Or perhaps did he need something from us? By no means; for “he is my God; he has no need of my goods” (Ps. 15:2). What then? [Col. 0819A] Truly, Lord, it was not my righteousness but your mercy; not your need but my necessity. For you said: “Mercy shall be built up in the heavens” (Ps. 88:3). Indeed, because misery abounded on earth, therefore at your first Advent “I will sing mercy to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1).

For it belonged to mercy that, made man, he took our infirmities upon himself; to mercy, that he confirmed faith in his divinity by miracles. Likewise it belonged to mercy that he uncovered for us the wiles of demons and rendered their power ineffective; to mercy, that he did not reject the touch of the prostitute, but approved her devotion. 556 Thus, that he showed himself humble in humanity, powerful in miracles, strong in the overthrow of demons, gentle in receiving sinners—everything came forth from the fountain of mercy, everything flowed from the depths of compassion. Therefore, at this your first Advent, I will sing mercy to you, O Lord. And fittingly, because “your mercy fills the earth” (Ps. 118:64).

3. Behold the oil at whose presence the yoke of our captivity rotted away, as holy Isaiah says: “On that day his burden shall be taken from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck, and the yoke shall rot away before the oil.” What is this day? What is this burden? What is this yoke? Hear what the same prophet says beforehand: “The Lord will raise up over him”—that is, over the king of the Assyrians—“a scourge like the blow of Midian at the rock of Oreb; and his rod over the sea, and he will raise it on the way of Egypt” (Isa. 10:26–27).

When, therefore, the devil—who is king [Col. 0819C] over all the children of pride (Job 41:25)—has been scourged and struck, the Lord raised his rod over the sea and raised it on the way of Egypt. The sea is the world; the rod is the cross; the way of Egypt is that broad and spacious way which leads to death. Thanks be to you, Lord Jesus, who raised your rod over the sea, casting down before your cross the pride of the world and subjecting principalities and powers to it. Truly, Lord, your cross presses down the waves of the world, calms tempests, and mitigates the storms of persecutions and temptations. You also raised it on the way of Egypt, so that, by blocking that broad way which leads to death, you might show the narrow and constricted way which leads to life.

Do you not know? Do you not feel it? Do you not experience it? The heat of desire burns in the flesh; sometimes anger rages fiercely [Col. 0819D] in the mind; words of indignation and bitterness burst forth; and, like a sea violently agitated by the wind, everything within a person is disturbed. But when Jesus raises his cross over this sea, all things are calmed, all things come to rest.

4. Moreover, dearest brothers, who led you into this way and narrow path of salvation except the example of the Lord’s cross and passion, which the Lord raised upon the way of Egypt? Rightly, on this day—that is, in the time of grace, the time of mercy, the time when the cross is raised, when the world is subjected to Christ, when the ruler of this world is cast out—on this day, I say, at this time, the burden shall be taken from your shoulder.

What burden? We read in the Scriptures of many kinds of burdens. For holy Isaiah describes for us eleven burdens in prophetic speech: 1, the burden of Babylon; 2, the burden of the Philistines; 3, the burden of Moab; 4, the burden of Damascus; 5, the burden of the desert sea; 6, the burden of Egypt; 7, the burden of Dumah; 8, the burden in Arabia; 9, the burden of the valley of vision; 10, the burden of Tyre; 11, the burden of the beasts of the south [Col. 0820A] (Isa. 13–23, 30). And what is a burden except a certain weight that presses down the soul and inclines it toward the earth, making it look toward lower things and neglect higher ones?

Sometimes such a burden comes to us from delight in the world, and this is the burden of Babylon; sometimes from the assault of unclean spirits, and this is the burden of the Philistines; sometimes from a certain natural and unavoidable necessity, and this is the burden of Moab; sometimes from the darkness of ignorance, and this is the burden of Egypt; sometimes from our inborn weakness, and this is the burden of Damascus; [Col. 0820B] sometimes from persecution by evil people, and this is the burden of the desert sea; sometimes from hidden distress of mind, and this is the burden of Dumah; sometimes from fear of death, and this is the burden in Arabia; sometimes from vanity when we make progress, and this is the burden of the valley of vision; sometimes from distress over what we endure, and this is the burden of Tyre; sometimes from charity when we desire to benefit others, and this is the burden of the beasts of the south.

5. The first burden, therefore, is that of Babylon, which must be taken from our shoulders. Babylon signifies the world, whose love is covetousness: thus it is a heavy burden pressing down many and bending them toward lower things. It burdens miserable people in three ways: by labor, fear, and grief. A person attains what he desires through labor; possesses it with fear; and loses it with grief. Come then, brothers: which king does not acquire what he desires with labor? Which king is so secure that he fears no one? Who does not lose something with grief?

But let us turn this parable upon ourselves. Does none of us groan beneath the weight of this burden? Have no worldly delights settled in us? What of the fact that those who have abandoned their own possessions are not afraid to seek those of others? For these they are exhausted by labors, tormented by griefs, and worn down by fears. Is even that person free from this burden who, though he brought nothing or little into the monastery, nevertheless does not cease to take things from the monastery in order to give whatever he can to others? He asks importunately; he grows angry if he does not receive; he grieves if corrected; he rages if publicly rebuked. [Col. 0820D]

What of those who are so bound by affection for their parents that they do not hesitate to undergo loss to their religious vocation and the greatest labors on their behalf, and for this reason even pass idle days and sleepless nights? What shall I say of those who seek honors? What burden do they not endure? Now they flatter, now they slander; now they rage at another’s advancement; now, frustrated in their own hope, they even rise up in curses against their own fathers. Thus, brothers, all these are conformed to this age. Hence they are designated by the name of Babylon, and are to be miserably crushed by that burden of punishment which the Prophet describes over Babylon.

6. The burden of the Philistines follows. Their name is interpreted “falling through drink,” and they signify those who, intoxicated with pride, fell from their heavenly dwelling. These burden miserable people, now through temptation, now through affliction. They burdened the Egyptians with many great plagues, as you have in the psalm: “He sent upon them the anger of his indignation, indignation and anger and tribulation, assaults through evil angels” (Ps. 77:49). They burdened the heart of Judas with avarice, the heart of the Pharisees with envy, and that of Pilate with folly. They burden the hearts of believers with many temptations, insulting the consenting soul and saying: “Bow down, that we may pass over” (Isa. 51:23).

7. The burden of Moab is added. Moab is interpreted “from the father.” It denotes that natural necessity which a father transmits to his son through generation: such as the unavoidable necessity of eating, drinking, and sleeping, and other things pertaining to the body’s necessary care. What a burden this is, dearest brothers, by which after the splendor of the sun we are forced to return to care for this flesh, as though to a foul-smelling corpse; and after the spiritual food of the mind, to provide the burdens of the belly! What a burden this is, which exacts from us every day the tribute of miserable servitude, and compels us to refill tomorrow the belly which we filled today and which has been emptied!

What shall I say? What a burden of anxieties and cares this necessity imposes on miserable mortals—so much so that the god of some people is their belly (Phil. 3:19), for whose sake—not, I say, for its pleasure, but for its burden—they regard justice itself and divine teaching as saleable! Such people, as the Apostle says, “do not serve the Lord Jesus Christ, but their own belly” (Rom. 16:18). What further burden they endure in the very discrimination of foods—desiring some and rejecting others—when some twist the belly, others weigh down the head, others obstruct the chest, and others oppress with so many corrupted humors! [Col. 0821C]

But what shall I say of those whom this necessity compels now to murmur, now to slander, and then even to quarrel? They are saddened if the food is too cheap, if the drink offered is less tasty, if it is prepared too slowly, or if it is attended to too negligently. Brothers of this sort, living according to carnal generation, may be called Moab; they are unhappily to be burdened with the weight of punishment which the prophet mentions in the burden of Moab.

8. Now the prophet adds the burden of Damascus. Damascus is interpreted “shedding blood,” and denotes the inborn corruption in us which in a certain way draws us to sin against our will and despite ourselves. This is the law in our members that wars against the law of our mind and leads us captive to the law of sin which is in our members. Every vital sensation in the body comes from blood; but vital perception in the soul comes from reason. And you know how the natural motion toward sin sometimes, in a kind of whirlpool of pleasure, almost swallows up reason’s very power and, so to speak, leaves it wholly bloodless.

But some feel it and do not consent; they are attacked but not conquered; burdened but not cast down. These indeed endure a burden from Damascus, but they are not Damascus. But the person who consents and presents his members to sin as weapons of iniquity is surely Damascus, shedding his own blood [Col. 0822A] and killing himself by his own hands. Such a one must know without doubt that he will be crushed by the weight of punishment described in the burden of Damascus.

9. The burden of Egypt is added. Egypt is interpreted “darkness.” Now there is darkness of ignorance, and there is darkness of iniquity. Come, brothers, this is no light burden that we bear from the blindness of our ignorance, not knowing in many matters what is expedient, what we should praise, what we should condemn; so that we often call evil good and good evil (Isa. 5:20). “For we do not know what we ought to pray for” (Rom. 8:26), and in the light of the Scriptures we walk gropingly as though by night.

Those who are such are burdened by Egypt; but they are not burdened together with Egypt, that is, with those who are Egypt and darkness, the children of darkness. Of them the Lord says in the Gospel: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3:20); and the Apostle says: “Those who sleep sleep at night, and those who are drunk are drunk at night” (1 Thess. 5:7). These indeed are weighed down by that burden of punishment by which the prophet teaches that Egypt is to be punished.

10. There follows the burden of the desert of the sea. The desert sea is the multitude of the reprobate, who, abandoned by God and separated from the number of the saints, oppress the holy Church by the weight of persecutions, though they themselves are afterwards to be punished by the weight of the penalties which the prophet denotes in this burden. Moreover, they are the sea who are shaken by diverse storms of passions and vices: always in motion and always wandering, never [Col. 0822C] stable, never remaining in the same state—now swollen with pride, now burning with anger; now sorrowful, now frivolous; now crushed by silence, now dissolved in laughter. They transgress the commands of their elders and disturb the peace of the brethren. Yet so long as they fear, so long as they grieve, so long as they admit correction and do not flee satisfaction, they are not a desert sea. But if, having come into the depth of evils, they become contemptuous; if, when corrected, they protest; if they answer nothing decent, nothing peaceable, nothing at all orderly, but, puffed up and inflated, rise even against the very person who corrects them with words of indignation, so that it becomes necessary to leave them to themselves—you should not hesitate to call them a desert sea. Woe to those who, abandoned by God and by men, are dismissed according to [Col. 0822D] the desires of their hearts, to go after their own devices! (Ps. 80:13.) To them too the Lord says through the prophet: “I will remove my jealousy from you, and I will no longer be angry” (Ezek. 16:42). You know, dearest brethren, what a heavy burden such people lay upon the shoulders of the saints. Under this burden the Prophet groaned when he said: “Sinners have built upon my back” (Ps. 128:3). Truly those of this kind build upon our back, loading us with their daily excesses: they add sin to sin, join contempt to contempt—insolent, proud, slanderous, hateful to God, disobedient to elders, and unwilling to live in harmony with their companions. Let such persons know that they will incur the weight of the sands contained in [Col. 0823A] the burden of the desert of the sea.

11. After this, the prophetic discourse describes the burden of Dumah. Dumah is interpreted “silence.” You know, brethren, that silence burdens many and rest weighs them down, so that, while they are silent and still, everything becomes burdensome: the head aches, the belly growls, the eyes grow dim, and the loins almost give way; but when they go out wandering here and there and talking, everything becomes pleasant, pains are forgotten, and each member is restored to its proper function. O how great is the power of the tongue, which clears the eyes, lightens the head, strengthens the loins, and braces weak knees! It makes one weak in labours tireless, patient under injuries, ready for a journey, prompt in obedience. Therefore, if you see [Col. 0823B] a monk sitting in the cloister, looking this way and that, yawning repeatedly, stretching hands and feet, now laying down a book, now taking it up again; finally, as though driven by certain spurs, running from place to place, from classroom to classroom—do not doubt that he is sighing beneath the burden of Dumah.

There is, moreover, another kind of silence which lays upon many the weight of eternal punishment. It is that silence which, arising from shame and confusion, obstructs the confession of sins or excludes forgiveness. The prophetic discourse does not fail to state what weight of punishment such silence deserves.

12. The prophet next adds the burden in Arabia. Arabia is interpreted “evening,” which is the end of day and the beginning of night: it fittingly signifies, I think, the hour of death, which lays no slight burden of fear upon nearly all mortals. For what human being escapes this burden, to which the Saviour voluntarily submitted himself as an example? For when death was imminent, he began, as the Evangelist says, to be afraid and distressed (Mark 14:33). The whole human race lives under this burden of fear, unless perhaps someone is such that blessed life after death is certain to him, and through longing for it he does not even feel the bitterness of death. Moreover, evening, which, as we have said, is the end of day and beginning of night, represents the fall of one who, after works of light, begins the works of darkness, whose latter state becomes worse than the former; such a person will certainly be crushed by the weight contained in this burden of Arabia.

[Col. 0823D] 13. There follows the burden of the valley of vision. “Vision” refers to contemplation; “valley,” to humility or abasement. For the contemplation of some is humble, and that of others is abased: humble in the saints, abased in philosophers. The saints, indeed, the more they advance, are wearied by the greater burden of vanity; and they raise themselves to higher things in such a way that they are sometimes drawn down, even unwillingly, to lower things. For if virtue advances, humility is preserved; if it weighs one down, it is vanity. You know, brethren, what a struggle the mind of one making progress must sustain: lest the favour of human praise creep in, lest flattery dissolve it, lest the heart swell with ambition.

But those to whom what is known of God is known, those who behold the invisible things of God through the things that have been made, “became vain [Col. 0824A] in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened,” and fell from the mountain of contemplation into the valley of error. Therefore “they changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed beasts, and serpents.” And if you wish to know what burden these deserve, hear what follows: “Therefore God gave them up to the desires of their hearts and to dishonourable passions, and God gave them up to a reprobate mind” (Rom. 1:19–28).

Likewise, those who turn knowledge of the Scriptures or heavenly doctrine to an improper end—for example, to human praise or temporal gain—are known to belong to the valley of vision: “knowledge” signifies vision, and “valley,” intention. What weight of punishment awaits all these, the prophetic [Col. 0824B] discourse declares.

14. In the next place is set the burden of Tyre, a name interpreted “narrowness,” whose burden lies in the bitterness of repentance, in the labour of continence, and in bodily sickness. What then? Is there no burden in bodily exercise or in observance of regular discipline? What of the labour of continence? What is more laborious, more difficult? What is guarded more precariously? What is more easily lost?

There is also a certain narrowness of heart produced by self-love; its opposite is the breadth of heart produced by love of God and neighbour. Self-love, however, proceeds from one’s own will. Therefore, one who loves his own will finds another’s will burdensome, and so seeks what is his own, [Col. 0824C] not what belongs to others. He is ready for everything which his own will suggests to him; for what is enjoined upon him he is sluggish and slow. Of such persons the Apostle says: “People will be lovers of themselves” (2 Tim. 3:2). They will certainly not escape the weight of punishment written in the burden of Tyre.

15. The final burden is that of the beasts of the south wind. The south wind, being a warm wind, signifies the Holy Spirit, as you have in the Song of Songs: “Let the north wind arise, and come, O south wind; breathe upon my garden” (Song 4:16). Blessed is the soul that is a beast of burden of this south wind, ruled by this bridle of moderation, and subject in all things to its will. Truly blessed is the soul over which the Holy Spirit presides, directing all its works, disposing its thoughts, ordering its impulses, and composing its habits. Of such persons it is written: “Wherever the impulse of the Spirit was, there they went, when they moved” (Ezek. 1:12). Of them the prophet says: “You made a way in the sea for your horses” (Hab. 3:15).

Paul was a beast of burden of this south wind, saying: “We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, 560 that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12). And see how the beast of the south wind is everywhere governed by the bridle of its rider. He is forbidden by the Spirit to preach in Asia (Acts 16:6); warned by the Spirit to visit Macedonia (Acts 20:1, 3); urged by the Spirit to proclaim the Gospel to the Athenians (Acts 17:16); and, bound in the Spirit, he hastens to Jerusalem (Acts 20:22). You see how the Holy Spirit, seated upon him as upon his beast of burden, now tightens the reins lest he go where he wishes, [Col. 0825A] now drives him with spurs that he may go where the Spirit wishes.

What do we think, my brethren? Do beasts of burden of this kind bear no load? But they are beasts of the south wind; therefore they are burdened by the south wind. “With what burden?” you ask. Hear the Apostle: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5). Let the Apostle himself say what a burden he bore in this love: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is caused to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11:29.) And again: “I have great sorrow and continual anguish for my brethren according to the flesh” (Rom. 9:2–3). Therefore he who is a beast of the south wind is burdened by another’s weakness, another’s iniquity, another’s need and perversity. The hunger of the poor is a burden; the oppression of the needy, [Col. 0825B] the misery of the sick, the temptation of one advancing, the cause of one failing. The distress of the people, the desolation of orphans, the groans of widows, and the affliction of captives had burdened him as well. Was not most blessed Paul, as though pressed by this burden, brought down from the secrets of heaven to the sickbed of the infirm?

But you also, brethren, who have fled from the north out of the midst of Babylon and now dwell in the land of the south wind, “bear one another’s burdens,” and thus, as a beast of the south wind, you will fulfil the law of Christ (Gal. 6:2). Certainly he is not a beast of the south wind who neglects to bear his brother’s burden—the infirmities both of character and of body—which we have mentioned in these burdens as best we could.

16. Moreover, brethren, by the beasts of the south wind we may understand those who receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0825C] not through merit but by reason of office, such as prophecy, healings, and other things of this kind. Those whom they ordain are ordained; those whom they curse are cursed; those whom they bless are blessed; those whom they bind are bound; and those whom they absolve are absolved—provided, however, that they do all this according to the laws of the Church, not according to the impulse of their own mind. Hence Balaam blessed the people of God (Num. 23–24); hence Caiaphas, though most wicked, prophesied (John 11:51); hence Judas, though most wicked, worked miracles like the other Apostles (Matt. 10:4, 8). Hence many will come on that day, saying, “Did we not prophesy in your name and perform many signs?” And then, the Lord says, “I will declare to them that I did not know you” (Matt. 7:22–23). Such persons are not to be called human beings, but beasts of burden, [Col. 0825D] since they do not serve the Lord Jesus Christ but their own belly, desire earthly things, and despise heavenly things. They will indeed be miserably punished by that burden which Isaiah terribly threatens against certain beasts of the south wind.

17. We have broken, as best we could, this barley bread; but because we broke it in haste, very many fragments have fallen from us. You, therefore, who have leisure, whom Christ has kept free from these occupations, gather up the fragments which remain, lest they perish. Let each person examine himself. Let him see both what burden he bears and what burden he ought to fear bearing in the future.

If he is under the burden of Babylon, let him detest and cast it away, lest, being conformed to her works, he not be exempt from her punishments. Under the burden of the Philistines, let him see that he is not made drunk by their potions, becoming like them in guilt and destined to be like them in punishment. But if he feels himself labouring under the burden of Moab, let him strive to indulge the body’s necessities in such a way that Nebuzaradan does not destroy the walls of Jerusalem (2 Kings 25:8–10), and not to satisfy them so that he burns with Moab eternally. But if the burden of Damascus presses upon his shoulder, let him beware lest he lay hands upon himself, and so, sowing in the flesh, reap corruption from the flesh.

Indeed, if the burden of Egypt rests upon him, let him cast off the works of darkness and put on the armour of light, lest, if he willingly delivers his mind here to inward darkness, he should someday unwillingly be tormented in outer darkness. Further, if the burden of the desert of the sea assails him with wicked persecutions, [Col. 0826B] let him not fail or be broken, lest what they inflict through malice he should suffer through impatience. If, however, the burden of Dumah—that is, silence—makes him impatient, or shame and confusion obstruct confession, let him beware the weight of punishment which the prophet threatens against those who are silent in this manner.

561 But if, pressed by the burden of Arabia, he fears death, let him remain according to nature, so that he may not fear it because of conscience; lest he be not only pressed by Arabia but also crushed, together with Arabia, by the burden of eternal condemnation. Moreover, if, sighing under the burden of the valley of vision, he struggles against vanity, let him beware lest he fall from the mountain of contemplation into the valley of error, to be overwhelmed by that very burden which the prophet describes in the burden of the valley of vision. But if, beneath the burden of Tyre, faintheartedness casts his mind down into despair because of present [Col. 0826C] labours and pains, let him beware above all the narrowness of his own will. Thus, with his heart enlarged, he may gladly pass through all the straits of this life and so escape the eternal weight of misery threatened against Tyre. Finally, if his affection fails from weariness under the burden of the beasts of the south wind, let him reflect and know that, if he throws off the burden of love, he will not undeservedly bear the burden of condemnation.

18. I also believe that the very order of the burdens is not without mystery; nor is the burden of Babylon put first, that of the Philistines second, and so on, without reason. For unless covetousness, known to be both the burden of Babylon and the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10), has first been driven from our hearts, we shall in no way be able either to avoid or conquer the other [Col. 0826D] burdens, or to advance to the summit of virtues. This expulsion of covetousness occurs either in those who wholly renounce the world, or in those who use this world as though they did not use it (1 Cor. 7:31), or as having nothing and yet possessing all things (2 Cor. 6:10).

Once covetousness has been conquered or excluded, our struggle is no longer against flesh and blood but against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in heavenly places (Eph. 6:12). But when he who does not allow us to be tempted beyond what we are able, but makes with the temptation a way of escape so that we may endure it (1 Cor. 10:13), has either lightened or removed this burden, the necessity of this [Col. 0827A] flesh will burden us—a necessity whose limits are as difficult to know as they are impossible to observe. Accordingly, once the fire has been conceived, natural impulses must trouble us and, unless resisted, drive us toward all kinds of unlawful acts.

But if, with the Philistines subdued, bodily necessity, like Moab, has been reduced within measure and temperance, and if one has thus overcome the impulses of the flesh, as it were the burden of Damascus, errors and blasphemies, like the darkness of Egypt, will immediately veil the eyes of the flesh, until darkness yields to the flashing light of wisdom; and immediately the desert sea—that is, the envy and malice of the perverse—will follow. When this ceases, though everything may seem quiet to him, rest itself cannot be quiet because of the spirit of acedia, as though beneath the burden of Dumah. Once that spirit has been expelled by steadfast labour, prayer, and reading, [Col. 0827B] the burden of Arabia—that is, fear of death—comes upon him. Yet when this too has been overcome through the strength of a good conscience and faith, vanity will burden him as one already near and approaching perfection [Col. 0828A]. If vanity is conquered by profound humility, nothing remains except that he be burdened by the needs of others, like a beast of the south wind.

19. Let these things said at present concerning the burdens suffice. Some of them Christ, in this time of grace, removes from our shoulders; some he moderates, some he lessens, and some he orders. He accomplishes all these things according to the abundance of his mercy, from whose presence, as from the face of oil, the yoke of diabolical domination has decayed. But let him who neglects the time of mercy fear the time of judgment, because he who redeemed us through mercy will judge through justice. Therefore, brethren, let us sing to the Lord of mercy and judgment: of mercy, which we experience; of judgment, which we await. Let us embrace the one and fear the other, so that we may be found devoted here and secure there, through the granting of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

[Col. 0827]

# Nicholas of Clairvaux: Three Sermons on the Nativity of the Lord

## Sermon I

[Note: [Col. 0827D] That some have wrongly attributed this sermon to Peter Damian is sufficiently evident from no. 3, since Peter Damian preceded Bernard by fifty years.]

On the words: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2).

[Col. 0827B]

1. The discourse which I have conceived in my mind cannot be unfolded. [Col. 0827C] For amazement at the miracles overwhelms me; and while I recount everything, everything becomes entangled. Who can conceive the day of his coming? Thus the tongue becomes speechless, memory forgetful, sense insensible. All things shine with an unfamiliar newness, and all things obey the Virgin’s childbirth. Wonders occur in heaven above and on earth below, because all things have sworn obedience to the God who is being born. The vault of heaven is marked by a brighter star, and places blazing with abundant light are struck through. More ruddy rays are poured over the fourfold world, and a new fire outshines the multitude of stars. The world marvels that the heavens have given birth to a new splendour and that their unchanging order has been changed into signs and wonders.

The Chaldeans see in heaven what Balaam left in the Scriptures: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel, and all the earth shall be his possession” (Num. 24:17–18). A star is born in the heights, and God on earth, whose possession extends from sea to sea. The kings of Tarshish prepare themselves, that with novel gifts they may behold a new Mother, a new Son, a new newness. A fountain of oil burst forth from the earth; the temple of Rome called the Eternal fell, wonderfully brought to completion at every expense of both city and world.

[Note: [Col. 0828D] This is refuted by Baronius in the *Annals*, at the beginning of volume I: that this temple was constructed by Vespasian long after Christ’s Nativity.]

For when the Romans, in memory of victorious antiquity, had resolved to make a temple of unique design, they asked the entire multitude of gods—or rather, demons—how long the laborious construction of so excellent a work might endure. The answer was: “Until a Virgin gives birth.” They, turning the oracle toward impossibility, called that solemn structure the Eternal Temple. But on the night when the virginal flower of Mary came forth from the virginal bridal chamber, that marvellous work of columns fell and was shattered so completely that scarcely any traces of its ruins appeared.

2. O Bethlehem, city of the most high God: in you and in your suburbs wonders have been seen today. God hangs at the breast, is laid in a manger, is bound in a cradle, wrapped in swaddling clothes; and, with the bands loosened, stretches out happy hands and holy little arms within the narrowness of the cradle. He plays with the Virgin, smiles upon his Mother, and turns his caressing eyes toward Mary. The Queen of heaven stands terrified by such great miracles, pondering in her heart the archangel’s greeting, the conception of God, and the birth of the child; and she marvels that he who could have come to us otherwise chose to help us in this manner.

Joseph too is present, though standing apart from both; in ecstasy of mind he marvels and cannot marvel enough at how he has been admitted into the mystery of such condescension. The multitude of the heavenly host is present; “Glory to God in the highest” is heard in glorious voices (Luke 2:14). The shepherds come and find the boy and the young woman; the star goes before, the kings approach, worship the Son, venerate the Mother, offer gifts, and render them to Majesty. Herod is tormented; Jerusalem is disturbed; the scribes are consulted; the place is foretold; deception is commanded; the deceiver is brought to nothing; the plots of fraud are uncovered; the Magi return by another way; peace unheard of from the beginning of the world reigns; the whole world is enrolled for the census; a stream of oil sweats forth from the earth, and the sanctified liquid boils up in a rich vein. What is this, except that true peace has appeared upon earth; except that citizens are enrolled for the heavenly kingdom; except that the fountain of mercy flows forth from the Virgin?

3. “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2). The Holy Spirit, the living author of Scripture itself, and a certain person have left beneath this heading no small sweetness of their richness. But you have been so wearied by the night watches that you can scarcely drive sleep from your eyes. Wake, nevertheless, for a little while and shake off the torpor of sleep: he of whose Nativity we speak will be present, that he may enlighten our eyes lest we fall asleep.

The entire meaning of this discourse will be borrowed from that treasury of him whose counsel is like the counsel of God: namely, that lord, the Abbot of Clairvaux, whose religious observance and discernment, wisdom, eloquence, life, and reputation deservedly extend throughout the whole Latin world. For I gladly take in the fragrance of his bundles. But let us return to the subject. That gracious Spirit, from whose more secret fountain the river of the Song of Songs flows, has left us in these three words three matters to investigate: namely, the name of the Bridegroom, why it is compared to oil, and how it is poured out—for he is silent about the name, says nothing of the comparison, and says nothing of the outpouring.

[Col. 0829C] 563 4. Let us first consider the name. Many names of the Bridegroom, I think, are scattered throughout divine Scripture; but I gather them all for you under two headings. You will find none, certainly, which does not sound either of the power of majesty or of the grace of loving-kindness. The servant of the Lord, whom I mention more frequently, having been introduced into the king’s chamber, heard two things, as it were more sublime, from the very mouth of divinity: “Power belongs to God,” he says, “and to you, Lord, mercy” (Ps. 61:12–13). The Saviour himself, attesting prophetic truth, says: “You call me Teacher and Lord” (John 13:13). “Lord” is a name of majesty; “teacher,” of loving-kindness. For if it is merciful to provide food for the body, it is much more merciful to impart food to the soul; and this is properly the work of teachers, who restrain disciplined minds under the rigour of discipline.

Let us see which of these names is poured out: whether the name of power into the name of grace, or the name of loving-kindness into the title of majesty. Far be it that mercy should be contained within power, for “his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9). It is certain, therefore, that today the power of God has been poured out into a greater loving-kindness, when the heavens distilled at the presence of God and the Ancient of Days arose from virginal members. No one can hide himself from this heat, for the more abundant outpouring of oil descended from the head into the beard and abundantly moistened even the lowest hem of the garment. So great is the abundance of the One who shows mercy that it is reckoned not only an outpouring but an emptying. “He emptied [Col. 0830A] himself,” says the Apostle, “taking the form of a servant on this day” (Phil. 2:7), and with the whole multitude of his mercies he sprang forth from the virginal chamber.

5. For that abyss of God’s counsels had no sweeter way of redeeming us, since whatever mercy is found in the treasury of divinity was all gathered into the Virgin’s womb. I cannot contain myself for joy that such majesty, assuming my nature, exalts me so greatly and receives miserable me into the riches of his glory, not for an hour but forever. My Lord becomes my brother, and affection for my brother overcomes fear of the Lord. Lord Jesus Christ, I gladly hear that you reign in heaven; more gladly, that you are born upon earth; most gladly, that you endure the cross, nails, and lance. This outpouring indeed carries away my affection; the memory of these things warms my heart, purified by the sharpness of the living and life-giving draught.

“This word is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the dividing of soul and spirit, and discerning also the joints and marrow” (Heb. 4:12). One of those belonging either to the prophetic choir or among its teachers marvellously, though subtly, prophesied about this outpouring under a sixfold division of divine names: “His name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9:6). My Lord was indeed wonderful among the angelic orders that hear the hymn of his glory; wonderful to that wonderful creature; performing wonders in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths. But I, wallowing in the mire of dregs and misery, miserable and pitiable, had lost every hope of rising again. He was in glory, I in misery; he wonderful, I miserable. How could I receive that holy and terrible name, shut up and whole, when the angelic eye can scarcely look toward it, much less look through it?

6. But see the outpouring. He who was wonderful to the hosts of angels bows the heavens and becomes the counsellor of human beings. The majestic name is poured out into a compassionate one: he who is wonderful in heaven comes to give counsel on earth, concealing purple beneath the garments of misery. He bends down to the mire where I lay, [Col. 0830D] yet is not immersed; and, if I dare say it, though I was fixed in the mud of the deep, he stretches out his right hand to the work of his hands. He draws me from the deep waters, washes the one drawn out, clothes the one washed, carries back the one clothed, and strengthens the one carried back. He stretches out his right hand when he is born; when he speaks, he draws out; he washes when he dies; clothes when he rises; carries back when he ascends; strengthens when he sends the Holy Spirit from heaven. A good counsellor indeed, who defends by his death the counsel he has given in speech. For, the Evangelist says, he taught as one having authority, not like their scribes and Pharisees (Mark 1:22).

“God” and “Mighty” are names of power; but God is poured out into “Father of the age to come,” and Mighty into “Prince of Peace.” I run through this briefly, because I speak to those who are both weary and acquainted with the law. What have you to do, muttering Lucifer, with such great flowing forth and outpouring? The whole itinerary of God is closed to you, and your malicious eye has become exceedingly dim here. Yet my Lord was Wonderful in his birth, Counsellor in his preaching, God in the radiance of miracles, Mighty in his Passion, Father of the age to come in his resurrection, and Prince of Peace in that eternal blessedness. Do not be alarmed by the novelty of the words, for nothing new is introduced. Names too were changed and poured out long ago: Abram into Abraham; Sarai into Sarah (Gen. 17:5, 15); and any other transformations which you remember reading in that ancient workshop.

7. I remember also finding, almost from the beginnings of the world, an outpouring of the divine name in a certain hidden place of Scripture. The Lord speaks to Moses concerning Israel’s deliverance; and after much conversation between God and Moses, the prophet subtly asks his name. The Lord says: “I am who I am; this is my name forever. Thus shall you say to the children of Israel: ‘He Who Is has sent me to you.’” Terrified by the authority of the inextricable title, Moses seems to say, “This surpasses my understanding; I cannot receive it unless it be poured out.” He hears from Majesty: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3:14–15). You see the outpouring: the God of angels calls himself the God of human beings.

Let us run, then, brethren, in the fragrance of these ointments; let us run to oil pressed from the beautiful olive tree in the fields, stained by no dregs and infected by no bitterness. This oil makes the human face glad, heals wounds, takes away pain, and restores sweetness. Did not our Samaritan bring wine and oil to us, wounded by that most wicked robber, in order to cleanse and soothe the greatness of the wound? But much oil, little wine: much mercy, little justice. For so it befitted the merciful One, and so it was advantageous for the miserable person. “Do not enter into judgment with your servant,” says the righteous man, “for no living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2); but crown me with mercy and compassions.

For today he came bringing five vessels of oil, but only two of wine. The Spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, knowledge, piety, sounds of sweetness, breathes mercy, and pours forth healing; strength and fear are wine. Yet that mighty one drank this wine when Christ, in the Spirit of strength, descended into hell—not fearful, but feared.

8. Let us now see why it is compared to oil. Oil, if you have nothing better, shines, nourishes, and anoints. Christ’s name does the same and accords in every respect with the comparison. When proclaimed, it shines; when remembered, it nourishes; when invoked, it soothes and anoints. See whether the most bright luminaries have not borne the light of this name upon the lampstand of eloquence; whether the flashes of God have not shone upon the world, and whether the earth has not been moved and trembled in the splendour of this radiance (Ps. [Col. 0832A] 76:19). “In the name of Jesus Christ, rise and walk,” says the Prince of the Apostles to the lame man. Did not a flash, as it were, leap from Peter’s mouth when the name was uttered—the name which the mouth of the Lord uttered? “And immediately,” it says, “his ankles and feet were strengthened” (Acts 3:6–7).

The name Jesus, as the more noble language of Origen defined it, is sweet and glorious, most worthy of every adoration and worship; it was fitting that it should not first be brought forth into the world by human beings, but by some loftier and more excellent nature. For all the Prophets either did not know this name or kept it wholly silent; and the dignity of that prerogative was reserved for the archangel Gabriel, who first disclosed it with holy mouth to the holy Virgin (Luke 1:31). Does not Isaiah, caught up in ecstasy of mind, agree with the archangelic words in almost the same syllables, even to the novelty of the holy name? (Isa. 7:14.)

It truly nourishes, and there is no happier feeding in the place of pasture where the Lord has set us. What equally fattens the mind that meditates? The name of Jesus is honey in the mouth, melody in the ear, jubilation in the heart. Every food not seasoned with this salt is tasteless. Scripture which has not been interlined with the oil of so great a devotion is insipid. Cicero once seemed sweet to me, Virgil was charming, and the Sirens—sweet even unto destruction—had enchanted my understanding. The Law, the Prophets, the Gospel, the Epistles, and all the glory of the sayings of my Lord and his servants seemed to me either slight [Col. 0832C] or nothing. Now I do not know what the son of Jesse murmurs more sweetly to me; by the varied harmony of words and thoughts he makes all those whom I was accustomed to love ineloquent and mute.

It soothes and anoints, because nothing refreshes so much in tribulation. Finally, it may also be proved: “Call upon me,” he says, “in tribulation; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49:15). This is the name; this is the oil; this is the outpouring of oil. Amen, I say to you: this flask of oil will not fail or diminish until, poured out, it rains down the voluntary rain reserved for his inheritance (Ps. 67:10), until it makes a new heaven and a new earth; for “his mercy is from everlasting unto everlasting upon those who fear him” (Ps. 102:17). But now let us rise and prepare ourselves for the rejoicing of the more solemn Mass, sparing neither hearts nor voices, in honour of the Child who has been born to us, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

## Sermon II

[Note: [Col. 0831] In volume III of the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis* it is entitled “On the Coming of the Lord,” etc.]

On the twofold generation of Christ.

1. Rejoice, brethren, in the Lord, because a discourse follows concerning that Sunday which claims a singular primacy in your hearts: the Sunday whose name you humbly honour by bowing, whose Hours you reverently attend, whose memorial you continually observe. It is that which sweetly delights your affections, because great is the multitude of its sweetness. For his Spirit is sweeter than honey; into it the Lord, with all his sweetness, comes in sweetly.

Though God made all his works very good, here he made something better, consecrating in her [Col. 0833A] a golden resting-place for himself, so that after the tumult of angels and human beings he might recline and find rest. This is what nature marvels at, the angel reveres, humanity fears, heaven is amazed by, earth trembles at, and hell shrinks from in horror. In her womb the majesty of the Most High, wonderfully liquefied, filled the earth as with fatness and richness, poured itself into heaven, and sprinkled the infernal regions.
