Here the lofty and immeasurable One emptied himself, casting into your bosom a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over. Here he was anointed by divine hands with the oil of gladness, and, like an altar, consecrated as the sign of priesthood. Ascending from this altar to the altar of the cross, soaked in his own blood as in an oil of another kind, now not consecrated but consecrating, he consecrated the whole body of the world’s fabric with a more abundant liquid.

Let grief therefore be rent asunder; let sadness flee; let pain be banished; let bitterness depart, so that we may be free to contemplate with Moses this great vision: how God is conceived in this womb; how the devil is deceived; how what was lost is received back; how what was not owed is received. My affection draws all of me, but speech fails. Rich thought is confounded by the poverty of speech. My inward parts burn and boil over into a wave-like depth, but the coldness of my tongue cools the overflowing billows. What is this, O most blessed one? Shall I sleep so silently in understanding that I am mute there where every creature speaks?

2. Nevertheless, I shall not be silent or rest until your countenance goes forth like brightness, and the word conceived concerning you [Col. 0833C] is kindled—if not as a lamp, at least as a spark. I confess that it moves me that, by God’s ordering, rational creatures sin, and that for so many thousands of years both heavenly and earthly things seem to stand in vain—the former half-ruined, the latter destroyed. That great city stands, robbed of the multitude of its citizens, while a manifold host of inhabitants is driven from its starry palaces. The fires of the stars—I mean sun, moon, and stars—are darkened and deprived of much of their bright radiance. The earth is cursed (Gen. 3:17) when the race of human beings is condemned; and every creature, according to the Apostle, labours and groans in childbirth (Rom. 8:22). Almighty God is silent, and his all-powerful ordering conceals so great a confusion.

At last Mary is born; and, when she has reached marriageable years, [Col. 0833D] she assumes a lovely beauty that draws God himself and turns the eyes of divinity toward her. See what that not insignificant explorer of God’s secrets says of this: “Hear, O daughter, and see; incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house; and the King will desire 566 your beauty, for he is the Lord your God” (Ps. 44:11–12).

Thus the rod of Jesse springs from the twisted root of the human race and the tree of the patriarchs; rising in height and straightness, it knows none of the knots of the children, knows no darkness, and has no bushy growth of any kind. That vehement Lover sees and burns; and he sings the entire bridal song in her praise, where [Col. 0834A] the Bridegroom is plainly introduced, breathing the sincerest love and no longer able to conceal what he suffers.

At once that heavenly assembly is summoned, and, according to the prophet, God begins a deliberation, gathers a council, and speaks with the angels concerning their restoration, the redemption of humankind, and the renewal of the elements (Isa. 16:1–3). While they stand astonished and rejoice in wonder, the manner of redemption is sought; and immediately the name of Mary is unfolded from the treasury of divinity. It is decreed that all this shall be accomplished through her, in her, from her, and with her, so that, as without him nothing was made, so without her nothing should be restored.

A letter is given to Gabriel, containing the Virgin’s greeting, the Redeemer’s incarnation, the fullness of grace, the greatness of glory, and an abundance of joy. Therefore the angel Gabriel, [Col. 0834B] sent by God, even before arriving at the Virgin, found God having entered the virginal womb, [Note: [Col. 0833D] A hyperbole, intended to signify speed.] and the majesty of God enclosed within the narrowness of a virgin’s womb. O womb more expansive than the heavens and greater than the earth, more capacious than the elements! You enclose him who encloses all things, in whom the God of glory reclines.

Indeed, the Archangel did not say, “Hail, Mary, who art to be filled,” but “full”; nor, “The Lord will come into you,” but “The Lord is with you,” because the Holy Spirit had already wholly taken her for himself and adorned her with heavenly ornaments. She had already been consecrated as the place of delight from which that fountain was to rise which would water the whole surface of the earth.

3. We have scattered words enough thus far and sown diverse matters in fleeting [Col. 0834C] discourse. Let us now dwell here, in case we may draw out something worthy. “A river,” says Scripture, “went forth from the place of delight to water the whole surface of the earth; and from there it divides into four heads” (Gen. 2:10).

This river is my Lord Jesus, who goes forth from two places of delight: from the womb of the Father and from the womb of the Virgin. Hence the prophet: “The Lord our God is a glorious river, leaping into a thirsty land.” Yet, by ineffable differences, he goes forth very differently from the Father than from the Mother; for although this temporal birth is glorious, the eternal one is far more glorious.

At your urging, I wish to disclose what I think concerning each generation—not presuming to expound anything, since this is beyond the powers of all, and how much more beyond mine [Col. 0834D]? It is the height of madness to wish to speak of ineffable things, especially for an unlearned man. For I have not forgotten Solomon’s saying: “Just as one who eats too much honey vomits it, so one who searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25:27). Of both, I think it may be said through the prophet: “Who shall declare his generation?” (Isa. 53:8).

For that generation from the Father is ineffable and inaccessible, open to no creature. In this sense I believe the Apostle said of God: “Who alone inhabits inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16), since even the purer natures are so struck back by that vision that they cannot break into the abyss of such brightness. The Son himself likewise declares: “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27). Yet this revelation is not according to what he is, but according to what the one to whom so great a condescension is granted can receive. Thus that exalted soul who had been caught up as far as the third heaven into the riches of God’s glory says: “I do not consider that I have comprehended” (Phil. 3:13).

4. The truest conclusion, then, is that no intellect at all penetrates the generation of the Begetter and the Begotten. I judge this generation from the Mother also to be inextricable for every human creature; and I do not know whether it can be comprehended even by that more excellent nature. For who can comprehend the union of flesh and Word—how God and man come together in one person while the properties of the natures remain intact and unconfused?

Each person abounds in his own opinion; I believe that this surpasses every understanding, following in the footsteps of the ancient men who left sound and unshaken judgments on these matters. Returning, then, to the paternal generation, we regard the Father as the place of delight, 567 although God is not contained in a place; but we cannot explain the workings of things except through ordinary language.

Whoever reads the Apostle saying, “For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:36), understands that every delight is in him; and likewise another voice from that twelvefold summit pours forth: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). The Son himself says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God” [Col. 0835C] (John 17:3). Therefore knowledge of the Father is eternal life; and where eternal life is, there is everlasting delight.

The river therefore goes forth from the place of delight, because from the Father’s womb is begotten God from God, light from light, Lord from Lord. It goes forth in identity, because he is the same as the Father. I say “the same” according to substance, not according to person. It goes forth also in equality, because it receives the Father’s omnipotence: whatever the Father can do, the Son can do also, as he himself testifies: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does; and the Son cannot do anything except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19).

It goes forth also in eternity, because although he is begotten, he is not later than the Begetter, but both are of one antiquity—if you do not recoil from the novelty of the term. Although it may in some way signify what is meant, it remains far beneath the majesty of the thought. It goes forth in likeness, because he is like the Father: the Father’s image, the radiance of his glory, and the impress of his substance. It goes forth in otherness, because he is other than he: “other,” I say, not “another thing.” “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). He said “one,” not “one person”: “one” signifies unity of substance, while “one person” signifies the distinct property of persons.

Thus, going forth from the Father in a mode far more exalted, the Son floods the angelic ranks; for, according to Solomon, “The fountain of wisdom is the Word of God on high” (Sir. 1:5). The boy harpist had drunk from this fountain with a full belly when he said: “With you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. [Col. 0836A] 35:10). “With you,” he says, “is the fountain of life,” because you are not only life, but your Son also is the fountain of life. And to show plainly what he meant, he added: “In your light we shall see light”—namely, for watering the whole surface of the earth.

What earth is set in that summit of the heavens, upon which the glorious river overflows and which it waters? The kingdom of heaven is the land of the living. Hence: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 26:13); likewise, “I shall please the Lord in the region of the living” (Ps. 114:9). This watering is beyond speech. For the angels are made drunk by the abundance of God’s house and are given to drink from the torrent of his delight.

5. Here I do not know what to say, because overwhelming astonishment crushes the understanding as it rises. Where are the speeches of orators, which that entire chorus of philosophers forged in the furnace of rhetoric? Where are the giants named from ancient times, who were mighty in stature from the beginning, skilled in war, exhausting themselves in contests of words? Was not that greatest giant—I mean Plato—repelled from the understanding of so pure a truth? Did he not, touching but not attaining the divinity of God with the keenest power of mind, say: “I found one thing which accomplishes all things; and another through which all things are brought about; but a third I could not find”?

Rightly was he ignorant of the Holy Spirit, who had not been poured into him—the teacher of holy revelations, who revealed to Paul things no eye had seen, as that same Apostle declares: “God has revealed them to us.” By what means, Apostle? By the Holy Spirit [Col. 0836C] (1 Cor. 2:10), not by our own spirit, through which philosophers were both deceived and deceived others.

Let us hear what our philosopher, who understood beyond the elders and beyond all who taught him (Ps. 118:99–100), thought concerning this: “Watering the mountains from his upper regions,” he says (Ps. 103:13). That is, he waters the higher angels, who behold God’s very substance with tireless lights, not in a mirror or in an enigma, but face to face.

6. It follows: “Which from there is divided into four heads.” Into which four heads? Let us speak briefly, for a long road remains to us.

Into wonder: for the more worthy creature, drinking from the torrent of delight, is wholly astonished at the Creator’s glory and at the reason for that glory, in view of the frailty of human constitution.

Into purity: [Col. 0836D] because they draw waters in joy from the fountains of the Saviour not in an earthen vessel, but with the veil removed.

Into satiety: because although they desire to look into him, desire does not bring need, nor does need bring misery; rather, in a more wonderful manner, they always desire in order always to be satisfied, and are always satisfied in order always to desire.

Into security: because, certain of their own stability, they are immersed in everlasting joys, awaiting the blessed hope and the appearing of the glory of the great God, when there shall be one fold and one shepherd, and that heavenly Jerusalem shall be consummated into one and the same reality.

But this river flows through the angelic orders. Yet faith apprehends all these things; reason does not know them, and human understanding is ignorant of them. Perhaps these are the [Col. 0837A] four things which the Vessel of Election saw in a happy quaternity in the Epistle to the Hebrews, saying: “You have not come,” he says, “to the smoking mountain, but to Mount Zion, to Jerusalem, the city of the living God, to the assembly of many thousands of angels, to the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven” (Heb. 12:18, 22–23).

7. Let us now prepare ourselves to see how he goes forth from the Virgin, because this going forth is sweeter and more tender for human misery: it shakes the breasts of those who behold it, moistens their eyes, and bathes the faces of lovers with blessed fountains.

Here I understand Mary’s womb to be the place of delight, in which the Lord accumulated every delight of delights. Of these delights the Holy Spirit, in an admiring utterance in the Song of Love, pours forth: “Who is this that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights?” [Col. 0837B] (Song 8:5).

Does the Most High take delight in the angels, in whom he himself finds perversity? (Job 4:18). Does he take delight in the constellation or glittering of the stars, of which some are turned to blood, others fall from heaven, and others are darkened in darkness? (Rev. 6:12–13). Does he take delight in air, fire, or winds? By no means: “The Lord is not in the fire; the Lord is not in the earthquake; the Lord is not in the spirit” (3 Kgs. 19:11–12), if true is he who was taken up into heaven in a fiery chariot and fiery horses (4 Kgs. 2:11). Does he take delight in the waters, where the raging and twisting Leviathan dwells (Isa. 27:1), or in the earth, which under Adam’s curse brings forth thorns and thistles? (Gen. 3:17–18).

[Col. 0837C] There is no place of delight except the Virgin’s womb. From it he goes forth in humanity, because, clothed in the haircloth of our mortality, he appeared visible to human eyes. Making a rod from the Virgin and a line from the book of generation, he fastened on the hook of divinity; this he covered with virginal flesh, so that the great dragon, drawn to the flesh, might feel the iron of the divine power.

He goes forth also in novelty, because never was a man born as he is born. The first human being is first formed from earth; second, woman is made from his side (Gen. 2:7, 22); third, Cain is begotten from both in the customary order of birth (Gen. 4:1). This one alone is born from the Virgin alone, and divinity made human seals the Virgin’s womb with a new and singular childbirth.

[Col. 0837D] Where now is the eloquent but barren verbosity of Aristotelian subtlety: “If she gave birth, she lay with a man”? Whether it wishes or not, privation turns into possession; and he who sets bounds to all things is not bound by dialectical terms—at whose command nature perishes and custom is unlearned.

He goes forth also in brightness. For when he is born, all that luminous serenity of the shining lights is eclipsed; and a star, whiter and sparkling with more brilliant rays, claims for itself the whole region of heaven. Kings walk in the brightness of his rising, for behold, kings are gathered and have come together as one. Seeing God and man thus born, a mother and virgin giving birth, they marvelled, were troubled, were moved, and trembling seized them in the light of such great miracles.

He goes forth [Col. 0838A] also in poverty, because, laid in the meanest swaddling-clothes, he was from that time foreshadowing in his most holy limbs the law of martyrdom. He goes forth secretly, because that most subtle investigator of fraud is excluded from the height of so great a condescension. Hence, wearied by alternating doubts, he tempts him; now he calls him, when tempting him, Son of the Most High; now he sets up the cross, now destroys it, commanding through a woman, his familiar instrument: “Have nothing to do with that righteous man” (Matt. 27:19).

8. It follows: “To water the whole surface of the earth”—that is, to cleanse earthly misery, which that first sinner had left us as an inheritance. I want the Apostle, here as above, to divide him for me into four heads, because I accept his exposition more confidently. “Who became for us,” he says, “wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption” (1 Cor. 1:30).

For, coming to us who were in prison, 569 he first of all drove away the darkness of our ignorance by the light of his wisdom; then, through the righteousness that is from faith, he loosed the bonds of our sins, sanctifying us in his body and redeeming us in the passion of his body: “The Lord releases those in bonds; the Lord gives light to the blind” [Col. 0838B] (Ps. 145:7–8), sanctifies the tabernacle, and redeems from the hand of the enemy.

He is divided also into patience, by which he endures sinners; mercy, by which he cherishes sinners; generosity, by which he raises those who make progress; and strength, by which he preserves those who attain perfection. Concerning this second [Col. 0838C] quaternity, throughout this whole Advent I have conversed with your Brotherhood, intertwining moral matters with mystical through the course of rivers and the interpretation of names. Whether I have done so worthily in any respect, you will judge. Yet we cannot compress everything into the present discourse, while avoiding weariness.

9. I have four heads sweeter than the former ones, which perhaps will please your hearts more sweetly. For your Lord, lifted up upon the cross, caused most abundant streams of blood to flow from four parts of his body. For as thorns pierced his most holy head bent back upon its snowy neck, nails his feet and hands, and a spear transfixed his side, precious blood flowed; by its sprinkling the judge becomes a father; wrath, gentleness; [Col. 0838D] the rod, mercy; captivity, a crown.

Christ therefore is a fountain hidden and concealed in heaven, a fountain open and revealed on earth: there he goes forth from the Father’s womb; here, from the Virgin’s womb. There, living, he waters the land of the living; here, dying, the land of the dying. There he is divided into a wonderful quaternity; here, into a sweet one. Sweet is the Lord; sweet the Lady: for he is “my Lord, my mercy”; she is my Lady, the gate of mercy. May the Mother lead us to the Son, the Son to the Father, the bride to the Bridegroom, who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

## SERMON III

[Note: [Col. 0839] In the *Bibliotheca Cisterciensis* it is entitled “On the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord,” etc.]

On the river of Egypt and its streams, allegorically.

[Col. 0839A]

1. At last we have come from sea to harbour, from promise to reward, from labour to rest, from despair to hope, from the road to our homeland. For the pen of the swiftly writing scribe had written us repeatedly in many letters: “Wait; wait again.” But we could say what follows: “A little here, and a little there” (Isa. 28:13). Runners rich in promise but utterly poor in fulfilment had gone before. One said: “Act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Ps. 26:14); another: “If he delays, wait for him, for he will surely come” (Hab. 2:3). By one and the same counsel they had gone forth from God’s sanctuary, carrying back with them nothing but a multitude of promises.

Thus our Harpist had already begun to slumber from weariness and, in silent reproaches, turned all the blame upon God himself in mournful strains: “But you,” he says, “have rejected and despised; you have delayed your Christ” [Col. 0839B] (Ps. 88:39). He turned from lamentation to the imperative, urged on by impatience, the mother of shamelessness and brazenness: “You who sit above the cherubim, manifest yourself” (Ps. 79:2).

And why do you sit so long upon your sovereign throne, surrounded and encircled by angels, without looking upon the children of men, whom iniquity has swallowed up and made deaf—iniquity committed indeed through Adam, but permitted by you? “Remember what my substance is” (Ps. 88:48), fashioned after the likeness of your substance; for although “every living human being is vanity” [Col. 0839C] (Ps. 38:6), yet, passing in your image, he cannot be vanity. “Have you then made all the children of men in vain?” (Ps. 88:48)—those of whom you say, “My delights are with the children of men” (Prov. 8:31)—so that that wicked deceiver might turn and divert them from you, though he could not deceive unless you permitted it? “Bow your heavens and come down” (Ps. 143:5), and bend those merciful eyes toward wretched sinners, lest you at least forget us for ever.

This, indeed, he said; but, tortured by groanings and distresses, he renounced the judgment of such presumption: “I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue” (Ps. 38:2).

2. That noble man also, lucid through the refinement of profound speech, growing warm in impassioned transports, says: “For Zion’s sake I shall not be silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I shall not rest” (Isa. 62:1), etc. “Would that,” he says, “you would tear open the heavens and come down!” (Isa. 64:1), and many other things which tedious length forbids us to insert.

This man too, held in suspense by the long delay of grace and carried beyond himself by the excess of grief, barks out impatiently: “Behold, the nations are before him as though they were not; they are accounted by him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. 40:17). Jeremiah also bursts into the voice of rejoicing praise with an adverb of demonstration: “Behold,” he says, “the Lord will make a new thing upon [Col. 0840A] the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22). Yet he is taught by tears of sudden submersion, taking up Christ’s lament before he becomes silent concerning his coming.

Daniel is told: “The vision is for days and for distant times” (Dan. 8:17, 19). And Ezekiel is wrapped in such darkness that one can scarcely discern whence he comes or whither he goes (Ezek. 12). Finally, that entire prophetic company, wearied by the long delay of lingering grace, varies its prayer now by petition, now by complaint, and often mixes indignant language with entreating words.

We too have heard them enough, and they are read again to us to weariness. Moses now flees, for he has become too impeded in speech for us (Exod. 4:10). Isaiah’s lips are unclean (Isa. 6:5). Jeremiah does not know how to speak, because he is a child [Col. 0840B] (Jer. 1:6). Ezekiel eats defiled bread (Ezek. 4:12). Hosea took a harlot and adulteress as wife (Hos. 1:2–3). Daniel becomes severely ill after the vision (Dan. 8:27).

3. All the prophets are tongue-tied and mute. We can no longer rejoice and exult unless he kisses us with the kiss of his mouth. You have been heard and answered: the kindness and humanity of God our Saviour are present, and they can no longer allow the love of those who languish to be delayed.

For what have you heard? “Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow, children of Israel, and be ready; for tomorrow the Lord will descend” (Josh. 7:13). The remainder of this day, and scarcely half the passage of the coming night, separates us from the face of glory, from the divine child, from the singular childbirth. Run with swifter and more rapid step; complete your courses, so that you may see the Son of God crying in the cradle and prepare whatever services you can for the Saviour’s birth.

I believe that you are children of Israel, purified from every defilement of flesh and spirit, prepared to receive tomorrow’s sacraments with watchful devotion and devout watchfulness. What else have you done during these holy days dedicated to his Advent? I saw old men, forgetful of old age, standing at the sacred vigils with youthful eagerness; and young men, their youth buried, standing with the grave reverence of old age before the divinity. The benches were full of singers, and voices resounded aloft in harmonious chorus, so that I would have believed, in happy envy, that you had sworn to rejoice to God with a voice of exultation.

Psalters were in your hands, psalms on your lips, devotion in your hearts. [Col. 0840D] The cheerfulness of your faces, the movement of your bodies, and your careful attention to work showed the solemnity of your minds. I watched the priests, with wakeful eyes carefully observing the first risings of day; putting on sacramental vestments; entering unto the altar of God to sacrifice the body and blood of the Redeemer. I saw the crowd of attendants, in ministerial devotion, now bending their knees, now kissing hands, and obeying the nod of those giving orders more swiftly than a nod.

I also watched boys who do not know the difference between right and left, envying one another their psalters, carrying them back to their beds, stealing sleep from their eyes, and upon their beds through the nights seeking him whom their souls loved. Although this may have been undertaken contrary to custom, it was not contrary to devotion.

I confess that amid all these things I thought: “These are the camp of God; this is nothing other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” [Col. 0841A] (Gen. 28:17). Whether I wished it or not, I was drawn along by your devotion; while you busied yourselves, I could not remain idle. I followed you, though from afar, either straying from the way or limping from my paths, grieving and sorrowful because I could not equal those who ran. That one alone knows [Note: [Col. 0841D] Namely Bernard, or Peter of Cluny.], with whom alone I began to be one in the Lord, how frequently I filled his ears with complaints that you were at noon with the Bridegroom while I remained with the bride in the evening chill.

4. Come then, brothers: if any still-flowing moisture from [Col. 0841B] the river of this mortality sprinkles your affections, wipe it away and cover it with the snowy garment of confession; and put on the readiness of the Gospel of peace (Eph. 6:15), so that you may be among those of whom the saint says: “They shall pass through the river on foot.” And what follows from this? “There we shall rejoice in him” (Ps. 65:6).

The prophet Isaiah discoursed more fully in the night readings concerning this river—or rather, these rivers. “The Lord,” he says, “will strike the river of Egypt into seven streams, so that they may pass through it shod” (Isa. 11:15). I wish to speak with you for a little while concerning the river and its streams: how and in what way it is struck, and what it is to pass through it shod.

Those who search the divine utterances maintain that Egypt figuratively signifies this world, which lies in the evil one and is filled with darkness and confusion. The river is the flow of the human race, bursting forth in an unhappy current from the first parents; bursting into a violent torrent, it has spread over the whole breadth of the world. It is drawn off into seven torrents, has overflowed valleys and plains in a deep whirlpool, and threatens to pour the same flood even over the very summits of the mountains. Hence one of the loftier voices cries: “The torrents of iniquity troubled me” [Col. 0841C] (Ps. 17:5), and, “The waters have entered even to my soul” (Ps. 68:2).

5. The first stream of this river is evil thought: an overflowing stream, checked by no barriers. It receives abundant rains through the windows of bodily senses, which worldly sluices pour in upon it as deadly showers. Before the mind’s sight there comes what it has seen and heard, smelled and tasted, handled and touched. And often what we saw with a simple eye, the twisting skin-changing deceiver turns into an occasion of offense and stumbling. It forms likenesses, paints images, applies colours, and rolls everything about in the chamber of the mind, if perhaps it may draw out consent and infect the affections.

It presents horrible things about divinity, terrifying things about faith, astonishing things about the institution of faith; and pours poisonous draughts into the channel of the mind, which the burdened sinner dreads to vomit out in confession. It comes into the oratory, occupies the dormitory, sits down in the refectory, goes around the cloister, revisits the workshops, and leaves no means of doing harm untried; everywhere it displays the subtleties of its own craft.

In choir, indeed, while praying and chanting psalms, it draws the mind in diverse directions, entangling purity of understanding in the recollection of the past. In the bedchamber it unfolds manifold impulses of lust, lying in wait for your watchfulness and attacking you with stronger weapons—would that it may not conquer you; let it prick, not wound. In the refectory it entices gluttony to look at what is brought in, and loads the distended belly with immense greed, so that you need greater labour to expel than to take in.

In the cloister it snatches books from your hands, unlocks the memory of Scripture, and carries you now from this person to that one, now from that person to this, with gestures and buffoonery. It makes you run about through the multitude of workshops and makes itself companion to your wandering, until it either opens or breaks down the door of silence. What more? In choir, the enemy of virtue uproots devotion; in bed, chastity; in the refectory, moderation; in the cloister, reading; in the workshops, the virtue of silence.

Nor is it enough for it to pierce the vital parts of the heart more subtly with its darts while you are awake: in sleep it displays and repeats a singular cunning. I leave all these matters to your conscience’s knowledge rather than to my pen’s knowledge. Even to the altar of the Lord of hosts those spirits follow us, flying before the eyes of the mind, so that scarcely any recollection can drive them away, whether of the God being born or hanging upon the cross.

That great patriarch could scarcely drive birds of this kind away from his sacrifices (Gen. 15:11); who are we, that we should presume to drive them away? Who would deny that in this stream he is either submerged or overwhelmed? You see how muddy this torrent is, how it surges back with slimy filth, and how scarcely, if ever, it is brought to complete dryness. I do not think that he who shut heaven by prayer (3 Kgs. 17:1) shut his mind against thought; it is easier to close heaven than the mind.

6. The second stream is perverse speech. “No human being can tame the tongue,” says James (Jas. 3:8): a restless member, a deadly member, ready to speak and readier still to speak ill. Notice that one is born from the other: the gate of perverse speech is opened by evil thought.

There is one kind of false speech: hence it is said, “You will destroy all who speak a lie” (Ps. [Col. 0842D] 5:7). Another is vain speech, of which it is written: “Each has spoken vain things to his neighbour” (Ps. 11:3). Another is indecent speech, of which the Apostle says: “Let no foul speech proceed from your mouth” (Eph. 4:29). Another is self-excusing speech, whence the Psalmist: “Do not incline my heart to words of wickedness, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4). Another is deceitful speech, of which the prophet says: “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the boastful tongue” (Ps. 11:4). Another is idle speech, of which the Lord himself says: “For every idle word which people have spoken, they will give account for it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12:36). And there are other kinds [Col. 0843A] of this plague which we cannot pass over in a brief leap.

7. The third is evil action. After thought and speech one comes to deeds, when we present our members to sin as weapons of unrighteousness and disgrace our bodies. For what is more shameful than to stain with lustful fires the members of Christ, consecrated by blood and buried in Baptism, without attending to the reverence due to God who is present, threatens punishment, and promises glory?

Far be it that any one of us should be laid beneath this idol: that he should receive the Son of the Virgin in Venus’s temple, set the ark of God beside Dagon, or—nourished on saffron—embrace dung. What has Peter to do with the Magician? What has Christ to do with Antichrist? What have virginity and lust to do with each other? Purity and corruption?

Far be it that any of you should walk in passionate desire like the nations that do not know God—you who either consecrate Christ’s body or minister to Christ’s body. Serve the chosen Emperor, so that you may sit with the Emperor when he sits upon the throne of his majesty. With what face, with what eyes could he see you or live among you, who served such obscenities in your midst? With what mind, with what conscience could one approach the Holy of Holies and sacrifice the Holy of Holies, if his reputation were contemptible, his life notable, and his speech blameworthy?

But if perhaps—humanly speaking, because of the weakness of your flesh—any one of you has folded up something of this kind in the chamber of conscience, unfold it through confession and penitence, and I promise him forgiveness through the mercy of the newborn child. And if he confesses and repents, the light of the world is born in him, so that, false darkness removed, he may receive the splendour of the true light.

For how will he deny mercy to the wretched on this night, on which the merciful and compassionate Lord is mercifully born? God and man are present; mother and virgin; flesh and Word; illuminating light; good and goodness; mercy and truth; fruitful virginity, virginal fruitfulness; eternal newness, new eternity; divine humanity, human divinity; humble sublimity—and in all these mercy is fashioned.

Therefore restrain pride from your eyes, talkativeness from your tongue, cruelty from your hands, pleasure from your loins, and your feet from a path that is not straight; come and accuse him if on this night he does not rend the heavens, descend [Col. 0843D] to you, and cast all your sins into the depths of the sea. Yet who is there who has not been immersed and re-immersed by the continual force of this third little stream?

8. The fourth stream is the defence of sins. In truth I tell you that nothing so exasperates the wrath of the Godhead as the defence of iniquity. For we contend with the Lord in an equal contest when we defend what he hates, when what displeases him pleases us. There is indeed a great difference between the proud and the humble sinner: he despises the one but looks upon the other, because he regards the humble and recognizes the lofty from afar. When can one be healed who scorns the physician, tramples the medicine underfoot, and inflames his sickly constitution by receiving contraries? You call evil good, [Col. 0844A] bitter sweet, darkness light, and heap insults upon the Creator: so that you condemn what he has praised and praise what he has condemned.

Nor should I pass over this in flattering concealment: I have seen some among you driven by such goads of impatience that, at the first words of a corrector, you offer not merely excuse and defence, but—unless the force of discipline intervenes—rush forth into uproar and quarrelling. This is the greatest impiety against God, the greatest offence; and it is what the simple and upright man, the servant of the Lord, avoids with the utmost circumspection. The prophet introduces a most elegant comparison concerning this, drawn from the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit: “There the hedgehog had its den” (Isa. 34:15). The hedgehog is so densely clothed in a most compact spikiness that it is armed everywhere with pricks and quills. But when it thinks it has obtained solitude, it uncovers its head, puts forth its feet, and displays the movements of life in its open walking. If anyone comes upon it, it immediately withdraws head and feet with the greatest speed into its inner hiding-place, so that, if you wish to seize it, you see your own blood before you see its body.

So too the sinner’s head with his feet—that is, intention with action—is watched by the vigilance of shepherds. Yet this is the fault of nearly all sinners: though seen by everyone, no one thinks himself seen. If you seek to cut away the vice and to detect, by corrective measures, the entrances of intention together with the exits of action, Cicero’s eloquence is immediately renewed: what you charge is excused and defended; you, who bring the charge, are accused and offended against. He asks concerning place and time when it was done, and the new dialectician, with tongue thrust out, bursts into the midst. He calls in his relatives; he seeks advocates; he declares himself oppressed; he announces that he will withdraw, that he would rather die than endure such things; denying what you saw, and retorting upon you insults that he did not see. Thus you feel the thorn and lose the fault; you incur hatred and make no correction; and him whom you thought to hold entirely, you lose entirely. Do you see with what manifold abundance this stream pours itself upon every person, and especially upon our Order?

9. The fifth is exultation in sins. O detestable joy, to be transformed into the sadness of everlasting pain: to exult in sins as in virtues! Do not thieves and every sort of criminal, when they attain the fulfilment of their desires, scarcely contain themselves for joy—so much so that they dare even offer thanks to the Godhead itself? “When they have done evil, they rejoice and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14). “Coals shall fall upon them, and they shall be cast into the fire” (Ps. 139:11). But how this stream, with its surging recurrence, overwhelms miserable souls is understood better by conscience than by eloquence.

10. The sixth is teaching others to do evil. This teaching flows from the chair of pestilence, which he who teaches humankind knowledge detests and condemns. O how vainly he receives his soul who hunts other souls unto death; who draws sins out like a long garment; who mingles blood with blood; [Col. 0845A] for whom it is not enough to perish for ever and ever unless he also drags others into everlasting destruction! For you know that many vices are stamped upon the tenderest ages, and that afterwards scarcely anyone can mitigate them, much less uproot them, in the mature person. Unhappy teachers who planted such seedlings! They shall be uprooted from that heavenly planting which the heavenly Father planted. Who shall boast that he has not been surrounded by the torrents of this stream?

11. The seventh is perseverance in all these evils. Here the sinner is sunk and swallowed up, and the pit has closed its mouth over him. For when he does not lift his eyes to heaven or remember the righteous judgments, he is dead and buried in the tomb [Col. 0845B] of his own conscience. Then “confession perishes from one dead, as though he were not” (Ecclus. 17:26); then “when the sinner comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:3). He is at the furthest extremity of the rivers of Egypt, and the multitude of the Lord’s mercies is removed from his sight.

12. O evil river, most wicked streams, streams that destroy! On this night the Lord passed through them shod, when, in the virginal substance, he assumed pure flesh immune from all the aforesaid plagues: shod with that footwear which he “stretched out over Idumea” (Ps. 59:10), whose strap the great Baptist could not unfasten (Luke 3:16). “He sent from on high his Son, and received me in the Virgin’s womb, and so at last took me up, even from deep waters.” We too shall strike them down if we grieve for our sin; if we keep our tongue from deceit; if we turn away from evil and do good; if we confess our injustice against ourselves to the Lord; if our sorrow is always before us; if we teach the unrighteous the Lord’s ways; and if his praise is always in our mouth.

And, that we may stitch something from the shoemaker’s art onto our conduct, let us have dense and finely sewn footwear, able to exclude the waters that come against us. Let us make our flesh firm and fastened [Col. 0846B] by the fear of the Lord, so that it may exclude the moisture of lust; and, baked by tribulations and thus made dense, let it become a new wineskin to preserve the new wine, of which it is said: “For I have become like a wineskin in the frost” (Ps. 118:83). But now let us leave your hearts and bodies prepared in peace to receive the Son of the Virgin, and let us all together embrace with innocent arms the light for the revelation of the nations, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0845]

## SERMON OF NICHOLAS OF CLAIRVAUX ON THE FEAST OF BLESSED STEPHEN, PROTOMARTYR

“Now Stephen, full of grace and power” (Acts 6:8).

[Col. 0845C] 1. We still hold the Son of the Virgin in our hands, and with dutiful attention honour the infancy of the crying God. The Virgin leads us to the venerable cradle; she who is fairer than the daughters of men brings us to him who is fair in form above the sons of men; blessed among women, she leads us to him who is blessed among men. She murmurs in our ear—if perhaps the rebellious house may hear and be at rest—that the veils of the Prophets have been uncovered and God’s counsel fulfilled. See the miracle of the Mother of the Lord: the creature creates, and the Creator is created. The star shines, the Magus worships, heaven exults, earth resounds, angels glory, shepherds rejoice, the Virgin gives birth, God is born, and the luminaries of heaven, with a brighter light, attend the light arisen in darkness.

We move amid these blessings: blessed is the man who fulfils his desire from them. I know that “In the beginning was the Word” is sweet to us; sweeter, “The Word was made flesh” (John 1:1, 14); sweetest of all, the Word hanging upon the cross. What madman would dare turn our eyes away, much less tear them away, from so great a childbirth, unless he himself commanded it who says: “Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away” (Song 6:4)? Behold, while he kisses us with the kiss of his mouth, while by such great miracles he makes us both astonished and attentive, Stephen, full of grace and power, performs [Col. 0846C] great wonders and signs among the people. Is it right to leave the king and turn our eyes toward his soldiers? By no means, unless the Emperor commands it.

The King himself rises, the Son of the King; but, breaking through the ranks of the stoners, he attends, not without grief of heart, the contest of his triumphant champion. He sees the first and foremost of the purple-clad cohort overwhelmed by the thick hail of stones; he sees streams of blood welling from the Protomartyr’s body. He sees that the whole fury overflows against himself and that the reproaches of those reviling are heaped upon him alone. Where are your compassion and mercy, Lord, if you do not suffer with the one who suffers? Where are your equity and justice, if you do not judge and avenge him upon the stoning people? Let us run to the spectacle to which he runs, he who exults as a giant to run his course; and let us see with what arms the standard-bearer of martyrs descends into the field to fight.

And, that the singular prerogative of his martyrdom may shine forth more clearly, let us recall the account of the Acts of the Apostles, in whose historical and figurative statements are contained the conversion and passion of this fighting soldier.

2. “Stephen,” they say, “full of grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people.” No small mystery lies hidden here, nor is the plain formulation of the simpler text to be despised. For the angel, speaking to the Virgin, addresses her with a new greeting [variant: brings one], using words drawn from heavenly treasuries and fashioned by no spirit other than God’s own: words that undoubtedly excel all others in loftiness, as unfolded from the choicest teachings of the Holy Spirit, and by whose announcement that unique mystery of Word and man, Godhead and flesh, was to be joined together. “Hail,” he says, “Strength of the Lord, full of grace” (Luke 1:28). But what is said of Stephen? “Stephen, full of grace and power.” Does not Luke speak of each in almost the same words? Yet although a far more excellent mode is proclaimed in the Virgin, it is nevertheless praised secondarily in the Martyr.

Stephen therefore has grace in a higher degree than the remaining multitude of martyrs: he is described as “full of grace,” [Col. 0847B] that is, overflowing and filled to abundance—a phrase which the subtle investigator will find rarely in the canonical Scriptures. Power is joined to grace through the infusion of the spirit of freedom. His fiery mind bursts into the voice of truth and by no means permits the rigor of justice ever to be lowered or abandoned. Thus armoured with grace and wisely brandishing the spear of power, he performed great wonders and signs among the people. He can perform wonders and signs in whom grace and power have established their firmest seat.

Thus Stephen speaks to murderers, to adulterers of the Law, to crucifiers of the Son of God the Father: to a sinful nation in Egypt, to a people burdened with iniquity in the wilderness, to an evil seed in the promised land, to criminal sons at the death of the Saviour. “Stiff-necked,” he says, [Col. 0847C] “and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit.”

3. Some arose from the synagogue—surely the synagogue of Satan—and surely they gather in a mass, whether to confute or to kill. They make one wall of impiety: “scale is joined to scale” (Job 41:6). Serpents hiss to one another; they have assembled as one against the Lord and against his Christ. Whether it wishes or not, impiety yields to piety, error to truth, folly to wisdom, and the presumption and vanity of the human spirit to the Holy Spirit. “They could not resist the wisdom and the Spirit speaking.” It does not say, “They would not,” which belongs to rational and perfect beings; but “they could not,” where ability is taken away from the evil mind, though its will is not changed. “They were rebuked,” it says, [Col. 0847D] “by him with all boldness.” He acts boldly; nor does the undaunted mind change or become changed, choosing justice rather than life, faith rather than blood, death rather than silence concerning justice.

Running together, they seize him, bring him before the council, and rejoice that they have enclosed him in their nets; but “the net is cast in vain before the eyes of those with wings.” Then his voice becomes freer, and from their own books the discourse of truth is sharpened. The Spirit of God wholly takes the martyr to himself and, through his mouth as a more resonant instrument, plays its melody. One face of the Scriptures appears to him; and he reduces the vast compass of the Old Testament to a concise summary. He recounts God’s promises and benefits, the people’s murmurings and evil deeds, good things bestowed and evil rendered in return. Finally, he reproaches them with the shedding of divine blood; calls them rebellious in spirit, stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart and ears, and, in a lofty voice, murderers and betrayers.

He does not fear their assemblies gathered for bloodshed; and, among the hands of those seeking his life, he ascends to the summit of truth by a justice yet freer. They are cut to the heart and gnash their teeth at him; they conceive pain, and are near to bringing forth iniquity. It is strange that they are not recalled to themselves by the unfamiliar novelty of the miracle, that the luminous face of the Protomartyr does not restrain the madmen. “They saw,” it says, “his face as the countenance of an angel standing among them.” What is this, senseless men? The glorious Levite is marked by the light of God’s countenance, Stephen is made radiant with flashing splendour, your eyes are dazzled, and yet the greatness of envy shuts out the majesty of the vision? Let them answer, while turning over the divine volumes, where they have found a human being placed on earth [the text reads *per*, sic] putting on an angelic countenance; and, since in both Laws they will find this rarely or never, let them stand amazed at the glory of the triumphant man. It follows:

4. “But being full of the Holy Spirit, and looking intently into heaven, he saw the glory of God,” etc. Wonderful to say, and surpassing every creature! He looks intently into heaven; now he sees not merely heaven, but the heavens opened; he sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God’s power. This fixed gaze moves me: flowing from purity of heart, it overpowers the heavens and penetrates and reaches the very court of the Godhead. The heavens are opened; God’s glory is seen; Jesus is beheld standing not merely at God’s right hand, but at the right hand of God’s power. This gaze was produced [Col. 0848C] by renunciation of the world, contempt of self, purity of heart, love of God, love of neighbour, defence of truth, and desire for Christ. All these things ought to be redirected to the common blossoms of moral teaching, unless the Martyr’s excellence had to be commended.

Blessed eyes, subtle sight, glorious vision. Mark carefully the arrangement of the words. He is full of the Spirit and thus looks intently into heaven, because he is inspired in the Spirit; having trodden earthly things underfoot, he longs for heavenly and eternal things. After this, the heavens are opened, and no barrier or closure can prevail against the mind which, eagerly cleaving to that supreme Mind, flies over or breaks through it. The heavens, therefore, are opened—and I think all the heavens—and their opening is followed by the vision of God’s glory. And the Lord God is seen standing at the right hand of God’s power, lest he be thought less than the Father. He stands with the one standing; with the combatant he fights, because he is stoned in the one being stoned.

5. No slight astonishment surrounds me as to whether the first flower of martyrs beheld these things with bodily or incorporeal eyes. It would indeed be a great miracle if, by mental vision, he immersed himself in the starry mysteries, if eyes pure of heart looked upon so solemn a vision. But if with bodily eyes, it is certain that by the surpassing difference of grace he outstripped the whole human race, and that by the wings of faith and virtues he reached the incorporeal with the bodily—if not comprehending it, yet apprehending it. I dare define nothing rashly or plunge abruptly into a conclusion, since I do not remember having read a decisive rule on such matters. Yet I more safely follow [Col. 0849A] the Apostle—indeed, the Spirit of God in the Apostle—who, with the utmost freedom of speech, entrusts these matters rather to safe ambiguity than dangerous definition: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Cor. 12:2–3).

They immediately cry out with a terrible shout, hold their ears closed and stop them against the truth, rush upon him unanimously, becoming friends in his death; and, casting him out of the city, they stoned him. The martyr is cast out of the city of blood, in which justice formerly dwelt but murders now dwell; of which the saint says: “For I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city. Day and night iniquity surrounds it, and toil and injustice are in its midst” (Ps. 54:10–11). The city is contemptuously called a little fortress, because it has been fortified with the hardest bars of unbelief against the apostles and the Lord of the apostles. The Lord suffered outside the gate of this city; outside it the servant is stoned, going out to him beyond the camp and bearing the likeness of his reproach. The martyr’s garments are laid at the feet of the persecutor, who was to be converted through the touch of the sacred garments and through the prayers of the man being stoned.

6. “And they stoned Stephen,” it says, “as he called upon God and said: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” They run to stones, and he to prayers. Stones strike the Stone, but a gentler Stone, from which flows the oil of charity and from which returns the sound of compassion. “Lord Jesus,” he says, “do not lay this sin to their charge.” He asks that his spirit be received—his spirit, indeed, [Col. 0849C] and holy: that spirit which the Apostle expressly commands to be preserved in the human being as a kind of seal: “May spirit and soul and body be kept whole without blame on the day of the Lord” (1 Thess. 5:23).

O what compassion, what affection, what integrity of most ardent love! Rightly does he claim for himself the flower of martyrdom, since in him the likeness of the Lord hanging on the cross is impressed in wondrous patterns. For, crowned with thorns upon the wood, pierced with the lance, fixed to the cross, he disregards that unique pain and forgets his imminent death. About to introduce a new example, he opens the breadth of charity and broadens, in a wider field, the boundaries of the law handed down: now not merely a friend to friends, but, whether they will or no, a friend also to enemies. “Father,” he says, “forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). The prayer of one dying could not be ineffective; hence the multitude of enemies also passed over into the number of friends.

7. See how Stephen, though he does not equal, nevertheless follows the Redeemer in a straight course. A shower of stones flies, and under the mighty hands of the envious the sites of his wounds are multiplied; yet our crowned one suffers patiently, to be transferred from the crown of his name to the crown of rule. He knows not the prompting of the flesh and is unaware of the hour of death. And see what he resolves to do. “Having bent his knees,” it says, [Col. 0850B] “he cried with a loud voice: Lord, do not lay this sin to their charge.” He cries with a loud voice because his charity is great indeed. With knees bent: because, praying for himself, he stands upright and is raised by a true and humble simplicity; for those stoning him he bends the knee. Who ever heard such a thing? Who saw its like? He grieves more over the sin of his persecutors than over his own wounds, more over their iniquity than over his own death. “And when he had said this, he fell asleep in the Lord.”

Blessed sleep with rest; rest with delight; delight with satiety; satiety with security; security with eternity. “He fell asleep,” it says, “in the Lord,” swallowed into the abyss of brightness and resting among his God’s arms. The Lord Jesus was seated at the right hand of God, but he was the head of martyrs to the first martyr. You recall what that tongue of the Church—I mean Augustine—thought of this martyr: after his death, he asserts, Stephen raised seven dead persons. Come then, you who shine in the Levitical order: sing to him a new song and acclaim so great a feast with festal voices. Perhaps, as you sing together, he will also commend you to his Lord, your Judge, that he may not lay anything to their sin—he who is God, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0849]

## TREATISE OF AELRED, ABBOT OF RIEVAULX, ON JESUS AS A BOY OF TWELVE

> [Note: [Col. 0849] It appears in volume XIII of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, Cologne edition.]

On the Gospel of the Lord for the Sunday within the octave of Epiphany: “When Jesus was twelve years old” (Luke 2:42).

[Col. 0849D] 1. You ask me, dearest son, to draw from the Gospel reading in which the deeds of Jesus as a boy of twelve are narrated some seeds of devout meditation and holy love, and, having entrusted them to the little baskets of writing, to send them to you for gathering. While this messenger was still speaking, behold, I felt in the very marrow of my heart with how great, what kind of, how ardent, and how sweet an affection your brotherhood asked this of me. Suddenly I remembered where I had once been, what [Col. 0850D] I had felt, and what the Gospel words had sometimes accomplished in myself, whether they were being read or sung.

I looked back, wretched man that I am; I looked back and saw how far behind me I had left those sweet and delightful things; how far the cords of occupations and anxieties had dragged me from those delights, so that things my soul then refused to touch are now, because of my distress, my food. I remembered these things and poured out my soul within me, when the Lord’s hand, stretched out to me, touched my heart and anointed it with the anointing of his mercy. You see from the very manner of your inquiry what light and splendour your affection flashes upon me, when you asked to be told, during those three days in which the boy Jesus was sought by his Mother, where he had been, in what lodging he had stayed, with what foods he had been nourished, in whose company he had delighted, and with what business he had been occupied.

I feel, my son, I feel how familiarly, how affectionately, and with what tears you are accustomed to ask these very things of Jesus himself in your holy prayers, when that sweet image of the sweet Boy moves before the eyes of your heart; when you paint that most beautiful face in a certain spiritual imagination; when you feel those eyes, at once most gentle and most mild, radiating delightfully upon you. Then, as it seems to me, you cry with inward affection: “O sweet Boy, where were you? Where did you hide? What lodging did you use? What company did you enjoy? Were you in heaven or on earth? Or meanwhile did you stay in some house, or perhaps stand in a secluded place with some little boys of your own age then, disclosing to them the mysteries of secrets according to your Gospel saying: ‘Allow the little children to come to me, and do not forbid them’?” (Matt. 19:14). Happy were they, if there were any such, to whom you granted your presence so familiarly for so many days.

2. But what is this, my sweet Lord, that you did not have compassion on your most holy Mother as she sought, grieved, and sighed? Indeed, she and your father sought you in sorrow. Or rather, my sweetest Lady, why did you seek the Boy, whom you did not fail to know as God? [Col. 0851C] Did you fear that he might be tormented by hunger, afflicted by cold, or injured by some other boy of his age? Is he not the one who feeds all things and nourishes all things, who clothes and adorns more gloriously than Solomon the grass of the field, which exists today and tomorrow is cast into the furnace? (Matt. 6:29–30).

Or rather, my Lady—forgive me for saying it—why did you lose your sweetest Son so easily, guard him so carelessly, and notice so late what was missing? Would that Jesus himself might deign to inspire me with what, in an inward and spiritual discourse, he answered her as she so sought, so begged, and so burned with longing, so that I might write it down for you as something known, and be able to utter what I have tasted.

3. Let us see, then, if you please, why the Lord Jesus is born in Bethlehem, hides in Egypt, is nourished at Nazareth, and from there, at twelve years old, goes up to the temple and the metropolitan city—yet not alone, but under his parents’ discipline. To what end are all these things? Because my Lord Jesus is truly a guide, a physician, and a teacher. [Col. 0851D] As our guide, “he exulted as a giant to run his course, for his going forth is from the highest heaven” (Ps. 18:6–7), and his descent reaches Bethlehem. There, leaving footprints full of heavenly fragrances, he “made darkness,” that is, Egypt, “his hiding place.” Having poured the light of heavenly grace upon those seated in darkness and the shadow of death, he also ennobled Nazareth by his holy presence. And, thus made a Nazarene, he enters the temple as a boy learning, not teaching, hearing and asking questions, and in all this not departing from his parents’ discipline.

Thus, Lord, thus you go before the wretched; thus you heal the sick, showing this way to the erring, this ladder to those ascending, this return to exiles. Who will grant me, good Jesus, to cling to your footsteps and so run after you that I may one day lay hold of you? I am that prodigal son who took my substance for myself, unwilling to preserve my strength for you, and departed into a far country, a land of unlikeness; I was compared with senseless beasts and made like them. There I squandered all my goods in riotous living, and thus began to be in want. Unhappy poverty, to which bread was lacking and the food of pigs gave no benefit! Following most unclean animals, [Col. 0852B] I wandered in a wilderness, in a waterless place, unable to find the way to an inhabited city. My hungry and thirsty soul wasted away in evils, and I said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house abound in bread, while I here perish with hunger!” (Luke 15:12–17).

As I thus cried to God, he heard me, leading me into the right way so that I might go to the city of habitation. What city could this be but that one abounding in bread, which is called the House of Bread—that is, Bethlehem? Let them give thanks to you, Lord, for your mercies, because you have satisfied the empty soul and filled the hungry soul with good things: namely, with that Bread which came down from heaven and, laid in a manger, became food for spiritual beasts of burden.

4. These, indeed, are the beginnings of conversion, as of a certain spiritual birth: that we may be conformed to the little one, take up the badges of poverty, [Col. 0852C] and, made as a beast of burden with you, Lord, enjoy the delights of your presence. But because it is written, “Son, when you approach the service of God, stand firm and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1), the Lord Jesus hides his face from us for a little while, not in order to depart but to remain hidden. And behold Egypt, behold darkness, behold disturbance. For, sitting in darkness and the shadow of death, suffering from the lack of experienced joy, bound and fettered with iron—that is, by the hardness of our own heart—we must cry to the Lord when we are troubled, and he will deliver us from our necessities.

For, dispersing the darkness of this temptation by the light of his consolation and breaking the bonds of inward hardness by the grace of inner compunction, he goes before us with a more serene countenance to Nazareth, so that there, nourished under the discipline of elders among the flowers of Scripture and the fruits of virtues, we may receive the delights of the twelfth year. For just as the Lord Jesus is born and conceived in us, so indeed he grows and is nourished in us until we all attain to a perfect man and to the measure of the age of Christ’s fullness (Eph. 4:13).

5. Therefore, when Jesus was twelve years old, as they went up to Jerusalem according to the custom of the feast day, and as they returned, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem. First, lest the wonderful sweetness of this narrative escape us, it should be known that the Jews had the custom, when going up to the feast day, of men walking separately and women separately, lest some defilement perhaps creep in; for the divine law prescribed that only the clean should take part in the sacred solemnities. Thus it is credible that at that time the boy Jesus gave the sweetness of his presence now to his father and the men accompanying him, now to his Mother and the women accompanying her. [Col. 0853A]

Let us therefore consider how great was the happiness of those to whom it was granted for so many days to see his face and hear his honey-sweet words; to observe certain signs of heavenly power radiating in a human being and a boy, and to see him introduce the mystery of saving wisdom into their mutual conversations. The old men are astonished, the young men marvel, and boys of his own age are held in awe by the gravity of his conduct and the weight of his speech. For I believe that in that most beautiful face such elegance of heavenly grace shone forth that it turned everyone’s gaze toward him, raised their hearing, and stirred their affection.

See, I pray, how he is seized and drawn by each group. Old men kiss him; young men embrace him; boys wait upon him. What tears were shed by the boys when he was kept longer by the men! What complaints from the holy women when he stayed a little longer with his father and his companions! I believe each cried inwardly: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1). And to the boys who longed for his presence but did not dare join the company of the elders, this is readily fitting: “Who will give you to me as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, so that I may find you outside and kiss you?” (Song 8:1).

[Col. 0853C] 6. Therefore, as all entered the holy city with this joy, consider, I pray, how pious and holy was the rivalry among the several households, all desiring that his most sweet presence should be granted to them. Happy was the household that prevailed. Perhaps for this reason, when all things had been completed and they were returning, the boy Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it. For each supposed that he was with the other, since he was loved by all and sought by all; and his parents did not know that he was absent until, after a day’s journey was completed, he was sought among the relatives and acquaintances in each of the households that had gone up together. Not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem; and after three days they found [Col. 0853D] him in the temple.

During those three days, then, where were you, good Jesus? Who supplied you food or drink? Who prepared a little bed? Who removed your sandals? Who soothed your youthful limbs with ointments and baths? I know certainly that, just as you voluntarily assumed our weakness, so, when you willed, you showed your own power; and therefore, when you willed, you did not need these services. Where then were you, Lord Jesus? It is pleasing to form some estimate, conjecture, or opinion about all this; but it is not permitted rashly to affirm anything.

What shall I say, my God? Was it that, in all things, you might conform yourself to our poverty and assume in yourself every misery of human nature, that you begged alms at doorways as one among a crowd of poor people? Who will grant me to share in those morsels so begged, or at least to be filled with the remnants of that divine food?

7. But to turn these things toward secrets of a more exalted meaning: perhaps on the first day he presented himself before his Father’s countenance, not to sit down, but to consult his Father’s will according to the order of the dispensation he had undertaken. Such an opinion does not seem absurd, if we consider that the Son of God, concerning those things which in the divine nature he himself, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit—equal and consubstantial with each—had arranged, consulted God as man in the servant’s form he had assumed, the little one consulting the great one: not in order to learn what he himself had eternally known with the Father in the form of God, but in order to yield to the Father in all things, offer obedience, and place humility first.

There, in that secret chamber of the Father, there is deliberation concerning the baptism to be received, disciples to be chosen, the Gospel to be established, miracles to be performed, and finally the endurance of the Passion and the glory of the resurrection. When all had been disposed in a divine manner, on the second day he granted the angelic and archangelic choirs the sweetness of his countenance. By reporting that the ancient ruin of the heavenly citizens was shortly to be repaired, he gladdened the whole city of God. On the third day, mingling himself with the ranks of Patriarchs and Prophets, he proved by the manifestation of his own countenance those things which they had long ago heard from the holy elder Simeon. Thus, consoling the delay of their expectation with the promise of redemption now at hand, he made them all more patient and more joyful.

[Col. 0854C] 8. Rightly, therefore, after three days he is found in the temple in the midst of doctors and elders, so that, just as he had disclosed—as seemed fitting—the Father’s merciful counsel concerning the restoration of humankind to angels and to saints freed from the flesh, so in the Jerusalem temple, the holiest of all places, and first to those who guarded in the sacred Scriptures the most precious treasure of this promise, he might gradually begin to unveil it: first hearing and asking questions, then revealing the most sacred mysteries. Finally, all marvelled at his understanding and answers.

Here is given to boys and youths a pattern of humility and reverence: that in the midst of elders they should be silent, listen, ask questions, and learn. Tell me, O most beloved Lady, Mother of my Lord, what disposition, what astonishment, what joy you then experienced, when you found your sweetest Son, the Lord Jesus, not among boys but among teachers; when you saw everyone’s eyes fixed upon him, everyone’s ears raised toward him; when little and great, learned and unlearned alike, spoke of his wisdom and answers. “I found him whom my soul loves; I will hold him and not let him go” (Song 3:4). Hold him, sweet Lady; hold him whom you love. Fall upon his neck, embrace him, kiss him, and repay his three-day absence with multiplied delights.

“Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I sought you in sorrow.” Again I ask you, my Lady, what were you grieving over? I believe you feared neither hunger nor thirst nor lack of food for the Boy whom you knew to be God; but you lamented only the ineffable delights of his presence, withdrawn from you, [Col. 0855A] even for a little while. For the Lord Jesus is so sweet to those who taste him, so beautiful to those who see him, so delightful to those who embrace him, that his brief absence is matter for the greatest sorrow.

9. “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be occupied with my Father’s affairs?” Here he begins to disclose the secret of the heavenly mysteries in which he had spent three days [or: “been observed”]. In order to commend more clearly and excellently an example of humility and obedience, and likewise of abandoning one’s own will and obeying the commands of elders—even when useful matters must be set aside—he subjects himself to the will of his elders, setting aside things so sublime, so useful, indeed so necessary. As the Evangelist says: “And he went down with them and was subject to them” [Col. 0855B] (Luke 2:51).

But what does the Evangelist mean when he says that they did not understand the saying which he had spoken? I do not think this was said of Mary, who, from the time when the Holy Spirit came upon her and the power of the Most High overshadowed her, could have been ignorant of no counsel of her Son. Rather, while those who did not know or understand what he had said were thus situated, Mary, knowing and understanding, kept all these words, pondering them in her heart. She preserved them in memory, ruminated upon them in meditation, and compared them with the other things she had seen and heard concerning him. Thus even then the most blessed Virgin mercifully provided for us, lest such sweet, health-giving, necessary words should slip away through some negligence and consequently neither be written nor preached, [Col. 0855C] so that followers might be deprived of the delights of this spiritual manna. Therefore the most prudent Virgin faithfully kept all these things, modestly remained silent, disclosed them at the fitting time, and entrusted them to the holy Apostles and disciples to be preached.

10. Concerning what follows—“Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace before God and men”—many have said many things, and different people hold different opinions; it is not ours to judge their opinions. Some have thought that Christ’s soul, from the moment it was created and assumed into God, possessed wisdom equal to God’s. Others, fearing to make a creature equal to the Creator, have said that, just as he advanced in age, so also he advanced in wisdom, relying upon the Evangelical authority which says: [Col. 0855D] “But Jesus advanced in age, wisdom, and grace.” Nor, they say, is it surprising if he is said to have been lesser in wisdom, since he is most truly proclaimed at that time to have been mortal and passible, and therefore lesser in blessedness.

Let each judge these opinions as he wishes. It is enough for me to know and believe that the Lord Jesus, from the moment when he was assumed with God into one person, was perfect God; and therefore possessed, and possesses, perfect wisdom, perfect justice, perfect blessedness, and, moreover, perfect power. I do not doubt that whatever may be said of God according to substance could be said of Christ, even when he was in his Mother’s womb. Yet we do not thereby deny him mortality or passibility before the resurrection, since we confess that he was not a phantom but truly [Col. 0856A] human, and possessed true human nature, in which he could advance in age. Whether he advanced in wisdom, let those who know how to contend about such matters determine.

11. But you, my son, seek not disputes, but devotion; not that by which the tongue is sharpened, but that by which the spirit is stirred. Therefore, setting aside for the moment matters belonging to the historical sense, let us proceed to unfold the spiritual understanding, insofar as he of whom we speak deigns to inspire us.

The Lord our God is one God. He cannot vary; he cannot change, as David says: “You are ever the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101:28). This our eternal, timeless, immutable God became mutable and temporal in our nature, [Col. 0856B] so that through the mutability which he assumed for us he might make a way to his eternity and stability for mutable beings; so that in one and the same Savior there might be both the way by which we ascend, the life to which we come, and the truth which we enjoy, as he himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Therefore, while the great Lord remained in his own nature, he was born little according to the flesh; through definite periods of time he advanced and grew according to the flesh, so that we, little in mind—indeed almost nothing—might be born spiritually, and might grow and advance through the distinct stages of spiritual ages. Thus his bodily growth is our spiritual growth; and those things which are described as done by him at every age are experienced by those who advance well as being spiritually enacted in us through each degree of progress. Let his bodily birth, then, be an example of our spiritual birth—that is, of holy conversion. Let the persecution he suffered from Herod signify the temptation which we endure from the devil at the beginning of our conversion; let his upbringing at Nazareth express our progress in virtue.

At first the prodigal son, wasting away with hunger, is summoned to the house of bread (Luke 15:16–17), where he finds not fine flour bread, but ash-bread, so that he may eat ashes with his bread and mingle his drink with weeping (Psalm 101:10). For fine flour bread is pure, clean, without ash, without leaven, without chaff: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” [Col. 0856D] (John 1:1).

12. But who is sufficient for these things? This is the bread of angels, whose palate was not numbed by the taste of sour grapes; therefore they taste fully and perfectly, and see that the Lord is sweet. But in order that man might eat the bread of angels, the bread of angels became man: taking up the chaff of our poverty, the ashes of our mortality, and the leaven of our weakness; the great became little, the rich became poor. Thus you, great in your own eyes, may become little through humility; rich in desire, may become poor by renouncing possessions; and may have no place in the inn where you are spiritually born, while you rely not upon your own will, judgment, knowledge, or industry, but upon another’s judgment.

Then you will eat ashes with bread [Col. 0857A] when the Lord feeds you with the bread of tears and gives you drink in tears by measure (Psalm 79:6). Thus you are born in Christ, and thus Christ is born in you. Herod—that is, the devil—is disturbed because Christ has invaded his kingdom, and he does not look with an equal eye upon his dwelling being changed into Christ’s lodging. He brandishes the sword, bends the bow, and prepares therein instruments of death, to shoot the upright in heart in darkness. He inflames the flesh with natural incentives, troubles the mind with harmful thoughts, and pierces with manifold temptation the thoughts of little ones still nursing upon their former sweetness.

Then Christ seems to you to have failed you, until Herod has been destroyed—not by your own strength, but by the grace of divine mercy—and Christ returns with greater peace and awaits your coming at Nazareth. For after temptation you must ascend with alacrity of mind to the pursuits of virtue and spiritual exercises, as it were to Nazareth, that is, “the flower.” For just as a flower is not indeed fruit, though fruit is produced from it, so these exercises are not themselves pure virtues, although true virtues are born from them through God’s working. From there one must ascend to Jerusalem, but in an appropriate manner and at a suitable time.

13. “When Jesus was twelve years old, he went up to Jerusalem.” Plainly, according to allegorical laws, Christ ascends from Nazareth to Jerusalem when, abandoning the Synagogue, he displayed the presence of his mercy to the Church of the Gentiles. Rightly he was then twelve years old, because he who had not come to dissolve the Law but [Col. 0857C] to fulfill it added the two of evangelical perfection to the ten of the Law: the word shortened, yet completing and bringing to completion upon earth, and enclosing both Law and Prophets within the twofold commandment of love.

14. Therefore the child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it. Christ is still in the Church, and the Jews—his parents according to the flesh—are ignorant of this. Joseph is still in Egypt, and the Savior of the world is called in the Egyptian, not the Jewish, tongue; and while he himself distributes the grain of his wisdom to the Egyptians—that is, to the Gentiles—his brothers waste away from hunger for the word of God among the Canaanites, that is, among unclean spirits. “They supposed,” it says, “that he was in the company.” [Col. 0857D]

What is this? Even now, O Jews, you presume that Christ is in your company, although, according to your own Jeremiah, he has abandoned his house and forsaken his inheritance, because his inheritance has become like a lioness’s den (Jeremiah 12:7–8). By what signs, mysteries, or sacraments is he in your company? Where is the Temple? Where is the continual sacrifice? Where is the priesthood?
