Where is that altar which was granted to you alone, in Jerusalem alone? Where is that perpetual fire, when, after its extinction, all the burnt offerings likewise perished—offerings which cannot be consumed by a strange fire? Either you possess none of these things; or, if perhaps you presume that you possess them, you do not possess them according to God’s command, and consequently you do not possess Christ either.

For in all these things, according to prophetic mysteries, you once possessed Christ; but when he whom they foretold appeared, the things that foretold him were removed—things upon which you relied in vain after his coming. O wondrous perversity! O wondrous blindness! Jews, paying heed to none of these things, still suppose that he is in their company and seek him among relatives and acquaintances.

Whom do you seek, O Jews? Whom do you seek? Already the stone cut from the mountain without hands has filled the whole face of the earth [Col. 0858A] (Daniel 2:34–35), and do you still seek? Behold, dispersed throughout the earth, everywhere you encounter Christ, and do you still seek? Everywhere among the Gentiles, in praises of Christ, your “Amen” resounds, your “Alleluia” is sung, your “Hosanna” rings out, and do you still seek? “He placed his tabernacle in the sun, and there is none who can hide himself from his heat” (Psalm 18:6–7), and do you still seek? You seek him among relatives and acquaintances.

You seek him in Isaiah; but, as he himself says, “The ox knows its owner and the ass its master’s manger, but Israel has not known me; my people have not understood” (Isaiah 1:3). Therefore you do not find him. You seek him in holy David; but according to him as well, “Their table became a snare before them”; therefore you do not find him. “For their eyes have been darkened that they may not see, and their backs are bent” (Psalm 68:24). You seek him in Jeremiah; but, as Jeremiah testifies, “The priests do not know the Law; they do not know the Seer” (Jeremiah 2:8). Therefore you do not find him. You seek him in Moses; but even to this day, when you read Moses, a veil lies over your heart. Therefore you do not find him.

15. Therefore return, return, O Shulamite; return to Jerusalem, and you will find him. Certainly it is reported to Jesus that his Mother and brothers stand outside seeking him: does he go out? Rather, you enter, and you will find him. “And returning,” it says, “they found him after three days in the Temple.” “Though the number of the children of Israel be like the sand of the sea, a remnant shall return”—a remnant, I say, of Jacob shall return to the mighty God. When? Certainly after three days.

O desirable time, when Israel shall know its God and shall fear David its king [Col. 0858C] (Hosea 3:5); when the two peoples shall make for themselves one head and shall ascend from the earth! When will this be, good Jesus? When will you look upon your own flesh, the members of your own blood, since no one hates his own flesh? Break your bread, Lord, for the hungry; bring the needy and homeless into your house. How long will wretched Cain be a wanderer and fugitive upon your earth, which opened its mouth and received your blood, O our Abel, from his hand? Have you not yet repaid him sevenfold into his own bosom, when everywhere the greater serves the lesser, when everywhere the yoke presses and the sword terrifies, and there is none to redeem or save?

I know that at last they shall return and suffer hunger like dogs, but at evening. For after three days they found him in the Temple.

16. The first day, on which the Lord Jesus entered our Jerusalem and hid himself from his mother, the Synagogue, and from his Jewish brothers, was the apostolic preaching among the Gentiles. Thus Paul speaks to the Jews themselves: “Since you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” [Col. 0859A] (Acts 13:46). Then heavenly light shone upon the dark hearts of the Gentiles; and, once the gloom of former unbelief had been struck down, the splendor of faith sent rays of its brightness into the minds of the lost.

But the most delightful light of this day was interrupted by the night of savage persecution, when the rulers of the world raged against Christians and crosses, beasts, racks, iron claws, heated pans, burning plates, and a thousand kinds of tortures were prepared for their destruction. Although the greater part of Christians overcame all these things by the strength of faith, yet no small multitude yielded to their torturers and inflicted lamentable grief upon the saints.

That night was followed by a day most bright with the light of divine mercy, when the kings of the world were converted to Christ, temples of the Gentiles were overthrown, shrines of demons were consecrated as memorials of martyrs, and, as truth gradually entered mortal hearts, the night of unbelief was shamefully driven away. Yet this most splendid day in turn was covered by the cloud of heretical depravity, until error was brought into the light by the labor of teachers and departed from Christian hearts. Then faith, long tested and proved by many arguments, brought back the sun of righteousness to a world in danger. [Col. 0859B]

And behold, it is now evening, and the day has already declined. O perilous times! The corrupt life of false Christians conceals the light of the third day and restores to the now-aging world a night darkened by overflowing iniquity. For iniquity abounds and charity grows cold. We await the day when, through the preaching of Enoch and Elijah, the Synagogue, Christ’s mother, shall find Jesus after entering the Temple—that is, the Church—where, seated in the midst of elders and teachers, is the mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus: hearing among little ones, questioning among youths, teaching among elders. [Col. 0859C]

17. Then a voice of joy and exultation shall resound in the tents of Jacob, when the true Joseph, recognized by his brothers, shall at the end of the world be announced alive to the Jewish people, as it were to an aged father, by those saying: “Joseph your son lives, and he rules over the whole land of Egypt” (Genesis 45:26).

“Son,” she says, “why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I were sorrowing and looking for you.” What have you done, O Joseph? Your mother dies; your father is worn away by unceasing weeping; your brothers are in danger; indeed, your whole paternal household languishes; and you, neglecting your own, provide salvation for Egyptians? “Son, why have you done this to us?” Your brothers go to Egypt and return; they see you as lord of the land, but do not recognize you. That beautiful face, which all Egypt admires, is hidden only from those of your own flesh. “Son, why have you done this to us?” You regard your own as strangers, lay crimes to their charge, threaten punishments; and those who are strangers find you most merciful, while your own find you most cruel. [Col. 0859D]

“Son, why have you done this to us?” That prodigal son of yours, who squandered all his substance [Col. 0860A] with prostitutes; who committed fornication with wood and stone (Jeremiah 3:9); who exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the image of corruptible man, birds, quadrupeds, and serpents (Romans 1:23)—once admitted into your house, behold, for so many years he has been fed on the flesh of the fattened calf, made drunk with the purest blood of the grape, and has played in symphony and dance amid the delights of our David. Yet we, to whom belonged the covenant, the giving of the Law, the worship, the promises, and the fathers, and from whom you came according to the flesh, have stood outside as strangers (Luke 15:11–32). “Son, why have you done this to us? Behold, your father and I were sorrowing and looking for you.”

We suppose that by a new miracle the Temple is to be rebuilt, the priesthood restored, and Israel’s dispersion brought back to Jerusalem, chosen for himself; and that thus Christ is to be found in the borders of Judea, whom we now find in the fields of the forest.

18. “We were sorrowing and looking for you.” We grieved that the ancient miracles had been removed, [Col. 0860B] prophetic oracles had fallen silent, no ruler came from Jacob’s thigh, and there was no anointing of kings or high priests. Although all these things bore witness to your coming, we nevertheless did not believe that, having left us, you had deigned to lodge among strangers; therefore we sorrowed and sought you.

We did not think that you, promised to us and given back to us, would leave those whom you begot and despise those whom you nourished for the salvation of a rival people; that you would prefer unclean Gentiles, devoted to idolatry, to those for whom the sea gave way, whom heaven fed, whom the rock gave drink, for whom water became a wall, for whom the wall became passable, whom the sun obeyed, and for whom the moon stood still. Therefore we sorrowed and sought you.

At times, indeed, your coming was proved to us by many signs; but because of the calling of the Gentiles and our rejection, it was again despaired of. Therefore we sorrowed and sought you.

And he says: “Why were you looking for me? Did you not know that I must be occupied with my Father’s affairs?” O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the Prophets spoke! Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer thus, enter into his glory thus, and that repentance should be preached in his name among all nations? [Col. 0860C] (Luke 24:25–26, 46–47). Have you not heard, through David’s mouth, the Father’s voice to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession” (Psalm 2:8)? Why did you seek me and not immediately find me among the nations? Was it not said to Abraham: “In your seed all the tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18)? Did you not know that I must be occupied with my Father’s affairs?

Hear the Father speaking to me through Isaiah: “It is too small a thing for you to be my servant, to raise up the tribes of Jacob and bring back the dregs of Israel. I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). Am I not, in the patriarch Jacob, “the expectation of the Gentiles” (Genesis 49:10), and in Malachi—

> [Note: [Col. 0859] A lapse of memory, or a scribal error; for this is Haggai 2:8.]

—their “Desired One”; and, as the same prophet says, “From the rising of the sun to its setting, my name is great among the nations” (Malachi 1:11)?

You grew swollen with my gifts and envied my compassion; and because an evil eye envied the salvation of the penitent, blinded by envy it could not see the author of its own salvation. Therefore I did not spare the natural branches; but, after they had been cut from the root of the natural olive, I grafted in foreign branches. But now, rising up, I will have mercy upon Zion, for the time to pity her has come; the time has come [Col. 0861A] (Psalm 101:14). I call back those whom I had rejected; I gather again those whom I had scattered; I receive those whom I had driven away. “And behold, I am with you all days, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). For the present, these allegorical remarks are sufficient.

19. Now I must return to you, dearest son, whose desire is to be conformed to Christ and to cling more closely to the footsteps of Jesus. Perhaps I may suffice to unfold for you your progress from the Gospel reading, so that you may read in these little pages what you experience more sweetly within yourself. For I believe that you have passed from the poverty of Bethlehem to the riches of Nazareth; and, now made twelve years old, have ascended from the flowers of Nazareth to the fruits of Jerusalem, where you can read these mysteries not so much in books as in your own conduct.

For just as Bethlehem, where Christ is born little and poor, is the beginning of the good life; just as Nazareth, where he is nourished, is the exercise of virtues; so Jerusalem, to which the Lord ascended when twelve years old, is contemplation of heavenly secrets. In Bethlehem the soul becomes poor; in Nazareth it becomes rich; in Jerusalem it overflows with delights. It becomes poor through perfect renunciation of the world; it becomes rich through the perfection of virtues [Col. 0861C]; and it overflows with delights through the sweetness of spiritual tastes.

One must ascend from the valley of weeping, amid the hardships of temptation, through the plains of spiritual exercise, to the heights of luminous contemplation. In Bethlehem the infancy of a new way of life is dedicated: an infancy incapable of reason, which harms no one, deceives no one, is free from desire, unaware of its own will, judges no one, speaks ill of no one, desires nothing, is neither anxious about present things nor troubled about future things, and is sustained only by another’s judgment. Commending this infancy to us, the Vessel of Election says: “If anyone among you wishes to become wise, let him become foolish that he may be wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless you are converted and become like little children, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 18:3).

20. Therefore, once any soul has been initiated into this infancy, after Herodian persecutions, if the flowers of virtues begin to spring up more abundantly in it, as in a most fertile field, it shall not undeservedly dwell in Nazareth—which is interpreted “Flower”—as though seven years old, and happily await the twelfth year. [Col. 0861D]

First, the field of our heart must be manured, as it were, by recollection of our sins and consideration of our weakness; then it must be repeatedly worked by the plowshare of temptations, so that the seeds of virtues may bring forth the flowers of spiritual exercises. Therefore, consider one in whom the spirit of fear has already cut off ancient vices and ingrained desires to be a child of one year. If afterward the spirit of piety has made him gentle and obedient, judge him spiritually to be two years old. If then [Col. 0862A] the spirit of knowledge has infused into him awareness of his own weakness and desire for divine help, do not doubt that he has reached his third year. If the spirit of fortitude has made him immovable and strong against all temptations and fleshly pleasures which wage war against the soul, admire him as a child of four years. Let the spirit of counsel be added, and by the power of discernment it will make him five years old. If the spirit of understanding grants him meditation on the sacred Law, he reaches the age of six years by happy progress. The spirit of wisdom brings the seventh year, proceeding from meditation on the divine Law and bringing into the advancing soul the light of four virtues, as it were, of four years; than which nothing is more useful to human beings in life, as is written of Wisdom itself: “She teaches temperance, prudence, justice, and fortitude, than which nothing is more useful” [Col. 0862B] (Wisdom 8:7).

These are the governors of the preceding virtues, without which the others can neither be possessed honorably nor retained steadfastly. Temperance—also called sobriety—ensures that the progress of the virtues themselves is not excessive. Prudence ensures that they are not confused without discernment. Justice ensures that the use of virtues is not disordered. Fortitude, also called strength, ensures that devotion to them is maintained perseveringly.

The twelfth year follows: namely, the light of contemplation, which raises the fervent soul itself to the heavenly Jerusalem; which opens heaven; which opens the gates of paradise; which presents for contemplation before the eyes of a pure mind the Bridegroom himself, the Bridegroom “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” as though looking through the lattice, so that it may deserve to hear that most sweet voice: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you.” For, spotless from the filth of sins and passions, flying from the nets of occupations, its memory of the past erased and images of outward things vanishing, it raises the lovely face of its heart with the utmost eagerness to behold him whom it loves. Therefore it deserves to hear: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you. Your lips drip honeycomb” [Col. 0862C] (Song of Songs 4:7, 11).

“Winter,” he says, “has passed; the rain has gone and withdrawn; flowers have appeared in our land.” These fragrant flowers are, of course, the virtues which, though still in a certain newness, happily arise in the field of the breast of one advancing well after the winter of persecutions and rains of temptations. Christ, delighted alike with their beauty and their fragrance, invites her from lower things to higher: “Winter has passed; the rain has gone and withdrawn; flowers have appeared in our land.” And because the life of contemplation is opened through the groaning of compunction, he adds in what follows: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song of Songs 2:11–12). [Col. 0862D]

21. Recall, son, what you are accustomed to whisper in corners when, following the likeness of the turtledove—a most chaste bird, solitary and mournful—you seek hiding places and, though placed among many people, build for yourself a daily solitude. Recall how you groan, how you burn, how you seek him whom your soul loves; how, suffering the force of love, you now desire to see him whom you love; how you now flatter him and now sweetly express indignation to intensify your greater longing. Now you accuse him of delay; now you complain that you are despised. Now you confess yourself unworthy of his visitation; then again you presume upon the goodness you have experienced so often. Now, as though you can bear it no longer, you try by a certain spiritual dispute or struggle to overcome him who delays.

What tears then! What groans! What sighs! What cries! Now eyes heavy with weeping are raised to heaven amid inward sobs; now hands and arms are stretched out; now the slowness of the soul is accused by beating the breast. Meanwhile words are uttered without beginning or end; their meanings do not cohere, their constructions are not alike, and no sense or idiom of any language is preserved, when the voice sometimes responds to affection and then affection interrupts the voice. [Col. 0863A]

That devout Jesus indeed delights to be overcome by such a struggle, and, pleased by such a soul’s such persistence, boasts to the angels standing around: “The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” For in the land of the living the voice of a soul thus burning is heard, and the most sweet fragrance of such great desire delights the whole city of God.

Thus, for you in the corner of your roof, as for Elijah in the cave, first there passes a great and strong wind, overturning mountains and breaking rocks; but the Lord is not in the wind. And after the wind, an earthquake; but the Lord is not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake, fire; but the Lord is not in the fire. And after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze—and there is the Lord (3 Kings 19:11–13). These, indeed, are the stages through which the compunct heart ascends in prayer, [Col. 0863C] like a little column of smoke from the perfumes of myrrh and frankincense and every kind of perfumer’s powder.

22. But I entrust these matters to you, not so much to investigate as to observe in your own prayer. Therefore attend carefully to the difficulty with which you sometimes first enter the chamber of your heart, so as to find for yourself a cave in which, in a sense, you may be buried from all worldly things and pray to your Father in secret. At times the heart seems to have hardened like flint. It seems as though a mountain lying between has excluded the inward gaze from all spiritual things, until the great wind passes by, overturns the mountains, and breaks the rocks before the Lord.

This wind is followed, of course, by an earthquake, when the mind is dissolved by a certain compunction and, as tears flow, stirred against itself by inward contrition, wipes away whatever uncleanness it perceives within itself. From the hope thus born, it burns with the fire of ineffable desire and begins a certain spiritual struggle with God, until the whisper of a gentle breeze, entering the heart, touches the affections with a soft contact and, imposing silence upon every thought, movement, distraction, and word, raises the contemplative mind to the very gates of the heavenly Jerusalem. [Col. 0863D]

Then he whom it had long sought, so often begged, and so ardently desired—beautiful in form beyond the sons of men—looks as if through the lattice and invites it to kisses, saying: “Arise, hasten, my beloved, and come” (Song of Songs 2:13). Then, entering Jerusalem, it passes “to the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God,” amid the voice of exultation and confession. Then come embraces; then kisses; then it sings: “I have found him whom my soul loves; I have held him and will not let him go” [Col. 0864A] (Song of Songs 3:4). Then it overflows with delights in Jerusalem, enjoys good things, and keeps the feast day with exultation.

23. Therefore, dearest son, I beseech you: remember me when things go well with you, so that you may ask your Beloved, your King who is in the sanctuary, to bring me out of this prison, these darknesses, these bonds, that at last I too may breathe again in the freedom of former joy. May I also feel how great is that abundance of sweetness which he has hidden for those who fear him. But alas, alas: the hour is rare and the stay short! Happy is the one who can remain amid these delights for three days.

In these three days I understand, not inappropriately, a threefold light of contemplation, since whatever my enlightened mind can perceive of God, we believe to pertain either to his power, his wisdom, or his goodness. Thus the Lord Jesus is sometimes seen strong and mighty in battle, so that you may know that, if you love him, his right hand will protect you against the world, the devil, and every principality and power. No one can resist him; beneath him those who bear the world are bowed. If he holds back the waters, all things shall dry up; if he lets them go, they shall overthrow the earth. [Col. 0864B]

24. Therefore, if a spirit possessing power comes upon you; if it drives the goads of sloth; if it kindles the stings of diverse passions; if it sets the world in motion against you; if it inflames persecutions; if you fear, tremble, dread defeat at every moment, and thus run anxiously to your Jesus, weep, lay out your dangers, and beg for help—then he whom you love cleaves to you in the form of the mightiest king. According to the prayer of holy David, he “takes up weapons and shield and rises to help you” (Psalm 34:2), and you shall hear: “Do not fear before them, for I am with you” [Col. 0864C] (Jeremiah 1:8).

But if you desire revealed to you the knowledge of secrets or the solution of some question; if you anxiously wonder at the causes and reasons of worldly disorder; if your feet are moved because you see the peace of sinners, who are not in the labor of men and are not scourged with men; then you seek a lodging where you may converse with Jesus alone with the Alone, and cry with Jeremiah: “Indeed you are righteous, Lord, if I dispute with you; nevertheless I speak just things to you: why does the way of the wicked prosper?” (Jeremiah 12:1).

Thus, as you seek, that Teacher will be present who alone teaches man knowledge; who opens our eyes, that we may consider the wonders of his Law; who has the key of wisdom and opens so that no one shuts, and shuts so that no one opens. He will be present in the form of the sweetest teacher, in whose right hand is a fiery law, so that he may enlighten you with knowledge of the Law and inflame you with the love which proceeds from meditation on the Law. In his left hand, moreover, is the rod of equity, the rod of his kingdom, that he may rebuke the presumption of the inquirer and restrain curiosity.

Finally, if you disdain all these things—although great, splendid, and sublime—for the desire of one kiss and those sweetest lips, [Col. 0865A] and begin to cry in plaintive tones with the prophet, “I have sought your face; your face, Lord, I will seek” (Psalm 26:8), and: “Who will give you to me as my brother, nursing at my mother’s breasts, so that I may find you outside and kiss you?” (Song of Songs 8:1), then he will surely come to you in the fragrance of ointments and spices. Thus impressing upon your mind a certain heavenly and divine kiss, he will fill all your inward parts with ineffable joy, so that you delight to cry: “Grace is poured forth upon your lips” (Psalm 44:3).

When you read the Law and the Prophets, observe carefully, and you will find these same appearances and contemplations repeatedly signified in certain figures and enigmas.

25. For there are many kinds of contemplation and [Col. 0865B] and spiritual vision, all of which, I think, are known to pertain either to God’s power, or to his wisdom, or to his goodness. For if God is considered as the cause of all things—of some, that they exist; of others, that they are rational and therefore capable of wisdom; and of many, that they exist well—the first belongs to power, the second to wisdom, the last to goodness. It belongs to power that no creature subsists without him; to wisdom, that no teaching instructs without him; to goodness, that the use of no thing is beneficial without him. With him all things are secure, since there is nothing by which his power can be disturbed. In him all things are certain, whose wisdom cannot be deceived. From him all things are right, whose nature no malice can corrupt. Therefore, in the creation of things [Col. 0865C] we contemplate his power; in their form, his wisdom; in their use, his goodness.

Indeed, if you prefer to contemplate him in the things he did in the flesh, you will easily behold this same splendour of threefold light. If, with the eyes of an illumined mind, you look upon him lying in the manger, crying in his mother’s arms, hanging at the breast, a little child in Simeon’s embrace, admire the works of his goodness. But if you delight to consider that fiery countenance, the whip made of cords, and the terrible voice by which he terrified the sellers and buyers in the Temple, overturned the money-changers’ seats, poured out their coins, and moreover drove out the sellers of doves, tremble before the power of such might. And if it pleases you to discern with the mind’s eye the snares of the Scribes and [Col. 0865D] Pharisees so often detected, and their crafty objections refuted by the prudence of his replies, you will perceive the light of his wisdom shining more clearly. Thus it was also an act of power that he drove out demons, fed the crowds, walked upon the seas, and called Lazarus from the tomb; yet it was no less an act of wisdom that, in order that the rulers of this world might be deceived, amid these divine miracles he allowed himself to be tempted by the devil; that he hungered as though needy, slept in the boat, and mounted the cross in order to die.

26. But since you more willingly linger in meditation upon his goodness, enter, I pray you, the house of Simon the Pharisee. Consider more attentively with how devout, how gentle, how gracious, how merciful a countenance he looks upon the sinner prostrate on the ground [Col. 0866A]; how compassionately he permits those most holy feet—which pride and wantonness had until then claimed for herself—to be watered with the tears of the penitent and wiped with her hair, [588] and to be sweetly kissed by lips defiled with the foulness of so many crimes. Kiss, kiss, O blessed sinner, those feet most sweet, most delightful, most beautiful: feet by which the serpent’s head is crushed; before which the ancient enemy goes forth; by which vices are trampled down; by which all the glory of this world is overthrown; by which the necks of the proud and exalted are pressed down with wondrous power. Kiss, I say, and with blessed lips lovingly touch the footprints which no sinner after you should dread, which none, however guilty, should shun, which none should fear himself unworthy to approach. Kiss, embrace, clasp those footprints, worthy of adoration by angels and human beings [Col. 0866B]; pour upon them the ointment of repentance and confession, so that the whole house may be filled with the fragrance of the ointment.

Woe, woe to you, O Pharisee, to whom this fragrance is “an odour of death unto death”; you fear being stained by another’s sins, while your own swelling pride befouls you more grievously and foully. You do not know how sweetly the confessed misery of this wretched sinner smells of mercy; how sweet the confession of sin tastes to compassion; how pleasing to him is the sacrifice of a contrite heart; how swiftly burning love consumes sin. Finally, “many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much” (Luke 7:36–50).

27. Thanks be to you, O most blessed sinner: you have shown the world a place sufficiently safe for sinners—the feet [Col. 0866C] of Jesus, which despise none, reject none, repel none, but receive all and admit all. There the Ethiopian woman changes her skin; there the leopard changes its spots; there the Pharisee alone does not cast off the foam of his pride. What are you doing, O my soul, O my wretched one, O my sinner? You surely have a place where you may pour out your tears; where you may cleanse your foul kisses with sacred kisses; where you may securely pour out the whole ointment of your devotion without any touch or stirring of tempting vice. Why do you hold back? Break forth, O sweet tears; break forth: let no one hinder your course. Water the most sacred feet of my Lord, my Saviour, my receiver. I do not care if some Pharisee mutters; if he judges that I ought to be kept away from his seats; if he considers me unworthy to touch even his fringe; [Col. 0866D] if he mocks, laughs, turns away his eyes, closes his ears. Nonetheless, good Jesus, I shall cling to your footprints; I shall clasp them with my hands; I shall press them with my lips; nor shall I cease from tears or kisses until I hear: “Many sins are forgiven her, because she loved much.”

28. Therefore the first day, on which the soul thirsting for God dwells, as it were, in Jerusalem amid contemplative delights, is the contemplation of divine power. The second is admiration of his wisdom. The third is a sweet foretaste of his goodness and sweetness. To the first belongs justice; to the second, knowledge; to the third, mercy. Justice terrifies; knowledge teaches; mercy cherishes. “I will enter into the powers of the Lord; O Lord, I will remember your justice alone,” says the prophet (Ps. 70:16). Behold justice. “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things [Col. 0867A] of your wisdom” (Ps. 50:8). Behold knowledge. “For your mercy is better than lives” (Ps. 62:4). Behold mercy.

On the first day fear, arising from the consideration of justice, cleanses the soul; on the second, wisdom illumines it when cleansed; on the third, goodness rewards the illumined soul by the infusion of its sweetness. You see, unless I am mistaken, how necessary and useful it is, amid the exercises of good works, to frequent for these three days the Jerusalem delights in which fear administers the bread of sorrow, knowledge the wine of rejoicing, and goodness the milk of consolation. I know that you do not wonder that I have called them delights when I have said that sorrow is not absent from them, since you have often experienced that a contrite mind prefers that sorrow which arises from chaste fear to all the delights of this world.

These things have been said according to the measure of our experience. But souls of more excellent merit, more capacious intellect, and greater purity explore subtler and deeper matters in these three: namely, in God’s power, his deep judgments; in his wisdom, his hidden counsels; in his goodness, the ineffable gifts of his mercy. Thus Paul, entering into the powers of the Lord and trembling at the abyss of his judgments, says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it, Why have you made me thus?” (Rom. 9:20). And, admiring the treasures of his wisdom, he exclaims: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable [589] [Col. 0867B] his ways!” (Rom. 11:33). Recalling also the riches of his goodness, he says: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness?” (Rom. 2:4).

29. “After three days they found him in the Temple”: beyond doubt, Mary and Joseph—the one his Mother, the other his Foster-father. Thus the spiritual contemplator of spiritual things is found not in just any place, but in the Temple. For Jerusalem has a court, gates, and a Temple. The court at times lies open even to enemies; the gates are opened only to friends; entrance into the Temple is granted only to the perfect.

Therefore, whoever can behold eternal things in temporal things, heavenly things in earthly things, divine things in human things—that is, the Creator in creatures—should rejoice as though introduced into the courts of the heavenly Jerusalem. Thus far philosophers, as enemies, could extend the force of their understanding into the courts, as the Apostle says: “What may be known of God is manifest in them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived through the things that have been made, including his everlasting power and divinity” (Rom. 1:19–20). But whoever can, in the Holy Scriptures, with the veil removed and with unveiled face, contemplate the glory of God, may glory in having entered through Jerusalem’s gates. Yet if the flame of heavenly desire kindles, upon the altar of the heart, the richness of inward love and the fatness of your devotion; if the smoke of spices rises from the fragrance of prayer; if thus the mind’s eye extends its ray into heaven’s very secrets, and the palate of the heart enjoys the blessed taste of that divine [Col. 0868A] love—then you have frequented the Temple of Jerusalem with a most pleasing holocaust.

30. But while the holy soul dwells amid these delights, the Mother and Foster-father grieve, complain, and search; when Jesus is finally found, they gently rebuke him and bring him back to Nazareth. These things are especially fitting for spiritual persons to whom the dispensation of God’s word or the care of souls has been entrusted. I would most readily call our Foster-father the Holy Spirit, and our Mother, more rightly, charity. They cherish and advance us, feed and nourish us, and refresh us with the milk of a twofold love: love of God and love of neighbour. They keep and sustain us in holy studies, as though in Nazareth; they console us in troubles; counsel us in doubts; strengthen us when weary; heal [Col. 0868B] the broken-hearted and bind up their wounds.

With their aid we pass from Nazareth to Jerusalem, from labour to rest, from the fruit of good action to the secrets of contemplation. By an eternal law they prescribe for us that, for the care of our neighbour, we must not wholly neglect the contemplation of God; nor, conversely, omit care for our neighbour for the delights of contemplation. Thus, not without reason, if we indulge repose more than we should, fraternal charity complains of us, as it were, and does not approve our dwelling in Jerusalem if it perceives that, through our excessive [variant: “too great”] repose, harm threatens others for whom it provides by our care.

For often, when, setting every action aside, we are intent upon secret meditations or private prayers, and linger more than is beneficial for those subject to us [Col. 0868C] amid these delights, while the Spirit works and charity suggests, there suddenly comes to mind the remembrance of the weak: one whom we consider sorrowfully awaiting consolation from a fatherly heart; another, tempted, who watches to see when his father will come out in public and bring him some comfort by his words; one agitated by the pricks of anger, who, having nowhere to release through healing confession the poison he has conceived, murmurs against his father; another, overcome by the spirit of sloth, who runs hither and thither seeking someone to whom he may speak and whom he may consult. Moved by such a prompting from fatherly hearts, we hear Charity, our Mother, as though rebuking us: “Son, why have you done this to us? Your father and I, grieving, were seeking you.”

Nor do we wrongly say that the Holy Spirit or charity in holy persons, even those still less than perfect, grieves or complains; since the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unutterable groanings (Rom. 8:26), and is accustomed in the saints to speak, to be grieved, and to perform other such acts.

31. But if, in the face of such necessities, the lover of repose murmurs within the soul’s own affections, saying, “Must I not be about my Father’s business?” nevertheless, considering that Christ died so that whoever lives should not live for himself, he goes down with them and is subject to them. He goes down safely with such a Foster-father, [590] and with such a Mother. [Col. 0868D] and with such a Mother. He goes down happily who, moved by the Spirit of God, condescends in charity to those beneath him.

I will gladly go down even into Egypt under these guides, provided that, if they lead me down, they bring me back; if they compel me to descend, they also cause me to ascend again. I shall gladly submit to such masters; gladly set my shoulders beneath the burden they impose; gladly receive the yoke to which they subject me, knowing that their yoke is sweet and their burden light. But you also, my son—although Christ still hides you, free from such cares, beneath his wings, as prelates ought to do lest their subjects be endangered—must provide for this same matter: that your companions may not be scandalized. At times they put necessities before the delights of contemplation; you must not put such necessities before the unity and peace of the community. Above all, in these changing seasons of spiritual life—whether you go down to Nazareth or ascend to Jerusalem—never act alone, that is, by the judgment of your own will, but always distinguish matters by the counsel of the elders. [Col. 0870A]

32. Behold, dearest son, you have what you asked for: though it is worthy neither of your desire, affection, and expectation, it is nevertheless, I think, some indication either of my will or of whatever effort I can make. Know, therefore, that we have taken care not so much to expound the Gospel reading as to draw from it, as you requested, certain seeds of meditation; and, by the help of the grace of him whose infancy we have been discussing, we have fashioned from the sequence of this Gospel reading incentives to devotion for its readers—Jesus Christ our Lord, who is full of power, grace, and wisdom, and who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0869]

## SERMON FOR PALM SUNDAY. Mystical expositions of Christ’s entry into Jerusalem (Matt. 21:1–9). (G)

[NOTE.]

William Estius judged this sermon, recovered from the Abbey of Marchiennes, to resemble Bernard in style and character as well as in piety; although, leaving aside any question of style, it is absent from the sequence of sermons *de tempore* in all manuscripts.

[Col. 0869B] 1. Our Redeemer, dearest brethren, our Lord Jesus, whom the Father sent into the world as a saving victim, when the time of his death drew near, chose, as you know, to present himself in the place where he would die. And just as he came in order to die, so he foresaw where, when, and by what kind of death he would die, having before him from eternity the manner, place, and time of his death. These three were Jerusalem, Passover, and the Cross. For if you ask concerning the place, he died in Jerusalem; concerning the manner, by the death of the Cross; and concerning the time, when the time of the Paschal solemnity was at hand.

As you have sufficiently learned through reading and hearing, the wicked Jews had wished at various times, in various ways, and elsewhere, to kill him before this. For when they led him away to throw him down, and he passed through their midst and went on his way, they neither came to Jerusalem, nor waited for Passover, nor sought the Cross. Yet in putting him to death they were unable either to alter the manner or the place, or to anticipate or postpone the time. Therefore on this present day he came to Jerusalem, namely five days before Passover, identifying himself with that prefigured lamb which was to be sacrificed on the fourteenth day of the spring month at evening, but was commanded to be taken on the tenth day of that same month and kept until the stated time (Exod. 12).

2. Many before us have said many things about this coming of his to Jerusalem. Since we know them to be true and Catholic, it is fitting that we approve them by our silence. The common interpretation is that his entry into Jerusalem is his coming to the Church. The two disciples who loose the ass [Col. 0870B] and colt and lead them to Jesus are the two orders of preachers, one sent to the circumcision and the other to the uncircumcision, loosing both peoples from the cords of sins and leading them to the knowledge of true faith. The garments placed upon the animal are the sacraments of faith entrusted to the Christian people, upon which Jesus sits because Christ dwells in [591] their hearts through faith. The very great crowd that spread their garments in the road is the multitude of holy martyrs, offering their bodies to sufferings in imitation of Christ. Those cutting branches from the trees are doctors drawing Catholic teachings from the Holy Books. Those who went before and those who followed, crying “Hosanna,” are the Jewish people going before and the Gentile people following in the same Christian faith, both confessing one and the same faith. This interpretation is in every respect to be approved, because it is sound and entirely Catholic.

But while approving it, let us seek in this holy Gospel another interpretation, not a foreign one; and, searching out its moral marrow, let us turn the service of our speech toward the edification of conduct.

3. I think that every day the Lord spiritually approaches Jerusalem, coming from Bethphage and Bethany to the Mount of Olives, and sending into the village opposite them two disciples, who may bring to him the animal upon which he may sit. For Christ the Lord is the Spirit before our face; and although we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer (2 Cor. 5:16). Therefore we must seek his spiritual coming to Jerusalem, and how what he did in his coming to Jerusalem on this day, as the time of his most holy Passion approached, he still deigns to perform daily in us.

“He approached Jerusalem,” says the Evangelist. His approaching Jerusalem is his approaching the soul. Indeed, not only is his approaching us our approaching him. For when we are far from him through sin, how could we draw near to him by living well unless he first drew near to us? For as John says that this is love—not that we loved God, but that he first loved us (1 John 4:10)—so we can and ought to say that this is grace: not that we drew near to God, but that he first drew near to us. As he approached Jerusalem, therefore, he came to Bethphage, Bethany, and the Mount of Olives, indicating to us, I think, in this holy journey that we cannot attain true peace unless we both disclose ourselves purely through confession, willingly and humbly obey commandments, and compassionately share in others’ necessities through mercy. [Col. 0871B]

4. For, as you know, Jerusalem is called “Vision of Peace.” We then proceed to it by the straight and royal road if we walk through the purity of confession, the humility of obedience, and the loftiness of mercy. Behold three outstanding virtues: the first we owe to ourselves, the second to our prelates, and the third to our neighbours. You owe confession to yourself, so that, having defiled yourself through sinning, you may cleanse yourself through confession. You owe the second to your superior: that you may obey and be subject to him who keeps watch as one who must render an account for your soul (Heb. 13:17). You owe the third to your neighbours: that you may meet their needs according to your ability, yet desire to benefit them even beyond your ability.

Bethphage signifies the first, for it means “House of the Mouth.” Bethany signifies the second, for it is called “House of Obedience.” The Mount of Olives likewise signifies the third, because oil in Scripture, as you know, customarily represents mercy. Brethren, whence come wars and strifes among us? Are they not from our own imperfection, because we are unwilling to render what we owe—to ourselves, to our superiors, and to our companions? For if we wished to go from Bethphage to Jerusalem, we could arrive within ourselves, since we can never have full peace while, concealing our guilt within ourselves, we do not expose it by pure and humble confession. Do I speak to those without experience? Almost always and everywhere conscience gnaws, continually presenting the hidden wound to the mind’s eyes and anxiously and harshly reproving the mind over its concealment. O worm that, as long as it lives, never ceases to eat and feed upon the heart’s inner parts; that never ceases to live and therefore never ceases to gnaw, unless humble confession slays it with the sword-point of its purity! [Col. 0871D]

5. If, however, we wished to go to Bethany, we could reach Jerusalem also in our superiors, because then we perniciously disagree with them when we proudly resist their commands that accord with God. But if we climbed [592] the Mount of Olives, we should undoubtedly come quickly to Jerusalem. For the Mount of Olives is near Jerusalem: service produces friends, and we would build Jerusalem among our companions, because we enjoy full peace when, in pious concern for one another, we compassionately accommodate ourselves to mutual needs and diligently give aid according to our ability.

You see, therefore, that it was not without purpose that the Lord, going to Jerusalem, chose to pass through Bethphage, Bethany, and the Mount of Olives. He thereby teaches us that the cause and occasion of peace are purity of confession toward ourselves, eagerness of obedience toward our superiors, and merciful compassion toward those who share our dwelling. [Col. 0872B]

6. He sends two disciples to go into the village opposite them. The village opposite Christ’s disciples is the sinful soul, which by obstinacy and pride is opposed to the inward and spiritual powers of our Redeemer. Such a soul possesses the tower of pride and the wall of obstinacy: enclosed by the ground of stubbornness and raised by the height of arrogance.

Long ago those sons of Adam undertook to build this tower, of whom Scripture says that, journeying from the East, they found a very broad plain in the land of Shinar (Gen. 11:2). Who are these but the reprobate, desirous of empty glory and swollen with the puffiness of pride? Departing in heart and deed from him of whom the prophet says, “Behold the man whose name is the East” (Zech. 6:12), they walk amid the contagions of a foul manner of life upon the broad road that leads to destruction; for Shinar means “Their Stench.” “Let us build a tower,” they say, “and make our name famous.” These are those who call their lands by their own names and who, building within themselves—or perhaps, “construct,” [*construunt*]—the height of pride, love the first places at feasts, the first seats in synagogues, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called Rabbi by men (Matt. 23:6–7).

And from what do they raise this ruinous tower? “They had,” says the truthful history, “bricks for stones and bitumen for mortar” (Gen. 11:4, 3). Stones signify the strength of good works; bricks are baked and hardened by fire. The reprobate are burned by the flame of lust and become stubborn. Bitumen is envy; mortar is concord. For they say that bitumen arises from earth struck by lightning, and we know that envy arises in a mind struck by the swelling of pride. Stones are joined together in a building by mortar. And what virtue other than concord joins together the living stones in the building of charity, from which the heavenly Jerusalem is built each day? Thus they have bricks for stones and bitumen for mortar, because, abandoning the strength of good action, they defile themselves with the mud of foul lust; and, casting aside the bond of concord, embrace the stubbornness of envy. [Col. 0872D]

7. This tower is indeed exceedingly huge. But lest it be easily cast down, not only its own height resists, but also the strength of the wall enclosing it. This is what often defeats our efforts when we fight against that fortress: for we could easily overthrow the soul’s swelling pride by the engines and battering-rams of holy preaching, unless the stubbornness of obstinacy resisted us within it so invincibly, if one may so speak. For what progress can you make with one who has been made diamond-hard by a kind of insensible hardness—one whom you can neither bend by commands, draw by counsel, soothe by persuasion, frighten by threats, correct by scourges, nor soften by benefits? Would you not say of such a person that it is almost impossible for him to be cured? Yet though this is impossible with human beings, with God all things are possible.

For the merciful Lord sends forth his word to the earth, infusing inspiration into such a soul; his word runs swiftly to it, not to return to him empty, but to accomplish whatever he wills and prosper in the matters for which he sent it. Thus here also he sends his disciples into this village opposite them. For what purpose? That they may loose the ass found tied there, and the colt with her, and bring them to him. Fulfilling the command, they not only loose them and bring them to him, but, so that the word going out from his mouth may prosper in the matters for which he sends it, they place their garments upon them and make him sit upon them.

This seems to correspond to the passage: “He sends forth his word to the earth; he gives snow like wool,” clothing through justice [593] those who were first cold through sin; “he scatters mist like ashes,” shaking in repentance those who were dark through ignorance by infusing into them knowledge of their corruption [Col. 0873C]; “he sends his crystal like morsels,” incorporating into himself through meekness those hardened by obstinacy. But how does he accomplish that work of salvation? “He will send forth his word and melt them; his Spirit will blow and the waters will flow” (Ps. 147:15–18), so that the two disciples going into the village opposite them may do with the ass and colt what we have just briefly touched upon.

8. But who are these two disciples? Perhaps they are those two outstanding virtues, fear and love. The former terrifies by threatening sad and harsh things, through severity; the latter soothes through sweetness by promising joyful and gentle things. The former is the beginning of wisdom, the latter its consummation. The former takes away what is evil so that you may be cleansed from guilt; the latter bestows what is good so that you may be adorned in righteousness. The former drains iniquity out of the soul; the latter pours holiness into it.

These are the two angels who lead Lot from the place of destruction (Gen. 19), rescuing from vices the soul God chooses. These are the two spiritual Levites who, when the camp moves, stand at the entrance of the tabernacle sounding silver trumpets (Num. 10:2–10): for fear and love sound at the very entrance of the mind with certain silent cries of the mind, stirring those inward assemblies of thoughts both to abandon evil and to practice good. Like a trumpet, the one lifts up [Col. 0874A] his voice and says, “Cease to do perversely”; the other says, “Learn to do good” (Isa. 1:16–17). The one says, “Root up and destroy, ruin and scatter”; the other, “Build and plant” (Jer. 1:10). Finally, the one says, “Turn away from evil”; the other likewise, “Do good” (Ps. 33:15).

These are the two men who bring a cluster from the promised land to the children of Israel (Num. 13:24), making known in our inward meditations the fruit of the heavenly homeland. These are the two messengers who rescue Rahab from the destruction of Jericho (Josh. 6:23), drawing away from such destruction the soul which God enlarges by his gifts. These also are the two disciples of whom we are now speaking, who, sent into this fortress, loose the tied ass and colt and bring them to Christ. [Col. 0874B]

9. It is rightly said of this fortress that it is opposite them. For what is more contrary to divine love than the swelling of pride? What is more contrary to fear than the stubbornness of pride and obstinacy? For pride, as some say, is love of one’s own excellence. And how, as long as you are desirous of vain glory and love your own excellence, can you perfectly seek the honour and glory of him of whom Paul says, “To God alone be honour and glory” (1 Tim. 1:17)? Obstinacy also, as they say, is a kind of insensitive persistence of the mind, unwilling ever to yield, and always more ready to resist. When this deadly evil fully possesses the soul, it makes it insensible to the goads of divine fear.

Yet while the fortress is outside them, it is opposed to these disciples; once they have entered it and remain within it for a while, it is already with them. For they powerfully subject it to themselves: love, by affirming that heavenly and eternal excellence, and therefore an excellence far better than any attainable there, is to be possessed elsewhere, overthrows the tower of pride. Fear, by threatening eternal punishment in Gehenna to those who are brazen-faced and hard-hearted, utterly breaks the wall of obstinacy. Thus this fortress, while they remain outside it, is opposite them; while they dwell within it, it is already with them. Hence, as Isaiah prophesies, the city once called a harlot, whose inhabitants were murderers, may now deservedly be called “the city of the righteous,” “the faithful city” (Isa. 1:21–26). [Col. 0874D]

10. But now these two disciples must enter in to loose the tied ass and colt and bring them to Jesus. There are two virtues, brethren, exceedingly necessary for a human being: humble simplicity and active freedom. The ass can represent the former; the colt, the latter. For the ass is placed beneath a yoke, whereas the colt still enjoys its own freedom. Hence the Lord Jesus, inviting us to the meekness of humility, offers us his yoke to take up: “Take my yoke upon you.” Immediately he indicates what it is to take up his yoke, adding: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29).

The author who says of the vain man raised up in pride that “he thinks himself born free like the colt of a wild ass” (Job 11:12) judged that the colt represents freedom [594] [Col. 0875A]. Although he understood this of a certain perverse freedom, of which Paul says, “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness” (Rom. 6:20), he nevertheless showed that, because the colt has not yet been put beneath a yoke, it can represent freedom, whose agility no obstacle impedes. These two animals, the ass and colt, are tied in the fortress when, in the sinful soul—which, as we have taught above, is signified by that fortress—these two virtues, simplicity and freedom, may perhaps be possessed in understanding but are not exercised fruitfully.

[Col. 0875B] 11. If you ask what are the bonds by which they are tied, understand them to be the embarrassment of shame and the inertia of fear. For in a wicked person, shame likewise impedes simplicity and fear impedes freedom, so that the former does not dare to show its true humility within itself, nor the latter presume to exercise its purity. For many clearly recognize that humble simplicity—or, if this is a more fitting expression, simple humility—is a very great virtue. Yet because their minds have not yet been stripped of the glory of this present life and they shrink from being held in contempt, they do not at all embrace it in practice.

Others understand what a lofty thing the purity of freedom is; but, trembling, they fear or desire what is not stable or in their own control; or, enticed by the perverse hope of acquiring it, or shaken by the sluggish fear of losing it, they dare not exercise that freedom either in speech or in action. Do you not recognize that, although simplicity and freedom are present in such persons so far as understanding is concerned, both are nevertheless tied in them so far as practice is concerned?

12. Moreover, the Holy Spirit, who appeared in a dove (Matt. 3:16) and in fire (Acts 2:3–4), makes his chosen ones simple in humility, lest they become proud through self-exaltation; and bold in purity, lest they grow numb through inertia. Recall those two men of virtue—the prophet David and the apostle Paul—and see whether they did not possess within themselves both these animals: both the she-ass of simplicity and the colt of freedom, neither bound, [Col. 0875D] but both unbound. For holy David says: “I will play before the Lord, and I will become more lowly than I have become, and I shall be humble in my own eyes” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 6:22). Rightly does the Holy Spirit say of him that he was “like a tender wood-worm” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 23:8). Therefore, addressing the Lord, he burst forth in these words: “O Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been raised up; neither have I walked in great matters, nor in wonders above me” (Ps. 130 [131]:1). Behold the she-ass in the little town of holy David. But see also the colt: “Did I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? With perfect hatred I hated them, and they became enemies to me” (Ps. 138 [139]:21–22).

Paul too is a little colt, in accordance with his name, and small among his disciples; and although he is afflicted on every side by torments, [Col. 0876A] the word of God is not bound in him. Though he entreats his disciples through the meekness and gentleness of Christ, affirming that he is indeed humble in presence among them (2 Cor. 10:1), he nevertheless withstands Cephas to his face at Antioch, because he sees that he is blameworthy (Gal. 2:11). Therefore admire him there as lowly through humility, and here as raised upright through freedom.

Holy Moses likewise—to linger for a while over these examples—both restrains the proud Pharaoh by authority (Exod. 7–14), and humbly obeys Jethro when he gives counsel (Exod. 18:13–26). Samuel, the man of God, considers that he would commit sin if he did not pray for the people who cast him down from leadership (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 12:23); yet he does not fear to cut the exceedingly fat Agag into pieces (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 15:33). How can we sufficiently admire most holy Elijah, when we see him now so bowed down in humility that, lowly in his own eyes and contemptuous of himself, girded about the loins, he humbly runs before Ahab; and now so raised up in authority that, being zealous with zeal for the Lord of hosts and wasting away over idolaters, he does not fear to deprive them of life? (3 Kings [1 Kings] 17–19.)

Following his master’s simple freedom and free simplicity, holy Elisha does not disdain to be touched by a little woman (4 Kings [2 Kings] 4), does not go out to Naaman the prince (ibid., 9–11), and would not even attend to or look upon the king of Israel, if he were not ashamed before the face of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah (4 Kings [2 Kings] 3:14). I would therefore say that these and other such men had the she-ass of humility [Col. 0876C] and the colt of freedom unbound: for, in order to humble themselves in all things, they are simple and meek; and, in order manfully to pursue whatever is against God, they are upright and free.

13. But if there is among you anyone who does indeed possess these two animals, yet has them bound, those above-mentioned disciples must enter in to unbind them. You have already heard who these disciples are, what these animals are, and also what the bonds are by which they are tied. And who is he who has these animals within himself but bound? When you see someone growing proud under the appearance of humility, adorning what concerns himself more for the brilliance of self-exaltation than arranging it for the beauty of propriety, know that this man has the she-ass, [Col. 0876D] but bound. He is well trained and instructed, so that he knows perfectly how humbly he ought to conduct himself in walking, standing, gesture and dress, expression and disposition—in short, in all his behavior. Yet, because he is ashamed to show himself thus in truth, he indeed has within himself the she-ass of simplicity, but bound by the chain of shame.

Likewise, when you discover someone who, like a wicked watchman, sees the sword and does not sound the trumpet (Ezek. 33:6); who, like a hireling, sees the wolf coming and flees (John 10:12); who, like a lazy and negligent cultivator, knows that thorns and briars and every other useless and harmful thing are growing up in the Lord’s garden, yet does not put his hand to rooting them out—or even, which is less, to cutting them down—recognize that this man has the colt, but [Col. 0877A] bound. For he sees evils, and perhaps does not wish to consent to them; nevertheless, he does not dare to rebuke them as person and matter, place and time require, and in him the colt is bound by the chain of fear.

14. But let the disciples see to it and loose the she-ass; let them loose the colt also, so that ordered love may drive out perverse shame, and simplicity may prevail; and likewise ordered fear may eliminate sluggish dread, so that freedom may flourish. Thus let the mind, made devout from being undevout, love truth so that it hates vanity; let it fear incurring what is penal, so that it fears failing, to the extent of its power, to pursue what is culpable. If this comes to pass in the little town which was formerly opposed to the disciples, the she-ass is loosed and the colt is loosed; because in the soul which formerly, through fear of self-exaltation, was opposed to love, and through the obstinacy of stubbornness was opposed to fear, [Col. 0877B] both simplicity prevails and flourishes, to cast down all arrogance within it, and freedom, to exercise devout zeal toward others.

15. “Loose them,” he says, “and bring them to me.” What is it for the disciples to loose the she-ass and the colt, except that simplicity is freed from perverse shame through the intervention of love, and freedom is freed from idle fear through the mediation of good fear? But these two animals, once loosed, are brought to Jesus when these two virtues are exercised with a pure intention for the attaining of the fruit of true salvation. For someone may, as it were, possess them loosed but not brought to Jesus when he exercises them manfully indeed, but seeks through them either human favor or some earthly advantage, rather than the reward of true salvation.

You see, then, that it is not enough for the she-ass in your little town and the colt to be loosed, unless, once loosed, they are also brought to Jesus. For, according to Paul’s statement, God “renders to each according to his works”: indeed, to those who, by perseverance in good work, seek glory and honor and incorruption, eternal life (Rom. 2:6–7). Therefore, in saying that God will render glory and honor and incorruption to those who persevere in good work, understand that the she-ass and colt have been loosed. But in hearing that he will render these things to those who seek eternal life, recognize that both the she-ass and colt have been brought to Jesus.

16. But these matters are lofty and profound, suited only to the perfect—yet they are also what make people perfect. For I shall call you perfect when I see you, with unceasing diligence, judging and reproving yourself with strict discernment in all your movements, and burning with devout zeal toward your neighbors. Therefore, if you desire to climb to the heights of this perfection, when your own faint-heartedness resists you so that you do not dare to exercise these things, know that [596] you cannot be perfect without them. Hence the Lord says to these disciples: “If anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord has need of them.” For who says anything to the disciples as they loose the she-ass and colt, except the foolish thought within us which, when it is swollen with pride, opposes love in us lest it free the purity of simplicity, and when it is fearful, opposes fear lest it liberate the strength of freedom? But the Lord [Col. 0878A] has need of them, because whoever desires to attain the spiritual lordship of holy perfection must necessarily exercise them.

For two things are especially necessary to the spiritual lord: power and daring—so that you may by no means acknowledge yourself to be lord unless you can both humbly judge yourself whenever you commit anything unlawful, and dare, inflamed as was said above, to rebuke others who act wickedly, according to the matter, the time, the person, and the place.

17. “And they brought the she-ass and the colt, and put their garments upon them, and made him sit upon them.” The disciples’ garments are the adornments of virtues. And what does it mean for their garments to be placed upon them, except that everything capable of stirring one toward the love and fear of God is brought to bear? Jesus himself sits upon them when the desire for true salvation takes precedence in all these things. First, the she-ass and colt are loosed by the disciples; second, they are brought to Jesus; third, their garments are placed upon them; and finally Jesus himself sits upon them. And for what purpose? Surely so that, first, we may do every holy thing, working good toward all; second, that in all these things we may desire to please God alone, seeking eternal life; and third, that we may always strive to advance more and more in goodness, stretching ourselves toward the things within, and so desire to come and appear before the face of God, having the desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ.

But a very great crowd spread their garments in the way, because good inward thoughts lay down their good things low within us. Others cut branches from the trees and spread them [Col. 0878C] in the way, because they humble themselves not only in good works belonging to bodily exercise, which, according to the Apostle, is useful for a little, but also cast down into the low places the very branches of spiritual understanding which they cut from the lofty trees of contemplation. These branches unquestionably pertain to godliness, which is useful for all things (1 Tim. 4:8).

18. Moreover, they humble themselves not only in every external good of the body and in all inward fruits of the spirit, but also, amid all the virtues they possess—whether implanted by nature or added by grace—they persist in devout prayers for eternal salvation. For “those who went before and those who followed cried out, Hosanna.” We pass quickly over these matters, [Col. 0878D] because we are hastening to the end of the sermon.

There are in us certain good dispositions, some by nature and some by grace. The former go before, while the latter follow. Nature implanted certain goods in us; but because these were insufficient for salvation, grace added what nature had supplied less fully. Yet it should be known that, just as the goods of conscience are from grace, so the goods of nature are from grace: the latter from creating grace, the former from saving grace. From the former, the goods of nature receive their beginning; from the latter, their increase, and, once increased, their completion. But in devout thoughts and in those who vigilantly attend to their salvation, both the antecedent gifts of nature and the subsequent gifts of grace cry out, “Hosanna,” so that, for the attainment of eternal salvation, they place their trust not so much in the quality and quantity of merits as in the pure constancy and constant purity of prayers.

For *Hosi*, it is said, means “Save”; while *Anna*, which is understood [another reading: added], expresses the fervent movement of one praying. Therefore, brothers, let us humble ourselves in all our goods, inward as well as outward; and amid the many virtues implanted in us by nature and added to us by grace, let us cry out, with all [Col. 0880A] the marrow of our hearts, “Hosanna.” Therefore, let us not answer him, not only if we have anything unjust, but even if we have anything just; rather, together with the good Job, let us entreat our judge (Job 9:15), whom dominions adore and powers tremble before: God almighty, living and reigning unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0879]

## Fifteen Sermons of Blessed Ogerius, Abbot of Lucedio, of the Cistercian Order in the Diocese of Vercelli, on the discourse delivered by the Lord to the disciples at the Last Supper

[Note.]

[597] The author, previously unknown, was first identified by Cardinal Bona of pious memory from an old manuscript of the Abbey of Staffarda in the Diocese of Saluzzo. That manuscript is now preserved at Turin in the library of His Serene Highness the Duke of Savoy. In Sermon 13, no. 1, there is a striking passage in support of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Mary. The author reveals himself to be a Cistercian in Sermon 10, no. 12. Some believe that Ogerius, or Oglerius, lived in the very time of St Bernard. But Manrique proves that he was somewhat later; and this seems to be supported by Ogerius’s view concerning the immaculate conception of the most holy Virgin, which had not yet been received in Bernard’s age.

## Prologue

[Col. 0879B]

Whoever, hungry, seeks to be satisfied with the Paschal feast, our little table has been set, and no eater is forbidden it. There you may be refreshed by the crumbs remaining from the Lord’s table. For that most sweet Bread, who said of himself, “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John 6:51), while he was in the world satisfied his children abundantly—those, namely, to whom, when about to ascend to the Father, he said: “Little children, yet a little while I am with you” (John 13:33).

But, ascending into heaven, he left his remains for his little ones. As I sought with groaning and weeping that most blessed bread of angels, my Lord Jesus, and resolved to give all the precious things of the world for that ineffable food, I received those remains from the evangelist John as he offered them according to the Lord’s will. But whoever wishes to sit at this little table of Christ’s servant, let him, I pray, not approach without tears; and if he has approached, let him at least not depart without groaning. For in it you will find food not for the belly but for the mind: not fattened burnt offerings, nor oxen with goats, but that Lamb born of the Virgin, who was silent before those striking him and did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7). My soul confesses to him, and he heals it, for it has sinned against him.

May he be my way in this little work and in all my actions, so that, under his guidance, I may begin and end whatever I undertake; so that I may proclaim the Lord’s name in Zion and his praise in Jerusalem; so that, when peoples are gathered together as one and kings to serve the Lord, I may merit to see him in the goodness of his chosen ones and rejoice in the joy of his nation—he who is blessed for ever.

## Sermon I

“Before the feast day of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end,” etc. (John 13:1–2).

[Col. 0880B]

1. The Word of the Father, the Son of God, who for the salvation of humankind “was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), desiring to instruct and form his disciples—and through them all who believe in him—in the practice of examples of humility, when that most merciful hour drew near in which the flesh he had taken from the undefiled Virgin Mary was to endure so sorrowful a punishment, rose from that noble final supper of his earthly life, laid aside his garments, put water into a basin, and washed the disciples’ feet. This is what John the evangelist says: “Before the feast day,” etc.

Such was the custom and observance of the Jews: they held that day solemn upon which the Lord divided the Red Sea for them into two parts, led them through its midst, and overthrew Pharaoh and his army in it. This is that feast day of Passover of which it is said, “Before the feast day of Passover”; for *Pascha* means “Passage.” For that most merciful Passover was drawing near, in which the true Moses was to pass through the Red Sea and enter the land of promise, not after forty years, but only after forty days. That Jewish feast day was the shadow, on which their fathers [598] passed out of Egypt; but this was the reality, on which Christ passed from this world. Thus he made us pass from vices to virtues, from death to [Col. 0881A] life, from the world to heaven, becoming victim and sacrifice for us, offering himself as a burnt offering to God the Father upon the altar of the cross.

“Before the feast day of Passover,” etc. What then is this, holy John, that you call a feast? Is not a feast day a day of joy and gladness? Do you suppose that day was one of happiness and delight, when the Lamb was lifted upon the wood of the cross to be sacrificed, made the reproach of men and the outcast of the people; when the sun was darkened by grief, the rocks split, and the whole circuit of the world trembled; when the Mother and her beloved John wept thus? Rather, that day was a day of mourning than of laughter and joy for the saints and elect; but it was joy for the Jews, and sadness for you and your Apostles. The Jews’ joy shall be turned into mourning, and the Apostles’ sorrow has been turned into joy. It follows:

[Col. 0881B]

2. “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come, to pass from this world to the Father.” Jesus, in Hebrew, is interpreted in Latin as Savior. This is that most mighty Savior who can no longer be conquered and who saves all who hope in him. Once, Christian, he was conquered for you—indeed, he died; but do not weep, because he rose from the dead, and death shall no longer have dominion over him. It was necessary for him to die for the salvation of the world and to rise on the third day; and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations (Luke 24:46–47), because he had so ordained. This is what is meant by, “Jesus, knowing that his hour had come,” etc.

This is that hour concerning which, above, fearing to die according to the flesh, he groaned and said: “Now my soul is greatly troubled. And what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour” (John 12:27). Christ feared to die so that you might not fear to die, trusting in him who raised Jesus from the dead on the third day. In him alone who raised Jesus must one place one’s trust.

You, Christian, must not despair because of this weakness. He taught what you ought then, and in all dangers of death, to say; to whom you should flee, whom you should invoke, in whom you should hope: in God the Father, who cannot despise those who hope in him when they have the testimony of good works. I say good works, because to hope for anything without merits should be called not hope but presumption. Therefore perform such works that, in the hour of death, you may truthfully say to him: “In you, O Lord, have I hoped; I shall not be confounded for ever” (Ps. [Col. 0881D] 30 [31]:2).

He foresaw this hour; he chose this hour, so that in it he might pass through death from this world to the Father according to his humanity, though according to his divinity he had never departed from the Father. That hour is the end of which it is said: “Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them unto the end.” Having loved his own, being made man for them, he loved them so much that love led him even to death. He loved you in death, so that through his love you might pass from the world to the Father. He loved you unto the end, so that you might remain in his love unto the end. And if you do this, without doubt you will pass to the Father; but whoever does not remain unto the end in his love shall, I say truly, perish for ever.

There ought to be no measure to love for him. He loved you without measure; you ought to love him without measure. In loving you he exceeded the measure of love, dying for you; how greatly you ought to love him, you cannot fully do. Love him with all your heart, with all your mind and all your soul, and with all your strength. This alone he asks; beyond this he asks nothing. Do this and you shall live. It follows:

3. “And supper having been made, when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas, son of Simon Iscariot, to betray him.” Here the supper is indicated as having been prepared but not yet completed, since afterward he reclined and gave the morsel to Judas. O unhappy Judas! O most wicked disciple, evil merchant! A supper was prepared for you, and by you the giver of the supper was betrayed. O wretched Judas! O evil confessor! O despairing penitent! You said, “I have sinned, betraying innocent blood” (Matt. 27:4), and, wretch that you were, you strangled yourself with the noose of despair.

This man, as I suppose, was the son of Simon Scharioth. Simon means “Obedient”; but what sort of man that Simon was, God knows, while I do not know. He is called Scharioth from the village in which he was born, which is also called Marmotis, or “evil death.” And rightly was he from “evil death,” because he perished by so evil a death.

The devil had put it into his heart by suggestion that he should betray him, because he did not believe him to be God. Do you not tremble, Christian, and you monk of Saint Benedict, when you consider what was done to Christ’s disciple? The devil put it into his heart to betray Life; and, betraying Life, he lost both himself and life by the noose of despair. If the wolf did not fear to enter the Lord’s flock and slaughter and destroy one out of twelve in so small a number, what will he do to the flock entrusted to a shepherd? [Col. 0882C]

Let each of you, dearest brothers, see that he is not like Judas. See how cautiously you walk, not as unwise but as wise, on guard against the snares of the cunning enemy. He put it into Judas’s heart to betray the Lord. What is it to betray the Lord? To sell the Lord. What is it to sell? To alienate. He sells the Lord who alienates the Lord from himself. You alienate the Lord from yourself if you drive him away from yourself.

O monk of God, O disciple of Christ, listen to me; listen to my counsel. The devil seeks to tear you away, to draw you out of the Lord’s flock. See that you do not consent to him; see that you do not believe him. He is a liar, and his father is one. He wishes to kill you, slaughter you, and destroy you with himself in Gehenna.
