Beware of money-boxes; beware of purses: they are the devil’s pits. Alas, how many he has ruined in them, how many he has slain in them! It is said of Judas that “he was a thief, and had the money-box” (John 12:6), etc. While he thirsts for gain, he goes toward the noose; while he loses life, he gains death.

Alas, how many money-boxes, alas, how many purses there are in the monasteries of Saint Benedict! Alas, how many hooded men, tonsured above the ears, have a purse of the mind; have a money-box of self-will; a purse of murmuring, detraction, wandering, pride and rancor, envy and ill will! But remember, most beloved brothers, that those who do such things follow Judas the betrayer; and therefore, unless they amend themselves, they shall not possess the kingdom of God.

4. Be, I beg you, beloved ones, disciples of Christ—not in falsehood, but in truth; not in dress, but [Col. 0883A] in heart; not in a high tonsure, but in a pure mind. Leave Judas despairing; follow Peter truly repenting. Leave Judas despairing in the abyss of hell; follow Peter, who is in the glory of paradise. Hold fast to Peter’s tears. If you do this, you will attain Peter’s glory through Jesus Christ the Lord, to whom my soul confesses, and who heals it because it has sinned against him; he who, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is blessed through all ages. Amen.

## Sermon II

On verses 3–19 of John, chapter 13.

1. As the ear cannot be satisfied with hearing, nor the eye with seeing, so we ought never to be satisfied with recounting Christ’s devout deeds. For they are sweeter to me than honey and the honeycomb, and dearer than thousands of gold and [Col. 0883B] silver pieces; and I cannot be satisfied with them. May the Lord increase my desire and make me joyful in the delight of his countenance, with all who love him. Of him it is said in what follows: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he came forth from God and goes to God, rises from supper and lays aside his garments. And when he had taken a linen cloth, he girded himself; then he put water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the linen cloth with which he was girded.”

Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, both good and evil—evil for use, good for fulfillment—he made the good of our redemption from the evil of Judas’s betrayal. Or, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, because he subjected all things beneath his feet: sheep and oxen, and moreover the beasts of the field. And knowing that he came forth from God, without forsaking him, and goes to God, without abandoning us, he rises from supper, etc.

He came forth from God because he came from the Father’s bosom into the womb of the blessed Virgin: because, “being in the form of God, he did not deem equality with God a thing to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men, and found in appearance as a man” (Phil. 2:6–7). He also came forth from God when he presented himself to men in such a manner that he could be seen and touched; indeed—what I ought not to commit to writing without great groaning of heart and a stream of tears—bound, struck, scourged, spat upon, and finally killed. This is what is meant by “he came forth from God.”

But do not weep, good monk, because it follows: “He goes to God.” He goes to God because, having risen from the dead, he dies no more; death shall no longer have dominion over him (Rom. 6:9). He ascended into heaven, sits at the right hand of the Father, and has been appointed by God judge of the living and the dead. And this is what is meant by “he rises from supper”; for he rose from supper because he came to humankind from the Father’s bosom, where he supped with the angels, taking upon himself the robe of our mortality.

2. In a certain manner he laid aside his garments when he emptied himself. By uniting human nature to himself, he took the linen cloth and girded himself with it: because, clothing himself with human nature, he girded himself with power in it, and, triumphing gloriously over the proud enemy, became King of glory and Lord of hosts. He put water into a basin and washed the disciples’ feet. What is the water? What is the basin? This is that blessed water [Col. 0884A] which washes away the filth of minds, cleanses lepers, enlightens the blind, heals the sick, justifies the ungodly, and raises the dead. To this water my Lord Jesus invites the thirsty, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7:37). This water is the Holy Spirit. This is the water of which Jeremiah says: “They have forsaken the fountain of living water and have dug for themselves broken cisterns which cannot hold water” (Jer. 2:13).

Give me to drink from this fountain, Lord, so that I may thirst no more. For my soul thirsts for this living fountain. O that I might touch this fountain! O that I might be filled with this most sweet fountain! Do you think the time will come when I can draw from it fully? And when? And if ever, why not now? What shall I say, what shall I do, because my Lord delays coming [Col. 0884B] to me? O most sweet Jesus, let tears be my continual refreshment until my soul is told: “Rejoice and be glad. Behold him whom you seek; behold him whom you desire; behold him for whom you weep. Behold your Lord; behold your God: Father and Son and the desired fountain, the Holy Spirit. Now be inebriated by the delights of paradise.”

This water, my brothers, is the Holy Spirit. May he so inebriate our minds from himself that we may love nothing else besides him. That basin in which the Lord placed the Holy Spirit is the Church of the faithful, in which, through the washing of regeneration, the Holy Spirit cleanses the filth of believers. When it is said, “He washed the Apostles’ feet,” understand the uncleannesses of those following in their footsteps.

Or we may say that the basin, or receptacle, [Col. 0884C] of the Holy Spirit was the hearts of the Apostles, into which the Lord poured the Holy Spirit. And he washed their feet because he strengthened them through the Holy Spirit in the Catholic faith, which carries the faithful to heaven—a faith which they had kept darkened by the dust of unbelief, once its rust had been wholly driven out.

3. We may also speak otherwise, if it delights you to listen with Christ’s love. But receive, I pray, not without tears what ought not to be written without tears. He put water into the basin because, counting death a delight for your love, he poured out his holy blood upon the wood of the cross. And he washed the Apostles’ feet, that is, he cleansed the footsteps of believers, which were filthy with sins. And he wiped them with the linen cloth with which he was girded—that is, with the human flesh in which he was clothed—because his passion is the true cleansing of our sins.

Or, whoever wishes to interpret the Lord’s supper as his passion should not think that he has wandered from the path of truth. This supper here signifies the passion. As breakfast does not follow supper, so Christ, once having suffered, does not suffer again. He rises from supper, after the passion; he lays aside his garments, namely his former weakness; he girds himself with the linen cloth, the same flesh now immortal. He puts water into the basin because, through the washing of baptism, he washes believers from sins. And he wipes them with the linen cloth with which he is girded because he intercedes for us before the Father with unutterable groanings, showing him his humanity.

O wondrous and unsearchable mercy! O inestimable goodness! O new and unheard-of humility! Christ, the Son of God, born of the pure and undefiled Virgin, [Col. 0885A] King of kings and Lord of lords, rises from supper, lays aside his garments, girds himself with a linen cloth, and puts water into a basin. Before the disciples he bends his venerable knees; lowly and bowed down, he washes the disciples’ feet. O who has ever heard such things? O how astonishing the mercy! Wondrous is God’s clemency! He who created all things out of nothing washes the disciples’ feet.

What do you think, whoever you are: you whom anger inflames, pride consumes, anger unsettles, pride ravages; you who are quick to anger and swift to pride? O proud one, O offspring of the devil, O apostate Christian, O wicked servant! What do you think of your Creator, of your God? Bowed down, he washes his disciples’ feet; and do you disdain to humble yourself before brothers who have offended you? O evil servant, seed of Canaan and not of Judah, deceived through the author of pride! Why do you not consider who he is whom you follow through pride, and who he is whom you disdain to imitate through humility? O how evil is he whom you follow, and how good is he from whom you turn aside! That one is the devil; this one is God. Choose whom it is better to imitate.

O proud one, does your brow not blush? Be ashamed, vessel of dung, to retain pride any longer. Do you not know that God resists the proud but gives his grace to the humble? Put off the old man and put on the new—namely, the Lord Jesus—and he will transform the body of your humility, making it conformed to the body of his glory. Learn, I pray, henceforth to possess humility through the author of humility. For the following is said of him:

4. “He comes to Simon Peter. And Peter said to him: [Col. 0885C] ‘Lord, do you wash my feet?’ Jesus answered and said to him: ‘What I do you do not know now, but you shall know afterward.’” When the Lord Jesus began to wash his disciples’ feet, he first came to the first of the disciples. And Peter himself is astonished that God washes a man’s feet. For, struck with fear, he could not bear that the Lord should humble himself at his feet. He had seen him put water into the basin and gird himself with a linen cloth, and perhaps wondered what he intended to do. But after he saw him carry a vessel with water before his feet, bend his knees, and prepare himself to wash them, he was astonished beyond all expression and was terrified. Struck with great fear, he groaned and cried out, saying: “Lord, do you wash my feet? The Creator [Col. 0885D] of a creature, God for a man, Lord for a servant, Master for a disciple—indeed, for one made from mud, he who made all things from nothing? Rise, Lord; rise, my God. What do you intend to do? I cannot endure it; I cannot bear it. My eyes shrink from seeing you so bowed down, so prostrate at my feet. Rise, Creator; rise, my God, light of the world, my life, my glory. Do not do what I see you intend to do.”

But Jesus says: “What I do you do not know now, but you shall know afterward.” As if he said: “Do not fear; do not be dismayed. Truly, Peter, these are great signs of humility, but you will soon see greater things. Allow it now, for so it must be done. Although you now do not understand the mystery of this matter, you shall understand afterward. It is a mystery, it is an example, which I leave you as I go to the Father. Therefore do not prevent what I wish [Col. 0886A] to do.”

Peter says to him: “You shall never wash my feet.” “Far be it from me, Lord, that you should wash my feet for ever,” that is, at any time. Jesus answered: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me.” In saying “you,” and not “your feet,” there is a synecdoche, when what belongs to a part is attributed to the whole. “I am the water that washes; I am the water that sanctifies. Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me.”

Peter, hearing, “You shall have no part with me,” trembled all over. Contradicting the Master no longer, he offers not only his feet but his whole self to be washed, saying: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and head.” “What is this that you say: ‘You shall have no part with me’? O how bitter is what you say: ‘I shall have no part with you’! Are you not my life, [Col. 0886B] my sweetness, my entire hope, my salvation, and all my desire? Behold me: do whatever you will with me; wash my feet, [602] and not only my feet, but also my hands and head.”

5. But, O Lord Jesus, since this is true—that no one can have a share with you unless you first wash him—have mercy on me, have mercy on me. I am that man wholly sinful, wholly unclean, wholly foul; I long to have a share with you, I desire to have a share with you. Do not despise me, God my Savior. Be gracious to me, a sinner; wash the filthy, wash the defiled; wash my feet, wash my hands, wash my head—indeed, my whole body; wash my mind, wash my soul, wash me inwardly and outwardly; wash me from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. If you [Col. 0886C] wash me, I shall be made whiter than snow (Ps. 50:4, 9). O Lord Jesus, who will grant that you may come into my heart and intoxicate me with your water, so that I may forget my past evils and embrace you, the good Word, O Life that shall never die for ever? Sweet food of my soul, come, Lord, and do not delay. My sinful soul awaits the inspiration of your grace, that it may repent sufficiently and live well. You said to Peter: “He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet.” I am not Peter, already bathed; I need to be washed wholly. I commit myself to you: do with me whatever you will. But may you, O Lord, remain blessed for ever. “He who has bathed needs only to wash his feet.” Here it is implied that the Apostles had been baptized, though we do not read where. He who has been washed in baptism is wholly clean. [Col. 0886D] But because he is again defiled by the dust of his earthly dwelling, it is again necessary to wash his feet. The Lord washes them by interceding for us; and we ourselves do so by prayer, through contrition of heart and the compunction of tears.

6. Even one who, in leisure, studies the truth, while he goes on opening to the Bride as she knocks in others, soils his feet: for truth is heard humbly, but it is not preached without danger. This the Bride shows in the Song of Songs, where, when her Bridegroom urges her toward preaching, she says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” He had said to her, the Bridegroom: “Open to me, my sister, my beloved, my undefiled one, for my head is full of dew, and my locks [Col. 0887A] with the drops of the night” (Song 5:3, 2). As if he said: O my sister, my co-heiress, my beloved, confidante of my secrets; my dove, illumined by the Holy Spirit; my undefiled one, stripped of earthly cares: “Open to me,” that is, by preaching make the hearts of those who wander accessible to me. “My head is full of dew,” that is, my divinity is surrounded by the ardor of charity. “And my locks with the drops of the night,” that is, the assemblies of the faithful are beset by the opinions of heretics. To him the Bride replies: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?” That is, I have abandoned worldly things; how shall I return to them? I have withdrawn from preaching; how shall I begin it again? I have washed my thoughts and affections; how shall I be defiled by the filth of the world? But the Lord washes these feet of the disciples through the pledge of his prayer, where it is said: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” [Col. 0887B] (Matt. 6:12).

7. The Evangelist explains what follows, “You are clean, but not all,” when he says: “Jesus knew who it was that would betray him; therefore he said: ‘You are not all clean.’” It follows: “After he had washed their feet and had taken his garments, when he had reclined, he said again to them: ‘Do you know what I, your Lord and Master, have done for you? For I have given you an example, that you also may do likewise.’” If you have committed this to memory, it has been explained. After he washed the feet of the disciples—that is, after purification had been accomplished through his blood—he took his garments, because he had become immortal. When he reclined—that is, when he sat at the right hand of the Father—he spoke through the Holy Spirit, sent in tongues [Col. 0887C] of fire. O blessed feet, O happy feet, which deserved to have so great and such a washer! I speak of the feet of the elect; I do not speak of the feet of Judas the betrayer. O blessed Peter, O happy Apostles, before whose feet the humble Creator of Angels stood! O blessed cleansing! O blessed washing, which cleanses lepers, heals the sick, cures wounds, makes scars sound, gives light to the blind, movement to the lame, beauty to the ugly, riches to the needy, joy to the sorrowful, pardon to penitents, life to the dead! O great joy, immeasurable gladness!

8. After Christ had washed, he took his garments; after the death of the flesh, he received the glory of the resurrection. After the shedding of his [603] blood, he received [Col. 0887D] the immortality of his body. Then he reclined; then he rested; he ascended into heaven, where he sits, blessed, at the right hand of God the Father. From that reclining-place he thunders forth to the disciples, instructs and teaches them through the Holy Spirit; and through them he thunders forth to all nations. And what does he say? “Do you know what I have done for you? You call me Master and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am.” This is what he had promised Peter when he said: “But you shall know afterward.” Here he invites them to know what they had not formerly known. What he says—“You call me Master and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am”—is not said arrogantly, but truthfully. For one who, under compelling necessity, speaks truly of his own good qualities is joined all the more truly to humility insofar as he is joined to truth. “You call me Master and Lord, and you speak rightly, for so I am.” I am [Col. 0888A] Master; I am Lord. I am a Master without error; I am a Master without falsehood. I am the Master of goodness; I am the Master of holiness. Whoever follows me goes rightly and cannot walk wrongly. I am Lord of life, Lord of death, Lord of heaven, Lord of earth, Creator of all things and Lord of all. “If therefore I, Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.” As before he instructed them by example, so now the Master of truth instructs them by word. Here, indeed, an argument for the practice of humility is drawn, as though he said: If I, who am Lord and Master, have washed your feet, then you, who are neither masters nor lords, ought to wash one another’s feet. “I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also may do.” [Col. 0888B] And the sense is: If I have washed your feet—that is, if I, Lord God, mighty in all things, have forgiven your sins, and Master, knowing all things before they happen—then you, who are servants and disciples, ought to forgive those who sin against you and pray for them. “I have given you an example, that as I have done to you, so you also may do.” You will not be good servants if you do not follow your Lord, nor true disciples if you depart from the teaching of your Master.

9. Hear, prelates, you who occupy the seat of government. Do you think that you possess the Lord’s example? Let each of us examine his own conscience; let him rejoice if he possesses it. If he does not possess it, he is no longer the Lord’s disciple. It would be better for him to have a millstone [Col. 0888C] around his neck and be drowned in the depths of the sea than to have obtained the title of abbot. It would be better for him to be a keeper of swine than an abbot of monks. O basin of the Lord! O humility of Christ, how far you have withdrawn! O how rare, how few are those who pour water into the basin and, bending the knee, seek to wash the feet of their disciples! A brother sins, a brother gives offense, he falls into some fault: there is no basin, no water, no one preparing himself to wash him, but rather to expel him. Learn, prelates, that this is not according to Christ’s rule. He washed the disciples’ feet with bent knees; and do you refuse to wash the filth of your fellow servants while your whole bodies are prostrate on the ground? “A disciple is not above his master.” A monk sins; a convert sins: he carries dust on his foot; indeed, perhaps his whole body wastes away in an eruption of the skin. Take water; take instruction from the basins of the Master, from the Lord’s commandments. Run to him, not upon Pharaoh’s horse, but in the humility of the Redeemer; with a kindly countenance and a tranquil mind hasten, as quickly as you can, to wash him, lest the dust become scabies, scabies become leprosy, and the leper be expelled from the Lord’s flock. But if he is obstinate and refuses correction, saying, “You shall never wash my feet,” then say to him also: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no share with Christ the Lord.” Afterwards, if he is willing to agree with Peter, wash him with all humility, gentleness, and mercy, so that you yourself may obtain mercy from God. If you do not do this, you do not hold to Christ’s example and are not [Col. 0889A] Christ’s disciple. Do you disdain to do what Christ did? Why does it weary the servant to do what the Lord did? “The servant is not greater than his lord, nor the apostle greater than him who sent him.” As I suffer, you also suffer; as I humble myself, you also humble yourselves.

10. “If you know these things which I have done and taught, you shall be blessed if you do them. I do not speak of all: I know whom I have chosen.” He did not speak of all because Judas was an apostate. He had chosen [604] twelve; but one was a devil—Judas Iscariot, who lifted up his heel against the Lord. Of him he himself said: “That the Scripture may be fulfilled: ‘He who eats my bread has lifted up his heel against me.’” O unhappy Judas! You eat the Lord’s bread, and lift up your heel against the Lord! Alas, how many Judases eat the Lord’s bread [Col. 0889B] and strike the Lord with their heel in their deeds. How many live from the altar who do not serve the altar; indeed, they count the Lord of the altar as nothing! Alas—what is more grievous—how many priests, false priests though they are, receive the bread of Christ, the body of Christ, in their mouths, and trample Christ underfoot: foul with the stench of lust, infected by the poison of wickedness! These are Judas Iscariot; unless they change for the better, would that they had not been born. But you, servant of God, monk of Christ, hold fast to the example and you shall possess the promise: do what he commanded, that you may attain the blessedness he promised. It follows:

11. “From now on I tell you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe that I am.” And the sense is: Until now I have endured and kept silent; but now I identify the betrayer [Col. 0889C] before what is soon to be done is done, so that, when it has happened, you may believe that I am he of whom that Scripture prophesied. Therefore, my brothers, disciples of Christ, consider what Iscariot did, and see that you do not do like things. Judas lifted up his heel against Christ; you, however, prostrate body and soul before him. Judas withdrew from him; you, however, follow him. Judas sold him to the Jews; you, however, sell what you possess, that you may be able to purchase him. Indeed, not only count what you possess as nothing for love of that pearl of such great beauty, but count even yourselves as nothing; and strive, as much as you can, to please him alone, so that I and you may be able to attain those joys, enduring without end, which he himself is, [Col. 0889D] through the same Savior of the world, who lives and reigns, blessed, with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. On verses 20–30 of John, chapter 13

1. Since, by the law of the human condition, every person must go forth to his work and to his labor until evening, and since Scripture cannot be broken, it is necessary that each person, while living in the body, should not cease to do what will profit him for eternity. For the time and hour will soon come when every labor and all concern with labor shall cease; and then every person shall receive a reward according to his labor. Therefore, since nothing is sweeter or more fitting than to consider the commandments of the Lord, I have chosen to meditate upon the law [Col. 0890A] of Christ, because the law of my Redeemer is good to me beyond thousands of gold and silver pieces, and to give from the fruit of my labors to anyone who asks. But you, my reader, listen attentively, and observe what Christ speaks to you through me. He is the one than whom none is greater, none better; than whom none is more beautiful, none sweeter, none dearer: the glory of the saints, the splendor of the Angels, author and creator of all things, who says to the disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you: he who receives anyone whom I send receives me; and he who receives me receives him who sent me.” After our Lord and Savior had taught humility and the passion of the flesh by his own example, he adds honor, in order to console them, affirming that he himself and his Father are received in those who are received for love of him. Here it should be noted [Col. 0890B] that in the person sent it is not the authority of the one sent, but of the sender, that is commended. Therefore, whoever receives Christ’s messenger receives Christ; and if he receives Christ, he also receives Christ’s Father.

2. What do you hear, O Christian? Truth speaks; Truth cannot lie. For he says: “He who receives anyone whom I send receives me.” Whom does he send? Who, indeed, is this messenger? A poor man comes; a beggar comes; he is a stranger and a traveler. He has nothing to wear, nothing to eat, nowhere to lay his head. He comes to your door, to your house, and asks for bread and requests clothing—not as one brother asks another, not as a companion asks his companion, but as a servant asks his lord; he seeks lodging with you for Christ’s love. What do you think? Who is that beggar, [Col. 0890C] that traveler, who so humbly and earnestly asks to lodge with you for Christ’s love? [605] He is Christ’s envoy; he is Christ’s messenger. He is not alone: Christ is with him. Receive him joyfully, feed him gladly, serve him devoutly with great fear and reverence: you receive Christ, you feed Christ. Rejoice and be glad that you have been worthy to have such a guest. Happy table, blessed table, at which Christ is a guest, at which God is refreshed; unhappy the table that lacks such a guest. O how wretched a table—indeed, how wretched the master of the table—who drives the poor man from his table, who closes to the poor the bowels of mercy! O wicked servant, whose heart neglects to open the purse of compassion! Ought you not to have had mercy upon your fellow servant? Who gave you what you possess? Was it not the Lord [Col. 0890D] of the poor? Was it not the Creator both of the poor and of you? Did not nature create you equal, and will you not depart under one and the same condition? Why do the common boundaries of your lot not move you? Receive the wretched man, take in the beggar and traveler; feed the hungry, clothe the naked, and devote yourself, insofar as you can, to works of mercy. When a poor person asks, do not delay to open your hand; for Christ receives your alms together with your poor brother. But you, my reader, I beg you, do not shrink from the poor man. Rather, as soon as you see him, do not neglect to reverence him: though he be scabrous or leprous, filthy in clothing, foul in breath, nevertheless embrace him with the arms of charity, and lovingly give what he asks of you. In truth you give to Christ; Christ receives. He himself is witness; he cannot lie, and on the day of judgment [Col. 0891A] he will render you an eternal reward. It follows:

3. “When Jesus had said this, he was troubled in spirit, and testified and said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, that one of you will betray me.’” Jesus was troubled because of our weakness, not because of any weakness in his own power. Our weakness was troubled in him, not his power, just as it truly suffered in him. He voluntarily accepts disturbance, lest a servant who is troubled by necessity should despair. His being troubled in spirit signifies that spiritual persons should be troubled out of charity when an urgent cause compels them to separate tares from wheat before the harvest—that is, compels them to excommunicate before the day of judgment. But it should be noted that there are two kinds of disturbance: disturbance of the flesh and disturbance of the spirit. Disturbance of the flesh is a passion of the flesh; disturbance of the spirit is fear, anxiety, and the like. The Lord was troubled not in flesh but in spirit [Col. 0891B] when he was about to say, “One of you will betray me.” This was not because he suddenly learned it for the first time then, and the unexpected evil troubled him; rather, because he was now about to reveal the man, so that he should not remain hidden; and because he was about to depart and bring the Jews. The betrayer’s imminent threat troubled him, as was said above; likewise his approaching passion troubled him, as is said below: “Now my soul is troubled, and what shall I say?” (John 12:27). He said these things as the hour of his passion approached. The Lord Jesus was troubled in spirit, and he made known what had been hidden and said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, that one of you will betray me.” As though he said: One of you will go out and betray me; one of you—but not one united to me by the bond of charity—will betray me. Therefore the disciples looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke. No slight disturbance, fear, and anxiety tormented the minds of the Apostles. Do you suppose that Peter and the holy Apostles searched the recesses of their minds, so that, if they had thought anything sinister against the Author of life even in thought, they would not have been greatly troubled? For the pallor on their faces showed the grief alive in their minds. But he who carried the cunning, rabid fox beneath his breast bore no grief; he was not sorrowful, though immense grief ought to have been within him.

4. O goodness of the Redeemer! O mercy of the Creator! He wills no one to perish but all to be saved. He does not identify his betrayer particularly, lest the man become more shameless or more brazen when openly exposed. [Col. 0891D] He therefore reveals the crime and allows room for repentance, so that the betrayer, seeing that he cannot remain concealed, may repent. But that man of perdition, admitting no lamentations of repentance, remained what he had been before, or worse, passing into the affection of his heart. Yet those whose hearts were shaken by the huge storm of grief looked at one another, uncertain of whom he spoke, because although each knew his own conscience, another’s was unknown to him. Now one of his disciples, whom Jesus loved, was reclining in Jesus’ bosom. Happy, I say, was that disciple to whom the Author of life, both present and future, was so intimate. [606] Exceedingly honored was that disciple whose head had as its resting-place that most venerable breast of Jesus—Jesus Christ, Creator of all things. And Jesus greatly [Col. 0892A] loved him whom he exalted with so great an honor. O how well he rested who rested upon Christ’s breast! O blessed Apostle of God, disciple of Jesus Christ, blessed John: would that I might deserve, by kissing them, to moisten with tears the most sweet feet of him upon whose breast you deserved to sleep! Would that I might at least be able to contemplate from afar the face of him upon whose breast you deserved to sleep so sweetly! For here he speaks of himself as though of another, so that, as writer of the events, he may not appear to be his own herald. By “bosom” or “breast” was signified that secret from which he drank the sacrament of divinity. He loved John not more than all the others, but more intimately, so that he might depart this life in peace rather than through passion. Simon Peter therefore signaled to him and said: “Who is it of whom he speaks?” [Col. 0892B] Peter knew that Christ loved John by a certain privilege of affection and would not conceal from him the secret of his divinity. Therefore Peter signaled to him to ask: “Who is it?” Thus, reclining upon Jesus’ breast, he said: “Lord, who is it?” And rightly he did not fear to ask his Master about the betrayer, since the Master of truth had already shown him, in the bosom of Divinity, how to search out the secrets of the heavens. And he says: “Lord, who is it? Who is that unhappy man? Who is that wicked man? Who is that accursed man? Who is your betrayer? I beg you, do not conceal him from me, to whom you have deigned to reveal the secrets of your divinity.” The Lord answered him: “It is he to whom I shall offer the dipped bread.” And, having dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. The dipping of the bread [Col. 0892C] signifies Judas’s deceit, for he came to supper as a feigned friend. For things that are dipped do not cleanse, but stain.

5. But as to what bread Judas received dipped, I shall not leave my reader in suspense, if he deigns to listen, with the help of the Lord. First, however, it must be known that “bread” is understood in many ways in Holy Scripture. By bread is sometimes understood the Lord; sometimes spiritual grace; sometimes instruction in divine teaching; sometimes heretical preaching; sometimes the support of this present life; sometimes the pleasure of human delight. The Lord is called bread, as he himself says: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:51). If we say that the Lord was that bread which the betrayer received dipped, we do not leave the path of truth. Judas therefore received dipped bread because he considered the Lord Jesus merely a man and not God. He ate the dipped morsel, or dipped hearth-bread, because, although he believed the Lord would die, he did not believe that he would rise again. This most blessed bread was dipped when his feet were nailed to the cross for our salvation: he appeared to have neither form nor beauty. The Jews, signified by Judas, eat this dipped bread because they believe that Christ Jesus was not God but a mere man; they grant his death, but do not yet accept his resurrection. He gnaws at dipped bread who denies that the Son of the Virgin existed before all ages. Dipped bread is gnawed by him [Col. 0893A] who departs from the firmness of faith; nor can one who wishes to weaken the Catholic faith worthily eat this solid bread. Bread signifies spiritual grace, as in that prophetic saying: “He who stops his ears lest he hear blood, and shuts his eyes lest he see evil—he shall dwell on high; the fortifications of rocks shall be his height; bread is given to him, his waters are sure” (Isa. 33:15–16). And the sense is: “He who stops his ears lest he hear blood,” that is, he who does not give consent to sins suggested by flesh and blood; and he who “shuts his eyes lest he see evil,” that is, who does not approach anything contrary to uprightness—he “shall dwell on high,” because although the flesh still holds him below, he has joined his mind to things on high. “The fortifications of rocks shall be his height,” because he who treads underfoot the base desires of earthly life raises himself toward the heavenly homeland by the examples of the fathers who have gone before; and because by the gift of contemplation he is filled with spiritual grace, there fittingly follows: “Bread is given to him,” that is, he has received the gift of spiritual grace because, by hoping for heavenly things, he has lifted himself above weak and lowly things. He therefore received this bread—[607] namely, the grace which the Lord had given him—dipped, because he exercised not love but hatred against Jesus, the perfecter of virtues. Dipped bread was due to him whose face hypocritically concealed his lack of holiness. For he feigned in his countenance the religious devotion that he did not possess in his mind; he displayed in his clothing the holiness that he banished from his heart: outwardly a lamb in public, inwardly a wolf in secret; outwardly Christ’s disciple, inwardly the devil’s disciple. For many eat this bread, because they do not show in deed the religious devotion that they profess in word. How many monks are there in Saint Benedict’s monastery who laugh at others’ mourning and rejoice at others’ grief; cloistered in body, wandering in mind, and never steadfast! Sluggish at reading, slow at prayer; sleeping in church, wakeful in the refectory; distressed by long vigils but delighted by a long feast; execrating the cloister, loving the lecture hall; more often remaining outside choir on account of illness; eyeing the infirmary with grim looks, not because of bodily illness but because of carnal desire; [Col. 0893C] ever grumbling and detracting. What else do these wretches do but eat dipped bread? Certainly such men follow Judas the betrayer; and unless they come to their senses, let them beware lest they be condemned with Judas. It follows:

6. “Then, after the morsel, Satan entered into him. And Jesus said to him: ‘What you are doing, do quickly.’” Some think that Judas then received Christ’s body. But it must be known that the Lord had already distributed to them all the sacrament of his Body and Blood, among whom Judas also was. Then, by the dipped morsel, the betrayer is made manifest. For many false religious and falsely tonsured men, when they receive the Lord’s Body together with piously religious people, cannot be distinguished from them except by the dipped morsel, which is [Col. 0894A] detraction, grumbling, disobedience, wanton speech, hidden money, and perhaps graver sins. Whoever is such a person is not a monk; indeed, he resembles Judas the betrayer. But whoever that wretched man may be, let him fear in repentance what follows, lest he be condemned with Judas the betrayer. For it follows: “Then Satan entered into him,” in order to possess more fully one into whom he had already entered. Then he entered in order to deceive him and draw him away from the fellowship of the Apostles, so that now, using him openly rather than secretly with unrestricted power, he might slaughter and destroy him in the abyss of perdition. And what he did to the betrayer, he does not cease to do to those like him. For one whom he has long possessed as a servant in a monastery, at the last he does not even leave among the company of monks; and the betrayer whom he held in the monastery he now kills outside [Col. 0894B] the monastery. But because he does not doubt that the end of the world will come quickly, he conceals the cunning of his wickedness from the minds of the depraved, so that he may strike with sudden death those whom he has long kept bound in the evil of wicked action. And he allows many to remain in the monastery until death, so that through their perversity he may corrupt and overthrow others. And since he counts it a matter of no consequence whether he kills and slaughters miserable souls in the monastery or outside it, let us avoid his snares under the Lord’s protection and carry out what is said, namely, “What you are doing, do quickly.” For when it is said, “What you are doing, do quickly,” he does not command Judas’s evil but cuts it short; it is good for us, because he wills it to occur sooner, not so much in haste toward Judas’s punishment as toward the salvation of the faithful.

[Col. 0894C] 7. O boundless love, O inestimable charity, O unfathomable affection: “What you are doing, do quickly!” This I desire, this I long for, this I seek; for this I came into this world. “What you are doing, do quickly.” Do you wish to sell me to the Jews? I wish to be sold. Do you wish to betray me? I wish to be betrayed. Do you wish me to be crucified? I wish to be crucified. Do you wish me to be killed? I wish to be killed. This I love, this I seek: “What you are doing, do quickly.” But, Jesus, my life, my whole desire, sweetness that does not deceive, delightful sweetness, glorious sweetness, splendor of Angels, brightness and glory of the saints: how greatly you loved those for whom you desired to die! For us you desired life; for yourself, death. O wretched me! Him whom until now I have offended so wickedly, whom once I so abhorred—alas, the Lord Jesus—he himself [608] [Col. 0894D] is my Lord and my God! Alas, would that I were to be tortured for a thousand years in purgatorial fire before the Lord Jesus should be so offended by me! O my reader, pour out tears to the Lord for me, that then he may hear me crying out, open to me when I knock, comfort me as I mourn, and graciously receive me in sorrow and repentance. O Lord Jesus, have mercy on me; restore to me the joy of your countenance. You who deigned to die for sinners, I beg you, do not allow me, a sinner, to be tortured in eternal fires. O most beloved brothers, observe and weigh with diligent thought how greatly he is to be loved, how greatly cherished, who endured such and so great reproaches for us; who thus encouraged the one delivering him to death, saying: “What you are doing, do quickly.”

[Col. 0895A] 8. It follows: “But none of those reclining knew why he had said this to him. For some thought, because he had the money-box, that Jesus was saying to him: ‘Buy the things we need for the feast day,’ or that he should give something to the needy.” For he had the money-box, in which offerings were kept for the needs of his own people and of other needy persons. In this is given the Church’s pattern for keeping necessities: she is commanded not to be anxious about tomorrow, lest she serve earthly things or abandon righteousness through fear of want. “When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night” when the son of darkness went out, doing the works of darkness. Therefore let us, who are disciples of Christ, see that we do not eat dipped bread; let us preserve in the mind the religious devotion we wear in our clothing; and let the soul inwardly maintain the holiness which outward garb conceals, lest in the hour of night [Col. 0895B] we go out from the Lord, rejected and to be burned with the devil in the lake of fire and sulphur. Let us cling to him with all our strength, because it is good to cling to him. Let my soul cling to you, O Lord; let it cling to you in such a way that you never permit it to depart from you, but swiftly bring it to be comforted by you, for whom it groans: to whom be honor and glory unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. On verses 31–33 of John, chapter 13

1. The more fully the word of God is chewed over in the mouth, the more sweetly it ought to taste in the heart. And a mind steeped in the savor of the divine word offers itself as an alabaster jar of ointment to those desiring to open it; nor does it allow the treasure to remain concealed for long, since it grows as it is distributed among more people. Therefore, not without reason, if anyone should desire to carry in his hands, for the fragrance of their sweetness, the fruits of divine utterances which we have gathered from the Lord’s orchard by his own bounty, we shall gladly give them to him. But I beg my reader not to cast them away from the affections of his heart. For from them proceeds a most sweet fragrance, which heals the contrite in heart and makes the scars of wounds whole. This fragrance holds within itself the sovereignty of all sweetness, because it surpasses every fragrance of balm and everything contained in fragrances. If you do not cease to smell so great and such a fragrance with the whole sense of smell of your heart, you shall undoubtedly never perish eternally, because he is the resurrection and the life: “He who believes in him, though he be dead, shall live” (John 11:25). [Col. 0895D] This fragrance, the sweetness of all fragrances, is the Lord Jesus: a good fragrance, a most sweet fragrance, sweeter than honey and milk, more delicious than nectar, more precious than gems and gold. This fragrance is that Word of which we are about to speak: “The Word which was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). From this Word may my words always proceed, and may they now be able to resound with nothing other than him—namely, the Lord Jesus—who says of himself: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.”

2. When Judas went out—the one concerning whom he had said, “You are not all clean”—only the clean remained with their cleanser. In this is signified Christ’s glorification, in which, when the wicked have been separated, he will remain eternally with the saints. This is so. But here Christ’s love requires another exposition, [Col. 0896A] which ought neither to be written without tears nor read without tears. Christ rejoices and exults over the approaching passion—indeed, the approaching death—which he had resolved to undergo for the salvation of the world, and says: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” O Lord Jesus, Son of Man, Son of the Virgin Mary, most glorious, most sweet, most beautiful, life of the saints and sweetness of the Angels: how are you glorified, how are you made illustrious? Do not bonds still threaten you, executioners’ blows, human reproaches, and the people’s rejection; spittle, nails, blows, a crown of thorns, a reed for a scepter, a cross, a lance? Is being bound with your hands behind your back, led bound before a judge, and set forth as a robber for mockery—is this your glorification? Or is it your glorification to mount the cross’s gibbet and bear so grievous [Col. 0896B] a punishment? Is dying—namely, for the salvation of humankind—your gladness, your joy? What shall we say to these things? What shall we answer, my brothers? Here speech should be silent and tears speak; here discourse should be quiet and weeping cry out. Christ our God regarded death as nothing—indeed, as joy—by which he frees us from perpetual death. And although he was to die so soon, he nevertheless called himself glorified, because in thus suffering—indeed, in thus dying—he glorified his members, his faithful people.

3. O good monk, O good Christian, recall your evil years in the bitterness of your soul. Set Christ, thus crucified, at one side of yourself and your sins at the other; and, placed between them, see what you do. Contemplate the Lamb; contemplate Christ [Col. 0896C] your Lord, stretched out thus upon the cross and suffering so impiously for you. Consider the shamefulness of your flesh and the wicked affections of your soul. Pour out tears to the Crucified One: he is ready to save you, he who endured such things for you. “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” And rightly, “Son of Man,” not “Son of Men,” because he was born without male seed from a pure and undefiled Virgin, and was begotten in heaven from the Father without a mother. His mother is a virgin; his Father knows no woman. This Son of Man, I say—the Son of the Virgin Mary—was greatly glorified, because whatever the Son of God possessed by nature, the Son of Man possesses by grace. In this Son of Man, namely of the Virgin Mary, God was glorified. In what was he glorified? In the healing of the sick, in the illumination of the blind, in the raising of the dead, and in [Col. 0896D] all his works, always doing the will of his Father. And God glorified him in himself, because he is one God with the Father: one divinity, one majesty; and this glorification is from eternity. Approaching death, according to his humanity he asked that this glorification be given him by God the Father, when he said: “Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had before the world was made” (John 17:5). For the glory which he possessed according to his divinity, he wished to possess according to his humanity, so that the human nature united to the Word, which was then capable of suffering and mortal, might soon become incapable of suffering and immortal. And this is what is meant by: “And immediately he will glorify him.”

[Col. 0897A] 4. Therefore you, Christian, who desire to have an inheritance with Christ, remember always to glorify God the Father—in pure thought, serene speech, ordered action, and in all your conduct—so that whoever sees you may glorify God and bless him, saying: “Blessed be God in heaven and on earth, because he works such things in his servants.” Certainly, if with Christ you glorify the Father, with Christ you will possess the inheritance of that same Father. Great is what I say. It surpasses the dignity of the human condition that a man, earthly from the earth, dust made from dust, should ascend into heaven to Christ and reign continually with Christ. Who has ever heard the like? Who has ever seen anything such? Truly it is great—indeed, exceedingly great; and though so great, nevertheless truly [Col. 0897B] great. Truth itself said: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John 12:26).

Therefore, monk of Benedict, be in truth a good servant of Christ: do not feign religious devotion, do not mask holiness, do not abandon humility; maintain obedience unto death, and so you will reign with Christ, who says to his disciples in what follows: “Little children, yet a little while I am with you.” He calls those little children whom, because of the tenderness of their minds, the full strength of faith had not yet made firm. For those accustomed to live on milk were not yet fit to feed on solid bread. Therefore they were little children because they were small, and, like little children in Christ, were nourished with milk, not solid food. They knew Christ according to his humanity; but, their minds veiled in darkness, they held uncertainly to [Col. 0897C] Christ’s divinity.

We may also say that he called his disciples little children because of the greatness of his love. For it is parents’ custom to rear their little children more tenderly than their grown ones, to embrace them more often, and to kiss them more frequently. And when the bitterness of death compels them to depart this life, they spread the whole bosom of their affection over the little ones; they clasp them in their arms and rush into their kisses, grieving more for the bereavement of little children than of adults. And those seem little who are bound together by the chain of unconquerable love when paternal protection can no longer aid them. Then they hold in their thoughts their little children, though they count them by no means small in love. So too our Lord called his disciples little children, [Col. 0897D] whom, as he was about to go to the Father, he loved with no small affection of charity. He loved greatly those whom he now called little children.

5. He says, “A little while I am with you”; that is, this is the little while during which I am with you in this mortal flesh and you can behold me present. But I shall take up the cross’s gallows; swiftly I shall break death’s dominion. The time and hour will soon come when I shall no longer be accounted as a man, but shall be as the reproach of men and the outcast of the people. Then you will seek me and desire to follow me; but struck by fear of death, and not yet clothed from on high with power, you will not be able to lay down your lives for me. And this is what is said: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now.” Its sense is: I go to the Father, but through the eye [Col. 0898A] of a needle, through the straits of suffering, through the pains of death. Yet you cannot follow me now, because you are fearful and timid, like kids still at their mother’s milk and not yet fit for sacrifice. But the time and hour will come when, fear wholly cast out, you will be ready, for love of me, to undergo not only the punishment of the cross but every torture that greater wickedness could devise.

“My little children, yet a little while I am with you.” O Lord Jesus, your love still compels me to repeat “a little while.” Jesus, Jesus, my Lord and my God, life of my sinful soul, reward of my pilgrimage: this little while was so bitter to you. In this little while you became the reproach of men and the mockery of the people; in this little while you were poured out like water and all your bones were scattered; in this little while the shepherd was struck and the sheep of the flock scattered. In this little while, so bitter, you who were fairer in form than the sons of men appeared to have neither form nor beauty (Isa. 53:2). In this little while my David—indeed, my Jesus, my Lord—outside the city gate beat the drum upon the drum of his flesh and sang, saying, “Heloi, Heloi, lamazabactani?” that is, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15:34).

In this little while, my Lady, your Mother—the incorrupt virgin, the undefiled virgin, virgin before your birth and virgin after your birth—your Mother, indeed your martyr, a martyr not by the executioner’s sword but by the bitter sorrow of her heart: how bitterly she wept, how bitterly she grieved! Nor is this surprising, when she saw you, her only one, all her desire, stretched upon the cross and near to death—indeed, with bowed head, yielding up the spirit. [Col. 0898C] This little while, Lord Jesus, bitter for you and bitter for your most sweet mother—would that it had been bitter for me in such a way that during this little while I might have stood beside the cross of my Lord, my God; so that, since I cannot yet see him abiding with the Father, I might at least have deserved to see him laid upon the cross and dead.

How blessed, how delightful, how glorious was this little while for that thief who in that little while deserved to hear from his Lord: “Today you shall be with me in paradise!” (Luke 23:43). O sweet voice, O delightful voice: “Today you shall be with me in paradise!” O Lord Jesus, what is sweeter, more delightful, more joyous than to be with you in paradise? Nothing at all, absolutely nothing. What then shall I say, [Col. 0898D] what shall I do, who, still placed amid the misery of this pilgrimage, am exiled so far from the delights of the paradise of my God? O good Jesus, be Jesus to me. Remember, Savior, what you suffered and why you suffered it, and have mercy on me. May compassion itself compel you to overcome our evils by forgiving, and to satisfy me, granted the fulfillment of my desire, with your countenance. Be my joy, you who are to be my reward. May my glory be in you through all ages forever—you who live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit (*In Hymno Ascensionis* [“In the Hymn of the Ascension”]), etc.

## SERMON V. On verses 34–35 of John, chapter XIII

1. “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another, as I have loved you.” Whoever does not ignore the Lord’s command must necessarily not neglect to live according to it. [Col. 0899A] “The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many stripes” (Luke 12:47); but whoever does it shall be enriched with many riches and honors, according to what the Lord of all says to his disciples: “You shall be blessed if you do what I command you” (John 15:14).

The sweet Lord has set forth a sweet command. For he says: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another as I have loved you.” He who loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood sets before us the commandment of love. O good commandment, sweet commandment, delightful commandment, commandment of life, commandment of eternal salvation! Upon this commandment hang the whole Law and the Prophets. This is the one commandment of which it was said: “Whoever keeps all the commandments, but offends in [Col. 0899B] one”—that is, in charity—“has become guilty of all” (James 2:10). Therefore the Apostle, having enumerated certain grades of virtues, immediately added concerning charity: “But if I do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

This is that precious pearl which, when the bride of the beloved found it, she gave all that she had and bought it (Matt. 13:46). This is that ladder which appeared to Jacob in a dream, stretching, as he saw it, even to heaven; by it some descended and some ascended (Gen. 28:12). For by it the angels descended and we ascend to the angels, because without this ladder no one can climb to the heavenly kingdom. And at the very foot of the ladder was found the Lord of angels himself, who says: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another [Col. 0899C] as I have loved you.” This, I say, is the Lord who gives the command to love one’s brother and who wishes to be loved from the whole heart by his servants. Nor is it a great thing if a servant loves his lord as much as the lord loves his servant; indeed, a lord ought to be loved more by his servant, since the servant cannot assist his lord, but the lord can assist the servant.

The servant who loves his lord with his whole heart strives with all his strength to observe his commandment. And when a commandment is despised, it follows beyond doubt that the author of the commandment himself is neglected. For whoever does not love his neighbor in truth despises Christ’s commandment; and whoever despises Christ’s commandment despises Christ also, the author of the commandment.

2. Therefore, most beloved brethren, let us love Christ [Col. 0899D] and keep his commands: the Lord’s commandment is radiant, enlightening the eyes of the mind. Christ’s commandments are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, and in keeping them there is great reward (Ps. 18:9, 11, 12)—the Lord Christ himself. Therefore, my reader, keep the rule of the commandment, and confidently await having the author of the commandment himself as your reward. Good is the commandment from which so great and such a reward proceeds. This commandment, I say, must be observed by us without contradiction, since through it we do not doubt that we shall merit the Lord Christ.

This is the commandment which, as he was about to go to the Father, he left to his disciples; indeed, it is the testament which, as he was about to die, he left to his heirs. For he says to his disciples: “A new commandment I give you.” In what sense new? Newly discovered? [Col. 0900A] Not because it is not written in the Old Testament, “You shall love the Lord your God” (Deut. 6:5). What then is new? It is new because it brings old things to newness and changes old people into young ones. It is new because it puts off the old man and puts on the new, who was created according to God in the holiness and righteousness of truth (Col. 3:9–10; Eph. 4:24). It is new because the human race, once expelled from the joys of paradise, now daily passes into heaven.

But because many love themselves with a love that does not rejoice in the path of truth, it is added: “as I have loved you.” The difference between *amor* (“love”) and *caritas* (“charity”) is like that between genus and species. There is a good love, an evil love, and an intermediate love. Good love is charity itself, by which we love [Col. 0900B] the Lord above ourselves and above everything that exists, and our neighbor as ourselves. Evil love is charity’s enemy: for example, filthy, wanton, and adulterous love. These loves, being opposites, have opposite effects upon one another: one gains merit for its possessor, the other punishment; one punishment, the other glory; one death, the other life; one paradise, the other hell; one God, the other the devil. Intermediate love is that which is neither united with charity nor defiled by filthy love: such as love for children, parents, relatives, and other things rightly and safely possessed. And so that these two loves may be excluded from the love which is charity, he added, “as I have loved you.”

3. But what human being ever could or can [Col. 0900C] keep such a commandment? Who ever loved his neighbors as Christ loved the Apostles? No one ever did. Therefore it must be noted that the expression “as” does not convey equality of quantity but similarity; and its sense is: As I loved you, so love one another. How did he love us? Hear.

“God so loved the world that he gave his Only-begotten [Son], that whoever believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). God the Father so loved us that he did not spare his only Son, but handed him over for us (Rom. 8:32). Christ loved us to such an extent that for us sinners he delivered his soul to death and washed us from sins by his blood, making us from sinners righteous, from dead persons living, [Col. 0900D] from earthborn people inhabitants of heaven, from earthly people heavenly, from companions of beasts companions of angels. Blessed be this lover, from whom we have in his commandments that we should love one another as he loved us.

4. But perhaps someone says: “I hesitate over this love, and understand rather imperfectly how one ought to love one’s neighbor. Certainly I cannot die for my brother, as Christ the Lord willed to die for our salvation.” To him I have already said above that the word “as” does not express quantity but quality. If you cannot walk equally with Christ, at least imitate his footsteps from a distance. If you are unable to love your neighbor more than yourself—as Christ did in dying for the salvation of humankind—at least love him as yourself, doing to him what you wish him to do to you. But perhaps you will say: “I cannot even do this, since it was said by way not of command but of counsel.” If you cannot keep this, see that you do not do to another what you do not wish to be done to yourself.

One must love one’s neighbor in such a way that God is always loved in him. If you love your neighbor thus, you have fulfilled the commandment. For one’s neighbor ought so to be loved that God is always the cause of love, not the neighbor himself. If a neighbor is loved solely for his own sake, it will no longer be charity, but intermediate love—or perhaps, God forbid, the worst love. And those blinded by such love, unless they repent, will be deprived eternally of Christ’s love.

5. Therefore, brethren, since we are called Christians by Christ and are so called, let us reject all earthly, transient, and perishable things, together with all their blind lovers. Let us desire to cleave to him alone, and be founded in brotherly charity, that we may deserve to be called and to be the disciples of him who commanded his Apostles, and us through them, saying: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” [Col. 0901B] For by this children of light are distinguished from children of darkness, disciples of Christ from disciples of the devil: if they extend the bosom of charity to one another and to all. Charity is unable to leave anyone outside the bosom of love. It embraces all, holds everything together, and gives itself commonly to all.

Charity is the affection of the mind embracing Christ with the arms of love. Charity is love embracing heaven and earth; charity is unconquerable love, which never knows how to yield to threats or punishments. Charity is the indissoluble bond of love and peace; [Col. 0901C] charity is contempt of the world and love of God. Charity, queen of virtues, fears no encounter with any vice; endowed with awareness of Christ’s blood and bearing the banner of the cross upon her forehead, she puts all adversaries to flight, and there is none who can resist her strength. No evil can befall her; she remains secure always and everywhere.

This is the armor and shield which the prophet, set in battle, asks the Lord to take up when he says: “Take hold of armor and shield, and rise to help me” (Ps. 34:2). The same prophet rejoiced that he had been protected by this shield when he said: “Lord, you have crowned us as with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5:3). Whoever is protected by such a shield will safely penetrate the ranks of enemies. [Col. 0901D] This is the adamantine stone which cannot be broken and breaks everything that breaks. This is the strong armed one, who casts down the enemy by her strength and destroys and kills her most wicked foe, with all his army, by the two-edged sword. She is the friend of the eternal King and does not fear to enter confidently before him. She disdains to enter Solomon’s bedchamber and rest anywhere but upon Christ’s breast.

6. If this queen of virtues reigns among us, brethren, surely all, little and great, will recognize that we are truly the Lord’s disciples. Whoever does not have charity no longer belongs to him who gave the commandment of charity. Charity is love of God and neighbor; and whoever does not love his neighbor consequently does not love God; and whoever does not love, hates. Therefore whoever hates [Col. 0902A] his brother hates the author of charity.

Therefore, brethren, whom Christ’s love has gathered into one, let us love the Lord Christ with all our heart and all our mind, and our neighbor as ourselves; and for love of him, let us love not only friends but also enemies—not merely refraining from hating them, but loving them as well. This is Christ’s school; this is the Holy Spirit’s teaching. If anyone departs from this school and does not persevere in this teaching, believe me, brethren, he will perish eternally. But to Christ’s disciples, lovers of charity, shall be given the very abundance of sweetness, the riches of eternal blessedness, and the joys of eternal happiness. May he himself deign to grant us these joys—he who, blessed God in perfect Trinity, lives and reigns through all ages of ages. [Col. 0902B] Amen.

## SERMON VI. On verses 36–38 of John, chapter XIII, and verses 1–4 of chapter XIV

1. It follows: “Peter said to him, Lord, where are you going?” Peter replied to what the Lord had said above: “Where I am going, you cannot come.” Peter could not hear the words “Where I am going, you cannot come” without bitter sorrow. Therefore he replied not to the present words, namely, “A new commandment I give you,” etc., but to the earlier words, namely, “Where I am going, you cannot come,” saying, “Lord, where are you going?”

For just as the hand, trained by frequent experience with its body, feels about a pain, so the tongue, the heart’s friend, does not allow the heart’s bitterness to be concealed; and what the mind conceives inwardly in sorrow, the tongue brings forth outwardly in disclosure. Hence sometimes the force of grief is conceived in the mind and disclosed through the palate of formed speech—that is, the tongue. Therefore Peter’s tongue could not conceal the grief which he held inwardly in his heart. Having heard, “Where I am going, you cannot come,” he could scarcely thereafter bear his Master’s speech. Thus, after the command concerning mutual love had been completed, overwhelmed by excessive grief at his Lord’s coming absence, he immediately interrupts the Master’s discourse of such authority and cries out, wholly sad in voice: “Lord, where are you going?” As though he said: “We shall keep, by your gift, the mutual charity which you commend to us, unharmed and undefiled; and whatever else you command, we shall do. But this word which you spoke, [Col. 0902D] namely, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ has filled us with great bitterness. And why are you going? Why do you leave us? To whom do you leave us desolate? I no longer wish to live without you. Do not abandon me; do not forsake me.”

2. To him the Lord says: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you shall follow afterward.” Its sense is: I do not leave you; I do not abandon you. I go before you, making a way out of the pathless place, a paved road out of the track, security out of fear, life out of death. You are fearful, you are timid, not yet strengthened; you cannot follow me now. I shall go before you to reproach, to the gallows, by dying, rising again, and ascending to heaven. You are not fit for the reward, because you are not yet ready for the gallows. You cannot follow me, who am life, because you are [Col. 0903A] not yet ready to die for me. “But you shall follow afterward.” I shall send into you the Holy Spirit, promised by the Father, who will strengthen you; “and you shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judaea and Samaria, and even to the uttermost part of the earth” (Acts 1:8). Then you will be ready to follow me.

Peter says to him: “Why can I not follow you now? I do not fear punishment; I do not fear death. ‘I am ready to go with you both to prison and to death’” (Luke 22:33). What is this that you say: “I cannot follow you now”? “I will lay down my life for you.” The Lord says to him: “Will you lay down your life for me? You are mistaken, Peter: you are not yet ready, not yet clothed with power from on high. When you have been clothed with power from on high, then you will give your life over to death. But now it is near that, through fear of my death, you will deny life and kill your soul; you will deny that you are my disciple and kill your spirit. The time and hour hasten in which you will deny me in order that you yourself may now be saved: the cock shall not crow until you deny me three times.” Whatever words you utter: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times.” Its sense is: Before the cock crows, you will deny me; and the denial will be threefold, whether before the cock’s first crow or its second.

3. When this had been said, fear, trembling, and great grief seized all the disciples. Nor is this surprising. They had heard the Lord say to Peter, “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times”—Peter, who surpassed all in holiness, was more devoted in love, and stronger in faith; who had already confessed Jesus to be the Son [Col. 0903C] of God, saying to him, “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16:16). They feared lest the same thing that would happen to Peter might happen to themselves. And because so great a man would deny him, they in a manner wavered in that matter; and they did not perfectly believe that he would rise from the dead on the third day. Moreover, they were grieved because they believed that the Lord whom they presently heard speaking would before long die.

There were mourning and lamentation there, a single voice of those weeping. They were certain of the departure of their sweet Master and of the future death of their most sweet Lord. Though they still beheld him living in the flesh, they nevertheless mourned him as if already dead. Then they recalled the most sweet streams of teaching which they had received from him; the healings he had given to the sick; and, beyond these, the life he had restored to the dead; the most kindly and sweet familiarity which he had always shown toward them. They saw themselves so suddenly abandoned by him. Then they wept most bitterly—believe me, brethren—so that they themselves could no longer be consoled.

4. When the Lord saw them weeping so bitterly, he wished to console them concerning his death. Yet I think that he did not wish this then; rather, he stirred them still further to lament when he said to them: “Let not your heart be troubled.” I wonder whether the Lord Jesus did not groan in spirit and trouble himself when he said to his weeping disciples: “Let not your heart be troubled.” I believe—and therefore I speak—that my Lord Jesus, blessed through every age, said to his weeping disciples: “Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.” As though he said: Do not be troubled at my departure, at [Col. 0904A] my death. I have power to lay down my life and to take it again. My body will lie dead in the tomb for three days, and after three days it will rise immortal and impassible. Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the whale, and the Son of Man will rise from the dead on the third day. Let not your heart be troubled: I who raised Lazarus can raise this body of mine; I who raised the widow’s son will not be held by death beyond three days. “You believe in God; believe also in me.” Do not fear on account of my flesh’s death: I am God, who will raise the flesh. The works which I have done bear witness concerning me. If you believe in God, it follows that you ought to believe in me, because I am God.

And lest they should doubt that they would abide with Christ before God in eternal life, he goes on and says:

5. “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” Its sense is: In eternal life you will reign with me, in which there are many dwelling places, that is, many ranks of dignity, for there is one glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars. The house of God the Father is his predestination and foreknowledge. In this house every perfect person has a dwelling place by reason of the counted denarius, which is given equally to all; and this denarius is one and not a different measure of life in eternity.

Or otherwise: My Father’s house is the temple of God, the kingdom of God—that is, righteous human beings—in whom there are many differences. These are the dwelling places of that house, namely, those dignities which are prepared in predestination, as the Apostle says: “He chose us before [Col. 0904C] the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4), by predestination; but they must be hoped for in action. Hence the Apostle says: “Whom he predestined, these he also called; and whom he called, these he also justified” (Rom. 8:30).

And this is what he says: “If it were otherwise, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you. And if I go and prepare a place for you, I shall come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be.” Its sense is: In my Father’s house there are diverse rewards for merits; and “if it were otherwise,” that is, if they did not exist, I would have told you this: “I go to prepare a place for you.” But because they are prepared there through predestination, there is no need for me to prepare dwelling places there anew through predestination. And because they are not yet present in action, he adds: “But if I go and prepare a place for you, I shall come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be.”

As though he said: You have a dwelling place in my Father’s house through predestination; but I go to the Father, and I shall prepare it for you through action. You have an eternal dwelling place in my Father’s house; but now you cannot come to it except through great labor. You have dwelling places in my Father’s house solely by God’s grace and gift; but I wish you now to possess them from me. I depart from you according to divinity, and according to my humanity I shall prepare for you [Col. 0904D] that ineffable blessedness which I prepared for you from the world’s beginning according to divinity. You cannot in any way attain those ineffable joys of everlasting life unless I have first been released from the flesh and again clothed with that same flesh. I shall ascend into heaven and send you the Holy Spirit, who will teach you to act through works and thanksgiving, so that through works you may come to possess the kingdom of eternal happiness which has been prepared for you through predestination.

6. The Lord Jesus daily prepares a place for his faithful when he shows that his flesh suffered for the salvation of humankind before God the Father. Thus he now grants us through his humanity the place that he had prepared through divinity. Whenever we do some good—fasting, praying, reading, meditating, mourning for sins or from longing to see Christ, visiting the sick, feeding the hungry, and so on with the other good works which would take long to recount—then that blessed place is always prepared for us in heaven by him who said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). But he will then bring us into those most blessed dwelling places if we have lived in his faith and love, when he comes to render to each according to his works. And this is what he says: “I shall come again and receive you to myself, that where I am, you also may be.” That is to say: I shall appear in judgment and introduce you into those dwelling places, that there you may abide with me eternally.

O supreme, O blessed happiness—to dwell with Christ! Who can attain this happiness, this so glorious blessedness? Who will be so happy, who so supremely blessed, as to be able to reign with Christ and behold [Col. 0905C] his glory and beauty?

7. O Jesus, Jesus, may I deserve to see you, my Jesus! I believe in God, and I believe in you; yet my heart is greatly troubled. My heart would not be troubled if I heard you say to me: “Let not your heart be troubled.” But now my soul is greatly troubled, not because I do not believe in you, but because I cannot now see you. I will nothing else, seek nothing else, desire nothing else, long for nothing else, except to see you, my Lord and God. And because I seek you and do not find you, I call, and you do not answer me. I desire to see you and cannot see you, although you yourself are my sole desire.

You, Truth, are my witness that my heart is greatly troubled. Yet I trust in your mercy, because my soul will still see you; and I shall be satisfied with you, by you, in you, and through you—not by my merits, but by your great and many mercies. I shall see you, God my Savior, when you come to judge the world through fire. But I beseech you by yourself and by that Mother who bore you: when you come to judgment, draw me to yourself, that where you now are I too may be with you and with your disciples, to whom, when you were about to go to the Father, you said: “You know where I am going, and you know the way.” For they knew that you were going to the Father and that you are the way by which one comes to the Father—you who live and reign with the same Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VII. On verses 5–14 of John, chapter XIV

1. The Lord had said to his disciples: “You know where [Col. 0906A] I am going, and you know the way.” Thomas said to him: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; and how can we know the way?” Thomas, who is called Didymus—that is, “Doubtful” or “Doubting”—because he himself doubted, believed that others doubted. Therefore he said: “Lord, we do not know where you are going.”

But the Master of truth proves that Thomas knows, because they knew him, since he himself is the way. Therefore they knew the way. And he is truth and life; and they knew him because they knew the truth and life to which he goes. He is the way insofar as he is man, and truth and life insofar as he is God. Therefore, by himself as way, he goes to truth and life, because according to glorified humanity he returns to himself as God. Thus he plainly proves that they know what they thought they did not know, when he says: “I am the way by which one must go, and the truth [Col. 0906B] to which one must come, and the life in which one must remain. I am the way without error, truth without falsehood, life without death. I am the way in the example, truth in the promise, life in the reward. I am the fitting way, irrevocable truth, endless life. I am the broad and spacious way, mighty and abundant truth, delightful and glorious life. I am the way of beginners, the truth of those making progress, the life of those who have arrived. I am the way of light and serenity, truth living without pain, life happy and pleasant. I am the way on the gallows, truth in hell, life in the joy of resurrection. I am the way in which there is no thorn or thistle, truth in which there is no sting of falsehood, life in which the dead live again. I am the straight way, perfect truth, life abiding without end. I am the way of reconciliation, truth of recompense, life of eternal blessedness.”
