2. “No one comes to the Father except through me.” As though he said: No one comes to me, truth and life, except through me, the way; and no one comes to me as God except through me as assumed man. By assumed mortal flesh, I make a passage for mortals through which one comes to truth and life; and I make the way by dying, rising again, and ascending to heaven, where I am truth and life, true God, eternal God.

Miserable man, earthly from the earth, always bent, always inclined downward, always sick, always weak, could not return by himself to the joys of paradise from which he had been expelled, nor could he ascend by himself to truth and life, which is God. But the Word came into flesh, God to man; the Word became flesh, and God became man. The Word bent down toward flesh, God toward man; and thus he carried the human race not only to paradise but even to heaven, where there is true being and eternal being: truth which always was and will be, blessed life ever blessed, which had no beginning and shall have no end. Therefore God-made-man became the way for us earthborn people, and led us to truth and life—namely, to himself, God and man. This is what he says: “No one comes to the Father except through me”; as though he said: No one comes to me as God except through me as man, man assumed by the Word; no one comes to the Father except through me, who am man and one God with the Father.

3. It follows: “If you had known me, you would surely have known [Col. 0907A] my Father also; and from now on you shall know him, and you have seen him.” If you had known me to be the same as the Father, you would surely have known my Father also, because “I and the Father are one”; and by knowing me, you will know him, and you have seen him with the heart, when you saw me to be like him in all things.

But Philip, not understanding that he was altogether like the Father, says to him: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” There were some among them who did not think that the Son was wholly like the Father, but thought the Father greater and better; and thus they knew neither Father nor Son. Philip was one of them. Therefore he says: “Show us the Father, who is greater than you, in whom sufficiency lies, and not in you.” Rebuking him, Jesus says that he does not even know the Son: “Have I been with you so long, [Col. 0907B] and you have not known me?” Truly you have not known me, because if you had known me, you would also have known the Father. He does not know the Son who believes the Father better—not because the Father is one thing and the Son another, but because the Son is altogether like him.

And therefore, because the Son is altogether like the Father, he goes on and says: “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father. How do you say, ‘Show us the Father’?” Since I am altogether like the Father, how do you say: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us”? I see the intention with which you speak: you do not seek another who is like me, but think that there is one better. Why do you wish to know separately those who are inseparable? “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” What you cannot see, at least believe.

“The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself,” because I who speak am not from myself. I attribute the works I do to him from whom I myself, who do them, am. “The Father abiding in me does the works,” among which are words—those words which are good works when they edify someone. And since the Father does works in me, do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? For if we were separate, we could by no means work inseparably.

4. “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever believes in me will himself also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father.” He repeats “Amen, amen” in order to affirm more truly what he says. *Amen* is Hebrew, and contains several distinct meanings in itself. *Amen* is called an adverb of affirmation and also an adverb of wishing, as when it is said, “May this good thing happen to you,” and the response is, “Amen.” And at the end of prayers, when it is said, “Through all ages of ages,” 617 the response is, [Col. 0907D] “Amen”; and the sense is, “What you ask from the Lord, that we desire.” It is an adverb of affirmation, as here: “Amen, I say to you”; that is, “Truly I say to you.” But when it is doubled, what is said is affirmed more strongly. “Amen, amen” is spoken by the Lord so that what he says may be believed true without doubt. For it could have been believed on his simple word; but because his disciples were still weak and feeble in the faith that works through love, not believing that he had one and the same power with the Father, “Amen” is therefore doubled by him, so that no doubt may undermine what he promises. “Amen, amen, I say to you”; that is, “Truly I say to you: whoever believes in me”—that is, believes that I am one God with the Father, worshipping and loving me—“will himself also do the works that I do” [Col. 0908A]; that is, the works which I do through myself, I shall afterward do through him; “and will do greater works than these.” For I shall indeed do them through him, because I am going to the Father. He goes to him from whom, according to his divinity, he has never departed.

5. It is of greater merit to believe in him now, because we do not see him, than if we saw him. After he ascended to the Father, greater miracles were performed through him than those which he performed in his own person. At the touch of the hem of his garment, only one woman suffering from an issue of blood is reported to have been healed (Matt. 9:20–22); but after he ascended into heaven, Peter’s shadow cured several people of every disease (Acts 5:15). He performed greater miracles through Peter than he himself had performed. Before he ascended into [Col. 0908B] heaven, few were converted to God through his preaching; but after he ascended into heaven, five thousand on one day and three thousand on another are reported to have been converted to the Lord through Peter’s preaching (Acts 4:4 and 2:41). Before he ascended into heaven, he was known only in Judaea; but after he ascended to heaven, he made himself known through his Apostles to the whole world, because “their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world” (Ps. 18:5). He came into the world, and the world did not know him; but after he left the world and ascended into heaven, his renown resounded throughout the world. This is what the prophet says in his person: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140:10); because I am unknown, and [Col. 0908C] shall remain unknown until I pass to the Father. “But when I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12:32). Greater, therefore, are the works which he now performs through his faithful ones, because he is at the Father’s right hand, than those which he performed while he sat in his Mother’s lap.

6. It follows: “And whatever you ask in my name, that I will do”; that is, whatever you ask for the salvation of your souls, I shall give you, either immediately or later. Many are hindered by the assaults of evil temptations; groaning and sorrowing, they ask in the Lord’s name to be delivered from them, since it is grievous and exceedingly laborious to wage war against them. They fear that they may fail; they ask help from the Lord [Col. 0908D] lest they be overcome. If they do not quickly receive from the Lord the help for which they implore, they think themselves abandoned by him; and because he delays in assisting them, they believe that the Lord does not care for them. But it is not so. Rather, he loves more those whom he permits, as though alone, to struggle long with temptations; for as the conflict increases, he will grant them a more glorious victory, and the stronger the contest, the more glorious a crown will be given them. Let the athlete of Christ not waver or doubt, as he fights against the wiles of the ancient serpent, as he struggles to obtain the joys of paradise. Let him not grow weary or withdraw from battle; let him persist courageously, fight fiercely, act manfully, and let his heart be strengthened. For the Lord will soon come, and with a mighty hand will break the arm of the sinner and the wicked one; afterward, when the crafty enemy [Col. 0909A] has been defeated, he will reign with Christ for ever and unto ages of ages. For let him remember that it is written through the prophet: “The Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart”; and, “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and out of all these the Lord will deliver them” (Ps. 33:19–20).

Let him ask whatever he wishes from the Lord, provided only that he asks for the salvation of his soul. Let him not be troubled if it is delayed: for if it is delayed, it is not taken away; indeed, once it begins to be possessed, it is possessed more dearly. Let us ask in his name for that which he taught his Apostles to ask from the Father, saying: “When you pray to the Father, say thus: Our Father who art in heaven” (Matt. 6:9), etc. But if we ask something else that conflicts with this petition, our petition is vain. If we ask for the salvation of our souls in his name, he will give it to us. And lest they suppose 618 that what [Col. 0909B] he promised he would do without the Father, it follows and says: “That the Father may be glorified in the Son”; because whatever the Son does, he does it so that the Father may be glorified in him.

Or otherwise: “Whatever you ask in my name, that I will do.” The name of the Lord is Jesus. This name was bestowed upon him according to his humanity. Thus the sense is: “Whatever you ask in my name, that I will do”; that is, whatever you ask of me insofar as I am man, I shall give you insofar as I am God, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son—God in the man united to him. What he added, “If you ask me anything in my name, I will do it,” merely confirms what he said above; for repetition of a saying is confirmation of the matter.

7. Therefore, most beloved brothers, let us ask this of him: [Col. 0909C] that his grace may go before and follow us, and may continually grant that we be intent upon good works. In his name let us ask for him alone. Certainly, he is excessively greedy for whom Christ is not enough. For one who possesses the Lord and says with the prophet, “The Lord is our portion” (Ps. 72:26), can possess nothing outside the Lord. That person is truly happy and blessed who is enriched by so great a gift; nor will he ever again be poor who holds as his inheritance the giver of all good things. If anyone asks for silver, gold, possessions, varied household goods, believe me: he does not ask in the name of Jesus. With such portions the Lord does not deign to become his portion or inheritance, unless he reckons all those things vile as dung for the love and affection of God. [Col. 0909D]

But we, for whom the Lord is our portion, ought to care for nothing except God, lest we be hindered by another’s gift of necessity. For whatever is allotted to other services is taken away from the worship of religion and from this our service. Therefore we ought to care for nothing else except how we may deserve to receive Christ as our inheritance, for whose love we have renounced what is our own and our own will. This, beloved brothers, is the inheritance which makes its heirs blessed. No distress of poverty will henceforth constrain the one who possesses such a great inheritance. This, I say, is the inheritance in the land of the living; this is the portion which the prophet asks from the Lord, saying: “May my portion, O Lord, be in the land of the living” (Ps. 141:6). The Apostle was preparing himself for this inheritance when he said: [Col. 0910A] “For me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” How happily he burned for it when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:21, 23)! Now he reigns with Christ because in this world he lived for Christ alone; now he reigns blessedly with Christ in heaven because he loved him with his whole heart on earth, and is now joined to him in his homeland whom he desired with all longing on his journey.

Therefore, beloved, let us ask from him for him alone, and seek nothing else but him alone with all our heart; and so we shall attain that great and such an inheritance, which he himself is. May Christ himself deign to grant this to us, he who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON VIII. On verses 15–17 of John chapter 14.

[Col. 0910B]

1. It follows: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it has not seen him and does not know him.” From this chapter alone we may infer whether we truly love God. We truly love him if we keep his commandments; and if we do not keep his commandment, certainly neither do we love him. He cannot be loved on one side and despised on the other. For he himself says: “He who is not with me is against me, and he who does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11:23). He deserves to dwell with the Lord who strives, according to his ability, to keep his commandments. For he vainly claims to dwell with the Lord who despises the keeping of his commandments. Let not religious dress deceive you, beloved. Believe me: you do not love God if you do not observe his commandments. How can we love the Lord in outward garb if we despise him in deed? God’s love does not seek clothing, but our mind; nor does it seek reputation, but our mind; nor does it seek reputation, but only good action. The proof of love is the performance of a work. For what the Lord says means this: “If you truly love me, you will keep my commandments.” In order that I may know perfectly that you love me, 619 keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father. For here he urges them to love and to keep the commandments, so that they may receive the Holy Spirit; without him they cannot love or keep the commandments. Hence it follows: “I will ask the Father, and [Col. 0910D] he will give you another Paraclete.” The man asks for what God gives; he asks for us who gives us the things asked for. God himself asks for us insofar as he is man, when he causes us to ask God. For then he asks the Father for us when we ask him, believing him to be one God with the Father.

2. What follows—“And he will give you another Paraclete”—means another as regards person, not as regards nature or essence. “He will give you”: not because they did not have him, but because they had him less fully and secretly, and were to receive him more fully and openly. “That he may remain with you”: that is, that he may enlighten you and teach you to preach the kingdom of God and proclaim the Gospel, and cause you to believe that I am equal to the Father, whom you now believe to be lesser. He will also remain with you [Col. 0911A] for ever, so that he may lead you into the sight of the brightness of eternal light, and so that you may contemplate face to face, as you will soon believe, that I am one God with the Father and with that same Paraclete.

*Paraclete* means advocate or comforter. This is the advocate of the faithful, this is the defender and protector of those who hope in him, without whom nothing is strong and nothing holy. He protects his own; he defends them; he fights for those whom he glorifies eternally. He, I say, is the comforter of mourners, the father of orphans, the husband of widows. Of what mourners is he the comforter? Of those mourning over committing sin, over the future punishment of what they have committed; mourning because by sinning they have ruined themselves and provoked Christ, the King of glory, to anger; mourning because in sin [Col. 0911B] they despised him who died upon the wood for them; mourning because they cannot see Christ, the hope of their life and author of salvation. The Spirit of Jesus comforts all these. He comforts them in this present life in hope, and will comfort them in the life of blessed happiness in reality. This Spirit, I say, is called the Spirit of truth, consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son: the Spirit of truth, the Spirit of goodness. All that he teaches is good, veiled by no error of falsehood.

3. Wicked and lying persons cannot receive this Spirit of truth. For all who have polluted hands—not hands of flesh, I mean, but of the mind; not with the filth of mud, but with the stench of sin—are unable to receive, cannot hold, and cannot possess him who is so pure, so radiant, so glorious. The world [Col. 0911C] does not receive him; that is, the worldly person, the worshipper of the world, the lover of the world. The Spirit of Christ hates a lover of the world. He flees from the one whom he recognizes as loving something other than himself. He wishes to be loved in such a manner that nothing else is loved for its own sake. He wishes to be loved perfectly who wishes to be loved alone. He does not wish to have a partner in love, for he has no equal in repaying love; yet he wishes to be loved in such a way that all things are loved together with him, and wishes to be loved in such a way that nothing else is loved for his sake. For every creature is from him by the right of creation, and every creature, inasmuch as it is a creature, is good. Therefore a creature ought to be loved so that the Creator may be loved in it—not it in itself, but through him who created it. For one who so loves gold, silver, possessions, and varied household goods that these things are the cause of his love, [Col. 0911D] certainly does not have the love of the Father in him.

Therefore the Creator is to be loved in all creatures, and all creatures through him; and so all things are loved with him, yet he alone is loved. He does not deserve to receive him who has an ulcerous scab upon his skin; nor can he now see him who has a cataract in the hidden places of his mind. Therefore the eye of the mind must be cleansed, so that we may deserve to see the Spirit of truth; and the body, like a vessel tested by fire, must be scraped for a long time of every scab, so that, fashioned with every art and well polished, it may deserve to become a temple of the Holy Spirit. Thus we must act, thus we must do, if we wish to attain the sight of the appearance of that brightness. If we do this, we shall know him with the Apostles of Jesus; he will remain with us in this present life, and will be with us [Col. 0912A] in everlasting life. O how happy the bride, how blessed the soul, which so diligently strives to wash away the filth of its mind that so great a guest of blessedness may deign to dwell with it!

620 4. Let whoever delights in reading our writing know that that beautiful Spirit of truth does not dwell in a soul subjected to sins. Only that soul is said to be subjected to sins which is held bound by the reins of its perversity in such a manner that it neither wishes nor seeks through the lamentations of repentance to break the bonds of its iniquity, nor implores the help of the Liberator of souls; but, like an immodest prostitute, freely and importunately returns and prostitutes herself to her corrupters. But that soul is not said to be under sins which, according to its strength, struggles with the sword-point of abstinence against every incitement of the flesh. Without this, one foolishly boasts of the flower of chastity who does not vigorously strive against those sins born from flesh and blood by affliction of the flesh and by the richness of the mind. [Col. 0912B]

For the arrows [or “needles,” *acus*] of desire perish when food and drink are withdrawn from our body; but while the belly is distended by harmful things, mind, flesh, and chastity must necessarily serve incontinence. For while the throat inclines itself to pleasure, and the hand, friend of the mouth, supplies the throat with fat beyond what nature requires, bodily fat is nourished and lust itself is strengthened. Therefore, that chastity may flourish in the mind, the flesh must be slain by the sickle of abstinence. It must not be spared if we wish to become a temple of the Holy Spirit. May he himself deign so to cleanse us from every defilement of flesh and spirit that we may deserve to become his worthy temple here and for ever, in whose unity Christ lives and reigns with God the Father, blessed through ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IX. On verses 18–26 of John chapter 14.

1. It follows: “I will not leave you orphans.” For everyone who is still compelled to walk the wretched paths of this miserable pilgrimage, and whom love and longing for Christ do not allow to forget his exile and the blessed life, will not, I think, be able to read this chapter without groaning and sighs. I believe, and therefore I speak. How can a lover of the Crucified restrain his tears while reading this chapter, when he is still unable to see his whole desire—the risen One sitting at the Father’s right hand? O Lord Jesus, unless your love gave me confidence, I would believe that I had been left an orphan by you, [Col. 0912D] because I cannot see you as you are. For you said to your Apostles: “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.” But I, wretched as I am, have not yet deserved to hear from my Lord: “I will no longer leave you an orphan; I shall soon come to you, and your heart will rejoice.” Let every joy meanwhile depart from me, until I come to see him whom my soul desires. I shall always have sorrow as my friend until I see God, my Savior; nor can joy now be mine, while the author of joy has happened to go so far away from me.

Blessed, I say, is that soul which daily groans and mourns because it does not see Christ, the author of all things and Savior of the world. It will indeed laugh on the last day and rejoice joyfully for ever with Christ. [Col. 0913A] But let the soul which does not groan at Christ’s departure beware lest it weep inconsolably at the coming of that same Christ. She does not love her bridegroom who does not sigh at some time from longing to see him. For one is not proved to love Christ perfectly who does not shed tears from his eyes through desire for Christ; but the one who has learned daily to weep for love of him cannot be separated from Christ for long. He will soon come to his sorrowing ones and wipe every tear from their eyes; and there will no longer be mourning or crying, but eternal joy at the sight of Christ, who said to his disciples: “I will not leave you orphans.” The sense is: “I will not leave you orphans”; that is, the Spirit will not be given by me in such a way that I am not with you. “I will not leave you orphans.” [Col. 0913B] *Orphani* is Greek; in Latin, *pupilli*, “fatherless children.” Here he indicates that he is their Father: “I will come to you after the resurrection of the flesh,” he who am always with you by the presence of divine majesty. “Yet a little while, and the world sees me no longer; but you will see me.” Christ appeared after the resurrection only to the good, not to the wicked and perverse lovers of the world. We may say that “a little while” means the whole duration of our mortality; when this is ended, the wicked person will be taken away, lest he see the glory of God, which the righteous will see.

621 2. But “I live, and you will live” should be understood thus: I live, who am life, and through me you will live life. He used this present word, “I live,” because the resurrection would soon come. He uses the future for those whose resurrection is yet to come at the end. “On that day you will know that [Col. 0913C] I am in the Father, and the Father is in me; and you in me, and I in you”; as though he said: On the last day, when your resurrection has been completed, you will know, as you believe, that I am now in the Father, one with him as a ray is in the sun; and that you are in me as branches in the vine, and I in you as the vine is in its branches. But the world neither now sees, nor then will see, God shining in his majesty. Who is this accursed world by which God cannot be seen? Accursed, I say, accursed, and more accursed than can be expressed, will be the one who does not see the Lord Christ eternally. The world will not see him: the world, that is, a lover of the world. For lovers of the world are called by the name of the world. [Col. 0913D] Let no one deceive himself: whoever loves the world, believe me, does not love God; and if he does not love him, how shall he see him? Whoever does not love God is blind. He cannot see him who does not have a pure heart, a gentle heart, a meek heart, a heart full of the sweetness of love. He has lost the light of his eyes and will not see the very author of true light. Therefore, if you desire to see God, do not neglect to cleanse your heart of every leprosy of sin. Remember that the mouth of Truth has declared: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). But the world does not see him because it does not have a pure heart.

3. “World” is said in several senses. The world is called the threefold structure of things—heavenly, earthly, and infernal—heaven and whatever is contained within heaven’s circuit. Love of the world is called “world,” as here: [Col. 0914A] “Yet a little while, and the world sees me no longer.” A person washed clean and pure from every defilement is also called *mundus*, “clean,” as in: “Being made clean through abstinence, let us sing glory” (*Hymn at Prime*). It is only of that world—indeed, only of those unclean persons, namely lovers of the world—that it is said: “The world does not see God.” For “if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15). The love of the world and the love of God are greatly opposed to one another. If love of the world dwells within, there is no place for the love of God to enter. God’s love calls a person back from the world, and love of the world calls a person away from God. One casts down; the other lifts up. One casts its possessor down into hell; the other raises him and carries him into heaven. Love of the world seeks the whole world and is never satisfied; indeed, the more it has, the more it always desires to have. [Col. 0914B] The love of God always desires to possess one thing alone; content with him, it no longer wishes to possess anything else. The love of God seeks nothing other than God alone. This love is exceedingly noble: it deigns to love no beauty except the flower of inviolate beauty, namely the one who says: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1). All things which are not Christ’s it not only does not seek, but rejects and scorns as putrid dung. It despises all, rejects all, and all things become cheap to it, because Christ alone becomes sweet to it. O happy love, O blessed love! Those who possess you are blessed; those who possess you are happy. Exceedingly happy, exceedingly blessed is the one whose only love is Christ. [Col. 0914C] Let us possess, beloved, this happiness; let us possess the love of our Creator. In this is a lover of Christ known: if he keeps Christ’s commandments. Hence it follows.

4. “He who has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me.” He has them in memory and keeps them in life; he has them by doing and keeps them by persevering; or he has them in words and keeps them in conduct; or he has them by hearing and keeps them by doing: he it is who loves me. For many have the Lord’s commandments and do not keep them at all: many have them in a book but do not hold them in their mind; many have them in speech but not in deed; many in memory but not in life; many in word but not in example. These certainly are not among the lovers of Christ. Such people, I say, [Col. 0914D] will be beaten with many stripes; theirs will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; fire, sulphur, and a stormy blast will be their portion of punishment with the devil and his angels. But for those who love Christ there will be great joy, great festivity, great exultation, great glorying. For it follows: “He who loves me will be loved 622 by my Father; and I will love him and reveal myself to him.”

What do you think, lover of Christ, worshipper of God, despiser of yourself, of the reward of your love? What evil can harm you, or what good can fail you, if he who created all things from nothing loves you? O exceedingly happy and blessed beyond all expression is the one whom God the Father lovingly loves, and his Son with the Spirit of Christ and God! What, I say, is happier or more blessed [Col. 0915A] than to be loved by him who is Lord of paradise, who has the power of life and death, to condemn and to save—to condemn those whom he hates and to save those whom he loves? For just as he cannot save those whom he hates, so he cannot condemn those whom he loves.

But, O Lord Jesus, what will you do for your lovers? Tell us, I beg: what will you do? Speak so that I may hear; for I too, although a sinner, am one who loves you. What shall be the reward of your love, and what fruit of your affection? Speak and gladden my soul with the reward. Whoever loves you with his whole heart attends to this and awaits it; because it is delayed so long, he groans and sometimes weeps. What is it? Speak, that the brothers may hear and understand, understand and seek, seek and find, find and receive, receive and hold, [Col. 0915B] hold and love—love as much as they can. What will you give to your lovers? What will you reveal to them? “I will reveal myself to them.” Where are those who groan, where are those who mourn for love of the eternal kingdom, for Christ’s absence? Let them rejoice and exult, because Jesus will reveal himself to them.

5. You have heard, brothers; you who sorrow, you who mourn from desire for Christ, from love for the most beloved Lord, Maker, Redeemer, Savior, the sweetness, glory, and splendor of all paradise, joy and delight: you have heard of the reward of your labor, of the gift that my Jesus—and would that he were mine—will give to his lovers. “To one who loves me,” he says, “I shall reveal myself.” O highest joy, O immeasurable gladness! What is sweeter, more glorious, or more blessed [Col. 0915C] than to see face to face him whose beauty the sun and moon admire; whom the holy angels see and always desire to see, yet are never filled with his sight; who is the beauty of heaven, the sweetness of paradise, the faith of the living, the hope of the dying, and the salvation of all—Jesus Christ our Lord? Nothing is dearer, nothing better, than the Lord himself to those who love him. He does not promise gold, silver, gems, precious stones, heaven, or earth; but himself, the Creator of all things and God of all. This is the reward of love, the merit of your affection, you who love the Lord Jesus above all things—I say, not in word but in deed; not in clothing but in mind; not in outward bearing but in affection; not in pretence but in truth. He will reveal himself to you; [Col. 0915D] he will give himself to you.

Do you want more? Do you seek something else? Whatever is without him is worthless. Do you love him? See, then, that you seek nothing from him except himself. He disdains the petitioner if he himself is not the principal cause of the petition. Though he gives every good thing, he gives himself more willingly. Do not fear the greatness or nobility of the gift. Love him with all your heart, with all your mind; and so you may safely approach him, enter unto him, and say: “I will, Lord, that you be my portion in the land of the living.” O happy portion, O blessed inheritance! O Lord Jesus, who will grant me that I may truly say: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15:5)? Would that you might be the reward of my labor, the recompense of [Col. 0916A] my pilgrimage, and the consolation of my sorrow. O Jesus, who are the cause of my love, be for me the sufficient cause for possessing so great a possession.

6. It follows: “Judas—not Judas Iscariot—said to him: ‘Lord, what has happened that you are about to reveal yourself to us, and not to the world?’” Having heard that the world would not see him but that they themselves would see him, Judas asks, on behalf of all who would inquire, the reason for this distinction. The reason, according to the Lord’s answer, is love, by which alone the holy people are distinguished from the unholy; and that love is the cause is proved by the keeping of words, as the Lord says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word.” For love of God is proved in the observance and keeping of Christ’s commandments, [Col. 0916B] because the proof of love is the performance of a work. He vainly claims to love God who contradicts his commandments by his deeds. Indeed, whoever does not obey his command hates him.

Let no one hide himself under religious garb; let no one presume to cloak supposed holiness beneath the covering of the monastic order. Only the one who strives, according to his ability, to observe Christ’s commandment loves Christ. For when you see a monk humble under insult, patient under reproaches, devoted to his priors, gentle in conduct, sparing in speech, constant in silence, reading attentively in the cloister, praising Christ in church with his own voice and with every devotion, shedding tears if not continually then daily, moderate at meals, [Col. 0916C] prompt to obedience, yielding everywhere, bowing everywhere, modest everywhere, striking heaven with his mouth, ever crying to the Lord in his heart, a servant of his neighbor and a despiser of himself, loving all and hating himself—then you may say: “This monk keeps the commandment of his Creator.” O how happy, O how blessed is such a monk! Truly, this monk will have the Lord Jesus as the reward of his labor. But one who does not have love, who does not keep his word, no longer belongs to him. What, then, will be that man’s reward? A stream of fire and sulphur, death and hell will be his reward. Would that you had not been born: such an inheritance is owed to you. Therefore, if you desire to have the reward which is Christ, keep his word, [Col. 0916D] namely: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another” (John 13:34). If you love Christ, you must love your brother. Therefore, lest you incur Christ’s hatred, keep your brotherly love uninjured.

7. A great reward follows from this. What reward? It has been stated above, and yet one delights to repeat it. The more this reward is chewed in the mouth, the more it becomes honey-sweet in the heart; and one who constantly labors according to his strength that he may now be able to possess it does not fail to know how sweet it is. Truth itself declares that the reward of brotherly love is the love of Christ and of God his Father: “If anyone keeps my word, he loves me, and my Father loves him.” If God the Father loves you, [Col. 0917A] what good can fail you? Nothing. Whatever you ask, you will obtain; indeed, you will possess without end the Lord himself, the giver of all good things, together with the holy angels. Is not he supremely blessed whom God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ his Son love? Exceedingly happy, I say, is the one whom God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit love. O, if my God, my Creator, my Redeemer loved me! I would seek nothing more in this world. In this life the love of Christ alone suffices for me. The love of Christ is sweet, delightful, and pleasant. It bestows and grants health to the sick, light to the blind, gladness to the sorrowful, pardon to sinners, life to the dead, heaven to those who dwell on earth, fellowship with angels to companions of beasts, and moreover the Lord of angels and Creator of all things himself. [Col. 0917B]

8. “He who loves me,” says the Lord Jesus, “my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him.” God comes to a person when a person comes to God. A person comes by believing, obeying, beholding, and receiving; God comes to a person by helping, enlightening, and filling. For this proceeds from the love of Christ; all this comes from the love of God. Love makes you the Lord’s house, and makes the Lord a house to you. “God is love; and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16). Happy artisan, love, which can build such a house for its Creator! This house is not made of mortar and brick, nor of stone, wood, gold, silver, or precious stone. It surpasses all gold and exceeds all silver. [Col. 0917C] Precious stones become cheap in comparison with it. Nothing can be compared to its beauty and loveliness. Honey, compared with its sweetness, is as wormwood compared with the sweetness of honey. All things, however beautiful or lovely, ought not to be reckoned anything in comparison with it.

This house is an eternal house, before all ages, before all times, containing all things, encompassing the universe, creating all things, giving life to all things. In this house all who enter receive light if blind, walking if lame, uprightness if crooked, health if sick, and resurrection if dead. No one is wretched in it; all are blessed in it. Whoever enters it enters into the joy of his Lord, which he himself is; and there he shall fare supremely well eternally in the supreme Good, who is God blessed through the ages. [Col. 0917D]

9. O most beloved brothers, does not this precious house become sweeter than honey and the honeycomb in your hearts? Do you not, Christian soul, beloved bride of Jesus Christ, commanding your attendants—the souls of the saints and the angelic spirits—by weeping and imploring them with tears, say: “Daughters of Jerusalem, tell my beloved that I am sick with love for him” (Song 5:8)? You love him little if you do not daily weep and groan for his love. For the absence of the beloved is customarily a river of tears to the loving bride. When she seeks him and does not find him, calls him and he does not answer, nothing delights her but weeping; and, that she may have greater cause to weep, she gathers together everything that is sorrowful. [Col. 0918A]

I know and am certain that God will wipe every tear from her eyes when the day of Christ’s marriage to the Church comes, at that time when the virgins have been brought into the chamber of the eternal King. But how will he wipe tears from your eyes if you do not groan and weep for his love? I believe that you love him little if you do not sigh and lament for his love. If you are such, you are no monk. But you say to me: “I cannot weep.” To this I reply: You do not weep because you do not love Christ perfectly. Tears, therefore, are witnesses of love. If you do not weep for love of your homeland, then at least weep for fear of Gehenna. But you say: “I cannot do even this.” To you I reply: If you cannot do this, you neither fear death nor love life; and if you feared, you would fear either little or not at all. But you, for whom [Col. 0918B] an inheritance in eternal life is reserved, fear God and keep his commandments. “He who does not love me,” says the Lord Jesus, Son of God, “does not keep my words.” Let us love him according to our strength and keep his commands, because a great reward follows from this.

10. What follows—“And the word which you have heard is not mine”—is to be understood thus: “The word which you have heard is not mine”; and there is here a figure called antiptosis, when one case is used in place of another. I beg you: do not be disturbed or troubled by this, you who place all your hope in the Lord Jesus Christ and love him with your whole heart as true God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, when he says, “The word which you have heard is not mine, but the Father’s”; for I am not from myself, but from the Father. I am God from God, [Col. 0918C] light from light, Son from the Father: one with him in essence, majesty, divinity, strength, power, and the creation of things—not later than he nor earlier, not greater nor less, but altogether equal to him. I am other in person, not other in nature; for the person of the Father is one, that of the Son another, that of the Holy Spirit another (Athanasius, in the Creed). “The words which I speak to you are my Father’s,” because he himself sent me; I am from him, and my words are from him.

Or, in another sense: “The word which you have heard is not mine,” that is, it is not that of the assumed man, but of the God who assumed him; it is not that of the Son of Man, but of the Son of God. It is not mine insofar as I was born of the Virgin, but it is mine insofar as I was begotten of God the Father; it is not mine insofar as I am the son of the Virgin, but it is mine insofar as [Col. 0918D] I am the Son of God the Father. Above I said, “He who does not love me does not keep my words”; but here he said, “The word which you have heard is not mine.” Above he says, “My words”; now he says, “The word which you have heard is not mine.” “It is” and “it is not”; “they are” and “they are not”; “they are mine” and “they are not mine”—these are very contrary. Yet it is so, just as Truth speaks. They are his insofar as he is Creator, not insofar as he is a creature; insofar as he is God, not insofar as he is man. They are his, because “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). They are not his but the Father’s, because “he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8).

[Col. 0919A] 11. Or perhaps he says this so that his disciples, who did not yet believe in him perfectly, might hold his commandments more firmly and observe them more earnestly, knowing that these commandments were those of God the Father, maker and creator of all things. For a father always seems to possess greater sublimity, excellence, and dignity than a son—this I say with reference to humanity, not divinity; for in divinity the Son is equal to the Father, neither later than he nor less than he: equal to the Father according to divinity, less than the Father according to humanity (Athanasius, in the Creed). Therefore, so that his own disciples, and their followers, might cherish more dearly the words they heard, he said that they were his Father’s. It is as though he said: “The things which I command you must be observed without dispute; no reasoning may allow them to be overthrown, either wholly or in part, [Col. 0919B] because they are not mine but my Father’s. For I am the Son from the Father; hence my words and works are not mine but the Father’s. The Father, abiding in me, performs his works; through me he gives you commandments.”

Earthly man, clothed in the robe of mortality in this valley of tears, expelled from the joys of paradise, did not deserve in this wretched exile to hear God speaking—he whose commandments he had despised while still in paradise; nor could he even devise what path remained by which he might return to his homeland. But his Lord, taking pity on him, came to seek the wanderer, console the grieving, heal the sick, raise up the fallen, restore a homeland to the exile, and give endless-abiding life to the dead. Thus the Word came into flesh, God to man; and “the Word was made flesh” [Col. 0919C] (John 1:14). God became man, and the Word through flesh, God through man, speaks mouth to mouth to man himself; and according to man gives to man the commandment of life, so that man may obey man and, through that same man, may return to God—to God who became man—from whom, that is, from God, miserable man had departed through disobedience.

Therefore God-made-man, dwelling among mortal human beings as mortal, gives mortals the commandment of life, so that, having now been made immortal through him, they may live blessedly and eternally with that Immortal One. Here two dwellings of the Lord should be noted: one on the way, the other in the homeland; one temporal, when he dwelt with us in flesh, the other eternal, in which we shall dwell with him, glorified in soul and body. Of the first he says subsequently: “These things I have spoken to you while remaining with you,” [Col. 0919D] namely, by bodily presence. But the time will come when I shall withdraw from you the presence of my flesh, and thereafter I shall speak to you through the Spirit. Hence it rightly follows:

12. “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all things whatsoever I have said to you.” The Lord Jesus says, “He will teach what I have said to you”—not because the Son says one thing and the Spirit teaches another, since what Christ says and teaches, the Trinity itself says and teaches; but because the Trinity exists, its individual persons must be indicated, whom we must hear distinctly and understand inseparably. Therefore, when we say Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we do not name them simultaneously, since they cannot fail to be together.

What he says—“the Paraclete, whom the Father will send,” and so forth—is to be understood thus: “I leave you in bodily presence, but I do not abandon you in the presence of the Spirit. I raise to heaven the body which I took from the earth; but through my Spirit I shall remain with you until the consummation of the age. The Father sent me to appear visibly in flesh; but the hour and time come for me to pay death’s debt, and, rising from the dead, to ascend to sit at the Father’s right hand. The world will no longer see me in mortal flesh. But the Paraclete Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will console you, by the abundance of his sweetness, for the absence of my flesh. He will be your teacher—not sounding words noisily outside, but teaching inwardly in the heart. [Col. 0920B] He will bring all things to your remembrance and will teach you all things whatsoever I shall say to you through him, that is, whatsoever I shall inspire in you. He will be your teacher and your consolation. You will be unable to grieve over the absence of my flesh while that Spirit remains in your hearts.”

Come, I beseech you, Lord Jesus: may that Spirit of yours, my God and Lord, come into my heart, and so intoxicate it with your love that I may seek no love but you, love no beauty but you, and be able to taste no sweetness but you. You are the honeycomb, God and man: honey from God the Father, honeycomb from the Virgin Mother; honey in the Father’s bosom, honeycomb broken on the cross; impassible honey reigning with the Father, honeycomb in the tomb; honey reigning with the Father and the Holy Spirit in heaven and in every place, blessed through all [Col. 0920C] ages of ages. Amen.

626. SERMON X. On verses 27–31 of John chapter XIV, and verses 1–2 of John chapter XV.

1. Whoever has learned to love the words of the Lord Jesus with his whole heart knows how sweet they are; nor will he now be able to close the entrance against them, who, in the treasury of his breast, holds Christ, the Lord of everlasting life, in close embrace and contains the delight and joy of all paradise’s beauty. They are the pastures of life, refreshment for the soul, draughts of sweetness, gladdening the hearts of Christ’s lovers; to those who love Christ they are dearer than much gold and precious stone, sweeter than honey and honeycomb; but to the negligent and those who live wickedly they are, like bile, bitter, hateful, and altogether exceedingly distasteful. For the latter they prepare [Col. 0920D] eternal punishment; for those who love Christ, everlasting glory; for the former torment, for the latter reward in blessed life; for the former death, for the latter life; for the former hell, for the latter the fellowship of angels. Whoever these people are, let them mourn and grieve, open the ear of the heart, receive the Word of God, and do what it commands. In him are treasures of wisdom and knowledge, abundant riches and glory. Therefore let those whom it delights to hear the words of Christ hear me, Christ’s sinner. Yet I ask that whoever prepares his hearing for Christ’s words should prepare himself to shed tears. How can he now restrain his tears when he learns that Christ was about to go to the Father after giving his disciples peace in the full embrace of charity? The Lord says to his disciples:

[Col. 0921A] 2. “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you.” For when the time came at which the Lord Jesus had ordained to save the human race by his death, to give his soul as a ransom for many, to leave the world and ascend to the Father’s right hand, he held his disciples—whom he was leaving in bodily presence—within the bosom of love with the fullest affection of charity. As though departing from them and almost abandoning them, he strove by every means possible to console them for his absence. Yet the more he wished to console them, the more he filled them with most bitter sorrow. Then, as though bidding them a final farewell, embracing them, perhaps he fell upon them with kisses. But who could estimate how great a river of tears was there? What heart, even if it were stony, would not have dissolved wholly into a fountain of tears at such an overflowing of charity? Love and grief were then the ministers of tears. O how great the love! O how great the grief! And because the love was great, the grief was great; for they were leaving with great sorrow him whom they possessed with great love. O how great was the love there! They wished for nothing else, sought nothing else, desired nothing else, except to be with the Lord, enjoy his sight, delight in his most sweet speech, and be filled by his honeyed companionship. When they considered all these things and recalled how soon they would be deprived of them all, then the most bitter griefs of their hearts flowed forth in rivers of tears.

[Col. 0921C] 3. How great was the sweetness of love there, and how great the charity of sweetness, when the Redeemer’s lips were pressed upon the lips of the disciples! Then they could truly say: “Honey and milk are under your tongue,” and “Your lips are a dripping honeycomb” (Song of Songs 4:11); “your fragrance surpasses every fragrance of balsam and whatever is contained in perfumes.” And indeed it was so. O how great was the fragrance there, where such abundance of love was present! And how great the sorrow at the future absence of such fragrance and sweetness! With what sobs, I suppose, were the disciples’ hearts afflicted as they heard: “My peace I give to you; my peace I leave with you”? There was grief and mourning there; all were lamenting with one voice.

The Lord Jesus says to his disciples: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace. Not as the world gives do I give to you. I, who am going to the Father, leave peace to you; and I, who shall bring you to the Father, give you my peace.” This is what the prophet says: “Peace upon peace”; and elsewhere: “Lord, you will give us peace—peace—because we have hoped in you” (Isa. 26:3, 12). There is peace in this age: remaining in it, we conquer the enemy, love one another, and do not judge one another over hidden matters. There will be peace in the future, when we reign without an enemy, where one cannot disagree with another, where all things will be naked [627] and open, and each one’s praise will come from God. Both kinds of peace are in him. He himself is our peace, because he reconciled us to God through his blood. Your peace will be in the future, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, and God will be all in all [Col. 0922A]—when there will be no struggle with flesh and blood, but rather palm and crown for the contest fought, when we see him as he is.

4. But perhaps our reader will wonder when, in this little book of Christ’s servant, he finds that Christ himself gave peace to his disciples. To him I, a sinner of Christ, say: What do you wonder at? What troubles you? What you hear is no great matter. Which do you think more lowly: that he washed the disciples’ feet with bent knees, or that he received them with a kiss of peace? He did not shrink from giving the kiss of peace to those for whom he did not fear to undergo the scaffold of the cross. But perhaps you say: “I read in the Apostle that Christ said to his disciples, ‘Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you’; but I do not read that he pressed his most holy lips upon the disciples’ lips.” To this I say: If it is established that it was uttered by the mouth of Truth, why should it not be established that it was fulfilled? It is not dangerous to believe this, nor damnable to think it; it is not contrary to faith. It follows:

5. “Not as the world gives do I give to you.” What kind of peace does this world give? False peace, feigned peace, sophistical peace, peace covered over. Peace is the bond of love and the indissoluble joining of charity. But what does the world love? Absolutely nothing. It loves nothing, cherishes nothing; it hates all things, destroys all things, and kills all things. From leaving the womb of his own mother until entering the belly of the mother of all, what does wretched man receive from the world? Hunger, thirst, nakedness, tormenting cold, distressing heat, scabs of the skin, headache, gout in the hands, gout in the feet, disease in the spleen, disease in the liver: misery everywhere, within and without. Outside, the sword kills him; and at home there is death like it (Lam. 1:20). At last cruel death strikes down and casts down all alike. Behold the world’s love.

Yet wretched people, not attending to the world’s deceit, love that which hates them and willingly submit their necks to its savage sword. These wretches are without counsel; but would that they were wise and understood, and foresaw the things to come in the last times! Certainly they would hate the world and not love it. “World” is also used in another sense, namely, for lovers of passing things. But any wise person can easily see what their peace and concord are like. Therefore, having despised the peace and concord of this world, let us return to the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ. It is not unreasonable to understand and believe that this peace is the love by which he loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood. This is that love by which God so loved the world that he gave himself, as man, to the world, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. This peace—that is, charity—he left to them when he gave his soul for their salvation: this is that most holy body, taken from the inviolate Virgin, which he placed upon the dreadful timber of the cross, despising shame. He left us this peace, as the blessed Apostle Peter affirms, saying: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we may follow [Col. 0923A] his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). Elsewhere he exhorts us to this charity, saying: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought” (ibid. 4:1).

By dying he left us this peace; by rising he gave us another peace. The first frees us from sin; the second reconciles us to the Lord. The first remits our sins; the second leads us to the joys of paradise. The first he gave us when he was to die upon the cross; the second he will give us when he reigns with the Father in eternity. The first was amid mourning and sorrow; the second will be in joy and exultation. The first is tearful; the second glorious. The first is in misery; the second will be in glory. In the first we weep for Christ; in the second we shall rejoice with Christ.

6. Hence the disciples rightly weep for their Master, the servants for their Lord, who was in a sense about to depart from them through death. Nor is this surprising. They saw what they could grieve over, but did not yet believe what they ought to rejoice over. They mourned because they knew Christ was to die; but they did not yet perfectly believe that he would rise again [Col. 0923B] and ascend to heaven. Each of them could truthfully have said—if indeed their grief allowed them to speak: “Therefore I weep, and my eye pours down water, because the comforter who comforts my soul has departed from me.” When the Lord saw them weeping most bitterly, I believe that, according to his humanity, he could not restrain his tears; yet he did not delay to console them by whatever means he could, saying: “Let not your heart be troubled, because I leave you in peace; [Col. 0923C] nor let it be afraid, as though a wolf might attack you because of the shepherd’s absence. For I go as man, but as God I am present. Let not your heart be troubled, nor be afraid concerning my death; for after three days I shall rise, come to you, and you will see me—the Life—in whom whoever believes cannot be subject to the dominion of death. I go, but I shall come again to you and receive you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be. You ought not be troubled or saddened by my departure, from which so great an honor and glory comes to me; rather, you ought to rejoice in it. You do not love me. If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice because I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I. Now command your tears, because you ought to rejoice at my departure. Do not indulge in weeping, for I go to the Father and do not leave you. I go to the Father according to the flesh; I do not leave you according to divinity. The assumed man goes to the Father, and the assuming Son of the Father will remain with you. I raise the body which I took from virginal earth above the choirs of angels, so that the Son of Man may sit at the Father’s right hand and possess by grace whatever God himself possesses by nature.

“I go to the Father so that I may place in heaven the human race deceived by diabolical fraud, slain by the sting of the ancient serpent, and buried in this valley of tears; and may bring back to the flock of angels the lost hundredth sheep, wandering for a long time. Therefore I ask that your heart not be troubled over my death, because this must so take place. It is expedient that one man die for the people and that the whole nation not perish. Only [Col. 0924A] for three days and three nights shall I be in the heart of the earth; afterward, on the third day, I shall rise, having destroyed the prince of this world. You will see me, and your heart will rejoice. On the fortieth day I shall ascend to heaven and sit at the Father’s right hand; and there I shall draw you to myself, to reign happily with me. Therefore, I ask you: rejoice.”

7. O good Jesus, Lord God, my life, all my hope, our whole desire: what do you say to us? What do you say to us who groan and mourn for you? You know, Life that shall never die, that you are our whole desire; therefore we groan and grieve greatly because we cannot see you as you are. Our heart is greatly troubled, Lord Jesus, sole hope of our salvation, because we have not yet deserved to see you, our Lord. We groan and grieve, and our heart is greatly [Col. 0924B] troubled; yet we have not deserved to hear from our Lord: “Let not your heart be troubled.”

O happy Apostles, O blessed disciples of the Lord! You deserved to see him present in the flesh: teaching in words, mighty in deeds, healing the sick, raising the dead; to walk with him, sit with him, take food with him; to see him rising from the dead and ascending into heaven. Now you see him shining in the bosom of his Father. For what is happier, or more blessed, than to enjoy the vision of God? How beloved is that vision of yours, Lord God! My sinful soul longs for it; and because it does not yet possess it, it languishes and fails in a sense. Yet I hope in the Lord Jesus Christ that in my flesh I shall see God, my Savior. This hope is laid up [Col. 0924C] in my mind. Meanwhile I shall rejoice with joy, and my soul shall always exult in Jesus my Savior, who, rising from the dead, ascended into heaven and sits in blessedness at the Father’s right hand. As he was about to ascend to the Father, he said to his grieving disciples: “If you loved me, you would indeed rejoice because I go to the Father, because the Father is greater than I.” It follows:

8. “And now I have told you before it happens, so that, when it has happened, you may believe.” “I now tell you before it happens that I am going to the Father, so that after I have ascended you may believe perfectly that I am the Son of God.” “That you may believe,” he says. You are to believe not what you have seen happen, for this is neither praise nor merit of faith; indeed, faith is not concerning what is seen. Rather, you are to believe that I am the Son of God—not with a new faith, because you believed before, but with a faith increased and made full. When he said these things, their faith was small; and when he died it was nonexistent [that is, explicit faith was nonexistent].

It follows: “I shall no longer speak much with you. For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” The time and hour are at hand when I shall pay death’s debt, and in this mortal flesh I shall no longer speak much with you. The devil is coming: prince not of creatures but of sinners, not of light but of darkness, not of life but of death, not of joy but of sorrow. “And he has nothing in me,” that is, there is nothing in me that belongs to him. For he committed no sin and never willed it; indeed, he could never sin. God did not will to possess anything that he might lose. He came poor, so that the devil might have nothing to take away. The prince of pride, envy, malice and deceit, rancor and every evil will came to the prince of humility, patience and kindness, the prince of life and resurrection, the prince of glory and everlasting blessedness. He came to him to see whether he could find in him any stain of sin. He saw him clothed in the garment of our mortality, near to death, and believed that he could find in him something which he might lay to his charge in death. But that miserable one was deceived, because he found nothing proper to him in Christ; rather, through Christ he lost the ancient right which he possessed over others.

May Jesus be blessed in all things—he who, in the days of his flesh, offered prayers and supplications to him who could [Col. 0925B] save him from death, offering them with tears and a loud cry; he was heard because of his reverence. Although he was the Son of God, he nevertheless learned obedience from the things which he suffered, and, having been made perfect, became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him (Heb. 5:7–9). In him the author of death found no sin, as Truth itself said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.”

9. But perhaps someone might say: “Why, then, do you die if you have no sin, since death followed only from sin?” Therefore here he makes an antipophora and answers this unspoken question, saying: “So that the world may know that I love the Father, and that I do the command which the Father gave me.” It is as though he said: “It is true that death would not yet exist if sin had not existed. Therefore I came into the world to die, so that by my death I might destroy sin. For this is my Father’s will: that I should undergo the punishment of the cross for the salvation of the human race. Therefore, so that the world may know that I love the Father, I do the command which he gave me.” This is what the blessed Apostle said: “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8).

It follows: “Rise, let us go from here.” He was still in the place where he had reclined with his disciples. Thus he said to those reclining, “Rise, let us go from here,” to the place where I am to be handed over to death. We must sit here no longer; the time of rest has passed, and behold, the time of the Passion hastens. [Col. 0925D] Rise and come after me. For you must follow me as I go before you to the Passion, because I am the vine and you are the branches. I am your head, of the same nature as you; and when the head suffers, the remaining members suffer with the sufferer. Insofar as I am man, I am the head of the Church, and therefore of the same nature as you.

10. “I am the true vine”: not that vine which turned into bitterness, which I expected to produce grapes but produced wild sour grapes. I am the fragrant vine, of wonderful beauty, fruitful in flowers, giving the sweetest cluster to all my branches that abide in me. I am the vine that produces wine which gladdens the human heart. I am the vine pouring out its own blood to God the Father for the salvation of my people. I am the flowering vine. I am the leafy vine, the fruit-bearing vine, needing no support from an elm or aid from any tree. I am the vine cultivated not by man but by God the Father: not only outwardly by cultivation but inwardly by grace; not only working externally but also giving growth inwardly.

Christ is the vine, in whom is all sap—that is, the whole fullness of the Holy Spirit bodily. His branches are the Apostles and all who cleave to him in faith. God the Father cleansed this vine—that is, Christ’s human nature—by making it free from sins and giving it virtues; and he does likewise to the branches, though not altogether as he does to Christ. Hence it follows: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take away; every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit.” For all who cleave to Christ by faith are branches abiding in Christ, the saving vine. But some bear fruit, while others persist in barrenness. Some flower and bud and produce a cluster of sweetness; others spread themselves out in the breadth of leaves, desiring to possess only the beauty of greenness. All who persist in barrenness, and who spread out in the breadth of leaves without fruit, if God the Father finds them fruitless at the time of pruning, he will cut them off from the vine, cast them into the fire, and they will burn.

11. But perhaps your mind is troubled by how those who cleave to Christ by faith can be cut off from him, when everyone who cleaves to Christ is one spirit with him. Therefore, that this may be clearer to you than light, you must know that faith is distinguished by diverse qualities. There is said to be dead faith, feigned faith, perverse faith, and right faith. All people, insofar as they are called Christians, are said to cleave to Christ. Insofar as they are Christians, they are believed to possess Christ’s faith; but in some it is dead, in some feigned, in some perverse, and in some Catholic. In the first are the proud and lustful, lovers of money, thieves, robbers, and others of this kind. In the second are those who do not obey spiritual fathers; those ungrateful for heavenly gifts, without brotherly affection, without the peace of charity, accusers of brethren, uncontrolled in anger, lovers of pleasures more than of God, having an appearance of godliness while denying its power. In the third are heretics, raised up against [Col. 0926D] God, proud of their errors, blasphemous against God, and in every respect worse than others. All these trample upon the Lord Jesus Christ and regard the blood of this sweetest vine as defiled.

In the Catholic faith are the meek, patient, gentle, humble, virgins, chaste, continent, lovers of God and neighbor, ready for every good work, awaiting the redemption of God’s children. May the Lord deign to number us among them. For, beloved, we ought greatly to fear what the Lord Jesus says: “Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take away.”

12. Therefore, dearest brethren, let us not trust merely in breadth of leaves, spreading of branches, or greenness of foliage. Unless we bear fruit in the Lord’s vineyard, we shall be cut down and cast into fire. Do you not know, my beloved, that when the hungry Lord saw beside the road a great fig tree, broad and spreading, having leaves and foliage, and found no fruit on it, he cursed it, and it withered? (Matt. 21:18–19.) Such is every hypocrite, because he has an appearance of holiness but lacks the power of holiness: he covers himself with a holiness in his clothing which he does not possess in his mind. It is not a white cowl [Note: [Col. 0927D] From this infer that the author was a Cistercian.] or a high tonsure, not a broad crown, but a pure conscience, purity of mind, renunciation of one’s own will, and charity inflamed in Christ that make a perfect monk.

Let us cleave, brethren, to the true vine, Jesus our Savior, with a true heart, in fullness of faith, our hearts sprinkled and washed from every defilement of flesh and [Col. 0927B] spirit; and let us hold unwaveringly the confession of our hope and faith. Let nothing now be able to separate us from the charity of the Lord Jesus. Thus we shall be among the vines of Engaddi, from which flows not the liquor of wine but the liquor of balsam; like the cluster of Cyprus, concerning which the bride, rejoicing in the Song of Love over Christ’s resurrection and bursting into a cry of delight and gladness, said: “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus in the vineyards of Engaddi” (Song of Songs 1:13). This means “spring of the kid.” “Spring of the kid” signifies repentance or baptism, in which, when someone enters as a kid, he ought to acquire the innocence of a lamb. Engaddi may be understood as a regular monastery: when someone comes there as a kid and puts off his goat-skin, then, cleansed in every respect, he will no longer be a kid but, if he perseveres, a lamb. God the Father cleansed such a one [Col. 0927C] so that he might bear more fruit, cleansing his heart and pouring upon his spirit the dew of truth and charity.

13. Every branch cleaving to the true vine and bearing fruit God the Father will cleanse, or prune, so that it may bear more fruit. God follows the practice and custom of a vine-grower in cultivating his vineyard. The Lord’s vineyard is the universal Church, Christ’s wife and bride, of whom God the Father says to the Son: “Your wife is like a fruitful vine on the sides of your house” (Ps. 127:3). When the time of pruning comes, a vinedresser who loves his vine because it bears seasonable fruit leaves in it nothing dry or withered. Then he digs about it down to [Col. 0927D] its lowest root, breaks up the ground with a sharp hoe, and, if it has put forth any small roots, cuts them away with the pruning knife. And the more the vine loses things of this sort—vain and less useful things—the more fruitful and abundant it grows for bearing fruit.

Thus God scourges and strikes the one whom he loves; for he scourges every son whom he receives. Those to whom it is granted to rejoice in eternity are the ones who receive these scourges here. But whoever murmurs at the blow does not draw near to him who is above him. Indeed, he loses the inheritance of heavenly blessedness if he does not receive the scourge of God the Father patiently and with love. And if he murmurs against the Lord’s scourge, [Col. 0928A] let him be certain that he has incurred the punishment of murmurers.

14. Therefore, dearest brethren, do not murmur if it happens that the discipline of our Lord is upon you, nor grow weary when you are reproved by him. For all discipline at the present time seems to be not joyful but grievous; afterward, however, it yields to those trained by it the most peaceful fruit of righteousness (Heb. 12:6, 11). By the Lord’s scourges the richness of carnal pleasure is worn down and the virtues of the soul are strengthened; the wanton flesh is restrained, and the soul is lifted to heavenly things on the wings of virtues. The flesh loses what it had in excess, and the spirit acquires virtues which it did not possess. Thus through the Lord’s scourges virtues increase and vices are cut away; earthly things are despised and heavenly things loved.

As we await the rewards of eternity, if some grave sickness, severe temptation, or even loss of temporal goods overtakes us, we ought to draw strength from all these things, because as the battle increases, we do not doubt that a more glorious victory awaits us. For in this we show how ardently we burn with desire for God: if we pass to him not only through quiet and pleasant things but also through harsh and difficult things. We cannot now return to eternal joys except through temporal losses; and therefore, in the hope of abiding joy, we ought to consider all adversities no small prosperity. Divine severity does not allow our sins to remain altogether unpunished; rather, the wrath of its judgment begins here with our correction, so that it may rest in the condemnation of the reprobate. For the physician is within, and he cuts away in us the infections of sins, which he thoroughly rejects; with the iron of tribulation he cuts off the poison of corruption.

This is what Truth says: “Every branch in me that bears fruit, God the Father will cleanse, that it may bear more fruit.” For when the mind placed in temptation considers that it is being driven from its former steadfastness in virtue, then it trembles anxiously lest it lose altogether what it had long begun to be. Then it seeks how it can resist temptation and labors to overcome it. Then it takes up the sword of prayer and the tears of compunction, and so weakens temptation and triumphs gloriously over it—not by itself, but by Christ’s grace through it. Thus the mind which lay sluggish and as though unfruitful [Col. 0928D] in prosperity rises stronger and more fruitful for bearing fruit.

15. Therefore, beloved, that we may deserve to have God the Father as our cultivator, let us cleave to the true vine, the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior: not with dead faith, feigned faith, or perverse faith, but with right faith, which works through love, without which no one can be saved. Let us cleave to him, because it is good to cleave to him; and let us place in him all our hope and all our desire, trusting in him who raised him from the dead, because he will also raise [Col. 0929A] our mortal bodies and make us sit with him at his right hand. May he deign to grant this to us through his same Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with the same Father, God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

632. SERMON XI. On verses 3–6 of John chapter XV.

1. Since we do not doubt that it was written by a disciple of Truth, “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (2 Cor. 9:6), we, who have been appointed as it were husbandmen in the Lord’s field, ought to sow according to our ability, so that, when the time of harvest comes, we may receive a hundredfold in the gathering of fruits for what we have expended in seed. For what he here calls “sowing” is, properly speaking, sowing through charity: since the person who scatters seed in order to gather it later goes without it for a short time, so that at harvest he may rejoice over the heap. Therefore, though poor and needy, from my small store of seed I shall gladly give in charity to one who desires it, that I may deserve from my Lord Jesus Christ the multiplied return of eternal blessedness. He does not sow sparingly who, possessing little, gives little, if his mind is ready to give more had he more. He gives generously who has the desire to give generously, even if he has nothing that he can give.

Therefore let us be ready to lend out, to those who desire it, that money which we have received from the Lord to distribute. But I ask that none of you fear the repayment of this interest; for this interest does not impoverish the rich, but enriches them with goods, and fills the destitute and poor. Let the thirsty person therefore come to this money, to the Gospel of blessed John, and draw with joy from the fountains of the Savior, who said to his disciples: “You are already clean because of the word which I have spoken to you.” And the sense is: You are clean, but you must be cleansed again, so that you may bear more fruit. You are clean not because of Baptism, but because of the word which I have spoken to you.

O how good is that word, which washes away the filth of minds, purifies the actions of the inner and outer person, heals wounds, strengthens scars; which raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dunghill, to set him among the princes of heaven, among the possessors of paradise! O how precious a word—indeed, how precious a treasure—which has learned to enrich its possessor, so as to make one who shared the lot of beasts a companion of angels! Blessed is this word and worthy of all acceptance. What is this word of such great blessedness? Hear, if you desire to keep it; but I command you not to delay in putting it out at interest. It is a most noble possession: when distributed, it receives increase, and it rejects an avaricious possessor; unless it is distributed, it quickly diminishes. It rejoices in generosity and flees grasping. It absolutely refuses to be hidden under a bushel, but desires to be set upon a lampstand, so that its beauty may appear to all. Its brightness is like lamps of fire and flame, which many waters cannot extinguish (Song 8:6–7). If a man were to give all the substance of his house for this possession, he would regard it as nothing.

[Col. 0930A]

2. This, I say, is charity; for wherever love of eternal things abounds, the possession of things that quickly pass away at once becomes cheap, and only the charity of Christ becomes sweet—the Christ who says: “A new commandment I give you, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John 13:34). This is that word of which the Lord said: “You are clean because of the word which I have spoken to you,” that is, because of the charity which I have commended to you; and because you are clean, “Remain in me, and I in you.”

“Remain in me,” says the Lord Jesus to his disciples, “and I shall remain in you.” Jesus, I say, sweet Jesus, delightful Jesus, endowed with every virtue and adorned with every beauty; sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, more beautiful in form than the children of men; by whose sweetness the angels are intoxicated, and whose beauty the sun and moon admire. Such and so great a one said to his disciples, and through them to all his faithful: “Remain in me, and I shall remain in you.”

O what great exaltation! O authority of great sublimity! That man should dwell with angels; that earth and dust should be raised to heaven; that man should be lifted from the dung of beasts and joined to the companies of angels! Indeed, that the creature should remain in the Creator, the work in its Maker, the redeemed in the Redeemer, the servant in the Lord, the sinner in the Just One, that which was made from clay in him who makes all things from nothing; the transient in the Eternal, the wretched in the supremely Blessed One—indeed, in him who makes blessed things wholly blessed and sanctifies all holy things: he who is truth and life and everlasting glory, the joy of the world, the delight of heaven, the sweetness of paradise and blessed eternity and eternal happiness—Christ, namely the Lord Jesus!

633

3. O wondrous and inexhaustible goodness! O unheard-of and immeasurable mercy! Who ever, my brothers—who, my beloved, my dearest fellow-servants, servants of the Lord Jesus Christ and, because of him, my lords—could explain in speech, or set down with pen and stylus, how greatly the author of mercy overflows with compassion, how abundantly that author himself abounds in goodness? Believe me, brothers: even if all men and angels strove, they could not draw for you even one smallest drop from the fountain of such mercy, compared with that very abundance of mercy.
