This, I say, is the immensity of the greatest mercy, the vast eminence of goodness: that God, Creator of all things, emptied himself, took the form of a servant, was made in the likeness of men, and was found in outward appearance as a man—remaining God in man, so that man might remain in God; life taking on death, so that death might take on life. Would that the abundance of this mercy so fragrantly filled our nostrils every day that we might truly say with the Bride in the Song of Songs: “I shall always carry a bundle of myrrh, my beloved, upon my breast” (Song 1:12). O sweet burden! O blessed medicine!

4. This burden, my brothers, is the blessed cross itself, namely Christ’s passion. It does not weigh down its bearer, but lightens him; it does not press him down, but lifts him up; it does not shake him, but raises him, and carries the one who carries it to where Christ is in the glory of the Father. This, I say, is the sweetest medicine: it drives out every illness and supplies strength and virtues to one who lacks them; it not only heals the sick but also gives life to the dead.

Let my hearer believe me—rather, let the lover of the cross believe me: he will no longer be harmed by the second death if in this life he has used such medicine. This is that prophetic wood which is among the joints of buildings; for this glorious cross binds earth to heaven, joins man to angel, and so reconciles the sinner to God that God himself deigns to remain in him and he deserves to remain in his God.

O highest rejoicing! O rejoicing joy, pleasant gladness and glad delight: that man should remain in God and God in man; the Redeemer in the redeemed and the redeemed in the Redeemer! To this joy of highest delight, to this glory of most joyful perpetuity, the author of glory, giver of blessedness, eternal salvation, blessed life, happy eternity, secure tranquillity, wholly sweet and wholly desirable, invites his apostles, urges his monks, and summons the whole Christian people, every holy assembly, caressing and comforting, consoling and strengthening, exhorting and saying to them: “Remain in me, and I in you.”

And the sense is: You who are clean, washed, and sanctified through the stone channel, through the sacrament of Baptism, through the banquet of virtues, through the proclamation of love—you are in me; but I ask you to remain in me. If you remain in me, I also shall remain in you. If you remain in me during this short time, I shall remain with you in eternity. Whoever remains in me through the exercise of love, I shall remain in him through the reward of eternal happiness. “I love those who love me”; and those who have loved me in this life will find me after this life, so that where I am, they too may be with me. Whoever has not loved me will certainly not find me for reward, but will find me for punishment.

But you, my disciples and friends, remain in my love. Let not the suffering of my humanity terrify you; nor my hanging upon the cross, the tortures of executioners, the punishment of the cross, the laying down of my flesh, or the tomb of my mortality. Let unconquered faith remain in you; let hope itself not languish; let charity for me flame within you. Remain in me through faith, hope, and charity; and I shall remain in you through the fruit of faith, hope, and charity. And if you do not remain in me, neither shall I remain in you.

[Col. 0931D]

5. You have heard, dearest ones, what Truth itself says—Truth which cannot lie, which never deceives and does not know how to deceive. For it says: “If anyone does not remain in me, he will be cast out”; and the ministers of torments will cast him into the fire, and he will burn. Therefore I ask you, beloved brothers, that each of you enter his chamber and sweep his conscience; let him search himself in the corners of his heart and go around the hidden places of his mind. If he finds that he remains in Christ, let him rejoice. If he perceives himself to be apart from Christ, let him groan and grieve, weep and lament; let him fear and shudder lest he be separated from the fellowship of the saints and be cast into eternal fire, to burn forever.

“Remain in me.” Alas, beloved brothers, how many wretched, how many unhappy persons come to Jesus, but, struck by the deadly venom of the serpent, deceived by the devil’s fraud, covered over by blindness of mind, and corrupted by malice, renounce fellowship with Christ and reject friendship with the Redeemer for love of the world. The necks that they were accustomed to bow before God, now that they have despised the Creator of the world himself, they are not ashamed to bend before the devil!

Alas, how many, after glorious conflicts in which they lawfully triumphed over the prince of this world, have turned their backs to the fleeing enemy and voluntarily bowed themselves, though victors, before one already conquered! How many come to the monastery to live there monastically, displaying signs of humility, enduring in peace every insult brought upon them, and ready, like good soldiers of Christ, for every good work; yet, after the joys of the contemplative life and a foretaste of honey-sweet delight, forget their profession and, like swine, return from their purpose itself to the wallowing-place of mud; and, like dogs returning to their vomit, carry back into their bellies what they had earlier vomited out! Such persons depart from Christ because they have departed from their holy purpose. If they observed the covenant which they had made with Christ, they would despise the poisons already vomited forth. Therefore they do not deserve to remain with Christ, because they did not fear to break the Lord’s covenant.

6. But would that they knew and understood how bitter it is to leave the fountain of life, the author of honey-sweet delight, the Lord of the world, the beauty of paradise, eternal joy—the Lord Jesus Christ, who saved us from death by his rosy blood. If you had quickly perceived how greatly you were preparing to offend:

> “Myrrha, your face would not be covered with bark.”
>
> (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 10.)

[Note: [Col. 0931D] Myrrha, daughter of Cinyras, king of the Cypriots, who, fleeing because of her unspeakable intercourse with her father, was changed into the tree bearing her name [Col. 0932D].]

O what a wretched exchange! O what blind desire, which makes a virgin a wasted-away girl and a prostitute;

[Note: [Col. 0932D] As though “eaten away by wasting disease” (*tabe esam*).]

which turns a woman into a tree, religious rule into apostasy, holy discipline into depraved wantonness, regular enclosure into fields of license, chastity into a filthy skin eruption, a monk into a fool, what is straight into what is crooked, what is level into what is rough, and a son of God into a son of the devil! This, my brothers, is not “the change of the right hand of the Most High.”

O how bitter a change, how harsh a transfer: to depart from Christ and cling to the devil; to despise the Redeemer and love the destroyer; to leave Christ’s footsteps and travel through the savage winding paths of the devil; to leave the way which leads to life and travel the way which leads to death! Whoever he may be who has thus changed, let him incline his mind to my words and not disdain to hear good counsel. “Have you sinned? Be still; do not add further sin” (Ecclus. 21:1). Thus says the Holy One of Israel: “If you return and rest, you shall be saved,” because “the Lord waits for you, that he may have mercy upon you” (Isa. 30:15, 18).

Return, then, to the Lord your God, and he will be merciful concerning your wickedness. Return to the Lord by the way through which one comes to him: the way of the heart, the way of the mouth, the way of deed, the way of fear, the way of sorrow, and the way of love—the way of the contrite heart, the way of the confessing lip, and the way of righteous action. The way of fear, lest you be drawn out to punishment; the way of sorrow, because you have so offended Christ; the way of love, that you may now love Christ himself perfectly, who has so long waited patiently for you to repent.

Groan, grieve, lament, weep. Do not spare yourself, so that the Lord may spare you. Do not indulge yourself, so that the Lord may deign to forgive you. Gird your loins, shave your hair, put on sackcloth, cover yourself with earth, and say to Christ your Lord, your God: “O good Jesus, have mercy upon me. Be Jesus to me; be my Savior. Have mercy upon me, who for my sake shed your gracious blood. Do not enter into judgment with your servant, because no human being will be justified unless through you forgiveness of his sins is granted him. Let not your judicial sentence weigh down one whom your abundant mercy lifts up. You who raised Lazarus when he already stank, raise also me, a sinner now confessing. You who spared sinful Mary, spare my sinful soul. You who gladdened the soul of the crucified Thief, gladden the soul of me, a sinner.”

If you do this, you will still remain with Christ, who says: “Remain in me, and I in you.” For he is charity, and “he who remains in charity remains in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16).

7. It should be noted that remaining in him is one thing, and remaining with him another; remaining near him is one thing, and remaining far from him another. The first is partly on the way and partly in the homeland; the second is wholly in the homeland; the third is wholly in this age; and the fourth wholly in hell. Let us therefore see what it is to remain in him, so that we may delight to remain in him and, not long hence, deserve to remain with him.

To remain in him is, out of love, to cleave to him alone; to love him with the whole heart; to keep his commands in all things and through all things; to place nothing before his love; and, for love of him, to reckon all things, even things not yet born, as nothing. Let him not doubt that he remains in Christ for whom all things besides Christ become cheap and Christ alone grows sweet. O with how great a happiness that person is endowed, with how great a blessedness made fruitful, for whom all things besides Christ grow cheap and Christ alone becomes honey-sweet! May Christ alone thus become honey-sweet in our hearts, and all transient things grow bitter to us, so that nothing but him may now please us, nor be able to please us.

Therefore, my brothers, that we may deserve to remain in Christ and with Christ, may Christ himself—the true light, goodness and life, joy of the world, boundless mercy—be our whole desire and all our hope, so that we may be certain that we shall yet remain with Christ and that, where he then is, we too shall be with him.

8. But “he who says that he remains in Christ ought to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). He no longer remains in him who strays from his path. Let no one deceive himself; let no one mislead himself; let no one trust in a religious garment. For it is not a religious garment but purity of mind that makes a monk; not the shaving of the head but love of Christ that makes a monk approved.

The Lord Jesus says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matt. 16:24); for unless someone departs from himself, he does not approach Christ the exalted King. Blessed is self-renunciation for Christ’s sake! Whoever does not possess it perfectly must not think that he is wholly pleasing to Christ. For he vainly believes that he pleases Christ who does not reject himself for Christ’s sake. And let him know that he perfectly pleases Christ who has perfectly learned, for Christ’s sake, to renounce himself.

Therefore, if we are to please Christ, self-renunciation is necessary for us—according to what our health permits, not according to what hatred of ourselves, pierced by the spear of sins, may at times eagerly desire to inflict upon us. This is especially so in taking food, where the strength of nature must be preserved and the appetite of seductive gluttony must not be followed. We cannot wage victorious war against the vices which issue forth to fight from fleshly loins unless we first firmly restrain the appetite of gluttony by the crushing force of abstinence.

After crushing the appetite of gluttony, we must take the greatest care lest the snare of human praise catch us and the poison of diseased praise make a smoking cautery in the ark of our heart and leave it there once made. Whatever breeze of praise about us may arise, whatever favor of flatterers may caress us, let humility, the empress of virtues, not depart from the ark of our mind, lest the twisting serpent which sometimes lies hidden in green grass—that is, in human favor—according to the poetic saying,

> “Flee from here, boys! A cold snake lies hidden in the grass.”
>
> (Virgil, *Eclogues* 3.93)

catch us in its venomous teeth and, having caught us, destroy and kill us. Therefore let us hold great humility in all things, so that we may remain in the author of humility and may as swiftly as possible be with him and reign with him. For everyone who remains in him through love need neither doubt nor hesitate: he will remain with him through love’s reward.

9. We have seen what it is to remain in him; now we must see what it is to remain with him. To remain with him is to be where he is; to rejoice with him in blessed glory; to reign with him on the throne of eternity; to contemplate him face to face, as the holy angels do, and as all the elect will see him after the resurrection of the bodies, according to the Apostle’s saying: “When Christ, our life, shall appear, then you also shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

To remain near him, but neither in him nor with him, is not to be in the way of faith, hope, and charity, but in the way of error; not to be in the way of commandment, but in the way of sin. Such a person, I say, if he is not in Christ or with Christ, is nevertheless near him, because he can quickly abandon error and immediately grow fervent in Christ through faith, hope, and charity. He has free choice and can direct it toward loving God. The Lord knocks at his door: let him open it, and the Lord will enter to him, remain in him, and he in the Lord.

To remain far from him is to have departed from him under the sentence of condemnation, although both expressions may also be understood in another way. Let us therefore remain in him, so that we may deserve always to bear the fruit of good work. Otherwise, unless we remain in him, we cannot bear fruit. Truth itself says, and cannot change: “As the branch cannot bear fruit unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me”; and: “If anyone does not remain in me, he shall be cast out as a branch and shall wither; and they shall gather him and cast him into the fire, and he burns.”

For we must greatly fear what follows: “If anyone does not remain in me,” and so forth. Whoever does not remain in the Lord Jesus Christ will be expelled from the fellowship of the saints, will wither from fear and expectation of everlasting condemnation, and the ministers of Tartarus will seize him and cast him into fire, to burn endlessly and forever. May Jesus Christ our Lord, author of everlasting glory, deliver us from this perpetual condemnation—he who lives and reigns as blessed God with the Father and the Holy Spirit unto ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XII. On John, chapter 15, verses 7–9

1. Everyone who desires to take up the way of truth plainly ought to stretch out the hand of his heart toward the commands of truth and live faithfully in them, so that that hand may be full of hyacinths and his belly ivory, set with sapphires; so that he may keep the Word’s word, Christ’s commandment, through love in the casket of his mind, and so that outwardly the flower of the word itself may give fragrance through the increase of good work. Certainly, one found to be such a person will necessarily obtain from God whatever he asks that would profit him.

The very rule of Truth, the complete pattern of holiness, has established this forever; its decree cannot be repealed or now altered from the book of Truth. For my Jesus—indeed my God—firmness of truth, removal of falsehood, avenger of sins, way of the way, life of life, wholly sweet, wholly good, wholly truthful, wholly true, says: “If you remain in me, and my words remain in you, you shall ask whatever you wish, and it shall be done for you.” Great are the gifts which Truth itself promises, for it knows how to deceive no one. “Whatever you wish,” says the Lord Jesus, “you shall ask, and it shall be done for you”—provided only that you remain in me and my words remain in you.

It is as though he said: If you remain in me through love, and my words remain in you through the performance of works, ask without hesitation whatever pertains to the advancement of the soul, and you shall obtain it and receive it. Those first two things necessarily serve each other and neither tolerates the absence of the other. Their mutual relation may be understood by an enthymeme. If someone remains in Christ, it necessarily follows that Christ’s commands should remain in him. Either of these propositions establishes this one conclusion: let him ask Christ whatever he wishes, and he will have it. Such an inference seems necessary: this person remains in Christ; therefore, whatever he asks from Christ toward such advancement, he will obtain. Likewise this other: Christ’s words remain in this person; therefore, and so on.

2. Yet we may say this, should some barking dialectician object by the force of the copulative conjunction, which makes a bond between equals, not between part and whole, but between whole and part, between opposites and contraries, and between things exceeding and things exceeded. We say, then, that some remain in Christ and his words remain in them; others remain in God, but God’s words do not remain in them.

He who remains in Christ, and in whom Christ’s words remain, is an ecclesiastical teacher who, by the instruction of doctrine, has from which to bring forth for his hearers things new and old—the fruits, namely, of the authorities of the Old and New Testaments—and who shows in his deeds, by living piously and devoutly, the good things which he preaches to his disciples. Another does not possess the word of God through learning, yet remains in Christ through a good life. Such a person, indeed, although he does not have Christ’s commandment in a book, nevertheless has it in a heart enlarged by charity. How happy and blessed are such people! The kingdom of heaven belongs to such as these.

Another who has the word of God but does not put it into practice is a monk of sophistical religion, under the pretext of a cloaked holiness; one who, by living perversely, contradicts what he has learned from the Rule of Benedict. Such a person neither remains in Christ nor do Christ’s words remain in him, because he neither loves Christ nor observes his commands, although he pretends both to love Christ and to keep his commands. But what kind of wretch he is, the day of the Lord will reveal, where there can be neither simulated religion nor counterfeit holiness, neither sophistical speech nor deceptive syllogism. All things will be naked and open before Jesus the Judge, who judges truly and strictly—not only concerning a perverse deed, but also concerning an idle word; not only concerning the movement of the feet or the labor of the hands, but also concerning the cast of the eyes.

3. Let one who is such consider, then, for what purpose he became a monk. “I have washed my feet; how shall I presume to defile them again? I have put off my tunic; how shall I put it on again?” If he changed his habit, why did he not also change his mind? If he is white outwardly, why is he black inwardly? If a white garment adorns him outwardly, why does the scar of conscience disfigure him inwardly? If he ought to devote himself to silence, why does he delight in talkativeness? He who promised contempt for the world—why does he still strive to please it?

Let him strive to please Christ; let him not delay to despise the world; let him heed what he promised; let him love Jesus above all things; let him place nothing before Christ’s love; let him keep Christ’s fear before his eyes wherever he may be, sitting or walking, speaking or silent, hungry or thirsty, drinking or eating, sick or healthy. In Christ are confidence of strength, hope of eternal blessedness, assurance of pardon, certainty of glory, remission of sins, bestowal of glory, acquisition of joy, and enjoyment of the highest and true God. “Blessed is the man,” says the Prophet, “who fears the Lord; he delights exceedingly in his commandments. His seed shall be mighty upon the earth” (Ps. 111:1–2), and he himself shall be blessed by the Lord.

That perpetual blessedness, that abundance of everlasting sweetness, and that eternal and delightful vision of God are the gift which those who remain in Christ ask from Christ. If you remain in Christ—that is, if you are grounded in Christ’s charity with a pure heart and pure conscience—nothing but Christ can satisfy you, and you will no longer be able to ask for anything but him. “Whatever you wish,” says the Lord Jesus—salvation that never ends, life that never dies, supreme delight, paradise’s glory, sweeter than all honey, more pleasant than any nectar, more precious than gems and gold—he says, I say, to those who love him: “Whatever you wish, you shall ask, and it shall be done for you.” Great is what he says.

4. But it must be observed that the universal expression “whatever” does not contain all things, but only him who contains all things: he whose being is such that it is always true being; God from God before all times, born as man from a Virgin at the end of times; eternal salvation of all believers, hope and refuge of those who fear him. This is that one thing which the elect seek, whom nothing can satisfy except God, who contains all things. They groan and mourn because they do not see Jesus, the author of blessedness; they do not behold what delights them. Everything they encounter is sad to them, for they seek the Lord Jesus and do not find him; they call, and he does not answer. They turn to tears, their companions in sorrow; and him whom they cannot follow with the steps of their feet, they pursue with tears and groans.

Blessed is the life of such people; blessed their course, whose goal deserves to possess such a great standard. This is not given to the lazy; the negligent do not attain it; it is denied to the lame. It is owed only to one running through the breadth of charity. Let each of us never cease to consider how he runs in the course of God’s commandments, how he strives in the Christian contest against the roaring lion. I believe none of you is unaware that no one can be saved unless he perseveres faithfully to the Lord Jesus until his departure from the dwelling of the body; nor can one attain the prize of eternal sweetness if he fails in the race before reaching the goal.

Our course is the observance of God’s commandments; the end of our course is charity, according to the Apostle’s saying: “The end of the law is charity” (1 Tim. 1:5). The end of our course is charity itself—not that charity by which we love God, but that by which we possess God; not that by which God is loved, but that which is God himself. In the course of God’s commandments, one person begins to run well and fails before he reaches the goal. Another begins sluggishly and afterward runs swiftly to the goal. Another both begins swiftly and finishes swiftly. Another begins sluggishly and always persists in his sluggishness. The prize is owed to two of these: namely, to the one who began sluggishly and afterward arrived swiftly, and to the other who both began energetically and arrived swiftly.

638

5. For many come to the monastery in order to live there boastfully, who begin badly and end badly: always wandering and never stable; always, when they do not possess what they want, grumbling and slandering; blessing the cellarers behind their backs; afflicting with insults the brothers with whom they live; undisciplined in manners, disordered in bearing and conduct, proud in dress, worthless in morals, and always ungrateful for benefits received. These will not deserve to possess the prize of eternal blessedness, because they refused to plant a straight step in the course of God’s commandments. For the form of holiness will not bring such persons to perfection when the depravity of their conduct confounds them through the poisons of disobedience.

Christ’s words do not remain in such persons, because they have devoted Christ’s commands, which they know or hear, to the vanity of winds. They despise the Lord’s orders and love the dining rooms of the belly; but God himself, the eternal and almighty God, they strike with the kicks of wickedness and malice, hating their neighbor, denying the Lord Jesus Christ, and not keeping what they promised him before all the saints on the day of their consecration. Let anyone who is such know that he is to be condemned by the God whom he mocks.

Another comes to the monastery in order to punish there the sins he committed in the world. But after entering, he not only fails to wash away in sorrow the sins he committed, but perhaps commits other and more grievous sins besides. Yet afterward he is pierced by great sorrow and cast down by great shame. Because he did not wash away by good living the sins which he committed, but ventured upon still more enormous deeds, he then recalls how great is the Judge’s severity toward sinners and how great, in those already condemned, is the punishment of condemnation itself. Moreover, he considers how great the Redeemer’s mercy is toward penitents and his kindness toward those who live rightly.

Then he counts every evil that he has done; then he heaps before his mind’s eyes every sorrowful thing. He is shaken by pains and distressed by torments as severe as those he fears will confine him in the punishments of hell, as severe as those by which he dreads being tortured in the furnace of fire and sulphur. Then indeed he sees nothing that delights; then everything he encounters is sad. Then with tears and grief he punishes what he committed with pleasures. Then he strives to discover how he may please the Lord Christ; devoting himself to fasting and prayer, he desires to please God alone. Whoever is such, let him ask the Lord whatever he wishes; he need not doubt: he will obtain it.

6. Therefore, my dearest brothers, whom Christ redeemed by his own blood, let us love, fear, and cherish without measure and beyond measure, with all heart, all mind, all strength, and all the marrow of our hearts, him who bestowed his blood, the Savior of the human race; and let us cling to his discipleship. For it is very sweet and delightful, joyful and pleasant, to become Christ’s disciple. “In this,” says the Lord Jesus to his disciples, “my Father is glorified: that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.”

We therefore, who are called Christians and are Christians, have been placed in the Church of Christ as in a field. Some bear fruit; others persist in barrenness. Some produce scant and few fruits: always lazy, always negligent—lazy in prayer, slow in reading, weighed down with long sleep at vigils, and too tender and delicate for labor. In these the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ is not greatly glorified, because they neither bear much fruit nor prove to be Christ’s disciples.

Others produce sweet fruits in abundance of fertility—sweet, I say, to God and sweet to men. These glorify God, and God will glorify them on the day of recompense for works, on the day of gathering the new harvest, when they shall come with exultation carrying their sheaves. These are meek and humble, devout and obedient; alert for vigils, fervent for every good work, exalted in prayer, subtle in sacred reading, sighing in meditations, groaning and weeping in contemplations. They sow indeed in tears; but let them rejoice and exult, because they shall reap in eternal joys.

7. Others there are who bear no fruit, but produce only shoots and leaves. These are those who have the appearance of holiness but not its fruit. The axe has been laid to their root. Why do they occupy the ground? Let them be cut down and cast into the fire. A hard and bitter sentence is pronounced upon fruitless trees. “Every tree,” says the Lord Jesus, “that does not bear good fruit shall be cut down and cast into the fire” (Matt. VII, 19). Let fruitless trees therefore fear: hypocrites, whitewashed tombs, carved and finely polished sepulchres. Let them root out what lies hidden within; let them confess and be healed. Let them change their strength, change their conscience, heal the branding of their conscience; let them direct their steps in the way of God’s commandments and bear fruit, so that through them the Father may be glorified in the Son, and Christ in his Father, and they themselves may be glorified in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Happy and blessed is he through whom God the Father is glorified, through whom Christ is praised and the Holy Spirit glorified. O exceedingly happy one, whose life and conduct thunder forth praises to the Creator! O blessed man, whose soul serves its Creator! O blessed soul, which strives, according to its strength, to please its Redeemer! Blessed be that soul whose entire love is Christ, whom nothing can satisfy apart from him who was slain for its love; [Col. 0939C] which knows how to love nothing apart from Christ, who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood, and gave himself as a ransom for us, in order that through his blood he might adopt us as children of God. In every way blessed be Christ, who so loved humankind as the Father loved him. For he himself says: “As the Father loved me, I also loved you.” O dear charity, O eternal truth, O sweet eternity, O blessed happiness, O glory of angels, O splendor of saints, good Jesus, holy Jesus, spotless life, eternal life, incorrupt salvation, everlasting glory, altogether sweet, altogether lovable! How you loved us, how you cherished us, you who gave yourself over to death! Your love knew no measure; and your charity, O Christ, could not be contained within limits. “As the Father loved me,” you say, “I also loved you.” Would that I too were one whom my Lord loved! Would that I had heard from my Lord’s mouth: “As the Father loved me, I also loved you!” What could now be lacking to me, if my Jesus loved me—mine, I say, and would that he were mine! O happy riches! O blessed wealth: to possess Jesus, to possess the Lord Christ!

8. Possess him, my reader, by love; and thus you shall possess him eternally through love’s recompense. Truth itself says: “I love him who loves me; and he who loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I will love him and reveal myself to him” (John XIV, 21). No living person suffices to recount how great was the love Christ displayed toward us by dying; let tears speak, because voices cannot explain it. “As the Father loved me, I also loved you.” Let us see how God the Father loved him, and how he himself loved us. For the Apostle says: “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross; therefore God also exalted him and gave him a name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II, 8–10). And the prophet, speaking of him to the Father, says: “You subjected all things beneath his feet: all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field; the birds of heaven and the fish of the sea, which traverse the paths of the sea” (Ps. VIII, 8–9). Behold how God the Father loved the Son: he himself judges no one, but has given all judgment to his Son (John [Col. 0940B] V, 22); and he gave him a name above every name, so that at his name, which is called Jesus, every knee should bend—of heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings: that is, every heavenly creature, such as angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, principalities and powers, virtues, cherubim, seraphim, every heavenly order, and every earthly creature. Nor do human beings alone tremble on hearing Christ’s name: even brute animals tremble; moreover, every infernal creature trembles and quakes at the invocation of a name so great. Great, therefore, is the Father’s love for the Son, since he has so raised him up, so exalted him, as to subject all things beneath his feet and place all things under his dominion.

9. We have seen how the Father loved Christ. [Col. 0940C] It remains for us now to see how Christ loved us. But who, I ask, can explain it? Who could ever unfold in words the abundance of love, the height of charity, which Christ showed toward us—he who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood; who destroyed our death by his death, choosing to die for us in order to free us from eternal death and draw us to that place where he himself is in the Father’s glory? For he says: “Father, I will that where I am, there also my servant may be” (John XII, 26). Behold how he loved us. He chose to die for us, lest we be condemned to eternal death. He rose from the dead so that he might make us participants in his resurrection. He ascended into heaven in order to lead us onward to the palaces of heaven; and he sits at the Father’s right hand, placing, crowning, [Col. 0940D] and gladdening there those whom he redeemed with his own blood, whom by the bond of charity he has secured with himself at that same right hand of the Father. Let us therefore love, venerate, and cherish Christ himself without measure, beyond measure, without limit, beyond limit, unceasingly, continually, with all our heart, all our mind, all our strength, and all our powers, that we may be able to come to him and reign with him, who lives as God with the Father and with the Holy Spirit, blessed for all ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIII. On John, chapter XV, verses 9–13

1. The more I drink of God’s love, the more I thirst; I cannot be sated with it, nor can anyone who loves Christ perfectly. The more it is eaten, the more [Col. 0941A] it increases hunger; and the more it is drunk, the more it kindles thirst. It so intoxicates the mind in which it dwells that it now seeks or loves nothing, nor can it love or have power to love anything apart from him who so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in and loves him may not die but live with him. The very author of immeasurable charity invites us to this love; he entreats and asks us to abide in it. For he says, “Abide in my love”; and thus he openly says: “Because I love you with that love by which the Father loves me, I ask you to love me with the same love. And because your love brought me even to death, yet not even the most cruel death separated me from your charity, love me and abide in my love.” But how we ought to [Col. 0941B] abide in his love follows, when he says: “If you keep my commandments, you shall abide in my love, as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love.” Let him who has ears to hear, hear; and let him who has a heart to understand, understand. This seems to exceed the measure of our capacity and surpass every strength and effort of soul and body. The command which the Lord enjoins upon us is counsel for our salvation, which the author of our salvation himself supplies to us. What human being, sprung from the apostate root of the first parent, has been or shall be able, without some blemish of transgression, to keep Christ’s commandments with every duty of charity, unshaken and unstained, as he himself wholly and in every respect kept his Father’s commands—he who committed no sin, could never sin, and did not even will to sin? Among the children of humankind there is none, great or small, endowed with such holiness or privileged with the honour of such religion, who was not conceived in sins, except the Mother of the Immaculate One who committed no sin but takes away the sins of the world; concerning her, when sin is under discussion, I will have no question whatsoever. Hence no one rightly shines with so great a prerogative of holiness as to be able to observe this “as” in all things and through all things, if it is indeed expressive of equality of degree.

2. But it should be noted that this adverb *sicut* (“as”), here, denotes a likeness of quality rather than quantity, as we explained above where it is said: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved [Col. 0941D] you” (John XIII, 34). The sense is: “If you keep my commandments as I too kept my Father’s commandments, and if you abide in my love as I abide in my Father’s love”—that is, if you are obedient to me in keeping my commandments until your departure from the dwelling-place of the flesh, according to the capacity of your frailty, as I was obedient to the Father unto death on the cross, according to the fullness of divinity which dwelt bodily in me—you shall abide in my love, and I in your love, as I too abide in the Father’s love and the Father in mine. Or we may say that this adverb *sicut*, in our case, does not here exercise the force of its full signification, but only indicates that Christ’s love and obedience toward God the Father are set before us as an admonitory likeness, so that we ought to keep Christ’s commandments [Col. 0942A] and abide in his love. It is as though he said: “I kept my Father’s commandments for your salvation, and therefore I abide in his love; you also keep my commandments for love of me, and thus you shall abide in my love.”

3. Love’s love still compels me—the charity of our lover, Jesus Christ our Lord, though would that we were loved—to repeat this chapter: “Abide in my love.” O Jesus, Jesus, resurrection of the dead, life of the living, eternal salvation of believers, wholly sweet, wholly lovable, wholly delightful to those seeking you, loving you, finding you: deign to let me, your servant, speak with the Lord; a human being with God; a thing formed with its Maker; a creature with its Creator; one redeemed with the Redeemer. Therefore hear me, and do not be troubled on my account. For I am one who loves you, though a sinner: your love gives me boldness to speak with you; your charity draws my mind; love urges me on. You said to your apostles—and let us understand that through them it was said to us—“Abide in me, and I in you.” I beseech you, lovely delight, honey-sweet sweetness, sweetness of fragrance, fragrant sweetness, highest joy, everlasting glory, life of the saints, glory of angels, Savior of the world, Son of the living God, most sweet, most beautiful, most dear, and most loving Jesus: tell me, I pray, what is the cause of your love, of your adhesive charity, for which you command us both to love you and to abide in your love? Tell us, so that those who do not [Col. 0942C] love you may hear and love, and those who love you may grow more and more fervent in your love. May your sweet voice sound in my ears. Say: “As the Father loved me, I also loved you; and because I loved you, render love to me in return: love me, and abide in my love.” What you say, Lord Jesus, what you command us, is just and right. Equity teaches everyone that one who is loved should love the one loving him, and that one who is loved should give reciprocal charity to the lover. Yet we seek another cause for your love, by which we ought to love you more. Tell us who you are and what you have done for us, whereby you have commanded us to love you. Tell us: “I am who I am” (Exod. III, 14). “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Rev. XXII, 13), creator of heaven and earth, air and seas, and of all [Col. 0942D] that is in them, maker and creator of all things, King of kings and Lord of lords. We have heard and rejoiced, and we are certain that you are God, blessed through all ages. But still our groans implore, and the tears of my sinful soul demand, what you have done for us. When I recall what you did for me and what I did to you, my inward parts collide with one another, my spirit trembles, my soul is disturbed, and I am wounded and pierced by many sorrows. Nor is this surprising. I consider what the servant has done to his Lord, and how many and what great punishments the Lord endured for the servant. My conscience bears witness to me, Lord Jesus, what I have done to you; and your cross testifies to me what you have done for me. You are God and [Col. 0943A] I am human; yet for me, you who are God became human. You are Creator and I am a creature; for me you deigned to become a creature. You are Lord, we are servants; and for servants you deigned to become a servant; a stranger for strangers, an exile for exiles, poor for the poor, humble for the humble; for mortals, not merely mortal, but dead—not by any ordinary death, but by the death of the cross, utterly harsh, utterly bitter, and utterly shameful. These are your works, O God. I consider these works and tremble. In them I know you to be merciful, and I come to life again; and therefore I trust in you, I place my confidence in you, I love you, I cherish you, I desire you with all my inward being.

4. These works, my brothers, are the cause of Christ’s love. Let each one of you consider whether he ought to love the Lord Jesus. What ought he to have done for us that he did not do? How could he have loved us more, and not have loved us? He could not have had greater love for us than he had, since he laid down his life for us unto death. Blessed Truth itself bears witness that no one has greater charity than that one should lay down his life for his friends. Let not Christ’s love, therefore, be cheap in our eyes, my brothers—he who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood. Let it not be cheap to you, my brothers; let Christ’s love itself, Christ’s charity itself, not become bitter to you. Christ’s love is wholly sweet, wholly delightful: it does not torment its possessor but delights him; it does not weaken but strengthens him. It scorns all earthly things [Col. 0943C] and seeks heavenly things alone; it seeks Christ’s commandments and strives to observe them according to its strength; and through observance of the commandments it advances with happy step to the receiving of joys, so that it may then rejoice perfectly with him for whose desire, while placed in this valley of tears, it often sighed so bitterly. Hence it rightly follows:

5. “These things I have spoken to you, that my joy may be in you and that your joy may be fulfilled.” It is as though he said: “For this reason I command and admonish you to keep my commandments and abide in my love: that my joy may be in you, and that your joy in me may be fulfilled; that I may have cause to rejoice in you because of the reciprocal charity you bestow on me, and that you may be able to receive and possess that joy which the elect will receive in the recompense of rewards.” Or otherwise: “That my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be fulfilled.” For everyone who, from the inmost marrow of the heart, purely, unstainedly, and unwaveringly embraces and binds Christ within the bosom of charity with the arms of love, will count all his joy as his own. Indeed, he rejoices more over the joy Christ received from the Father by rising again, ascending to heaven, and sitting at his right hand, than over that joy which he himself will receive from Christ on the day of judgment. Therefore, dearest brothers, let Christ’s joy remain in you, whether active or passive, whether that of the lover or of the beloved: that is, whether it is the joy by which Christ rejoices in us or the joy by which we rejoice in Christ. Let us keep Christ’s commandments, [Col. 0944A] so that he may be able to rejoice in us and we in him. Let the joy of his blessedness remain in us—not only that by which he blesses or makes blessed those who rejoice in himself, but also that by which he was glorified by the Father—so that we may deserve to reign with him in eternity, through the same Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit, blessed through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON XIV. On John, chapter XV, verse 12

1. Since our tongue ought not to be silent concerning our Redeemer—and lest what is to come soon be upon those who are silent concerning him—I consider it greatly concerns us that, speaking of him day after day, we should not conclude perfunctorily, and that, conversely, we should not incur the sentence of dreadful damnation by setting our tongue free for empty words. Therefore, condemning in every place of eternal confinement empty words that do not resound with Christ or possess the weight of religion, let our lyre stretch forth its strings to the sweet utterances poured forth by the Word of the Father; and let the tongue, the mistress of speech, sound the trumpet of the Savior with the plectrum of the mind—those sweet utterances of life which flowed from Christ’s honeyed mouth. Yet would that no clouding of uselessness or contempt might obscure what is set before you; but that, bound more closely by charity, it might become dearer to you than a precious stone and taste sweeter on the palate of your heart than every honey and every honeycomb. May the author of sweetness himself, for whom all desired things are forthcoming, whose will all things obey, who can even do what seems impossible, [Col. 0944C] become so sweet in your hearts that you may always delight to hear of him; and may he inwardly teach me the wisdom that concerns him, and through the lance of my mouth wound and pierce the enemy of humankind, who labours with all his might to make Christ’s very words become cheap to us through hearing, and, though preached and taught by me and others, to bring upon us a sentence of damnation. May Jesus always aid, protect, and defend us from him—Jesus who loved us and washed us from our sins in his own blood, instructing us by word and forming us by example; establishing an ordinance and enacting a commandment; an ordinance of sweetness, a commandment of life; an ordinance of love, [Col. 0944D] a commandment of charity—establishing and fulfilling, commanding and accomplishing, in himself, I say, and in us.

2. This is the commandment which Jesus commanded, which he established for his disciples: namely, the commandment of charity, the commandment of love, which reads thus: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” He sets before us a sweet and pleasant commandment. That which love commands and affection draws us toward seems sweet and pleasant. For where charity is, no difficulty appears; where true love is, there is no labour. All willingly obey love and submit their necks to its yoke: the perverse to the perverse, the sensual to the sensual, the holy to the holy, the chaste to the chaste—each in accordance with his own desire. Therefore the Lord gives a commandment of love, a commandment of charity, so that all may obey [Col. 0945A] his commandment and hasten to tame the neck of their pride under the yoke of his humility. Therefore, my brothers, as good disciples of Christ, be ready to hear; gladly receive Christ’s commandment, which the evangelical trumpet sounds forth to you, and fulfill it effectively in all things and through all things, so that through love you may be able to return to him from whom you departed through the swelling of pride.

3. Now let your charity attend to what true charity commands you: proven charity, unprecedented charity, merciful charity, good charity, charity wholly sweet and wholly delightful—the beautiful bridegroom, fair, radiant, ruddy, chosen from thousands: Christ, judge of the age to come, prince of peace and Lord of life. The Lord Jesus, blessed through all ages, says: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you.” A light commandment, a pleasant commandment, a sweet commandment: light to bear, pleasant to embrace, sweet and delightful to hold. What is lighter, more pleasant, or sweeter than to love? Every person can do this: healthy and sick, rich and poor, foolish and wise, noble and low-born, slave and free. Let no one make excuses; let no one offer a defence in this matter. This capacity, namely to love, is common to every human being. It follows, therefore, from the Lord’s commandment that we ought to love one another.

4. But because many love one another, not with that love which is charity, but with a love that is blasphemy against the Lord—love which is “skin for skin,” which conceives pain and gives birth to iniquity; like blind lust and prostituted desire, which drives its steed [Col. 0945C] with the spurs of malice and wickedness toward an eruption, so that it cannot foresee or avoid the abyss of hell in which it lies—the words “as I have loved you” have been added. How did Christ love us? As he himself gave it, we have set it down above. But, to bring you back to yourself for knowledge of this matter, let your love, your holy devotion, know that Christ’s flesh and blood, received and offered by the faithful upon the altar, bears testimony to you of how Christ loved us. Let your love therefore know that one’s own advantage must sometimes be set aside for the advantage of one’s neighbours. But if your holiness still seeks another instance of Christ’s love, you can find it also in the temporal goods bestowed on you by him. It should therefore be observed that there are two loves of Christ: one temporal, the other spiritual; one common, the other special. The Creator’s mercy has bestowed the first, the temporal love, generally upon the just and the ungodly; the spiritual or special love he grants only to those who live piously and justly. This special love is distributed in two ways. One kind concerns the bestowal of virtues; the other, the recompense of merits. One is that by which he strengthens us with virtues against the weapons of the most wicked enemy; the other, that by which he enriches us with everlasting glory when we have lawfully triumphed over our tyrant. Christ’s own merciful love gave us these two kinds of love—he who loved [Col. 0946A] us and washed us from every defilement of flesh and spirit in his own blood.

5. Therefore, as Christ loved us with a twofold love, so he commanded us to burn with a twofold charity: love of himself and love of neighbour. If we show charity toward God and human beings with a pure heart, good conscience, and unfeigned faith, we easily resist sin, abound in every good thing, reject the enticements of the world, and accomplish in love even all things difficult or harsh to human frailty—provided, however, that we love God with perfect charity, which is from him, with all our heart and all our soul. If we love him with all our heart, nothing will be in us by which we might serve sinful desires. And what is it to love God? To be occupied with him alone; to conceive in the mind a longing for the enjoyment of his vision; to have hatred of sin and disdain for the world; to love one’s neighbour, whom he has declared worthy of love in himself; to preserve in that love the lawful measure, and not overturn the established order of love. They overturn the order of love and do not preserve the measure of loving who either love the world, which ought to be despised, or love their own bodies—which should be loved less—more; or do not love their neighbours as themselves, or perhaps do not love God more than themselves. We ought to love our body so that we provide naturally for its health and weakness; so that it may serve the spirit in an orderly manner [Col. 0946B] in its movements and contradict the soul and reason in nothing; and so that, on the day of resurrection, it may live forever with the Lord in blessed glory.

## SERMON XV. On John, chapter XV, verse 14

[Col. 0946C]

1. We love our neighbour as ourselves when we love him not for some advantage to ourselves, expected or received benefits, family connections, or blood relationship, but only because he shares our nature. Accordingly, on this ground we should love all our neighbours, providing as far as we can for their welfare in good conduct and in attaining eternal life, just as for our own, and helping their needs as our resources permit. We love God with all our heart if we strive, according to our ability, to please him alone; if he alone is our desire, our hope, our aim, our entire love, our entire charity. Otherwise we do not love him perfectly and do not possess charity; and one who does not possess charity no longer belongs to him, nor will he possess as the reward of his labour the one whose straight path of charity he did not keep in this distressing solitude. This, I say, is the path of charity: not only to love the one who loves us, but also the one who hates us—not less than oneself, but as oneself. This path is narrow and strait, and few travel upon it. Only those travel upon it who despise themselves for Christ’s sake and to whom everything besides Christ himself is worthless. If these encounter some diabolical thorns seeking to conceal the wayfarers of charity, then, like stags running swiftly and strongly, led by love of their heavenly homeland, they leap over them and reduce to nothing the devil himself, who suggests brotherly hatred. And when the stirrings of their minds are in some way disturbed by an injury inflicted on them and seek to rage against a reviling brother, they constrain them with the bit of charity and dash them against Christ. Such people indeed lay down their lives, who through charity humble themselves before friends and enemies in order to win all people for Christ. Whoever acts thus both obeys Christ’s commandments and renders him reciprocal charity; such a person is truly Christ’s friend. And because for Christ’s sake he hates himself, loves him above all things, and for his sake embraces all who hate him in charity, let whoever is such rejoice.

2. Whoever is such is truly a monk; and whoever is not such, though hooded, though clad in rags, whether shaven or tonsured, let him have whatever you please and be whatever you please: he is an image or picture of a monk, but is not a monk. I say this to shame the frenzied. There are certain people in the monastery suffering from a frenzied sickness: quick to anger, prepared for wrath, hasty toward hatred; they draw the itch of the heart through the scraping of the tongue into a scab of the skin—corrupt in mind, wandering and unstable, roaming about to spy, whisperers, gluttonous, murmuring, envious, puffed up and proud, ungrateful to God for benefits bestowed, clothed in the skins of transgressing Adam and stripped of the garment of salvation, of him who was created according to God in righteousness and holiness of truth. These people

> Retain the old skin, and beneath a polished brow  
> Bear a crafty fox within their raging breast.

[Col. 0947C] Let the brow of such persons blush; let it be confounded and blush very swiftly. Let them confess and be healed; let them change their mind and direct their steps in the paths of eternity, in the ways of most chaste love, along the most glorious way of charity. Let them render mutual charity to their brothers, love God above all things, lay down their lives for love of him, and obey his commandments in all things and through all things, that they may deserve to be called and to be Christ’s friends, he who says: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you.” O great condescension, immeasurable overflow of charity, innate goodness, mercy beyond interpretation! We are found unworthy, by virtue of our creation, even to be his servants, and yet he deigns to have and call us friends. Giver of sweetness, lover of charity—indeed, dear charity itself, blessed delight, delightful tranquillity, secure security, happy eternity, eternal happiness—the Lord Jesus, altogether desirable, altogether lovable, incomparable treasure, priceless pearl, life of the living, hope of the dying, the eternal happiness of those who for love of him have made themselves unhappy in this world. O how happy is the one who for love of him has made himself unhappy! And how blessed the one who for his sake has made himself wretched! Truly happy and worthy of eternal happiness is the one who despises himself, scorns himself, and is displeased with himself so that he may truly please his Creator. Let every proud person know, every exalted person, befouled in the Gilgals (*Galgalis*) of vices, scabbed in lustful flesh, defiled in a perverse conscience, pleasing himself and setting himself above himself: [Col. 0948A] he will no longer please his Creator unless he first becomes displeasing to himself because of his error. Therefore, my brothers, let us be displeased that we have been evil and perhaps still are; and let it please us that we are not yet perfect, but, through the gift of the Lord Jesus Christ—and would that he were ours—we shall be perfect, keeping his commandments and becoming friends from his enemies, as he said to his disciples: “You are my friends, if you do what I command you.”

3. I still address you, monk of Benedict. O man, swift to the table, slow to church; vigorous at drinking, but feeble at singing; wakeful for tales, sleepy at vigils; forward in speech, but mute in psalmody; prompt to anger and detraction, slow to prayer; a lover of envy, a persecutor of Christ; seeing the speck but not considering the beam; you rebuke others but do not correct yourself; inventor of malice, destroyer of discipline; friend of vices, enemy of virtues. These are the things that blind the eye and separate from God. These are what make one who has converted perverse, a monk demoniac. When, from the depth of my heart—which is rare, yet exceedingly dear—I consider in the health granted me by him how fervently a true lover burns toward the beloved with the love of charity in those whom he redeemed by his holy blood, I confess that I am wholly displeased with myself and ashamed within myself of myself. I am ashamed—and would be ashamed; indeed, I would altogether despair—unless the Word who was made flesh and dwelt [Col. 0948C] among us, and who, having ascended into heaven, sits at the Father’s right hand, were the propitiation for our sins. Yet while I lie weak in the very abyss of my shame and suffer from the fever of vices, he stretches out from his royal seat his healing hand and says: “Come to me, you who labour in the toil of sins and are burdened by their weight; and I will refresh you by sparing you and bestowing the grace of my love. For you shall be my friend, if you do those things which I have commanded you to do.” What? Are you not ashamed at this? For what applies to me applies also to you. Let Christ’s enemies be ashamed, be converted, and blush very swiftly, and they will be Christ’s friends. We are his friends if we love him with all our heart; you are not his friend if you do not love him in every respect. If on one side you are chaste and on another proud, you must remember that “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV, 6). Therefore you must love him in every respect; you must cleave to him with all your heart. For to cleave to him is good and secure. What is it to cleave to him? To place one’s hope in him, love nothing apart from him—indeed, to despise everything for his sake, hate all things, disdain all things, and count every transitory thing as nothing. This is good; this is delightful: thus to love the Lord Jesus Christ. Whoever is thus is his friend.

4. Let us therefore consider, my brothers, how great is the mercy of our Redeemer. We are not worthy to be reckoned his servants, and yet we are called and are his friends if we remain in his love. Therefore let us now keep the commandments of our Lord, true friend, creator of all things, maker of [Col. 0949A] all things, so that we may deserve to be reckoned and to be not only among the number of friends but also in the lot of sons: denying ourselves for the sake of him who emptied himself and took the form of a servant for our salvation, in which he paid what he had not stolen—he who willed to be scourged, slain, crucified, and killed for us. This is why Christ ought to be loved; this is how the Lord Jesus shall be ours: if for his sake we deny ourselves. Happy self-denial and blessed contempt, which makes a sinner righteous, an enemy a friend, a servant a son—indeed, what is exceedingly great, a slave of the devil a son of God. Therefore, monk of Christ, despiser of the world, be a despiser [Col. 0950A] of yourself: despise the world, despise yourself. Exceedingly great is that which is owed to your contempt, owed to your self-denial. Inestimable is the abundance of sweetness, the abundance of happiness, of glorious eternity, which Christ will give to those who love him—namely, himself. Nothing is dearer, sweeter, more precious, or more beautiful than Christ. He is health without illness, life without death, joy without sorrow, beauty without tarnish, sweetness without bitterness. Such a reward is owed to those who deny themselves for his sake. May Christ himself grant us this reward—namely, himself—he who lives and reigns as God without end, blessed unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0949]

## ANOTHER SERMON FOR THE LORD’S SUPPER. (G)

**[Note.]**

646 This sermon, listed among the Bernardine writings in earlier editions, has seemed fit to be placed here together with the following sermon, since it is foreign to Bernard’s style and character. It is not found in manuscripts of better authority containing only genuine sermons of Bernard, nor in the earliest printed editions of Bernard.

[Col. 0949B] 1. “Have you sat at the table of a rich man? Carefully consider what is set before you; and know that you must prepare such things” (Prov. 23:1–2). In these words the Spirit of counsel speaks with a voice that is gentle, yet terrible. Gentle is the voice to those who obey; terrible to those who despise it. Rewards are due to those who receive it; punishments are threatened to those who reject it. Those who receive it shall live; those who reject it shall be condemned. “You have sat,” he says. See what a mark of great sweetness the beginning of such words bears. The preceding words sound sweetly, soothe the affections, and enrich the mind from the abundance of the senses. But what follows—“know that you must prepare such things”—the more it exercises the understanding, the more it terrifies; and, by the height of its mysteries, wonderfully humbles us because of our incapacity.

[Col. 0949C] Therefore that rich and most mighty one is the Lord of hosts, himself the King of glory, to whom it is said through the prophet: “That I might see thy power and thy glory” (Ps. 62:3). He is the one “who takes away the spirit of princes, terrible among the kings of the earth.” The table at which the faithful sit in order to feast with him is his incarnation: “Thou hast prepared before me a table,” that is, the remedy of thy incarnation, which I always contemplate and recall, “against those who afflict me” (Ps. 22:5), lest those who formerly used to insult the wretched exile should prevail according to their ancient custom.

2. Moreover, at and from the table of the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0949D] rich refreshment is obtained. There royal dishes are taken, prepared with the most careful art and diligence: most delightful to the taste, substantial for nourishment, and effective as medicine. The first dish, therefore, [Col. 0950B] is filial obedience, woven with three cords: humility in the heart, patience in the mouth, and perseverance in good work. For Christ became obedient to the Father. Hence he himself says, “I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 5:30); and elsewhere, “My food is to do the will of my Father who sent me” (John 4:34).

Do you ask about humility? The Lord of all put on the form of a little servant; he was born of a poor virgin. Therefore, though free from the law, he was made subject to the law and lived under it without complaint. He ate with tax collectors and sinners; he washed the feet of the disciples whom he had chosen. From his birth to the end of his life he strove for this: that, as virginity in his Mother was special [Col. 0950C] and without example, so humility in the Son might be singular and unique.

If patience is asked about: “Like a sheep he was led to slaughter,” “he was wounded for our iniquities,” and “was reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. 53:7, 5, 12). For that he, though invisible, might be seen by us, and that he, though immortal, might die for us, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). This Word dwelt among us veiled by the flesh which he assumed from us for our sake: the Word in flesh, the sun in a cloud, honey in wax, light in an earthen vessel, a wax taper in a lamp. In assumed flesh he bore our infirmities without the sinfulness of flesh, bearing our sins in his flesh; and all this not for himself but for us, that he might restore us [Col. 0950D] from sickness to health, from strangers to co-heirs, from slaves to freedom.

If you ask concerning perseverance, he was “obedient unto death.” Obedience is the garment reaching to the ankles which Joseph—whose name means “increase” or “augmentation,” that is, any person made perfect by the gift of the more merciful grace, which is the mother of believers—distinctively put on.

[Col. 0951A] 3. The second dish is spiritual poverty, constituted by three things: laying aside and despising possessions; lowliness and self-abasement; and the renunciation of one’s own will in all things. Voluntary poverty, therefore, possessed without ownership or desire, is safer in proportion as it is freer from encumbrance. Such poverty is the guardian and teacher of virtues; conversely, immoderate abundance of possessions is the root of vices. It is expedient to be naked when we are to wrestle with the devil, who is naked. A naked athlete fights more vigorously; a swimmer strips himself in order to cross a river; a traveller runs well when he has cast aside his little burdens.

Noble, then, is the title of voluntary poverty [Col. 0951B] which Christ taught in word, saying, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3), and so forth, and consecrated by example. For he had no house of his own in which to lay his head or eat the Passover with his disciples, nor had he anything of his own with which to pay the tax. He also commended it by the prophetic utterance: “I am the man who sees my poverty” (Lam. 3:1). The first Apostles after Christ set forth an example of this poverty, when in the primitive Church “the multitude of believers had one heart and one soul, and all things were common” (Acts 4:32). This poverty was enjoined upon religious followers of the Apostles.

That poverty which neither possesses nor wishes to possess seeks an accompanying poverty: namely, the breaking down of hidden pride [Col. 0951C]. Thus one who is a member of God may be poor in spirit—that is, may think and judge lowly and contemptibly of himself; may not applaud himself, swell with the eminence of his merits, or insult others. Christ possessed and kept this above all others; hence he said to his disciples: “When you have done all these things, say: We are unprofitable servants” (Luke 17:10). Thirdly, the religious person should be poor in spirit, never doing anything from his own will, but made subject in all things and through all things to the yoke of obedience. These are the three marks of true religious life which we set forth beforehand: they make a human being conformed to God and the angels, enroll him as a citizen and heir of the heavenly homeland.

4. The third dish is the death of Christ, worthy of reverence, [Col. 0951D] the most moving of all mysteries. In this mystery piety shone forth more brightly, grace gleamed more fully, and charity radiated more abundantly. Three matters especially belong to Christ’s death, to be pursued not without fear, tears, and groaning: the infliction of manifold insults; the fastening of his hands and feet upon the cross; and the guarding, beneath the watch of soldiers, of the tomb and of him who was buried.

Now sitting signifies two things: judicial authority and voluntary subjection. You have fitting examples of each at hand. “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1); “I saw the Lord sitting” (Isa. 6:1); and “When the Son of man shall sit on the seat of his majesty” (Matt. 19:28): these are signs of judicial authority. But Scripture itself cries, “Rise up after you have sat, you who eat [Col. 0952A] the bread of sorrow” (Ps. 126:2); “Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept” (Ps. 136:1); and Christ’s words to the disciples, “Sit here until I pray” (Mark 14:32): these are words of due subjection. Therefore, while Christ is still praying, we must not rise through any self-exaltation; rather, we ought to be humbled and exercise ourselves in good works, so that after enduring the labours by which we are afflicted here, we may one day rise, advanced in its proper place and time to heavenly glory.

5. Therefore you who sit at the rich man’s table, subjecting and humbling yourself by the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, with the dishes set before you which we have mentioned, consider carefully, not negligently, what is set before you. Consider, I say, that you may learn not to be slow or sluggish in returning thanks; that you may learn to give thanks for each gift. Consider, I say, that none of God’s gifts may lack the thanksgiving due to it—not great gifts, not moderate, not small. Indeed, we are commanded to gather up the fragments lest they perish: that is, not to forget even the least benefits. What is given [Col. 0952B] to an ungrateful person never fails to perish.

What follows is terrible because it is burdensome and seems almost impossible. But to whom? To the soft, effeminate, and idle—those in whom, with the reins of self-control broken by destructive liberty, drunken desire and intoxicated affection go where they please, while they wander after the flesh in an ever more carnal fashion, excessively court and pursue the world. But what is that which they judge terrible? This: “Because you must prepare such things.” Note that you must prepare such things by suffering with him, dying with him, and being buried with him, and so forth. For it is fitting, and very beneficial for you, to suffer with, die with, and be buried with him who suffered, died, and was buried. These things were done for this purpose: that the Christian life might be configured and conformed in all these respects to them. For whoever, as a member of Christ, says that he abides in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked. For the sake of the cross it was said to the godly: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24). For the sake of burial it was said: “We have been buried with Christ” (Rom. 6:4), and so forth.

6. Therefore, that we may be more powerfully pierced with compunction, more deeply moved, and run through everything, let us review [Col. 0952D] each detail: weaving a little cord, binding a rope, joining a bundle from all and each of the things related concerning the humble Son of God, the Father’s supreme Only-Begotten, the most merciful Redeemer, our most loving brother. Let the Lord Christ, then, spiritually come before us and press himself upon our hearts: betrayed and sold by a disciple; bought by the Jews as a worthless slave at a very trifling price; seized, dragged, and bound, like a man without help; his back torn by scourges, his cheeks plucked, his face smeared with spittle, his head pierced with thorns, his side wounded, his palms bored through, and his feet transfixed. As though mocking his own murderer, he offered himself without resistance and patiently stretched out his naked body as an anvil for the strokes of smiths, while, in order to convey us through the sea of this life from exile to our homeland, he paid rapacious pirates the fare of his own death.

Nor shall I pass over the myrrh with which he was given to drink upon the cross, nor that with which he was anointed for burial. In the first he took to himself the bitterness of my sins; in the second he consecrated the future incorruptibility of my body. This is the most renowned and royal banquet, in which the righteous feast and rejoice before God, or delight in gladness.

7. Beyond all this, a sweet spice is set before those invited, to make them joyful: wine of Cyprus, seasoned with precious and foreign spices, foreign because they are still untried by us. “My beloved is to me a cluster of Cyprus,” he says. In the preceding verse it had been said, “My beloved is to me a bundle [Col. 0953B] of myrrh”—namely, Christ according to the flesh; but the cluster of Cyprus is Christ according to his divinity. The bundle of myrrh is Christ in the Passion; the cluster of Cyprus is Christ in the Resurrection. The bundle of myrrh is the hail and thunder of the Jewish storm; the cluster of Cyprus is the destruction of the whole opposing power. The bundle of myrrh is the multitude of afflictions; the cluster of Cyprus is the abundance of joys: bitter there, intoxicating here.

8. But we must not pass over what is said: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh; he shall dwell between my breasts” (Song 1:13, 12). For there is the heart; and where the heart is, there is love; and where love is, there is the dwelling of the beloved.

> [Note: [Col. 0953D] What follows, as far as the words “And therefore, if you love your soul,” occurs above in almost the same words in the *Letter to the Brethren of Mont-Dieu*, book I, no. 30, [Col. 0954D].]

Everyone of sound judgment knows how greatly it benefits Christian piety, how fitting it is for God’s servant, faithfully to recall the benefits of Christ’s most holy Passion: to enjoy them sweetly in conscience and to store them more fully in memory through imitation. This is spiritually to eat the Lord’s body and drink his blood, out of love and reverence for him who commands believers in him, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (1 Cor. 11:25). It is plain to all how impious it is for a person to forget such great divine mercy, since it is wicked to forget the memory entrusted under some sign by a friend who is dying or departing for a distant land.

Indeed, it is permitted to few persons, to whom this mystery has also been entrusted, to celebrate the mystery of this venerable remembrance in its proper manner, time, and place. But all believers may at every time and in every place of God’s dominion enact, handle, and receive unto salvation the reality of the mystery in the manner in which it has been handed down [Col. 0954A]—that is, with the affection of due piety and the effect of holy imitation. For just as the worthy person receives the sacrament unto life, so the unworthy receives it unto judgment and his own death. The sacrament without the reality of the sacrament is death to its recipient; but the reality of the sacrament, even apart from the sacrament, is eternal life to its recipient.

Whenever, in remembrance of him who suffered for you, you are piously and faithfully moved and devoted to imitating Christ, you eat his body and drink his blood. So long as you abide in him through love, and he in you through the working of righteousness and holiness, you shall be reckoned among his body and his members. Therefore, if you love your soul, you must lose it for Christ—either by laying it down as a martyr, if necessity requires; or by afflicting it more strictly as a penitent. Indeed, it is also a kind of martyrdom to mortify by the Spirit the deeds of the flesh: less harsh in horror than that by which limbs are cut with the sword, but more burdensome in duration.

Let us therefore hold a continual and unceasing remembrance of the things contemptibly inflicted upon Christ: certainly not an idle, lukewarm, or sluggish remembrance, but one that delights us above all things through the ardour of compassion and obtains all things through the privilege of imitation. Hence the prophet says, “Delight in the Lord”: that, once every pleasure of worldly vices has been despised, the remembrance of him may be sweeter; “and he shall give thee the petitions of thy heart” (Ps. 36:4), not of the flesh.

9. There are, moreover, three spices from which is made the seasoning set forth for the festive rejoicing of the royal banquet: Christ’s triumphal return from hell, the glory of his resurrection, and his session at the right hand of God the Father. The foods already mentioned strengthen; these three make joyful. Those believed to feast and to be invited above others in the time of grace are the Apostles and martyrs, who, showing themselves neither ungrateful nor forgetful of the banquet furnished by Christ, return and offer from themselves things like those which they received, in heavenly strength and spiritual exultation. In this desire and contest they sweat, run, and labour; God chooses them that they may offer themselves as a living sacrifice acceptable to God. May Christ grant us, by however small an accomplishment of good works, humbly to venerate [Col. 0954D] their footsteps—he who is God blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 0953]

## Sermon on the Life and Passion of the Lord. (G)*

[Note.]

650 Trithemius, Bellarmine, and others attribute this to Saint Anselm under the title *The Spur of Love*. Certainly, it does not have Bernard’s style, and it is found neither in ancient manuscripts nor in the first Lyons edition under Bernard’s name.

[Col. 0953D] 1. Let Christians honour Jesus of Nazareth, innocently condemned by the Jews and crucified by the Gentiles, with divine acts of service. It is worthy, salutary, and honourable for us Christians reverently to venerate, lovingly embrace, and steadfastly imitate the weaknesses of the Saviour. For these are the most powerful instruments by which the omnipotent power and unsearchable wisdom of God has powerfully and wonderfully accomplished, and still accomplishes, the restoration of the world. Christ the Lord was made lower than the angels so that he might make us equal to angels. Who, then, would not humble himself for Christ? Christ the Lord was crucified for our sins and sweetened the bitter cross for those who love him. He died and destroyed death so that we might live through him. Who would not love Christ the Lord? Who would not suffer for Christ? Through the shame of the cross Christ passes into the glory of heavenly brightness; and for his reverence all power in heaven and on earth was given him by God the Father, so that all God’s angels may worship him and every knee bend at Jesus’ name—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.

2. Where is your boasting, O Christian, except in the name of your crucified Lord God, and in Christ’s name, which is above every name, in which whoever is blessed upon earth shall be blessed in heaven? Glory in the name of the Son, the Redeemer, and give honour to him, our Saviour, who has done great things in us. Magnify his name with me, saying: “We worship thee, O Christ, King alike of Israel and of the Gentiles, prince of the kings of the earth, Lord God of hosts, most mighty power of Almighty God. We worship thee, precious price of our redemption, peace-offering, who by the inestimable sweetness of thy fragrance alone didst incline the Father, who dwells on high, to look upon lowly things, and didst render him so gracious toward his children. We proclaim thy mercies, O Christ; in abundance we pour forth the remembrance of thy sweetness.
