To thee, O Christ, we offer the sacrifice of praise for the multitude of thy goodness, which thou hast shown to us—an evil seed, wicked and lost children.”

While we were still your enemies, Lord, and unjust death exercised dominion over all flesh—every seed of Adam being subject to it through the law of original guilt—you remembered your word of mercy and looked down from your lofty dwelling upon this valley of our tears and misery. You saw the affliction of your people and, touched inwardly by the sweetness of charity, began to devise concerning us thoughts of peace and redemption.

[Col. 0955D] 3. And although you were the Son of God, true God, coeternal and consubstantial with God the Father and the Holy Spirit, dwelling in inaccessible light and upholding all things by the word of your power, you did not disdain to bow down your loftiness into this prison-house of our mortality, where you might taste and absorb our misery and restore us to glory. Your charity did not think it enough, for completing the work of our salvation, to send a Cherub or Seraph, or one of the angels: you yourself deigned to come to us at the Father’s command; in you we have experienced his exceeding charity.

You came, I say, not by changing place, but by showing us your presence in flesh. You came from the royal throne of your sublime glory into a humble maiden, lowly in her own eyes, sealed by the pious vow of virginal continence. In her sacred womb the ineffable power of the Holy Spirit alone caused you to be conceived and born in the nature of true humility, so that the occasion of birth violated neither the majesty of your divinity nor the integrity of your Mother’s virginity. O loving, O wondrous condescension! God of immeasurable glory, you did not disdain to become a despised worm; God of all, you willed to appear as fellow-servant of servants. It seemed too little for you to be our Father and Lord: you deigned also to be our brother.

And you, Lord of all, who lack nothing, did not shrink, at the very beginning of your birth, from tasting the hardships of most abject poverty. For, as Scripture says, when you were born, “there was no place for thee in the inn” (Luke 2:7); nor did you have a cradle to receive your tender body. Instead, you who encompass the earth with your palm, wrapped in little cloths, were laid in the wretched manger of a filthy stable. Even this your Mother borrowed from brute animals.

Take comfort, you who are brought up amid the filth of poverty, because God is with you in poverty. He does not lie in the delights of a splendid chamber, nor is he found in the land of those who live pleasantly. Why do you still glory, O rich man, in a muddy thing, in the rolling luxury of a painted and delicate bed, when the King of kings preferred to honour his resting-place with the straw of the poor? Why do you detest harsh straw when the tender infant, in whose hand all things are, preferred hard animal-straw to your silks and your feathers?

Yet your tender infancy, O Christ, was not safe from persecutors’ swords. For while you still hung at your Mother’s sweet breasts, an angel appeared in a dream to Joseph, saying: “Arise, take the Child and his Mother, flee into Egypt, and remain there until I tell thee. For Herod will seek the Child to destroy him” (Matt. 2:13). From that time onward, good Jesus, you began to suffer hard things. Nor did you bear only in yourself that affliction of your infancy, [Col. 0956C] but also the death of your little ones, many thousands of whom Herod’s savagery slaughtered for your sake between their mothers’ breasts.

4. When your tender infancy had passed, you humbly gave us an example of truth. You did not sit with the council of vanity, but in the midst of the teachers, questioning and hearing them, although you were the Lord of knowledge and the Wisdom of God the Father. You also gave us the pattern of obedience, when you, Emperor of the world, humbly became subject to the command of your parents.

But when the fullness of stronger age came, about to set your hand to mighty deeds, you went forth for the salvation of your people, like a great giant running the course through the whole extent of our misery. And indeed, that in all things you might first be made like your brethren, you approached your servant, who baptized sinners unto repentance, as though a sinner: you asked to be baptized, innocent Lamb of God, whom no drop of sin had ever stained. But when baptized, you sanctified not yourself in the waters but the waters in yourself, so that through them you might sanctify us.

From baptism you went out into the wilderness in a spirit of strength, so that an example of the solitary life might not be lacking in you. You patiently endured the wilderness, the forty-day fast, the sharpness of hunger, the temptations and deceits of the spirit, that you might make all these things bearable to us. At last you came to the lost sheep of the house of Israel, openly raising the lamp of the divine word for the enlightenment of the world. You proclaimed God’s kingdom to all who obeyed the word; you confirmed your word by accompanying signs; you displayed the power of your divinity in all things; and, healing the sick, freely bestowed on all peoples everything suited to the salvation of sinners, that you might gain all.

But their foolish heart was darkened, Lord, and they cast your words behind their backs. They paid no heed to all your wonders which you had worked among them, except for a very few noble athletes whom you chose from among the weak and despised things of the world, that through them you might wonderfully overthrow the strong and lofty. Not only were they ungrateful for your gratuitous benefits; they also heaped insults upon you, Lord of lords, and did to you whatever they wished. For while you performed works of God which no one else had done, what did they say? “This man is not from God”; “By the prince of demons he casts out demons”; “He has a demon”; “He deceives the crowds”; “He is a glutton, a drinker of wine, and a friend of tax collectors and sinners.”

Why do you weep, why do you sigh, O man, when you endure injuries of speech? Do you not hear how great the reproaches were that fell upon the Lord your God on your account? “If they have called the master of the house Beelzebub, how much more his household?” But while they uttered these and similar blasphemies, and sometimes assaulted you with stones, good Jesus, you endured them patiently and became before them like one who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth.

5. Finally they valued your righteous blood—delivered up by your disciple, the son of perdition—at thirty silver coins, in order to cast down your soul into death without cause. The treachery of your utterly lost betrayer was not hidden from you when, at the supper of washing, you even knelt and bowed before him, deigning with your most holy hands to touch, wash, and wipe his accursed feet, swift to shed your blood.

Why, O earth and ashes, do you still walk with your neck stretched out? Does pride still raise you up? Does impatience still agitate you? Look upon the Lord Jesus, Lord of humility and gentleness, maker of the whole creation, the dreadful judge of the living and the dead, bending his knees before the feet of a man and his betrayer. Learn that he is meek and humble of heart; be ashamed in your pride and blush for your impatience.

This too, Lord, was an act of your gentleness: you did not wish to expose and publicly shame that faithless man in the company of the brethren, but gently admonished him and told him to hasten what he was preparing. In all these things his wrath against you was not turned away; instead, he went out and busied himself with the frequent crime. “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, who didst rise in the morning?” (Isa. 14:12). You appeared glorious amid the delights of paradise, a companion of heaven’s citizens and a fellow-guest at the divine word’s banquet: how were you reckoned among the children [Col. 0958A] of darkness? You who were nourished in saffron-coloured garments, why did you embrace dung? (Lam. 4:5).

Then your household, O Christ, was made glorious when the unclean one went out from the assembly of angelic fellowship. Then at last that blessed gathering was watered with the most abundant flood of divine discourse, since that corrupted man, whom you knew unworthy of an infusion of this most limpid drink, had truly been sent outside.

6. Having given the saving commandment of charity and patience, and arranged for your brethren the kingdom of your Father, you withdrew with them to a place known to your betrayer, knowing all things that were to come upon you. There you did not blush to declare in your brethren’s hearing the sorrow of your soul, which you voluntarily assumed from your impending Passion, just as you assumed the other things you suffered, saying: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.”

You also fell face down with your knees upon the ground, praying in agony and saying: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me.” That bloody sweat which, during prayer, ran drop by drop from your most holy flesh to the earth most certainly showed the anguish of your heart. O sovereign Lord Jesus, what is the source of this anxious prayer of yours? Did you not willingly offer yourself wholly as a sacrifice to the Father? Indeed you did, Lord. Yet we think that you assumed this for the consolation of your weak members, lest anyone despair if weak flesh murmurs where the spirit is ready for suffering.

Doubtless, that we might have stronger incentives of love and gratitude toward you, you expressed in yourself natural weakness of the flesh by these signs, teaching us that you truly bore our infirmities and underwent the sufferings of the Passion not without feeling pain. For that utterance seems to be the voice of the flesh, not the spirit, because you added: “The spirit indeed is ready, but the flesh is weak.”

7. You clearly showed that your spirit was ready for the Passion when, as men of blood came by night with your betrayer, lanterns, torches, and weapons, seeking your life, you went out voluntarily to meet them. So that they might receive nothing from the leader of the crime, you made yourself known to them. You did not recoil from the savage beast approaching to kiss your most holy mouth; rather, you sweetly applied the mouth in which no deceit was found to the mouth that overflowed with malice. Innocent Lamb of God, what have you to do with that wolf? What fellowship is there between you and Belial?

This too was part of your kindness, Lord: you displayed everything that might soften the obstinacy of a wicked heart. Not forgetful of the old friendship, you admonished him, saying: “Friend, for what have you come?” (Matt. 26:38, 39, 41, 50). You also wished to strike the impious man’s heart with horror at his crime when you said: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). And behold, the Philistines are upon you, Samson. They were not deterred from you by the fact that, at the hour of your arrest, you threw them to the ground by your almighty arm—not in self-defence, but so that human presumption might know that it could do nothing against you except insofar as you permitted it.

[Col. 0959A] 8. Who can hear without groaning how, in that hour, murderers laid hands upon you, and, binding your innocent hands, good Jesus, dragged you—the gentlest Lamb, saying nothing—as though a thief, dishonourably to the sacrifice? Yet even then, Christ, you did not cease to pour out your mercy upon your enemies and to distil the honeycomb of your sweetness. For touching the ear cut off by your own disciple, you healed your enemy, and you restrained your defender’s zeal from injuring those who were dragging you away.

Accursed be their rage, because it was obstinate: neither the majesty of the miracle nor the mercy of the benefit could break it. You were presented before the high priests in their council of evildoers; having confessed the truth as was fitting, you were condemned to death as though for blasphemy. Most loving Lord, how many unworthy things did you endure there from your own people! Your desirable face, into which angels desire to look, which filled all the heavens with joy, before which all the rich of the people shall pray, they defiled with the spittle of their polluted lips; they struck it with sacrilegious hands, covered it with a veil in mockery, and slapped you, the Lord of all creation, as though you were a contemptible slave.

9. Still further, they delivered your soul to be swallowed up by the uncircumcised dog. For they brought you bound before Pilate, demanding that you, who knew no sin, be put to death by the punishment of the cross; and they demanded that a murderous man be given to them, preferring a wolf to a lamb and mud to gold. O shameful and miserable exchange [variant: *concambium*, “exchange”]!

Nor was that wicked man unaware that these things were being done to you out of envy; yet he did not withhold his reckless hands from you, but filled your soul with bitterness without cause. He sent you to Herod to be mocked and received you back after you had been mocked; he ordered you to stand naked before your mockers and did not spare your virginal flesh from being torn by most bitter scourges, cruelly adding wound to wound and bruise to bruise. O chosen servant of the Lord my God, what had you committed that deserved such bitterness and such shame? Absolutely nothing. I—I, a lost man—was the cause to you of all your crushing and all your shame. I, Lord, ate sour grapes, and your teeth were set on edge, because you then paid what you had not taken.

In all these things the impiety of the faithless Jews was not satisfied.

10. Finally you were handed over to the hands of uncircumcised soldiers to be consumed by a most shameful death. It was not enough for those sacrilegious men to crucify you unless they first also filled your soul with mockeries. For what does Scripture say of them?

“And they gathered the whole cohort around him. And stripping him of his clothes, they put a purple tunic upon him and wrapped him in a scarlet cloak. And plaiting a crown of thorns, they placed it upon his head, and a reed in his right hand. And, bending the knee, they mocked him, saying: ‘Hail, King of the Jews!’ And they struck him with blows, and spitting upon him, they took the reed and struck his head. And after they had mocked him, they put [Col. 0960A] his own garments upon him, that he might carry his cross to be crucified. And they bring him to Golgotha; and they gave him wine mixed with myrrh and gall to drink, and when he had tasted it, he would not drink. Then they crucified him, and with him two thieves, one on either side, with Jesus in the middle. But Jesus said: ‘Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do.’ Afterwards Jesus, knowing that all things had been accomplished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said: ‘I thirst.’ And one of them ran, took a sponge, filled it with vinegar, put it on a reed, and gave it to him to drink. Therefore, when he had received the vinegar, he said: ‘It is finished.’ And crying with a loud voice, he said: ‘Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit.’ And bowing his head, he gave up the spirit. Then one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came forth [Col. 0960B] for the redemption of our salvation” (Matt. 27; Mark 15; Luke 23; John 19).

11. Awake now, my soul; shake yourself from the dust, and contemplate this memorable man, whom, behold, you gaze upon as though present in the mirror of the Gospel narrative. Attend, my soul: who is this who enters bearing the appearance of a king, yet proceeds filled with the shame of a most despised servant and crowned? Yet even his crown is a torture to him, wounding his beautiful head with a thousand punctures. He is clothed in royal purple, yet is thereby despised rather than honoured. He carries a sceptre in his hand, yet with that very object his venerable head is struck. They worship before him with their knees placed upon the ground, and proclaim him king [Col. 0960C]; then immediately they leap up to spit upon his lovely cheeks, buffet his jaws with their palms, and dishonour his noble neck. See, my soul, how this man is troubled and despised in every way. His back seems bent beneath the burden of the cross, as though he were carrying his own disgrace. Led to the place of punishment, he is given myrrh and gall to drink; he is raised upon the cross and says, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” What kind of man is this, who amid all his afflictions did not even once open his mouth to utter against those accursed dogs a word of complaint, defence, threat, or curse, but at last poured forth over his enemies a word of blessing such as had not been heard since the beginning of time? What have you seen, my soul, gentler or kinder [Col. 0960D] than this man? Yet look more intently still: how greatly worthy he appears of wonder and of tenderest compassion. See him naked and torn by scourges, fastened with iron nails to the shameful cross between thieves, given vinegar to drink upon the cross, and after death wounded in his side by a lance, pouring forth abundant streams of blood from the five wounds of his hands, feet, and side. Let tears flow, my eyes; and melt, my soul, in the fire of compassion over the brokenness of this beloved man, whom you see afflicted by so many sorrows in such great bitterness.

12. And now, indeed, my soul, you have seen his weakness and have felt compassion; now attend to his majesty, and you will marvel. For what does Scripture say? “Now from the sixth [Col. 0961A] hour darkness came over the whole earth until the ninth hour. And the sun was darkened; and the veil of the temple was torn from top to bottom; and the earth was shaken; and the rocks were split; and the tombs were opened; and many bodies of the saints who slept arose” (Matt. XXVII, 45, 51–52; Luke XXIII, 44–45). What kind of man is this, for whom both heaven and earth suffer together, and whose death gives life to the dead? Know, my soul, know: this is the Lord our God, Jesus Christ, your Saviour, the only-begotten Son of God, true God and true man, who alone was found without blemish beneath the sun. And see how he was reckoned among criminals and esteemed, as though a leper, the least of men; and, like an untimely birth cast out from the womb, so he was cast out from the womb of his mother, the unhappy Synagogue. How disfigured has this one, beautiful beyond the children of men, become! “He was wounded for our iniquities, crushed for our crimes” (Isa. LIII, 5), and was made a burnt offering of sweetest fragrance in your sight, Father of eternal glory, so that you might turn away your indignation from us and make us sit with you in heavenly places.

13. Look down, Lord, holy Father, from your sanctuary and from the lofty dwelling-place of heaven, and behold this most holy sacrificial victim, whom our great High Priest, your holy servant, the Lord Jesus, offers to you for the sins of his brethren; and be merciful toward the multitude of our wickedness. Behold: the voice of the blood of our brother Jesus cries to you from the cross. For what is it, [Col. 0961C] Lord, that hangs upon it? It hangs there, I say, because things past are as present before you. Recognize, Father, the tunic of your true son Joseph. Alas! “A most evil beast has devoured him” (Gen. XXXVII, 33), and in its fury it has trampled his garment, staining all its beauty with the remnants of gore. Behold, it has left five lamentable rents in it. See, Lord, the cloak which your innocent child left in the hand of an adulterous generation—that is, of the Egyptian harlot—judging the loss of a garment better than the loss of chastity, and choosing rather, stripped of the cloak of flesh, to descend into the prison of death than to consent for worldly glory to the adulterous voice (Gen. XXXIX, 7, 20): that voice, I say, to which it was said, “All these things I will give you, if you fall down and worship me” (Matt. [Col. 0961D] IV, 9). And this indeed would have occurred had he slept with the adulteress.

14. And now, Lord Father, we know that your Son himself lives and rules throughout all the land of Egypt and in every place of your dominion. For, brought out from the prison of death and hell into your rule, and shorn into the crown of immortality, he flourished anew in the beauty of immortality, the garment of flesh having been changed; and you received him with glory. For he subjected Pharaoh’s dominion to himself and, in noble triumph, penetrated the heavens by his own power. And behold, crowned with glory and honour, he stands at the right hand of your majesty before your face for us. For he is our flesh and our brother. Look, Lord, upon the face of your Christ, who became obedient to you unto death; and let his scars never depart from your sight [Col. 0962A], so that you may remember how great a satisfaction you received from him for our sins. Would that, Lord, you weighed in the balance the sins by which we deserved wrath, and the affliction which your innocent Son endured for us. Surely, Lord, this latter would appear the weightier and more deserving reason for you to pour out your mercy upon us than the former was for you to restrain your mercies in anger on account of our sins. Let every tongue give thanks to you, Lord Father, for the superabundance of your goodness: you did not spare the only Son of your heart, but delivered him up to death for us all, that we might have him as a faithful advocate before you in heaven.

15. And to you, Lord Jesus, most mighty zealot, what thanks shall I return? What recompense shall I, a human being, dust and ashes, and a worthless creature, worthily render in return? What ought you to have done for my salvation that you did not do? From the sole of your foot to the crown of your head, you immersed your whole self in the waters of suffering, that you might draw me entirely out of them; and they entered even unto your soul. Indeed, you gave up your soul to death, so that you might restore to me mine, which was lost. And behold, you have bound me by a double debt. For I am your debtor both for what you gave and for what you lost on my account. For that soul which you gave me twice—once in creation and once in redemption—I have nothing that I could more justly give back to you than that very soul. But for your precious soul, so afflicted, I cannot discover what could worthily be repaid by a human being. For [Col. 0962C], even if I could give in return heaven, earth, and all their adornment, surely I could not thereby in any way attain the measure of the debt. But that I should render to you, Lord, both what I owe and what lies within my power, is your gift. You must be loved by me with all my heart, all my soul, and all my strength; and I must follow your footsteps, you who deigned to die for me. And how will this come to pass in me except through you? Let my soul cling close after you, for all its strength depends upon you. And now, Lord my redeemer, I worship you as the true God; in you I trust, in you I hope, and with such desires as I can I sigh toward you. Help my imperfection. Before the glorious emblems of your passion, by which you accomplished my salvation, I bow my whole self. [Col. 0962D] In your name, Christ, I worship the royal standard of your victorious cross. I humbly worship and glorify, Christ, your crown of thorns, your nails reddened with blood, the lance plunged into your sacred side, your wounds, your blood, your death, your burial, and your glorious and victorious resurrection and glorification. For in all these things the fragrance of life breathes upon me. By their life-giving fragrance, Lord, raise my spirit from the death of sin; by their power guard me from Satan’s wiles, and strengthen me, so that the yoke of your commandments may become sweet to me, and the burden of the cross which you command me to carry after you may be light and bearable upon the shoulders of my soul. For what is my strength, that I should endure with unconquered spirit the manifold pressures of the world according to your command? Are my feet like those of deer, that I may follow the swift runner through the thorns and rugged places of sufferings? [Col. 0963A]

16. But hear my voice, and lay upon your servant that sweet cross which is the tree of life to those who lay hold of it, so that I too may run eagerly in spirit. I shall tirelessly carry after you the cross that comes from enemies. Lay upon my shoulders, I say, that most divine cross, whose breadth is charity, whose length is eternity, whose height is omnipotence, and whose depth is unfathomable wisdom. Fasten my hands and feet to it, and conform your servant wholly to your passion, Lord. Grant, I beseech you, that I may refrain from the works of the flesh which you hate, do the righteousness which you have loved [Col. 0963B], and seek your glory in both; and I reckon that my left hand is fixed upon that lofty cross by the nail of temperance, and my right by the nail of justice. Grant that my mind may meditate continually upon your law, cast all my thought upon you, and fasten my right foot to that same tree of life with the nail of prudence. Grant that the unhappy prosperity of fleeting [variant: present] life may neither weaken sensuality, the handmaid of my spirit, nor happy adversity disturb it from the rewards of everlasting life; and so too my left foot shall be held upon the cross by the nail of fortitude.

17. Moreover, so that some likeness of the thorns of your head may appear in me, grant, I beseech you, to my mind the compunction of saving repentance, compassion for another’s misery, and the spur of zeal emulating what is right [Col. 0963C] before you; and let me turn to you in my distress while the threefold thorn is driven in. I desire that you should also offer to my mouth a sponge upon a reed, and apply to my taste the bitterness of vinegar. I desire that through your Scriptures you should enable my reason to taste and see how this flourishing world is empty like a sponge, and all its desire more bitter than vinegar. So let it be in me, Father, that this golden cup of Babylon which intoxicates all the earth may neither seduce me by its empty splendour nor intoxicate me with false sweetness, as it does those who think darkness light and light darkness, bitter sweet and sweet bitter. Wine mingled with myrrh and gall is suspect to me because you refused to drink it; perhaps because it signified the excessive bitterness of the envy and wickedness of those who crucified you. Conform your servant also to your life-giving death, bringing it about in me that I may indeed die to sin according to the flesh, but live [Col. 0963D] to righteousness according to the spirit.

18. And so that I may glory in bearing the complete image of the Crucified One, imprint upon me also a likeness of that which, after your death, the insatiable malice of the impious Jews inflicted upon you. Let your living and effective word wound my heart, more piercing than every sharpest lance, reaching even to the division of my soul; and let it bring forth from it, as from my right side, in place of blood and [Col. 0964A] water, love for you, Lord, and for my brethren. Finally, wrap my spirit in the clean linen cloth of the first robe, in which I may rest, going out and coming in to the place of the wondrous tabernacle; and hide me until your wrath has passed by. Then, on the third day after the day of labour, after the day of punishment, on the morning of the first Sabbath, raise me, unworthy though I am, forever among your children, that in my flesh I may see your brightness and be filled with the joy of your countenance. O my Saviour and my God, let the time come—let it come, I pray—when I may at last behold with unveiled eyes what I now believe; grasp what I now hope for and greet from afar; embrace and kiss with the arms of my soul what I now desire according to my strength; and be wholly swallowed up in the abyss of your love, O my Saviour and my God!

[Col. 0964B] But meanwhile, my soul, bless your Saviour and magnify his name, which is holy and full of delights most holy. O how good, how sweet you are, Lord Jesus, to the soul that seeks you! Jesus, redeemer of captives, saviour of the lost, hope of exiles, strength of those who labour, expansiveness for the anxious spirit, sweet consolation and gentle refreshment to the tearful soul running after you in sweat; crown of those who triumph, sole reward and joy of all the citizens above; most abundant fountain of every grace; illustrious offspring of the highest God! Highest God, all things which are above in heaven and below upon earth bless you, because you are great and your name is great. O unfading beauty of the most high God, and most pure brightness of eternal light [Col. 0964C], life giving life to every living thing, light illuminating every light and preserving in perpetual splendour the thousand thousands of lights shining before the throne of your divinity from primeval dawn! O eternal and unceasing, bright and sweet outpouring of the fountain hidden from the eyes of all mortals: its wave without origin, its depth without bottom, its height without limit, its breadth incapable of being bounded or explored, its purity incapable of disturbance! The heart of God Most High brought you forth from its impenetrable abyss: life from life, light from light, God from God, the eternal from the eternal, the immeasurable from the immeasurable, and in all things equal to himself. And from your fullness we have all received.

[Note: From [Col. 0963D] to the end, it differs in Anselm.]

[Col. 0964D] 20. For you, most generous fountain of every good, send forth from your treasures the precious river of sevenfold grace, by whose sweet delight you deign to soften the saltiness of this sea of ours, that is, our weakness: a river of the oil of gladness, a river of purest wine, a torrent of fiery vigour. The Paraclete Spirit, from you and from the Father, equal to both, is poured over the whole world, filling all things and containing all things: Spirit from you, Spirit from the Father, one from both, uniting both, as the indivisible bond of both, the unifying glue, the indissoluble embrace, and the peace surpassing all understanding. This is your torrent of delight, Lord, by which you continually give drink to that lovely and glorious city, Jerusalem [Col. 0965A] above, and make it surge in joyful intoxication, so that those radiant and flaming instruments may sing to you an unceasing hymn with the voice of exultation and the sound of feasting. And the thirsty throats of your exiled people continually await from you, Lord, refreshment from its desirable drops. Permit, Father, that the little dogs may drink from the drops falling from their masters’ table. Drop down, heavens, from above; and let the clouds rain down that righteous one, Lord, whom you have made to overflow. With that fiery sprinkling, we beseech you, cleanse, renew, enlighten, inflame, gladden, and strengthen the illustrious firstfruits of your people, the distinguished solemnity of ours [Col. 0966A]; and grant one heart to those who believe in you, that they may be one, think one thing, seek one thing with one accord, so that they may grasp, see, and bless you, the God of gods, in Zion. To the undivided Trinity be glory, thanksgiving, honour, and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0965]

## MONDAY OF EASTER. SERMON On the Two Disciples Going to Emmaus. (G)

[Col. 0965B] 657 “Two of Jesus’ disciples were going to a village named Emmaus, sixty stadia from Jerusalem. And they spoke with one another about all the things that had happened. And the rest” (Luke XXIV, 13–35).

1. Return, my soul, to your rest, because Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep. By the remembrance of such sweetness, soften the sorrows of your tears, that you may offer to the risen one, together with roasted fish, a honeycomb, and that the sweetness of the paschal Lamb may temper the bitterness of wild lettuces. Choose whether you would rather see Jesus with Mary Magdalene under the appearance of a gardener, or with the two disciples in the garb of a traveller. For either vision and conversation is joy and sweetness to a faithful conscience. The account of the two fellow disciples seems sweeter in flavour. For this reading [Col. 0965C] is honey in the mouth and jubilation in the heart, the ecstasy of a devout mind. Its sweetness surpasses all eloquence, absorbs the whole conscience, and transforms it into the image of heavenly jubilation and the newness of celestial delights. The wondrous sweetness considered in this reading intoxicates the very marrow of the soul. For from each phrase a certain fire seems to burst forth, hidden and enclosed in the bosom, consuming every corner of the loving conscience in its bones. If it sparkles outwardly, it seems to shine more brilliantly than the sun’s ray. “Two were going.” The historical text does not state the reason for this journey; but I judge that it was by divine providence that those who were so desolate over the Lord’s death might receive consolation on the road they travelled [Col. 0965D] from the sight of him, most sweet. And perhaps for this reason the two walked together: that they might soften their sorrows by mutual conversation and recall despairing hearts to the refreshment of hope. Thus they are said to set out for Emmaus, which is interpreted “desire of counsel.” For they desired to relieve the bitterness of their wavering by salutary counsel.

2. But let us endeavour, as it were, to press honey from the comb and set flame-breathing gems in gleaming gold, seeking whether something still sweeter lies hidden in so sweet a history. I think that these two may be called Prayer and [Col. 0966B] Meditation, joined to one another by a necessary union. Meditation is enlightened through prayer, and prayer is set ablaze in meditation. Therefore, whenever we are absorbed in contemplation of the Lord’s passion, the recollection of so great a marvel moves us to compunction in prayer. Meditation chews over the bruises of the wounds, the piercings of the nails, the lance and vinegar, the persecutors’ savagery, the Apostles’ flight, the most shameful death, and the burial of the body. Prayer pours forth sighs, distils the spices of pious devotion, and wholly dissolves into lamentation. “And it came to pass, while they conversed and questioned together, that Jesus himself, drawing near, went with them. But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him.” Jesus draws near to those engaged in such conversation. What is Jesus but life and salvation? For in such discourse are the life and salvation of the soul; and Jesus is said to have drawn near to them because “the Lord is near to those who are troubled in heart” (Ps. XXXIII, 19). But [Col. 0966C] their eyes were held so that they could not recognize him, because even if they are righteous and wise, and their works are in God’s hand, “man nevertheless does not know whether he is worthy of hatred or love” (Eccl. IX, 1). “If I say,” says Job, “My bed will comfort me, and I shall be relieved by speaking with myself on my couch, you will terrify me through dreams and shake me with horror by visions” (Job XIII, 14). The bed signifies peaceful meditation, and the couch on which one is relieved while conversing signifies the power of prayer, because in these two, troubled in heart, the repose of true consolation is found. But when we seek inward refreshment beneath their silvered wings [Col. 0966D], and the images arise in our minds of how strict the Judge’s sentences will be at the last judgment, we find sorrow where we sought consolation.

3. Yet in the statement that Jesus, drawing near, went with them, nothing could be signified more delightfully. For in that drawing near is signified that whisper of a gentle breeze which Eliphaz boasts of having heard while the rest slept (Job IV, 13–16), by which Scripture also tells us that the Lord came to Elijah as he stood at the entrance of the cave: for he was seen to pass by not in the earthquake, not in the fire, not in the wind, but in the whisper of a gentle breeze (III Kings XIX, 9–13). This is that sweetest ray of contemplation by which the soul is lifted by a lock of the head. When meditation burns and prayer sparkles, a certain jubilation is born in the heart: namely, a honey-sweet laughter of the heart, which no one knows except one who experiences it; nor even that person truly knows it, because it passes so quickly. A happy hour, but a brief stay, for “there was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. VIII, 1). Those who have experienced it know what I say, having learned these things by experience of inward sweetness: when the ardour of meditation is mingled with the fervour of prayer, that ray of contemplation bursts forth from their midst like the appearance of electrum—that is, from the midst of fire—and sparks like glowing bronze [Col. 0967B], namely, the sighs of a jubilant conscience.

4. “But their eyes were held, so that they did not recognize him.” Conscious of its weakness, the human conscience trembles before the ineffable glory of such great sweetness. Hence Elijah covered his face, Eliphaz was wholly terrified, and Moses did not dare to look upon the Lord (Exod. III, 6). “And if he comes to me,” says Job, “I shall not see him” (Job IX, 11). Their eyes were held. O, if they knew the Lord, how greatly they would rejoice! How greatly we ourselves would rejoice if we saw him more closely in his own form! Who would not approach—indeed, run—and grasp his feet? But Joseph still speaks to his brothers through an interpreter; he still conceals from us his most sweet vision. For what else could it be? We are mortal, we dwell in exile, and because of the abundance of glory we cannot receive that joyful blessedness of perfect vision [Col. 0967C]. For who could breathe amid those joys of overflowing jubilation which shall be given in the homeland, when even that drop of sweetness which he offers us on the way, in this land foreign to our true homeland, intoxicates the whole mind and constricts the entire breadth of the heart with new delights? Therefore their eyes were held because the Lord was in a traveller’s garb. And when we daily perceive him at the altar under the appearances of bread and wine, he dwells with us in a traveller’s garb. May we not understand by the eyes love and desire? For we love God and neighbour; we desire the King and the kingdom. But because, as blessed Gregory says, while we are in this body it is unknown to us how much we love God and neighbour, and when, departing from this exile, we shall attain the kingdom and see God, we suffer blindness of the eyes. Hence it is said in Ezekiel that the gate and chamber have a roof (Ezek. XL, 13).

5. Nor should we pass over the fact that, conversing together, they travel to the village of Emmaus, sixty stadia from Jerusalem. Sweet discourse and happy conversation, when prayer treats of meditation. For honey and milk are on their tongue. Their lips are like a scarlet ribbon, while the one invites to contempt of the world and the other urges to love of God. Thus they are said to set out for Emmaus, which is interpreted “desire of counsel.” “Will two walk together unless they have agreed?” [Col. 0968A] O blessed meeting, in which prayer and meditation whisper to one another. Certainly they desire to go to the village Emmaus, which is sixty stadia from Jerusalem. The number sixty consists of ten and six, which six times ten, or ten times six, make sixty. A stadium is a place in which one runs. The number ten signifies the Decalogue, in which the sequence of the ten commandments is contained. 659 In the number six, however, are figured renunciation of the world and conversion of conduct; the abandonment of one’s own will and the unfeigned rejection of pretence; the guarding of the heart and watchfulness in speech. One must run in these stadia, so that when the Lord has enlarged our heart, we may run in the way of his commandments and afterwards roll onward upon the way. And on these paths the Lord, drawing near, will come to us, as is written of Wisdom: “She anticipates those who desire her; she shows herself cheerfully to them in the ways, and reveals herself to them in every forethought” (Wis. VI, 14, 17). And he said to them:

6. “What are these words that you exchange with one another as you walk, and why are you sad?” This question supplies the fuel of love and is like oil cast upon a flame. For while the traveller asks what sad matters they discuss together, the one whom they had loved so much and still love is recalled to mind; sweet sorrow is increased, and love, half dead, breaks forth from its little spark into a furnace and rages more violently in their hearts. “What are these words that you exchange,” and so forth. Do you suppose that in the traveller’s address they felt no sweetness of divine love? Rather, the love of Christ wholly revived and blossomed anew in their marrow. “What are these words that you exchange,” and so forth. God, O God, how many jubilations these sorrows engendered, how sweet the sweetnesses when chewed over, and how sweet the sighs that run through the heart! Good Jesus, with what delightful whisper you console those whom you see saddened by your absence! How willingly you stand with those who pray and attend those who sigh, looking through the windows, peering through the lattice! How pleasantly you hide behind our wall, in order to hear the voices of those who pray, that the sorrows of those who love may become sweet to you, and that you may smile at the sufferings of the innocent!

7. And one of them, whose name was Cleophas, answered and said to him: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have you not known [Col. 0968D] the things that have happened there in these days?” Cleophas, which is interpreted “rebuking with the mouth,” seems to represent prayer, which sets judgment before God and fills its mouth with rebukes: now accusing the heart’s hardness, now its inconstancy; now constricted by the chill of sloth, now dissolved in foolish joy. “Are you the only stranger?” The sorrow of compunction is accustomed to affect loving hearts more familiarly when they see so many especially despise such pursuits and, growing lukewarm in their desire for the heavenly homeland, retain the appearance of piety only in outward habit. Thus Cleophas answers whenever, grieving inwardly over the ruin of such people, they pour out complaints like these in prayer: “Lord, you were alone in the time of the passion, when Peter denied you, when the disciple whom you loved fled, forgetful of the privilege of your love, and when the rest also fled. But alas, alas! In this present time of passion we see religious persons not only failing to share your sufferings through compassion, or to flee, or to deny you through the disturbance of some sudden temptation; rather, ‘their iniquity proceeds as if from fat; they have passed into the desires of their heart.’ For adding iniquity to iniquity, they are not ashamed to add to the pain of your wounds, though with the holy women they ought to have soothed them with the spices of pious devotion. ‘Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem?’ All your friends have abandoned you; those who knew you have become far from you; they have made you an abomination to themselves. All seek their own interests and love themselves; they have made a homeland out of exile; by their deeds they deny that they are strangers and sojourners on earth. [Col. 0969B] ‘Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem?’ Even we, who are thought by the privilege of a more eminent profession to be more expressly conformed to the humility of your pilgrimage, are placed in darkness like the dead of old. Yet we are shrewder in enlarging possessions, more glorious in erecting buildings, and more cunning in gathering money. Few can be found who faithfully walk the paths of truth. ‘Are you the only stranger?’ Behemoth no longer wonders if the river is swallowed up (Job XL, 18), because the greater part of the Jordan flows into his mouth; he has cast down from their strength and from the stars, has strewn gold for himself like mud, and beneath him are the rays of the sun.”

8. “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem”—that is, in the Church militant for God, which plainly does not yet possess peace—“and have you not known the things that have happened there in these [Col. 0969C] days?” In these days you shed your blood for the salvation of humankind, endured so many pains and reproaches, and at last the punishment of the cross. And although in these days you suffered such things for the world and promised, if you were lifted up from the earth, to draw all things to yourself, behold, you have been lifted above the heavens. Indeed, why do you not deliver those who are led to death? Why do you not return from Bashan? Why do you not draw all? Why do you choose so few from among many, as though forgetful of your passion? “Have you not known the things that have happened in Jerusalem in these days?” In Jerusalem in these days, you, that lofty and wondrous one, were killed—you to whom Moses and Elijah spoke in the most beautiful vision of your transfiguration [Col. 0969D] (Matt. XVII, 3). Truly, Lord, you went beyond all measure: for although you are the brightness of the Father’s glory and the image of his substance, although you are the Lord of majesty, yet while the elements trembled, the lights of heaven were darkened, and the angels stood astonished, you deigned to endure the torment of a most abject passion. Truly it was an excess, when you gave your cheeks to those who struck you, when you did not turn your face away from those who rebuked and spat upon you (Isa. L, 6), when you were numbered among the wicked (Isa. LIII, 12). “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem?” Why do you not draw us after you, that we may run in the fragrance of your ointments? Why do you give your honour to strangers, when for us you consumed your flesh and body? Why do you not remember the throne of your glory, on which you judged the prince of this world? Why do you not pour out upon us the spirit [Col. 0970A] of grace and prayer, so that, confessing not only with the tongue but also in deed and truth that we are strangers and pilgrims upon earth, we may abstain from fleshly desires and be drawn to you in the cords of Adam, in the bonds of charity?

9. While Cleophas says these things in tribulation of spirit and bitterness of mind, how greatly, do you think, do these words fill the conscience of the questioner? To them he said, “What things?” It is not the question of one ignorant, but of one encouraging them, a certain reciprocal stirring of grief. And they said: “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people; and how our chief priests and rulers delivered him up to condemnation of death and crucified him.” At first Cleophas alone is recorded as answering. [Col. 0970B] Now both he and the one whose name is not given in the history answer. Since he is unnamed, he seems to represent meditation, which we are accustomed at times to call thought and at times contemplation, as though by its proper name. But according to blessed Gregory, some thought this man was Luke. Luke, whom the Apostle calls a physician (Col. IV, 14), and whose name is interpreted “Rising” or “Lifting Up,” by the meaning of his name presents an image of meditation, which is medicine for the afflicted spirit and ailing conscience. Like the gecko, it supports itself on its hands so as to remain in royal palaces (Prov. XXX, 28); rising from low things by choosing what is suspended above, it abandons transitory things and lifts itself to what is heavenly. Meditation is therefore joined to prayer, so that from the response of them both the balm of a sweeter melody may breathe fuller delights into the traveller’s ears.

10. “Concerning Jesus,” they say, “of Nazareth.” “His name is poured-out oil.” Poured-out oil, I say: ointment of spices, jubilation of hearts, Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews. But let the alabaster vessel be broken; let the south wind blow through the garden of spices; let myrrh give forth its fragrance; let streams of balsam flow. Let the Crucified One be in our memory; let the Crucified One’s injury be rehearsed; let the Crucified One’s reproaches be chewed over; and let charity be unwearying. Let all that is within us speak of Jesus of Nazareth, who washed us from our sins in his blood, so that we may be mighty in deed and word. Some are mighty [Col. 0970D] in deed but not in word; others in word but not in deed; some are mighty in both. One who is vigorous in bodily exercise does not neglect to do the good which he has strength to do. Patient in tribulation and rejoicing in the labour of obedience, he may be called mighty in deed. But if constancy in prayer gives him little delight, if he is not devout in vigils through pious concern, or perhaps lacks the grace of preaching, he is mighty in deed but not in word. You may see someone frequently devout in prayer, whose eyes are “pools in Heshbon” (Song VII, 4) because of the multitude of tears, but who refuses to bear the yoke of obedience and thinks he offers his vow by offering a victim with an ear cut off. In prayer he laments his pride, but when the hour of compunction has passed, he is as proud [Col. 0971A] as before. Or, if he is frivolous in conduct, after the devotion of his prayer he falls back into the same frivolity; his bones are filled with the vices of his youth, so that he is never mature in his conduct, though for a short time in prayer he is devout. “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau” (Gen. XXVII, 22). Such persons seem mighty in word but not in deed. Mighty in deed and word are those who have decency in conduct, strength in works, knowledge in speech, devotion in constancy of prayer, seriousness in behaviour, and perseverance in love. For devout prayer is the support of pious activity, and the practice of devout prayer provides the foundation of good works. This is the saving compunction in its fullness which the breadth of conscience commends. Hence, when the Lord gave Solomon wisdom and riches, he also gave him breadth of heart (III Kings IV, 5–14), because wisdom is nothing and riches are nothing if the river of charity, which cannot be crossed, does not overflow in the heart. Nor does the Lord spare those powerful words, composed for supplication.

11. If you are thus powerful in deed and word, be so before God and before all the people. Let purity of intention commend you before God, and usefulness of work before the people, so that the loins of your mind may be girded and a lamp burn in your hands. And fittingly, “before all the people,” because charity knows no corner, does not love what is its own, and desires to serve the advantage of every individual. Hence the Apostle commends himself to every human conscience [Col. 0971C], “providing things good, not only before God, but also before all men” (II Cor. VIII, 21), so that he may be acceptable both to God and to all the people.

But let no one dare compare himself with the most blessed Apostle. For as far as the east is from the west, so far were his ways from our ways, and his paths exalted above our paths: because, as Isaiah says, “We have all become unclean; all our righteousnesses are like the cloth of a menstruous woman” (Isa. LXIV, 6). We are not powerful in deeds; and we do not know what we ought to pray for (Rom. VIII, 26). He alone, “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV, 3), was by singular privilege a prophet powerful in deed and word, who powerfully accomplished our salvation [Col. 0971D] in the midst of the earth. He was full of power in word when he created all things; when “he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. CXLVIII, 5). He was mighty in deed when he restored humankind and, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, “to accomplish his work, his strange work,” he made his work an alien work (Isa. XXVIII, 21).

Truly it was an alien work, if you consider how the chief priests handed him over and crucified him. “Lord, I heard thy report, and was afraid” (Hab. III, 2): I considered thy works, thy ways, and was terrified. They mocked you with mockery; they gnashed their teeth against you; they rejoiced and assembled against you; the chief priests and rulers handed you over. Those who ought to have guided the flock in the way of salvation became a snare and a ruin unto the precipice of damnation. [Col. 0972A] From them the flame of envy burst forth, because, as is read in Job, “The fire of God fell from heaven and consumed the sheep and the servants whom it touched” (Job I, 16).

12. Therefore, we who seek the Crucified One should consider the mystery of the cross. It is the balance of Christ’s body, which he desired who said: “Would that my sins, by which I have deserved wrath, and the calamity which I suffer, might be weighed in a balance.” The cross became the balance of Christ’s body, which is the Church. For while he himself was crucified, the sins we committed and the calamity we incurred were hung with him. He was innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and his manner of life was higher than the heavens; for “he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” And because one so great and such as he deigned to suffer such unworthy things [Col. 0972B] on the cross, calamity began to outweigh, and crimes to be made lighter.

Yet while he still stood raised upon the cross, the balance seemed to waver, nor was it fully known to which side it ought to fall, until, bowing his head, he gave up the spirit, so that calamity might fall by outweighing and appear heavier “than the sand of the sea” (Job VI, 2–3). The nations “were reckoned as the small weight of a balance.” 662 For they fell in the balance, because the adverse parties lost the bond of our condemnation. Moab was crushed under its lord; he spread out his hands over him as a swimmer spreads them to swim, lest he sink into the deep. And so that he might lift us up on high, he spread out his wings, took us up, and carried us upon his shoulders, like an eagle stirring its young to fly (Deut. XXXII, 11). Thus ascending [Col. 0972C] above all heavens, he sent fire from on high into our bones, so that we might set our minds on things above and our citizenship might be in heaven. He was powerful before God and all the people, because he became the Angel speaking for us and, becoming an intercessor, reconciled the human race to the Father; he alone was able to rebuke both parties and to lay his hand upon them both.

13. And how the chief priests and rulers crucified him. By the persuasion of the priests, the people cried out that Barabbas should be released and Christ crucified; and Pilate adjudged it to be done. They crucified him with tongues, not hands. Hence David says that “they sharpened their tongues like a sword” (Ps. CXXXIX, 4). In this they are perhaps less blameworthy than the new crucifiers [Col. 0972D] who summon death upon him by hands and words; they kill the Immortal One and crucify him who cannot be crucified. It is shameful even to speak of what they do in secret, or even openly. I fear to set my mouth in heaven—indeed, not to say in filth—and to kill Saul, bent down to relieve himself; it is enough if I cut off the hem of his cloak (I Kings XXIV, 4–5) with Jeremiah’s sword, when the Lord says through Malachi: “You pierce me, namely the whole nation” (Mal. III, 8–9).

Jeremiah shows how the chief priests and rulers crucify him more cruelly. “I will go,” he says, “to the great men and speak to them; for they know the way of the Lord and the judgment of their God. And behold, these have all together broken the yoke and burst the bonds” (Jer. V, 5); and “from prophet even unto priest, all deal deceitfully” [Col. 0973A] (Jer. VI, 13). Behold how the chief priests and rulers crucified him.

14. “But we hoped that he would redeem Israel,” which means “the man who sees God.” By this are signified the learned and religious, who more particularly than others ought to see God through understanding and affection. Hence we have no small cause for sorrow, because even the learned and those who seem religious are compared to beasts and have become more unclean than they. For they not only crucify God with the thorns of their own sins, but have become a proverb and an example to others. “But we hoped that he would redeem Israel.”

It would not be a cause for grief, nor a thing so astounding, if the people who do not know the law alone fell into error, because they could be raised up [Col. 0973B] by the prudence of the learned and religious, if these themselves had not been foremost in bringing about ruin. “But we hoped that he would redeem Israel.” For if Scripture calls a king an apostate and rulers impious, if it supplants great men and leads priests away without glory, perhaps they are not learned and do not know the law of the Lord; they are children of distrust, and we are not astonished at them. But we are amazed at the learned and at those who put on the appearance of religion, who have tasted the good word of God, the heavenly gift, and the powers of the age to come; and behold, they have become the fat cows of Samaria, autumnal trees, uprooted, twice dead—those who ought to have taught the way of life have become enemies at the head. “But we hoped that he would redeem Israel.”

[Col. 0973C] 15. “And now, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened.” The first day, on which Christ was crucified, signifies the time of persecutors and heretics, who afflicted the primitive Church, which is his body, with the harshness of torments. The second day, on which he was buried, signifies the time of hypocrites, who regard Christ as though buried in the earth, yearning after earthly advantages and honors, and expecting no glory for their labors except that of earthly happiness. “Besides all this, today is the third day”: on it we ought to consider another and graver danger, namely false brethren.

And on this third day Christ ought to have risen, because we supposed that in these days the power of true faith would be spread everywhere and that the rays of charity would be extended through religious places, so that [Col. 0973D] after the Orions and Hyades the inner regions of the south wind might appear. But because almost all have turned aside and still crucify Christ in their iniquities, 663 we grieve, besides all this, because today is the third day since all these things happened.

16. “But certain women of our company terrified us, who were at the tomb before dawn; and, not finding his body, came saying that they had also seen a vision of angels, who say that he lives.” The devout women are thoughts. By the tomb may be understood the cloister of religious persons, in which we are buried with Christ through mortification of temporal delights and through the bond of holy profession. Then the women go to the tomb to seek [Col. 0974A] the Lord, when we consider whether at least in cloisters there may be a religious person seeking and loving God. They came before dawn and found his body. O how sweet it is to rise before dawn to seek the beloved! He is sweet to the one who seeks him. “Upon my bed I sought by nights him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find him” (Song III, 1). It remains, therefore, that I should go to the tomb—that is, to the cloister of religious persons, to the vigils of cloistered people—because there I shall find the beloved, though not according to the body. For “even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (II Cor. V, 16).

These watchmen guard the city; they are the angels whose vision the women claim to have seen, who say that he lives and, through the fervor of true love, show [Col. 0974B] Christ dwelling in their hearts. These are the watchmen observing the watches of the Lord at all times. They keep watch at the door of the tabernacle; they are the Orions and Hyades and the inner regions of the south wind. How delightful it is to share in their vigils! They rise by night at the beginning of their watches, to pour out their heart before the Lord, and their prayer is before the Most High. There, among young women playing tambourines, princes are joined with those who sing psalms; there, in ecstasy of mind, is the young Benjamin (Ps. LXVII, 26, 28); there the heavenly harmony resounds together. There are the Seraphim crying, “Holy, holy, holy,” and the Cherubim looking toward the mercy-seat with faces turned toward one another. There all the sons of God shout for joy; the morning stars praise the Lord [Col. 0974C]. They are truly like angels through their pursuit of an angelic manner of life.

To them has been entrusted the guarding of the tomb: that is, the regular observances of the cloister. Christ does not abandon this tomb, he who promised that he would be with us until the consummation of the age; and then we shall be with him when he receives us to himself. The women say that they did not find him, but saw a vision of angels who say that he lives, whenever we turn over in our thoughts the fact that, although those who sing the praise of the Lord day by day and by night on earth, as the angels do in heaven, are truly like angels, they nevertheless do not yet possess the glory of eternal blessedness brought to perfection in supreme holiness. “A little while after I had passed by them, I found him whom my soul loves” [Col. 0974D] (Song III, 4).

But what does it mean when it says, “They terrified us”? It is not terror that produces horror, but that which brings forth a new exultation or wonder in the heart. For while we consider how abundant are the happy delights in the cloister, our heart is astonished at these things and is moved from its place with a certain sweet reverence.

17. “And some of our company went to the tomb and found it so, as the women had said; but him they did not find.” “Some of our company went.” These are the affections of a religious mind, which find all things as the women do, yet do not return, as is said of the women. For when we merely treat in our hearts with thoughts concerning the love of religion, the women go to the tomb and return. [Col. 0975A] But when the affections of the mind are turned toward desires of conversion, no longer merely women, but some of our company go to the tomb; they do not return, and yet do not find him.

We know this by experience: when, in the fervor of a novice, we come to conversion, we suppose that we shall find Jesus here, because we hope to attain the joys of perfect tranquillity and holiness. But when with the passage of time we experience the miseries of human frailty, then we recognize that we have not found the Lord; nevertheless, we behold a vision of angels—that is, the examples of fervent monks.

18. And he himself said to them: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe 664 all that the Prophets have spoken! Ought not Christ to have suffered these things and so to enter into his glory?” These words seem to pour forth the tenderness of love and, like new wine bursting fresh wineskins, to proceed from the marrow of one who loves. The Lord gave his voice a voice of power, so that his words might be like a hammer breaking the rock and like fire, according to Jeremiah’s testimony (Jer. XXIII, 29). His words are like fire and a hammer: that from the fire there may rise a little column of smoke from spices and the powder of the perfumer, and that the hammer may break.

It is pleasant to incline the eyes of the mind a little toward the sweetness of the story. While he interprets the Scriptures, while he expounds Moses and the Prophets, a wonderful sweetness proceeding from his mouth refreshes minds struck down by sorrow and weariness. Inestimable elegance of speech flowed from the lips of Jesus [Col. 0975C], sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; his eloquence became sweeter than all spices. Surely he knew the order of heaven and set forth its reason upon earth. Their hearts, filled with mourning, rejoice as their grief is changed into gladness. Now the Lord’s resurrection shines forth in their consciences. They begin to rejoice more at his rising than they had grieved at his crucifixion.

Hence they drew near to the village to which they were going, because the desire of the purpose they sought had begun to be fulfilled. And he pretended to be going farther, so that, when he seemed willing to leave them, they might burn more wonderfully with the fire of love by which they had begun sweetly to burn. What disposition of mind do you suppose they then had when he pretended to go farther? Perhaps, I think, they addressed him with such complaints: “Do not depart, most sweet one; do not leave us. Let your voice still sound in our ears concerning Jesus of Nazareth. [Col. 0975D] Speak, we beseech you, of the joy of the resurrection. Stay with us, for it is toward evening and the day is now declining; but we shall keep the watches of the night. The day is not sufficient for the ear to be satisfied with hearing of most sweet Jesus.” And they constrained him, because the force of love could not restrain itself.

9. Let us now return to the delights of mortality. “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the Prophets have spoken! Ought not Christ to have suffered these things and so to enter into his glory?” The time has been fulfilled of which the Lord said in the Gospel: “Where two or three are gathered together in my name, there am I in the midst of them” (Matt. XVIII, 20). Two are gathered in his name, namely Prayer and Meditation, so that, like the turtledove [Col. 0976A] and the dove, they may softly murmur sweet complaints in the cleft of the rock, in the hollow of the wall, grieving over the Lord’s passion.

But these whisperings, these devout sighs, are so pleasing in the eyes of him who searches hearts and reins that he cannot long conceal the abundance of his sweetness which he has hidden for those who fear and love him. Rather, by hidden inspiration and by the reading of sacred Scripture, he is accustomed frequently to change such sorrow into jubilation. “O foolish and slow of heart to believe!” As I consider the sweetness of this rebuke, I would rather weep than say anything, because a balm of wondrous fragrance breathes through the little garden-bed of my mind. I desire to reason with God—not indeed as an equal, but by setting forth the frailty of human conscience.

Lord, [Col. 0976B] whenever we chew over in our hearts the bitterness of your passion, we are terrified for ourselves, because “you gave a sign to those who fear you, that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Ps. LIX, 6). For if you passed from this world to the Father amid such torments, what will become of us sinners? “If these things are done in the green wood, what shall be done in the dry?” (Luke XXIII, 31 [printed: 23].) While we pour out such complaints in prayer, true and supreme charity sweetly consoles us by rebuking us, through the authority of the Scriptures or through hidden inspiration: “Why are you so sorrowful over my passion? Do not fear, little flock; I suffered so that you might rejoice. I have stored up for you treasures of exultation, because parents ought to lay up treasures for their children. For I have worked all your works for you; [Col. 0976C] I rose again so that you might rejoice. I tell you: why do you not believe?”

20. “Beginning with Moses and the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” Blessed are those who know by the taste of happy experience how sweetly and wonderfully the Lord deigns to reveal the Scriptures in prayer and meditation. Indeed, he is the Lord of all knowledge and can distribute it as he wills. “Beginning 665 with Moses and the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.” He does this when he illuminates our hearts with rays of charity. The person who keeps charity in conduct possesses both what is hidden and what is manifest in the divine sayings. “On love alone hang Moses and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 40).

Then we draw near to the village [Col. 0976D] toward which we are tending, because through the infusion of charity we obtain the desired purpose of life. “But he pretended to be going farther.” “I said, ‘I shall become wise’; and wisdom itself withdrew far from me!” (Eccles. VII, 24). The ways of the Lord seem difficult to the beginner, but one runs in them when the heart begins to be enlarged. Hence they constrained him. For one does not lightly reach the summit of perfection; rather, by the steps of virtues one arrives by force, little by little, at the height of charity.

21. “They constrained him.” Do not wonder if the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, when its Lord himself does so. If, then, you find your heart undevout through a certain natural hardness, persist in prayers, devote yourself to meditations, run where the impulse of the spirit is, lest you [Col. 0977A] give assent to the flesh. Press yourself into vigils; conquer the Lord of majesty by the violence of tears, and say to him: “Stay with us, Lord, for it is toward evening and the day is now declining.”

We can understand this clause in many ways and find many delights in it. “Stay with us, for it is toward evening.” When we prosper in successes of virtue, we are in daytime; when the straits of tribulations darken us, evening begins to come upon us; when sorrow confounds us, evening comes upon us. And because we flee to you, who alone consider labor and grief, stay with us, for it is toward evening. Now waters have come even unto the soul; now the delights of devotion are turned into misery; now the wind of temptation shakes every corner of our mind: stay with us, for it is toward evening.

[Col. 0977B] You are refreshment for troubled hearts; you are refuge; you are consolation. Power is yours, dominion is yours. The eyes of all are directed toward you; the thirsty soul desires you alone: stay with us, for it is toward evening. Without you we can do nothing. You alone give songs in the night; you are a tower of strength against the oppressor. The eye of your mercy looks upon the things beneath heaven: stay with us, for it is toward evening. Through you a noonday brightness rises for us at evening, and we arise like the morning star when we think ourselves consumed; none who trusts in you is put to shame: stay with us, for it is toward evening.

The day is now declining; evenings have grown longer, because, as the end of the world approaches, iniquity increases beyond measure and charity grows cold. Let not our lamp be extinguished in the night [Col. 0977C]; stay with us, for it is toward evening. As the evening of the world inclines, O sun of righteousness, the cold of iniquity oppresses humankind. The night of faithlessness occupies all; the light of truth fails. Lest we fail with those who fail, stay with us, for it is toward evening.

The evening of my life is now at hand; grievous sickness consumes my body; harsh death now threatens; fear and trembling shake my whole conscience; it dreads the terrible sentence of judgment. But you, Lord, to whom the Father has given all judgment, stay with us, for it is toward evening. Into your hands I commend my spirit. Do not hand over to the powers of darkness a soul confessing you. In you alone is our salvation; our eyes are upon you, lest we perish. From the abundance of your mercies the mind conceives confidence: stay with us, for it is toward evening.

[Col. 0977D] Or by “evening” we may understand refreshment for an afflicted mind, so that, when every heat of tribulation has withdrawn, prayer and meditation may prepare for God a tranquil lodging within it, constrain him to remain, and invite him to supper, according to what is written: “If anyone opens the door to me, I will enter in to him and will sup with him, and he with me” (Apoc. III, 20). He became like a traveler turning aside to stay; and therefore he entered with them.

22. “And it came to pass, when he reclined with them, that he took bread, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to them; and their eyes were opened, and they recognized him.” This bread is the bread of grace. He receives this bread in himself, because, not as an inferior but as equal to the Father, he received the gifts [Col. 0978A] of grace according to his will, not by measure. He blesses the bread when, as lawgiver, he gives us his blessing, that we may go from strength to strength. He breaks it and gives it to them, because it depends “not on one who wills nor on one who runs, but on God who has mercy.” Nor does he give the bread whole, but broken, because there are divisions of graces but the same Lord, who sends forth his ice like morsels.

And what does it mean when it says: “Their eyes were opened and they recognized him in the breaking of bread”? In the breaking of bread there is a certain diminishment and emptying. Understand in the breaking the virtue of humility, by which he who is the bread of life himself broke, diminished, and emptied himself. And because he emptied himself, he gave us his thought. He is the desirable bread which Daniel did not eat for many days [Col. 0978B] (Dan. X, 3), because many righteous persons and prophets desired to see, but did not see, the incarnate wisdom of God the Father. They burned with many sighs from desire to see the Son of Man, but he was hidden in the Father’s bosom. “The little ones asked for bread, and there was none to break it for them” (Lam. IV, 4). What profit is there in the hidden wisdom of the Father and in the whole, concealed treasure alike?

Break your bread, Lord, for one who hungers—yourself as bread—so that the eyes of humankind may be opened, and it may not be reckoned as sin to a human being if he wishes to be like you, knowing good and evil. Let him recognize you in the breaking of bread, who from the beginning wished to attempt or touch what was whole. Break yourself, so that he may learn to break himself, since you are not recognized except in the breaking of bread. Balaam heard the sayings of God and beheld the visions of the Almighty; [Col. 0978C] but he fell with open eyes (Num. XXIV, 4), because he did not recognize the Lord in the breaking of bread.

Thus today you see many studying the Scriptures, teaching from chairs, and preaching in churches, but their works do not agree with their words. They profess in words that they know God, but deny him in deeds, because he is recognized only in the breaking of bread. Indeed, the Lord became bread for us, and we are his bread. He deigned to eat his bread in the sweat of his face, so that we might eat ours in joy. If you wish to recognize him, break yourself as he broke himself; for “he who says that he abides in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked” (I John II, 6). The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power. Therefore break yourself to the labor of obedience, to the humility of penitence. Bear [Col. 0978D] in your body the marks of Jesus Christ, taking the form not of a prelate but of a servant. And when you have emptied and broken yourself, you will recognize the Lord in the breaking of bread.

23. But since we have begun to speak of the bread of grace: while it is broken, the eyes are opened and the Lord is recognized, because with the other gifts of grace the virtue of humility is infused. Then we recognize him because, from the gifts received, we humbly submit ourselves to him, when we refer to him whatever good we have received. The wise man attests that God is honored by the humble (Ecclus. III, 21). See how blessed Gregory agrees with our words: “He,” he says, “who gathers the other virtues without humility carries, as it were, dust which he has found” [Col. 0979A] (*Morals*, book XXXV, ch. 10), so that from what ought to have enabled him to carry something, a worse consequence follows.

True humility, therefore, opens the eyes while it breaks and diminishes the other virtues, through which a person could be blinded by the wind of pride; and a person knows himself to be nothing of himself. And the more anyone decreases through contempt for himself, the more he advances in the knowledge of God. Therefore, in order that the Lord may be recognized in the breaking of bread, let a person break whatever virtues he possesses in himself; let him break his own wills, imitating him who for us became obedient even unto death on a cross.

“And he vanished from their eyes.” A wonderful thing! When the master begins to become sweet to the heart, then he flees, in order by his absence to make us sweetly grieve. Such are the delights of love: the eyes of love make him fly away. “Flee, my beloved, and be like [Col. 0979B] a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of spices” (Song II, 17; VIII, 14). Ascend above the Cherubim and walk upon the wings of the winds. Yet be like a roe and a young hart, so that you do not turn the eyes of your love away from us, even if you withdraw yourself from ours—you who look upon lowly things and know lofty things from afar.

24. And they said to one another: “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus, while he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” This clause is not to be expounded but chewed over. Whenever our soul withers within us and days of affliction take possession of us, whenever we are wounded by weariness or by the arrows of temptations, let us recall what we once felt in prayer, what we tasted in meditation [Col. 0979C], and how the Lord spoke to us when we passed into the delights of contemplation. 667 “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus?”

O sweet burning, sweet brightness, sweet love! Burning that strengthens, brightness that illumines, love that intoxicates. How sweetly you burn, how wonderfully you shine, how sufficiently you fill the whole human heart! “Who among us can dwell with devouring fire, with everlasting burnings?” (Isa. XXXIII, 14), when there will no longer be fire in Zion but a furnace in Jerusalem, amid the splendors of eternity? Then we too shall remember this little flame which we feel in the valley of weeping; we shall sing and chant, and say to one another: “Was not our heart burning [Col. 0979D] within us concerning Jesus?”

When we lived in the poverty of regular warfare, stood to sing psalms in the night vigils, and after the vigils secretly devoted ourselves to prayer in those most blessed intervals, how great then was the abundance of sweetness in our hearts! “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus?” Was not the night an illumination amid delights? Was not our heart then burning within us when, sitting in the cloister, we meditated in silence, when God was secretly in our tabernacle, when our heart ascended above Jerusalem, and we thought upon the joys of our homeland while the harmony of heaven resounded in conscience? “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus?” When we refreshed our souls with the sweetness of the divine Scriptures, finding in them marvelous delights [Col. 0980A] beyond all riches?
