Did not the anointing of Christ then teach us all things, pouring marrow-rich delights into us? “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus while he spoke to us on the way?”

25. “And rising in that same hour, they returned to Jerusalem and found the eleven gathered together, and those who were with them saying: ‘The Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.’” They are not inappropriately said to rise at that same hour, because such delights cannot remain in the soul except for an hour—not even for an hour. They swiftly pass, depart, vanish. Therefore they flee, so that we may desire more fervently their fullness, which is due [variant: is possessed] in the homeland; therefore they attract and inflame the mind, that we may rise, not descend to Jericho. There those who descend are ambushed, to be stripped or killed.

But the soul accustomed to heavenly delights ought, with a certain noble pride, to despise these temporal things, which are changeable like the moon. [Col. 0980B] Therefore Prayer and Meditation, rising, return to Jerusalem when, after being refreshed by spiritual delights, they possess the rest of inward peace. By the eleven gathered in Jerusalem may be understood the sevenfold gifts of the Spirit and the four principal virtues. Those who are with them may be called faith, hope, charity, and whatever other gifts of grace are there. Prayer and meditation find these persons gathered; they do not gather them. For although we strive, as far as we can, to gather virtues, we can do nothing without the Father of lights, who works in us both the willing and the accomplishing. When prayer and meditation are joined to these, they say, “The Lord has truly risen,” when he breathes the joy of the Lord’s resurrection into a loving conscience.

26. But what is meant by the addition, “He appeared to Simon”? See whether perhaps it was said for our sake, we who are especially children of obedience, debtors to wise and foolish alike, bound to obey without contradiction of speech and without the resentment of murmuring. It is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance, bringing forth a great abundance of joy for the obedient: the Lord appeared to Simon, to him alone with a special prerogative above all others.

O, if we turn over in the memory of a devout mind how sweet his appearance is to the children of obedience in that terrible struggle and miserable hour when [Col. 0980D] the soul is compelled to be separated from the body! We do not presume to assert what we do not know; yet we may imagine something such as this with devout thoughts. Perhaps Christ then appears to some with the banner of obedience, cheers the obedient soul with ineffable exultation amid that tribulation, and comforts it with words such as these:

“Do not fear, child of obedience; do not fear to behold hands fastened to the cross for obedience’s sake. Consider the feet exposed to the piercing of nails, and the side pierced by the lance. Attend to the fact that I died for obedience. And if, through the frailty of the human condition, your obedience possesses something less than perfection, I will that the fullness of my obedience be the supplement for your obedience, which is less than sufficient.”

What can be sweeter in that hour than such consolation? [Col. 0981A] What could be impressed more sweetly upon the human heart? Lay these things upon your hearts, children of obedience; rejoice and exult, because “the Lord has truly risen and has appeared to Simon.”

27. “And they related what had happened on the way and how they recognized him in the breaking of bread.” We may refer this final clause to the joys of that blessed rest, when each shall sit beneath his own vine and fig tree amid the beauty of peace, in tents of confidence and abundant rest; when the streets of Jerusalem will be paved with gold and Alleluia will be sung through all its lanes, and it will be filled with boys and girls following the Lamb wherever he goes, clothed in white garments.

Then we shall recount what happened on the way, how we recognized the Lord in the breaking of bread; how sweetly [Col. 0981B] he humbles us here in the place of affliction, so that he may delight in our hearts—he who hides his secrets from the wise and prudent and reveals them to little ones. [Col. 0982A] Then we shall remember the dangers amid which we live, the tribulations by which we are afflicted, the miseries in which we are entangled; and we shall rejoice wonderfully, because all these things have passed like a shadow, and from the splendors in which we shall be our bones will put forth jubilation.

Then we shall plant vineyards on the mountain of Samaria, hear the voice of joy and the voice of gladness, the voice of bridegroom and bride, and see the glory of the king and the beauty of the queen. Then the Virgin will rejoice in the choir, bearing the diadem of the kingdom upon her head, and will show us the fruit of her most holy womb. In our humanity the Lord of majesty will be seen. Then our heart shall see, flow abundantly, wonder, and be enlarged; together we shall praise him, because eye to eye, gaze answering gaze, we shall see; face to face we shall know; [Col. 0982B] mouth to mouth we shall speak, saying:

“To you, Lord, belong power and dominion; to you honor and glory. Let every spirit praise you for ages of ages. Amen.”

[Col. 0981]

**SERMON ON THE EXCELLENCE OF THE MOST HOLY SACRAMENT AND THE DIGNITY OF PRIESTS.** 668 It is not by St Bernard, but by someone who was not a priest, as may be inferred from nos. 3, 5, and 16.

“Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 25).

[Col. 0981C]

1. Let it not escape you, reverend priests, that this passage recited to you, concise in words, is exceedingly fruitful in the majesty of its spiritual meanings. Above all others it is incumbent upon you to hear what we set forth; and not merely to hear, but to store it more faithfully and, like clean animals, to chew it over more diligently. Blessed David, outstanding among the Prophets and most dear to the living God, caught up in the spirit before Him who sits upon the thrones, had read in a certain treasury of mysteries what great things, and of what kind, the Lord was mercifully to provide for a shipwrecked world through your ministry. As the holy interpreter of the heavenly counsel, he sings with joy: “Man ate the bread of angels” [Col. 0981D] (Ps. 77:25).

Thus, to express clearly the certainty of so fruitful a matter, he significantly used the past for the future, saying, “Man ate the bread of angels.” O astonishing mercy of God! The Word puts on flesh; God, ashes; the potter, clay; life, mortality—so that beasts might eat the bread of angels. Men were beasts. For “man, though he was in honour, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13, 21). It is not unfitting, indeed it is joyful, to recall in what high estate man was created.

669 Yet it is worthwhile next to consider how grievously he fell because he gave insufficient thought to what he was in himself and what he was from God. For our first parent was appointed an inhabitant [variant: dweller] of paradise, established lord of the earth [Col. 0982C], designated a citizen of the heavenly Jerusalem, and made a member of the Lord’s household. He was enriched by love and knowledge of Him, a companion of angels, brother and co-heir of the heavenly powers, experiencing absolutely no want and no distress. What he requested was ready at hand—not only what necessity [variant: necessity] required, but even what devout will [variant: will] desired—since there was nothing in his soul to offend and nothing in his flesh to shame him. Such was man’s honour and dignity: to prosper and flourish in the blessings just mentioned. And these came from God.

2. Yet, while in honour, he did not understand what he was in himself: namely mud, dust, a dry leaf, parched stubble, an earthen and fragile pot, dead skin. But he swelled with pride and was plainly made foolish, delighting in the height of his honour. [Col. 0982D] And at once he discovered in himself what, much later, a man from among the children of captivity wisely perceived and truthfully declared: “He who thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3). Woe to the wretch that there was then no one to say to him: “Why are you proud, earth and ashes?” (Ecclus. 10:9). By a sudden reversal, therefore, man found himself lying because of weakness in a stable. What is the stable? It is the world. And because of his likeness to cattle, he needed hay. Therefore heavenly food changed itself into fodder for cattle, since man had changed into cattle. For the bread of angels became hay: the Only-begotten of the Father, the Son of Man. “For the Word was made flesh” (John 1:14); and, according to the prophet, “All flesh is hay” (Isa. 40:6).

Therefore [Col. 0983A] angels eat the Word born of God; men eat the Word made hay. Angels live on their bread in heaven and are blessed; men live on their hay on earth and are holy. For this hay, gathered from the meadow of the virgin womb, became refreshment for beasts. In order that the Word might become hay, He lay hidden in the Virgin: the Sun in the star, the Craftsman in His work.

3. This gift of more generous excellence was bestowed upon us in the first place by the most holy incarnation of the Word of the Father; and in the second place you minister it to us day by day by virtue of the office of authority conferred upon you. O your splendid, venerable power! Certainly, after God there is no power such as yours. Perhaps you wish to know, and take pleasure in hearing more plainly, what this great power is, to which nothing in heaven [Col. 0983B] or on earth can be compared. To this I reply: namely, to consecrate the body and blood of the Lord.

At your power, at so notable a spectacle, at so solemn a privilege of your dignity, heaven is astonished, earth marvels, man trembles, and the angelic height shows deep reverence. But whence is this granted to us, most merciful Jesus: that we, little worms crawling upon the face of the earth—we who are dust and ashes—should deserve to have You present before our hands and before our eyes, You who whole and entire sit at the right hand of the Father; who, even within the moment of one hour, are available to all from the rising of the sun to its setting, from north to south: one among many, the same in different places? Whence, I say, is this? Certainly not from our due or our merit, but from Your will [Col. 0983C] and the good pleasure of Your sweetness. “For in Your sweetness, O God, You prepared for the poor” (Ps. 67:11). The human race is poor, and to it this good has been granted from heaven. This is truly heavenly indulgence; this is truly heaped-up grace; this is truly the surpassing glory of priests: to hold their God and to extend Him to others by giving Him. O new and divine power, by whose ministry the bread of angels and of life is prepared daily for mortals!

4. This bread is called, by excellence, the Eucharist—that is, good grace. For in this sacrament not merely some grace, but He from whom all grace comes, is received. Christ was once made the saving victim for the salvation of the world, the universal reconciliation; He gave power and efficacy to all [Col. 0983D] sacraments, both preceding and following, so that all who were to be delivered through Him might be sanctified by so great and such a victim. Hence we read that “the Lamb was slain from the beginning of the world” (Rev. 13:8), namely for those who have been from the beginning; so that by the phrase “from the beginning” the text determines not the time of His slaying but the time of salvation. For His death was beneficial before it occurred; first came the promise, and then its fulfilment.

From the beginning of the world, therefore, O most gracious Jesus, You were slain; You granted Your bride a most noble marriage portion, that by this means Your dove might possess a sweetest memorial of her beloved. For Christ, on the day before He suffered, prescribed for His disciples the form of this sacrament and supplied its efficacy—that is, He commanded it to be done. The prescription of the form lies in bread and wine. Mark [Col. 0984A] the order. While supper was still in progress, He rose from supper; the Lord of all washed the feet of His disciples; then, returning to the table, He established the sacrifice of His body and blood, giving the bread separately and the wine separately. Of the bread He said: “Take and eat; this is my body.” Of the wine likewise: “Drink of this, all of you. This is my blood, which shall be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26:26–28).

“It shall be poured out” was said because it was to be shed abroad and without restraint. The puncturing of thorns, the piercing of hands and feet with nails, and the opening of His side by a soldier’s lance more forcefully express how they poured it outward like a torrent. That blood was more precious and dearer than balm; through it our filth was cleansed. At that supper Christ was both giver and gift; feeder and food; guest and banquet; offerer and offering.

5. You have heard the form of the sacrament; hear its efficacy and the communion of the Lord’s body and blood. Jesus Christ and we are joined in an inexpressible unity, as He Himself says: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:57). This must be understood of the good who receive worthily, not of the wicked and depraved. Indeed, at one table, at the Lord’s supper, Peter and Judas received from one consecrated bread: the good man unto life, the utterly wicked man unto punishment; the good man unto benefit, the wicked man unto testimony against himself; the good man unto salvation, the wicked man unto death.

All this is still fulfilled in the Church in the sacrament [Col. 0984C] of the altar: for the good who receive it unto good; but not so for dogs and the unclean. Dogs are those who approach irreverently, and therefore depart under judgment. For those who live according to the flesh and wander after fleshly things, fettered by a chain of vices, receive poison with Judas the betrayer and incur the noose of spiritual hanging. They are to be most grievously condemned, both for their manifold guilt and for contempt of the sacrament, which they truly receive, but in its essence, not in its saving efficacy. Will He who distinguishes between clods not also distinguish between stars? Surely He will assay silver who has also tested and rejected gold itself.

Behold, you have heard the fruit and benefit for the good; you have also heard—and, I think, shuddered at—the destruction of the wicked. [Col. 0984D] Now hear and marvel in astonishment that the celebration at the altar of so great a sacrament, which Christ performed with His own hands at the Paschal supper, has been entrusted not to any angels or heavenly spirits, but to men—and not to all men, but to your Order alone.

6. The form and efficacy of the sacrament having thus been set out, it remains to say in what words Christ commanded it to be celebrated. “Do this,” He says, “in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). O words overflowing with affection! O words piercing and penetrating to the very soul! “Do this,” He says, “in remembrance of me.” The prophet likewise says: “They shall utter the remembrance of the abundance of Your sweetness” (Ps. 144:7). O supremely merciful and truly sweet remembrance: to proclaim the Lord’s death [Col. 0985A] until He comes! Christ’s death is a work without example, humility without measure, a gift without price, and grace without merit. He who bore our sins upon the wood of His cross willingly underwent it for us: namely, the punishment of sins, by whose wound we have been healed.

What are you doing, unworthy man? What are you doing, ungrateful man? Worship more devoutly, and more frequently recall in the sacrament of the altar the salvation of the world that suffered for you, the life that died for you, the strength that was made weak. If you are a member of Christ, suffer with your head. If you are Christ’s brother, die with your brother. Weep; grieve with sighs and tears over the precious death of the Only-begotten Son of God the Father. Otherwise, if you do not grieve, do not weep, do not suffer with Him, you are delirious, you have become degenerate, you savour of a beast, you suffer lethargy, you deny that you are human.

Moreover, that you may be moved more deeply—or rather, that you may grow warmer in love for your Redeemer—Christ willed that He should be continually worshipped through the mystery which was once offered as the price; that the perpetual victim should live in remembrance and always be present in grace. And so it is. Although sin is renewed in many persons, nevertheless the universality of original guilt has been wholly [Col. 0985B] removed, 671 since Leviathan, the venomous serpent, was pierced by the power of the flashing spear—the death of Jesus Christ (Isa. 27:1). Thus Christ need not be crucified anew to expiate what is committed daily; rather, He is the sufficient remedy for all, if the remembrance of His past death is retained through faith and imitation.

7. O Christ Jesus, the remembrance of Your death is like the work [Col. 0985C] of a perfumer; like incense fragrant in summer days; like a royal place of spices cleansed by the heat of the sun; like rose-flowers in spring days; and like lilies beside running water (Ecclus. 50:8). Rejoice, bride; exult beyond measure. You have as your presiding lord and ruler the Bridegroom amid the warfare of this present exile. You have a pledge and hold an earnest, by which you may be happily united with the Bridegroom in your homeland. Glorious and beloved bride, on earth you possess the Bridegroom in the sacrament; in heaven you shall possess Him without a veil. Here and there alike is truth; but here it is veiled, there manifest. Here indeed the Church possesses the Bridegroom according to her present order, not yet in the majesty of purity or the security of eternity. Here is truly a sweet prelude and joyful betrothal; there [Col. 0985D] will be the wedding banquet and blessed union, when we pass from faith to sight, from month to month, from sabbath to sabbath, from the warmth of bread to the warmth of the eternal banquet.

Hence the bride sighs and says with Moses: “Show me Yourself” (Exod. 33:13, 18). Nor without reason. For Jesus Himself—sweet in speech, sweet in face, sweet in name, sweet in deed—will appear sweeter in the vision of the Godhead. Truly sweet in speech, from whose mouth milk and honey flow: “Grace has been poured upon His lips.” Truly sweet in face: for He is beautiful not only beyond the sons of men (Ps. 44:3), but also beyond thousands of angels. Truly He is sweet in name. For the name Jesus is sweet and pleasant, consecrated from eternity, announced by an angel, prophesied by Solomon’s oracle, [Col. 0986A] who says: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song 1:2). Nor is there any other name in which salvation must be found. For He is salvation, who “will save His people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). Sweet in deed: in the miracles He performed, in sinners converted, and in the sacrament of His precious death, which gently accommodates human weakness. For therein love shone forth, mercy gleamed more brightly, and grace radiated more abundantly.

8. Yet He will be far sweeter in the vision of the Godhead, when He manifests Himself seated upon a throne exalted above all. Then our desire will be satisfied. Desiring this, the prophet said: “My heart said to You: My face has sought You; Your face, O Lord, I shall seek” (Ps. 26:8). “For what have I in heaven, and what have I desired from You upon earth?” (Ps. 72:25). And elsewhere: “You will fill me with joy by Your countenance” (Ps. 15:11). Therefore the sight of the face is called more precious than the repeated image in a mirror. For the outer covering of the sacrament and the marrow of wheat, faith and sight, remembrance and presence, eternity and time, mirror and face, the image of God and the form of a servant, are by no means received with equal delight.

Here, however, we walk by faith, not yet by sight. Meanwhile we ought to delight and rejoice in the sacrament of the altar. In its consecration, the faithful minister finds himself in the midst of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, with the heavenly orders standing on every side. A most noble sacrament, a mystery of surpassing glory, demands and requires a most festive [Col. 0986C] celebration for persons so illustrious. Whatever can be thought or said concerning the priest’s ascent or advance at that hour lies far beneath the dignity of the truth. There the soul of the good priest delights, having been raised above itself; it strives, hastens, ascends, and grows in desire. And the more it is lifted upward, the more it is emptied, so that, evaporating every cloud of earthly desire, wholly spiritual, it puts off the man within the man and glories in the secret place of the Lord’s countenance.

For a pious mind offering incense and a devoted soul sacrificing are not excluded from the sight of the mercy-seat in the Holy of Holies; but few are those whom purity admits to the threshold of this depth, whom integrity snatches up and raises to such a height of holiness.

[Col. 0986D] 9. Thus the holy minister sees and spiritually perceives God, who is Father of all by creation, to be more specially his Father by gracious condescension, because He is the Father by grace of all orphans—those whose wicked father, that is, the world, has died, and whose most evil mother, that is, fleshly desire, has died. Blessed is he who dares, who is able, to say: “My father and my mother have forsaken me, but the Lord has taken me up” (Ps. 26:10).

672 He also sees and perceives the Son of God to be his most loving brother, who, made little for us, is truly the brother of the little ones—that is, of the humble. “I shall declare Your name to my brethren; in the midst of the church I shall praise You” (Ps. 21:23). He sees [Col. 0987A] and perceives the Holy Spirit, proceeding from the Father and the Son, to be a member of his household, his helper and defender, because He is the comforter of those truly repentant and the advocate of those who hope in Him. Again, he sees and perceives the angelic spirits applauding his progress and ardently desiring that he may deserve to be enrolled as their fellow-citizen.

This Church is indeed the treasury of those enrolled in heaven. To this Church, that other Church which, with its instruments hung up, still sighs to God beside the rivers of Babylon, is joined by original kinship and united by natural affinity, habits, and vows. By such a minister the fatted calf, whole and perfect; the yearling lamb, full and spotless, is received with every sweetness, most delightful flavour, and most welcome joy—and, when received, is not consumed. For it is the food of life that descended from heaven.

10. Can you estimate what or how great is this Holy of Holies and sacrament of sacraments, love of loves, sweetness of all sweetnesses? These truly are the Paschal feasts; these are the joys and life-giving dishes of the righteous; these are the spiritual delights of the righteous and saints. Here, in a fertile place, are drunk torrents of milk, rivers of honey, streams of heavenly balm. Here the bride becomes one flesh with the Bridegroom; the holy soul becomes one spirit with Christ. The experience of these and like things is spirit and life; the merely natural person enjoys neither their perception nor their access.

The friends of the Bridegroom—that is, good bishops, good abbots, [Col. 0987C] and other God-fearing and religious men—have tasted and fully experienced what we say. Therefore they approach the table of the altar more frequently, keeping their garments—that is, their bodies—white at all times, as best they can, since they are about to touch their God with hand and mouth and to hear Him speaking to them. For there a familiar conversation takes place between God and Moses His friend—that is, the good and faithful minister.

11. Yet that speech is not sounding but penetrating; not verbose but effective; not clamorous in the ears but soothing to the affections. It is not public speech, but singular and private. It does not sound in the marketplace and is not heard in public. Secret counsel seeks a secret friend. It will doubtless bring joy and gladness to the hearing, if it is received by the sober ear of the heart. “Hear, O Israel,” says the Lord, “and be silent.” The faithful friend and faithful servant answers with the boldness of devout familiarity, yet not with a vocal response but with sweet weeping, saying with Samuel: “Speak, Lord, for Your servant hears” (1 Sam. 3:10); and with the prophet: “I will hear what the Lord God speaks in me” (Ps. 84:9).

Certainly there Christ speaks with His minister: “Ponder continually,” He says; “store faithfully; lovingly embrace what you see, what you do, what you hold. Embrace it, I say, with the affection of devout remembrance and the effect of devout imitation, knowing that you must prepare such things. The preparation of this table is not that of man, but of faith; not of a deed, but of a mystery; [Col. 0988A] not of temporal food, but of eternal food. I who am the author of the gift am myself the witness of its truth. The altar at which you stand represents the cross which I endured for you; the chalice, the tomb in which I rested dead; the paten, the stone laid over it; the corporal, the shroud; the coverings beneath the corporal, the linen cloths in which I was wrapped.

“The victim which you see is no longer bread but my flesh, which hung upon the cross for the life of the world. Indeed, this change is the work of blessing, not of origin; power accomplishes it, not custom; it is an effect of might, not of natural usage; gracious condescension, not reasoning; mercy, not misery. It is not common but solely divine, not human; a sacrament of mercy, not a diminution of the Godhead. Let physical nourishment perish here. This food is not for the belly but for the mind. [Col. 0988B] For it was given not for the ruin of this life, which is a vapour appearing for a little while, but for the bestowal of the soul’s eternal life. This is the bread of angels, which does not know decay: it does not pass into the privy, but rises to what is on high. It brings man back to the place from which he derived his image. ‘For my flesh is truly food.’

“Likewise, this liquid which you see is no longer wine but my blood, which I poured out for you as the price, reserving for you at the altar a cup, in your pilgrimage a protection, in your departure from Egypt a guide, and in heaven provision for the journey. I am the cluster of flesh carried to the winepress of the cross for your salvation; from it was pressed out the new wine of your redemption. ‘For my blood is truly drink’” (John 6:56).

12. Wonderful, brothers, are the things said concerning this sacrament. Faith is necessary; knowledge through reason is superfluous. Knowledge is gathered through reason and understanding; faith alone is induced by authority. Augustine, *Against Felicianus*: “Let faith believe this; let understanding not seek it, lest it either judge what has not been found incredible, or fail to believe what has been found singular.” These, brothers, are matters which necessarily require faith and admit reason not at all. They require a simple believer and rebuke an impious investigator. And therefore one must believe simply what cannot profitably be investigated. This is that torrent which Elisha could not ford.

Do not, therefore, do not ask how it happens; do not doubt whether it happens. Do not approach irreverently, lest it become death for you. For it is God; and although bread possesses the mysteries [Col. 0988D] of bread, it is nevertheless changed into flesh. He who testifies that bread truly becomes His flesh is God and man. The chosen vessel is he who threatens judgment upon one who does not discern so holy a flesh. O Christian, think the same concerning wine; honour the same reality in wine. He who advances wine into Christ’s blood is the Creator of wine. He is the Teacher of the Gentiles, on whose assertion the person who drinks Christ’s blood unworthily drinks death (1 Cor. 11:29).

13. It must be known that water mixed with wine signifies the union of the members with their head. For “many waters” are “many peoples” (Rev. 17:15). The three portions made at the altar from Christ’s body have a mystical meaning. For the whole Church is Christ’s body—namely, the head together with its members—and in this body there are, as it were, three [Col. 0989A] parts, of which the entire body consists.

One part is the head itself. For the head is both head and likewise a part of the body. Thus the head itself is one part of the body: the head, I say, which has now risen immortal and incapable of suffering, to die or suffer no more. Another part of the body consists in those members who already rest, as it were, in the sabbath of the soul with their head, possessing the one robe of immortality as regards their souls in heaven. Of such persons it is said: “The souls of the saints rejoice in heaven” (*Office of the Church for Martyrs*). Thus these two parts are together: the head, namely Christ; and the other part of the body, namely the good departed, whose bodies rest in tombs and whose souls are with Christ. Therefore at the altar two portions are reserved [Col. 0989B] outside the chalice, as though outside suffering, because the blessed now feel no pain, since the former things have passed away.

The third portion, which we put into the blood, signifies that part of the Church which drinks the Lord’s cup—that is, imitates Christ’s suffering. To this part the Lord said in the Apostles: “In me you may have peace; in the world you shall have tribulation” (John 16:33).

14. Smell, appearance, taste, and weight remain for the rite of the mystery and for the support of taste, so that horror may wholly be removed and merit may be obtained. For, lest human weakness should shrink from eating flesh and drinking blood when receiving them, Christ willed that these two should be veiled and covered beneath the appearances of bread and wine, which in some manner hold first place among the provisions of the human race. For literally, above all foods [Col. 0989C] bread strengthens the human heart and wine makes it glad. Therefore He set forth His body and blood to be received in such a way that sense might be comforted in one respect and faith built up in the other. Sense is comforted in one respect while it sees only what is familiar and customary; faith is built up in the other, while the eye of flesh sees one thing outwardly, but the eye of the heart inwardly perceives and reveres another. One thing is hidden; another lies open. “He made darkness His hiding-place” (Ps. 17:12).

For just as appearances are seen there whose things or substances are not believed to be there, so the thing whose appearance is not seen is truly and substantially believed to be there. The appearance of bread and wine is seen, and the substance of bread and wine is not believed to remain. But the substance of Christ’s body [Col. 0989D] and blood is believed, though its appearance is not seen. Thus the appearance of bread and wine is offered in order to teach that receiving 674 Christ’s body and blood is a full and perfect refreshment, the full refreshment of food and drink. Now bread and wine are the principal substances of food and drink.

15. Although the sacrament is one, three distinct things are offered in it: the visible appearance, the truth of the body, and the power of spiritual grace. One thing is the visible appearance, which is visibly seen; another is the truth of the body, which is invisibly believed under the visible appearance; and another is spiritual grace, which together with the body and blood is received visibly and spiritually by those alone who communicate worthily. For in the sacrament of the altar you must attend to three things: the appearance of bread, [Col. 0990A] the truth of flesh, and the power of spiritual grace. The outward sense reaches as far as the appearance of bread; inward faith, to the truth of flesh; higher love, to the power of spiritual grace. The tiniest mouse sometimes gnaws the appearance of bread; even the worst Christian receives [supplied: the truth]; only the predestined person receives the power of spiritual grace.

Therefore what we see is the appearance of bread and wine. But what we believe under that appearance is the true body and true blood of Christ, which hung upon the cross and flowed from His side. Sacramental eating, therefore, as regards the visible appearance and the truth of Christ’s body, belongs alike to good and bad persons. But there is another eating, as we have already said, belonging only to the good. Through God’s grace and faith working through [Col. 0990B] love, it produces the merit of life and the dispositions of the minds in the hearts of those receiving or ministering, through a certain spiritual and subtler union of head and members intervening.

Hence comes the phrase: “May it become for us the body and blood of Your Son.” “For us,” it says, “may it become.” For without doubt the Lord’s body is always made upon the table of the altar when that solemn mystery is celebrated in the due rite; but it does not always become so for those through whom it is made. Hence likewise the phrase in the Canon: “That as many of us as shall receive the sacrament of Your Son through this participation at the altar may be filled with every heavenly blessing and grace” (*from the Canon of the Mass*). For not all who receive the Lord’s body through participation at the altar are spiritually filled with that heavenly blessing and grace. Hence there is the phrase: “That what we perform temporally [Col. 0990C] we may attain in eternal joys”; likewise: “That what we have received to be taken under visible mysteries we may attain in invisible effect” (*in the common prayer*); and many phrases of this kind.

16. Therefore this sacrament, laid up from eternity, hidden from the devil, revealed to the prophets, and entrusted to your care, must be pursued with due thanksgiving. O your sacred, heavenly ministry: praiseworthy desire, notable spectacle, solemn miracle! God, who is wonderful in all things, shows Himself certainly more wonderful in relation to you, while He works more wonderful things through you. What more need be said? Priests of God, bless the Lord, striving for things worthy of God, lest that which has been provided as a remedy for worthy recipients become your ruin.

Not without reason would I call you priests of God, if you live priestly lives in the house of the Lord. For dignity does not arise from the name “priest.” Not from the name, I say, but from virtue; from conduct, not office; from merit, not title; from holiness, not ministry. Hence Scripture says: “We seek priestly men, though we have many priests.” Many, I say, in number, not in merit; in pretence, not in faith; in outward appearance, not in virtue; in bodily association, not in a spiritual bond; in joining of flesh, not in unity of heart.

For there are those who, with hands washed but deeds unwashed, approach the divine sacrifices with a blood-stained conscience. They eat without fear and reverence the flesh of the Lamb who presides in heaven, as though it were meat sold [Col. 0991A] in the marketplace. They stand at the altar not as priests, but as butchers in a slaughterhouse. Great, therefore, is the burden; great is the danger of this honour. This rank is a rank from which one may fall, a rank subject to judgment, unless the dignity of anointing is made illustrious by merits, nobility of character, the exercise of virtues, and persistence in good works.

Therefore, beloved, dig through the walls of your households—that is, set your hearts upon your ways. Strive, as far as you can, swiftly to make amends for the things in which [Col. 0992A] you have offended. For the day of the Lord will come like a thief (1 Thess. 5:2). For as nothing is more certain than death, so nothing is more uncertain than the hour of death. Weigh this as it deserves, and keep more watchfully awake to weigh it. It will be glory to God, joy to the angels, a fragrance leading to life for your subjects, and a crown for you. May Christ deign to hear Christ and His anointed ones in this, by ministering the help of His grace—He who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 0991]

# SERMON ON THE NATIVITY OF ST JOHN THE BAPTIST, CONCERNING HIS TEN PRIVILEGES

[NOTE.]

675 This sermon is listed among the works of Peter Damian and is attributed to Nicholas of Clairvaux in the *Library of the Cistercian Fathers* (where material lacking in that edition has here been enclosed in brackets) and in manuscript codices. But the fact that in section 5 the author says that, in his time, only the Nativity of Christ and that of St John had been received as feasts in the Church seems to conflict with this attribution. For both St Bernard’s Letter 86 and also Letter 174 to the Canons of Lyons establish that the Nativity of Blessed Mary was solemn at that time; indeed Nicholas himself has a sermon for it. Unless perhaps one should say that the statement is to be understood of the universal and more ancient custom or rite.

[Col. 0991B] 1. Today, beloved, a notable day has dawned upon us, holier than other days by as much as it gave forth to earth a holier man. For on this day was born the splendour of saints, the glory of the righteous, the joy of angels, a most excellent man, Christ’s kinsman, the Bridegroom’s friend, the bride’s preparer. He is one and has no equal: admitted into the angelic choirs, he surpasses the ascent of all humanity by the distinctions of a more exalted crown. For, “Among those born of women none has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11).

Happy is the man who, happily traversing the workshops of heaven, follows the Redeemer in most blessed course; no summit of dignity excludes him, whom the immensity of supreme blessedness has more abundantly drenched. The angels rejoice, and the multitude of both natures marvels at the man [Col. 0991C] who has thus entered the abyss of light and been absorbed into the inner depths of divinity, so that he reflects back the very brilliance of angelic purity. Let all be raised up and exult before the court of Majesty in the prerogatives of their merits; yet there shall be none who dares aspire to the privilege of blessed John the Baptist.

Come then, let us now begin to enter upon the marks of virtue which the God of majesty distinguished in His friend with glorious abundance. For from the rising of his life to its setting he conducted himself among men in such a way that he might be held to be a pattern of life and an instruction in character. And although the golden beauty of this sermon does not gleam, we shall nevertheless attempt to sketch the truth of the matters in whatever style we can, keeping in view that saying of the wise man: “Men of prudence take pleasure not in ornamented trifles, but in things of strength.”

[Col. 0991D] 2. The first honor, then, is glory in the announcement. It must not be passed over in concealing silence with what solemn glorification the entrance of this child into the world is announced. The angel Gabriel is present; [Col. 0992B] the strength of the Lord, descending from the hinge of the higher heavens, stands at the right side of the altar of incense. Nor is it just any angel, but that higher one who brought the singular message to the blessed Virgin, and was also chosen to announce the soldier who was to announce the King.

The priest stands arrayed in priestly vestments, and, by the manifold variety of his garments prefiguring the image of heavenly mysteries, signifies the cleansing of sins by the sprinkling of mystical blood. He stands before the ark of the covenant, before the tablets of the testament, the golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s rod, the Cherubim, and the mercy-seat; solemnly vested with the mitre, he offers up vows before the countenance of God—the glory of majesty, the Lord of all things.

A solemn day is at hand, more celebrated among the multitude of the Jews than other days, exalted by the attestation of the Lord’s command, indeed splendid and festive: the one day on which the high priest alone was permitted to enter the Holy of Holies and, by manifold sprinkling, to appease the wrath of the supreme Divinity. People gather from every side into the holy city, and the denser crowd of peoples adds to the occasion for rejoicing.

Amid these sacred rites the Archangel stands and says: “Do not fear, Zechariah, for a son shall be born to you” (Luke 1:13): the joy of his parents, nobility of lineage, an example to the world, the end of the Law, the beginning of the Gospel, the expulsion of death, the gate of life, the glory of humankind, the splendor of holy conduct, the leader of all righteousness. And lest, through a more extended treatment, we obscure the excellence of these matters, the integrity of his birth and manner of life is more fully set forth in the books of the Gospels.

Consider the exalted rank of the messenger, [Col. 0992D] the dignity of the place, and the reverence due to the day; then you will be able to understand with what surpassing glory the birth of John the Baptist is proclaimed. Therefore, with due reverence for the Redeemer preserved—for we do not detract from the King if we honor the King’s soldier—since he is Lord and John servant, he Creator and John creature, John is announced with a more distinguished preliminary manifestation than Christ. Christ perhaps was in a chamber; John, in the Temple—and not merely in the Temple, but before the Holy of Holies, on a notable day of their solemnity. John is proclaimed by the same Archangel, in a more dignified place, at a holier time, and by a more evident miracle.

Recall Isaac, announced by angels (Gen. 18:10); Samson, proclaimed by an angel (Judg. 13:3); look upon the entire order of Nazarites. You will find the Baptist alone more eminent, both in this respect and in others.

3. The second honor is sanctification in his mother’s womb. Whoever enters the world from the fallen mass draws with him [Col. 0993B] a long train of original sin. He alone who committed no sin is excepted: he whom the bridal chamber of a virginal womb, unacquainted with a man, brought forth into the world. For he was conceived far otherwise than we and in a different manner, when the Holy Spirit, flooding the Virgin with all majesty, surpassed the use of flesh, the order of nature, and union with a man. For it was fitting that he who took away sin should know no sin; that he should assume the likeness of sinful flesh, but not sinful flesh itself.

Since, therefore, all are conceived in iniquities, we never read that any mortal was sanctified within the maternal womb except Jeremiah and John the Baptist. Yet concerning the unique Virgin also there is no doubt that she, enclosed within her mother’s womb, was cleansed by a more exalted kind of sanctification, since she was that sanctuary [Col. 0993C] in which God and the Son of God was to assume flesh. But Jeremiah’s sanctification was far less than John’s. Jeremiah was indeed sanctified in his mother’s womb; John, however, is known to have been filled with the Holy Spirit. To be filled with the Holy Spirit is much more excellent than to be sanctified. There, sanctification signifies cleansing; here, filling signifies an overflowing flood.

Finally, even the Apostles, who handled with their own hands the Word of life, though they received the Holy Spirit through the Savior’s breathing, could scarcely attain, on the fiftieth day after the resurrection, to that degree of which it might be said: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:4). And although at that time the Holy Spirit filled believers’ hearts with a more abundant gift, John is nevertheless read to have attained in the womb [Col. 0993D] what the apostolic eminence at last deserved to obtain after a longer promise.

Observe carefully, I pray, with what ordered dispensation that manifold Spirit sanctifies Jeremiah, fills John, and comes upon Mary. Jeremiah’s sanctification is indeed wondrous: though conceived in sin, he is nevertheless born without sin. For he was sanctified before he came forth from the womb. Nor could one be born other than holy who had been sanctified in his mother’s womb (Jer. 1:3). A marvelous thing, unheard of in preceding ages: a person conceived in sins is born without sin!

But a far more glorious power filled John, who was both sanctified from sin and so overflowed under the Spirit’s dominion that he came forth both cleansed and filled. Truly great before [Col. 0994A] the Lord is he whom the angel announces, God sanctifies, the Spirit fills, and whose life commends him.

The Spirit came upon the Virgin in a more ineffable manner: the entire fullness of divinity flooded her without measure or distinction, so that he who made all things might be wholly contained, so that she might be believed not merely washed from sins and filled with the Holy Spirit, but also to have conceived from the Holy Spirit: “for that which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20). Hence, by a singular prerogative, the Catholic faith confesses that the Son of God was born of the Virgin and conceived of the Holy Spirit, so that the inseparably united connection of divinity and humanity may be indicated by the interchangeability of these expressions.

You see, then, by how much more remote a privilege he who was “fairer in form than the children of men” was set apart from the children of men in conception. For they were conceived from sins [Col. 0994B] and in sins; he is conceived in the Holy Spirit and from the Holy Spirit.

Let these things, indeed, be said concerning John’s conception. But if they seem to conflict with the authorities of any saints, we wish them to be overthrown without any support of excuses or defenses.

4. The third honor is excellence in exultation. From the beginning of the world it has not been heard that anyone exulted in his mother’s womb, whereas this one is read to have exulted in joy. Truly astonishing condescension: that a child scarcely conceived should burst forth into an exultant movement and eagerly meet, in sweeter service, him whom he perceived infused into the virginal substance.

Blessed the soul which did not stand in the path of sinners, but, departing by a more secret path from the heavenly workshops, obtained the sweetness [Col. 0994C] of unheard-of rejoicing! Blessed Elizabeth, to whom the Mother of the Savior hastens, upon whom the Empress of heaven bestows [or: seeks] the service of greeting! Yet far more blessed is the child, who, recognizing the majesty of the one greeting, rejoices with joy amid the dark enclosures of the womb because he attends to the power of so blessed a greeting.

“And it came to pass,” he says, “when Elizabeth heard the greeting of Mary, the child leaped for joy in her womb.” The Virgin went up in haste into the house of Zechariah to greet Elizabeth, carrying in her womb the Son of God, the King of glory, the Lord of majesty. Elizabeth comes to meet her and, free from the reproach of ancient barrenness, carries in her most happy womb the Bridegroom’s friend, the herald of the Word. Their embraces are joined, they come to kisses, and the blessed wombs are united: only two most tender walls separate the King and his soldier.

What wonder if the child marvels and exults at the touch and breath of divinity so near? Could anything miraculous be absent where the King’s presence was present—the Mother of the reigning King, the Redeemer of the world? Moreover, this union of such holy embraces was celebrated not once only. “Mary remained with her about three months,” says the Evangelist (Luke 1:41, 56). For so long, virginal integrity remained with Elizabeth and consecrated and distinguished the child John now by sweeter speech, now by a happier embrace.

[And perhaps the glorious Virgin stayed with her kinswoman until the day of his birth, so that she might cherish the newborn child in her most blessed bosom and, with one wall removed, [Col. 0995A] make him nearer to the presence of the Creator. This may readily be inferred from the Gospel, because six months had already elapsed from John’s conception when the Archangel was sent to the Virgin, bringing to virginal modesty, in a new greeting, the renewal of the world. Thereupon the Virgin hastened to Elizabeth and deigned to visit her kinswoman’s lodging for three months, until, the end of the ninth month being completed, the Patriarch’s birth was imminent. Others who have examined the Book of the Just with more careful eyes testify that they saw that the Mother of God herself first lifted the blessed child from the ground and attended her kinswoman’s delivery with every service. But however the truth of this matter may be determined, this] is certainly certain: the happy and prolonged companionship of the undefiled Virgin contributed no little to the child about to be born.

5. John’s fourth honor is joy at his birth. Blush, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning; frustrated in your attempts [variant: your impulses broken], understand at last that in the last days you will remain like a most foolish partridge. By your devices it came about that the entire human race should be conceived in sins and born in sorrow. But behold, this one is sanctified in the womb, arises in joy, and pours back joy upon the world by his birth. Behold, the kind of weaponry that you had established for victory is born to John as a crown.

Take up your arms and shield, and rage with the full spirit of your malice—[Col. 0995C] yet you will not be able to break into John’s privilege, which the kindly hand of the writer has sealed with its own character. You have been greatly deceived, greatly mocked. Do you not know that a warrior rises against you from his youth, indeed from his mother’s womb? Do you not know that from these days the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it? (Matt. 11:12.) Have you forgotten that this man is sent to prepare a perfect people for the Lord? (Luke 1:17.)

Look at the order of events, and from the first beginnings of his conception you will find that he has broken through your strength by a mightier effort. You caused Cain the fratricide, who was first-born, to come forth defiled and wrapped about, stained by the disgrace of original sin. The terrified world received this; and the birth of the human race that followed passed onward into an accumulation of infinite sorrow. But the birth [Col. 0995D] of this John is for joy and for a splendid solemnity. The world rejoices, and throughout the four regions of the earth resounds the approach of a glorious festival, celebrated and renowned even in heaven. “What, do you think, will this child be?” (Luke 1:66.) The Bridegroom’s friend; his own enemy; more powerful than you.

One must consider also with what dignity the devout celebration of this birth excels, and how much favor it can find in the eyes of the Church. The Church has admitted the birth of no human being, save that of God alone, to the summit of authoritative observance, this one exception being preserved. For she knows that “the day of death is better than the day of birth” (Eccles. 7:2), and that sorrow accompanies human birth. Hence the Church solemnizes the day of martyrs’ death, not their birth; yet she calls their deaths “birthdays,” since through death a birth has come to be theirs. Then, indeed, they began through death to be born into life, when they laid down life for Life.

But Christ’s bride received this man’s birth with so much the more secure and most gracious condescension because the incontrovertible authority of Gospel truth commends it in so singular a way.

6. The fifth honor is singularity in conversion and manner of life. In the tenderness of his years this blessed child was led, under the Spirit’s guidance, into the wilderness; nor did the weakness of age stand in the way, for the majesty of the Lord made it fruitful. For the Holy Spirit pays no heed to difference of sex, bodily frailty, or the length of years; but fills whomever, whenever, [Col. 0996B] and however he wills with most gracious kindness.

John leaves the world, flees people, knows no homeland, disregards his parents, and fixes his gaze upon the summit of Divinity alone. A wondrous reversal of things: that a person who had scarcely entered the world should flee the world’s glory; should not merely forget but not know the desires of the age; and should have perpetual fellowship with divinity! Mountain retreats, winding woods, and the desolate stretches lying beneath the valleys provided dwellings for the patriarch’s child when night compelled him.

Let not Jeremiah be set against me, nor let the vigor of his youthful preaching dare to oppose this; for if Jeremiah was consecrated as a prophet, John was consecrated as more than a prophet. And although Jeremiah foretells the future to the people, he nevertheless does not turn away from the sight of human society. John, however, [Col. 0996C] having passed beyond infancy and forgotten the nobility of his eminent lineage, devotes himself to Divinity alone: he becomes a pattern of life, the model of monks, the origin of anchorites, and the champion of all religious life.

These things concern his conversion. But how great was the sublimity of his way of life ought not to be expounded in the fluency of a running tongue, but demonstrated by the Gospel’s authoritative speech. “John,” it says, “had a garment of camel’s hair and a leather girdle about his loins; and his food was locusts and wild honey” (Matt. 3:4). “Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11:8).

A harsh garment, woven of the roughest bristles, afflicts the patriarch’s body with grim severity; and the untimely rigour of discipline, with savage harshness, constrains his most tender flesh, while the long duration of martyrdom continually shakes his delicate limbs, suffused with a more sacred spirit. [Col. 0996D] And what was his food? Partridges, pheasants, and other birds are not sought; no one runs through the whole country to fill the patriarch’s stomach. His food was locusts and wild honey. He feeds on heaven’s dew and is satisfied with the fare of a most lowly creature; the austerity of his fasting received nothing cooked. Variety of dishes was unknown to the chastened belly, stretched by prolonged mortification; nothing entered his mouth that could entice the appetite, stuff the belly, or flatter the stomach.

Elijah ate meat, and whatever else was set before him he received with thanksgiving (3 Kings 17:6); nor do we read that anyone from that old dispensation attained the summit of this observance. Rough clothing, scant food, a devout mind—these indeed consecrate a perfect patriarch.

7. The sixth honor is novelty in preaching. Here I wish your charity to attend, because the greatness of the subject requires that the matter be unfolded somewhat more subtly. After Adam’s sin and that momentous devastation of the flood, an almost countless multitude of righteous persons was chosen, with whom God is known to have spoken face to face. Enoch is translated, Noah is chosen, Abraham is called, Isaac is loved, Jacob beholds God face to face, Joseph is called the savior of the world; yet neither in God’s speech to them nor in theirs to humankind is any mention made of the eternal dwelling of the kingdom of heaven.

Moses is taken up as leader of the Jewish people [Col. 0997B] and made a god to Pharaoh. Through him God performs great deeds in Egypt, wonders in the land of Ham, terrible works in the Red Sea. Moses ascends into the darkness where God was, and on the mountain is given a manifold body of commandments. He speaks with God as a man speaks to his neighbor. Nothing that God did in secret is hidden from Moses, and the glorious name *Adonai*, veiled from all others, is revealed to him; yet amid all these things the kingdom of heaven is neither remembered nor named nor heard of.

Aaron stands as high priest, bearer of the mighty rod, anointed and consecrated with the anointing of heavenly sanctuaries. Joshua succeeds him, and all that multitude of Judges; yet there is not even the slightest mention of the kingdom of heaven. The Lord finds David a holy man after his own heart; he endows Solomon his son with singular wisdom; and the Holy Spirit orders and fills that entire prophetic choir—yet nothing is prophesied concerning the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

Elijah shuts heaven for three years and six months (3 Kings 1; Jas. 5:17). Elisha, even dead, restores a dead man to life (4 Kings 13:21), and from them not even a spark of the blessed dwelling shines forth. Why say more? Review the chosen ones of the entire human race from the beginning of the world to John, and in the speech or works of that sanctuary you will not be able to find its sweetness.

8. Come then to John and hear a voice of exultation, a voice of newness, a voice of joy, a word of mercy, a speech of glory, an abundance of grace—[Col. 0997D] what God had concealed, the angel had kept silent about, what had lain hidden from the Patriarchs and been unknown to the Prophets. “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3:2). The word “repentance” is sweet and glorious; the word “kingdom of heaven” joyful and worthy of adoration; it befitted him alone, first, who first laid the foundations of the New Testament.

This is the voice of which that greatest contemplator of heavenly visions speaks in these words: “And the first voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing on their harps” (Rev. 14:2). From Adam’s days until John, our instrument was turned into the voice of those who weep, because the multitude of sins and the absence of any place for repentance provided a double cause for lamentation. Do you kill? You are commanded to be killed. Do you gather wood on the Sabbath? You are commanded to be stoned. And he whose own property [Col. 0998A] is always to show mercy and to spare knows nothing but to strike. For the giver of commandments had given them commandments that were not good, and ordinances by which they could not live (Ezek. 20:25). This is what the righteous man wonders at when he says: “Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord?” (Ps. 88:50).

John’s birth shows the remedy for the wound: repentance for sin, pardon for iniquity. This is the first voice which the voice crying in the wilderness set forth, and “the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land” (Song 2:12). From then on he placed in our mouth a new song, a hymn to our God; thanksgiving and the voice of praise resound in our mouth. Mercy exalts itself above judgment; sinners are spared, loving-kindness reigns, justice is overlooked, and the merciful and compassionate Lord seeks an occasion to show mercy rather than to strike.

Therefore they play harps on their harps who beat back the outflow of pleasure by the restraint of repentance; and, breathing again from the deep abyss of sins, with Pharaoh drowned, they sing in the ways of the Lord, for great is the glory of the Lord.

9. The seventh honor is dignity in baptism. A singular humility indeed! The Word became flesh and, coming forth as a perfect man, leaves the whole multitude of humankind, seeks John, desires John, comes to John. God is terrible in his counsels over the children of men (Ps. 65:5), and, bearing all things by the word of his power and making purification for sins (Heb. 1:3), he comes from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him.

John is astonished and shaken with fear; boundless [Col. 0998C] dread comes upon the patriarch. “I ought to be baptized by you,” he says, “and do you come to me?” The Savior says to him: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:14–15). Both submit to this saving instruction, and John girds himself to baptize, to receive the Lord, the King of Angels.

The King of glory, the splendor of light and image of God’s substance, is stripped of his garments. That flesh taken from the Virgin, derived from a more radiant substance, is bared in the river to receive the pouring of water from the blessed Baptist’s hands. Angels descend, and all the hosts of heaven hasten reverently to the Creator. Ruling divinities surround the baptizer and the baptized. The nobler creature pours water upon the Creator’s head; a mortal hand touches and handles God’s brow.

Heaven trembles, earth is astonished, the Jordan smiles, and the angels marvel that the Lord of hosts is enclosed within the baptizer’s hands. What is this, John? You dare to hold naked him whom Cherubim and Seraphim scarcely dare to behold? This is he into whom angels desire to look; to whom the assembly of the blessed city repeats, in the lofty music of its melodies, “Holy, holy, holy”; he who alone inhabits inaccessible light: the Lord of powers, the God of knowledges, the Father of mercies. And are you not afraid?

You have been given what has been denied to all others: to baptize him who baptizes all in the Holy Spirit and fire, and to bathe—or, according to the variant, sprinkle—the virgin Son of a Virgin with virginal hands. I am wholly astonished; I revere the baptizer and the man who is God; I marvel at the Master’s condescension, I stand in awe of that condescension, and I see a man doing violence to heaven itself.

Further, what is the nature of this: that in this baptism the Law is completed, prophecy receives its end, and the entire multitude of sacrifices is driven away and expelled? Here begins and is established the cleansing of new regeneration, destined to endure; and the expenditures of legal figures pass over into a single form of baptism. For in the washing with water and the renewal of the spirit, the bloody heap of goats and calves is buried; and we leave that to sinful Jews, attending to David’s words: “You did not require burnt offering or sin offering” (Ps. 39:7).

10. The eighth honor is the first revelation of the Trinity. [Col. 0999B] From the creation of heaven and earth until this point the Trinity never appeared manifestly to human beings; rather, the eternity of such great radiance lay wrapped in coverings of things and words. Finally, when the Creator of things commends the creation of man with the highest dignity: “Let us make man,” he says, “in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). A privilege truly worthy of reverence, bestowed on no other creature! That more exalted multitude of angels is created, and the varied connection of all the elements is ordered; but the presence of the Almighty regards so great a work in profound silence. But when humankind is reached and a noble creature is about to be created, the Trinity prepares itself to create, and Wisdom takes counsel, so that the creature’s dignity may be shown illustrious by the Creator’s privilege.

[Col. 0999C] [Yet even there the names of the divine majesty did not shine forth clearly enough, since some refer the oracle of the Lord’s speech to the ministering angels. Or, if this is less carefully stated, signs of plurality are declared without a distinction of names; variant: “a marked plurality … is proclaimed.”]

Abraham saw three and worshiped one; but there the reverence of sacred Scripture veils its language now jointly, now separately, so that it chooses at one time to call them the Lord and at another men.

[Yet the Jews here devise a great polemical fiction, maintaining that three angels were sent by the Lord: one assigned to announce Isaac’s birth, two delegated to overthrow Sodom. They imagine that the righteous man, speaking with one of them and saying, “Lord, if I have found favor [Col. 0999D] in your eyes” (Gen. 18–19), knew by the prophetic Spirit that he was the herald who had come to announce Isaac’s birth. Abraham worships him as Bathsheba worshiped King David, and tirelessly waits upon his companions out of reverence for him. Thus only two are numbered in the overthrow of the faithless cities, since the aforementioned one had already returned, having faithfully fulfilled the task of announcing Isaac’s birth. For three men command Sarah to be called, but it is one who reveals the hidden mystery of the unexpected promise. Such is the Jews’ account—and that of those who chose rather to Judaize than to believe.]

But to conclude briefly: the entire company of Patriarchs and Prophets is nowhere read to have made any open mention, whether in words or deeds, of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Come, then, and behold [Col. 1000A] the son of Zechariah touching God and man with his own hands. See that there the heavens are opened; the Holy Spirit descends in bodily form, like a dove, upon Christ; and the Father’s voice is heard: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3:16–17).

You see that, at the new disclosure of the most sacred names, the palaces of heaven are opened. The Father is heard in the voice; the Son is baptized in the river; the Holy Spirit is displayed in the dove’s form. John stands amid the whole Trinity; and the Baptist is gloriously marked as having put on the open names of the substance. The name of the Trinity, veiled in former ages, shines forth without the shadowing of its whole veil. Lord, who is this, that you have made yourself known to him?

11. The ninth honor is the testimony of Truth. Hear [Col. 1000B] what Truth testifies concerning him. When John heard in prison of Christ’s works, he sent his disciples to him, and they were answered: “The blind see,” and the rest that the abundant Gospel narrative of truth continues to recount. When the messengers had departed—lest praise in their presence perhaps seem to smell of flattery—Jesus began to speak concerning John: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?”

O wondrous testimony of the Redeemer! Who has entered the world and not known the world in some respect? Who is there whom windy prosperity, turbulent adversity, or the faintest breath of any sin has not bent? At the end he adds that John surpasses earth, passes beyond heaven, and reaches the very summit of angelic dignity. “Among those born of women,” says the Lord, “none greater than John the Baptist has arisen” (Matt. 11:2–11).

What more do you want? “Of no one,” Augustine says, “could what was said of John be said.” Do not set against me the Evangelist more beloved than the other disciples, nor the Prince of the Apostles preferred to all apostles; not the Vessel of Election carried into the secrets of the third heaven; nor let apostolic splendor dare to stand against the Forerunner. For all these had already passed the bounds of youth when Truth declared, “Among those born,” and so forth. Consider the dwellings of the kingdom and survey the entire order of human generation: you will see John alone set above, or made equal to, the Patriarchs of both the Old and the New Testament. Yet God is blessed above all.

12. The tenth honor is the affirmation of Mother Church. [Col. 1000D] The hem of the robe is woven, and ointment poured upon the head flows down in abundance upon the lowest fringe of the garment. For that Church, mother and teacher of all Churches—the Roman Church—to which it was said, “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), has been consecrated and marked in honor of John the Baptist after the Savior’s name. For it was fitting that the bride’s authority should follow the sentence of the Bridegroom, and should raise his singular friend to the place where she herself ascended to primacy.

This choice is undoubtedly singular: to claim for John the primacy of the Church in that very city which two luminaries of heaven consecrated by their most glorious deaths. Peter is crucified, Paul dies by the sword, and the dignity remains with the Forerunner. [Col. 1001A] Rome is made purple by the multitude of martyrs, and all its sublimity is bestowed upon the blessed Patriarch. John is greater everywhere, singular in all things, wonderful above all.

Who was announced so gloriously? Who is read to have been filled with the Holy Spirit so specially in his mother’s womb? Whom have you read to have exulted in his mother’s womb? Whose birth have you seen celebrated in God’s Church? Who so desired the wilderness? Who is read to have lived so sublimely? Who first showed repentance and the kingdom of heaven? Who baptized the King of glory? To whom did the Trinity first reveal itself? To whom did Truth give such testimony? Whom did the Church honor in this way? See whether all these things are not so uniquely singular that no mortal ought to aspire to those things stated above.

Perhaps you intend to object to me [Col. 1001B] that this man has his own distinctive privileges, but does not share in the common attributes of the other saints. Hear, then. John is a patriarch—indeed, the end and head of the Patriarchs. John is a prophet—indeed, more than a prophet, because he pointed with his finger to him whose coming he announced. John is an angel, but one chosen among the angels, as the Savior testifies when he says: “Behold, I send my angel, who shall prepare the way before my face” (Matt. 11:10).

John is an apostle, but also the first and chief of the Apostles, because he was the first man sent by God. John is an evangelist, but also the first inaugurator of the Gospel, preaching the Gospel of the kingdom. John is a virgin—indeed, the outstanding mirror of virginity, an emblem of modesty, an example of chastity. John is a martyr, but the light of martyrs, a most steadfast model of martyrdom between Christ’s birth and death.

I pass over the fact that he is the voice crying in the wilderness, the herald of the Word, the Forerunner of the Judge. I likewise leave aside that the Law and the Prophets were until John; that John himself is Elijah; that he is a burning and shining lamp; that he is the Bridegroom’s friend and the bride’s preparer. I pass over in silence [Col. 1002B] that he was so admitted among the nine orders of angels as even to be raised to the summit of the Seraphim. But this is a work so laborious that the poverty of our understanding is unequal to it. Let these things that have been said at present concerning John’s praise suffice for the glory of the Redeemer, who is blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 1001]

682. SERMON FOR THE ASSUMPTION OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY. SERMON G)

[NOTE.]

This sermon, formerly the fifth among Bernard’s Sermons on the Assumption of the Virgin Mother of God, has seemed fit to be assigned to this place, since in the manuscripts it does not occur among the genuine sermons of the holy Father. It is nevertheless found again among the doubtful works in the Lyons edition of 1514. It closely imitates Bernard’s third sermon on the Dedication of a Church.

On the Gospel of Luke, “Jesus entered into a certain village,” etc. (Chapter 10, verses 38–42.)

[Col. 1001C]

1. What our Lord and Savior once deigned visibly to do at that time and in one place, he now also works daily, invisibly, everywhere throughout the world in the hearts of the elect. For, as the Gospel speaks, we have heard that Jesus entered into a certain village, and a woman named Martha received him—and the rest.

But what is this fortress except the human heart, which, before the Lord comes to it, is surrounded by the ditch of desire, enclosed by the wall of obstinacy, and raises within its broad interior expanse a Babylonian tower? Three things are especially necessary in every town: provisions, by which its inhabitants are sustained; a fortification, by which they are protected; and weapons, by which they resist enemies.

Thus the inhabitants of this fortress have as their sustenance bodily pleasure and the vanity of the world, on which they feed. They also have the hardness of their own heart as that by which they are covered, so that they can scarcely, or never, be pierced by the mighty arrows of God’s word. They are girded with weapons, namely the arguments of carnal wisdom, with which they fight against enemies. Hence it is written: “The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16:8).

[Col. 1002C] 2. But when Christ visits and enters, this fortress is overthrown, and in its place another is built—new, beautiful, and spiritual. Thus is fulfilled what is said: “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creature; the old things have passed away, and behold, all things have become new” (2 Cor. 5:17).

For when desire has been removed, a vast capacity for longing is expanded, so that at Christ’s coming the mind pants much more eagerly for heavenly things than it previously had clung to earthly ones. The wall of self-restraint is now erected, and the outer wall is patience. This work rises from the foundation of faith and grows through love of neighbor up to the love of God, which is on the upper level and upon the battlements of that wall. For self-restraint is then perfect virtue when, living together with our neighbors in the unity of faith, we restrain ourselves from sins not through fear of punishment or desire for human praise, but solely for the sake of divine love.

Or certainly the love of God—that is, the love by which he loves us—seems to be above the wall in order to signify that he fights for his self-restrained people; and because self-restraint cannot resist the frequent and powerful blows of the tempter unless it is protected by his grace. Therefore patience is placed as an outer wall, lest the devil have easy access to attack self-restraint.

Those, then, who live in self-restraint under patience’s protection fittingly protest and say with the Apostle: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or peril? Or the sword?” You see how solid is the wall of the self-restrained: neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities nor powers nor virtues, neither things present nor things to come, neither strength nor height nor depth nor any creature can separate them from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:35, 38–39).

3. But now let us knock at its gates—the gates, namely, of righteousness—that they may be opened to us; and, entering through them, let us behold within the great works of the Lord, sought out in all His purposes. For there, through His working, that evangelical tower is built, as it were upon Mount Zion, by which the saints, with humbled heart, ascend into heaven from the valley of weeping. They ascend, I say, not by their own strength, but by God’s help and grace, as the Holy Spirit says through the prophet David: “Blessed is the man whose help is from thee; he has disposed ascents in his heart.” You ask, where? “In the valley of weeping,” that is, in the humility of the present life. And he repeats this same grace, saying: “For the lawgiver will give a blessing.” But immediately afterward he adds how far that ascent reaches, and to what fruit grace itself brings those who ascend: “They shall go,” he says, “from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. 83:6–8).

This is the reward, the end, and the fruit of our labor: namely, the vision of God. Who would not incomparably prefer this one fruit to all things visible and invisible? Whose breast, however cold, would not this desire inflame? For this is that grace commended to us by blessed John the Evangelist when he says: “And of his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace” (John 1:16).

4. From these words it is understood that we have received three kinds of grace from God: one by which we are converted; another by which we are helped in temptations; a third by which, having been proved, we are rewarded. The first initiates us, by which we are called; the second advances us, by which we are justified; the third completes us, by which we are glorified. The first, indeed, is good pleasure; the second, [Col. 1003D] merit; the third, reward. Of the first it was said: “And of his fullness we have all received.” Of the two remaining it was said: “And grace for grace,” that is, the gifts of eternal glory in return for the merit of temporal warfare.

Let the first grace, then, be in the wall of continence to which we are called; let the second be in the ascent of the tower which we climb; let the third be at its summit, to which we arrive. Here, therefore—that is, at this summit—when those who make good progress arrive there, they become a place and dwelling for the Lord, such as those of whom it is written: “For thither the tribes ascended, the tribes of the Lord, a testimony to Israel, to confess the name of the Lord: because there seats sat in judgment” (Ps. 121:4–5).

And indeed, while they were still on the wall of continence and stood in battle array, they could be attacked, and at first God was known in Judaea as a helper. But when they now stand in this station, where they contemplate the Lord, “his name is great in Israel, and his place has been made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion.” There “he broke the powers of bows, shield and sword and war,” because there no movement of the flesh resists, but it is wholly subjected to the spirit. The Prophet ardently desired this place when he said: “If I give sleep to my eyes, or slumber to my eyelids, or rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord” (Ps. 131:4). Desiring also to fly there, he says: “Who will give me wings like a dove, and I shall fly and be at rest?” (Ps. 54:7).

5. Now if inquiry is made concerning the inhabitants of this little fortress—what food they have for sustenance, what defense for protection, or what arms are available for resistance—we may answer quite reasonably that, just as works of the flesh were food for the carnal, so for these a much better food is the fruit of the Spirit. Their food also is to do the will of the almighty Father. Their food is the word of God, by which all the saints, both human beings and angels, are fed. Hence it is written: “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. 8:3; Matt. 4:4).

Their defense is, as has been said, the wall of continence and the outer wall of patience. Against their enemies they possess the arms described by the Apostle: the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6:13–17). Let no one be troubled [Col. 1004C] that I have said the same word is both food and sword, as though this were impossible or absurd. In material things, this is one thing and that another; one is sought in one place, another elsewhere. But in spiritual things this is not other than that, nor is one sought in one place and another elsewhere; rather, all things are for us in God, and God is all things in all.

For behold, in the nature of things, what is more different than bread and stone? Yet if you refer them to mystical understanding, both signify the same thing. For the same Christ is called both bread and stone: living bread, namely (John 6:35), and “the stone rejected by the builders” (Acts 4:11). Both are so by signification, though neither is so in its proper sense.
