It follows: “And the lord praised the steward of iniquity because he had acted prudently.” Some wonder whence this praise arose, since he is not said literally to have paid the debt, but to have reduced it. Whoever does such a thing should consider that he ought rather to imitate the steward than marvel at him. For he acted prudently in a worldly manner: what he could not repay, he cautiously concealed, lest he be accused of theft concerning it; and, in the words of someone who says, “If not chastely, at least cautiously”—for it is a lesser fault for anyone to deliver himself alone to death than to carry others away with him by the contagion of sin—[Col. 1029D] he did what was highly beneficial and supremely prudent for himself, because he arranged that there should be persons with whom he would be received if he were removed from the stewardship.

But let me speak more deeply. According to the moral sense, one is entirely worthy of much praise when, abandoning the error of his former manner of life, he makes satisfaction to the rich God and returns to grace. And for this reason the lord praised him: whether he is said to have acted in this way or in that way, he acted prudently. Nor should anyone be troubled because he is called “of iniquity.” The expression is used not because he acts in a praiseworthy manner, but to remove the despair of those who heard it, as the Lord testifies when he says through the Prophet: “Their infirmities were multiplied; afterwards they hastened. I will not gather their assemblies from blood, nor will I remember their names with my lips” (Ps. 15:4). For this reason Matthew retained his surname, “the Publican.”

What follows—“the children of this age are more prudent in their generation than the children of light”—was said to us so that we might imitate the otherwise useless prudence of worldly people. Moses teaches us this mystically when he says: “When you go out to battle, if you see a beautiful woman and love her, shave her hair,” and so forth, “and she shall be your wife” (Deut. 21:10–13). It was likewise said for our great shame, as if the prophet had said to us: “Be ashamed, Sidon, says the sea” (Isa. 23:4). For we ought indeed to be greatly ashamed that the children of perdition are more prompt in pursuing evils than we are in seeking heavenly joys. Of these blessed Gregory says: “Whoever has perfectly known, so far as capacity permits, the sweetness of heavenly life, willingly leaves behind all that he had loved on earth.”

13. We are urged to this when it is said: “Make for yourselves friends from the mammon of iniquity, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into eternal dwellings.” A good saying, worthy of all acceptance, teaching us to join friendship with those who can place us with themselves in eternal dwellings. And who are these, if not those whom I briefly noted above: Christ’s little ones and poor? Since the Lord loves them—as he himself testifies when he says, “You are my friends” (John 15:14)—let us make them love us by means of that concerning which the same Lord taught us, when he said, “from the mammon of iniquity.”

The price is low, but the purchase is great. For *mammon* is the name given to riches, which are called iniquitous not in themselves, [Col. 1030C] but because of the effect of iniquity that arises from them. So too that tree was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, not because it possessed any knowledge, but because those who touched it contrary to the commandment would become acquainted with both good and evil. This sufficiently shows how easily friends among the citizens above may be obtained. Truth then shows what fruit comes to us from their friendship when he says: “That they may receive you into eternal dwellings.”

A question seems to arise here, because receiving and repaying those who do good to them are attributed to the poor, although this gift belongs to God alone and comes from his abundant compassion and grace. The question is very easily resolved if one considers that the Son of God, taking our flesh, became poor for us; that he declares what is distributed to the poor to have been done to himself; and that he will repay those who do good. He testifies to this when, speaking of the little ones, he says: “Whatever you did to one of my least ones, you did to me. I was hungry and you gave me food; I was thirsty and you gave me drink,” and so forth. “Come, therefore, and receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34–40).

14. Let us therefore be diligent, my brothers, let us be diligent in distributing to the poor, according to the Lord’s counsel. But because one poor person differs from another—as the Lord seems to have indicated there when he said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit”—we must distinguish the kinds of poverty so as to indicate to whom we ought especially to give. Poverty, then, is one thing when natural, another when wealthy, another when spiritual. [Col. 1031A] Each member of this division is itself subdivided in two ways. We leave this to those who know how to draw great matters from small ones. We say only this: we are urged especially to extend the hand of mercy to those naturally needy and to the spiritual poor, in the words of the Apostle Paul: “Whoever does not provide for his own, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. 5:8).

But because today we do not know who is worthy of hatred or love before God’s eyes, let us give to these and give to those, according to the voice of the same Apostle: “Let us do good,” he says, “to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6:10). And because there are those who ask and those who are ashamed to ask, when there is enough to give, let us give to both. For the Lord says of those who ask: “Give to everyone who asks you” (Luke 6:30). Of those who are ashamed, blessed Augustine says on the verse, “Who brings forth grass for the cattle and plants for the service of men” (Ps. 103:14), as follows: “Blessed is he who anticipates the voice of one about to ask” (*Expositions on Psalm 103*, sermon 3, §10). [Col. 1031B; Col. 1032A]

Of all people without distinction the Lord says: “Give, and it shall be given to you” (Luke 6:38); and also: “Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you” (Luke 11:41); and again: “Water extinguishes a blazing fire, and almsgiving resists sins” (Ecclus. 3:33); hence also: “Store up almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will pray for you” (Ecclus. 29:15). And a good father says to his son: “If you have much, give abundantly in return; if little, share even that gladly” (Tob. 4:9). Let us strive to do all these things with such diligence [the printed text uncertainly suggests *omnes*, “everyone,” rather than *omnia*, “all things”] that we may deserve to be received into the eternal dwellings through our Lord Jesus Christ, [Col. 1032B] our Saviour, who lives and reigns as God with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1031]

702. SERMON on Wisdom 7:30 and 8:1: “Wisdom conquers malice. Therefore she reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things sweetly.” (G)

[NOTE.]

This is not Bernard’s; rather, as I think, it is by Guibert, abbot of Nogent, who delivered an extended sermon on that passage of Wisdom, from book 1, chapter 16, of *His Life*.

[Col. 1031C] 1. As wisdom is called the taste of good, so malice is called the taste of evil. One nail is driven out by another; so wicked things are removed when good things come upon them. For by the power and Wisdom of the Father—Christ Jesus, mediator between God and human beings, undergoing the cross for us—our old human being was crucified with him, according to the Apostle, “that the body of sin might be destroyed” (Rom. 6:6).

What, then, shall I call the body of sin? I rightly call it the image which the stone cut from the mountain without hands struck and shattered. Its head was gold, while its other limbs are described as being partly silver, partly bronze, partly iron, and partly clay mixed with iron (Dan. 2:32–34). The head is malice, which above we called the taste of evil; hence it is expressed by gold, by which wisdom is doubtless signified in the Scriptures. The middle of the body—that is, the breast and arms—is said to have been silver. Silver is bright and resonant: its resonance delights the hearing, and its brightness pleases the sight. Thus curiosity is signified by it, for curiosity is especially vigorous in these two senses, sight and hearing, because through them, being the principal windows of the body, death more frequently and readily enters our souls.

By the belly and thighs, where lust rules, pleasure is signified. These are described as bronze, 703 likewise bright and resonant, because the frenzy of malice has burned so fiercely that shameful and defiled people are accustomed not merely to delight in filthiness but even to boast in disgrace. They “rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2:14). By their evil example they corrupt both those far away and those near: their neighbours by wicked conduct, the distant by the evil reputation of that conduct; shining in the eyes of the former and sounding in the ears of the latter. [Col. 1032C]

The shins, which support the mass of the body, are called iron. “Scale is joined to scale” (Job 41:6–7), and a perverse will, hardened like iron, sustains the entire structure of sin. Why do you sin? Because you do not know what you are doing? Far from it. Because you are compelled to do it? Far from it. Rather, because you like to act thus. Therefore, the desire of the will, steeped and choked in the devil’s poison—the tinder of crime and venom of wickedness—is the only thing that stops the ears from hearing “the voice of charmers and of the enchanter who charms wisely.”

By the feet, partly iron and partly clay, are signified the works of darkness by which people become known. Clay and iron do not adhere well to each other. By clay is signified the uncleanness of works; by iron, the obstinacy of the mind. Though joined together for a time, they cannot remain joined for long. For “you spend your days in prosperity, yet in a moment you descend into hell” (Job 21:13). [Col. 1032D]

2. Therefore the stone first crushed the feet, because Jesus Christ, our strength and foundation, gives to his voice a voice of power. Hence the thunder of his voice, made in power, shakes the inward parts and breaks the mind’s obstinacy through fear. Then, once the sinner has been torn away from the vanity of the world, he destroys works through confession; next, by implanting good desires and fulfilling them in good deeds, he heals the will. Under the yoke of discipline, by stopping the ears so that they may not hear blood and closing the eyes so that they may not see evil, he drives out curiosity. Thus at last the person wise and pleasing to God shatters the statue’s golden head, when he utterly plucks from the soul’s inmost parts the taste of evil which we called malice.

Wisdom conquers malice. For one to whom Christ begins to be sweet must surely find the world bitter. He is the bread which comes down from heaven, containing every delight and sweetness of taste. He is the taste of the Father through that eternal and ineffable nature; the taste of angels through grace; our taste through mercy. [Col. 1033A–B]

3. Wisdom conquers, therefore; but let us see how. “She reaches mightily from end to end and disposes all things sweetly.” There must therefore be found at least two ends, positioned on either side, which mediating wisdom reaches. Let us seek these ends in the Gospel parables: those, namely, in which first there is discussion of the treasure which, when a man finds it, he sells all he has and buys that field. Afterwards follows the precious pearl which the merchant, finding it, purchases after selling all that he possesses. Finally, there is discussion of the net cast into the sea, which gathers good and bad fish (Matt. 13:44–48). Let us examine these likenesses more diligently, that from them the truth proposed may be elicited.

The field of which the first parable speaks is the discipline of the Order. A field is cultivated land which, when the bushes have been cut down and the roots of trees uprooted, is fit to receive seed and bear fruit. Such is the discipline of the Order, which, after the thorns of sins have been pulled out and occasions of scandal removed, is indeed worthy for God to send forth his word into it. In it, surely, his word is not bound; but, impediments having been removed, his saying runs swiftly through the humble and meek in heart. This is the full field which the Lord has blessed (Gen. 27:27), having upper irrigation [Col. 1033D] and lower irrigation (Judg. 1:15): certainly, the fountains of Israel, by which the Lord is blessed in the churches.

These are the fountains of the Saviour: one is divinity, namely the upper irrigation; the other humanity, namely the lower irrigation. From the fountain of humanity we drink the waters of confidence, because through it we have access to the Father through confidence in faith in him. From the fountain of divinity flow waters of mercy, whose stream gladdens the city of God—gladdening it fully in heaven, and on earth according to the measure of faith God has apportioned to each. 704 Christ Jesus sprang from the hidden places of the Prophets into the fields of the poor. Through the merits of his humanity he grants, as a reward, participation in his divinity. For he will give us peace by transferring [Col. 1034A] us into the hidden depths of his divinity, because in the humility of his humanity he has wrought all our works for us. If, therefore, his humanity has wrought our salvation, what does his divinity work? Certainly our delight, because “delights are at his right hand for ever” (Ps. 15:11).

4. Those labouring in the field of poverty therefore have two irrigations, by which the dryness of their hearts is watered and the barrenness of our earth made fruitful. Without the refreshment of these waters, there would surely be no possibility of making progress; rather, necessity would press upon us to fail. For when, returning to yourself, you consider on the one hand the power of offended majesty and on the other the obstinacy of offending iniquity, would not despair immediately steal in, unless the incarnation and passion of Jesus Christ, the man who is mediator between God and human beings, came to your aid? But when the tribulations of the world and attacks of the devil come upon you, and storms of temptation rise upon the plain of your mind, would you not succumb to the sufferings of this present time unless the hope of future glory sustained you?

Therefore, just as in Christ’s humanity you have merits in which you may trust and not despair, so in his divinity there are rewards in the expectation of which you may not only breathe amid tribulations but even glory. For he has shown us his mercy not only by forgiving debts but also by promising rewards. “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” For all, indeed, that he has bestowed on me for my conversion? In my very conversion he has rendered me my body [Col. 1034C] and my soul—indeed, restored them; indeed, though I was sluggish and resisting, he himself wrested me from myself.

But for all that he has given me from the beginning of my conversion—compunction of tears, devotion in meditations, consolation in labours, delight in meditations—for these, I say, and innumerable other benefits, what shall I in turn render him? He who has given all, what more have I to offer? “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 115:12–13). What is it, “I will take the cup”? “My soul desires you in the night; my spirit also within my inmost heart. Your name and your memorial are in the desire of my soul” (Isa. 26:9, 8).

The name of my Saviour, my brothers—the name of my flesh, [Col. 1034D] of my blood; the name hidden from the ages but revealed at the end of the ages; the wonderful name, the ineffable name, the inestimable name—or rather, the more wonderful because more inestimable, the more welcome because gratuitous. This name, I say, I shall praise with my lips, no longer living myself, but with Christ living in me; so that my soul may be filled as with marrow and fatness, and that I may call upon the name of the Lord not only with outward but also with inward lips. For whoever does not merely call, but invokes, the name of the Lord shall be saved (Joel 2:32). Let not only the name, but also the memorial of his passion, always be in the desire of my soul, that I may become a participant in his passion, if somehow I may know as I am known.

[Col. 1035A] 5. Thus I shall take his cup, because I shall always turn over the memorials of his passion within my soul’s bosom, within the chambers of my memory. I shall behold King Solomon in the crown with which his mother crowned him (Song 3:11). I shall behold him bound, scourged, spat upon, filled with reproaches, and nailed fast. In this wilderness of exile I shall behold the bronze serpent raised upon the pillar of the cross, so that the serpents which bite me may die; for no one who believes in him shall perish but shall have eternal life (Num. 21:9; John 3:14–15). These and other memorials of my Lord suffering and dying I shall commend more closely to my memory; bringing them back to the mouth of thought, I shall chew them over at length, that I may be more richly nourished in devotion.

Let these signs of his cross and passion, I say, be present, so that his left hand of love—than which none has ever had greater—may be under my head, lest my mind bend down toward carnal desires, until the right hand of his divinity embraces me (Song 2:6); so that “what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:4), and this mortal may put on immortality and this corruptible incorruption (1 Cor. 15:53). [Col. 1035B]

By the left hand here I understand his humanity, in which he displayed to us the charity, as we have said, than which none has greater, laying down his life even for his enemies. The right hand is divinity, by which I desire to be embraced and surrounded. “Then,” he says, “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:13); and: “You will fill me with joy in your presence, because delights are at your right hand for ever” (Ps. 15:11). [Col. 1035C]

6. But as much as the right hand surpasses the left—namely, as eternal things surpass transient, incorruptible things corruptible, immortal things mortal—so much greater must be the charity which he will show us in the glory of his divinity than the charity which he showed us in the misery of his humanity. For the latter “eye has seen, ear has heard, and it has entered into the heart of man”—not that which he has prepared for those who love him. Yet what is that charity? Listen. Although no one has greater love than this, that one lay down his life for his friends (John 15:13), he nevertheless laid down his own life for enemies. For while we were still enemies, he reconciled us to God in his blood (Rom. 5:10). If man did this, what will God do? If the poor man did this, what will the rich man do? If he did this for enemies, what will he do for friends? If he did this on the way, what will he do in the homeland? If he did this in exile, what will he do in the palace? If he did this on earth, where his own did not receive him, what will he do in heaven, where all obey him?

If at any time we are drawn back, by the devil’s suggestions or the importunate cries of our flesh, to care for the flesh in fulfilment of its desires, let us set before our eyes Christ’s anxieties and the punishment of the cross; and at once experience itself will teach us what the Apostle meant when he said: “The word of the cross is the power of God to those who are being saved” (1 Cor. 1:18); and, “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14). Why? Because, as wax flows away before fire, so every impurity perishes before the cross. For God’s weakness is our strength, and in his foolishness we have been made wise. Since the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe (1 Cor. 1:21). “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). He became flesh for those who are fleshly, just as he is spirit for angelic spirits. Let flesh recognize him in the flesh, man in the man. Let it recognize him, I say, and imitate him, that it may deserve to see him in majesty, because through humility it will reach sublimity. “For if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him; if we die with him, we shall also live with him” (Rom. 8:17; 2 Tim. 2:11–12).

Let us recognize him according to the flesh, until, with the movements of the flesh trodden down and all fleshly desires extinguished or conquered, we can say with the Apostle: “Even if we have known him according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer” (2 Cor. 5:16). For although it is glorious to see, or to hold in memory, even according to the flesh, him who is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men, still his flesh is set before us more for healing than for glory, more for need than for blessedness. For another blessedness has been bestowed upon the soul, for which no created thing can suffice, even if it possessed heaven together with earth. Nor can its desire be satisfied until it possesses him whose image it is, who alone can fill every recess of its longing.

7. Now just as our Mediator joined two natures, humanity and divinity, in one person, so each of his works must belong to one nature or the other. Misery belongs to the former, power to the latter. Whatever he suffered in misery, therefore, he derived from man; whatever he worked in power, he had from the Father. With humanity and divinity thus placed on either side, you have two middle things: the Passion and the Resurrection. The former belongs to mercy and misery; the latter to power.

Do you wish to be proclaimed among the wings of the dove—that is, among the perfect members of holy Church, by whose example the weak are strengthened and the downcast raised up? You must sleep between the two lots, that is, between the Passion and the Resurrection, here surrounded by fruits, there supported by flowers. Fruits pertain to the Passion; flowers to the Resurrection. “What a man sows, that shall he also reap. He who sows in the flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh” (Gal. 6:8). The old man sowed in the flesh and afterward reaped corruption. What corruption? Christ’s Passion. For unless the old man had transgressed, the new man would not have suffered. O deep and inscrutable counsel of our redemption! Truly, “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Rom. 8:28).

Lord Jesus Christ, if Adam’s disobedience worked together for our good—and for a good so great and so wonderful that you became corruptible—into what good will your obedience work together for us? Surely, that man may become incorruptible. If, by sowing in the flesh, we reaped your corruption, by sowing in the Spirit we shall reap our own incorruption.

8. Therefore the fruit of all the times which we spent in the manner of life of the old man is Christ’s Passion, to which we ought to be conformed, carrying his mortification in our mortal flesh. Hence, as from the beginning of his life, so from the beginning of his preaching, he set repentance before us: “Repent,” he says, “for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matt. 3:2). He had experienced great refreshment who said of the fruit of repentance: “My tears became my bread day and night” (Ps. 41:4); and elsewhere: “You will feed us with the bread of tears, and give us drink in tears by measure” (Ps. 79:6); and again: “You have given us wine of compunction to drink” (Ps. 59:5).

Why, then, should I not call repentance a harvest or fruit, since it is called bread and wine? This fruit is bitter, but health-giving; for repentance is indeed bitter to endure, but most healthful for recovery. Therefore let the faithful soul, desiring to forget what lies behind and to stretch forward to what lies before, desire to be surrounded and strengthened by these fruits, so that, with them interposed, it cannot turn back toward worldly desires and the enticements of the flesh.

But just as, in recalling the temporality of our old state, we have repentance as its end and fruit, so, in meditating beforehand upon the eternity of our new state, we feel a certain fragrance of joys, rightly compared to flowers. For when the flower is seen, hope of fruit is conceived; likewise, through this foretaste of joys we are encouraged more surely to await things to come. “For what we do not see, we hope for; and through patience we await it” (Rom. 8:25). Thus compunction is the fruit of time past; devotion is the flower of the age to come.

9. You must therefore sleep between the two lots, that is, between the Passion and the Resurrection; between fruit and flower, between compunction and devotion. Who are those who sleep? Those who weep as though not weeping; who rejoice as though not rejoicing; who use this world as though not using it (1 Cor. 7:30–31); who, “as deceivers and yet true, as unknown and yet known, through dishonour and good report” (2 Cor. 6:8), pass through both the prosperity and adversity of this life as though they did not feel them.

Blessed indeed is the people to whom a sabbath-rest has been left even in this world. One who sleeps lies exposed, taking no care for himself, and yet rests. So too, casting all our care upon him (1 Pet. 5:7), let us lie open alike in adversity and prosperity, rejoicing under his guidance over smooth paths and rough alike. For this reason he bowed the heavens and came down: that he might bring us back into the straight way, so that we might go from the place of pilgrimage to the city of habitation.

If this way is steep and narrow, do not fail, for by so much it is safer and straighter. Moreover, your guide is strong and merciful, certainly ready, in your weakness, to place you upon his sacred shoulders and carry you back to the flock; for he who is your guide and Lord is also your ass. “Issachar is a strong ass” (Gen. 49:14), and “the hinder parts of his back are in the pallor of gold” (Ps. 67:14). He is our back, upon whom burdens too heavy for the other members are laid; just as he himself is also our scapegoat, upon whom our sins were laid (Lev. 16:8–10), because “he truly bore our infirmities, and himself carried our sorrows” (Isa. 53:4).

Therefore, by turning Christ’s Passion over in our memory, let us regard every blandishment of the world as dung, that we may be conformed to Christ’s sufferings. And by firmly holding, in hope, the glory of the Resurrection, let us not fail, but glory in tribulations; for “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that shall be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:18).

10. The field of poverty, therefore, is rightly called full: spring adorns it with flowers, while autumn fills it with fruits. The Father rightly compares his Son to it, saying: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a full field” (Gen. 27:27). In him, indeed, every perfection of poverty and the fullness of virtues overflowed, so that “from his fullness we have all received” (John 1:16). For though he was rich, for our sakes he became poor, that by his poverty we might be enriched (2 Cor. 8:9).

This field, watered with streams, fragrant with flowers, and abundant in fruits, has a treasure hidden within it: namely, continence of the flesh. It is indeed a precious treasure to possess one’s vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of desire like the Gentiles who do not know God (1 Thess. 4:4–5). Do not seek this treasure among the thorns and briars of worldly enticement, nor in the forests of ancient brutishness. It is hidden not in a forest but in a field. Seek it in the field, where the trees of the countryside are satisfied and where sparrows build their nests: that is, where the incontinent come to their senses by producing fruits worthy of repentance; where they bring forth offspring, making progress not only for themselves but for others also.

Believe continence necessary for you, so that the Holy Spirit may become in you a fountain of water springing up into eternal life. Water does not spring upward unless it first comes from above. “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1:17). Therefore that which springs up into eternal life surely descends from eternal life. Thus, although water comes from above, unless it has a channel that is continent and whole, it does not return upward, but flows away. The Holy Spirit descends into you and gives life to your soul, that he may spring up in you into eternal life. Your body must be continent, so that you may “stop your ears lest you hear blood, and shut your eyes lest you see evil” (Isa. 33:15), lest the grace granted to you from above flow outward through your insufficiently guarded senses, while your spirit is poured out into vanities and false madnesses.

11. Observe that to be continent is one thing, to be chaste another. The luxurious person and the chaste person are opposites. It belongs to the luxurious person both to feel impulses and to consent to them; to the chaste person neither to feel impulses nor to consent to them. The continent person stands in the middle, sharing in both: with the one, the feeling of impulses; with the other, the refusal of consent to impulses.

This person, standing in the midst of the house, placed below in relation to the luxurious person but above in relation to the modest person, though he does not walk in purity of flesh, nevertheless sings of mercy and judgment in innocence of heart. Judgment, because he feels impulses; mercy, because he does not consent to them. Such a one, unwilling at the dawning of the new light to release the Angel of Great Counsel, but earnestly seeking the blessing of perseverance, deserves, if not to be wholly deprived, at least to limp on one foot (Gen. 32:24–32).

What are the two feet? To feel impulses and to consent to impulses. The former is natural; the latter culpable. Although, therefore, he cannot yet be unaware of the perverse impulses of desire, and this foot still remains vigorous in him, nevertheless through the grace of the heavenly blessing the foot of consent is so weakened in him that, even if it draws him, he cannot lean upon it. He is not wholly without it, because when a sudden thought arises, a certain pleasure frequently accompanies it; yet, once felt, it draws from him a groan rather than consent.

12. Having found such a treasure in the field of poverty, go, that the treasure may become your possession; sell all that you have and buy that field. What does “sell all that you have” mean? Renounce everything you possess; go out to Jesus outside the camp, that you may bear the reproach of his cross. Thus, by the merit of such great humility, coming out from the forest in which are entangled the paths of the wicked who walk round about (Ps. 11:9), you may possess the field of which we have spoken. There, having cast aside worldly occupations and cares, with body composed and heart enlarged, you may run eagerly in the way of God’s commandments, which are desirable and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Why? Because “in keeping them there is great reward” (Ps. 18:11–12). Truly great, because eternal life is owed to those who keep them. Hence Truth says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17).

At this degree of continence, in which you restrain what delights you and do what does not delight you, great tribulation lies upon you; for while reason resists your will, an inward war is waged. Therefore do not grow sluggish, but lift your eyes to him who dwells in heaven, from whom help will come to you, so that you may not only endure but even glory in tribulations. Yet this cannot happen otherwise than if God becomes sweet to you.

13. You must therefore seek wisdom, through which God becomes sweet to you and the world tasteless; wisdom which is signified by the precious pearl, which, when a man finds it, he goes and sells all that he has and buys it (Matt. 13:45–46). Would that you tasted and saw how sweet the Lord is! Would that you tasted the bread which came down from heaven, containing every delight and sweetness of flavour! (Wis. 16:20.) Surely, if you had anything, you would sell it and buy it.

But what have you to sell, you who sold all that you possessed in order to buy the field of poverty, in which you found the treasure of continence? Consider whether perhaps you have a double possession: one inward, the other outward. Outward possession is worldly wealth; inward possession is one’s own will. You renounced worldly wealth by going out to Jesus outside the camp of this world. Yet, still unformed and wrapped in the darkness of your old state, you had not understood the vice of your own will; and this assuredly is not abandoned whenever external renunciation is made. For property is left more swiftly and easily than desire is lost. Hence the Lord calls blessed not just any poor persons, but “the poor in spirit” (Matt. 5:3). Who are they? Certainly not all who possess nothing, but those who love poverty.

14. Thus external renunciation without inward renunciation, whether accompanying it or following it, profits very little—indeed, nothing. For one’s own will fights against God and raises itself against him. It is that which despoils paradise and enriches hell; which empties the blood of Christ of effect and subjects the world to the dominion of the devil.

See how one’s own will opposes God. “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24). You cannot obey both the divine will and your own will at once. For if your will agrees with the divine will, it is no longer your own will but a common will: it belongs not merely to man, but to man and God. Yet you are necessarily bound to God’s will by the debt of your creation. Why? Because God’s will alone is the reason why he created and re-created you, as the Apostle James says: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth” (Jas. 1:18). You do what you owe when you obey him. You also faithfully discharge the obligation of virtue when you both desire his will and keep it in obedience.

But behold: while the devil deceives you and the world seduces your senses, you go out curiously toward things outside. When you are drawn by the concupiscence of your own will to delight in them, you in some measure renounce God, as though, in denying him, you said: “Thus far I have served you; I have done your will. But henceforth place no confidence in me, for I have resolved to serve another master and keep faith with him.” Behold: by the iniquity of your own will you have denied your God. Yet that denial itself does not suffice you; rather, becoming afterward a most shameless robber, you violently ravage his possessions, both food and clothing, which he prepared not for his despisers but for his servants, shamelessly abusing them to the injury of so great a majesty.

If you are in a monastery, you eat nothing, drink nothing, wear nothing, that you do not first take away. And while you seize provisions from the sacristy, you join sacrilege to theft. Yet you approach the altar, and, handling the Lord’s body and blood, find nothing criminal in yourself—though, if truth is closely investigated, you are proved to have denied God and shown to be a thief and sacrilegious person.

A third thing follows, and it is the gravest: him whom you have denied and plundered, you finally attempt to kill. For while remaining in your iniquity, you wish your sin to go unpunished, in which you wish God to be unjust. His justice requires that he render to each according to his works (Rom. 2:6). Whoever wishes God to be unjust wishes God not to be God. And whoever desires God not to be, does he not, so far as lies within him, kill God himself?

15. Therefore, you who sold your outward possession in order to buy the hidden treasure of continence in the field of regular discipline, go and sell your inward possession as well—far more burdensome to abandon, and altogether ruinous to retain—that you may acquire the precious pearl of wisdom. Whoever finds it is blessed if he holds it fast. Do you wish to possess it? Keep the commandments. For it is written: “Have you desired wisdom? Keep the commandments, and the Lord will give her to you” (Ecclus. 1:33). Devote obedience, then, and you will receive wisdom. For how can we please God, or how can he be sweet to us, if we scorn to obey his commandments?

Hence he immediately sets divine commandments to be kept before the young man questioning him in the Gospel (Matt. 19:17), showing that we must do the will of him from whom we hope for eternal recompense. Accordingly he says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21); and elsewhere: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

You must advance in this order. Cannot you be continent in the world? Flee the world and embrace discipline, where you will indeed find continence. Then, after the fleshly desires have been slain through confession, you will be able more freely to judge the vices of the soul, from whose roots shoots of shameful deeds spring up and grow into a complete body of foulness. The Apostle calls these vices of the soul “spiritual wickednesses” (Eph. 6:12), which you could scarcely discern while you were occupied with fleshly desires and delighted in outward things.

Therefore, after you have lost outward delight, unless you feel inward delight, you cannot stand long. What is it? The visitation of the Holy Spirit. You will find that this is taken from you through your own will. Sell that will by diligently obeying God’s commandments, and in exchange for it you will find eternal life. For Truth says: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17).

16. Behold, you have continence, by which you possess your body in sanctification; you have wisdom, by which you please God in devotion. You have something for yourself and something for God; but what have you for your neighbour? What does the Apostle mean when he says: “Whether we are sober-minded, it is for you; whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Cor. 5:13)? To whom does he speak? He speaks to the neighbour. Therefore, the one who gives his ecstasy to God and his sobriety to his neighbour—what does he keep for himself? “Charity does not seek its own” (1 Cor. 13:5). Why? Because it is not needy: it possesses and overflows.

So you too must have something for your neighbour’s service, that you may prove what is “the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” You prove God’s good will in yourself through continence; his well-pleasing will through wisdom. It remains that you prove his perfect will through mercy, which is signified by the net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind (Matt. 13:47).

For the net of mercy is drawn through the sea of brotherly charity, and gathers both good and bad fish—that is, both bitter and sweet dispositions—conforming itself to all and passing through itself the adversity and prosperity of all, weeping with those who weep and rejoicing with those who rejoice. When it finally reaches the shore—that is, when it is freed from the servitude of this body into the liberty of the glory of the children of God—it will destroy and cast off whatever is bitter, sad, or adverse; for it will then have joy, and everlasting light will shine upon it.

Do not think it absurd that I call the community a sea. For when the breeze of temptation blows, it is often dashed by storms of disturbances. In it are very many who ascend to the heavens through presumption and descend into the abysses through despair; when their soul melts away within them, they are troubled and stagger like drunken men, and all their wisdom—indeed, their conscience—is swallowed up (Ps. 106:26–27). Yet although the liftings of the sea are wondrous, “the Lord is wondrous on high” (Ps. 92:4), because, even if he sometimes endures to sleep in the ship, he nevertheless knows how to rise at the fitting time; and at his command to the waves and sea, a great calm returns.

17. To discover the bounds of wisdom, as we proposed, we set forth three Gospel parables and expounded them as the Lord granted: the first concerning the treasure, the second concerning pearls, the third concerning the net. Now that the density of so great a darkness has been overcome, it is clear how Wisdom “reaches strongly from end to end.” Indeed, according to the course we have followed, wisdom holds, as it were, the middle place, with continence on one side and mercy on the other. It reaches now toward the one, now toward the other, furnishing strength to both.

Luxury attacks continence; avarice attacks mercy. Luxury is a disgraceful vice; avarice is spiritual wickedness. Thus the former is a vice of the body, the latter of the soul. See that no sin defiles the body as luxury does: “Every sin that a man commits is outside his body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18). Likewise, above every sin avarice defiles the soul; hence it is called idolatrous service (Col. 3:5). For it bends down toward the low and needy elements a soul which, subject to the Creator alone, ought to rule over all other things.

Those who persevere in continence, therefore, feel the assaults of luxury, but find in wisdom the strength to resist. For because God becomes sweet to them, and because at times they are granted to taste how sweet the Lord is, they reject that most miserable and foul sweetness of luxury, and find refreshment in him whom they desire within themselves. Likewise, avarice strives to overthrow mercy and, under a seeming appearance of good, forbids the goods of the monastery to be sold for the needs of the sick, as if the monastery must collapse if care is undertaken for the sick. But to those for whom God is sweet, earthly property is not so sweet that they fail to have compassion on the sick.

Avarice, while it urges superfluities, wishes to cut off necessities; but the net of mercy, made from the threads of compassion, both devotes charity to meeting necessities and exercises discernment in rejecting superfluities. Thus wisdom gives virtue and strength to his people: virtue against avarice, strength against luxury. Yet amid so many disturbances and so many distresses it orders matters so that “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. 8:28). Amen.

[Col. 1043]

## SERMON ON THE GOSPEL PARABLE OF THE TEN VIRGINS

It is sufficiently elegant, but does not appear to be Bernard’s. (G)

[Col. 1043B]

“The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins,” etc. (Matt. 25:1–13).

1. The bridegroom is Christ, at whose voice the friend stands and listens, rejoicing with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. The Apostle betrothed us to him when he said: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2). Yet I fear that he may be unable to do what he promised: that is, to present our soul to Christ as a virgin—and as a chaste virgin. He adds “chaste,” because there are certain virgins in body who are deflowered by adulterous thought and defile the sweet-smelling flower of virginity with the shame of lustful affection. These are signified by the five foolish virgins, whom an affection lacking right intention renders foolish.

Christ is a virgin and the Son of a Virgin, and he wishes to have a virgin as his bride. If you possess the grace of angels—indeed, more than this, the grace of Christ and of his mother—rejoice, exult, and, hastening eagerly and yearning for Christ’s embraces, cry out with amorous sighing: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song 1:1).

You are therefore the bride of Jesus Christ; but attend carefully to this name of yours. Grammarians derive the names *sponsa* and *sponsus*, bride and bridegroom, from *spondere*, “to promise.” Bridegroom and bride are so called because they pledge themselves reciprocally to one another, so that neither he nor she may marry another. Now between the day of this betrothal and the wedding there is sometimes a short interval, sometimes a long one; yet the day on which they are to meet is fixed and appointed. This has been wisely and beneficially established, so that meanwhile mutual love may increase and grow, and impatient longing for the desired union may burn more fiercely the longer it is delayed; and so that, since, as Sallust says, “nothing is hurried enough for a desiring mind,” they may desire the appointed day of the wedding to come sooner.

Thus Jacob, from the day of his betrothal, toils for Rachel for seven years; he sleeps beneath the open sky, is chilled by frost, scorched by the sun, and, a vehement lover, does not yield to the hardship of labour so great and so long (Gen. 29:18–28). But to what end is all this? That you too, if you are now Christ’s bride, may burn with love, glow with desire, pant with sighs while the day of the desired union is delayed.

Someone says: “Let every lover grow pale”; let pallor and emaciation be the surest signs of love. What have you to do with rich banquets? What have you to do with wine? This is not for monks. Let the citizens of Babylon feast magnificently. If your bridegroom sees you wasting away, growing pale, burning with impatient longing because of love for him, he will hasten the day of union, offer kisses, and join embraces. O joyful wedding day! O happy bride in such a marriage! Take the kisses, blessed bride; join the embraces; sing: “Behold, what I desired I now see; what I loved I now hold. I am joined in heaven to him whom, while still on earth, I loved with my whole devotion” (*In the Office of St Agnes*).

2. “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins,” whom the King of heaven, should they meet him with shining lamps, will lead into that heavenly bridal chamber, into the sanctuary of the inner room. But what are we to do, since five are foolish and five wise? I think that there are more, and that the multitude of foolish virgins far exceeds the number of prudent ones. Yet all went out, having taken lamps, to meet the bridegroom and bride.

They went out. From where did they go out? Clearly from worldly property and manner of life, according to the words: “Depart, go out from there, and touch no unclean thing” (Isa. 52:11). Abraham too hears: “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. 12:1). Lot likewise is commanded to leave Sodom and forbidden to look back, lest he be caught up together with the Sodomites in their burning fires. But what did he say to the angel? “There is a city nearby to which I can flee; it is small, and I shall be saved in it” (Gen. 19:20). “Is it not a little one, and my soul shall live?” The small and nearby city—that is, not far from the world—in which Lot is saved while Sodom burns, is the monastery. Is it not small in comparison with that city which, occupying the world’s expanse, populous and exceedingly wicked, burns with the fire of greed and lust?

We leave it and flee to the little city nearby, abandoning Sodom, burning with its inhabitants. “I shall be saved in it,” he says. Certainly we shall be saved in this little city if we do not look backward, if the sparks of flaming Sodom, which rightly burns nearby, neither seize nor set us ablaze. From this Sodom the virgins went out to meet the bridegroom and bride; for the flame of the Sodomites is far from virgins.

3. They went out with lamps, with their loins girded and burning lamps in their hands, so that the girdle of chastity may be tightened upon the body and the light of example may shine brightly in action, for the benefit of the neighbour and the glory of the Father. Thus Gideon concealed lamps in jars, but, at the hour of battle, displayed them by breaking the vessels; with their sudden light he terrified the enemy and put them to flight (Judg. 7). For the princes of darkness are terrified when they see the light of good works, because darkness cannot stand before light.

The prudent virgins took oil in their vessels with their lamps. Consider the prudence of these virgins. They knew that the night would be prolonged; and, not knowing at what hour of the night the bridegroom would come, they were not content with the oil in the lamps, but took oil also in vessels, so that if the oil in the lamps should be consumed and fail, they might fill the lamps from what they had stored in vessels to preserve the light.

Oil in the lamp is a good work publicly displayed. But when neighbours see the brightness of the deed, admire and praise it, the worker’s proud mind often grows exalted and rises up; and when it glories in itself rather than in the Lord, the lamp’s light is extinguished. Deprived of suitable fuel, the lamp which shines brightly before people is darkened before the Lord. But the prudent virgins, besides the oil they have in their lamps, store another oil in vessels; for holy souls, while awaiting the coming of their bridegroom and daily crying to him with all desire, “May your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10), perform some works in secret, where the Father alone sees, besides those works which shine for their neighbours to God’s glory and are seen. Thus, if the breath of human praise should extinguish the conspicuous and shining works, the oil of hidden conscience may support them.

This is the glory of the king’s daughter from within: she glories more in the oil that shines in the vessels of conscience than in that which shines outwardly; she judges all that is seen to have perished, and does not consider worthy of reward what is pursued by human favour. Therefore she performs whatever she can secretly, seeks solitude, knocks at heaven by prayers, pours out tears that bear witness to love, and speaks with her beloved in sighs and groans. This is glory—but inward, unseen—of the king’s daughter and beloved. The foolish virgins do not have this oil, because they perform good deeds only for the splendour of vainglory and human favour. This is the oil in which the prudent put their trust, stored in the hidden vessels of their consciences.

4. But while the bridegroom delayed, they all grew drowsy and slept. The good virgins sleep in the Lord, resting sweetly upon Christ’s breast, and await that final morning. “In the morning,” he says, “I will stand before you and behold” (Ps. 5:5). Oh, with what pleasant sleep they are meanwhile lulled, whose flesh rests in hope and whose spirit rejoices in hope! (Isa. 51.)

It is pleasant here to recall that holy Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, while travelling to Rome, came to Autun and turned aside to the tomb of Saint Cassian. Calling him by name, he said: “How do you fare, dearest brother?” And the other replied from the tomb: “Sweetly I rest in peace, and await the coming of the Redeemer.”

> **Note: [Col. 1045D]** Constantine the priest, *Life of St Germanus*, book II, chapter 7, in Surius, 31 July.

Behold the sleep of the prudent virgins, to whom the heavenly Spirit says: “That they may rest from their labours” (Rev. 14:13). But this is not said to the foolish virgins, nor is their intervening sleep of this kind. For they do not rest from their labours: their flesh sees corruption, so that decay enters into their bones and swarms beneath them. This concerns the flesh. But how does the soul, buried in hell, sleep in turmoil? It is set amid torments, parched by thirst, hopes for no drop of refreshment, and, conscious of evil, dreads the day of resurrection and the coming of the Judge.

5. Therefore they all became drowsy and fell asleep. But at midnight a cry arose: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming! Go out to meet him.” O cry sweeter to the prudent virgins than every melody and all musical measures: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming!” Do you suppose that this is the voice of the Son of God, which, when that blessed hour comes, all who are in the tombs will hear, and those who hear will live? (John 5:25.) Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God [Col. 1046C], grant that in that hour my hearing may receive joy and gladness, and that my humbled bones may exult. Let me not then, I pray, Lord, fear the evil report which those will hear to whom you will say: “Depart from me, you cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25:41). Perhaps it will be the voice of that trumpet-sounding archangel, at whose voice and at the last trumpet the Lord will descend from heaven (1 Thess. 4:15). For the trumpet will sound, and at its blast, to use Jerome’s words, the whole world will tremble. Thus the crash of that trumpet, while the angel sounds it and men awaken, will shake even dark Tartarus. The wretched who are there, held in that prison, will hear; then those who now hear and refuse to act will hear: “Go out to meet him.” Great indeed is that cry, because, as the Sibyl says [Note: [Col. 1046D] See Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 23.], when the trumpet [Col. 1046D] sends forth its mournful sound from the high heaven, and the Lord summons heaven above and earth, wishing to distinguish his people before him and separate the prudent virgins from the foolish, he will summon heaven above, so that those powers of heaven may move from their dwelling places and all the angels gather with him for judgment. The Psalmist says, “He will summon heaven above” (Ps. 49:4): that is, the spirits and souls of the righteous, to whom it had previously been said that they should rest a little longer, until the number of their brethren should be fulfilled (Rev. 6:11). Then, leaving that heavenly dwelling, those holy souls restored to their bodies will rejoice all the more securely because more incorruptibly [Col. 1047A].

Then, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, according to Ezekiel, in the field full of bones, the bones of the dead will again be joined bone to bone, sinew to sinew, and joint to joint (Ezek. 37); because the spiritual body will rise which was sown as an animal body (1 Cor. 15:44), and, risen from the dead, will die no more: death will no longer have dominion over it. Then, at that instant, at the dawn of that day, when the bridegroom comes, a great cry will awaken all who sleep and will cry with great and most effectual power: “Go out to meet him.” Go out, sleepers, and hasten to meet the Judge. Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn. Then they will say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” (Luke 23:30). Go out from the tombs, you whom the memory of conscience does not accuse, and behold the Judge [Col. 1047B] with rejoicing, conscious of your good standing and good merit.

6. But the reprobate will be brought forth not so much by their will as by the Judge’s power, and will not so much come out of their tombs as be dragged out. Rightly is that day proclaimed a day of wrath, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom (Zeph. 1:15), on which:

> With the sign of judgment, the earth will be wet with sweat;  
> A stream of fire and sulphur will fall from heaven,  
> And the earth, gaping open, will reveal Tartarean chaos.  
>
> [Note: [Col. 1047D] See Augustine, *City of God*.]

For fire will go before the Lord and will burn his enemies round about (Ps. 96:3; Luke 12:49), whom he will then find, like the Sodomites, naked and uncovered. Thus a flooding rain of fire and sulphur will ignite and burn them as they rise again. Then it will be altogether pitiable to see that the incorruptible and incombustible [Col. 1047C] body burns yet does not perish; it is consumed by fire yet is not diminished. Not even a hair of the head will perish, because nothing of the body which has put on incorruption can either be cut away or burned. Look at the salamander walking bodily unharmed over glowing, burning coals. Moreover, asbestos stone is said to be of such a nature that, once ignited, it burns unquenchably, the fire clinging to the stone without consuming it [Note: [Col. 1047] See Augustine, in the place cited, book XXI, chapters 4–5.]. In such a manner, I think, that sulphurous fire will burn the Lord’s enemies. But it will not touch the righteous at all, just as it did not touch the three Babylonian youths (Dan. 3); nor will it grieve them or inflict any injury, when the Lord reforms the body of our lowliness so that it is conformed to the body of his glory. I ask: what will be the state of mind [Col. 1047D] of sinners amid these things—those who now delight in doing evil and exult in the worst deeds? (Prov. 2:14). What spirit, I say, will they then have, when the elements burn, the earth opens, and its terrible gaping reveals Tartarean chaos; when the dead arise and that Judge comes down from heaven with all the angels—the Judge to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5:22)? Wretched man that I am! While I think and write of these things, my heart pounds with fear, my eyes grow moist, and I would be excessively distressed, if I did not know the mercies of the Lord.

7. But let us return to our subject. Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps—that is, their consciences—by thoughts accusing [Col. 1048A] or even defending them: “I will rebuke you,” he says, “and set you before your face” (Ps. 49:21). While living here, we put our sins behind our backs and, as though no examination of our deeds were to take place before Christ’s tribunal, through negligence consigned many sins to oblivion. But what does he say? “I will set you before your face”: that is, I will bring before the face of your mind your entire life, whatever you have sinned in thought and deed. When you see all these things together, I shall say, “These things you did, and I kept silence.” I think this is what will happen in that hour; this is the judgment that will take place, when Truth—which is Christ—judges in the hearts of each individual. Alas, how many things will then come to mind which we now, considering them nothing at all, leave unconfessed and unpurged! Fearing this, the devout and prudent king Hezekiah said: “I will review all my years in the bitterness of my soul” [Col. 1048B] (Isa. 38:15). “I will review”—that is, I will think again—lest perhaps I have forgotten anything and something remain unjudged and unexamined.

8. The prudent virgins therefore trim their lamps with the oil which they had stored in vessels; but the lamps of the foolish virgins go out, and, because they had performed works of darkness, they remain in darkness. “Give us,” they say, “some of your oil.” A foolish request. “The righteous man is scarcely saved” (1 Pet. 4:18), and even for the saints the oil of their own righteousness scarcely suffices for salvation: how much less for both themselves and their neighbours? Noah, Daniel, and Job will not save even a son; rather, just as the soul that sins shall itself die, so the soul that has done righteousness shall alone be saved [Col. 1048C] (Ezek. 18:4, 20–30). The prudent answered: “Lest there not be enough for us and for you, go instead to the sellers and buy for yourselves.” It is too late: the oil of righteousness is no longer for sale. The prophets and apostles and other teachers, who once used to distribute it and offer it for sale, now rest from such commerce and no longer say: “Take up the psalm and give the timbrel” (Ps. 80:3). What more need be said? Those who were ready entered with him into the wedding feast. Virgins enter the wedding feast, whom the King will bring into his chamber, because he desired their beauty. There, from the heavenly wine-cellar, the new wine is brought out and offered, which the Son of Man will both drink and show forth.

[Col. 1048D] 9. And the door was shut. What door? The one now open to those coming from East and West, that they may recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; the one which says, “The one who comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6:37). See how it now stands open, though then it will be shut forever. Murderers come and are admitted; tax collectors and prostitutes come and are received; Sodomites, effeminate men, adulterers, thieves, and all such persons come, and the open door is not denied them. For he is abundant in forgiveness, surpassing in goodness every evil, whatever and however great it may be. But what does he then say? “The door was shut.” The door of Christ’s loving-kindness and mercy, now easily opened by the tears, [Col. 1049A] groans, sighs, and prayers of penitents, is shut. No one’s repentance, no one’s prayer, no one’s groaning will thereafter be admitted. That door was shut which received Aaron after idolatry, admitted David after adultery and homicide, and after Peter’s threefold denial not only did not [Col. 1050A] reject him, but entrusted his keys to him for keeping. Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour; for the kingdom of heaven is granted to those who watch and pray, not to those who sleep and are slothful, through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1049]

## Nicholas of Clairvaux: Sermon on the Feast of Saint Andrew

[Note: [Col. 1049D] Compare Sermon 40, *On Various Subjects*.]

“With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. 10:10).

[Col. 1049B] 714 1. Both your peaceful application and attentive silence, and the great solemnity of so great a man, urge—indeed compel—me to say something that displays the glory of divinity, the grace of apostolic dignity, and the power of confession. Let us give glory to the praise of him whom all nations praise, who both praises his ministers and makes them praiseworthy. He is the one whom angels stand by, to hear the voice of his utterances; who calls the stars and they say, “Here we are”; whose hand stretches out the heavens; who founded the earth upon its stability; who walks upon the waves of the sea; who alone has wrought wonders; into whom angels desire to look. He is the one who made all things and, in all that he made, did whatever he willed. To serve him is to reign; he who served for us under harsh and grievous necessity, covering the purple [Col. 1049C] of his divinity with the sackcloth of our mortality, came poor and needy into our land. Does it not seem like a game to you, Jews, pagans, heretics, and all that throng of scoffers—or rather madmen—when we say that the Son of God endured flesh, death, nails, and a lance? It is indeed a game through which we are so played with that you are made sport of. That one and only Wise One, not ignorant of this mystery, rehearsed this game in graceful speech: “I was delighted day by day, playing before him in the world of the earth” (Prov. 8:30). For he played before God when, at his command, he took flesh; and in the world of the earth, because, delighting in the redemption of the world, he rejoiced day by day in each of the Apostles, while to one he gives the kingdom of heaven and to another makes his breast a resting-place.

2. “And my delights were to be with the sons of men.” I had thought, Lord Jesus, that your delights were not to be with the sons of men but with the choirs of angels, where, wondrous in the glory of divinity, you strike the eyes of the higher natures—the Thrones and Powers—with reflected splendour; where you inhabit inaccessible light and, by the majesty of your light, veil the encircling host of most radiant lights. But that most merciful compassion and adorable kindness of yours says that its delights are with the sons [Col. 1050B] of men. These are the sons of men who hoped under the shelter of your wings, whom you chose from the people, whose feet you washed, upon whom you poured your Spirit, and who carried the faith of your name in the four-horsed chariots of the Gospels through the fourfold world. Observe, however, that he does not say “with men,” but “with the sons of men.” I think that “men” belong to the old man, while “sons of men” belong to the Son of Man—according to the understanding in which the boy harpist thus sings: “What is man, that you are mindful of him? Or the son of man, that you visit him?” (Ps. 8:5). Do you see that he affirms that God is mindful of man, but visits the son of man? We presume and hope that he will show us his mercy in the sight of the sons of men, provided that meanwhile he protects us [Col. 1050C] in the hiding-place of his face from the disturbance of men. Therefore our Lord also, whose school is on earth and whose chair is in heaven, chose from among all those whom he chose and fore-chose Andrew as apostle, whose feast we celebrate aloud with both voices and hearts. O sweet Apostle and first calling of the Lord and Saviour, distinguished in the apostolic choir itself by the lofty eminence of so great a primacy! It does not escape us that he is in some manner most tender and sweeter in the hearts of the faithful, since his Passion distils with so great a devotion of spirit that it seems to fill the minds of hearers with fatness and richness. Thus, not without reason, it has been received into a unique height of authority: those who saw it wrote it down for the world and were ministers of the word. His calling, his life, and his Passion are known to you: what, then, remains [Col. 1050D] for you to expect further from me?

3. Nevertheless, the apostolic reading moves me to speak of it for a little while to your reverence. For it says: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.” Scripture says: “Everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame.” Three things are set forth here: believing with the heart unto righteousness; confessing with the mouth unto salvation; and believing in him, in whom whoever believes shall not be put to shame. The human heart alone is capable of prayer and receptive of God’s mysteries [Col. 1051A]; once purified and polished, it contemplates the very substance of divinity. Though it does not comprehend it, it nevertheless apprehends it. The heart is in the breast, the soul in the heart, the mind in the soul, faith in the mind, Christ in faith. And this, I think, is what the Apostle means when he says that Christ dwells through faith in our hearts (Eph. 3:17). This, then, has been refined into the purest purity when you grasp by unshaken faith all the mysteries of Christian faith, and nothing causes you doubt, although you do not see the reason. This is consummate righteousness, perfect truth, and true perfection—provided that confession by the mouth follows. For faith of the heart without faith of the mouth is either nonexistent or slight, as the Saviour says: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed” (Luke 9:26), and so forth. And [Col. 1051B] the prophet says: “Faith has perished and has been taken from their mouth.” He did not say, “from their heart,” but “from their mouth,” because faith of the heart is of no avail without faith of the mouth, nor faith of the mouth without faith of the heart: since the one grants righteousness and the other salvation, for salvation cannot be separated from righteousness, nor righteousness from salvation. Therefore believe and confess; likewise confess and believe: for faith is unto righteousness, and confession is made unto salvation.

4. Since we have come to this point and the occasion of confession has presented itself, we must render what we promised elsewhere and set forth all that we think concerning confession. Be patient; and if I perhaps extend my discourse at too great a length, attend to what is said, since it is offered for your benefit. For confession is a way without which no one comes to the Father; whoever loses it loses God. When you resolve to emerge from the abyss [Col. 1051C] of vices, let your chief refuge be the one to whom your soul has been entrusted, whom God has set over your head. And do not be troubled if he is unlearned or undiscerning, since this itself is a sign of the humility which gives rise to confession. Remember that there is no authority except from God. “The scribes and Pharisees,” he says, “sit upon the chair of Moses.” Attend, then, not to the one sitting, but to the seat; to the chair, not to the person. But if perhaps his permission allows you to go over to another, nevertheless first disclose to him the secret of your heart; for there is no complete salvation if one flees or despises him to whom one ought to adhere and whom one ought to honour. If his instruction seems insufficient to you, the way is open for you freely [Col. 1051D] to pour out your heart before another who is learned and discerning, while preserving his privilege for the one to whom you entrusted your soul.

5. Do not flatter yourself if, when you have sinned gravely, a lighter penance is imposed by one who does not know or who connives; for whatever you do too little here must be completed in purgatorial fires, because the Most High seeks worthy fruits of repentance. Although the one who does not fully provide for you will not escape the hand of the Almighty, reason, your teacher, nevertheless presides over you and teaches you to abstain from lawful things as much as you remember having committed unlawful things. Therefore we exclude from the threshold of this most sacred virtue all those whom fear compels to confession, because forced confession is not confession; whom accusation of others draws on, [Col. 1052A] because it is not confession but offence; whom self-excuse leads, because it is not confession but defence; whom empty boasting carries away, because it is not confession but mockery; and whatever other plagues there are which, under a shadowy covering, imitate the holiness of so great a sacrament. A heart contrite and humbled in itself and of itself can ascend to the purity of this purification. I shall show you one of the righteous confessing most righteously. Whom do you ask? It is the Lord’s Psalmist. “I said,” he declares, “I will confess against myself my unrighteousness to the Lord” (Ps. 31:5). “I said,” that is, I proposed it in my heart: not forced, not compelled, but voluntarily. “My unrighteousness,” he says, not another’s, reproving and accusing himself. You see that the saint confesses himself [Col. 1052B] to the Lord, not from fear of someone else nor in order to accuse another. “For such confession you will forgive, O Lord, the ungodliness of my sin.” “For this every saint will pray to you at a fitting time.” It first sprouts in the heart unto righteousness; after this, it is born in the mouth unto salvation.

6. Its first step is knowledge of sin. “The beginning of salvation,” says someone, “is knowledge of sin” (Seneca, *Letters*). In this knowledge one must consider what one has done, with how many insults one has afflicted one’s body, walking in the passion of desire like the Gentiles who do not know God, possessing one’s vessel in uncleanness and vileness, not in sanctification and honour. One must also consider what one has deserved: namely, that fire prepared for the devil and his angels, and all kinds of punishments which vie with and increase one another in those penal places [Col. 1052C]. And one must examine what one has lost: namely, those good things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him.

7. Terrified, therefore, by reflection on all these things, pass on to repentance, the avenger of vices and nourisher of virtues. Repent that, entangled in so many and such great crimes, you lay so long in the mire of filth and misery. In repenting, wear down your body; withdraw the seeds of provocation from the raging little ass of the flesh, and admit no more things needing repentance, lest repeatedly adding wound to wound you break the bones of your soul, which the Lord preserves in the righteous: “Not one of them,” I say, “shall be broken” (Ps. 33:21). [Col. 1052D] For these two things are so joined to one another that no one can know himself unless he repents, nor repent unless he knows himself.

8. Thus, once known to yourself and repenting within yourself, soar to the third step: sorrow of heart. Then righteousness will already have been planted by that planting which your heavenly Father planted. Grieve, therefore, because you have offended the Creator, whose law heavenly and earthly things, except for you, keep in unwearied observance; and in so great a commonwealth of God you alone are an exile and do not care for the decrees of imperial majesty. Let a keener sorrow arise because, together with your Creator, you have also offended your Father—him who ministers to you the courses of the stars, the fruitfulness of the earth, and the abundance of its fruits. Let an even sharper sorrow enter and pierce your soul [Col. 1053A]: that you have despised so great a benefactor, who endured the pain of the cross so that you might no longer endure the pains of hell. Thus, while righteousness sprouts in the inner person, let the shoot grow into a tree, and let the tongue speak what knowledge spoke.

9. The fourth step, therefore, is confession of the mouth. This must be made purely: for one part of one’s sins must not be spoken and another kept silent; nor must light sins be confessed and grave ones denied. Neither must another be accused while oneself is excused; rather, one must say with the righteous man: “Do not incline my heart to words of malice, to make excuses for excuses in sins” (Ps. 140:4). For these are words of malice—and grievous malice, than which scarcely anything can be graver or worse. It must also be spoken humbly, so that what is in the heart is the same as what sounds from the mouth. For there are [Col. 1053B] some who in confessions habitually recount the clever feats they performed in literary contests and their brave deeds in armed combat—alas!—clothing pride in the cloak of humility and thinking that they can escape the eyes of the Judge who sees all things. Were not Kings Saul and David, rebuked by the prophets Samuel and Nathan, alike said, “I have sinned”? Yet Samuel heard, “The Lord has transferred the kingdom from you and will give it to your rival” (1 Sam. 15:28); while David heard, “The Lord has transferred your sin, and you shall not die” (2 Sam. 12:13). What does this mean, except that what Saul had in his mouth was not in his heart, whereas the humility which was in David’s mouth existed in his heart and shone forth from it? It must also be spoken faithfully, so that one believes, in the faith of the Church, that one’s sins are forgiven. For Cain and Judas confessed purely and humbly [Col. 1053C], but not faithfully at all: one of them, despairing, ran to the noose (Matt. 27); the other uttered that great crime: “My iniquity is greater than I can deserve forgiveness for” (Gen. 4:13). You lie, thief: God’s mercy is greater than any iniquity, because his mercies are above all his works.

10. The fifth step follows: mortification of the flesh, which must be reduced by fasts and vigils, lest it fly back through fresh itching to its pleasure-loving perversity. This, however, must be done with permission, because what is done without permission will be reckoned to vain glory rather than reward. Do it secretly, so that your left hand does not know what your right hand does. Do it with discretion, on account of bodily weakness and manifold illnesses. For we have seen many at the beginning of conversion so break down the barriers of discretion that [Col. 1053D] they made themselves unfit for the solemn services of praise and thereafter needed to be sustained for long periods with more sumptuous provision. Now, thus enlightened, let him proceed to the sixth step, which is amendment of conduct. Restrain your tongue from evil; do what is good; bridle your sensual impulses with the reins of continence, and thus there will be peace in the land of your flesh. Rebuke the wicked in accordance with the office you hold, and do not allow righteousness to be buried while you are present. Come to the seventh step: it is perseverance in goodness. In this seventh step the Lord will call you with Moses from the midst of the cloud (Exod. 24:16), and you will fix your inner eyes upon the very substance of divinity. Perseverance is produced by expectation of rewards, remembrance of punishments, the firstfruits of the Spirit [Col. 1054A], and the heavenly gift, of which the Apostle speaks—something which one who has experienced it does not fail to know, and one who has not experienced it cannot understand (Heb. 6). For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand the things of the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14).

11. Hear also, briefly, what sort of person ought to be ordained for the administration of this mystery. He must be no less learned than religious, so that he has zeal for God according to knowledge; for undiscerning religious devotion usually harms more than it helps. He must be learned, so that he knows what penance to impose, whom to spare, when he ought to spare, and what consolation to offer from the Scriptures. He must be religious as well, so that he may lift pure hands to God and intercede confidently for sinners. Let him take care never to make [Col. 1054B] any mention of what he has received under the seal of confession, or agree with anyone discussing it. Let him also take care not to become contemptible in the eyes of the person who has revealed his own contemptibility; let him not become suspicious, nor judge a sinner’s future life by the past. If, by chance, a case concerning matters heard in confession comes before him for discussion, he must not take a side as one who knows, but permit the judicial process to proceed as though he knew nothing. Yet he should be disposed to show compassion and to free the person, and should strive to lessen severity in some way, imitating the sweetness of his Lord, of whom the saint says: “For you have executed my judgment and my cause” (Ps. 9:5). But alas! In our times a pestilential disease has grown throughout the world: men are preferred to churches whom neither learning nor life commends—blind [Col. 1054C] guides of the blind, themselves fallen and leading others to the precipice.

12. We have heard concerning the confessor and the one who receives confession; now let us hear what impedes confession. So far as I can gather, four things chiefly arise: shame, fear, hope, and despair. Nothing is stronger in assaulting God’s grace than human shame, because while we blush to confess what we have committed, we revere God less than human beings. This is the shame that brings sin (Ecclus. 4). Let us set against it rational reflection, reverence for the God who beholds us, and comparison with the greater shame. Reason urges us to confess; God, who has seen, compels us. And if we are ashamed to speak here, what [Col. 1054D] will it be in that great shame, when everything will lie open to everyone? Fear overwhelms many, lest they be struck with a grievous penance that they cannot bear. Truly, “He who fears frost, snow will fall upon him” (Job 6:16). Here one must consider how grievous, how long, and how fruitless the punishment of Gehenna is; and, conversely, how light, brief, and fruitful present repentance is.
