Hope also ruins many: while they desire present goods, they refuse to disclose their consciences, lest, if people knew what they were like, they might not rise to any goods of this present life. They must be reminded that the goods of this age are small, uncertain, and momentary, whereas those of the other life are greatest, most certain, and eternal. Despair kills very many, who fear only that they will not be able to remain continent. It is true [Col. 1055A] that “when a sinner has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18:5). We must crush this by the strength of confession, the grace of humility, and the compassion of the one to whom we disclose our conscience. But it must be known that one kind of confession laments sin, and another sings praise. Confession is a good ornament of the soul: it both cleanses the sinner and makes the righteous person more clean.

13. It follows: “Whoever believes in him shall not be put to shame.” To believe God is to give credence to his words. To believe God is to confess that he is everywhere. To believe in [Col. 1056A] God is to direct all one’s hope to him. Demons believe God and believe that God exists, but they do not believe in him—in whom whoever believes shall not be put to shame—because they do not place their hope in him. Behold, so far as I could, though not so fully as I wished, I have spoken concerning the sacrament of confession. But we have drawn out the discourse at length; let us also hear the end of our speaking. May the Bridegroom of the Church, Son of Mary, who is God blessed for ever, grant us to believe unto righteousness, to confess with the mouth unto salvation, and to believe in himself. Amen.

[Col. 1055]

## The Same Nicholas: Sermon on the Feast of St Nicholas, Bishop of Myra

[Note: [Col. 1055D] Compare Sermon 40, *On Various Subjects*.]

“A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom” (Luke 19:12).

[Col. 1055B] 718 1. This Nicholas, mine—indeed yours—chosen from the womb, holy from childhood, glory of the young, reverence of the old, honour of priests, splendour of bishops, gladdens our assembly by his feast. This is Nicholas whose miracles are spread through the whole breadth of the world; whom the earth and its inhabitants praise. So many and such great miracles are accumulated that all the ingenuity of learned men scarcely suffices to write them down, much less do we suffice to read them. And although a multitude of scholars, on the rhetorical anvil beneath the hammers of Quintilian or Cicero, stretches out the thinnest sheets of their speeches, the glory of the confessor nevertheless exceeds voice and mind, tongue and conscience. For wonders multiply daily, and the Spirit of God does not cease, in memory of his soldier, to continue his miracles [Col. 1055C]. He is glorified at sea and praised on land; he is invoked in every danger. Finally, those who go down to the sea in ships and do their work upon many waters have themselves seen the works of the Lord and Nicholas’s wonders through the Lord in the deep. Is not, after the commemoration of the singular Virgin, such sweet compassion—or compassionate sweetness—is observed in the hearts of the faithful [variant: *obversatur*, “is before the mind”] that, in the day of tribulation, Nicholas’s name is held in the mouth and rests in the heart? If lightning flashes and, amid thundering storms, vengeance proceeds from above, Nicholas is taken as patron; Nicholas is sweetly invoked. If a raging storm and the cruelty of the sea threaten sailors, 719 Nicholas is tearfully entreated to hear; he is suppliantly invoked to come; he is acclaimed that he may mercifully deliver [Col. 1055D] them. If we are struck by troubles or grieve over hindrances, at once the holy Confessor’s name leaps to our mouths: Nicholas is repeated; Nicholas’s patronage is sought.

[Col. 1056B] 2. Do not think, however, that I speak merely as a declaimer or exaggerate this splendour by the rhetorical charm of words, since the whole world experiences the confessor’s benefits and there is no one who can hide himself from his love. Witnesses are the pilgrimages undertaken from the ends of the earth to his holy body, so that the miracles wrought through him may be seen. Nor has the authority of his holy name flown into such great reverence among Christians alone: pagans too flock eagerly, competing to praise and glorify his holy name. Above all, the throng of priests and clerics is stirred with such devotion in his worship that, throughout the entire world, they gather and assemble from every direction to serve so great a solemnity. Boys rejoice, young people congratulate one another, virgins are adorned, old people are cheered, [Col. 1056C] and every age joins personally [variant: *personanter*, “with resounding voices”] in the celebration. Each, moreover, has material for rejoicing: boys praise the boy who fasted; young people the young man who delivers; virgins the defender who repels virgins’ disgrace; old people the old man who redeems an old man’s need. “Young men and virgins, old men with the younger, let them praise his name.”

3. But after his deeds, so remarkably celebrated in the excellent tongues of the Greeks, what can a poor, stammering discourse now dare to say? Yet, lest I appear to offer evasive excuses, I return to the Gospel reading and set forth for the common good what I have received from the common store. For it says: “A certain nobleman went into a far country to receive for himself a kingdom and to return. And he said to his servants: ‘Trade until [Col. 1056D] I come.’” I shall trade securely at my Lord’s command, nor shall I fear the Psalmist saying: “Because I have not known trade, I will enter into the powers of the Lord” (Ps. 70:16). For it gives no small strength to my confidence [Col. 1057A] that the supreme Emperor himself became my merchant and conducted my business without leisure as long as he was on earth; carrying loads of precious wares to the Father, he showed to the very countenance of God what he bought, what he redeemed, and from what he redeemed it. Do you, then, intend to be idle while he is trading, and to rest while he labours? He came to trade in a far country, and do you disdain even to walk to neighbouring regions? Enter upon and go into the land of unlikeness—namely, this world—and see how frequent its markets are, how great are the vanities that spring up and spring up anew there. It is indeed a land of unlikeness, because we know that we have lost the land of likeness, where we were made in God’s likeness. Is there not a great unlikeness in passing from paradise to hell, from angel to beast, from God to devil?

4. Go through the turmoil of the marketplaces, and look around at those contending on every side; and, so far as I can gather, all pleasure is occupied with three pursuits: some rely on riches, others on honours, others on glory. You run to India, travel through Ethiopia, cross seas, and by sailing disclose another world to yourself, in order to amass wealth. You flee your homeland, neglect your children, tear yourself from your wife, and, forgetting every tie, seek in order to acquire, acquire in order to lose, lose in order to grieve. You climb mountains besieged by snow, and traverse their dreadful heights as though they were level ground. You give no thought to the face of the hidden abyss; you pass the swords of robbers and ambush-filled roads as though they were smooth; and, forgetting your humanity, you make little account either of the thundering face of heaven or of heat [Col. 1057C] or cold. You heap up treasure and do not know for whom you gather it. Nor is there generally lacking the power of someone stronger, who, openly confronting you, may seize or snatch it away and in one hour make poor and lowly the man whom a long lifetime had raised rich and exalted. “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3).

Hear briefly also about honours. You have yourself appointed duke; and power has been given you in order that you may be wretched and no longer have rest. The material of anxieties is piled up, and amid troubles that consume the very heart you must put on a face of joy. No one can ever be in honour without pain, in pre-eminence without disturbance, in exalted rank without vanity. Wretches that we are, according to the philosopher, we love the reward of miseries and curse the miseries themselves. We put on the minds of kings, and whatever does not conform to our will immediately calls forth anger; nor is our shared humanity considered. Then there is the gnawing worm, the fear of higher power, which continually torments the conscience. This is the most just law: live with your inferior as you wish your superior to live with you.

Hear also concerning glory. If you seek glory, you have furnished all men with seeds of envy. You are puffed up and, filled with windy spirit, are bursting apart; nor do you consider how many follow you, but how many go before you. All gather together to disparage you and sharpen their tongues to curse you; and you are very shrewd if you can escape either the hand or the tongue of the envious. Behold: from the source from which you wished to be glorious, you are proved inglorious [Col. 1058A]. For the multitude persecutes no one more relentlessly than the one who arrogates to himself leadership over the multitude. Add to these three power and pleasure, which themselves are carried away by thin and fleeting delight; and you will see that abundance is poor, honour lowly, favour cheap, power weak, and pleasure burdensome—so that, according to the Apostle, we may bring every understanding into the obedience of Christ (2 Cor. 10:5). Read again that greatest of Latin philosophers, Seneca, and in his words you will find my judgment. Therefore despise all these despicable things; and from them all make your burden: contempt for the world.

5. Having therefore traversed this region, and—what is more precious—having been lifted out of it, pass to the second, which is the paradise [Col. 1058B] of the cloister. Truly, the cloister is paradise. Here are the green meadows of the Scriptures; the flowing flood of tears, which that heavenly love draws forth from the purest affections. Here are the most upright trees, the choirs of saints, and there is none that does not rejoice in abundant fruitfulness. Here is that lofty table, at which God is both feeder and food; giver and gift; offerer and offered; fellow-diner and feast. Here the riches of the Almighty are heaped up; here the glory of angels is poured out.

Do you think that there are no markets here, and that those who dwell in the house of one rule are idle? You may see one intent upon sacred reading, another absorbed in prayer; one weeping for his own transgressions, another exulting in the praises of God; one keeping vigil, another fasting; and mutually outdoing one another in the office [Col. 1058C] of devotion. At night they rise to confess him; in evening, morning, and midday they recount and proclaim his praise; and all their diligence revolves within the orbit of divine service. Run therefore through them all, run through each one, and from all and each make your burden: a pattern of life.

6. Therefore, having left the world and embraced a way of life, pass to the third, which is the region of expiation. In it the gracious Father tests his rust-stained children as silver is tested; he leads them through fire and water in order to bring them out into refreshment. There are three divisions of places which souls receive according to the diversity of their merits. For those who have used the dwelling-place [Col. 1058D] of the body as a prison, who have kept the substance of both the inner and outer person cleansed and pure, immediately fly up to heaven. Conversely, those who have done, even unto death, deeds worthy of death are assigned without mercy to the places of Gehenna. But those who are neither one nor the other, but are between the two—who indeed have committed mortal sins, but repented near death without completing their penance, unworthy to rejoice immediately yet not deserving always to burn—receive purgatorial places. There they are scourged, but not to their own folly, so that, wrenched free, they may pass over to the kingdom.

For those in heaven we should not pray, because we ought to pray to them, not for them. For those in hell prayers must be withheld: from them the door of mercy has been shut and every hope of salvation cut off. Only for those [Col. 1059A] who are cleansed in purgatorial places must we keep vigil in prayer and bring aid by the singular sacrifice, so that the gracious Father may swiftly convert their repentance into satisfaction, and that satisfaction into glorification. Run again through these with the gaze of compassion, and make your burden: fellow-feeling in suffering.

7. The fourth region is that of Gehenna: a hard and dreadful region; a land of affliction and forgetfulness, a land of miseries and darkness, a land of tempest and gloom, a land of curse and death, a land of thirst and hunger, a land of burning 721 and cold, in which no order dwells, but everlasting horror. I wholly tremble and shudder at the memory of this region, and all my bones are shaken. There is fire that is not kindled; the worm that does not die; dreadful cold [Col. 1059B]. There an intolerable stench rises, striking hammers resound without ceasing, and dense darkness grows ever more thickly heaped up. There are the confusion of sinners, the horrible faces of demons, the teeming multitude of inextricable chains. There are weeping and gnashing of teeth, lamentation and groaning; and alternating evils tear the impious apart without pity.

Nothing so avails to tear up the roots of pleasures as the memory of these things and the recollection of the wounds of my Lord: who stood before the judge; who received blows; who was scourged and spat upon; who was crowned with thorns; who was struck with fists; who was hung upon the wood; who, while hanging, was mocked; who died on the cross; who was pierced by the spear; who was buried; who rose again; who ascended into heaven; who made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father. Run through these tumultuous markets, so that while alive you may descend [Col. 1060A] into hell; and make your burden: hatred of sin.

8. The fifth region is the paradise above heaven: a blessed and glorious region, full of delight and grace, sweetness and joy, kindness and glory. There is rest from labour, delight in newness, security in eternity. There all live; none dies; all exult with the voice of exultation. David had entered his sanctuary and had been carried beyond in mind to God; yet he could bring away nothing else except: “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. 86:3); and: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). I know not what great thing is promised: to see God and to praise him. “I too rejoiced at the things said [Col. 1060B] to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’” (Ps. 121:1). Already we stand in the courts of Jerusalem; already from the threshold of the great city we dream of [alternative: sow] joys. Run therefore also through this region, and make your burden: love of God.

9. Therefore trade until that nobleman comes who went into a far country to receive a kingdom and return. He will certainly return, and then will exact with interest the money he entrusted to us. He loses nothing, forgets nothing, leaves nothing unpunished.

10. Let us therefore beseech the confessor, that he may deign today to beseech our Redeemer, his friend, for us—he who is God, blessed for ever. Amen.

[Col. 1059]

# Four Sermons on the Antiphon *Salve Regina* (G)

[Note.]

722 Although certain passages in these sermons are drawn from Bernard—for example, in the third sermon—nevertheless they must decisively be denied to him, both because of their difference in style and genius and because of the frequent citations of poets, whom the holy doctor is less accustomed to use. They are attributed to Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo, by Claudius de Rota in his Notes on Pseudo-Liutprand, p. 451; there the author of the aforesaid antiphon is called Peter of Compostela. William Durand had earlier advanced this latter opinion in book IV, chapter 22 of the *Rationale*: “But Peter, bishop of Compostela, composed that antiphon,” *Salve Regina misericordiae*, omitting *mater* (“mother”), as likewise in the sermons mentioned above. On this antiphon see book II of the *Life of St Bernard*, by John the Hermit, no. 7. (See the note below.)

# Sermon I

[Col. 1059D]

1. “Hail, Queen of mercy, our life, sweetness, and hope, hail.” Lady, you will open my lips. The Lord be with you, and you with me. Deign that I may praise you. I flee beneath your protection, where the weak have received strength [Col. 1060D]. Be to me a tower of strength against the face of the enemy. Let our voice first sound you forth, and let us open our mouths to you.

We have undertaken, brothers, to examine for our edification this sweet song and most noble melody, which our Order sings with deepest devotion four times yearly in honour of holy Mary [Note: [Col. 1059D] Namely, at the four solemnities then instituted in honour of the Blessed Virgin: the Purification, Annunciation, Assumption, and Nativity; for others were introduced later. But of what Order is this passage finally to be understood? That, under Peter the Venerable, this use of the antiphon had been adopted among the Cluniacs on the principal feasts is established by his final statute; and the same will shortly be said of the Cistercian Order.], because we find it filled with much special sweetness through continual meditation. For this song came poured forth from the highest lips. It has a foundation: “its foundation is in the holy mountains”; its foundation is the sweetness of inward delight. And where is this, unless in the holy mountains—that is, in our minds? Composed by saints, instituted by saints [Note: [Col. 1061C] Wion, in *Lignum Vitae*, book V, chapter 105, proves by many testimonies of later writers that the author of this antiphon was Hermann the Cripple, a Benedictine monk; yet the present context appears somewhat to conflict with this, for I nowhere read that Hermann was distinguished by the title “saint.” Moreover, John the Hermit, book II of the *Life of St Bernard*, no. 7, relates that St Bernard “heard the antiphon *Salve Regina* sung with angelic voice, from beginning to end; and, it is reported, afterwards wrote it down from his heart and sent it to Pope Eugenius, so that by command of apostolic authority it might be solemnly observed in the churches … And this was done,” etc. From this passage the angels of that vision ought to be called the authors of the prayer; and certain other words of this sermon, immediately near those quoted above, seem to allude to this: “This song came poured forth from the highest lips.”

Alberic recounts the story somewhat differently in his *Chronicle* under the year 1130. He records that St Bernard, once received as a guest at St Benignus in Dijon—“an abbey,” he says, “which he always loved because his mother is buried there”—heard before the hour, near the altar, angels sweetly chanting the antiphon *Salve Regina*, and at first believed that it had been the community. The next day he said to the abbot: “You sang the antiphon of Le Puy very well last night near the altar of the Blessed Virgin.” It was called the Antiphon of Le Puy because Haimerus, bishop of Le Puy, had composed it … Hence at a certain general chapter of the Cistercian Order, he obtained permission for this antiphon to be received by the whole Order; and this was done.

Haimerus, or Aimarus, or Ademarus, was bishop of Le Puy, especially devoted to the Blessed Virgin, in the time of Pope Urban II. But William Durand, in book IV, chapter 22 of the *Rationale*, reports that Peter, bishop of Compostela, composed this antiphon; Claudius de Rota likewise maintains this in his notes on Pseudo-Liutprand. The same writer there also asserts that these four sermons were published by Bernard, Archbishop of Toledo. But since certain matters from St Bernard’s sixteenth sermon on the Song of Songs are quoted word for word in sermon 3, these sermons cannot be ascribed to Bernard of Toledo, who flourished before St Bernard—that is, from the pontificate of Gregory VII to the end of the eleventh century.], it will worthily be frequented also by saints. And indeed, unless it is sung by religious persons fervent in holy affection, it can neither be understood subtly nor sung effectively. For it is so sweet in grace, so fruitful in meaning, and so profound in mysteries. It is such that we are unable to consider and examine it as worthily as it deserves.

But because it sounds sweetly, it soothes affection; from the abundance of its meanings it enriches the mind; and, as it greets the Holy of Holies—namely our Advocate—as though she were present, it inflames all our inward parts to the marrow. For we must say that she is present to us when we greet her as present; and we must direct toward her the whole trinity of our soul, whom we entreat with such devout prayers. Certainly she acknowledges and loves those who love her, and is near to those who invoke her in truth—especially those whom she sees made like herself in chastity and humility, provided that they add charity, place all their hope in her after her Son, and seek her with their whole heart, praying and frequently saying: “Help, Lady, those who continually cry to you.” (From the Church’s responsory for the Blessed Virgin.)

She does not disdain the most sweet affection, the great longing, the flood of tears, or the constancy in prayer of any persons, however sinful, if only they have washed their hearts from malice, loosened the bonds of impiety, untied the oppressive bundles, set free those who are crushed, and cast off every burden. To her has been given power in heaven and on earth—a power able to act; in her hands are our life and spirit; the eyes of all Christians hope in her; and she gives them, at the fitting time, the food of grace with which she is full.

[Col. 1062A]

2. Therefore, brothers, let us lift our hearts with our hands toward her, approach her with steps of love, offer her the sacrifice of praise, and render our vows to her from day to day and hour to hour, continually saying: “Hail, Queen of mercy.” Who will worthily unlock for me the mystery of this hymn? Who will worthily explain for me the beginning of so unusual a greeting? Holy Mary, the knowledge of holy forms of knowledge, is the source of springs and rivers, the sea, and the author of virtues; for just as the sun surpasses all lights of heaven by the prerogative of extraordinary brightness, so she surpasses, after her Son, every rational creature by the splendour of virtue and knowledge.

Not unfittingly we say of her what is written: “How good is the Lady of Israel to those who are upright of heart!” (Ps. 72:1.) Those are upright of heart who are upright and agree rightly in all things. To these persons our Advocate, by her goodness alone at work, often grants so abundant a manifestation of her presence, and by the bestowal of grace teaches how readily she may be entreated, that, renewed in spirit, they may cry out through the consolation of experience: “Hail, Queen of mercy.” In such persons understanding grasps only as much as experience tastes. The anointing of the Spirit alone teaches these things. Here the heart’s jubilation is stronger than the mouth’s noise; the movement of joys than the sound of lips; the harmony of wills more than that of voices.

For such reasons I thought it prudent to say: “Who will unlock for me the mystery of this hymn?” *Who* is customarily said of something rare. For it is indeed a rare bird on earth that merits such familiarity in the eyes of Majesty that, recognizing by experience of bestowed grace her presence, one can exultantly say: “Hail, Queen of mercy.” She is rightly called Queen of the world and Queen of heaven, through whom the Creator and Ruler of both was born.

3. But in what way is she called “Queen of mercy,” since mercy is not a substance but the compassion of heavenly clemency, or the benevolent disposition of a rational creature? It may therefore be understood metonymically—that is, by the efficient cause for that which is effected—so that the work of mercy [Col. 1063A] is understood in place of mercy. The work of mercy is the restoration of nature. “The mercy of the Lord” fills the earth of the living and the dying. That angels were created and confirmed, and that human beings were formed and restored, belongs to mercy, which from eternity and unto eternity is itself the primordial cause of all things and the most causative of causes. Its effect is the work of saving those who are to be saved; this salvation is the adoption of the children of God. In this way the Holy of Holies is Queen, whose virginal childbirth is the source of all these things.

Queen is a name of glory and honour, magnificence and beauty, sweetness and compassion, love and magnificence, sublimity and power, governance and justice, defence and grace. The Holy of Holies is all these things to us and for us all, she whom we continually sing: “Hail, Queen of mercy.” We may also understand it thus: she is called “Queen of mercy” so that we may attribute solely to divine mercy, and not to merits, the fact that she, surpassing every creature in holiness and dignity, is further exalted by the title and honour of queen. She is fittingly also called “Queen of mercy” in this respect: she is believed to open the abyss of divine compassion for whom she wishes, when she wishes, and as she wishes, so that no monstrous sinner may perish for whom the Holy of Holies grants the aid of her patronage. Therefore let us all say it, let each say it, let all say it, let us say it continually: “Hail, Queen of mercy.” It follows:

4. “Our life, sweetness, and hope, hail.” A most beautiful order: life precedes sweetness, and hope follows. For you do not taste unless you live, nor do you hope unless [Col. 1063C] you live and taste. Taste is the seat of sweetness, and the sense of taste is the seat of savour. We have resolved to aim at brevity and therefore refrain from speaking of life’s varied condition.

We believe that this passage speaks of that life of which John’s Gospel says: “He who eats me shall himself live because of me.” Why should not the one who eats Life live? “I am,” he says, “life” (John 6:47–60); and, “Blessed is he who eats this bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke 14:15), which is within. The kingdom of God is charity, joy, peace. And life, bread, and charity are one. Charity is a great delight, which casts out fear. Whoever abides in it both eats it and is eaten by it. It is that which feeds among the lilies, both feeds and is fed—feeds us and is fed by us. “How?” you ask. If God loves us, he draws us into himself, and conversely. This food is the charity of God; and the God of virtues and source of knowledge grants life to the soul, both present and future. This the Holy of Holies grants us metonymically, namely she who both bore this life for us and pours it into us through her prayers.

This is she of whom the Apostle says: “For me, to live is Christ” (Phil. 1:21); and: “Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20). Of this life, in Deuteronomy’s account of carnal circumcision: “Your life shall hang before your eyes, and you shall not believe your life” (Deut. 28:66). This life gives sweetness, but gives itself from itself. “If I have found grace in your eyes,” Moses says, “show me yourself, unto the fullness of grace.” And conversely: “I will show you all good” (Exod. 33:13, 18, 19). He asked for one thing, and an all-embracing fullness was promised. What could be more different than one thing and all things? Different in sound, one in reality; different in utterance, one in identity.

5. Therefore God is every good and the highest good; likewise sweetness, and the most universal genus of sweetness. “Those who eat me,” he says, “will still hunger; and those who drink me will still thirst” (Ecclus. 24:29; John 6:35). Why? Because he is good and sweet. God is good to Israel, to the upright in heart; but he is also sweet and upright. Neither goodness nor justice exists without uprightness. Whoever drinks from the former will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the latter will become within himself a fountain of water springing up to eternal life. For with him is the fountain of life, and he himself is the fountain of life, even the rush of the river which makes glad the city of God. Be the city of God, and this rush will make you glad. For God prepares in his sweetness for the poor.

For the fruit is sweet to the throat, and his throat is altogether delightful [Col. 1064B], all things ineffable. This is the white stone that no one knows except the one who receives it. For in it are joys of inward festivity, which the inward and eternal sweetness daily impresses upon our minds through the inspiration of its love. “I have made known to you,” he says, “all things whatsoever I heard from the Father” (John 15:15); and to Moses: “I will show you every good” (Exod. 33:19). All that he heard from the Father and what he promises Moses are the one denarius promised to those who labour in the vineyard (Matt. 20), that one thing which David asked (Ps. 26:4), and the one thing necessary (Luke 10:42). It is honey which Israel sucks from the rock and oil from the hardest stone (Deut. 32:13). It is joy which no one takes away (John 16:22). 724 It is the kiss of which it is written: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth” (Song [Col. 1064C] 1:1). It is the taste and sweetness of inward delight, the hidden manna, and the treasure hidden in the field; compared with it, everything sweet is bitter, every beautiful thing ugly, every pleasant thing sad, every precious thing cheap, and everything desirable in the eyes of lovers of this passing world is filthy.

For the Holy of Holies obtained the precious pearl at the cost of every delight of earthly things; she prepared it for us in her Son and always prepares, by her intercession, for us who pray, the poured-out oil of this sweetness. It will not be unfitting, but very fitting, if we call that Queen of mercy our life and sweetness: we have as yet experienced little of this life and sweetness, but through her hope that we may attain whatever grace the maker of all goodness deigns to impart to us.

6. It follows: “Our hope, hail.” Hope is in virtue as a spark in tinder. A spark cannot endure without tinder. Remove the tinder: it perishes and dies; supply it: it lives. Likewise hope collapses without a foundation, dies without food, fails through hunger, is extinguished without nourishment, and dries up when its root is cut off. For hope without the life of virtues and the sweetness of devotion is not hope but presumption. Hope lies between fear and security, and is the name of an uncertain good. Life and sweetness drive away the face of fear and give strength and beauty to security. Therefore he says to God: “You have made me dwell alone in hope,” and: “In peace, in the selfsame thing, I shall sleep [Col. 1065A] and rest” (Ps. 4:9–10).

For her charity, which casts out fear, is supported by flowers and surrounded by apples, and will say: “His left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6). The left hand is the threat of punishment; the right, the promise of the kingdom. Between these hope lies upon the soft bed of charity; life and sweetness spread it. This is that middle part of Solomon’s litter of which Scripture says: “Its middle he paved with charity” (Song 3:10). You now see the sublimity of this hymn. First it sets forth life, which consists in the integrity of virtues; second, the sweetness of spiritual joys; then it introduces hope of eternal things. All these things the Queen of mercy, Lady of the world, Queen of heaven, bestowed upon the world: Virgin of virgins, Holy of Holies, light of the blind, glory of the righteous [Col. 1065B], pardon of sinners, restoration of the despairing, strength of the failing, salvation of the world, the age of all integrity. May she intercede for our sins, through the grace of the Lord, her only Son, whose kingdom and dominion remain without end for ever and ever. Amen.

# Sermon II

> If a hundred tongues resounded, and a hundred mouths,  
> an iron voice were mine [Note: [Col. 1065D] An imitation of Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.625–626.], yet, Mary, I could say nothing worthy of you,  
> you who are called the blessed Virgin, Star of the Sea.

1. O Virgin, how shall I name you? With what praises shall I exalt you? My most unspeakable tongue, defiled among the dead, uncircumcised in lips, not purified by the altar’s fire—a restless evil, having breath in its nostrils and flowing out everywhere through its cracks—what worthy praise can it offer to your praises [Col. 1065C]? Your magnificence is exalted above the heavens and your glory above all the earth, so that no creature in heaven can be found capable of worthily praising your magnificence, nor any on earth able to express your glory. For none was found worthy, either in heaven or on earth, to open the book of your prerogatives and worthily loose its seven seals.

Who will recount the fullness of grace—the coming of the Holy Spirit into you, the overshadowing of the power of the Most High, the conception of the Word—so that without burden you were pregnant, without pain a mother, virgin and fruitful alike? Many rich men, from the city of the Lord of powers, have set their hands to these mighty matters; yet they have not been able fully [Col. 1065D] to comprehend the height of these riches, because these ways are unsearchable and all things inscrutable. They have attempted it, and it was not granted them to go further. While they were still beginning, they were cut off. For who shall speak the powers of the Lord and make heard all his praises? And, if no one can do so worthily, still let each do so according to his strength.

> Each, with all the strength of his abundant resources, strove for himself,  
> as someone has said. (Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.552.)

Finally, all ran in the fragrance of your ointments. Draw us also after you, O Holy of Holies, and show us the light of your mercies. Protect us beneath the shadow of your wings.

2. “To you we cry, exiled children of Eve.” This is the second division of the hymn which we have undertaken to explain [Col. 1066A], and it seems to us to have been composed in the manner of a drama. For here speaks the varying disposition of different persons; here is found the condition of the perfect and of those still advancing toward better things. For a life animated by integrity of virtue, the sweetness of inward delight, and such confidence of holy hope—what are these but fruits of the Spirit and attractions of virtue? They are gifts bestowed on veterans, the accumulated reward of a long struggle.

But the lamentation of exile, longing for homeland, and the penal sting of original sin are signs of beginners or of those making progress. Let the exile be this present life, the false show of vanity; the homeland, truth’s solidity. The false show of vanity is the brilliance of temporal glory; truth’s solidity is the unchanging knowledge of eternity. The false show of vanity is the pleasing splendour of visible creation; truth’s solidity is the inextinguishable light of inward sweetness. Of this homeland a certain wise man said: “O Truth, homeland of exiles, end of exile, I see you, but am not allowed to enter: unworthy of admission, stained with sins. How long shall we smell and not taste, journeying toward our homeland and not attaining it, sighing and greeting it from afar?”

3. The first human being was created for this purpose: that, if he had not sinned, he might always stand before the countenance of his Creator through the presence of contemplation; know truth’s solidity; love what he knew; hold what he loved; delight in what he held; and, always cleaving to him who is immortal, himself possess life without end. For the true and highest good of human beings is the full [Col. 1066C] and perfect knowledge of the Creator.

But hemmed in by the serpent’s cunning and deceived by the false show of vanity—that is, by the appearance of visible creation—he descended from Jerusalem into Jericho, abandoned the fountain of truth, and inclined his affection toward the beauty of things. At once, struck by the blindness of ignorance, he came forth into exile; and, separated from the inmost light of contemplation, he became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth: a wanderer through disordered desire, a fugitive through sinful conscience. For whatever temptation attacks a mind abandoned by divine help overthrows it.

Therefore the human heart, which first remained fixed and steadfast in divine love and, loving one thing, remained one, once it began to flow away through earthly desires, established for itself in exile as many dwelling places as the pleasures it found there. Thus the mind that does not know how to love the beauty, sweetness, peace, security, and perpetuity of the first light can never be stable. Finding no enduring joy in what it embraces in the false show of vanity, it ever stretches itself out in desire, pursues what it cannot attain, and never rests while wavering in exile.

Now it slips out through the eyelids and feeds curious gazes, considering the immensity of things in their mass and bulk; now it investigates the beauty of things in position and motion, appearance and quality; now it tests their usefulness through what is necessary, convenient, suitable, and agreeable. It also emerges through the nostrils and, through smell, seeks the pleasant delights of varied odours [Col. 1067A]. Fed by these, it proceeds through the organs of the ears and draws inward, captivated through hearing, sweet melody and the disciplines of harmony, music, and arithmetic. By touch, too, it examines subtle, light, and smooth things by feeling them, and stores its felt desires in the hall of memory. Nor does it less sample through the taste of the throat the variety of flavours.

The mind that does not know itself or God feeds these its kids beside the shepherds’ tents amid the vanities of times and temporal things, begging from the passing form of this world something that may in some degree console its hungry curiosity. For it has been compared to senseless beasts and made like them, because, when it was in honour, it did not understand that it was mud, delighted by the pinnacle of honour. From this arises, in the exile of vanity [Col. 1067B], movement without stability, labour without rest, running without arrival; so that the heart is always restless until it begins to return to the homeland of truth—needy, and wishing to be filled with the husks of swine, until it sighs for the Father’s house, where the hired servant has bread in abundance and all the household servants are clothed in double garments.

4. From this exile, O Holy of Holies, “to you we cry, exiled children of Eve,” that through your intercession, guidance, and aid we may be able to return to the chamber of truth, our homeland. We know beyond doubt that human beings have nothing more from all their labour under the sun than vanity; nevertheless, ensnared by the bonds of perverse habit, we cannot by ourselves return to the freedom of truth.

But by truth in this passage we do not mean knowledge of God and of the knowledge that accords with godliness, but that pure, naked, and solid mean which consists in the love of virtue [Col. 1067C]. For although authorities define human restoration as the knowledge of truth and love of virtue, perfect virtue is not without knowledge of truth, nor truth without love of virtue. One is vain who dwells in vanity, whether in the vanity of curiosity or of error. The vanity of curiosity proceeds from the vanity of mutability and generates the vanity of mortality. The first is the cause of sin; the second, sin; the third, sin’s punishment. The first is in things made for human beings; the second, in things made by human beings; the third, in things that are in human beings. One is in created things, another in minds, another in bodies.

The vanity of error is found in all things contrary to Catholic faith and sound doctrine, and which do not attain religious discipline in that solid truth which restrains human willing and unwilling between the narrow limits of too little and too much [Col. 1067D]. All these are vanity: they deceive those who embrace them and do not bring them to the truth of eternity. In this exile nearly every kind of human being, from the beginning until the coming of the Queen of Heaven, delighted to wander, remembering the homeland of truth with no sighs or longing. She first opened the way to the homeland; and, giving birth to Truth, which is the true homeland, made it manifest to all the world.

[Col. 1068A] **5.** Therefore we too, O Queen of mercy, “cry to thee, banished children of Eve.” There is one cry of the mouth and another of the heart. The cry of the mouth is loud shouting; the cry of the heart is a strong and supplicating direction of the intention toward God. God is within, man without. The cry of the mouth is directed to those who are without; the cry of the heart to God and to those who are with him within. Within where? In the spirit. How, you ask? In two ways. By what means? By knowledge and love, revelation and devotion, sharpness and warmth. By these means God dwells in the heart, though not alone. “For where the body is, there will the eagles also be gathered together” (Matt. 24:28). For what purpose? That the youthfulness of the heart may be renewed like that of an eagle. There too are that great eagle of mighty wings, the innocence of the Holy of holies, and equity, which hears when invoked, if it is continually stirred by hidden cries.

And we, still children of Eve—children of transgression, children of disobedience, children of the ancient mother—cry to thee, Queen of mercy. Return, visiting in us thy nature; return, displaying that love which thou hast for Christians; return through thy singular power given to thee by God on our behalf; return through that prerogative which was specially infused into thee in the fullness of grace, so that we may behold thee—not such as the angels desire to look upon, saying, “Thou art all fair, my beloved, and there is no spot in thee” (Song 4:7)—but behold thee bestowing benefits, granting remedies, healing the brokenhearted, establishing strength for the mourners of Zion, giving a crown instead of ashes, the oil of joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of grief.

[Col. 1068C] Nor is this a slight vision: to experience thee as merciful and approachable, and to console the sighs of mourners by the gift of grace. May this thy voice sound in our ears. This thy voice is sweet, and this thy face beautiful. For to see thee in that beauty with which the Lord has clothed thee in strength and girded thee is not for this present time, nor for the time of our life, defiled by the stench of vices. We are unworthy, Lady, to see thee clothed in the robe of immortality; show us the face of thy mercies, and we shall be saved. May he deign to grant this to us, whose kingdom and dominion endure without end for ages of ages. Amen.

727

## SERMON III

> While rivers run into the sea, while shadows  
> Roam the mountain slopes, while the sky feeds the stars,  
> Ever thy honor, thy name, and thy praises shall remain  
> [Note: [Col. 1067D] Virgil, *Aeneid*, book I, lines 611–614.]

My hope, gracious Virgin—O sacred Virgin, Virgin Mary!

**1.** And no more? Much more, indeed, and in every way. For forever and beyond, thy praise shall not fail from the mouth of men, and even of angels. “The heavens declare the glory of God.” And what is greater in all the glory of God than the ineffable fullness of heaven? And we, together with it—that is, with angels and archangels, with Thrones and Dominions, and with all the host of the heavenly army—sing the hymn of glory of the Holy of holies. They declare glory; we, the hymn of glory. They mutually recount in the rejoicing of their hearts the glory which they see present before them; we utter only a hymn of glory—that is, we pour forth the memory of the abundance of thy sweetness. “And the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18:2).

[Col. 1069A] “Let there be a firmament,” he says, “and let it divide the waters from the waters” (Gen. 1:6). O Lady, thou art a firmament firmer than all firmaments: thou didst receive and conceive, carry without failing, bear, nourish, feed, suckle, and rear him whom the heaven of heavens could not contain. In the midst of the waters thou didst divide waters from waters: that is, the affections for eternal things from affections for temporal things. For a sword passed through thy soul, “that the thoughts of many hearts might be revealed” (Luke 2:35). God set in this firmament the sun and moon, Christ and the Church; and the stars, the many prerogatives of graces.

“We praise the Lord in his saints.” Her firmness, strength, constancy, and fortitude of mind are shown because she despised the glory of the world and trampled the enticements of the flesh. She is the power of the Most High, of which it is written: “And the power of the Most High shall overshadow thee” (Luke 1:35).

**2.** Yet, Lady of all things, she is understood not only as heaven and firmament, but is fittingly called by other names and designated by the names of things. She is the tabernacle of God, the temple, the house, the court, the chamber, the bridal chamber, the bride, the daughter, the ark of the flood, the ark of the covenant, the golden urn, the manna, Aaron’s rod, Gideon’s fleece, Ezekiel’s gate, the city of God, heaven, earth, sun, moon, and morning star; she is dawn and lamp, trumpet and mountain, the fountain of gardens and lily of the valleys; she is the desert and the promised land flowing with milk and honey, the star of the sea, likewise a ship, a path in the sea, a net, a vineyard, a field, an ark, a granary, a stable, a yoked manger, a storehouse, a hall, a tower, a camp, a battle-line, a people, a kingdom, a priesthood.

[Col. 1069C] She is a sheep, a pasture, paradise, a palm tree, a rose, a river, a drink, a dove, a column, a garment, a pearl, a lampstand, a table, a crown, a scepter, bread, oil, wine, a tree, a rod, a cedar, a cypress, a plane tree, cinnamon, balsam, myrrh, incense, an olive tree, nard, saffron, a pipe, a reed, and storax; she is sister and mother. And, to conclude briefly: all Scripture was made concerning her, because of her, and for her; the whole world was made for her; she is full of the grace of God; through her man was redeemed, the Word of God became flesh, God was humbled, and man exalted.

**3.** Therefore to thee, so great and such a one, Lady of all things, Holy of holies, Queen of heaven, “we sigh, mourning and weeping in this valley of tears.” This is the third phrase of the hymn which we have undertaken to explain. Sighs, groans, and tears are forms of compunction, seeds of righteousness. “Sow for yourselves unto righteousness,” he says; “reap the hope of life, and enlighten for yourselves the light of knowledge” (Hos. 10:12). “Going they went and wept, casting their seed” (Ps. 125:6).

[Col. 1070A] A sigh is an inarticulate voice; groans belong to those who groan, tears to those who suffer pain. These have their places. These are the three things which go well in the lower watering-place, and the fourth which proceeds happily: namely, the valley of tears. This is the seat of the upper watering-place (Josh. 15:19). The true Caleb gives both to his daughter seated upon an ass. And if thou aspirest to these things, restrain the irrational motions of sensuality and of the body by the motion of reason. Cut away from thyself the concupiscence of the flesh, of the eyes, of power, and of honor. Cast off the pomp and burden of the world; tame the flesh by the discipline of the spirit; constrain thy desires into narrow bounds. “Do not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the chair of pestilence” (Ps. 1:1). Embrace humility, that thou mayest be poor in spirit; correct thy savage habits, and be meek. Then, having crossed Jordan, thou shalt enter the promised land, which is that of compunction. Thus, in the third place among the eight beatitudes, it is said: “Blessed are they that mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5; Isa. 61:2).

**4.** Lazarus was raised on the fourth day; at the fourth watch Jesus came to the disciples. And make for thyself four watches, that thou mayest be raised and Jesus may come to thee: two of fear and two of shame. Consider God thy Creator; consider him as benefactor; consider him as Father; consider him as Lord. In each respect thou art guilty [Note: [Col. 1069] These and the following passages are from St. Bernard’s sixteenth Sermon on the *Song of Songs*.]; weep in each respect, keep watch in each respect. Let the several understandings of these things be as so many days in the mind, during which thou wast, as it were, Lazarus dead and stinking.

[Col. 1070C] As thou dost weep over each of them, thou art, as it were, raised on the fourth day. The first and the last produce fear; the two in the middle, shame. The Father, indeed, is not feared precisely because he is Father: it belongs always to a father to have mercy and spare. The paternal voice says: “I will strike, and I will heal” (Deut. 32:39). Therefore there is no reason to fear the Father. If he sometimes strikes, he corrects; he does not take vengeance. But when thou reflectest that thou hast offended thy Father, there is certainly reason to be ashamed, even if not to be terrified. “Of his own will he begot thee by the word of truth” (James 1:18); then he did not spare his Only-begotten Son, that it might benefit thee whom he had begotten (John 3:16). He thus showed himself to thee as Father; but thou didst not show thyself to him equally as a son. With what face dost thou now raise thine eyes to the countenance of so good a Father, being so evil a son? Be ashamed to have acted unworthily of thy race; be ashamed to have lived as a degenerate son of so great a Father.

[Col. 1070D] “Let streams of waters run down thine eyes”; let confusion cover thy face. Let shame suffuse thy countenance and darkness seize it; let thy life fail in sorrow and thy years in groaning. Alas for grief! What fruit hadst thou in those things of which thou art now ashamed? If thou hast sown in the flesh, thou hast reaped corruption from the flesh. If the world itself passes away, and its concupiscence, be ashamed at that voice which says: “If I am a father, where is my honor?” (Mal. 1:6).

This concerning the Father’s honor. Now we must come to his benefits. To pass over innumerable others: the sustenance of this body, the use of this present time, and, above all, the blood of his beloved Son crying from the earth—these call thee to shame for ingratitude. “What hast thou rendered to the Lord for all that he has rendered to thee?”

**5.** Let us come also to fear. If shame performs its part too weakly, let fear be aroused to rouse it. Put aside the gentle titles of Benefactor and Father; turn to more severe ones. For he who is called “the Father of mercies and God of all consolation” (2 Cor. 1:3) is nevertheless called “the Lord God of vengeance” (Ps. 93:1), and is called “terrible in his counsels over the sons of men” (Ps. 65:5). That he is Father, that he is beneficent, is for thee; that he is Lord and Creator is for himself. For “he made all things for himself” (Prov. 16:4). He who defends and preserves for thee what is thine—dost thou suppose that he will not demand the honor due to his sovereignty? He will demand it to the last farthing; he will demand it, and “will richly repay those who act proudly” (Ps. 30:24).

[Col. 1071B] He will demand service from one redeemed, honor and glory from one whom he formed. Suppose that the Father overlooks and the Benefactor forgives—but the Lord and Creator do not. Consider what fear and horror it is to have despised thy Maker and the Maker of all, to have despised the Lord of majesty. “He touches the mountains and they smoke”; and vile dust, to be scattered by one light breath and never gathered again, dares to provoke so dreadful a majesty!

Fear Gehenna; fear the countenance of the Judge. Tremble at the anger of the Mighty One and the face of his fury; at the crash of the falling world, the conflagration of the elements, the violent tempest, the voice of the archangel, and the harsh word. Tremble at the teeth of the infernal beast, the belly of hell, and the roaring creatures prepared for food. Fear the gnawing worm, the rushing fire, smoke and vapor, sulphur and stormy winds; fear the outer darkness, and say: “Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. 9:1), that I may forestall with tears the weeping and gnashing of teeth, and the hard bonds of hands and feet, and the weight of chains pressing, constricting, burning, yet not consuming? Alas! My mother, why didst thou bear me a son of sorrow and bitterness, indignation and lamentation?

**6.** Whoever is thus affected by this twofold fear and twofold shame keeps four watches in the mind, or is inwardly illuminated through four days, on the fourth of which he is raised, like Lazarus four days dead. And as four rivers arise from the one fountain of paradise and water the earth (Gen. 2:10–14), so these four affections, arising from the one fountain of compunction, consume [perhaps: “complete”] the fullness of the lower watering-place. For they give birth to sighs, groans, and tears, which, insofar as they are made over a lack of virtues, are called the lower watering-place. The upper watering-place, however, is the valley of tears: a rich outpouring sprinkled from heaven, neither forced out nor artificial, the voluntary rain which God set apart for his inheritance (Ps. 67:10).

[Col. 1072A] These are the waters that go out from the temple at its right side (Ezek. 47:1), that flow violently from Lebanon (Song 4:15), and that flow from the fountain of paradise into four heads. Paradise is the conscience of the righteous person, which piercing care does not burn, remorse of guilt does not bite, deficient understanding does not impoverish, and the rushing phantasms of bodily things do not batter with hail; it is flowering in faith, fruitful in virtues, fragrant in reputation. In its midst a fountain rises when virtue is strengthened by integrity. It is then divided into four heads: justice, prudence, fortitude, and temperance. Justice digs deeply and seeks the waters of the upper watering-place; prudence finds them; fortitude claims them for itself; temperance possesses them.

By justice I mean the genus embracing all God’s commandments; by prudence, knowledge of divine and human things; by fortitude, the vigor of the mind held erect amid adversity and prosperity; by temperance, knowing moderation and excess between willing and unwilling, between too little and too much, on this side and beyond discretion. When these are lawfully preserved, they make the perfect man, who desires “to be dissolved and to be with Christ,” and who says: “Alas for me, for my sojourning has been prolonged!” (Ps. 119:5), and: “My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Ps. 41:3).

[Col. 1072B] This fountain is the open fountain of the house of David, for the washing of the sinner and the menstruous woman (Zech. 13:1). This is the fountain which the princes of the multitude—namely justice, fortitude, and temperance—whom we have mentioned, dug in the giver of the Law, that is, in compunction; and with their staffs, that is, with the firm strength of perfect integrity.

**7.** Therefore the mind cleansed of vices, continually thirsting for God and receiving his coming into itself, often delighted by the ineffable sweetness of so great a delight, is afflicted by a wondrous sorrow because it cannot at will possess this sweetness continually. Its consolation is that, because of its continual desire, it is fed on the bread of tears. Thus it becomes a valley of tears, when, having a humble opinion of itself, it abounds in the full richness of weeping. And it possesses this upper watering-place, by which, dead to the world, it is sweetly and gently nourished, because, having already been cleansed through the lower watering-place, it is ineffably delighted by the contemplation of heavenly things.

[Col. 1072C] These two watering-places are the two olive trees and the two lampstands shining before God. They are the two lights, the two altars, the two scouts, the two cherubim, the two little doors, the two breasts, the two testaments, the two goats, the two lions, the two mites, the two tablets, the two columns, the two sisters, the two hands, and whatever pairs may plausibly be found corresponding to these.

In such sighs, groaning, tears, and valley of tears, “we cry to thee, banished children of Eve,” O Lady of all things, Holy of holies, our strength and refuge: splendor of the world, glory of heaven, chosen as the sun, beautiful as the moon in brightness; acknowledge all who love thee. Hear us, for thy Son honors thee by refusing thee nothing. And do thou save us, Lord Jesus, for whom thy Virgin Mother prays to thee [Note: [Col. 1071] From the Sequence concerning the Blessed Virgin according to the Cologne and certain other missals.], whose kingdom and dominion endure without end for ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV

> Before, with the limits of each land traversed, the Parthian exile  
> Shall drink the Arar, or Germany the Tigris,  
> [Col. 1073A] Than thy countenance shall slip from my breast  
> [Note: [Col. 1073D] Virgil, *Eclogue* 1, lines 61–63.]

Virgin Mother of God, whom the whole world cannot contain.

**1.** Most certainly and necessarily. “All the rich among the people shall entreat thy countenance”; how much more the poor of the people? And if the poor of the people, how much more the needy and poor man, the reproach of men and outcast of the people? My heart said to thee: “I have sought thy face; thy face, Lady, will I seek. Turn not thy face from me; decline not in anger from thy servant. Show thy face; let thy voice sound in our ears, for thy voice is sweet and thy face beautiful.”

We have heard thy voice four times in the Gospel, O Lady of all things: first, to the angel; second, to Elizabeth; third, to thy Son: “Son, why hast thou done thus to us?” (Luke 2:48); fourth, again to thy Son: “They have no wine” (John 2:3). Which of these do we seek? Certainly that one: “They have no wine.” This is necessary for us. Wine has failed in our vessels: namely, the wine “which makes glad the heart of man” (Ps. 103:15). We do not complain about the wine in which is debauchery (Eph. 5:18); we seek that of which the prophet speaks, which makes virgins flourish (Zech. 9:17). Thou art their cupbearer; thou art their standard-bearer. The banners of the King go forth among us through thy action on our behalf.

[Col. 1073B] A cup of pure wine is in thy hand—in thy hand, that is, in thy power—of pure wine, of divine love. Say, Lady of all things, say to thy Son for us: “They have no wine.” How excellent is the intoxicating cup of this wine! It intoxicates, warms, sharpens, makes men bold and strong, forgetful, discerning, sleepy. Love of God intoxicates to contempt of the world; it warms because it makes men fervent; it sharpens because it instructs; it makes them bold against adversities and strong, invincible against flesh, world, and demons; forgetful, that is, of things behind and stretching forward to things to come; discerning, by teaching them righteousness; sleepy and weary toward temporal things, yet inclined and ready to contemplate invisible things.

**2.** This wine makes glad the heart of man. We hope for this from thee and through thee—not wine alone, but bread as well. “For bread strengthens the heart of man” (Ps. 103:15): that bread of which Scripture says, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25). This bread is the sweet remembrance of thy Son; thou art full of his presence. And the table of proposition dedicates the number of twelve loaves. The twelve loaves are the twelve prerogatives of grace in which thou art filled with grace and the Lord is with thee.

[Col. 1073D] Lest I seem to prophesy from my own heart, the apostle Paul both names and enumerates these thy prerogatives, saying: “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity, joy, peace, patience, long-suffering, kindness, meekness, fortitude, mercy, continence, chastity” (Gal. 5:22–23). These loaves are certainly exceedingly bright and savory: bright in their own nature, savory in the experience of souls. In short, these are the highest spiritual delights. For the soul is strengthened and delighted by them more than the body by any carnal delights. Nor do they arise in man from himself; indeed, they are fruits of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, blessed Virgin, after the heavenly messenger declared thee full of the aforesaid prerogative of graces, he immediately added the cause of those graces, saying: “The Lord is with thee” (Luke 1:28). But the Lord is Spirit. Therefore the Holy Spirit performed great things with thee. He performed, I say, two works in thee. One was that he made thee worthy to conceive and bear the Son of God; the other was that from thy holy and worthy flesh he formed the flesh of the Son of God. Thus he made thee great and chaste: great indeed, that thou mightest contain the immeasurable; chaste, that thou mightest worthily contain him. He made thee great through humility and chaste through virginity.

**3.** Thus thou art holy; thou art the castle into which Jesus entered, possessing the tower of humility—for “he who humbles himself shall be exalted”—and the wall of virginity.

[Col. 1074B] Certainly it is a most strong wall, for it could be violated neither before childbirth, nor in childbirth, nor after childbirth. The stones of thy wall were thy discipline and continence, without which the wall of virginity is never firm. In thee were the two sisters Mary and Martha (Luke 10:38–39), who received the Lord. Mary was thy special understanding, by which thou understoodst that the one whom thou didst bear was God and the Son of God. Martha, however, was thy rational prudence, by which thou didst serve him in the flesh as thy Lord and Son.

Therefore, Lady, thou art the beautiful nose, to whom the Bridegroom says: “Thy nose is like the tower of Lebanon” (Song 7:4), “which is built with battlements: a thousand shields hang from it, all the armor of the mighty” (Song 4:4). The nose has two nostrils through which it emits breath from the head. So thou, Lady, through thy virginity and humility didst draw down from heaven the Son of God, “the breath of our mouth,” of whom the prophet says, “Christ the Lord” (Lam. 4:20). Now Christ the Lord is Spirit, since, as the breath of our mouth, he warms love, cools our covetousness, moves us toward a good will, and justifies us by faith.

[Col. 1074C] Therefore thou art the nose of the Church, like a tower—lofty in dignity, firm in gravity. Thou art the tower of Lebanon. Lebanon is a mountain whose name means “Whitening,” and it signifies thy innocence, higher than all others. Thou wast innocent from original and actual sins. No one was so apart from thee. Hence the authority of Augustine:

> “When sins are under discussion, we do not wish any mention to be made of the blessed Mary. For we believe that a greater grace was bestowed on her for overcoming sin in every respect, since she deserved to conceive and bear him who had no sin.” (*On Nature and Grace*, book 36 [recte chapter 36], no. 42.)

By “in every respect,” he means both in respect of original and actual sin. With her alone excepted, what can all the rest say but what the apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)?

I too hold, in pious faith, that thou wast freed from original sins in thy mother’s womb. This faith is not vain, nor is the opinion false. For reasons and authorities are found supporting it. The argument is this: if others were sanctified in their mother’s womb, much more thou, Mother of the Lord. But Jeremiah is read to have been sanctified, and John to have been filled with the Holy Spirit, in their mothers’ wombs (Jer. 1:5; Luke 1:64). Therefore thou also, Mary Mother of God, who alone didst possess the whole grace of the Holy Spirit, which others possessed in parts. For the angel Gabriel declared thee full of grace (ibid., 28).

[Col. 1075A] Long beforehand, the patriarch Isaac perceived thy fragrance in his son, saying: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a full field” (Gen. 27:21). Thou art the full field, full of virtues, full of graces. Thou didst bring forth the grain of the elect, which is also the food of angels. The Lord blessed thee. He blessed thee, I say, so that through thee blessed life might come, just as accursed death had proceeded through Eve.

Solomon, who was acquainted with heavenly secrets, says concerning thee: “Who is this that comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in battle?” (Song 6:9). Dawn always follows night; night precedes dawn. What is cold and dark night but original sin—cold through concupiscence, dark through ignorance? Therefore thou didst come forth as a bright and ruddy dawn, because, having overcome original sins in thy mother’s womb, thou wast born bright with knowledge of truth and ruddy with love of virtue. Hence the holy Church honors thy holy nativity with festive celebrations, which it would not do otherwise. For it celebrates the nativity of no one except thee, thy Son the Lord, and John the Baptist—who, of course, were born holy.

**4.** Since, then, divine authorities so clearly bear witness to thy innocence from the womb, who can any longer doubt that thou wast born holy and immaculate into this world? Thou art therefore the tower of Lebanon, built with battlements. From thy earliest age thou didst love righteousness and hate iniquity. Thus delight in righteousness and hatred of iniquity, with which thou didst grow, were thy battlements. When the enemies saw these, thou wert surely an object of dread to them. For they feared not a little that perhaps thou wast—and indeed thou wast—the one through whom they were to be conquered and condemned; on this account thou wert terrible to them as an army arrayed in battle.

[Col. 1075D] But the enemy gains no advantage at all against thee, because a thousand shields hang from thee: all the armor of the mighty. A solid ten is one thousand, since ten squared makes one hundred. Now there are ten commandments of the Law. The first is: “Thou shalt worship the Lord thy God, and him alone shalt thou serve” (Deut. 6:13). In this the worship of God alone is commanded. For service which in Greek is called *latria* is owed to no other. Indeed, when it is rendered to demons, it is called idolatry; this is forbidden by the next commandment: “Thou shalt not take the name of thy God in vain.” As though it said: Render to no creature the honor due to God; seek nothing through incantations or divinations.

Moreover, special service is offered to God by observing holy solemnities; hence the third commandment is joined: “Observe the Sabbath day,” that is, occupy thyself on sacred festivals, so that through present rest thou mayest learn to hope for eternal rest. These three pertain solely to God; for this reason they were written on one tablet only. But the remaining commandments concern a person’s conduct toward the neighbor, and therefore they were contained on the second tablet.

**5.** The first of these concerns one’s nearest neighbors, namely parents: “Honor,” he says, “thy father and mother.” By the name of honor is meant not only the reverence of submission, but also the service of assistance. Children therefore ought to honor their parents, both by obeying in what is good and by providing temporal assistance when they have need of it.

“Thou shalt not kill.” This is the greatest evil that can be inflicted on neighbors, and therefore it ought to have been forbidden before all else. Homicide, however, is committed in many ways: by hand, command, counsel, consent, or neglect. For if thou canst in some way preserve someone who is going to die and neglectest to do so, thou art without doubt held guilty of that person’s death.

[Col. 1076B] Afterwards it says: “Thou shalt not commit fornication” (Deut. 5:11, 12, 16, 18). One fornication is of the spirit; another is of the body. Fornication of the spirit is to abandon God and cleave to the devil. Hence: “Thou wilt destroy all who commit fornication away from thee” (Ps. 72:27). Bodily fornication, however, is indiscriminate sexual union with prostitutes, or with women separated from their lawful husbands, solely for satisfying lust.

Then is added: “Neither shalt thou commit theft.” Under theft are comprehended robbery, usury, unlawful seizure, and, in short, whatever is possessed to another’s loss. Next it says: “Thou shalt not bear false testimony.” False testimony properly means the support of another’s lie. Nevertheless, it seems likely that in this place it stands for every form of lying. For he who expressly forbade false testimony permits neither perjury, failure to fulfill a vow, nor any lie in general.

The ninth commandment is: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s wife.” There it plainly forbade adultery and the abuse of women consecrated to God. For they are brides of God; and it is surely no less serious to violate God’s bride than a man’s. The tenth is: “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor’s property” (Deut. 5:19–21). By this last commandment he forbids every deceit and circumvention through which wretched mortals deceive one another and deprive one another of earthly goods.

**6.** These ten commandments of the Law fortify their observers as shields and defend them from the torments of hell; for this reason they are most excellent ten shields. The number ten, moreover, is a linear number, having length alone, which is apprehended only by understanding. Thus it has ten shields. But if ten is extended upward and squared, it produces one hundred. Likewise, if the Decalogue is established in memory after knowledge and expanded by affection, one certainly possesses a hundred shields. Finally, ten raised and solidified makes one thousand: so also, when one brings the Decalogue forth from affection into good action, one begins certainly to possess the desired thousand shields.

[Col. 1077A] There is no doubt that thou, blessed in understanding, affection, and act, didst possess and observe this Decalogue beyond all mortals; hence, with complete justice, a thousand shields are said to hang from thee. And not shields alone, but all the armor of the mighty. For there is no virtue that does not shine forth from thee; and whatever the individual saints possessed, thou alone possessedst. Thou art Solomon’s bed, of which the *Song of Songs* says: “Behold Solomon’s bed; seventy mighty men from the mightiest of Israel surround it, all holding swords and most skilled in battle” (Song 3:7–8).

[Col. 1077]

## MEDITATION ON THE *SALVE REGINA* (G)*

**[NOTE.]**

It is a fragment of chapter 19, part III, of the *Stimulus amoris*, among the minor works of St. Bonaventure. Some think it is by Anselm, bishop of Lucca, who died before Bernard was born. Bernard, therefore, would not be the author of the conclusion of this antiphon, “O clement,” etc., since it is cited by this author.

[Col. 1077A] **1.** In greeting the Virgin, I ought first to consider her greatness. For she could not have been raised higher in relation to her Son than to be called Mother of God. Therefore, admiring the magnificence of our Mother, I say devoutly and reverently: “Hail, Queen.” Under thy protection, Lady, I wish henceforth to serve as a soldier. I commit myself wholly to thy dominion, that thou mayest govern me completely, leaving to my own foolishness nothing of the rule of myself. For whatever thou leavest to me, thou knowest will be destroyed most miserably.

But since I am full of misery from the crown of my head to the soles of my feet, and am putrefied, how wilt thou deign to govern such heavy stench and horror, thou so noble a creature? Because thou art “Queen of mercy”; and who are subjects of mercy if not the miserable? Thou art greatly concerned for the miserable; thou hast adopted them as thy children; thou hast willed, Lady, to govern them. Therefore thou art called “Queen of mercy.” Let us miserable ones, then, henceforth console ourselves with thee; henceforth, Lady, let us dwell with thee; let us embrace thee with the inward affections of the mind, because thou art “life.”

[Col. 1077C] Truly life, since thou hast humbly conquered the death of pride and hast obtained for us the life of grace. O certainly lovable life, desirable life, delightful life! O life that nourishest thy own with heavenly food! Whoever wishes to possess thee, let him afflict himself, reject pleasures, and despise all delicacies; and the more mortified he is, the more fully he will possess thee.

**2. “Sweetness.”** Truly sweetness, thou who drivest away the bitterness of sin by obtaining grace, who gainest for us the sweetness of grace, who introducest us, as we contemplate, into the sweetness of the heavenly homeland. O sweet Lady, whose memory alone sweetens the affection, whose meditation upon greatness raises the mind, whose beauty gladdens the inward eye, whose boundless loveliness intoxicates the heart of one who meditates!

O Lady, thou who dost ravish human hearts by sweetness, hast thou not ravished my heart, Lady? Where, I ask, hast thou put it, that I may be able to find it? O ravisher of hearts, when wilt thou restore my heart to me? Why dost thou thus ravish the hearts of the simple? Why dost thou use violence against thy friends? Dost thou wish always to keep it? When I ask for it, thou smilest upon me; and immediately, lulled by thy sweetness, I rest. When I return to myself and ask for it again, thou embracest me, most sweet one, and immediately I am intoxicated by thy love. Then I do not distinguish my heart from thine, nor know how to ask for anything other than thine.

[Col. 1078A] But since my heart has thus been intoxicated by thy sweetness, govern it together with thine, preserve it in the blood of the Lamb, and place it in the side of thy Son. Then I shall attain what I intend and possess what I hope, because thou art “our hope.” Therefore let those who know thy name hope in thee, because thou hast not forsaken those who seek thee, Lady. Surely those who hope in thee “shall renew their strength; they shall take wings as eagles; they shall fly and not fail.” Who will not hope in thee, who even helpest the desperate? I do not doubt that if we come to thee, we shall have what we desire. Therefore let the despairing hope in thee; let one who fails run to thee.

**3. “Hail.”** Who, then, will henceforth be able to prevent us from greeting thee, since thou art thus our life, sweetness, and hope? “Hail.” Who, then, since thou art our Queen, can separate us from or hinder us in reverencing thee? First thou art to be greeted as Lady, that grace may be obtained through thee; secondly, that glory may be reached through thee. “To thee.” Truly to thee, because thou alone didst bear God; thou alone didst destroy every heretical perversity; truly to thee, who raisest us from the dregs of sins, consolest us as we cry in our cradles, and sucklest hungry little children.

[Col. 1078C] “We cry.” Why should we not cry, Lady, when we endure wounds, feel blows, and are surrounded on every side by enemies? We cry in distress, oppressed by infinite miseries. We cry through anxiety of heart, emptiness of stomach, bitterness of pain, or perhaps through immense love for thee. For why dost thou sleep, Lady? Rise, help us. We cry also in order to make known our need, because necessity compels us to cry out. Why dost thou afflict us further? If thou delayest too long, I shall lose my voice with crying and shall no longer be able to call out to thee. Alas for me! What shall I then do, when thou canst neither hear me nor heed me?

Quickly, quickly, Lady, come to the aid of one crying out, lest I perish in the hands of the enemy. Run, hasten, Lady; and in thy mercy aid thy most wicked and faithless servant crying to thee, and rescue him from the hand and dangers of thine enemy. If nothing else, Lady, should move thee, except that thine enemy dares fraudulently to attack us thy servants, thou oughtest to hasten to us with all speed. Run and free us, Lady, to repress their pride. Run, lest they say: “Where is their Lady, in whose clemency they trusted?”

4. Do not wonder, Lady, that we cry out, because we are too far removed from you. In a far country we squandered our portion 734, and therefore “to you we cry, exiles.” Exiles from our homeland, exiles from the vision of God—and would that we were not exiles from grace, exiles from a mother’s consolation! O soul, why are you not rather [Col. 1079A] separated from the body than made an exile from your Lady? Alas for me! Why have I been banished into so long an exile? O Lady, while we are here, make us exiles, lest, trusting here as though in our homeland, we cease to seek you and your Son; yet make us exiles in the body in such a way that we may always be fellow citizens with you in mind. “Children of Eve.” Truly children of Eve: proud, presumptuous, ambitious, greedy, gluttonous, carnal, disobedient; and, briefly, following Eve herself in all things, we are prone to evil but slow toward good. And if it happens that we bring forth any child of good works, we give birth with a certain pain and sorrow of heart. But we commit evil with delight; nor are our evils enough for us: rather, like Eve herself, we incline others toward evil; and [Col. 1079B] likewise, like her, we excuse ourselves in our failings, or at least, if we can, shift them onto others. We prefer to acquire worthless things amid much sweat and labor, rather than to taste the Lady of glory and possess her with the greatest ease—indeed, with the greatest sweetness. For unless you, Lady, had helped us, perhaps by now we should have descended into the deepest hell.

5. Nor is there anything that can excuse us, who imitate not you but Eve in all things, and therefore “we sigh to you.” We sigh because of the absence of so good a Mother, desiring to come to you, Lady: “we sigh to you,” longing to see your Son. Thus the excessive love with which we are inwardly intoxicated toward you compels us, Lady, to sigh to you. To all you are lovable, to all approachable, to all delightful: seat of wisdom, river of mercy, ray of the Godhead; nor is there anyone who can hide himself from your warmth. Who, then, Lady, will not sigh to you? We sigh from love, and also from sorrow. Distresses press upon us on every side. How then should we not sigh to you—consolation of the wretched, refuge of the expelled, deliverance of captives, Queen of warriors, Lady of all, even of enemies?
