And there is none able to resist your will. Thus afflicted, thus wretched, we sigh to you: “groaning and weeping in this valley of tears.” Alas, Lady! Do you not see that we are wholly filled with bitterness? Within, we groan; outwardly, we weep, lying in a place of tears. Burdened by sins we groan; weighed down by troubles we weep; abounding in [Col. 1080A] miseries, we are in the valley of tears, asking for your aid. What more shall I say? I neither can nor know how to recount all the abominations of this valley.

6. “Come then, our advocate.” O praiseworthy mercy of the Savior, who deigned to bestow so noble an aid upon those so afflicted! Therefore there is no cause to fear that you will not have mercy on the wretched, inclining toward that side the judgment which you plead, so as to show us the glory which you bore. Nothing therefore remains, Lady, except that you turn those merciful eyes toward us. “Come then, our advocate, turn toward us those merciful eyes of yours.” We do not doubt, Lady, that if you look upon our miseries, your compassion cannot delay its effect. Wondrous also and lovable are those rays of your eyes, by which [Col. 1080B] you draw us to love and lead us to complete salvation, so that we may not fear the venomous eyes of the basilisk. O venomous eyes of Eve! Why do you not offer yourselves to the eyes of the Virgin, if you wish to receive perfect healing? For the brightness of her eyes drives away darkness, puts the hosts of demons to flight, cleanses the vices of minds, kindles frozen hearts, and finally draws them to heavenly things. O how blessed, Lady, are those whom your eyes have seen! Turn these eyes, therefore, Lady, toward us. “And after this exile show us Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb.” O wondrous womb, able to contain the Savior! O praiseworthy womb, able to receive the Redeemer! O desirable womb, from which flowed the desire of minds, the river of graces, the reward of glory! O lovable womb and sweetness of the soul, elevation of minds, intoxication of hearts, health of sinners! Your fruit, Lady, is surely the blessed fruit from the beginning of his birth. This is Jesus, Son of the living God. This is our Savior, the Lord God. “Show us Jesus, the blessed fruit of your womb, after this exile,” so that, beholding him, we may possess him; beholding him, may be filled with blessedness. “O clement, O pious, O sweet Mary!” O clement to the needy, pious to those who entreat, sweet to those who love! O clement to penitents, pious to those making progress, sweet to contemplatives! O clement in delivering, pious in giving, sweet in giving yourself! O clement in consoling, pious in caressing, sweet in kissing! You are clement to the subject, pious to those now corrected, sweet to the beloved. Amen.

[Col. 1079]

## SERMON TO THE CLERGY ASSEMBLED AT THE COUNCIL OF REIMS

[NOTE.]

735 This is not by Bernard, to whom it would have seemed proud and insolent to call bishops and all prelates “brothers,” much less “devils,” as is done here in no. 3. Whoever its author may be, it is composed throughout of passages from Bernard; it was delivered before the Pope and at his command, as no. 1 shows.

[Col. 1079D]

1. The task imposed upon me is grave: namely, that I should teach teachers and instruct fathers—especially since it is written, “Ask your fathers, and they will tell [Col. 1080D] you” (Deut. 32:7). But this Moses, whose hands are weighty, commands me; and he must be obeyed not only by me but also by all. And this man is more than [Col. 1081A] Moses. One people of Israel was entrusted to Moses; but to this man, the whole Church. And this man is more than an angel. For to which of the angels did God ever say, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19)? I say this with respect to office, not merit. Apart from God, there is none like him either in heaven or on earth. This is Peter, who cast himself into the sea (John 21:7), while the other disciples sailed toward Jesus. Each of you is content with his own little boat—that is, his own archbishopric, abbey, or provostship; but he has cast himself into all archbishoprics, abbeys, and provostships. “This great and wide sea; there are creeping things without number” [Ps. 104:25]. And I say to you, my brothers the bishops: God has greatly exalted you. [Col. 1081B] “You are the salt of the earth,” as the Lord says in the Gospel. “You are the light of the world” (Matt. 5:13–14). “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High. Nevertheless, you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes” (Ps. 82:6–7). “Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the disputant of this age?” (1 Cor. 1:20). Will they not die like men? Will they not fall like one of the princes? From where will they fall, or whereunto? From the Lord’s side into the depths of hell.

2. Brothers, two great evils remain: death and judgment. For the condition of death is hard, and therefore rare is the person willing to die. But why take care about dying, when this is the way of all flesh? “Where shall I go from your spirit? Or where shall I flee from your face?” (Ps. 139: [Col. 1081C] 7), when the Apostle says, “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may render an account of the things he has done in his body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10; Rom. 14:10). Brothers, I announce to you another synod, where the Lord God will sit in judgment; and there we must all appear, and there God will judge the world justly. Here justice is enclosed in a purse; but God will judge justly in that judgment. And there we must all appear—unless, perhaps, a thing it is impious even to say, the Apostle lies—whether Pope, cardinal, archbishop, bishop, rich person, poor person, learned person, or unlearned: “that each may render an account of the things he has done in the body, whether good or evil.” And if an account must be rendered [Col. 1081D] of what each has done in his own body, alas, what will become of what each has done in Christ’s body, which is the Church? God’s Church has been entrusted to you, and you are called shepherds when you are plunderers. And we have few shepherds—alas!—but many excommunicators. Would that wool and milk were enough for you! For you thirst for blood.

3. Yet I consider four things especially necessary for those who preside in the Church of God: that they enter through the door; that they keep themselves in humility; that they avoid avarice; and that they endeavor to preserve purity both of heart and body. But what use is it if they are elected canonically—which is to enter through the door—if they do not live canonically? The Lord said to the Twelve: “Have I not chosen you twelve? And one of [Col. 1082A] you is a devil” (John 6:71). Lord Jesus, when that election was in your hand, if you had no one contradicting and protesting against you, why did you choose a devil as bishop? Why, good Jesus, did you not choose one good, just, and holy, as Peter was good, just, and holy? Or if you chose a devil, why do you boast of having chosen? Brothers, 736 Jesus does this today, choosing for himself many devils as bishops. Where, alas, shall we find bishops who, after obtaining dignity, keep themselves in humility? Surely pride gives them occasion to aspire to so great a dignity, to burst shamelessly into Christ’s sheepfold, though the Lord says through the Psalmist: “He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house” (Ps. 101:7). But Jesus is in the midst, not in a corner. Hence he himself says in the Gospel, “Where two or three are gathered in my name, I am in their midst” (Matt. 18:20); and again, “Jesus, passing through their midst, went away” (Luke 4:30); and in the book of Wisdom, “In the midst of the church he opened his mouth” (Ecclus. 15:5); and again the Gospel says, “Jesus stood in the midst of his disciples” (Luke 24:36). Woe to me, Lord Jesus, if I am with you in your house and not in the midst of your house. But these men are not so. They are indeed with Jesus, but not in the midst of his house, because they love and practice pride, exalting their relatives but neglecting and oppressing the poor. They live badly [Col. 1082C] and wish those subject to them to live badly. Therefore they are compared to the apostate angel, who said in his heart: “I will set my throne in the north” (Isa. 14:13), and so forth. What does it mean for the devil to wish to set his throne in the north, except that some proud and impious man, estranged from the warmth of charity or the light of wisdom, should seek or hold an authority over those like himself? Such was Absalom over the children of Israel, rebellious against his father and seeking rule (2 Sam. 15). Such was Jeroboam, who sinned and caused the children of Israel to sin through the golden calves (1 Kgs. 12). Such were the scribes and Pharisees, against whom the Lord says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who shut the kingdom of heaven before men; for you do not enter, and you do not allow those entering to enter” (Matt. [Col. 1082D] 23:13).

4. Moreover, how do the bishops of this age avoid avarice? For, what cannot be said without pitiful groaning, they melt Christ’s reproaches, spittle, scourges, nails, lance, cross, and death in the furnace of avarice, and expend all these upon acquiring shameful gain; they hasten to enclose in their purses the price of the whole world. In this alone they differ from Judas Iscariot: he assessed all their profit by a number of coins; they, with a greedier appetite for gain, demand limitless sums of money. They crave these with insatiable desire; they fear lest they lose them, and when they lose them, grieve. In love for them they rest, so far as the free [lacuna] will of hoarding or the care of increasing [Col. 1083A] them permits. The ruin or salvation of souls is not reckoned. Certainly they are not mothers, who, though they have become excessively fat, stout, and swollen from the patrimony of the Crucified, do not sympathize with the affliction of Joseph. An archpriest goes through the obedience entrusted to him, and, in order to fill his bag, he sells innocent blood. He sells, indeed, homicides, adulteries, incest, fornications, sacrileges, perjuries, and fills his pouch to the brim. The report of such gain accordingly flies abroad and becomes known to the bishop; and, summoning the archpriest, he says, “Give me my share.” But the other says, “I will give you nothing.” In reply the bishop says, “If you do not give me my share, I will take everything from you.” A very great quarrel arises, and greed causes discord. But afterward the archpriest, reflecting [Col. 1083B] that he exercises this power by the bishop’s authority and can do nothing without his favor, changes perversely and says, “I repent; take your share, and in addition whatever you please from my own.” And they are reconciled. Alas! As Herod and Pilate were reconciled and Christ was crucified, 737 so these likewise are reconciled and Christ’s poor are stripped.

5. Behold, these are times altogether foul because of “the thing that walks in darkness” [Ps. 91:6]. Therefore woe to this generation from the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy—if indeed it ought to be called hypocrisy when, through excess, it can no longer lie concealed, and through shamelessness does not seek concealment. Thus today the putrid corruption creeps through the whole body of the Church: the more widespread it is, the more desperate it is; and the more dangerous, [Col. 1083C] the more inward it is. For if an open heretic should arise, he would be cast out and wither; if a violent enemy, perhaps one might hide from him. But now how shall one cast him out, or how shall one hide oneself? All are friends and enemies; all are dependents; all are members of the household—and none are peaceful; and all seek what is their own. They are ministers of Christ and serve Antichrist. They go in honor on the Lord’s resources, to him whom they do not honor. Hence comes that meretricious glitter which we see daily among them, that theatrical dress, that royal display. Hence gold on bridles, gold on saddles and spurs. The spurs shine more brightly than the altars. Hence splendid tables, both in food and cups. Hence feasting and drunkenness. Hence cithara, [Col. 1083D] lyre, and pipe; overflowing winepresses and full storehouses, belching out from one thing into another. Hence jars of spiced wine; hence stuffed purses. Such are, and wish to be, the provosts, deans, bishops, and archbishops of churches. These things do not come to them by merit, but by that thing which walks in darkness. It was predicted long ago, and now the time of fulfillment has come: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. 38:17). Bitter first in the slaughter of martyrs; more bitter afterward in conflict with heretics; most bitter now in the conduct of household members. They cannot be driven out or exterminated: they have become so strong, so multiplied beyond number. The wound of the Church is internal and incurable; and therefore, “in peace my bitterness is most bitter.” But in what [Col. 1084A] peace? There is peace, and there is no peace. Peace from pagans, peace from heretics, but certainly not from her children. The voice of one lamenting in the time of Israel: “I have nourished and exalted children, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1:2). They have despised and prevailed through shameful life, shameful gain, shameful commerce, through the thing that walks in darkness. It remains that the “noonday demon” should now arise, to deceive any who remain in Christ and still persist in their simplicity; for it “swallows rivers of the wise and torrents of the mighty, and is confident that the Jordan may flow into its mouth” (Job 40:18), that is, the humble and simple who are in the Church. For he is Antichrist, who falsely claims to be not only day but even noon, and “exalts himself above that which is worshiped as God”; whom [Col. 1084B] the Lord Jesus “will slay with the breath of his mouth and destroy by the brightness of his coming” (2 Thess. 2:4, 8).

6. Behold, we have said what kind of shepherds we have on this path on which we walk, not what kind we ought to have. Not all who today are seen standing here and there like the Church’s bridegrooms are friends of the Bridegroom; and, as people say, are seen as though to stand at her right hand. Very few among all those dear to her fail to seek what is their own. They love gifts and cannot at the same time love Christ, because they have given their hands to Mammon. Look how splendidly and ornamentally they proceed, wrapped round with varied apparel, like a bride coming out from her chamber. If you were suddenly to see one of them approaching from a distance, [Col. 1084C] would you not think him a bride rather than the bride’s guardian? Whence, indeed, can you suppose that this abundance of possessions, splendor of clothing, 738 luxury of tables, and heaps of silver and golden vessels overflow to them, unless from the bride’s resources? Meanwhile she is left poor, needy, and naked—a pitiable sight—unkempt, shaggy, and bloodless. Therefore at this time they do not adorn the bride, but despoil her; they do not guard her, but destroy her; they do not defend her, but expose her; they do not instruct her, but prostitute her; they do not feed the Lord’s flock, but slaughter and devour it. Of them the Lord says: “They devour my people as bread for food” (Ps. 53:5); and again, “They have devoured Jacob and laid waste his place” [Col. 1084D] (Ps. 79:7); and in another prophet, “They eat the sins of my people” (Hos. 4:8)—as if to say: they exact the price of sins and bestow no care upon sinners. Whom will you give me from among the bishops who keeps watch more eagerly to empty the purses of his subjects than to root out their vices? Where is one who turns away wrath? Where is one who proclaims the year acceptable to the Lord? Therefore let us leave these men, because they are not shepherds but betrayers; and let us imitate those who, living in the flesh, planted the Church with their own blood. Indeed, these have obtained the place of ministry, but not its zeal. All wish to be successors; few to be imitators. Would that they were found as watchful in their care as eagerly as they run to the episcopal chair! They would surely keep watch, carefully guarding the Church entrusted to them; indeed [Col. 1085A] they would keep watch over themselves, and would not allow it to be said of them: “My friends and my neighbors drew near and stood against me” (Ps. 38:12). A wholly just complaint, and one to be applied more justly to no age than our own. It is too little for our shepherds not to preserve us unless they also destroy us. For, deeply submerged in the sleep of forgetfulness, they awaken at no thunderclap of the Lord’s warning, even to dread their own danger. Hence they spare not their own people because they spare not themselves, destroying and perishing together.

7. But now it must be said how the bishops and priests of this time strive to preserve the holiness of chastity—without which no one shall see God (Heb. 12:14)—both in heart and body. Certainly [Col. 1085B] the Lord says in the Gospel to bishops, doubtless those of the primitive Church, “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12:35), approving not only but also commanding chastity. The Holy Spirit also bears witness to this in the Law, allowing no one except the pure, and especially those pure from women, to eat the bread of the Presence. Therefore Ahimelech did not permit King David, who wished to take these loaves [Col. 1086A] with his soldiers, to do so until he had learned that they were clean from women, David the king saying: “If it is a question of women, they have been clean since yesterday and the day before” (1 Sam. 21:5). Even then the Holy Spirit signified that no one should approach Christ’s table and that bread of angels unless purified in mind and body, lest what divine grace prepared for believers unto salvation become judgment and condemnation to unworthy recipients. But how do these preserve the distinction of chastity, who, handed over to a reprobate mind, do things unfitting? For it is shameful to speak of the things done in secret by bishops. I think it better, therefore, to pass over and refrain from the subject than to say anything by which the innocent and inexperienced might be scandalized. [Col. 1086B] But why am I ashamed to say what they are not ashamed to do—indeed, what the Apostle is not ashamed to write and preach? The eminent preacher says thus: “Males committing shameful acts with males, and receiving in themselves the recompense of their error” (Rom. 1:27). Brothers, I have become foolish; you compelled me.

[Col. 1085]

## SERMON TO PASTORS ASSEMBLED IN SYNOD

739 Whoever its author may be, it is neither inelegant nor unworthy of reading.

[Col. 1085C]

“He who does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs up another way, is a thief and a robber. But he who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep,” etc. John, chapter 10, vv. 1–16.

1. Most reverend Fathers and Lords, behold, the words of the holy Gospel have been read in your hearing; and would that they had been carefully understood by you all! “Good understanding belongs to all who do them.” Secular people are accustomed to recognize, in their mirrors, their beauty or ugliness by sight. Your mirror is of another kind, in which you can attend more by hearing than sight to what is fitting and what unfitting; what hinders, what helps, and what the obligation of your office requires of you. Your mirror is the holy Gospel. Consider, I beg you, not the face of your birth, but the state of your daily conduct. [Col. 1085D] Consider, and do not go away negligently, but stand in more diligent inquiry; having searched your consciences to the depths, either glory in their testimony or be afraid. For as the testimony of conscience is glory to many, so it is shame to many. Behold, the sacred Gospel comprehends the entire multitude of prelates under three persons. For it sets before us a good shepherd, a hired hand, and a thief. If you are good shepherds, rejoice, because your reward is abundant in heaven. If [Col. 1086C] you are hired hands, fear, because your danger is great on earth. If you are thieves, groan, because your place is great in punishments, unless you hasten to repentance and worthily render what you have vowed to the Lord your God. Especially you who are about the Lord and bring and offer gifts before him—not corruptible gold and silver, but the precious blood and body of the spotless Lamb. What dignity God has bestowed upon you! How great is the prerogative of your order! God has set you above kings and emperors; he has set your order above all others; indeed, to speak more exaltedly, he has set you above angels and archangels, thrones and dominions. For as he did not take hold of angels but of Abraham’s seed in order to effect redemption (Heb. [Col. 1086D] 2:15–16), so he entrusted not to angels but to men—and to priests alone—the consecration of the Lord’s body and blood. For all, as the Apostle says, are “ministering spirits sent forth to serve those who shall inherit salvation” (Heb. 1:14). But your office is far more excellent, wondrous not only in your own eyes but also in those of angels.

2. These are the most unhappy times, which the apostle Paul foresaw: times in which people do not endure sound doctrine, but heap up teachers for themselves according to their own desires; in which they turn away from truth and turn to the tales and vanities of this age (2 Tim. 4:3–4). These are, I say, the last times, in which charity grows cold and the iniquity of many abounds. Why do I say this? Because, as you have heard, the holy Gospel describes three persons—or, to say more plainly, three kinds of teachers. The first kind includes only some part of the multitude of prelates, but each of the two following kinds includes a plentiful and destructive multitude; yet their number protects them. In the first kind alone charity abounds; in the other two it wholly grows cold, where iniquity indeed abounds. You have heard the characteristics of each. The good shepherd is he who lays down his life for his sheep; [Col. 1087B] the hired hand is he who sees the wolf coming and flees; the thief is he who slaughters and kills. The good shepherd seeks not to do his own will, but the benefit of his Lord. To him alone he keeps faith, for him he labors, him he honors. He seeks glory for him, not for himself. “To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, to God alone, be honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen” (1 Tim. 1:17). “Not to us, 740 O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113:1). To us wretches grant pardon, grant grace; preserve glory for yourself, since from you come pardon for sins and grace for merits. In every labor of his stewardship, the good shepherd seeks not his own interests but those of Christ; this is charity’s special mark. Hence, if he should at any time fail, “charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Pet. 4:8; Prov. [Col. 1087C] 10:12); and he also has an advocate in heaven, Jesus Christ our Lord, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins (1 John 2:1–2).

3. The hired hand, as we have said, is one who sees the wolf coming and flees. He therefore seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. Otherwise, surely he would not flee, but would rather lavish his possessions—indeed himself—than expose his flock to plunderers. There are many hired hands who in prosperity cannot easily be distinguished from good shepherds. For they have much in common with them. They have had a sound election at their entrance; nevertheless, they maintain a clean manner of life as they proceed. They love and seek the Church’s peace; they involve themselves profitably and vigorously in ecclesiastical [Col. 1087D] affairs; they do not refuse the burdensome weight of office—but this is because they seek the glory of honor. For they love the chief places at feasts, greetings in the marketplace, and to be called rabbi by men (Matt. 23:6; Mark 12:39). Often they also feed on the bread of tears and drink the wine of compunction in remembrance of sins, as the younger son testifies, who spent all his substance in a far country by living extravagantly. Hence he said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have bread in abundance!” (Luke 15:17). If hired hands abound in bread, will laborers perish by hunger? I mean those laborers who, the rarer they are on earth, are the dearer they are held in heaven. Truth complains of their scarcity, saying: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers [Col. 1088A] are few” (Luke 10:2). The harvest is certainly plentiful, and priests are many; hired hands too are many, but laborers are few. Few indeed are laborers, and exceedingly rare are those who are unashamed, who, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith, do not destroy by the example of evil conduct those whom they instruct by the word of holy preaching, preaching more effectively by deed than by word.

4. It should be noted that the son does not say, “Make me one of your hired hands,” but “Make me like one of your hired hands” (Luke 15:19), so that he may receive for himself those benefits in which they share at present. The Psalmist says: “He fed them with the fat of wheat” (Ps. 81:17). Whom did he feed? Hear what precedes: “The enemies of the Lord lied to him.” These are those whom he feeds with the fat of wheat and satisfies with honey. Who are they? Hired hands, who, though they believe for an hour, nevertheless withdraw in the time of temptation (Luke 8:13). Hence it is clear that they are friends of the world. But “the friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4). Again, they seek what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s (Phil. 2:21); and if they do not seek what is his, they are not with him. Those who are not with him are against him, because he says: “He who is not with me is against me” (Luke 11:23). And those against him are his enemies. These lie to God outwardly concerning their inward state. For when they preach soundly and live cleanly, they speak of soundness of intention, as though they had God as their motive and all that is within them blessed his holy name; whereas in fact they have not God but the world, not the Lord but [Col. 1088C] themselves, as their motive. They lie to God rather than to men, since such a bestowal of graces is an insult to him when it is evidently used to gain not God’s honor but human honor, and to serve not charity but cupidity. Therefore the unashamed laborer asks not merely for two things but for three, because “a threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. 4:12). For he asks not for discipline and knowledge, which hired hands may also have, but says: “Teach me goodness, and discipline, and knowledge” (Ps. 119:66). These three are required only in sons. For what would it profit to have discipline 741 in conduct and knowledge in preaching unless goodness of intention were present? Nowhere is it written that either service to the flesh [Col. 1088D] or knowledge of reason is sufficient; rather, a good will is sufficient. Once the will is healed, both the chastening of the flesh through discipline and the illumination of reason through knowledge will be useful and reward-bearing.

5. For the reasons stated above, therefore, and others of the same kind, we said that in prosperity the hired hand cannot easily be distinguished from the good shepherd, because while the security of peace smiles upon him, the weakness of his intention is concealed. “Nothing is hidden that shall not be revealed” (Matt. 10:26). “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels” (Ecclus. 27:6). When the wind of adversity blows, the effect of conduct immediately reveals what is weak in the intention. For he sees the wolf coming and flees. Who are these wolves? The tyrants and plunderers of the age, who, tempted by their own desire or driven by inborn malice, [Col. 1089A] burn churches, lay waste Christ’s sheepfolds, strip orphans and widows, bring proscription upon the poor, and blaspheme God in their actions. Once they have committed robberies and broken churches, when the sword of vengeance is drawn against them, they come either flattering or threatening. And the hired hand flees, whether from love of the flatterer or fear of the persecutor. From where does he flee? From the straight path of justice, from defense of the Church, from liberation of the homeland, from vengeance for orphans and widows. Where does he flee? To protect what he possesses—or rather what possesses him: namely, purses, granaries, and cellars; certainly not to reserve them for the poor, but to empty them for thieves or let them be consumed by fire. For one may have relatives placed within the province of tyrants, and therefore often flatters plunderers in order to provide for his relatives; so that they may have peace and flourish among tyrants, the holy Church is permitted to be afflicted and justice trampled underfoot.

6. And what shall I say of thieves? Thieves are heretics. These are the thieves and robbers who come in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves (Matt. 7:15). “All who came before me are thieves and robbers.” Thieves, because they harm secretly; robbers, because they rage openly. Heretics disseminated perverse doctrines among the people; by the perversity of their teaching they obscured the Catholic faith and led the simple into error. I do not believe that any one of you is a heretic. You all believe in God, three and one; that he suffered and was buried, that he descended and ascended. Yet does this faith make one Catholic? By this faith, demons themselves would certainly be Catholics; for, as James says, “they believe—and tremble” (James 2:19). But what truly makes one Catholic is not the faith shared by demons and human beings, but only that which is shared by human beings and angelic spirits. What is that faith? The [Col. 1089C] faith which works through love, of which the Apostle says: “Neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith which works through love” (Gal. 5:6). He himself was endowed with this faith when he said: “While we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6:10), not of the world.

Do you have this faith? Would that you did! But this is the faith which conquers the world, because “this is the victory that conquers the world—our faith” [Col. 1089D] (1 John 5:4). Shall I say that you conquer the world, or that you are conquered by the world? I see your churches badly treated; I see some half-ruined and some utterly overthrown. I see desolation in the villages, silence in the fields, and devastation everywhere. I see insolence among soldiers, disobedience among men, and folly in all. Yet you gladly endure such fools, though perhaps you yourselves are wise. For you endure their reducing you to slavery, devouring you, taking from you, exalting themselves over you, and sometimes even striking you in the face (1 Cor. 11:19–20), or squeezing money from you even when you have been shut up in prison.

Do you suffer these things so that through your patience you may possess your souls? For patience is necessary to us, so that, doing the will of God, we may bear fruit with joy [Col. 1090A]. Do you endure these things in order to do God’s will? Certainly not; rather, in order to fulfil your own will, to provide more freely for the desires of your flesh, to make more convenient provision for your children and parents, and to dwell upon the estates of tyrants in their peace, using their woods and cultivating their fields. For this reason you flatter princes and the powers of this darkness, both men and demons. Men, because you speak according to their will; according to their will you bind and loose. They themselves are half-bishops and half-archdeacons; indeed, to tell the truth, with all due respect to everyone, they are above bishops, above archdeacons, above priests. And truly, those who wield power are today called benefactors (Luke 22:25).

You flatter demons because you make them like the Most High within yourselves. “I will set,” he says, “my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:14). And he who is king over all the children of pride has frozen your inward parts with the cold of his wickedness; and, like a strong man armed, guarding his own court, he peacefully occupies the throne of your will, where the Most High ought to sit. “On earth,” it says, “peace to men.” To whom? To those of great learning? Of great nobility? No, but to those of good will (Luke 2:14). And where there is peace, there is God, because “his dwelling is made in peace” (Ps. 75:3). Thus it is clear that his seat is good will. Does one therefore conquer the world who has, not God, but the devil dwelling inwardly, and serves tyrants and robbers outwardly? Rather, he is conquered by the world; he is conquered by the devil [Col. 1090C]; he is conquered by his own flesh. “He is fixed in the mire of the deep, and has no firm footing” (Ps. 68:3), nor power to rise again.

7. Lord God of hosts, stir up your power and come, that you may draw us out of the pit of misery and the mud of filth. Stretch forth your right hand to the work of your hands. Draw our souls out of prison, that they may no longer obey the world but confess your name. Be gracious to your officials, who must render you an account of your sheep. Come, Lord, and do not delay. The devil is raging; the enemy of the human race is raging, knowing that he has but a little time. We have faith, but without works it is dead, and we are dead along with it. Increase our faith, that in your vicars [Col. 1090D] it may work through love, so that at their command mountains may be moved and demons driven from possessed souls—so that they may first be cast out of those souls, before they are cast with them into eternal fire. Increase, I say, our faith, because “this is the victory that conquers the world—our faith” (1 John 5:4). By this faith the saints conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, quenched the violence of fire, put the edge of the sword to flight, and were made strong from their weaknesses (Heb. 11:33–34).

In our regions there is fire everywhere, the sword on every side. Why do you not work righteousness? Why do you not quench the fires? Why do you not put the edge of the sword to flight? Why? The reason is ready to hand: because you seek to please men, not God. Hence Paul says: “If I were still pleasing men, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. [Col. 1091A] 1:10). You are not strengthened from your weaknesses, but grow numb through your sloth; nor can you administer justice upon evildoers. Why? Because there is no strength in your fortitude; for “the Lord scatters the bones of those who please men.” Flesh is weak, but bones are strong. Therefore he has scattered the bones—that is, the strength—of those who seek to please men. “They were put to shame, because God despised them” (Ps. 52:6); and you are put to shame in your actions, not honoured but burdened with your dignities, because God has despised you. For God has despised all who depart from his judgments (Ps. 118:118).

You have faith, but I call you to works—especially you who are Christ’s vicars, shepherds of souls, who ought to instruct others, not destroy them. You especially, I say [Col. 1091B], because you cannot perish alone, since you ought to go before others by teaching and doing. Many are Catholics in their preaching who are heretics in their conduct. What heretics did by perverse doctrines, most people today do by evil examples. They deceive the people and lead them into error; and they are so much the graver than heretics as works prevail over words.

8. Did not the Only-begotten, who is in the bosom of the Father, come forth from his secret place into your public sphere? Did he not descend from heaven to earth, that by his preaching and manner of life he might persuade men to despise the world? Are you not his vicars? Ought you not also to preach what he preached, dissuade from what he dissuaded, and persuade to what he persuaded? You are called Christians from Christ. Ought you not walk in the same way [Col. 1091C] in which Christ walked? Ought not you, his vicars, to live as he lived? Certainly so—unless perhaps you are wiser or holier than he.

Therefore speak, archdeacons; speak, priests; let bishops also speak: what is gold doing on bridles and saddles? What is such ornament doing on garments? What is such excessive display doing in food? “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them” (1 Cor. 6:13). There was great brilliance of clothing and delicate provision of food with that rich man of the Gospel, who was clothed in purple and fine linen and feasted splendidly every day (Luke 16:19). Yet he died and was buried in hell. O dreadful, execrable, and horrible tomb, where there is weeping [Col. 1091D] and gnashing of teeth; where are waters of snow; where the worm does not die; where the fire is not quenched! This tomb received the rich man, but Abraham’s bosom received poor Lazarus. “Who is wise and will keep these things?” (Ps. 106:43). “A senseless man will not know, nor will a fool understand these things” (Ps. 91:7).

Who, I ask, among laypeople seeks temporal things more eagerly than clerics, or uses what he acquires more foolishly? When laypeople see such extravagance in the furnishings of clerics, are they not thereby invited rather to love the world than to disregard it? “Physician, heal yourself” (Luke 4:23). If you preach that the world is to be despised, first despise it yourself; then you will invite others to this more effectively. Give your voice a voice of power; let life accord with words; and at once the word of God will be living and effective in your mouth [Col. 1092A], sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb. 4:12).

But it is certainly not so: rather, as the people, so the priest; as the layman, so the cleric. Both desire, both love the world and the things in the world. Yet the layperson must labour, whereas clerics wish, without labour, to possess the whole world. They wish to share in men’s greed and excess, but not in their labour. They wish to sin, but not to be scourged with men. Therefore it must be feared that they will be scourged with demons.

9. How could secular people fail to spend their substance in luxurious living, even in the presence of priests? How could they fail to give themselves to the vanities and enticements of this age? How could they fail to be insolent and puffed up, when they see such extravagance and such insolence [Col. 1092B] among clerics? Do you not, in their presence, irreverently misuse the alms of the poor? From the patrimony of the Crucified One you do not make books for churches, but feed concubines in your chambers; you fatten dogs and adorn horses, decorating their breasts with trappings and gilding their heads.

And truly, “the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4:1). Streets are broad, and broad is the way that leads to death. The stones of the sanctuary—that is, priests—stand at the heads, that is, at the entrance of broad ways; for by evil examples they teach peoples to enter broad ways which lead to death and plunge them into the depths of hell. Pain in the head flows down into the limbs. The priests are the heads of the people. “Every head is sick, and every heart sorrowful” (Isa. 1:5) [Col. 1092C]. The prelates of the Church are sick in their desires. Since sickness is therefore in the heads, sorrow arises in the hearts. The hearts are the religious men of the Church, who, understanding their honour, do not look to vanities and false madness; neither are they compared to senseless beasts, nor made like them. Weeping, they weep in the night of this adversity, when greed grows strong among the prelates of the Church and love grows cold.

10. And with good reason the holy Church cries today: “Behold, in peace my bitterness is most bitter” (Isa. 38:17). Today there is a persecution of holy Church, far greater and more severe than can be believed; and such a persecution presses upon her as there has not been from the beginning. The devil has persecuted her in many ways, but never more grievously than today [Col. 1092D], because there has never been a greater destruction of Christians, nor a freer or safer transgression of the divine commandments. He persecuted the Church in her beginning through tyrants; as she advanced, he persecuted her through heretics; now, joyful and flourishing, he persecutes her through unlawful impulses.

There are three elements in the soul: reason, will, and sensuality. Judgment belongs to reason; desire to will; the flesh ought to render obedience. Thus he tortured the flesh in martyrs; disturbed reason in the simple; but today he generally corrupts the will in all. Therefore the Church’s bitterness was bitter indeed under the persecution of tyrants, more bitter under the craftiness of heretics, but most bitter today through the perversity of desires. Woe to those who say, “Peace,” when there is no peace. The Church has peace among outsiders [Col. 1093A]; but wicked, criminal sons rage against her—sons who disembowel their own mother in order to give themselves birth in honour. She has outward peace everywhere, but inward peace in few, because everywhere, or almost everywhere, the will does not consent to the judgment of reason, but takes it captive under the law of sin. For although reason may be sound in judgment, the will is nevertheless perverse in desire; and in it, as we have said above, the devil sits like the Most High.

11. Awake, righteous ones; cast out the devil and cleanse God’s seat, because righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne. Owing to your sins, he has gone out from his temple. Bring him back to his holy temple. “For the temple of God is holy, which temple you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). The soul of the righteous person is God’s seat and temple [Col. 1093B]. The Lord works wonders in his temple and gives oracles. Let the Lord, whom you seek, come to his temple, so that you may rule over fleshly desires and resist diabolical temptations. Let the Angel of the Covenant, whom you desire, come (Mal. 3:1), to announce his will to you and confirm the promised inheritance.

Let his parents bring him into his temple—namely, his father, mother, and brothers. Who are they? Let him himself answer: “Whoever does the will of my Father who is in heaven, he is my father and mother and brother and sister” (Matt. 12:50). Father, by begetting through the word of preaching, as the Apostle says: “Through the Gospel I begot you in Christ” (1 Cor. 4:15). Mother, by giving birth through the example of holy conduct [Col. 1093C]. Brother and sister, by loving chastely in brotherly love. You are, or ought to be, these parents.

The people have appointed you mediators between themselves and God, that God may speak to you and you may speak to him. For this reason they give you their alms and firstfruits: that through your prayers and merits God may be gracious to them, and they may be brought to him. But how will you render him appeased to others when you render him offended to yourselves? Your prayer is not clean before God. Therefore seek for yourselves parents of Jesus Christ, who may bring him to you and lead him into his temple. Seek those who do God’s will from the heart, who have despised worldly life, who chastise their body and reduce it to servitude, not so as to please men but God.

12. Learn not only to receive alms, but also to distribute them [Col. 1093D]. “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke 16:9). Do not merely speak, but do good to all; and, as the Apostle says, “Do not forget beneficence and sharing, for by such sacrifices God is won” (Heb. 13:16). Let such persons therefore bring Jesus into his temple through righteousness and lead him through judgment. Open to him the gates of righteousness; otherwise he will not enter to you. “Love righteousness, you who judge the earth.” It belongs to you to exercise judgment, because you are the senators of the whole world. Therefore love righteousness (Wis. 1:1), and “judge rightly, sons of men” (Ps. 57:2).

Why do you hesitate to lay hold of discipline? Restrain yourselves from your wicked deeds, possessing and practising righteousness; for “he who holds fast to righteousness will obtain her, and she will meet him as an honoured mother” (Sir. 15:1–2) [Col. 1094A]. Without righteousness, not only a commonwealth but not even a small household can stand. Why do you fear the princes and powers of this darkness? Why do you subject yourselves to them? Do you wish to be exalted on earth? Do you wish to be exalted among nations? Lay hold of righteousness and practise it. Lay hold of it by restraining yourselves; practise it by justifying the humble and poor; and surely in righteousness you shall be exalted.

For the Psalmist says: “And in your righteousness they shall be exalted.” Who? Clearly, the blessed people who know jubilation. In jubilation diverse voices harmonize. Therefore those know jubilation who know how to give peace to nations, free the people of God, and preserve the unity of peoples in the bond of peace. Such persons, Lord [Col. 1094B], shall not wander in the darkness of this world, but shall walk in the light of your countenance; they shall rejoice, not in their own countenance, but in your name; they shall be exalted, not in the friendship of tyrants, but in your righteousness (Ps. 88:16–17).

You fear being trampled by lions if you hold to righteousness. Daniel cries out in the lions’ den, “They did me no harm.” Why? “Because righteousness was found in me before God” (Dan. 6:22). “Your right hand is full of righteousness” (Ps. 47:11). By the right hand spiritual things are received; by the left, temporal things. “Length of days is in her right hand; in her left are riches and glory” (Prov. 3:16). At the judgment, the goats will be at his left, to whom he gives glory and riches in this age; but at the Lamb’s right will be those for whom length of days has been prepared (Matt. 25:33–46). Do not thirst for the gifts in his left hand, because [Col. 1094C] those who desire his left hand in this age will be placed at his left hand in judgment. Cling to his right hand, so that in judgment you may sit at his right hand upon the seats of judges, and in the present life press down the necks of the proud and exalted—not by your own strength, but by the strength of his right hand—because “the right hand of God has wrought might” (Ps. 117:16).

13. Yet do you wish to receive double gifts from his hand, that is, spiritual and temporal goods? First seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, which belong to the right hand; and all these things shall be added to you (Matt. 6:33), which belong to the left. First seek God’s kingdom, that God may dwell and reign within you; then seek his righteousness, that the people may seek and receive the law from your mouth [Col. 1094D]. From so great a grace of merits there shall be rendered to you a glory of rewards “which eye has not seen,” etc.; and besides these, these temporal things shall be added to you, because “glory and riches are in his house.” Whose house? Without doubt, that of the righteous generation of which it was said above: “The generation of the upright shall be blessed” (Ps. 111:2–3). Blessed in predestination, it is blessed in justification, and it shall be blessed in glorification. “The blessing of the Lord is upon the head of the righteous” (Prov. 10:6), because “the mercy of the Lord is from everlasting” (Ps. 102:17) through predestination, and unto everlasting through glorification.

Therefore practise righteousness, yet not according to your own judgment, but according to the judgment that dictates it, because “righteousness and judgment are the correction of his throne” (Ps. 96:2). If you only exercised judgment and possessed no dominion [Col. 1095A], you would be judges only, not makers of righteousness, and therefore could not practise righteousness. For this reason he who gave you judgment also gave you dominion, as the prophet foretold: “They shall judge nations and rule peoples” (Wis. 3:8). The dominion of prelates is twofold. For they possess the keys of the Church, by which they shut and none opens; they open [Col. 1096A], and none shuts. They also possess royal rights, because they are lords of cities and towns. They hold not only bishoprics but also consulships, so that it may rightly be said to them: “What more ought I to have done, and have not done?” But what was given them for help has become for them an occasion of stumbling.

Something appears to be missing.

[Col. 1095]

## SERMON TO THE PRELATES CONVENED IN COUNCIL

On this text: “For we must all be made manifest before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10). (G)*

[NOTE.]

746 This sermon was delivered a few years after the death of Eugenius III, from no. 3; and indeed during the schism, under the pontificate of Alexander III, from nos. 10 and 11. The author was a Cistercian monk, no. 11, perhaps Gilbert, abbot of Cîteaux, to whom Alexander III wrote. In the earlier editions it bore the title “Sermon in a General Council.” But “general” appears to have been added from no. 4, where the supreme judgment is called a “general council.”

[Col. 1095B] 1. Not because of any wisdom in me, but because of the shadow of a name lately great on earth above the name of great men who either then existed or exist on earth today, there is laid upon me a burden too great for me: to deliver a discourse in a great church. Would that nothing be expected from me which will not be found in me—nothing keenly devised, nothing eloquently demonstrated! I am not he to whom it was said: “Your lips drip honeycomb” (Song 4:11). And even if I were what I am not, I should nevertheless have cause for fear from what the Wise Man says: “A full soul treads honeycomb underfoot” (Prov. 27:7).

Sometimes even bodily distaste may be relieved by a small amount of somewhat sharp food. And what is so sharp to every rational spirit as that terrible expectation of judgment? The remembrance of death does indeed sting, but this pierces much more deeply. Yet we also read concerning death that the Lord said to the prophet: “Cry out.” “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is grass, and all its glory like the flower of grass: the grass withers and its flower falls; but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isa. 40:6, 8).

Hence the wisest Solomon, wisely admonishing each shepherd, says: “Diligently know the countenance of your flock, and consider your herds. For you will not always be prince, but the crown is given from generation to generation. The meadows are opened, green plants have appeared, and hay has been gathered from the mountains” (Prov. 27:23–25). “Diligently know,” he says, “the countenance of your flock.” For this is your concern, Scripture saying: “Man sees in the face; God sees in the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7, and Ps. 7:10) [Col. 1095D]. Therefore, just as it is rash to judge the hidden things of another’s heart, so a shepherd may not disregard the things which are apparent in the face. Moreover, the countenance possesses a certain credible indication of the will, whence it is also said to have received its name. To this also belongs what the Lord says: “By their fruits you shall know them” (Matt. 7:20).

2. Therefore a shepherd must take care not to be found suspicious in judging the intention of the heart; but he must nevertheless take heed not to be negligent in considering outward conduct. For he is commanded not merely to know, but diligently to know, the countenance of his flock, lest he presume that he has easy knowledge if he has not applied diligence. “For you will not always be prince,” but will someday render an account of your stewardship to the supreme Prince, when you can no longer be steward. “The crown,” he says, “is given from generation to generation.” Thus, as the Apostle says, “they became many priests because, death intervening, they could not remain.” Nor is it surprising that they succeed one another in turns, since they approach to discharge the duties of the eternal Priest, of whom the Apostle adds: “But Jesus, because he remains forever, has an everlasting priesthood” (Heb. 7:23–24) [Col. 1096C].

Therefore the crown is given from generation to generation to those from whom an account of that same crown is required; and this succession is found among those to whom a vicarious stewardship is entrusted. What would human ambition not do to obtain this crown if it were perpetual? But now this crown has an end, while desire has no measure. Would that the crown of life, which God will render to those who love him, were sought and desired as this crown is sought and desired, which he has permitted many to obtain who neglect him!

[Col. 1096D] 3. But if it is given from generation to generation, how many are these generations today? If it does not endure forever, perhaps it lasts for a long time. Observe what follows, and observe what you see daily: “The meadows are opened, and green plants have appeared” [Col. 1097A]. Behold a meadow most delightfully springing forth, most gloriously flowering, most pleasantly green. But where there is so much verdure, how much vigour is there? A few years ago, under our father Pope Eugenius of good memory, the Church likewise assembled, and it shone splendidly with a great abundance of green plants. Where are those who were flourishing then? Today we see here few of those whom we saw seated together then, and we know no few seats which afterward changed their occupants many times. Very many pass away; and amid such great learning, knowledge is not yet manifold, but condemnable negligence is, according to that saying: “You will not see destruction when you see wise men dying; the foolish and the senseless perish together” (Ps. 48:11).

“The meadows,” he says, “are opened.” But how often have these meadows been shorn and yet must be shorn! How often do they change their fleeces! How often have they already been cut down, and must still be cut down, from generation to generation! “And green plants have appeared”: thus in some today dignity flourishes; in others authority flourishes; bodily elegance flourishes, abundance of possessions, favour with princes; but it does not flourish for long. Finally, he says, “they have appeared,” not “green plants appear.” For appearing is so brief that the time during which they have appeared does not seem long. They appeared and vanished; they appeared and passed away, and their places were not found. Indeed, their places will be found, nor will they be empty for long. For whoever depart, people are readily and abundantly found to be placed in their stead at once. “Green plants have appeared,” he says, “and hay has been gathered from the mountains” [Col. 1097C], because all verdure has withered and the loftiness of men has been brought low.

4. These things should indeed suffice for contempt of the world. But if we do not sufficiently disregard things that perish, let us fear things that destroy. For today the trumpet of salvation sounds something more terrible for us through the Apostle: “We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ.” We are in a council, and we are invited to a council: a wholly general council, where no one will be absent, where all must stand, and where not only the merits of all but also the works of all will be judged. If more people seriously considered this, as they ought, they would not so seek provostships in addition to archdeaconries; they would not so seek deaneries for themselves or their own dependants in addition to treasurerships; nor would miserable men, with such dreadful lust, add hump upon hump, when one hump alone could more than sufficiently hinder a camel from entering the kingdom of heaven through the eye of a needle [Col. 1097D].

They ought rather to have considered what they read: “Do not become many teachers, my brethren, knowing that you shall receive a greater judgment” (James 3:1). Nor ought those spiritual men to have forgotten this, who boast that meanwhile they judge works indeed and are judged by no one (1 Cor. 2:15): “A most severe judgment shall be for those who rule, and the powerful shall suffer powerful torments” (Wis. 6:6–7). For mercy is readily granted to the lowly person, who now prefers to be judged by men, knowing how dreadful it is to fall into the hands of the living God.

[Col. 1098A] 5. He is the one before whose tribunal we must all stand, that each may receive according to what he has done. For there will not then be what is now said of some people, namely, that numbers seem to defend them. Nor will there be any respect of persons there; no evasion will be able to avail, when all things are naked and open to the eyes of him to whom we must then give account; no concealment will be possible there, where an account must be rendered even for an idle word.

Therefore, in the body of Christ, which is the Church, it must be examined much more closely what rank each person has held; how he entered it, with what intention, by what merits, and through what support; how he himself lived in it; how he perhaps presided over others or benefited them; how he acquired worldly substance and how he distributed what he acquired [Col. 1098B]. For each shall receive according to what he did while he was in his own body, whether good or evil.

O good—good indeed! Evil—evil indeed! How happy are those who receive evil in this life, that they may deserve to receive that good! And how miserable are those who pass their days meanwhile in good things, that in a moment they must descend to that evil! Lord, deliver us from that evil which will come at the end, as you taught us to ask at the end of the prayer (Matt. 6:13). For that good will be the supreme good, full good, and every good, of which God says to Moses: “I will show you every good” (Exod. 33:19). And that evil will be every evil: fire and worm—the latter immortal, the former unquenchable—chains and darkness, weeping and gnashing of teeth; pain without remedy, death without end, perpetual repentance without fruit, eternal damnation without hope of pardon.

6. And what will those do there who meanwhile nourish their bodies in pleasures? Let the wealthy man fear at the remembrance of death, and not possess with love what he will quickly leave with grief. For he brought nothing into this world, and without doubt will carry nothing more away. Let the ambitious man fear the future judgment at the consummation, where perhaps he will begin, though mighty, to hold the lowest place, when he sees the powerful cast down from their seat and the humble exalted. Let the pleasure-lover fear eternal evil, eternal punishments, where moth will be spread beneath him and worms will be his covering. If all these things, so clearly set forth beforehand [Col. 1098D], are not believed, I ask, why are they read? And if they are believed, how are they not feared? Or how can a cleric, wealthy from poverty and glorious from obscurity, fear them today? And rightly the Wise Man long ago warned us to flee such persons as a plague; but who now will flee this plague? It is found even on the small islands. You may see for yourselves whence it arises.

7. For this truly is a plague which has now occupied the whole world. It is a wasting disease which has now infected—if I may not say killed—the whole body of the Church. “From the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it,” says the prophet. “Wound and bruise and swelling sore have not been bound up, nor treated with medicine [Col. 1099A], nor softened with oil” (Isa. 1:6). Let the wound be referred to guilt, the bruise to disgrace, the swelling tumour to pride. There is a wound when conscience is injured inwardly; there is a bruise when life is also discoloured outwardly; there is a swelling sore when shamelessness is also added, according to the saying: “They were not ashamed with shame; they did not know how to blush” (Jer. 8:12).

There is wound and bruise when good things are insufficiently provided before God and men. There is a swelling sore when neither fear of God follows from the wound nor shame from the bruise, but men rejoice when they have done evil and glory in wickedness; finally, they neither fear God nor respect men. Sometimes there is a wound without a bruise, when something is done less chastely but cautiously. There is wound and bruise without swelling when those who have transgressed begin not to think highly of themselves, but to blush and to fear [Col. 1099B].

But nothing so repels that most merciful Samaritan as this swelling, so that he does not bind up the wound or pour in wine and oil. Hence it is also pointedly added concerning that same swelling sore: “It has not been bound up, nor treated with medicine, nor softened with oil.” “It has not,” he says, “been bound up,” because there is no one to restrain it; “nor treated with medicine,” because there is no one to rebuke it; “nor softened with oil,” because no one dares to confront them even with a mild admonition. Yet perhaps it may seem to be warmed with a certain reprobate oil—the oil of the sinner. For those who favour vices foster vices. But the sore is fostered for destruction, not salvation, when the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul and the wicked man is blessed.

The Apostle does not foster in this way when, sounding forth terribly, he says: “Each shall receive according to what he has done.” Knowledge, riches, and no human favour whatsoever will avail there. No unjust person, no unworthy person, shall occupy those second seats, which we read have long since been prepared for those who sit in judgment [Col. 1099C].

8. Would that those who today love the first seats, seize them wickedly, and ambitiously pursue them shamelessly, desired those seats instead! For we call prosperous things “favourable” (*secundae*), and the Lord, like good wine, keeps every good thing for us until later, contrary to human custom. I call them, then, those “second seats”: the seats which John the Evangelist testifies in the Apocalypse were placed around the throne of God for the twenty-four elders (Rev. 4:4) [Col. 1099D]. If anyone observes there the doubled apostolic number, perhaps he will not find it difficult to recognize for whom the Judge has prepared those seats.

For in some are found both apostolic life and doctrine; in others, life only. In some, I say, merit together with office; in others, merit without office. If anyone should say that some are also found who lack apostolic perfection but are heirs only of probation, let them see where they sit—indeed, let them beware lest perhaps they are that third part of the stars which the dragon’s tail is said to have dragged down from heaven to earth. The promise of those seats is read as having been made to profession alone, when Simon Peter said to the Lord: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you: what then shall we have?” And the Lord said to him: “You shall sit upon twelve seats, judging” (Matt. 19:27–28) [Col. 1100A].

As we said, the twelfth number is doubled because this profession seems to be found both in prelates and in subjects, as it were in Noah and Daniel. These also are the two seraphim in Isaiah (Isa. 6:2), who are read as standing above the throne upon which the Lord was seated. For the name itself is interpreted “Burning Ones” or “Kindling Ones”; and to burn belongs to religious persons, to kindle to prelates.

9. But in the form of the four living creatures (Ezek. 1:5), which are likewise recorded as having appeared in the prophetic vision, we believe that only the shepherds and preachers of the Church are signified. In them appeared together the likeness of a lion, an ox, a man, and an eagle, so that by these four [Col. 1100B] we might be taught what manner of men such shepherds and rulers ought to be. For everyone who presides over the people of God must show himself a lion, sternly correcting offences; an ox, vigorously managing earthly matters; a man, kindly sympathizing with men; an eagle, soaring on high and subtly contemplating divine things.

Would that no one today among prelates were found to have too much of the lion and too little of the man, raging immoderately against his subjects, ruling with severity and power, and neither showing nor recognizing himself as a man toward men! Would that no one displayed too much man and too little lion, so sympathizing with men that he is not even indignant at crimes! Would that no one had too much of the ox and too little of the eagle, being too immoderately occupied with earthly things [Col. 1100C] and less eager for heavenly and divine things! Would that no one showed himself too much an eagle and imitated the ox less than he should, seeking heavenly things in such a way that he refuses to administer earthly things.

Hence blessed Gregory also, in the *Pastoral Rule*, admonishes that a ruler should be near to each person in compassion and, above all, absorbed in contemplation: in these qualities the face of man and eagle are together commended to him. Next, that he should be, through humility, a companion to those who do well; but, through zeal for justice, raised up against the vices of offenders: thus displaying both the lion’s face and the human face. Thirdly also, that he should not diminish care for inward things amid outward occupations, nor abandon care for outward things amid concern for inward things [Col. 1100D] (*Part* 2, ch. 5): that is, that he should temper the face of the ox and the eagle in a proportion suited to each other.

10. Let him therefore who reads this concerning the faces of the four living creatures consider whether he employs all these fittingly and moderately; let him also consider in what respect he especially exceeds the rule of equity, having either less or more than he ought. For if each quality were fittingly apportioned among those who are seen to hold pre-eminence in the Church, then the one wheel having four faces upon the earth beside these living creatures (Ezek. 1:15) would not merely exist but would be visible. The Church would not today be torn apart—or rather, the tunic of Christ would not appear to be torn, nor would it ever have been torn or be torn in the future.

Although individual shepherds seem to preside over certain individual churches [Col. 1101A], and the holy living creatures in some fashion draw several wheels, yet their appearance ought to be as though there were a wheel within a wheel, so that it may be found to encompass together all churches within the compass of one Catholic Church. Let their appearance therefore be as though there were a wheel within a wheel, in order to avoid dissimulation; let there be works, in order to guard against pretence. For some today conceal what they think and have no true appearance; others perhaps feign what they are, but works are not found in them. By their fruits we recognize those who abase themselves wickedly, while their inward parts are full of deceit.

Certainly every prelate ought in this respect to become a model for the flock, so that those whom the Church has nourished and exalted might not despise her in her need. And when the living creatures went, the wheels went; when they stood, the wheels stood; and when they were lifted from the earth, the wheels were likewise lifted—provided, however, that the spirit of life was in the wheels. Otherwise, however much the shepherds advance in virtue, however steadfastly they persevere, however much they seek the things above rather than those upon the earth, their peoples will never follow through the effectiveness of their efforts unless they are drawn by the Spirit. But now, alas and grievously, in many places, when the living creatures retreat, the wheels return with them; when they fall, the wheels fall; and when they bend down to the earth, the wheels likewise bend down [Col. 1101B].

11. Forgive us, Reverend Fathers. Many have been angered with us and scandalized by us because, from the beginning of this schism, our lowliness has not dissembled with them, has not kept silence, and has not remained inactive. This was done [Col. 1101C] not by human presumption, but by fear of God: lest this small wheel of the Cistercian Order should thereafter be of no use to us at all if it were not a wheel within a wheel. But it ought to be so, as we have said, both in appearance and in deed. For monastic life would contribute nothing to the eternal salvation of souls—for which we live to God and have resolved to keep hard paths—if ecclesiastical communion were not present to us. Nor is it doubtful that a member cannot belong to the body if it refuses to be under the head.

If the Church has set rulers over the earth from her children in place of her fathers [Col. 1102A], she does this not by her own presumption but by divine authority, just as the Holy Spirit once ordained for her in the Psalm, saying: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them rulers over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17). You, I say, shall appoint them—not secular power, but ecclesiastical unity—so that everyone who enters the sheepfold by another way is not a shepherd, not even a hireling, but a thief and robber. Therefore he resists the divine ordinance who does not obey the ruler appointed by the Church; since the Lord has appointed him to her, so that in place of her fathers she may appoint rulers for herself from her children. Finally, whoever does not listen to the Church is judged a heathen and a heretic; and not only this, but he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

[Col. 1102B] 12. For this is the profession of faith which we profess in Baptism: that we believe in God the Father, and in the Son, and in the Holy Spirit, and immediately thereafter in the holy Catholic Church. Therefore, just as he makes the first faith void who does not believe in the most holy Trinity, so also does he who abandons ecclesiastical unity. For the saints teach that it is an unforgivable blasphemy against the Holy Spirit to separate oneself from that same holy Church which has been gathered through the Holy Spirit.

For there is a great correspondence between the Holy Spirit and the Church. Just as the angel said of the blessed Virgin, “That which is born in her is of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 1:20), so also what we see reborn from water and the Spirit: the water itself is the Church, as John says, “The waters are peoples” (Rev. 17:15). If this is true [Col. 1102C]—indeed, because it is true—he is immersed in water to no purpose who is not united to the peoples of the Church.

Therefore, turning to the Lord our God, let us render him manifold thanks for this most devout assembly of ours; and let us also offer humble prayers, that in his mercy he may deign to correct the practices of Catholics and the errors of schismatics, through Jesus Christ his Son, our Lord, who lives and reigns with him as God in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1101]

## SERMON ON FLEEING THE IMPURITY OF HEART AND BODY. 750

On Luke 12:35: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands.” It consists almost entirely of centos from the Fathers, especially Guerric, Abbot of Igny. (G)\*

[Col. 1101D] 1. God, the lover of chastity and integrity, himself a virgin and Son of a Virgin, has set before us a discourse on avoiding impurity of heart and body and seeking purity: brief indeed in words, but weighty in mysteries; plain in expression, but full of meaning. [Col. 1102D] In it we should note that God’s words to us are often not so much sounds of spoken utterance as effects of deeds; for in those things which are seemingly stated simply, we must seek not a simple but a manifold meaning; and that which outwardly sounds corporeal overflows with spiritual mysteries.

For he says: “Let your loins be girded.” If we wished to take literally this saying of the Lord concerning girding the loins, we could find no spiritual benefit in it. For it would contribute little to the eternal salvation of the soul if someone merely girded his loins bodily or held a burning lamp in his hands. Therefore another spiritual understanding must be sought in girded loins and burning lamps—one worthy of the divine command and found fitting and beneficial to our salvation. For the spiritual Master, whose words are spirit and life, would not take such pains to instruct us concerning the girding of bodily loins.

The loins which the Lord commands us to gird are our unlawful appetites; he desires them to be girded in us because he wishes the unlawful motions of the flesh to be calmed within us. We gird our loins, therefore, when we restrain carnal desires within ourselves. Then we gird our loins when we avoid evil desires and wicked deeds: when the mind resists lust, when its effect is denied to sensuality, when sensuality is trodden down, 751 when impurity is subdued. Then we gird our loins when we do not yield to carnal desires, when we struggle against their pleasures [Col. 1103B].

2. It should also be noted that what the Lord himself set forth, he had long before deigned to set forth through his servant. For among the other commandments which Moses delivered to the people of God, he commands them to guard against impurity: “You shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20:14; [Col. 1103C] Matt. 5:27). Indeed, if we examine attentively, we find that in both Testaments the Lord condemned sensuality by words and by figures. In the Old Testament he condemns sensuality by words, as in the passage just mentioned: “You shall not commit adultery.” He condemns it by figures, as we read in Daniel, who himself testifies: “I lifted up my eyes and saw; and behold, a man clothed in linen, and his loins girded with fine gold” (Dan. 10:5).

What is understood by the loins except the pleasure of the flesh? Hence the Psalmist prays, saying: “Try my loins” [literally, “Burn my loins”] (Ps. 25:2). Had he not known that the pleasure of lust lies in the loins, he would never have asked that they be burned. Hence, because the power of the devil has prevailed most greatly over humankind through sensuality, the Lord’s voice says of him to blessed Job: “His power is in his loins” [Col. 1103D] (Job 40:11). Thus, by the girdle around the loins is signified the restraint of carnal fornication.

In the New Testament, however, the Lord condemns sensuality by words when he says: “Let your loins be girded”; that is, let the effects of carnal sensuality in you be restrained. But because the evil of sensuality is committed either in thought or in deed, the crafty adversary, when expelled from the desire for action, tries to defile the secret realm of thought. As bodily sensuality is forbidden through Moses, so sensuality of the heart is forbidden through the Redeemer. Through Moses, completed sensuality is forbidden; through the author of purity, sensuality merely thought is condemned.

Our Redeemer, coming, surpassed the precepts of the Law. From his elect he removed not only sensuality of the flesh but also sensuality of the heart [Col. 1104A], commanding them not only to gird the loins of the flesh—that is, to restrain sensuality from its effect—but also to gird the loins of the mind—that is, to restrain it even from thought. Hence John the Evangelist, having been banished in exile to the island of Patmos because of his unconquerable steadfastness in preaching the Gospel, announces among the other things he saw that our Redeemer was girded at the breasts, saying: “I turned and saw seven golden lampstands; and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like the Son of Man, clothed in a long robe, and girded at the breasts with a golden belt” (Rev. 1:12–13).

*Podes* in Greek is called *pedes* in Latin; hence a *poderis* is called a garment reaching to the ankles, because it touches the middle of the feet. What then is signified by the belt around the breast [Col. 1104B], except the restraint of sensuality in the heart? Since, therefore, in the former Testament only bodily adultery seems to be restrained by the Law, the prophet is shown girded about the loins. And because the purity of the later Testament also curbs sensuality in the heart, our Redeemer appeared girded at the breast.

3. Although these and many other commands against impurity are found in both Testaments, people in this age of grace nevertheless serve the pleasure of the flesh and their own lust as though they had never heard any of Christ’s or his saints’ commands concerning such matters. They do not know that no works of righteousness and piety are acceptable in God’s sight when they are shown to be defiled by the contagion of sensuality. Therefore, unless the flame of lust is extinguished through purity of heart, whatever virtues may arise do so in vain.

Why, then, are they overwhelmed by the enormity of this crime and do not even fear lest that pestilential fire, wickedly kindled in their flesh and members, has been kindled in the wrath and fury of the Lord, as he threatens through the prophet: “A fire has been kindled in my fury, and it shall burn to the lowest depths of hell; it shall devour the earth with its increase” (Deut. 32:22). The fire of the Lord is kindled in fury when the itch of the flesh and the incitements of lust so dominate the members of the wicked that, because they do not try to extinguish them with God’s grace, they are utterly unable to extinguish them.

By “earth” is understood this earthly body or earthly flesh, to which it is said in the case of the first sinner: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19). The shoots [Col. 1104D] of the earth are good works performed through this earthly body, but they are wholly burned up by the fire of lust. In this way the fire devours the shoots of the earth together with the earth, and the earth with its increase: for the Lord often brings the fire of sensuality to its end in the fire of Gehenna, which will devour the wicked man—a fire that is neither kindled nor extinguished—because “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. 66:24; Mark 9:45). For the Lord will give fire and worms to their flesh, that they may burn and suffer for ever (Judith 16:21).

But those who now violate in their bodies the temple of God and, by the impurity of lust, exclude themselves from the solidity of Christ’s body, which is the Church of the faithful [Col. 1105A], now burn delightfully through the sweetness of the flesh; but shortly they will burn miserably. As the Lord himself threatens in the Gospel: “If anyone does not abide in me, he shall be cast out like a branch and shall wither; and they shall gather him and cast him into the fire, and he burns” (John 15:6). He burns now indeed through God’s foreknowledge, but shortly will burn through the justice of recompense. Yet he would not burn there in experience unless he had first burned here through sensuality or through wickedness of heart.

4. That the enemies of the Lord burn even in this life is testified by the prophet Isaiah, who says: “And now fire consumes the adversaries” (Isa. 26:11).
