For he torments the wicked not only after this life by the avenging fire of Gehenna, but even now the flame of lust burns them up; and those who are afterwards to be punished by the penalty of recompense now afflict themselves by the torment of sensuality. Does it not seem a torment to them to serve lust enervatingly? That it is a torment and disgrace to the body is testified by the Apostle, who says: “The Lord gave them over to impurity, that they might dishonour their own bodies among themselves” (Rom. 1:24); and elsewhere: “Whatever sin a man commits is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:8) [Col. 1105B].

For what sinners account pleasure, these men regard as punishment. For as the flesh is fed by soft things, so the soul is nourished by hard things. Pleasant things cherish the flesh; harsh things train the soul. The flesh feeds upon delights; the soul is refreshed by bitterness. And as hard things wound the flesh, so soft things kill the spirit; as laborious things destroy the flesh, so delightful things extinguish the spirit. Thus the spirit perishes eternally from that by which the flesh rests sweetly for a time [Col. 1105C].

5. Since we have begun to speak of sensuality and fornication, it should be known that fornication is understood as fourfold—indeed, it is subdivided into four kinds, and in every one of these kinds it is most emphatically taught that it must be avoided, although one of them is understood to involve lesser guilt.

The first kind of this fourfold fornication is that by which a person desires in mind alone to mingle with obscene pleasures of the flesh. Of this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5:28). The second is that by which he brings to completion the desired act of pleasure, joined in carnal intercourse; concerning it the Apostle warns: “Flee fornication, brothers. For whatever sin a man commits is outside the body; but he who fornicates sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18) [Col. 1105D].

The third is that by which, burning with earthly desires, a person loves the creature more than the Creator of creatures. Of this the aforesaid Apostle of the Gentiles testifies, saying: “And covetousness, which is the service of idols” (Eph. 5:5). The fourth is that by which, venerating images as God, a person renders service to demons. Of this the Lord complains through the prophet against the Jewish people, saying: “Because she committed adultery with wood and stone” (Jer. 3:9).

And indeed fornication now flourishes most greatly in its three forms: in the desire for obscene intercourse [Col. 1106A], in the inclination to bodily sensuality, and in the pursuit of earthly happiness. But even the fourth has not been wholly extinguished, which consists in the worship of images. For we see that many pass from a particular form to the general category when they give themselves immoderately to an evil suggestion, so as to proceed through it to shameful action. They would not have come to the performance of evil unless evil thought had first preceded within them. For one comes to action through thought.

But when someone engaged in action does not possess what he may furnish to those serving him in this activity, he must necessarily advance even to avarice. And when even through avarice the things he desired are not available for him to expend sufficiently on lust, he does not care from what persons [Col. 1106B], or even from what demons, the things may be bestowed upon him which are wickedly consumed in the pleasure of the flesh.

6. After he has climbed all these steps of fornication and thereby descended—or rather fallen—into the depths of sins, with the eye of his heart closed the wretched man gives himself wholly to and attends to the pleasure of the flesh, like horse and mule, which have no understanding. He is likened to those whose flesh, according to the prophet, is like the flesh of asses (Ezek. 23:20). For the wantonness of asses is found to be such that they often mate with another species of animal. The flesh of fornicators is therefore compared with the flesh of asses because they sometimes engage not only in natural but also in unnatural embraces. The Apostle fittingly rebukes the shameful vices of men in honourable terms, in order honourably to recall many from dishonour to the pattern of honour (Rom. 1) [Col. 1106C].

Such people are clothed in purple and fine linen, if they can afford it; if not, in whatever is more delicate that they can afford. And they feast daily as splendidly as they can. But after the Lord had praised John the Baptist’s frugality in food and roughness of dress, he said: “Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses” (Matt. 11:8). He evidently wished it to be understood that those who pursue the delights of the flesh serve the kingdom of this age, not the kingdom of God.

But alas, what a terrible sentence from heaven was heard against the softness of that great harlot who contains in herself the character of all lovers of luxury: “As much as she lived in luxury and glorified herself, give her so much torment and mourning” [Col. 1106D] (Rev. 18:7).

7. Yet would that the effeminacy of Babylon’s more luxurious people were content with such delights—with merely soft garments and pleasant feasts—and that the branch of pleasure did not produce in them other thorns of vices; would that their entire sin were to indulge in pleasures and not to practise sensuality! For concerning the great harlot Babylon, from whose midst these pleasure-lovers seem to have gone forth to seduce God’s elect, I perhaps dare say this: however much she has lived in luxury, however much she has been clothed in purple, let her not therefore be a harlot, nor, according to the prophet, spread her legs to every passer-by (Ezek. 16:25).

Let them see for themselves whether that innate and pestilential fire has been so extinguished in them that, amid so many surrounding stimulants, it cannot be rekindled—especially with winds blowing from the opposite direction, that is, tempting words and lascivious laughter [Col. 1107A]. Yet I am accustomed to hear that it always lives in one who is dying, flourishes in an old man, and I know that it is stirred and rises even without fuel, and rages when nothing provokes it.

And when these lovers of luxury indulge in banqueting and drunkenness, or in the beds and indecencies of the age, should any adversity happen to them, they mark their foreheads with the sign of the cross, as though all their conduct appeared to accord with the precepts of the Crucified One. But let us observe how great is the perversity and abuse: that enemies of Christ’s cross wish to protect themselves by the sign of Christ’s cross, while, having followed sensual indulgence contrary to the godliness of Christ’s cross, they wish in danger to be defended by the power of Christ’s cross.

Plainly, the enemies of Christ’s cross are the friends of their own belly [Col. 1107B]: their god is their belly; their idol is money; their sweetness is the worm; their glory is vanity; all their striving is for human favour. But why do they glory so greatly in praise and human favour? For what is human favour except a scorching wind, a corrupting breeze, pestilential air, a little robber who despoils, a lurking murderer, a serpent in the road, a horned viper on the path, biting the horse’s hoofs so that its rider falls backward? A vain man is indeed lifted up into pride and, by the vanity of his own understanding, like a headlong horse he is carried into ruin. The serpent surely wounds and overturns his footsteps, provided that, flattering the flesh, it afterward draws the soul down with itself into Tartarus.

8. But if any religious person should rebuke or reprove them in order to correct them, saying: “Why do you deceive and neglect yourselves, and fail to regard the works of the Lord within yourselves? ‘Turn away from evil and do good’” [Col. 1107C] (Ps. 36:27). “‘Cease to act perversely’” (Isa. 1:16). “‘Take hold of discipline, lest the Lord at any time be angry, and you perish from the right way’” (Ps. 2:12), and similar things—they reply: “Will monks alone, or cloistered persons alone, obtain the kingdom of heaven? Will not secular persons also?” Indeed, secular persons also.

For what is the meaning of the Lord’s command to his disciples in the Gospel: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved” (Matt. 28:19; Mark 16:15–16)? “We have been baptized; we believe; therefore we shall be saved by this faith, according to the words of the Saviour.”

They fail to observe that, as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead. They rely too much on the name of faith while denying works. For today, if you ask about the mystery of faith, you will find almost everyone most Christian; if you examine consciences, you will find few truly Christian. The entire world confesses in words that it knows God, but denies him in deeds, so that those who seem to have the hope of godliness are often found to deny its power [Col. 1107D].

I know, indeed, that the earth is full of the confession of the Lord (Jer. 7); yet I hear the Prophet lamenting that faith has perished from the earth. “Do you suppose that, when the Son comes, he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8). Will he count as faith this faith of the negligent and contemptuous, by which he judges more lightly the blindness of unbelievers and judges the belief of demons better? For demons believe and tremble; people believe and do not tremble. Demons fear him in whom they believe; people, because they neither fear nor revere him in whom they believe, will be judged more severely for their contempt.

Therefore, brothers, let us not be deceived by the general name of faith, as though every faith ought to be counted unto righteousness. Rather, let us remember what kind of faith the Doctor of the Gentiles, in faith and truth, defined as that by which God is pleased. “Faith,” he says, “is the substance of things hoped for” (Heb. 11:1). This is the faith that works through love, so that hope may arise from faith at the prompting of a conscience conscious of merits, and faith may be laid down as the underlying foundation upon which the eternal goods to be hoped for are built [Col. 1108B]. Without this faith it is impossible to please God; with this faith it is impossible to displease him.

9. But if we, brothers, behave as though without faith, we put God behind our back, so that, disregarding his fear, we look rather upon vanities. For this reason, do we suppose that we deserve to be looked upon? Indeed, we shall be looked upon. But with what countenance? “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. 33:17). Yet how angry, how terrible, how unbearable that face is will then at last be known when those who hate him flee from before it. And from your face, Lord, where will they flee, except into the outer darkness, into that great and deep chaos which separates the region of life from that of death; into an abyss of darkness, burning sulphur, and consuming fire?

And which of us can dwell with consuming fire? Or who can endure to dwell with everlasting burnings? Then they will say to the mountains, “Fall upon us,” and to the hills, “Cover us” (Luke 23:30), judging it lighter to be swallowed by the gulf of hell than to endure the face of an angry God [Col. 1108C]. I confess to your Holiness that I am confounded and ashamed in myself, and even shudder to utter such harsh but truthful things to any persons whatsoever. But as the Lord lives, I dare not flatter; I have not dared to sew cushions and lay them under every elbow, knowing that the Lord says through the prophet to the people: “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you” (Isa. 3:12). The Lord stands to judge. For if I had heard good things of those whose vices I rebuke, I would certainly have praised them.

10. For how can I praise those who are called Christians in name alone, vainly taking Christ’s holy name upon themselves, while in their whole and unrestrained profession they pursue the things hostile to that name; those who by every manner of conduct and way of life declare themselves enemies of Christ? Are these the things that we should praise in them: a harlot’s dress and gait, clownish speech, an immodest eye, a belly worshipped as God, and every disgrace of life publicly inflicted in the face of God [Col. 1108D]? For the things done by them in secret are shameful even to mention. Let him who was sent to prophesy to them, and not I, dig through their wall, that he may see still greater abominations which they do not blush to commit before that dread Majesty.

What good things can I extol [Col. 1109A] in those whose every outward deed declares manifest hatred of God; whose life is not a temptation or warfare against sin, but voluntary slavery to sin; who seem to serve the law of sin both in mind and in flesh; who, with the prudence of the flesh—which is not subject to God’s law, nor indeed can be—and friendship with this world, both of which are enemies of God, seem plainly to have concluded a wretched pact with death and an agreement with hell? O miserable pact, miserable indeed, yet not beyond cancellation! For we know that it is written: “Your covenant with death shall be abolished, and your pact with hell shall not stand” (Isa. 28:18), because the sides of the north are the city of the great King (Ps. 47:5). For the number of the elect has always been increased from the number of the wicked.

[Col. 1109B] 11. But what right have I, who appear to be a monk, to judge those who are outside? My soul is troubled within me concerning myself. Let them see to themselves; it is nothing to me to judge the consciences of others, since I know that many have lived temperately and chastely amid every abundance and glory of the world, while conversely some have behaved wickedly under a harsher habit and a more sparing diet. Attend to yourselves, brothers. Do not judge secular persons; do not condemn them. Restrain the loins of mind and flesh, lest you fall through thought into the evil that threatens them through deed; for perverse thoughts separate from God (Wis. 1:3).

One thing is sensuality of the flesh, by which we corrupt chastity; another is sensuality of the heart, by which we glory in chastity. And we are so much the more sensual in God’s sight [Col. 1109C] the more chaste we appear in the sight of men, if we are not truly chaste. For you, who have in some measure withdrawn from bodily action, it is easy to avoid wicked deeds; but it is less easy to cleanse the heart of unlawful thought.

Yet it is one thing if we think in order to obtain something, and another when we are tempted in thought by the hidden adversary. For the heart is often tempted and takes delight in the wickedness of the flesh, yet through reason resists that very wickedness; so that in the secret of thought it is grieved by what it finds pleasing, and finds pleasing what it grieves over. But sometimes the mind is so swallowed by the abyss of temptation that it offers no resistance at all. Rather, by deliberate choice it follows what first assails it through delight; and, if outward opportunity is available, it immediately fulfils its inward desires by outward effects. If you consider the judgment of the strict Judge, this is no longer the guilt of thought but of deed; for although the delay of circumstances postponed the sin outwardly, inwardly the consenting will accomplished it in action [Col. 1110A].

12. But the mercies of the Lord are many. For the merciful Lord often washes away sins of the heart more swiftly precisely because he does not permit them to issue into deeds. Wickedness conceived in thought is more quickly loosed because it is not bound more strictly by the effect of deed; so that, where guilt has not proceeded as far as action, repentance may not proceed as far as suffering [Col. 1110B]. Rather, let affliction conceived in thought cleanse the mind which wickedness conceived in thought alone has defiled.

But when anyone has proceeded to wicked deeds through the sweetness of thought, it is fitting that penitential affliction should follow against the sweetness of carnality. “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands; and be yourselves like men waiting for their lord, when he returns from the wedding. Watch, therefore, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come—at evening, or at midnight, or at cockcrow, or in the morning—so that, when he comes and knocks, you may immediately open to him; lest perhaps, when you have knocked and cried, saying, ‘Lord, Lord, open to us,’ he answer you sternly, as to sleepers and the negligent: ‘Truly I say to you, I do not know you’” (Luke [Col. 1110C] 12:35–36, 39–40; Matt. 25:11–13; 24:42, 44). Rather, may he open to us the door of the kingdom and bring us with him into the wedding.

Strive, therefore, to be present at the wedding of bridegroom and bride, that you may see the bridegroom rejoicing over the bride, where thousands upon thousands praise the bridegroom in sweet melody; and that you may see the King in his beauty and be able to live and reign for ever with the Bridegroom, who lives and reigns with God the Father in the unity of the Holy Spirit, through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1109]

## SERMON ON HUMAN MISERY. (G)

[Col. 1109D] 736 1. O human being, who subsists from a rational soul and human flesh, of miserable condition and filled with many miseries! Wretched and pitiable human being, poor, blind, naked, subject to countless necessities: return to your heart. Why do you wander outside? Why seek outside? Why do you devote yourself to these carnal things? Why entangle yourself in secular matters? Why wrap yourself in vanities and delight in lower things? Why do you estrange yourself from all things lower and higher, scattering yourself abroad through outward things?

The closer you draw to the world, the farther you withdraw from God. The wiser you are outwardly, the more foolish you become inwardly [Col. 1110D]. The more you gain outwardly, the more you lose inwardly. The more you wander in outward things, the more you are emptied within. The more anxious you are about temporal things, the more impoverished you are in spiritual things.

What is this, O human being: you order everything, yet refuse to order yourself? You are prudent in all things, yet foolish concerning yourself. Why are you anxious to make all outward things good, while allowing yourself always to be evil and useless? The Spirit of God sleeps within you, and the spirit of the world keeps watch within you. Reason lies idle within you; sensuality is vigorous within you. The Spirit of God is extinguished within you; love of the world rules within you [Col. 1111A]. Love of earthly things burns in your heart, and love of eternal goods dies within you. You love the world and abandon God. You remember everything and forget yourself. You desire and love what is upon the earth, but take no care for heavenly things. You draw near to destruction and withdraw from salvation. You run to the devil and withdraw from God.

Return, return, transgressing human being, to your heart, because God speaks peace to those who return to their heart. God gave you all things of this world, and you abandon him because of all things. God made all things for you, and you abandon yourself because of all things. Because of every thing that comes before you, you abandon God; and for that reason all things abandon you. You leave the Creator for creatures; and therefore all creatures will rise up against you. Because in offending the Creator [Col. 1111B] you have offended every creature, the creatures made for your service and benefit will be turned into your vengeance and punishment. And woe without end shall be yours, because you refused to possess the good without end.

2. Therefore recognize yourself, wretched man; recognize yourself. Reflect that you were nothing; observe how vile and evil you are; consider what you will become. Weep, wretched man; weep unceasingly for your sins. Wipe away your wickednesses and miseries with tears, because you have sinned by your own will. Let it displease you above all things, let it displease you with your whole heart and continually, that you dared to offend the Lord of immeasurable majesty, who has power over all flesh and can cast body and soul into Gehenna. [Col. 1111C] Let your heart be most bitterly bitter to you, because you have willingly, gladly, and with delight offended God, the supreme Father of incomprehensible goodness, who is kind and merciful toward the ungrateful and the wicked. Let your whole self displease you, so that you may wholly please him who is the supreme, true, and only God: no one pleases him except one who displeases himself; and no one displeases him except one who pleases himself. For God scatters the bones of those who please men (Ps. 52:6). And what is lofty and beautiful in the sight of men is abominable before God. It is astonishing concerning you, wretched man, that you are wholly eager, wholly ready, wholly compliant, wholly clever, and wholly anxious for evils; but for good things you are wholly hard, wholly lazy, wholly lukewarm, [Col. 1111D] wholly foolish, wholly unbelieving, and rebellious. Whence comes this to you, except from the flesh that you love and follow? Since you love the flesh, you follow the flesh; and since you follow the flesh, you do the works of the flesh and will be punished with it. The fruit of your flesh is lust, concupiscence, envy, infirmity—that is, frailty and pain—the worm, stinking decay, and foul stench.

3. Are you yourself so blinded by the darkness of ignorance that you do not know what you are? Do you not attend to where you are going, consider what you have done, or understand the snares of the enemy and his deceitful temptations? You are wholly negligent and do not consider where you ought to be heading: you do not know the way and do not seek it. For a great journey still lies before you. You diligently seek food, clothing, rest, and every necessity of the flesh when you need them; [Col. 1112A] but you care, with excessive lukewarmness, nothing for the life and salvation of your soul, though you always need it, full as you are of wickedness and malice. Wretched man, in order to feed and clothe your wretched body, and satisfy the pleasures of the flesh—which after a few days will be devoured by worms—you labor anxiously, run about, keep watch, and allow no sleep to your eyes, so as to fill your belly; yet for your soul, which must be presented to God in heaven, you do not anxiously weary your heart in order to feed it with good works and clothe it with virtues, lest its nakedness appear. Sad man, you always seek to fill your belly; why do you not feed your hungry soul? You are always concerned for the vessel of excrement; why are you not concerned for the image of God? You feed what is barren and does not bear fruit, but do not satisfy with good things the hungry soul. Woe will be yours, because your soul [Col. 1112B] will fail within you through hunger. Woe is yours, and woe will be yours, because you render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, but do not render to God the things that are God’s; and therefore you are cursed by God and will be put to shame by him.

4. See, wretched man, that everything is vanity, everything folly, everything madness—whatever you do in this world—except only that which you do in God, for God, and for the honor of God. Whatever you do without God is wholly wickedness and vanity, because nothing is good without the supreme good. And it is the great misery of a human being not to be with him without whom he cannot exist. Therefore, wretched man, you who were created in the likeness and image of God, who through the exceeding love of our Lord Jesus Christ were redeemed and delivered from most shameful eternal death, who were called by his mercy alone—an inestimable mercy—to behold the brightness [Col. 1112C] of the supreme God; you who, from the time you began to be, have been invited by the most high Father of all goodness, through his only Son, to possess eternal life, and with very many benefits: wretched man, recognize this honor; understand your dignity, you who have been honored by such majesty. For the eternal and immeasurable God created you, formed you, redeemed you, and invited you. Great is the honor and abundant the love. Know, O man, your honor, and run with thanksgiving to him who invites you; lest perhaps, if you refuse to go in ingratitude, or if an estate, oxen, or a wife should hinder you, the angry Lord command you to be cut down and close to you forever the gate of life. Know, therefore, O man, your honor, and honor [Col. 1112D] your Creator.

5. But alas! Today it may rightly be said: “Man, though he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). Certainly it is fitting and just that one who refused to be a companion of angels should become like beasts; and that one who destroyed in himself the image and likeness of God should deservedly have the image and likeness of beasts adhere to him. Know yourself, then, wretched man; know yourself to be better than birds, better than all living creatures. Do not be like senseless beasts, which think only of the present life and love only fleshly and temporal things, because they know no others. Man, do not subject yourself to the flesh; do not be a lover of the world. Do not endure to be a son of the devil, for the sake of the honor [Col. 1113A] of your most mighty, most wise, incomprehensible Father, the eternal most high God. For the sake of God’s wonderful name, do not set yourself up as your own adversary and murderer. For the love of the most kindly God, do not make yourself an enemy of almighty God. For the sake of his only-begotten and beloved Son, Jesus Christ, do not make yourself a companion of demons and of the burning of eternal fire. You who have been redeemed by the most precious blood of the spotless Lamb, do not despise so great a price, which the Son of God deigned to pay for you, lest you be wrapped in everlasting fires. For then you will undergo the greatest punishment without remedy; then you will suffer unimaginable pain without end, and be filled with torment. Yet you will never be relieved, because one who did not weep when it was time to weep [Col. 1113B] will mourn in eternal grief, but without profit.

6. Return therefore to yourself, man; return to spiritual things; return to eternal and heavenly joys; return, wretched man, return to the Son. Do not delay in turning to him who made you by his power and wisdom, redeemed you by his ineffable goodness, called you to himself, and still waits daily in order to crown you. What do you seek apart from him? What do you desire besides him? What pleases you without him? He made all things; he possesses all things; he is all things. Whatever good you desire, whatever beauty you seek, whatever sweetness and delight you require, you will find it all in him and enjoy it in him. If you wish to rejoice, he is joy; if you delight in striving, he is the palm of victory; if you wish to be crowned, he is the crown; [Col. 1113C] if you desire to conquer, he is victory; if you desire power, he is power; if you seek strength, he is strength; if you wish to possess justice, he is justice; if you love wisdom, he is the fountain of wisdom; if you wish for charity, God is charity; if you seek riches, he is rich; if you wish to possess beauty, he is supreme beauty; if you seek the fullness of every good, he is fullness; if you desire glory and [Col. 1114A] honor, God is true glory and supreme honor; if you desire peace, he is eternal peace. Whatever good you seek, he is the supreme good and every good. Indeed, he is always wholly desirable, wholly sweet, wholly lovable, wholly pleasant, and wholly delightful. He is always, everywhere, wholly present. Wherever you are without him, you will be ill and it will go ill with you; wherever you are with him, you will be well and it will go well with you.

7. Therefore submit your whole self to him who made your whole self, from whom you have all things and whose grace you use at every moment. Always serve him who does not permit all the things that would gladly harm you to harm you—whether infirmities, human beings, beasts, demons, or anything else. Always serve [Col. 1114B] him who does not allow you to fall into every sin, because he does not permit you to inflict upon yourself all the evils and injuries that you would gladly commit. Always love wholly the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the sole, true, and supreme good, who alone always truly and supremely loves you. Therefore let your will please him, and let his will always please you. Always make yourself accord with him; always follow his will in all things—he who always wills your good, who cares for nothing but your salvation, whose will is kindly disposed to show you mercy and delights in doing you good. Do you think that you yourself are a great friend to yourself? God is more a friend to you than you are to yourself, because he loves you more than you love yourself. Do you believe another’s help stronger, or [Col. 1114C] another’s counsel more useful? You are mistaken if you believe this. You are most foolish and most mad, because you follow your own desires or those of others and abandon the counsel of him who is always a sweet friend, a wise and loving counselor and Savior, and, above all, a strong and mighty helper, Father of the age to come and Prince of Peace. Amen.

[Col. 1113]

758. SERMON ON THE SEVEN GIFTS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT. (G)

[Col. 1113D] 1. The first grace is the fear of the Lord. Whoever possesses this grace hates every iniquity, in accordance with the Psalmist’s words: “I have hated and abhorred iniquity”; and elsewhere: “I have hated every way of iniquity” (Ps. 118:128, 163). For it is written: “The fear of the Lord hates evil” (Prov. 8:13); and likewise: “Fear God and depart from evil.” And of Job it is said: “A man fearing God and departing from evil” (Job 1:1). Without this grace, the first of graces and the beginning of all religion, no good can spring up or flow forth. For just as security or negligence is the cause and mother of all offenses, so the fear of the Lord is the root and guardian of all goods. Hence it is written: “Unless you steadfastly maintain yourself in the fear of the Lord, your house will quickly be overthrown” [Col. 1114D] (Ecclus. 27:4). For the whole edifice of virtues immediately tends toward ruin if it loses the protection of this grace. Thus Solomon says: “Be in the fear of the Lord daily, because you shall have hope at the end, and your expectation shall not be taken away” (Prov. 23:17). Hence also the Apostle: “Work out your salvation with fear and trembling” (Phil. 2:12). And what more need be said? Fear and religion are joined together, and neither can remain without the other. Thus Cornelius was “a religious man and one who feared God” (Acts 10:22), and Simeon was “just and God-fearing” (Luke 2:25). Thus Solomon says: “Fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccl. 12:13). We ought to possess this fear as the most blessed Job declared that he possessed it: he feared God always [Col. 1115A] as though swelling waves hung over him (Job 31:23). Through this fear of God we forsake all things, renounce the world, and deny ourselves, as the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9:23). This divine fear, then, which subjects one whom it wholly permeates to poverty and separates him from evil, is first in the order of graces just as poverty is first in the sequence of beatitudes. Setting it as the foundation of the other virtues, the Lord says of it: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3; Luke 6:20).

2. The second charisma is the Spirit of piety, corresponding to the second beatitude set forth in the Gospel, of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for [Col. 1115B] they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5:4; Ps. 36:11). Of such persons the Lord says in Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; he sent me to proclaim good news to the meek” (Isa. 61:1). Moses too was the meekest of all men dwelling upon earth (Num. 12:13). Of such persons Job says: “The Lord sets the humble on high and raises the mourners to safety” (Job 5:11). Hence it is said of the Lord: “He will save the humble in spirit” (Ps. 33:19). Conversely, it is said of the proud: “The Lord resists the proud” (James 4:6; Prov. 3:34; 1 Pet. 5:5). “Before ruin the heart is lifted up” (Prov. 16:18). Pride casts down from high places to the depths; humility raises from the depths to high places. For the angel, proud in heaven, fell into Tartarus; the human being, humbling himself on earth, ascends to heaven. [Col. 1115C] The higher one is, the more humble one ought to be. Hence it is written: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things, and you shall find grace before God” (Ecclus. 3:20). Thus the Lord himself says to his disciples: “Whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your servant” (Matt. 20:26); likewise: “When you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants’” (Luke 17:10); likewise he himself says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11:29). Without the virtue of humility, the other virtues cannot avail. Hence blessed Gregory says (*Homily 7 on the Gospels*): “He who gathers virtues without humility is like one who carries dust into the wind.” For as dust is scattered by the blast of a strong wind, so every good without [Col. 1115D] humility is swept away by the empty wind of glory. It is even much better to be a humble sinner than an arrogant righteous person. This is plainly shown by the Lord when the Publican and Pharisee are offered as an example (Luke 18), as a certain wise man says: “Humble confession amid evil deeds is better than proud boasting amid good deeds.”

3. The third gift is the Spirit of knowledge, concerning which Solomon says: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18). For true knowledge is to know that we are mortal, perishable, and frail, and that in this exile, this prison-house, this pilgrimage, this vale of tears, we ought to grieve and mourn. Thus it is said in the third beatitude, corresponding to this third gift: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” [Col. 1116A] (Matt. 5:5; Isa. 6:2); likewise: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall weep” (Luke 6:25). Hence Solomon says: “Laughter shall be mingled with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Prov. 14:13).

4. The fourth grace is the Spirit of fortitude, corresponding to the fourth Gospel beatitude: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6). For one who hungers and thirsts for righteousness stands strong, invincible, and fearless against every adversity. Thus Solomon says: “The righteous is confident as a lion and shall be without fear” (Prov. 28:1); likewise: “The righteous shall not be distressed by whatever may happen to him” (ibid. 12:21). All those of whom the Apostle speaks were endowed with this Spirit: “The saints suffered mockeries and scourging, and even chains and prisons; [Col. 1116B] they were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, and died by the slaughter of the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted—of whom the world was not worthy—wandering in deserts, mountains, caves, and caverns of the earth” (Heb. 11:36–38). The Apostle himself likewise speaks of these things when he says: “Who shall separate us from the charity of Christ? Shall tribulation?” (Rom. 8:35), etc. This Spirit endures every evil inflicted from without and equips and fortifies against hostile snares. Thus the bridegroom, in praise of his bride, says: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army arrayed in battle order” (Song 6:3).

5. The fifth gift is the Spirit of counsel, which makes a person so compassionate and merciful toward others, corresponding to the fifth beatitude, of which it is said: [Col. 1116C] “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7). Solomon likewise says: “He who is inclined to mercy shall be blessed” (Prov. 22:9). We exercise this chiefly in three ways: either when we fulfill the six works mentioned in the Gospel (Matt. 5:4–10), or when we strive to correct offenders and lead them back to goodness, or when we readily forgive injuries inflicted upon us. This second manner of clemency, or counsel of the Spirit, caused God to empty himself and take the form of a servant, namely so that he might correct the wandering sheep and bring it back to its own fold. Hence the Apostle says: “He gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from the present wicked [Col. 1116D] age” (Gal. 1:4). We must devote ourselves to this manner of giving counsel as the Apostle commands in his exhortation: “Press on in season and out of season” (2 Tim. 4:2). There is also another manner of counsel: namely, the virtue of discernment, by which we distinguish genuine virtues from those that are disguised and feigned, and by which we also recognize Satan himself as the author of hypocrisy. For Satan himself, as the Apostle says, “transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14); and, according to the saying of blessed Cyprian, he suborns ministers of injustice, bringing night in place of day and destruction in place of salvation. This virtue, indeed, the teacher and mistress of the other virtues, regulates and governs all the others from above, preserving them imperiously and with discernment lest they wander freely beyond or short of their proper bounds. Thus Boethius says: “Virtues hold to the mean. If anything is done either beyond [Col. 1117A] or below what is proper, one departs from virtue.”

6. The sixth grace is the Spirit of understanding, corresponding to the sixth beatitude: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8; Ps. 23:4–5). Unless the sight of the mind has been diligently purified, it cannot clearly understand mystical and divine things. For it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit and withdraw from thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1:5). Hence Solomon says: “Evil thoughts are an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. 15:26). “Perverse thoughts separate from God” (Wis. 1:3). Therefore, whoever wishes to possess a sincere and lucid understanding should strive to flee the phantasms and clouds of depraved thoughts, and should guard the heart with every diligence and caution. [Col. 1117B] Hence Solomon says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for life proceeds from it” (Prov. 4:23).

7. The seventh gift is the Spirit of wisdom, a certain inward savor and most sweet taste. Hence the Psalmist says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” [Col. 1118A] (Ps. 33:9); and again: “Be still and see” (Ps. 45:11); and again: “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6). By this inward taste of divine wisdom we taste beforehand the things above, contemplating, that is, how delightful it is to be present among the angelic companies, where nothing that can displease can exist. This seventh grace corresponds to that true beatitude of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matt. 5:9). For those who possess a peaceful and serene mind savor heavenly things more sweetly and see more subtly. For whoever is found wiser is wiser than he [the reading is uncertain in sense]. Hence Solomon says: “A man’s teaching is known through patience” (Prov. 19:11). Elsewhere it is said of such people: “Great peace belongs to those who love your law, and there is no stumbling-block for them” (Ps. 118:165). These seven [Col. 1118B] graces are the seven women laying hold upon one man; the seven spirits resting upon the flower; the seven lamps shining in the lampstand; the seven eyes in the stone; the seven spirits before the throne of God.

[Col. 1117]

## SERMON ON THE TWELVE GATES OF JERUSALEM

This sermon, in the manuscript of the Carthusian house at Cologne (from which Horstius extracted it), bears the name of St Bernard, abbot, to whom, however, it does not appear to be attributable. (G)

[Col. 1117C] 1. “Strive to enter through the narrow gate, because strait and narrow is the gate that leads to life” (Luke 13:24; Matt. 7:13–14). Oh, how terribly and beneficially this voice of supreme Truth frightened slow and lukewarm travelers, faint-hearted and lazy climbers! It imposed even upon the most perfect disciples, entering the heavenly Jerusalem in free flight, striving, the singleness of the gate, the difficulty of entry, and the fewness of the elect. “Narrow,” he says, “is the way that leads to life.” It is narrow, indeed, in the washing away of sins; but far narrower in the separation of body and soul; and narrowest in the final examination by the Judge. Yet blessed be the God [Col. 1117D] and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all consolation (2 Cor. 1:3; Eph. 1:3; 1 Pet. 1:3), who mingled consolation with terror lest we despair, and set breadth against narrowness, so that we might venture, and in venturing run, and in running arrive beforehand. For elsewhere the Lord himself says: “I tell you, many shall come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8:11). David too, prophet and herald of truth, a man after God’s heart, says: “Let those redeemed by the Lord say so, whom he redeemed from the hand of the enemy and gathered from the regions: from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and the sea” (Ps. 106:6–7). By the sunrise he signifies [Col. 1118C] innocence for us; by the south, righteousness; by the west, repentance; by the north, mercy.

2. From the east—that is, through the gate of innocence—the Innocents entered: those who, knowing how to die before they could speak, were slaughtered for the Lord. Through this gate enter little children reborn through Baptism, who, having received the sacrament of regeneration, are separated from the body immediately or shortly afterwards: without doubt they enter the heavenly Jerusalem through the gate of innocence. From the south—that is, through the gate of righteousness—the Apostles and martyrs entered. And rightly all who are perfect are compared to the south, because there the sun’s course is more prolonged, the heat’s ardor more intense, and the light’s brightness more abundant. The sun of righteousness neither sets nor [Col. 1118D] cools in them, but grows stronger and warmer, as it is written: “The wise man remains like the sun; the fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27:12). Furthermore, how great a splendor of works and fervor of love shone in those saints is evident and needs not so much exposition as imitation. From the west—that is, through the gate of repentance—Mary Magdalene entered. By the merit of her sins she had once been a dwelling-place of demons; but afterward, visited by divine grace, she was pierced with compunction, and by weeping and repenting and honoring her Savior with singular love, she became a temple of the Holy Spirit. Through this gate also enter penitents, who, as though dwelling in [Col. 1119A] western regions and hastening from inner darkness to a land dark and covered by the shadow of death, are illuminated by the Sun of righteousness. If they perfectly renounce all the pomps of Satan and works of darkness, they enter the heavenly Jerusalem through the gate of repentance. From the north—that is, through the gate of mercy—entered that thief of the Gospel, who, drawn from the depth of iniquity and ignorance by God’s goodness alone at the very moment of death, was brought back from the mouth of the pit of Gehenna to the delightful loveliness of paradise. Through this gate perhaps also enter those who, serving vices and iniquities throughout their whole lives, when they are assigned to death because of their crimes, offer God full satisfaction for their evil deeds through true contrition of heart; they are at some time to enter the heavenly Jerusalem through the gate of mercy. For it is written: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18); and elsewhere: “Where I find you, there I shall judge you” (Eccl. 11:3); again: “A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God; a contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 50:19). It remains, therefore, to see how contrary and opposed to one another these four are found: namely, innocence and repentance, righteousness and mercy, and conversely. For one who is innocent does not seek repentance, and one who is penitent does not possess innocence. Likewise, one who is righteous does not invoke mercy, and one who is miserable does not possess righteousness.

[Col. 1119C] 3. Now we must consider and delightfully recall what the Apostle John, Christ’s intimate companion, beloved friend among the rest, and more deeply imbued than all others with heavenly mysteries, says about this glorious and eternal city. “On its east,” he says, “three gates; and on the south three gates; and on the west three gates; and on the north three gates” (Rev. 21:13). The eastern region is described as having three gates. Innocence is known to be threefold. There is innocence according to power, innocence according to age, and innocence according to will. Christ possessed innocence according to power: he alone could truly say, “The prince of this world comes, and has nothing in me” [Col. 1119D] (John 14:30); and of him it is written: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Pet. 2:22; Isa. 53:9). For he neither contracted nor committed sin: both his birth, by which he was begotten God from God the Father before the ages, is ineffable; and likewise that birth by which he was born man from a Virgin Mother at the end of time is incomprehensible; and the life by which he lived in the world was singular. Innocence according to power—that is, the first gate of innocence—is closed to others but open to Christ alone, as the prophet Ezekiel testifies: “The eastern gate,” he says, “shall be closed to all; the prince alone shall enter and leave through [Col. 1120A] it” (Ezek. 44:1–4). Innocence according to age belongs to those who, both through bodily weakness and through the undiscerning simplicity of their heart, neither know how nor are able to perpetrate evil. Innocence according to will belongs to those who, although they sometimes offend in certain light sins—without which this life can scarcely, or not at all, be passed—nonetheless preserve the purity of innocence in their good will. Therefore, the first innocence is inability to do evil; the second, ignorance of how to do evil; the last, unwillingness to do evil.

4. It follows: “And on the south three gates.” The southern gate, by which righteousness is signified, has three gates; and therefore righteousness too is threefold. There is righteousness according to obligation, righteousness according to [Col. 1120B] merit, and righteousness according to purpose. Righteousness according to obligation belongs to all the faithful, especially monks, because day by day they strive to pay the vows that their lips have uttered, following the prophet’s counsel: “Make vows and pay them to the Lord your God” (Ps. 75:12). Righteousness according to merit belongs to those who commit virtually no unlawful acts and yet do not wish to make use even of lawful things; rather, forgetting the things behind and stretching themselves toward those before, they climb by holy desires, tireless steps of faith, and daily advances to the summit of perfection. Truly such persons can say as happily as confidently: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; having entered them, I shall confess to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord: not the innocent, not the wretched, not the penitent, but [Col. 1120C] the righteous shall enter through it” (Ps. 117:19–20); and: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness” (2 Tim. 4:7–8). Righteousness according to purpose is maintained by those who, although they are afflicted with superfluous thoughts and drawn away by alluring desires, nevertheless seek, to the best of their powers, to resist sin and preserve the strength of their purpose in an unbroken course; humbly confessing that all adverse events befall them because of their deserts, they believe that all things cooperate for their good. For of such persons it is written: “We know that all things work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called saints according to purpose” (Rom. 8:28).

[Col. 1120D] 5. It follows: “And on the west three gates.” The western region, by which repentance is signified, is written to have three gates, because repentance is known to be threefold. There is gratuitous repentance, voluntary repentance, and compelled repentance. John the Baptist, and more than a prophet, practiced gratuitous repentance. Foretold by a prophet, promised by the archangel Gabriel, sanctified in the womb by the Holy Spirit, and placed above all mortals before him by the truthful voice of the Savior, this man—such and so great as he was—like the righteous man of whom we read [Note: [Col. 1119] Namely, St Benedict, *Dialogues* of St Gregory, book 2, chapter 1.], sought rather to suffer the evils of the world than its praises. Preferring to be wearied by labors for God [Col. 1121A] rather than enjoy the blandishments of this life, and wishing to devote himself to God alone, he left his father’s house and possessions, sought the desert, and by his own example left posterity an almost admirable model of repentance to follow. This repentance is called gratuitous because it is suffered freely—indeed, offered freely; for the rule of repentance is that one who has committed no unlawful act may use lawful things as he pleases. Voluntary repentance belongs to those who, after sins committed and crimes perpetrated, when illuminated by the Sun of righteousness, confess to the Lord no longer from necessity but by their own will. By willing diligence they take care that sin may not reign in their mortal body, but righteousness may reign; and those who had formerly presented their members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity now present them to serve [Col. 1121B] righteousness unto sanctification; those who were children of night while they followed the works of darkness become children of light through worthy fruits of repentance. Compelled repentance belongs to the lukewarm and to people like myself, who, kindled by no fire of charity and animated by no fervor of devotion, do not yet follow the spirit of freedom; but, remaining in a condition of habitual faint-heartedness in the body, are again weighed down by the spirit of servitude and are scarcely compelled by the severity of their superiors to fulfill the required measure of regular observances. Yet such persons must by no means be despaired of; for if they bear with patient perseverance the yoke of Christian servitude once assumed, possessing their souls in their patience, they enter the heavenly Jerusalem through the gate of repentance.

[Col. 1121C] 6. It follows: “And on the north three gates.” The northern region, by which mercy is signified, has three gates. One is exterior, another interior, and the third posterior—that is, final. The exterior is the distribution of alms. For lovers of this world, who have Christ merely as a foundation, although they serve with all their heart’s desire the acquisition of temporal goods and do not fear in every respect to obey the pleasures of their flesh, when the hour of death approaches and they are inwardly shaken by consideration of their sins and fear of everlasting retribution, distribute to needy and poor persons and to servants of God what they had acquired unjustly and possessed unlawfully for the salvation of their souls. [Col. 1122A] We must therefore believe that persons of this sort are greatly helped by the suffrages of Holy Church and also by the good offices of the faithful, since they receive from those persons the aid of intercession whom, in accordance with the Lord’s command, they had made friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that from them they might receive eternal things, to whom they had given temporal things. The interior gate is called confession of the mouth. For Catholic faith and Christian piety hold this: that any sinner, however unclean and however criminal, if cleansed through true confession when the danger of death is at hand, will by no means enter the punishments of eternal fire; for if all things are washed away in confession, surely those who confess are not excluded from the kingdom of mercy. For the prophet says: “I made my offense known to you and did not conceal my injustice. I said: ‘I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Ps. 31:5). The final gate of mercy is called contrition of heart, because when the sinner’s heart is pierced by contemplation of supreme clemency, it is offered before the eyes of divine mercy like an evening sacrifice. He too, whose nature is loving-kindness and whose work is mercy, is believed to save many such people. This gate is called the final one because it is shown to come to aid after all the others. [Col. 1122C] For if the giving of alms is absent and oral confession is lacking, God, who knows hidden things, nevertheless does not despise a contrite and humbled heart, but sometimes gladly receives the sacrifice of a humbled spirit, according to the saying of the instrument of the Holy Spirit: “At whatever hour the sinner groans, he shall be saved” (Ezek. 18).

[Col. 1121]

## SERMON ON THE CANTICLE OF THE BLESSED VIRGIN MARY

(G)

[NOTE.]

764. Horstius excerpted this sermon from a manuscript codex of the Cistercian monastery of Hortus Mariae, which names Bernard as its author, as does our Gemmeticensis manuscript, from which it is published in a more corrected form; although it does not wholly attain Bernard’s style.

[Col. 1121D] 1. *My soul magnifies the Lord.* It magnifies by voice, by deed, and by affection; it magnifies by praising, loving, and proclaiming. It magnifies, at once giving the form and material of praising, loving, and magnifying. *My soul magnifies the Lord*, because it is made magnificent by the magnificent Lord. First, my soul was wonderfully created by the Lord in the image and likeness of God; but afterwards it was miserably disfigured in Adam, and now it has been renewed by the Lord more wonderfully, more gloriously, and more magnificently.

[Col. 1122D] *My soul magnifies the Lord.* Every creature magnifies the Lord, but my soul magnifies the Lord beyond every creature. For in all creation the Lord made nothing so magnificently as my soul. But the Lord is: as he willed, so it was done. *My soul magnifies the Lord.* Magnify the Lord, not yourself. Whoever magnified himself, so far as lay in him dishonoured God; and therefore he did not exalt himself, but cast himself down. Your task is to humble yourself and to exalt the Lord.

[Col. 1123A] 2. *And my spirit rejoiced in God my Saviour.* Observe the order. She touched the lyre first and then the psaltery; she named the soul first and then the spirit: for “that which is spiritual” is not first, “but that which is natural; afterwards that which is spiritual.” *And my spirit rejoiced*: beyond every creature, and even beyond itself, it leapt at the immensity of joy. In whom? Not in myself, but in God my Creator, burning with the knowledge and love of him; and this not through myself, but through my Saviour Jesus, my Son, who mediates and saves me—uniquely mine. God is mine; my Saviour is mine; my Son is mine. He is indeed the Creator of all and of me, but he is the Son of me alone; and through me he is the salvation of all.

*For he has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid.* His handmaid would not dare even to lift her eyes to him, unless he had first deigned to look upon his handmaid.

[Col. 1123B] Mercy first looked down upon us from him, because our misery had rendered us altogether despised. But he looked especially upon me among all, to whom he granted a singular privilege above all. Notice that she was not content to say, “He regarded me,” or “He regarded his handmaid,” or “He regarded my lowliness”; rather, she humbled herself greatly and laid the firmest foundations where she might securely receive and preserve ornaments of such magnitude and beauty: “He has regarded,” she says, “the lowliness of his handmaid.”

Every word must be weighed according to its own gravity. There are handmaids who are not humble. Hagar was a handmaid, but proud: she despised her mistress (Gen. XVI). There are many who are sufficiently humble but not to the point of being handmaids; there are also many humble handmaids, but not the Lord’s.

[Col. 1123C] Thus humility commends contempt of oneself; handmaidship commends service by its devotion. *He has regarded the lowliness of his handmaid.* By regarding me through his grace, he made me both humble and his handmaid. His—yes, his—he made me, he who made of me and in me his own special work.

3. *For behold, from henceforth all generations shall call me blessed.* O heart enlarged! With what piercing eyes you suddenly beheld all creation together, destined to be placed in true blessedness! “Behold,” she says. This is the word of one who sees and points out. “Behold, I see what shall come to pass concerning me, what fruit shall proceed from me, how many and how great goods shall reach, through me, not to myself alone but to every generation.”

*All generations shall call me blessed.* They would not call me blessed unless they attained something of that same blessedness which I possess.

[Col. 1123D] How shall one who does not eat belch forth? They shall call me blessed, from whose good all generations shall receive fruit. They shall be blessed from my fruit; and though all are made blessed, all shall nevertheless call me, in a singular manner, blessed. All generations, I say: the generations of heaven and the generations of earth, all angels and all the elect. For among the angels too there are generations. Hence he is called “the Father of spirits,” and it is said: “from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. IV, 6).

For some in heaven are fathers to others, presiding over them with fatherly charity; in them they generate and express every affection of fatherhood. Their fatherhood receives its name from the highest Father, because, just as the highest and true Father loves, teaches, and governs all in a fatherly way,

[Col. 1124A] so they too, according to the gift of fatherhood which they have received, love, teach, and govern in a fatherly way those subject to them. Likewise good fathers on earth receive the gift of their fatherhood from the highest Father, insofar as they themselves approach, more or less, knowledge and love of the highest fatherhood.

*All generations shall call me blessed.* For the number of angelic generations shall be restored through the One begotten; and the human generation cursed in Adam shall be regenerated to eternal blessing through the blessed fruit of my womb. Among and above all these generations, all those generations shall call me blessed. Rightly, therefore, Lady, shall all generations call you blessed, who have borne true and eternal blessedness for all generations.

4. *For he who is mighty has done great things to me, and holy is his name.* That all generations call me blessed, I ascribe not to myself, nor do I attribute it to my merits, but to him who has done great things to me. For I am called blessed by all because I have been made blessed by him, set before all as though a mirror of blessedness.

*For he has done great things to me.* He did not do merely one great thing to me, but many great things. It is in itself a great thing that I am a virgin; in itself a great thing that I am a mother; a great thing that I am both at once, virgin and mother. And whose mother? The mother of God’s Only-Begotten, the Fashioner and Saviour of all.

[Col. 1124B] *He has done great things to me.* The greatness and multitude of the good things he has done to me cannot be narrated or conceived.

And who is he that has done such great things to you? *He who is mighty, and holy is his name.* Do not wonder; do not say, “How can these things be?” He who has done these things is mighty—mighty, indeed almighty. Consider his power, for he is able to do whatever he wills. Great are the things which you observe in me; but great is the power which has done such great things to me. From the great and wonderful things which he has done in me, consider his great and wonderful power.

And why has he done such great things to you here? *Because holy is his name.* For the sake of his name, not for the sake of my merit, he has done such great things to me. His name, which is wonderful, holy, and ineffable, he willed to make manifest in me. What is this name? “Good.” For no one is good

[Col. 1124D] except God alone. Therefore he has done such great things to me solely because of his goodness; for he wished to manifest in me both his power and his goodness: for he is uniquely mighty, and holy is his name. Yet, as his name is holy in himself, so may it be sanctified in us; as it has been predestined in him from eternity, so may it be fulfilled in us.

5. *And his mercy is from generation unto generations upon those who fear him.* Behold, his mercy is called his name. Where? “From generation unto generations”: from Judaea to all nations; or, from the beginning of the age until its end, his mercy is bestowed, not indiscriminately, but on those who fear him. With God there is no respect of persons. Jew and Greek, barbarian and Scythian, slave and free, male and female—in every nation and generation, if one fears

[Col. 1125A] God and works righteousness, that person is acceptable to him (Col. III).

*His mercy is upon those who fear him.* One begins with fear in order to arrive at love. Let those who still fear because of their sins not despair, for his mercy is upon those who fear him. His mercy forgives the sins of those who fear him; the forgiveness of sins nourishes love in those who thirst for him; and those who love him know his name. Love itself is knowledge; yet the farther we remain from his knowledge, the less we love him. But if we cannot yet love him perfectly because we do not know him perfectly, let us at least fear him with love. Whoever fears without love is not a son but a slave; and this fear has punishment, not knowledge.

6. *He has shown strength with his arm.* By nature indeed we were children of wrath; but through the redemption of Jesus Christ we have become children of mercy, because he showed strength with his arm, binding the strong man and plundering his goods. Otherwise, unless the Son had set us free and reconciled us to God through his death, mercy would not be gently disposed toward those who fear him, but justice would punish those who fear him.

*He has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.* Since, therefore, all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth, as above he treated of the mercy by which he redeemed the humble, so now he treats of the justice by which he judges the proud, and, by treating each in turn, establishes as it were a double wall from both.

[Col. 1125B] *He has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart.* From the beginning of the world, both proud human beings and proud angels have been scattered. The great dragon, Satan, was cast out of heaven and scattered

[Col. 1125C] through this dark air, because he refused to stand in the unity of truth. Whoever is not gathered together in God’s truth is scattered in his own vanity. The proud builders of the tower of Babel were scattered because the unity of their language was divided into a multitude. Every proud person is scattered by that very fact that he is proud. What is pride but dust raised on high and scattered on the wind? *He has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart*—that is, those who are proud in the thought of their heart. How clearly he has opened the hidden lurking-place of the worst self-exaltation!

7. There is a certain coarse and vile pride, evident even to all fools, which chiefly dwells in the pleasure of carnal senses: for example, rejoicing in a polished body, fine clothing, or the satisfaction of appetite or some unclean desire.

[Col. 1125D] There is another pride which seems fairer to itself and is yet far more shameful: to be exalted over others because of knowledge, power, or subtlety of intellect, and to regard everyone else as cattle in comparison with oneself. This commonly occupies the eminent people of this world.

There is a third and most foul kind: glorying inwardly in virtues, miracles, an understanding of the tongues of angels, or heavenly mysteries. These are they who are proud in the thought of their heart. The mind is the subtlety of intelligence; the heart is the affection of vain glory. And “their” was well added, because although some have knowledge from God, nevertheless they have their self-exaltation from themselves.

Thus he has scattered the proud of every kind: the beasts of the field, the birds of heaven, and the fish of the sea.

[Col. 1126A] These fish, who break nets, investigate subtle matters, and seem among the faithful to be humble as though in waters, are fish of the sea rather than of the river’s sweetness, for they are of the sea’s bitterness. Therefore they travel the paths not of heaven but of the sea. Even if they apprehend something heavenly, as though leaping into the air, they plunge it all down with themselves into the depths of the sea.

But the birds of heaven are lifted up in manifest pride: for temporal glory, they seem to themselves almost to touch the stars with their summit. Sacred history describes Antiochus as such a person (I Macc.), and Herod (Acts XII); and many such people may still today be seen and lamented rather than read about. But the beasts of the earth—that is, persons devoted only to gluttony and luxury—more readily recover their senses from the devil’s snare than those who are wise in their own eyes.

Therefore he has scattered the proud in the thought of their heart, because from every kind of proud person he crushes some so that they perish eternally, and humbles others so that they may return to life.

8. *He has put down the mighty from their seat, and exalted the humble.* First he weakened, from their power, the demons who rule these darknesses and who were mighty through their affection for evil; and, driving out the Jebusite from Jerusalem, he established there the seat of his kingdom.

[Col. 1126B] *He has put down the mighty from their seat* when the word reached the king of Nineveh—that is, even the rulers of this world—and he descended from his throne, clothed himself in sackcloth and ashes, and humbled himself, that he might turn aside God’s wrath (Jonah III). He put down Saul and exalted David (II Kings VI). He also put down proud Ahab from his seat, as he says to his prophet: “Have you not seen Ahab humbled before me?” (III Kings XXI, 29). But because he did not remain in humility, he did not exalt him as humble, but condemned him as proud.

He also daily puts down the mighty of this world: some indeed to eternal punishment, others to the kingdom of humility. For he has his balance in his hand; he has mercy on whom he wills, and hardens whom he wills (Rom. IX, 18). Why he condemns this man after putting him down, and saves that one after restoring him, he keeps hidden for himself in his treasuries. This one thing may certainly be known: unless we are humbled, we are not saved.

9. *He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty.*

[Col. 1126D] First he humbled; afterwards he fed. It is the Spirit of prophecy: it relates future things as though already past. For the hungry have not yet been filled with good things. If they have been filled with good things, how are they hungry? And if hungry, how are they filled with good things? Unless perhaps we speak according to that saying: “into which angels desire to look” (I Pet. I, 12). Yet they always behold the face of the Father, and are hungry; and, though filled with good things, they have desire in satiety and satiety in desire. But that satiety is without disgust, and that hunger without suffering—indeed, that blessed hunger itself always satisfies them.

But the case is not the same in the homeland as on the way. On the way they thirst and hunger for righteousness; in the homeland they shall be satisfied

[Col. 1127A] when glory is manifested. Meanwhile, here on the way, the hungry are filled with good things, because he gives them food in due season. They are filled with goods and emptied of evils; they are filled with goods, that is, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit. The hungry who are not disgusted are filled; the poor are satisfied; for he has sent the rich away empty.

Esau was rich; therefore he did not value his brother’s gifts. “I have plenty,” he said; “keep what is yours” (Gen. XXXVI, 9). Jethro, Moses’ priestly kinsman, was rich; therefore he would not consent to go with him to the good things God had promised Israel (Num. X). Hiram, king of Tyre, was rich; therefore he thought little of the cities which Solomon allotted to him (III Kings IX).

Therefore never appear full and rich to yourself, lest you be dismissed empty and void. Always say to the Lord your God: “I am needy and poor” (Ps. LXXIX, 6): “In your hand, Lord, are bread and clothing for my soul. If you give me bread to eat and clothing

[Col. 1127B] to cover me, you shall be God to me, and this stone shall be a sign” (Gen. XXVIII, 20–22). But if we give our hand to Egypt and the Assyrians in order to be satisfied with bread (Lam. V, 6), we have already stretched out our hands to a foreign god. God therefore feeds and clothes us on this way, and fills the hungry with his good consolations, so that we may finally become Israel—that is, contemplative persons.

10. Then, that is, in contemplation, *he has received Israel his servant*. So long as he is called Jacob, he sweats in labours: he serves faithfully indeed in a foreign land. But when he returns to his father with his possessions, he now receives another name, namely Israel, because he has received Israel his servant. He received him returning from Syrian Mesopotamia, worn out by labour

[Col. 1127C] and hardship, now longing to see his father’s face. He received him to nourish, received him to perfect, and to bring him unto his own face. He received Israel his servant: not proud but humble; not hairy but smooth; not a hunter but a shepherd.

And why did he receive him? *Remembering his mercy.* This alone is the reason why he received him: to show the riches of his grace in vessels of mercy prepared for glory. God seemed to have forgotten to show mercy when he delayed sending his Son until the end of the ages; but he remembered what he had never forgotten, so that we may always remember and may sing the mercies of the Lord for ever.

*He has received Israel his servant.* He received his nature; he took up his cause; he took up his affair; the Father received his Son. In the Son he received his servant, that is, his whole body, from the first righteous person to the last.

[Col. 1128A] He received him as an evening sacrifice, a sweet-smelling offering; he received him into an inheritance unfading and undefiled, reserved in heaven. Note that the final word of this canticle is “mercy.” It began with mercy, ends with mercy, and everywhere turns upon mercy.

11. *As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever.* This is the final verse, which completes the Decalogue and finishes the tabernacle with ten curtains. In this verse are confirmed the truth of God’s promises, the authority of both Testaments, and the unity of all believers; and it is suitably referred to all and each of the things said above, as though she said: “He who is mighty, merciful, just, and true in all his words

> [Note: Col. 1127C. Here the Gemmeticensis manuscript ends.]

[Col. 1128B] and works has done this and this for me.” Thus, I say, he completed all things in deed, *as he spoke to our fathers.*

God, who created all things, did indeed speak once; but what was eternally accomplished once in him could not be declared once through the things which he decreed in time. Hence God “spoke to the fathers in many portions and in many ways” (Heb. I, 1); yet wrongly and obscurely, and very few knew of this Word, until at last he spoke to us in the Son, who made himself known more clearly.

Yet even now that Word is seen only “through a mirror, in an enigma,” and by very few, until at last, “in the splendours of the saints,” begotten from the Father’s womb before the morning star,

[Col. 1128C] he shall be known by the elect.

From the beginning, therefore, he spoke to our fathers what he began to disclose at the end of the ages, so that one and the same stone might gather both ancient and new children into the structure of one faith and love; and there might be one dove and one fair one—both she who believed that he would come and she who received him as he came.

Among those fathers, Abraham was certainly eminent, chief, and greatest; in his seed all the faithful are reckoned. To them God does not now speak through a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, and he shall speak in the ages to come—not through a mirror, vision, or dream, but he shall speak once through himself to all, face to face, when he has delivered the kingdom to God and the Father, and God shall be all in all (I Cor. XV, 28).

[Col. 1127]

## SERMON ON THE WORDS OF THE GOSPEL: “BEHOLD, WE HAVE LEFT ALL THINGS.” (Matt. XIX, 27.) (G)*

> [Note.]

It is ascribed to Bernard at the end of a certain codex printed at Cologne in 1577, which contains the four Rules most widely received in the Church, together with the commentaries of Torquemada and Smaragdus on the Rule of the holy Father Benedict.

[Col. 1127D] 1. *Behold, we have left all things and followed you.* Here is set before us an admirable example of true conversion, to be imitated.

[Col. 1128D] For one who truly professes the religious life must leave all things and follow Christ.

[Col. 1129A] Blessed indeed is the person who so leaves all things as to follow him in whom all things are. Those who wish to follow Christ with an unencumbered mind must abandon three impediments: avarice, pride, and lust—avarice of the world, pride of heart, and lust of the flesh. Peter teaches us by his example that these especially must be left behind. For he left nets, a boat, and marriage.

The net, which gathers and encloses fish, signifies covetousness, by which a person, improperly stretched out in desire, joins house to house and field to field. The boat, which is borne upon the waves, denotes pride, by which a person sets himself above others. The wife represents carnal pleasure. These three joined together rob a person of himself. Through avarice he wanders outside himself; through pride he is lifted above himself; through lust he is defiled within himself.

[Col. 1129B] He wanders in anxiety, is elevated in self-estimation, and is defiled by delight in impurity. Outside, he fears; above, he swells; within, he stinks. He fears that what he has acquired may diminish; he fears that he cannot obtain what he desires. He swells, despising inferiors, preferring himself to equals, and making himself equal to superiors. He stinks in thought, stinks in action, stinks in habit. Avarice alienates a person from the neighbour; pride from God; lust casts him away from himself.

2. Intent upon and detained by these three vices, those three most wretched men of whom the Evangelist speaks refused to come to the supper of the householder (Luke XIV). The first, in order to test oxen; the second, to see an estate he had bought; the third, because he had taken a wife. The testing of oxen is the cultivation of earthly things; an estate is bought when the power of dominion is desired; he takes a wife who satisfies the desires of the flesh.

[Col. 1129C] Unless such people are converted, they can neither come to the supper of the householder nor follow Christ. For the first remains on this side of the Jordan; the second migrates to the north; the third swims in the river of Babylon. When the other tribes entered the land of promise, Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, having much livestock, remained on this side of the Jordan (Josh. XXII), foreshadowing those who, occupied with earthly things after the manner of cattle, despise heavenly things.

“Jordan” means “descent.” There is one descent that is good and another that is evil. Evil is the descent of which Isaiah says, “My people went down into Egypt” (Isa. LII, 4), and the Gospel: “A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke X, 30). A good descent is sometimes made through humility and more often through compassion.

[Col. 1129D] It is made through humility, as in Rebecca, who, seeing Isaac, descended from the camel (Gen. XXIV, 64), signifying—or openly declaring—the humble submission which the bride owes to the bridegroom, the Church to Christ, and the soul to God. Descent takes place through compassion, as we have in the Creed of faith, that Christ “for our salvation came down from heaven.” In a moral sense, we may understand by the Jordan the descent of mercy by which a person is led to have compassion upon a neighbour.

3. It should be understood that one person is on this side of the Jordan, another within it, and another above it. One who has compassion on no one and receives compassion from no one is on this side; one who pities another and is pitied by another is within; one who has compassion on others and needs no one’s compassion

[Col. 1130A] is above. On this side is the devil; within is man; above is God. Thus the avaricious person, because he does not know how to show mercy and consequently cannot obtain mercy, is on this side; for “judgment without mercy shall be upon him who has shown no mercy” (Jas. II, 13).

4. It follows that the proud person migrates to the north. As holy teachers affirm, the north signifies the swelling of pride. For just as “all evil is opened from the north” (Jer. I, 14; IV, 6), so “pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. X, 15); likewise, in it every perdition took its beginning. Hence the apostate angel says in his heart: “I shall sit upon the mount of the covenant, in the sides of the north” (Isa. XIV, 13).

The proud person, therefore, migrates to the north because, in pride, he departs from God, who resists the proud,

[Col. 1130B] and follows the devil, who is king over all the children of pride.

5. It next follows that the lustful person swims in the river of Babylon. The river of Babylon is the flow of lust. Whoever, carried away by the pleasure of lust, wallows in it through habit, swims in this river.
