The devil suggests these three vices to human beings. Through avarice the devil takes possession of a person, because “those who wish to become rich fall into temptation and the snare of the devil” (I Tim. VI, 9). Thus we read that when Judas, intoxicated with the poison of avarice, was about to betray Christ to the Jews, having received money from them, “then Satan entered into him” (John XIII). Avarice excludes generosity, knows no kindness, and detests mercy.

Pride is the throne of iniquity, the vice of man, and the ruin of the devil.

[Col. 1130C] Pride is hateful to God, detested by angels, and intolerable to human beings. Pride is the origin of sin, the mother of discord, and the stepmother of concord; pride is the support of vices and the destruction of virtues. Thus through pride the devil reigns in a person; through lust he rests in him, because, as we read, he sleeps in moist places (Job XL, 16), that is, in hearts subject to lust. Lust dissolves the flesh, afflicts the mind, and turns the whole person into mourning. Lust is the dung of impurities, the filth of vices, the dregs of pleasures.

6. If you please, let us consider still more attentively how shamefully a person is treated by the three vices just mentioned. Through avarice he is blinded, through pride he hangs, and through lust he rots.

[Col. 1130D] He is blinded through avarice, as we read. For when the aforementioned Judas, led by avarice and intending to betray the Lord, had left the company of the disciples, the Evangelist, wishing to show his inner blindness, said: “And it was night” (John XIII, 30).

Through avarice a person is blinded; through pride he hangs, because, while he considers himself wealthier than others, attending not to equality of condition but to glory in the abundance of riches, he inwardly exalts himself above others. Hence we read that two women, whom blessed Gregory calls pride and vain glory, lifted between heaven and earth an amphora, which signifies avarice (Zech. V, 9). Unless this were so, the Apostle would never have said: “Charge those who are rich in this world not to think proudly, nor to hope in the uncertainty

[Col. 1131A] of riches” (I Tim. VI, 17).

Suspended through pride, a person is dissolved into lust. When he sees himself as richer than others, and is therefore suspended upon the rack of pride—where he neither fears God nor respects man—then, like the horse and mule that have no understanding, he enters the stall of pleasure and, lying in the dung of his condition, rots away. Hence it is said: “The beasts have rotted in their dung” (Joel I, 17). Moreover, the two women bore the elevated [supplied: amphora] between heaven and earth, in order to build it a house in Shinar, that is, in stench.

7. Considering these things, beloved, let us give praise to the Creator, by whose aid and grace we seem to have left them behind. This is attested by the way of poverty which we have entered,

[Col. 1132A] the garb of humility which we have received, and the observance of purity which we have vowed. Entering upon the way of poverty, we have put away avarice from ourselves; receiving the garb of humility, we have put away pride; vowing purity, we have put away lust.

Let us know, therefore, that as in the things we have left lies the ruin of all honourableness, so in those to which we pass lies the sum of all honourableness. For religious life is founded upon humility, preserved by poverty, and adorned by purity. Every affection is base in the love of money. A soul greedy for money does not fear to perish even for a trifling gain; nor does any trace of justice remain in the heart where avarice has fixed its dwelling.

[Col. 1131]

## HOMILY ON MATTHEW 13:45: “THE KINGDOM OF HEAVEN IS LIKE A MERCHANT SEEKING GOOD PEARLS.” (G)

> [Note.]

It is commonly attributed to Bernard, although it does not appear to be his. It is absent from Horstius.

[Col. 1131B] 1. “Kings of the earth and all peoples, princes and all judges of the earth, young men and maidens, old men together with the young”: hear, I beg you, the word of the Lord, who says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking fine pearls; and when he had found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it.” But what, I ask, my dearest brothers, is this pearl so precious that we ought to give everything for it—that is, ourselves—for he gave all to God, he who offered himself, so that we may possess it? Is it not holy, pure, and undefiled religious life, in which a person lives more purely, falls more rarely, rises more swiftly, walks more cautiously, is refreshed more often, rests more securely, dies more confidently, is cleansed more quickly, and is rewarded more abundantly?

O glorious and wonderful religious life! [Col. 1131C] What mind can conceive you, what understanding fully know you, what human tongue sufficiently and worthily extol you? For this, my brothers, is what, through God's mercy, forgives sins and opens Paradise; what heals the contrite person and cheers the sorrowful; what calls life back from ruin, restores one’s condition, renews honor, reforms confidence, and pours forth strength and more abundant grace. O religious life adorned with virtues! O brightly gleaming pearl! What new thing shall I say of you? You loose all things that are bound; you open all things that are shut. You soften every adversity; you revive everything despaired of. O religious life, more radiant than gold, more splendid than the sun! If it is truly kept, sin does not overcome, slander does not prevail, despair does not cast down; but, with God’s help, it perseveres to the end, that it may seize the prize.

[Col. 1131D] This is what rejects avarice, abhors lust, flees rage, strengthens love, tramples pride, restrains the tongue, orders conduct, hates malice, excludes wickedness, and compels a person gladly to endure all things for love of God. O religious life [Col. 1132B] most welcome and to be sought with one’s whole heart! Is it not through you that the blind see, the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the poor receive the Gospel? O peaceful religious life, far removed from the tumult of this evil age, and, for Christ’s sake, dead to the world: there the Holy Spirit comes upon the humble and quiet, and Christ descends upon the devout. O religious life, dwelling-place of God and his angels! Here his fellow-servants make their abode. O blessed life, life of angels! The Holy Spirit himself says: “Mary has chosen for herself the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” (Luke 10:42).

O most blessed solitary life, contemplative life! When the Virgin Mary was contemplating in solitude, then you came, and in her and from her assumed flesh. O my God! O good Jesus! What more shall I say? Truly, my brothers, the cloister—truly, [Col. 1132C] religious life—is Paradise. O religious life fortified by the rampart of discipline, in which is the fruitful fertility of precious virtues! “It is a glorious thing for people of one disposition to dwell in a house” (Ps. 67:7); “It is good and pleasant for brothers to dwell together as one” (Ps. 132:1). You may see one weeping for sins, another rejoicing in God’s praises; one serving people, another instructing others; one praying, another reading; one showing mercy, another correcting another’s sins; one burning with charity, another excelling in humility; one humble in prosperity, another exalted in adversity; one laboring in the active life, another resting in the contemplative life—and you may say: “These are the camps of God. How awesome is this place! Truly this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28:16–17).

[Col. 1132D] O most glorious gate, through which one enters the holy city, through which the kingdom of heaven is seized and possessed! O most noble religious life! You are the chastity of religious persons, the cord of clerics, a treasure beyond gold! O blessed solitude! O wilderness, [Col. 1133A] death of vices and life of virtues! The Law and the Prophets marvel at you, and all who have attained perfection entered Paradise through you. O blessed solitary and contemplative life, what more shall I say of you? The very Son of God, our Savior and teacher, gave us an example by fleeing into the desert and remaining in solitude, where there are roses of charity that always flame and always live in holy fragrance.

There is the wondrous perfection of those who have mortified themselves, and thanksgiving: namely, to consider what and how great are the things promised us in heaven, which make everything possessed on earth seem worthless, and to say: “What does it profit a man if he gains the world but loses himself?” (Matt. 16:26). O solitude, storehouse of heavenly occupations! In you transitory and earthly things are changed into heavenly and [Col. 1133B] eternal things. Through this brief purgatory are wrought the eternal heavenly banquet and everlasting pastures. Finally, in you tears are changed into laughter and bring forth eternal joy. From earthly possession, which is abandoned to mortal worms, one comes to the inheritance of eternity.

O religious life, struggle of the spiritual army, wondrous workshop! In you the faithful soul restores within itself the image of its Creator and returns to the purity of its image. You are the furnace in which the vessels of the heavenly King are formed, where sins are dissolved, and where people toil with angels in divine praises. O holy life, bath of souls, death of sins, and purgatory of defiled souls! You cleanse the hidden places of minds; you wash away [Col. 1133C] the filth of consciences and enable souls to reach the purity of angelic cleanness. You are Jacob’s ladder, bringing souls to Paradise. You are the royal road of Paradise, [Col. 1134A] bringing human beings to their homeland. You are the stadium of contestants and wrestlers who run well; you lead them to lofty crowns.

O religious life, burial of the Lord’s Passion! Of you the prophet Jeremiah says: “It is good to wait silently for the saving help of God. He shall sit solitary and be silent” (Lam. 3:26, 28) in the wilderness, because a person becomes wise through resting and keeping silence. Certain things concerning these matters have been proved, whence it is said: “O man, flee people, choose religious life, and you shall be saved.” Rise, you who sleep in the world; rise from the dead, and leave the dead to bury their own dead. O wonderful life, spiritual dwelling-place, which makes the proud humble, the gluttonous sober, the cruel devout and holy, the angry gentle, the lustful chaste, the disobedient obedient, and those who hate [Col. 1134B] fervent in brotherly love! You put a bridle upon the tongues of the talkative; upon the unclean you place the girdle of chastity, the sweet love of Christ; you are the nurse of fasts and vigils; you bind the wandering with chains; you are the guardian of patience and the teacher of most pure simplicity.

Those who flee you are deprived of God’s light; those who love you perceive and taste how sweet and pleasant the Lord is. You lead to eternal joys which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor have entered into the human heart; nor can the tongue express what you, Lord, have prepared for those who love you. Therefore enter in, my most beloved brothers, since the Angel of Great Counsel calls you; and do not delay, for the reward is great and the danger in delay is not small. Hasten, then, into the holy religious life of Christ; and the [Col. 1134C] Son of God will enlighten you through worthy satisfaction—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1133]

## SERMON

On Micah, chapter 6, verse 8: “I will show you, O man, what is good,” etc. It is attributed to Bernard in a Speyer codex printed in 1501, incorrectly entitled *On the Threefold Character of Tears*. (G)*

[Col. 1133D] 1. “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” “I will show you, O man, what is good,” and what God requires of you: namely, to do justice, to love mercy, and to walk solicitously with your God. These are the three things that you must offer, because God, who is Trinity, can be pleased only by a threefold sacrifice. Offer judgment, then, to the Son who is Judge; offer mercy to holy charity; offer solicitude to fatherhood. Discernment belongs to wisdom; piety to charity; solicitude to fatherhood. Yet offer them in such a way that you neither divide the unity of the Trinity in distinguishing the gifts, nor confuse the Trinity of unity in sharing the gifts; but render what belongs to each individually, and all things to the One together.

If you judge justly, you honor the righteous Judge. If you love mercy, you venerate him who is merciful with an acceptable sacrifice. If you always walk solicitously in the fear of God, [Col. 1134D] you appease for yourself the heavenly Father whom you had offended by your sins.

2. Now listen to the kind of judgment that you are commanded to make. First, you must render judgment upon yourself; next, between yourself and your neighbor; finally, concerning your neighbor. In that judgment by which you judge between yourself and your neighbor, you ought to be the greater one.

You should judge yourself as follows: carefully consider what you do and do not do; what you ought to do and what you ought not to do. Then, comparing these things with one another, weigh whether what you do is the same as what you ought to do, and whether what you do not do is the same as what you ought not to do. If you find that it is so, rejoice. But if you discover that you do what you ought not to do, or do not do what you ought to do, fear.

You should judge between yourself and your neighbor as follows. See what you do for your neighbor and what your neighbor does for you. If he does you good and [Col. 1135A] you return good to him, you are not evil. If he does you evil and you return evil to him, you are not good. If he does you good and you return evil to him, you are evil. If he does you evil and you return good to him, you are good.

You should judge concerning your neighbor as follows. See what he does: whether it is certain good, doubtful good, certain evil, or doubtful evil. If certain good is small, regard it as greater. If certain evil is great, regard it as small; if small, judge it still smaller. If good is doubtful, regard it as true; if evil is doubtful, regard it as good. This is true judgment, good judgment, judgment pleasing to God. And if you offer this to him as a sacrifice not merely by discerning but also by doing it, you will appease wrath and obtain grace.

3. Then follows loving mercy, so that [Col. 1136A] the good you do may proceed not from fear but from love. Finally, walk solicitously, lest you either fail to deserve to receive the good you do not yet possess or lose the good you possess. In these three things, moreover, you cooperate with the Trinity working in you. Wisdom enlightens you to the knowledge of truth; charity kindles you with desire for goodness; fatherhood preserves in you what it created, lest it perish. Thus, through illuminating wisdom, you discern rightly together with the One who gives light; through enkindling charity, you show mercy together with the One who burns; and through provident fatherhood, you guard yourself together with the One who protects. By cooperating with the Trinity, you become an image of the Trinity cooperating with you; and then you offer yourself to God as a true sacrifice when you are reformed into his likeness. Amen.

[Col. 1135]

## BOOK OF SENTENCES (G)

### [NOTE.]

Horstius, following Bellarmine’s counsel, relegated the following *Sentences*, which had been appended to the sermons *On Various Subjects* in the earlier editions, to the class of doubtful works because of their difference in style.

[Col. 1135B] 1. A rational creature ought to direct itself toward being blessed, and toward God, through whom alone it can be made blessed. His pursuer and rival labors to corrupt it in both aspects of its nature. Therefore he utterly spoils and corrupts its bodily aspect through the appetite of gluttony and the overflow of lust; and, driving the beast of the flesh with these two goads, he hurls it into the precipices of death. But he attacks the invisible portion of human substance with spiritual weapons and, infecting it with a double plague, stains it with the swelling of pride and the blot of avarice. Thus, corrupting the whole mass by the pollution of this leaven, he wrests from humanity the blessedness which he himself lost.

2. There are four masters whose service we perform in this life: the flesh, the world, the devil, and God. We serve the flesh by yielding to the enticements of gluttony and obeying the prompts of lust. [Col. 1135C] We serve the world by panting after the heats of avarice and aspiring to the height of honor. We serve the devil by envying the progress of the good and swelling against God with a spirit of pride. We serve God by humbly persisting in works of piety and attacking the powers of the air by the strength of the spirit. Each of these rulers also has his own gifts for his soldiers. The flesh grants its recruits momentary pleasure; the world, transitory eminence; the devil, everlasting captivity; God, unending happiness. This alone outweighs all the rest.

[Col. 1135D] 3. By Gospel ordinance we are commanded, in the course of this mortal life, to greet no one who clings to earthly affections (Luke 10:4; 11:43). But to those whom we see detached from this life, [Col. 1136B] let us offer the joy of a confident greeting. Hence in the Gospel we find three kinds of greeting. The Virgin Mary greeted Elizabeth (Luke 1:40); the angel greeted Mary (ibid., 28); and the Lord Jesus greeted the disciples after the Resurrection (John 20:19).

Therefore, when we see those who have served in the barrenness of this life ascending the mountains of confession and conceiving, as it were, the fervor of penitence as a certain son, we ought to offer them the voice of greeting, and, in the Lord’s word, the abundance of remission, grace, and pardon. But to those whom we perceive serving the Lord in holiness and chastity, we must promise blessing and the fruitfulness of grace by inviting them to better things. And to those whom we see in the inner chamber of withdrawal striving toward the apostolic height, [Col. 1136C] let us pledge, by the ministry of the living voice, the twofold firmness of rest and peace, of which they already feel certain foretastes in their own body.

4. Three principal things, by a voluntary compulsion, moved the Lord Jesus Christ to undergo the disgrace of the cross and death. Filial and pure obedience, by which the guilt of the earlier disobedience might be paid. Compassionate and common misery, which urged his inflexible justice—his rod of iron—toward mercy. That misery was weighty and grievous, pressing human necks beneath the condition of common sin and death; it was public and universal, [Col. 1136D] binding just and unjust alike under the same sentence of condemnation; it was continuous and everlasting, so that unless the grace of redemption were accomplished through Christ, it would swallow the whole race of Adam [Col. 1137A] in the abyss of condemnation by an irremediable bond of captivity. Finally, the third thing voluntarily compelling him to death was the most celebrated and solemn victory, by whose success the unavoidable power of the devil and death was to be gloriously and effectively diminished in the tomb.

5. The Lord exalts our head in three ways: by lifting the mind above earthly affections, so that in hope of heavenly things we may despise transitory things; by conferring divine knowledge, so that we may possess knowledge of things not seen in time; and by raising us to love of heavenly things, so that, though placed in the flesh, we may transcend even the flesh by the height of divine love.

6. Human beings have a threefold condition of life: not to sin, which servile fear accomplishes; not to wish to sin, which filial fear displays; and not to be able to sin, which everlasting blessedness alone confers.

7. Four things are said to increase the grace of our devotion: the remembrance of sins, which makes a person humble in his own eyes; recollection of punishments, which urges him to act well; consideration of pilgrimage, which exhorts him to despise visible things; and desire for eternal life, which, inciting a person toward perfection, compels him by a change of will to withdraw from earthly affections.

8. The Lord instructs the slowness of our ignorance in three ways: by the abundance of a bestowed benefit, which softens the hardness of our mind and awakens it to love; by the frequent severity of blows, which, giving understanding to the ear, strikes fear into us; and by the public humiliation of contempt, by which, filling our faces with disgrace, he produces in us shame and blushing.

9. The stirring and titillation of our flesh occur for three reasons: from a preceding thought, when, drawing unlawful forms and images inward, we are shamefully aroused in reconsidering them; from fullness of the belly, because, when the stomach is distended by an abundance of food, the wanton flesh is stirred to the motion of lust; and from the assault of an evil spirit, because, the less it finds itself able to overcome the righteous, the more heavily it attacks them through fleshly titillation.

10. By the authority of the Scriptures, we are forbidden to think evil, speak evil, and do evil. For in thinking evil there is either uncleanness, when filthy and impure matters are turned over in the memory; or pride, when the mind raises and puffs itself up as though superior to its neighbors; or avarice, when, at the devil’s instigation and contrary to God’s commandment, one covets a neighbor’s property. For something of these three must always be present in an evil thought.

In speaking evil, moreover, speech is either superfluous, lacking reason and usefulness; or slanderous, diminishing a brother’s goods with envious corrosion and the prompting of hatred; or flattering, [Col. 1137D] caressing someone’s head with the false anointing of oil. In doing evil, likewise, a deed is either hypocritical, when we intend something other than what we display in our deed; or impious, when we harm our neighbors; or indecent, when we defile ourselves in some way.

[Col. 1138A] 11. As those about to ascend from the valley of weeping, we must always strive and pant after higher things. For this mortal life is, as it were, a desert, of which it is said: “A deserted land, trackless and without water” (Ps. 62:3). But deserts have a threefold form. There is a desert, namely momentary vanity, which we ought to despise through moderation of life. From this desert we must ascend, as it is said: “Who is this that comes up from the desert, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song 8:5). We abound in delights when we abound in virtues. We lean upon the Beloved when we ascribe to God whatever good we do.

There is another desert: the humility of Christian simplicity. It is called a desert because scarcely anyone is an imitator of Christ who endeavors to practice this good. Through [Col. 1138B] this desert we must ascend. Hence it is said: “Who is this that ascends through the desert like a little column of smoke from aromatics?” (Song 3:6). We ascend like a little column of smoke from aromatics when, trained by the pursuit and discipline of virtues, we encourage our neighbors to imitate good action.

There is also another desert: the simplicity or integrity of purer innocence. We must ascend to this, because we ought to long for true purity, so that we may be holy in body and spirit. Let us therefore ascend from the desert of momentary vanity through the desert of most humble simplicity to the desert of most complete purity.

12. Our Lord has his own arrows, by which he wounds his enemies and overcomes them with the arm of strength. [Col. 1138C] There are three arrows by which enemies are wounded. The sting of lost money: for one is greatly crushed who remembers that he has lost wealth, the means of living and attendants of pleasures. Then comes the pestilence of bodily affliction, which, in order to hedge in his ways on every side, scourges even with bodily suffering the one whom it sees hastening toward sin. Then comes the hammer of the memory of hell: for, when someone considers himself hemmed in on every side by the burden of bodily punishments, he turns his eyes also toward that distress which has no end and ponders with fearful reflection the horrible furnace of Gehenna.

13. There are also three other arrows by which the Lord wounds even those whom he invites to taste the sweetness [Col. 1138D] of his love. The first is chaste fear. It is so called because it commands that the Lord be feared even by a servant and continually persuades the servant, through regard for the Lord, to refrain from unlawful things. Then follows devout love, which, when it has occupied the mind, sets the whole person aflame with the fire of most sweet love. Then follows the power of desire, which, when it has breathed upon the breadth of the conscience like a gentle breeze, makes the mind forget what lies behind and pant for the Creator’s face alone; and because it does not attain the end of its desire, it wastes away.

14. The offering of our praise, which we sacrifice to God, ought to be threefold: affectionate, so that the mind agrees with the voice; fruitful, so that it produces edification in the beholder; gracious, so that it pleases the Creator who gave freely.

[Col. 1139A] By the decrees and exhortations of the holy Fathers we are continually admonished to think well, speak well, and act well. For in thinking well, thought is either honorable, contracting no impurity; humble, savoring nothing proud; or devout, devising nothing cruel. In speaking well, speech either brings benefit to the hearer; or is humble, swelling with none of the charm of empty eloquence; or is plausible, putting forward beneath its covering nothing overlaid with the cosmetic of pretence. In acting well, likewise, a deed is either pure, showing cleanness; pious, breathing mercy; or modest, not offending or violating the eyes of those who behold it.

16. It is a very common and worn-out usage that this world, deservedly because of its blindness and ignorance, is called by the name of Egypt. When we go out from it through a change of will, three things meet us. The sting of desires, which, like the Red Sea, envelops the sense of our reason in the swollen, stormy waves of thoughts; and unless the waters above are separated from those below by the rod of discerning judgment, it utterly overwhelms and drowns us.

[Col. 1139B] Then comes the mass of temptations, like another Jordan overflowing the bounds of its channel and occupying the land of our body more abundantly than usual. Unless the ark of the covenant—that is, the sentence of truth—intervenes, it restrains its violence and thoroughly dries it up. Then comes the sting of afflictions, which, when it comes upon us like Jordan again meeting Elisha, requires us to take up Elijah’s cloak and oppose it to the waves [Col. 1139C] in their midst, so that whatever torments us in time may, by a changed savor through regard for the Lord’s Passion, become sweet to us with a new sweetness.

17. The paths that lead to death are divided in a threefold way: one is miserable, another laborious, another pleasurable. The miserable path is found in the poor who, swelling in their poverty with a royal spirit and wealthy mind, are transferred from temporal want to eternal misery. The laborious path is found in the avaricious and greedy, who, while they are miserably stretched out by anxiety over diverse cares, forget to seek the things that are God’s; panting with the heats of avarice, they are transferred at life’s end from temporal restlessness to the straits of eternal labor. The pleasurable path is found in delicate rich people, who, nurturing their bodies and hearts amid luxuries and pleasures, are carried after momentary sweetness and hourly delights into everlasting bitterness.

[Col. 1139D] 18. The way leading to life is likewise distinguished in a similar manner. One is bloody, another purple, another milky. The bloody way is in martyrs, who washed the garments of their bodies in the blood of the Lamb and, by the path of martyrdom, reached the throne of triumphant exaltation. The purple way is in confessors, who impressed in their flesh the traces of the Lord’s Passion through abstinence and bore in their bodies the marks of Christ’s wounds. The milky way is in virgins, who consecrated in themselves the brightness of angelic purity and the virtues of holiness, and [Col. 1140A] by the way of purity happily flew, upon the wings of virtues, to the embraces and bridal chambers of the true Bridegroom.

19. Death of the soul is forgetfulness; from this death it is raised in the following way: through memory it feels; through obedience it hears; through understanding it sees; through circumspection it smells; and through love it tastes.

20. There are four kinds of human will. Dry will is in the reprobate and earthly-minded, whose hearts are sprinkled with no dew of grace. Straight will is in beginners, who, leaving behind the strength of their former life, rise by a change of will to the rectitude of good work. Devout will is in those making progress, who through the practice of continual prayer are raised from heaven to the love of doing good. Blessed will is in the perfected, who, thinking of scarcely anything except God, place in him the fulfillment of their whole desire.

[Col. 1140B] Between dry and straight will a certain chasm has been fixed, namely perverse intention, so that one who wishes to cross cannot. Between straight and devout will lies ingrained habit. Between devout and blessed will lies bodily inclination. These three, like certain stones placed in the path of our work, hinder us from ascending from virtue to virtue.

21. All the righteous are trees, planted in the midst of the temporal Church, and they ought to bear enduring fruits of life. Let each person see that he chooses for himself a watered place, in which, bearing fruit, he may bring forth the fruit of life in its season. There are three streams of waters: the urgings of the Scriptures, which through threats and promises awaken an upright will in a person; the charisms of graces, which make a person spiritual from being animal-like, training him in provision and care for himself and teaching all truth, and which provide fruitfulness of works; and the droplets of tears, which, watering and soaking the veins of intention and purpose with their dew so that the tree may not die, grant perseverance.

[Col. 1140C] Whoever has been rooted beside these streams will bear fruit every month, and the leaves of that tree will be for the delight of the nations.

22. Not all who have been made drunk are intoxicated in one and the same way. One wine is the wine of malice, which flows from the grape of gall and had its beginning from the devil, who offered the human race the bitterness of sin and death; the wicked are made drunk by it when they are made like him. Another wine is the wine of affliction, which flows from the wild vine of human condition, which offered its Lord the vinegar of iniquity. Whoever is intoxicated by this wine is shown to suffer it from God not unjustly but deservedly, on account of his sin. Another is the wine of grace, which flows from the cluster of *cyprus*—that is, from the Creator’s bounty. This is the new wine by which the sons of the bridegroom are made drunk, [Col. 1140D] and which is also put into new wineskins.

23. All the elect are kings and priests, and they ought to be anointed with the oil of anointing. Now the oil is threefold. One oil is the oil of pouring forth: namely, the word of God, by which they are initiated as they put off the old person, so that, like young maidens, they may rise in love for the Bridegroom. Another is the oil of purity, with which the vessels of our works ought to be filled and which ought continually to nourish the fire in the lamp of divine fervor. The other [Col. 1141A] is oil of exultation, namely principal charity; when it has filled the mind, it enlarges it, so that, tasting how sweet the Lord is, seated on the summit of justice, it may glory and rejoice in God alone.

24. Christians have received their name from Christ; and it is fitting that, as they are heirs of his name, so they should be imitators of his holiness. Therefore there are three things that, being displayed to us in Christ, we ought to practice with all our strength: vigorously to reject the world’s vanity, for Jesus fled lest he be made king by the crowds; manfully to practice penitence, for Jesus was slain like a lamb; and truly to possess twofold charity, for Jesus prayed for his enemies.

25. Humility has seven steps of descent: renunciation of possessions, after the example of the Apostles; renunciation of clothing, like Elijah and John; bodily discipline, like Paul; right conduct in prosperity, after the example of David, both poor man and king; patience in adversity, like Job and Tobit; abhorrence of one’s own counsel; and abhorrence of attachment to one’s own will.

[Col. 1141B] 26. The weapons of virtue by which the weapons of wickedness are overcome are these: full knowledge of sin, which drives out the darkness of pleasure; penitential affliction, against the sweetness of carnality; humble and true confession, against the poison of iniquity; sufficient and worthy correction through a change from one’s former will; and a full attainment of perseverance, so that perfect safeguarding of health may be established.

27. These three are necessary for penitence: abstinence, through which the pride of the flesh is subdued; reading, by whose fruit the mind that must be restored to strength is nourished; and prayer, by whose defense and protection the swarms of virtues are guarded.

28. The virtue of humility has these three things: to be subject to a superior, so that it may not be seized by any ambition or envy for equality with him; not to be preferred to an equal, lest one appear to wish to become superior through unlawful desire; and rather to submit to an inferior than to take precedence over him, so that the truth of humility may thereby be proven.

[Col. 1141C] 29. Not all advance toward God at the same pace. Some walk step by step, like those entangled in the cares of earthly things, who scarcely ever take breath to remember the Lord. Some proceed at a moderate pace, like those devoted to the Lord’s service, who indeed serve God and yet are more indulgent toward themselves. Others move swiftly—that is, with rapid course—like those who look beyond their flesh and, despising both themselves and transitory things, make quick progress toward God, desiring only to rest in peace in the same reality.

[Col. 1141D] 30. There are three places—heaven, earth, and hell—and each has its inhabitants: heaven, the good alone; earth, a mixture; hell, the evil alone.

31. The human race suffers from a threefold sickness: at its beginning, middle, and end—that is, in birth, life, and death. Birth is unclean, life perverse, death perilous. Christ came and brought a threefold remedy against this threefold sickness. For he was born, lived, and died; and his birth cleansed ours, [Col. 1142A] his death destroyed ours, and his life instructed ours.

32. Three things await the elect in the world to come: inward satiety, eternal gladness, and delightful pleasure. Of these it is said, “Let the righteous exult” (Ps. 67:4), etc.

33. The desire of the elect is threefold: to dwell with one heart in the house, whence: “One thing have I asked of the Lord” (Ps. 26:4); to gain victory over the world, whence: “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” (Rom. 7:24); and to enjoy God in his presence, whence also: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1:23).

34. The fear of prelates is threefold: lest more elaborate display disturb the minds of their hearers; lest more immoderate use offend the eyes of the inward Judge; [Col. 1142B] and lest the recompense of justice be rendered to them in the present.

35. The sorrow of the saints is threefold: because they fell from Paradise; because they are held in exile; and because they are delayed from the kingdom.

36. In Christ, the mountain of mountains, there were these two things: the curd of the Passion and the richness of holiness.

37. There are three calves that we must sacrifice to the Lord: the effect of new conversion, like a young calf growing horns and hooves; the progress of holy religious life, which is the most tender calf from the herd; and the disposition of perfected virtue, which is the fattened calf.

38. Our oppression is fourfold: the straits of corruptible flesh, which are the pains of death; [Col. 1142C] the afflictions of temporal pressures, which are the torrents of iniquity; the hidden snares of the secret enemy, which are the pains of hell; and the deceptive appearances of worldly glory, which are the snares of death.

39. Smoke comes from God’s anger, because the elect are pierced with compunction in considering God’s anger. Fire comes from his face, because through knowledge and presence they are kindled to love. Darkness is beneath his feet [*nedibus*, presumably *pedibus*], because the reprobate is darkened by clouds of despair through his strict judgment.

40. The Lord walks upon the wings of the winds when his elect touch his sweetness, even lightly. He flies when they perceive nothing of his unbounded substance. Hence: “Flee, my beloved” (Song 8:14). The Lord makes the darkness of depth and height—the hiddenness of his divinity—his hiding-place; the light of purity and holiness, the dwelling-place of his habitation.

[Col. 1142D] 41. The world has its gates by which we enter into it: corrupt sensuality and incestuous desire; whence: “They drew near even to the gates of death” (Ps. 106:18). The gates of hell are blind despair and hard obstinacy; whence: “The gates of hell shall not prevail” (Matt. 17:18). The gates of heaven are humble patience, which is “the iron gate leading into the city” (Acts 12:10), and harmony of love, which is “the eastern gate” (Ezek. 45:1).

42. There are four kinds of recompense: two in this age and two in the age to come. The recompense of the prosperity and abundance of the wicked—whence: “They have received [Col. 1143A] their reward” (Matt. 6:5)—and that of their condemnation and disgrace; [and] the recompense of the righteous, namely intimacy and grace, sweetness, love, and glory. There are two things that receive reward: justice in deed and purity of heart.

43. There are three lamps: Christ, the rule of discipline, which is lit so that the lost drachma may be found; the form of truth in the Gospel, which is placed upon the lampstand; and purity of knowledge in a good heart, which is illuminated by the Lord.

44. Our feet ought to be like those of deer and like those of calves.

45. Some are foreign sons, who lie; others are sons of Belial, who do not know God; others are sons of Israel, who do know him.

46. Seed is threefold: that of truth and justice, [Col. 1143B] which, cast into the earth, yields a hundredfold fruit; that of iniquity and malice, which is a brood of vipers; and that of error and malice, which is Canaan and not Judah.

47. The wisdom of God, like a partridge, broods over children whom it did not bear; like a hen, gathers chicks beneath its wings; like an eagle, urges them to fly.

48. Our garment is threefold: penitential anxiety, which is the widow’s garment; religious maturity, which is the garment of rejoicing; sincere integrity, which is the garment of virgins.

49. Esau’s garments are uprightness of life and maturity of discipline; the kids’ skins are the casting off of harmful oldness and the mortification of one’s own will. The foods are cheerful obedience and humble abstinence. The father touches the son with the applied hand of testing; he kisses him by the prompting of secret inspiration [Col. 1143C]; he blesses him through progress in religious life.

50. Three things are necessary for purity: integrity of action, simplicity of intention, and tranquillity of devotion.

51. Purity bestows three things: the spirit of freedom, the joy of security, and the firmness of charity.

52. The reprobate are sometimes like smoke, because they vanish in their own height; sometimes like dust, because they produce no moisture of charity; sometimes like wax, because at heat—that is, at the onset of temptation—they melt easily.

53. The gates of Zion, that is, of the Church, are the sacraments [p. 778], without which we do not enter the Church. The gates of righteousness are the intermediate virtues which we exercise in time. [Col. 1143D] The everlasting gates are the principal virtues which we shall possess also in the life to come.

54. There are three things by which we are bound to God: the seal of nature, by which we were made in God’s likeness; the talent of faith, which through good work we must return to God whole and intact; and the title of profession, by which we are bound, through the bonds of a promise, to serve God.

God questions us in three ways: by the promulgation of a commandment, so that our obedience may become known to ourselves; by the infliction of a scourge, so that our patience may become known to our neighbours; and by the revelation of a secret, so that the virtue of humility may reveal itself to us.

55. Tribulation bestows three things: exercise, lest the virtue of love grow cold in a time of idleness; testing, so that the strength of our constancy may become known to people as an example; [Col. 1144A] and reward, so that it may receive an immeasurable weight of glory in proportion to tribulation.

Three things must be set against adversity: the struggles and distresses of the elect, endured by those who live devoutly; the afflictions and troubles of the Redeemer, inflicted upon him by most savage rulers; and the ordering of governing justice, whose height we ought not scrutinize, any more than the summit of Joseph’s rod, but adore. These are those three doors, bars, and boundaries by which the Lord surrounds the sea of this age.

56. The exercise of the elect is threefold: the austerity of fasts, by which the soil of the flesh is cultivated so that it may bear fruit; assiduity in reading, by which the soul is refreshed so that the inward person may grow fat; and persistence in prayer, by which [Col. 1144B] the mind rises toward a desire for heavenly things.

57. God, the author of wonders, worked three remarkable wonders in Mary. He wondrously raised up the integrity of purity, so that the ark of the covenant might be covered with the purest gold. He powerfully made virginal purity fruitful, so that the burning bush might not be consumed. He ineffably joined the lowest things to the highest, so that, through the mediation of Jacob’s ladder, earthly things might be united with heavenly things.

58. Mary’s fruitfulness bestowed three things upon us: it removed the yoke of ancient captivity; it remitted the wrath of divine indignation; and it erased the mark of human iniquity.

59. The elect await three things in the future: that what is mortal in them may be utterly swallowed up by life; that they may be enriched by the recompense of everlasting glory; and that they may contemplate God as he is without satiety.

[Col. 1144C] 60. The reprobate are said to hope for three things: to heap up bodily pleasure for themselves to sufficiency; to obtain blessedness through momentary glory; and to have their habits and deeds condemned by no judgment.

61. An imitator of Christ ought to do three things: retain the disposition of simple innocence, so as to become a child with Christ; love a lowly and humble condition, so as to be wrapped with Christ in the poor swaddling-clothes of infancy; and walk simply in discipline, so as to be found placed with Christ in the manger.

62. There are ministering spirits, who have care for our salvation; operative spirits, who are the authors of human well-being; and contemplative spirits, who stand before the face of divine majesty.

[Col. 1144D] 63. Blessed spirits are satisfied by vision, intoxicated by sweetness, and united by charity.

64. Those awaiting God ought to be in suspense as to when he will come, uncertain what he will bring them, cheerful and devout, more diligently adorned; hoping for three things in him: a nuptial presence, familiar favour, and generous munificence.

65. There are three kinds of nuptials. The first is reconciliation through faith, in which are three dishes: cleansing from sins, the attainment of grace, and the reformation of nature. The second is adoption through hope, in which likewise are consolation from the divine word, participation in heavenly nourishment, and a foretaste of inward sweetness. The third is perfect glorification through charity, whose [Col. 1145A] dishes are eternal incorruption, true glorification, and the everlasting vision of God.

66. There are three kinds of horses: worldly pride, whose rider falls backward; spiritual knowledge, around whose neck are set neighings; and integral purity [p. 779], which the whole army of heaven follows in white garments.

67. The words of God’s consolation are the washing away of guilt, restoration of grace, escape from exile, attainment of the kingdom, fellowship in divinity, and acquisition of eternity.

68. The faithful have three weapons: fullness of wisdom, which is David’s sling, from which stones of judgments are cast; steadfastness of patience, which is the staff by which the fury of wolves is driven off; and breadth of charity, which is David’s bag, from which prayers are brought forth.

[Col. 1145B] 69. Three things are necessary for prelates: living sincerity of faith and teaching, that they may dwell in the same region; diligent zeal in doing good, that they may keep watch with the shepherds; and careful concern for the salvation of their subjects, that they may guard their flock.

70. An ox-driver ought to have two things: sweetness of voice, to soothe those who labour; and the prick of a goad, to shake the slothful out of torpor.

71. There are three kinds of penance: feigned and fruitless, exemplified in Esau and Saul; cruel and despairing, as in Cain and Judas; and useful and complete, as in Mary and Zacchaeus. Its five parts are contrition in the heart, confession on the lips, mortification in the flesh, correction in action, and perseverance [Col. 1145C] in virtue.

72. Three things are found in Peter: unity of faith, truth of penitence, and firmness of love.

73. There are three kinds of change: sublimity into humility, when the Word assumed flesh; contemptibility into majesty, when God the man transformed himself before the disciples; and mutability into eternity, when, rising again, he ascended to heaven to reign.

74. What we do, we do either in the light of people’s faces, to please people; or in the light of our own face, believing that we do good when we do evil; or in the light of God’s face, humbly ascribing to him alone whatever good is in us.

75. Three things undermine patience: excessive anxiety of suffering, the just cause of an innocent person, and the unworthiness of the one inflicting it.

[Col. 1145D] 76. One who withdraws from fellowship loses the consolations of those assembled; in pursuing companions he incurs annoyances; in wandering, he easily follows byways and more often suffers shipwrecks of life.

77. There are three taskmasters of Pharaoh’s works: the foul heat of seething lust, the anxious fury of raging avarice, and the harmful appetite of empty glory.

78. There are three rulers in us who must die so that Christ may live: the prudence of worldly people, which is Joseph; the eloquence of spiritual people, which is Moses; and abundance of temporal things, which is Joshua.

79. The refuge of the wicked is threefold: the teaching of deceiving falsehood, which is Pithom; the fortification of worldly power, which is Rameses; and the semblance of feigned righteousness, which is the city of the Sun. Pharaoh commands these to be built.

[Col. 1146A] 80. There are three cups which the Lord offers us: that of penitence and sorrow, which is full of mixed wine; that of patience and labour, which Jesus drank; and that of goodwill and love, which is intoxicating and splendid.

81. There are five torrents: that of cruelty and malice, which is Kishon, by which Jabin is killed; that of philosophical eloquence, which is Kidron, beyond which Jesus goes forth; that of suffering and distress, which is on the way, and from which Jesus is said to have drunk; that of heavenly wisdom, beside which Elijah is fed; and that of delight and joy, by which the elect are given drink.

[Col. 1146B] 82. We are renewed in three ways: in the flesh, through the mystery of Baptism, from original sin; in deed, through the remedy of penance, from actual sin; and in flesh and spirit, through the gift of resurrection.

83. The kind of earth is fourfold: the flower and greenery of temporal goods, watered like paradise; the useful life and conduct of the elect, from which bread arises; the pleasantness of heavenly dwellings, flowing with milk and honey; and the condition of infernal places, which is a land of misery and darkness.

84. The desert is fourfold: the trackless solitude of worldly exile, concerning which David says, “In a desert land, trackless and waterless” (Psalm 62:3); the difficult height of Christian discipline, in which the children of Israel wander; the delightful expanse of the heavenly Jerusalem, [Col. 1146C] in which the ninety-nine sheep are left; [p. 780] and the dreadful condition of infernal misery, which is the desert of desolation.

85. There are four kinds of chariots: that of pride and dominion, in which Pharaoh is drowned; that of humility and zeal, in which the Eunuch sits; that of devotion and service, in which Joseph, seated, meets his father; and that of love and desire, in which Elijah is carried away.

86. The Lord’s ascent is threefold: victorious, by which he ascends above the west; beautiful, by which he ascends above the heavens of heavens; and glorious, by which he ascends upon the wings of the winds.

87. Some seize the kingdom of heaven violently, as the poor in spirit do; some purchase it, as those who make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity; some steal it, as [Col. 1146D] the woman who touches the fringe; and some are compelled to enter, as the poor of this world.

88. Four things confer true humility: lowliness of work, constancy in subjection, comparison with one better, and judgment by the Creator.

89. There are three judgments: another’s, one’s own, and God’s.

90. Sometimes life makes death precious, as in confessors; sometimes the cause does, as in martyrs; sometimes both life and cause do, as in most cases.

91. There are three foreskins which are cut away: the foreskin of the flesh in the Jew; the foreskin of the heart in the Christian; and the foreskin of the tongue in the perfect person.

[Col. 1147A] 92. There are four times: of prefiguration, prediction, visitation, and redemption.

93. God visits us in four ways: by the giving of a commandment—for one commandment is carnal and another spiritual; by the harshness of a scourge, which has five causes: to correct someone from iniquity, lest anyone grow proud of virtue bestowed, to make virtue known to people, to restrain others by that person’s example, and to accumulate and increase a crown; by the novelty of a miracle, which is visible; and invisibly, by subtle inspiration.

94. Jacob wrestled four times: in the womb with Esau, in youth with the same man, in Mesopotamia with Laban, and at Bethel with the angel.

95. Jesus is said to have wept three times: at his very birth, for the human race; in the course of time, for Lazarus; and finally [Col. 1147B] over Jerusalem, for its future fall.

96. On our forehead we sometimes bear leprosy, sometimes the *tau* (Thau), and sometimes a golden plate.

97. The Lord sometimes sits in the valley of Jehoshaphat, sometimes on a mountain, and sometimes upon a high throne.

98. One thunderclap is fiery; another is rainy.

99. There are two spurs with which the prophet urges his ass: shame, lest it be defiled in time; and fear, lest it be punished eternally.

100. There are three things which restrain and curb us, and may be called belts: remembrance of the body of death, which is the leather girdle with which Elijah and John were girded; the commendability and beauty of chastity, with which Aaron is girded when approaching God; and the love of religious devotion and righteousness, which is the golden belt with which [Col. 1147C] Jesus is girded about the breasts.

101. There are four virgins whom we ought to join in marriage: philosophical eloquence, which is Zilpah, Jacob’s handmaid; juridical judgment, signified through Balaam; practical innocence, which may be called Leah; and spiritual contemplation, understood as Rachel.

102. There are two eyes of the bride: consideration of passing things, which is like a flame of fire; and worthy estimation of the heavenly homeland, by which the bridegroom’s heart is wounded.

103. There are three common garments for ministers of God: heavenly wisdom, which is the ephod and covers the head; enduring righteousness, which is the *poderis*, covering the whole body; and bodily continence, which girds the loins.

104. Three lampstands are found in the Scriptures: legal obscurity, which has little globes and lilies; prophetic subtlety, which has two olive trees on its summit; and evangelical truth, which has in its midst one like a son of man.

105. The fortifications by which the soul is defended are three: diligent watchfulness, which is a hedge; the intercession of the saints, which is a very strong rampart; and divine protection, which is a wall defending against the assaults of enemies.

[p. 781] 106. A threefold reasoning examines and strengthens our hope: the humility of wisdom bestowed, which is to boil an egg in water; the firmness of constant patience, which [Col. 1148A] is to roast an egg in fire; and the truth of hidden inspiration, which is to fry an egg in fat.

107. There are three means by which God exercises vengeance on enemies: the remedy of saving baptism, which, like the Red Sea, kills the Egyptians; the exercise of worthy penitence, which, like sulphur, destroys sinners; and the judgment of final strictness, which, like fire at Elijah’s word, envelops them.

108. The bed of the soul, on which it rests, is threefold. The gravity of bodily weakness, which the sick man, once healed, spreads beneath himself. The tranquillity of a peaceful conscience, in which, while David flees, a statue is placed. This is that beneath which two mattresses are laid: amplitude of security and confidence concerning the past, and certainty of recompense and reward concerning the future. The pillow placed [Col. 1148B] beneath the head is the abundance of divine intimacy and grace. The third bed is humility amid higher glory: it is the flowering bed surrounded by sixty mighty men.

109. There are three panes of glass through which the sun’s ray is poured in: integrity of charity, through which forgiveness of sin enters; purity of humility, through which heavenly grace entered Mary; and subtlety of understanding, through which the ray of wisdom illuminates the heart.

110. Seven lamps illuminate the throne of the chosen mind: namely, the charisms of the Spirit, which the prophet expounds more fully. While these consume, with heavenly fire, the oil of glory and the reed of fear and weakness, they unceasingly provide the light of truth.

111. What is set before us to eat is a threefold food of flesh: a kid from the goats in the fruit [Col. 1148C] of penitence, which Jacob offered Isaac in order to be blessed; a calf from the herd in the act of righteousness, which Abraham expended on food for the angels; and the fatted calf in the abundance of glory, which the father is read to have sacrificed when his son was received.

112. The garden in which chosen souls walk is threefold: the distress of corruptible life, which is the garden of nuts, in which Susanna bathes; the pleasantness of heavenly delight, which is the garden of delights, in which Adam is placed to work and guard it; and the sweetness and pleasantness of the divine vision, which is the enclosed garden in which Joseph set up for himself a tomb hewn in the rock. A clean conscience also receives these gardens into itself, according to its diversity.

[Col. 1148D] 113. Three things are set upon the table for our hunger: the sacrament of Law and Gospel, in which the foods of wisdom are taken; the mystery of Catholic instruction, where the flesh of a roasted fish and a honeycomb are received; and the secret of eternal satisfaction, which is within the veil and contains the bread of presentation and of life.

114. There are three treasures which we ought to store up: the desire of piety in the heart, which is hidden in a field so that it may be bought; the doctrine of truth in the mouth, which is the treasure of snow and hail; and persevering assiduity in a person, which has wheat and barley, oil and honey. These are the treasures of the Magi, who offered gold, frankincense, and myrrh to the Lord at his birth.

115. Four kinds of bread are found in the Scriptures [Col. 1149A], by which the different miseries of humankind are lamented: bread baked in human dung, bovine dung, ashes, and an oven, by which different human dispositions are expressed.

116. There are three altars upon which we must place vows: fulfilment of divine ordinances, which is made from shittim wood in the desert; the manifold invocation of the blessed, which is made from stones untouched by iron; and the Redeemer’s humble incarnation, which is made from earth.

117. There are three girls who overthrow our understanding: the weakness of our flesh, which is Delilah, who tore out Samson’s eyes; the attractiveness of worldly glory, which is Jezebel and kills Naboth; and distrust of the future life, which is Herodias’s daughter and removes the prophet’s head.

[Col. 1149B] 118. There are two tribes, Levi and Judah, from which priests are taken—Aaron and Christ—and their succession. How this is fitting may be inferred from the interpretation of the names.

[p. 782] 119. There are three eagles attending the Lord’s body: the greatness of lay power, large and with great wings; the misuse of clerical purpose, which places its nest in heaven; and the spiritual subtlety of the humble, which provokes its young to fly.

120. Priestly office is fourfold: to sacrifice the living offering of the flesh, which is Levitical; to offer God the charisms of virtues, which is to burn incense and belongs to Aaron’s sons; to enter heaven with the fervour of martyrdom, which is to enter the Holy of Holies with [Col. 1149C] blood; and to convey the vows of grace and prayers to heaven, which is to offer bread and wine to God.

121. There are three fountains by which souls are washed: the anguish of contrition, which waters the surface of the earth; the humility of confession, which is placed outside the city; and the devotion of compunction, upon which Jesus stays and sits.

122. There are three breads by which we are nourished in this life: purgative bread with bitterness, which the woman of Zarephath serves in famine; consoling bread with sweetness, which the angel sets before one resting in the shade; and substantial bread with strength, which leads to God’s mountain Horeb. These are contained in the three portions of the Lord’s body [Col. 1149D].

123. There are three lamps that illuminate the night of this life: vigour of understanding in the mind, lit so that the drachma may be found; splendour of wisdom in speech, set on high so that its light may be seen; and the form of righteousness in one’s neighbour, borne before one coming to the wedding so that it may be carried in lampstands.

124. Three streams of salvation flowed from Jesus’ body: the word of suffering, in which is confession; the blood of sprinkling, in which is affliction; and the water of cleansing, in which is compunction.

125. Three pools are found in Scripture: the oldness of error, which is behind two walls; the sensuality of the flesh, in which the sick lay; and the perspicacity [Col. 1150A] of reason, which is on the road of the fuller’s field. In these sheep are watered and burnt offerings washed.

126. Three fuels of fire are in us: the straw of unclean thought, the hay of wicked speech, and the wood of unlawful action. These feed us to the fire unless they are extinguished by the higher fountains.

127. There are three windows of contemplatives: the original, which faces east; the governing, which inclines south; and the consummating, which looks west.

128. Four fountains water God’s garden: lamentation for one’s own guilt, which circles the land of Ethiopia; compassion for a brother’s transgression, which goes toward the Assyrians; consideration of grace bestowed, which cuts through the midst of Babylon; and the longing affection of charity, [Col. 1150B] which circles the whole land of Havilah. These fountains have upper watering and lower watering, possessing the waters of sea, river, spring, and snow.

129. Three dishes are contained in God’s bowl: clarity of brightness, which will shine like the sun; integrity of purity, which will be like the angels; and firmness of eternity, which will be like God.

130. There are three doors through which one passes to life: truth of faith, behind which Sarah laughs; firmness of hope, which is in the side of the ark; and solidity of charity, which the Cherub guards with a flaming sword.

131. The wine in God’s cup is threefold: red, in the long-suffering of the saints, which gladdens Isaac in sickness; white, in the recompense of the righteous, by which Noah is made drunk; and black and sour, in [Col. 1150C] the condemnation of the wicked, which Jesus tastes but does not wish to drink.

132. The garment which a priest ought to use is threefold: the coarseness of outward work, with which Aaron is clothed before the people; the condition of spiritual holiness, which Rebecca hides at home and with which Aaron serves in the tabernacle; and the beauty of contemplative sweetness, which is seamless and is used by Jesus.

133. There are three tunics with which we are clothed: chastising subjection of the body, which is of skins and clothes Adam; the extent of steadfast perseverance, with which Joseph is clothed by his beloved; and the abundance of rewarding grace, with which Jesus is clothed.

134. The Seraphim have six wings: two for the feet—shame concerning past things and fear concerning future things; lateral wings, by which they fly—fear that presses down and hope that lifts up; and head-wings—humility that advances and charity that perfects.

[p. 783] 135. God has two thrones: angelic substance, which is the high throne; and human nature, which is the exalted throne.

136. The four living creatures have four wings: fear and penitence, which cover the body; and love and hope, which are joined together and fly.

137. The living creatures of the New Law possess six wings: natural prompting, legal instruction, prophetic affirmation, evangelical ordinance, apostolic command, and ecclesiastical custom.

138. Jesus’ bed is threefold: unity of the Testaments, [Col. 1151A] which is like a virginal womb; the Church of the elect, which is like a manger; and the conscience of those purified, which is like a tomb in rock.

139. Three things are set before us in the saints to eat. First, the outward disposition of the body, consisting of three measures: gravity in the face, lowliness in dress, and maturity in gait. This is the barley bread with which five thousand are satisfied. Then follows the inner disposition of the spirit, likewise consisting of three measures: humility in prosperity, firmness in adversity, and moderation in all things. This is the rye bread with which four thousand are satisfied. Then follows the higher beauty, like unto God: its measures are constituted by the threefold character of charity in relation to God and human beings, which embraces friend and enemy and loves for [Col. 1151B] God’s sake. This is the wheat bread, baked by the breath of the Holy Spirit, and called the bread of angels.

140. There are two houses of God: the outer one, the inquisitive concern that ministers to temporal things, which is the tabernacle over which the glory of the Lord appears and departs; and the inner one, devout simplicity, free for and serving God, which is the temple and does not move from its place.

141. There are two arks in the Old Law: the text of literal history, which contains people and animals; and the spiritual sense of what is contained, which contains manna and Aaron’s rod.

142. Three chariots are found in Scripture. The first is the exaltation of temporal power: its charioteer is the swelling of presumption [Col. 1151C] and audacity; its horse is the strength of self-confidence; its wheels are the headlong instability of vanity and the happy success of prosperity. This is Pharaoh’s chariot, in which Rechab dies (Exod. XIV). Next is the loftiness of conduct and life: its charioteer is the word of divine admonition; its horse, the vow of perseverance; its wheels, the dreadful terror of torments and the wonderful delight of rewards. This is the chariot in which the Eunuch reads with Philip (Acts 8). Next is the height of contemplation and grace: its charioteer is love of the heavenly homeland; its horse, desire for blessedness and life; its wheels, disapproval of worldly glory and reverence for divine majesty. This is the fiery chariot in which Elijah is carried up to heaven (4 Kings 2).

[Col. 1151D] 143. There are three coverings of the altar: penitential affliction for sins, which is sackcloth; the greatness of praise and joy for forgiveness, which is like sounding bronze; and heartfelt jubilation for grace, which gleams like gold.

144. There are three keys which unlock hidden things for us: the austerity of anxious time, which opened the pit of the abyss; the subtlety of presumptuous hope, which unlocks the kingdom of heaven; and the brightness of true love, which is David’s key.

145. There are two rivers in which sinners wash themselves: the flow of corruption and wantonness, and the pest of flattery and deceit—these are the rivers Abana and Pharpar of Damascus. There are two in which the righteous bathe themselves: the assault of corruption and insult, and the sweetness of consolation [Col. 1152A] and grace—these are the rivers Jor and Dan of Judaea.

146. There are four songs of the faithful: of victory, sung when Pharaoh is drowned (Exod. 15); of exhortation, sung when they are about to enter the land of promise (Num. 3); of joy, sung by Hannah concerning the reception of her son (2 Kings 1); and of strength, sung by David when rescued from Saul’s hand (Psalm 69).

147. There are four kinds of herbs in God’s garden: purity of bodily cleanness, like a lily; the grace of spiritual innocence, like hyssop; the truth of generous eloquence, like a violet; and the righteousness of continuous action, like a rose.

148. Bloodless martyrdom is threefold: moderation in abundance, which David and Job had; generosity in poverty, [Col. 1152B] which Tobias and the widow exercised; and chastity in [p. 784] youth, which Joseph practiced in Egypt.

149. There are two feet which we ought to use: nature and custom.

150. There are three horses by which we are carried to heaven. The first is sorrow arising from penitence, whose hoofs a serpent bites. Its saddle is presumption based on receiving forgiveness; its bit and halter are the consolations of the Scriptures and examples of the ancients; its spurs are shame at the enormity of guilt and dread arising from consideration of punishment; its pitfall is despair. Next is fervour arising from religious devotion, on which Mordecai sits in royal dress. Its saddle is the moderating gravity of discernment; its bit and halter are distrust of one’s fleshly condition and a profitable emergence into perseverance; [Col. 1152C] its spurs are eagerness to practise uprightness and desire for a brother’s benefit; its pitfall is intemperance. Next is desire arising from love, to which strength is given and around which neighing is set. Its spurs are the transient instability of present things and the stable eternity of future things; its guide is the affection of seeing God; its pitfall is indiscretion.

151. Three caves are found in the sacred books: the perverse ungodliness of the will, which is the cave of robbers, in which Saul relieves himself; the solid firmness of even-mindedness, which is made in the altar and is one cubit in size; and the exercise of twofold piety. This is the double cave in which the Patriarchs are buried.

152. There are four weapons by which we are chiefly fortified: prudent and humble understanding, which is like a helmet and covers the head; moderate and sparing temperance, which is a breastplate and covers the chest; persevering and patient constancy, which is like a shield and protects the right hand; and the justice of retributive equity, which is a sword cutting on both sides for the division of soul and spirit.

153. There are three sacrifices: devout contrition, having the butter of humility and the wormwood of indignation; worthy action, having the oil of discernment and the vinegar of shame; and thanksgiving, having the balsam of devotion and the poison of ingratitude.

154. There are four things in which the soul is held captive: worldly wickedness, useless sadness, vain glory, and hidden pride.

[Col. 1153A] 155. There are three heavens to which we are carried: the dignity of ecclesiastical purity, to which Elijah is carried in body; the truth of angelic subtlety, to which Ezekiel is carried in spirit; and the unboundedness of the supreme Deity, to which the souls of the elect are carried.

156. There are six cities of refuge: caution against forbidden transgression, obedience to a command that must be followed, and eagerness to propitiate divinity—these are in the land of Canaan; consideration of the worldly structure, continual observation of the tyrannical city, and surpassing knowledge of the word of God—these are beyond the Jordan and belong to the Levitical allotment.

157. There are three kinds of paradise: the pleasurable sweetness of visible things, watered like the garden of delights; the sincere purity of spiritual things, which preserves the human being within itself; and the delightful truth of things above heaven, where Paul hears secret words.

158. There are four kinds of mountains: the mountains of Gilboa, where Saul’s shield is cast away (2 Kings 1); the mountains of Samaria, which rise too high (Amos 3); the mountains of Armenia, upon which the ark rested (Gen. 8); and the mountains of Israel, which spread forth their branches (Ezek. 36).

159. There are two things that call us back from our purpose: shame at the work begun and despair of carrying virtue through. These are Rechab and Baanah, who kill Ish-bosheth in his bed (2 Kings 4).

160. There are four cloaks with which our nakedness is covered: the oldness of error and wickedness, like a loincloth for shameful parts; newness of conduct [Col. 1153C] and life, by which Rebecca, descending from the camel, covered her face (Gen. 3); integrity of heavenly holiness, which Elijah left to Elisha and which divides the Jordan (Gen. 24); and the brightness of eternal immortality, the sapphire cloak which Mordecai wears on a feast day (4 Kings 2).

161. God is good in generously bestowing temporal benefit; patient in mercifully postponing punishment for sins; and long-suffering in inviting the guilty to repentance.

162. There are three enemies to whom we are delivered: the impurity of unclean desires, like mice gnawing the hind parts; the filthiness of bodily passions, like locusts striking with a scorpion’s manner; [Col. 1153D] and the stubborn perversity of reason and sense [p. 785], like fiery serpents.

163. There are four thieves who steal every good thing from us: the sluggishness of dulled understanding, taking from us knowledge of truth—this thief is called by the Psalmist “the business in darkness”; the lust of untamed flesh, snatching away the merit of integrity and called the “noonday demon”; boastfulness in a favourable breeze, taking away fullness of holiness and called “the arrow flying by day”; and love and desire for this life, snatching away the reward of eternity and called “the terror by night” (Psalm 90:5–6). These are the thieves of Syria.

164. There are three kisses: the reconciliatory kiss, by which the Lord’s two feet, mercy and justice, are touched; the rewarding kiss, by which the two hands—the work of creative [Col. 1154A] justice and the manner of continual governance—are embraced; and the contemplative kiss, received upon the mouth, which joins the Word of God and humanity in wonderful unity. They may also be called natural, when we are led spontaneously by the will toward good; doctrinal, when another’s admonition invites us to God; and gracious, when pleasant inspiration draws us to do good.

165. There are three callings: divine, as in Paul; human, as in the five thousand converted at the Apostles’ voice; and necessary, as in Paul the first hermit.

166. Contemplation is called food in this life, where we eat our bread in sweat; drink in the future life, where it is received freely and without pain; and intoxication at the end, when the soul, having received its body, rejoices together with it. Hence it is said: “Eat, friends” (Song of Songs 5:1), etc.

167. Of contemplatives, some ascend and fall (Exod. 19), like the beast that touches the mountain; others are caught up and descend, as Peter, after the ecstasy, came down from the upper room (Acts 10).

168. There are two breasts: compassion, from which flows the milk of consolation by which the weak are nourished; and shared joy, from which flows the milk of exhortation by which the strong are sustained.

169. There are three ointments: compunction from remembrance of sins, which anoints Jesus’ feet; devotion from recollection of benefits, by which Jesus’ head is anointed; and piety from consideration of the wretched, which women prepare for anointing Jesus’ body.

170. There are three rods: Moses’ rod, which divides [Col. 1154C] the Red Sea (Exod. 4); Aaron’s rod, which confers priesthood (Num. 17); and David’s pastoral rod, which drives off the adversary (1 Kings 17).

171. Jesus’ form was threefold: common and despised; brighter than the sun and wholly splendid; spiritual and divine, yet tempered to human sight.

172. Israel has three foods: unleavened bread of secular knowledge at the departure from Egypt; manna of understanding in the desert; and the palm of triumphant victory in the kingdom of promise.

173. There are three who know divine secrets: the most steadfast executor of recognized faith; the vigorous overthrower of encroaching vices; and the humble confessor of grace received. These are Peter, James, and John.

[Col. 1154D] 174. Three are delivered from every people: Noah, Daniel, and Job.

175. Three are assumed into the priesthood: Moses, Aaron, and Samuel.

176. Thieves strip us of the garment of innocence, pierce us with arrows of temptations, and deprive us of heavenly consolation.

177. From our Lady the guilty receive forgiveness, the righteous grace, and the angels joy.

178. We ought to provide good things before people: in dress, lest it be conspicuous; in action, lest it be blameworthy; and in speech, lest it be contemptible. Before God, we ought to do so with holy thought, pure affection, and right intention.

179. There are two in Christ: the divine generation and the human generation; and in the Holy Spirit, procession and grace.

180. The Holy Spirit works one thing in us for our own sake—for example, compunction by forgiving sins; devotion by healing our deeds; love by revealing heavenly things. For the sake of our neighbours He works another thing: the teaching of words, the grace of healings, and so forth.

181. There is a twofold danger: either that we divide among our neighbours things meant for ourselves, or reserve for ourselves things meant for our neighbours. This is the discernment of spirits.

182. The gatekeeper of memory is recollection of one’s profession; the gatekeeper of the will, memory of the heavenly homeland; the bearer of intention, consideration of Gehenna.

183. There are four ways of loving: to love the flesh carnally, the spirit carnally, the flesh spiritually, and the spirit spiritually.

[Col. 1156A] 184. There are three loaves which the friend coming from the road seeks (Luke 11): continence, humility, and charity.

185. Peace is threefold: feigned, as in Judas; disordered, as in Adam and Eve; true, which Christ left to His disciples.

186. There are three kinds of those who pursue peace: the peaceable, who possess their land in peace; the patient, who possess their souls in their patience; and the peacemakers, who make peace between those at variance.

187. Some contemplatives ascend and fall, as those who “became vain in their thoughts”; others are caught up and descend, as where it says, “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God” (2 Cor. 5:13), etc.

188. A square stone consists in loving heavenly things above, despising earthly things below, holding prosperity in contempt at the right, and bearing adversities with equanimity at the left.

[Col. 1155]

## A Certain Just Man’s Dialogue with God; or, of One Drawn from the Body for a Time and Restored to the Body, or Caught Up in Ecstasy and Afterwards Recalled to Himself. (G)

[Col. 1155B] It once seemed to this man—whether in the body or outside the body, God knows—that he had now been granted rest from his labours and the keeping of sabbath with the people of God: to sit at Jesus’ feet and fix his gaze upon the beauty of His countenance; that he had now obtained for ever Mary’s better part, and Rachel’s beauty, never to be torn away from the embraces of the heavenly Bridegroom.

But behold, suddenly the Lord looked down from heaven and saw little children weeping and seeking bread; their mother, widowed of her husband, pouring out tears upon her cheeks, seeking consolation for herself and her children and finding none. And He looked at the man of His own will, exulting nearby in singular joy and seeming no longer to care for the common sorrow. Looking upon him, I say, the Lord—the Father of mercies and God of all consolation, charity that does not seek its own—said: “Your rewards are safe for you, nor will delay diminish them. Have pity rather upon those whom you abandon. Shall your brothers go to battle while you sit here? Shall they stand outside seeking you while you have entered into the joy of your Lord? You must go out to them, rise for the Lord’s battles, and help them.”

The Lord therefore said: “Rise, and depart from here.”

The man: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. Where shall I go from Your presence?”

The Lord: “Depart from here, and return to your sick man—your body—which I entrusted to you to guard and watch over. It is already wasting away.”
