The man: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death? Lord, have mercy. My sick man is burdensome and intolerable: shameless in demanding necessities, and anxious and importunate for superfluous or harmful things.”

The Lord: “See that you care for him, but not according to his desires; for this is expedient for his infirmity.”

The man: “A harsh providence.”

The Lord: “Depart from here. If you take from him anything that is his, you will be compelled to restore it fourfold. Moreover, the children are already crying and asking for bread, and there is no one to break it for them.”

The man: “But when will it be for me?”

The Lord: “For you, afterwards.”

The man: “What, Lord—what? I cannot feed them or care for them unless I give my hand to Egypt and to the Assyrians, that they may be filled with bread.”

The Lord: “The creation was subjected to vanity, not willingly, but on account of Him who subjected it in hope. Yet it shall be delivered from the bondage of corruption into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.”

The man: “Lord, this Assyria not only devours our flesh but strips us to the bone. Not only is the body tortured by weariness: the sword reaches even to my soul.”

The Lord: “If I gave My soul for you, you also ought to lay down your souls for your brothers.”

The man: “And why do You not avenge our blood?”

The Lord: “Then you are a child, who will not cease weeping unless you see the rod with which you have been struck itself struck.”

The man: “I beseech You, Lord, permit me still to speak to my Lord, though I am earth and dust. You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived; You were strong and prevailed” (Jer. 20:7). “For You said to me: ‘Come to Me, all who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you. For My yoke is sweet and My burden light’” (Matt. 11:28, 30). “I believed; therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115:10). I fled willingly and joyfully beneath Your yoke; and behold, with Your permission, they possess me, Lord, apart from You. Crushed beneath their iron yoke, they drive me to their threshing-floor; and the Egyptians force a citizen enrolled in Your city to build cities from mud and brick.”

The Lord: “Be patient until My coming.”

The man: “Until when, Lord?”

The Lord: “Moses and Aaron, go to your burdens” (Exod. 5:4).

And, feeling himself cast out from the presence of so happy a blessedness, just as Moses and Aaron were cast out from Pharaoh’s presence by these words, the man returned to himself and said with a groan: “I said in the ecstasy of my mind: ‘I am cast out from before the sight of Your eyes’” (Ps. 30:23), Lord. “You have changed toward me into one cruel, and in the hardness of Your hand You oppose me” (Job 30:21).

[Col. 1158A] Thus, lamenting that he must return to the burden and heat of the day and again undergo the defilements of mud and brick, he spent what remained of his life in sorrows, awaiting the time when he should be wholly taken up and perfectly brought into the joy of his Lord.

[Col. 1157]

## Soliloquy. (G)

[Note.]

It is not by Saint Bernard. Nevertheless, it was published under his name by Gretser at Ingolstadt in 1617, from the Library of the Carthusians of Erfurt.

[Col. 1157B] **1.** My heart, I beg you, do not be a foolish heart, that is, a broken heart which will not retain all wisdom. Rather, remember your ways, and see how far apart are the ways through which you have walked hitherto and those through which you ought to walk toward God. See how, as far as the east is from the west (Ps. 102:12), these ways are separated from one another. For the way in which you have walked is full of frivolity, idleness, bodily dissipation, and certain vain pleasures; although you know well that one who is soft and undisciplined is brother to one who wastes his works (Prov. 18:9), and that your works truly do not flourish thereby but are rather scattered.

I admit that you sometimes think that you wish to reform your habits; that you wish more and more to resist fleshly desires; that you wish to devote yourself more watchfully to God’s praises; to subject the flesh wholly to the spirit; to flee idleness; to avoid vain and useless things; and to attend more ardently to prayer and meditation. You indeed propose these things, but I see you never, or very rarely, put them into effect. Indeed, even when you begin at some time, you end so miserably that your enemies may rightly say to you: “This man began to build and was not able to finish” (Luke 14:30).

Sometimes, when you ought to give yourself to prayer or meditation, you are weighed down by lethargy, overcome by sleep, or led astray by a superfluous thought. Sometimes you sleep in order that the time of prayer may be spent in desires. And if some strengthening grace ought to be granted you, the sloth of the flesh steals it from you, so that the flesh itself is strengthened while the spirit remains weak. O truly godless and exceedingly harsh cruelty: that the handmaid should voluptuously consume the substance of her mistress while the mistress remains hungry! What remains, then, when battle is imminent, is that the weaker is overcome by the stronger. For what else is it when the body, after time has been spent upon its own comforts, refuses to be content with food, drink, and sleep, and even, by abusing the time of prayer, wishes to deprive the spirit?

**2.** O truly blessed time, worthy of every reverence and discipline: in which all time is gathered up, and, for time uselessly spent, groans and tears are offered; for time usefully spent, praise, honour, and glory are rendered to God! Who can adequately say how great is the usefulness of this time? When pure prayer knocks, as though it were the soul’s messenger, not Paradise now, but the gate of the kingdom of the Son of God, is powerfully opened: what is sought is shown; what is asked is granted.

At this time also, if the soul is blind, it is enlightened; if infirm, it is healed; if poor, enriched; if naked, clothed; if weak, strengthened; if wavering, made steadfast; if doubtful about any matter, made certain; if cold in the love of God, inflamed by the warmth of holy love; if foolish and senseless, it becomes wise and learned beyond all who teach it. At this time also one tastes and sees how sweet the Lord is (Ps. 33:9).

It is also a time of spiritual leisure, which is the refreshment and exercise of all holy labours. For when that for which one labours, though only a little, is sweetly tasted at this time, the fire for labour is kindled as sweetly as it is strongly. What more need be said? This too will be the end of all tribulations and the strength of every virtue. By the merit of perfect prayer at this time all enemies are manfully subdued, so that their power is reduced to nothing. The virtues, moreover, are increased through the grace of the Holy Spirit and most firmly strengthened.

At this time also, those things which must be pruned and cut away in the mind and in one’s conduct are shown, so that they may afterwards be removed through confession. Indeed, then even stained things are cleansed by the water of tears, and superfluities are utterly uprooted by the ploughshare of sacred contrition. Sometimes also, when Jesus sees the cultivator of the vineyard attentive to such labours, He Himself descends into His vineyard and begins to help the labourer: uprooting what is harmful, destroying and dispersing what is superfluous. Then He begins also to exalt the lowly, plant what is useful, water what is dry, build what is necessary; and, as I have said, to illuminate what is dark and bring hidden things into the open. In short, He begins to reform all things so that nothing crooked can be found in that vineyard.

O truly blessed vineyard into which You have descended even once with so great a fullness of graces, O good Jesus! For I shall never call its cultivator unacquainted with inward joys if he has once merited happily to glory in so great a guest—indeed, in so great a fellow-worker. Nor thereafter will he be unlearned who has merited to have such and so great an instructor. What, after all, did He not know whose wisdom is without number? O how much he could learn from Him who was the companion of his labour!

**3.** But when Jesus withdraws, will the vineyard be harvested by the enemy? I say no—provided Jesus withdraws of Himself and has not been driven away by the vineyard’s cultivator. For I believe rather that he who has experienced the so sweet presence of Jesus is kindled with such a fire of love for Him that he does not let Him go without His blessing him, assigning angelic guardians to the vineyard, and promising to return swiftly.

I say also that such a man is ready and diligent in every way by which he may most quickly merit Jesus’ presence. Thus he is watchful in guarding; devout in prayer; strong in patience; humbly prostrate at the feet of all; diligent in subjecting himself to everyone, so that scarcely even the least work passes him by without his being a helper in it. He becomes fervent in charity, serviceable to people, and untiring for Jesus’ love, so that he may rightly and properly be called Jesus’ bride.

O how often, do you think, does he call Jesus back with most holy desires, crying out after Jesus in pure and continual prayer and saying, “Return, my Beloved” (Song 2:17)? Sometimes you will find such most holy desires standing at the doors of the kingdom, knocking and saying, “We wish to see Jesus” (Luke 8:20). Nor is it surprising that they are admitted without delay. For the doorkeeper opens to them, because he knows that Jesus wills this and recognizes them by their frequency.

They enter and advance, adorned with poverty and humility as though with most precious garments. They come to the throne of the Son of God, stand in reverence, and say: “O Lord Jesus, You said: ‘A little while, and you shall not see Me; and again a little while, and you shall see Me.’ But this little while is truly long and burdensome to a soul longing for You. You also said, ‘I go and I come to you.’ When will You come to us? O good Jesus, we have adorned the bed, piled flower upon flower; and what could be prepared by us has been prepared. The bride can no longer endure the delay of Your absence, for she languishes with love and desire to see You.”

O truly blessed messengers, who bear so good a report concerning your lady before the eyes of Him who examines the secrets of hearts! For her reverence, access to such great glory is open to you; you are gratefully received by Jesus and given drink from the torrent of such delight. Afterwards Jesus says to them, “I will come again to you” (John 16:5, 10, 16–19), giving them jewels (*clenodia*, pledges) both to keep for themselves and to carry to the bride.

The bride’s messengers run ahead rejoicing and with wondrous bearing: if you saw them running, you would think them utterly drunk. And truly they are—not with wine, but intoxicated with the abundance of that house. With their cries they stir the entire heavenly court, from the cherubim and seraphim down to the lowest orders of angels. Jesus says to the bride: “[lacuna] Gird yourselves, and be ready, that you may come together to the bride.” They come, filled with astonishment and still suspended in wonder at what they have seen. They begin to tell how graciously they were received, and say, “We have seen wonderful things today” (Luke 5:26)—indeed, wholly ineffable things, at which, as we considered them, reason halted and understanding grew dull.

**4.** And truly, “as we have heard, so we have seen” (Luke 8:18), and more besides. We had heard glorious things spoken concerning the city of God (Ps. 76:3) and its inhabitants; but we saw things far more glorious and praiseworthy in the city to which we had gone. Its walls and streets are of the purest gold; its towers are built with jewels; all its stones are precious; its ramparts are of jasper; it is founded upon sapphires; its gates shine with pearls; and the whole circuit of its wall is of emerald and precious stone.

All its inhabitants are most joyful and glad, because everlasting joy is upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and exultation. There will be neither death, mourning, cry, nor sickness there; nor old age, deceit, or terror from enemies. Rather, there is one voice of those rejoicing and one ardour of hearts—O how secure! For all sit in the beauty of peace, in tents of confidence, and in abundant repose (Isa. 32:18). O abundant—exceedingly abundant—wealth: eternity! Whatever delights is present at a nod; whatever causes sorrow is far away.

There the instruments of the saints sound continually; there the sweet harmony of musicians resounds; there angels and archangels sing a hymn to God before God’s throne. God Himself is there for His people: the garland of exultation and the crown of joy. He Himself is their reward, their shepherd, and their pasture. There they are fed and do not weary of it. Every delight is poured forth for them. He is all sweetness, all freedom; and, to say it briefly, He is all things in all things for them.

O how sweetly the songs of songs resound before Him! Here and there one hears: “Great is the Lord and exceedingly worthy of praise” (Ps. 47:1). In short, there is no place in which a song of joy is not sung; and throughout all its streets, by everyone, are spoken praise, honour, glory, blessing, and every thanksgiving to our God for ages of ages. Amen (Rev. 7:12). These things we have seen and speak—not as things that are like parables, but as things that are true: things which eyes have not seen, ears have not heard, nor have ever entered into human hearts (1 Cor. 2:9; Isa. 64:4).

**5.** While the messengers thus speak sweetly with the bride of the bridegroom’s glory and announce His coming, a certain divine fire arrives, which is accustomed to precede the bridegroom’s face. It illuminates dark things, inflames cold things, restores their former warmth to lukewarm things, and prepares the way to the body by utterly burning up even the slightest rust of sin, if there is any.

Therefore the glorious Bridegroom descends from the lofty throne of His kingdom and hastens humbly to the bride. The Queen of Heaven, the bridegroom’s mother, more praiseworthy than all praise, in a garment embroidered with gold and adorned among virgins with variety like the brightest jewels, deigns to accompany her Son on His journey. Michael the archangel, with a multitude of the heavenly host, meets them in praise and exultation. O how sweetly rings out the melody of those praising the bridegroom and congratulating the bride!

The bride is not unaware. She too goes eagerly to meet the Bridegroom with her companions, singing: “Let my Beloved come into my garden” (Song 5:1). The Bridegroom enters the bride’s chamber; and who can explain with how much glory and grace He enters? O how flowery He finds it, sprinkled with the flowers of good works and holy meditations! This holy soul now dines with her Beloved. O happy banquet, where the Lord of the table is banquet and guest alike, and where the splendid ministries of angels are not lacking!

I leave it to those who have experienced this banquet to speak of it. Who can doubt that the Bridegroom has brought the keys of His treasures, so that He may immediately open for the bride what she most desires, and she, entering confidently without fear, may receive what she wishes, enjoy it as she wishes without lack and without weariness? And what further things He has brought, I am unable to say, and perhaps do not know.

[Col. 1161B] **6.** My heart, you have heard things unexperienced and wholly unknown; but know that the bride now enjoys the longed-for embraces of her Beloved. You have heard all these things, my heart; but you should truly be ashamed, and repent of having let this precious time pass so wholly without profit. How often in the day of battle did the enemies find you weak? The hardness of your coldness did not permit you to flee. And why was this? Because you neglected the time in which you ought to have armed yourself against enemies, been enlightened amid darkness, and been clothed against cold.

What more need be said? You yielded, you were bent down, your gates were destroyed and your bars broken; the enemies entered into you and laid hands upon all your desirable things. Alas, how often, amid the very darkness, was your light no longer merely obscured but wholly extinguished in your tent! For, oppressed by lethargy, you ceased to add wood to wood—that is, good works to good works. And there was fulfilled in you what is said: “Let their light be taken away from the wicked” [read: *impiis*] (Job 38:15), in contrast to that sweet and blessed fire which, once kindled, always longs for more.

How blessed is the one who, after once feeling within himself this fire of Jesus’ love, does not cease to cherish it with continual good works lest it be extinguished; for when these fail, the fire is truly withdrawn. O miserable and despised heart! If you had walked in the way of God’s commandments from the time when you first began, and had not often been deceived by prosperity or broken by adversity, nor listened on the road to the tales of the wicked who detained you, you might have experienced far more of the things you have heard and have become a pathway of the King of angels. You would no longer be a den of thieves. You might already be a vessel worthy of heavenly treasures stored continually within you [perhaps: “stored up”], surrounded and fortified by many thousands of angels.

**7.** But you have been double-minded and inconstant in all your ways (Jas. 1:8); therefore I see you still set amid the ministers of hell. O truly foolish heart of mine! Although you can enjoy heavenly and eternal things in such abundance, you strive so brutishly to be entangled in earthly and passing things, which have occupied your mind during the time of prayer. If the beauty of a transient creature and the deceptive riches of this world occupy you, why does the beauty of the eternal Creator and the glory of the heavenly kingdom, which remains without end, not occupy you instead? It is a certain sign that you do not love your Creator when you prefer love of His creature to love of Him.

If you say that you love both, you lie; for “the friend of this world is made an enemy of God” (Jas. 4:4). Whenever you come to prayer and perhaps bring the ointment of contrition to anoint Jesus’ feet, dead flies that come immediately spoil the sweetness of the ointment (Eccl. 10:1). If you have resolved to do something good and abandon evils, you do not fear in a moment to do what is contrary to these.

**8.** It remains, therefore, that you too should similarly be defrauded of the fulfilment of whatever good things Jesus had proposed to do for you. Indeed, often, when He gave grace, He did nothing other than one who gathered wages and put them into a bag with holes (Hag. 1:6). For just as that man finds nothing in time of need, so Jesus, when He was praised by His lovers for benefits bestowed, received no praise whatever from you. Instead, all His benefits perished with you, deprived of praise and thanksgiving.

Alas, how often during the time of praise could Jesus have said to you: “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matt. 21:13; Luke 19:46); and again, “Take these things away from here, and do not make My Father’s house a house of trade” (John 2:16); and again, “This people honours Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me” (Matt. 15:8; Isa. 29:13; Mark 7:6). How often, then, has that curse come upon you which says, “Cursed is the man who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48:10)!

All these things come upon you because you did not listen to His voice, who said: “I will show you, O man, what is good, or what is required of you: to do judgment and justice, and to walk carefully with your God” (Mic. 6:8). In you I see wholly fulfilled that prophetic saying: “The heart of man is crooked and inscrutable” (Jer. 18:9).

Sometimes, when the Lord Jesus stood at your door knocking and crying that “the time of pruning has come” (Song 2:12), so that you might rise and go to the vineyard with the other brides—or perhaps rise and pray lest you enter into temptation (Matt. 26:41)—you, like a sleeping helmsman, slept in the midst of the sea. And like him whose temples were pierced with a nail (Judg. 4), you had either wholly gone out without doubt, like Dinah (Gen. 34), or, to say more, gone out to arrange worldly business.

O how often, at the time of praise and prayer, you fortified camps and built strongholds for others, while you alone, standing in prayer, could have stormed the camps which princes could not storm with their entire military host! Tell me, I ask you: while you were building camps for others, to whom had you entrusted the keeping of your own camp, already surrounded by the princes of darkness? Certainly the man who said, “I will stand upon my watch and set my foot upon my stronghold, and I will listen to what may be said to me and what I shall answer to him who reproves me” (Hab. 2:1), had not left his own [camp].

Or were you attending to other people’s vineyards, not from zeal of charity but from vain curiosity, wishing to cast the speck from another’s eye while leaving the beam in your own (Luke 6:41; Matt. 7:3)? You returned at some point, but late. Indeed, alas, sometimes you did not know how to return at all to your own vineyard. At last you entered it to work. But what had happened? The enemies had come up, broken down the wall, and harvested the vineyard, so that they had scarcely left a few clusters in it. Briers and thorns had grown over it (Isa. 5:5–6), so that whatever remained from the enemies appeared to be choked by them all.

**9.** You could have avoided all these worst evils had you gone with the Bridegroom to the vineyards. For He did not say, “Go,” but “Let us go.” The others went, and you have heard how great their profit was in going. Thus those brides happily and joyfully, and certainly very fruitfully, awaited the time of grace’s visitation, because they have fruits most pleasing with which to feed the Bridegroom. But what else did He find in you but wild grapes? Certainly, unless you amend yourself, you will tremble as you await the fearful day of the Judge.

I fear that Jesus often says of you: “Would that you were cold or hot; but because you are lukewarm, I will begin to vomit you out” (Rev. 3:15–16). Certainly, because you often pursue idleness, or, if you have read at some time, have done so more to teach others than to correct yourself. O truly a teacher of error, who were never a disciple of truth: why do you teach others and not instruct yourself? O surely an unjust study, in which you prefer to stammer with the tongue rather than preserve in the heart and show in deed! O truly, for this reason you have never attained wisdom!

Hear that your bow must be renewed in your hand (Job 29:20), because Jesus began to do and to teach (Acts 1:1). O my heart, you have heard many of your miseries and have often seen very many of your own evils occur. Yet I fear that He will find more of these things when He searches Jerusalem with lamps (Zeph. 1:12). This is the way through which you have walked hitherto; but I counsel you to go with me to Jesus’ bride and learn wisdom from her, because she walks the way of God. Let us learn this from her by becoming her imitators.

**10.** Let us first consider her active way and imitate it, so that through her merits we may also approach the contemplative way. Let us see how manfully she chastises her body and brings it into slavery (1 Cor. 9:27), compelling it to serve the spirit in all that the spirit desires. O what strength in her actions! Obedient to all and burdensome to none, she always has compassion on the needs of her brothers. She does not consider in what respect anyone is in need or ought to be helped, but in what respect anyone can be helped.

However tireless her hand may be, it is always fruitful in work, first and last. If she cannot apply her hand, she applies at least a finger. If not even a finger, she shows herself wholly prepared, in her very affection, to undertake every task. Therefore she neglects her own concerns in order to fulfil those of others. Indeed, the more things are common, the more she judges them to be her own particular concern. Thus you never see her attending to her own affairs so long as even the least work of charity or mercy remains to be done.

No work is so base, humble, small, or great that she is reluctant to fulfil it for the Bridegroom’s love, always meditating upon this: that Jesus came not to be served but to serve; and also: “Whoever wishes to be greater among you, let him be the servant of you all” (Matt. 20:28, 26). “Who is weak, and she does not suffer with him?” (2 Cor. 11:29). Who is in pain, and she does not grieve with him? Certainly, she weeps with those who weep and rejoices with those who rejoice (Rom. 12:15). She labours likewise and does not grow weary; she endures likewise and does not complain. At times she suffers under a burden and does not perceive it. She is mocked and does not heed it. Truly, she has become to herself like a lost vessel (Ps. 30:13), so as always to hasten forth ready for the needs of all.

**11.** O holy and wondrous charity, which changes bitter into sweet, hard into gentle, and rough into pleasant—how it also delights! O how gracious her appearance, how pleasing her face! Her eyes are chaste and always fixed upon the ground, certainly not curious to see the negligences of others. Indeed, if she saw some great evil in another, her most chaste heart would by no means consent to believe it evil. If the deed could not be excused by the evidence, she would excuse it entirely by the intention. Few, chaste, and holy are always her words.

She meditates on Jesus, speaks of Jesus, and imitates Jesus in deed. O how late, to say nothing of detraction, lies, and shameless words, could you hear a worldly word from her mouth! Her laughter is always modest, her walk humble. She desires nothing other than to please Jesus. In sum, there is such custody of her outward and inward senses that nothing may enter her heart which offends its Possessor.

O how greatly the virtue of patience flourishes in her! For the more she is shaken by tribulations and inconveniences, the more unconquerable she is found. I believe that her patience can in no way be disturbed, not only by words, but not even by blows, outward or inward. She is more pleased to be reproved and corrected than praised. O how peaceable she is! With those who frequently strive to take peace from other hearts, and even from her own, she always keeps peace both in heart and in deed.

We have seen the bride working outwardly in wonderful ways and doing things beyond telling. What will it be if we see her inward parts? Let us pray to the Bridegroom that we may be permitted to enter the bride. What consolations, do you think, will she receive when she, wearied by labours, reaches the time of rest and descends beneath the shade of the tree and cross of Jesus?

**12.** O with what reverence will she occupy herself with the Bridegroom’s praises in His presence, she who outside has pursued Him so ardently in good works! She certainly turns over in her heart what she speaks with her mouth. There she will no longer be divided in half: as she is present in body, so she will be present in heart. All senses are commanded to enter; foreign things are removed; and the chamber is shut, so that, secure and attentive at once, they may apply themselves to Jesus’ praises.

The heart, despising everything else, is directed toward Jesus alone. The tongue praises, propitiates, prays, and invites Jesus. At times all the senses likewise are there, in great reverence and discipline. After the day has been spent in Jesus’ praise and good works, she then draws near to rest; but first comes a time of careful examination.

For the bride enters the chapter-house together with her attendants and asks whether the vineyard has been kept well or badly. If perhaps she finds its wall broken down through the negligence of some guardian, she carefully investigates through whose guardianship the vineyard’s fruit has been ruined. When she finds him—whether sight, taste, hearing, smell, tongue, touch, or step—she sharply reproves or corrects him, commanding him henceforth to be more watchful in guarding it. And if any of them is found negligent in God’s praises or in any other work belonging to him, he too is similarly corrected and ordered to take care in the future.

**13.** Afterwards the bride examines whether there is light, because darkness is imminent; clothing, because of the cold; and help, because of the terrors of night. If all these are not sufficiently present, then, though it be late, she still sends messengers to report their lack in the bride’s tent to the Bridegroom and to pray that, in His accustomed mercy, He may be present as its guardian until, with His aid, she provides for her own necessities in the future.

But if she finds everything ready, she blesses the Bridegroom in His gifts. Having poured out devout prayer for her own protection and that of her household, and having firmly shut all the doors of the chamber, she proceeds into the chamber’s secret places; and what she does there, I do not know. Yet if Jesus deigned it, I would ask that I might be permitted, at least as the bride’s handmaid, to enter the secret places of the chamber with her, that I might be more fully instructed.

But so long as the bride sits—or rather, labours—beneath the shade of the tree, although it is not useful for her to remain there, it will nevertheless protect her from the heat of temptations. But when will she eat its fruit? Perhaps that time now arrives, since she has now entered the chamber’s secret places. It seems altogether necessary: she had laboured diligently for a long time and perhaps was now hungry.

O good Jesus, that I might see her fare! Is her food perhaps to do Your will? It certainly is; indeed, all her labour’s consolation is never to depart even slightly from Your will. For this is the sole reward she desires for her labour: that she may be allowed to love You alone, follow Your footsteps, obey Your commands, and never be separated from You for ever.

O good Jesus, if Your love delights so greatly in the racecourse, how greatly will it delight her in the prize, when You are the joy of all the blessed? We have not yet seen the secrets of the bridal chamber. O who will lead us in, that we may see the flowers with which the chamber of so great a King ought to be adorned? Are not the violets in the bride’s chamber the humble beginnings of Your birth, and the budding lilies the emblems of Your most beloved chastity, and the roses by which that chamber was made rosy the blood of Your most sweet Passion?

**14.** Certainly we have not yet seen the bride’s jewels; but neither are we permitted to see them. O if you enter the bride’s chamber, you will find there a table most worthy: the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ. Upon it is indeed the most holy bread, containing every delight and every sweetness of taste (Wis. 16:2). This bread, which Jesus gave to His disciples at supper—namely, His own little body—was so miserably handled by the hands of the ungodly. Who could regard this bread as worthless to the bride, when even the multitude of blessed spirits feeds upon it?

O truly blessed earth, which brought forth this bread for us! I would gladly praise you, but I do not know with what praises I may extol you. Yet you bore Him in your bosom, whom heaven and earth could not contain. May your name be praiseworthy for ages of ages. Amen.

15. O what a sweet drink you will find before the bride: the blood of Jesus, poured out from his body, so fresh as though it had been shed yesterday or today. Will she be content with bread or drink alone? By no means: she will have other precious dishes—the scourge, the bridegroom’s crown of thorns, nails, and spear; and certainly the little cloths in which he was wrapped as a child, in which he was laid in the manger, will not be lacking to her. On these indeed she feeds; strengthened by these dishes, she is made stronger than all her enemies. Delighted by them, she becomes pleasing to her beloved. Occupied with them always, she becomes a companion of the angels. Nor should they appear to you in any way cheap; rather, know that they are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, and more pleasing than gold and topaz. I would not praise humility in the bride to you; nevertheless, know that it is not absent from her. For unless upon the firm foundation of humility, the spiritual structure of such praiseworthy virtues as you have seen could not stand. Let no one suppose that this bride is ever left by the bridegroom without protection. Rather, let him know that the bed of Jesus is surrounded by sixty valiant men, of the mightiest of Israel (Song 3:7), who will not be silent day or night in praise (Isa. 62:6); or, if you prefer, I shall say that she is encircled by a wall of constancy, built up with the battlements of patience, with an angelic guard upon her walls; and that the tall, strong, and most beautiful tower in the middle of the fortress may rightly be called charity. Upon it the bride remains continually, and sometimes the bridegroom with her, so that, foreseeing dangers from afar, she may more safely avoid them through the bridegroom’s aid.

16. O my heart, I have depicted for you, however inadequately, the bride of Jesus—indeed, according to what God in his sweetness has given to the poor man—urging you in the Lord to imitate her more devoutly. If you do this and diligently sit beneath the shade of the oft-mentioned tree, you too will experience greater things than these. And if you cannot grasp all this at once, I chiefly urge three things upon you. First, shun greatness altogether. Second, humbly follow the humble Jesus. Third, quickly lay hold of charity. Do not fear: you will not sit long—provided that you sit perseveringly—without obtaining the fruit of this tree. Beware lest these words pass vainly over you, like the many words of Jesus himself warning you: namely, that you should love him with your whole soul, with your whole heart, with all your strength (Luke 10:27); that you should renounce all that you possess (Matt. 19:59–61); deny yourself, take up your cross, and humbly follow him (Luke 9:23), so that at last you may become his co-heir (Rom. 8:17). For he says: “Whoever wishes to be first among others, let him be servant and minister of all; just as he came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 20:26–28). These things and many like them you have passed by with a deaf ear until this day, because your love, stretched out toward many things, does not seek at all to embrace Jesus. Indeed, even if it had been directed wholly toward Christ Jesus a thousand times over, it still would not in any way have attained the deserts of his love. And if you have loved Jesus a little, you have not done so with all your strength; for he is to be loved in and above all things. So too you have renounced some things, but not all, so long as your own will retains power within you.

17. O if you considered how many evils your will has caused you! You would surely see that it has been the cause for you of every sin, every misery, every estrangement, and every war between God and you. It always fought against the Lord’s will and, alas, very often prevailed; and with it every evil entered into you. Have you renounced everything, when you have held so firmly the root of everything? No virtue or salvation will send down roots in you until this most corrupt root of sins has been wholly uprooted. Therefore do not be a forgetful hearer; but read the passion of Jesus day and night, and in all your actions imitate the bride of Jesus, taking up your cross and, in imitation of her, running with her in ardent desire strongly after Jesus. Pray, beg, entreat that this ruinous and destructive will of yours may be taken away from you; cry out and say: “May your holy, well-pleasing, and perfect will be done, Lord Jesus, as in heaven” (Matt. 6:10), so also in me, wretched man that I am, dust and ashes—until Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, who is more praiseworthy than all praise, accomplishes all his will in me; so that, as he is one with the Father, he may make me, perfected in himself by the bond of charity, to be one, so that I may never depart from his will through the endless ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1167]

## FORMULA FOR AN HONEST LIFE. (G)

[Note.]

In a Cistercian codex this work occurs under the heading: “Formula for an honest life, given by St Bernard, as is believed.” It is likewise attributed to him in a manuscript codex of the Church of Paris, but wrongly.

1. You ask of me, dearest brother, what I have not yet heard anyone ask of his superior. Nevertheless, because your devotion urgently requests it—and I cannot rightly and reasonably refuse something to one who asks in Christ’s name—I shall sketch for you in brief words a formula for an honest life. If, burning with love or affection for Christ, you persevere in keeping it, you will without doubt obtain eternal life. Therefore, that the discourse may proceed from the inward person to the outward, you must labour unceasingly for the purity of your heart, so that God, the lover of all purity, may deign to establish there his dwelling, as though in heaven, according to the saying: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1), and: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wisdom 7, Old Latin section). You must therefore vigilantly strive always to direct your thoughts toward what is good and honorable, so that you may fear to think or meditate before God what you would rightly blush to say or do in the presence of people. Know that, just as we become known to a human being by words or deeds, so certainly do we become known by our thoughts to the Spirit who searches all things; for thoughts do for God what spoken words do for human beings. “God knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain” (Ps. 93:11). And just as no creature is invisible to him, so absolutely nothing can be thought which escapes him. For the word of God is living and effective, sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of soul and spirit, of joints also and marrow, and discerning the thoughts of the heart (Heb. 4:12).

2. Let Jesus likewise always be in your heart, and let the image of the Crucified never depart from your mind. Let him be your food and drink, your sweetness and consolation, your honey and desire, your reading and meditation, your prayer and contemplation, your life, death, and resurrection. Think of him always: now laid in the manger and wrapped in swaddling-clothes; then presented by his parents in the Temple to the Father; now fleeing into Egypt; there dwelling long in the utmost poverty and need, and returning thence with the greatest hardship; then in the Temple hearing and questioning the teachers—he who teaches human beings knowledge—and afterward subject to his parents, though every creature is rightly subject to him; then hungering and thirsting in the desert—he who is the bread of life and the fountain of wisdom (Ps. 35:10), who feeds among the lilies (Song 2:16), and fills every living creature with blessing (Ps. 144:16); then, weary from the journey, sitting beside the well and speaking alone with a woman, though he governs the state of the entire world; afterward in agony, praying at greater length, though supplying all things sufficiently to all. Consider also him who is the sweetness and consolation of angels and human beings receiving consolation nonetheless from an angel; him who is the support of the whole world bound to a pillar and scourged; him who is the splendor of angels smeared with spittle, struck on the face with palms, crowned with thorns, and sated with reproaches; finally, reckoned among the wicked, hanging and dying for you on the cross, and commending his spirit into the hands of the Father. Thus indeed your beloved will be a bundle of myrrh; thus he will dwell between your breasts (Song 1:12). Gather, then, from all the anxieties and bitter sufferings of your Lord, as it were, a bundle, so that you may prepare for yourself a bitter cup of tears. But if, kindled with most ardent love of Christ, you should wish, with the Apostle, now to know him “not according to the flesh” (2 Cor. 5), raise the eyes of your mind a little toward the victory of his resurrection, the glory of his ascension, and the glorious majesty of his sitting and reigning in the glory of God the Father—having your mind on things above and seeking things above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God (Col. 3:1–2). Yet do not linger there long, lest perhaps, if you search the Majesty too long, you be overwhelmed by glory (Prov. 25:27).

3. Above all, you should know that you must flee every exaltation, vainglory, and arrogance of heart as venomous asps, knowing without doubt that everyone who exalts his heart is unclean before God. Therefore despise no one, harm no one, speak ill of no one, and strive, for Christ’s love, to benefit all. Believe yourself not only from the innermost affection of your heart, but also openly, to be lower and more contemptible than all others; do not say that you have made progress, nor think yourself to be anything, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Whoever thinks himself to be something when he is nothing deceives himself” (Gal. 6:3).

4. Let your manner of walking be full of gravity, sober and honorable: do not walk with affected steps, twist your shoulders to right or left, hold your neck erect, thrust out your breast, or incline your head onto your shoulder. All such things either suggest frivolity, display pride, or savor of hypocrisy. Therefore, walking, standing, and sitting, keep your face always cast down, turning over in your mind that you are dust and shall return to dust; but keep your heart above, where Christ sits at the right hand of God the Father. Look in no direction out of curiosity, but only from necessity. You ought, especially in community, to conceal sadness, presenting a certain cheerfulness of countenance; in private, however, let your expression never change into varying forms. If at some point, before others, you are compelled—as often happens—to laugh for some reason, let your laughter not be uncontrolled. For according to the Wise Man, “The clothing of the body, the laughter of the teeth [or: let your witticisms be toothless], and a person’s gait declare what he is” (Sir. 19:27). Let your joys sometimes interrupt your cares.

5. Never be idle; rather, either read, meditate upon something from the sacred Scriptures, or, better still, ruminate upon the Psalms, while nevertheless continually doing whatever work has been enjoined upon you, so that the devil may always find you occupied. For idleness has taught much wickedness (Sir. 33:29). Read especially willingly those writings that more greatly inflame your understanding toward your Christ. Understand what I say. For the Lord will give you understanding in all things if, in sound judgment, you reflect upon God’s watchful care. When you pray, do not fill the ears of your hearers with sobs and sighs; rather, pray intently to God in the chamber of your heart. Yet it will help toward gaining devotion and compunction if you are so secluded that, lifting pure hands to God, you can hear even your own voice. Sometimes, to raise your attention, look up toward heaven, where your heart is to be—where Christ sits at the right hand of God. From prayer return again to reading; and when reading dispels weariness, return again to prayer.

6. Avoid, as far as you can suitably do so, the company of young men, especially those who are beardless. Never fix your eyes upon anyone’s face.

7. Approach food as you approach the cross: that is, let necessity, never pleasure, feed you; let hunger, not flavor, provoke your appetite. Flee singularity and be content with what is common, knowing that the flesh must be fed and vices extinguished. If something extra is set before you, receive it as divinely provided; but always keep this in mind and will: that it might rather have been set before another.

8. Set a limit to your prudence, lest you seem wise in your own eyes. Always, everywhere, and in all works, fear lest perhaps you exceed in something. Hence blessed Job says: “I was afraid of all my works, knowing that you would not spare the offender” (Job 9:28).

9. When, weary, you have come to bed, arrange yourself most decently in lying down. Do not lie on your back; nor, lifting your knees, join your heels to your shins. But if the parade of lust should shake you, remember your beloved laid upon the bed of suffering, and his whole couch turned in his infirmity; say in your heart: “My Lord hangs upon the gallows, and shall I give myself to pleasure?” Thus, invoking the Savior’s name and often repeating the name of salvation, the agitation will at last cease, with God’s help. Let sleep overtake you while you ruminate upon Psalms, so that in sleep you may dream yourself reciting Psalms.

10. When you rise for vigils, praise your Creator with all your strength, and raise your voice mightily in praise of your Redeemer. Finally, always keep the purest love toward Christ, and remember to love nothing besides him except for his sake. I have described for you at greater length than I expected things that I myself cannot do, desiring them to be fulfilled in you, though I recognize that they are lacking in me; for your progress is my joy and crown in the Lord.

## USEFUL ADMONITION ON THE CONSIDERATION OF DEATH

Whenever you are afflicted by weariness, place yourself in meditation beside the stone upon which bodies are washed, and carefully consider how those to be buried are handled: now they are turned onto their back, now onto their face. How the head nods, the arms fall, the legs stiffen, the shins lie prone; how they are clothed, sewn up, and carried out for burial; how they are laid in the tomb, covered with dust, devoured by worms, and consumed like a rotten sack. Let continual meditation on death be your highest philosophy. Carry it with you wherever you are and wherever you go, and you will never sin.

[Note: At Col. 1169D, read “onto the back.” Edition.]

## BRIEF AND MOST USEFUL ADMONITIONS

In all your thoughts, words, and actions, say to yourself: “Would you act thus if you knew with certainty that this was the final hour of your life?” Take care, servant of God, lest you seem to condemn those whom you do not wish to imitate. [Note: At Col. 1171D, read “whom you do not refuse.” Edition.] It is uncertain in what place death awaits you; therefore await it in every place. Know yourself, and preserve the time which the mercy of your Creator has granted you for doing penance and meriting glory. Be a cheerful giver, a rare petitioner, and a modest receiver. Let your speech be timely, or later [variant: late], or absent; your look either dutiful, or lowered and held within itself. “Let your eye be in your head” (Eccl. 2:14). Let your laughter either indicate gentleness of spirit or invite it, yet be rare. Let it indeed be elicited sometimes, but never poured out. Be so modest that you are not suspected of frivolity. Be kind to all, flattering to none, intimate with few, fair toward everyone—which may God grant us. Amen.

[Col. 1171]

## INSTRUCTION ON HOW A PERSON MAY MAKE PROGRESS IN GOODNESS AND PLEASE GOD. (G)

First, let him strive, as far as he can, to regard himself as utterly worthless and unworthy of God’s favor. Let him displease himself. Let him desire to please God alone. Let him wish to be regarded by others as lowly and not humble; and, since he is lowly of himself, let him recognize God’s mercy in deigning to take into his service so worthless a person—one almost ready for every evil and slow for every good—and, what is greater, to adopt him as a son. Therefore do not regard it as a great thing that you serve God; rather, regard it as the greatest thing that he deigns to take you into his service.

Second, let him grieve over nothing except sin, what leads into sin, and what draws away from good; indeed, let him rejoice in every tribulation, injury, and affliction. Let him love his enemies most earnestly and offer special prayer for them. Then let him render abundant praises to God on account of this, recognizing himself unable to give sufficient thanks for so great a benefit; for whom God loves, he reproves and scourges. Tribulations themselves compel us to go to God.

Third, let him seek or desire nothing from temporal things except strictly for his need, and let him strive to conform himself to Christ the Lord in every deprivation of bodily consolation. He should regard it as the greatest thing that Christ, King of kings and Lord of lords, does not disdain to clothe so lowly a servant in his own adornments and to liken foul mud to himself. Therefore, the richer he sees himself to be and the more he abounds in bodily comforts, the more deeply and inwardly he ought to grieve, seeing himself thereby further removed from Christ’s likeness.

Fourth, in matters that are indifferent, whether good or bad, let him strive to fulfill another’s will rather than his own. Indeed, let him always strive to deny himself in outward acts, desiring what pleases others and, with all vigilance, performing every permitted thing. Let him strive to observe this toward all, but especially toward his superiors.

Fifth, let him despise no one, however miserable; rather, let him be moved toward all with maternal affection, so that he may sympathize inwardly with everyone as a mother would sympathize with her only child. Let him regard all their miseries as his own, and, if he can, assist them as he would himself. He should also revere all poor persons as patrons, because they are those who receive others into eternal dwellings.

Sixth, let him judge no one for sin, since he does not know what divine mercy is doing in that person’s soul. But if by clear signs he should infer that someone is a sinner, let him first grieve over that person’s sin as if death threatened his own body. Let him reflect that a soul so mortally wounded is more precious than all the bodies of the whole universe considered by themselves. And just as I ought to preserve my own body from death, so—indeed far more—I ought with all diligence to protect my neighbor and draw him back from sin by prayer, exhortation, and example.

Seventh, let him love his neighbor’s good as his own. And as a mother rejoices in the good qualities of her children, so he ought to rejoice in the good of all, especially in what is spiritual and leads to spiritual things. Let him procure others’ good as his own, and strive to advance it when procured. Let him always believe more good of his neighbor than he himself can see.

Eighth, let him love nothing but God, so that in all things God alone may be sincerely loved without a companion. Let no degree of another person’s holiness, nor the immensity of benefits, entice him to love anyone with a special love; rather, let him refer all persons to God by a love for all, that is, by charity. Otherwise, let him love the better person more. Yet he may repay benefits with benefits and offer prayers to God in return for them.

Ninth, whatever affairs a person may be involved in, let him strive to keep God in mindful remembrance in his heart, and always place God’s honor before everything. But especially let him endeavour always to understand God as present, as though he saw him who is present in his essence. Thus let him fear and reverence him, be carried toward him with intense love, enjoy him as far as possible on the way, and rest in him rather than in another.

Tenth, if he can attain the things mentioned above, let him recognize them as God’s benefits. He should also remember other benefits as he is able: first, that God marked him with his own image; second, that God assumed his nature and deigned to die for him; third, that he gives himself as food and will give himself in the future as a reward. And because he has not yet attained him as reward, let him nevertheless behold him on the way upon the gallows, and sympathize with him as though he himself bore all Christ’s wounds in his own body. Above all, he ought to grieve because he sees so many deprived of this immense benefit.

[Col. 1173]

## VARIOUS BRIEF INSTRUCTIONS FOR LIVING PIOUSLY OR RELIGIOUSLY. (G)

1. If you wish fully to attain what you intend, two things are necessary for you. First, withdraw yourself from all transient and earthly things, so that you care for them as little as though they did not exist. Second, give yourself to God in such a way that you say or do nothing except what you firmly believe pleases God.

You will attain the first in this way. By every means you can, make yourself lowly, regarding yourself as nothing; believe all people to be good, better than you, and more pleasing to God. Whatever you hear or see in religious persons, suppose it to be said or done with a good intention, even if it appears contrary; for human suspicion is easily deceived. Displease no one. Never say anything about yourself that carries praise, however intimate the person to whom you are speaking may be; rather, labour more to conceal virtues than vices. Speak maliciously of no one whatsoever, however true or manifest the matter may be, except in confession, and then only where you cannot otherwise reveal your sin. More willingly lend your ear when someone is praised than when someone is blamed. When you speak, let your words be few, true, weighty, and about God. If a secular person speaks with you and proposes idle matters, cut off the conversation as quickly as you can and turn yourself to matters of God. Whatever happens to you or to another person, however closely connected to you, do not concern yourself; if it is adverse, do not grieve; if prosperous, do not rejoice. Rather, regard the whole as nothing and praise God. Take the greatest care you can to attend diligently to lowliness. Flee places of conversation as far as you can, for it is better to be silent than to speak. After Compline do not speak until the following day’s Mass has ended, unless some very serious reason intervenes. When you see something displeasing to you, see whether it is in yourself and cut it off; when you see something pleasing to you, see whether it is in yourself and keep it; if it is not, acquire it. Thus all things will be a mirror to you. Do not complain about anything with anyone unless you believe it will be beneficial, however grievous what you endure may be. Never obstinately affirm or deny anything; let your affirmations and denials be seasoned with the salt of doubt. Always abstain from loud laughter; laugh rarely, and offer your mouth only to a few. In short, conduct yourself in all your speech so that matters which are uncertain remain uncertain.

2. You will attain the second in this way. Attend to prayers with great devotion, strive to say them at the proper hours, and remember in your heart what you offer in prayer. And, to confirm what you read, reflect on it diligently and picture the condition of those in whose commemoration you have said these things. Always keep these three things in mind: what you were, what you are, and what you will be. What you were: foul-smelling semen; what you are: a vessel of excrement; what you will be: food for worms. Likewise picture the punishments of those in hell: that they will never end, and for how slight a pleasure they suffer such great evils. Likewise picture the glory of paradise: that it will never end, how briefly and swiftly it is won, and how great the grief and pain of those will be who have lost so great a glory for a small thing. When you have something displeasing to you, or fear having it, think that if you were in hell you would have that and whatever you did not want. When you have something pleasing to you, or wish to have it, think that if you were in paradise you would have that and whatever you wanted. But if you were in hell, you would have neither that nor anything you wanted. Whenever it is the feast of a saint, consider how great the things were that the saint endured for God’s sake, because they were brief; and what things the saint attained, because they are eternal. Likewise consider that the torments of the good pass away, as do the joys of the wicked. The former, through these torments, attained eternal glory; the latter, through unlawful pleasures, eternal punishment. Whenever sloth overcomes you, take this writing and picture all these things carefully. Consider the time that you thus lose, for which those in hell would give the whole world, if they had it. When you have tribulations, consider that those in paradise lack them. Likewise, when you have consolations, consider that those in hell lack them. Every day when you go to bed, carefully examine what you thought and said during the day, and how usefully you dispensed the time and space given for acquiring eternal life. If you passed it well, praise God; if badly or negligently, grieve, and do not delay confession until the next day. If you thought, said, or did anything that severely gnaws at your conscience, do not eat before you have confessed. I place this at the end: picture two cities—one full of every torment, which is hell; the other full of every consolation, which is paradise. To one of them you must run. See what can draw you toward evil or hinder you from good. I believe you will find nothing. I am certain that if you keep well what is written here, the Holy Spirit will dwell in you and perfectly teach you to do all things. Therefore keep these things well and neglect nothing. Read them twice in the week, namely on Wednesday and Saturday; and insofar as you find that you have done what is written, praise God, who is gracious and merciful unto ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1175]

## ARNULF, MONK OF BOERIES: MIRROR OF MONKS

R. P. Tissier identified the author in the *Bibliotheca Patrum Cisterciensium*, vol. VI. (G)

1. Whoever, touched by the desire for a more reformed life, diligently examines his thoughts, words, and works and strives to correct all his transgressions, should contemplate, in the frequent reading and continual meditation of this page, as in a mirror, the face of his inward person.

First, then, from the time he rises for vigils, the monk ought to calculate the span of his life moment by moment, always taking care to do good and avoid evil in every action, and say to himself: “If you were about to die now, would you do this?”

At psalmody, let him have his heart present, unless perhaps he is carried away to something more sublime. Yet he should certainly know himself bound to say in his own choir, or hear in another, every single thing said there, down to one letter.

During the interval he ought to stand for prayer or provide for bodily necessity, yet in going let him know how to say to himself: “Lift up your hearts.” It is, however, a loss to the spiritual purpose if infirmity compels the former strictness to be relaxed somewhat.

After reading one should pray; and if one comes to read, let him seek not so much knowledge as savor. Sacred Scripture is Jacob’s well, from which are drawn the waters poured out in prayer. Nor must one always go to the oratory, for during reading itself one can contemplate and pray.

If he is a priest, let him stand at the sacred altars wholly present in spirit, like one of the highest angels. If he is a minister, let him minister to the Lord as an angel.

Let him go with the others to work, where he should consider not what he is doing but for what purpose he has come. If the hand ceases, let the spirit work through prayer or meditation, although he is bound to do the same even during the work itself.

At table, let not only the throat receive food, but let the ears also drink in God’s word. For the whole person ought not to eat; rather, let the heart be so occupied with God’s word that only the throat takes food and the ears take the word. Let him greatly rejoice, moreover, if food more inferior than that of others is set before him. For those are truly happier who have been stronger in enduring scantiness.

In giving thanks, let him know that he must pray for two things: either for the sins of those by whose alms he is sustained, or perhaps for himself, because he has indulged his body beyond necessity.

If he is called to conversation, according to the Rule (Rule of St Benedict, ch. 7), let him speak gently and without laughter, in few and reasonable words; before he brings words to his tongue, let them come twice to the file. If he must speak with a secular person, let him then especially set a guard upon his mouth, so as to utter nothing that does not edify the hearer.

Let him conduct himself in all things so as to edify those who see him; and let no one doubt, when he sees or hears him, that he is truly a monk.

After Compline, every day let him hold chapter with himself; and, having summoned his thoughts, let him carefully render account of whatever he has sinned that day in thought, word, or work, publicly or privately. Washing his bed each night—that is, having carefully cleansed each individual sin with tears and sorrow—let him make account of each; on the following day he is to make public confession of open sins, but secret confession of hidden ones.

2. For confession to be perfect, it must have three qualities: it must be voluntary, naked, and pure. Voluntary: that is, from one’s own deliberation and purpose. Naked: that one confess one’s sin plainly as one committed it. Pure: that one not proclaim one’s sin like Sodom, but rather weep and accuse oneself with a simple intention.

In chapter, whoever has offended publicly should reveal it openly, as one standing before the judge. In all things let him speak, promise, or make complaint there in such a way that his speech, inwardly and outwardly, is anointed with the oil of charity.

Let him accept no gift from anyone whatsoever.

Let him have no intimate friend.

In all things let him flee the appearance of singularity or of being remarkable.

When speaking, let him say nothing by which he might be considered especially learned or especially religious.

Let him answer questions briefly. If Scripture or morals are under discussion, let him offer his ear, not his tongue.

When he speaks, let him not cultivate eloquence; rather, let his speech be rustic rather than polished.

In everything he does, let him not strive to appear courtly.

Without compromising propriety, let him avoid all persons in authority, especially secular persons.

Let him pursue common observances, work, labour, reading, and the rest, in which he may not be like Ephraim’s heifer, “trained to love threshing” (Hos. 10:11): that is, let him be drawn to such things not by habit but by devotion.

Let him put first the prayers that are prescribed; and let him not flatter himself about his private prayers, which he should rank second when he has been negligent in the prayers commanded him.

But if intimacy with men is forbidden, how much more is intimacy with women?

Let his outward appearance be common with the others, but inwardly different: that is, let it be governed by a sound moderation, neither constricted by excessive severity nor dissipated by excessive speech. Thus it is written of St Martin: “Sorrow did not raise his face, nor did laughter smooth it.” For it belongs to a prudent soul, carefully guarding its treasure, after Moses’ manner, to veil its horned face, and by a certain smile—yet a modest one—to conceal the glory of the inward person and the gravity of the mind.

Let the day at hand be compared with the preceding day, so that by comparing them a monk may perceive either his progress or his decline.

In every act and thought let him remember that God is present to him; and let him reckon as lost every time in which he does not think of God.

When afflicted by weariness, let him place himself in meditation upon the stone where the dead are washed, and consider how those to be buried are handled there: now turned on their back, now on their face; how the head nods, arms fall, legs stiffen, and shins lie prone; how they are clothed and sewn up, carried away for burial, placed in the tomb, covered with dust, devoured by worms, and consumed like a rotten sack.

The highest philosophy is continual meditation on death. Let him carry it with him wherever he goes, and he will never sin. Let the monk be like Melchizedek, without father, without mother, without genealogy; let him call no one his father upon earth. Indeed, let him regard himself as though he and God alone existed.

Behold, in the first place we have the order and manner of life; the remedy, however, is promised by the constant holding of the spiritual chapter described above. Let him confess at least once a week, that he may obtain pardon for sins committed and be given greater grace for avoiding evils. Amen.

[Col. 1177]

## ALSO, OTHER INSTRUCTIONS FOR THE RELIGIOUS LIFE  
*(Otherwise: Teaching of Blessed Bernard.)* (G)*

When it is time to rise for vigils, the mind must be prepared for devotion, so that you may leap fervently from bed and, shaking off torpor, give thanks to divine mercy for the rest granted to you and for angelic guarding and protection.

Then, when you come to church, place your hand upon the door and say: “Wait here, evil thoughts, intentions and affections of the heart, and appetites of the flesh. But you, my soul, enter into the joy of the Lord your God, that you may see the Lord’s will and visit his temple.” And when you come before the cross, say: “We adore you, O Christ, and bless you,” etc.

Then, whenever you recite a verse in your choir, say silently the verse recited in the other choir; and season every verse at least with some spice, namely some spiritual meditation, because your mind is delicate and its foods ought to be choice.

And do not fix your eyes farther ahead than the height of your body reaches; for this greatly hinders the wanderings of the mind. There depict, as it were, the Lord lying stretched out before you upon the cross; and sigh now for the nails, now for the thorns, now for the spittle, now for the piercing of his side, and give thanks.

When it is time to leave choir, say to the Lord: “I still have, Lord, private praises and blessings to say to you; these, as I now leave the public worship, I shall sing and chant to you in my glory.”

When the time for Mass has come, welcome one inviting you to private Masses as though you saw the bread of angels descending for you from heaven.

[Col. 1178C] If you see anyone wishing to keep you away, flee as though he were trying to snatch a morsel of bread from the mouth of one dying of hunger.

When you come to chapter, carefully take up the armour of God: the helmet of foresight, the breastplate of patience, and the shield of meekness, by which you may repel either just or unjust reprimands. If you have sinned, say only: “I shall amend.” If not, say: “I do not remember.” Let neither more nor less than this be extracted from you, whether by shouting or by blows.

As you approach the judgment of chapter, think of God and the Prior as Pilate and the Pharisees crying out against him, and the soldiers beating him without cause. Think of the harsh chapter endured by the holy martyrs, when they stood before kings and governors with their *pertinentiae*, that is, [Col. 1178D] with the punishments and torments which they suffered. Think of your future chapter at death before God, when thousands of demons will cry out against you, and ten times a hundred thousand against you; so that, if anything rather severe is done to you here, it may be made lighter by considering them. Think that he who reproves you is God’s razor, and wishes to remove your unsightly hairs so that you may become beautiful. Think that correction is a *pitantia*—a special allowance—sent from heaven.

Whoever reproves you, reward him that same day with whatever service you can, because he wished to free you from the ugliness of sin.

When you come to work, so moderate the task to be done that concern for the work does not turn your mind’s attention away from the things of God.

When it is time to rest, do not seek out corners [Col. 1179A] or sit apart from the others; rather, let your eyes be upon the faithful of the land, that they may sit with you; and sit down yourself in the midst of the teachers. A certain brother, while the rest among us were resting, sat alone at a distance and began to be pressed by a most grievous stirring of the flesh; and he heard a voice saying to him: “Go to the camp.” When he came where the others were, the stirring ceased.

When you come to the meal, enter neither first nor last. If you cannot eat what is set before you, do not permit it to be changed altogether; instead, take even a little, so that you may appear to have eaten. If anyone presses you to eat, answer only by this sign: “It is good; it is much; it is done.” Think that herring, fish, and other necessities are procured for you through the labour of many and the countless dangers faced by seafarers, so that the desires of your flesh [Col. 1179B] may be satisfied; and give thanks with every morsel. Meanwhile, think that Christ crucified is awaiting your thanks, or that a poor person is waiting at the gate for your leftovers.

Do not impose abstinence upon yourself at all by your own decision; instead, eat daily according to measure.

If a nocturnal illusion befalls you, do not be distressed; but confess it the next day. If someone invites you to Mass to serve, cautiously excuse yourself before everyone by the customary sign, so that all may understand that pollution of yours. Someone among us did this even when no one had invited him to Masses, so that he might be more ashamed; and he was freed from the temptation of the flesh, so completely that afterward he scarcely experienced anything of the kind, and suffered such an itch only once or twice a year. [Col. 1179C] From this it is clear how true is God’s saying: “Those who glorify me I will glorify” (1 Sam. 2:30); and: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 4:11; 18:14; and Matt. 23:12); and: “He gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6; 1 Pet. 5:5; and Prov. 3:34).

When it is time to read, turn your face toward the church; with the book set before you, employ your private dialogue. Wherever God’s benefits occur, say: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115:12). “How much you owe, my soul!” Then, turning to the angels, say: “Come, hear, and I shall relate, all you who fear God, how great things he has done for my soul” (Ps. 65:16); and, turning your eyes toward him, say: “Truly, [Col. 1179D] Lord, your mercy is great toward me” (Ps. 85:13). But if, while you thus earnestly seek him with your heart and knock at the gate of paradise, some evil thought makes a disturbance, immediately put before it and say: “Whose image and inscription is this?” (Matt. 22:20). And, hearing that it is Caesar’s—that is, the ruler of this world, namely the devil—say: “May your money be with you unto perdition” (Acts 8:20). The door is now shut, and the Lord is eating the Passover here; I have no leisure to open to you. But if the evil thought still remains, set the sign of the cross against it.

A certain nun among us held the sign of the cross in such veneration that, when she was being carried out to burial, the face of the crucified figure turned after her on the side by which she was carried out; and thus the head of the image, [Col. 1180A] directed toward that side, remained permanently so, contrary to its usual position. Another revealed to someone that her hands had decayed, but that the thumb with which she had been accustomed to make the sign of the cross upon herself could not decay.

Beware lest, by touching someone or by consent, you do—or allow to be done to you—something for which you must be ashamed.

Neither avoid nor seek private conversations; nevertheless, think of them as wild apples.

When you see someone diligent in prayer, reading, silence, patience, obedience, and the like, give thanks to God because he has sent you a mirror; and do not envy him.

When you see someone troubled, give thanks that that cloud has not passed over you, and say: “What would that temptation have done to me, if God had permitted it?” Do not judge [Col. 1180B] another’s imperfection, nor dig through the wall of his conscience.

When you come to ask something of the Prior, always prepare yourself for refusal. If what you request happens to be denied you, say within yourself: “What befits a little ass except bridle and goad? I can claim as my own in this house nothing except a hair-shirt at death and a cross in the grave: this is my inheritance—provided only that a small clod of earth covers the cross.” Keep this in mind when you go to bed.

And when you see the blanket and covering, compare the bed with a tomb, and enter it as one about to be buried. If you can sleep, it is well; if you cannot, experience shows that, if you strive by reflection, you will sleep.

Above all, hide such practices of yours, and conceal from others, as far as possible, your holy meditations; and in all things show yourself diligent in service to everyone.

[Col. 1180C] Especially value the gains of others in public and private services. Moreover, be ready to obey with a cheerful mind and countenance.

Think of that monk named Gerard, who, despairing beyond measure of God’s mercy, fell mortally ill and lay for three days with closed eyes in an ecstasy of mind. When visited by the abbot, he opened his eyes and said: “Obedience is good. I was before Christ’s tribunal; I saw the souls of the saints, and I saw him himself face to face, saying to me: ‘Behold your place among your brethren. None of your Order shall perish if he loves the Order: either he shall be purified at death, or shortly after death. But those of your Order who are saved shall receive a lot in the order of the apostles, martyrs, or confessors.’” Having said this, he received Communion and died.

Learn to apply some remedy against everything that rises up against you.

803 When you are weighed down by sluggishness, think that today you are able to work; tomorrow perhaps you will not be able.

When you are assailed by lust, think of eternal fire.

If disobedience holds you fast, think that unwillingness to submit is as the crime of idolatry.

If impatience vexes you, think what Christ endured for you.

When pride tempts you, think of those better than yourself; when an evil will assails you, think how a person is condemned for a trifling matter when he is rejected for will alone, without the deed being carried out.

When vanity assails you, think of the many things you have not done; and the more you are now hidden, the more gloriously you will become known at the judgment.

When you rejoice in bodily strength or beauty, recognize how swiftly the slightest fever may take it away.

When the weight of religious life and the constancy of discipline trouble you, think of that saying of blessed Jerome: “No labour should seem hard, no time long, by which the glory of eternity is acquired.”

My dear son, flee before all the wiles of the ancient enemy that thing which I most earnestly warn you to avoid as the noonday demon: from the time [Col. 1181B] when you enter religious life, never admit, cherish, or trust the thought which suggests that it is less useful for you to remain in the religious life you have undertaken, and that in another state or habit you might make greater progress for yourself or others. For if you incline the ear of your heart to fantasies of this kind, they will divide and stretch your mind, so that you cannot retain any seasoning of spiritual savour; and your heart will be like a broken vessel, unable to hold any wisdom. [Col. 1182A] Hence not only weariness but horror and despair of the good work previously undertaken must necessarily come upon you, while your mind is divided among many professions and diverse pursuits.

Accordingly, one of the Fathers says in the *Conferences*: “Fickle and wholly ungrounded minds, when they hear certain persons magnificently praised for diverse virtues and good pursuits, are commonly so inflamed by their praise that they immediately desire to imitate their way of life. But in vain; for from such change and variety of purpose they receive loss, not progress, because one who pursues many things will attain nothing completely. Therefore it is advantageous for each person, according to the purpose he has chosen and the grace he has received, to hasten with the utmost zeal and diligence toward the perfection of the work he has undertaken; to love the praises and admire the virtues of others, yet by no means depart from the vocation he has once chosen. For many roads lead to God; and therefore each person should complete the road once undertaken with an irrevocable purpose in his course, so that he may at least be perfect in some vocation” (Cassian, *Conference* 14, chs. 5–6). But the singular remedy against all evils is remembrance of death.

[Col. 1181]

## EIGHT POINTS FOR ATTAINING PERFECTION. (G)*

[Col. 1181C] 1. If you cultivate these eight points well, you will attain, through the grace of God, the perfection and completion of all virtues.

First: that you frequently confess your sins purely and fully, with great sorrow and a resolve not to commit them again.

Second: that you are not broken by adversity or temptation, but stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation. For there is no place or religious order which permits a person to serve as a soldier and live without conflict. For the whole life of humankind is warfare upon earth; and all who wish to live piously in Christ shall suffer persecution. For, as blessed Gregory testifies, the Lord permits his elect to be torn by slanders, that they may be preserved in humility.

[Col. 1181D] Third: that, as far as you can in a good manner, you do not mingle with people, whether insiders or outsiders; but keep yourself solitary with your bridegroom Christ, flee worldly rumours and vain, secular conversations, which distract the mind, make it restless, and do not permit it to remain at peace.

2. Fourth: at all times you must strive for purity of heart; 804 that is, continually, as though the bodily senses were shut, turn back into yourself, and carefully keep the doors of your heart, as far as possible, closed against sensible forms and images of earthly things. For purity of heart is, among all spiritual exercises, in some manner the final aim and the recompense of all labours, which the veteran soldier of Christ is accustomed to receive in this life; it claims the first place for itself. With every diligence restrain your affection from all things that could impede its freedom, and from every thing capable of binding and holding that affection so that it clings to it, in accordance with the saying of the Mosaic law: “Let each person remain in his own place; let no one go out from the door of his house on the Sabbath day; and the people shall keep Sabbath” (Exod. 12:22).
