For to be within oneself is to gather together and keep gathered the dispersions of one’s heart and its affections toward the one true and most simple good. But to keep Sabbath is for the heart to be free from fleshly affection that defiles it and worldly cares [Col. 1182D] that distract it, and sweetly to rest in the peace of its own heart, as in a harbour of silence, in love and enjoyment of the Creator.

Yet above all else, let your chief effort always be to keep your mind lifted upward in contemplation of divine things, so that your mind may continually be directed to divine things and to God. Whatever differs from these, although it may appear more conspicuous—such as bodily mortification, fasting, vigils, and similar exercises of virtue—must be judged secondary and inferior, useful only insofar as it advances purity of heart. Hence very few now attain true perfection, [Col. 1183A] because they expend time and strength upon intermediate things that are not very profitable, neglecting and postponing the necessary remedies. But since you desire to arrive at the intended end, you must yearn unceasingly, by practice, for perpetual purity of heart and tranquillity of mind, and keep your heart continually raised to the Lord. Nevertheless, no mortal can remain continually attached to this contemplation. It has been said so that you may know where to keep the intention of your mind fixed and toward what goal always to recall the gaze of your soul. Whenever the mind can attain it, let it rejoice; whenever it finds itself distracted and separated from that gaze, let it grieve and sigh. If, in a complaining voice, you should object that you cannot remain long in the same state, you ought to know [Col. 1183B] that divine power can do more than a human being can conceive, and that repetition of an act commonly generates a corresponding habit. Thus it often happens that what perhaps a person initially undertook with a certain force and difficulty, he will afterward do easily, and finally with great delight—provided that he does not give up.

3. Hear, my son, the discipline of my father. Attend carefully to these words, and write them in your heart as though in a book. Do not emulate the multitude who have already turned back after the desires of their own hearts: in them devotion has grown lukewarm, charity has cooled, humility fails, and obedience has been cast down. They desire to please people, seek honours, and serve their bellies; [Col. 1183C] loving gifts beyond measure, they pursue recompense. In this world they receive as the reward of their work the very thing they seek, and in the future they will remain empty. But look to those excellent flowers, the most holy Fathers, who burned with an incomparable zeal for holiness; hasten to embrace their purpose, by an equivalent zeal and manner of life, as has already been set before you. Therefore, whether you eat or drink or do anything else, let this voice of a loving father always resound in your ears, exhorting and saying: “My son, return to your heart. Withdraw yourself, as far as possible, from all things; always preserve the eye of your mind in purity and tranquillity, guarding the understanding against the forms of frail things; wholly free the affection of your will from earthly cares, always clinging with ardent love to the highest good. Keep your memory also continually lifted upward, striving heavenward through contemplation of divine things, [Col. 1183D] so that your whole soul, gathered into God with all its powers and capacities, may become one spirit with him, in whom the highest perfection of life is known to consist.” 805 Let this brief rule of your life, then, be handed down to you. If you diligently study it and faithfully wish to put it into effect, you will be blessed and will in some sense begin eternal happiness in this frail body. This, my son, is the way of salvation which your Arsenius, instructed by an angel, observed and commanded his disciples to observe: “Flee, be silent, be at rest.” These, I say, are the beginnings of salvation. [Col. 1184A] These are eternal wisdom to the disciple. Then it is immediately added: “For the spiritual person, the fountain and origin of all good is to remain continually in the cell.”

4. Fifth: that you neither grieve, rejoice, nor anxiously concern yourself over your friends and relatives; but entrust them to God, and render them spiritual assistance, namely the aid of your prayers. Reckon yourself crucified to the world and the world to you; stretch out toward inward things, as though deprived of all friends.

Sixth: that you are fervent in prayers and holy meditations, and do not grow lukewarm from the purpose with which you came to religious life or from the first fervour of your novitiate. For a slack person, if he begins something, acts somewhat vigorously at the start; then he proceeds by diminishing, because many begin and few finish. Yet perseverance alone will be crowned; it alone will receive the prize. No virtue exists without labour, and great rewards are not reached except through great labours. For the kingdom of heaven is seized not by the idle, slack, or self-indulgent, but by the forceful, who inflict noble force not upon others but upon their own wills. For those who are soft and fluid in their habits descend to the depths like rushing water. But those who are steadfast, firm, and fervent grow daily toward the citadel of virtue. Fools are pleased by nothing for long: they desire what they do not have and disdain what they have. Therefore be constant, and do not be moved by the examples of the lukewarm to imitate them. [Col. 1184C] Do not involve yourself in what is not observed by others under the strictness of the Order; rather, see that you walk without offence before your fellow brethren, correcting them more by example than by words, so that everything belonging to the Order may be sound and whole in your own person. Therefore do not be severe toward others; do not rebuke or reprimand others sharply or harshly. For fraternal correction has no place where amendment is not hoped for; and sound comes to the ears in vain unless God speaks in the heart, because God alone turns the hearts of the children of men.

Fraternal correction ought to be performed with great moderation, with groaning and goodwill, in its proper place and time, always preceded by prayer. Therefore, if some have not fulfilled all that belongs to the Order, provided that you are a good and discerning imitator, do not judge the deeds of others. Do not be disturbed if you see some less discerning, others ignorant, others untaught, others negligent in the Hours, or infected with any vices whatsoever. Close your eyes, as far as you can, to investigating the actions of others. Certainly, do not seem to condemn those whom you do not wish to imitate, for there is great danger in judging others, and such suspicions are often false. They also diminish the affection and charity that a person has for a neighbour. [Col. 1185A] You must take great care that anyone’s charity toward you or anyone else is not corrupted or even diminished, because no plunder or loss is greater than the removal or diminution of charity. For all things, however useful or necessary they may seem, must nevertheless be despised in order to avoid disturbance; and all things that are adverse, or thought adverse, must be endured in order to preserve the tranquillity of peace and love. For nothing should be thought more destructive than anger, nor anything more useful than charity, nor anything more precious than tranquillity of mind. For their sake not only bodily and transient comforts, but even spiritual ones, seem to be despised, if they cannot otherwise be acquired or perfected.

5. Seventh: that you be silent and not talkative; wherever you are, speak or answer gently and slowly, with a subdued voice, calm countenance, and disciplined manners, speaking few and reasonable words. Let words come twice to the file rather than once to the tongue. [Col. 1185B] Love hearing more than being heard, so that questioning may open your mouth more often than answering things not asked. Do not rely on your own prudence or trust your own perceptions, and do not 806 be wise in your own eyes. Do not seek things higher than yourself, nor investigate things stronger than yourself; but show yourself discerning, modest, and orderly in all things. For nothing immoderate, unstable, confused, or disordered has ever pleased God; but the Spirit of the Lord rests upon the humble and quiet.

6. Eighth and last: never be idle, for every idle person lives amid desires. Therefore love knowledge of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh. Let your mind not lie vacant for various disturbances, which, if they settle in your breast, will rule you and lead you into the gravest sin. Therefore always either read, pray, or meditate upon something sacred. For idleness has taught many evils: it is the death of the soul, the burial of a living person, and the sink of all evils. Assign its proper exercises to each hour and day: spiritual exercises to spiritual matters, bodily exercises to bodily matters. In all things guard yourself against sin and your neighbour against scandal. As soon as you feel yourself pricked by vainglory or any temptation, resist its beginnings; and be prompt in doing whatever you understand, whether from another’s admonition or divine prompting, must be done. Learn to preside over and govern yourself, not others. Order your own life, compose your habits, judge yourself, accuse and condemn yourself before yourself, and leave no transgression unpunished. Be hard toward yourself, never toward others. In the morning exact an account from yourself of the night that has passed, and prescribe caution for the coming day. In the evening demand an account of the day that has passed, and make provision for the approaching night. Consider how much progress you make and how much of the journey still remains: for a great road remains for you before the God of gods is seen in Zion. But when you have exercised yourself in these eight things already set forth, advancing from virtue to virtue, be on guard against the devil’s snares, lest he lead you away from them.

[Col. 1185]

## LETTER OF A CERTAIN PERSON ON THE INSTRUCTION FOR CONDUCTING ONE’S LIFE, OR ON THE GOVERNMENT OF HEART, SPEECH, AND DEED. (G)*

[Col. 1185C] 1. Your devout and frequent importuning presses me to comply with your requests, which seek instruction for the life to be lived, or what is expedient for a traveller—that is, what should be diligently thought in the heart, what should more fittingly be uttered, and what may more honourably be brought into action. This is a very lofty matter, though a common one. It has many inquirers, few who arrive, and far fewer who search it out thoroughly. But, as I seem to understand, I shall set forth something for your condemnation or mercy, and that of the other readers—though sufficient neither to your request nor to my intention as I would wish. Our heart can accomplish nothing more worthy than to restore itself to him by whom it was made; and this the Lord requires of us, saying: “My son, give me your heart” (Prov. 23:26). The human heart is given to God when every thought [Col. 1185D] ends in him, turns and bends about him, and wishes to possess absolutely nothing besides him. Thus, with the mind bound to him, it loves him, so that every love without him is bitter. Nor would I say that giving one’s heart to the Lord is anything other than taking it captive into every service of him and subjecting it wholly to his will, so that it wills nothing except what it knows him to will. Therefore a heart given to the Lord will worship him in all things [Col. 1186C] and for all things, and will give thanks even if many things seem burdensome to our senses. It will admit no disturbance from the novelty of events. When tested by the Lord through tribulations and harsh conditions, it will not be moved. When in want—that is, poor—it will rejoice. Whatever is brought upon it, even if it feels harsh, it will accept as impelling it toward heavenly things. Whoever has given his heart to God will sing melodiously and say with the prophet David: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready; I shall sing and chant in my glory” (Ps. 56:8). There is indeed a first and a second glory: the first, of virtue; the second, of blessedness; one on the journey, the other in the homeland. Therefore all who have given their hearts to God are made a proof and sign in that they sing, and chant in the glory of virtues amid tribulations, [Col. 1186D] pressures and straits, hunger and thirst, nakedness and humiliation, curses, reproaches and mockery, scourges, and even impending death; in their hearts they rejoice the more. They do not take back for themselves authority over that which they have given to the Lord. No crime of sacrilege is found worse than taking back authority over a will once offered to God. Those who have consecrated their hearts to God ought not to live for themselves, [Col. 1187A] but for him who gave his life for all. Nothing worthier can be thought than to refer one’s heart to him who chose to die so that you might live. For the righteous person also gave his heart to watch early for the Lord who made him (Ecclus. 39:6). The righteous watchfulness and thought of the heart are to meditate continually on what it has received in the goods of nature, in the goods of grace, and in God’s Son made human, suffering, dead, and buried for us; on what it has received in promise; from what evil it has been delivered; what it renders to the Lord for all that he has rendered to it; what we love, what we fear, what we do; by what impulse of nature we proceed, by what free will, and by what guidance of grace given to us.

2. There is also a threefold direction of our heart according to the teaching of Scripture. The first is total conversion to God, as the Lord requires of his people through the prophet, saying: “Return to me with your whole heart” (Joel 2:12). For that person is converted to God with his whole heart who first turns away with his whole heart from every evil of corruptible things. No one can be converted to God with his whole heart unless he has first turned away from the whole world. Indeed, earthly entanglements do not allow a person to turn to God with an undivided mind. The total conversion of our heart to God is estrangement from the world and from oneself; it is being borne toward God by virtue and resting in him through an unseen, inward, and withdrawn peace of mind. One converted to God with his whole heart delights in him; if he could receive anything further that is delightful, he does not seek it. He considers it an irreparable loss if for an hour he turns the inward invisible sight away from him; and, by turning aside to another, he has committed apostasy.

3. The second is total confession, as the Psalm declares: “I shall confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart.” This confession, moreover, in the lowliness it receives from you, casts down the misery contracted by sinning; it knows nothing for itself except to attribute every evil to itself, while it refers all praise, thanks, and blessing to God, and ascribes to him, from whom all good things proceed, every good thing. Whoever knows how to make this confession, becoming vile in his own eyes, finds nothing in himself over which to rejoice, but only something over which to mourn and grieve, because he is guilty of death. He rejoices only in him from whom he has received what he possesses; nor does he glory in himself, [Col. 1187D] but in God. Such a person remains one and undivided in prosperity and adversity: prosperity does not exalt him, nor adversity break him. The mind of one who confesses to God with his whole heart is not changed, but blesses the Lord at all times; and, without being blinded by an emotion of the heart, he confesses Christ the Lord, beyond even what is common to human beings, in life, conduct, and speech—abhorring what Christ abhorred and embracing what he deigned to embrace. The third direction of our heart is perfected love: that we love God with our whole heart. But that love will not be perfect if human hearts are touched by any uncertainty.

4. Why, then, was this so expressly commanded in this life if it is not fulfilled on the way as in the homeland? Yet it is best to consider the height of the virtues. Although they are often handed down under precept or counsel, no one has been able to touch their summit except him who, God and man, chose to be born, live among people, and die. For virtue has always remained above the attainable capacity of every saint, and the ascent toward it is always open until one comes into the homeland. Thus, although we cannot possess this direction of the heart—that is, total love—in its entirety, we should nevertheless practise it at once, turning away from every vice. Even though unable to aim at every perfection, the Saviour says: “He who has my commandments and keeps them, he is the one who loves me” (John 14:21). The lover of God is the enemy of the world, because the friend of the world is the enemy of God. An enemy [Col. 1188B] receives no joys in his heart from an enemy except when he sees him oppressed, or when, having become stronger, he can send him into exile or kill him. This image shows by what covenant one is bound to the world. A lover in this manner, with a perfect heart, does not savour lofty things but consents to the humble; occupied with God himself, he will have no leisure for human judgments. He will not devise evil against the upright, contend, or envy those who possess human prosperity. The cleansing to be practised in relation to our speech is that nothing irrelevant be uttered from it, and that moderation be maintained in matters which necessity itself compels us to say; for Wisdom says: “He who moderates his lips is most prudent” (Prov. 10:19). Nothing is more fitting for it than one’s own accusations, prayers, praises, [Col. 1188C] and blessings to the Creator of all; and humble, modest, and exhortative speech should be directed toward one’s neighbour, not in contention or disputation of words, not presumptuously, but with all meekness of spirit and sweetness of tongue. Yet it is safer to hear than to speak, to be taught than to teach. Sometimes a flattering demon lies hidden in uttering speeches from which the detestable pursuit of reputation and the breeze of vanity are often sought; and the Holy Spirit frightens us, because “a man of the tongue shall not be directed upon the earth” (Ps. 139:12). If anyone, beyond necessity and clear usefulness, addresses listeners even about good things, let the finger of prudence always be upon his mouth, lest he belch forth undisciplined words; and let him be joined with David in this virtue, who said: “I said: I shall guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I set a guard upon my mouth when the sinner stood against me” (Ps. 38:1–2).

5. Honourable human actions proceed only from an honourable heart, aided by divine grace and through the law of Christ. Such are: a sincere guarding of all the senses, so that nothing shameful may slip through them into the soul; and ordered manners, lest they become conspicuous through singularity of life, but may be such as befit a servant of Christ who wishes to seek heavenly, not earthly, things. Let one’s intercourse be not importunate, but infrequent, according to personal or common necessity; not burdensome, nor marked by hypocritical signs, excluding every doubleness and indirectness; subject to one’s neighbour in all things except sin. Take delight in yourself: do not think highly of yourself in anything. Be humble and gentle under the burden of poverty, by which Christ’s servants must properly be assailed daily. Sustain your life from labour and sweat. But where infirmity exists and impossibility prevents it, do not be ashamed to seek a humble livelihood. For through a livelihood gained humbly the needy person is aided, heavenly merits are acquired, and one is formed for the saints. Frequently wash yourself in the saving Sacraments, and refresh your soul with these and the divine [Col. 1190A] words. Endeavour to live as you desire to be found at the last judgment. I write no more to you. Exercise your soul in these few things. Seek no further from me or from others things that are curious and not beneficial to you. What I know to be useful to you, I have written; and if you asked anything else of me, I usefully refused it, unwilling to entangle your soul in great matters, but in small and few ones. As far as you can, nurture your children in God, and pray for me. May patience, which is expedient for you, always be with you. Amen.

> **[Note:** [Col. 1189A] Another letter of similar subject, “On the Care and Management of Household Affairs,” is also attributed to St Bernard. It begins: “Bernard, grown old, sends greetings to Raymond, gracious and fortunate knight, lord of the castle of Amboise. You ask us to instruct you concerning the care and management of household affairs,” etc., as in Jean Picard. [Col. 1190A] But this letter is as unworthy of new publication as it is of Bernard as author. Whether it is by Bernardus Silvestris, whose unprinted metrical work is entitled *Megacosmus et Microcosmus* and dedicated to “the most famous doctor Gerricus,” let others determine.**]**

[Col. 1189]

## LITTLE TREATISE ON THESE WORDS: “FOR WHAT HAVE YOU COME?” (G)*

**[NOTE.]**

809 Gerardus Vossius, provost of Tongeren, first published it at Rome in 1594 under this title: “A Little Treatise Ascribed to St Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux.” Those who first attributed it to Bernard may perhaps have been prompted by the fact that he repeatedly used the phrase, “For what have you come?”, as appears from Book I of the *Life*, chapter 4. But, with a few alterations, it is found in the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. XIII of the Cologne edition, among the works of David of Augsburg of the Order of Friars Minor, under the title “Rule for Novices,” preceded by a dedicatory letter to Berthold.

### I.—On Reflecting upon One’s Aim and End.

[Col. 1189B]

First, you must consider why you have come, or for what purpose you have come. Why have you come, except solely for God, that he might be your reward in eternal life? For just as you came for no other, so for no other should you neglect what is good or grow lukewarm through anyone’s example, rather than striving toward that for which you came. For you came to serve God, whom every creature ought to serve. First, because no one has anything except from him; and therefore every human being, as rational, owes him above all the gift of what he is and what he can do. And just as all things serve the Creator according to their power, much more should man do so—man whom God not only created, as he created other things, but moreover endowed with understanding, ennobled with free choice, made lord of the world, [Col. 1189C] made in his own likeness, whose nature he assumed; whom he instructed by word and example, redeemed from eternal death by his own blood, filled with the Holy Spirit, gave his flesh to as food, cares for as a mother cares for her little child, and has resolved to give an eternal inheritance. See, then, how greatly we are bound to serve him above other creatures, since he loved us above all creatures of the world.

## II.—On obedience

And because you do not trust yourself sufficiently to presume that you know what the Lord wills, you have entrusted yourself to your superior, so that he may govern you; and in confession you have given him your hand, so that he may lead you in the way of God. Hence you will not be permitted to live according to your own will; rather, where your guide [Col. 1189D] commands you to go, there you must go; and what he forbids, you must avoid. For one who desires to learn any craft [Col. 1190B] must observe the rule of his instructor and abandon personal inventions. Just as a sick person suffering an attack or exacerbation must keep the diet prescribed by the physician if he wishes to be healed quickly, so you too should say or do nothing which you presume your master does not wish.

For you gave yourself to him for the kingdom of heaven; therefore you are not your own, but his. You sold yourself to him, and therefore you may not dispose of yourself without his will. For he is the master of your will, and taking possession of another’s property against the owner’s will is theft. But a thief does not draw near to heaven. Those rulers themselves, because they are the Lord’s vicars over us, are to be obeyed as the Lord, not as men; for we submit to them not for their sake but for God’s. Therefore the servant is not greater than his master (Matt. [Col. 1190C] 10:24; John 13:16 and 15:20). Show yourself, then, such toward him that he may freely command you to do or leave undone whatever seems expedient to him. For if he fears you, the servant has already become greater than his master, and the disciple above his teacher.

## III.—On reverence toward prelates

Maintain peace with your prelates. Do not speak ill of them, nor willingly listen to others speaking ill of them; for God especially punishes this fault in subjects, even in the present life. Do not weigh their failings harshly, but forgive them as human beings; for amid many concerns negligence cannot sometimes be avoided, and often what another does for good, because we do not understand his intention, we judge to be evil. Honor them in [Col. 1190D] your heart, and do not despise them, lest perhaps you despise God also, whose place they hold. For your own benefit [Col. 1191A] and that of your soul, observe their ordinances and constitutions, and do not disdain what they do not without reason, even though you do not know the reason. Such matters do not harm one who walks simply in the way of God, but benefit him and become an occasion of greater merit.

A true servant of God ought to walk in the royal way and in God’s commandments in such fashion that human statutes do not constrain him in anything; for he ought to constrain himself, so that, even if that statute did not exist, he would nevertheless guard himself from everything that is not expedient. For by such statutes the excesses of those who transgress the boundaries [810] of discipline are restrained. Having set forth these matters concerning obedience, which are the beginning of good religious life, I pass to other matters: first bodily exercises, then spiritual ones in consequence; for “not that which is spiritual is first, but [Col. 1191B] that which is natural; afterward that which is spiritual.”

## IV.—On offering God the first fruits of the day and of one’s thoughts

Accustom yourself, as is fitting, to wake a little before Matins, so that your spirit may be directed to the Lord in prayer, and afterward you may be more sober and devout in God’s service and praises. Upon waking, immediately drive away every thought and dream with which the devil wished to occupy you; and offer to God the first fruits of your thoughts in prayer, with heart uplifted or knee bent, until you conceive some feeling of devotion and your spirit grows warm. Then throughout the whole day you will be more devout and fervent.

## V.—On reverence and attention in the divine office

In the divine office do not be sluggish or listless; [Col. 1191C] rather compel both your body and your spirit. Psalm the Lord reverently and cheerfully before the angels, who stand there present. Detest laughter and useless words where you ought to stand with fear and reverence before the eyes of supreme majesty. Pronounce the words of the psalmody distinctly and completely. Do not willingly wander about the choir, nor leave before the end of the Hours unless great necessity compels and forces you. Strive to arrive before the office begins, so that you may stir yourself to some devotion. For this is why we are so indolent in the office: we have not been stirred beforehand; and thus we leave cold and distracted, as we entered.

Therefore strive, at the very beginning, to cast away varied thoughts and attend to what is sung; otherwise you will scarcely be able later to escape their tumult. [Col. 1191D] After the office, strive to preserve the devotion you have conceived, and do not immediately pour yourself out upon empty matters. But if you have no inward devotion, at least preserve outward discipline and gravity of conduct, for reverence toward God and as an example to the other brethren and neighbors.

## VI.—On accusing oneself and others in chapter

In chapter, do not speak much unless it is very useful; and say even this in the same manner. When corrected, answer gently, and do not excuse yourself when you are reproved, like Adam, who cast his blame upon God and the woman, saying: “The woman whom you gave me deceived me” (Gen. 3:12). If you are asked for counsel, freely and humbly answer what seems expedient to you. [Col. 1192A] If your counsel is neither sought nor received, do not concern yourself about it, nor wish stubbornly to defend your opinion. Let it suffice you to satisfy your conscience.

Do not be anxious in accusations. Nevertheless, say what has been done against the Rule and the statutes of the Order, without hatred toward anyone, and with gentle words and a placid expression. You are not bound to speak about what you do not know. Do not accuse on the basis of conjecture, for conjecture often deceives. Let the person who told you what you do not know say it himself, if it is true. But if he is not present, you cannot prove it either, since you have no witness.

Do not burden yourself over accusations made against you. Say only your fault, if it is true; or, if slight, even if it is not true. Otherwise, greater shame will arise for you if you excuse yourself defiantly than if you confess humbly. But if the charges [Col. 1192B] were serious and untrue, especially such as might scandalize others, then, having humbly requested leave to speak, state to them in few and gentle words that you are not conscious of the matters of which you are accused. A servant of God ought not to fear shame before human beings where conscience does not accuse before God; rather, he ought patiently to endure whatever the Lord wills him to endure.

## VII.—On carefully observing good institutions

Accustom yourself, wherever you are corrected by superiors, whether in chapter or elsewhere, immediately to kneel and humbly acknowledge your fault. This is a law of ancient religious life handed down by the ancient [811] Fathers. Therefore you ought to strive to hand on to your successors, as far as lies within you, in word and example, the order handed down to you by your elders [Col. 1192C]. Do not introduce or teach any bad custom; nor, through negligence or the devil’s carelessness, omit any good one, whether in yourself or in others whom you can exhort with moderation. For whoever leaves any example to others, whether good or bad, will share in the reward or punishment of those who imitate him.

## VIII.—On maintaining rule and moderation at table

At table let your eyes not rove, nor look here and there, so as to see who sits beside you, what he is doing, or what stands before him. You ought to attend to yourself alone and to God. Eat with discipline, silence, and fear, not in the rush [Col. 1192D] of gluttony, as though you could not be satisfied. Do not throw your whole self upon food like a hungry dog, nor seek first to satisfy your eyes before your palate. Let what is present suffice you with thanksgiving; and at table always prefer to suffer want rather than to abound.

Despise none of the things set before you, nor be indignant if there is some deficiency in seasoning, salt, or cooking. Rather, consider that many better than you are content with fewer and poorer things, and would receive as great delicacies whatever you reject. It is difficult to give a fixed rule concerning the measure of eating, unless you observe the mean between these two extremes: do not take so little that you lose strength and are broken by labor; nor so much that after food you cannot pray, read, meditate, or be swift for all [Col. 1193A] works of virtue. Between these two, personal experience will be the better teacher.

## IX.—On pursuing poverty

Let poverty, the friend of Christ, please you in all things, and embrace it with utmost effort—in food, clothing, utensils, books, buildings, in everything. Observe how humble are the bearing of the poor, how simple their answer, how fearful their disposition. Let no complaint ever be heard from you about any lack in food or drink, or about cheap clothing. Always consider yourself unworthy of what you possess. For outward deficiency grows into an increase of inward grace and into the riches of a good conscience; whereas outward abundance produces inward poverty.

## X.—On the manner of lying down or sleeping

[Col. 1193B]

In the dormitory be quiet, and let no one be disturbed through you. Whenever you awake, let the remembrance of God immediately occur to you with thanksgiving, because he watches over us when we sleep, in order to guard us. When you wish to sleep, you should first give yourself to prayer or meditation, and thus fall asleep in this occupation. Your sleep will be sweeter and more useful; you will dream, and even wake, more fervent in the same devotion; you will rise more cheerfully and return more easily to the devotion in which you were previously engaged.

Although sleeping persons do not seem accountable for what they unknowingly do or suffer, it is nevertheless very unbecoming for a religious person to be wholly overwhelmed by sleep [Col. 1193C] like a beast, lying with arms stretched out and other limbs disorderly contracted beneath the breast. We lie clothed and girded precisely so that we may not have the freedom to move our hands this way and that upon the naked body, and may be more ready for prayer or for rising. Discretion is necessary in these matters: by it you chastise the body prudently, lest the flesh rebel against the spirit; and nourish the spirit wisely, lest it fail under the burden and, through excessive weakness, impede spiritual progress.

## XI.—On lowly work and service at Mass

Be ready for common labors and humble duties, in church and kitchen; and offer yourself especially for those services which others despise or shrink from because of their lowliness: carrying wood, [Col. 1193D] cleaning the house, shaking out tunics, and washing feet. Serve willingly at Mass, since this is the office of angels. For they serve and minister most devoutly to the Lord.

This ministry bears a threefold fruit. First, it is the exercise of a good work. Second, it is a work of charity, because it encourages one’s neighbor in good. Third, it is a work of devotion: when you stand before the table of the highest King, speak with him in prayer, and minister with the angels, with whom you will become more familiar through this ministry. Consequently, the priest in particular and all present generally ought to pray for you [812]; indeed, the whole Church everywhere throughout the world ought to pray for you, because you perform the role of all those who ought, if they could [Col. 1194A] be present, to minister fervently to their Lord from heaven with most devout thanksgiving.

And it can scarcely be otherwise than that God rewards in the present life with some special grace one who devoutly and willingly ministers at that most saving Sacrament, than which nothing can be better or holier in heaven or on earth, and which is in some fashion the chief indication of divine condescension and love toward humankind. What less does God do by coming daily upon the altar than when, descending from heaven, he assumed human form? Therefore he left in himself a memorial of all his love: of the Incarnation, Redemption, and Glorification.

It is wholesome for the person who diligently seeks to make himself fit for this, through every devotion, pursuit of virtue, and guard over himself—not only from grave sins but also from carelessness in words, deeds, and thoughts—to communicate often. Although at every time [Col. 1194B] we ought to be attentive to spiritual works, it is especially fitting that we prepare ourselves for receiving so great a Sacrament and reverently preserve it once received.

## XII.—On properly establishing confession

Confess your sins often, at least twice or three times in every week; and state your fault simply, as to a single angel who knew the secrets of your heart. Add no veil of excuse or mitigation, nor confess obscurely so that your confessor cannot understand what you mean. Specify what you have done, and confess nakedly and purely. Do not recount stories and deeds of others; rather, briefly and purely state whatever transgressions you remember from the time when you most recently confessed. [Col. 1194C] Do not weave an elaborate account of some long, affirmative general confession, because it produces weariness in the confessor. You may make such a confession daily to the Lord in your prayer.

Set before him your faults as you perceive them in the individual virtues, and it is very profitable to seek from him a remedy of mercy for these. For confession is of little value unless you resolve henceforth to guard yourself against the things you confess and strive to amend yourself.

## XIII.—On love of the cell and renunciation of one’s own will

Be willingly in your cell, and do there some good work that builds up your heart or mind, or which has been enjoined upon you by your superior. You should be so ready for obedience that, if every hour you were left [Col. 1194D] to your own judgment as to what you should do, you would more willingly and with an even mind accept service under the command of obedience, and not be your own master. Thus, even if you had free choice, you would neither speak without permission nor go to attend to any personal necessity. So, we read, the holy fathers lived in Egypt; if we desire to attain their glory, let us imitate their virtues.

## XIV.—On reading Scripture and devout books

Apply yourself often to the divine utterance of sacred Scripture. This should be your first foundation and also the way that leads to life. Read the lives and teaching of the saints, so that you may be instructed by their good works and deeds, humbled, kindled to devotion, or stirred to zeal; so that you may be formed in understanding of the Scriptures and illumined in faith, [Col. 1195A] knowing how to distinguish truth from falsehood, good from evil, vice from virtue; and may find remedies for temptations and reformation of morals. Do not read so as to be called a teacher, nor from curiosity. Do not read books that do not edify, such as poets’ fictions; for new reading generates new thoughts and extinguishes devotion of mind.

## XV.—On not seeking preeminence or the office of teaching

Do not seek a prelate’s office or any office whatsoever; and however worthy you may be, do not presume great things concerning yourself. Rather, strive always to lower and humble yourself to the ground. Yet if you are worthy, the Lord will call you even if you resist. For “no one takes the honor to himself, but he who is called by God, as [Col. 1195B] Aaron was” (Heb. 5:4). If you are inadequate and unworthy, great shame will be yours.

Why is it that we sometimes obtain little fruit from our preaching or confessions? Because we come without being called by God, and run without being sent. We wish to bear fruit in others before we have fixed roots in the earth of charity and truth. Therefore the fruit is not lasting, because it does not proceed from a root of charity. Hence it is said in Leviticus: “When you have entered the land and planted fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins; the fruits they produce shall be unclean to you, and you shall not eat of them. But in the fourth [813] year all their fruit shall be sanctified, praiseworthy to the Lord. And in the fifth year you shall eat the fruit, gathering the fruits which they produce” [Col. 1195C] (Lev. 19:23–25).

The tree planted in the ground is the person taken from the world and planted in religious life, who should bring forth fruits of salvation in himself and in others at the appropriate time. If he produces untimely fruits, they will be regarded as unclean and useless for spiritual fruit because of presumption. The first year is true penitence for past sins. The second year is a perfect turning to a state of amendment. The third year is practice in a good manner of life. The fourth year is despising praise and human honors, seeking glory for God alone and the salvation of souls. But whoever thrusts himself forward before this year so as to bring forth fruit in souls will be neither acceptable to God nor meritorious for himself, because of his [Col. 1195D] frivolity, nor profitable to others.

After this year, however—that is, in the fifth year—they will eat the fruits of pure charity and gather fruit; for then preaching will be fruitful and meritorious for them, so that they may gather fruit unto eternal life. Strive first to shape yourself inwardly in good habits and to order yourself in holy affections and thoughts; then proceed to teach others. It is unsound teaching when one presumes to teach someone before he has learned.

## XVI.—On continual self-discipline, because God and the angels behold us everywhere

Never consider yourself secure, even when hidden, from the obligation to conduct yourself with discipline and chastity in everything—in sight, hearing, touch, taste, and smell—as though you were seen by a friend. [Col. 1196A] Know that the holy angels are with us, and always and everywhere see all that we do; we ought to fear their gaze and reverence their presence. God himself also sees us, our Lord and Judge; our own conscience sees us as well, the witness to what we do, and it accuses us.

But one who fears human eyes more than God, the angels, and his own conscience is not a chaste lover of good but a seeker of temporal honor. Such a person is not a true servant of God, since he still desires more to please human beings than God. For those whom you fear displeasing more are also those whom you seek more to please. “No one can serve two masters” (Matt. 6:24; Luke 16:13).

## XVII.—On shamefastness and modesty

[Col. 1196B]

Among the brethren show yourself shamefast, gracious, modest, affable, gentle, and rather strict, so that you preserve discipline without becoming burdensome to anyone by severity. Never indulge in loose jokes, utter secular words anywhere, or willingly listen to them; for what delights you to hear, you would, if you dared, also willingly say. A servant of God should be so chaste in all words and deeds that he abhors not merely indecent speech, but also things which suggest anything shameful, even if they are cloaked in some appearance of propriety.

All your gestures, speech, habits, looks, and manner of walking ought to be adorned with a certain humble shamefastness. Let nothing lofty or pompous appear in you, nor anything notable for boldness or presumption. For shamefastness is [Col. 1196C] the greatest ornament of a religious person, especially of the young; so much so that there is scarcely any hope that those who set it aside will become good and virtuous. As fear of the Lord composes human beings and inwardly orders all things toward blessedness, so shamefastness outwardly orders them toward discipline.

Let no one be so intimate with you that before him you entirely forget shamefastness. Let your gait be measured: do not run lightly without necessity; do not hold your face raised, but moderately lowered; do not let your eyes wander; do not swing your arms excessively; and do not walk, after the manner of secular people, with disordered stride, but with a level and humble bearing. When sitting, do not lazily lean to one side, nor stretch your legs far out, especially when others are present. For outward disorder of the body is an indication of an undevout mind. [Col. 1196D] Let your laughter be restrained and infrequent, without loud guffaws. For the Lord desires goodness rather than dissipation. Strive to have a serene countenance, not a troubled or angry one, for this vice greatly displeases God.

## XVIII.—On circumspect speech and avoiding detraction

Let your words be gentle; your answer humble, without the sting of bitterness, indirect reproof, or mockery. So frame your words when you speak of anyone else as though you saw that person listening and standing near. Let no one fear that in his absence you will tarnish his reputation in any respect. It is a great fault in a religious person to say something evil of [Col. 1197A] an absent person which he would be ashamed to say [814] if that person heard it. Do not willingly listen to detraction against anyone; either flee the detractor or restrain him if you can.

It profits nothing to hear detractions. Therefore, if you can, choose some praiseworthy person who may edify you and the other hearers by his words rather than harm you by detraction. Know nothing of rumors, because they disturb the heart, distract the mind, exhaust devotion, and consume time without benefit. Nor should you pour out everything you know like a vessel without a lid, which, as soon as it is tilted, pours out whatever it contains. Do not willingly remain in a crowd unless God and matters that edify the soul are being discussed. Do not be loud in speaking or impetuous in venting what you keep within.

Take care, however, that just as you speak ill of no one, [Col. 1197B] so you do not betray a detractor to the person against whom he has spoken, lest you burden the detractor more heavily and sow discord through yourself. It may be that the one who spoke of another did not intend to disparage him, though the other perhaps suspects this, is stirred to hatred against him, and is provoked to revenge. Or perhaps the speaker said it simply, without intent to detract; or perhaps he immediately repented and resolved henceforth to guard himself from similar things.

But if such things were said about someone that it would entirely be expedient for him to know what was said, you may, if you wish, tell him what is said without identifying the speaker, so that he may know what he ought to avoid and may not burn with hatred against the detractor.

## XIX.—On avoiding boastfulness

[Col. 1197C]

Avoid boastfulness most diligently. Never take pains to know what good qualities are in you; nor should you disclose to anyone anything praiseworthy in yourself; nor wish vainly to glory in yourself because there may be something praiseworthy in you of which others are unaware, even though you are silent and conceal it. If you reveal and praise yourself, you will be mocked and despised; and those who were formerly edified by you will afterward look down upon you. For all praise grows foul in one’s own mouth.

Curses and insults, trivial and frivolous lies, every oath, and every shameful word, even if spoken in jest, must be banished from a religious person’s mouth by perpetual anathema. The apostle James says: “If anyone thinks himself religious, yet does not restrain his tongue but deceives his own heart, that person’s religion is vain” (Jas. 1:26).

## XX.—On avoiding joking words

[Col. 1197D]

Joking words must be avoided everywhere. Though their sin is not grave, continual habit produces harm to the soul. For often, while we relax the tongue, as though with permission or unnoticed, into idle words and do not pay attention, we gradually slip into harmful things, from which arise detractions, murmurings, dissipation, and grave wounds of conscience.

## XXI.—On the practice of hearing devout and useful things

Willingly listen to talk about God, and speak of him likewise yourself; for such speech stirs pursuit of virtue and the affection of devotion. Humbly hear words from those who speak, and do not argue against them. There are some [Col. 1198A] who, upon hearing something good, immediately wish to dispute about it so that they may not seem ignorant of the good proposed by another, but may appear also to know something about it. They seek not edification but display; and therefore many good things are more often left unsaid because of such people.

## XXII.—On avoiding contention

Do not be contentious. Quickly believe when what another proposes is good and true. It is not your role to resist for the sake of display when it is good and true. But if it is not good, you will persuade him of the truth better by demonstrating it peacefully and calmly than by rebuking sharply.

## XXIII.—On the manner of religious persons’ speech and care for time

[Col. 1198B]

When you speak, speak in a subdued voice and with a calm countenance. Strive to be disciplined and peaceful in conduct, and whatever you then say will be more authoritative and useful. Do not be bold before elders, but modest, listening to their teaching. It belongs to elders to teach, but to the young humbly to listen.

Do not sit idle, attending to rumors and tales, for two principal evils arise from this. You waste time uselessly, and thus suffer loss, since on the last day you will have to render account of it to God; every moment granted to you will be demanded of you on the day of judgment. The other evil is that you do not provide others with a good example in this matter, and for that too you will render account.

## XXIV.—On the mirror of all virtues set before us, namely the life of Christ

[Col. 1198C]

In every virtue and good habit, always set before yourself that most excellent mirror of holiness and most perfect example: namely, the life and death of the Son of God and our Lord Jesus Christ, who was sent from heaven for this purpose [815], that he might go before us in the way of virtues, give us in his own example a law of life and discipline, and form us after his own likeness. For just as we were naturally created in the image of God, so let us, according to our ability, be conformed to the likeness of his character—we who have defiled his image by sin. The more each person strives to conform himself to Christ through imitation of virtues, the nearer he will be to him in the heavenly homeland and the more like him in the brightness of glory.

Set down in your heart his manner of life: [Col. 1198D] how humbly he conducted himself among people; how kindly among his disciples; how modestly in eating and drinking; how mercifully toward sinners, to whom he made himself like in all things; how he despised or recoiled from no one, even a leper; how he did not flatter the rich; how he was not anxious over bodily necessities; how shamefast in his gaze, patient under insults, and gentle in his answers. For he did not seek to avenge himself with biting and bitter speech; rather, by a mild and humble answer he healed another’s malice. Likewise, how solicitous he was for the salvation of souls, for whose salvation, though he was God, he deigned to be born and to die. He is blessed above all things for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 1199]

# BOOK ON THE WAY OF LIVING WELL, ADDRESSED TO A SISTER (G)*

[NOTE.]

The following treatise belongs neither to Bernard nor to his sister Humbeline, who was married in the world before professing the monastic life. At no. 65 the author advises his sister “not to despise married women coming from the world into religious life.” He does not appear to have been subject to the Rule of St Benedict. For among the psalms customarily recited at Prime, he mentions the psalm “O God, in thy name,” etc., which followers of the Benedictine Rule do not recite at Prime except during Holy Week. Whoever he may finally have been, he wrote this book in old age, as appears from no. 170. But enough—more than enough—has been said about this rather lengthy treatise, which it seemed fitting to relegate to the end of this volume.

## PREFACE

[Col. 1199A]

Sister most dear to me in Christ, long ago you asked me to write words of holy admonition for you. But since it is written, “It is pride for anyone to wish to teach one better than himself,” I judged myself unworthy for this work, and therefore delayed for some time doing what you asked. But because you asked again and again, I recalled anew the Lord’s saying: “Whoever compels you to go a thousand paces, go with him two thousand; and give to everyone who asks of you” (Matt. 5:41–42). Compelled from every side, at last driven by charity and aided by your prayers, I gathered crumbs from beneath the table of the Fathers; and, if not as I ought, yet as I could, I offer them in this book to your holiness.

Now then, dearest sister, [Col. 1199B] receive this book, place it before your eyes as a mirror, and contemplate it every hour as though it were a mirror. For God’s commandments are mirrors in which souls examine themselves, recognize whatever stains of ugliness they possess—for no one is clean from sin—and correct the faults of their thoughts, composing their radiant faces as though from a restored image. For while they attend with their whole mind to the Lord’s commandments, they undoubtedly discern in them what pleases or displeases the heavenly Bridegroom in themselves.

Therefore, venerable sister, read this book willingly, and read it again and again. In it you will learn how to love God and neighbor; how to despise all earthly and transitory things; how to desire eternal and heavenly things; [Col. 1199C] how patiently to endure for Christ the adversities of this world and to despise its prosperity and blandishments; how to give thanks to God in your infirmities and not to be proud in health; how neither to be exalted in prosperity nor broken in adversity.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, let your prudence diligently run through this little book and continually mourn my sins, so that I, who am unworthy to obtain pardon, may at least through your prayers receive forgiveness for my sins. May almighty God keep you safe, defend you from every evil, and lead you, together with all who serve God with you, [Col. 1200A] to eternal life, venerable sister. Amen.

## I.—On faith

1. The Lord says in the Gospel: “All things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9:22). No one can come to eternal blessedness except through faith. Blessed is the one who believes rightly [816], lives well through right belief, and by living well preserves right faith. Hence blessed Isidore says: “Without faith no one can please God. Faith is by no means extorted by force, but is commended by examples and reason. Those from whom it is demanded violently can by no means persevere in it, as the example of a young tree shows: if anyone forcibly bends down its top, when it is released it immediately returns to the position in which it was before.”

“Faith [Col. 1200B] without works is dead” (Jas. 2:17); and one who is not adorned with good works vainly comforts himself concerning faith alone. Whoever carries the cross must die to the world, for to carry the cross is to mortify oneself. To carry the cross and not die is the pretense of hypocrites. Whoever does not doubt in his heart, but believes, will have whatever he asks done for him. Whoever believes in the Son of God has eternal life (John 3:36; 1 John 5:10). But whoever does not believe will not see life; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him. As the body without the soul is dead, so faith without works is dead.

Dearest sister, faith is great, but it is worth nothing without charity. Therefore, venerable sister, preserve right faith within yourself; hold fast sincere faith; guard undefiled faith. Let right faith remain in you; let faith of incorrupt confession be in you. Speak nothing rashly concerning Christ; think nothing false or impious concerning God; entertain no perverse thought; do not offend his love. Be righteous in faith; maintain holy conduct in right faith. Do not deny by works the God whom you invoke by faith. Evil mixed with good contaminates very much; one evil destroys many goods. Do not sin in works when you are perfect in faith. Do not pollute faith by evil living. Do not corrupt the integrity of faith through perverse habits. Do not mix vice with virtues or join evil to good. Beloved sister, may God keep you safe. Amen.

## II.—On hope

[Col. 1201A]

2. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not despair, but have faith in God within yourselves” (Mark 11:22). Hope that is seen is not hope; for what a person sees, why does he hope for it? (Rom. 8:24). But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it through patience. Hence Solomon says: “The expectation of the righteous is joy, but the hope of the wicked shall perish” (Prov. 10:28). Therefore, dearest sister, you too await the Lord and keep His way, and He will exalt you so that you may inherit the kingdom of God. Await the Lord, dearest one, and depart from evil, and He will exalt you on the day of visitation—that is, on the day of your death, or on the day of judgment. Those who do not cease to do evil await God’s mercy in vain; they would rightly await it if they departed from evil.

[Col. 1201B] 817 Hence blessed Isidore says: “We ought to fear lest, through the hope which God promises us, we sin persistently.” Yet neither, because He justly punishes sins, should we despair of God’s mercy; rather, what is better, let us flee both dangers: let us turn aside from evil and hope for pardon from the mercy of God. For every righteous person is sustained by hope and fear: now hope raises him toward joy, now the terror of Gehenna calls him back to fear. For whoever despairs of forgiveness for sin condemns himself more by despair than by sin. Therefore, beloved sister, let your hope be firm in Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, because “mercy shall surround those hoping in the Lord” (Ps. 31:10). Hope firmly in the Lord and do good; dwell in the land, and in the heavenly kingdom you shall be fed upon His riches [Col. 1201C] (Ps. 26:3). Venerable sister, put away injustice and hope in God’s mercy; remove iniquity from yourself and hope for salvation. Correct yourself and hope in God’s clemency. Drive perversity from yourself and hope for pardon; amend your life and hope for eternal life. May He who chose you before the ages deign to lead you to it. Amen.

## III.—On the Grace of God

3. The Apostle Paul says: “Where sin abounded, grace also abounded exceedingly, so that, as sin reigned unto death, so grace also might reign through forgiveness unto eternal life. For the wages of sin are death, but the grace of God is eternal life” (Rom. 5:20–21). “But grace has been given to each one of you according to the measure” [Col. 1201D] “of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4:7; 1 Cor. 12:10; Rom. 12:3, 6). Dearest sister, as blessed Isidore says, human progress is God’s gift. Therefore, if we make progress by God’s gift, we must praise not ourselves but God for good works. Nor can anyone be corrected by himself, except by God. A person possesses no good as his own; his way is not his own, as the prophet testifies when he says: “I know, O Lord, that a man’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man, as he walks, to direct his steps” (Jer. 10:23). And when someone receives a gift, he should not seek more than he has received, lest, while trying to seize the office of another member, he lose what he has merited. For he disturbs the entire order of the body who, not content with his own office, seizes another’s. In the distribution of gifts, diverse gifts of God [Col. 1202A] are received. Nor are all gifts granted to one person; rather, for the sake of humility, one person possesses what another may admire in him. For where, in Ezekiel, the wings of the living creatures strike one another (Ezek. 3:13), the virtues of the saints are signified: they mutually incite one another by affection and instruct one another by reciprocal example.

4. Honorable virgin, I do not wish you to be unaware that without the grace of God preceding, accompanying, and cooperating, we can do no good whatever. God’s grace goes before us, that we may will the good; it accompanies us, that we may begin the good; it cooperates with us, that we may complete the good. Therefore, from God we receive the power to will, begin, and complete what is good. Thus virtues are given us by God; but vices and sins arise from ourselves. Charity, [Col. 1202B] chastity, and honorableness are given us by God; but pride, avarice, and covetousness are from ourselves. Without God we can do no good; but through God’s grace we can perform many good works. Without the grace of God, we are slow, lazy, and lukewarm in doing good; but through God’s grace we are eager, diligent, and devout in good works. Without God we are immediately ready to sin; but through God’s grace we are set free from sin. Without God we love earthly and passing things more than we ought; but through God’s grace we despise all that belongs to this world and desire heavenly things. Through the sin of the first human being we were cast out of paradise; but through God’s grace we believe that we shall reach paradise. Through the sin of the first human being we descend into hell; but through God’s grace we trust [Col. 1202C] that we shall ascend into heaven. For even our being powerful, rich, or wise comes only through God’s grace.

5. Meanwhile, most reverend sister, I want you to know that all the good things we have in this age we have through God’s grace. For all evils happen to us because of our sins. God, through His holy mercy and grace, gives us good things; but 818 evils befall us because of our sins. Prosperity is bestowed upon us through God’s grace; but adversity comes upon us because of our iniquities. Necessities are given us through God’s grace; but contrary things happen to us because of our vices. Therefore, O bride of Christ, we must always [Col. 1202D] call to mind with thanksgiving God’s benefits toward us. Hence the Church speaks in the Song of Songs concerning Christ her bridegroom, saying: “Mindful of your breasts more than wine, the upright love you” (Song 1:3). It is as if she said: Those mindful of your grace, your mercy, and your benefits love you—that is, those who are upright in heart love you. Those are upright in heart who ascribe nothing of righteousness or holiness to their own merits, but attribute all things to the gift of your grace. Those who have been saved, mindful of your grace, love you. Honorable virgin, always remember that whatever good is in you is through God’s grace. Hear the Apostle Paul speaking of himself: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). Thus you too, dearest one, are whatever you are by God’s grace. For your having despised the world, left your father’s house, wished to be a handmaid of God, resolved to serve God in a monastery, and now vowed to live among God’s handmaids—all these good things have come to you through God’s grace. For even your virginity, prudence, and wisdom are yours not through yourself, but through God’s grace.

6. **Question.** Tell me, I beg you, my brother: why do we read in Sacred Scripture that no one is holy, no one good, no one righteous, except God alone? (Mark 10:18.)

**Answer.** Beloved sister, it is truly as it is said. God alone is good, holy, and righteous, because He is good through Himself; human beings, however, are good not through themselves but through God. Thus God alone is good because He is good through Himself. Human beings [Col. 1203B] are good, righteous, and holy not through themselves but through God’s grace. This the bridegroom of the Church, namely Christ, fittingly indicates in the Song of Songs, saying: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song 2:1), because I spread the fragrance of my virtue throughout the whole world. “I,” He says, “am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys”; that is: I am the holiness, goodness, and righteousness of those who trust in me with humility, because none of them can be holy or good without me, as I said in the Gospel: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys. For as a field is adorned with flowers and comes into bloom, so the whole world is adorned by faith in and knowledge of Christ. I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys, because I bestow my grace more abundantly upon those persons [Col. 1203C] who trust not in their own goodness or their own merits, but in me. Venerable sister, therefore I urge you: attribute nothing to your own merits, presume nothing of yourself. Place nothing in your own virtue; do not trust in your own strength; have no confidence in your own boldness. Ascribe all things to the divine gift and divine grace. Give thanks to God in all your works. Render thanks to God in all your actions. Return thanks to God in all your manner of life. Let your confidence always be in Christ, who created you from nothing.

## IV. On the Fear of God

7. Dearest sister, hear what I say and what I urge; listen to what I speak. Fear God above all things, and always observe His commandments, for behold, “the eyes of the Lord are [Col. 1203D] upon those who fear Him, and upon those who hope in His mercy” (Ps. 22:18). And Solomon says: “Fear the Lord, and depart from evil” (Prov. 3:7). “Whoever fears the Lord neglects nothing” (Ecclus. 15:1). Another Wise Man also says: “The fear of the Lord is glory, boasting, joy, and a crown of exultation. The fear of the Lord will enrich the heart and give joy and gladness in length of days; for one who is without fear cannot be justified. The fear of the Lord is wisdom and discipline. Do not be unbelieving in the fear of God, and do not approach Him with a double heart” (Ecclus. 1:11, 12, 28, 34, 36, 37). “You who fear the Lord, await His mercy, and do not turn aside from Him, lest you fall. You who fear the Lord, believe in Him, that His mercy may come to you in delight. You who fear the Lord, [Col. 1204A] believe in Him, and your reward shall not be made void. You who fear the Lord, love Him, and your hearts shall be enlightened. Those who fear the Lord will not disbelieve His word, and those who love Him will keep His ways. Those who fear the Lord seek what is pleasing to Him, and those who love Him shall be filled with His law. Those who fear the Lord will test 819 their hearts and sanctify their souls in His sight. Those who fear the Lord keep His commandments and will have patience until His visitation” (Ecclus. 2:7–10, 18–21). “The eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear Him, and He Himself knows all their works” (Ecclus. 15:20). “The consummation of the love of God is wisdom” (Ecclus. 21:13). “No evils shall meet one who fears the Lord, but in temptation God will deliver him from evil” (Ecclus. 33:1). “The spirit of those who fear God shall be sought out, and it shall be blessed in His regard” (Ecclus. 36:14). “The fear of the Lord is like paradise; blessing and every glory shall cover it” (Ecclus. 40:28). “Blessed is the person to whom it has been granted to possess the fear of the Lord” (Ecclus. 25:15). “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of His love” (Ecclus. 1:16; Prov. 1:7).

8. O beloved sister, nothing keeps us so free from every sin as the fear of hell and the love of God. To fear God is to do no evil and to omit none of the good things that ought to be done. The fear of the Lord is the fountain of wisdom. “It shall be well with one who fears the Lord at the end, and he shall be blessed on the day of his death” (Ecclus. 1:19). Venerable sister, it is good for us to fear God, for the fear of the Lord drives out sin. The fear [Col. 1204C] of the Lord always reforms. The fear of the Lord restrains vice. The fear of the Lord makes a person cautious and diligent; but where fear is absent, there is destruction of the soul. Where fear is absent, there is dissolution of life; where fear is absent, there is an abundance of sins. Therefore, honorable virgin, let fear and hope always be in your heart; let fear and confidence alike be in you. Let hope and fear endure together in you. Hope thus in God’s mercy: fear His justice.

9. Yet, sister beloved to me in Christ, I wish you to know that there are four kinds of fear: namely, human, servile, initial, and chaste. Human fear, as Cassiodorus says, is when we fear suffering bodily dangers or losing worldly goods, and for that reason sin. This worldly fear is evil, and it is abandoned with the world at the first stage; the Lord forbids it in the Gospel, saying: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10:28), etc. The second fear is servile, as blessed Augustine says: when through fear of Gehenna a person withdraws from sin, and does all the good he does not for God’s sake but from fear of hell. That person fears like a servant who performs the good which he does, not for fear of losing a good which he does not love, but for fear of suffering an evil which he dreads. He does not fear losing the embraces of the most beautiful bridegroom, but fears being cast into the punishments of hell. Of this servile fear Paul says: “For you have not received the spirit of slavery again unto fear, [Col. 1205A] but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons” (Rom. 8:15; 2 Tim. 1:7), that is, the filial Spirit. This servile fear is good and useful, although insufficient and imperfect; through it the habit of righteousness gradually grows. When a person begins to believe, he begins to fear the day of judgment. If he has begun to believe, he has also begun to fear; but one who still fears does not have perfect confidence on the day of judgment. Perfect charity is not yet in the person who still fears, because if perfect charity were in him, he would not fear. Perfect charity would produce perfect righteousness in a person; then he would have nothing to fear, but would have reason to desire that iniquity pass away and the kingdom of God come. What is perfect charity but perfect holiness? Whoever lives perfectly possesses perfect charity within himself. Whoever [Col. 1205B] lives perfectly has no cause to be condemned in hell, but rather cause to be crowned in heaven. Whoever possesses perfect charity within himself does not fear punishment in hell, but hopes to be glorified with God in heaven. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “All who love your name shall glory in you” (Ps. 5:12). Therefore fear is not in charity, but “perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18). Fear comes first into the human heart, so that a place may be prepared for charity.

10. A third fear follows this servile fear: namely, initial fear, when a person begins to do good for love of God which he formerly did from fear of hell. Of this initial fear David the prophet says in the Psalm: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ps. 110:10). Initial fear is when [Col. 1205C] a person begins to love the God whom he had formerly feared; and so servile fear is driven from the heart. A fourth fear follows this initial fear, namely chaste fear, through which we fear lest the bridegroom, namely Christ, delay; lest He depart from us; lest we offend Him, sin against Him, and lose Him. This fear, namely chaste fear, descends from love; this fear is born of love. Of 820 this fear it is read in the Psalm: “The holy fear of the Lord endures for age upon age” (Ps. 18:10). Fear comes first into the human heart. And why does it come? To prepare a place for charity. But the more charity begins to dwell in the human heart, the more fear decreases. The greater charity is in a person’s heart, the less fear is there [Col. 1205D]. Why? Because charity casts it out. Hear, beloved sister, an apt comparison. We often see thread introduced by means of a bristle. When something is sewn, the bristle enters first, and the thread enters after the bristle. Thus fear enters the human mind first, and charity after fear. Fear enters in order to introduce charity; but after charity has entered, it casts fear out. This fear is holy because it produces holiness in the human mind. This fear is holy because it introduces perfect charity into human minds. For perfect charity is perfect holiness. This fear is chaste because it admits no adulterous love; that is, because it loves God above all things and puts nothing before His love. This fear is also called filial, because it does not [Col. 1206A] fear God as a servant fears a cruel master, but as a son fears a most loving father. This fear is called filial because it fears not as a servant, but as a son.

11. But what is meant by David the prophet’s saying, “The holy fear of the Lord endures for age upon age,” when John says, “Perfect charity casts out fear” (1 John 4:18)? This is what we said above: one possesses chaste and holy fear who fears God not because of the punishments of hell or the torments of Gehenna, but with reverence and love. And this fear, namely reverence for God, endures for age upon age. But one who fears God because of the punishments of hell does not possess chaste fear, but servile fear, because he does not possess perfect charity. [Col. 1206B] For if he loved God perfectly, he would have perfect righteousness within himself; and he would fear God not because of punishment, but with reverence and fear. Thus the fear of punishment is not in charity, because perfect charity casts it out. A servant fears his master in one way, and a son fears his father in another. A servant fears his master with despair and hatred; a son fears his father with reverence and love. Therefore now, most reverend sister, I urge you to fear God with love and reverence. For I do not want you always to lie crushed beneath the yoke of fear, but to rise through love to the Lord your Father, who created you as a daughter. I also urge you to love God chastely and put nothing before His love, but for His love despise all things that are in this world. Again [Col. 1206C] I exhort and beseech you, most honorable virgin, amend your life with every effort: let your speech be chaste, your walk honorable, your countenance humble, your tongue gracious, your mind full of love, and your hands full of work—with the Lord’s help, without whom you can do no good. Sister most dear to me in Christ, if you heed me as a brother and fear God with your whole heart, you will possess many good things not only in this life but also in the life to come. Amen.

## V.—On Charity

12. “The king brought me into the wine-cellar, and ordered charity in me” (Song 1:3; 2:4). The wine-cellar is the Church, in which is the wine of evangelical preaching. Into this cellar, therefore, the bridegroom’s beloved—namely, the holy soul—is brought, [Col. 1206D] and in it charity is ordered, because not all things are to be loved equally, but differently. We ought not to love all things equally, but some less and some more. For to know what we ought to do, yet not to know the order in which it ought to be done, is not perfect knowledge. If we do not love what we ought to love, or if we love what we ought not to love, we do not have ordered charity. And if we love more what we ought to love less, or love less what we ought to love more, we do not retain ordered charity. This, then, is ordered charity: that we love God before all things and above all things. We ought to love God with our whole heart—that is, with our whole understanding, with our whole soul, with [Col. 1207A] our whole will, with our whole mind, and with our whole memory—so that we direct all our understanding, all our thoughts, and our whole life toward Him from whom we have all good things; so that no part of our life is left idle, but whatever enters the soul may be directed to the place toward which the impulse of love runs. Therefore, dearest sister, it is most fitting and very necessary for us to love God in all things and above all things, since He is the highest good. To love the highest good is therefore the highest blessedness. The more anyone loves God, the more blessed that person will be. Whoever loves God is good. If good, then blessed. Hence Solomon says in the Song of Songs: “Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). God’s love is truly said to be strong as death because, as death violently separates the soul [Col. 1207B] from the body, so God’s love violently separates a person from the world and from carnal love. God’s love is truly strong as death because, while we are mortified to vices through love of God, what death does in the bodily senses, God’s love does in worldly desires. God is to be loved for His own sake, because He is supremely good and because He created us from nothing. Charity is the love by which God is loved for His own sake and one’s neighbor for God’s sake. In the first place God is loved, as has already been said, in all things and above all things. In the second place one’s neighbor is loved in God, that is, in goodness.

13. Charity has two commandments: one concerning love of God, which is the greatest commandment; the other concerning love of one’s neighbor, [Col. 1207C] which is like it, as it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God, and your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. 6:5; 11:13; Matt. 22:37, 39; Mark 12:30–31). It is as if He said: You ought to love your neighbor for the end for which you love yourself: namely, that he may be good and may be able to attain eternal life. Concerning this love of God and neighbor, in the Song of Songs the bridegroom—namely Christ—speaks to the bride, namely the Church or holy soul, saying: “How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride; and the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices” (Song 4:10). What is more fittingly understood here by the breasts than the very love of God and neighbor of which we spoke above? By these breasts [Col. 1207D] the holy mind nourishes all its senses through its love, when it is bound to its God by the union of charity and bestows on its neighbors whatever good it can. “And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices.” By the ointments, indeed, we understand those very virtues which are born from charity. We must love our neighbors in goodness, because one who loves a neighbor in evil does not love the neighbor but hates him. “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” By no means. Therefore let us love one another, because charity is from God. And whoever loves his brother is born of God and sees God (1 John 4:20, 7). Whoever loves the brother whom he sees with bodily eyes sees with the eyes of the mind God abiding in himself, namely charity; [Col. 1208A] for God is charity. And whoever does not love the brother whom he sees with bodily eyes does not see with the eyes of the mind God abiding in himself, namely charity: for if charity were in him, God would be in him, because God is charity. We ought also to love our kindred, if they are good and serve God. We ought to love strangers joined to us by the bond of Christ’s charity more than kindred who do not love God and do not serve God. Why? Because the bond of hearts is holier than that of bodies. We ought to love all faithful people; but since we cannot benefit everyone, we must give especial care to those who, by the opportunities of place, time, or any circumstances, are joined to us more closely, as though by some particular lot. Eternal life is to be desired with equal love [Col. 1208B] for all people. We must love all people with the affection of charity, namely that they may serve God and be saved.
