But we ought not to bestow works of mercy equally upon all people, but less upon some and more upon others.

14. Beloved sister, if we wish to preserve true and perfect charity, by God’s help we can reach our eternal homeland. Moreover, we ought to love our enemies for God’s sake, just as He Himself says in the Gospel: “Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, 822 and pray for those who persecute and calumniate you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven” (Luke 6:27, 28, 35; Matt. [Col. 1208C] 5:43–45). Therefore, venerable sister, charity is necessary for us, without which no one can please God. Whoever hates a human being does not love God. Nor does one love God who despises God’s commands. Charity is the root of all virtues. For whatever we do without charity profits us nothing. Our striving is empty if we do not possess charity, because God is charity. Carnal desire reigns where God’s charity is absent. Then a person is perfect when he is full of charity. Without the love of charity, however rightly one may believe, one cannot attain blessedness. Such is the power of charity that, if it is absent, the other virtues are possessed in vain; if it is present, all things are possessed rightly. Whoever does not love God does not love himself either. Therefore I now urge you, most honorable [Col. 1208D] virgin, to be united by love to the invisible bridegroom Jesus Christ and to burn with longing for Him. Desire none of the things now in the world. Regard the length of this present life as a punishment; hasten to depart from the world. Receive no consolation from the present life, but sigh, burn, pant, and be anxious with your whole mind for Christ whom you love; and let even the well-being of your body become cheap to you for the sake of Christ’s love. Be pierced through by love’s wound, so that you may rightly say: “I am wounded by charity.” Sister beloved to me in Christ, hear the words of Jesus Christ your bridegroom: “Whoever loves me shall be loved by my Father, and I shall love him and reveal myself to him” (John 14:21). Love Him, therefore, dearest one, in this life, so that He may deign to love you with the Father in eternal blessedness. Amen.

## VI.—On the Beginnings of Converts

[Col. 1209A]

15. A reward is promised to those who begin, but it is given to those who persevere, as it is written: “Whoever perseveres unto the end, that person shall be saved” (Matt. 10:22). For our conversion then pleases God when we bring the good which we begin through to the end. Thus it is written: “Woe to those who have lost endurance” (Ecclus. 2:16); that is, who have not completed a good work. There are many people who turn to God solely from devotion of mind. Many also, who did not turn through devotion, are compelled by afflictions to turn to God, as is read in the Psalm: “Bind their jaws with bit and bridle, those who do not draw near to you” (Ps. 31:9). Everyone who turns must begin with weeping over sins, and then pass [Col. 1209B] to longing for heavenly goods. Dearest sister, we must first wash away by tears the evils we commit, so that we may then contemplate with the pure gaze of the mind what we seek; so that, once the darkness of sin has first been wiped away from us by weeping, the whitened things may be seen with the cleansed eyes of the heart. It is necessary that everyone who turns, after fear, rise to God through love as a child, lest he always lie under fear like a servant. Those newly converted should be consoled with gentle words, lest, if they begin to be embittered, they flee back in terror to their former sins. Whoever does not teach and correct a novice with kindness and gentleness knows better how to embitter than to reform. A novice must first be corrected and disciplined in wrongful action, and then in thought.

[Col. 1209C] 16. Every new conversion still retains an admixture of the former life. Therefore no virtue should ever be displayed before human eyes until the old manner of life has been utterly uprooted from the mind. Then each person recognizes himself to be more heavily burdened by the assault of vices when he enters God’s service. Thus the people of Israel are pressed under a heavier burden by the Egyptians when divine knowledge is revealed through Moses (Exod. 5). Before conversion, vices have peace in a person; but when they are driven out, they rise more fiercely against him. Many after conversion endure the stirring of lust; yet they endure it not for condemnation but for testing: namely, that they may always have an enemy to resist, shaking off sluggishness, provided that they do not consent to it. Slack conversion leads many back into their former errors and dissolves them in the torpor of living. One who is lukewarm in conversion does not perceive idle words and vain thoughts to be harmful; but when the mind has awakened from its mental torpor, it immediately fears as hostile and dreadful those things which it had considered trivial. Deceit and sloth must be feared in every work of God. We deceive God when [Col. 1209D] we praise not God but ourselves for our good work. We practice sloth when, through languor and torpor, we perform God’s works. Every art of this world has earnest lovers, most ready to carry it out. Why? Because it has the present reward of its labor. But the practice of divine fear has many followers who are timid, languid, [Col. 1210A] and frozen by the inertia of sloth. This happens because the reward of their labor will be given not in the present life but in the future one. Those newly converted to God ought not to be advanced into outward concerns. For if they become entangled in them, they are immediately shaken and wither, like a little tree newly planted and not yet firmly rooted. A change of place is not always effective for converts’ salvation of soul. Yet for some, when the place is changed, the disposition of the mind is changed also. It is fitting, indeed, that each person should physically withdraw from the place where he remembers having been enslaved to vices.

17. Venerable sister, hear what I say. Many turn to God not so much in mind as in body—a thing which we cannot say without deep groaning. They have the habit of religion, but not a religious mind. Many do not have the spirit of religion. For many come to conversion not so much for the salvation of the soul as from bodily necessity; they worship not God but their belly, of whom the Apostle says: “Whose god is their belly” (Phil. 3:19). Their intention is not to serve God worthily, but to eat and drink well, be well clothed, and fare well in this age. And because they love earthly things, they lose heavenly things. As the Lord says in the Gospel: “They receive their reward in this age” (Matt. 6:5). Therefore, beloved sister, we must beware of loving transient and earthly things more than we ought. For this reason the Psalmist warns us: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:11). Earthly things ought indeed to be for our use, [Col. 1210C] but heavenly things for our desire; we ought to expend earthly things and desire heavenly ones. For there is a certain wonderful and great abundance of sweetness, which God has hidden for those who love Him, of which it is written: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, neither has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love Him” (1 Cor. 2:9; Isa. 64:4). Hence the Prophet says: “They shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16:15). Sister beloved in Christ, therefore let that satisfaction be our happiness. Amen.

## VII.—On Conversion

18. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). But what is it to [Col. 1210D] deny oneself, except to renounce one’s own pleasures? Thus, one who was proud should become humble; one who was wrathful, gentle; one who was lustful, chaste; one who was drunken, sober; and one who was avaricious, generous. For if anyone renounces all that he possesses but does not renounce his evil habits, he is not Christ’s disciple. Whoever renounces his possessions denies what is his; whoever renounces his evil habits denies himself. Things which lovers of the world love, God’s servants flee as though they were hostile. God’s servants rejoice more in the world’s adversities than they delight in its prosperity. Dearest sister, the things of this world are hostile to God’s servants, so that, when they feel these adversities, they may sigh with the greatest longing for the heavenly kingdom. Great grace shines before God [Col. 1211A] which is contemptible to this world. For indeed what the world hates must be loved by God. Holy men are strangers and sojourners in the world; thus Peter is reproved for wishing to make a tent on the mountain (Matt. 17), because the saints have no tent in this world, whose homeland and house are in heaven. Venerable sister, all temporal things wither and pass away like fading grass; and therefore, in comparison with eternal things that never wither, God’s servants rightly scorn and despise these things, because they see no permanence in them.

19. Holy people who perfectly despise the world die to this world in such a way that they delight to live for God alone. And the more they withdraw themselves from the manner of life of this age, the more they behold with the eyes of the mind the presence of God and the frequent company of angels. For although [Col. 1211B] God protects the life of the elect amid carnal people, it is nevertheless very rare for someone placed amid worldly pleasures to remain free from sins. One who is near danger will not always be safe. Beloved sister, it is good for a person to be physically removed from the world, but much better to be separated from the world in will. Therefore, one is perfect who is separated from the world in mind and body. Hence blessed Job says: “The wild ass despises the city” (Job 39:5, 7). So God’s servant despises the society of worldly people. Those who perfectly scorn the world seek the adversities of our life and despise its prosperity; and when this life is despised by them, the heavenly life is found. For that mind is far from God to which this miserable life is sweet. Such a person does not know what heavenly things to desire or what earthly things to despise. For, as it is written: “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18). The more a person is able to know the heavenly things that he should desire, the more he ought to grieve over the earthly and transitory things in which he is entangled.

20. Servants of God who attend to the advantage of their parents separate themselves from the love of God. Therefore, one who is spiritual ought so to benefit his or her parents that, while striving to render them the service due to the flesh, he or she does not depart from spiritual work or purpose. Sister beloved to me in Christ [Col. 1211D], hear the judgment of blessed Isidore:

> “Many canons, monks, and consecrated women, through love for their parents, become entangled in earthly cares, frenzies, quarrels, and business affairs, and for the temporal welfare of their parents lose their own souls.”

Yet sound discernment requires that what is mercifully bestowed upon strangers should not be withheld from parents. It is fitting that we give our parents what we mercifully give to strangers. For what is devoutly bestowed upon strangers is rendered to parents in a bodily way. Honourable sister, we ought not to hate our parents, but rather the hindrances they create when they turn us aside from the straight path.

By the Philistine cows that led the ark of the Lord to the land of Israel, we understand a figure of those who have left the world for God’s sake [Col. 1212A]. For just as the Philistines yoked the cows to the cart, shut up their calves at home, and placed upon the cart the ark of the Lord’s covenant (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 6), so the light and sweet yoke of Christ has been laid upon the necks of God’s servants. And just as the cows lowed in love for their calves, yet turned neither to the right nor to the left, but proceeded by a straight road as far as Beth-shemesh, which lay at the entrance of the land of Israel, so servants of God ought to proceed by the straight road. Out of love for their parents they ought not turn either to the right or to the left from a good work or purpose, but should reach Beth-shemesh—that is, the entrance into the heavenly kingdom—by the straight path. And just as the cows went on lowing for their young [Col. 1212B], so it is fitting for God’s servants to low for their parents; that is, they should pray for them, that it may go well with them, that they may be delivered from evil, and strengthened in good.

21. Sister beloved to me in Christ, as I said to you above, we ought not to hate our parents, but to love them. Yet, as blessed Augustine says, if they oppose us on God’s way, not even burial is owed them by us. You, dearest one, have gone out with Abraham from your land, your kindred, and your father’s house; and you have come into the land which God showed you (Gen. 12), that is, into the monastery. I therefore beseech you to persevere there in right living, and to rest in the bosom of that same Abraham—that is, in blessed repose—so that after your death you may be able to rest.

You, sister beloved to me in Christ [Col. 1212C], have gone out with Lot from Sodom (Gen. 19), that is, from secular life. Therefore I urge you not to look back with his wife, lest—God forbid!—you become an example of perversity to all people. Rather, I ask you to save yourself with Lot upon the mountain, that is, in the monastery, and to provide others with an example of holiness.

You, honourable virgin, have gone out with Joshua from Egypt (Exod. 13 and 14), that is, from the world; and you remain with him in the wilderness (Exod. 16), that is, in the monastery, where God rains manna upon you: that is, he gives you the bread of the heavenly word. Therefore, sister most beloved to me in Christ, I urge you to persevere in the monastery as you have begun: there keeping watch, praying, singing psalms, and fighting manfully against the devil [Col. 1212D], so that at last, when all enemies have been conquered and every worldly delight overcome, you may reach with that same Joshua the land of promise—that is, the blessedness of heavenly life—and there be found worthy to behold the face of the unfailing Sun. Amen.

VIII.—On contempt for the world

22. Dearest sister, hear the Lord Jesus Christ saying in the Gospel: “Everyone who has left house, or father, or mother, or brothers, or sisters, or fields for my name’s sake, shall receive a hundredfold and shall possess eternal life” (Matt. 19:29). Therefore it is very good for us to leave all earthly things for the Lord’s name, so that we may receive heavenly things from him. Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world will be God’s enemy [Col. 1213A]. Therefore, sister beloved in Christ, let us not love the world, lest we have God as our enemy.

“He readily despises all things who judges that he will die daily” (St Jerome, *Epistle* 1). If we daily bring our death to mind, we willingly despise all earthly things. If we keep the day of our death in mind, we quickly despise everything that is in this world.

*(Question.)* O my brother, I would gladly leave everything in this world for the Lord’s name, if I possessed anything; but since I have neither gold nor silver nor this world’s riches, I do not know what I may leave for the Lord’s name.

*(Answer.)* O bride of Christ, you leave much if you abandon the will to possess; you give up much if you set aside the desire to possess [Col. 1213B]; you leave much if you forsake fleshly desires; you leave much if for God’s sake you despise this world’s pleasure; you give up much if you renounce earthly covetousness and desires. God loves human souls more than earthly riches; God loves a mind that is clean and holy more than worldly substance (St Gregory, *Homily* 5 on the Gospels).

Venerable sister, the kingdom of God is worth as much as you possess. God does not require of you what he has not given you. Therefore give him what he gave you: namely, a mind holy, chaste, clean, modest, devout, God-fearing, and adorned with good conduct. Thus, honourable sister, the kingdom of God is worth as much as you are. Hand yourself over to Christ, and purchase his kingdom from him. Do not be troubled about the price [Col. 1213C]. Let the price not trouble you; let it not seem difficult to you; let it not be burdensome to you. For Jesus Christ, king of heaven, gave himself in order to free you from the devil’s power and win you for God the Father. Therefore willingly give yourself to him who redeemed you from the hand of the enemy. Give yourself wholly to him, because, in order to save you, he gave himself wholly.

23. Sister beloved to me in Christ, despise earthly riches so that you may acquire heavenly ones. Riches lead a person into danger of body and soul; riches drag a person as far as death. Many have been endangered through wealth, and many have fallen into peril through riches. Riches prove destructive to many; wealth has brought death to many people [Col. 1213D].

Those who entangle themselves in earthly cares never have rest of mind. For concern over possessions disturbs the mind. A mind occupied with earthly cares is always in distress. Venerable bride of Christ, therefore, if you wish to be at peace, seek none of the things that are in the world. You will always have rest of mind if you remove yourself from worldly care. You will always have peace of mind if you withdraw yourself from the tumult of earthly business, because riches are never acquired without sin. No one administers earthly affairs without sin. It is very rare for those who possess riches to attain rest.

Whoever entangles himself in earthly cares separates himself from the love of God. Whoever is fixed in love for temporal things takes no delight in God. Care for temporal things turns the mind away from attention to God [Col. 1214A]. No one can embrace at once the glory of God and the glory of the world. No one can love Christ and the world at the same time. It is difficult to serve at once heavenly concerns and earthly business; difficult to love God and the world at once. No one can love God and the world perfectly at the same time. The two cannot both be loved equally at once.

24. Honourable virgin, hear what I say. Though a person shine in the world’s glory, though clothed in purple and gold, though dressed in costly garments, though appearing adorned in secular clothing, though gleaming with jewels and precious stones, though walking crowned with splendid attire, though surrounded by a multitude of servants, though protected by the arms of guards [Col. 1214B], though crowded about by innumerable ranks of attendants, though guarded by companies, he is always in punishment, always in distress, always in mourning, always in danger. He remains always on silken coverings, yet lies troubled upon golden beds; he lies sick upon silver beds; he lies frail upon down, yet he is frail and mortal.

Sister most beloved to me in Christ, I have said these things so that you may know how vain the glory of this world is. The happiness of this world is brief. The glory of this age is slight, temporal power transitory and fragile. Therefore, venerable virgin, so that you may acquire heavenly riches, despise earthly ones. Gladly reject earthly things, that you may attain heavenly goods. Spurn transitory things, that you may be worthy to possess eternal ones. Give little, that [Col. 1214C] you may receive great things from God. Flee the society of people on earth, that you may have the fellowship of angels in heaven. May he deign to lead you there who redeemed you by his precious blood. Amen.

IX.—On clothing

25. Our Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospel: “Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings” (Matt. 11:8). Garments are called soft because they make the mind soft. The court of a king delights in soft garments; Christ’s Church, however, delights in rough and humble ones. Such ought to be the garments of God’s male and female servants: nothing in them should be marked by novelty, excess, vanity, or anything belonging to pride and vain glory [Col. 1214D]. Hence blessed Jerome says: “A delicate garment does not adorn a cleric, but purity of mind.”

Dearest sister, therefore let us adorn ourselves with spiritual ornaments: charity, humility, meekness, obedience, and patience. These are the garments by which we may please Jesus Christ, our heavenly bridegroom. Christ, the invisible bridegroom, does not seek beauty outwardly but inwardly, as is written in the Psalm: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within” (Ps. 44:14). Therefore, sister beloved in Christ, let your riches be good conduct, and your beauty a good life.

Dearest one, I desire that there may be said of you what is read in the Song of Songs: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you”; and again: “Come from Lebanon; come, you shall be crowned” (Song 4:7–8) [Col. 1215A]. Truly blessed is the soul that serves Jesus Christ, the heavenly bridegroom, without blemish. So too, venerable sister, you will be blessed if you serve Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, without blemish.

Strive, therefore, to please Christ not with costly garments but with good conduct; not with beauty of flesh but with beauty of mind. Strive to please him not in the face but in the heart. Let your garments and shoes be neither excessively costly nor too mean, but of moderate and suitable dress. For blessed Augustine says of himself: “I confess that I blush at costly clothing”; and again: “It does not become this profession; it does not become this exhortation; it does not become these limbs; it does not become these gray hairs.”

Honourable virgin, let a clean garment surround you, not for beauty but for the body’s necessity [Col. 1215B], lest, while you clothe yourself in costly garments, you fall into the ugliness of the soul. For the more the body is arranged and adorned outwardly for vain glory, the more the soul is inwardly made foul and defiled.

26. Therefore, sister beloved in Christ, show your profession by your dress and bearing. Let simplicity be in your step and propriety in your manner of walking. Let nothing disgraceful, wanton, insolent, presumptuous, or frivolous appear in your bearing. For the mind appears in the body’s carriage; bodily bearing is a sign of the mind. The mind is disclosed by the body’s carriage, dearest sister.

Therefore let your walk bear no image of frivolity; let it not offend another’s eyes. Do not make a spectacle of yourself; do not give others an occasion to speak ill of you [Col. 1215C]. Beloved sister, cleanse your conscience of all malice, so that Jesus Christ, your heavenly bridegroom, may happily say to you: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are doves’ eyes” (Song 1:14). Beautiful, namely, through bodily integrity and purity of thought. Behold, you are beautiful, having a clean and simple intention of heart, because you do every good thing not in order to be seen by people, but in order to please God alone. You have doves’ eyes because you keep yourself free from every malice, pretense, and deceit.

27. Sister most beloved to me in Christ, I have said this so that you may rejoice more inwardly in your soul over holy virtues than outwardly in your body over costly clothing [Col. 1215D]. For, as blessed Gregory says, no one seeks costly garments except for vain glory: namely, so as to be praised for them and to appear more honourable than others. No one wishes to be clothed in costly garments except where he may be seen by others. Thus costly clothing is sought solely for vain glory.

Venerable virgin, in this we recognize that we love the world: that we love costly garments. Whoever does not love the world does not seek costly clothing. When a person delights in bodily beauty, his mind is removed from love of the Creator. The more we rejoice in adorning the body, the more we are separated from heavenly love. The more we rejoice in earthly and transitory things, the less we desire heavenly things.

A consecrated woman truly has a blemish in herself if she loves costly garments [Col. 1216A]. Christ’s bride is not without blemish if she loves an expensive dress. The handmaid of Christ who has perfectly left the world seeks humble clothing. The handmaid of Christ who desires costly garments has not yet perfectly despised the world. A black garment signifies humility of mind; plain clothing declares contempt for the world. The blackness of the veil shows the mind’s cleanness and purity; a black veil is a sign of chastity and holiness.

Now, therefore, most reverend sister, I urge you to fulfill in deed the habit which you display in appearance. I beseech you: adorn the habit of your Order with good conduct. The habit is holy; let the mind be holy. As the garments are holy, so let your works be holy; as the veil is consecrated, so let your work be holy [Col. 1216B]. Do not hide one thing within and show another without; do not be one thing in private and another in public. Be such as you wish to be thought; as you are in appearance, so be in action; and as you are in countenance, so be in deed. Amen.

X.—On compunction

28. Compunction of heart is humility of mind arising from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment. That compunction is perfect which drives away from itself every delight in fleshly things and fixes, with the whole effort of the mind, its attention upon contemplation of God. We read that compunction is twofold: first, that by which the soul of every servant of God is moved on account of God—that is, when it calls to mind the evils it has done; second, when it sighs from desire for eternal life.

The mind of a righteous person is pierced by compunction in four ways: by remembrance of sins, recollection of future punishments, consideration of this life’s pilgrimage, and longing for the heavenly homeland, so that it may swiftly reach it [Col. 1216C]. Every sinner then knows that he or she is visited by the Lord when moved to tears. Thus Peter wept when Christ looked upon him, as it is written: “And the Lord turned and looked at Peter, who immediately went out and wept bitterly” (Matt. 26:75). Hence the Psalmist also says: “He looked, and the earth was moved and trembled” (Ps. 17:8). The earth trembles when the sinner is moved to tears.

Therefore I urge you, dearest sister, in prayer and with tears to call your sins to mind. For one who does not have compunction or contrition of heart does not have pure prayer. Sister beloved to me in Christ, hear the examples of the saints, who through compunction and tears obtained from God forgiveness of their sins. Hannah, Samuel’s mother, through compunction and tears deserved to have a son; moreover, she received from God the gift of prophecy (1 Kings [1 Samuel] 1). Through compunction and tears David obtained forgiveness for the murder and adultery he had committed. For through the prophet he heard: “You shall not die, because the Lord has taken away your sin” (2 Kings [2 Samuel] 12:13). Father Tobit, through compunction and tears, deserved to receive healing from blindness [Col. 1217A] and consolation in poverty. Thus the angel Raphael said to him: “May joy always be yours”; and he added: “Be of good courage; it is near that you shall be healed by God” (Tob. 5:11, 13). Mary Magdalene likewise, through compunction and tears, deserved to hear from the Lord: “Your sins are forgiven” (Luke 7:48). Venerable sister, I have set these examples of the saints before you so that tears through compunction may be sweet to you.

29. Good compunction is a desirable treasure and an inexpressible joy in the human mind. The soul that has compunction in prayer advances toward salvation. A strong person is no less praiseworthy in mourning than in battle. Therefore, because after baptism we have defiled our life, let us baptize our conscience with tears. Where there are tears, the spiritual fire is kindled which illumines the mind’s hidden places [Col. 1217B]. The tears of penitents are counted as baptism before God.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, if you have compunction according to God, you will be blessed. Compunction of heart is health of the soul; compunction of mind is illumination of the soul, because the soul is then illuminated when it is pierced into tears. Compunction in tears is forgiveness of sins, because sins are then forgiven when they are called to mind with tears. Compunction draws the Holy Spirit back to itself, because when the mind is visited by the Holy Spirit, a person immediately weeps over his or her sins.

30. *(Question.)* O my brother, I ask you: tell me what are the causes of our sorrow, for which we weep in this mortal life?

*(Answer.)* For our sins [Col. 1217C], for the misery of this world, from compassion for our neighbour, and from love of the heavenly reward. He wept for sins who said: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall drench my couch” (Ps. 6:7). The same man groaned over this world’s miseries when he said: “Alas for me, for my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt among the inhabitants of Kedar; my soul has long been a sojourner” (Ps. 119:5–6).

The Lord wept from compassion over Lazarus (John 11:35), and over the city of Jerusalem, saying: “For if you too had known” (Luke 19:42). The apostle Paul also, who commands us to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. 12:15), grieved from compassion, saying: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. 11:29). The righteous wept in love of the heavenly reward, saying the Psalmist’s words: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept while we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. 136:1).

The present life is death, because it is full of miseries; for it is not in our homeland but on the road, not at home but in exile. In this world we are not in our own city but on pilgrimage, as it is written: “We do not have here an enduring city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13:14; cf. Mic. 2:10) [Col. 1217D]. Therefore, beloved sister, I urge you first to mourn for your sins; then for this world’s miseries and in compassion for your neighbour; and finally, for love of God and the heavenly reward.

Honourable virgin, pray to God with all devotion [Col. 1218A] that he may give you true compunction of mind and contrition of heart. Compunction causes one to have within oneself Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, as the Lord himself says: “I and the Father will come, and we shall make our dwelling with the one who loves me” (John 14:23). Where tears abound, grave thoughts do not draw near; and if at some time they draw near, they take no root there. Tears always give us great confidence before God.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, hear the voice of Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, saying: “Arise, my beloved, and come, through love; for now winter has passed, the rain has gone and departed, flowers have appeared in our land, the time of pruning has come, the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land” (Song 2:10–12). That is, the voice of the preaching Apostles in the Church.

The turtledove [Col. 1218B] is a most chaste bird, which is accustomed always to nest or remain on high and in trees; it signifies the Apostles and other teachers, who can say, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). It has groaning rather than song, and signifies the weeping of the saints, who urge their own people to lamentation and tears, saying: “Be wretched and mourn” (Jas. 4:9).

31. Therefore, honourable virgin, take the example of this turtledove, and mourn for love of Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, until you can behold him reigning upon the throne of his kingdom. It is better for you to mourn with love of Jesus Christ than with fear of hell. “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove” (Song 1:9). It is the nature of the turtledove that, if by chance it loses its mate, it seeks no other thereafter. O bride of Christ, make yourself like this turtledove [Col. 1218C], and apart from Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, seek no other lover.

O bride of Christ, be like the turtledove, and mourn day and night with longing for Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, because he has now ascended to heaven, so that one day you may deserve to behold his face at the Father’s right hand. “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.” Modesty is customarily found in the cheeks. Venerable sister, you have cheeks like those of a turtledove if, out of modesty before Jesus Christ your bridegroom, you do nothing contrary to his will; you have cheeks like those of a turtledove if, with love and reverence for Christ, you put aside what displeases him; you have cheeks like those of a turtledove if, apart from Christ, you love no other friend.

Therefore, dearest sister, unceasingly wash your sins with tears [Col. 1218D]. Daily wash your negligences through compunction and tears. Without ceasing cleanse the transgressions of your Order with tears; and through tears and compunction obtain forgiveness of your sins; through tears and frequent sighs obtain eternal joys. Weep for your iniquities; lament the evils of your crimes; remember in weeping the evils you have done. Let a flood of sorrow water you; let a river of tears compel you to weep. Blot out by tears what you have done wickedly; wash away with tears what you have committed unlawfully.

Honourable virgin, if you do not weep for sins in this age, when will you say to God: “You have placed my tears before your sight?” (Ps. 55:9). Dearest one, if you do not weep for your iniquities in this mortal life, when will you say: “My tears were my bread day and night?” (Ps. 41:4) [Col. 1219A]. Therefore I urge you, bride of Christ, to mourn for your sins in this mortal life, that you may deserve to be comforted in the heavenly homeland, as it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5; Isa. 61:2). Amen.

XI.—On sorrow

32. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, amen, I say to you: you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you indeed will be sorrowful, but your sorrow shall be turned into joy” (John 16:20). Solomon also says: “A joyful heart makes the face cheerful, but a sorrowful spirit is cast down into the grief of the soul” (Prov. 15:13). “A joyful mind makes one’s age flourish, but a sorrowful spirit dries up the bones” (Prov. 17:22). “My son, in good things make no complaint, and in every gift do not add the sorrow of an evil word” (Ecclus. 18:15). “Every wound is sorrow of heart” (Ecclus. 25:17). “Joyfulness of heart is the life of a person” (Ecclus. 30:23). “A perverse heart will give sorrow, and a wise person will resist it” (Ecclus. 36:22). “Through sorrow death hastens; sorrow bends the neck of the heart” (Ecclus. 38:19). “A joyful heart makes good health, but the bones of a sorrowful person are dried up.”

Blessed Athanasius also says: “A sorrowful person is always devising evil, and grieves the Holy Spirit given to him by God.” The Apostle also teaches this, saying: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, in whom you were sealed on the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:30). See, then, dearest sister, that you do not grieve the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, lest perhaps he abandon you. Put away from yourself doubtfulness and resentment, because both grieve the Holy Spirit [Col. 1219C]. Put away sorrow from yourself, because it is the sister of doubtfulness and resentment.

Certainly worldly sorrow is the worst of all evil spirits and harms God’s servants. Worldly sorrow wounds, crushes, and entices God’s servants. For the Holy Spirit does not endure carnal sorrow. Therefore, beloved sister, put on always spiritual joy, which has favour with God. Every spiritual joy is always good: it thinks good things and despises vain sorrow. If spiritual joy were not good, the prophet would never say: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous; glory, all you upright in heart” (Ps. 31:11); and again: “The righteous shall rejoice in the Lord and hope in him, and all the upright in heart shall be praised” (Ps. 63:11) [Col. 1219D].

33. *(Question.)* O dearest brother, if sorrow is evil and harms God’s servants, what does Solomon mean when he says: “The heart of the wise is where sorrow is, and the heart of fools where joy is” (Eccl. 7:5)?

*(Answer.)* Venerable sister, Solomon’s saying, “The heart of the wise is where sorrow is, and the heart of fools where joy is,” must be understood only of spiritual sorrow and worldly joy. It is as though he said more plainly: The heart of the wise is where spiritual sorrow is, and the heart of fools where worldly joy is. Those who have sorrow according to God are wise; those who have sorrow according to the world are foolish.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Rejoice and exult, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke 10:20). And the apostle Paul says: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (2 Cor. 6:10); and again: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4) [Col. 1220A]. Therefore spiritual sorrow is good, but sorrow born from desire for temporal things is evil. Of spiritual sorrow it is written: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5; Isa. 61:2). But of worldly sorrow Solomon says: “Sorrow has killed many, and there is no benefit in it” (Ecclus. 30:25; cf. 2 Cor. 7:10). Again, of spiritual joy it is said: “Let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice” (Ps. 104:3). And again, concerning worldly joy, we read: “Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep” (Luke 6:25).

Dearest sister, hear also what blessed Paul says: “The sorrow which is according to God works the salvation of repentance, but the sorrow which is according to the world works death” (2 Cor. 7:10). The prayer of one who is always sorrowful has no power and cannot ascend to God. Where sorrow has overshadowed the Holy Spirit, prayer is not acceptable there, because it is weak and cannot ascend to God [Col. 1220B].

Therefore, sister beloved to me, abandon sorrow. Cease to be sorrowful; drive sorrow away from yourself. Do not give yourself over to much sorrow; do not persist in sorrow; do not give your heart to sorrow. Sorrow is one of the seven principal vices, and therefore must be avoided by all God’s servants. Hence blessed Isidore says: “If you live well and devoutly, you will never be sorrowful. A good life always has joy.”

Honourable sister, therefore cast sorrow out of yourself, because just as a moth eats a garment and a worm gnaws wood, so sorrow harms the heart [Col. 1220C]. Cleanse your heart, then, of every carnal and worldly sorrow, and your prayer will be acceptable to God.

Therefore, venerable sister, mourn in remembrance of your sins, but rejoice in love for Jesus Christ, your bridegroom. Weep at the memory of your former offenses, but exult in hope of heavenly goods. Grieve over your past faults and negligences, but rejoice in the promise of the heavenly kingdom. Be sorrowful for your past offenses, but become glad at the joy of eternal recompense. May he deign to lead you to this, he for whom you have prepared a pleasant dwelling in your virgin body. Amen.

XII.—On the love of God

[Col. 1220D]

34. Our Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospel: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). And the apostle John says: “We love God because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Whoever loves God will pray for forgiveness of his or her sins and will restrain himself or herself from them.

Dearest sister, love God and call upon him for your salvation, because love is life and hatred is death. God does not wish to be loved only in words, but with a pure heart and good works. One does not love God who despises God’s commandments. The mind of a person who loves God is not on earth but in heaven, because it continually desires heavenly things.

I urge you, dearest sister, to love God above all things [Col. 1221A], because he himself chose you before the ages. We ought to love God more than our parents. Why? Because God made us and our parents with his own hands—that is, by his own power—as it is written: “He made us, and not we ourselves” (Ps. 99:6). Christ has bestowed greater things on us than our parents have; therefore we ought to love Christ above our parents.

It is foolish to love anything more than God, because one who loves the creature more than the Creator sins. And one who sets love of the creature before love of the Creator goes astray. Therefore God must be loved above all things.

Say, I pray, honourable virgin, with love and affection concerning Christ: “My beloved is mine and I am his, he who feeds among the lilies, until day breathes and the shadows incline” (Song 2:16–17). Bride of Christ [Col. 1221B], I ask you to say it more plainly: “May my beloved be joined to me by the bond of charity and love, and may I be joined and united to him in the reciprocity of mutual affection—he who feeds among the lilies,” that is, who delights and rejoices among the white and fragrant virtues of the saints and among the choirs of virgins, “until day breathes and the shadows incline”: until the clouds of the present life pass away and the day appears—that is, until the brightness of everlasting blessedness comes.

35. Dearest sister, righteousness is to love God with one’s whole heart and to cling to him with one’s whole will, for he is the highest good. To love the highest good is the highest blessedness. Whoever loves God is good; if good, then blessed also. The more a person loves God, the more blessed he or she will be. Love is the special and proper virtue of the saints [Col. 1221C].

Sister most beloved to me in Christ, I have said these things so that no love of the world may separate you from Christ’s love. Bride of Christ, I also ask you to tell us something of the love of your heavenly bridegroom: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he shall remain between my breasts” (Song 1:12).

Tell us more plainly, dearest one, so that we may understand what you say: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me; he shall remain between my breasts.” The place of the heart is between the breasts—that is, between the nipples. Therefore, “my beloved shall remain between my breasts”; that is, the remembrance, affection, and love of Jesus Christ, my bridegroom, shall always be between my breasts, that is, in my heart. And whether in prosperity or adversity, I shall always call to mind [Col. 1221D] all the good things he has bestowed upon me: for he loved me and died for me; he ascended to heaven; and, that I may reach him, he calls me daily, saying: “Come from Lebanon, bride; come, you shall be crowned” (Song 4:8).

“The left hand of Jesus Christ, my bridegroom, is under my head”; that is, may the gift of the Holy Spirit rest in me in this present life, and may understanding of the holy Scriptures be in my mind, so that I may know him and understand him perfectly. “And his right hand shall embrace me”; that is, may it cause me to attain eternal blessedness.

36. Dearest sister, ask the handmaids of Christ who are with you, and say to them: “Strengthen me with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love for Jesus Christ, my bridegroom” (Song of Songs 2:5). O my holy sisters, who now love Christ above all things and set nothing [Col. 1222A] before his love, strengthen me by the examples of your good deeds, and show me how I may find Christ, my beloved, for I grow weak through love of him. This love is sweet; this languishing is pleasant; this weakness is holy; this affection chaste; this union undefiled; this bond inviolate; this embrace unstained. And you, holy sisters, strengthen me with flowers—that is, with the examples of your way of life—for I am weak through love for my bridegroom.

Honorable virgin, you truly languish and grow weak through love for Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, if, for love of him, you despise and reject everything that is in the world. You truly lie weak upon the bed of contemplation through love for Jesus Christ, if you love Christ above all things. You are truly weak through love for Christ if you love heavenly things more than earthly. You truly lie languishing upon the bed of the soul’s love and sweetness because of [Col. 1222B] Christ’s love and affection, if you are strong in holy works and weak in earthly pursuits.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, if you love Christ with your whole heart and set nothing before his love, you shall rejoice with Jesus Christ himself, your bridegroom, in the heavenly kingdom. If you follow Christ with your whole mind and love him with your whole mind, without any doubt you shall rejoice with him in the heavenly homeland, and with the holy virgins you shall follow him wherever he goes. If you cling to Christ with all devotion and sigh after him day and night in this present age, without doubt you shall exult with him in the heavenly palace and sing sweet hymns to him among the choirs of virgins, as it is written:

[Col. 1222C]

> You who feed among the lilies,  
> Surrounded by choirs of virgins,  
> Bridegroom beautiful in glory,  
> Bestowing rewards upon brides.  
>
> Wherever you go, the virgins  
> Follow; and, singing praises after you,  
> They run on,  
> And resound sweet hymns.

(*In the hymn of Virgins, Roman Breviary.*)

I have said this, dearest sister, so that you may love Christ above all things and set nothing before his love. I beseech you, beloved sister, seek no love except Christ and love no beauty except Christ. Mourn for love of Christ; weep for love of Christ, until you deserve to see him reigning at the right hand of [Col. 1222D] his Father. Amen.

## XIII.—On Love of Neighbour

37. Dearest sister, hear what the Lord Jesus Christ says to his disciples: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:35). All believers are Christ’s disciples. Each person is the disciple of the one whose teaching he follows. Therefore, whoever wishes to be Christ’s disciple should strive to love his neighbours as himself. Love of neighbour does no evil. Why? Because “love is the fulfilment of the law” (Rom. 13:10).

And the apostle Paul says: “Walk in love, as Christ also loved you and gave himself for you” (Eph. 5:2). The apostle John likewise says: “He who loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no stumbling-block in him; but he who hates his brother [Col. 1223A] is in darkness and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:10–11). “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar, and truth is not in him. And we have this commandment from God: that whoever loves God should love his brother also. For how can one who does not love his brother whom he sees love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 4:20–21; 2:4.)

Solomon likewise says: “A friend loves at all times,” and, “A brother is proved in adversity” (Prov. 17:17). And blessed Augustine says: “You conquer a human being by human kindness; you conquer the devil by love for an enemy.”

Yet, beloved sister, there ought not to be carnal affection among God’s servants, but spiritual affection. Nothing is more precious to God than the virtue of love. [Col. 1223B] Nothing is more desirable to the devil than the extinction of charity. Holy love has no occasion for offence. Judge every faithful person to be your brother. Remember that one Maker created us. True love has no bitterness of offence.

38. Venerable sister, in love of neighbour you shall learn how you ought to attain love of God. As love raises the mind, so malice sinks it. You can neither truly love God without your neighbour nor your neighbour without God. You possess true charity if you love a friend in God and love an enemy for God’s sake. The more generous you are in love of neighbour, the more exalted you shall be in God’s assembly. If you truly love your neighbour, your heart is at peace. But the person who hates his neighbour [Col. 1223C] is surrounded by darkness; and therefore, by loving your neighbour, you cleanse the eye of the mind for seeing God.

Nevertheless, most reverend sister, I warn you not to love any person carnally. Hence blessed Isidore says: “He is deeply sunk in the earth who carnally loves a mortal human being more than is fitting.” We cannot remain with God if we are unwilling to be of one mind in this world. A friend is proved in adversity. If we wish to keep God’s commandments, we must love our neighbours as ourselves; for if a person loves his brother without pretence, he quickly appeases God the Father. One who loves his neighbour cannot commit murder, adultery, theft, perjury, false witness, robbery, envy, or quarrelling.

[Col. 1223D] Therefore, honorable virgin, let us always meditate upon and carry out in deed love for God and neighbour, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend. But if our neighbour suffers any tribulation, illness, loss, or imprisonment, and we grieve for him, we are in the body of the Church; but if we do not grieve, we have already been cut off from the body of the Church. Charity, which gathers together and gives life to all the Church’s members, if it sees us rejoicing in a neighbour’s downfall, immediately cuts us off from the body. A member suffers so long as it remains joined to the body. But if a member has been cut off from the body, it can neither feel nor suffer. If a hand, a foot, or any member has been cut off from the body, and then the whole body [Col. 1224A] is divided into many parts or cast into the fire, that hand no longer feels, because it has been separated from the body. Such is every Christian who does not grieve at another’s loss, affliction, distress, or need, but—what is worse—rejoices in it: for such a person is already alienated from the body of the Church.

39. But we, honorable virgin, if we wish to preserve true and perfect charity, should love rightly. Let us strive to love all believers as ourselves, so that, because Christ is our head, we may deserve to be his members; and so that, when Christ appears, who is our glory, we may appear with him in glory through the harmony of charity and through love for God and neighbour. A friend is truly loved when he is loved not for his own sake but for God’s. Hence blessed [Col. 1224B] Isidore says: “Whoever loves a friend without restraint loves him more for his own sake than for God’s.”

Each person becomes opposed to goodness and divine justice when he despises a friend struck by some adversity. True friendship is excluded by no circumstance and erased by no time; wherever time may turn, it remains steadfast. Few friends remain dear to the end. That is true friendship which seeks nothing from a friend’s possessions except goodwill alone: namely, that one may freely love the person who loves one.

Therefore, sister beloved in Christ, I exhort you to love your friends in God—that is, in goodness. Love even your enemies for God’s sake, as it is written: “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6:27; Matt. 5:44); and again: “If your enemy [Col. 1224C] is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink” (Rom. 12:20; Ecclus. 25:21); and again: “Bless those who persecute you; bless, and do not curse” (Luke 6:28; Rom. 12:14).

Love is charity’s sister. Charity has never existed without love, nor love without charity. Honorable virgin, love is therefore necessary for us; in it so great virtues consist, and from it so great blessings are born. Love has two wings. The right wing is love of God; the left wing is love of neighbour. No human being can fly to heaven with one wing. Why? Because love of God alone, without love of neighbour, does not suffice to attain eternal blessedness. Prudent virgin, take for yourself these two wings, namely love of God and [Col. 1224D] neighbour, so that you may freely fly by doing good works and reach the homeland of the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

## XIV.—On Compassion

40. Dearest sister, hear what our Lord Jesus Christ says: “All the good things that you wish people to do to you, do them to them” (Matt. 7:12; Luke 6:31). For this is the Law and the Prophets. And Paul says: “Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep” (Rom. 12:15); and again: “Receive the weak; be patient with all” (1 Thess. 5:14). Solomon says: “Whoever despises his neighbour sins” (Prov. 14:21). Keep faith with your neighbour in his poverty, so that you may also rejoice in his prosperity. Remain faithful to your neighbour in time of affliction, so that you may be a co-heir in his inheritance (Ecclus. 22:28–29).

[Col. 1225A] Whoever digs a pit for his neighbour shall fall into it; and whoever prepares a snare for his neighbour shall perish in it (Ecclus. 27:29). Hence the Psalmist says: “He opened a pit and dug it, and fell into the hole that he made” (Ps. 7:16). A person does not love his neighbour perfectly if he does not help him in need. The more we assist our neighbours in need through compassion, the nearer we come to our Creator. We must care for ourselves in such a way that we do not neglect care for our neighbour.

Therefore, beloved sister, do not desire your neighbour to suffer what you do not wish to happen to yourself. Sympathize with the misfortunes of others. Wound yourself with tears over another’s sorrows. Be sorrowful in another’s affliction; be weak with the weak. Thus mourn others’ sorrows as though they were your own: weep with those who weep; mourn with those who mourn [Col. 1225B]; cry with those who shed tears; lament with those who lament. Be toward others such as you wish others to be toward you. Do not do to another what you do not wish to suffer; do not do evil to another, lest you suffer like things yourself.

Be as merciful in others’ faults as in your own, so that you do not judge yourself one way and others another. If your enemy falls, do not rejoice at your adversary’s ruin or exalt yourself. Do not delight in an enemy’s destruction, lest evil perhaps come upon you as well. Do not exalt yourself over an enemy’s downfall, lest God turn his wrath upon you. For evil quickly comes upon one who rejoices in an enemy’s fall. Let there be humane feeling toward the wretched, compassionate sorrow toward the poor, and merciful love toward the beloved. If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him drink.

Do not despise the poor (Prov. [Col. 1225C] 17:5); do not scorn the needy (Prov. 22:22); do not disparage orphans (Prov. 23:10). Let no one receive sorrow from you; let no one depart from you ashamed. Visit the sick and console the faint-hearted, so that you may deserve to be consoled by the Lord in eternal blessedness. Amen.

## XV.—On Mercy

41. Dearest sister, hear Jesus Christ saying in the Gospel: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5:7); and again: “Be merciful, as your heavenly Father also is merciful” (Luke 6:36). And the apostle Paul says: “Be kind and merciful to one another, and clothe yourselves, as God’s elect and holy ones, in holy compassion” (Col. 3:12; Eph. 4:32). “Piety is useful in every respect” (1 Tim. 4:8). And [Col. 1225D] Solomon says: “To do mercy and judgment is more pleasing to God than sacrifice” (Prov. 21:3).

Mercy assigns to each person a place according to the merit of his works. A human being’s compassion concerns himself and his neighbour; but the Lord’s mercy is over all flesh (Ecclus. 18:12). The one who performs mercy offers sacrifice (Ecclus. 35:4). The word *misericordia* (“mercy”) derives its name from compassion for another’s misery. Whoever is not merciful toward another cannot find God’s mercy.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, let mercy and truth go before you. Never abandon mercy. You will do good to your own soul if you are merciful. Whoever has mercy [Col. 1226A] on another shall obtain mercy from the Lord. Venerable sister, hold what you possess for mercy. Show mercy without grumbling. Your work will be such as your intention has been. There is no mercy where there is no goodwill. Do the good you do out of mercy, not for empty glory. Do nothing for praise, but for eternal recompense. Do nothing for temporal reputation, but for eternal reward. Do nothing for fame, but for eternal life. May almighty God deign to bring you to this, most reverend sister. Amen.

## XVI.—On the Examples of the Saints

42. Dearest sister, the examples of the saints greatly assist the conversion or correction of believers. [Col. 1226B] Therefore the falls and restorations of saints are written down, so that we wretched people may not despair because of the multitude of our sins, but may have hope of rising through repentance even after a fall; so that no one may despair of God’s goodness after sin, when he sees that saints too were restored after their ruin. For this reason God set the virtues of the saints before us as examples, so that we may reach the heavenly kingdoms by following their footsteps; or, if we refuse to follow them in doing good, we may be without excuse in punishment.

The holy men of God, so long as they were in this world, did not cease to run in good works: namely, in fasting, vigils, almsgiving, chastity, continence, [Col. 1226C] long-suffering, patience, gentleness, prayers, persecutions, goodwill, hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and many labours for Christ’s name. Holy people despised the present world in order to acquire the eternal kingdom. They did not receive here the promises or the miserable riches of this age, which bring those who misuse them to the torments of hell; rather, leaving this homeland with their whole intention, they raised their eyes toward the heavenly Jerusalem.

Holy people avoided sin in word, deed, thought, sight, hearing, gesture, eyes, hands, anger, feet, quarrelling, fury, dissension, vainglory, pride, [Col. 1226D] self-exaltation, greed, gluttony, sleepiness, fornication, and drunkenness. Guarding their bodies and souls, they fasted in two ways: from vices and from food. Abstinence from food is good, but abstinence from vices is far better.

Therefore the Church says of her members, that is, of these same holy fathers: “My hands dripped myrrh” (Song 5:5). What do we understand by “hands” except the works of the saints? And what is signified by “myrrh” except mortification of the flesh and mortification of vices? The Church’s hands are holy people who do good works, of whom it says: “They worked righteousness” (Heb. 11:33). Therefore the Church’s hands drip the myrrh of good works, because they show us examples of living well and preach that we should [Col. 1227A] mortify the vices of our flesh.

Thus one of them said: “If you live according to the flesh, you shall die” (Rom. 8:13); and again: “Mortify your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3:5). And again the Church says: “My fingers [drip] the finest myrrh” (Song 5:5). Myrrh is truly finest when the flesh is perfectly mortified and vices and sins are extinguished.

43. Therefore, sister beloved in Christ, if we desire the fellowship of the saints, we must follow their examples. If we sin, we now have no excuse for sin. Why? Because God’s law daily admonishes us to live well, and the examples of the holy fathers always invite us to do good. But if at some time we have followed [Col. 1227B] the examples of evil people, why do we not follow the examples of the holy fathers? And if we have been ready [perhaps “eager”] to imitate the evil in doing evil, why should we be slow to imitate the good in doing good?

Venerable sister, let us therefore beseech God that the holy virtues which he prepared for his saints as a crown may not bring us punishment or condemnation, but advancement and salvation. We believe without doubt that if we follow the examples of the saints, after this life we shall reign with them in heaven. The more we read the lives of the holy fathers, if we refuse to follow their examples, the more guilty we are.

Now, honorable virgin, I pray almighty God to give you these virtues of the holy fathers: [Col. 1227C] Christ’s humility, Peter’s devotion, John’s charity, Abraham’s obedience, Isaac’s patience, Jacob’s endurance, Joseph’s chastity, Moses’ gentleness, Joshua’s steadfastness, Samuel’s kindness, David’s mercy, Daniel’s abstinence, and the other worthy deeds of the earlier saints, so that after this mortal life you may reach their fellowship.

44. Virgin of Christ, consider daily by what discipline, what intention, and what compunction Christ’s people pleased God. Hence, in the person of Christ, the Church is addressed in the Song of Songs: “How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince!” (Song 7:1). Christ, by the power of his divinity, is the ruler of all creatures; and [Col. 1227D] therefore the holy Church is called the prince’s daughter, because through Christ’s preaching she is regenerated into new life.

What, then, are the Church’s sandals except the examples of the holy fathers, by which we are protected on the road of this age, so that these sandals may pass through every tribulation? Sister beloved in Christ, we too put shoes on our feet spiritually when we take examples of good living from the holy fathers, so that, in likeness to them, we may overcome this world’s temptations.

Again, in the same Song of Songs, Christ, the Church’s bridegroom, speaks, saying: “I went down into my garden, to see the fruits of the valleys and to observe whether the vines had flowered and the pomegranates had budded” (Song 6:10). The vines flower [Col. 1228A] when children are newly begotten in faith in the churches and are prepared for holy conduct, as for the solidity of good works. The pomegranates bud when perfect people build up their neighbours by examples of good works and renew them in the newness of holy conduct by their preaching and the display of a good life through holy works. Therefore I exhort you, spiritual friend in Christ, to give every person a good example of yourself throughout your whole life.

45. Venerable virgin, I desire that by living well you may shine before all God’s handmaids who are with you in the monastery. For, as blessed Gregory says, those who conceal their good life from others are kindled within themselves but do not serve as examples of light for others. But those [Col. 1228B] who display to others the example of virtues, light by the way of holiness, and light through the word of preaching, are burning lamps, because they show others the way of salvation.

Hence the Lord says: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16); for all glory must of course be rendered to God alone. Virgin of Christ, I nevertheless advise you to ensure that your work is public in such a way that your intention remains hidden.

Therefore, sister most dearly beloved to me in Christ, as I have said above, in all your actions, every work, and every manner of life, imitate the saints and emulate the righteous. Keep before your eyes the examples of the saints; consider them by imitating the examples of the righteous. Set the examples of the righteous [Col. 1228C] before yourself; let the fathers’ examples be incentives to discipline for you. Attend to the saints’ virtue in doing good; attend to living well. Attend to the teachings of the saints. Let no disgrace scandalize your life; let no hostile report make you sad. Learn to burn with a good reputation; have a good testimony; guard your good name. Let no foul odours obscure your good reputation; let no reproaches tear your good reputation apart. Amen.

## XVII.—On Strife

46. The apostle Paul says: “For when jealousy and strife are among you, are you not walking according to man and being carnal?” (1 Cor. 3:3). And Solomon says: “Among the proud there are always quarrels” (Prov. 13:10). [Col. 1228D] “An evil person always seeks quarrels” (Cor. 17:11). An evil angel is sent against him. Whoever goes through dangerous places falls quickly; so one who contends daily with neighbours quickly falls into offence. Gentle people always despise disputes; those who argue and quarrel every day are loved by few people. Therefore peace and concord are loved by everyone; therefore peace and concord are necessary for everyone.

Dearest sister, hear blessed Augustine saying: “Oh, how blameless we might be if we corrected our own faults as diligently as we criticize those of others!” But if we examine ourselves properly, we can find much in ourselves to criticize. [Col. 1229A] I want you to know that nothing is more shameful than disputes among religious persons, who ought through harmony and love to shine in the world like lights in heaven. Strife is customarily produced and arises from envy and detraction.

But if detraction and quarrels are in the cloister, where is regular silence? Where is the holiness of religious life? Where is the silence of the Order? Where is the religious character of the monastery? Where is the bond of charity? Where is the peace of unity, the concord of brotherhood, social love? Alas, alas! Regular silence has perished; the holiness of religious life has been removed; the silence of the Order has failed; the religious character of the monastery has come to nothing; the charity of brotherhood has been annulled.

But if those who ought to live in peace begin to contend, quarrel, and speak ill of one another, where is tranquil life? Where quiet [Col. 1229B] life? Where peaceful life? Where honorable life? Where modest life? Where chaste life? Where contemplative life? Where angelic life? Certainly there can be no whole peace where a slanderous tongue rules; where quarrels and strife rule, perfect religious life cannot exist.

47. See, then, beloved sister, that you do not lose your labours through disputes and strife. Beware lest you lose your days through detraction and quarrelling. Watch yourself carefully, lest through quarrels and contentions you lose the heavenly promises. Be vigilant lest through foolish words you lose eternal joys. Therefore restrain your tongue, and you will be religious; for if you do not restrain it, you will not be religious.

But if perhaps you do not believe me, hear the apostle James saying: “If anyone thinks himself religious and does not restrain his tongue but deceives [Col. 1229C] his heart, that person’s religion is vain” (Jas. 1:26). The tongue is a small member of the human body, but if it is not restrained, it stains and corrupts the whole body (Jas. 3:5–6). For just as a little leaven corrupts the whole lump, and as a small spark of fire burns a great forest, so an unbridled tongue gives offence to everyone—superiors and prelates, equals and companions, subjects and little ones—and provokes them to anger.

If a contentious tongue has no bridle, no one can live in peace with it. A quarrelsome tongue is full of poison; unless it is corrected, it will lead all its companions into offences. Venerable sister, it is therefore good for you to keep your tongue from evil and your lips [Col. 1229D] from speaking deceit.

48. Consider whence you came and to what you came. You left the world and fled to God’s camp, that is, to the monastery. You set aside the riches of the age and came to merit heavenly riches; and therefore you chose poverty. You chose poverty freely, and therefore you ought to consign to oblivion everything that you left for God’s sake. Beware, then, lest you wish to prefer yourself to others. The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things. Renounce gatherings for conspiracy and detraction. Flee grumbling and whispering; do not listen to whispering. Do not lend your ear to grumblers; separate your ears from detractors as from serpents. Flee detractors: like serpents, detractors pour deadly poison [Col. 1230A] into the ears of those who listen to them.

Both the one who speaks ill of another and the one who willingly listens to the detractor sin. Not only does the detractor sin, but also the person who voluntarily listens to him. Honorable virgin, hear what the perfect man in Christ says: “I have not sat with the council of vanity, and I will not enter with those who do iniquity” (Ps. 25:4). Therefore do not sit with the council of vanity, and do not associate with those who speak evil.

Do not contend in any matter; do not strive to fight in any matter. Strife produces disputes; strife extinguishes peace of heart; strife begets quarrels; strife sows wrangling; strife kindles the torches of hatreds; strife breaks concord; strife troubles the eye of the mind, as David says: “My eye is troubled by fury” (Ps. 6:8). Therefore, [Col. 1230B] sister beloved in Christ, I exhort you not to contend in any matter. Do not contend over food, drink, or clothing; but receive without grumbling from the hands of your superiors what they give you; receive without grumbling what your superiors have supplied to you.

If your sister receives better garments than you receive, do not concern yourself about it. If your superior gives you a cheap garment and gives your sister a costly one, do not grumble about this. Whether better garments are given to your sisters while you receive poorer ones, do not contend over it.

49. In no temporal matter choose the better things; do not seek better things among passing possessions; do not desire better things among the [Col. 1230C] world’s goods. Why? Because you did not come for riches but for poverty. You did not come to the monastery to have earthly riches but to acquire spiritual virtues. You did not come to the cloister to shine in costly garments but to serve God in simplicity. You did not come to the Order to appear glorious in clothing before human eyes but to please God through humility. You did not come to the holy community to fulfil your own will but to obey another’s will and despise all earthly things for God’s sake.

Otherwise, it would have been better for you to remain in your father’s house than to seek costly garments in a monastery; it would have been better to have comfort in your parents’ home than to stir up offence among God’s handmaids over earthly [Col. 1230D] and passing things; it would have been better to remain in your own land than to contend, quarrel, or grumble in God’s house over temporal things. Therefore, dearest sister, as I said above, strive to fight in no cause except to please God alone. Amen.

## XVIII.—On Discipline

50. The most wise Solomon says: “Hear, my son, your father’s discipline, and do not forsake your mother’s law, so that grace may be added to your head and a necklace to your neck” (Prov. 1:8–9). “Hold fast discipline, and do not let it go; keep it, for it is your mother” (Prov. 4:13). “Receive discipline, and do not reject it” (Prov. 8:10, 33). “Whoever hates correction is foolish” (Prov. 12:1). Whoever abandons reproof goes greatly astray. [Col. 1231A] Whoever despises discipline sins. Whoever keeps discipline shall find life; but whoever refuses to keep discipline shall find death (Prov. 10:16–17). “Poverty and disgrace shall be his who abandons discipline; but he who accepts correction shall be glorified” (Prov. 13:18). “A fool mocks his father’s discipline, but whoever keeps reproofs is wise” (Prov. 15:5).

A prudent person profits more from a thought expressed by the tongue than a fool does from a hundred blows. A wise and disciplined man will not grumble against one who corrects him (Ecclus. 10:28). Yet correction ought to be moderate. Hence blessed Ambrose says: “One corrected gently shows reverence to the corrector; but one corrected or rebuked cruelly receives neither the rebuke nor salvation.” Those who, because of their weakness, cannot be reproved [Col. 1231B] must be borne with in gentle kindness.

51. Because sinners differ, some must be borne with and others corrected, since the character of sins differs. The prelates of the Church ought to bear their subjects whom they correct, and correct those whom they bear. Thus Solomon caused images of a lion, an ox, and cherubim to be carved upon the bases in the temple of the Lord (3 Kings 7). What do the bases in the temple signify except prelates in the Church? Whoever undertakes the responsibility of governance bears, like a base, the burden placed upon it. *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge.” The cherubim on the bases show that the prelates of the Church ought to be full of heavenly knowledge. The lion signifies the terror of severity; the [Col. 1231C] ox, however, displays the patience of gentleness.

Thus on the bases lions are not represented without oxen, nor oxen without lions, because prelates of the Church ought sometimes to correct their subjects strictly, sometimes gently, sometimes harshly, sometimes by words, sometimes by lashes. For one who is not reformed when corrected with gentle words must necessarily be corrected and rebuked more sharply. Wounds which cannot be healed gently must be cut away with pain. Whoever neglects to amend after private admonition concerning sin must be rebuked publicly; and a wound that cannot be healed secretly must be treated openly. Those who do harm openly must be rebuked openly, so that when they are healed by public reproof, those who sinned by imitating them may be corrected; so that, when one person is reproved, the rest may amend. It is better that one person be condemned for the salvation of many than that many be endangered through one person’s license.

[Col. 1231D] Blessed Gregory also says: “There are many who hear words of rebuke and scorn to return to repentance.” Let everyone hear about God’s kingdom, that he may love it; let him hear about hell, that he may fear it; so that, if he does not come to the kingdom through love, he may at least come through fear. These are Isidore’s words: “The righteous kindly accept correction when they are rebuked for their faults.”

52. Dearest sister, discipline is corrective and must not be despised. Therefore we ought to love our prelates and kindly receive their words, [Col. 1232A] since by their reproofs and corrections they remove from us our self-will and the world’s desires. Hence, concerning these same prelates, the Church—or any faithful beloved woman—says in the Song of Songs: “The watchmen who guard the city found me; they struck me and wounded me; the watchmen of the walls took away my cloak” (Song 5:7).

By the watchmen of the city we understand the prelates who guard the condition of the holy Church. They find the faithful soul, strike it by their preaching, exhortations, and threats, and wound it with love for Christ’s charity. Nor does this suffice them: they also take away its cloak—that is, they remove from it every earthly delight and temporal possession—and send it, naked of sins and stripped [Col. 1232B] of riches, to the heavenly kingdom.

Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, it is very fitting that we love our prelates as fathers, so that we may willingly receive from them the discipline of our salvation, according to David’s counsel: “Lay hold of discipline, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the righteous way” (Ps. 2:12). Therefore, if we do not wish to perish from the righteous way, we must receive discipline. If one who does not receive discipline shall perish from the righteous way, then without doubt one who receives discipline shall be confirmed in the righteous way.

Now, venerable sister, I urge you willingly to receive discipline, so that you may be delivered from God’s wrath and confirmed in the righteous way. Give many thanks to one who corrects you; repay thanks to one who rebukes you. If the abbess [Col. 1232C] or prioress rebukes you for your salvation, do not be saddened. When she shows you the way of your salvation, receive her instruction freely. When anyone shows you the means of your salvation, do not be rebellious. Love those who reprove you for your transgressions; love those who correct you for your negligences; love as mothers those who reprove you for your transgressions.

Do not answer those who correct you with injury. Do not speak insult to those who rebuke you. Do not return evil for good. Do not answer good counsel with quarrels. Do not answer good words with evil. Why? Because whoever loves discipline loves wisdom. Therefore, if you love discipline, you shall be wise. [Col. 1232D] You shall be prudent if you endure reproofs patiently; you shall be patient if you bear corrections humbly.

53. Honorable virgin, it is for this reason that we are corrected in this life by the Lord and by our prelates: that we may not be condemned with this world. It is far better for us to be corrected in this life by our prelates for our negligences than to be condemned in the life to come. It is better for us to be chastised in this age by our superiors for transgressions and faults than to be punished in the age to come. Sister dear to me in Christ, it is better for you to be beaten with whips by the hand of the abbess than to suffer punishments in hell; it is better for you to be scourged in this life by the hand of the abbess or prioress than to be tortured in hell hereafter; it is better for you to be struck with lashes by the hand of the abbess [Col. 1233A] than to be tormented in hell; it is better for you in this world to endure lashes from the hand of the abbess or prioress than to suffer eternal punishments in Gehenna; it is better for you to be temporarily afflicted with rods by the hand of the abbess or prioress than to be burned in eternal fires. May he who redeemed you by his precious blood deign to free you from these. Amen.

XIX.—On Obedience.

54. Dearest sister, hear the words of the Apostle Paul: “There is no authority except from God; and those which exist have been ordained by God. Therefore, whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance” (Rom. XIII.1–2). Therefore we ought not to despise authorities, whether they belong to the world or to the Church, because all are ordained by God. Thus, when through disobedience we oppose our prelates, [Col. 1233B] we wrong God; when through pride and disobedience we rebel against our prelates, we act against God’s commandments; when we are obstinate and disobedient toward our prelates, we despise God, who says: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke X.16)—that is, whoever obeys you obeys me, and whoever despises you despises me. Sister dear to me in Christ, therefore whoever despises her prelate despises God; whoever honors her prelate honors God; and whoever is obedient to her prelate is obedient to God.

The prophet Samuel praises this virtue, namely obedience, saying: “Obedience is better than sacrifice, and to obey better than to offer the fat of rams; for resistance is like the sin of divination, and refusal to comply [Col. 1233C] like the crime of idolatry” (1 Kings [1 Samuel] XV.22–23), that is, refusal to obey. Miriam, Aaron’s sister, through pride and disobedience murmured against Moses her brother, and was immediately struck with leprosy (Num. XII). Miriam, who through disobedience and rebellion murmured against Moses her brother—that is, against her prelate—signifies the soul of any person who murmurs against her prelate, whom she will not obey or accept commands of salvation from. Because she will not receive in obedience the commands of her prelate, she is struck and defiled by the leprosy of sins.
