Likewise Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who rose up against Moses and Aaron through pride, insult, and disobedience, immediately suffered punishments for their presumption [Col. 1233D] (Num. XVI), as is written in the Psalm: “The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered over the company of Abiram”; and again: “Fire blazed up in their assembly; flame consumed the sinners” (Ps. CV.17–18). Likewise King Uzziah, when through pride, disobedience, and obstinacy he took a censer and wished to offer sacrifice contrary to God’s law, was struck by God with leprosy and marked upon his forehead (2 Chronicles XXVI). Likewise King Saul, because he was disobedient, lost his kingdom and fell into the hands of his enemies (1 Kings [1 Samuel] XV). Likewise the prophet Jonah fled through disobedience; a fish swallowed him and cast him into the depths of the sea [Col. 1234A] (Jonah I–II). We must therefore beware lest we dare rise against our prelates in disobedience, lest the Lord should wish to punish us severely through them, since each acts in his stead.

55. Venerable sister, for our salvation God has placed prelates in the Church: that they may provide for us, render an account to God for us, and guard us lest we do evil. Hence the Apostle Paul: “Obey your superiors and submit to them, for they keep watch as those who must render an account for your souls” (Heb. XIII.17). Prelates ought to guard and govern the Lord’s flock with great vigilance and concern. Of them it is read in the Song of Songs: “Sixty strong men surround Solomon’s bed, from among the strongest of Israel; all holding swords and most skilled [Col. 1234B] in war; each one’s sword upon his thigh, because of the terrors of the night” (Song III.7–8).

The true Solomon is understood to be Christ, because he is indeed peaceable, having restored peace between God and humankind. Solomon’s bed is the congregation of the faithful, in which God dwells and rests. Solomon’s bed is surrounded by sixty strong men, namely prelates, who go about and guard God’s Church against vices and against visible and invisible enemies by defending, chastising, rebuking, correcting, and admonishing. They are called strong because the prelates of holy Church are perfect in observing God’s commandments. “All holding swords”: that is, the spiritual word, because through preaching they ought to restrain the vices of their subjects. “Most skilled in war” [Col. 1234C] because they must be trained for spiritual warfare. “Each one’s sword upon his thigh.” The prelates of holy Church hold swords upon their thighs because they ought first to cut away vices in themselves, and then in those subject to them. And they do all this because of the terrors of the night: that is, because of the hidden snares of evil spirits, who especially lie in wait during the night of this age for holy prelates, so that, once these have been deceived, they may be able to defile and stain Solomon’s bed—that is, the congregation of God’s servants.

56. Dearest sister, I have said these things to you so that you may know how devoutly and humbly we ought to obey our prelates. Obedience is the one virtue that implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves them once implanted. [Col. 1234D] Solomon says of it: “Obedience is better than victims” (Eccles. IV.17; 1 Kings [1 Samuel] XV.22), because by victims another’s flesh is slain, whereas by obedience one’s own will is bound. Hence, “An obedient man speaks of victories” (Prov. XXI.28), because one who humbly obeys another’s voice for the Lord’s sake conquers herself in her heart.

Adam fell into hell [Note: [Col. 1233] Understand this with respect to guilt or the debt of sin; otherwise the Fathers’ unanimous opinion is that Adam was saved.] because he was disobedient; Christ, however, ascended into heaven because he obeyed God the Father even unto death (Phil. II.8–9). Just as through Adam’s obedience many were made sinners, so through Christ’s obedience many were made righteous. And just as through Adam’s sin all people are subject to the condemnation of death [Col. 1235A], so through Christ’s righteousness all people are subject to the justification of life (Rom. V.19, 18). And again: just as the disobedience of the first parent produced death, so Christ’s obedience produced life (1 Cor. XV.22).

Therefore, beloved sister, if for Christ’s sake you are obedient to your prelates, you will reign with Christ in heaven. Never speak a harsh word against your mother, that is, the abbess or prioress. Never be rebellious against your prelates; in no matter contradict your superiors. Reverence people of greater learning and better life. Reverence each person according to the merit of her holiness. Give appropriate reverence to the higher rank. Give each person honor according to her dignity. Do not present yourself as equal to a superior rank. Give obedience to your elders [Col. 1235B] and humbly serve their commands. Yield to the authority of your betters; render fitting services to those greater than yourself. Be obedient to all in good commands. O bride of Christ, obey a human being in such a way that you do not offend God’s will. Never obey in evil deeds. Do not obey one who commands you to do evil; do not consent when ordered to do evil. Do not obey any authority in evil, even if punishment compels you, penalties threaten, or tortures confront you. It is better to suffer death than to carry out evil commands; better to be slaughtered by a human being than condemned by eternal judgment. For one who obeyed in order that evil might be done is not without guilt. Therefore, venerable sister, be obedient unto death, and God will give you the crown of life. Amen.

XX.—On Perseverance.

[Col. 1235C]

57. Dearest sister, hear blessed Jerome saying: “In Christians, beginnings or first starts are not sought, but the end and perseverance.” The Apostle Paul began badly but ended well; Judas Iscariot began well but ended badly. Judas’s beginning is praised, but the end of his life is condemned. Hence blessed Gregory: “Perseverance is the fruit of good work. Good is done in vain if it is abandoned before life’s end.” Blessed Isidore also says of this: “God judges a person not by past life, but by that person’s end.” For everyone will be justified or condemned on the day of her death. Hence it is written: “Where I find you, there I shall judge you.”

[Col. 1235D] Likewise blessed Mary Magdalene deserved to see the risen Christ first because she persevered in seeking him (John XX). Thus also it is said in the Song of Songs: “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves” (Song III.1). Therefore, honorable virgin, I urge you to seek that same Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, upon your bed—that is, in repose of mind and tranquil contemplation. Seek him by nights, that is, in this life, sighing toward him and desiring him, so that you may be able to find him perfectly in the life to come and see him reigning upon the Father’s throne. Seek him without ceasing by living well, that you may deserve to see his face in the heavenly kingdom. I ask you, bride of Christ, to say with the prophet David: “My soul thirsted for God, the living fountain: when [Col. 1236A] shall I come and appear before the face of the Lord?” (Ps. XLI.3). Truly your soul thirsts for God if it loves him above all things. Truly your soul thirsts for God if, for love of him, it despises all earthly things. Truly your soul thirsts for God if it longs for him reigning at the Father’s right hand.

The same prophet also admonishes us, saying: “Seek the Lord and be strengthened; seek his face always” (Ps. CIV.4): that is, in prosperity and distress, poverty and abundance, sickness and health, youth and old age. We ought to seek God with our whole mind and whole purpose, that we may deserve to be strengthened by him in holy conduct, and that we may deserve to find and see him in the heavenly kingdom. Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, because none but those of chaste body will be able to be raised to heaven [Col. 1236B] on the day of resurrection, nor will any see the glory of the divine majesty except those who are pure in heart.

58. Beloved sister, believe me: the kingdom of heaven will not be given to the idle and wandering, but to those who ask, seek, and knock. For the Lord says: “Ask, and you shall receive; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. VIII.7; Luke XI.9). Therefore the door of the kingdom must be asked for through prayer, sought through right living, and knocked upon through perseverance in God’s service. It is not enough to begin good things, unless each person also strives to carry through to the end of life what she has rightly begun; for it is better not to know the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back (2 Pet. II.21). Hence the Lord in the Gospel: “No one who puts a hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” [Col. 1236C] (Luke IX.62).

Therefore, venerable sister, through desire for eternal blessedness we must daily knock upon the ears of Almighty God, and not fall away from the good things we have begun, before, with him opening, we deserve to be freed from the prison of this death and arrive at the gate of the heavenly homeland. Sister dear to me in Christ, it is good to persevere in God’s service, for those who return from the monastery to the world become blacker than coals. Those who descend from the monastery into the world become black like cold coals. Why? Because through the torpor of their minds they have died and been extinguished from the fire of God’s love. Hence blessed Isidore:

> “Those who return from a good life to an evil one through desire for the world are darkened, defiled, and blackened by the blackness of vices, and are strangers to the lamp of God’s brightness. Those who flee from the monastery into the world are separated from the fellowship of angels and joined to demons. Those who leave the holy congregation and descend to secular life are removed from God’s fellowship and subjected to the devil’s dominion.”

59. Sister most beloved in Christ, consider what you have done. Daily call to mind whence you came, for what you came, and why you came. For God you left and despised everything that exists in this world, and for love of him chose the monastery. You purchased the kingdom of heaven and gave yourself as its price [Col. 1237A]. Therefore strive with utmost vigilance not to lose the kingdom you purchased, but to possess forever what you desired and hoped for. Take care not to lose the kingdom for which you gave yourself as the price. Hear the Apostle Paul saying: “No one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully” (2 Tim. II.5). The one who labors lawfully is the one who perseveres in good works until the day of death. The one who competes lawfully is the one who perseveres in God’s service without deceit or pretense. The one who serves God worthily is the one who brings the good work begun to completion. The one who toils well in good works is the one who completes what she rightly began.

Hence the Church says in the Song of Songs of her members who persevere in God’s service: “The timbers of our houses are cedar, and our ceilings cypress” (Song I.16). The houses of the Church are gatherings of the faithful who serve God and persevere in matters belonging to God. Cedar and cypress are trees of incorruptible nature; they signify God’s saints, who burn with an untiring and unfading desire for their Creator and persevere in good works until life’s completion. Therefore, venerable virgin, be also a cypress in God’s house by persevering in a good life. You will also be a cedar in God’s house if you give in yourself an example of good life and the fragrance of good conduct to your sisters [Col. 1237B].

60. Prudent virgin, I have said these things so that with your whole mind you may despise love of the world; I have said them so that you may never wish to leave religious life and seek secular life [Col. 1237C]; I have said them so that you may never wish to abandon monastic life and, like a dog returning to its vomit, return to the world. I urge you to persevere in the monastery all the days of your life and never desire secular life. I urge you to love the monastery with the highest desire and set the world aside with all your heart. I urge you to remain at every time in God’s house and never seek to return to the world. Why? Because in the monastery there is the contemplative life; in the world, the laborious life. In the monastery there is holy life; in the world, criminal life. In the monastery there is spiritual life; in the world, carnal life. In the monastery there is heavenly life; in the world, earthly life. In the monastery there is [Col. 1237D] quiet life; in the world, turbulent life. In the monastery there is peaceful life; in the world, quarrelsome life. In the monastery there is tranquil life; in the world, contentious life. In the monastery there is peaceful life; in the world, a life full of disputes. In the monastery there is chaste life; in the world, lustful life. In the monastery there is perfect life; in the world, vicious life. In the monastery there is a life full of virtues; in the world, a life full of vices. In the monastery there is a life of holiness; in the world, a life of iniquity.

61. Revered sister, you have heard the good things that are in the monastery; you have heard the evils that are in the world. You have heard the virtues of the monastery; you have heard the vices of the world. You have heard the salvation of the monastery; you have heard the perdition of the world. You have heard life; you have heard death. Now therefore, behold [Col. 1238A] good and evil before you; behold the soul’s destruction and salvation before your eyes; behold life and death before you; behold fire and water (Ecclus. XV.17–18). Stretch out your hand and choose what you wish. Behold the way of paradise, and behold the way of hell; behold the way that leads to life, and behold the way that leads to death. Walk, therefore, by whichever you choose. I ask only that you choose the better.

—My brother, I shall accept your counsel and choose the better way. It is good for me to accept counsel and, with God’s help, walk by the way that leads to paradise.

—Honorable virgin, because you choose the better way, I give thanks to God. Therefore do not abandon the good life which you have begun to follow. Preserve henceforth the good purpose of your life on every day of your life. Then your work will be perfect if it endures to the end [Col. 1238B]. Salvation is promised to those who persevere; reward is given to those who persevere. The good person is not the one who does good, but the one who does it without ceasing. Therefore, if you persevere in good works until the end of life, you shall be saved.

XXI.—On Virginity.

62. “The prudent virgins took oil in their vessels with their lamps.” Dearest sister, hear what I say. Those who are virgins in mind and body are not foolish but prudent, and they can go out to meet the bridegroom because they have oil in their vessels—that is, chastity in their minds. But those who are virgins in body and not in mind are not prudent but foolish, nor can they go out to meet the bridegroom, because they have no oil in their vessels—that is, they have no chastity in their minds. [Col. 1238C] Thus blessed Isidore says: “A virgin in body and not in mind has no reward in recompense.” And the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the foolish virgins: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. XXV.4, 12).

For this reason, sister dear to me, I urge you to be a virgin in mind and body, so that after this life you may deserve to be placed in the heavenly bridal chamber by Jesus Christ, the heavenly bridegroom. Virginity is not commanded but advised (1 Cor. VII.25–26), because it is exceedingly lofty. The good of virginity is twofold, because in this world it is free from worldly care, and in the future it will receive the reward of chastity. Without doubt, those who persevere chaste and virginal will be equal to God’s angels. Virgins will be happier in eternal blessedness, as Isaiah testifies, saying: “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs: I shall give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I shall give them an everlasting name which shall not perish” [Col. 1238D] (Isa. LVI.4–5). Every sin receives pardon through repentance. But if virginity falls, it is in no way restored; for although one may receive forgiveness through repentance, one never receives back one’s former incorruption.

63. Venerable sister, bodily virginity is of no value where there is no integrity of mind. Virgins who glory in their merits are compared with hypocrites, who seek outwardly the glory of a good work which they ought to have within their conscience. This is what it means in the Gospel for virgins not to have oil in their vessels: that is, not to preserve in conscience the testimony of a good work, but to glory in appearance before human beings, not in heart before God [Col. 1239A]. These are the words of blessed Augustine: “Bodily virginity profits nothing where anger of mind dwells.” There is a great difference between the purity of a virginal soul, defiled by no contamination, and one subjected to the lust of many.

Venerable sister, hear blessed Jerome saying: “It profits nothing to have virginal flesh if someone has married in the mind; nor does it profit to preserve the virginity of a virginal body if she will not restrain her eyes from lust. Virginity in the body will profit nothing if charity or humility has departed from the heart.” Therefore, honorable sister in Christ, I urge you to be a virgin in mind and body. I also urge you to take with you the oil of good works [Col. 1239B], adorn your lamp with good works, and illuminate it with holy virtues, so that when the cry has been made, “Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. XXV.6), you may be able to meet Jesus Christ, your heavenly bridegroom, and be placed by him in the heavenly bridal chamber.

XXII.—On Continence.

64. Dearest sister, I ask you to hear with all devotion the words of this admonition. The thirtyfold number is the first rank and signifies the bonds of marriage. The sixtyfold number is the second rank and signifies the continence of widows. The hundredfold number is the third rank, assigned to virgins for the crown of virginity. Blessed Isidore says: “Some, having lived lustfully in youth, wish to become continent in old age; and then they wish to keep chastity, when lust has disdained to keep them as slaves.” Such people have no reward, because they have had no contest of labor. But glory awaits those whose struggles were glorious. For the fruit of chastity is sweetness. Chastity is the inviolate beauty of the saints. Chastity is security of mind and health of body. Lust weakens the flesh and swiftly carries it, once broken, into old age. Long continence is counted as virginity. [Col. 1239D]

Therefore, venerable sister, the beauty of chastity must be loved. Those who live continent and chaste prepare in themselves a dwelling-place for God. Hence the Apostle: “Those who live chastely are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in them” [Col. 1239C] (1 Cor. VI.19; 2 Cor. VI.16). Continence makes a person near to God. God dwells where continence abides. Chastity joins a person to heaven. Chastity leads a person to the kingdom. The kingdom of heaven is promised to those who live chastely. Those who live chastely will have an inheritance in heaven.

Marital chastity is good, but widowly continence is better; virginal integrity is best. A humble widow is better than a proud virgin. A widow with humility is better than a virgin with pride. A widow mourning her sins is better than a virgin boasting before people of her virginity. A widow weeping for her iniquities is better than a virgin exalting herself because of her merits. A virgin ought not boast before people of the gift of her virginity, for if she does this, she does not have oil with her: her lamp has been extinguished [Col. 1240A]. A virgin ought not despise widows. A virgin who wishes to please God ought not despise women living chastely, because if she does so, she will displease God and harm herself. A virgin who despises women living chastely and serving God acts proudly. Why? Because a humble sinner is better than a proud righteous person.

65. Therefore, venerable sister, do not despise women who came from the world, had husbands, and bore children; for if you despise them, you will be exceedingly guilty before God. Anna the prophetess had a husband, yet she prophesied concerning Christ and deserved to see him (Luke II). Mary Magdalene too was secular, yet she saw the risen Christ and deserved to become the apostle of the Apostles (John XX). Honorable virgin, I have said these things so that you may in no way despise Christ’s handmaids [Col. 1240B] who came from secular life to serve God. Therefore you ought not despise honorable women who came from the world to the monastery, but honor them; for those whom God has deigned to choose you ought not despise. Therefore, venerable sister, I urge you to serve them for Christ’s love and love them as mothers. Sister dear to me in Christ, you ought to serve them as a daughter because God converted them to himself from secular life. Thus you wrong God if you despise God’s handmaids.

But you, sister dear to me in Christ, do not say, “Behold, I am a dry tree”; do not say, “Behold, I am a fruitless tree.” For if you love and fear Christ your bridegroom as you ought, you have seven sons. The first son is modesty; the second, patience; the third, sobriety; the fourth, temperance; the fifth, charity; the sixth, humility; the seventh, chastity. Behold, venerable sister, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, without pain, from an incorrupt womb you have borne seven sons to Christ, so that what is written may be fulfilled in you: “For the barren woman has borne seven” (Jer. XV.9) [Col. 1240C]. Therefore, sister beloved in Christ, you ought to nourish, cherish, suckle, refresh, strengthen, and discipline these sons whom you have borne to Jesus Christ your bridegroom. Nourish them with good habits; cherish them in the bosom of inward contemplation; and give them the breasts of eternal sweetness. Refresh them with the love of heavenly delight and strengthen them with the bread of the heavenly word. Discipline them with the lashes of the fear of God, and command them not to be proud, frivolous, or transgressors, and never to depart or separate themselves from you.

[Col. 1240D] You see, beloved sister, that virgins hold the principal place in God’s kingdom. And not without reason: because they have despised the present world, they have attained the heavenly kingdom. May he, in whose service you consecrated your body and soul, deign to lead you there. Amen.

XXIII.—On Fornication.

66. Sister dear to me in Christ, I urge you to hear with all devotion these words of our Lord Jesus Christ: “Let your loins be girded, and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke XII.35). We gird our loins when we restrain the flesh’s lust through continence. We hold lamps in our hands when we show our neighbors examples of light. [Col. 1241A]

As blessed Isidore says, fornication of the flesh is adultery; fornication of the soul is slavery to idols. The first fornication is the darts of the eyes; the second, of words. But one who is not taken captive by the eyes can resist words. Every unclean defilement is called fornication, although people may enjoy different pleasures of shamefulness. Various crimes arise from the pleasure of fornication; by these the kingdom of God is shut and a person separated from God. Among the other seven vices, fornication is the greatest crime, because through the uncleanness of the flesh it violates God’s temple and, taking Christ’s member, makes it the member of a prostitute. Therefore, honorable virgin, if it is true that God lives in you, let fornication be dead in you. Lust is an enemy of God and the ruin of paternal blessing and property. Fornication [Col. 1241B] stains not only the body but also the conscience. Whoever lives lustfully, though seeming alive, is nevertheless dead. God will judge—that is, condemn—fornicators and adulterers.

Therefore hear, dearest sister, the words of blessed Isidore:

> “To be defiled by fornication is worse than every sin; fornication is greater than all sins. Fornication is a grave sin; fornication surpasses every evil; fornication is more grievous than death. It is better to die than to commit fornication; better to die than to be stained by fornication; better to die than to lose one’s soul through fornication. Lust leads a person to the punishments of hell; lust plunges a person into hell; lust sends a person to Tartarus.”

67. The eyes are the messengers of fornication. Sight is [Col. 1241C] the first occasion of fornication. For the mind is captured through the eyes. Through the eyes the arrow of love enters the mind; the sight of the eyes shoots arrows of fornication. Therefore, sister in Christ, restrain your eyes; accordingly, withdraw your gaze. Do not fix your eyes upon bodily appearance. Do not look at any person with the intention of desiring that person; do not look at any person in order to love that person carnally. Do not look upon a man’s face in order to love him evilly. “Turn away your eyes, lest they see vanity” (Ps. CXVIII.37); do not desire a person’s beauty.

Tell me, venerable sister, what benefit is there in bodily beauty? Does not a person wither like hay, and does not her beauty flee like a shadow? And when death comes, tell me, I ask, [Col. 1241D] how much beauty will remain in the body? When you see the entire body swollen and transformed into stench, do you not close your nostrils so as not to endure the foulest odor? Tell me, then: where is beauty of face at that time? Where are the pleasant words that softened the hearts of listeners? Where then are the sweet speeches that made people glad? Tell me, honorable virgin, where then will immoderate laughter and shameful jesting be? Where then will be vain and useless merriment that moved people to laughter? It has perished and come to nothing; it has vanished like smoke. Such is the end of bodily beauty, the end of the body. Know therefore, venerable sister, that beauty is vain. Hence Solomon also says: “Charm is deceptive, and beauty is vain” (Prov. XXXI.30).

Therefore, sister most beloved in Christ [Col. 1242A], if bodily beauty is vain, if bodily beauty is rot and a worm, if the beauty of the body is ash and earth, beware lest for that reason you look at people and desire their beauty. Why? Because the world passes away, and its desire. Everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes (1 John II.17, 16). Therefore the world, with all things in it, must be despised for Christ’s sake. But you, honorable virgin, who left the world for Christ’s sake, ought not delight in the beauty of people.

68. Therefore I urge you, sister dear to me in Christ, to love Jesus Christ your bridegroom above all things, that you may be able to reign with him in the heavenly court. Certainly, if the desire of fornication delights the mind more than love of chastity, sin still reigns in the person. But if the beauty of chastity delights the mind more than the foulness of fornication, sin no longer reigns in the person, but righteousness reigns. Although a person may be chaste in body, if she is lustful in mind, sin reigns in her heart. Fornication of the heart is slavery to idols. There is also another, spiritual fornication, concerning which the Lord says: “Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” [Col. 1242B] (Matt. V.28). Human beings are subjected to the devil chiefly through the lust of the flesh, more than through the other vices. Chastity is the beauty of the soul, and by this virtue a person is made equal in merits to the angels. Sister dear to me in Christ, believe me: many have fallen through carelessness of the eyes [Col. 1242C] into danger to their souls.

69. *(Question.)* Dear brother, tell me: do you know anyone deceived through the sight of the eyes?

*(Answer.)* O venerable sister, how many I know who have been deceived by sight and sent into the devil’s snare! Yet of those I have heard of, I shall tell you of some. Because Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, went out to see the women of the region, Shechem loved her, seized her, and shamefully violated her virginity (Gen. XXXIV). Thus the unhappy girl, because she heedlessly looked at what she ought not to have looked at, lost her honor and virginity. David likewise, one day standing on the roof of his house, saw a woman and loved her; for love of her he committed adultery and homicide, and [Col. 1242D] thus, deceived, became guilty under God’s law (2 Kings [2 Samuel] XI). Because he heedlessly saw what he ought not to have seen, he contracted a stain for the whole time of his life.

The mighty Samson went down into the land of the Philistines, saw a woman there and loved her, and slept in her lap. But she shaved the hair of his head and delivered him into the hands of his enemies, who immediately gouged out his eyes (Judges XIV–XVI). Thus the unhappy man, because he saw what he ought not to have seen, lost his eyes and fell into peril of body. Know then, beloved sister, how many have fallen through the sight of the eyes into danger to their bodies and souls. Therefore, sister dear to me in Christ, I urge you to make a covenant with your eyes, lest you heedlessly look at what you ought not to see. Beware also lest death enter through the window [Col. 1243A] of your eyes into your soul (Jer. IX.21).

And so, sister most beloved in Christ, as I have already said to you above: if your flesh still assaults you, if lust still tempts you, if desire still invites you, if the memory of fornication still torments you, set before yourself the remembrance of your death. Place the end of your life before your eyes; set before yourself the day of your departure. Set before yourself the torments to come; think daily upon the judgment to come. Let the image of the judgment to come be ever before your eyes. Recall the horrible punishments of hell. Let the heat of Gehenna extinguish in you the heat of lust; let remembrance of eternal judgment shut out the heat of your body; let hell’s unquenchable flame drive from you the memory of fornication. Let the greater heat overcome the lesser heat; let the greater heat conquer the lesser heat. Let the dreadful crackling of the flames drive away love of desire. As one nail drives out another, so the heat of Gehenna often drives out the heat of lust [Col. 1243B]. Venerable sister, I pray Almighty God to grant you true chastity of mind and body. Amen.

XXIV.—On Abstinence.

70. This is perfect fasting: when our outward person fasts, while the inward person prays. Prayer more readily pierces heaven through fasting. Through fasting and prayer the human mind is joined to the Angels and united with God. Fasts are strong weapons against the temptations of demons. Demons are overcome through fasting and prayers. Sister beloved in Christ, do you wish to know by what means lust is most effectively restrained?—My brother [Col. 1243C], I do; and I ask you to show it to me.—Listen then, beloved sister in Christ. Fornication is overcome through fasting; lust is restrained through fasting: when satiety is removed, lust does not rule. Abstinence overcomes the flesh; abstinence restrains the flesh; abstinence breaks the movement of desire; abstinence destroys the power of fornication. Through hunger and thirst lust is destroyed; hunger and thirst overcome lust. A mind wearied by an abundance of food loses the vigor of prayer. As is flesh which does not receive food for a long time, so is the soul which is continually fed on the word of God. Jerome says thus:

> “Fasts ought to be moderate, lest they weaken the stomach excessively, because moderate and temperate food is beneficial to body and soul. A fat belly does not produce a subtle understanding. It is much better [Col. 1243D] to take a little daily than to eat enough rarely. Sparing food, and a belly that quickly becomes hungry, are preferable to fasts of three days. That person fasts well who turns aside from every vice. Abstinence from vices is better than abstinence from foods. Abstinence is not reckoned as such where fullness of the belly follows.”

And blessed Isidore:

> “The person who prepares delicacies for himself in the evening to satisfy his gluttony chews over feasts in his thoughts throughout the whole day. An empty stomach keeps one wakeful in prayer. For one who is full brings on the heaviest sleep; hence we cannot keep watch well when our stomach is filled with food.”

71. Venerable sister, keep your body lean for the desire of the heavenly kingdom, so that you may fulfil what is written in the Psalm: “My soul thirsted for God; [Col. 1244A] how manifoldly my flesh [thirsts] for him” (Ps. 62:2). For the flesh then thirsts for God when it abstains and dries up through fasting. Sister beloved in Christ, believe me: if in this life you hunger and thirst perfectly for God, you will be satisfied with him in the heavenly homeland. Abstinence gives life and kills: it gives life to the soul and kills the body. Abstinence builds virtues in the soul and destroys the vices of the body. With every effort we must despise the gluttony of food; the desire for dishes must be scorned; care for the belly must be avoided. For when the belly is refreshed immoderately, the body is stirred to lust. We ought not to eat in order that the belly may be filled, but that the body may be sustained. Where the belly is filled with food, there the fire of lust is kindled. But the fire of lust does not burn up the body which abstinence disciplines. That rich man [Col. 1244B] clothed in purple, who feasted splendidly every day, because he would not abstain from food in this world, was therefore set among the flames and sought a drop of water, but did not deserve to receive it (Luke 16). Just as through abstinence all spiritual virtues take root and are built up in the soul, so through the pleasantness of foods all vices are nourished and strengthened in the body. No one can attain perfection in the virtues unless he has first subdued in himself the gluttony of the belly. Therefore the three youths did not burn in the fiery furnace, because they were abstinent (Dan. 3). Daniel too was delivered from the mouths of lions because he preserved abstinence from food within himself (Dan. 14). No one can drive the temptations of demons away from himself unless he has restrained within himself [Col. 1244C] the appetite of gluttony.

72. *(Question.)* Dearest brother, I ask you to tell me how I ought to discipline my body through abstinence. *(Answer.)* Beloved sister, you ought so to nourish your body that it does not become proud; and again, so to restrain it that it does not fall. Thus you ought to refresh your flesh that it may serve, and thus to discipline it through abstinence that it may not perish. If you afflict your flesh beyond measure, you kill your fellow citizen; and again, if you refresh it more than is fitting, you nourish your enemy. My most beloved sister, this you must always observe in every abstinence: do not kill your flesh, but its vices. Therefore, sister most beloved to me in Christ, discipline your body through abstinence: fast and abstain from food; keep [Col. 1244D] your face pale, not ruddy; let your face not be red, but pale. Keep your body lean, not fat: let your body not be fat but dry. Do not feed your flesh to the worms. Eat in such a way that you are always hungry; eat in such a way that you always retain hunger: let your belly 847 by no means be filled with food. Hunger and thirst; abstain and grow lean. Believe me, venerable sister: you will not be able to conquer temptations unless you discipline your whole body through abstinence. Lust grows through food and drink. Fullness of food arouses the lust of the flesh: lust is always joined to satiety. The cold of vigils extinguishes the heat of lust. Malignant spirits enter more readily where they see more food and drink. Sister beloved in Christ, as I told you, if [Col. 1245A] you wish perfectly to flee the temptations of the flesh, abstain not only from food but also from all worldly pleasures, so that after this life you may rejoice in heaven with the Angels. Amen.

## XXV.—On Drunkenness

73. My dearest sister, hear the words of our Lord Jesus Christ: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with carousing and drunkenness” (Luke 21:34). The Apostle Paul also, reproving his disciples, says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is lust” (Eph. 5:18). And Solomon: “Wine is a luxurious thing, and drunkenness tumultuous” (Prov. 20:1). “Do not look upon wine when it turns yellow, nor when its colour shines in the glass. For it goes down smoothly, but in the end it will bite like a snake and pour out venom like a serpent” (Prov. 23:31–32) [Col. 1245B]. There is no secret where drunkenness is. Wine has ruined many and led them into danger of body and soul. Wine was created for gladness, not for drunkenness (Ecclus. 31:35). Wherever abundance of food prevails, there lust will rule. Pleasure in lust follows a belly distended with foods and irrigated with draughts of wine. Drunkenness weakens the body and ensnares the soul; drunkenness produces disturbance of mind; drunkenness increases the madness of the heart; drunkenness feeds the flame of fornication; drunkenness so estranges the mind that a person does not know himself: a drunken person is so estranged from himself that he does not know where he is. For many, it is a boast to drink much and not become drunk; the prophet rebukes them, saying: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, and strong men at [Col. 1245C] mixing drunkenness”; and again: “Woe to you who rise early to pursue drunkenness, and to drink until evening, so that you burn with wine” (Isa. 5:22, 11). The prophet Joel likewise cries out: “Awake, you drunkards, and weep; and howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness” (Joel 1:5). He does not say, “You who drink wine from necessity,” but, “you who drink wine in sweetness,” that is, for pleasure. Drunkenness is a mortal crime; drunkenness is a grave sin; drunkenness is reckoned among murders, adulteries, and fornications; drunkenness casts a person out of the kingdom of God; drunkenness drives a person from paradise; drunkenness plunges a person into hell. Noah drank wine and uncovered the genitals which he had concealed for six hundred years (Gen. 9:21). [Col. 1245D] Lot likewise, made drunk with wine, slept with his daughters, yet did not perceive the sin, because he was estranged from himself (Gen. 19:32–36). Consider therefore, beloved sister, how greatly drunkenness must be detested and fled by all servants of God.

74. *(Question.)* My brother, is it a sin to drink wine? *(Answer.)* Venerable sister, it is not a sin to drink wine temperately, that is, with sobriety. For the Apostle Paul says thus to his disciple Timothy: “Drink a little wine for your stomach’s sake and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5:23). Hear also what Solomon says: “Wine drunk in measure is health for soul and body” (Ecclus. 31:36). Immoderate wine is poison. Wine without measure overcomes the mind; through much [Col. 1246A] wine the mind is weighed down. Through wine lust grows; through wine lust is aroused; through much wine lust is nourished. For God gave us wine for gladness of heart, not as a gift for drunkenness. Therefore, honourable virgin, let us drink not as much as gluttony demands, but as much as necessity requires. Let us beware lest we reckon to the vice of gluttony that which God has granted us as a remedy for the body; let us beware lest we turn into an instrument of vice the wine which God gave us for bodily health; let us beware lest we transform the medicine of the flesh into the vice of drunkenness. Many have been taken captive by demons through wine, and drunkenness is nothing other than a most manifest demon. You therefore, sister beloved in Christ, drink wine temperately, and it will be health for your body and gladness for your mind. Drink wine [Col. 1246B] with sobriety, and it will take away from you sluggishness and idleness, and make you diligent 848 and devout in God’s service. Why? Because wine drunk temperately makes a person diligent in prayer and keen in God’s service. Therefore, dearest sister, if you listen to me as to your brother and do all these things as I have said, you will be wise.

## XXVI.—On Sin

75. Dearest sister, hear the Lord saying in the Gospel: “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34). Sin is committed in two ways: namely, either from the love of desire or from fear; while a person either wishes to have what he desires, or fears lest he incur the evil which he fears. Sin is committed in the heart in four ways, and likewise carried out in deed in four ways. Sin is committed in the heart by the suggestion of demons, the delight of the flesh, the consent of the mind, and the defence of pride. It is also committed in deed sometimes secretly, sometimes publicly, sometimes by habit, sometimes through despair. Thus in these ways we sin in heart and perpetrate sin in deed. Sin is committed in three ways: through ignorance, through weakness, and through deliberation—that is, knowingly. Eve sinned through ignorance in paradise, as the Apostle says: “The man was not deceived, but the woman was deceived” (1 Tim. 2:14). Adam therefore sinned deliberately, but Eve through ignorance. But one who is deceived does not know to what [Col. 1246D; alternatively, “what”] he consents. Peter sinned through weakness when, through fear of the serving-maid, he denied Christ (Matt. 26). To sin through weakness is more grave than to sin through ignorance; but to sin through deliberation is far more grave than to sin through weakness. One who sins publicly also sins more grievously than one who sins in secret. One who sins publicly sins doubly, because he both sins and shows others how to sin.

76. It is already some part of righteousness for a person to know his own iniquity and to feel shame in himself for his own sins. It is better not to sin through love of God than through fear of hell. It is also better not to sin than to correct sin. Everyone who sins is proud [Col. 1247A]. For the person who does forbidden things despises the divine commandments. Hear then, dearest sister, what I say; hear what I urge: through one evil many goods perish. Guard your soul from sin: one who has sinned in one matter has become guilty of all; through one sin many righteous deeds perish. Do not incline your heart to that in which the body delights. Do not give your soul into the power of the flesh; do not consent to fleshly pleasure. Venerable sister, if you live according to the flesh, you will die. Cleanse therefore your conscience from every sin: let your mind be pure, and let your body also be cleansed from every iniquity. Let your body be unstained; let no stain of sin remain in your heart. The body cannot be corrupted unless the mind has first been corrupted. If the soul slips, [Col. 1247B] the body is immediately ready to sin. The soul goes before the flesh; in wrongdoing the soul is the first to go into sin. The body can do nothing except what the mind wills. Cleanse therefore your heart from iniquity, and your flesh will not sin.

77. *(Question.)* My brother, I ask you to tell me whether the soul of a sinful person is foul and black, or whether the soul of a righteous person is beautiful or fair. *(Answer.)* Sister beloved in Christ, there are three things in this world blacker and worse than every evil: namely, the soul of a sinner persisting in sin, which is blacker than a raven; the evil angels who seize it on the day of its death; and hell, into which it is cast. There are no things fouler or blacker than these three in this world. Again, there are three things than which there are none better: [Col. 1247C] namely, the soul of a righteous person persisting in good works, which is beautiful as the sun; the holy Angels who receive it on the day of its death; and paradise, in which it is placed. Among created things there are none better than these three. The holy Angels present the soul of the righteous person before God, saying: “Behold him whom you chose, Lord, and received; he has always dwelt in your courts” (Ps. 64:5). Sister beloved in Christ, if you cleanse your mind from all iniquity and persevere in the service of God, as you promised, you will without doubt rejoice in the heavenly bridal chamber with Jesus Christ, your bridegroom. Amen.

## XXVII.—On Confession of Sins and Repentance

[Col. 1247D] 78. A person begins to be righteous when he begins to accuse himself of his own sins; hence it is written: “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning” (Prov. 18:17). Nothing, however, is worse than to know one’s fault and not bewail it. Every sinner ought to weep for his sins in two ways: first, because through negligence he did not do good; second, because through boldness he committed evil. He did not do the good which he ought to have done, and he did the evil which he ought not to have done. That person does worthy repentance who laments past sins and does not again commit deeds requiring lamentation. For one who laments sin and commits sin again is like one washing an unbaked brick: the more he washes it, the more mud he makes. Thus, when a person able to sin repents and, while living, reforms [Col. 1248A] his life from every crime, without doubt, when death comes upon him, he will attain eternal rest. But one who lives badly and repents at death: as his condemnation is uncertain, so too is his forgiveness doubtful. Therefore, whoever wishes to be secure at death concerning pardon should repent while healthy and lament his sins while healthy. Since God’s mercy is hidden, it is necessary to weep without ceasing. Dearest sister, hear the words of blessed Isidore: “A penitent ought not to have confidence concerning his sins.” Why? Because confidence produces negligence, and negligence often leads an unwary person back to former sins.

79. Therefore now, dearest sister, accept my counsel, and amend your life while you can. While God gives you opportunity, disclose your sins; while space is granted you, weep for your sins. While you can, repent; while you can, confess your sins; while you still live, mourn your sins. Let the summons of those who are dying be your correction. While you can, amend the evils you have done; while you can, draw yourself away from sin and vice; while there is time, cry to God for yourself; while you still live in the body, obtain for yourself pardon of your sins. Before the day of death comes upon you, repent; before the pit swallows you, repent; before hell seizes you, mourn your sins; before you are plunged into the depths of hell, lament your negligences—where there is no longer a place for pardon, where there is no longer joy, no permission to repent, where there is no longer an opportunity for amendment, [Col. 1248C] where there is no longer a place for confession. Why? Because in hell there is no redemption. Although you are a sinner, nevertheless through repentance you will have pardon. No fault is so grave that it does not receive pardon through repentance. Despair increases sin; despair is greater than all sins; despair is worse than every sin. Therefore, beloved sister, believe with complete certainty that there is hope in confession. Do not doubt in any way; do not in any way despair of God’s mercy. Have confidence in confession because of God’s goodness.—Dearest brother, you speak well; you give me good counsel.

80. Alas for me, a sinner; alas for me, wretched one! Into so many sins, so many crimes, so many negligences [Col. 1248D] have I fallen! What shall I lament first? What shall I weep for first? What shall I mourn first? Wretched that I am, what mourning shall I take up first? Unworthy that I am, what tears shall I pour out first? Memory is not sufficient to recount the deeds of so many crimes. O tears, where have you withdrawn yourselves? O tears, where are you? Where are you, fountains of tears? I beseech you, stir yourselves to my weeping: fountains of tears, flow over my face, moisten my cheeks, grant me bitter lamentation. Help me, my God, before I die, before death overtakes me, before hell seizes me, before flame burns me, before darkness enfolds me. Aid me, my God, before I come to torments, before the fire of Gehenna devours me, before I am tortured without end in hell. My God [Col. 1249A], what shall I do when your dreadful judgment comes? What shall I answer when the examination of your judgment comes? What shall I say, wretched and sinful as I am, when I am brought before Christ’s tribunal? Woe to the day on which I sinned! Woe to the day when I did evil! Woe to the day when I transgressed God’s commandments! 850 Would that the sun had not shone upon me! Would that the sun had not risen over me! O detestable day, abominable day, O day not to be named at all, which brought me forth into this world and opened for me the confines of the womb! It would have been better for me not to have been born into this world than to be tortured perpetually in hell; it would have been better for me not to have been begotten than to suffer the eternal punishments of Gehenna; it would have been preferable for me not to have been brought forth in this world than to suffer eternal evils. [Col. 1249B] Weep over me, heaven and earth; mourn for me, all creatures; and you that can possess the sense of life, pour out tears over me. For I have sinned grievously, I have sinned unhappily, I have sinned wretchedly: my sins are innumerable. I freely promised that I would live well; but I never kept the good things which I promised. I always returned to my sin; I always multiplied my sins; I always repeated my offences; I never changed my conduct for the better; I never ceased from evil deeds.

81. Pray to the Lord for me, holy men; intercede with the Lord for me, all saints. All souls of the righteous, intercede for me, if perhaps God may have mercy on me, if perhaps he may take away my iniquities. O my wretched soul, who will pity you? Who [Col. 1249C] will comfort you? O wretched soul! O soul, who will give lamentation for you? Where are you, guardian of humankind? Where are you, redeemer of souls? Where are you, good shepherd? Why have you despised me? Why have you turned your face away from me? My God, do not forget me unto the end. Do not abandon me forever; do not abandon me into the power of demons. I am sinful, I am unworthy; nevertheless, I flee to you, my God. You are merciful; you are compassionate; you are abundant in mercies. You despise no one, detest no one, refuse no one mercy. Lord, show your mercy in me. I beseech you, Lord, do not deny me what you have mercifully given to many. I do not defend my crimes; I do not conceal my sins. The evil I have done displeases me. [Col. 1249D] Wretched that I am, I have sinned. I confess my error, make known my fault, acknowledge my iniquity. I have sinned; my God, be gracious to me, a sinner. Spare my evils; forgive my sins; pardon my crimes, Lord. “If you observe iniquities, Lord, who shall stand?” No one will stand before your judgment, nor will even the righteousness of the righteous person be secure. For what righteous person dares call himself without sin? No human being is without sin; no one is clean from offence; no one is clean in your sight; behold, among the saints no one is unstained. Behold, those who served God were not steadfast, and in the Angels iniquity was found; the stars are not clean before you, the heavens are not clean in your sight (Job 25:4–5; 15:14–15; 4:17–19; and 14:1–2, 4). Therefore, if no one [Col. 1250A] is holy in your sight, no one unstained, how much more I, a sinner, rot and a worm, a daughter of human beings, who drank iniquities like water and multiplied my sins; who sit in dust, who dwell in a house of clay, who have an earthly foundation. My God, stretch out your right hand to me, a sinner.

82. Remember, I beseech you, Lord, what my substance is. Remember, Lord, that I am earth; remember that I am ashes and dust. Grant the medicine by which I may be healed; bestow the medicine by which I may be cured. Wretched that I am, I have fallen into the pit of my sins; unworthy that I am, I have fallen into the depths of hell. My God, free my captive soul from hell: let not the deep shut me in, let not hell swallow me, [Col. 1250B] let not the pit press its mouth over me, let not the abyss deny me an exit. Behold, the fearful day is now imminent; the last day has now come; the day of death is now near. Nothing remains for me but the grave mound, nothing but the tomb. Spare me, Lord, before I go to the land of darkness; aid me, my God, before I go to the land of misery and darkness (Job 10:20–22). Redeemer of souls, help me before I die; loose the bonds of my sins before I come to death.

83.—Sister beloved to me in Christ, may God have mercy on you and forgive you all your sins; may God grant you pardon for your offences; may God pardon whatever you have sinned; may God wash you from every sin. Therefore now do what is fitting: resolve [Col. 1250C] in your heart that you will sin no more; determine in your heart that you will do evil no more. Beware of repeating your faults; do not defile yourself after sin; after the mourning of repentance do not return to sin; 851 do not again do what you must again lament. That person is not penitent but a mocker who still does deeds for which he must repent. He does not seem humbly to entreat God but proudly to mock him, who still does the evil for which he has already received repentance. Hence blessed Isidore says: “Repentance which a subsequent fault defiles is vain”; and again: “A repeated wound is healed more slowly.” One who frequently sins and weeps scarcely deserves pardon. Be therefore steadfast in repentance. Do not abandon the good life which you have begun to maintain. Salvation [Col. 1250D] is granted to those who persevere. Hence it is said: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do righteousness at all times” (Ps. 105:3); and again: “He who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13). Honourable virgin, I urge you always to bear shame in your countenance from the recollection of sin; bear modesty in your face from the memory of transgression. Through shame for sin, blush to raise your eyes. Walk with downcast face, sorrowful in grief; go with a cast-down expression. Let haircloth and ashes enfold your limbs; let haircloth cover your body. Let the earth be your bed; let the ground be your couch. You are dust: sit in dust. You are ashes: sit in ashes. Be always weeping, always mourning, always sending forth sighs of the heart; let compunction always be in your heart. Let lamentation be in your breast, groanings in your [Col. 1251A] heart; let tears flow frequently from your eyes; always be ready for tears.

84. Venerable virgin, believe me: servants of God ought never to be secure in this life, even though they are righteous. Servants of God must always keep watch and recall their sins with tears. Hence, in praise of the Bridegroom, namely Christ, it is said in the Song of Songs: “His locks are like the loftiness of palm trees, black as a raven” (Song 5:11). What do we understand by Christ’s locks except faithful people, who, while they keep the faith of the holy Trinity in their mind and, cleaving to God, do what they believe, like hairs upon that wise head confer honour upon him? The palm indeed prospers by growing upward and, by its signification, displays victory. Christ’s locks therefore are like the loftiness of palm trees, because all the elect, while they always raise themselves to the heights of virtues, are at times brought through God’s grace to victory. But they are black as a raven because, although they raise themselves to heaven by virtues, they nevertheless always recognize themselves to be sinners. So you also, sister most beloved to me in Christ, although you live well and religiously, although you serve God justly and devoutly, I nevertheless urge you never to abandon tears. Therefore, if you wish to wash away the stains of your sins, always love tears. Let tears be sweet to you; let mourning and grief always delight you; never abandon mourning and grief. Be as inclined to lamentation as you were inclined to fault; let your devotion to repentance be as great [Col. 1251C] as was your intentness upon sinning. The remedy must be applied according to the weakness; grave sins require great lamentations. Venerable sister, may he whom the Angels adore in the heavenly court deign to help and console you in this present life. Amen.

## XXVIII.—On Communion

85. “Whoever eats the bread and drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord.” That is, he will incur sin and stain for himself. Why? Because he approaches a good thing badly. “But let a person prove himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup.” As though he said: Let each person consider his life and cleanse his heart of every malice, so that he may be able worthily to approach so great a Sacrament. For whoever eats and drinks the Body and Blood of the Lord unworthily [Col. 1251D] “eats and drinks judgment to himself” (1 Cor. 11:27–29), namely, the cause of his own condemnation. Hence blessed Isidore also says:

> “Those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease to communicate, thinking that they can be cleansed from sins by such communion, should know that this does not profit them for cleansing, as the prophet says: ‘What is it that my beloved has done in my house, committing many crimes? Will holy flesh take away your evils from you?’ (Jer. 11:15). Therefore, whoever wishes to receive Christ’s body should first strive to remain in Christ’s faith and love. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘He who eats my flesh [Col. 1252A] remains in me, and I in him’ (John 6:57). As though he said: He remains in me who fulfils my will in good works. Otherwise, unless he first remains in me through faith and good action, and I in him, he cannot eat my flesh or drink my blood. What then do people eat? Behold, all plainly receive the Sacraments of the altar frequently; but one person eats Christ’s flesh spiritually and drinks his blood, while another does not, but receives only the Sacrament—that is, Christ’s body under the Sacrament—and not the reality of the Sacrament. This Sacrament is called Christ’s own body born of the Virgin, but the reality is Christ’s spiritual flesh. The good person therefore receives both the Sacrament and the reality of the Sacrament; but the evil person, because he eats unworthily, as the Apostle says, eats and drinks judgment to himself, not first proving himself nor discerning the body of the Lord. What, then, does the sinner eat and drink? Certainly not the flesh and blood spiritually for his salvation, but judgment for his condemnation, although he appears with the rest to receive the Sacrament of the altar. Thus one receives the Lord’s body for salvation, another for condemnation. The person who receives the Lord’s body with Judas the betrayer is condemned with Judas; the one who devoutly and faithfully receives it with Peter and the other faithful is without doubt sanctified in Christ’s body with Peter and the other Apostles.”

Hear therefore, bride of Christ, the words of blessed Augustine:

> “Whoever comes with a chaste body and clean heart, with a pure conscience and devout mind, to this communion of the altar, will attain, by a blessed passage, to that altar which is Christ in heaven before the eyes of God.”

[Col. 1252C] 86. Sister beloved in Christ, I ask you to heed the serpent’s prudence. For when a serpent begins to go to drink, before it comes to the spring it vomits out all its venom. Therefore, dearest one, imitate this serpent in this respect: before you come to the spring—that is, to communion in the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—vomit out every venom from your heart: namely, hatred, anger, malice, envy, evil will, and harmful thoughts. Forgive also all your companions and all your neighbours whatever they have sinned against you, so that your sins may be forgiven you by God, as the Lord himself says: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). Thus, if you do all these things as I have said, you will be able to approach the living spring, that is, Christ, who is the source of all goods. [Col. 1252D] He also says of himself: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven” (John 6:51). David says of this bread in the Psalms: “Man ate the bread of Angels” (Ps. 77:25). Otherwise, that food, although it came from heaven, and that drink, because it was bodily, were not suitable for Angels; but certainly the bread and drink which were prefigured through them were suitable. Christ indeed is the bread of Angels, and this Sacrament is his true flesh and true blood, which a person eats and drinks spiritually. Thus, that by which Angels live in heaven is that by which a person lives on earth, because everything in what a person receives is spiritual and divine. But, as the Apostle says, some in the wilderness ate the same spiritual food and nevertheless died (1 Cor. 10:3–5). So also now in the Church the Lord’s body is life for some, while for others [Col. 1253A] it is punishment and the penalty of sin. The Lord’s body is without doubt life for those to whom Christ is life; but it is death for those who through fault, ignorance, and negligence are members of the devil.

87. Therefore, sister most beloved to me in Christ, I urge you, when you receive the Lord’s Body, to understand something other by tasting than you perceive by smell. Hear also, honourable virgin, what the priest says in the consecration of Christ’s body. “We ask,” he says, “that this offering be made ‘blessed,’” through which we may be blessed; “‘enrolled,’” through which we may all be enrolled in heaven; “‘ratified,’” through which we may be numbered among Christ’s inward parts; “‘reasonable,’” through which we may be stripped of brutish understanding; “and that you may deign to make it ‘acceptable,’” so that, through that by which we are displeasing in ourselves, we may be acceptable in his only Son Jesus Christ. Therefore, honourable virgin, as has already been said above, Christ feeds the holy Angels in heaven in himself; Christ also refreshes all the faithful on earth in himself. Christ satisfies the holy Angels in their homeland by sight; Christ feeds us on earth by faith, lest we fail on the way. Christ [Col. 1253B] refreshes Angels and humans from himself, yet remains whole in himself. How good and wonderful is that bread, by which Angels are satisfied in heaven and people are refreshed on earth! The Angel eats it with full mouth in the homeland; the pilgrim human being eats that same bread in his measure, lest he grow weary on the way. Christ, the living bread, who is the refreshment of Angels, is himself the redemption and medicine of human beings. Therefore now, dearest sister, entreat the Lord with your whole mind that he may cleanse your conscience of all malice, so that you may be able worthily to receive the mysteries of the Body and Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## XXIX.—On Thought

88. Dearest sister, hear what the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “Remove the evil of your thoughts from before your eyes” (Isa. 1:16). Although a person ceases from an evil deed, nevertheless, if he has an evil thought in his heart, he is not without guilt. Hence blessed Isidore: “We sin not only in deeds, but also in thoughts, if we delight in them when they occur unlawfully.” For as a viper is killed by its offspring still enclosed in its womb, so our thoughts, nourished within us, kill us, because they consume our soul with viper’s venom. Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, I urge you to guard your heart with every care, since there is the beginning of good or evil work. Hence it is written: “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it life proceeds” (Prov. 4:23). Hear also, I ask, honourable virgin, what the Bridegroom says in praise of the Church in the Song of Songs: “The locks of your head are like royal purple bound in channels” (Song 7:5). The locks of the head of the Church [supplied: “signify”] the little bed of the holy soul and [supplied: “are”] said to be like royal purple bound in channels. Purple, indeed, is bound in bundles in channels; when water is poured over them, it runs through channels to the garment above, so that the garment may be dyed. From this it received its name: *purpura* is called “purple” because it is dyed with a purple colour. All these things are fitting for the holy mind. For the locks of the head are the thoughts of the mind; they are bound in channels because they are restrained in the divine Scriptures, lest they flow away uselessly.

89. Therefore guard your heart, venerable virgin, against harmful contamination; let no shameful thought steal upon your mind; let your mind be pure. For God examines not only the flesh, but also the mind: the Lord judges the consciences of men; God the Judge judges the soul even concerning its thoughts. When an evil thought tickles you, do not consent to it; do not allow an evil thought to remain in your heart. At whatever hour an evil thought comes, cast it out. As soon as the scorpion appears, [Col. 1254B] crush its head; crush the serpent’s head—that is, the head of the evil thought. Correct the fault where it is born, namely in the heart: drive the head of the perverse thought from your heart. Sin [perhaps: “you sin”] where you do not know God to be. For nothing is hidden before God. He who made hidden things sees what is secret. The Lord is present everywhere; the Spirit of God fills all things; the majesty of almighty God penetrates all the elements: no place is outside God; the Lord knows the thoughts of men.

Beloved sister, do you wish never to be sad?—My brother, I do.—Then live well. If you live well, you will never be sad. A secure mind bears sadness lightly; a good mind always possesses joy. For if you persevere in a good life, sadness will depart from you; if you persevere in holiness, [Col. 1254C] sadness will not meet you; if you live rightly and devoutly, you will fear neither stroke nor death. But the conscience of sinners is always in punishment. A guilty person is never secure: for a mind conscious of evil is agitated by its own stings.

Venerable sister, hear what the Lord says concerning the woman and the serpent: “She herself shall crush your head” (Gen. III, 15). The serpent’s head is crushed when the fault is corrected where it is born. May almighty God cleanse your heart from every evil contamination, so that you may serve him without stain. Amen.

XXX. — On Silence

90. The prophet Isaiah says: “The service of righteousness is silence and security for ever” (Isa. XXXII, 17). And again David asks in supplication, saying: [Col. 1254D] “Set, O Lord, a guard upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. CXL, 3). The holy fathers, guarding silence with the greatest vigilance, laboured to be free for contemplation and to see how sweet and pleasant the Lord is; laying aside the concerns of the active life, they devoted themselves to the contemplative life.

Dearest sister, reject dishonourable words; flee indecent talk. Idle speech quickly pollutes the mind, and what is gladly heard is easily done. Let nothing ever proceed from your mouth that can hinder you; never say anything unfitting. Let nothing proceed from your lips that offends the hearer’s ears; flee the foulness of speech. Idle speech displays an empty conscience; the tongue reveals the conscience; the tongue [Col. 1255A] reports a person’s conscience. As one’s speech is shown to be, so one’s disposition is proved to be: for the mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart. Therefore restrain your tongue from idle speech; hold your tongue back from an idle word. Do not tell shameful tales; do not chatter empty words. Idle speech will not be without judgment. Each person will render an account of his words (Matt. XII, 34–37; Luke VI, 45). On the day of judgment, each person’s words will stand before his face.

Let the things you say be worthy of seriousness and instruction. Let your speech be irreproachable; let not your tongue destroy you or condemn you. Do not say what an adversary may receive to your shame. Let silence be your friend. Set a guard upon your mouth; put a seal upon your lips; place the bars of silence upon your tongue. Know at what time you should speak; consider at what hour you should talk. Speak at a fitting time; be silent at a fitting time. Be silent until you are questioned; let the question open your mouth. Let your words be few; do not exceed the measure of speech. Much speaking does not escape fault; verbosity does not avoid sin (Prov. X, 19). A talkative virgin is foolish; a wise virgin uses few words. Wisdom makes speech brief; to speak much is folly. Therefore let there be measure in your word and a balance in your speech. Do not exceed the proper limit of speaking. Venerable sister, may he who chose you as his bride deign to set a guard upon your mouth.

XXXI. — On Lying

91. Liars cause even those who speak truth not to be believed. Every kind of lie must be avoided with the greatest care, although there is a certain kind of lie of lighter fault—for example, if someone lies for the safety of human beings. But because it is written, “A lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. I, 11), perfect persons flee even this kind of lie with the utmost care, so that they may neither defend anyone’s sins through their deceit nor harm their own soul while wishing to help another’s body. Yet we readily believe that this kind of lie is forgiven.

Dearest sister, I exhort you to flee every kind of lie with all your strength. Neither on an occasion nor from deliberate purpose speak falsehood; do not seek to lie, not even in order to help someone. Do not defend another’s life by a lie. No lie is just; every lie is sin in all cases; everything [Col. 1255D] that departs from truth is iniquity. The laws of the world condemn deceivers; the laws of the world punish liars. If lying is condemned among human beings, if falsehood is punished by human judgment, how much more before God, who is witness of words and deeds, before whom every person will render an account even for an idle word, and before whom each will suffer punishment even for idle speech (Matt. XII, 36, 37)? “You will destroy those who speak a lie” (Ps. V, 7), and a false witness shall not go unpunished.

Venerable sister, therefore turn aside from lying; do not speak falsehood. Speak what is true; never lie. Be truthful; deceive no one by lying. Do not say one thing and do another. Beloved sister, may God grant you to speak truth. Amen.

XXXII. — On Perjury

[Col. 1256A]

92. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Do not swear by heaven, for it is God’s throne; nor by the earth, for it is his footstool; nor by your head, because you cannot make one hair upon it white or black. But let your speech be, Yes, No. What is more than this is from evil” (Matt. V, 34, 37). Just as one who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not desire to swear cannot commit perjury. By whatever verbal artifice anyone swears, nevertheless God, who is witness of the conscience, takes it in the sense in which the person to whom the oath is sworn understands it. We ought not to fulfil an evil act which we have sworn to perform.

Venerable sister, do you wish me to tell you how you will never commit perjury?—Never swear. If you do not swear, you will never commit perjury. If you fear perjury, [Col. 1256B] never swear; forbid oaths to yourself also; remove the habit of swearing. For it is dangerous to swear: the practice of swearing produces the habit of perjury; the practice of swearing leads a person to perjury. Let “Yes” be in your mouth; let “No” be in your mouth. Truth has no need of an oath; trustworthy speech holds the place of a sacrament. Let the faith of your oath also be firm. Most beloved sister, may the Holy Spirit, who has made your virginal body his temple, place upon your mouth the seal of moderation. Amen.

XXXIII. — On Detraction

93. Sister beloved to me in Christ, hear what I say, listen to what I exhort, attend to what I speak. Detraction is a grave vice; detraction is a grave sin; detraction is a grievous condemnation; detraction is a great crime. All rebuke the detractor; all blame the slanderer; all dishonour one who speaks ill of another. And the prophet David says: “Him who secretly detracted from his neighbour, I persecuted” (Ps. C, 5). This is utter disgrace; nothing is more foul. Those who slander bark like dogs; as dogs gnaw the feet of passers-by, so slanderers gnaw the lives of their neighbours. Dogs are accustomed to bite people and tear apart passers-by with a deadly tooth.

Venerable sister, therefore cut from your tongue the vice of detraction. Do not gnaw at another’s life; do not censure another’s life; do not tear apart another’s life; do not defile your mouth with another’s evil. Do not speak ill of a sinner, but grieve with them. What you criticize in another, fear rather in yourself; [Col. 1256D] what you rebuke in others, correct in yourself. With as much care as you criticize another’s life, with that same care correct yourself. When you speak ill of another, examine yourself; when you bite another, rebuke your own sins. If you wish to speak ill, speak ill of your own sins. Do not scrutinize the sins of others, but your own. Do not attend to others’ vices, but to your own. You will never speak ill of others if you look well to yourself. Therefore be concerned for your own amendment; be attentive to your own correction and salvation.

Do not listen to slanderers. Give no hearing to whisperers. Slanderers and their hearers are held guilty by an equal charge; equally culpable are the one who slanders and the one who listens to the slanderer. The revilers shall not possess the kingdom of God. A virgin who desires to reach the heavenly bridal chamber ought not to speak ill of others. O [Col. 1257A] venerable virgin, if you keep your ears apart from slanderers, and restrain your tongue, as I have said, from every perverse utterance, you will be counted among the prudent virgins.

XXXIV. — On Envy

94. An envious person is a member of the devil, through whose envy death entered the world (Wis. II, 24). Envy burns up every shoot of virtue; envy devours every good thing with its pestilential heat. Envy is the moth of the soul. Envy bites itself before it bites another; envy first bites its own author. Envy consumes a person’s understanding, burns the breast, tears the mind, and feeds upon the human heart like a certain plague. Therefore let goodness meet envy; let charity be prepared against envy.

Sister most beloved to me in Christ, do not grieve at another’s good; do not waste away over another’s progress; do not torment yourself over another’s prosperity. There is no virtue that does not have envy as its contrary evil. Misery alone is without envy. Why? Because no one envies the wretched. A virgin who desires to dwell in heaven ought not to envy people; a virgin who desires to enter the marriage feast with Christ ought not to be saddened by another’s honour. Dearest sister, may God cleanse your heart from every wickedness and envy, so that you may serve him without stain. Amen.

XXXV. — On Anger

95. Honourable virgin, hear what Solomon says: “A gentle answer breaks anger; a harsh word stirs up fury” (Prov. XV, 1; XXV, 15); and again: “A sweet word softens enemies and multiplies friends” (Ecclus. VI, 5). The less patient a person is, the less wise that person is proved to be. Through anger the eye of the mind is disturbed; through anger the wise lose wisdom; through anger a person is estranged from oneself.

Some become angry quickly but return quickly to peace; others become angry more slowly and return more slowly to peace; while others, which is more serious, are more quickly stirred to anger and more slowly inclined to peace. Yet one who becomes angry quickly and returns quickly to peace is better than one who becomes angry more slowly and is more slowly stirred toward peace. Dearest sister, hear James also saying: “Let every person be swift to hear, but slow to speak and slow to anger.” [Col. 1257D] Why? “Because the anger of a man does not work the righteousness of God” (Jas. I, 19–20); certainly neither can a virgin’s anger work God’s righteousness.

A virgin who ought to become God’s temple should by no means become angry; it is not fitting for Christ’s bride to be irascible. A virgin who prepares a dwelling for Christ in her breast must in every way drive anger from her heart; a virgin who desires to reach the heavenly bridal chamber with Christ must utterly cast anger out of her heart. Most beloved sister, if irascibility comes before you, restrain it; if anger seizes you, calm it. Moderate fury; moderate indignation. Restrain the movement of irascibility; curb the onset of anger. If you cannot avoid or moderate anger, let fury not carry you away, let anger not inflame you, let indignation not move you. Let not the sun [Col. 1258A] go down upon your anger (Eph. IV, 26). Amen.

XXXVI. — On Hatred

96. Honourable virgin, hear what I say. Hatred separates a person from the kingdom of God; hatred separates a person from paradise; hatred removes a person from heaven. Hatred is not destroyed even by suffering, is not purged even by martyrdom, is not washed away even by shed blood. We ought not to hate persons, but vices. “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness and walks in darkness” (I John III, 15, 14). One who hates a human being does not love God. As great as the difference between a straw and a beam, so great is the distance between anger and hatred: for hatred is anger grown old. Through anger the eye of the mind is disturbed; through hatred the eye of the heart is extinguished.

Sister most beloved to me in Christ, hear what I say. If you have caused your sister grief in any matter, make satisfaction to her; if you have sinned against your sister, do penance before her; if you have caused scandal to any of God’s handmaids, ask her to forgive you. Hasten to reconciliation; do not sleep until you have first made satisfaction; do not rest until you have returned to peace. If your enemy falls, do not rejoice; do not be glad at your enemy’s destruction, lest similar things perhaps come upon you, [Col. 1258B] lest God turn his anger from that person upon you (Prov. XXIV, 17–18). Let it please you to grieve for one who is afflicted; share the suffering of others; be saddened in another’s distress; weep with those who weep; mourn with those who mourn.

Venerable sister, do not be hard; let not your heart be hard. Do not repay one who sins against you according to that person’s fault, because God’s judgment will come upon you as well. Forgive, that you may be forgiven: for you will not receive pardon unless you grant forgiveness. Cast hatred out of your heart; let hatred not remain in your mind.
