Beloved sister, may God grant you love of himself and of your neighbour. Amen.

XXXVII. — On Pride

97. Pride is the root of all evils. “A proud person is hateful to God and to men” (Ecclus. X, 7). A proud person is like the devil. Pride and covetousness are so much one evil that neither pride can exist without covetousness nor covetousness without pride. Through pride and covetousness the devil said: [Col. 1258D] “I will ascend into heaven” (Isa. XIV, 14). Christ said with humility: “My soul has been humbled into the dust” (Matt. XXVI, 38; Mark XIV, 34). Through pride and covetousness the devil said: “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIX, 14). Through humility Christ became obedient to the Father unto death (Phil. II, 8). Finally, through pride the devil is cast down into hell; but through humility Christ is raised to heaven.

What is every sin but contempt for God, by which we despise his commands? Dearest sister, believe me: the vigils, prayers, fasts, almsgiving, and labours of many years, if they end in pride, are counted as nothing before God. Therefore, venerable sister, do not spread the wings of pride; do not raise the feathers of pride [Col. 1259A]. Why? Because pride cast down angels, struck down the mighty, and brought down the proud: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (Luke I, 50–51; Jas. IV, 6).

I exhort you also, bride of Christ, to rejoice more in the fellowship of angels and God’s handmaids than in the nobility of your lineage. I ask you, most beloved sister, to rejoice more in the fellowship of poor virgins than in the nobility of your wealthy parents. Why? Because with God there is no respect of persons. Whoever despises the poor does injury to God. Whoever scorns the poor reproaches their Maker (Prov. XVII, 5; XIV, 31). Venerable sister, may God give you profound humility and true charity. Amen.

XXXVIII. — On Boasting

98. In deeds as well as in words we must beware [Col. 1259B] of boasting. Therefore, dearest sister, examine yourself, and claim nothing among the things that are in you as your own except sins. Beware of boasting; flee the desire for vain glory; beware the pursuit of empty glory. Do not claim anything for yourself; do not boast; presume nothing concerning yourself; do not insolently exalt yourself; attribute no good to yourself; do not glory in a good work; do not be puffed up by the wind of popular favour. Despise human praise; do not seek whether anyone praises or blames you. Let praise not deceive you, nor blame break you. One who does not seek praise does not feel insult.

Virgins who glory in their merits before people have no oil in their vessels, because through their desire for vain glory they have lost the reward which they deserved from the Lord. Let them always look upon their own foulness, because they love vain glory; and let them grieve that they have lost the good work which they did for human praise. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 2). Through the pursuit of empty glory the virtues of saints are subjected to the dominion of demons. Thus King Hezekiah, because he boastfully showed his riches to the Chaldeans, heard through the prophet that they would perish (IV Kings XX). Likewise the Pharisee who had come to the Temple to pray lost his good deeds because he boastfully displayed them (Luke XVIII). As an eagle descends from on high to its food, so a person is plunged down from the height of good conduct to lower things through the desire for vain glory.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, do not place your conscience in another’s tongue. If another tongue praises you and not your own, if another mouth praises you and not your own, nevertheless judge yourself by your own judgment, not by another’s. No one can know better what you are than you, who are conscious of yourself.

99. Venerable sister, do you wish me to tell you how you can increase all virtues?—Beloved brother, I do; and I ask you to show me.—Listen, then, venerable sister: if you wish to increase all your virtues and not lose them, conceal your virtues against self-exaltation; conceal your good deeds against arrogance. Flee being seen for what you have merited. Hide your virtues; make your sins known; reveal the vices of your heart. Conceal your good works; never bring forward publicly anything good that you have done or said. Immediately make known perverse thoughts: for a sin that is made known is quickly cured, [Col. 1260A] but a crime is enlarged by silence; if it is hidden, it becomes great from being small. Sin decreases by being confessed; it grows by silence. Virtues increase in secret and decrease in public. Virtues are annihilated when boastfully displayed; they are multiplied when humbly concealed.

Therefore, honourable sister, always direct your counsel and action toward God. In every work of yours, place God’s help. Ascribe everything to divine grace and to God’s gift; attribute nothing to your own merits; presume nothing upon your virtue; place no confidence in your own boldness. Dearest sister, hear the Apostle saying: “Whoever glories, let that person glory in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31; II Cor. X, 17). Therefore, venerable virgin, let your glory and your praise always be in Christ Jesus, your bridegroom.

XXXIX. — On Humility

[Col. 1260B]

100. Dearest sister, hear your bridegroom, the Lord Jesus Christ, saying in the Gospel: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matt. XI, 29). Venerable sister, humble yourself under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in the time of tribulation (I Pet. V, 6). A virgin’s conscience ought always to be humble and sad: humble, that through humility it may not become proud; and sad, that through useless sadness the heart may not dissolve into wantonness. Humility is the virgin’s highest virtue. For pride is the greatest reproach.

Though a humble virgin be lowly in garb, she is glorious in virtues before God. But a proud virgin, although beautiful, lovely, and well-composed before human eyes, is nevertheless lowly, despised, and rejected before God’s eyes. Why? Because [Col. 1260C] the soul of the righteous is God’s seat, as the Lord himself says: “Upon whom shall I rest, but upon one who is humble and quiet, and fears my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

Sister beloved to me in Christ, be humble; be founded in humility; be the last of all. Dearest one, set yourself above no one; account yourself superior to no one; reckon all to be above you. The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things. If you keep humility, you shall have glory (Prov. XI, 16; XV, 35): for the humbler you are, the greater height of glory will follow you. Descend, that you may ascend; humble yourself, that you may be exalted, lest, having exalted yourself, you be humbled. For “whoever exalts himself shall be humbled, and whoever humbles himself shall be exalted” (Matt. XXIII, 12; Luke XIV, 11; XVIII, 14). Whoever is lifted up shall be humbled. A fall is heavier from a height; ruin is greater from on high. Humility knows no fall; humility never incurs ruin; humility has never suffered a slip.

O bride of Christ, recognize that God came in humility; recognize that he humbled himself in the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death (Phil. II, 6–8). Beloved sister, walk as he walked; follow his example; imitate his footsteps. Be lowly, be despised, be rejected; be displeasing to yourself. For one who is lowly in one’s own eyes is great before God; one who displeases oneself pleases God. Dearest one, be little in your own eyes, that you may be great in God’s eyes. The more despised you are in your own sight, the more precious you shall be before God’s eyes. Venerable sister, if you keep profound humility, [Col. 1261A] you will rejoice with the prudent virgins in the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

XL. — On Patience

101. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (Matt. V, 9). Therefore, dearest sister, if peaceful people are blessed and will be called children of God, patience is necessary for you. “Patience has a perfect work” (Jas. I, 4). A peaceful virgin is wise; an angry virgin is not prudent but foolish. Venerable sister, without the sword you can be a martyr, if you truly preserve patience in your soul. One who is not peaceful will not deserve fellowship with the angels; the envious and angry person will be a companion of demons. One who is not peaceful drives concord away; indeed, the angry person raises quarrels.

A kindly virgin, even if she suffers injuries, counts them as nothing. A peaceful virgin prepares a dwelling for Christ in her heart. Why? Because Christ is peace, and is accustomed to rest in peace. A child of peace ought to love peace. Prepare yourself more to receive an injury than to inflict one; learn rather to bear evils than to do evil. Be patient, gentle, gracious, modest, and meek. Love peace, cherish peace, preserve peace with all. Embrace all in meekness and charity. Show yourself to love more than you are loved; show yourself to cherish more than you are cherished. Do not be fickle in friendship; always keep the bond of friendship. Always maintain patience of mind. Be kind; be ready in affection; be agreeable in speech; appear to all with a gracious spirit. Remove the occasion for quarrelling; scorn strife; always live in peace.

Dearest sister, if possible, preserve peace with all people. Overcome the reproaches of slanderers through patience; shatter the arrows of insult with the shield of patience; offer the shield of conscience against the sword of the tongue. You possess great virtue if you do not harm the person by whom you have been harmed; you possess great strength if, even when injured, you forgive; you possess great glory if you spare the person upon whom you could have taken revenge. Venerable sister, may the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, guard your heart and your soul. Amen.

XLI. — On Concord

102. “There are six things which my soul hates,” says the Lord, “and a seventh which it detests,” namely, one who sows discord among brothers (Prov. VI, 16, 19). [Col. 1261D] Cursed is the person who sows discord among God’s servants. Whoever breaks peace and concord acts against God; one who sows discord among God’s servants does injury to Christ. Why? Because Christ is our peace, “who makes the two one” (Eph. II, 14), namely because he made angels and human beings to be in concord.

The concord of the wicked is the opposition of the good. As we desire good people to have peace, so we ought to desire the concord of the wicked to be broken. Concord in committing sin is evil; but concord in doing good, pursuing righteousness, and serving God is good. For this reason we have been gathered together as one: that, in God’s service, we may all have one spirit and one mind. All who dwell in God’s house ought to have one soul [Col. 1262A] and one heart in God. It profits nothing if one house contains us while differing wills divide us. God loves unity of mind more than unity of place. Behold, many people are in this house: diverse customs, diverse hearts, diverse souls. All these ought to be joined into one by life, purpose, and one love for God.

Therefore we ought to be of one mind and one will in this: to serve God, to love God with our whole heart and whole soul, and our neighbour as ourselves. Thus the virtue of concord is necessary to us. But if I wish to do my will, and this person theirs, and that person theirs, divisions arise, disputes arise, as also anger and quarrels, which are works of the flesh; and, as the Apostle says, “Those who do such things shall not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. V, 21).

Dearest sister, believe me: our fasts, prayers, and sacrifices do not please God as much as concord. Therefore God says in the Gospel: “First go to be reconciled to your brother, and then, coming, you shall offer your gift.” Venerable sister, great is the virtue of concord before God, without which our sacrifices, by which sins are wiped away, do not please God. We should know that when we come to conversion, we undertake a struggle against the devil.

103. *(Question.)* Beloved brother, tell me whether the devil fears anything. *(Answer.)* Beloved sister, there is nothing that the devil fears as much as concord and charity. For if we give all that we possess for God, the devil does not fear this, because he himself has nothing. If we fast, the devil does not fear this, because he himself never eats. If we keep vigil, the devil does not fear this, because he himself never sleeps. But if we maintain charity and concord, the devil fears this exceedingly. Why? Because we possess this on earth, whereas he refused to possess it in heaven.

This also is why holy Church is said to be “terrible as an army arrayed in battle order” (Cant. VI, 3): for just as enemies are afraid when they see battle-lines of camps well arranged for war, so indeed the devil is terrified when he sees spiritual persons, girded with the arms of virtues, living in the unity of concord. Defeated and confounded, he grieves bitterly when he cannot divide and penetrate them through discord. Therefore we must all live unanimously and concordantly in [Col. 1262D] God’s house, so that we may conquer the devil.

A handmaid of God who wishes to live concordantly must first abandon perverse habits, lest she be perverse, disorderly, or undisciplined, and lest by her perversity she trouble or scandalize the other handmaids of God. She must also measure her actions, movements, words, and her whole life, so that she may be able to live in harmony, according to God, with those among whom she lives. Therefore, beloved sister, I exhort you to live concordantly and humbly in the monastery with all God’s handmaids. Venerable sister, invite those who hate to peace; call the discordant back to concord. Let there be no speech of quarrelling that divides concord. O bride of Christ, may the charity which separated you from the world itself join you to God. Amen.

XLII. — On Forbearance

[Col. 1263A]

104. Dearest sister, learn modesty from Christ; learn forbearance. Attend to Christ, and you will not grieve over injuries. For he suffered for us and left us an example (I Pet. I). Struck with palms, beaten with scourges, mocked with spittle, pierced with nails, crowned with thorns, condemned to the cross, he always remained silent (Isa. LIII). When anyone abuses you, it happens to you because of your sins; when anyone wrongs you, your evils bring this about. Whatever adverse thing happens to you, it happens because of your sin. You will bear it more lightly if you consider the things for which it is inflicted upon you.

Therefore, when someone speaks ill of you, pray; when someone curses you, bless that person; bless the one who curses you. Add a blessing [Col. 1263B] for one cursing you; soothe the angry person by patience; dissolve the anger of raging fury by gentleness. Conquer wickedness by mildness, malice by goodness. Overcome others’ evils by your good. Destroy others’ insults by your tranquil mind. Venerable sister, prepare your heart for good and evil; and bear good and evil as they happen to you. Endure adversity and prosperity, so that whatever may meet or happen to you, you may bear it with an untroubled mind. Reject the reproaches of inflicted insult; overcome the reproaches of mockery by despising them. By overlooking them, despise the faults of slanderers.

105. Honourable virgin, although anyone may provoke you, incite you, embitter you, insult you, abuse you, accuse you, summon you to a dispute, call you to a quarrel, speak abuse, commit an injury, or afflict you with insults: be silent, keep silence, overlook it, despise it; do not speak; maintain silence. Do not answer injury; do not utter evil words; do not return abuse; do not answer insult. Keep the peace of silence: by silence you will conquer more quickly.

O bride of Christ, undertake the struggle against temporal hardships. Be steadfast in every circumstance; bear all things patiently. What happens to many must be patiently endured by one person. Both the one who afflicts and the one afflicted are mortal; both the one who does evil and the one who bears evil will die. Beloved sister, believe me: no one could have opposed you unless the Lord had given that person power. Nor would the devil have had power over you unless God permitted it. “Through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV, 21). “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory” (Rom. VIII, 18).

Dearest sister, it is impossible for you to be a woman and not taste distress. In this world we all endure things with a like outcome. There is no one placed in this life who does not sigh. This life is full of tears; this life begins with weeping. When an infant is born, it begins life with crying; when it emerges from the womb, it begins to mourn before it begins to laugh. Weeping, we are cast into this wretched life. Tribulation is useful; the pressures of this life are useful. The more we are broken in this world, the more firmly we are established in eternity; the more we are afflicted in the present time, the more we shall rejoice in the future. [Col. 1264A] If we are worn down here by scourges, we shall be found purified at judgment. Amen.

XLIII. — On Illness
106. The Lord speaks in the Apocalypse, saying: “Those whom I love I rebuke and chastise” (Rev. 3:19). God chastises human beings in this life in three ways. That is, he strikes the reprobate for condemnation; he corrects for purification the elect whom he sees going astray; and he chastises the righteous to increase the glory of their merits. God struck Egypt with plagues for condemnation (Exod. 5 and 14); poor Lazarus was scourged for purification (Luke 16); Job too was scourged for testing (Job 5). He also scourges a person before sin, lest that person become wicked, as he scourged Paul, who, at the prompting of the angel of Satan, endured the stings of the flesh (2 Cor. 12 [Col. 1264B]). A person is also scourged by God after sin, in order to be corrected, as was the man handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved (1 Cor. 5).

For those who are robust and healthy, it is beneficial to become ill, lest through the vigor of health they take greater delight than they should in transient and earthly things. Bodily health is bad when it leads a person into sickness of soul; and bodily sickness is very good when it brings a person to health of soul. The Apostle praises bodily infirmity, saying: “For when I am weak, then I am stronger” (2 Cor. 12:10), namely in spirit. A person ought not to murmur under God’s scourges, because through being chastised he is corrected from sin. We shall endure bodily illnesses more lightly if we call to mind the evils we have done.

[Col. 1264C] A person ought not to murmur in illness. Why? Because that person is judged by him whose judgments are always just. Whoever suffers illness and murmurs against God accuses the justice of the Judge, and thereby provokes God’s wrath against himself or herself. What pleases the just Judge cannot fail to be just. For whom God loves, he chastises; and he scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6), and, as a father, takes pleasure in his 861 son. In this life God spares sinners and does not spare the righteous. In the life to come he will spare the righteous and will not spare sinners. Whoever does not deserve to be scourged in this life will be tormented in hell.

Dearest sister, pain and sorrow are common to all: there is no one in this world who does not suffer. [Col. 1264D] God continually chastises those whom he prepares for everlasting salvation. Venerable sister, do not be sorrowful in your illnesses. In your weakness give thanks to God. Desire to be strong more in soul than in body; desire to be more vigorous in mind than in flesh. The adversities of the flesh are remedies for the soul: sickness wounds the flesh but heals the mind. For weakness burns out vices; weakness breaks the powers of lust. Know that you are being tested in pain; do not be broken. Gold is tested in the furnace (Wis. 3:6), so that it may be free of filth; you are purified in the kiln of tribulation, so that you may appear purer; you are melted in the fire of persecution. You are melted so that you may be cleansed of every stain of sins. All these things that you endure are for testing (Rom. 5:3–4). Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, do not murmur in your illnesses, [Col. 1265A] do not blaspheme, do not say, “Why do I endure evils?” Do not say, “Why am I afflicted? Why do I suffer evils?”

107. My brother, I beg you to tell me what I ought to say in my illnesses, or how I ought to accuse myself. — Honorable sister, accuse yourself in this way: “I have sinned. I have not received what I deserved. I do not feel punishment equal to my sin; I feel myself struck less severely than I deserve. In proportion to my deserving, the tribulation of retribution is less; according to the deserving of my sins, the cause of my punishments is unequal. The sufferings are not as great as the sins have been.”

O bride of Christ, do you wish to be cleansed of your sins? Accuse yourself in punishment, and praise God’s justice. It suffices for your purification if you refer what you suffer to God’s justice; if, for the infirmity imposed upon you, [Col. 1265B] you humbly glorify God. For God corrects you with the scourge of loving chastisement and exercises discipline upon you; and he who, by sparing you, was rejecting you from himself, cries out by striking you that you may return.

Venerable virgin, consider any sufferings of the world; direct your mind toward whatever worldly punishments, whatever pains of torments, whatever bitter agonies there may be. Compare all this with Gehenna, and what you suffer will be light. Beloved sister, if you fear, fear the punishments of hell. For these punishments are temporal; those are eternal. In these punishments, by dying, the torments depart; in those, by dying, eternal pain follows. For if you have been converted, what you suffer is correction. For one who has been converted, present blows lead to purification. Whoever is corrected here by chastisement [Col. 1265C] is freed there; but those who are not corrected even under the scourge are condemned both to temporal punishment and to eternal punishment. They are first judged in this world, and then again there in the life to come. Theirs is a double punishment and condemnation; theirs is a twofold blow, because here they undergo judgments of torments and there the completion of punishments.

Therefore God’s hand has delivered you over to punishment; God’s indignation has commanded that you be afflicted. He himself, in anger, commanded you to experience every evil, reverend sister. For the fact that you are broken by bodily weakness, afflicted by diseases of the flesh, tormented by the stings of infirmities, shaken by sufferings of soul, tortured by distress of mind, and agitated by the growing assault of evil spirits—this very thing divine justice pours upon you for your sin. Your own weapons fight against you; you are struck by your own arrows, [Col. 1265D] wounded by your own missiles. For by the things through which you sinned, through those very things you are tormented. Because you followed the flesh, you are scourged in the flesh; you groan in that very flesh in which you sinned. Beloved sister, you are tortured in the very flesh in which you transgressed; in it is your assessment of punishment, in which was the cause of sin. From where you fell into vices, from there you endure torments. O bride of Christ, you are justly rebuked, justly scourged, judged by a just judgment. The storm justly crushes you; the penalty of justice weighs upon you.

### XLIV.—On Avarice

108. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of all avarice, because a person’s life upon earth does not consist in the abundance of the things that he possesses” (Luke 12:15). And Paul the Apostle says: “Let every fornication and uncleanness and avarice not even be named among you”; and again: “Every fornicator, or unclean person, or avaricious person—which is the service of idols—has no inheritance in the kingdom of God” (Eph. 5:3, 5). Hence Solomon says: “He who pursues avarice troubles [Col. 1266A] his own 862 house” (Prov. 15:27). The avaricious person will not be filled with money. Whoever loves riches will gain no fruit from them (Eccl. 5:9). Nothing is worse than loving money, for thereby a person holds his own soul for sale (Eccl. 10:10).

As avarice sinks a person into hell, so generosity in almsgiving altogether raises one to heaven. An avaricious person is like hell: as hell never says, “It is enough,” so the avaricious person is never satisfied with money. As a person with dropsy, the more he drinks, the more he thirsts, so the avaricious person, the more he acquires, the more he desires. Avarice and greed are sisters; pride is their [Col. 1266B] mother. Pride has never existed without greed, nor greed without avarice.

Venerable sister, let your hand not be extended to receive and withdrawn in giving; let giving delight you more than receiving. It is better to give than to receive. Dearest sister, let avarice not strike roots in your heart; let there be no avarice in you. Cast avarice out of your heart. Thus you will rejoice perfectly for Christ, your bridegroom, in the heavenly homeland. Amen.

### XLV.—On Greed

109. “Greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). No one can undertake spiritual battles perfectly unless first he or she has subdued the pleasures of the flesh. A mind cannot be free to contemplate God [Col. 1266C] when it desires the earthly and transient things of this world; the eye of the mind cannot see high things when it is closed by the dust of earthly greed. Greed is a grave sin, the material of all crimes. It is no wonder if those who did not extinguish the flame of their greed while living are assigned, when dying, to the fires of hell.

Dearest sister, even though you have no money, if you have the desire to possess it, it avails you nothing. Bodily nakedness avails you nothing if you have a desire for clothing. Through greed Judas sold Christ. We are born naked into this life, and naked we shall leave this life (Job 1:21; Eccl. 5:14). Why, then, do we desire earthly and transient things? If we believe the goods of this world will perish, why do we love them with so great an affection? If we love the earthly and transient things of this world more [Col. 1266D] than we should, we sin.

Therefore, beloved sister, consider your course, and recognize that the few things you have can suffice for you. If, then, greed is the root of all evils, as we said above, you must cast it out of your heart, lest the other offspring of vices sprout up: let perverse greed not be in you. Venerable sister, may almighty God enable you, for his own sake, to despise the world’s prosperity and fear none of its adversities. Amen.

### XLVI.—On Poverty

110. “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:3; Luke 6:20). There are many poor people whom poverty itself does not make blessed but miserable, because they endure poverty not for [Col. 1267A] God’s sake but by compulsion. There are likewise some poor people whom poverty does not make miserable but blessed, because they endure it for God’s sake; of these it is said: “Blessed are the poor in spirit.”

Dearest sister, I return once more to address you. You have heard of Job’s tribulation and patience; therefore I warn you neither to be broken in tribulation nor exalted in prosperity. You read that the patriarchs were rich in possessions but humble in mind. Such was Abraham, who said: “I will speak to the Lord my God, though I am dust and ashes” (Gen. 18:27). Therefore, venerable sister, you will be blessed if you always give thanks to God in prosperity and adversity, and regard the happiness of this temporal life as smoke and vapor that vanishes. For Paul the Apostle says: “If in this life [Col. 1267B] only we have hope in Christ, we are more miserable than all people” (1 Cor. 15:19).

For Christ, lest we love gold, taught us to despise gifts offered in life; lest we fear hunger, he fasted for forty days (Matt. 4); lest we fear nakedness, he commanded his disciples to have a single tunic (Matt. 10:10); lest we dread tribulations, he endured tribulations for us; and lest we fear death, he endured and accepted death for us. All that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and worldly ambition. And the world will perish, and its desire (1 John 2:16). Therefore, beloved sister, let us not love the things that are in the world, lest we perish with the world.

Certainly David reigned; and although he possessed treasures [Col. 1267C] 863 of silver and commanded peoples with a strong hand, he nevertheless knew himself humble and said: “I am poor, and in labors from my youth” (Ps. 87:16); and again: “I am needy and poor” (Ps. 69:6). Likewise he says: “I am a resident alien on earth and a stranger, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38:13).

111. Venerable sister, let transient allurements not delight you; take no delight in earthly advantages or worldly gains, and you will not be grieved at earthly losses. For thus it is written: “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. 61:41). What we possess with love, we lose with sorrow. Hear, bride of Christ, what I say. He whom heavenly and earthly things serve became poor for us. [Col. 1267D] Why? So that by his poverty he might make us rich.

Therefore, honorable virgin, walk by the way on which Jesus Christ your bridegroom went before, and follow the heavenly leader with untiring steps. Without doubt, if you follow him, you will reign with him in heaven. Venerable sister, look to the virginity and poverty of the blessed Virgin Mary. She was so rich in the Lord that she deserved to be the Lord’s mother; yet she was so deprived of outward resources that at the time of birth she had neither midwives nor maidservants to attend her, and she was so poor in possessions that she had even an inn so cramped that she laid the infant not in a little bed but in a manger. Joseph also, to whom she had been betrothed, though he was righteous, was nevertheless poor, so that he sought food and clothing by a trade. [Col. 1268A] Certainly he is read to have been a craftsman. We also read of the holy Apostles that they served God in hunger and thirst. Hence Paul the Apostle says: “In hunger and thirst, in many fasts, in cold and nakedness, and in many vigils” (2 Cor. 11:27).

112. O bride of Christ, you have examples by which you may despise earthly riches and desire heavenly ones. For those who wish to become rich in this world fall into temptation and the devil’s snare, and into many harmful desires that plunge a person into destruction (1 Tim. 6:9). Those who perfectly hope for heavenly riches willingly despise earthly riches, because voluntary poverty introduces a person into the kingdom of heaven. We did not come to the monastery in order to live there in delights, but so that, by watching, praying, fasting, [Col. 1268B] chanting psalms, and fighting against our adversary, we may, with Christ’s help, attain the kingdom promised to us.

For this reason we are born naked into this world, and we also approach baptism naked: so that naked and unencumbered we may attain heaven. How unfitting, absurd, and shameful it is that one whom a mother bore naked and earth received naked should wish to enter heaven rich! “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of heaven” (Mark 10:25). It is better to have greater need than to have more possessions. Excessively avaricious is the person for whom the Lord does not suffice. Beloved sister, if in this world we endure hunger, thirst, and nakedness for Christ, we shall rejoice more graciously with that same Lord Jesus Christ in the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

### XLVII.—On Murmuring

[Col. 1268C]

113. The lodging of our heart is sanctified through God’s grace and the indwelling of the Holy Spirit, when love, peace, goodness, humility, concord, gentleness, and other such things are within us. These are our riches, namely good habits and virtues. But if we begin among ourselves to quarrel, murmur, and contend, we immediately remain empty and naked of these spiritual goods. Why? Because virtues cannot remain with vices. For even a little leaven corrupts the whole mass.

Every servant of God should weigh in his or her heart how great an evil is incurred by murmuring over temporal things: one who ought to have been rich becomes poor. What are our riches? Virtues, certainly. Therefore we lose virtues if we murmur over food or drink. Murmuring is a grave sin. Hence Gregory says: “No murmurer receives the kingdom of heaven; no one who receives it can murmur.” The inward parts of a fool are like a cartwheel, carrying hay and creaking [or “murmuring”]. Such are many brothers and many sisters in a community: subject to fleshly desires, they never cease to murmur.

Therefore, dearest sister, the counsel of Paul the Apostle is very necessary for us: “Do not murmur, as some of them murmured”—namely in the wilderness—“and were destroyed by the destroyer.” Therefore it is dangerous for us to murmur, lest perhaps we perish through the destroyer in the monastery, as they perished in the wilderness. [Col. 1269A] Let us therefore guard our tongues from murmuring, lest—God forbid—as they perished in this world, we perish in the life to come. Let us not murmur, then, lest perhaps, as they perished in this life, we perish in the future one. Let us beware of every kind of murmuring, lest perhaps we suffer in our souls what they suffered in their bodies.

114. Again the Apostle speaks in advising us: “Do not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10:10, 9). Whoever murmurs over food, drink, or clothing tempts Christ. Thus it is written of that same people: “They tempted God in their hearts, that they might ask food for their souls” (Ps. 77:18); and again: “They murmured in their tents and did not heed [Col. 1269B] the voice of the Lord” (Ps. 105:25). Whoever murmurs in the monastery by demanding superfluities tempts Christ. Whoever demands more than is fitting in the monastery acts against Christ. Whoever, by seeking earthly and transient things in the monastery, scandalizes superiors sins against Christ. “And they perished by serpents” (Judith 8:25). Why did they perish by serpents, if not because the serpent is poisonous and every murmurer has the devil’s poison on the tongue? Hence James the Apostle says: “The tongue is an unruly evil, full of deadly poison” (Jas. 3:8). Therefore we must beware of murmuring, lest we perish through deadly and diabolical poison.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, hear what our Lord Jesus Christ says in the Gospel: “I say to you, do not be anxious for your life, what [Col. 1269C] you shall eat, nor for your body, what you shall wear” (Matt. 6:31). It is as though he said more plainly: God who gave you a soul will also give food; and he who gave a body will give clothing. And he added: “Look at the birds of heaven: they neither sow nor gather nor store in barns or cellars, and God feeds them.” That is: if God governs birds which exist today and will not exist tomorrow, whose souls are mortal, will he give food and clothing to his male and female servants, whose souls are immortal and to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised? And again: “Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither labor nor spin”—that is, they neither weave nor spin thread—and God thus clothes them. How much more will he clothe his male and female servants? [Col. 1269D] God will not kill the souls of his servants by hunger, thirst, or nakedness.

And he added: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you.” It is as though he said: Serve the Lord in fear; sing and exult for him day and night with trembling; and he himself will give you all things necessary in this life and the next: “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Ps. 33:11). Dearest sister, God who brought you out of your father’s house, if you persevere in his service, will grant you the good desires of your heart. Amen.

### XLVIII.—On Private Possessions

115. Dearest sister, let a personal possession held among servants of God never be found in you, for it is a great crime. Everything in a monastery is common to all. [Col. 1270A] Therefore, if a handmaid of God has something hidden or held as her own, unknown to the other handmaids of God, it is theft; it is the sin of theft. Why? Because she has all things in common with the other handmaids of God, yet hides something for herself as though it were her own. To possess furtively something not shared with the other handmaids of God, and to hide something as though it were one’s own, is theft; it is manifest fraud. It is a great sin; it is the road to hell. By this path thieves have gone down into hell. For Paul the Apostle says: “Neither thieves nor robbers shall possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. 6:10).

A handmaid of God who separates herself from the monastery’s common life by hiding something as though it were her own necessarily separates herself from the fellowship of heavenly life. Many come to the monastery’s common [Col. 1270B] community; but, what we cannot say without heavy groaning, not all live in it according to the Gospel. In a monastery are the holy Apostles of Jesus Christ; Judas Iscariot, betrayer of the Lord, is also there. Ananias is there with his wife Sapphira. Gehazi, Elisha’s disciple, is there also. 865

Those, therefore, who for God’s sake leave behind everything they possess in this world, in imitation of the Apostles and for the sake of eternal life alone, will rejoice with those same Apostles and be rewarded in eternal blessedness. But whoever, after coming to the monastic conversion, presumes to commit fraud with the monastery’s goods is Judas, and will bear Judas’s punishment in hell, because he presumes to defraud what is common by making it private property. Therefore those who turn from [Col. 1270C] secular life to God’s service, if they reserve one portion for themselves of the things they possessed in the world and commit the other portion to the monastery with them, deserve the sentence of curse with Ananias and Sapphira. But if one who comes from the world to a monastery wishes or demands to have in the monastery what he could not have in his own home, Gehazi’s leprosy will without doubt cling to him; and the leprosy which Gehazi bore in his body, that person will bear in the soul.

116. Honorable sister, as I told you above, there is a great difference between those who live in a monastery and those who live in a monastery according to the manner of the Apostles. To those who conceal nothing from what they had in this world, or have in the monastery, the Psalmist’s saying applies: “But it is good for me to cling to God and to place my hope in God” (Ps. 72:28), and this: “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Ps. 54:23).

To those who, like Judas Iscariot, retain private possessions or hide goods belonging to the monastery, this saying applies: “They go up to the heavens and go down to the depths; their souls wasted away in evils” (Ps. 106:26). To those who, like Ananias and Sapphira, give one portion to the monastery from what they possessed in the world but retain another as private property, this saying applies: “Who trust in their own strength and boast in the multitude of their riches” (Ps. 48:7). Likewise, to those who, like Gehazi, seek in [Col. 1271A] the monastery things which they could not have in the world, this saying applies: “Behold the person who did not make God his helper, but hoped in the multitude of his riches and prevailed in his vanity” (Ps. 51:9).

Therefore, venerable sister, conceal nothing, hide nothing; store away nothing concealed, retain nothing in secret, let nothing remain hidden with you. Whatever you have, have it by permission; if you possess anything, have it with a blessing. Have nothing without the permission of the abbess or prioress; receive nothing without a blessing; give nothing without permission. Honorable virgin, “Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he will nourish you” (Ps. 51:9).

### XLIX.—On Prayer

117. Dearest sister, hear what I say. To pray before the appointed time is foresight. To pray at the appointed time is obedience. [Col. 1271B] To let the time for prayer pass is negligence. Prayer ought to be more frequent in proportion as it is more beneficial. The Lord says in the Gospel: “Whatever you ask in prayer, believing, you will receive” (Matt. 21:22). And Paul the Apostle says: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thess. 5:17). And James says: “The persistent prayer of a righteous person has great power” (Jas. 5:16).

Venerable sister, before prayer prepare your soul, and do not be like a person who tests God (Sir. 18:23). In prayer prepare yourself and disclose the conscience of your heart, that you may obtain greater grace from your God. You pray truly when you think of nothing else in your heart. A judge is more quickly inclined toward a plea if the sinner is corrected from wickedness. [Col. 1271C] Prayer belongs to the heart, not to the lips. It is better to pray with the heart’s silence than with words alone and without the mind’s attention. Prayer is pure when superfluous thoughts do not disturb it at its proper time. The mind is indeed far from God when, in prayer, it is occupied by worldly thoughts.

Prayer is hindered in two ways, so that one cannot obtain what one asks: namely, if the person still commits evils, or if that person does not forgive from the whole heart one who sins against him or her. Our mind is heavenly; and it contemplates God well in prayer when it is hindered by no earthly cares or errors. When anyone prays, that person calls the Holy Spirit to himself or herself; but after he has come, all the demonic temptations that plunge themselves into human minds flee at once, unable to endure his presence. Whoever is injured should not cease praying for those who injure him or her (Luke 6:28). Otherwise, according to the Lord’s judgment, whoever does not pray for enemies sins. As medicine does no good in a wound if the iron 866 still remains in it, so the prayer of one who has hatred in the heart does no good. A person culpably stretches out hands to God who, in prayer, boastfully makes his or her deeds known, just as the Pharisee in the Temple prayed boastfully and praised himself more for good works than he praised God (Luke 18).

118. Beloved sister, pray ceaselessly with tears. Pray continually; entreat God by day and night. Let prayer be without stopping; let prayer be frequent; let the weapons of prayer be constant; let prayer not fall from your mouth. [Col. 1272A] Persist in prayer; devote yourself often to prayer. Always groan and weep. Rise in the night for prayer; keep watch and pray; spend the night in prayer and entreaty; devote yourself to night vigils. After closing your eyes for a short time, pray again. Frequent prayer repels the devil’s darts; daily prayer overcomes the devil’s weapons. Prayer is the first virtue against the assaults of temptations; prayer overcomes the temptations of enemies; it conquers demons and overcomes unclean spirits. Through prayer demons are conquered; prayer prevails over every evil demon.

Honorable virgin, let your prayer be pure. I urge you, dearest one, to pray for good people, that they may persevere in goodness. I also ask you to pray for evil people, that they may turn from evil to good. Pray for your friends; pray also for your enemies. Pray also [Col. 1272B] for all faithful persons, living and dead. “Let your prayer be directed like incense in the sight of God” (Ps. 140:2).

### L.—On Reading

119. Through prayer we are cleansed from sins; through reading we are taught what we should do. Both are good, when permitted. But if it is not permitted, it is better to pray than to read. For when we pray, we speak with God; when we read, God speaks with us. Dearest sister, if you wish always to be with God, always pray and always read. Sacred reading is very necessary for us. For through reading we learn what we ought to do, what we ought to avoid, and toward what we ought to strive. Hence it is said: “Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light [Col. 1272C] to my paths” (Ps. 118:105).

Through reading perception and understanding are increased. Reading instructs us for prayer and action; reading forms us for the active and contemplative life. Thus it is said in the Psalms: “Blessed is the person who meditates on the law of the Lord day and night.” Reading and prayer are weapons by which the devil is overcome; they are the instruments through which eternal blessedness is acquired. Through prayer and reading vices are destroyed and virtues nourished in the soul. A handmaid of God should always pray and read. Hence it is read in the Psalms: “Then I shall not be put to shame, when I look upon your commandments.”

Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, persist frequently in prayer; persevere in meditation on the Scriptures; be constant in God’s law; devote yourself to the divine laws; make reading habitual; let reading be your daily meditation on the law. Reading removes life’s error and draws a person away from the world’s vanity. Through reading perception and understanding grow: for reading teaches what you should do, distinguishes what you should avoid, and shows where you should strive. You make great progress when you read—provided that you do what you read. Venerable sister, may God open your heart in his law and in his commandments.

### LI.—On Work

120. Jeremiah the prophet says: “Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God” (Lam. 3:41). Whoever prays and works lifts heart and hands to God. But whoever prays and does not work lifts the heart to God, but not the hands. Whoever works and does not pray lifts the hands to God, but not the heart. Therefore, dearest sister, [Col. 1273A] we must lift our heart to God in prayer and stretch out our hands to God in work. Why? Lest we be reproved for neglect of the commandments while seeking to obtain salvation by prayer alone or by work alone. Hence Paul the Apostle says: “Whoever does not work shall not eat” (2 Thess. 3:10).

A handmaid of Christ ought always to pray, read, and work, lest the spirit of fornication deceive an idle mind. The pleasure of the flesh is overcome by labor. Dearest sister, divide the day into three parts: in the first, pray; in the second, read; in the third part, work. Through idleness King Solomon entangled himself in many 867 acts of fornication, and through lustful desire worshiped idols. Venerable sister, these three things are very necessary for you: [Col. 1273B] prayer, reading, and work. By prayer we are cleansed; by reading we are instructed; by work we are made blessed, as the Holy Spirit says in the Psalm: “Because you shall eat the labors of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. 127:2).

If you should at any time cease from reading, you must work, so that you are never idle, because idleness is the enemy of the soul. The devil quickly deceives one whom he finds idle. The devil enters the enclosure every day; and if he finds anyone idle, he immediately accuses that person. O bride of Christ, see to it that when the devil enters the enclosure and examines each person’s deeds, he finds nothing by which he can accuse you. For this reason I urge you, sister beloved to me in Christ, never to be idle, for love of Jesus Christ.

[Col. 1273C] 121. I ask that you show Christ’s love to your companions not only in words but also in good works. Then you truly love God, if for love of him you perform the good things that you can. Every holy soul ought to show God’s love in itself through holy words and deeds. Thus, in the Song of Songs, the bridegroom—that is, Christ—adorns the bride, that is, the holy soul, saying: “Set me as a seal upon your heart and upon your arm” (Song 8:6). In the heart are thoughts; in the arms are works. Therefore the beloved is set as a seal upon the bride’s heart and arm, because in the holy soul the degree to which he is loved is indicated both by will and action. God’s love is never idle. If love is real, [Col. 1273D] it accomplishes great things; if it does not act, it is not love.

Therefore I ask you, venerable virgin, to love God perfectly, and never to sit idle for love of him. If you truly love God, you will not be idle for any hour; if you love God in truth, for love of him you refuse idleness; if you love God with your whole heart, at all times you despise idleness. Whoever loves God with the whole mind sets idleness aside for God’s sake. The kingdom of God will not be given to the idle, but to those diligent in God’s service; the kingdom of God will not be given to wanderers, but to those who work worthily for God. Those who are sluggish and lukewarm in good works will not have a place in the kingdom of God.

Lust quickly deceives people given to idleness; lust quickly deceives a person who is idle and wandering; lust burns more grievously one whom it finds idle. Lust yields to occupations; sensuality yields to works; sensuality yields to diligence and labor. By work a person often overcomes sexual desire, for a body wearied by labor takes less pleasure in vice. Therefore, beloved sister in Christ, beware of idleness; do not love idleness. Wear out your body with labor; perform good work; seek a useful task for yourself, by which your mind’s attention may be occupied. Let your good work and your intention always be in God. Amen.

### LII.—On Psalms and Hymns

122. Dearest sister, when you sing Psalms and hymns in God’s presence, consider in your mind what you sing with your voice. Let your mind agree with your voice and agree with your tongue: do not think one thing and sing another. If you sing one thing in your mind and another with your voice, you lose the fruit of your labor. If your body [Col. 1274B] stands in church while your mind wanders outside, you lose your reward. Hence it is said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Matt. 15:8; Mark 7:16; Isa. 29:13). For, as the Apostle says: “I will sing psalms with the spirit; I will sing psalms also with the mind” (1 Cor. 14:15). I shall sing with my mouth and with my heart.

It is good, therefore, always to pray to God in the mind. It is also good to glorify God with vocal sound, hymns, Psalms, and spiritual songs. As prayers help us, so the melodies of Psalms delight us. The practice of singing consoles sorrowful hearts. Singing in church gladdens people’s minds, pleases the weary, rouses the sluggish, and invites sinners to lamentation. For although the hearts of worldly people are hard, as soon as they hear the sweetness of Psalms, [Col. 1274C] they turn to the love of piety. Many, pierced by the sweetness of the Psalms, lament their sins.

Prayer alone is poured forth in this life for the remission of sins; but the singing of Psalms signifies the everlasting praise of God in eternal joys, as it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ages of ages they shall praise you” (Ps. 83:5). Whoever faithfully sings Psalms with an attentive mind is in some measure joined to God’s angels. 868 How? Because the person praises on earth, according to his or her own measure, him whom the angels adore and glorify without ceasing in heaven. The singing of Psalms sometimes moves us to tears and sometimes invites us to prayer.

[Col. 1274D] **123.** The Psalms make the watches of the night pleasing to us, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord, O righteous; praise befits the upright” (Ps. 32:1). The Psalms proclaim to us the first hour of day with the joy of light, saying: “O God, save me by your name, and judge me by your power” (Ps. 53:3). The Psalms consecrate for us the third hour of the day when they say: “Let your mercy come upon us, O Lord—your salvation according to your promise” (Ps. 118:41). The Psalms gladden us at the sixth hour of the day in the breaking of bread. At the ninth hour the Psalms break the fast and satisfy us with spiritual sweetness and delight. At the evening hour the Psalms commend us to God, saying: “Let my prayer be directed, O Lord, like incense in your sight; let the lifting up of my hands be an evening sacrifice” [Col. 1275A] (Ps. 140:2). At Compline the Psalms exhort us to bless the Lord, saying: “Behold, now bless the Lord, all you servants of the Lord” (Ps. 133:1).

Sister beloved to me in Christ, hold firmly in your memory that which sounds well in the ears of God when it comes from a holy soul. Through affection, love, and devotion, sing to God psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. Thus the Bridegroom—that is, Christ—in the Song of Songs exhorts the bride, that is, the Church or the holy soul, saying: “Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears, for your voice is sweet and your face beautiful” (Song 2:14). “You,” he says, “my beloved, who lie upon the couch of sweetest contemplation, upon which you desire to please me in psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, [Col. 1275B] and prayers—come and show me your face.” That is, come forth from the secret place of your heart, and display to others, as an example, the beauty of your good works, so that, when they see your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5:16).

“Let your voice sound in my ears”: namely, the voice of preaching, the voice of divine praise, the voice of rejoicing, which causes others to advance in my praise and glory. The singing of Psalms delights the ears of hearers and teaches the souls of the faithful to live well. Let the voice of those who sing be one, and let us mingle words of praise with the angels of God, whom we cannot see.

**124.** The servants of God ought always to praise the name of God, as the upper waters also indicate, concerning which it is said: “Bless the Lord, all waters that are above the heavens” (Ps. 148:4–5); for the elect shall not cease eternally to praise the Lord’s name. But concerning the lower waters it was said: “Let the waters which are under heaven be gathered into one place” (Gen. 1:9), because the reprobate, now scattered throughout the whole world, will be gathered into hell to be tormented. Without ceasing, the faithful ought to render praises to God, because God takes delight in them.

That God takes delight in the praises of the faithful is attested by the Bridegroom—that is, Christ—who speaks in the Song of Songs to the bride, that is, the holy soul, saying: “You who dwell in the gardens” [Col. 1275C] (Song 8:13). The Church, or any holy soul, dwells in gardens when it is already filled with the flourishing growth and hope of good works. Therefore she who now dwells in gardens ought to make her Bridegroom hear her voice—that is, the song of good preaching or holy rejoicing—or to send forth the voice of divine praise, in which he delights, which he desires, and to which his friends listen: namely, all the elect, who desire to hear words of life—that is, readings, psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs—so that they may be revived unto the heavenly homeland.

Therefore, most reverend sister, as I have already said above, it is very necessary for you throughout your whole life to praise almighty God, your Creator, because pardon is promised to you from the very source from which you praise him. Praise him, then, in your heart; praise him with your voice. Praise him with the voice of rejoicing; praise him also in the secret place of contemplation. Praise him in the chamber of the mind, in the rejoicing [Col. 1276A] of the voice. For although we are sinners and unworthy to praise God, yet we ought not cease from praises, because we believe that from this very source—from which we praise God—we obtain forgiveness of sins. Hence the divine voice says in the Psalms: “The sacrifice of praise will glorify me, and there is the way by which I shall show him the salvation of God” (Ps. 49:23). As if it said more plainly: In the Psalms is the way of praise by which you may arrive at eternal praise. But unless I show it to you, you cannot find it.

Therefore, dearest sister, because the way of our salvation lies in the hands of the Creator, I exhort you that the praise of God may never depart from your mouth. Sister most dearly beloved to me in Christ, God is your praise; therefore be his praise also, so that his praise may always be in your mouth. Amen.

## LIII.—On the Active and Contemplative Life

[Col. 1276B]

**125.** Jacob saw a ladder standing upon the earth, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon it; and its summit touched the heavens (Gen. 28:12). Upon this ladder are placed all those predestined to eternal life, and everyone who looks toward the kingdom of heaven has a place upon this ladder. This ladder is the universal Church, which in part still serves as a militant body on earth and in part already reigns in heaven.

On this ladder are three orders of people: the worldly, the active, and the contemplative. The worldly are on the lowest rung; the active are in a higher place; the contemplative are at the summit. Among these three orders of people, some are at the mill, some in the field, and some in bed. The mill is the worldly life. [Col. 1276C] The field is the mind of the worldly person. In the field are the preachers of God’s word. In bed is love for the Bridegroom, that is, Christ. Those who are at the mill go round the earth: they seek and love earthly things. Those who are in the field cultivate the earth: they sow the word of God in human ears. In bed are those who despise and scorn [worldly things; the object is unstated in the source].

At the foot of this ladder are worldly people; in the middle of the ladder are the active; at its summit are the contemplative, as though already placed in heaven, because they think upon heavenly things. These are the angels of God ascending the ladder, because through contemplation they ascend to God and through compassion descend to their neighbour. The active life is the innocence of good works; the contemplative life is the contemplation of things above. The active life belongs to many; the contemplative to few. The active life makes good use of earthly things; the contemplative life, renouncing the world, delights in living for God alone.

**126.** *(Question.)* Beloved brother, I ask you to show me the differences between the active and contemplative life.

*(Answer.)* Dearest sister, there is a very great difference between the active and contemplative life. The active life is to give bread to the hungry; to teach one’s neighbours a word of wisdom; to correct the erring; to bring the proud back to the way of humility; to recall the discordant to concord; to visit the sick; to bury the dead; to ransom captives and those confined in prison; to distribute whatever is fitting to each person; and to provide each person with necessities.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, you have heard the works of the active life; now, if you please, hear the virtues of the contemplative life. The contemplative life is to hold fast with the whole mind to love of God and neighbour; to rest from outward activity; to cling to the desire of the Creator alone. It is such that one no longer wishes to do anything, but, scorning all worldly cares, the mind burns to behold the face of its Creator; such that it already knows how to bear the burden of corruptible flesh with sorrow, and longs with all its desires to join the hymn-singing choirs of angels, desires to be mingled with the citizens of heaven, and rejoices before God in eternal incorruption.

Venerable sister, you have heard of the active life, and you have also heard of the contemplative. I now ask you, with Mary Magdalene, to choose the better part: namely, the contemplative life. The [Col. 1277B] active life is good, but the contemplative is far better. Whoever first advances in the former life ascends well to the contemplative. Whoever still seeks temporal glory or fleshly desire is barred from contemplation.

Take Jacob as an example of the active and contemplative life. While he loved Rachel, who signifies the contemplative life, Leah was given to him (Gen. 29), and she signifies the active life. The active life serves God amid the labours of this world when it feeds, receives, gives drink to, and clothes the poor; visits and consoles them; buries them; and bestows upon them the other works of mercy. Yet Leah is fruitful in children, because there are many active persons and few contemplatives. Rachel, however, is interpreted “a sheep” or “seeing the beginning,” because contemplatives are simple and innocent [Col. 1277C] like sheep, and are free from every turmoil of the world, so that, clinging to divine contemplation alone, they may see him who says, “I am the Beginning, who also speak to you” (John 8:25).

**127.** Rachel has two sons (Gen. 35), because there are two kinds of contemplatives. Some live in common in monasteries; others are solitaries, separated from everyone. But the contemplative life is more blessed and more perfect than the active. Just as the eagle fixes its eyes upon the rays of the sun and does not turn them away unless it wishes to refresh its body with food, so the saints sometimes return from contemplation to the active life. They consider those sublime things to be useful in such a way that these humble things are nevertheless, for a little while, necessary for our need.

Therefore in the Song of Songs the Bridegroom—that is, Christ—exhorts the bride, that is, the holy soul devoted to contemplation, saying: “Arise, hasten, my friend, my dove, my beautiful one, and come” (Song 2:13). As if he said more plainly: “Arise, hasten, my friend through love and faith; my dove through innocence and simplicity; my beautiful one through virtue and chastity. Rise from that most sweet couch of yours—that is, from the repose of contemplation—in which you desire to please me alone with psalms, hymns, prayers, and spiritual songs. Hasten, then, and come”: that is, go forth for the benefit of your neighbours, so that through the office of preaching and through examples of good works you may make them also your imitators and lead them [Col. 1278A] to the salvation of their souls.

The vision of the living creatures in Ezekiel, which went and did not return, pertains to perseverance in the active life. Again, the creatures which went and returned pertain to the measure of the contemplative life: when anyone directs himself toward it, struck back by his own weakness he immediately descends; and then, with the mind’s sight renewed, he rises again to those things from which he had descended (Ezek. 10). This cannot happen in the active life: if anyone descends from it even a little, he is immediately entangled in the defilements of vices.

**128.** Often the mind is raised from earth to heaven, and again, weighed down by the weakness of the flesh, descends from heaven to earth. God visits many worldly people and through his grace raises them to the height of contemplation; and, by his just and hidden judgment, God leaves many contemplatives fallen into earthly actions. Just as one buried in a tomb ceases from every earthly business, so the contemplative person ceases from every earthly work or ministry. And just as people ascending from the active life are buried in the repose of contemplation, so those withdrawing from the worldly life are received by the active life as though to be buried within it.

Accordingly, just as the active life is the tomb of the worldly life, so the contemplative life is the sepulchre of the active life. Just as holy persons sometimes leave the secret place of contemplation for the active life, so they return again from the active life to the secrecy of inward contemplation, in order that they may praise God within, where they received what would enable them to work outwardly for his glory. Just as God sometimes wills contemplatives to go forth into the active life so that they may benefit others, so at other times he wills that no one should disturb them, but that they should rest in the secret place of sweetest contemplation. The Bridegroom fittingly indicates this in the Song of Songs when he adjures the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken the bride, saying: “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and the hinds of the field, do not rouse or awaken my beloved until she herself wills it” (Song 2:7).

That is: Do not rouse or awaken the soul devoted to divine contemplation and occupied with prayers and divine readings; nor wish to disturb it for outward works until it itself wills it—that is, until, when the time of contemplation has been completed and bodily frailty gives warning, it itself wishes to be awakened [Col. 1278D] from the sleep of inward repose and inward sweetness.

**129.** Yet in this mortal life no one can contemplate God perfectly. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8:1). For heaven is the soul of the righteous, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1). Therefore, when the repose of the contemplative life is practised in the mind, silence occurs in heaven—that is, in the soul—because the clamour of earthly things and activities ceases in thought. But because the contemplative life cannot be perfect in this world, Scripture does not say that silence occurred in heaven for a whole hour, but for about half an hour.

Whoever wishes perfectly to maintain the contemplative life ought to cease from every earthly work. Hence, in the same Song of Songs, the bride says of herself: “I sleep, but my heart watches” (Song 5:2). As if the holy mind plainly spoke, saying: “While outwardly I sleep from worldly tumults, inwardly I consider in thought those things which are heavenly and spiritual.”

The ark of Noah, too, which is said to have two chambers (Gen. 6), signifies the active and the contemplative, of whom the active stand below and the contemplative above. Its being called three-chambered also signifies the three orders in the holy Church: the married, the continent, and virgins. Of this contemplative life the Lord says in the Gospel: “If you wish to be perfect, sell everything that you have and give to the poor, and you shall have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19:21). And he says of Mary Magdalene: “Mary has chosen the best part, which shall not be taken away from her” [Col. 1279B] (Luke 10:42).

The contemplative life will not be taken away, either in this age or in the age to come. The active life will be taken away from a person in the age to come; the active life has an end in this age, but the contemplative does not, because it endures always. The active life will fail in this age; the contemplative life begins in this age but is perfected in heaven.

Honourable virgin, I exhort you for God’s sake to despise the present age; for God’s sake, withdraw yourself from all worldly cares. Strive to serve God without the hindrance of the world. Let no worldly care draw you away from the fear of God. Let no concern for possessions draw you away from attention to God. Cast away from yourself whatever can obstruct your good purpose. With your whole soul hate [Col. 1279C] and condemn what the world loves. Be dead to the world, and let the world be dead to you. As one dead, separate yourself from love of the present life; as one dead, do not desire the world’s glory. Sister beloved to me in Christ, like one buried in a tomb, have no concern for the world. Like one deceased in a grave, deprive yourself of every earthly occupation. Sister beloved to me in Christ, despise while living what you will not be able to possess after death. If you do this, after your death you will have eternal life.

## LIX.—On Curiosity

**130.** Dearest sister, I exhort you to strive day by day to advance in good works, and not to consider the evils that others do, but to consider the good that you yourself ought to do. Hence a certain wise man says: “Do not investigate superfluous matters excessively” (Ecclus. 3:24). You have no need to know things remote from human understanding. It is altogether fitting that one should cease judging people’s minds when one does not know how perfectly to know the hearts of others. Why? Because we judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who “will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4:5).

It is also fitting that one who wishes to criticize another’s life should cease sinning. Foolish people, while wishing to criticize the errors of others, display their own. A person remains ignorant of the sins that he ought to have bewailed and acknowledged as long as he curiously investigates the vices of others; but when he returns to himself and considers himself well, he does not seek what to criticize in others, because in himself he finds much to mourn. Whoever considers himself well finds in himself much to lament.

Hence blessed Gregory says: “We ought to criticize the hearts of others all the less because we know that our sight cannot illuminate the darkness of another’s thought.” Blessed Isidore also says: “We more readily criticize the vices of each person than attend to their virtues; nor do we desire to recognize what good each has done, but we scrutinize what he has done badly.”

**131.** Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, I exhort you to criticize your own vices more than those of others. See your own faults before those of others. Be diligent about your own correction; attentive to your own salvation; provident for your own amendment. Do not seek what does not concern you. Never desire to know what people say among themselves. Do not ask what each person says or does. Beware of curiosity; lay aside concern for another’s life. Let no curiosity deceive your mind; let no desire for detestable curiosity creep upon you, lest, forgetting your own conduct, you investigate that of others.

Bride of Christ, correct your own vices with as much care as you devote to criticizing those of others. Let there be no concern in you to know hidden things. Beware of inquiring into what you ought not know. Pass over as secret that which you have not learned on the authority of Holy Scripture. Seek nothing beyond what is written; inquire into nothing more than the divine Scriptures show. Never desire to know what you ought not know.

Venerable sister, know for certain that curiosity is a dangerous presumption; curiosity is harmful expertise. It incites toward heresy and hurls the mind into sacrilegious fables; it makes people bold in obscure matters and rash in matters unknown. Most beloved sister, amend your life with every effort, so that after this life you may deserve to attain eternal joys. Amen.

## LV.—On Watchfulness

**132.** Beloved sister, hear the Lord Jesus Christ saying in the Gospel: “Watch, because you do not know when the Lord will come” (Matt. 24:42); and again: “I say to all: Watch” (Mark 13:37). And the apostle Peter says: “Be prudent and watchful in prayers” (1 Pet. 4:7). “When people say, ‘Peace and security,’ then sudden destruction will come upon them” (1 Thess. 5:3). Solomon also says: “The righteous and the wise and their works are in the hand of God; yet no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred.” Why? Because all things are reserved as uncertain for the future (Eccl. 9:1–2).

Sister beloved in Christ, the Lord concealed from us the time of his coming so that, uncertain through our long expectation, we may always believe that the true Judge will come, because we do not know when he will come. These are the words of blessed Gregory: “The joy of the present life must be conducted in such a way that the bitterness of the coming judgment never departs from memory. The devil often deceives a person into sinning, and, when he sees him afflicted by his fall, deceives him again by false security.”

Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, it is always necessary that when we do good, we recall to mind the evils we have done, so that, while we certainly recognize our fault, we may never rejoice heedlessly in a good work. The Lord therefore willed that the final hour should be unknown to us, so that we may always remain in suspense, and, because we cannot see it, may prepare ourselves for it every day.

Blessed Isidore also exhorts us not to be secure in this life, saying: “Neither should the righteous person place confidence in his righteousness, nor should the sinner despair at all of God’s mercy; rather, both hope and fear should be held together in the heart. Let one hope for God’s mercy in such a way as always to fear his justice.” Although the conduct of saints is commendable, it remains uncertain to people to what end they are destined. Therefore a person should never be without fear, because the adequacy of penitential satisfaction is assessed by divine judgment alone, not by human judgment. Hence Caesarius says: “The more secure we are concerning the past, the more anxious we ought to be concerning the future.” Venerable sister, hold firmly that the whole life of a wise person is meditation upon death.

**133.** Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, if you keep watch toward God at every hour, you will be wise. If every day you raise your mind to God and bring the day of your death to remembrance, you will be blessed, according to what a certain wise man says: “Blessed is the person who is always fearful” (Prov. 28:14). For this reason, honourable virgin, I exhort you always to be fearful and always in suspense; always be vigilant and shrewd against the devil’s temptations; always watch and fight without ceasing against the ancient enemy. Pray by day and night with all watchfulness, and struggle manfully against the devil’s snares. Throughout your whole life be provident and contend with every diligence against the enemy’s wiles.

Hear also, honourable virgin, what Jesus Christ, your Bridegroom, says in the Gospel: “Blessed is that servant whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching” (Luke 12:43). Therefore, if with your whole mind you watch toward the same Lord Jesus Christ, you will be counted among the blessed in eternal blessedness. You will be blessed if with all devotion you raise the eyes of your mind to the true light, which is God. Truly you will be blessed if you watch toward God with all earnestness, because God has promised a crown to those who watch.

Hence in the Song of Songs it is said of the Bridegroom’s eyes: “His eyes are like doves beside streams of water, washed with milk, and sitting beside overflowing channels” [Col. 1281D] (Song 5:12). The Bridegroom’s eyes are holy persons, who live in simplicity like doves and show others the way of salvation by their preaching and examples. They are said to be beside streams of water because they are always occupied with the refreshment of the holy Scriptures. They have been washed with milk because, through the grace of God, they have been cleansed from their sins in baptism. What do we understand by the overflowing channels beside which they sit, except the deep and hidden sayings of Holy Scripture, by which we are refreshed as we draw them in by reading or hearing?

For just as doves commonly sit beside streams of water in order to see in the water the shadow of birds flying above, and by this means escape the rapacious claws of those that swoop upon them, so holy persons discern the deceits of demons in Holy Scripture; and, from the description which they see, they recognize the enemy as if from a shadow and flee his deceptions. Therefore you also, most honourable sister, be constant in meditations upon the holy Scriptures, because in them you will be able to learn how you can avoid the snares of enemies.

Honourable virgin, I again exhort you to entrust yourself wholly to the counsels of Holy Scripture: namely, to do nothing except what you have heard from the answer of the Scriptures, because there you will find how to flee the deceits of demons. I also exhort you, from fear of rapacious birds—that is, demons—to sit beside the streams of Holy Scripture, lest you become an unsuspecting prey to your enemies [Col. 1282B] (which may it never be). I ask you to keep watch unceasingly beside the streams of Holy Scripture, and to avoid the enemies’ deceptions with the greatest diligence.

**134.** Alas, foolish people! Why do we not know or understand that our thoughts, before they proceed to action, are manifest and open in the sight of the Lord? For the Psalmist says: “God searches hearts and reins” (Ps. 7:10). Therefore, most beloved sister, let us consider that we always stand in the sight of God, and let us acknowledge that we are earth and ashes. Behold, our terrible God, who repays each according to his works, is near and will not delay; he himself will come and save us.

Let us therefore watch with all perseverance and devotion, so that, when he comes and knocks, he may not find us sleeping but watching in his praises, in his love, and in his holy service (Matt. 24:42–51). Let us run while we have the light, lest darkness overtake us (John 12:35). Thus the Wisdom of God says in Proverbs: “Blessed is the one who hears me and watches daily at my doors and waits at the posts of my doorway. Whoever finds me finds life and draws salvation from the Lord” (Prov. 8:34–35).

Virgin of Christ, I therefore exhort you to watch toward God with every effort, so that on the day of your need you may find him gracious. Therefore, honourable virgin, let no misfortune find you unprepared; let there be no event which your reflection has not anticipated. Set before your eyes that there is nothing which cannot happen. Always call future miseries to mind; amid prosperity reflect how you will meet adversity. Always consider in your mind lest something adverse occur.

It belongs to a wise person to foresee the loss caused by danger. All things that have been thought over happen with a lighter outcome. Expected evils are borne tolerably; a foreseen event is accepted when it comes. Premeditation breaks the force of approaching attacks; forethought lessens future troubles; foresight softens the arrival of evils. An unexpected evil strikes hard. Serious are the things that have not been considered. Bitter are the things into which we fall unawares. Unforeseen evils wound severely. Sudden evil quickly breaks one; what has not been foreseen afflicts grievously. A sudden storm at sea arouses terror; an unexpected enemy [Col. 1283A] causes grievous disturbance. All sudden things are more burdensome; what happens suddenly confronts us more severely.

Therefore, sister most dearly beloved to me in Christ, prepare your heart both for good and for evil. “In the day of prosperity do not forget adversity, and in the day of adversity do not forget prosperity” (Eccl. 11:27). Be most watchful in understanding, lest you be defiled by vain thoughts. Love knowledge of the Scriptures and despise the vices of the flesh.
