Dearest sister, if you watch toward God with your whole heart and serve him throughout your life with all devotion, then without any doubt you will reign with him in the heavenly court. Amen.

## LVI.—On Prudence

**135.** Dearest sister, hear the Lord Jesus Christ saying in the Gospel: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves” [Col. 1283B] (Matt. 10:16). Solomon also says: “The simplicity of the righteous shall guide them, but the perversity of the deceitful shall destroy them” (Prov. 11:3). “The way of the simple is the way of the Lord, but terror is for those who work evil” (Prov. 10:29). “The righteousness of the simple shall direct his soul, but the wicked shall fall in his wickedness” (Prov. 11:5). “The innocent believes every word” (ibid. 14:13). “But whoever deceives the righteous into an evil way shall fall into his own destruction, and the simple shall possess his goods” (Prov. 28:10). “Men of blood hate the simple person, but the righteous seek his salvation” (Prov. 29:10).

Holy lack of sophistication benefits itself alone; and insofar as it builds up the Church of Christ by the merit of its life, it destroys it if it does not resist those who destroy the truth. Blessed Jerome also says: “In male and female servants of God one should not seek bodily adornment but simplicity of mind.” Let neither the simple nor the unlearned person, therefore, suppose that holiness consists in his language, but only in a pure and simple conscience. Of two imperfect things, it is far better to possess holy lack of sophistication than sinful eloquence. Holy lack of sophistication is more worthy of reverence than wordy talkativeness.

Sister beloved in Christ, if our intention is simple before God, our action will not be dark in his judgment. Those who do not know how to be chaste through righteousness cannot possibly be innocent through simplicity. The Church of the holy elect begins the paths of its uprightness and simplicity with fear but completes them with love. For God is the examiner not only of words but also of the heart, and he loves those who serve him in simplicity of heart. Hence the Bridegroom speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “My dove, my perfect one, is one; she is one to her mother, chosen for her who bore her” (Song 6:8).

Our mother is the grace of God that regenerates us; with her one dove is chosen, because she gathers only those who remain in simplicity and are not divided from unity. For many believers, while directing themselves to him, while nourishing one another by the single desire for Christ, and while joining themselves in love with one heart and one soul, make one body from many members. In that body all who live in the simplicity of unity are one dove. Those things that are despised among people and held in contempt are in great glory with God.

**136.** Therefore, venerable sister, let us pray almighty God to send us the Holy Spirit from heaven, who may grant us the simplicity of the dove and the prudence of the serpent, so that we may be simple in malice and prudent in good works. For the serpent is a shrewd animal, as is related of the asp: when it sees the charmer coming, it presses one ear to the ground and stops the other with its tail, so that it may not hear the charmer’s voice. Thus the prophet says of those who are cruel and clever in evil: “Their fury is like that of a serpent, like the deaf asp which stops its ears, so that it may not hear the voice of charmers or of a skilful enchanter” [Col. 1284B] (Ps. 57:5–6).

Therefore, beloved sister, imitate this serpent in this respect: close your ears so that you may not hear evil words. Honourable virgin, pray to God that “the oil of the sinner may not fatten your head” (Ps. 141:5; cited as Ps. 111:5 in the source). The oil of the sinner is the praise of the flatterer. The serpent closes its ear lest it hear the charmer; similarly close your ear, so that you do not hear the slanderer. The prudent person, like the asp, does not listen to the word of death lest he die. Therefore be prudent, lest evil words enter your soul through your ears and you die.

Thus, bride of Christ, neither the prudence of the serpent without the simplicity of the dove, nor the simplicity of the dove without the prudence of the serpent, ought to be in you: so that the serpent’s shrewdness may stir up the dove’s simplicity to avoid evil, and the dove’s simplicity may temper the serpent’s prudence in doing good.

**137.** Sister most beloved to me in Christ, the dove also has seven virtues, as we read, which you may possess through the grace of the Holy Spirit:

1. The dove often sits beside streams of water, so that, on seeing a hawk approach, it may plunge into the waves and escape.
2. Among wheat, it chooses the better grains.
3. It often feeds the young of another.
4. It does not strike with its beak.
5. It has no gall.
6. It makes its nest in the openings of walls.
7. It has groaning instead of song.

Therefore, honourable virgin, pray to God with the greatest diligence that he may give you these virtues of the dove: namely, that you may sit beside the streams of Holy Scripture and, through their admonition, escape the devil’s assault. In Holy Scripture choose the better sayings, from which you may be nourished. Feed the young of another; that is, convert to God by your words and examples people formerly estranged from God. Do not strike with your beak; that is, do not do evil to your neighbour or speak evil. Have no gall; that is, have no anger within you. Make your nest in the openings of rocks—that is, make there your hope. Have groaning instead of song: namely, just as worldly people delight in the songs of the world, so you should delight in groaning and spiritual sorrow.

Therefore, venerable sister, as I said to you above, you must at once understand and avoid the enemy’s snares with every diligence. Thus, through innocence of life, you must be prudent. He who does not unite prudence [Col. 1285A] with simplicity is, according to the prophet’s saying, “a deceived dove, without heart” (Hos. 7:11). He is a dove because he is simple; but he has no heart because he has no prudence.

Again, dearest sister, I exhort you to prepare in your heart a worthy dwelling for Christ, so that he, coming with the Father and the Holy Spirit, may deign to make his abode with you in the dwelling-place of your breast. Amen.

## LVII.—On Avoiding Worldly Women
138. Dearest sister, flee the company of worldly women. Let secular women, who do not share one profession with you, not enter into your company, because they commend to you what they love. Behold: they tell you what they cherish. Therefore you ought to avoid the company of worldly women, because they love the world [Col. 1285B] and speak of worldly things; they love earthly things, and therefore announce earthly things to you; they desire transitory things, and therefore expound transitory matters in your ears. For it is written: “Each person praises what he loves.” And therefore a worldly woman praises the world because she loves the world; certainly, if she loved heavenly things, she would praise heavenly things. Without doubt, if she loved heavenly things, she would approve heavenly things and preach heavenly things; if she desired eternal things, she would urge eternal things upon you. And therefore, sister, I admonish you to drive the company of worldly women away from yourself. Why? “Evil and corrupt conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. XV, 33). What has a man’s wife to do with Christ’s bride? Or what has a married woman to do with a virgin devoted to God? What has a worldly woman to do with [Col. 1285C] Christ’s bride? What has a secular woman to do with a religious woman? Or what has a woman who loves the world to do with a woman who has left the world? What has a married woman to do with a woman beloved of Christ? What has one who loves a husband to do with her who loves Christ?

Why does a woman who does not maintain your purpose come into your company? Why does a worldly woman who does not wear your habit approach your fellowship? What has a worldly woman to do with you, when she does not bear Christ’s yoke with you? Why does a woman who has not submitted her neck with you to Christ’s yoke come to converse with you? She differs in dress; she differs in disposition; and as she differs in clothing, so too in mind. A worldly woman is Satan’s instrument [Col. 1285D]. She sings to you in order to stir up the enticements of the world and show the paths of the devil, as we read. Such is the siren of the sea: above the navel she is like a most beautiful and lovely virgin; but from the navel to the feet she is like a fish. The siren has a virgin’s head and a fish’s hind parts. She sings sweetly in loud voices and in many melodies, and with great sweetness produces harmonious sounds; but through her sweet songs she often deceives sailors and brings them into danger. Sailors crossing the sea often hear the sweet voices of sirens, and are deceived through their sweet voices and pleasant songs, and are brought into mortal peril. As the siren deceives sailors by sweet songs, so the worldly woman deceives Christ’s servants by her deceitful words. [Col. 1286A] And as the siren, through pleasant songs, is accustomed to turn seafarers aside from the right course and bring them to destruction, so the worldly woman, through flattering and seductive words, is accustomed to draw those serving God back from their holy purpose and lead them into danger to their souls.

139. Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, flee the songs of sirens, lest, while you delight in hearing earthly pleasures, you be turned from the right way. For what are the words of worldly women but the songs of sirens? Therefore flee the siren’s song, and separate your ears from the evil tongue of a woman who gives harmful counsel. Avoid a worldly woman’s words as though they were a serpent’s hiss. Beware lest, as the serpent deceived the woman in paradise, so the poisonous tongue of a woman giving evil counsel deceive you [Col. 1286B] in the monastery. Take care lest a vain and talkative woman pour the poisons of death into your ears. Beware lest death enter through your windows—that is, through your eyes and ears—into your soul.

Venerable sister, when you see a woman unlike you in purpose, fortify your heart with the shield of faith, and arm your forehead against her with the trophy of the cross. Honorable sister, I permit you conversation with a worldly woman for this purpose alone: that by holy admonitions you may persuade her to leave the world and come to the monastery. For this purpose only do I grant you permission to speak with a woman of the world: that you may teach her to despise earthly things, to love heavenly things, to leave the world, and to serve God. Likewise, that through your address she may despise transitory things and desire eternal ones. Dearest sister, if you do this [Col. 1286C] as I have told you, you will keep yourself from evil in this world and in the future receive from the Lord a crown in heaven. Amen.

LVIII.—On guarding against the company of men.

140. Dearest sister, if you flee women with such diligence, how much more ought you to flee men? And if you avoid the company of women so carefully, how much more ought you to avoid the company of men? And if you avoid women’s conversations with such care, how much more ought you to avoid men’s deceptions? And if you separate your ears so thoroughly from women’s words, how much more ought you to separate them from men’s seductive words?

Sister beloved to me in Christ, I admonish you that, however holy a man may be, he should nevertheless have no association with you [Col. 1286D]. Though he be holy and righteous, let him have no familiarity with you; though he be religious, let him have no constant intercourse with you; though he be good, let him have no continual sharing of life with you. Why? Lest, through the familiarity of mutual visiting, the chastity of both perish; lest, through frequent seeing of each other, the honor of both be destroyed; lest, through habitual seeing of each other, the religious reputation of both be defamed; lest, through mutual intercourse in life, the person of each be dishonored. He falls away from the love of God who gives occasion for sinning. He also falls away from love of neighbor who provides an opportunity for wrongdoing; for although he does not commit evil in deed, he nevertheless fosters the worst opinion. A person often sins through constant association. Familiarity often conquers those whom vice could not overcome. Opportunity for sin often has made—and makes—the will [Col. 1287A]. Those whom pleasure could not overcome, constant association overcomes. When different sexes are placed together, they provoke the impulse of the flesh that arises from this. Even the natural flame of the flesh is kindled if it touches what is forbidden. Man and woman differ by nature; if they are placed together, even though they do not sin, yet through their intercourse they foster an evil reputation between themselves.

141. “Who will bind fire in his bosom and not be burned?” (Prov. VI, 27). Fire and tow placed together nourish flames. Although they are opposites, if placed together they produce flames. So man and woman, if placed together, although they do not do evil, nevertheless through constant association foster an evil reputation between themselves and cause others to murmur about them. [Col. 1287B] If a religious man and a religious woman unite with one another without moderation, they give others occasion to murmur about them. The sex of man and woman is different; and therefore, if they are joined together, an occasion for sin immediately arises from this.

What then have fire and tow to do together? Why is a serpent placed in one’s bosom? Why is fire placed in clothing? Why does a woman who has promised chastity to God have association with a man? Why does a woman who has despised the world for God’s sake love familiarity with a man? Why does she who desires to enter the heavenly bridal chamber with Christ love the presence of men? Why does a woman devoted to God seek to hear men’s deceitful words? Why does she who in the world did not wish to have a husband, once placed in a monastery desire to see men’s faces? Therefore, [Col. 1287C] sister beloved to me in Christ, if you wish to be secure from fornication, be separated in mind and body from the company of men. If you wish perfectly to preserve chastity for love of Christ, keep far from the company of a man. If you are stationed near a serpent, certainly you will not be safe for long; sitting near a fire, even if you are iron, you will at some point melt; placed near danger, you will not long remain unharmed or secure.

Hear then, sister most dearly beloved to me in Christ, words of good counsel. Let men not know your name; let them not see your face; let them not recognize your face, even though they hear your name. Hear also, honorable virgin, the words of the Apostle Paul: “We ought to have a good testimony from those who are outside” (1 Tim. III, 7): a good life within, indeed, for our own sake; but a good reputation for the sake of others. [Col. 1287D] Venerable sister, if for God’s sake on earth you avoid the company of men, through God you will have the company of angels in heaven. Amen.

LIX.—On fleeing the company of young men.

142. My dearest sister, if even holy men must thus be avoided, lest the holiness of both perish through habitual intercourse, how much more must young men be avoided, who follow the dark paths and pleasures of temporal life? And if you must flee the frequent company of holy men with such care, how much more ought you to flee young men who follow the desires of this world? For this purpose the devil sets young men before the eyes of a religious woman: that she may meditate at night upon the forms of those whom she has seen by day [Col. 1288A], and that the recent vision—the sight of a body observed—may continually turn in her mind. Thus Satan’s arrow enters through the gateways of the eyes into the mind. Hence the prophet says: “Death has entered through your windows; it has entered your houses” (Jer. IX, 21). The devil’s arrow does not enter the inward parts of the mind except through the bodily senses.

Sister beloved to me in Christ, men are to be loved, but while absent; people are to be loved not within the house but outside; we ought to love people in the mind, but not in the home; love people in your thoughts, but from afar; men are to be loved because they are God’s work, but outside the house; men are to be loved not because of bodily beauty, but because they are the work of the Creator. Again, venerable sister, I admonish you never to speak alone with a man alone. Let no one speak with you privately; nor should you speak with anyone except in the presence of two or three witnesses [Col. 1288B]. Christ’s bride ought not to speak alone with a man alone, except with her confessor when she is doing penance for her sins. A religious woman who desires to speak alone with a man has folly reigning in her mind. Hear, therefore, beloved one, if you wish perfectly to preserve chastity for love of Christ, keep far from the company of men. If you perfectly despise the company of men on earth for Christ’s sake, without any doubt you will reign with him in heaven. Amen.

LX.—On avoiding the company of the wicked.

143. Most honorable sister, hear Solomon’s words: “My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent to them” (Prov. I, 10); “do not emulate an unjust man, nor follow [Col. 1288C] his way” (Prov. III, 31). “Depart from an iniquitous man, and you will have peace” (Ecclus. VII, 2). Let righteous men be your companions; let your glory be in the fear of God (Ecclus. IX, 22). Whomever you know to observe the fear of God, let him be joined to you in friendship. Do not associate with evil people.

Blessed Ambrose: “The life of holy people ought to be a norm of good living for other people.” For one who has associated with a holy man will receive from that companionship the practice of good speech and the example of good work, so that day by day his mind may be kindled in the love of God. He is not greatly praiseworthy who is good among the good; but he is truly praiseworthy who is good among the evil. Truly praiseworthy is the person who is good in the company [Col. 1288D] of the wicked. As one is blameworthy who is evil among the good, so one is to be praised who is good among the evil. The words of God-fearing people are words of life, and health of soul to those who follow and love them. As the rising sun drives away darkness, so the teaching of the saints drives the darkness of vices from our senses. Hence David the prophet says: “With the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will be perverted” (Ps. XVII, 26–27).

Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, if you wish to live well, avoid the company of evil people. Avoid the bad, beware the wicked, flee the depraved, reject the idle from yourself. Flee crowds of people, especially age-groups inclined to vice; do not join yourself to frivolous persons or mingle with vain ones. Join yourself to the good, seek the fellowship of the good, look for the company of the good [Col. 1289A], cling inseparably to the saints. If you are their companion in manner of life, you will also be their companion in virtue. “He who walks with the wise is wise; he who goes with fools is foolish” (Prov. XIII, 20). Like is accustomed to be joined with like. It is dangerous to live with evil people; it is ruinous to associate in life with those of perverse will. It is better to have the hatred of the wicked than their fellowship. As the common life of saints has many goods, so the company of the wicked brings very many evils. Whoever touches what is unclean will be defiled; whoever touches what is filthy will become filthy. Therefore, venerable sister, if you gladly hear my words and fulfill them in deed, you will be numbered among God’s elect. Amen.

LXI.—On not secretly accepting letters or little gifts.

[Col. 1289B]

144. Dearest sister, hear what I say. A handmaid of Christ who receives letters or gifts in secret breaks her Order. She does great evil and commits a grave sin if she receives letters or any other gift from men, because she breaks her Order. She commits a great wrong who, for temporal gifts, becomes a transgressor of her Order. A religious woman who desires to enter into marriage with Christ ought not to give men handkerchiefs, combs, belts, mirrors, or bands. She who awaits Christ with a burning lamp ought not to receive worldly gifts from men—namely [Col. 1289C] combs, mirrors, and other such things. She who is veiled for love of Christ ought not to receive gifts of vanity from her friends. She who, for God’s sake, has placed the sacred veil upon her head sins greatly if she receives worldly gifts from men. A religious woman who delights in such things is deceived by great vanity and displays the sign of a prostitute.

Hence blessed Jerome says: “Holy love does not have sweet letters, handkerchiefs, and frequent little gifts.” As though he said: If holy love were in the mind of a religious woman, she would not receive from men gifts of vanity and superfluity. A chaste and religious mind does not desire to receive gifts from worldly friends, but from Christ, for whose love it despises all earthly things; and it ought to desire [Col. 1289D] gifts from him alone, with whom it hopes to rejoice in the heavenly homeland. A chaste woman does not seek earthly gifts, but heavenly ones. The more a person delights in earthly gifts, the more he is removed from the love of God.

145. If religious women do in the monastery what secular women are accustomed to do in the world, they are sufficiently blameworthy before God, and there is no difference between secular and religious women. Therefore, if there is no distinction between those who are in the monastery and those who are in the world, neither is there any difference between religious and secular women. Therefore, if religious women give delightful gifts to their friends, as prostitutes are accustomed to do, where are honor, religion, chastity, purity, and holiness? If religious women, who ought to please God through [Col. 1290A] good works, please their friends in evil by giving luxurious gifts, where are modesty, self-restraint, reverence, and shame? Thus, if religious women prefer to please people in the world rather than Jesus Christ, the eternal king in heaven, where are observance of religion, the rigor of the Order, ardor in contemplation, purity of mind, contrition of heart, diligence in prayer, groaning of the breast, and monastic habit? If religious women rejoice in temporal gifts as secular people are accustomed to rejoice, where are contempt for the world, fear of hell, remembrance of judgment, recollection of eternal fire, and love of God? Therefore, if religious women desire to receive from men gifts of vanity, [Col. 1290B] where are remembrance of sins, tears of the eyes, and recollection of transgressions? All are held cheap, despised, scorned, annihilated. Truly, a religious woman who receives from men things in which she may delight despises her Order. She who rejoices more in her friends’ gifts than in the precepts of her Order is a transgressor of her purpose.

Of such people the prophet says: “Their right hand is full of gifts” (Ps. XXV, 10). As though he said: Although their works appear good, nevertheless they rejoice more in gifts than in good works. They prefer to receive gifts from men rather than eternal goods from Christ. A religious woman who loves Christ perfectly does not receive delightful and superfluous [Col. 1290C] gifts from men, because she places Christ before all gifts. Hence in the Song of Songs it is said of the Church: “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove” (Song I, 9). The Church, or any holy soul, is compared to a turtledove because it loves Christ perfectly and places nothing before his love. Once through some mischance the turtledove has lost its mate, it never seeks another, because it does not accept an adulterous love. So a religious woman who loves Christ perfectly does not thereafter accept adulterous love—that is, she no longer loves evil people. A religious woman who loves a person more than Christ is not chaste but adulterous, because she despises Christ, to whom she had been betrothed. When a religious woman first comes to the monastery, [Col. 1290D] she receives Christ as her bridegroom. But if afterward she loves a person carnally above Christ, she commits adultery; and even if not in body, she is already an adulteress in mind, according to the saying: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V, 28). So too a woman commits adultery with a man if she desires him in her heart or loves him carnally.

146. Therefore, sister most beloved to me in Christ, I admonish you to love Christ, your bridegroom, above all things and to desire to receive gifts from him alone. I beg you to love Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, above all things, and for his love not to receive worldly gifts. Without doubt, one who seeks earthly gifts does not hope for heavenly ones. “Gifts blind the eyes [Col. 1291A] of the wise and change the words of the righteous” (Deut. XVI, 19). Certainly, if gifts blind the eyes of the wise, they also blind the minds of religious men so that they do not see God. If, as is true, gifts blind the eyes of the wise, they likewise cloud the eyes of God’s servants so that Christ is not seen.

Hence blessed Isidore says: “The eye of the mind, which dust closes, cannot see lofty things.” As though he said more plainly: the eye of the mind, closed by the dust of desire, cannot perfectly behold heavenly things. The mind of God’s servant cannot be free for contemplation of God if it is still darkened by earthly desires. If the mind of a religious woman still delights in earthly gifts, she does not perfectly contemplate heavenly things. If, by receiving or giving, she desires to please people, she does not perfectly love God [Col. 1291B]. For those who desire to please in these vanities are also despised by God. Hence David the prophet says: “God will scatter the bones of those who please people; they have been confounded, because God has rejected them” (Ps. LII, 6).

I also ask you, venerable sister in Christ, to hear with every devotion the prophet Isaiah saying: “He who shakes his hands free of every gift shall dwell on high; his eyes shall see the King of saints in his beauty” (Isa. XXXIII, 15–17). As though he said: whoever for God’s sake shakes his hands free of every gift will dwell in heaven and see the King of saints in his glory. Whoever, because of love for God, does not receive from people gifts of vanity and superfluity [Col. 1291C] will see God in his majesty and rejoice eternally with all the saints in his splendor. Therefore, sister beloved in Christ, I ask you to take this holy prophet’s counsel and shake your hands free of every gift. If you wish to dwell on high, shake your hands free of every gift. Again, through God’s grace I admonish you to strive to imitate him who says: “I shall appear in your presence with righteousness; I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. XVI, 15). Amen.

LXII.—On rendering vows to God.

147. Dearest sister, consider carefully what you vow to God, and render it. Vow and render yourself whole. Accuse yourself concerning sins; praise God concerning benefits. Attribute no good to yourself; say that you have received from him every good thing that you possess. Confess [Col. 1291D] him merciful, yourself sinful; him truthful, yourself false. I ask you, beloved sister, to say with the prophet: “I shall enter into your house,” that is, the monastery, “with burnt offerings”—that is, in a spirit of contrition and compunction. “I shall render my vows to you” (Ps. LXV, 13): that is, there I shall offer you myself, ungrateful as I am, on the altar of my heart, as I vowed myself to you.

It is necessary that one who desires salvation render with every devotion the good things vowed to God. Whoever desires to attain eternal joys must strive to fulfill the good things promised to God. Hence the prophet says: “Vow and render to the Lord your God” (Ps. LXXV, 12). As though he said: vow and render yourselves, because one who vows must also render, since by vowing one has made oneself a debtor. And it would be better not to vow than, after [Col. 1292A] a vow, not to fulfill what was promised (Eccl. V, 4).

There are also certain vows common to all and others that are special. The common vows are those we promised in Baptism: namely, that we would not sin and that we would renounce the devil and his works. Special vows are made when someone promises to become a monk, a canon, a hermit, or something else. If the one who vows does not render it, he cannot be saved. Why? Because one who has promised God that he will live well cannot be saved if he does not fulfill these promises in good works. Whoever neglects to fulfill the good things promised to God cannot attain those good things God has promised. How does one who does not wish to render to God the good things vowed to him wish to receive from God the good things God has promised him? [Col. 1292B] How does one who does not wish to render his vow to God wish to receive the heavenly gift from God? Or how does one who neglects to pay his vows to God think that he will receive heavenly gifts from God? Because he is not faithful but unfaithful, the one who neglects to render his vows to God will be condemned among the unfaithful; he who does not bring his vow to completion in good works will perish among the unfaithful.

148. Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, I admonish you to do the good you promised. Do not be easy in words and difficult in deeds. Do not readily promise before God to do anything; undertake nothing without considering your strength. Do not promise what you cannot do. You will be greatly culpable in God’s sight if you do not render the good you promised. Those who do not fulfill their vows displease God. Among the unfaithful will be reckoned [Col. 1292C] those who have not fulfilled what they vowed. For it is better not to promise than not to fulfill the faith of a promise.

Nevertheless, venerable sister, break faith in evil promises; alter your resolution in a disgraceful vow. Do not do the evil that you promised; do not fulfill what you vowed incautiously. A promise fulfilled by a crime is impious. Therefore now, bride of Christ, as I have already told you, if with all devotion you render to God the good things you promised him, you will receive from him the eternal good things that he has promised you. Amen.

LXIII.—On always considering the end and purpose of one’s state.

149. Dearest sister, know well what you are; know yourself. Recall why you were born; remember why you came into being, for what purpose you were brought forth, under what condition you were created, and to what end you have been called in this world. Remember your condition, preserve the order of your nature, be what you were made. Be such as God made you; be such as your Maker established you. Keep measure in every work; maintain moderation in everything. Do nothing without temperance; do nothing either too little or too much, beyond what is fitting or below it. Even in good things nothing ought to be excessive. All things moderate are useful and, in their proper measure, perfect. Things done with moderation are wholesome; but good things become harmful through immoderate use. For every excess is counted as a vice. To do everything temperately is prudence. Do not make evil out of good.

Beloved sister, [Col. 1293A] consider also what is suitable to each time. First see what you ought to do, where and when, how, and for how long you should do it. By discernment know the causes of things. With every care distinguish all that you do; carefully consider how you may begin and complete a good work. Keep discernment in every action of yours; when you have rightly ordered your work, you will be most rightly just. Whatever good you do with discernment will be virtue; what you do without discernment will be vice. For indiscreet virtue is reckoned a vice; virtue without discernment holds the place of vice. Through perverse custom many things have been corrupted; through evil usage many things have been profaned. Many things have been unlawfully appropriated contrary to modest conduct. Therefore custom must yield to authority. Let law and reason overcome evil custom.

Honorable virgin, I admonish you to [Col. 1293B] keep firm faith in your heart, the helmet of salvation on your head, the sign of the cross on your forehead, the word of truth in your mouth, good will in your mind, fear and true love of God and neighbor in your breast, the girdle of chastity on your body, honorableness in your actions, sobriety in your conduct and goodness, humility in prosperity, patience in tribulation, simplicity in manner of life, certain hope in the Creator, love of eternal life, and perseverance in good works until the end. Amen.

LXIV.—On guarding against striving to please people through beauty.

150. Dearest sister, let us avoid destructive beauties, lest the seeds of all evils sprout from them. [Col. 1293C] Whoever loves bodily beauty deceives himself. Why? Because bodily beauty is deceptive, vain, earth and ashes, a deception of humankind. Hence Solomon says: “Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain” (Prov. XXXI, 30). Many have been and are deceived by bodily beauty. Foolish people, while they contemplate bodily beauty, fall into the devil’s snare; while they attend to the beauty of flesh, they are entangled in the devil’s nets. Many are bound in sins through bodily beauty. God does not seek the adornment of the body, but the beauty of the soul. God loves spiritual beauty more than carnal beauty. Christ does not delight in bodily beauty but in purity of soul.

Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, I admonish you [Col. 1293D] to love that beauty in which God delights. Never look upon people with the intention of loving their beauty; do not consider people with the purpose of delighting in their beauty; never behold people in order to desire their beauty. I also ask you never to arrange your face in order to please people; never adorn your face in order to please in the eyes of people. Let it not be your intention to wish to appear beautiful before people; because if you do this in order to seem beautiful in the sight of people, you wrong Jesus Christ, your bridegroom. Since you are betrothed to Christ, if you wish to appear before people’s eyes, you are not chaste but adulterous. Like an adulteress, you wrong Christ if you display your beauty in order to be loved by people. [Col. 1294A] How are you not adulterous when you love people more than Christ? Or how do you not commit adultery when you love people above Christ? How can you say, “I am not an adulteress,” when you gave yourself to Christ in the monastery and now wish to please people by the beauty of your face? When you do this, you display the sign of a prostitute. Prostitutes and worldly women are accustomed to do this: that is, they arrange their faces in order to appear beautiful in people’s eyes. O how shameful and absurd it is for religious women to do what prostitutes and worldly women are accustomed to do!

151. Therefore, honorable virgin, hear what I say; attend to what I admonish. Never arrange your face in order to please people; but adorn inwardly the face of your [Col. 1294B] conscience with good virtues, so that you may be able to please Jesus Christ, the heavenly bridegroom. God does not delight in bodily beauty, but in beauty of mind; not in the arrangement of the face, but in good morals; not in bodily adornment, but in holy conduct. When a holy soul is inwardly adorned for Christ with good morals, it is loved and cherished by Christ. This the bridegroom aptly intimates in the Song of Songs, where he speaks to the bride, saying: “How beautiful you are, my friend; how lovely, dearest, in delights!” (Song IV, 1). As though he said: How beautiful you are, my friend: that is, by living justly, holily, and religiously you are beautiful; and by loving me above all things you are my friend. Therefore you are beautiful and lovely, because you live well in good works; [Col. 1294C] and therefore you are my friend, because you love me perfectly, because you do not love another friend more than me. And you are not only my friend, but also dearest in delights. A holy soul is called “dearest in delights,” namely, in the delights of the Holy Scriptures, because one who despises being rich in the delights of Holy Scripture does not perfectly attain Christ’s love and intimacy. One who has refreshed himself with the delights of the Scriptures may perfectly attain Christ’s love, and loves Christ and is loved by Christ. But whoever desires more to please people through the beauty of his face [Col. 1294D] than Christ through good works neither loves Christ perfectly nor is loved by Christ.

Therefore I admonish you, dearest sister, to love Christ above all things, because God the Father chose you in him before the ages (Eph. I, 4). I also ask you to desire to please him alone and not to receive temporal praise from people. Amen.

LXV.—On fleeing immoderate laughter.

152. Dearest sister, hear the words of most wise Solomon: “I counted laughter an error, and I said to joy: Why are you deceived in vain?” (Eccl. II, 2). An error is said to occur when one thing ought to be done and another is done. Therefore an error occurs when one who ought to weep laughs. Thus laughter is called an error because, while someone laughs, that person does not keep the day of death in mind. Truly [Col. 1295A], one who rejoices and is glad in temporal pleasures is vainly deceived. Those who rejoice in this world’s prosperity are deceived, since, if they recalled the day of their death, they would first weep for their sins rather than laugh at vain things. Those who laugh at vain things, if they kept in mind the evils they will suffer, would not laugh but mourn. Hence Solomon also says: “Laughter will be mingled with sorrow, and mourning will occupy the end of joy” (Prov. XIV, 13). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. V, 5). He did not say, “Blessed are those who laugh,” but “Blessed are those who mourn,” because those who mourn their sins are truly blessed, not those who laugh at vain things. Those who mourn according to God are blessed, because they shall be comforted.

And the apostle James rebukes foolish people who laugh, saying: “Your laughter shall be turned into mourning, and your joy into grief” (Jas. IV, 9). “A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise person will scarcely laugh silently” (Ecclus. XXI, 23). Therefore, beloved sister, avoid laughter as an error, and change temporal gladness into mourning. Why? Namely, that you may make yourself blessed if you weep in this pilgrimage; that you may be found blessed on the day of your death if you weep for yourself in this world. Know that you are a pilgrim in this world, because this is not your homeland, but heaven is. You have no abiding city here, because God has promised you the heavenly Jerusalem, to which David the prophet desired to come when he said: “I rejoiced in those things which were said to me: ‘We shall go into the house of the Lord’” (Ps. CXXI, 1). Christ’s servant also burned with such desire [Col. 1295C] when he said: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. I, 23). He too desired to reach heaven when he said: “Alas for me, because my sojourn has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. CXIX, 5). When he said these things, he did not laugh at this world’s vanities, but mourned over this pilgrimage.

153. Therefore, honorable virgin, let your joy always be in heaven. Let the gladness of your heart always be modest and tranquil, according to the Apostle’s saying: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4:4); and elsewhere he says: “But the fruit of the Spirit is joy” (Gal. 5:22). Such joy does not disturb the mind by an abundance of laughter, but raises the soul [Col. 1295D] through longing to reach the heavenly homeland, where it may hear: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21). A person’s face is the mirror of the heart. By laughter one can recognize the heart of a religious woman. Useless laughter and jokes reveal the vain conscience of a religious woman; often laughter and shameful jesting show what the heart of a religious woman is like. For she would not laugh thoughtlessly if she had a chaste heart; she would never laugh lasciviously if she did not have lasciviousness in her mind. For thus the Lord says: “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” (Matt. 12:34). Therefore the virgin’s face laughs from the abundance of an utterly vain breast. If vanity were not in a woman’s mind, she would never laugh at vanity. A chaste mind rejoices more in mourning than in laughter. Certainly, [Col. 1296A] if a religious woman had true chastity in her mind, she would love tears more than temporal joy. If she recalled her negligences and the punishments of hell, she would love tears more than laughter. Where laughter and joking abound, perfect charity does not reign. If a religious woman loved Christ perfectly, she would not laugh, but would weep unceasingly with longing for him; for one who perfectly loves and fears Christ does not laugh, but mourns through love of him. I wonder why she seeks jokes and laughter who came to the monastery for the purpose of shedding tears for her sins. I wonder why she has no shame, she who raises her voice in laughter. How shameful it is for her to laugh when she ought, in this pilgrimage, to have wept for her sins! Why do we wretches laugh, who must render an account to God, in the sight of the angels and all the saints, for [Col. 1296B] all our deeds? Therefore it is better for us in this life to mourn our sins, so that we may obtain forgiveness from the Lord in the life to come. I beseech you, venerable sister, to beware of laughter and jokes, and to shed tears without ceasing for your sins: flee jokes and laughter, and mourn your sins continually. Hear, bride of Christ, what the bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon” (Song 7:4). The bride’s eyes are rightly called pools, because, when the holy soul weeps over this pilgrimage, through God’s grace it washes itself from sins. Thus a religious woman ought to mourn without interruption, so that she may wash herself from her sins. Therefore, dearest sister, if [Col. 1296C] in this life we mourn our sins perfectly and withdraw from the vanities of this world, we believe that we shall obtain forgiveness for our sins.

## LXVI.—On Not Wandering Outside

154. Most honorable sister, hear how the prophet Jeremiah laments our iniquities, saying: “How the gold has grown dim, how its finest color has changed! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4:1). By the gold we understand the life of religious persons, which formerly was bright through the glory of virtues, but now is dark through shameful practices. The gold’s finest color signifies the habit of holiness, which formerly was precious and excellent through good works, but now through [Col. 1296D] vices and worldly activities has been altered and become cheap and despised. Truly the excellent habit of religious men—that is, monks, canons, and religious women—has been altered when it is more carefully arranged to please in the sight of the people than to please in the sight of God. Truly the finest color of gold has been altered when the habit of religious men is more adjusted to please through vain glory in human sight than to please God through humility. Certainly today the finest garments of religious persons have been changed, when they are adorned more to please in the royal court than in the sight of the Creator. It follows: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street.” The stones of the sanctuary signify religious men, who should never [Col. 1297A] wander abroad but should always remain in the seclusion of the monastery before God’s eyes. Yet today the stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street when religious men wander abroad in search of vain and worldly things. The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street when religious men desire more to frequent the royal court than to remain within the monastery enclosure. They are scattered when they desire more to hear the superfluous words of rich people than the commands of Scripture. They are scattered at the head of the streets when they take more delight in the banquets and conversation of the wealthy than in the poverty and abstinence of religious brothers. Servants of God ought to love vegetables in the monastery more than sumptuous banquets in the world. Religious men ought to love [Col. 1297B] greens among their brothers more than an abundance of foods among the rich. Religious men ought to rejoice more at the table of poor brothers than at the table of kings. Why? Because, as Augustine says, it is better to lack less than to possess more. 884 It is better to endure poverty for Christ in the monastery than to possess many riches in the world.

155. Therefore it is necessary that every religious person who desires salvation should despise the world and shut himself within the monastery’s enclosure. A religious man ought to flee the gatherings of worldly people and seek the fellowship of God’s servants. Religious men ought to love the cloister more than the court. Now hear what I say; listen to what I advise. It is better for you to sit in the cloister than to go about the streets of the city; [Col. 1297C] love remaining in the monastery more than seeing cities. It is better to rest within the monastery walls than to appear before the people. If you shut yourself within the cloister, you will be loved by Christ. This the bridegroom aptly suggests in the Song of Songs when he says to the bride: “A garden enclosed, my sister, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4:12). Every holy soul is understood to be an enclosed garden, because while it nourishes virtues it produces flowers; it nourishes and refreshes itself with virtues, and it preserves the fruits which it brings forth. For the holy soul is called an enclosed garden because, through love of eternal life, it withdraws itself from worldly noise; because it avoids human eyes; because it hides the good it does from the praise of men; [Col. 1297D] because it encloses itself for God’s sake, lest it be seen by people; because it despises human praise. It surrounds itself with the intention of despising such good things, lest the ancient enemy break in to seize its inner possessions. It is also called a sealed fountain because, while it constantly thinks on heavenly things and continually stores the knowledge of the Scriptures in the womb of memory, the holy mind never ceases, as it were, to produce within itself living waters by which it may refresh its thirsty neighbors. Therefore, dearest sister, as I said to you above, if while you live you shut yourself within the cloister walls for Christ’s love and adhere perfectly to the commands of the Rule, after this life you will rejoice with the same Lord Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, in the bridal chamber. Amen.

## LXVII.—On Temptation

[Col. 1298A]

156. Most honorable sister, hear the apostle James saying: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (Jas. 4:7). And blessed Jerome says: “Nothing is stronger than one who conquers the devil, and nothing is weaker than one conquered by his own flesh.” The devil’s arrows must be extinguished by the cold of vigils and the moderation of fasts. Our cunning enemy always seeks how he may deceive us, and he is concerned not merely to kill bodies but souls, like a wolf attacking the flock. The devil scatters souls when he kills the faithful people through temptation; nevertheless, the devil does not tempt the elect beyond what God permits (Job 1). When the devil tempts God’s servants, he serves their benefit, since through his temptations he does not deceive them but instructs them. [Col. 1298B] God often turns to the advancement of souls those temptations which the devil stirs up for human destruction. God’s servants could never endure the devil’s temptations if God’s mercy did not moderate or restrain their wickedness. Although the devil always desires to tempt God’s servants, nevertheless, unless he receives power from God, he cannot accomplish what he seeks. Hence every will of the devil is always unjust, yet his power is just when God permits it. The devil unjustly seeks of himself to tempt God’s servants; but he cannot tempt those whom he wishes to tempt unless God grants him permission. Hence it is written in the books of Kings concerning the devil that “an evil spirit from the Lord tormented Saul” (1 Sam. 16:14): in this respect it was rightly, as it were, a spirit of the Lord [Col. 1298C]—but why was it evil? If it was evil, why was it the Lord’s? In this passage both God’s just power and the devil’s unjust will are comprehended in two words. For the spirit was evil through its evil will, and the same spirit was the Lord’s through the most just power it had received. The devil is not the commander of vices, but only their instigator; nor can he kindle the fuel of concupiscence anywhere except where he has first seen weighty delights in thoughts. But if we cast out the delights of evil thought, the devil at once withdraws in confusion, and the weapons of his temptation are broken.

157. The devil often wishes to deceive God’s servants under the appearance of good, when he pretends to be an angel of light [Col. 1298D] (2 Cor. 11:14); but the discernment 885 of the saints must be such as to distinguish good from evil, lest the devil be able fraudulently to deceive them. This is the inquiry of Joshua, who says: “Are you one of us, or of our adversaries?” (Josh. 5:13). For this reason the prophet Jeremiah is also told: “If you separate the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth” (Jer. 15:19). The devil is terrible in the eyes of worldly people, but contemptible in the eyes of God’s elect. Unbelievers fear the devil like a lion; but those strong in faith despise him like a little worm and, when they see him, scorn him. The devil is a slippery serpent; but if his head—that is, the first suggestion—is not resisted, he slips wholly into the depths of the heart as he is perceived. The vices of diabolical temptations [Col. 1299A] are fragile; but if they are not guarded against and through practice pass into habit, in the end they grow very strong, so that they are never, or only with difficulty, conquered. When the devil seeks to deceive anyone, he first observes each person’s nature, and then applies himself where he sees that person is inclined to sin. Hence blessed Isidore says: “The devil tempts a person more in that part in which he sees him, through an excess of humors, readily inclined to vices; so that he applies temptation according to the mixture of the humors, like one who directs water: he does not send it by another route except where he knows it will flow more readily.” Throughout life the devil desires to deceive a person, but especially at the end. This is what was said to the serpent in the beginning: “You shall lie in wait for his heel” (Gen. 3:15). [Col. 1299B] The devil lies in wait for a person’s heel when he attempts to deceive him at the end of life; for assuredly the devil plans to deceive at the end the person whom he has not deceived during the course of life. Therefore, although one may be righteous, one must never trust oneself so much as to be secure in this life; rather, one must always beware humbly and always fear anxiously lest one be deceived at the end.

158. Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, we must pray to almighty God not to permit us to be tempted beyond what we can endure, because God always restrains the devil’s strength, lest he harm as much as he wishes. Hence in the Song of Songs the Holy Spirit rebukes the devil, [Col. 1299C] saying: “Arise, north wind; and come, south wind; blow upon my garden, and let its spices flow” (Song 4:16). By the north wind, which constricts with cold and makes people numb, what else is signified but the unclean spirit, which, while it tempts and possesses all the reprobate, makes them numb toward good work? But by the south wind, namely the warm wind, the Holy Spirit is signified; when it touches the minds of the elect, it releases them from all numbness and makes them fervent in God’s love. Therefore let the north wind arise—that is, let the evil spirit depart from the Church or from every faithful soul—so that it may not tempt beyond what is fitting; and let the south wind come and blow upon the bridegroom’s garden, and let its spices flow: that is, let the Holy Spirit come and pour the fire of charity into minds, [Col. 1299D] and free the mind from temptation and from the numbness of negligence. When it does this, the spices flow, because at the Holy Spirit’s coming the heart that had previously been numb rouses itself to good works, blossoms like a garden, and after the flower produces fragrant and refreshing fruits, by which it refreshes both itself and its neighbors through good examples.

159. **Question.** Dearest brother, I ask you to show me what remedy there is against the temptations of demons.

**Answer.** Sister beloved to me in Christ, this is the remedy for one who is inflamed by temptations of vices or demons: the more one is tempted, the more one should hasten to prayer. Therefore, if evil and foul thoughts of this world disturb your heart and persuade you to commit something unlawful, let them be driven [Col. 1300A] from the soul by pure prayers and holy vigils. With all devotion, stand continually before the Lord at the time of your prayer, so that you may more easily escape the devil’s imminent temptation. Know, venerable sister, that we must fight not only against the devil’s temptation, but also against the vices of the flesh. Why? Because the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh. Therefore we must pray so perseveringly until, by God’s grace, we are able to conquer the suggestions of fleshly desires and the temptations of demons. Frequent prayer extinguishes the assault of vices. Continual prayer overcomes the devil’s darts. Prayer is the foremost strength against the assaults of temptations. Therefore, dearest sister, as I have already told you, through prayers you will conquer diabolical temptations. But if you still feel the disturbances of the flesh, if you are touched by the flesh’s goads, if the memory of lust still tickles your mind; if your flesh still attacks you, if luxury tempts you, if lust invites you to sin: set before yourself the memory of your death; place before yourself the future judgment; call future torments to mind; set before yourself eternal punishments; and also place before your eyes the perpetual fires of hell, and set before yourself the dreadful punishments of Gehenna. May the memory of Gehenna’s burning extinguish within you the burning of lust. Amen.

## LXVIII.—On Dreams

160. Most honorable sister, listen to the things that are said. Demons often appear by night and disturb people’s senses through visions; they often also rage in open attack and beat human bodies. Dreams arise in different ways. Some dreams occur through surfeit or through emptiness, and these are known also by experience. Some arise from deliberate thought; for we often recognize at night what we have thought during the day. Many dreams occur through the illusion of unclean spirits, as Solomon testifies when he says: “Dreams have led many astray, and those who hoped in them have fallen” (Ecclus. 34:7). But some visions occur to the righteous in a just manner—that is, by the mystery of revelation—as is read in the Old Testament concerning Joseph son of Jacob, who was declared through a dream to be preferred above his brothers (Gen. 37); or as is read in [Col. 1300D] the Gospel concerning Joseph, Mary’s husband, who was warned in a dream to flee with the child into Egypt (Matt. 2). Sometimes mixed visions also occur: thoughts together with illusions, and likewise thoughts together with revelations, as Daniel says: “He who reveals mysteries has shown you what is to come” (Dan. 2:29).

161. Although some dreams are true, we nevertheless ought not readily to believe them, because they arise from diverse imaginings and we do not fully know whence they come. Therefore we should not readily place faith in dreams, lest perhaps Satan, transforming himself into an angel of light, deceive some unwary person. Sometimes demons deceive certain curious persons who observe dreams with such deceptive art that [Col. 1301A] some dreams turn out exactly as they predict; and therefore they sometimes announce true things in order to deceive in many things. But although dreams come about as demons announce, they are nevertheless not to be believed, lest they proceed from illusion, according to Scripture’s testimony: “If they tell you, and it so happens, do not believe” (Deut. 13:2–3). Dreams are like auguries, and those who observe them are known to practice divination. Therefore faith is not to be placed in dreams, even though they seem true. One who places hope in dreams or auguries does not trust in God; such a person is like one who follows the wind or endeavors to grasp a shadow. False auguries and deceptive dreams are both vain. We ought not believe dreams, lest we be deceived by them. Let our hope [Col. 1301B] always be firm in God, and let us have no concern about dreams. It is most fitting that we place our hope in God and have no confidence in dreams. Therefore, dearest sister, I advise you that your mind should not be intent on dreams or auguries, but should be steadfast in almighty God. For if you observe auguries or dreams, you will quickly be deceived. Throughout your life despise auguries and dreams, and place your hope wholly in God’s providence; and prosperity will come to you both in this life and in the life to come. Amen.

## LXIX.—On the Brevity of Life

162. Dearest sister, hear Solomon’s words: “Whatever your hand can do, do diligently; for there will be neither work, nor reasoning, nor knowledge, nor wisdom in the underworld, to which you are hastening” (Eccl. 9:10). For it is permitted to do good only in this present life. In the future life, indeed, action is no longer expected, but the recompense of honorable works. This life is brief and passing. Hence blessed Isidore says: “One who considers the length of this present life not by its duration but by its end makes a very useful assessment of how brief and wretched it is.” Therefore, sister beloved to me in Christ, if you seek true life, strive toward that life which is true, for which you are a Christian—that is, eternal life. Eternal life is truly living; this life is mortal. Therefore you ought to die to the world in the flesh, lest you die to Christ in the soul. A person is then believed to live when, dying according to the world, that person lives in God alone, in whom he has promised to live. The righteous person suffers weariness at the delay of this life because he reaches the desired homeland slowly. Ignorance of the coming end leaves human beings uncertain; and while someone supposes that he will not die, he suddenly dies. Therefore let each person hasten to correct the evil that he has done, lest he die in iniquities and life end together with guilt. The devil inflames people to vices while they live, and when they die he strives suddenly to drag them to torments. Although a person is righteous in this life, nevertheless, when departing from this body, he fears greatly lest he be worthy of punishment. A peaceful summons commends the end of righteous people, so that they may be understood to have the fellowship of the holy angels from the fact that they depart from this mortal body without grievous distress. Jesus Christ, the Son of God, [Col. 1302A] receives his servants who depart this life with great honor into eternal blessedness. Hence the bride speaks in the Song of Songs, saying: “My beloved has descended into his garden, to the bed of spices” (Song 6:1). He descends because, in visiting the Church, he comes with greater grace to those whom he knows, by holy works and examples of virtue, to send forth to their neighbors the fragrance of a good reputation. He feeds in gardens when he delights in the virtues of souls. He gathers lilies when he cuts down his elect from this life and causes them to pass into the joys of eternal life. Of such persons it is said: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). Cloth is worn away by threads, and human life is spent day by day. [Col. 1302B] On the day of death, the souls of the elect are terrified by excessive fear, uncertain whether they are passing to reward or to punishments. But some of the elect are purified at their end from slight sins; others, at the very hour of death, become cheerful and rejoice in contemplation of eternal goods.

163. Therefore almighty God wished the day of our death to be unknown to us, so that it may always be unknown, always believed near; and so that each person may be as diligent in good work as he is uncertain of his calling. Demons receive the souls of evil people on the day of their death, so that those who were counsellors in vices may themselves be torturers in punishments. Then evil spirits demand their own works, when the soul departs the body; and they now rehearse the evils they urged, so that they may drag it with them to torments. The wicked person is led after death to be tortured, but the righteous person rests secure after [Col. 1302C] labor. For just as blessedness gladdens the elect, so it must be believed that from the day of their departure fire burns up sinners. Sister beloved to me in Christ, I set these matters forth in your hearing so that you may know that we must always despise earthly things and always keep the day of our death in mind. Hear also what the apostle James says: “What is our life except a vapor appearing for a little while?” (Jas. 4:15). Again Solomon says: “Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what the coming day will bring forth” (Prov. 27:1). Therefore, venerable sister, you ought to live diligently and consider the end of your life daily, so that you may despise this world’s allurements and acquire heavenly goods. “In all [Col. 1302D] your works consider your last things, and you shall never sin” (Ecclus. 7:40). For if you always consider them, you will never, or rarely, sin. For this reason I advise you, sister, not to rejoice in this world’s vain things, because you will certainly die. Nor should you place hope in temporal things, because by no means can you escape death. Why does wretched flesh rejoice in earthly things when it is prepared to be eaten by worms? Most honorable sister, I have said this so that you may never forget the condition of your nature. Remember that you are ashes, and shall return to ashes. You are dust, and shall go into dust (Gen. 3:19). For thus the Lord spoke to the first man. Recall also what Job said of himself: “I shall be consumed as rottenness, and like a garment [Col. 1303A] eaten by moths” (Job 13:28). Set the memory of your death before yourself; place before yourself the day of your departure; let the day of your death always be in your memory; and by remembrance of it guard yourself perfectly against sins and vices. Amen.

## LXX.—On Death

164. Venerable sister, I ask you to hear the words of a certain wise man: “O death, how bitter is your memory to a person at peace amid his possessions!” And again: “O death, how good is your judgment to the needy person, and to one diminished in wealth and strength!” (Ecclus. 41:1, 3). Similar to this is what blessed Isidore says: “O death, how sweet you are to the wretched; how pleasant to those who live bitterly; how welcome to the sad and mourning!” Death puts an end to every evil in this life. It gives an end to evils in this world [Col. 1303B] and removes every calamity. Death provides an end for people in tribulations in this world; but alas, the death for which one waits comes slowly. Therefore, dearest sister, it is better to die well than to live badly; it is better not to exist than to exist unhappily.

165. **Question.** Dear brother, I ask you to say whether we ought to mourn the dead or make lamentation for dead friends.

**Answer.** Dear sister, let blessed Isidore answer you on this point: “Although,” he says, “affection commands that we weep for the faithful departed, faith forbids that we mourn for them.” Therefore we ought not weep for the faithful departed, but give thanks to God because he has deigned to free them from the misery of this world and, as we believe, has caused them to pass to places of refreshment, light, and peace. We ought not mourn the faithful departed, whom we do not doubt have gone to rest. Honorable virgin, hear what I say. Those people are to be wept for in death whom demons seize with disgrace, not those whom angels receive with honor; or rather, those are to be mourned whom demons drag to the punishments of hell, not those whom angels lead to the joys of paradise. Or, those are to be wept for who after death are buried by demons in hell, not those whom angels place in heaven. Those are to be mourned who die badly, not those who end well; those are to be lamented who are overtaken by an evil death, not those honored by a precious death. Virgin of Christ, hear what I say. When I mourn the dead who die well, I harm myself and do them no benefit; when I weep for the dead, it does not benefit them [Col. 1303D] but harms me. Therefore let those mourn their dead carnally who deny the resurrection or do not believe in resurrection after death. Therefore, dearest sister, we who believe that our dead reign with Christ ought not to weep for them, but to pray: we ought not mourn the dead carnally, but pour out prayers to the Lord for them, that he may deign to rescue them from punishments.

## LXXI.—On Judgment

166. Divine judgment is twofold: one by which people are judged in this life; the other by which they will be judged in the future. For this reason, are some judged here through illnesses, poverty, and various tribulations of this world, lest they be judged in the future? [Col. 1304A] (1 Cor. 11:31–32). Thus for some, temporal punishment contributes to purification; but for others condemnation begins here, and complete destruction is prepared there. Some are judged in this world through tribulation; others will be judged in the future through fire. Before the examination of the strict Judge, not even righteousness will be secure. Hence Job speaks of the Lord: “He consumes the innocent and the wicked alike” (Job 9:22). For the innocent is consumed by God when that very innocence is examined more clearly and compared with divine innocence, and is found to amount to nothing. The wicked too is consumed by God when his impiety is examined by the subtlety of the divine scrutiny, and he is justly condemned. At judgment Christ will appear gentle and gracious to the elect according to the diversity of their merits, but terrible to the reprobate. On [Col. 1304B] the day of judgment each will have such a judge as the conscience that person has had, so that, while Christ remains tranquil in himself, he appears terrible only to those whom an evil conscience accuses. Dearest sister, hear blessed Isidore: “No one is without sin, nor can anyone be secure concerning God’s judgment, since an account must be rendered even for idle words” (Matt. 12:36). Alas for us wretched sinners! Alas for us unworthy ones! What shall we say on that day, when we sin daily not only in idle words but also in deeds, and never cease from evil acts? If the righteous person will not be secure in the judgment of almighty God, what will become of us sinners? If, at the examination of the strict Judge, not even the righteousness of a righteous person will be secure, what shall we wretches do [Col. 1304C] on that day, we who multiply our sins daily? If the righteous will scarcely be saved on the day of judgment, where shall we appear on that day, we who have committed innumerable sins? (1 Pet. 4:18; Prov. 11:31.) No one will be able to be without fear on that day, when heaven and earth are to be shaken and all the elements dissolved by heat; concerning it too it is said: “That day: a day of tribulation, a day of misery and vengeance, a day of cloud and darkness, a day of trumpet and blast; on it even the strong man shall be distressed” (Zeph. 1:15, 16, 14).

167. **Question.** Alas, my brother, what shall we say on that day when that strict Judge comes? For by recalling his coming you have made me weep; by recalling the terrible day of judgment, you have compelled me to tears. [Col. 1304D]

**Answer.** Sister beloved to me in Christ, you have done well if you wept in fear of the strict Judge; for before the day of judgment appears, we must go before his face in confession and set our tears before him. In this life is the acceptable time and the day of salvation. Hence it is said: “Seek the Lord while he may be found; call upon him while he is near” (Isa. 55:6). In this life the Judge is not seen, yet he is near; in the future life he will be seen, yet he will be far away. Therefore, dearest sister, it is necessary that we seek the Lord with all our heart and all our mind in this present life, if we seek to find him in the future. If in this life we seek him with every devotion and withdraw from evil works, we shall obtain mercy from him on the day of judgment, because [Col. 1305A] he is kind and merciful. For it is written of him: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. 144:9). Therefore, dearest sister, let us implore that terrible and most just Judge with tears and every devotion, that on the day of judgment he may not repay us according to our iniquities but according to his mercies, and that he may not permit us to hear with the wicked that terrible sentence, “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire,” but may cause us to hear with his elect: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:41, 34).

## LXXII.—Epilogue

[Col. 1305B] 168. Dearest sister, by God’s grace I now steer the ship of my discourse toward harbor; yet I return again to speak to you. For you asked me to write words of holy admonition for you. Although not as I ought, yet by God’s grace as I was able, I have gathered from the sayings of the holy Fathers judgments for your admonition, which I have presented to your Love in this book. Behold, then, sister beloved to me in Christ, you have counsels for a good life. You have been given both advice for living well and a rule. No ignorance now excuses you from sin. You are no longer unacquainted with a good life. You can no longer say, as one inexperienced or ignorant of how to live well: “I have sinned through ignorance.” Why? Because the law which you ought to follow has now been laid down for you; the precepts for living well have now been shown to you; it has now been demonstrated [Col. 1305C] how you ought to conduct yourself in God’s house; what sort of person you ought to be has now been shown to you. You now have knowledge of the commandments; you now know what it is to live rightly. Take care, therefore, not to offend further; take care henceforth not to disregard the good that you know. By living badly you despise the good that you read. If by living badly you despise the good things that you read, you will be exceedingly blameworthy before God. Why? Because it is better not to know the way of salvation than, after knowing it, to turn back. Therefore retain in mind and deed the received gift of knowledge; fulfill in action what you have learned by instruction. Venerable sister, again and again I command you to observe with the utmost care the admonitions of this book.

## LXXIII.—He Requests His Sister’s Intercession for Him before God

[Col. 1305D]

169. I beseech you, dearest sister in Christ, not to be reluctant to hear what I wish to say to you with great longing: because I love you greatly in Christ, I reveal my conscience to you. But while I disclose my sins to you, I fear lest I defile your ears. Nevertheless, beloved sister in Christ, I ask you to pardon me, an unworthy sinner. I, wretched and sinful, have defiled my life from almost my earliest years. I have always joined new sins to old ones; I have always added sins to sins; I have never ceased to sin. The good that I ought to have done, I did not do; the evil [Col. 1306A] that I ought not to have done, I did. I, wretched man, am unworthy to look upon heaven’s height because of the multitude of my iniquity, since I have provoked the anger of almighty God against myself and have thought, spoken, and done innumerable evils before him from my infancy until the present day. I, unhappy man, sinned in infancy; I sinned in childhood, adolescence, and youth; but also, what is more grievous and dangerous, I sinned in old age. Wretched as I am, I fell into the mire of shameful deeds. Guilty as I am, I fell into the pit of sins. Blameworthy as I am, I fell into the well of iniquity. Unhappy as I am, I fell into the abyss of evils; wretched as I am, I descended into the wallowing-place of vices. Alas, wretched man! Alas, unhappy man! I have fallen, and by myself I cannot rise. Therefore I beseech you, sister beloved in Christ, to raise me by the hand of your [Col. 1306B] prayer. Stretch out to me the hand of your prayer, and draw me out from the depth of vices. Extend the hand of your intercession, and rescue me from the pit of iniquity. Dearest sister, I am certain that if you keep the covenant which you have made with Christ, both a crown for eternal joys will be given to you and forgiveness in this life will be granted to me, a sinner. If you fulfill with a devoted mind the things you have vowed to Christ, you will obtain pardon for me, unworthy as I am, and you will rejoice with the holy virgins in the heavenly bridal chamber.

170. Honorable virgin, I am certain, nor do I doubt, that your virginal prayer can obtain forgiveness of my sins for me, though unworthy. Venerable sister, if you persevere in God’s service, as you have promised, [Col. 1306C] you will obtain pardon for me, a sinner, and you yourself will be exalted forever among the choirs of virgins. Honorable virgin, I ask you to hear attentively what I say. You are my most devoted sister in Christ, through whose intercession I do not doubt that I may be cleansed from the filth of my sins. If you, honorable virgin, are accepted by God as a virgin, and if you have lain in a chaste bed with Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, whatever you ask of him for my salvation you will obtain. If you, sister, have embraced Christ in chaste embraces, you will surely be able to obtain pardon for me, a sinner. If you cling in Christ’s embraces with the most fragrant scent of virginity, you will obtain forgiveness for me, though unworthy. If you love Jesus Christ, the heavenly bridegroom, above all things, and rest in his sweetest love, you will be able to obtain absolution for my sins. [Col. 1306D] Jesus Christ, your bridegroom, will not make you sorrowful; rather, he who has joined you to his union will give you whatever you ask: for he greatly loves you, whom he redeemed by his blood. Therefore your love in Christ will be the remission of my sins. I have hope of forgiveness if you, dearest sister, whom I love greatly, enter with Christ into the heavenly bridal chamber for the wedding. You, venerable sister, will be my consolation on the day of God’s strict and terrible judgment, when I must render account for my faults and negligences. For the merit of your holy virginity will lessen the punishment of my iniquity. Amen.

## Various Rhythms

### Notice concerning the following verses and rhythms

[Col. 1307]

891 Berengar the schoolman, in his *Apology for Abelard against St Bernard*, states that Bernard himself, “from almost the first rudiments of adolescence, composed little mimetic songs” (thus he speaks in accordance with his innate insolence) “and fashioned polished tunes, and competed with his brothers in rhythmic contest.” Yet I do not think that the following verses and rhythms should be attributed to Bernard. For the Cistercians admitted nothing constrained by metrical rules. Accordingly, when Bernard composed the office of St Victor, he entirely disregarded not only the rules of metre but those of rhythm as well. Therefore I do not think his to be the hortatory poem addressed to Rainald, which Peter Possinus of the Society of Jesus published from the Chigi Library at Rome in 1663; nor the following rhythm, edited by Charles de Visch, monk of the Dunes. Nor have we anything certain concerning the rhythmic *Jubilation on the Name of Jesus*, long ago ascribed to Bernard; in a certain manuscript of Vaux-de-Cernay of the Cistercian Order it bears the title, “Meditation of a certain holy virgin on the love of Christ.” Some attribute the hymn “Ave, Maris stella” to the same holy Doctor. But it is clear that this is by an earlier author, both from our older German manuscript and from the Cassinese Breviary, now preserved in the house of formation of the Fathers of the Oratory at Paris, written in the time of Abbot Oderisius the First, who died in 1105; this hymn is found in both books.

## Hortatory Poem to Rainald (G)*

[Col. 1307A]

892 Our little letter brings you greetings, Rainald;  
You will see more therein, if you do not reject these gifts.  
Sweet are the consolations of the soul which I send you;  
But they profit nothing unless you keep them in practice.  

Do not cast my admonishing words to the wind;  
Let them sound in the ear of your heart, and remember to retain them,  
So that our counsels may work great good for you,  
And through God’s gift may prepare heavenly kingdoms for you.  

These words can please a sincere mind.  
They show the way; they exhort, not reproach.  
The divine voice declares that no one should place hope  
In worldly things, which furnish the cause of perishing.  

Whoever loves Christ does not love this world;  
But, scorning its allurements as foul smells,  
He judges foul what the world thinks pleasant;  
[Col. 1307B] and all that glitters in the world becomes cheap to him.  
He avoids earthly splendor as mortal poison;  
And, having cast off the mire of carnal love outside,  
He longs with faithful mind for the kingdom of heaven,  
And already, full of faith, hopes for the delights of paradise.  

You too, brother, avoid in this way the contagions of the flesh,  
That you may please Christ while living in this world.  
Things that quickly slip away and are sought with great labor  
Must not concern you: they will return to nothing.  
Do not rejoice now, because perhaps tomorrow you will die;  
By no fate will you be able to drive death away.
